The author of a computer program shall retain exclusive rights pertaining to the reproduction and distribution of said program, subject to the provisions herein relating to fair dealing. An author may grant a license permitting the use, adaptation, or commercial exploitation of their copyrighted work in exchange for royalty payments as agreed upon between the parties; such licenses shall be assignable in whole or in part by the author. Provided that any assignment of copyright must be executed in writing and attested to by at least one witness competent to testify under this Act. Further, where an author has entered into a contractual agreement granting rights to a third party, subsequent assignments relating to those specific rights are void unless expressly authorized by the original assignee. The right to control the manner of distribution remains with the author, even when copyright is assigned for other purposes.

Where a claim is made before a High Court alleging infringement of copyright in respect of a published work, the determination of whether an individual qualifies as the *author* for the purposes of establishing ownership shall be subject to rigorous scrutiny. The claimant must demonstrate, by clear and convincing evidence, that they conceived of and executed the substantial elements of originality within the work, or alternatively, held exclusive contractual rights over the creation process, provided that such contracts were duly registered under this Act. Disputes concerning joint authorship may be resolved through expert testimony regarding contribution levels; however, any challenge to the claimant’s assertion of *author* status is appealable to a higher appellate bench if it involves questions of fact impacting the underlying validity of the copyright itself.

Where any person infringes upon the copyright in respect of a work, being a photograph, and such infringement involves the reproduction thereof for commercial purposes, the owner of the copyright shall be entitled to claim damages proportionate to the loss suffered by him as a consequence of the said infringement. For the purpose of determining such damages, regard may be had to any profits earned by the infringer which he could not have made but for the infringing act. The author of the work shall also be empowered to apply to the District Court for an injunction restraining further acts of copyright infringement. Provided that where a trade mark recognised under the Trade Marks Act is incorporated within the photograph, the remedies available to the owner are subject to limitations as provided herein.

The author of a computer program shall retain all rights pertaining to authorship under this Act unless such rights have been explicitly assigned or licensed. Where an assignment is made, it may be absolute or subject to limitations as agreed upon between the assignor and assignee. An exclusive licensee, having received a license granting them sole right to exploit certain copyright works, shall be deemed for all purposes relating to enforcement of those rights to be the author in relation to the specific acts licensed. This provision does not prejudice the original author’s ability to grant further licenses concerning non-licensed aspects of their work. Any subsequent assignment or license granted by an exclusive licensee shall require express written consent from the original author, provided that such consent may be withheld only for demonstrable reasons relating to artistic integrity and commercial viability.

Where a claim is made before the relevant adjudicating authority alleging that a person has falsely presented themselves as the author of an artistic work, and such presentation has caused demonstrable prejudice to the rightful owner’s ability to exercise their exclusive rights under this Act, the authority shall provide both parties with an opportunity for full argument. The claimant may submit evidence demonstrating misrepresentation and resultant financial loss or reputational damage. Provided that the alleged author is given reasonable notice of the claim and a chance to rebut the allegations, the adjudicating authority may issue an order cancelling the registration of the work in the name of the falsely claiming individual. Any party aggrieved by such an order cancellation may appeal against it before the appellate forum as provided herein.

Where an infringement of copyright subsists due to unauthorized reproduction of a substantial portion of a published book’s board use layout, the author shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief restraining further acts of such infringement. Provided that, where the alleged infringer demonstrates good faith belief in their right to utilize the said layout and promptly ceases the infringing activity upon receiving notice of the copyright violation, damages may be limited as determined by the competent court. Furthermore, any person found guilty of contributory infringement, meaning knowingly inducing or enabling another’s copyright violation concerning the author's work, shall also be liable for appropriate remedies under this Act. The right to claim damages includes compensation for loss of royalties and demonstrable harm to reputation arising from the unauthorized reproduction.

A copyright society is constituted for the administration of rights vested under this Act in creators of literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic works, and in producers and authors of cinematograph films. Such a society shall be registered with the central government and may undertake collective bargaining on behalf of its members relating to royalties and other remuneration payable for any right administered by it. The objects of a copyright society include the collection and distribution of sums paid as royalty under this Act, subject to adherence to equitable principles and transparent accounting procedures. Membership in a copyright society shall be voluntary, provided that no member shall have the right to unilaterally terminate their membership without providing six months’ notice.

The registration of a copyright society shall be undertaken by an applicant fulfilling the criteria as provided herein, including demonstration of representation of not less than seven authors or owners of rights in musical works. An application for registration must include detailed particulars regarding the proposed name of the society, its objectives, geographical area of operation, and the rules governing membership, distribution of royalties, and dispute resolution mechanisms. The applicant shall furnish a list of members with their addresses and details of the works they control. Upon review, if the Registrar is satisfied that the proposed society complies with these requirements and does not contravene any provisions under this Act, registration may be granted, subject to payment of prescribed fees.

A copyright society established under this Act shall be liable to compensate owners for acts of infringement committed by licensees operating within its jurisdiction, provided that the society maintains adequate funds to meet such obligations. Failure to remit royalties collected from users to the registered owners as determined by the relevant provisions herein constitutes a breach of contract and renders the society subject to civil suit for damages. Any owner aggrieved by the actions or omissions of a copyright society may petition the designated appellate authority, seeking redressal concerning distribution of royalties or alleged mismanagement of funds. The society shall furnish detailed accounts annually to its registered members, allowing for scrutiny under this Act. Further, any member demonstrating demonstrable prejudice due to the society’s conduct may pursue legal remedies as provided herein.

The registration of a copyright society shall be undertaken by the designated Registrar, following an application submitted in the prescribed form accompanied by the requisite fee. An applicant seeking to establish a copyright society must demonstrate that it possesses a substantial membership base comprising authors or owners of rights in literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic works. The Registrar may require such further information as deemed necessary to ascertain the genuineness and representational capacity of the proposed society. Upon satisfaction that the application complies with all provisions under this Act, the Registrar shall issue a certificate of registration. Any aggrieved party may appeal against a refusal of registration within sixty days from the date of notification of such refusal, to the Appellate Authority constituted for adjudicating disputes relating to copyright. The copyright society’s operational procedures and distribution mechanisms are subject to periodic audit as provided herein.

A copyright society established under this Act shall not register any literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work unless it has obtained prior written consent from the authors and owners of all rights therein, confirming their voluntary affiliation with said society. Such consent shall explicitly detail the scope of works to be administered by the society, including but not limited to specific categories of musical compositions and sound recordings. The copyright society may collect royalties on behalf of its members only in proportion to their respective contributions as determined through a transparent accounting system maintained and audited annually. Further, any member withdrawing from the society shall be entitled to receive a full and accurate statement of royalties accrued attributable to their works within ninety days of such withdrawal, provided that the society maintains adequate records for this purpose.

Any collecting society established under this Act shall maintain detailed accounts of all royalties collected from users and distributed to right owners, subject to audit by an independent chartered accountant appointed by the central government. Failure to provide these audited accounts within three months of the close of each financial year shall attract a penalty of one thousand rupees for each day of default, recoverable as civil debt. Furthermore, any society found to have improperly withheld royalties or distributed them unfairly may be ordered to pay compensatory damages to affected right owners, determined by the relevant High Court. The central government may, after due inquiry, revoke the registration of any copyright society failing persistently to comply with these provisions and regulations as provided herein.

Any copyright society established under this Act may grant non-exclusive licenses to users of works for which it collects royalties, subject to terms and conditions approved by the relevant governmental authority. Such licenses shall be offered on reasonable cost principles, considering administrative expenses and the needs of right holders. A member of a copyright society who wishes to assign their rights in any musical work or literary work may do so with the prior written consent of the society, provided that such assignment includes a detailed accounting mechanism for royalty distribution proportionate to usage data collected by the society. The society shall have the power to enter into reciprocal representation agreements with foreign copyright societies facilitating international licensing and collection activities. Further, rights holders retaining ownership under this arrangement may specify limitations on sub-licensing granted through the copyright society.

The distribution of royalties collected by a copyright society shall be determined according to the terms of its constitution, provided that any dispute arising from the interpretation or application of those terms may be referred for resolution to an adjudicating authority constituted under this Act. Such adjudication shall consider representations made by both right owners and users whose interests are affected by the royalty distribution scheme. The copyright society shall maintain detailed records pertaining to all collections and distributions, accessible for inspection upon request by any aggrieved party seeking to challenge its actions. Any order passed by the adjudicating authority may be appealed against within a period of ninety days, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed.

The operation of a copyright society established under this Act shall be subject to rigorous oversight by the designated governmental authority, ensuring equitable distribution of royalties amongst its members and adherence to prescribed guidelines concerning licensing practices. Any member aggrieved by the actions or decisions of such a copyright society relating to royalty allocation, licensing terms, or membership disputes may appeal directly to the appellate forum as provided herein. The appellate forum shall consider evidence presented by both the copyright society and the aggrieved member, with particular regard to whether the society’s conduct demonstrably deviates from principles of fairness and transparency. Decisions of the appellate forum are final, subject only to further judicial review on grounds limited to jurisdictional error or violation of fundamental rights.

A Copyright Society is hereby defined as an association formed under this Act for the collective management of copyright in musical works, literary works, or dramatic works, and which is registered with the Trade Marks Registry. Such registration shall be subject to conditions prescribed herein relating to governance, financial transparency, and equitable distribution of royalties amongst its members. A Copyright Society may enter into licensing agreements on behalf of its members for the utilization of their respective copyrighted works, provided that such agreements adhere to principles of fair dealing as understood under this Act. The functions of a Copyright Society shall include the collection and disbursement of royalty income.

The registration of a copyright society shall be subject to approval by the designated governmental authority, following an assessment of its proposed operational procedures and adherence to principles of equitable distribution amongst its members. Any member aggrieved by a decision regarding royalties or licensing terms determined by a copyright society may appeal such determination under this Act. The appellate process shall involve submission of written representations and supporting documentation to the relevant adjudicating officer. Such officer, after affording an opportunity for hearing to both the appellant and the copyright society, shall issue reasoned orders detailing findings and remedies. An order issued under an 112a order appellate may be reviewed by a higher judicial forum as provided herein, subject to limitations on grounds of legal error only.

A mark shall be deemed a well-known trade mark if, through association with the goods or services of its proprietor, it has acquired substantial recognition in India, irrespective of whether such recognition is direct or indirect. The determination of distinctiveness under this provision shall consider factors including the duration and extent of use of the mark, the geographical area where it is used, the nature of the goods or services for which it is used, and evidence of reputation enjoyed by the proprietor thereof. A mark may also be considered a well-known trade mark if its inherent character indicates that it has such recognition, even without extensive prior usage as provided herein.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed to include an assertion that the mark is capable of distinguishing the applicant’s goods or services from those of others. Where the Registrar has reason to believe that a proposed trade mark qualifies as a well-known trade mark in relation to particular goods or services, he may direct the applicant to furnish such further information as he deems necessary to substantiate this claim. Such direction shall specify the geographical area and the relevant consumer perception within India which supports the assertion of ‘well-known’ status. The Registrar is empowered to request evidence demonstrating extensive prior use and recognition of the mark, provided that the applicant demonstrates a genuine and reasonable basis for believing it enjoys such reputation.

Where a trade mark has acquired substantial recognition of the public as being distinctive and representative of particular goods or services, it shall be deemed a well-known trade mark for the purposes of this Act. Any use of an identical or confusingly similar indicator in relation to goods or services not identical with those associated with the well-known trade mark shall constitute infringement, subject to limitations imposed by equitable considerations. The owner of a well-known trade mark may apply to restrain any such infringing use even if there is no direct competition between the goods or services involved, provided that the infringing indicator creates a likelihood of confusion on the part of the public or otherwise dilutes the distinctiveness of the well-known trade mark. Damages shall be awarded as provided herein, taking into account the extent of the dilution and any resulting loss of reputation.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed on the ground that it conflicts with a previously registered well-known trade mark, the Trade Marks Registry shall give notice of the opposition to the applicant and the proprietor of the well-known trade mark. The proprietor may then file their case in support of the opposition, including evidence demonstrating the extent of recognition and reputation enjoyed by the well-known trade mark within India and any dilution or likelihood of confusion arising from registration of the impugned mark. Subject to this, the Registry shall afford both parties an opportunity to be heard, either in person or through duly authorized representatives. The Registrar may, after considering all evidence presented, direct that the application for registration proceed, be rejected, or be amended as deemed appropriate to resolve the conflict with the well-known trade mark, provided that such direction is consistent with the provisions of this Act concerning unfair competition.

A mark shall be deemed a well-known trade mark if, through association with the goods or services of its proprietor, it has acquired substantial recognition amongst the relevant public in India, and such recognition is such that use of the mark by another person, without the consent of the registered proprietor, would likely create confusion or cause detriment to the distinctive character or repute of the well-known trade mark. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating this association and recognition, including but not limited to market surveys and consumer perception studies. Provided that a mark’s reputation is established in another country shall not, of itself, be sufficient grounds for it being classified as a well-known trade mark under this Act; consideration must be given to its impact within the Indian marketplace.

Notwithstanding anything contained elsewhere under this Act, any mark which has acquired substantial recognition within India as a well-known trade mark shall be entitled to protection irrespective of whether it is registered in India. Any person who, without due cause and with intent to deceive or tarnish the reputation of the proprietor of the well-known trade mark, uses an identical or confusingly similar mark relating to goods or services identical or closely related to those for which the well-known trade mark is recognized shall be liable for damages. The amount of such damages shall be determined by the Court, subject to a minimum penalty of five hundred thousand rupees and may extend up to ten million rupees, as deemed appropriate considering the extent of infringement and loss suffered.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, any proprietor of a well-known trade mark shall be entitled to grant licenses for the use of such trade mark in India, specifying the geographical area and duration of such license, as they deem fit. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and the terms thereof shall be subject to registration with the Trade Marks Registry. Assignment of rights pertaining to a well-known trade mark is permissible, provided that the assignee undertakes to maintain the distinctiveness and reputation associated therewith. Further, any use of a registered trade mark which creates confusion or misrepresentation in relation to goods or services offered by the proprietor of the well-known trade mark shall be deemed an infringement under this Act, irrespective of intent. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating continued usage to ensure validity.

Where an objection is raised before the Registrar alleging that a proposed trade mark has become a well-known trade mark in relation to particular goods or services, the Registrar shall give notice thereof to the applicant and any proprietor claiming rights under the registered trade mark. Such proprietors may appear and be heard against the objection, presenting evidence demonstrating consumer recognition and distinctiveness acquired through extensive use and advertising. The Registrar may require further submissions from both parties before reaching a determination. An appeal lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days of the date of the order; provided that the Board shall consider only questions of law arising out of the Registrar’s decision, subject to any evidence deemed relevant by the Board itself.

The Registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for registration of a trade mark, investigate whether the proposed mark qualifies as a well-known trade mark in relation to the goods or services specified in the application. Such investigation shall include consideration of all relevant factors, including duration of the mark’s use, geographical extent of recognition, and reputation enjoyed by the proprietor thereof. Where an applicant seeks to assign a well-known trade mark, the governing assignment denomination must be clearly stated within the instrument of transfer presented for registration under this Act. The Registrar may require further evidence substantiating the claim of ‘well-known’ status, provided that such requirements are reasonable and proportionate to the nature of the application.

Where a proprietor establishes that a mark has acquired substantial recognition of the mark as being distinctive for particular goods or services in India, and such recognition is prevalent enough to elicit immediate public association with the proprietor’s goods or services, then that mark shall be deemed a well-known trade mark. Any person seeking registration of a trade mark identical or confusingly similar to a well-known trade mark shall be refused registration under this Act. The application registrar shall consider evidence presented by the proprietor of the well-known trade mark and any other interested parties in determining whether such confusion is likely to arise. Provided that, nothing herein prevents an application for registration if use does not constitute taking unfair advantage of or being detrimental to the distinctive character or repute of the well-known trade mark.

For the purposes of this Act, a geographical indication shall mean an indication identifying goods originating in a specific territory and used to designate the quality, reputation, or characteristics of those goods, which are essentially attributable to their geographical origin. An agricultural product, foodstuff, wine, spirit, handicraft, or manufactured good may constitute a geographical indication as provided herein. The distinctiveness of a geographical indication shall be assessed based on its recognition by consumers within the territory of origin and in relevant markets. Any alteration or modification that misleads consumers regarding the true geographical origin of goods bearing a registered geographical indication shall be prohibited under this Act.

An application for the registration of a geographical indication may be filed with the Registrar in such form and manner as may be prescribed, containing particulars relating to the name of the geographical indication sought to be registered, the goods or services to which it relates, the area of entitlement, and the collective body representing the interests of producers or users concerned. The applicant shall furnish evidence demonstrating that the quality, reputation, or other characteristics of the goods or services originate from a specific geographical origin. A geographical indication shall not be registrable if it is non-distinctive due to its common usage or lacks sufficient link with the specified geographic area. Any person claiming an interest may oppose the registration under this Act within the prescribed period.

A proprietor of a geographical indication, aggrieved by any infringement of the rights conferred under this Act, may institute civil proceedings in the competent District Court for redress. Such remedies shall include an injunction restraining further acts of infringement and recovery of damages sustained by the proprietor as a direct result of the infringing activity. The court may also order the destruction or disposal of goods bearing the falsely applied geographical indication, subject to regulations framed by the Central Government. Further, any person who, without authorization from the registered proprietor, uses a geographical indication in connection with goods not conforming to the standards prescribed for that indication shall be liable to pay compensation to the proprietor. A geographical indication shall not be deemed to infringe upon these provisions if its use is solely descriptive of the origin of the goods and not used in an attempt to falsely represent their quality or characteristics.

An application for the registration of a geographical indication shall include particulars specifying the name of the geographical indication as it is proposed to be registered, a map of the area corresponding to the alleged origin of the goods, and a statement indicating the qualities, reputation or other characteristics which the applicant claims are unique to the goods attributable to the geographical origin. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further information deemed necessary for assessing the distinctiveness of the indication. Where an objection is raised by any interested party under this Act against the registration of a geographical indication, the Registrar shall provide the applicant and the objector with an opportunity to be heard. A geographical indication shall not be registered if it is contrary to public order or morality. The Registering Authority may, after due inquiry, reject an application if satisfied that the proposed geographical indication does not meet the criteria as provided herein.

A geographical indication shall, upon application and subject to the provisions herein, be registered in respect of goods originating from a specific territory within India, where the quality, reputation or characteristics of such goods are essentially attributable to the geographical origin. The applicant must demonstrate, through verifiable documentation and established production practices, that the good’s qualities derive uniquely from its defined geographic location. Furthermore, an application for registration may be refused if it contains a representation which is contrary to public order or morality. Any registered geographical indication shall remain valid for a period of ten years, renewable by subsequent application demonstrating continued adherence to prescribed standards and maintenance of distinctiveness as provided herein.

Any person who, without due cause and in contravention of the provisions herein, applies for registration of a geographical indication which falsely suggests an association with any goods originating from a place different than the one claimed, shall be liable to pay a pecuniary penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees. Further, where a registered proprietor of a geographical indication discovers that another person is using the said indication in relation to goods not conforming to the standards as prescribed under this Act, they may apply to the relevant authority for an order restraining such use and recovering damages sustained. A geographical indication shall be deemed infringed if it is used in a manner which misrepresents the origin of the goods or services.

A proprietor of a geographical indication, desiring to grant a license for use of the said indication in relation to goods or services falling within the scope of its registration, shall execute an agreement specifying the terms and conditions thereof. Such agreement may include provisions regarding royalty payments, quality control measures applicable to the licensed products, and territorial limitations on usage. The proprietor retains ownership of the geographical indication; however, assignment of such rights, including any associated licenses, is permissible subject to prior approval from the Registrar. Any assignee shall be bound by all existing conditions attached to the geographical indication as provided herein. A geographical indication shall not be assigned without a registered instrument and notice published in the Trade Marks Journal. Further, sub-licensing may only occur with express written consent of the original proprietor.

A geographical indication shall, upon registration, confer upon the registered proprietor exclusive right to use the indication in relation to goods for which it is registered. However, any person who prior to the date of such registration has been using a sign identical or similar to the registered geographical indication in an honest and contemporaneous manner may continue to use that sign, subject to conditions as provided herein regarding potential consumer confusion. An appeal against this allowance may be made within sixty days from the date of order by the Registrar, and shall lie before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The Board’s decision is final, but remains open to challenge under this Act on grounds of manifest error or perversity.

An application for registration of a geographical indication shall include particulars relating to the name of the collective body or organization making the application, its address and constitution. The applicant shall furnish evidence demonstrating use of the good or product in relation to the proposed geographical indication by persons interested in ensuring the quality and maintenance of its characteristics. Where an objection is raised against registration under this Act, the registrar person may require the applicant to submit further documentation substantiating the distinctiveness of the goods or products associated with the claimed geographical indication. The application shall also specify the area constituting the geographical unit for which the indication seeks protection, as defined by established local practices and traditions.

Any person seeking to use a protected geographical indication, including in connection with a lease patented article derived from the indicated goods, shall be liable for infringement under this Act. An aggrieved party may institute civil proceedings before the relevant jurisdictional court claiming damages proportionate to the loss suffered by them as a direct result of such unauthorized use. The remedies available include an injunction restraining the infringing activity and the recovery of costs incurred in bringing the action. Further, where the infringing use constitutes a misrepresentation likely to mislead consumers regarding the origin of goods, enhanced damages may be awarded. A geographical indication shall not be deemed to lose protection merely by reason of its prior description or reference in any publication; however, such references will not constitute permissible use under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, “sound recording” means a recording of sounds fixed in a medium capable of being reproduced and shall include exclusively those recordings which originate from an audio visual work. A sound recording is deemed to be authored by the producer who undertakes the arrangement for its creation, provided that where such arrangement is undertaken on behalf of another person, that other person shall be considered the author. The rights conferred under this Act in respect of a sound recording are distinct and independent from any rights subsisting in an underlying work incorporated within it, subject to provisions relating to synchronization.

For the purposes of registration under this Act, a sound recording shall be deemed to comprise all sounds fixed on any medium of expression. An application for registration of a sound recording may be filed by the owner of the copyright in such sound recording, or by an authorized agent acting on their behalf. The Registrar shall require particulars relating to the date of first publication, if any, and details of the producer responsible for the creation of the sound recording. Where a sound recording incorporates elements previously existing, the applicant shall provide evidence demonstrating ownership of rights pertaining to those incorporated elements, subject to provisions regarding fair dealing under this Act. Any alteration or modification to a registered sound recording requires notification to the Registrar within thirty days.

The owner of copyright in a sound recording shall be entitled to restrain any person from infringing such copyright, including but not limited to the reproduction, distribution, communication to the public, and adaptation of the said sound recording. Provided that, where an infringement involves the making of copies for private use or other non-commercial purposes, remedies available under this Act shall be proportionate to the nature and extent of the infringement and may include a direction to cease such infringing activity and pay damages not exceeding a sum as determined by the relevant adjudicating authority. Further, any person aggrieved by an act of infringement may institute legal proceedings seeking injunctions, accounts of profits derived from the infringement, and general damages. The right to claim special damages shall be subject to proof of actual pecuniary loss suffered due to the infringing conduct.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, copyright in a sound recording shall vest initially in the producer thereof. For the purposes of this section, “producer” means the person who undertakes the arrangement, manufacture and publication of a sound recording. Any aggrieved party may file an appeal before the Controller within sixty days from the date of order sought to be challenged, detailing grounds for reconsideration and submitting supporting documentation as prescribed by regulations framed under this Act. The Controller shall provide an opportunity for hearing to both the appellant and the respondent, and shall pass reasoned orders within ninety days of receipt of the appeal. Further, any person making a sound recording infringing on existing copyright may be liable to damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the owner of the copyright, as determined by civil court jurisdiction.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, copyright in a sound recording shall subsist until sixty years from the end of the year in which the work is first published. Provided that, where the ownership of the sound recording vests in a person other than the producer thereof, such copyright shall endure for a period not exceeding fifty years from the date of publication, unless a longer term is agreed upon in writing between the producer and the owner. The right to reproduce a sound recording shall be deemed an exclusive right, subject to any license granted under this Act or as provided herein. Any person infringing upon said rights may be liable for damages commensurate with the extent of commercial loss suffered by the copyright holder.

Any person who, without authorisation from the owner of the sound recording, reproduces the said sound recording in any medium, including but not limited to digital formats for distribution or commercial use, shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall be assessed at an amount equivalent to three times the reasonable licensing fee that would have been payable had the reproduction been authorised, subject to a minimum penalty of fifty thousand rupees. Further, where such infringement is committed with the intent to deceive or cause undue gain, the offender may also face imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years. The owner of the sound recording shall be entitled to seek an injunction restraining further acts of infringement as provided herein.

The owner of a sound recording shall be entitled to grant licenses permitting the reproduction, distribution, and communication to the public of the sound recording, subject to such terms and conditions as may be specified in the license agreement. Such agreements may include provisions relating to royalty payments, duration of rights granted, and geographical limitations on exploitation. Where a sound recording is created through collaborative effort involving multiple individuals or entities, the assignment of rights under this Act shall require the consent of all co-owners unless otherwise stipulated by written contract executed prior to the creation of the sound recording. Any license granted for a sound recording may be assigned to any person or entity with the prior written approval of the licensor, provided that such assignee adheres to the original terms and conditions of the grant. The right to control the rental of a sound recording remains vested solely with the owner as provided herein.

The right in a sound recording shall vest initially with the producer thereof, and such producer may assign or transfer said right subject to appeal under this Act. Where a dispute arises concerning the ownership of a sound recording, it shall be presumed that the individual or entity responsible for financing the initial creation and commercial distribution of the recording is the rightful owner unless demonstrable evidence to the contrary is presented before an adjudicating officer. Any party aggrieved by a decision regarding ownership may appeal to the appellate forum established under this Act within sixty days from the date of notification of the order, provided that such appeal shall be accompanied by a security deposit as determined by regulations framed in accordance with this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, a sound recording shall be deemed registered for copyright upon successful completion of the registration process as prescribed herein. The Registrar may require submission of detailed metadata pertaining to the original master recording and all subsequent derivative works incorporated within the submitted sound recording. Any alteration to a registered sound recording following initial registration requires notification to the Registrar and may necessitate re-evaluation of the effect registered status, particularly where such alterations materially impact the integrity or originality of the underlying artistic work. The owner of an effect registered trade mark incorporating elements derived from a previously registered sound recording shall be subject to conditions as determined by the Controller, ensuring equitable recognition of both intellectual property rights.

Where a sound recording has been commercially released without authorization, and it is established that such release was facilitated through the actions of an individual acting as an agent for another party, then said agent shall be deemed liable under this Act. This liability extends to instances where the agent knowingly participated in, or had reasonable grounds to suspect, the unauthorized distribution of the sound recording. Provided that, if the principal party demonstrates due diligence in preventing the release and proves lack of direct involvement, the agent’s commission offence attributable may be mitigated by a competent court. Any person found guilty shall be subject to penalties as provided herein, without prejudice to civil remedies available to the copyright owner of the sound recording.

Any person who, without authorization from the owner of the sound recording, reproduces, distributes, publicly exhibits, or communicates to the public any sound recording, shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall be assessed at an amount not less than ten thousand rupees nor more than fifty thousand rupees per instance of infringement ascertained by the Civil Court. Where a restoration patent relating to the digital enhancement of a sound recording is registered, unauthorized use thereof constitutes a distinct violation, attracting enhanced penalties as determined under this Act. The owner may further seek injunctive relief preventing future acts of infringement and recovery of costs incurred in pursuing legal remedies. Failure to comply with a court order regarding cessation of infringing activity shall result in daily fines until compliance is achieved.

For the purposes of this Act, an “application patent” shall mean a patent granted under this Act which confers upon the patentee exclusive right to make, use and sell the patented invention in India for a term commencing from the date of grant, subject to the provisions regarding compulsory licenses as provided herein. An application patent is distinct from a process patent, wherein the scope of protection relates specifically to a method or process of manufacturing a substance or article rather than the substance or article itself. The right conferred by an application patent shall be assignable and may be transmitted by will or succession, subject to any conditions prescribed under this Act.

An applicant seeking registration of an invention under this Act shall file a request for grant of an application patent accompanied by the prescribed fee and particulars specifying the priority claim, if any. The request shall clearly identify the inventor or inventors and state whether the invention has been previously published or used in the territory extending to one year before the date of filing. Where an applicant is not the original inventor, the request must disclose the basis for claiming inventorship, subject to verification by the Controller. Any alteration to the particulars disclosed in the initial request shall require a formal notification and payment of additional fees as provided herein. The application patent shall be deemed abandoned if the prescribed formalities are not completed within the stipulated timeframe.

An applicant whose application patent has been rejected under this Act shall have the right to appeal against such rejection to the Controller. The appellate body may, after affording the applicant a reasonable opportunity of being heard and considering all relevant evidence presented, either allow the appeal and direct that the patent be granted as originally applied for or modify the claim(s) in the application and grant the patent accordingly. Where an appeal is allowed, the date of filing of the original application shall be deemed to be the date of filing for the purposes of determining priority under this Act. Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the appellate body may further appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within a period of sixty days from the date of such order, subject to payment of prescribed fees and fulfilling other conditions as provided herein. The Board’s decision shall be final.

An applicant seeking protection under this Act shall file a complete application patent specifying the invention and its claimed subject matter. The application must include a clear and concise description of the invention sufficient to enable a person skilled in the art to practice it, accompanied by any necessary drawings or diagrams. Where an application relates to a process for producing a substance, the application shall also disclose the best method known to the applicant for carrying out the process on an industrial scale. The Controller General may require the submission of additional information or clarification at any stage during examination. An applicant is permitted to request provisional protection for a period not exceeding twelve months from the date of filing, subject to fulfilling prescribed formalities and payment of requisite fees. Any amendment to claims after the first statement in reply shall only be allowed if such amendments do not substantially alter the original invention disclosed.

An application patent shall be deemed invalid if it is determined, under this Act, that the invention was not novel at the time of filing. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating prior publication disclosure has been adequately addressed, provided that such requirement shall only arise where a credible challenge regarding novelty is presented by an interested party. Further, an application patent will be rejected if it contains subject matter which is solely comprised of a discovery relating to living organisms or naturally occurring substances, unless it incorporates a process by which the substance can be extracted or produced. The applicant bears the responsibility for demonstrating compliance with these conditions throughout the examination procedure.

An applicant seeking protection under this Act shall file a complete application patent disclosing the invention clearly and concisely. Failure to do so, or submission of information deliberately misleading to the Controller, renders the application liable for rejection and subjects the applicant to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Any person aggrieved by an order rejecting an application may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The Board’s decision is final, subject to further appeal under the Supreme Court Act. Where infringement of a patent is established, damages shall be assessed based on reasonable royalty and lost profits, with enhanced penalties for wilful infringement exceeding one hundred thousand rupees.

An applicant seeking grant of an application patent shall, upon request by any third party demonstrating legitimate industrial interest, provide a reasoned explanation regarding the scope and terms proposed for compulsory licensing under this Act. Such request must specify the nature of the technological field involved and the potential public benefit to be derived from the license. The Controller may, after affording the applicant an opportunity to be heard, direct the applicant to negotiate in good faith with the requesting party concerning a non-exclusive license on patent protected terms. Any assignment or transmission of the application patent shall include a covenant binding the assignee to adhere to any existing compulsory licensing arrangements previously agreed upon by the original applicant. Failure to comply with such directions may render the patent liable for revocation as provided herein.

An applicant seeking grant of an application patent shall furnish such particulars and documents as are required under this Act, and any failure to do so accurately and completely may render the application liable for rejection. Where a person aggrieved by a decision of the Controller relating to the acceptance or refusal of an application patent, or the determination of priority between two applications, appeals may be made to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of that decision. The Appellate Board shall hear arguments presented by both the applicant and the Controller, and may require further evidence to be submitted. Any order passed by the Appellate Board shall be final, subject to a further appeal to the High Court on grounds specified herein relating to jurisdiction or violation of natural justice.

An application patent shall be deemed to be filed on the date the prescribed forms and accompanying documents are received by the Controller. Where an applicant submits multiple versions of an application within a period of twelve months from the initial filing date, only the first such submission shall constitute the official date filing application under this Act. The Controller may require further particulars or clarification regarding any aspect of the application, and the applicant shall be obliged to provide these within the timeframe specified by the Controller. Failure to comply with such requests may result in the application being deemed withdrawn. Any communication from an applicant relating to a pending application must be submitted electronically unless specifically exempted under rules framed for this purpose. The date filing application is critical for determining priority rights and subsequent examination procedures as provided herein.

An applicant seeking grant of an application patent shall furnish with the request, a declaration specifying the claim of originality and novelty pertaining to the invention. The Controller may require further documentation substantiating these claims, including detailed experimental data and comparative analyses against prior art disclosures. Where the invention relates to a process for producing a substance intended for use as a foodstuff or medicinal purpose, the applicant must demonstrate through certified testing procedures that such use is safe and efficacious. Furthermore, any entity intending to utilize a patented product or process commercially shall obtain a use certification trade mark from the relevant authority, confirming adherence to prescribed quality standards, provided that this requirement does not preclude patent enforcement actions under this Act.

The Controller may, upon receipt of an application patent and after due consideration of the invention’s merits, grant permission to a third party to utilize the patented process or product subject to a royalty payment scheme determined by the Controller. Such permission shall be documented in a license agreement annexed to the patent record, outlining the scope of permitted activities and duration of the license. The applicant for the application patent may assign their rights under this Act relating to the service derived from the invention to any person, including a body corporate, provided that such assignment is recorded with the Controller. Any subsequent transfer or sub-license shall also be subject to prior approval and registration as per procedures prescribed herein. Failure to adhere to the terms of the license agreement may result in revocation of the permission granted under this Act.

A person shall be deemed to be a patent agent if, and only if, such person has applied for registration under this Act and possesses qualifications as may be prescribed. A patent agent shall possess either a degree in engineering or technology from a recognized institution or a diploma of not less than three years’ duration in any branch of engineering or technology, provided that the applicant has passed an examination conducted by the Controller to assess their competence relating to patents law and practice. Any person registered as a patent agent may appear for or on behalf of applicants before the Controller under this Act.

Every application for registration as a patent agent shall be accompanied by a declaration verifying that the applicant possesses the prescribed qualifications, including demonstrable experience in matters relating to intellectual property rights. The Controller may require such further documentation as deemed necessary to ascertain the applicant’s competence and understanding of patent law principles. Upon receipt of an application, the Controller shall publish a notice inviting objections from any person having knowledge of the applicant's suitability. Any objection received must be addressed by the applicant in writing, providing reasoned responses and supporting evidence. Registration as a patent agent confers upon the registrant the right to represent applicants before the relevant authorities under this Act.

Any person acting as a patent agent shall be deemed to have committed an offence if, having knowledge that any false statement or material particular has been incorporated in the application for a patent, he proceeds with prosecution thereof. Such person shall be liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, and also be subject to a fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees. Further, under this Act, a patent agent found guilty of professional misconduct, including but not limited to wilful negligence in the performance of his duties or improper solicitation of patent business, may have his name removed from the Register of Patent Agents. The Controller shall provide an opportunity for the patent agent to be heard before making such an order. Any aggrieved party may seek redressal through civil remedies as provided herein against a patent agent’s actions.

An application for registration as a patent agent shall be made to the Controller in such form and containing such particulars as may be prescribed. Every applicant for registration under this Act shall, subject to any exemptions provided herein, furnish proof of possessing qualifications deemed sufficient by the Controller, including evidence of academic attainment in science or engineering, or practical experience equivalent thereto, relevant to patent law practice. The Controller may require an applicant to undergo and pass such examinations as he deems necessary to assess their competence in matters pertaining to patents. Upon satisfactory completion of these requirements and payment of the prescribed fee, the applicant shall be registered as a patent agent and entered into the Register maintained for that purpose. A person whose name is so entered shall be entitled to exercise the rights and perform the duties of a patent agent under this Act.

A person shall be deemed to be a patent agent if, and only if, such individual has satisfied the Controller that they possess qualifications prescribed under this Act relating to scientific or technical education and practical experience in the field of patents. An applicant seeking registration as a patent agent must submit an application in the form specified by the rules made hereunder, accompanied by evidence demonstrating compliance with these requirements. The Controller may require further documentation or interviews to ascertain suitability. Registration shall be conditional upon adherence to ethical guidelines promulgated under this Act and subject to revocation if professional misconduct is established. A registered patent agent shall not represent clients in matters relating to inventions outside their area of specified expertise, as determined by the Controller.

Any individual acting as a patent agent without possessing a valid certificate of registration, obtained through examination conducted by the Controller, shall be deemed to have engaged in unauthorized practice and will be liable for penalties not exceeding fifty thousand rupees for each instance of such activity. Furthermore, any person employing an unregistered individual as a patent agent shall face a similar penalty, recoverable from both parties jointly and severally. The Controller may, upon receiving credible information regarding violations under this Act, issue notices requiring production of registration certificates; failure to comply will result in summary suspension of the alleged agent’s activities pending investigation. Repeated or willful contravention may lead to prosecution for offenses punishable with imprisonment for a term not less than six months.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any assignment or license of a patent, or of any right or interest therein, may be effected by instrument in writing and under seal, or where the assignor or licensee is a company, by an instrument executed electronically as provided herein. Where such assignment or license relates to the entire patent, including all claims, it shall be deemed absolute unless the instrument specifies limitations on the scope of the rights granted. Any person seeking to act as a patent agent may execute assignments and licenses on behalf of their clients, subject to fulfilling conditions prescribed by regulations made under this Act. Such agents shall hold no personal interest in any royalties or benefits arising from such assignment or license, except where expressly agreed upon with the client through a written agreement registered with the Controller. The Controller may require disclosure of all related parties involved in an assignment for scrutiny and verification purposes.

Where any question arises concerning whether a person is, or is not, entitled to be registered as a patent agent under this Act, the Controller may, subject to appeal to the Appellate Board, determine such question. An application for appeal against an order made by the Controller determining entitlement shall be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of that order and shall state specifically the grounds on which the applicant alleges the order to be erroneous in law or fact. Provided that if the appellant satisfies the Appellate Board that sufficient cause existed for the delay, the Board may entertain the appeal notwithstanding the delay. The Controller’s decision regarding registration as a patent agent shall be final pending such an appeal.

Any individual acting as a patent agent without possessing a valid certificate of registration, obtained through examination conducted by the Controller, shall be deemed to have engaged in unauthorized practice and subject to penalties under this Act. Such individuals may face fines not exceeding two hundred thousand rupees for each instance of such activity, and further, imprisonment extending up to one year. Where an unregistered person facilitates the filing of a patent application on behalf of another, that applicant shall also be liable to a fine of fifty thousand rupees. The Controller may, ex officio, initiate proceedings against any suspected individual. This provision applies irrespective of whether the individual is acting under the auspices of a registered firm and remains applicable even when dealing with applications filed under the Budapest Treaty International system.

Where any question arises regarding the validity of a representation made by a patent agent on behalf of an applicant for a patent, such question shall be determined solely based on the information available to the Controller at the time of grant and subsequent examination under this Act. Any party aggrieved by a decision concerning the competence or conduct of a registered user shall have recourse to appeal as provided herein, subject to demonstrating prejudice directly attributable to the actions of the patent agent. The burden of proving such prejudice rests upon the appellant. Further, any claim that a registered user acted outside the scope of their authorized activities will be considered in determining whether the patent remains valid and enforceable against third parties.

For the purposes of this Act, “International Bureau” means the International Bureau of the World Intellectual Property Organization. A person shall be deemed to be a patent agent if such person has been duly registered as a patent agent under this Act and possesses the qualifications prescribed herein for registration. No individual other than a person so registered shall use the title of "patent agent" or any words likely to suggest that he is a patent agent, subject to exceptions provided for in the regulations framed under this Act. A patent agent may represent clients before the Controller and perform acts relating to applications for patents as authorized by rules made under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, a collective mark shall mean a mark adopted by an association of persons engaged in providing common services or carrying on activities for mutual benefit. Such a mark may indicate membership in that association, or otherwise identify goods or services provided by members. The use of a collective mark is subject to conditions as provided herein relating to quality control and adherence to standards established by the association. Any alteration to a registered collective mark shall require prior approval from the Registrar. Further, the rights conferred under this Act regarding a collective mark extend only to the association itself, not individual members using the mark.

An application for registration of a collective mark shall be made to the Registrar in the prescribed form and shall include a statement of all those who, at the time of application, are members of the association seeking registration. The applicant shall furnish such documents as may be required by the Registrar demonstrating that the association is a legal entity duly constituted under the relevant laws and possesses the requisite authority to use the mark collectively for the benefit of its members. Further, the statement must specify the goods or services in relation to which the collective mark proposes to be used by the members of the association. The Registrar may require the applicant to submit evidence demonstrating the geographical area within which the members operate, provided that this requirement does not impede registration otherwise compliant with this Act.

The proprietor of a collective mark shall be an association incorporated by law or otherwise recognised as such, and may include cooperatives, societies registered under the Cooperative Societies Act, and other similar bodies. Any person who ceases to be a member of such association shall immediately cease to have any right in relation to the collective mark. The association is entitled to institute proceedings for infringement of the collective mark on behalf of its members, and any damages recovered shall be distributed amongst them as determined by the association’s governing council. Further, an aggrieved member may pursue remedies independently under this Act if the association fails to adequately protect the mark's integrity or enforce its rights against infringers. The association is responsible for ensuring that all goods or services offered under the collective mark conform to prescribed standards and maintain the reputation of the mark.

The Registrar may register a collective mark upon application made by an association conforming to the requirements prescribed herein. Such application shall state the objects of the association, the geographical area of its operation and the rules governing the use of the collective mark by members. The applicant shall furnish evidence demonstrating that the association is a body corporate or a society registered under relevant legislation and possesses the requisite authority to regulate the quality and characteristics of goods or services associated with the mark. Registration of a collective mark does not grant exclusive rights to any individual member, but rather vests such rights in the association itself, subject to adherence to the prescribed usage guidelines. Any dispute concerning eligibility for membership or infringement of the collective mark’s standards may be referred to an Arbitrator appointed by the Registrar.

The Registrar may register a collective mark upon application made by an association conforming to prescribed conditions and demonstrating that its members engage, or propose to engage, in activities giving rise to a common characteristic. Such registration shall be subject to the applicant association furnishing proof of its constitution, bylaws, and a list of current members, updated annually as provided herein. The collective mark shall not be used by any member except under terms stipulated within the association’s bylaws, ensuring uniformity in quality or services rendered. Any alteration to the association's bylaws concerning usage guidelines must be notified to the Registrar for approval prior to implementation; failure to do so may result in cancellation of the registration. Further, members found violating these conditions are liable for penalties as determined by the association and reported under this Act.

The registration of a collective mark shall not be refused solely on the ground that members of the association are engaged in activities unrelated to the goods or services indicated by the mark, provided that such activities do not detract from the distinctiveness or reputation thereof. Any person who uses a registered collective mark without authorization from the proprietor association, or alters the mark in any manner which affects its identity and distinctive character, shall be guilty of an offence and liable to prosecution under this Act. Furthermore, where infringement occurs, the proprietor may seek injunctive relief preventing further unauthorized use and recover damages proportionate to the loss suffered by members of the association due to the deceptive practice as provided herein.

The proprietor of a collective mark may grant licenses to use the mark to members of the association entitled to its benefit, subject to such terms and conditions as are specified in the license agreement. Such agreements shall clearly delineate the scope of permissible activities under the mark, including geographical limitations and product categories. Any assignment of rights relating to a collective mark requires prior approval from the Registrar, who may condition such assignments on maintaining the integrity and quality standards associated with the mark. The association shall provide the Registrar with details of all licenses granted and assignments made, as provided herein. Further, any sublicensee or assignee shall be bound by the original license terms and conditions, and remain subject to disciplinary action under the association’s internal regulations for misuse of the collective mark.

The Registrar may refuse registration of a proposed collective mark if he considers that the conditions for eligibility are not met, and such refusal shall be accompanied by an order specifying the reasons therefor. Any applicant aggrieved by such an order may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. Further, where a collective mark is registered, any member of the association entitled to use the mark may challenge a decision of the Registrar regarding the scope of permissible usage or the conditions for maintaining registration, through a similar process of appeal before the Appellate Board. The Association shall be responsible for ensuring compliance with these conditions and may face revocation proceedings under this Act if it fails to do so.

The owner of a collective mark may grant licenses to authorized users for the use thereof upon such terms and conditions as are specified in writing, provided that such terms do not conflict with the fundamental purpose of maintaining uniformity and quality control amongst those utilizing the mark. Any license granted under this Act shall be assignable subject to the prior consent of the owner of the collective mark, which consent shall not be unreasonably withheld. Further, where a registered breeder variety is incorporated into the production process or characteristics defining goods eligible for use under the collective mark, any assignment of rights relating to that breeder variety must explicitly acknowledge and respect the existing licensing agreements pertaining to the collective mark’s usage. The owner may revoke licenses if an authorized user fails to adhere to these conditions as provided herein.

The Registrar may entertain an application for registration of a collective mark even if a prior respect filing application exists concerning identical or similar indicia, provided that the applicant demonstrates a clear and established organizational structure representing a defined group of users. Any party aggrieved by such acceptance shall have standing to appeal under this Act within sixty days from the date of publication in the Trade Marks Journal, asserting that the collective mark’s use would create confusion with existing marks or unfairly prejudice prior respect filings. The appellate authority shall consider evidence pertaining to the applicant's organizational constitution and the potential for dilution or misrepresentation arising from registration, subject to principles of fair trade and consumer protection as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, “register” shall mean the official record maintained by the Controller General under this Act, detailing particulars relating to applications for patents, granted patents, and other relevant information as provided herein. The register shall be deemed a public document, subject to any restrictions imposed in accordance with regulations framed under this Act concerning confidential or commercially sensitive data. Any entry made in the register shall be presumed correct until proven otherwise through due process of law. An applicant seeking inclusion of an invention in the register must satisfy all requirements pertaining to novelty and inventive step as determined by the Controller.

An application for registration shall be accompanied by a declaration specifying the name and address of any legal entity claiming assignment or license relating to the invention, and such declaration shall be verified in the prescribed manner. The Controller may require further particulars regarding the ownership interest claimed, including documentation substantiating the transfer or grant of rights. Upon receipt of an application, the Controller shall record a provisional registration on the register, noting the date of filing and assigning a unique identification number. Any person aggrieved by a decision relating to the entry of an invention onto the register may appeal under this Act to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of such decision. The register shall be deemed public record and accessible for inspection as provided herein.

Any applicant aggrieved by a decision relating to the acceptance or rejection of his application for registration shall have the right to appeal to the Controller within three months from the date of communication of such decision. The Controller may, after giving the appellant an opportunity of being heard and after considering the evidence submitted, confirm, vary, or reverse the decision appealed against. Where an appeal is preferred under this Act, the applicant shall be deemed to have waived any objection which he could have raised but for the provisions of section 105. The Controller’s order on such appeal shall be final, subject to further appeals as provided herein. Any person whose interests are adversely affected by an entry in the register may apply to the Appellate Board for redressal of his grievances.

An application for registration shall be accompanied by a statement setting forth the priority date, if any, claimed under this Act, and such statement shall be verified by the applicant declaring that as at the date of filing the application, no earlier identical application has been filed or published anywhere in the world. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish further particulars relating to the invention, including details regarding experimentation conducted and data generated, if deemed necessary for assessing novelty and inventive step. Any alteration made to the application after its publication shall be noted by the Registrar in the register. Objections raised during examination shall be communicated to the applicant within a prescribed time frame, allowing opportunity for response or amendment. The register maintained under this Act shall be open to public inspection at all reasonable hours, subject to such regulations as may be prescribed.

An application for entry on the register shall be accompanied by a declaration specifying the right to priority under this Act, provided that such declaration complies with the prescribed form and contains a statement verifying the accuracy of the particulars relating to the earlier application. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish further documentation substantiating the claim to priority, including certified copies of official records from the jurisdiction where the initial application was filed. Failure to submit satisfactory evidence as directed by the Controller shall render the application liable for rejection under this Act. Any alteration to the details recorded on the register relating to a registered invention requires prior approval from the Controller and must be made in accordance with prescribed procedures.

Any party aggrieved by any entry in the register relating to a patent shall have the right to appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date on which such entry was made, provided that the appeal must specify the grounds of objection and be accompanied by the prescribed fee. Failure to comply with this time limit shall render the appeal inadmissible. The Board may, after affording an opportunity for hearing to all concerned parties, direct rectification of the register or dismiss the appeal. Any person found to have knowingly misrepresented facts during proceedings concerning the register shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding one lakh rupees and may also face prosecution under relevant provisions relating to false evidence.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any patentee may grant a license to use the patented invention under conditions specified in the license agreement, which shall be recorded with the Controller. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and the terms thereof, including royalty rates and duration, are entirely at the discretion of the parties involved, provided that the license does not contravene any other provision of this Act or rules made thereunder. Furthermore, a patentee may assign their entire interest in the patent, or part thereof, to another party by way of an assignment, which shall also be recorded in the register. The recordation of such licenses and assignments is mandatory for them to be legally binding against third parties and creates a public notice of the transfer of rights relating to the invention as it appears on the register.

The Controller shall maintain a comprehensive register of all inventions for which patent applications have been filed under this Act, distinguishing between pending applications and those patents granted; provided that any party aggrieved by an entry, or omission thereof, in the said register may within sixty days from the date such entry is published, or the relevant record becomes accessible online, file an appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be on grounds demonstrably affecting the applicant’s right to a patent, including but not limited to errors in classification, misstatement of inventorship, or improper notation regarding priority claims. The Board's decision on such appeals shall be final and binding, subject to further judicial review under established principles of law concerning decisions made by administrative tribunals.

Where any person aggrieved by an entry in the register relating to a patent believes that such entry has been made erroneously or without due cause, he may apply to the Controller for rectification of the said entry. Such application shall specify the nature of the error and the rectification sought. The Controller may, after affording the applicant and all other interested parties an opportunity of being heard, direct rectification of the register as deemed appropriate. Failure to comply with a direction under this Act concerning the register may render the defaulting party liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees, and further action for passing off or unfair competition arising from such non-compliance shall be actionable under the relevant provisions of law.

The Controller shall maintain a comprehensive register of all patent applications received under this Act, detailing particulars including the applicant’s name and address, the title of the invention, the date of filing, and any priority claims asserted. Entries in the register shall be deemed prima facie evidence of the matters therein contained, subject to proof to the contrary. Any person aggrieved by an entry or omission in the patent office register may apply for its correction or amendment as provided herein. The Controller may, upon application and after due notice to all concerned parties, rectify any errors or make necessary additions to the register. Furthermore, the public shall have access to inspect the register during normal business hours, except where such access is restricted under this Act to protect trade secrets.

For the purposes of this Act, an integrated circuit shall be defined as a set of circuits manufactured on a semiconductor material and includes three-dimensional arrangements of such circuits. An integrated circuit may incorporate active and passive elements, including but not limited to transistors, diodes, resistors, capacitors, and inductors. Subject to any modifications notified under this Act, the term "integrated circuit" shall also encompass layouts depicting structures intended for use in manufacturing an integrated circuit, provided that these layouts are capable of being reproduced or used directly in the manufacture of such a circuit. The definition excludes circuits solely designed for military applications as determined by the Central Government.

An application for registration of an integrated circuit layout-design shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the drawings and documentation pertaining to the fabrication process, detailing all layers and masking techniques employed. The Registrar may require further clarification regarding the technical specifications if deemed necessary for proper assessment under this Act. Any prior publication or commercial exploitation of the integrated circuit design outside India shall be disclosed in the application, subject to provisions relating to grace periods as provided herein. An applicant seeking registration shall affirm that they are the rightful owner of the layout-design and possess exclusive rights over its reproduction and use. The Registrar may reject an application if it finds that the submitted documentation is incomplete or fails to adequately describe the integrated circuit.

Where any person unlawfully makes, imports, distributes, displays for sale, offers for sale, or uses an integrated circuit infringing upon the layout-design rights of another, such person shall be liable for damages. The amount of damages recoverable shall be determined by considering the loss suffered by the owner of the layout-design right, taking into account the reasonable royalty that would have been payable had the infringer obtained a license under this Act.
