Further, the Court may grant an injunction restraining the infringing party from continuing such acts, provided that it is satisfied that irreparable injury has been caused to the registered proprietor. Subject to appeal to the High Court, any order made by the Court concerning damages or injunctions shall be final. The owner of a layout-design right may also seek account of profits derived from the infringement as provided herein.

An application for registration of an integrated circuit layout-design shall be accompanied by a declaration verifying the originality of the design and confirming that the applicant is the first owner thereof, subject to any prior assignments. The Registrar may require such further information as he deems necessary to ascertain compliance with the provisions of this Act relating to ownership and inventorship. Where an application relates to an integrated circuit incorporating elements previously registered under this Act, the declaration shall specifically address the nature of those incorporated elements and demonstrate that the overall layout-design constitutes a novel work. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar regarding the acceptance or rejection of an application may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of communication of such decision. The Tribunal’s determination shall be final, provided that it does not contravene any provision under this Act.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, an integrated circuit shall be deemed to have been infringed where a person, without authorization from the registered proprietor, makes, imports, distributes, sells, hires or offers to sell or hire any integrated circuit that is substantially similar to the original layout-design. For the purposes of determining substantial similarity, consideration shall be given to the overall impression created by comparing the infringing integrated circuit with the registered layout-design, taking into account features such as masking layers and interconnecting elements. Provided that this determination shall not extend to minor variations or adaptations necessary for compatibility with existing manufacturing processes, unless those variations directly reproduce a protected element of the original design. Any person alleging infringement may apply to the relevant authority seeking redressal as provided herein.

Any person who, without authorization from the registered proprietor of an integrated circuit layout-design, makes, imports, distributes, sells, hires or offers for sale or hire any infringing copy shall be liable to pay damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the proprietor. Such damages may include compensation for lost profits and reasonable costs incurred in pursuing legal remedies under this Act. Further, where infringement is established, the Court may order the destruction of the infringing integrated circuit layout-designs and related materials. The registered proprietor shall have the right to apply for an injunction restraining any person from continuing such acts of infringement, subject to demonstrating a likelihood of irreparable harm. Penalties for repeat offences shall be doubled as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder, the owner of an integrated circuit layout-design may grant a license conferring upon the licensee the right to make, use, or exploit the design for specific purposes. Such licenses shall be assignable in writing, provided that the assignment includes a detailed description of the licensed rights and limitations as determined by the Controller. Any subsequent assignment of such license requires prior notification to the original licensor, allowing them a period of thirty days to object based on material breach of the initial licensing agreement. The owner may also grant an exclusive license, restricting all other uses of the integrated circuit design during the term specified in the written agreement. Failure to adhere to these stipulations renders the assignee liable for damages as provided herein.

Where an allegation is made that a person has engaged in an act restricted under this Act concerning an integrated circuit layout-design, such allegation shall be deemed substantiated only upon presentation of prima facie evidence demonstrating substantial similarity between the alleged infringing layout-design and the registered layout-design, taking into account the overall impression created. The respondent may challenge the sufficiency of said evidence by presenting expert testimony establishing differences in functionality or intended purpose; provided that such challenge must specify with particularity the aspects of difference relied upon. Any order made under this Act concerning infringement shall be subject to appeal before a High Court, and the appellate determination shall consider whether the original finding was manifestly arbitrary or based on an erroneous interpretation of the criteria for assessing substantial similarity as provided herein.

The owner of an integrated circuit layout-design shall be entitled to grant licenses permitting the manufacture of semiconductor devices incorporating such design, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated within the license agreement. Such agreements may specify limitations on geographic territory, field of use, and duration of validity. Any assignment of rights in an integrated circuit layout-design, whether partial or complete, requires execution by a registered power of attorney duly authorized by the assignor. The permitted use of a licensed integrated circuit design for research purposes is expressly allowed without requiring prior consent from the owner, provided that such research does not involve commercial exploitation and the results are published in a recognized scientific journal. Further, any licensee may sub-license rights under this Act with the written approval of the layout-design owner.

Where an integrated circuit layout-design is alleged to be a copy of an existing layout-design, the determination of infringement shall proceed upon a finding that the allegedly infringing design incorporates substantially all elements of the original, and that such incorporation demonstrates a clear intent to reproduce the inventive features therein. It is provided that the mere presence of common or standard components within both designs does not, in itself, constitute evidence of copying. The burden of proving substantial similarity rests with the claimant; however, where the claimant establishes prima facie evidence of unauthorized reproduction, the respondent may demonstrate that the design incorporates elements derived from an invention means new and independently conceived, thereby negating the claim subject to a detailed technical comparison as provided herein. Appeals against such findings may be made before the relevant judicial forum.

An application for registration of an integrated circuit layout-design shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the first published version of the said layout-design, if any. The applicant shall furnish such particulars as are required under this Act relating to the ownership and prior history of the integrated circuit. Where an application is received, the Application Registrar may require the applicant to submit further documentation clarifying aspects of the design or its derivation. Subject to compliance with these requirements, the Application Registrar shall record the date of filing of the application in a register maintained for that purpose. Provided that if the layout-design incorporates elements already registered under this Act, the Application Registrar shall notify the applicant accordingly and request details regarding those incorporated features.

Where any person has contravened clause (a) of section 13 relating to unauthorized reproduction of an integrated circuit layout-design, the registered proprietor shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief restraining such acts and further damages as provided herein. The measure of damages recoverable shall take into account the loss of profits suffered by the proprietor due to the infringement, as well as any unreasonable profit made by the infringer as a consequence thereof. Subject to an application being made within three years from the date of first proven infringement, the Court may grant a register effect order compelling the infringing party to deliver up or destroy all copies of the integrated circuit layout-design in their possession or control. Provided that such delivery or destruction is carried out under the supervision of a designated officer appointed by the Court.

For the purposes of this Act, "layout design" means the three dimensional representation of an integrated circuit upon a mask used in the manufacture of semiconductors; provided that such representation includes distinctive topological features which define the arrangement of elements comprising the integrated circuit. A “registered layout design” is one accepted for registration under this Act and entered into the Register of Layout-Designs, as provided herein. An application for registration of a layout design shall disclose whether it incorporates any previously registered layout design, and if so, specify such prior registrations. The term "layout design" excludes features solely attributable to achieving technical effects or producing manufacturing results.

An application for registration of a registered layout design shall be accompanied by such particulars and documents as may be prescribed, including detailed schematics illustrating the arrangement of elements within the integrated circuit. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further information or clarification regarding the layout-design’s novelty and originality, provided that any such request must be substantiated with reasoned justification. Upon receipt of a complete application, an examination shall be conducted to ascertain whether the design meets the criteria for registration under this Act, specifically concerning its distinctiveness from prior published works. If deficiencies are identified during examination, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to address them within a stipulated timeframe. The registered layout design confers upon the proprietor exclusive rights as provided herein.

Where any person infringes a registered layout design, such person shall be liable to pay damages to the registered proprietor. The amount of damages shall be determined by considering the loss suffered by the registered proprietor as a consequence of the infringement, taking into account profit made by the infringing party and any other relevant factors as provided herein. Subject to appeal to an appropriate judicial forum, the Court may also grant an injunction restraining the infringer from further acts of infringement. It is provided that in determining damages, the Court shall consider whether the infringer acted in good faith or with knowledge of the registered layout design. The remedies available under this Act are without prejudice to any other remedy available to the registered proprietor under general principles of law.

An application for registration of a registered layout design shall be accompanied by such particulars and documents as the Office may require, including detailed schematics illustrating the topological features of the integrated circuit. The applicant shall furnish an address for service in India; failure to do so will render the application void. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar may direct the applicant to amend any deficiencies within a period not exceeding sixty days from the date of such direction. If the applicant fails to comply with such directions, the application shall be deemed rejected. The Registrar may, after giving notice to the applicant and other interested parties, refuse registration if he considers that the layout design does not involve an original work or is contrary to public interest. Any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days of receipt of such order.

An application for registration of a registered layout design shall be deemed to satisfy the requirements of this Act if it contains a clear and accurate representation of the integrated circuit layout-design, accompanied by a declaration verifying its originality and absence of prior publication. The Controller may reject an application if he is satisfied that the layout-design lacks sufficient novelty or infringes upon any existing right under this Act or any other law for the time being in force. Furthermore, where a layout-design incorporates elements already registered as a separate registered layout design, the applicant shall provide explicit details of such incorporation and demonstrate compliance with the provisions regarding derivative works as provided herein. The Registrar may require additional documentation to ascertain these conditions are met before proceeding with examination.

Any person who knowingly and without authorization makes, uses, imports, or offers to sell any product incorporating a registered layout design shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall be assessed at an amount not less than five per centum of the cost of production of the infringing article nor more than ten per centum thereof, as determined by the relevant civil court. Further, where infringement is established, the Court may order the destruction or disposal of the infringing products and materials used in their manufacture. The registered layout design proprietor shall have the right to apply for interlocutory orders restraining any acts that would constitute an infringement under this Act, subject to just terms. Repeated contravention of these provisions may result in imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years.

The registered layout design shall remain the exclusive property of the registrant, subject to any license granted as provided herein. Any assignment of rights pertaining to a registered layout design must be executed in writing and attested by at least one witness competent to testify under this Act; such assignment shall include a detailed description identifying the specific layout-design being transferred and the scope of rights conveyed. The Registrar may require submission of documentation demonstrating due diligence regarding any proposed sublicensee, particularly where the sublicense involves commercial exploitation outside territorial jurisdiction. Further, an owner of a registered layout design may grant non-exclusive licenses permitting reproduction or adaptation, provided that such licenses do not conflict with existing contractual obligations and are duly recorded with the Registrar to maintain transparency amongst interested parties.

Where any question arises as to whether a layout design infringes a registered layout design, the Tribunal shall determine such question based upon an examination of the substantial similarity between the two designs, considering both their overall appearance and the interplay of their constituent elements. It shall be presumed that a registered layout design is infringed if the alleged infringing layout design copies or has been derived from the registered layout design, subject to proof by the registered proprietor demonstrating lack of such copying or derivation. The respondent may adduce evidence establishing independent creation of the allegedly infringing work, provided that such evidence demonstrates a clear absence of access to the registered layout design prior to its creation. Any appeal against an order made under this Act shall lie to the High Court within ninety days from the date of such order.

Where an appeal arises from any decision of the Registrar relating to the registration of a registered layout design, or concerning objections filed under this Act, such appeal shall lie before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The appellant may submit documentary evidence not previously considered by the Registrar, provided that such submission is accompanied by a duly signed affidavit explaining the reasons for its late presentation and demonstrating material prejudice resulting from the initial failure to present it. Decisions of the Intellectual Property Appellate Board concerning applications filed with the patent office central shall be final subject only to appeal to the High Court on grounds specified under this Act relating to jurisdiction or other substantial questions of law.

For the purposes of this Act, "registered layout design" shall mean a layout design that has been entered into the Register as provided herein and relates only to features essential to the functioning of an integrated circuit or specifically designed to improve its performance; nothing in this definition shall be construed to include elements solely for aesthetic appeal. An application for registration of a layout design shall disclose all such features, and the particulars thereof, as are prescribed by regulations framed under this Act. The Registrar may reject any application if it contains matter which is not directly related to the registered layout design.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder, an infringement of a registered layout design shall occur where any person, without authorization from the registered proprietor, directly or indirectly makes, imports, sells, hires, displays for sale, or distributes any article embodying the protected layout-design. Where such infringement has occurred, the registered proprietor may apply to the relevant Commercial Court for relief, including an injunction restraining further acts of infringement and damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the proprietor. The court shall also have power to order the destruction of infringing articles found in the possession of the infringer. Furthermore, if the registered layout design is subject to an effected international registration under the International Design System, remedies available under this Act shall be extended to cover acts committed within the territories designated in such international registration.

Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication shall be entitled to grant licenses relating to the use of such indication under this Act, provided that any such license may be exclusive or non-exclusive and may relate to specific goods or services as defined in the register. Assignment of the right to use a registration geographical indication is permissible subject to prior approval from the Registrar, who may require demonstration of due diligence regarding continued adherence to standards of quality and authenticity associated with the indicated product. Further, any assignee shall be bound by all conditions and limitations applicable to the original proprietor’s use of the geographical indication. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint, investigate whether licensed or assigned usage is detrimental to the reputation or distinctiveness of the registered geographical indication and may impose remedial measures as deemed appropriate.

For the purposes of this Act, "registered" shall mean that a trade mark has been formally recorded in the Trade Marks Register maintained by the Registrar and is accompanied by an entry confirming such registration. A trade mark shall be deemed registered upon the date specified in the certificate of registration issued under this Act, provided that the applicant has complied with all prescribed conditions for registration as stipulated herein. Any alteration to a registered trade mark’s particulars, including but not limited to changes in ownership or address, shall also be recorded and maintained within the Register. The status of any trade mark as registered is subject to periodic review under this Act.

An application for registration of a proposed trade mark shall be refused if it is deemed deceptive and likely to mislead or cause confusion amongst the public regarding the nature, quality or origin of goods or services. Where an objection is raised under this Act, the applicant may submit counter-arguments and evidence in support of the distinctiveness of the mark. The Trade Marks Registry shall consider such submissions before making a determination on whether to proceed with registration. A trade mark once registered confers upon the proprietor exclusive rights to use the mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered, subject to any limitations specified during the registration process. Any subsequent application featuring a substantially identical mark will be refused if it conflicts with an existing registered trade mark.

Where any goods or services are offered or provided infringing a registered trade mark, the owner of the registered trade mark shall be entitled to seek an injunction restraining such infringement. Such injunction may include orders preventing the erasure or alteration of marks, labels, signs, or packaging used in connection with the infringing goods or services. Further, under this Act, damages adequate to compensate for the loss suffered by the registered proprietor as a result of the infringement may be awarded. It is provided that where the defendant proves having acted in good faith, the amount of damages shall be reduced accordingly. The remedies available to a registered proprietor are without prejudice to any other right or remedy which they may have under this Act or otherwise. Any person desiring to enforce a registered trade mark shall provide evidence satisfying the court regarding ownership and validity.

An application for the registration of a proposed trade mark shall be refused if the Registrar has reason to believe that the mark is likely to be confused with an earlier registered trade mark or any other trade mark used in India, and such confusion would be detrimental to the interests of consumers or the owners of the earlier marks. The applicant may submit evidence rebutting this belief, and the Registrar shall consider all submitted material before issuing a decision. Where a trade mark is deemed descriptive of the goods or services with which it is associated, registration shall only be granted if the applicant demonstrates acquired distinctiveness through extensive use and consumer recognition. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of that decision. The register maintained under this Act shall clearly indicate whether a trade mark is registered and, where applicable, specify any limitations on its scope of protection.

A trademark shall be deemed *registered* upon successful completion of the examination process and subsequent entry into the Register of Trade Marks, subject to compliance with all applicable provisions under this Act. The Registrar may require further documentation or clarification from an applicant if any discrepancies are identified during examination relating to distinctiveness or prior use. Provided that a notice of acceptance is dispatched to the applicant, and no request for personal hearing is received within the prescribed period, the trademark shall proceed to registration. Any opposition filed against a proposed mark must be resolved according to established procedures as provided herein; failure to do so may result in delayed registration. The registered proprietor shall maintain accurate records pertaining to the goods or services associated with their trade mark.

Any individual or enterprise employing a deceptive or false representation in connection with any goods or services offered under a registered trademark shall be liable for damages. Such liability extends to instances where the use of an identical or confusingly similar sign creates a likelihood of confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin, quality, or characteristics of those goods or services. Further, upon complaint by the registered proprietor, the High Court may issue injunctions restraining such deceptive practices and order the destruction of infringing materials. The court shall also be empowered to award compensation reflecting the loss suffered by the registered proprietor due to the infringement, subject to limitations as provided herein regarding contributory liability.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any registered proprietor may grant exclusive licenses relating to the use of their registered trademark for specific goods or services within defined geographical territories. Such licenses shall be documented in writing and filed with the Trade Marks Registry, specifying the licensed rights, duration, and royalty structure. The grantor retains ownership of the underlying trade mark and may revoke a license upon material breach by the licensee, as provided herein. Further, a registered proprietor may assign their trademark, or any part thereof, to another person, either wholly or partially, subject to prior approval from the Registrar where such assignment involves use outside India. Any assignee shall be deemed the new registered proprietor with all attendant rights and obligations under this Act.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act, and the Hearing Officer determines that the opponent has established relevant grounds for opposition, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to submit written arguments rebutting such findings. The Trade Marks Registry may, at its discretion, require both parties to attend a personal hearing to further clarify disputed facts relating to distinctiveness or likelihood of confusion. Any party aggrieved by an order made by the Hearing Officer concerning the acceptance or rejection of a trade mark application, or regarding any condition imposed upon registration, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Board’s decision shall be final, subject to further appeal under the provisions relating to appeals to higher courts as provided herein and pertaining to matters concerning a registered trade mark.

Where an application for the registration of a trade mark is refused under this Act, the applicant may appeal against such refusal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be made within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order of refusal by the applicant. The Board shall give notice to the Registrar and any other party who appeared in the opposition proceedings relating to the trade mark, affording them an opportunity to be heard. If the Board allows the appeal, it shall direct that the trade mark be registered as requested, or with such modifications as it deems fit. Notice of the decision of the Board shall be published in the Official Gazette. Any person aggrieved by any order made by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board may further appeal to the High Court within sixty days, subject to the provisions regarding costs as provided herein. A trade mark once registered remains so until removed from the register under this Act.

Where any performer demonstrates that goods or services are being offered using an imitation of their artistic style or persona, and such use is likely to cause confusion amongst the public regarding endorsement by said performer, then the Registrar may, upon application, direct the cancellation of a *registered* trade mark. Such direction shall be accompanied by an order requiring the proprietor of the offending trade mark to pay damages to the aggrieved performer, calculated as if this Act were an action for passing off. The amount of such damages shall reflect the diminution in value of the performer’s reputation and any lost opportunities arising from the misleading use. Any appeal against such direction or order may be made under provisions relating to appeals.

Where the owner of a design registered layout seeks to grant a license conferring rights to use such registered design layout for commercial purposes, the agreement shall be executed in writing and specify the scope of permitted uses, including but not limited to manufacturing, distribution, or display. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as determined by the licensor; provided that any assignment of the entire registered trade mark, encompassing the associated design registered layout, requires prior notification to the Trade Marks Registry. Further, under this Act, a licensee shall be deemed an agent of the registered proprietor for the purposes of enforcing rights relating to the licensed use, subject to the terms outlined in the licensing agreement. The registered proprietor retains ultimate control over quality assurance and may terminate the license if the licensee’s actions damage the reputation associated with the trade mark.

For the efficient execution of functions under this Act, there shall be an office known as the Office of the Registrar, headed by a Registrar appointed by the Central Government. The Registrar shall exercise such powers and perform such duties as may be delegated to him or her by the Central Government, including but not limited to receiving applications for registration of trade marks and conducting searches relating thereto. Any communication required to be made under this Act with any person shall be deemed to have been duly made if sent through registered post or email, as determined by the Registrar. The Registrar may also appoint such officers and staff as are necessary for the proper functioning of the Office.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall contain such particulars as are required to identify the trade mark clearly, including a representation of the marks applied for, and shall be accompanied by a statement of disclaimer of any portion of the trade mark which the applicant does not desire to register. The Registrar may require an applicant to amend or clarify any description or representation contained in the application if he deems it necessary for proper understanding. Further, the Registrar shall record all documents filed with the application and maintain them as part of the public record pertaining to the registration process. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to acceptance or rejection of an application may appeal under this Act to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is refused under this Act, the applicant shall have the right to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. The appellant shall specify the order appealed against and the grounds upon which such appeal is based, and shall serve a copy of the appeal on the Registrar within sixty days from the date of receipt of the refusal notice. Failure to comply with these procedural requirements may result in the dismissal of the appeal.

The Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal may, after affording the applicant and the Registrar an opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify or reverse the decision appealed against. Any party aggrieved by any order made by the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal may further appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such order. The Registrar shall be bound by the decisions of both the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal and the High Court in relation to the trade mark application.

Applications for registration of service marks shall be examined in accordance with the provisions relating to trade marks, subject to any modifications deemed necessary by the Registrar having regard to the nature of the services. The Registrar may require an applicant to furnish further information or clarification regarding the goods or services for which registration is sought, and such requirements shall be complied with within a period specified by the Registrar. Any failure to comply with such directions may result in the rejection of the application. Where any objection is raised against a proposed trade mark under this Act, the Registrar shall issue a notice to the applicant detailing the grounds of objection. The applicant shall have an opportunity to file their response and present arguments within the timeframe stipulated by the Registrar. Decisions made by the Registrar concerning applications are subject to appeal as provided herein.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall contain a clear representation of the marks sought to be registered and shall state whether the mark is being used in relation to any goods or services. The applicant shall furnish proof of ownership satisfactory to the Registrar, provided that where the applicant is a partnership firm, such proof shall include a certified copy of the partnership deed. Further, if the trade mark includes a depiction of a geographical indication as defined under this Act, the application must be accompanied by an affidavit confirming compliance with all applicable regulations pertaining to such indications and demonstrating non-infringement of any existing rights. The Registrar may require additional documentation or clarifications at any stage before proceeding with examination.

Any person aggrieved by an adverse decision of the registrar relating to the acceptance or rejection of a trade mark application, or concerning any rectification proceeding under this Act, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such decision. Failure to comply with prescribed forms and fees during the appeal process shall render the appeal inadmissible. The Board may, after affording an opportunity for hearing to all parties concerned, confirm, reverse, or modify the order appealed against. Any party dissatisfied with the order of the Intellectual Property Appellate Board may further appeal to the High Court within a period not exceeding ninety days, subject to imposition of costs as determined by the court. Deliberate misrepresentation to the registrar shall attract penalties as provided herein.

The owner of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to grant licences conferring the right to use the trade mark in relation to specified goods or services, subject to any conditions stipulated in the licence agreement. Such licences may be exclusive or non-exclusive as determined by the licensor; provided that an exclusive licence shall be recorded with the Registrar and shall specify the territorial extent of such exclusivity. Assignment of a registered trade mark, or of the benefit of any registered trade mark, including assignment of any licence granted thereunder, requires prior notification to the Registrar, accompanied by prescribed fees. The Registrar may request further information to verify the authenticity of the assignee and the terms of the transfer. Any subsequent dealing with the assigned right shall also be notified as provided herein.

The application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed to be refused if the Registrar considers that the proposed mark is descriptive of the goods or services with which it seeks association. Any party aggrieved by such refusal may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the notice of refusal. The Board, after affording an opportunity for a hearing to both the appellant and the Registrar, shall determine whether the grounds for refusal were justified under this Act. Further, if the applicant fails to satisfy the Board that the mark possesses distinctive character, the appeal shall be dismissed, and the original order of the Registrar shall stand affirmed.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed to include an indication of use relating to India if the applicant demonstrates, through documentary evidence acceptable to the Registrar, that the goods or services specified in the application have been offered for sale or provided within the territory of India. Provided that such demonstration need not extend beyond a period of three months immediately preceding the date of filing the application. The Registrar may require further clarification regarding the nature and extent of this use if deemed necessary to ascertain compliance with these requirements. Failure to adequately substantiate the claim of India relates use, as determined by the Registrar, shall render the application liable for rejection under this Act.

The assignment of a registered trade mark shall require execution of a formal instrument in the prescribed form, attesting to the transferor’s complete relinquishment of all rights and title pertaining to the mark. Such instruments must be presented to the Registrar for registration within thirty days of the date of assignment; failure to do so renders the assignment voidable at the assignee's option. Where an agreement purports to grant a license to use a registered trade mark, such license may be assigned subject to conditions stipulated in the original agreement and as provided herein. The Registrar shall appear before any court or tribunal claiming jurisdiction over disputes arising from assignments or licenses under this Act, upon request by either party involved, to provide clarification regarding registration details and procedural compliance. Any alteration of terms within a licensed trade mark usage requires prior written consent from both licensor and the registered proprietor, duly acknowledged by the Registrar.

Where an application for registration is refused under this Act based on objection from any person claiming proprietary rights in respect of identical or similar marks used in connection with patented articles, the applicant shall have the right to appeal to the Appellate Tribunal. Such appeal may only be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the refusal order and must specify the grounds upon which the decision is challenged. The Registrar shall provide a reasoned statement outlining the basis for the objection and the evidence considered in reaching the determination. Failure by the appellant to demonstrate, through admissible documentary or testimonial evidence, that the claimed proprietary rights are invalid or do not extend to the goods or services specified in the application will result in dismissal of the appeal as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, “design” means a three-dimensional pattern or arrangement which is applied to a semiconductor integrated circuit layout design or constitutes its topography, and includes features of shape, configuration, colour or association, or relative placement of components. A design shall be considered original if it embodies skill and ingenuity and is not solely dictated by functional considerations or technical necessity inherent in the manufacture or use of the said layout design. The term “design” excludes elements which are minor or standard and commonly used in semiconductor integrated circuit layout designs as provided herein, subject to any modifications made thereto.

An application for registration of a layout-design shall include a copy of the layout-design represented in a form specified under this Act, along with a statement by the applicant claiming entitlement to the design. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further particulars relating to the design and the circumstances giving rise to the claim of ownership, provided that such requirements are reasonable and do not unduly delay the registration process. Where the layout-design incorporates elements which themselves constitute designs, the application shall clearly identify these incorporated features. Any person claiming an interest in a registered design may file a caveat against the proposed registration, subject to provisions regarding frivolous caveats as prescribed herein. The Registrar shall maintain a register of registered designs accessible for public inspection.

Where a person alleging infringement of a registered design establishes that another has reproduced the design in question without leave, or has done any act amounting to reproduction as provided herein, the owner shall be entitled to relief. Such relief may include an injunction restraining the infringing party from further acts of reproduction, and damages calculated by reference to the loss sustained by the owner as a result of the infringement, or where such loss cannot be readily ascertainable, a reasonable sum determined by the court. The court may also order the delivery up or destruction of any articles made in relation to the infringing design. Nothing in this Act shall prevent the defendant from proving that their use of the design was for experimental purposes relating to the design itself.

An application for registration of a layout-design relating to an integrated circuit shall be accompanied by particulars specifying the name and address of the applicant, the title of the design, and a statement indicating whether the design is original. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish such further information as he deems necessary for determining entitlement under this Act. Where any question arises regarding the originality of a layout-design, the Registrar shall afford an opportunity to both the applicant and any other person claiming interest in the design to present evidence and arguments. Subject to the provisions herein, the determination of the Registrar on matters relating to originality shall be final. An appeal against such determination may be made to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within a period of sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The applicant shall provide adequate documentation demonstrating the layout-design’s technical features and intended functionality.

A layout-design shall be deemed original if it was created independently by the claimant or derived from a prior work with substantial modifications that constitute an original design. Subject to compliance with prescribed standards regarding technical documentation, registration of a layout-design is permissible only after a period of six months has elapsed from the date of its first commercial exploitation anywhere in the world. Any person claiming infringement under this Act must demonstrate that the infringing layout-design possesses a striking similarity to the registered design, considering both overall appearance and component arrangement. Provided that such similarity does not arise solely from features dictated by functional considerations or technical necessity, the claimant shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief and damages as provided herein.

Any person who knowingly makes, uses, imports, or offers to sell any layout design which infringes a registered *design* shall be guilty of an offence under this Act. Such infringement includes the reproduction of the protected layout design in whole or in part, and its use for the manufacture of semiconductor devices. Upon conviction, the offender shall be liable to imprisonment for a term not less than six months but which may extend to three years, and with a fine which may extend to ten lakh rupees; furthermore, any profits made from the infringing activity are recoverable as damages. The Central Government may, by notification, prescribe standards for determining reasonable royalties in cases of compulsory licensing relating to registered designs, subject to due process.

The right to exploit a registered design shall vest initially with the registrant, who may grant non-exclusive licenses conferring specific rights relating to manufacture, import, sale, or distribution of articles incorporating that design. Such licenses may be assigned freely, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated within the license agreement itself; however, any assignment shall not prejudice existing rights held by third parties under prior valid licenses granted by the original registrant. Where a design is jointly registered, all registrants are deemed joint owners and must consent in writing for any licensing or assignment of the design as a whole. The Central Government may, upon application from an aggrieved party demonstrating substantial reliance on a design previously licensed without proper authorization, issue directives compelling disclosure of license terms. This power shall be exercised cautiously to avoid undue interference with contractual arrangements concerning designs.

Where a claim for infringement of a registered design is contested upon grounds that the alleged infringing layout-design incorporates elements derived from pre-existing works or designs not incorporated into the original registration, the claimant shall bear the onus of demonstrating, by clear and convincing evidence, that such prior art did not substantially influence the creation of the protected design. It is provided that a finding of similarity between the registered design and the alleged infringing layout-design alone shall not constitute conclusive proof of infringement; instead, an assessment of overall impression and freedom of artistic expression must be undertaken. The respondent may appeal any determination regarding originality or substantial similarity to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal, subject to demonstrating demonstrable prejudice arising from the initial finding.

An application for registration of a layout-design relating to an integrated circuit shall include a representation of the design, certified as true by a qualified person. The Registrar shall examine whether the layout-design is original and not infringing under this Act; if satisfied, he may proceed with registration. An established registry shall maintain a record of all registered designs, accessible for public inspection subject to prescribed fees and conditions. Where an applicant has previously filed an identical or substantially similar design, the application shall be deemed withdrawn. The Registrar may require further clarification from the applicant regarding any aspect of the layout-design’s functionality or aesthetic features. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to registration of a design may appeal under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, “cinematograph film” means any visual recording produced by processes involving cinematography and includes works which, by such process, have been combined and edited together. A cinematograph film shall be deemed to be an artistic work for the purposes of copyright protection under this Act; provided that elements incorporated therein through literary or musical works remain subject to separate rights as provided herein. The term “cinematograph film” does not include any amateur recordings made solely for private use, subject to such conditions and limitations as may be prescribed by regulations framed under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, registration of a cinematograph film shall be deemed conclusive evidence of ownership of copyright therein, subject to the provisions relating to joint authorship. An application for such registration may be made by the producer who is recognized as the owner of the film under this Act, or by any person claiming ownership through assignment or license. The application shall include particulars regarding the title of the cinematograph film, the name and address of the applicant, details concerning the principal director and author of the script, and a synopsis of the work. Provided that, where the copyright in musical works incorporated within the cinematograph film is separately owned, such ownership shall be clearly indicated on the application form.

The owner of copyright in a cinematograph film shall be entitled to restrain any person from infringing such copyright, including but not limited to the reproduction, distribution, adaptation, and public exhibition of the film. Provided that where a cinematograph film has been made from an underlying literary or dramatic work, the producer shall be deemed the owner of copyright therein only to the extent provided herein; the authors of the underlying work retaining rights as they would otherwise possess under this Act. Any infringement of copyright in a cinematograph film constitutes a violation and renders the infringer liable for damages, which may include compensatory damages, punitive damages not exceeding ten times the actual damages or statutory damages as determined by the court. Further, subject to any order made by the Controller, the court may grant an injunction restraining the infringing activity.

For the purposes of this Act, a cinematograph film shall be deemed as an artistic work and copyright therein shall vest in the producer who owns the rights necessary for the creation of the film. Where such producer is not the author of the cinematograph film, the right to claim ownership shall be subject to demonstration before the Controller that all requisite permissions and assignments relating to underlying works incorporated within the film have been duly obtained and recorded. Any person desiring to reproduce, distribute, exhibit or trade in a cinematograph film contrary to the provisions herein shall first apply for permission from the Controller, furnishing details of the intended use and providing evidence of compliance with applicable regulations. The Controller may grant such permission upon payment of prescribed fees and subject to conditions as deemed appropriate, provided that no permission shall be granted which would infringe on any existing copyright.

For the purposes of this Act, a cinematograph film shall be deemed as comprising visual sequences and accompanying sounds permanently recorded on any medium. The producer of a cinematograph film shall, subject to compliance with prescribed guidelines issued by the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trademarks, be considered the owner of copyright therein, unless registration demonstrates otherwise. Provided that where such film incorporates pre-existing copyrighted works, including literary, dramatic, musical or artistic works, the copyright in those incorporated elements remains vested in their respective owners. Any person desiring to reproduce, distribute, exhibit or communicate a cinematograph film commercially shall obtain prior written permission from the producer, demonstrating adherence to stipulated royalty payment schedules as determined under this Act.

Any person who, without authorisation from the owner of copyright in a cinematograph film, reproduces the film in an infringing copy, whether for sale or distribution, shall be liable to pay damages as determined by the civil court. The amount of such damages shall reflect the reasonable costs incurred by the copyright owner in discovering and proving the infringement, including expenses related to forensic analysis of digital copies. Further, any person found guilty of commercial exploitation of a cinematograph film without due license is subject to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with a fine that may extend to ten lakhs rupees, or both, as provided herein. This penalty applies irrespective of the medium through which the infringing copy is disseminated.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, the owner of copyright in a cinematograph film shall be entitled to grant licenses granting rights to reproduce, distribute, and publicly exhibit the said film. Such licenses may be granted for specific territories or for all territories as determined by the licensor. Any assignment of copyright under this Act relating to a cinematograph film shall include, unless otherwise expressly stated within the instrument of assignment, the right to exploit ancillary works derived from the original film, including but not limited to soundtracks and trailers. Provided that any license granted prior to the date of this amendment shall remain valid until its natural expiration, as per its original terms. The remuneration for such licenses shall be determined through negotiation between the copyright owner and the licensee, taking into consideration prevailing market rates and the scope of rights being assigned.

The right of copyright under this Act in a cinematograph film shall extend to the producer thereof and where such film has been produced subject to a written agreement assigning to any person the exclusive right to reproduce the film, that person shall be deemed the owner for the purposes of infringement proceedings. Provided that, if the ownership of the underlying literary or musical work incorporated within the cinematograph film is disputed, the court may require evidence establishing the rightful claimant prior to adjudicating on the validity of the producer’s copyright claim relating to the entire film. Any appeal arising from a determination under this provision shall lie to the appellate forum as provided herein, subject to the satisfaction of conditions regarding deposit and costs.

The owner of copyright in a cinematograph film shall be entitled to grant licenses granting rights to reproduce, distribute, and exhibit the said film, subject to the conditions specified herein. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as determined by the grantor, and the terms thereof shall be binding on all parties involved. Where a license is granted for the synchronization of copyrighted musical works within a cinematograph film, the licensee shall ensure that appropriate royalties are paid to the owners of those underlying copyrights, as per established practice. Furthermore, any assignment of copyright in a cinematograph film must be registered with the Designs Office, and such registration shall serve as prima facie evidence of ownership for the purposes of enforcing these rights under this Act. Provided that, where a design element is integral to the visual presentation of the cinematograph film, its protection may also extend through the design registry exercise.

For the purposes of this Act, "cinematograph film" shall mean any visual recording produced by means of a cinematographic apparatus and includes works incorporated therein, whether protected under this Act as artistic works or musical works. The term shall extend to compilations of such recordings, provided that they are presented in an integrated manner for public exhibition. An amendment claim specification relating to a cinematograph film shall be deemed to include all elements contributing to the overall aesthetic presentation, including but not limited to camera angles, editing sequences, and sound design, subject to any restrictions as may be prescribed under this Act regarding originality and substantial similarity.

For the purposes of registration under this Act, a cinematograph film shall be deemed registered on the date specified in the application, provided that the applicant furnishes proof satisfactory to the Registrar that all necessary permissions and clearances relating to the exhibition of the said cinematograph film have been obtained from relevant authorities. Where such a film incorporates elements derived from works protected under copyright or otherwise, the applicant shall declare within the registration documentation the nature and extent of those incorporated elements, along with details pertaining to any licenses or assignments secured in relation thereto. The Registrar may require further information concerning the date accorded patent for any novel apparatus utilized in the creation of the cinematograph film.

For the purposes of this Act, an exclusive licence shall be deemed to be a grant of rights enabling the licensee to exercise certain copyright owner’s prerogatives concerning a work, subject to conditions stipulated in the licensing agreement. Such conditions may include limitations on territory, duration, or specific acts permitted under the licence. An exclusive licence does not transfer ownership of the copyright; the copyright owner retains ultimate control and responsibility for the work. Provided that the terms of the exclusive licence are clearly defined and documented, the licensee shall be entitled to enforce those rights against any infringement, as provided herein.

Where the copyright in any cinematograph film or sound recording has been assigned under this Act, the assignor may, subject to the terms of the assignment, apply for registration of such assignment. Upon receipt of the application and after satisfaction that the provisions herein relating to assignments have been complied with, the Registrar shall register the same and issue a certificate accordingly. Such certificate shall be prima facie evidence that the copyright has been validly assigned. An exclusive licence granted in respect of any work or sound recording shall be deemed to be an assignment for the purposes of registration under this Act, provided that the terms of such licence expressly state it is intended as an exclusive grant and specify the duration thereof.

Where an exclusive licence is granted under this Act, the licensee shall be entitled to exercise all copyright owner’s rights pertaining to the work licensed exclusively for the term specified in the agreement. The grantor shall not, during that period, directly or indirectly exploit the same right within the territory defined in the license without the licensee's written consent. Any infringement of copyright committed by a third party subsequent to the grant of such exclusive licence shall be actionable at the suit of the licensee as if they were the sole owner of the copyright. Provided that, where the grantor materially contributes to any infringing act occurring after the grant, both the infringer and the grantor may be held jointly liable for damages. The licensee shall have the right to seek injunctive relief against such infringement. Further, the license agreement shall specify remedies available to the licensee in case of breach by the grantor.

Where an exclusive licence is granted under this Act, the terms and conditions thereof shall be recorded in writing and presented to the Controller for registration. Such recording shall specify the duration of the exclusivity conferred, the geographical territory covered by the license, and the specific acts relating to copyright which are reserved exclusively to the licensee. The grantor of the exclusive licence shall provide an undertaking confirming that they possess the necessary rights to grant such a license and that no prior conflicting agreements exist. Any party aggrieved by the terms of registration may file an appeal with the Controller within sixty days from the date of publication of the registration details, outlining grounds for objection. The Controller may, after affording an opportunity for hearing, modify or reject the registration if it finds the terms unreasonable or contrary to the provisions herein.

Where an exclusive licence is granted under this Act, the licensor shall retain the right to terminate such licence if the licensee fails to exploit the copyrighted work in a commercially reasonable manner within a period of three years from the date of grant, subject to conditions prescribed by regulations. The licensee may, prior to the expiry of the aforementioned three-year period, apply for an extension provided that they demonstrate substantial progress towards commercial exploitation and provide supporting documentation as required under this Act. Any assignment of rights granted pursuant to such exclusive licence shall be deemed void unless approved in writing by the copyright holder and registered with the designated authority. The copyright holder retains the right to audit the licensee’s accounts pertaining to the copyrighted work, as provided herein.

Where an exclusive licence is granted under this Act, the licensee shall be entitled to exercise all copyright owner’s rights pertaining to the work licensed, subject to the terms specified in the agreement. Any infringement of these rights by third parties during the term of the license shall constitute a violation actionable at law. The grantor of such an exclusive licence shall not, without the prior written consent of the licensee, grant any further licences or assignments affecting the same rights within the scope of the original exclusivity. Failure to obtain such consent will render the subsequent grant void and subject the grantor to penalties as provided herein, including damages and injunctive relief. The aggrieved party may also seek recovery of legal costs incurred in enforcing these provisions.

The copyright in all literary works created by employees during the course of their employment shall vest initially in the employer, provided that such employment agreement expressly stipulates this arrangement. The employer may grant an exclusive licence to third parties for specific acts fixed by the agreement, including but not limited to reproduction, distribution, and public performance. Such exclusive licences shall be assignable subject to the terms outlined within the original employment contract and any subsequent licensing agreements. Further, where a work is jointly authored, the rights of each author shall remain distinct unless otherwise agreed in writing; however, an employer’s exclusive licence granted under this Act shall extend to all such joint authors' contributions as part of the assigned works. Any sub-licensing by the licensee shall require prior written consent from the copyright owner, and any breach of these conditions may render the license voidable.

Where an exclusive licence is granted under this Act, the licensee shall be entitled to exercise all copyright rights in respect of the licensed work as if they were the sole owner thereof, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated within the licensing agreement. Any dispute arising from the interpretation or enforcement of such an exclusive licence may be referred to arbitration by a single arbitrator appointed jointly by the licensor and licensee; provided that either party may petition the High Court for judicial review of any arbitral award if it demonstrably suffers material prejudice due to demonstrable error apparent on the face of the record. The licensor shall remain liable for acts constituting copyright infringement committed prior to the commencement of the licence period, notwithstanding the grant of exclusive rights as provided herein.

Where an exclusive licence is granted under this Act, the licensee shall be entitled to exercise all copyright rights comprised therein as if they were the sole proprietor of the work in question, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated within the licensing agreement. Any dispute arising concerning the scope or validity of such an exclusive licence may be referred for adjudication to a court of competent jurisdiction. Furthermore, provided that the licensor fails to register the details of the grant of the exclusive licence with the designated office as provided herein, the licensee shall have recourse to challenge the enforceability of said agreement before any judicial forum. The register shall brought up-to-date within thirty days of the execution of such a license.

The grant of an exclusive licence under this Act shall be subject to registration with the Copyright Office within ninety days from the date of execution of the agreement. Such registration shall be deemed conclusive evidence of the validity of the license, provided that a copy of the underlying work and the terms of the license are submitted alongside the application. The Registrar may require further documentation pertaining to the consideration paid or promised for the grant of the exclusive licence, particularly where the licensed work is demonstrably capable of industrial application, such as in the manufacture of goods incorporating copyrighted designs. Any challenge to the validity of an exclusive licence shall be brought before the relevant High Court within six months of its registration. The Registrar may refuse registration if the terms are deemed manifestly unfair or contrary to public interest, affording the applicant an opportunity for representation prior to any decision.

For the purposes of this Act, “good quality” with reference to any agricultural product or foodstuff means that the product or foodstuffs conform to standards specified by an appropriate authority and are free from defects which render them unsuitable for consumption or use. A geographical indication is deemed registered upon publication in the Geographical Indications Journal and shall confer upon the registered proprietor exclusive right to use the registration geographical indication to indicate origin of goods in relation to which it has been registered, subject to any conditions or limitations as may be prescribed under this Act. Any alteration to a registered geographical indication requires prior approval from the Registrar.

An application for registration of a geographical indication shall include particulars specifying the name of the geographical indication sought to be registered, the agricultural product or good relating to which the geographical indication is used, and the area comprising the origin of that goods. The applicant shall also furnish a map of the geographical territory of origin, clearly delineating its boundaries. Where an objection is raised against the registration under this Act, the Registrar may require the applicant to submit further evidence demonstrating the link between the product’s qualities or characteristics and its unique geographical environment. Any prior registration of a similar indication relating to identical goods shall be considered during examination for registration geographical protection.

An application for registration of a geographical indication shall include particulars specifying the name of the agricultural product or good indicating its origin, along with a map of the area where the good is produced or processed. The applicant must demonstrate that the quality, reputation, or other characteristic of the goods are essentially attributable to their geographical origin as provided herein. Prior use of the proposed indication by others shall not disqualify an application, subject to demonstrating continued adherence to established production standards and practices within the defined geographical area. Any alteration in these standards requires prior notification to the Registrar and approval based on a determination that such changes do not compromise the distinctiveness linked to the registration geographical indication.

The registered proprietor of a geographical indication shall have the exclusive right to use the registration geographical indication for the goods specified in the register, and no person shall be entitled to use or authorize the use of any word, mark, seal, symbol or other indicia which falsely suggests an association with goods identified by that geographical indication. Any authorised use mark employed by a licensee under a contractual agreement with the registered proprietor may be permitted subject to conditions prescribed by the Registrar, provided that such use does not create confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of the goods. Infringement of these rights shall constitute a civil wrong and the registered proprietor may seek remedies including injunctions and damages as provided herein. Further, any person found guilty of falsely representing goods as originating from the indicated geographical area is liable to prosecution under relevant penal laws.

For the purposes of this Act, “artistic work” shall include, but not be limited to, graphic works, sculptural works, architectural designs and photographic works, irrespective of whether such works are produced or rendered digitally or through traditional means. An artistic work shall be deemed fixed when it is in a form discernible by sight or sound, having been deliberately created with the intention of being reproduced or communicated to the public. The reproduction of an artistic work which incidentally results from any other act permitted under this Act shall not be considered an infringement provided that such incidental reproduction does not constitute a substantial extraction of the original creative expression.

For the purposes of registration under this Act, an “artistic work” shall include graphic designs, architectural works, photographic works, and sculptures, provided that such works are fixed in a tangible medium. The Registrar may require submission of detailed specifications regarding the creation process and intended use of the artistic work during the application review. Where an artistic work incorporates elements derived from pre-existing sources, the applicant shall provide a comprehensive declaration affirming originality and demonstrating substantial independent creative effort. Registration of an architectural work extends only to the design itself and does not confer rights over the building constructed embodying that design. An applicant seeking registration for a photographic work must attest to being the author or having obtained lawful authorization from the author.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, copyright in an artistic work shall endure during the lifetime of the author and extend for sixty years from the beginning of the calendar year following the author's death. Where an artistic work is created during employment under a contract of service, the employer shall be deemed the author for the purposes of assignment of rights as provided herein; however, any subsequent sale or transfer of such copyright requires written consent from the original creator. Infringement of this right may be remedied by injunction and damages, calculated at the discretion of the court based on the extent of reproduction and commercial impact. Further, a person found to have knowingly dealt with an infringing copy shall be liable for compensation equivalent to the reasonable licensing fee that would have been payable had the use been authorized under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, an “artistic work” includes, but is not limited to, graphic works, photographic works, three-dimensional objects, and architectural designs. The ownership of copyright in an artistic work shall vest initially in the creator of the work; provided that where the artistic work has been created during the course of employment, the employer shall be deemed to be the owner of such copyright unless otherwise agreed between the parties in writing. Any person claiming rights under this Act may file a complaint with the designated Copyright Grievance Redressal Officer appointed by the competent authority for investigation and adjudication. The Registrar shall maintain records pertaining to all complaints received and actions taken, accessible for inspection subject to reasonable restrictions as determined by the Registrar. Decisions of the Copyright Grievance Redressal Officer are appealable to a High Court under this Act.

An artistic work shall be deemed to include photographs, architectural designs and models used in architecture, irrespective of whether such works are fixed on any medium. Provided that an architectural design or model used in architecture shall not be considered an artistic work if it is solely functional in nature and lacks aesthetic merit discernible by a reasonable person exercising due care. The right of the author to issue copies of the artistic work shall subsist until sixty years from the beginning of the calendar year following the author’s death, subject to compliance with prescribed conditions regarding public display and reproduction for educational purposes as provided herein. Any commercial exploitation exceeding fair use guidelines requires prior authorization and adherence to stipulated royalty structures.

Where an artistic work has been reproduced or disseminated without authorization, and such reproduction or dissemination constitutes infringement under this Act, the owner of the copyright shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief restraining further acts of infringement. Any person found guilty of knowingly enabling or assisting in the commission of such infringement shall be deemed as having committed a violation punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and with a fine which may extend to ten lakhs of rupees. The court may, subject to appeal, order the destruction of infringing copies and materials used in their creation. Further, damages equivalent to actual loss suffered by the copyright owner or statutory damages as determined by the court, whichever is higher, shall be recoverable.

Where an artistic work has been created under commission, the right to assign the copyright therein shall vest initially in the party commissioning such work, provided that a written agreement exists specifying the terms of assignment. Such agreement may stipulate a period during which the copyright remains with the commissioner, after which it automatically reverts to the creator unless further extended by mutual consent. The commissioner shall be obligated to provide the creator with a copy of the assignment document upon request. Any subsequent assignment of the copyright, whether by the original commissioner or the creator, must be in writing and duly registered under this Act. Failure to register such an assignment shall render it void against third parties claiming rights under the artistic work. The creator retains moral rights as provided herein, irrespective of any assignment made.

Notwithstanding anything contained herein, where an individual claims copyright in respect of an artistic work incorporating pre-existing elements demonstrably within the public domain, such claim shall be subject to rigorous scrutiny by the relevant adjudicating authority. The onus lies upon the claimant to affirmatively establish that the creative contribution constituting originality transcends mere rearrangement or trivial modification of those preexisting materials. Further, any assertion of infringement relating to said artistic work may be challenged on grounds of fair dealing for purposes of criticism or review, provided that such use is accompanied by due acknowledgement and does not prejudice the commercial exploitation rights vested in the copyright holder under this Act. Decisions regarding originality shall be appealable to a higher appellate forum.

Where any person is found to have infringed upon the exclusive right under this Act relating to an artistic work, such person shall be liable for damages sustained by the owner of the copyright. The amount of compensation may be determined by the High Court, taking into consideration the extent of the infringement and the loss suffered by the copyright holder. Provided that in cases where the alleged offence is committed without reasonable knowledge or belief that such act would constitute an infringement, the court may award a reduced sum as it deems just and equitable. Further, any person who reproduces, distributes, exhibits, or otherwise exploits an artistic work in violation of these provisions shall be subject to additional penalties as provided herein. The owner of copyright is entitled to seek injunctive relief to restrain further acts of infringement.

An application for registration as an owner of copyright in respect of an artistic work shall be made to the Copyright Office in such form and containing such particulars as may be prescribed. The Registrar shall, upon receipt of an application, proceed to examine it under this Act. If the Registrar is satisfied that the applicant is indeed the first owner of the copyright claimed and that the work fulfills the requirements for registration as an artistic work, he may register the same in the Register of Copyrights maintained by the Office. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to the refusal or conditional registration of any such application may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The particulars recorded in the Register shall be deemed prima facie evidence of the ownership of copyright and validity of the register patents pertaining to that artistic work, subject to proof to the contrary.

Where an artistic work has been created under commission, the right to assign the copyright therein shall vest initially in the party commissioning the work, provided that such commission is evidenced by a written agreement specifying the scope and nature of the assignment. This assignment may be granted wholly or partially, and may include the exclusive right to reproduce, distribute, communicate to the public, and adapt the artistic work. Further, where an inventor incorporates elements of an existing artistic work into a patented device, the patent shall not extend to the underlying copyrighted material unless explicitly licensed by the copyright holder. Any subsequent transfer of ownership of the commissioning party shall include such assignment rights as provided herein. The assignee may further assign or license these rights subject to applicable law and any restrictions outlined in the original commission agreement.

Where the originality of an alleged artistic work is disputed, the burden shall lie upon the claimant to establish that the work was created independently and embodies sufficient skill, judgment, or labour as to warrant its protection under this Act. It shall be a material consideration in determining originality whether the claimed work bears substantial similarity to any pre-existing work, and if such similarity is demonstrated, the claimant must further prove that the alleged copying did not arise from an innocent or unintentional source. For the purposes of assessing infringement, it is hereby declared that an invention means invention, irrespective of its technical application or commercial viability; therefore, derivative works incorporating elements demonstrably derived from a protected artistic work shall be deemed infringing, subject to arguments regarding fair dealing and transformative use as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, "royalty" means consideration payable to the owner of copyright in respect of the use of that copyright, whether by way of payment for performance, reproduction, distribution, broadcasting, or otherwise as provided herein. Such consideration may be expressed as a fixed sum, a percentage of net revenue derived from exploitation of the work, or any other mutually agreed arrangement between the copyright owner and the user. The term "royalty" shall include any sums paid in advance to secure the right to use copyrighted material, subject to adjustments based on actual usage. Any agreement relating to royalty payments shall be governed by principles of fairness and transparency as determined under this Act.

The Registrar may, upon receipt of an application accompanied by the prescribed fee, register details pertaining to agreements concerning the exploitation of copyrighted works where such agreements involve the payment of a royalty. Such applications shall include particulars of the work, the name and address of the copyright owner, and the identity of the licensee authorised to receive royalties.
