The Registrar shall, upon receiving an application for the transmission of the ownership of a trade mark already registered under this Act, verify that the proposed assignee is capable of satisfying all requirements for registration as if they were the original applicant. Such verification shall include confirmation of the assignor’s legal title and consent to the transfer, evidenced by a duly executed instrument. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating the relationship between the transferor and transferee where unusual circumstances exist. Transmission is deemed effective from the date specified in the instrument of assignment unless otherwise stipulated, and notice thereof shall be published in the Trade Marks Journal. Any subsequent dealings with the trade mark shall reflect the new ownership as recorded by the Registrar.

Where the registered proprietor of a trade mark desires to divest himself of his rights therein, he shall be entitled to effect such transmission by way of assignment, license, or other instrument in writing. Such transmission may occur inter vivos or by testamentary disposition, and shall only be effective upon registration thereof with the Registrar, as provided herein. The Registrar may require such evidence as is deemed necessary to establish the validity of the transferor’s title and the transferee's consent to assume the obligations incident to ownership of the trade mark. Failure to register a transmission shall render the purported assignee or successor incapable of enforcing rights under this Act against any third party deriving use from prior registration. Any person claiming through such unregistered transmission shall be deemed a licensee only, subject to the rights of the registered proprietor.

The Registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for registration of a service mark relating to services rendered exclusively through electronic means, verify that the applicant possesses the requisite legal capacity to effect such transmission of services. Where a proprietor seeks to assign or otherwise transmit ownership of a trademark registered under this Act, the assignment deed or other instrument evidencing the transmission shall be executed in accordance with the principles of law governing contractual obligations and shall specify both the cedent and the assignee clearly. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating the legal standing of parties involved in any such transmission, including but not limited to certificates of incorporation and board resolutions. Any alteration or modification to a registered trademark following a transmission requires prior approval from the Registrar, subject to conditions as provided herein regarding maintaining distinctiveness.

The right to use a registered trade mark, as provided herein, shall be deemed to vest initially in the applicant named on the register. Such right may be transmitted by way of assignment, express or implied, subject to compliance with prescribed formalities and payment of requisite fees. Transmission under this Act requires execution of a written instrument conforming to the form specified in Schedule III, duly stamped as per applicable law. The assignee shall, upon registration of the transmission, become entitled to all rights and privileges previously enjoyed by the assignor relating to the trade mark. Further, any subsequent transmission of the same right shall be subject to similar conditions regarding documentation and fees, ensuring a clear chain of title is maintained on the register.

Where the transmission of a registered trade mark occurs through operation of law, such as by way of inheritance or dissolution of a partnership, the successor in title shall be deemed to have acquired the exclusive right to use the trade mark subject to any prior registrations or applications. Any person utilizing the trade mark without express written consent from the assignee following such transmission shall be liable for damages and account of profits made through the infringing activity. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint regarding unauthorized use after transmission, issue an injunction restraining further infringement. Failure to comply with this restraint constitutes a civil offence punishable with a fine not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees, and imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years.

The owner of a registered trademark shall be entitled to grant licenses for the use of the mark upon such terms as may be agreed between the parties, provided that any such license agreement expressly specifies the geographical territory and the goods or services in relation to which the licensee is authorized to utilize the trademark. Where a license granted under this Act includes a provision for assignment, the assignee shall be deemed to have stepped into the shoes of the original licensee and subject to all limitations contained within the initial licensing agreement. Further, any transmission of a registered trademark, whether by way of assignment or otherwise, shall require prior notification to the Registrar, accompanied by evidence demonstrating consent from all existing licensees. The Registrar may reject such transmission if it deems it detrimental to consumers or unfairly prejudices the interests of other trade mark proprietors.

Where the ownership of a registered trade mark is transferred under this Act by way of assignment or other instrument, such transmission shall be deemed to include all rights and privileges pertaining to the said trade mark, subject to any limitations expressly stated in the instrument effecting the transfer. Provided that, if the Registrar receives notice from a person claiming an interest in the trade mark adverse to the purported transferee, the Registrar may require both parties to furnish evidence and arguments regarding the validity of the transmission. Any dispute arising concerning the completeness or accuracy of such transmission shall be subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, as provided herein, notwithstanding any conflicting provisions under other statutes relating to property law.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any assignment of a trademark shall be valid if it is made by a written instrument signed by or on behalf of the assignor and delivered to the assignee. Such an assignment may include the goodwill of the business connected with the trade mark. Where a trade mark has been registered, the transmission of the entire interest in such registration, including any associated rights relating to prior use, shall require recording in the Register Book. It is provided that transient incidental storage of data necessary for the operation of online services utilizing the trademark does not constitute an assignment or transfer of ownership under this Act. The Registrar may, upon application and subject to verification, register such assignments and transmit details thereof electronically.

The right to transmit ownership of a registered trademark shall vest initially in the registrant named on the register. Such transmission may occur by way of assignment, operation of law, or other lawful means, provided that any such transfer is recorded within thirty days thereof with the Registrar, accompanied by prescribed documentation establishing the prior ownership and the identity of the new proprietor. Failure to record a transmission shall render the transferee not a true proprietor for all purposes under this Act, and subject to an action for damages sustained as a consequence of such unregistered status. The remedies available to a person claiming rights through an unregistered transmission are limited to equitable relief and may not include recovery of profits earned by the infringing party; however, the Registrar may, at his discretion, afford temporary recognition pending judicial determination under the section 41 scheme.

Where the ownership of a registered trade mark is transmitted by operation of law, including but not limited to inheritance or dissolution of a partnership, the Registrar shall be notified within ninety days of such transmission. The notification shall include particulars of the new owner and evidence satisfactory to the Registrar establishing the legal basis for the transfer. Upon receipt of such notification and verification of its contents, the Registrar may update the register proposed to reflect the change in ownership. Failure to notify the Registrar as provided herein will not invalidate the transmission but may affect the ability of the new owner to enforce rights under this Act relating to the trade mark. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all notifications received and actions taken concerning transmissions of registered trade marks, accessible for public inspection subject to reasonable restrictions.

For the purposes of this Act, “pharmaceutical substance” shall mean any novel chemical entity or biological product intended for use in diagnosis, mitigation, or cure of disease, or for improvement of health conditions in human beings or animals. Such a pharmaceutical substance shall be deemed to include salts, esters, ethers, and other derivatives thereof, provided that such derivative possesses substantially the same pharmacological activity as the parent compound. The determination of novelty under this Act shall consider prior public knowledge relating to the chemical structure, method of manufacture, or intended therapeutic application of the pharmaceutical substance. Any process for producing a pharmaceutical substance may be patented subject to fulfilling all requirements as provided herein.

For the purposes of registration under this Act, a pharmaceutical substance shall be deemed eligible for inclusion on the Register of Pharmaceutical Innovations if it demonstrates novelty and involves an inventive step beyond that which is obvious to a person skilled in the art. The Controller may require submission of comprehensive data pertaining to the manufacturing process, including detailed specifications of excipients utilized and quality control measures implemented during production. Such data shall be considered confidential and protected from public disclosure subject to provisions regarding challenges to validity under this Act. An applicant seeking registration must provide evidence demonstrating that the pharmaceutical substance is capable of industrial application; furthermore, any prior publication or use relating to the claimed invention shall be disclosed as provided herein.

Where an infringement of patent rights relating to a pharmaceutical substance has occurred, the patentee shall be entitled to injunctive relief restraining the infringing party from further acts of manufacture, use, sale or importation. Such injunction may include terms prohibiting the infringing party from exploiting any data generated through reverse engineering of the patented process, provided that such exploitation would constitute an infringement under this Act. The remedies available to a patentee are without prejudice to claims for damages and compensation for losses suffered as a direct consequence of the infringement. Any person found to have knowingly induced or assisted in the infringement shall also be liable for appropriate relief. Further, where the infringing activity involves a substantial misrepresentation concerning the efficacy or safety of the pharmaceutical substance, additional penalties may be imposed as determined by the Controller.

Applications for patents relating to a pharmaceutical substance shall be examined to determine compliance with the provisions of this Act and the Regulations framed thereunder. The Controller may require the applicant to submit further information or clarification regarding the nature of the invention, including details concerning its composition, method of manufacture, and intended use. Where an objection is raised under this Act pertaining to the patentability of a pharmaceutical substance on grounds of prior publication or public knowledge, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to demonstrate that the claimed invention is novel and non-obvious. The Board constituted as provided herein may hear appeals arising from decisions made by the Controller concerning the acceptance or rejection of such applications. Evidence presented before the Board shall be admissible subject to the rules of procedure established for patent proceedings.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and the regulations framed thereunder, an application for a patent relating to a pharmaceutical substance shall be deemed to be non-compliant if it fails to adequately disclose the methods of manufacture employed. Such disclosure must enable a person skilled in the art to reproduce the process without undue experimentation, provided that the applicant demonstrates sufficient evidence of clinical trials conducted in accordance with Good Clinical Practice guidelines. Furthermore, where the claimed invention incorporates a known therapeutic agent, the application shall explicitly detail any novel formulation or delivery system and substantiate its improved efficacy or safety profile through comparative data. The Controller may require submission of additional information to verify compliance with these requirements prior to granting patent rights as provided herein.

Any person found to have manufactured, imported, distributed, sold, or offered for sale any pharmaceutical substance infringing upon a patent granted under this Act shall be liable to pay an indemnity of not less than ten times the value of goods produced or imported or dealt with. Such infringement includes acts that directly or indirectly exploit the patented invention without authorization from the patent holder. The Controller may, after giving notice and opportunity for hearing to the accused party, issue an injunction restraining further infringing activities. Failure to comply with such an order shall render the offender subject to a daily penalty of fifty thousand rupees until compliance is achieved. Further, any property used or acquired in connection with the infringement shall be liable for seizure by enforcement officers as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and the regulations framed thereunder, any patentee of a pharmaceutical substance may grant exclusive licenses authorizing specific acts relating to the manufacture, use, sale, or importation of the patented invention. Such licenses shall be assignable, both absolutely and conditionally, by instrument in writing duly executed and registered with the Controller. Where an assignment or license is made without disclosing the names of all reversionary interest holders, it shall be void unless such disclosure is subsequently rectified as provided herein. The patentee shall provide a copy of any licensing agreement to the Controller within thirty days of its execution; failure to do so may render the license unenforceable against third parties. Further, any licensee granted rights under this Act shall adhere to quality control standards prescribed by the relevant regulatory authority and be subject to inspection accordingly.

Where an application for a patent relating to a pharmaceutical substance is opposed under this Act, the grounds of opposition shall include, but not be limited to, allegations that the invention lacks novelty or involves an obvious modification of existing knowledge. Provided that, where such an allegation concerns the formulation of a known active ingredient, the opponent must demonstrate, with clear and convincing evidence, that the claimed process results in a significant and unexpected improvement in efficacy or safety. The patentee shall be afforded an opportunity to rebut this evidence and present counter-arguments pertaining to the inventive step. Any appeal against a decision upholding such an opposition may only be entertained if it is shown that the appellate authority was demonstrably swayed by extraneous considerations or misapplied established principles of patent law as provided herein.

Where an application for a patent relating to a pharmaceutical substance is rejected under this Act on the grounds of novelty or inventive step, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to submit written arguments and evidence demonstrating the contrary. Such submissions may include expert testimony regarding prior art disclosures and comparative data establishing non-obviousness. The Controller, while considering such arguments, shall give due weight to any evidence presented by third parties claiming a conflicting right arising from a deceptively similar substance already in public use. Any order of rejection or grant shall be subject to appeal before the Appellate Board, where the Board may direct further inquiry into the matter and consider additional expert opinions as it deems necessary for just determination.

For the purposes of registration under this Act, a pharmaceutical substance shall be deemed to include any novel chemical compound or formulation exhibiting therapeutic efficacy and fulfilling all criteria for patentability as provided herein. The Controller General may require submission of detailed manufacturing processes, stability data, and clinical trial summaries demonstrating safety and effectiveness prior to grant of registration. Any entity engaged in the commercial production, distribution, or sale of a pharmaceutical substance registered under this Act shall be subject to periodic inspections by designated authorities to ensure compliance with prescribed quality standards. Failure to adhere to these standards may constitute infringement, leading to penalties as determined under this Act. Further, any alteration to the registered formulation without prior approval from the Controller General shall also be deemed an act of infringement.

Where an objection is taken to the grant of a patent for a pharmaceutical substance on the ground that the invention is not novel or does not involve inventive step, the Controller shall issue a notice to the applicant and any other person interested in making representations. Such representations shall be filed within a period specified in the notice, and the Controller shall consider all submissions received before proceeding with examination. The Controller may, after giving an opportunity of being heard to both sides, either allow the patent as applied for or reject the application entirely. Any party aggrieved by an order passed by the Controller under this Act may appeal to the appellate board. The appellate board shall hear appeals from the orders of the Controller and may confirm, vary, or reverse such orders, subject to the provisions herein.

“Semiconductor” with reference to this Act means any material or device embodying circuitry originating from a semiconductor substrate; "layout-design" means a three-dimensional representation of the arrangement of elements, accurately depicting their relative positions and connections on an integrated circuit. The term “means registrar semiconductor” shall refer to the officer appointed by the Central Government under this Act, who is responsible for receiving applications for registration of layout-designs, conducting examinations as provided herein, and maintaining the Register of Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout-Designs. An application filed with the means registrar semiconductor shall include detailed technical specifications subject to guidelines issued from time to time.

For the purposes of this Act, “person” includes any individual, whether Indian citizen or not, firm, company, society, association, co-operative committee, trust, legal entity registered under any law for the time being in force and any body incorporated under a statute. A partnership firm shall be deemed to be a person for the purposes of suits relating to patents; provided that such firm is duly registered under the Indian Partnership Act. Where an individual ceases to be a partner in a partnership firm, the firm shall continue as a “person” subject to its continued registration and operation as defined herein. The term "person" also extends to include any entity acting on behalf of or representing another person.

For the purposes of this Act, “person” shall include any individual, firm, company, society, or association incorporated under the laws for the time being in force and may also include bodies corporate and authorities established by law. A person shall be deemed to be registered as a patent agent if such person has satisfied the Controller that he possesses the requisite qualification and experience as prescribed herein. Any application for registration of a patent agent shall contain particulars relating to the applicant’s educational background, professional training, and details of any prior engagement in intellectual property matters. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, specify conditions regarding continuing professional development required of registered persons.

Where an application for patent is rejected under this Act, and the applicant seeks redressal through appeal, the appellate authority shall consider whether the rejection was based on misinterpretation of evidence presented or a flawed assessment of prior art. Any person aggrieved by such a decision may petition the High Court within ninety days from the date of the order, provided that the petitioner demonstrates demonstrable prejudice resulting directly from the appellate authority’s determination. The term "person" for the purposes of this appeal includes not only the applicant but also any individual or entity holding a relevant interest in the subject matter of the patent application, such as assignees or licensees. Further, the High Court may grant interim relief to prevent further action on the rejected application pending final adjudication, subject to just cause and security being furnished as deemed appropriate by the court.

For the purposes of this Act, “person” includes any individual, firm, company, society, or association incorporated under the laws for the time being in force and shall extend to include bodies politic. Where an application for a patent is filed by a partnership, the Central Government may require such partnership to disclose the names of all partners who are jointly claiming inventorship. Any communication required to be made under this Act shall be deemed to have been duly made if sent by registered post with acknowledgment due or delivered personally to the address as notified by the applicant or patentee. The Controller shall, upon receiving a request from any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act, afford him an opportunity of being heard and may consider such representations as he deems fit before making any further determination. Any appeal against an order of the Controller may be made to the Appellate Board within a period prescribed herein.

For the purposes of this Act, a “person” shall include any individual, firm, company, or association incorporated under the laws for the time being in force and may also include bodies corporate and societies registered under the Societies Registration Act. A person shall be deemed to have made, used, or sold an invention if it has been done by another acting on their behalf with their knowledge or consent. Subject to compliance with prescribed formalities, any person claiming to be the inventor of a process or article may apply for a patent as provided herein. Provided that where an application is filed by a legal representative of a deceased person, such representative shall satisfy the Controller regarding their entitlement to file the application and manage the patent rights accordingly. Any assignment of patent rights shall require registration under this Act to be valid against third parties.

For the purposes of this Act, “person” shall include any individual, firm, company, society, or association incorporated under the laws for the time being in force and may also include bodies corporate and authorities established by law. Any false representation made to the Controller with intent to deceive, or which is likely to deceive, as to the identity of a person claiming to be the inventor shall render such person liable to prosecution under this Act and subject to a penalty not exceeding five thousand rupees for each instance of misrepresentation. Further, any officer of a company found complicit in such deceptive practices shall also face similar penalties, without prejudice to their individual liability as provided herein. The Controller may issue notices requiring disclosure of true ownership where reasonable doubt exists regarding the declared person.

Where an invention has been assigned under this Act, and the assignee is a person engaged in the manufacture or importation of patented articles, that assignee shall be deemed to hold such assignment subject to any conditions expressly stipulated therein. Any subsequent transfer of rights relating to the patent, whether by way of further assignment or otherwise, shall require prior notification to the Controller, who may, after due inquiry and providing an opportunity for objection from the original assignor, impose reasonable royalty obligations on the transferee. A person acquiring a license to make, use, or sell a patented invention is empowered to sub-license such rights, provided that the terms of the sublicense are not more favourable than those granted in the initial license agreement. The Controller may require disclosure of all assignments and licenses relating to a patent within six months of their execution.

For the purposes of this Act, “person” shall include not only an individual, but also any body corporate or association of individuals, whether incorporated or unincorporated. Where a dispute arises concerning whether an entity qualifies as a "person" under this definition, the Controller may require submission of relevant constitutive documents and operational records for examination. An appeal against such determination by the Controller lies to the Appellate Board, subject to the condition that the appellant demonstrates demonstrable prejudice resulting from the initial assessment. Provided that, in cases involving foreign entities claiming “person” status, verification of domicile and principal place of business shall be mandatory, and any challenge to this verification may be raised before a designated tribunal as provided herein.

Where an application for patent is rejected under this Act, and the applicant desires to appeal against such rejection, the appellate authority shall require the appellant to furnish proof of having paid the prescribed fee within thirty days from the date of communication of the order of rejection. Failure to comply with this requirement shall render the appeal void ab initio. Any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act relating to revocation or surrender of a patent may prefer an appeal to the appellate authority, subject to demonstrating standing and prejudice arising directly from the impugned decision. The register patents shall be maintained in accordance with regulations prescribed; any alteration to such entries must be certified by a duly authorized officer. A person found to have made false statements in relation to a patent application or proceedings may be liable for damages as determined by the relevant court.

Where an application for patent is assigned or licensed under this Act, the assignee or licensee shall be deemed to be a person for all purposes relating to the continued prosecution of that application. Provided that, where such assignment or license is granted prior to the sealing of the patent, the assignor or licensor retains the right to participate in proceedings concerning the application’s validity subject to the terms stipulated within the agreement. Any subsequent transfer of rights under this Act pertaining to a patented invention shall be recorded with the Controller and shall operate to substitute the original assignee or licensee as a person holding title. The Controller may, upon receiving an application sub section detailing such substitution, issue a certificate reflecting the change in ownership, which certificate shall be binding on all parties.

For the purposes of this Act, “person” shall include any individual, firm, company, or association incorporated under the laws for the time being in force and may also extend to bodies politic or corporate. Where an international registration makes a claim for protection within India, the determination of whether such a person is indeed entitled to enforce rights arising from that registration shall be subject to verification by the Controller, considering factors including domicile and place of business at the time of filing the initial application abroad. Any appeal against this determination may be made to the Appellate Board, provided that the appellant demonstrates demonstrable prejudice resulting directly from the Controller’s decision; otherwise, such appeals shall be deemed frivolous under this Act.

An application for registration of a layout-design shall be deemed incomplete if it does not include a declaration specifying the name and address of the applicant claiming ownership rights. The Registrar may require further particulars regarding the technical aspects of the layout-design from the applicant, provided that such request is made within thirty days of receipt of the application. Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Registrar relating to registration or refusal thereof may appeal to the Appellate Board. The Appellate Board shall be constituted with a CIAL Member or a Technical Member of the Appellate Board and shall hear appeals under this Act. Decisions of the Appellate Board are final, subject to revision by the High Court on a point of law.

Subject to the provisions herein, any member so appointed shall hold office for a term of three years from the date on which they assume charge, provided that a member may be removed from office if found guilty of misconduct as determined under established procedures. The Board’s decisions shall be binding and final, subject to appeal to the High Court only on grounds of legal error.

An appeal shall only be admitted if the appellant deposits with the Appellate Board such sum as may be determined by the Board, representing costs incurred by the respondent. Failure to comply with this provision will render the appeal inadmissible. The Appellate Board shall consist of a Chairperson and not less than two members, one of whom shall be a cial Member or a Technical Member of the Appellate Board and possess expertise in semiconductor technology. Decisions of the Appellate Board are final subject to further appeals under the relevant provisions concerning judicial review.

context: For the purposes of this Act, an “invention” shall be defined as a novel concept transformed into tangible form through technical skill and ingenuity. An invention is deemed non-obvious if, prior to the date of filing of the patent application, it did not exist or become known in any part of the world, subject to exceptions provided herein relating to grace periods. The term "invention" specifically excludes discoveries, scientific theories, mathematical methods, literary or artistic creations, and schemes for performing mental acts. An invention shall also include an improvement of an existing process or product, provided that such improvement possesses inventive step as determined under this Act.

An application for registration of an invention shall be accompanied by a detailed description sufficient to enable a person skilled in the art to make and use the invention. The Controller may, under this Act, require the applicant to furnish further particulars concerning the nature of the invention, including diagrams or drawings where appropriate, to ascertain its compliance with the requirements of novelty and inventive step. Such particulars shall be submitted within the time specified by the Controller. Failure to provide the requested information may result in the application being deemed abandoned. The description must clearly define the scope of protection sought for the claimed invention, distinguishing it from prior art disclosures. Any ambiguity in the description shall be resolved against the applicant.

Where any person considers that another has infringed his patent, he may institute proceedings for relief under this Act. Such proceedings shall be commenced within three years from the date when the infringement is reasonably suspected to have taken place, subject to just and equitable considerations as determined by the relevant judicial authority. The remedies available to the patentee include an injunction restraining the infringing party from further acts of infringement, damages sustained by the patentee due to the infringement, and delivery up or destruction of the patented article constituting the infringement. It is provided that a finding of non-infringement shall not preclude a subsequent action based on substantially identical facts. The determination of whether an alleged act constitutes an *invention* requires consideration of its novelty and inventive step as defined herein.

An application for a patent shall be accompanied by a declaration, made under this Act, stating whether the applicant is claiming priority from any earlier publication or application relating to the subject matter of the invention. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish such further particulars as he deems necessary for the purpose of determining novelty and inventive step. Where an objection is taken on the ground that the invention lacks an inventive step, the applicant shall be given a reasonable opportunity of being heard. Evidence pertaining to prior art relevant to assessing the inventive step may be presented by any party interested in opposing the grant of patent. The determination of whether an invention constitutes an *invention* requires consideration of technical knowledge available at the time of filing and assessment of obviousness to a person skilled in the art, as provided herein.

An application for a patent shall be deemed invalid if it is demonstrated, under this Act, that the claimed invention was previously known or used by others within India, provided that such prior knowledge or use was not made public through any written or oral description accessible to the public before the date of filing of the patent application. Furthermore, an invention shall not be considered novel if its essential features are disclosed in a document published anywhere in the world, unless it can be established that the disclosure occurred without the applicant’s knowledge and consent. The determination of whether an invention constitutes a true *invention* requires consideration of whether it involves sufficient technical advancement over existing knowledge and is capable of being applied to an industrial process.

Where any person is aggrieved by an order passed under this Act, such person may appeal against such order within sixty days from the date of communication thereof to the Appellate Board. The Appellate Board shall consider all evidence presented and may, subject to provisions regarding natural justice, affirm, modify or reverse the order appealed against. Any act done in contravention of a patent, including but not limited to making, using, selling, importing or offering to sell an invention without authorization from the patentee, shall constitute infringement. Infringement proceedings may be initiated by the patentee and are subject to penalties as provided herein, which include monetary damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the patentee due to such unauthorized exploitation of the invention.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any patentee may grant exclusive licenses under their patent for an invention, specifying the field of use, territory, or other limitations as they deem fit. Such license shall be assignable by the patentee, either wholly or partially, and such assignment shall vest in the assignee the right to exercise the licensed rights to the extent specified therein. Where a patentee has granted multiple licenses relating to the same invention, the Controller may intervene if disputes arise concerning priority of enjoyment of the patented invention amongst the licensees, acting as an arbiter to ensure equitable distribution of benefits derived from exploitation of the intellectual property. Further, any licensee may, with prior written consent of the patentee and subject to conditions prescribed herein, sub-license their rights pertaining to the granted invention.

An application for a patent shall be deemed invalid if it is demonstrated, through evidence presented before the Controller, that the claimed invention was previously described in a publication accessible to the public, notwithstanding any assertion by the applicant regarding independent conception. The burden of proving prior publication and its impact on novelty rests upon the petitioner challenging the validity of the patent. Provided that, such challenge may be successfully sustained only if it is established that a person skilled in the relevant art would have been motivated to reproduce the invention based on said publication. Further, any appeal against an order determining lack of inventive step shall require demonstration of manifest error in the Controller's assessment of obviousness, subject to prevailing case law.

An application for registration of an invention relating to genetically modified organisms shall include detailed particulars regarding the source material utilized, including its geographical origin and any traditional knowledge associated therewith. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating benefit-sharing arrangements with communities possessing such traditional knowledge, remitting a portion thereof to the National Gene Fund as determined by regulations framed under this Act. Provided that, where the invention is derived from publicly funded research, the applicant shall disclose the extent of public funding received and demonstrate compliance with applicable guidelines regarding access to research data. The Controller may reject an application if it appears that the claimed invention inappropriately exploits traditional knowledge without equitable benefit-sharing.

An application for a patent shall be deemed to disclose the matter described therein sufficiently if it contains a clear and complete description of the invention, enabling any person skilled in the relevant field to make and use the same. Where an applicant seeks protection for both a process and the product obtained therefrom, the claims defining the scope of the invention must clearly distinguish between these aspects. Further, where a mark separately registered under the Trade Marks Act is incorporated as an integral element within the claimed invention, the application shall include a declaration confirming freedom to use said mark in relation to the patented article or process. The Controller may require further clarification regarding such integration and its impact on patentability. Any alteration made to the description after the initial filing date is permissible only with the written consent of the Controller, provided that it does not broaden the scope of the original invention claimed.

The registration of a trademark shall not be invalidated solely upon demonstration that use of an identical or similar mark exists for dissimilar goods, provided that such prior use does not create confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of the goods or services. Justified registration, as contemplated under this Act, requires evidence establishing consumer recognition and association with the applicant’s goods or services at the time of application. The Registrar may consider factors including duration of use, geographical extent of trade, and advertising expenditure in determining whether a mark warrants justified registration. Further, any challenge to such registration must demonstrate demonstrable prejudice resulting from the continued protection afforded by this Act.

The Registrar shall, upon receiving an application for registration of a proposed trade mark, conduct such examination as is deemed necessary to ascertain whether the mark fulfills all requirements under this Act. Where the proposed trade mark comprises a geographical indication already registered or capable of being registered under this Act, the Registrar may proceed with registration only if satisfied that use by the applicant does not constitute misleading practices or unfair competition. Justified registration shall be granted where the applicant demonstrates acquired distinctiveness through extensive and continuous use following initial application, provided that such use has created a significant association between the mark and the goods or services for which it is proposed. The Registrar may require further evidence to substantiate claims of acquired distinctiveness as deemed appropriate.

Where a trade mark is registered subject to a condition limiting its use to a specified geographical area, any person claiming damages for infringement shall be entitled to recover such damages as are reasonably attributable to the infringing use within that defined territory. Provided that, where the proprietor of the trade mark has failed to exercise due diligence in preventing unauthorized use extending beyond the initially justified registration, the remedies available under this Act may be limited accordingly at the discretion of the adjudicating authority. The Registrar shall provide an opportunity for both the proprietor and the alleged infringer to present evidence concerning the extent of such unauthorized use and its impact on the claimant’s business interests. Furthermore, a finding that the trade mark's scope was unduly restricted at registration does not preclude subsequent expansion subject to procedural requirements as provided herein.

The Board shall, upon receiving an objection under this Act from any person asserting a right or interest in relation to a proposed trade mark, afford such objector an opportunity for a hearing. The applicant for registration shall be notified of the objection and the time, date, and place fixed for the hearing at least thirty days prior to the appointed date, by registered post acknowledgement due. If, following such hearing, the Board is satisfied that the grounds raised by the objector are substantiated and that the proposed trade mark would infringe any right or interest possessed by the objector, registration may be refused. However, if the Board finds that the applicant has demonstrated a genuine use of the mark in accordance with the provisions herein, or otherwise provides compelling justification for registration notwithstanding the objection, justified registration may nonetheless be granted subject to such conditions as the Board deems appropriate to protect the interests of both parties.

The registration of a trademark shall not be deemed to confer upon the registered proprietor any right to use the trademark in relation to goods or services which are substantially identical or confusingly similar to those in respect of which an earlier trade mark is registered under this Act, provided that such earlier trade mark enjoys justified registration. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating continuous and genuine use of the trademark for a period not less than five years from the date of registration before considering any application for rectification based on non-use. Further, where the applicant demonstrates prior honest intent to use the mark in relation to specified goods, but was prevented by circumstances beyond their control, such impediment shall be considered when assessing whether justified registration exists.

The registration of a trademark shall not be invalidated solely upon demonstration that another party previously used an identical or deceptively similar sign, provided that such prior use was limited to sporadic promotional activities and did not establish substantial reputation within the Indian territory. Any party claiming damage resulting from the unjustified registration of a trademark may institute civil proceedings seeking injunctive relief and compensation for losses incurred directly attributable to the infringing mark’s presence in commerce. The Registrar shall, upon receiving evidence of such detrimental impact, conduct an inquiry into the validity of the registration, with due consideration given to the extent of prior use and any demonstrable consumer confusion. Failure to comply with orders issued under this Act may attract penalties as determined by the adjudicating authority.

The owner of a registered trade mark shall, subject to this Act and the regulations made thereunder, have the right to grant licenses for the use of their trade mark, either generally or relating to specific goods or services, provided that such license agreements explicitly state the scope and duration of permitted usage. Any assignment of rights pertaining to a justified registration, including but not limited to the right to exploit the trade mark commercially, shall be in writing and executed as per the prescribed formalities; failure to adhere to these requirements renders the assignment void. Further, where a license is granted, the licensor retains the power to audit the licensee’s use of the trade mark to ensure compliance with the terms agreed upon, and may revoke such license if material breaches are detected. The Registrar shall maintain records of all assignments and licenses relating to registered trade marks as provided herein.

The registration of a trademark shall not be invalidated solely upon demonstration that prior use existed, provided that such prior use did not constitute honest concurrent use as defined under this Act. An appeal against an order refusing justified registration lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of said order. The Board may, after affording opportunity for a hearing to all parties concerned, substitute its own decision in place of that of the Registrar. Further, any party aggrieved by an order of the Board under this provision may prefer an appeal to the High Court within ninety days thereafter, subject to demonstrating substantial grounds for such challenge and payment of prescribed fees.

Where a trade mark is registered following an international application form filed under the Madrid Protocol, and opposition proceedings are initiated based on prior conflicting rights existing in India, the registration shall not be deemed invalid solely due to the absence of earlier use within Indian territory. Justified registration, in such circumstances, requires demonstration by the applicant that the adoption of the mark, despite lack of prior use, does not create confusion amongst consumers or otherwise unfairly prejudice the interests of those possessing pre-existing rights. The Registrar may require submission of evidence substantiating this justification, including market surveys and consumer perception studies. Failure to provide satisfactory evidence shall render the registration vulnerable to revocation under this Act. Any party aggrieved by a decision regarding justified registration may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board as provided herein.

Where a trade mark is registered under this Act, and such registration is deemed justified registration due to prior use or other exceptional circumstances as provided herein, the owner shall retain exclusive rights pertaining to the representation of those goods or services for which the mark identifies them. However, the owner may grant licenses permitting third parties to utilize the registered trade mark in connection with specific purposes identifying goods, subject to conditions stipulated within the licensing agreement and approved by the Registrar. Any assignment of such license shall require notification to the Registrar prior to its effective date, detailing the assignee’s identity and scope of permitted use. Further, sub-licensing is permissible only with express written consent from the original trade mark owner, ensuring continued adherence to quality standards associated with the registered mark.

For the purposes of this Act, “farmer” shall mean a person who cultivates land for agricultural purposes and includes a tiller, cultivator or sower. A farmer may be an individual, a partnership firm, a co-operative society or any other legal entity engaged in cultivation. The term "farmer" excludes individuals primarily engaged in seed production for commercial gain unless they also cultivate land as defined herein. Subject to the provisions of this Act, a farmer shall retain the right to save, exchange, share or sell farm saved seeds of varieties cultivated by them, provided that such actions do not infringe upon any extant intellectual property rights relating to plant varieties.

An application for registration of a plant variety shall include particulars relating to the breeder, which, where the applicant is a farmer claiming rights under this Act, shall specify the extent of their involvement in the selection and maintenance of the variety. Such farmer applicants must provide documentation demonstrating continuous cultivation of the variety for a period not less than three years prior to the date of application, evidencing their contribution towards its distinctiveness or stability. The Authority may require further evidence substantiating the farmer’s claim, including records pertaining to seed saving practices and local adaptation observations. Any person aggrieved by a decision regarding registration based on a farmer's involvement may appeal under this Act.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, a farmer shall be entitled to save, use, exchange, share or sell farm saved seeds of any variety which they have legally obtained, including varieties protected under this Act. Provided that such sharing or selling shall not include offering for sale branded seed products unless the farmer is registered as a seller with the appropriate authority and complies with all applicable regulations regarding quality control and labeling. Any person who obstructs or prevents a farmer from exercising these rights may be liable to pay compensation, determined by the Authority, reflecting loss of livelihood and associated costs. Further, any false claim made against a farmer concerning their seed practices, intended to deprive them of their legitimate activities as a farmer, shall constitute an actionable wrong under this Act, entitling the aggrieved party to seek redressal through civil courts.

A farmer shall be deemed to include any individual cultivating land solely as an occupation and engaged in seed saving and exchange, provided that such cultivation is not undertaken for commercial purposes exceeding the limits prescribed by the Central Government. Any application made under this Act by a farmer claiming rights relating to a variety shall be accompanied by a certificate from the District Collector or other designated officer verifying the applicant’s status as a farmer and confirming their engagement in traditional agricultural practices. The Authority may, at any time, require a farmer to submit further documentation substantiating their claim, including records of seed saving activities and landholding details. Failure to comply with such requests shall render the application liable for rejection. Rights granted to a farmer under this Act are subject to conditions regarding traceability of seeds and adherence to bio-safety protocols as provided herein.

A farmer shall be deemed to have fulfilled the conditions for recognition under this Act if, and only if, they possess documented proof of continuous cultivation on a specified parcel of land for a minimum period of three cropping seasons immediately preceding an application for registration. Such proof may include, but is not limited to, revenue records, agricultural receipts, or affidavits duly attested by recognized village authorities. Provided that, in cases where documentary evidence is unavailable due to circumstances beyond the farmer’s control, the Authority may consider oral testimony corroborated by at least two independent witnesses familiar with the farming practices of the applicant. Further, a farmer claiming rights under this Act shall disclose any prior agreements regarding seed usage or distribution and demonstrate compliance with relevant regulations pertaining to bio-safety protocols.

Any person found to have knowingly and willfully infringed upon the rights of a registered plant variety, including unauthorized commercialization or distribution thereof, shall be liable for penalties as determined by the relevant authority. Such penalties may include fines not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees and imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years. Where the infringement is committed by an employee or agent acting within the scope of their employment, the employer shall also be deemed guilty and subject to similar penalties. A farmer who utilizes propagating material of a registered variety without authorization from the breeder, except for legitimate farm practices as provided herein, will face administrative action including suspension of access to subsidized inputs. Repeated offenses may result in permanent revocation of farming privileges.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, a farmer who has multiplied, sold, exchanged or otherwise distributed plant material of a variety protected under this Act may grant a license for such activities to any other person, including seed companies, on terms and conditions as agreed upon in writing. Such licenses shall specify the geographical area within which the licensee is authorized to operate, the quantity of plant material that may be handled, and the royalty payable to the farmer. The farmer retains ownership of all rights pertaining to the variety, and any assignment of these rights must be registered with the Authority. Provided that a license granted under this provision shall not restrict the farmer’s right to save, reuse, exchange or sell farm-saved seed of the protected variety for their own direct agricultural use. Any transfer of such licenses requires prior notification to the Authority.

Notwithstanding anything contained herein, an appeal shall lie to the Appellate Board under this Act if any authority determines that a farmer has acted in contravention of a Plant Variety Protection order relating to saved seed. Such appeal may be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order and shall state specifically the grounds upon which it is based. The Appellate Board, after affording an opportunity for hearing to all parties concerned, may confirm, vary or reverse the order appealed against. It shall be presumed that any action undertaken by a farmer in traditional farming practices, utilizing locally adapted seeds, was not intended as commercial exploitation unless proven otherwise before the Appellate Board. This presumption shall apply subject to demonstrating adherence to customary agricultural practices.

Where an application for registration of a plant variety is opposed by any person claiming to be affected by such proposed registration, including but not limited to a farmer alleging infringement of their traditional rights or knowledge relating to the variety, the Authority shall give notice of the opposition to the applicant and afford both parties an opportunity of being heard. The applicant may present evidence in support of their claim, and the opponent shall be permitted to rebut such evidence and submit counter-evidence as provided herein. In determining whether to grant or refuse registration, the Authority shall consider all relevant factors, including the extent to which the variety is demonstrably new, distinct, stable, and uniform, and any demonstrable impact on the livelihoods of farmers cultivating traditional varieties. Should the Authority find sufficient grounds for concern regarding the potential adverse effects on a farmer’s rights, it may initiate a procedure cancelling registration, subject to appeal under this Act.

Any person found to have knowingly and willfully infringed upon the rights of a registered plant variety, including unauthorized commercialization or distribution thereof, shall be liable for penalties as determined by the Controller. Where such infringement is demonstrated to have been facilitated through misleading representations concerning the origin or characteristics of the harvested material, the penalty may be enhanced up to three times the assessed damages. A farmer utilizing propagating material of a registered plant variety obtained in contravention of this Act shall be subject to remedial action including mandatory reporting and potential forfeiture of subsequent harvests. The Controller may issue directives for the cessation of infringing activities and order compensation payable to the right holder, taking into account the scale and duration of the offense.

A farmer possessing rights under this Act relating to a plant variety shall be permitted, subject to conditions prescribed by the Authority, to grant licenses for the commercial use of propagating material derived from that variety. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive and shall specify the geographical area within which the licensee is authorized to operate. Where a farmer offers propagating material for sale, accompanied by an advertisement indicating acceptance of specific terms regarding liability for crop failure attributable to the variety’s characteristics, such advertised acceptance shall constitute binding notification to any prospective purchaser. The Authority may, upon receiving complaints from other farmers alleging unfair licensing practices or misleading advertisements, initiate inquiries and impose penalties as deemed appropriate. Assignment of farmer's rights relating to plant varieties is permissible with prior approval from the Board, provided that the assignee undertakes obligations equivalent to those originally held by the transferring farmer.

Where an application is filed by a person claiming to be a farmer for registration of a plant variety, and such claim is disputed on the grounds that the applicant does not fulfill the definition of “farmer” as provided herein, the Authority shall give notice thereof to all interested parties. Any party aggrieved by this determination may appeal under this Act to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The Appellate Board shall consider any evidence submitted regarding the applicant’s farming activities and landholding records, subject to verification through a designated officer appointed for that purpose. An India application shall be deemed invalid if the farmer's claim is ultimately found unsubstantiated by the Appellate Board.

For the purposes of this Act, “farmer” includes any individual cultivating land for agricultural purposes, whether as an owner, tenant, or otherwise, and shall encompass traditional farming communities and marginal farmers engaged in seed saving, exchange, and cultivation practices. A farmer shall be entitled to save, use, exchange, share or sell farm saved seeds of varieties including those protected under this Act, provided that such activities do not violate any conditions stipulated on a certificate registration produced by the breeder. The rights of a farmer as defined herein are subject to limitations imposed by regulations framed under this Act concerning intellectual property protection and bio-safety protocols.

The proprietor of a registered trade mark may grant a license to use the trade mark for goods or services, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated in the licensing agreement. Such agreements shall be in writing and clearly define the scope of permitted use, geographical territory, duration, and royalty payments payable by the licensee. Any assignment of the registered trade mark, whether partial or complete, must be executed in the prescribed form and filed with the Trade Marks Registry for registration as provided herein. The assignee shall become the new proprietor and acquire all rights and privileges associated with the register trade marks, including the right to enforce against infringers. Further, a license granted under this Act may be assigned by the licensee subject to prior written consent of the original proprietor, unless otherwise specified in the initial licensing agreement.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act, the Registrar may, at any time during the opposition proceedings, require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating continuous use of the proposed trade mark in relation to the goods or services specified in the application. Such evidence shall be submitted within the period prescribed by the Registrar and must clearly establish the extent and duration of such *use trade mark*. The Registrar may allow the opponent an opportunity to file a counterstatement addressing any issues raised concerning the veracity or relevance of the applicant’s evidentiary submissions. Failure on the part of the applicant to comply with the Registrar's requirements regarding evidence of use, as provided herein, shall be considered by the Registrar when determining the merits of the opposition and may result in the rejection of the application for registration. The Registrar shall record reasons for any such decision.

Where the registered proprietor of a trade mark desires to grant a license for the use thereof, he may execute an assignment agreement in writing, specifying the goods or services in relation to which the right to use the trade mark shall extend. Such license shall be valid only for the duration explicitly stated within the assignment agreement and subject to any conditions imposed by the registered proprietor concerning quality control or territorial limitations. The registrar may, upon application by a third party demonstrating substantial investment predicated on a belief of exclusive usage rights, investigate whether the continued use trade mark aligns with the terms initially recorded during registration produced registrar. Any sub-licensing shall require prior written consent from both the original registered proprietor and the assignee, failing which it is deemed invalid under this Act.

In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires,— (q) “package” includes any container, wrapping, band, label, and such other materials as are customarily employed for enclosing or identifying goods; (r) Any proprietor who, knowing that a registered trade mark is being used in relation to identical or similar goods without his consent, shall knowingly permit the use thereof, or offer any inducement for such use, shall be guilty of an offence cognizable by a Magistrates Court and liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or both. Further, where such knowing permission or inducement results in damage to the reputation of the registered trade mark, the proprietor shall also be liable to pay damages as determined by the Commercial Courts. This liability is without prejudice to any other remedies available under this Act.

context: Where a proprietor of a registered trade mark institutes proceedings under this Act for infringement, and obtains a judgment against a defendant found guilty of such infringement, the court may, in addition to any damages awarded, order the forfeiture of any property used or adapted for making or vending the infringing goods. Such order shall specify the items subject to forfeiture, which may include packaging materials, advertising displays, and stock-in-trade. The proprietor shall provide a detailed inventory to the appropriate authorities for disposal as directed by the court. “Permitted use”, in relation to a registered trade mark, means the use of the trade mark with the consent of the proprietor, expressly granted in writing, or arising from a contract under this Act. Any goods produced or services provided following a convicted order forfeited shall be deemed an infringement and subject to further remedies as provided herein.

context: For the purposes of this Act, a registered trade mark shall be deemed to confer upon the proprietor thereof the exclusive right to the use of the said trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered, and to prevent the use of any identical or confusingly similar marks relating to such goods or services. This right extends to all forms of representation of the registered trade mark, including but not limited to its graphical depiction and textual presentation. Provided that, nothing herein shall restrict the use of a registered trade mark by duly authorized users as may be permitted under this Act, subject to conditions prescribed therein.

An application for registration of a proposed registered trade shall include a representation of the marks as applied and intended to be used, accompanied by a statement clearly identifying all colours claimed as part of the mark. Where the applicant seeks to register a three-dimensional shape, the application must provide detailed specifications outlining the precise contours and dimensions thereof, sufficient to allow for unambiguous assessment under this Act. The Registrar may require further clarification regarding any aspect of the representation or specification if deemed necessary for proper examination. Any alteration made to the registered trade mark after registration shall be subject to approval by the Registrar and will constitute a new application, provided that such alterations do not fundamentally change the distinctive character of the registered trade.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person desiring to prevent, or continuing to prevent, the use of a registered trade mark which is liable to cause confusion in relation to the goods or services for which the registered trade mark is registered shall be entitled to institute legal proceedings against such person. Such proceedings may seek an injunction restraining the infringing party from further acts of infringement, and damages commensurate with the loss suffered by the proprietor of the registered trade mark as a direct result of the unauthorized use. Where the infringement has been willful and malicious, the court may award aggravated damages not exceeding three times the amount of compensation it deems appropriate. The proprietor shall be deemed to have established prior rights in the registered trade mark for the purposes of such remedies. Further, any goods bearing the infringing mark are liable to be seized and destroyed under this Act.

An application for registration of a proposed registered trade shall be refused if the representation of the trade mark is such that it does not comply with the prescribed standards regarding clarity and distinctiveness, as determined by the Registrar. The Registrar may require an applicant to amend the representation of a proposed registered trade to bring it into compliance with these standards; provided that any amendment so made shall not substantially alter the identity of the trade mark. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar refusing registration or requiring amendments may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of such decision. The Board’s determination shall be final, subject to further appeals as provided herein. Furthermore, the Registrar shall maintain records pertaining to all applications and registrations, accessible for inspection by interested parties upon payment of a prescribed fee.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any proprietor of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to institute proceedings for relief against any person infringing their exclusive right in the registered trade mark. Such infringement is deemed to occur where an identical or confusingly similar sign is used in connection with goods or services identical or similar to those for which the registration is effective, without the consent of the proprietor. Provided that, use in accordance with honest practices in industrial commerce and reasonably acquired prior public knowledge shall not constitute infringement under this Act. The Registrar may, upon application by an interested party demonstrating demonstrable consumer confusion, issue an order restraining further use of the infringing sign. Any such order shall be subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Any person who, without due cause and with intent to deceive, uses a registered trade mark identical or confusingly similar to a registered trade mark for the sale or advertising of goods or services shall be guilty of an offence. Such offender shall be liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. Further, any goods bearing such infringing mark are deemed counterfeit and subject to seizure and destruction as provided herein. The owner of a registered trade mark may apply to the relevant authority seeking injunctions restraining further acts of infringement and claiming damages commensurate with the loss suffered due to the unauthorized use. This provision shall not preclude civil remedies available under this Act.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any proprietor of a registered trade mark may grant a license to use such registered trade mark, specifying the rights granted and the duration of the license. Such licenses shall be assignable subject to registration with the Trade Marks Registry, provided that no assignment shall prejudice existing rights of registered users. Where a registered trade mark is assigned, the assignee shall become entitled to exercise all rights and privileges as if they were the original proprietor. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating due diligence in ensuring continued quality control by licensees using the registered trade mark, failing which revocation proceedings may be initiated under this Act. Any sub-license granted without prior written consent of the proprietor shall be deemed invalid unless ratified within six months from the date of such sub-licensing.

Subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal, any person claiming damages for the use of a registered trade mark without consent shall be required to demonstrate that such use has resulted in actual financial loss attributable directly to the infringement. The Registrar may, upon receiving evidence of misleading similarity between an unregistered mark and a registered trade mark, issue a notice to the proprietor of the unregistered mark, affording them opportunity to submit their response within sixty days. Failure to adequately respond shall be deemed conclusive acceptance of the Registrar’s determination regarding likelihood of confusion. Further, any party aggrieved by such determination may petition the Tribunal for review, provided that the petitioner demonstrates demonstrable prejudice resulting from the Registrar's action.

An application for registration of a registered trade mark shall include particulars identifying the applicant and specifying the goods or services in connection with which the trade mark is sought to be registered. Where an applicant is acting through a practise patent agent, such agent shall provide verification as per prescribed forms attesting to the accuracy of the information provided within the application. The Registrar may require further documentation demonstrating distinctiveness if the proposed registered trade mark bears similarity to existing marks or names. Any alteration to the list of goods or services following initial filing requires consent from the applicant and notification to the Registrar, subject to provisions regarding acceptable amendments. Opposition proceedings against a pending registration shall be conducted as provided herein.

An application for renewal of a registered trade mark shall be made to the Registrar not earlier than six months before the date of its expiry and not later than six months after such expiry. The applicant shall furnish with the application, a copy of the notice published under this Act prior to the registration. Where the registrar is satisfied that there are sufficient grounds for believing that the registered trade mark is still being used in relation to goods or services, he may renew the registration for a period not exceeding ten years from the expiry date. Any person may, within two months from the date of publication of notice of application for renewal, file with the registrar an objection to such renewal, stating the grounds thereof. The Registrar shall give due opportunity to the applicant and objector to be heard under this Act before passing any order regarding the renewal.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any proprietor of a registered trade mark may grant licenses authorizing others to uses trade mark for specific goods or services. Such licenses shall be documented in writing and filed with the Trade Marks Registry within thirty days of their execution, providing details of the licensed territory and duration. The grantor retains full ownership of the registered trade mark, and any sublicensees must adhere to the terms stipulated by the primary license agreement. Assignment of a registered trade mark or a right to uses trade mark under a license requires prior written consent from the Trade Marks Registry. Further, where a registered trade mark is assigned, all existing licenses relating thereto shall automatically pass to the assignee unless expressly excluded in the assignment deed. The Registrar may require security deposits for certain licenses deemed commercially sensitive.

For the purposes of this Act, the term “Trade Mark Registrar” means the officer appointed by the Central Government and includes any person acting temporarily in his place or deputed by him; the Trade Mark Registrar shall exercise such powers and discharge such duties as may be delegated to him under this Act. The Trade Mark Registrar is responsible for receiving applications for registration of trade marks, examining them according to prescribed procedures, and making decisions on their acceptance or rejection. Any appeal from a decision of the Trade Mark Registrar shall lie before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, subject to any conditions provided herein.

An applicant for registration of a trade mark shall furnish such particulars relating to the goods or services in respect of which he seeks to register the trade mark as may be required by the Registrar. For the purposes of this Act, an “applicant” includes any person or body corporate claiming through variation or transmission of interest. The registrar may require the applicant to submit further information if deemed necessary for assessing distinctiveness. An application shall not be considered complete until all prescribed fees have been remitted and all required documentation is submitted by the applicant registration process. Any alteration to an application must be notified to the Registrar as provided herein.

An applicant for registration of a trade mark shall be entitled to relief in proceedings under this Act where it is established that any person has made use of a trade mark identical or confusingly similar to the registered trade mark without due cause. Such relief may include an injunction restraining the infringing party from further use of the impugned trade mark, and damages commensurate with the loss suffered by the applicant as a direct result of the infringement. Provided that where the infringing activity was undertaken unknowingly and ceases promptly upon notification of the registration, the Court may consider mitigating factors in determining the appropriate level of damages. The Registrar shall have power to order the destruction of any goods bearing the infringing trade mark, subject to due process and an opportunity for the infringer to be heard. Any appeal from an order made under this Act regarding applicant registration lies to the High Court.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark shall submit Form TM-A, duly completed and supported by all requisite documentation as specified in the First Schedule, demonstrating distinctiveness and non-infringement under this Act. The Registrar may require further evidence substantiating the claim to inherent or acquired distinctiveness, including but not limited to market survey data and declarations from relevant stakeholders. An applicant shall be deemed to have knowledge of any prior conflicting marks existing on the trade mark registry. Provided that an application for registration is refused solely due to a finding of deceptively similarity, the applicant may appeal under provisions as provided herein. The Registrar’s decision regarding acceptance or rejection of the applicant registration shall be final, subject to judicial review.

An applicant for registration of a trade mark shall furnish such documentary evidence as the Registrar deems necessary to substantiate the claim of use of the mark in relation to the goods or services specified in the application. Failure to provide satisfactory documentation within the time prescribed may result in rejection of the application under this Act. Any person aggrieved by a decision relating to an applicant registration, including decisions concerning acceptance or refusal based on non-use, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such decision. The Registrar shall impose a penalty for any false representation made by an applicant in connection with their application, as provided herein.

Where any person, being aggrieved by an order made under this Act relating to the rectification of the Register, or by any other action taken by the Registrar affecting his rights as a registered proprietor trade, alleges that such order or action is without due cause and in contravention of the provisions herein, he may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The Appellate Board shall consider the alleged offence reason presented and may, after affording the parties an opportunity for being heard, confirm, vary, or reverse the order appealed from. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Appellate Board may further appeal to the Supreme Court within sixty days from the date of such order.
