Repeated contraventions may result in revocation of licenses and prohibition from engaging in plant breeding activities under this Act.

Any person holding an extant license granted prior to the effective date of these amendments under this Act relating to the commercial use of a distinct denomination variety shall continue to be entitled to exercise those rights subject to the terms and conditions stipulated in the original licensing agreement. Such licenses may be assigned by the licensee, provided that any proposed assignee possesses demonstrable expertise in agricultural practices relevant to the registered variety’s cultivation. The Assignor shall provide written notification to the Authority of any such assignment, including details of both the assignor and assignee, along with a copy of the amended license terms. Further, sub-licensing of a distinct denomination variety is permitted only with prior consent from the original holder, recorded as per procedures outlined herein. Any breach of these provisions shall render the license liable for revocation.

Where an objection is raised by any person claiming proprietary interest in a plant variety concerning the distinctness of its proposed denomination, the Appellate Board may entertain such objection if it demonstrates reasonable grounds for believing that the proposed denomination falsely suggests or comprises a connection with another registered variety or infringes upon existing trademark rights. The Authority shall provide the applicant and the objector an opportunity to present evidence and arguments pertaining to the alleged lack of distinctness in the proposed *distinct denomination variety*. Decisions regarding the suitability of a denomination are final, subject to appeal under this Act within sixty days from the date of notification; failure to demonstrate genuine novelty during such appeal will result in automatic rejection.

For the purposes of this Act, a distinct denomination variety shall mean a plant variety that exhibits stable heritable characteristics differentiating it from other known varieties and for which a unique designation is applied under the prescribed procedures. The Authority may refuse registration if the proposed distinct denomination variety’s name bears similarity to an existing trademark or trade name registered in India, or any foreign country, impacting its commercial viability; provided that such refusal shall be subject to appeal before the Appellate Board. Further, the application of this provision shall not preclude consideration of the effect India patent laws may have on plant breeding innovation.

An application for registration of a plant variety shall include a detailed description of the distinct denomination variety, encompassing its botanical characteristics and expression as observed across multiple generations and environments. The applicant must provide evidence demonstrating that the proposed denomination is unique and does not resemble any existing denominations already registered under this Act or pending consideration. Further, an application patent shall be submitted alongside the registration request, detailing the method by which the distinctiveness of the variety was initially established. Subject to verification by the Authority, a provisional acceptance may be granted; however, final registration will only occur upon successful completion of the DUS testing protocol as provided herein and confirmation that the denomination meets all stipulated requirements.

Any person aggrieved by an order granting protection for a distinct denomination variety may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appellate Board shall hear appeals arising under this Act and may allow or dismiss the appeal, reverse the order appealed against, or substitute its own order in lieu thereof. Where infringement of farmers’ rights relating to a protected distinct denomination variety occurs through unauthorized use or reproduction, the aggrieved farmer shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief and damages as provided herein. Further, any registered layout design incorporating elements derived from an unregistered distinct denomination variety shall be deemed infringing if it creates confusion amongst breeders regarding the source of the plant material. The remedies available under this Act are without prejudice to any other remedy available to the aggrieved party in civil law.

An applicant for registration of a plant variety shall propose an *assignment denomination* that accurately reflects the characteristics of the variety and does not comprise descriptive terms relating to such characteristics. The proposed denomination must be unique within the Register and may not contain any trademark or geographical indication without prior authorization from the relevant authority. Further, the assignment denomination shall not include words which are offensive or contrary to public order as determined by the Authority. Any subsequent transfer of rights in a registered variety shall not affect the validity of the existing *assignment denomination* unless expressly agreed upon in writing between the assignor and assignee.

An applicant seeking registration of a plant variety shall propose an initial denomination for consideration by the Plant Variety Protection Appellate Tribunal. This denomination must be descriptive of the variety’s characteristics and not contrary to morality or public order, as determined under this Act. The Authority may reject a proposed denomination if it is identical or confusingly similar to an existing registered denomination or one already applied for concerning another plant variety. Upon successful registration, the assignment denomination becomes legally protected property, transferable subject to conditions prescribed by regulations. Any subsequent transfer of rights in the plant variety shall not affect the validity of the assigned denomination unless expressly agreed upon in writing between all relevant parties and notified to the Authority.

Any person claiming rights in a plant variety shall, upon application for registration, propose an *assignment denomination* that complies with all requirements as provided herein. The proposed denomination must not include any statement of fact or description of the variety's characteristics; nor may it contain any word or phrase which is likely to give rise to confusion with existing registered varieties or common names. Subject to approval by the Authority, a denomination once assigned shall remain associated with that plant variety for its duration of protection. Further, if an applicant seeks to assign a denomination identical or nearly identical to one already in use for another plant variety, they must demonstrate to the satisfaction of the Authority that such assignment does not constitute unfair competition under this Act and will not mislead farmers.

Any person applying for registration of a plant variety shall propose an initial denomination that is distinct and readily recognizable, and such denomination shall not include descriptive terms relating to the variety’s characteristics or those of its seed. The Authority may reject a proposed denomination if it finds that it conflicts with existing denominations registered under this Act or any other law, or if it is likely to cause confusion amongst farmers. Failure to comply with these provisions regarding assignment denomination will render the registration application liable for rejection and subsequent penalties as provided herein. Furthermore, unauthorized use of a protected denomination by any third party shall constitute an infringement subject to civil remedies and criminal prosecution under this Act.

Subject to the requirements of novelty and distinctiveness as provided herein, an applicant seeking registration of a plant variety may grant licenses relating to the commercial use of the assigned denomination. Such licenses shall be documented in writing and specify the geographical territory, duration, and permitted activities concerning the denomination’s application. The assignor retains ownership of the assignment denomination unless explicitly transferred through a further written agreement registered with the Authority. Any sub-licensing undertaken by a licensee shall require prior consent from the original assignor, such consent not to be unreasonably withheld. Further, where an assignment denomination is found to infringe upon existing trademarks or geographical indications under other Acts, the Authority may direct its modification or revocation. The terms of any license agreement relating to an assignment denomination are governed by contract law principles and shall remain confidential unless otherwise ordered by a competent court.

An application for registration may be rejected if the proposed denomination is deemed deceptively similar to an existing denomination already in use for another plant variety, subject to the proviso that the Registrar shall provide the applicant with written reasons for such rejection and afford them a reasonable opportunity to submit representations against the finding. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Registrar rejecting an application on grounds of denominational similarity may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order, provided that the appeal shall be accompanied by a fee as prescribed. The burden of proving distinctiveness and freedom from deceptive similarity in respect of an assignment denomination shall lie upon the applicant.

An application for registration of a plant variety shall include particulars relating to the proposed *assignment denomination*, including its transliteration where not in Devanagari script. The applicant shall provide justification for the selection of the denomination and demonstrate that it does not constitute deceptive or misleading information regarding the variety’s characteristics, geographical origin, or any other relevant attribute as determined by the Authority. Where an applicant utilizes a design agent person to prepare drawings or representations associated with the application, such individual's involvement must be disclosed in writing. The Authority may require further documentation substantiating the uniqueness of the proposed denomination and its compliance with existing regulations concerning trademarks and geographical indications. Any challenge to a granted assignment denomination shall be filed within ninety days from the date of publication of the registration notification under this Act.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, any person holding an assignment denomination for a registered plant variety may grant a license conferring specific rights relating to the commercialization, propagation, or distribution of such variety. Such licenses shall be documented in writing and specify the territory within which the licensee’s rights are exercisable, as well as the duration of the license agreement. The assignor retains ownership of the assignment denomination unless explicitly transferred through a further written assignment executed prior to the date filing specification for any subsequent application relating to derived varieties. Any sub-licensing shall require the prior written consent of the original assignor, and such consent may be withheld or granted subject to conditions deemed appropriate by the Authority. Failure to adhere to these stipulations renders the license voidable at the discretion of the assignor.

An application for registration of a trade mark, if found to contain matter which is likely to deceive or cause confusion as to the origin or character of goods or services relating to another registered trade mark, shall be rejected by the Registrar. The applicant may appeal against such rejection under this Act within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. Where any person, having been notified of a pending application for registration and intending to use a sign identical or confusingly similar to the proposed trade mark, institutes proceedings to impugn the application, they shall be subject to penalties as provided herein. Any such person found guilty of wilfully obstructing the registration process may also face a punishable imprisonment term extending up to one year and a fine which may extend to fifty thousand rupees.

Where any proprietor of a registered trade mark institutes proceedings under this Act against any person for alleged infringement, and fails to establish such infringement notwithstanding evidence presented demonstrating a confusing similarity between the impugned layout design consisting of distinctive graphical elements and representations used in connection with goods or services identical or closely related to those for which the trade mark is registered, the proprietor shall be liable to pay costs incurred by the defendant. Further, any person convicted under this Act for knowingly making false statements relating to infringement proceedings may be subject to a punishable imprisonment term of up to one year and a fine not exceeding seventy-five thousand rupees; provided that an appeal against such conviction lies to the High Court within ninety days from the date of judgment.

For the purpose of this Act, "design" shall mean any wholly original artistic creation relating to the shape, configuration, pattern or composition of lines or colours applied to any article whether two-dimensional or three-dimensional, and capable of being reproduced in any material other than by an industrial process. A design shall not include a trade mark under this Act or a property mark as defined therein. The term "industrial application" with respect to a registered design signifies its use or exploitation for the manufacture of articles, subject to conditions prescribed herein regarding novelty and originality; provided that such application does not infringe upon any prior copyright existing in relation to the underlying artistic work.

The Registrar shall register designs relating to articles of manufacture, including integrated circuits, where such designs are original and not merely aesthetic. An application for registration may include multiple design variations pertaining to a single article, provided that each variation demonstrates a distinct visual feature. Designs shall be deemed registered upon the issuance of a certificate by the Registrar, subject to objections filed under this Act. The term "industrial application" in relation to a design signifies its use or incorporation into a commercially produced item for sale or distribution. Any person claiming ownership of a design may apply for registration, including legal representatives and assignees. Designs used solely for artistic expression without practical utility are excluded from protection as provided herein.

Where an artistic work is applied industrially, the owner shall retain exclusive rights regarding reproduction, adaptation, and public display for the duration specified under this Act. This right extends to any process involving the use of such work as a master or model in creating goods intended for sale or hire, subject to limitations concerning fair dealing for research or private study. Any person infringing upon these rights may be liable for damages equivalent to the reasonable royalties that would have been paid had proper license been obtained. Further, the owner shall be entitled to seek an injunction restraining further acts of infringement and recovering costs incurred in pursuing legal remedies. Provided that this protection does not extend to works already within the public domain or where the industrial application is solely functional and lacks artistic merit as determined by a competent court.

Where an artistic work is incorporated into an article as its functional element, and such incorporation constitutes industrial application, the rights of the author of the artistic work shall not extend to prevent exploitation of that functional aspect. The Registrar may, upon receipt of a written representation from any person claiming right or interest in respect of such industrial application, initiate inquiries to determine whether the use falls within the exception provided herein. Such inquiries shall be conducted according to procedures prescribed by regulations framed under this Act. Any party aggrieved by the decision of the Registrar may appeal to the relevant High Court. The author of the artistic work shall be entitled to claim reasonable compensation for the industrial application, as determined by the High Court, subject to demonstrating substantial dependence of the article’s utility on the incorporated work.

Where an artistic work is incorporated into a product for the purposes of industrial application, and such incorporation constitutes an essential feature contributing to the commercial utility or aesthetic appeal of that product, copyright therein shall subsist only in respect of elements demonstrably separable from the functional aspects. This provision applies where the design of the product relies significantly on the artistic work’s visual representation. Provided that, if the industrial application involves a process directly and substantially derived from an underlying technological innovation, the rights accruing under this Act shall be subordinate to any patent protection lawfully obtained for said innovation. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint, investigate whether such incorporation unduly restricts competition or constitutes unfair trade practice, subject to due process as provided herein.

Any person who, without due authorization from the copyright owner, makes, distributes, imports into India, or offers for sale any article embodying an infringing copy of a work protected under this Act, and such article is demonstrably employed for industrial application, shall be guilty of an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and with a fine which may extend to ten lakhs rupees. The right holder may, subject to the provisions herein, seek injunctive relief against any party engaged in such infringing activity. Further, where the infringement involves commercial reproduction intended for profit, enhanced penalties as determined by the relevant judicial authority shall apply. Damages recoverable shall be assessed based on demonstrable loss suffered by the copyright owner.

Any person holding copyright in designs incorporated into an article for industrial application shall be deemed, subject to this Act and any rules made thereunder, to possess exclusive rights regarding the commercial exploitation of such incorporation. Such rights extend to granting licenses permitting reproduction, adaptation, and distribution of the copyrighted design element within the manufactured article. A license granted under this provision may specify a duration, geographical scope, and permitted field of use, as agreed upon by the copyright holder and licensee. Assignment of these rights is permissible through written instrument, duly executed and registered with the designated authority. Provided that any assignment shall not prejudice existing licenses unless expressly consented to by the affected licensees. Further, the right to grant licenses or assignments relating to industrial application does not extend to functionalities inherent in the article itself, but solely to the design aspects protected under copyright.

Where an artistic work is incorporated into an article for its industrial application, and such incorporation constitutes a substantial alteration of the original work’s character, rendering it primarily functional within the manufactured article, any subsequent claim asserting copyright infringement shall be subject to review by the relevant High Court. The aggrieved party may petition the High Court demonstrating that the claimed derivative work lacks sufficient originality beyond the technical requirements for its intended use and that the industrial application diminishes or obscures the artistic merit of the original creation. Provided that a finding of substantial alteration requires expert testimony establishing the functional necessity of the modification, and further provided that such testimony must convincingly demonstrate absence of reasonable alternative design solutions.

Where an artistic work is incorporated into an article for its industrial application, and such incorporation constitutes a substantial part of the aesthetic appeal of the finished product, the right of copyright therein shall extend to prevent reproduction of that article solely for the purpose of extracting and utilizing the embedded artistic element. This protection shall not apply where the industrial application serves a purely functional purpose and does not primarily rely on the originality of the artistic work. Furthermore, registration of a services trade mark depicting an image substantially similar to the incorporated artistic work shall not, by itself, negate copyright protection under this Act; provided that such trademark registration was obtained in good faith and without knowledge of the underlying copyright. Any infringement shall be subject to remedies as provided herein.

Where an invention incorporates elements derived from a copyrighted work, and such incorporation constitutes industrial application, the copyright holder shall be entitled to claim equitable relief against any party exploiting said invention commercially. This right is subject to the condition that the inventive step in the process or product demonstrably transcends the originality of the underlying copyrighted material. Any dispute concerning whether an element’s use represents permissible adaptation or actionable infringement may be referred to a civil court registry for preliminary assessment, and the decision of such registry shall be appealable before the High Court. Provided that this provision does not preclude claims arising from direct copyright violation under this Act, irrespective of any subsequent industrial application.

For the purposes of determining entitlement to equitable remedies relating to acts of plagiarism or unauthorized adaptation of literary works, the term "court having jurisdiction" shall mean a High Court exercising original civil jurisdiction where the cause of action arose wholly or in part, or a District Court within the local limits of whose territorial jurisdiction the defendant resides or carries on business. Subject to any reciprocal arrangements between States as provided herein, no suit for damages may be entertained by a court lacking such jurisdiction. The determination of whether a particular court possesses jurisdiction shall be governed by principles of ordinary civil procedure and precedence established under this Act.

Applications for registration of literary works, musical works, dramatic works, cinematograph films and sound recordings may be filed electronically through the designated online portal as provided herein. Where an applicant seeks rectification of a register entry concerning copyright ownership, such application shall be made to the High Court having jurisdiction over the place where the registered work was first published or where the cause of action arose. The Registrar shall forward copies of all applications and documents relating thereto to the relevant High Court upon request. Any appeal against an order passed by the Registrar under this Act may be preferred before a High Court, subject to such conditions as are prescribed. Proceedings related to disputes concerning registration shall be governed by the principles of natural justice.

Where an aggrieved party alleges a violation of copyright under this Act, they may institute legal proceedings to seek redress for damages sustained and injunctive relief against further infringement. The determination of entitlement to such remedies is subject to demonstrating reasonable efforts undertaken to mitigate actual losses attributable directly to the infringing activity. Provided that the claimant demonstrates standing as a registered proprietor or rightful beneficiary of the copyrighted work, the suit shall be brought before a court having jurisdiction over the place where the alleged infringement occurred, or where the cause of action arose. Further, any such court may award compensatory damages not exceeding an amount determined by reference to the license fee which would have been payable had the defendant lawfully obtained permission to use the work.

Where an action is brought before a civil court alleging violation of rights vested under this Act concerning literary, dramatic, musical or artistic works, or any other right as provided herein, the plaintiff shall satisfy the court that reasonable efforts have been made to resolve the dispute through mediation as prescribed by the rules framed under this Act. The determination of jurisdiction in such proceedings shall be governed solely by the geographical location of the defendant’s principal place of business at the time the cause of action arose. Subject to any order passed by a High Court, appeals from decrees or orders made by district courts shall lie only to the High Court within whose territorial jurisdiction the suit was originally filed. The court having jurisdiction may, in its discretion, require security for costs before admitting an appeal under this provision.

Where an action is brought under this Act concerning alleged copyright infringement relating to a cinematograph film, the suit shall be deemed to accrue where the defendant resides or carries on business, or where the cause of action arose. Provided that, if the plaintiff is a non-resident and the defendant has placed the work online for access or download within India, the suit may also be instituted in any High Court having jurisdiction over any place within India where such infringing act occurred. Further, subject to compliance with prescribed rules regarding service of summons, a court having jurisdiction shall not be deemed to lack such jurisdiction solely by reason of the defendant’s server being located outside Indian territory if the infringement demonstrably originates from within India.

Any person found to have reproduced, distributed, exhibited, or performed any work in violation of the provisions of this Act shall be liable for damages, calculated at the option of the copyright owner as either actual loss sustained or a sum not less than fifty thousand rupees but not exceeding two hundred thousand rupees. Further, where such infringement is committed by an employee acting within the scope of his employment, the employer shall also be held vicariously liable unless it proves that it exercised due diligence to prevent the infringing act. Suits for recovery of damages and injunctions relating to copyright infringement shall be entertained only by a court having jurisdiction over the place where the infringement occurred or where the cause of action arose. The aggrieved party may apply to such court for interim relief pending determination of the suit.

Where an assignment of copyright in a musical work or dramatic performance is made subject to a condition restricting its exploitation within India, such restriction shall be deemed part of the assignment and enforceable as if incorporated therein. Any subsequent license granted by the assignee relating to the assigned rights shall respect this pre-existing limitation unless expressly agreed otherwise in writing with the assignor. Provided that, where an exclusive license is granted permitting reproduction of a work, the court having jurisdiction may, upon application by the copyright holder or any other person claiming through them, determine whether the terms of the license are unduly restrictive and contrary to public interest. The assignee shall be deemed to have knowledge of all conditions attached to the assignment at the time of acceptance; failing which, the assignor may seek redress under this Act.

Any action brought before a judicial forum alleging violation of exclusive rights granted under this Act concerning literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic works, or any adaptation thereof, shall be subject to the provisions regarding territorial limits. It is provided that where the place of origin of the alleged infringement is uncertain, or spans multiple jurisdictions, the aggrieved party may initiate proceedings in a court having jurisdiction over any location where the infringing act occurred or was reasonably likely to have taken effect. The defendant shall not be precluded from challenging this assertion of jurisdiction by demonstrating, on clear and convincing evidence, that such forum selection is manifestly inconvenient and lacks substantial connection to the cause of action, subject to judicial discretion. Appeals against orders concerning jurisdiction may be made as provided herein.

Where an action arises alleging copyright infringement relating to a musical work, subject to compliance with sub-section (2), such action may only be brought before a District Court situated within the local limits of either the place where the alleged infringing act occurred, or the place where the cause of action arose. Provided that, if the defendant has placed on record a form filed patent claiming priority over elements incorporated into the allegedly infringed musical work, the plaintiff shall demonstrate to the satisfaction of the court having jurisdiction that the patented invention does not encompass the entirety of the copyrighted material. Further, service of notice of the suit must be effected upon the defendant within thirty days from the date of institution and failure to do so will render the action void ab initio.

Any action for damages arising from the unauthorized reproduction or distribution of works protected under this Act shall be brought before a civil court having jurisdiction over the place where the infringement occurred, or where the cause of action arose. The plaintiff must provide evidence demonstrating reasonable belief that the defendant has engaged in acts contrary to the provisions herein relating to copyright ownership. Failure to do so may result in dismissal of the suit with costs. Where marks registered accordance with the Trade Marks Act, 1999 are demonstrably utilized to create confusion regarding the origin or authenticity of copyrighted works, such actions shall be considered aggravated infringements subject to enhanced penalties as provided herein. The court shall have power to issue injunctions and award compensatory damages reflecting the commercial harm suffered by the copyright owner.

Where an action is brought before a judicial forum alleging violation of exclusive rights pertaining to a registered design, it shall be incumbent upon the claimant to demonstrate prima facie evidence of such infringement. The determination of whether a particular court has jurisdiction under this Act shall be subject to challenge by either party through appropriate legal mechanisms. Provided that, in instances where multiple courts may ostensibly possess concurrent jurisdiction, the defendant may elect the forum of their choice, notwithstanding any prior proceedings initiated elsewhere. Furthermore, it is clarified that a patentee includes exclusive licensees and assignees who assert these rights; consequently, such parties are empowered to initiate suits concerning design infringement before a court having jurisdiction.

Registration of a layout-design shall confer upon the registrant exclusive rights within India pertaining to the manufacture, reproduction, adaptation and sale of integrated circuits corresponding to that design. For the purposes of this Act, “adaptation” includes the modification or alteration of a registered layout-design in such a manner as to produce an equivalent layout-design. An application for registration may be made by the creator of the layout-design or any person authorized by him; however, where multiple persons jointly create a layout-design, they shall be deemed joint applicants under this Act. The register sub section pertaining to rectification of entries is governed by principles of natural justice and procedural fairness.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall contain particulars as prescribed and accompanied by the requisite fee. Upon receiving an application, the Registrar may direct the applicant to rectify any defects or ambiguities therein; failure to comply with such direction within the stipulated period shall render the application liable to rejection. Where a layout-design is found to be substantially similar to an earlier registered design, the application shall be rejected and the applicant notified of the reasons for rejection. Any person aggrieved by an order rejecting an application may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board under this Act. The register sub section provides that rectification of entries in the register may be applied for by any interested party demonstrating a material error or omission.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout design shall be accompanied by such particulars and documents as the Registrar may require, including certified copies of any relevant prior publications or disclosures. The applicant shall furnish an execution specifying the layout design claimed to be registered and identifying its salient features. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall issue an acknowledgment containing a date of filing. Subsequently, the Registrar may serve notice on the applicant requiring further particulars within a prescribed period; failure to comply will result in rejection of the application. The register sub section pertaining to rectification proceedings allows for applications to be made by any person aggrieved by an entry or omission in the Register. Such applications must specify the nature of the grievance and provide supporting evidence as provided herein.

An application for registration of a layout-design shall accompany an affidavit verifying the originality of the design and confirming that no prior publication or unauthorized disclosure thereof has occurred, subject to exceptions as provided herein regarding exhibition at officially recognized trade fairs. The Registrar may require such further information as is necessary to ascertain compliance with these requirements under this Act. Upon receipt of the application and after satisfying himself concerning its completeness and adherence to prescribed formalities, the Registrar shall publish a notification in the Official Gazette indicating the acceptance of the layout-design for registration. Any person aggrieved by such publication may, within sixty days, file an objection with the Registrar; the register sub section process will then proceed according to established protocols.

The owner of a registered integrated circuit layout-design shall be entitled to grant licenses conferring rights to utilize the design, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated therein. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and may relate to any aspect of the design’s reproduction, adaptation, or commercial exploitation as provided herein. Assignment of ownership interests in a registered layout-design, including all associated license agreements, requires registration with the Controller General of Patents, Designs, and Trademarks. The register sub section pertaining to assignments shall record details of both assignor and assignee, alongside the effective date of transfer. Any subsequent modification or revocation of such licenses must also be formally documented within the register, ensuring transparency for third parties. Failure to adhere to these registration requirements may render any contractual agreement unenforceable under this Act.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be deemed invalid if it incorporates an identical reproduction of a certification trade mark lawfully used in connection with goods or services, subject to demonstrating reasonable use and lack of consumer confusion. The Registrar may entertain objections to such applications from aggrieved parties claiming prior rights under this Act or any other law for the time being in force; however, the applicant shall be afforded a full opportunity to rebut these claims through written submissions and a hearing before the Registrar. Any decision made by the Registrar concerning the validity of a registration, particularly relating to the register sub section pertaining to trade mark conflicts, is subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such decision.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design may be made in the prescribed form and shall include particulars relating to the applicant, the nature of the layout-design, and its intended use. The Registering Officer shall examine such an application and if satisfied that the layout-design is original and not infringing any existing right, including rights arising from a patent invention, he may proceed with registration. Upon acceptance, the layout-design shall be entered in the register as provided herein, specifying the date of entry and the name of the applicant. Any person aggrieved by a refusal to register or by an erroneous entry in the register sub section (2) may appeal to the Appellate Board within a period of sixty days from the date of communication of such decision.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, a trade mark shall be deemed accepted for registration upon publication thereof in the Official Gazette. Acceptance is conditional; specifically, such acceptance remains provisional until the expiry of three months from the date of such publication. During this period, any person may, under this Act, file a notice of opposition to the proposed registration. The Registrar shall consider all oppositions filed within that timeframe and determine their validity according to established procedures as provided herein. Failure to adhere to gazette subject conditions renders the acceptance liable for revocation.

The Registrar shall, prior to publication in the Official Gazette under this Act, furnish a copy of every proposed acceptance of a trademark application to the Advocate-General of India for his opinion. Such opinion, if received within thirty days from the date of furnishing, may contain objections to the registration of the mark. The Registrar shall consider any such objection and provide the applicant with an opportunity to respond in writing within fifteen days thereafter. Following consideration of the response, the Registrar may proceed with publication or decline acceptance. Publication in the Official Gazette is subject to conditions regarding clarity of description and representation of the trademark. Any person aggrieved by a decision declining acceptance may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board as provided herein. The gazette subject conditions shall be deemed fulfilled upon completion of these procedural requirements.

The Registrar shall, prior to publication in the Official Gazette under this Act, verify that an application for registration of a trade mark satisfies all requirements as provided herein. Such verification shall include confirmation that the proposed mark does not conflict with any existing registered trade marks or pending applications, and that the applicant possesses the requisite legal standing to claim ownership. The Registrar may require submission of further documentation substantiating these claims before proceeding. Publication in the Official Gazette is conditional upon adherence to prescribed formatting standards for clarity and accessibility. Any deviation from such standards shall render the publication invalid, necessitating re-submission and subsequent gazette subject conditions review by the Registrar.

Where a trade mark is accepted for publication in the Official Gazette under this Act, the Registrar shall publish particulars of the application as provided herein. Any person considering himself aggrieved by such acceptance may, within sixty days from the date of such publication in the gazette subject conditions, file notice of opposition with the Registrar. Failure to comply with the prescribed form and fee for such opposition shall render it inadmissible. The Registrar shall afford due opportunity to both the applicant and the opponent to be heard, and may direct the production of evidence. Any wilful or negligent failure to appear at a hearing may result in penalties as determined by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal, a trade mark shall not be advertised in the Official Gazette under this Act if the application relates to goods or services that are deceptively similar to those for which an identical or confusingly similar trade mark is already registered. The Registrar may, notwithstanding any representation made by the applicant, refuse publication if he considers there exists a reasonable likelihood of confusion arising amongst consumers due to such advertisement. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar refusing gazette subject conditions may appeal within sixty days from the date of receipt of that decision; and the Appellate Tribunal shall consider all relevant factors including prior use evidence presented by third parties.

Where a trade mark is accepted for publication in the Official Gazette under this Act, the Registrar shall publish particulars of such acceptance as provided herein. Any person having grounds to believe that the acceptance is erroneous or contrary to law may, within sixty days from the date of such publication in the gazette subject conditions, file notice of opposition with the Registrar. Such opposition must specify the grounds upon which it is based and provide supporting evidence. The Registrar shall promptly record the opposition in the inspection register for public access. Failure to comply with these procedural requirements will render the opposition void. Further, any party aggrieved by a decision regarding an opposed trade mark may appeal to the relevant intellectual property tribunal as provided under this Act, subject to prescribed timelines and fees.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, where an application for registration of a trade mark is refused under section 29, the Registrar shall direct the applicant to file within three months from the date of the direction, such further particulars or amendments as may be required. Such direction shall be published in the Official Gazette and deemed to satisfy the conditions of gazette subject conditions prescribed herein. The publication shall include a concise statement of the grounds for refusal and an indication of the period within which compliance is expected. Failure to comply with the Registrar’s direction within the stipulated time shall render the application liable to rejection. Where the trade mark relates to an invention disclosed in a patent application filed under the Patent Cooperation Treaty, the Registrar may request relevant information from the Controller-General of Patents, Trade Marks and Designs for verification purposes.

An application patent shall relate only to one invention or a group of inventions relating to the same or similar kind and having their subject matter linked functionally by being conceived as a whole. The specification of an application patent must disclose the invention and enable any person skilled in the art to put it into practice, provided that such disclosure does not compromise trade secrets essential for implementation. Further, where the invention is or includes a process for producing a substance, the specification shall, or where applicable may, describe an example embodying the process as applied to the production of the substance.

An application patent shall relate only to one invention or a group of inventions relating to the same or similar kind and use thereof. The applicant for such registration shall furnish a declaration as to the true inventor or inventors, subject to any rights they may have assigned or otherwise transferred. Where an application incorporates by reference matter which has previously been made available to the public either orally, in writing, by use or in any other form, the applicant shall provide evidence demonstrating that the invention was novel and non-obvious as on the date of filing. The Controller may require further particulars regarding the claimed invention if deemed necessary for assessment under this Act. Provided that, an application filed jointly by two or more applicants shall be treated as a single application.

Where any person considers that another person has contravened any provision of this Act or rules made thereunder, he may present a complaint to the Controller alleging such contravention and seeking appropriate remedies. The Controller shall afford the accused an opportunity of being heard and shall record his findings on all material placed before him. Subject to appeal under this Act, the Controller may order that the person found to have contravened any provision be restrained from continuing such infringement, and may direct them to pay compensation to the complainant for losses suffered as a consequence of the infringement. An application patent shall confer upon the applicant the exclusive right to make, use or sell the invention in India, subject to the provisions regarding compulsory licenses as provided herein. Any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board.

An application patent shall relate only to one invention or a group of inventions relating to the same or similar kind and having a single inventive concept; provided that the inventions are linked functionally dependent on each other. The applicant for such an application patent shall furnish, along with the application, a declaration as to priority, if claiming right of priority under this Act. Any person may file a request for pre-grant opposition against any application patent within a period of six months from the date of publication of the application or before the grant of the patent, whichever is earlier. The Controller shall consider such requests and provide an opportunity for the applicant to be heard. Subject to the provisions herein, the procedure for examination of the application patent shall follow that prescribed under this Act.

An application patent shall relate only to one invention or a group of inventions linked by a single inventive concept; provided that the claims are clear and concise. The applicant shall disclose the best method known to them for carrying out the invention, unless such disclosure would involve the use of confidential information as defined under this Act. Further, an application may be amended only once during the pendency of the proceedings before the patent office, subject to the condition that the amendment does not substantially alter the scope of protection sought. Any request for re-examination shall be accompanied by a statement specifying the grounds on which the invention is considered invalid, as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Controller relating to the grant or refusal of an application patent shall have the right to appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. Failure to comply with prescribed timelines for filing appeals will render them inadmissible, subject to any relaxation granted by the Board due to sufficient cause demonstrated. The Board may, upon hearing all parties involved and considering relevant evidence, affirm, reverse or modify the Controller's decision. Any party dissatisfied with a final order of the Appellate Board may further seek redressal under the provisions relating to writ petitions in the High Court. Penalties for non-compliance with directions issued by the Appellate Board shall be determined as provided herein.

Where an application patent shall relate to an invention already claimed in a previously filed application, the controller may grant such patent subject to the condition that the applicant provides written consent from the holder of the earlier application allowing for the subsequent claim. Such consent must explicitly detail the scope of permitted use and commercialization relating to the licensed technology. Further, any assignment or license granted under this Act shall be recorded in the prescribed manner with the Controller, and such recording shall create a public record accessible to all interested parties. The applicant may also offer a cross-license agreement as part of fulfilling requirements for novelty assessment. Failure to provide accurate details regarding licensing arrangements during examination will render the patent liable for revocation proceedings under this Act.

An application patent shall be refused if the invention is not novel, unless it is established that the prior teaching did not involve working or use of the invention in India. The burden of proving such working or use shall lie upon the applicant. Where a determination under this Act finds an invention to lack novelty due to prior publication by the applicant, the Controller may allow the application patent if satisfied that the publication was made honestly and without intention to deceive. Any party aggrieved by such a determination may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days of the order’s communication, subject to payment of the prescribed fee. The Board's decision shall be final, provided that it does not contravene any provision as provided herein.

An application patent shall relate only to one invention or a group of inventions linked by a single inventive concept; provided that the claims relating to such group are clear and concise. Where an applicant seeks protection for multiple inventions not so linked, separate applications must be filed accordingly. The term "invention" as used herein encompasses any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof. Further, an application patent may incorporate subject matter disclosed in prior art accessible to the public anywhere in the world; however, such disclosure shall not invalidate the patent unless it demonstrates a lack of novelty or inventive step as provided herein, considering obligations under the Madrid Agreement concerning the international registration of industrial designs.

An application patent shall relate only to one invention or a group of inventions relating to the same subject matter and having their source in the same idea. Where an applicant seeks to register a process for producing a substance by means unknown at the time of filing, the description accompanying such application must disclose the best method known to the applicant at that time for carrying out the invention. Upon satisfactory examination and fulfillment of all requirements under this Act, the Controller may grant patent letters. Each patent letter shall be accompanied by a certificate purporting to be a verification of compliance with prescribed standards relating to novelty and inventive step, signed by an authorized officer.

For the purposes of this Act, a “manner registered proprietor” shall mean the person entered as the registered owner of a trademark under this Act, and where such registration is jointly held, it shall include each joint registered proprietor. The rights conferred upon a manner registered proprietor are subject to any conditions or limitations endorsed on the register relating to the trade mark. An application for rectification concerning a registered trade mark may be made by any person claiming interest, including but not limited to, a party alleging dilution of distinctiveness, provided that such claim is substantiated as provided herein and does not prejudice existing rights under this Act.

Subject to the provisions relating to rectification, a registered trademark shall remain valid for a period of ten years from the date of registration, and such validity may be extended under this Act for further periods not exceeding fifteen years each upon application made by the manner registered proprietor. The Registrar may require evidence of continued use of the trade mark in connection with the goods or services specified in the register before granting any extension of time. Any alteration to the list of goods or services associated with a trademark, following registration, shall be permissible only with the consent of the Registrar and subject to conditions as provided herein ensuring no confusion arises among consumers. The registered proprietor is deemed to possess exclusive rights within India relating to the trade mark for the specified goods or services.

Where a registered trademark is used exclusively for the export of goods, the owner shall, upon filing an application with the Registrar in the prescribed form and furnishing such evidence as the Registrar deems appropriate to demonstrate continued exclusive use for export purposes, be entitled to maintain registration under this Act. The Registrar may require periodic submissions from the manner registered proprietor demonstrating ongoing compliance with these conditions; failure to provide such documentation within the stipulated timeframe shall render the trademark liable for review and potential removal from the register of trademarks. Any party aggrieved by a decision regarding the continued registration of an export-only trademark may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, subject to the provisions herein relating to timelines and procedural requirements for appeals. The Registrar’s determination on whether exclusive use has been maintained is final, barring such appeal.

Subject to the provisions regarding consumer protection, a registered proprietor shall not assign or pledge their rights under this Act unless such assignment or pledge is made in accordance with the prescribed form and duly executed before a notary public. Further, any subsequent registered proprietor acquiring title through such an assignment or pledge shall be deemed to hold the trade mark subject to all existing licences and encumbrances affecting the same at the time of acquisition. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating compliance with these stipulations prior to registering any transfer of ownership. Where a manner registered proprietor seeks to alter the specification of goods or services for which registration is accorded, they must provide an affidavit confirming no deceptive similarity will arise from such alteration.

Any person seeking to institute proceedings under this Act for infringement of a registered trademark shall first serve upon the alleged infringer a notice specifying the nature of the infringement and demanding that such infringement cease. Failure to comply with this requirement shall render the proceeding manifestly frivolous and subject the claimant to costs incurred by the defendant, as determined by the relevant court. Where a *manner registered proprietor* has assigned their rights in a trademark, subsequent proceedings relating to that assignment must be initiated within six months of the date of such assignment; otherwise, the right to enforce against infringers shall vest solely with the assignor. Any wilful and knowing misrepresentation regarding ownership during enforcement actions may attract penalties as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, a manner registered proprietor shall have the right to grant non-exclusive licenses relating to the use of the trademark for which registration is granted. Such license agreements may specify the territory within which the licensee operates and the duration of the permitted usage. Provided that any assignment or sub-license undertaken by the manner registered proprietor must be executed in the prescribed form and shall be subject to approval from the Registrar, who may require evidence demonstrating adequate safeguards for existing licensees. The Registrar’s decision regarding such approvals is final, subject to appeal under this Act. Furthermore, a license granted under these provisions does not confer upon the licensee any right to sue for infringement of the trademark unless expressly authorized in writing by the manner registered proprietor.

Subject to appeal under this Act, a registered proprietor shall not, without leave of the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, institute any suit or other proceeding relating to the remedies available under this Act against any person alleging infringement of the trade mark unless such proprietor has previously given notice specifying the alleged infringement and demanding that it be discontinued. Provided that where the defendant in such suit or proceeding claims right to use the impugned sign under section 47, the registered proprietor shall demonstrate clear evidence of ongoing damage attributable directly to the continued use. The Appellate Board may, upon application by any party aggrieved, direct a stay of proceedings pending determination of the appeal; and the manner registered proprietor is deemed to have consented to such stay.

Subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal, any person employing a design registered layout identical or deceptively similar to a trademark for which another is the manner registered proprietor shall be deemed guilty of an offence. Such offender shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees and may also be subject to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years. Where the infringing use continues after conviction, a further daily penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees shall be imposed until compliance is secured. The Registrar may issue injunctions restraining such use, provided that evidence of consumer confusion or likelihood thereof is presented.

An *order appellate* shall be deemed final subject to a further appeal to the High Court under provisions relating to writ jurisdiction. The Board constituted under this Act may, upon receiving an application from any person aggrieved by an order appellate, direct that the matter be referred for reconsideration if it appears that there is an error apparent on the face of the record. Such direction shall not preclude subsequent appeals as provided herein. Any party dissatisfied with a decision following reference shall have recourse to appeal under this Act within sixty days of notification of the revised order.

Where an application for registration of a geographical indication is opposed by any interested party, the Registrar shall provide notice to the applicant and the opponent, affording them each a reasonable opportunity to present their respective arguments and supporting documentation. The Registrar shall then record his findings on the objections raised, taking into consideration all relevant evidence submitted. Any party aggrieved by an order passed by the Registrar under this Act may prefer an appeal to the *order appellate* authority as provided herein. Such appeals shall be filed within a period of sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The appellant shall deposit such fees as may be prescribed, and the appellate authority’s decision shall be final subject to further appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal.

Where an invention is rejected under this Act based on grounds specified in section 35, the applicant shall have the right to prefer an appeal to an *order appellate* within three months from the date of communication of the refusal. Such appeal may be directed against any decision or direction made by the Controller relating to the grant of a patent, including but not limited to objections raised during examination or opposition proceedings. The Appellate Board shall hear parties de novo and may confirm, vary, or reverse the order appealed from. 

Provided that, if the appellant fails to deposit the prescribed fee within the time specified by the Appellate Board, the appeal shall be deemed abandoned. Further, any party aggrieved by an order of the Appellate Board may prefer further appeals as provided herein, subject to limitations on successive appeals and costs awarded at the discretion of the appellate forum.

An appeal shall lie to the Controller from any order made by him under this Act, provided that no appeal shall be entertained unless a sum equal to twenty-five per centum of the fee specified in Schedule I has been deposited with the Controller. The Controller may, at his discretion, require the appellant to furnish security for costs. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Controller may, within sixty days from the date of such order, file an appeal before the *order appellate* authority constituted under this Act. The authority shall give notice to all parties concerned and afford them a reasonable opportunity of being heard. Decisions of the appellate authority shall be final subject to further appeals as provided herein. The appellant shall satisfy the appellate authority that he has a locus standi to file the appeal, and failure to do so will render the appeal incompetent.

Where an appeal is preferred under this Act against any decision or order made by a Controller, the Appellate Board shall give notice to all parties concerned and opportunity of being heard. The Board may, after affording such parties a reasonable opportunity for presenting their views, confirm, vary, or reverse the decision or order appealed from, subject to compliance with principles of natural justice. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Appellate Board may further appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of communication of the order; provided that the delay in filing such subsequent appeal shall not be a ground for dismissal unless the Appellate Board has certified that the delay is unreasonable and causes prejudice. The Board’s decision on any question of fact or law shall be final, pending review under an *order appellate* procedure.

Any party aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to infringement of patent rights, including but not limited to orders for damages, injunctions, or account of profits, may prefer an appeal to the Controller. Such appeal shall be filed within sixty days from the date of service of the order. The Controller may, after giving notice to all parties concerned and affording them a reasonable opportunity of being heard, affirm, modify, reverse, or set aside the order appealed against. Failure to comply with any order issued by the Controller regarding discovery of documents or attendance of witnesses shall render the defaulting party liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees for each such default. The decision of the *order appellate* authority is final and binding.

Where a patentee desires to grant an exclusive license or assign his patent, or any right therein, relating to a pharmaceutical formulation, he shall provide prior notice to the Controller detailing the proposed terms and conditions of such license or assignment. This requirement is waived only where the license or assignment is granted to a public institution engaged in research and development related to public health. The Controller may, after considering representations from interested parties, issue an order requiring modification of the proposed terms if they are deemed detrimental to promoting innovation or access to essential medicines. Any party aggrieved by such an order may prefer an appeal before the *order appellate* authority constituted under this Act, subject to such fees and timelines as prescribed. The Controller shall maintain a public register of all licenses and assignments granted relating to pharmaceutical patents.

Where any party aggrieved by an order passed under this Act is dissatisfied therewith, he may prefer an appeal to the Controller. Such appeal shall lie only on a question of law and not otherwise, subject to the proviso that where the findings of fact affect a substantial question of law, the appellate authority may examine such findings notwithstanding their nature as findings of fact. The Controller may, after giving notice to all parties concerned and affording them an opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify, or reverse the order appealed from. Any party aggrieved by any order passed by the Controller in exercise of his powers under this Act relating to an *order appellate* may further appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within a period of sixty days from the date of such order.

Where any party aggrieved by an order passed by a Controller under this Act is dissatisfied, that party may prefer an appeal to the *order appellate* board. The Board shall give notice to all parties concerned and opportunity for them to present their cases in writing or orally, subject to just rules of procedure as it deems fit. An appeal lies only on a substantial question of law arising out of the order appealed from; however, the Board may, at its discretion, examine the matters of fact decided by the Controller if necessary for proper disposal of the appeal. The appellate board shall consider any evidence submitted and may direct further inquiry where deemed essential. Any party failing to appear before the *order appellate* board on a date fixed may have their appeal dismissed.

Any party aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to revocation of patent, infringement proceedings, or rectification of the register shall have the right to prefer an appeal to the *Order Appellate* Board. Such appeal must be filed within sixty days from the date of service of notice of the order. The Board may, after giving all parties concerned a reasonable opportunity for being heard, confirm, vary, or reverse the order appealed against. Failure to comply with any direction issued by the Board shall render the appellant liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees and may also attract further action under this Act. A certified copy of the *entry register document* pertaining to the patent in question shall be submitted alongside the appeal.

For the purposes of this Act, “biotechnological process” means a process employing biological systems or organisms, whole or modified microorganisms, cells or cellular components to produce, modify, or control substances or processes; provided that such process does not involve manipulation at the molecular level. The patent office shall, when examining an application for a patent relating to a biotechnological process, consider whether the claimed invention is novel and non-obvious, subject to the provisions regarding exclusions from patentability under this Act. Further, the patent office shall require detailed description of the biological material employed in such processes, sufficient to enable its reproduction by persons skilled in the art.

The Registering Authority, upon receiving an application for registration of a layout design, shall verify that the design fulfills all requirements under this Act and rules made thereunder. Provided that, if the applicant is not resident in India, the application must be accompanied by evidence of representation by an attorney or agent duly authorized to act on behalf of the applicant within India. The patent office shall then proceed with examination of novelty and originality as per prescribed procedures. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registering Authority regarding rejection or acceptance of a layout design may appeal to the Appellate Board. Further, the Registering Authority is empowered to require submission of additional information or clarification from the applicant at any stage during processing.

Where an aggrieved party alleges that a decision of the patent office is manifestly unjust or erroneous, they may institute proceedings before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board seeking redressal. Such proceedings shall be initiated within ninety days from the date of communication of the order to the claimant. The Board shall afford both the applicant and the patent office an opportunity for being heard, and shall consider all relevant evidence presented. If, upon review, the Board finds that the decision of the patent office was indeed flawed, it may direct the patent office to revise its determination or grant such other relief as deemed appropriate under this Act. The patent office shall comply with any order issued by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within a period not exceeding sixty days. Failure to do so will render the officer in default liable for penalties as provided herein.

Where an application for patents is filed, the applicant shall furnish such particulars concerning the priority of the invention as may be prescribed. The patent office shall, upon receipt of the application and after conducting a preliminary examination under this Act, issue a written communication to the applicant indicating any deficiencies or objections observed in relation to compliance with procedural requirements. Such communication shall provide an opportunity for the applicant to respond and rectify the identified issues within the time specified therein. Further, if the patent office deems it necessary to ascertain the prior art relating to the invention, it may request additional information from the applicant. The Controller of Patents shall maintain a register of all applications filed and patents granted, accessible for public inspection subject to any restrictions as provided herein.

Where an application for a patent relates to a method or process applicable to agriculture or horticulture, the patent office shall examine whether such method or process is novel and involves an inventive step in relation to the cultivation of plants, trees or shrubs. Provided that, if the applicant demonstrates compliance with prescribed guidelines regarding bio-safety assessments and environmental impact studies, as determined by the relevant governmental authority, the application may proceed for further consideration. The patent office shall also require disclosure of any genetically modified organisms utilized within the claimed method, along with a detailed explanation of their potential effects on biodiversity. Further, under this Act, an applicant failing to provide such information is deemed to have abandoned the application.

Where an application for patents is found, upon examination, to relate to a substance declared under this Act not to be patentable, the patent office shall issue a notice to the applicant specifying the grounds on which such determination is based and affording him an opportunity of being heard. Failure by the applicant to demonstrate, within the time specified in the notice, that the invention does indeed fall outside the scope of non-patentability as provided herein will result in rejection of the application. Any person aggrieved by a decision under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board; however, such appeals shall be subject to penalties for frivolous or vexatious proceedings, including costs and legal fees awarded against the appellant.

Where the proprietor of a patent has granted a license, whether exclusive or non-exclusive, relating to the patented invention, such license may be assigned by the proprietor subject to the provisions herein. The assignor shall provide written notice to the Controller within thirty days of any assignment affecting the rights conferred under the patent, detailing the assignee’s name and address, and specifying the extent of the assignment. Further, where a patent has been surrendered or revoked, any license granted prior thereto shall remain valid unless expressly terminated by agreement between the licensor and licensee. The patent office shall maintain a record of all assignments and licenses affecting patents, which shall be open to public inspection upon payment of prescribed fees. Any person seeking to enforce rights under an assignment must provide evidence satisfactory to the Controller confirming the validity of said assignment.

Where an application for a patent is rejected by the patent office, the applicant may appeal to the Appellate Board constituted under this Act within sixty days from the date of communication of the order of rejection. The Appellate Board shall hear arguments presented by both the applicant and the Controller, and may require further evidence or clarification as deemed necessary to determine the merits of the case. Subject to provisions regarding frivolous or vexatious appeals, any party aggrieved by an order of the Appellate Board may prefer an appeal from that order to the High Court within a period of ninety days from the date of such order; provided that the High Court shall admit such appeal only if it involves a substantial question of law. The patent office shall be bound by the decision of the High Court on any matter determined in appeal.

Where an application for a patent is finally rejected by the patent office, the applicant may appeal to the Appellate Board constituted under this Act. The patent office shall serve notice of such rejection on the applicant within thirty days of the date of the order and shall specify therein the grounds upon which the rejection is based. Upon receipt of the notice of appeal, the Appellate Board shall afford the patent office an opportunity to file its written submissions in response to the appellant’s case. The trade marks proprietor may be impleaded as a party to such proceedings if their interests are demonstrably affected by the subject matter of the patent application. Provided that the applicant demonstrates sufficient cause, the patent office may extend the time limit for filing its submissions, but only with prior notification to the Appellate Board and the appellant. The decision of the Appellate Board shall be final, subject to further appeal under this Act.

Where an application for a patent is granted, and subsequently challenged under this Act on grounds of prior publication or lack of novelty, the patent office shall conduct a review in accordance with prescribed procedures. Such review will consider all documentary evidence submitted by both the patent holder and the challenger. The Controller may, after affording both parties an opportunity to be heard, determine whether the grant was justified. Provided that, if the Controller finds that the challenged invention infringes upon existing intellectual property rights, including but not limited to design registrations or trade secrets, an injunction subject terms relating to the scope of the patent shall be considered. The patent office is obligated to maintain records pertaining to all such reviews for a period of ten years from the date of determination.

Where a patent has been granted, the patentee may, by instrument in writing, assign or license the invention subject to this Act and rules made thereunder. Such assignment or license shall include provisions for indication certification trade relating to the use of the patented invention, ensuring adherence to quality standards as prescribed by the Controller. The patent office shall maintain a register of all assignments and licenses executed under this Act, accessible for public inspection upon payment of the prescribed fee. Any subsequent assignee or licensee may further assign or license the rights acquired, provided that such transfer is also registered with the patent office. Failure to register an assignment or license shall render it void against any third party deriving title under a prior registration. The Controller may require specific clauses regarding royalty payments and enforcement mechanisms in licenses relating to essential inventions.

Where an objection is taken by any person under this Act against the acceptance of a patent application, the applicant may appeal to the Appellate Board constituted as provided herein. The Appellate Board shall hear appeals from orders passed by the patent office relating to the determination of novelty or inventive step and shall determine whether the grounds for objection were substantiated. Further, where an aggrieved party disputes the assessment of copyright society fees levied against them, they may file a petition before the relevant High Court, challenging the methodology employed in calculating such fees. The patent office shall provide reasoned orders on all appeals received, detailing the findings upon which the decision is based and affording parties opportunity for rejoinder.

An application made under this Act shall be deemed to include all documents filed by the applicant with the Registrar in support thereof, including but not limited to claims of prior use, evidence of reputation, and declarations of consent from registered proprietors. For the purposes of processing a registrar application, ‘applicant’ means the person or entity making such application for registration of a trade mark, and shall be taken to include their authorized agent acting on their behalf. Any alteration to particulars within an existing registrar application requires notification to the Registrar in writing, subject to regulations prescribing the manner of such notification.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark shall furnish with their registrar application a representation of the mark sufficient for reproduction thereof under this Act. The Registrar may require such further particulars as he deems necessary for proper adjudication of the application, including details regarding colour claims and disclaimers of particular elements within the mark. Provided that where the mark consists exclusively of a word or words, a representation is not required unless the applicant specifically requests it to facilitate clarity during examination. Any alteration made to the trade mark after the initial registrar application is filed shall be subject to approval by the Registrar, who may require payment of an additional fee for such amendments. The Registrar’s decision on any amendment request is final, subject to appeal under this Act.

An applicant aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar refusing registration of a proposed trade mark, or requiring amendment thereof, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. Such an appeal shall be accompanied by such fees as may be prescribed under this Act. The Board may, after giving notice to all parties concerned and affording them an opportunity of being heard, confirm, reverse or modify the decision appealed against, or substitute it with a new decision. Failure to comply with the procedural requirements relating to a registrar application, including timely payment of requisite fees, shall render the appeal incompetent. Any order made by the Board shall be final, subject to further appeals as provided herein and in accordance with the general principles of natural justice.
