An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark shall file an application with the Registrar in the prescribed form and manner, providing all information deemed necessary by the Registrar for assessment under this Act. The application must include a clear representation of the mark and a list specifying the goods or services with which it is associated. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar may direct the applicant to make such alterations as are considered expedient to conform to the provisions herein. Any deficiency in the particulars furnished shall be brought to the attention of the applicant, who shall have a period of thirty days to rectify them, failing which the registrar application may be rejected. The Registrar shall record all documents filed and maintain an accurate register of applications received. Further, any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to a registrar application may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board as provided herein.

An application made to the Registrar shall be deemed complete only upon submission of all prescribed forms and requisite fees, and compliance with the requirements detailed under this Act regarding representation of the trademark. The Registrar may require further clarification from the applicant concerning the classification of goods or services associated with the proposed mark, provided that such request is made within thirty days of receipt of the application. Failure to respond adequately to a query issued by the Registrar shall result in the application being held in abeyance until satisfactory information is furnished. Any alteration to the details initially presented in the registrar application after its deemed completion will necessitate a fresh filing and associated fees, subject to conditions regarding minor clerical errors as provided herein.

An applicant seeking registration of a trademark shall furnish all information required by the Registrar under this Act and shall be deemed to have made a false statement if such information is subsequently found to be untrue. Any person making a misstatement in a registrar application shall be liable to pay a pecuniary penalty, not exceeding fifty thousand rupees, and may also face criminal prosecution for offences cognizable by a Magistrate first class. The Registrar may, at any time, require an applicant to submit further documentation substantiating the distinctiveness of the mark or its use in commerce; failure to comply within the stipulated period shall render the registrar application liable for rejection. Repeated non-compliance with these provisions will result in disqualification from filing future trademark applications for a period determined by the Registrar.

An applicant seeking registration of a trademark under this Act shall be deemed to hold a revocable license granting limited rights to use the mark pending final determination of their application by the Registrar. This license is assignable subject to prior approval from the Registrar, who may require demonstration that the assignee possesses sufficient resources and technical expertise to properly manage the trademark portfolio. Further, any subsequent assignment or sub-license granted without such consent shall be deemed void. The Registrar may, upon receiving a registrar application for assignment, request detailed information regarding the proposed assignee’s business operations and reputation. Provided that the original applicant retains responsibility for ensuring compliance with all relevant regulations during the pendency of the trademark registration process, this licensing arrangement does not preclude further commercial exploitation of the mark by the applicant.

An applicant aggrieved by any decision of the Registrar regarding the acceptance or rejection of their registrar application, or by any direction issued under this Act concerning the examination of such application, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The Board shall hear appeals arising under this provision and may allow a party to adduce further evidence if it considers that such evidence was not reasonably available at the time of the original decision. Provided that any appeal against an order directing amendment or refusal of a trade mark shall be accompanied by a fee as prescribed, and failure to pay said fee will render the appeal inadmissible. The Board’s decision shall be final, subject to further appeals under the provisions relating to judicial review.

An application made to the Registrar shall be deemed incomplete if it does not include a clear representation of the proposed marks and a detailed specification of the goods or services with which such marks are associated. The Registrar may require further clarification regarding the nature of the goods or services listed, provided that such request is made within thirty days of receipt of the application. Any alteration to the marks after initial filing shall be subject to approval by the Registrar and may necessitate a revised examination fee. Failure to respond to a notice issued under this Act concerning deficiencies in the application within the stipulated timeframe will result in the rejection of the registrar application. Marks means trade names, service marks, geographical indications, collective marks or public domain works as defined herein.

An application filed with the Registrar for registration of a trademark incorporating a design relating to a semiconductor integrated circuit shall be deemed invalid if it is shown that an identical or confusingly similar design has previously been registered under this Act, or is currently subject to a pending registrar application. The applicant may appeal against such determination within sixty days from the date of notification of the Registrar's decision. Provided that, the appellate authority shall consider whether the similarity between the designs constitutes a likelihood of confusion on the part of consumers, taking into account the overall impression created by the marks and the nature of the goods or services with which they are associated. Any party aggrieved by an order made under this provision may further appeal to the relevant High Court.

An application for registration of a trademark shall be deemed complete upon receipt by the Registrar of the prescribed fee and all requisite forms, subject to verification under this Act. The term "registrar application" includes any subsequent amendment filed pursuant to these provisions. Upon completion, the registrar may proceed with examination and publication as provided herein. An application registration notice shall be published in the Trade Marks Journal indicating acceptance for opposition or refusal. Any party aggrieved by a decision regarding an application’s status may appeal under this Act. The Registrar's determination of completeness is final, barring judicial review on limited grounds.

Any person who knowingly makes, uses, imports, or offers to sell an infringing copy of a registered design shall be guilty of an offence and liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine which may extend to fifty thousand rupees, or both. Where the infringement is committed by a company, any director, manager, secretary, or other officer thereof in default shall be deemed to be guilty of the offence. Further, where an infringing copy has been placed on the market as a result of the act of such person, he shall also be liable to pay damages equivalent to the loss suffered by the registered proprietor. The right to seek injunction and account of profits remains available under this Act, subject to procedural guidelines prescribed herein. A design shall registered only upon satisfying all conditions stipulated in these regulations.

Where an application for registration of a design is rejected under this Act, the applicant may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order of rejection. Such appeal shall be accompanied by a fee as prescribed and shall state specifically the grounds on which the order is contested. The Tribunal may, after affording an opportunity for hearing to both the appellant and the respondent, confirm, modify or reverse the order appealed against. Any party aggrieved by the decision of the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal may further appeal to the Supreme Court within sixty days, subject to just cause shown. It shall be a condition precedent that every design shall registered before it can enjoy protection under this Act.

Where a copyright infringement has been committed by a corporate body incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013, or any other law for the time being in force relating to companies, the expression "company" shall be construed as including its directors, managers, and officers who were directly involved in the decision-making process leading to the infringing act. For the purposes of determining liability under this Act, a company proved offence shall include acts such as unauthorized reproduction, distribution, or adaptation of copyrighted works. The responsibility for ensuring compliance with copyright law rests upon those individuals authorized to manage the company’s operations and intellectual property assets.

Where any work is registered under this Act in the name of a company, and it is subsequently established that an infringement of copyright relating to such work has occurred, the determination of liability shall proceed as follows. If the company proved offence was committed by its agents or employees acting within the scope of their authority, the Registrar may issue notices requiring the company to demonstrate due diligence in preventing such infringements. Failure to provide satisfactory evidence of preventative measures, including employee training and internal compliance protocols, may result in the imposition of penalties as provided herein. The Registrar shall consider the nature of the work, the extent of the infringement, and the company’s overall copyright management system when assessing culpability.

Where a copyright infringement has been established through due process, and it is demonstrated that such infringement was undertaken by a corporate entity acting through its agents or employees, the liability for damages shall extend to both the infringing company and any individual proven to have directed or knowingly participated in the infringing activity. The court may, upon consideration of the scale and duration of the infringement, award compensatory damages as prescribed under this Act, alongside reasonable attorney’s fees incurred by the copyright owner. Furthermore, if it is shown that a company proved offence was committed with the intent to gain an undue commercial advantage or to undermine the market for the copyrighted work, punitive damages may be assessed up to three times the amount of compensatory damages awarded. The court shall consider evidence pertaining to the corporate structure and internal policies in determining individual culpability.

Where a copyright infringement has been established through due process under this Act involving a corporate entity, it shall be presumed, subject to rebuttal by affirmative evidence presented before the relevant adjudicating officer, that the actions constituting the infringement were undertaken with the knowledge or consent of at least one director or principal officer of the company. Such director or officer shall be deemed to have been in default unless they demonstrate, through verifiable records and testimony, that reasonable steps were taken to prevent the infringing activity. The company proved offence will attract penalties as determined by the adjudicating officer, considering factors including the scale of infringement and demonstrable efforts at remediation. Further proceedings may be initiated against any individual found to have actively concealed information relevant to the investigation.

Where an infringement of copyright subsists due to acts committed by a corporate entity, such company shall be held accountable under this Act. The liability of the company shall extend to encompass every director, manager, secretary, or any other officer demonstrably involved in the decision-making process that led directly to the infringing activity. It is provided that for a company proved offence, it must be established beyond reasonable doubt that the aforementioned officers possessed knowledge of, and actively participated in, the actions constituting copyright infringement. Further, where such an offence involves the reproduction or distribution of works without authorization, the burden shall lie upon the prosecution to demonstrate the requisite level of involvement by the corporate officers.

Where a copyright infringement has been established through due process under this Act, and it is demonstrated that such infringement was carried out by a corporate entity, then the company itself shall be held accountable as a first offender. Every director, manager, or other officer of the company who knowingly authorized, permitted, or participated in the infringing activity shall also be deemed to have committed an offence. The court may, subject to provisions regarding proportionate penalties, impose fines and imprisonment upon both the corporate body and individual officers found culpable. Further, where a company proved offence is established, recovery of damages for copyright holders shall be pursued against the entity as a whole, without prejudice to actions against implicated individuals.

Where an infringement of copyright has occurred and it is established that a company proved offence by means of acts carried out by its employees or agents, the prosecution may proceed against both the company and any director, manager, secretary, or other officer thereof who was directly involved in the decision-making process relating to the infringing activity. Such officers shall be deemed guilty participants unless they demonstrate, to the satisfaction of the court, that they took all reasonable steps to prevent the infringement from occurring. The burden of proving such due diligence rests upon the accused officer. Further proceedings against any individual shall not preclude concurrent prosecution of the company under this Act, subject to principles of fairness and proportionality as determined by the adjudicating authority.

For the purposes of this Act, a “trade mark” means a mark capable of being represented graphically and shall include a device, brand name, heading, label, sign, word, letter, numeral, shape, configuration, air mark, colour or combination thereof adopted to distinguish goods or services of one undertaking from those of others under this Act. A trade mark may incorporate three-dimensional shapes, provided that such shapes have acquired distinctiveness through the use of the trade mark in relation to the goods or services and are capable of distinguishing them. The registration of a india trade mark confers upon the registered proprietor exclusive rights to use the trade mark for the goods or services specified in the register.

An application for registration of a india trade mark shall include a representation of the marks applied for, distinguishing clearly those parts thereof which the applicant claims to be distinctive. The Registrar may require the applicant to amend the representation if it is deemed unclear or does not adequately reflect the proposed marks. Where the india trade mark consists exclusively of a shape resulting from the nature of the goods, the necessary characteristics of the goods themselves, or results from the intended use of the goods, registration shall be refused unless such shape enjoys reputation among consumers and has acquired distinctiveness through use. An applicant may submit evidence demonstrating acquired distinctiveness as part of their application, subject to verification by the Registrar. The acceptance of an india trade mark is conditional upon compliance with these requirements.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to the rectification of a india trade mark register may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order and shall state specifically the grounds on which it is based. The Appellate Board may, after giving notice to all parties concerned and affording them an opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify or reverse the decision appealed against. Further, where a trade mark is used in contravention of the rights conferred by registration, the registered proprietor shall be entitled to seek remedies including injunctions and damages as provided herein. The measure of damages shall be determined having regard to all relevant factors, including but not limited to lost profits and reputation.

An application for registration of a india trade mark shall be refused if it contains only such matter as is or are capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one undertaking from those of another by some fairly distinctive means, and that matter is commonly used in describing those goods or services. The Registrar may require an applicant to amend the representation of a mark where he considers the depiction unclear or ambiguous; such amendment shall not alter the identity of the trade mark as intended by the applicant. Further, any person claiming ownership of a trade mark applied for registration under this Act may file a caveat against the application, provided that the claimant demonstrates prior use of an identical or confusingly similar india trade mark in relation to goods or services. The Registrar shall give notice of such caveat to the applicant and afford them both an opportunity to be heard.

An application for registration of a india trade mark shall be refused if it contains any matter which, to the satisfaction of the Registrar, is likely to deceive or confuse the public relating to the nature, quality or geographical origin of goods or services. Provided that, where a proposed trade mark includes only descriptive terms, such refusal may be waived if the applicant demonstrates acquired distinctiveness through use subsequent to the date of application and furnishes evidence establishing widespread recognition of the mark as indicating the source of the goods or services. Further, any representation of a geographical indication shall not be registrable unless it is duly authorized by the proprietor of the geographical indication and complies with conditions prescribed under this Act regarding fair trade practices.

Any person who, without due cause and with intent to deceive or injure, uses a trademark identical or confusingly similar to a registered india trade mark shall be guilty of an offence under this Act. Such offender shall be liable to imprisonment for a term not less than six months but which may extend to three years, and also to a fine which shall not be less than fifty thousand rupees but may extend to two hundred thousand rupees. Further, any goods bearing the infringing trademark are deemed misbranded and subject to seizure and destruction as provided herein. The Registrar may, ex parte, issue an injunction restraining such use if it is established that the infringement causes demonstrable damage to the reputation or goodwill associated with the india trade mark.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, no india trade mark shall be deemed invalid solely on the grounds that its use by the proprietor following registration resulted in confusion amongst consumers with a prior unregistered mark employed within a geographically limited area. However, where such confusion is demonstrated to have caused demonstrable financial prejudice to the possessor of the prior mark, an appeal may be made to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board asserting dilution of distinctiveness. The Board shall consider evidence pertaining to consumer perception and market share data; provided that the proprietor of the india trade mark demonstrates bona fide intention to use the mark throughout India. Any order issued by the Board is subject to further appeal before the High Court.

A ‘trade mark’ as defined under this Act, shall include any word, symbol, device, name, monogram, signature, or amalgam thereof, used to distinguish the goods or services of one undertaking from those of others. For the purposes of determining deceptiveness, a trade mark shall be considered in relation to not only the goods or services with which it is directly associated but also those that are similar or related thereto. Where infringement of a registered india trade mark is established, the Intellectual Property Appellate Board may grant an order injunction restraining the defendant from any further acts of infringement and directing him to deliver up for destruction the infringing materials.

An applicant seeking to register a india trade mark shall furnish, along with the application, a detailed description of the goods or services associated with the proposed mark. Where the application relates to a package comprising multiple articles, the description shall clearly delineate each element of the package and its intended function in relation to the goods or services. The Registrar may require further clarification regarding the nature and composition of such a package if deemed necessary for proper examination under this Act. Registration shall be granted subject to the condition that the applicant demonstrates continued use of the india trade mark on all elements of the package, as described in the application, for a period not less than six months from the date of registration.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person aggrieved by a notice issued under section 59 relating to rectification of a india trade mark shall have the right to file counter-statement within such time and manner as may be prescribed. Such counter-statement must specifically address the grounds raised in the rectification notice and present relevant evidence supporting the continued validity or distinctiveness of the registered trade mark. Failure to file a timely and adequate counter-statement may result in the rectification proceeding continuing without further opportunity for objection. Furthermore, where a respect registered application has been opposed under section 40, the applicant shall be entitled to submit written arguments rebutting the grounds of opposition, and the Registrar may afford both parties an opportunity to present oral submissions before rendering a decision. The Registrar’s determination is final subject to appeal under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, “territorial extent” shall mean the territory of India and any other place within the jurisdiction india trade marks are used or proposed to be used. This territorial extent includes, but is not limited to, the Exclusive Economic Zone of India as defined under the Maritime Zones of India (Regulation of Sea-Based Activities) Act. An application for registration of a trademark shall be deemed to be made in any state within India if the applicant has his principal place of business or residence therein. Subject to appeal under this Act, jurisdiction over matters relating to trade mark infringement shall vest with the District Court having local jurisdiction.

For the purposes of this Act, "registration" shall mean the entry of a mark in the Register of Trade Marks under section 21, conferring upon the proprietor exclusive rights to use and obtain benefit from the mark within India. An application for registration shall be deemed to be pending until the Registrar either accepts or rejects it, or makes an order relating thereto. The Registrar may require such further particulars as he deems necessary in relation to any proposed trade mark. Provided that a mark already registered under this Act shall not be subject to challenge solely on the basis of its prior use before the date of registration. Any alteration to a registered mark requires notification and approval by the Registrar, as provided herein.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall include such particulars relating to goods or services, as are necessary to determine the scope of protection sought. The Registrar may require an applicant to amend any specification of goods or services if he considers it too wide or ambiguous; and such amendment shall be made in accordance with the Trade Marks Rules. Where an application relates to more than one class of goods or services, each class shall be separately specified. Upon receiving an application, the Registrar shall record a date of filing for registration. The applicant shall furnish all information required by the Registrar, failing which the application may be rejected. Any person claiming right in a trade mark applied for under this Act may oppose the registration. The grant of registration is subject to fulfilling requirements as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person who, without due cause and after receiving notice from the Registrar that a trade mark has been registered, uses a trade mark identical or confusingly similar to the registered trade mark in relation to goods or services for which the registration is effective, shall be liable to pay damages. The amount of such damages shall be determined by the Court, taking into consideration the loss suffered by the proprietor of the registered trade mark and any measure of benefit gained by the infringing user. Further, where an injunction has been granted restraining the use of a particular trade mark, subsequent infringement may be deemed as willful under this Act, attracting enhanced penalties. The Registrar shall maintain a publicly accessible record of all registrations and pending applications for registration.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark shall file the application in the prescribed form and manner, specifying clearly the trade marks proposed to be registered, the goods or services associated with each mark, and the relevant class under the International Classification of Goods and Services. The Trade Marks Registry may require the applicant to furnish further particulars deemed necessary for examination of the application. Where an objection is raised by the Registry concerning distinctiveness or any other ground as provided herein, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to submit a written response addressing the concerns articulated in the objection notice. Failure to respond within the stipulated period may result in the rejection of the application. The Registrar shall consider all submissions and issue an order either accepting the registration for publication or rejecting it entirely. Any party aggrieved by such an order may appeal under this Act.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be refused if the proposed mark is deemed descriptive of the goods or services with which it is associated, unless such use has acquired distinctiveness through extensive and continuous employment prior to the date of application. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating this acquired distinctiveness, including but not limited to market survey data and sales figures reflecting consumer recognition. Further, registration shall be conditional upon compliance with prescribed advertising requirements within six months of grant; failure to adhere to these stipulations will render the mark liable for removal from the register. Any person aggrieved by a decision concerning registration may appeal under this Act to the relevant intellectual property tribunal.

Any person who, without due cause and after being served with a notice to cease doing so under this Act, continues to use a trade mark identical or deceptively similar to a registered trade mark in connection with goods or services for which the registration is valid shall be liable to pay damages of such amount as may be determined by the High Court. The amount of damages shall reflect the loss suffered by the proprietor of the registered trade mark and account for any benefit accruing to the infringing party. Further, where a false representation has been made to the public regarding the association or connection with goods or services offered under an unregistered trade mark, penalties may be imposed as provided herein, subject to considerations of intent and demonstrable harm. The grant of registration does not preclude claims based on passing off.

A proprietor seeking to grant a license relating to a registered trade mark shall execute a written instrument specifying the scope and duration of such license, including particulars of the licensed goods or services. Such license may be granted exclusively or non-exclusively, as determined by the grantor. Any assignment of registration under this Act shall include all rights and privileges pertaining to the mark, subject to any limitations expressly stated in the assignment deed. Where a trade mark has been assigned, subsequent licenses granted by the assignee shall remain valid unless explicitly revoked through written notice served upon the licensee. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating the validity of any such license or assignment, provided that this requirement shall not impede legitimate commercial transactions. Further, sub-licensing is permitted only with prior consent from the original proprietor and documented as part of the initial registration record.

An application for registration of a mark shall be refused if it is demonstrably identical or confusingly similar to an earlier mark already registered under this Act, provided that the proprietor of the earlier mark can adduce evidence establishing repute thereof. The Registrar may, however, allow such registration if the applicant demonstrates distinctive character acquired subsequent to the earlier registration and satisfies the Board that a likelihood of confusion is obviated by factors including differences in goods or services. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar refusing or allowing registration may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order, subject to payment of the prescribed fee; and the Board’s determination shall be final.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark shall submit all prescribed documents and forms as detailed in the First Schedule to this Act. The application must be accompanied by a certified copy of any prior registration, if the mark is identical or confusingly similar to an existing registered trade mark under this Act. Provided that, where the applicant demonstrates due cause for failing to provide such a certified copy, the Registrar may, at his discretion, waive this requirement following written justification from the applicant and after opportunity has been afforded to any potentially affected party to object. The prescribed manner for submitting these documents is electronic filing through the designated online portal, unless an exemption is granted by the Registrar due to demonstrable technological limitations. Any alteration made to submitted documentation post-filing shall be deemed a withdrawal of the original application.

Any person aggrieved by a refusal to register a trademark relating to a pharmaceutical substance may appeal such refusal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. Such appeal shall be accompanied by a fee as prescribed, and the Tribunal may entertain the appeal if it is satisfied that the appellant has made a prima facie case for registration. Failure to comply with this provision will render the appeal inadmissible. Where an infringing use of a registered trademark relating to a pharmaceutical substance occurs, the proprietor shall be entitled to seek injunctions and damages under this Act, subject to demonstrating actual financial loss or potential harm to reputation. Any wilful infringement shall attract enhanced penalties as determined by the adjudicating officer.

An amendment to an application for registration of a trade mark is deemed permitted under this Act where such amendment relates only to the representation of the mark and does not alter the identity of goods or services for which the mark is sought. The Registrar shall consider any proposed amendment permissible if it conforms with the provisions regarding clarity and distinctiveness as provided herein. Further, an application permitted amended may be subject to objection from any interested party within a period specified by the Registrar; such objections shall be considered before proceeding further with registration. Any alteration affecting the scope of protection sought requires fresh filing.

An applicant whose trade mark application is pending before the Registry may, at any time prior to opposition, file a request for amendment of the representation of the marks as applied for, or for alteration of the description of goods or services associated with the trade mark. Such an *application permitted amended* shall be considered only if the proposed changes do not substantially affect the identity of the original trade mark and are consistent with the provisions relating to acceptable representations under this Act. The Registrar shall notify all parties who have previously received notice of the application, providing them opportunity to submit objections to the amendment. Any such objection may be determined by the Registrar after hearing the applicant and objector.

An applicant whose trade mark application has been refused under this Act may submit a request for reconsideration within sixty days from the date of communication of the refusal order. Such request shall specify the grounds upon which the applicant relies and provide supporting documentation as deemed necessary by the Registrar. The Registrar, after reviewing the request and any relevant materials submitted, may direct that the application be reconsidered.

Where an application permitted amended pursuant to a direction under this Act incorporates alterations affecting the representation of goods or services, or substantially changing the nature of the trade mark itself, the Registrar shall provide notice of such amendment to all interested parties for comment. Any objections received within thirty days of publication may be considered by the Registrar prior to proceeding with further examination. The Registrar’s decision on any objection is final and binding subject to appeal under this Act.

An applicant whose trade mark application is pending before the Registry may submit a request for amendment of particulars specified in the application, provided such amendment does not substantially alter the character of the goods or services for which registration is sought. The Registrar shall consider any such request and may allow it if satisfied that the proposed amendment is merely clerical or typographical in nature, or if the applicant demonstrates that the alteration is necessitated by a change in the relevant classification of goods or services under this Act. Where an application permitted amended, the Registrar shall issue a fresh examination report reflecting the changes made, and such report shall be subject to objection as provided herein.

An applicant whose trade mark application has been refused under this Act may submit a request for reconsideration and propose amendments to the representation of goods or services, or other aspects of the mark itself. Such an amended application is deemed a fresh application permitted amended, subject to the provisions relating to examination and advertisement as if it were originally filed. Failure to comply with prescribed forms or pay requisite fees during this amendment process shall render the request invalid, and any costs incurred by the Registry in processing the initial refusal will be recoverable from the applicant. Any person aggrieved by a trade mark registration resulting from an application permitted amended may institute proceedings under Chapter VI seeking rectification of the register.

An applicant whose trade mark application is pending before the Registry and who seeks to introduce amendments to the representation of goods or services specified in their initial application shall submit a request for amendment detailing the proposed changes. Such request must demonstrate that the amended specification remains consistent with the original intention underlying the application, as assessed by the Registrar. The Registrar may permit an *application permitted amended* only if satisfied that the user party proceeding with the amendment has not materially altered the scope or nature of the trade mark sought to be registered. Further, any such permission shall be subject to a fee prescribed under this Act and publication in the Trade Marks Journal for public inspection.

Where an applicant seeks to amend a pending application permitted amended under this Act, such amendment shall not alter the fundamental character of the goods or services for which registration is sought. Any alteration intended to circumvent existing registrations or create confusion amongst consumers will be deemed a falsifying trade mark and shall be rejected outright. The Registrar may, at any time, require an applicant seeking amendment to submit evidence demonstrating the continued distinctiveness of the amended mark in relation to the specified goods or services. Failure to provide such evidence within the prescribed period shall result in rejection of the application and imposition of a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees; repeated offences will attract enhanced penalties and potential prosecution under relevant provisions relating to trade malpractices.

An applicant whose trade mark application is pending before the Registry may, at any time prior to opposition, file a request for amendment of the representation of goods or services specified in the application. Such an *application permitted amended* shall not alter the character of the goods or services sought to be registered and must remain within the scope of the original specification as understood at the date of filing. The Registrar may require clarification regarding the nature and extent of any proposed amendment. Further, where an amended trade mark is deemed by the Registrar to conflict with a prior right, an order cancellation against the amended representation may be sought under this Act.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be refused if the proposed mark, or any element thereof, is likely to be perceived as a falsifying trade mark in relation to any existing registered trade marks. The Registrar may require an applicant to submit evidence demonstrating that their proposed mark will not cause confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of goods or services. Where an application incorporates a representation which, though technically distinct from a prior registration, creates a false impression concerning affiliation or endorsement by the proprietor of that earlier mark, it shall be considered a falsifying trade mark under this Act. Such representations are deemed to mislead and prejudice the public interest in maintaining clarity within the marketplace.

For the purposes of this Act, "registered proprietor”, in relation to a layout-design, means the person entered in the Register as the owner of the registered layout-design and includes the legal representatives of a deceased registered proprietor. A registered proprietor shall be entitled exclusively to exercise the rights provided herein relating to the registered layout-design. The right to assign or license a registered layout-design remains with the registered proprietor, subject to any conditions stipulated in the assignment deed or license agreement filed under this Act. An application for registration shall not confer upon the applicant the status of a registered proprietor until the layout-design is formally entered on the Register as provided herein.
primary_entity: registered proprietor”, in relation to a layout-design

context: Application for registration of a layout-design shall be accompanied by such particulars and documents as are prescribed. Upon receipt of an application, the Controller may direct that the applicant furnish further information or submit revised drawings if deficiencies exist. Where the Controller is satisfied that the layout-design fulfills all requirements under this Act, including originality and distinctiveness, he shall proceed with registration. The register shall record details pertaining to each registered proprietor, including their address for communication of notices. Any person claiming rights in a layout-design may challenge the validity of a registration before an intellectual property tribunal as provided herein. A “registered proprietor”, in relation to a layout-design, is entitled exclusively to exploit the design and prevent others from doing so without consent.
primary_entity: registered proprietor”, in relation to a layout-design

context: Where an appeal arises from any decision or order made by the Controller relating to the registration of a layout-design, or concerning the validity of a registered layout-design, such appeal shall lie to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The appellant may seek review of findings pertaining to novelty and originality under this Act, particularly where evidence presented contradicts the initial assessment. It is provided that any party aggrieved by an order affirming the rights of a “registered proprietor”, in relation to a layout-design, may petition the Appellate Board demonstrating substantial prior use or publication undermining the claim of exclusive right. The Controller shall provide detailed reasoning for all decisions regarding registration and validity, which reasoning shall be accessible to all parties involved subject to confidentiality provisions as provided herein.
primary_entity: registered proprietor”, in relation to a layout-design

context: For the purposes of this Act, "registered proprietor”, in relation to a layout-design, means the person entered in the Register as the owner of the registered layout-design and includes the legal representatives of a deceased registered proprietor. The rights conferred under this Act shall binding upon any person infringing the exclusive rights of the registered proprietor. A registered proprietor may assign or otherwise transfer their interest in the registered layout-design subject to such conditions as are prescribed. Any license granted by a registered proprietor shall be valid only for the term specified therein, as provided herein. The application for registration shall contain particulars relating to the applicant and the layout-design.
primary_entity: registered proprietor”, in relation to a layout-design

context: For the purposes of this Act, a “layout design register” means a public record maintained by the Registrar, containing particulars of registered layout designs. The register shall include, but not be limited to, the name and address of the registrant, the title of the layout design, the date of registration, and any modifications or extensions subsequently recorded under this Act. Access to the layout design register shall be open to inspection by the public during normal business hours, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. Any person seeking to ascertain whether a particular layout design is registered may consult the layout design register for that information. The Registrar may provide copies of entries in the layout design register upon payment of the prescribed fee.

An applicant seeking registration of a layout design shall submit detailed technical documentation pertaining to the integrated circuit, including schematics, mask data, and manufacturing processes employed. The application must clearly identify the features constituting the original layout design for which protection is sought, distinguishing them from standard or commonly used elements. Upon receipt of the application, the Registrar may require further clarification or modifications to ensure compliance with the requirements under this Act. If the applicant demonstrates that the layout design is novel and possesses aesthetic merit as defined herein, the Registrar shall proceed to enter it into the register of layout designs. The entry in the layout design register shall include particulars of the applicant, the date of registration, and a concise description of the layout design.

Any person aggrieved by an order relating to the revocation of a layout design register, or any other decision made under this Act concerning the validity or enforceability of registered rights, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. Such appeals shall be filed within ninety days from the date of communication of the order and accompanied by such fees as may be prescribed. The Tribunal shall consider all relevant evidence presented by the appellant and the respondent, including expert testimony where necessary, and shall pass a reasoned order affirming, reversing, or modifying the original decision. Failure to comply with the procedural requirements for filing an appeal may result in its rejection. Remedies available under this Act for infringement of registered layout designs include injunctions, damages, and account of profits derived from the infringing activity, as provided herein.

An application for registration as a layout design register may be made to the Registrar by any person claiming to be the first owner of the integrated circuit layout-design. Such an application shall contain particulars specified under this Act, including a verified statement attesting to the originality of the layout-design and detailing its intended use. The Registrar shall examine the application for compliance with the prescribed formalities and may require the applicant to submit further information or clarifications as deemed necessary. If the Registrar finds that the layout-design is already registered or contains elements substantially similar to a previously registered design, the application shall be rejected, providing reasons for such rejection in writing to the applicant. Any person aggrieved by an order of rejection under this Act may appeal to the Controller within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order.

An application for registration as a layout design register may be refused if the particulars disclosed therein do not comply with the prescribed format or contain any information which is false or misleading. Subject to this Act, an applicant seeking registration of a layout-design shall furnish a sworn statement verifying the correctness of the information contained in the application and affirming that the applicant is the rightful owner of the layout-design. The Registrar may require such further particulars as are necessary for the proper examination of the application; provided that any alteration to the layout-design after the date of the application shall be disclosed clearly within the register. Failure to comply with these requirements renders the registration liable to cancellation under this Act.

Any person aggrieved by a decision relating to the registration of a layout design may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of such decision. Where an unauthorized copy of a registered layout design is manufactured or imported for trade or commercial purposes, the owner of the layout design register shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief and damages as provided herein. Failure to comply with an order issued by the Tribunal under this Act shall render the defaulting party liable to a penalty not exceeding ten lakhs rupees, and further penalties may be imposed at intervals not less than thirty days until compliance is secured. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint, initiate investigations into alleged infringements of registered layout designs.

The holder of a layout design register may grant non-exclusive licenses to third parties enabling them to reproduce the registered integrated circuit layout design for commercial purposes, subject to such terms and conditions as are specified in the license agreement. Such license agreements shall be executed in writing and may include provisions regarding royalty payments, duration of use, and geographical limitations. Assignment of a layout design register is permissible with the prior written consent of the Registrar, provided that the assignee undertakes all obligations and liabilities incumbent upon the original registrant under this Act. Any transfer or assignment made without such consent shall be deemed void. Furthermore, where a license has been granted, subsequent assignments of the layout design register are permitted but must clearly identify all licensees benefiting from the transferred rights as provided herein.

The determination of whether a layout design infringes upon a registered layout design shall be predicated on substantial similarity, assessed considering both the overall impression and individual features as provided herein. An aggrieved party asserting infringement may file an appeal with the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of order; such appeal shall specify grounds demonstrating error apparent on the face of the record or manifest injustice arising from the Registrar’s decision regarding the layout design register. The Tribunal may, after affording the respondent a reasonable opportunity for being heard, affirm, reverse, or modify the order appealed against. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Tribunal may further appeal to the Supreme Court within sixty days.

The holder of a layout design register may grant non-exclusive licenses to third parties permitting the manufacture integrated circuits embodying the registered layout design, subject to conditions specified in the license agreement. Such licenses shall be documented and advertised publicly through publication in the Official Gazette, constituting an advertised acceptance of the terms therein. Any assignment of rights pertaining to a registered layout design, whether partial or complete, requires prior notification to the Registrar and is only valid upon confirmation by the Registrar following due process as provided herein. The assignee shall be deemed to hold title subject to any existing licenses granted under this Act. Further, any licensee may sub-license their rights, provided that such sub-licensing agreements adhere to principles of fair dealing and do not unduly prejudice the interests of the layout design holder.

A layout design register is deemed to be complete when it contains particulars relating to each registered layout design including, but not limited to, the name and address of the registrant, the date of registration, a copy of the layout design, and any relevant claims made by the registrant regarding originality. The register shall also record details pertaining to any article patented process utilized in the creation of the layout design, as provided herein. Any modification or alteration to a registered layout design requires notification to the Registrar, subject to guidelines issued under this Act concerning minor variations not affecting the overall topology. Access to information contained within the layout design register may be granted upon application and payment of prescribed fees.

For the purposes of this Act, a “design register” means an official record maintained by the Controller General under his authority, containing particulars of registered layout designs. The design register shall include, but not be limited to, the name and address of the applicant, the date of registration, the class of the integrated circuit layout-design, and a representation thereof as filed with the application. Any person may inspect the design register upon payment of such fees as may be prescribed. Information pertaining to confidential commercial matters shall be protected from public disclosure subject to regulations issued by the Controller General. The maintenance of the design register is crucial for ensuring transparency and facilitating searches under this Act.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be accompanied by such particulars as the Registrar may prescribe, including detailed schematics and a description of the fabrication process employed. The Registrar shall examine each application to ascertain whether the layout-design is original and not contrary to public interest or morality. Upon satisfactory examination, the applicant shall be notified for payment of the prescribed registration fee. Following successful payment, the layout-design shall be entered into the design register maintained by the Registrar, along with the date of entry and the name and address of the registrant. Any modification to the registered layout-design requires a fresh application under this Act, subject to provisions regarding minor alterations deemed inconsequential as provided herein.

Subject to appeal under this Act, a proprietor of a design register shall be entitled to sue for relief by way of injunction, damages, or both, against any person who without leave from the proprietor makes, uses, offers to sell, sells, or imports into India any article embodying the registered layout-design. Provided that in determining whether an infringement has occurred, the court shall consider not only the exact reproduction of the design but also designs which are substantially similar thereto. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint from any person aggrieved by an act of infringement, direct the proprietor to institute proceedings for redressal; failure to do so within a reasonable time as determined by the Registrar may result in the Registrar’s power to initiate such proceedings on behalf of the complainant, recovering costs incurred therefrom from the proprietor.

An application for entry into the design register shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the drawings or other representations of the integrated circuit layout-design sought to be registered, conforming to the standards prescribed under this Act. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further particulars or clarification regarding the layout-design and its representation as deemed necessary for proper examination. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall assign it a serial number and intimate the same to the applicant by post or electronic means. Any alteration made to the drawings or representations after the assignment of the serial number shall be inadmissible unless sanctioned in writing by the Registrar. The design register shall be maintained electronically and shall be accessible for public inspection subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. Information pertaining to pending applications shall not be disclosed, provided that this does not impede due process.

An applicant seeking entry of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design into the design register shall submit detailed technical specifications conforming to the prescribed format, including but not limited to representations depicting all layers and interconnection patterns. The application must be accompanied by an affirmation verifying originality and absence of prior registration under this Act or any equivalent legislation in another jurisdiction. Provided that the Registrar is satisfied with the completeness and accuracy of the submitted documentation and adherence to established standards, a provisional entry shall be made pending verification of non-infringement of existing registered designs. Any third party possessing evidence suggesting similarity to an already registered layout-design may file an objection within sixty days of the publication notice as provided herein.

An unauthorized reproduction or importation for sale with intent to sell of a registered design shall be deemed an infringement under this Act. Any person infringing a design registered in the design register shall be liable to pay damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the registrant, and such amount as may be determined by the relevant adjudicating officer. Further, where an infringement is established, the Court may order the destruction of the infringing articles, packaging materials, and advertising matter related thereto. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint regarding suspected infringement, issue summons requiring the alleged infringer to appear before the Court for adjudication, provided that such summons shall be accompanied by evidence supporting the claim.

The holder of a design register relating to an integrated circuit layout-design may grant licenses conferring rights to use, manufacture, or import articles incorporating the registered design, subject to conditions specified in the license agreement. Such licenses shall be assignable, either wholly or partially, by instrument in writing and may include provisions for royalty payments, non-compete clauses, and limitations on field of use as deemed appropriate by the licensor. Any assignment under this Act requires registration with the Registrar within thirty days of execution; failure to register an assignment renders it void against subsequent dealings. The registered owner shall provide a copy of any license agreement relating to the design register upon request from the Registrar for verification purposes, provided that confidential commercial information may be redacted as permitted by regulations framed thereunder. Further, sub-licensing is permissible with the prior written consent of the original registrant.

Subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal, an entry in the design register shall be deemed conclusive evidence of the validity of the registered layout-design and prior right of the registrant therein, provided that any person aggrieved by a decision relating to the registration or rejection of a layout-design may, within sixty days from the date of such decision, file an appeal as provided herein. The Appellate Tribunal may allow such appeal if it is satisfied that there has been an error apparent on the face of the record; however, this shall not preclude consideration of other grounds where the applicant demonstrates substantial prejudice due to a demonstrable procedural irregularity during the registration process. An application for rectification of entries in the design register may be made by any interested party and will be subject to similar appellate review.

For the purposes of this Act, a “design register” means a public record maintained by the Controller General, containing particulars of registered layouts and designs, including but not limited to the name and address of the registrant, the date of registration, the class and description of the layout-design, and copies or representations thereof. An application for inclusion in the design register shall be refused if the layout-design incorporates a condition declared unlawful under this Act, namely, that it is substantially similar to an existing registered layout-design or contains elements which are dictated solely by technical function or process, thereby lacking originality as provided herein.

An application for entry into the design register may be made by any person claiming to be the owner of an original layout-design. Such application shall contain particulars as prescribed, including a representation of the layout-design and a statement of ownership. The Registrar shall examine each application to ascertain whether it complies with the requirements under this Act and the regulations framed thereunder. If satisfied that the applicant is entitled to registration and the design is registrable, the Registrar may proceed with registration. A design registered shall be deemed for all purposes to be the property of the registrant. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application for registration, or concerning the validity of a design registered, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

An applicant seeking entry of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design into the design register shall submit detailed schematics conforming to prescribed standards, accompanied by a declaration affirming originality and non-infringement of existing intellectual property rights. The application must specify the intended field of use for the layout-design and declare any modifications made from previously published designs. Prior to registration, the Registrar may request further technical documentation or clarification regarding the design’s functionality. Registration shall be conditional upon compliance with these requirements; a failure to adequately demonstrate novelty may result in rejection under this Act. Furthermore, an existing India patent pertaining to the underlying technology of the layout-design must be disclosed and its status verified by the applicant.

An applicant seeking to respect filing application for a layout-design shall submit Form LD-A along with a certified copy of the drawings constituting the layout-design. The Registrar may, upon receiving an application, issue a provisional registration certificate if satisfied that the layout-design is capable of being registered under this Act and does not conflict with any existing registered layout-designs. Provided that, the applicant shall declare in the application whether or not the layout-design incorporates elements derived from another source, and furnish details thereof as may be prescribed. Failure to provide such declaration will render the application liable for rejection. The Registrar shall maintain a register of applications received, noting the date of receipt and any correspondence relating thereto.

Where a person aggrieved by an order passed by the Controller relating to the grant or refusal of registration of a layout-design believes that the said order is manifestly erroneous in law, they may prefer an appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. Such appeal shall be filed within ninety days from the date of communication of the order. The appellant shall, along with the memorandum of appeal, pay such fee as may be prescribed. Failure to respect filing application requirements, including timely payment of fees, will render the appeal inadmissible. The Tribunal may, after giving notice to all parties concerned and affording them an opportunity of being heard, pass such orders as it deems fit, which shall include affirming, modifying or reversing the order appealed against.

An applicant seeking to obtain protection for a layout-design shall submit an application to the Controller under this Act. The application must be accompanied by a certified copy of the drawings constituting the layout-design, executed in triplicate, along with a statement specifying the nature of the layout-design and its intended use. Any person claiming to be the first inventor or creator of the layout-design may respect filing application, provided that such claim is substantiated by appropriate documentation demonstrating originality and inventive step. The Controller shall prescribe the form for the application and the fees payable in respect thereof. Failure to comply with these requirements will render the application liable to rejection. An applicant may be required to furnish further information or clarification at any stage of the examination process, as deemed necessary by the Controller.

An applicant seeking to respect filing application for a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall submit Form IC-LA along with a declaration verifying originality and freedom from prior publication. The Registrar may require further documentation, including detailed schematics and manufacturing process descriptions, if deemed necessary to ascertain compliance with the provisions of this Act regarding substantial similarity. Failure to provide requested information within thirty days of notification will result in suspension of processing until such time as complete data is furnished. An application shall be accompanied by a non-refundable fee payable to the Government, and any subsequent amendments must adhere to prescribed formatting guidelines. The applicant’s identity and address details provided at the time of respect filing application are deemed accurate for all official correspondence under this Act.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Controller refusing to accept a filing application relating to a layout-design shall have the right to appeal under this Act. Such appeal must be filed within ninety days from the date of communication of the order, subject to payment of the prescribed fee. Failure to comply with this time limit will render the appeal inadmissible. The Appellate Tribunal may, after giving notice to all parties concerned and affording them an opportunity for being heard, confirm, modify or reverse the decision appealed against. Any attempt to circumvent these provisions through fraudulent misrepresentation in respect filing application shall be deemed a cognizable offence punishable with imprisonment and fine as provided herein.

The owner of a layout-design right may grant a license conferring specific rights to utilize, reproduce, and commercially exploit the said design, subject to the terms stipulated within the licensing agreement. Such licenses shall be assignable, either in whole or in part, provided that any assignment is executed through a formal instrument registered with the Controller General under this Act. The owner shall respect filing application for compulsory license relating to the layout-design, and such applications must clearly delineate the intended use and duration of the proposed license. Further, where an assignment includes rights pertaining to pending applications for extension of protection, the assignee’s obligations regarding maintenance fees and renewal charges shall be explicitly defined within the assignment document. The Controller General may require submission of detailed financial records relating to royalty payments associated with any licensed utilization.

An applicant aggrieved by a decision of the Controller refusing to accept a filing application concerning a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design may appeal to the Intellectual Property Tribunal. Such an appeal shall only be maintainable if the applicant demonstrates, through duly authenticated documentation submitted with the appeal, that the reasons stated by the Controller were manifestly erroneous or based on a misinterpretation of the provisions under this Act. The Tribunal may, after affording both the applicant and the Controller an opportunity to present their respective arguments and supporting evidence, direct the Controller to respect filing application or uphold the original decision. Costs associated with such appeals shall be determined at the discretion of the Tribunal.

An applicant seeking to respect filing application for a layout-design relating to an integrated circuit shall furnish with the prescribed application a detailed technical description including all layers comprising the said layout-design, along with requisite drawings conforming to standards specified under this Act. The Controller General may require further clarification or amendments to the submitted documentation if deficiencies are perceived that impede proper examination of the layout-design’s novelty and originality. Failure to comply with such directions within the stipulated timeframe shall constitute grounds for rejection of the application. An alleged offence reason relating to non-disclosure of prior art during the filing process will be considered a material misrepresentation, subject to penalties as provided herein.

Where a person aggrieved by an order appellate relating to infringement of layout-design rights believes that the Appellate Tribunal has acted without due consideration of material facts presented during proceedings, that person may file an application seeking review. Such application shall be made within ninety days from the date of communication of the order appellate and must specify the errors apparent on the face of the record which are alleged to have occasioned a miscarriage of justice. The applicant shall further demonstrate how the omission or misdirection impacted the ultimate determination of infringement. Failure to respect filing application requirements, including payment of prescribed fees, will render the review application inadmissible. Any counter-claim arising from such an application shall be dealt with expeditiously under this Act.

Applications for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be examined by the Registrar in accordance with the prescribed procedures. The Registrar may require the applicant to submit further particulars or modifications to the application, provided that such requirements are communicated in writing and accompanied by a reasoned explanation. Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Registrar relating to the examination of an application may prefer an appeal to the Controller within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The Controller shall consider all relevant materials presented during the original proceedings and any additional evidence submitted with the appeal. Decisions regarding matters relating registered layout-designs, including but not limited to extensions of term or rectification requests, are subject to judicial review under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, “form issuing” with respect to a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall mean the process by which an applicant submits documentation and data demonstrating compliance with the technical requirements for registration, as prescribed by the Registrar. This includes, but is not limited to, detailed schematics, mask information, and verification reports pertaining to the layout-design. The Registrar may require further clarification or supplementary materials during form issuing to ascertain complete adherence to these stipulations. Any deliberate misrepresentation or omission of material facts during form issuing shall render the application liable for rejection under this Act, subject to appeal as provided herein.

Where a person claims right in a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design and applies for form issuing, the Controller shall examine whether the layout-design satisfies the requirements of novelty and originality as provided herein. If, upon examination, it appears that the applicant has not demonstrated sufficient distinctiveness to warrant registration, the application may be rejected, and the applicant shall be notified in writing with reasons for such rejection. Any person aggrieved by an order rejecting a form issuing application may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days of receipt of the order. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final and binding subject to further judicial review under law. Failure to comply with procedural requirements during form issuing, including timely submission of prescribed documentation, may render the application liable for dismissal without further notice.

An application for a form issuing from the Controller shall be made in the prescribed manner and shall contain a statement specifying the particulars of the integrated circuit layout design, including its title, date of creation, and the name and address of the applicant claiming to be the first maker. The application must be accompanied by such documentation as the Controller deems necessary for verification purposes, relating to ownership or right to apply. Any person aggrieved by an order refusing a form issuing may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of that order. The Controller shall consider any representations made by the applicant or any other interested party during the pendency of the application and may require further information as deemed appropriate. Subject to this, the Controller’s decision on whether to issue a form is final.

An application for a form issuing under this Act shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the relevant documentation establishing ownership or right to the semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design. The Registrar may, subject to compliance with prescribed formalities, require the applicant to furnish further particulars relating to the design’s creation and initial public disclosure, provided that such requirements are proportionate to the complexity of the layout-design involved. Failure to provide requested information within the stipulated timeframe shall render the application liable for rejection. Any alteration made to a submitted form after its registration is deemed invalid unless expressly authorized by the Registrar following due process as provided herein. The applicant must demonstrate adherence to all relevant technical specifications outlined in the prescribed guidelines.

Any person who, having obtained a form issuing from the Controller, reproduces an integrated circuit layout-design in violation of the conditions specified therein shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall be assessed at twice the reasonable royalty that would have been payable had the reproduction been authorized under this Act, or such higher amount as the Court may deem just and appropriate considering the extent of infringement and resultant loss to the registered proprietor. Further, where a continuing infringement is established, an injunction may be granted restraining the infringer from further acts of reproduction. The Controller shall maintain records pertaining to all forms issued and any subsequent modifications thereof, accessible for inspection subject to reasonable restrictions as provided herein.

The owner of a registered semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be entitled to grant licenses granting rights to utilize the design for any purpose. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and may relate to the manufacture, import, sale, hire, or use of integrated circuits incorporating the layout-design, as determined by the terms of the agreement. Any assignment of ownership under this Act shall be deemed to include all rights pertaining to form issuing, including but not limited to the right to grant licenses. Provided that any licensee may further assign their license subject to obtaining prior written consent from the original owner unless such assignment is explicitly permitted within the initial licensing agreement. The terms and conditions governing such licenses and assignments are governed by contract law as provided herein, and no approval of the Controller General shall be required for their validity.

An application for a form issuing from the Registrar shall be accompanied by a declaration verifying the originality of the integrated circuit layout design and affirming that no prior publication or unauthorized disclosure has occurred, subject to exceptions permitted as provided herein. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating this claim, including evidence demonstrating due diligence in safeguarding confidential information. Any party aggrieved by a decision regarding form issuing, whether granting, refusing, or imposing conditions, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days of receipt of notification thereof. Such an appeal shall be on grounds alleging misinterpretation of the Act’s provisions concerning originality or procedural irregularities during the examination process.

An application for form issuing shall be submitted to the Registrar in the prescribed manner and accompanied by the requisite fee. The applicant must demonstrate that the integrated circuit layout-design is original, hitherto unregistered under this Act or any corresponding law registration referred, and does not contain any unauthorized reproduction of an existing layout-design. Provided that a layout-design incorporating minor modifications to a previously registered design shall be considered original if such modifications are demonstrably inventive and do not substantially replicate the prior design’s overall appearance. The Registrar may require further documentation or clarification from the applicant to ascertain compliance with these conditions, and failure to provide satisfactory responses within the stipulated timeframe will result in rejection of the application.

Any person desiring to obtain a form issuing from the Registrar shall submit an application in the prescribed manner, accompanied by the requisite fee. The Registrar may require such applicant to furnish further information or documentation as deemed necessary for verification of entitlement. Failure to comply with this requirement within thirty days of notification shall render the application liable for rejection and forfeiture of any fees paid. Where a dispute arises regarding eligibility for form issuing, the aggrieved party may appeal to the civil court registrar having jurisdiction over the matter. The Registrar’s decision in such cases is final, subject to judicial review under established principles. Any attempt to fraudulently obtain a form or misuse its contents shall be deemed an offence punishable with imprisonment and monetary penalties as provided herein.

Where an application for form issuing is rejected by the Layout-Design Registrar, the applicant shall have the right to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. Such appeal may be made within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order of rejection and must specify the grounds upon which the decision is challenged. The Tribunal shall give notice to the Registrar and afford him an opportunity to present his case in response to the appeal, subject to just cause shown. Further, if the applicant subsequently obtains a granted new patent relating to elements disclosed within the layout-design application, the Tribunal may consider this factor when determining the merits of the appeal, provided that the patent does not invalidate the original form issuing request as provided herein.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall include particulars verifying ownership and detailing the date of first commercial exploitation, if any, outside India. The Registrar may reject an application if it is determined that the layout-design incorporates elements substantially derived from a previously registered design under this Act or another jurisdiction, provided that evidence demonstrating independent creation is submitted alongside the application. Any modification to a registered layout-design following registration requires notification to the Registrar within thirty days, detailing the alterations and their impact on the original claim of novelty.
