An applicant shall provide evidence of prior use of the mark in India, where claimed under this Act, and failure to do so may prejudice the registration process.

Where an india application is filed relating to a trade mark that includes a geographical indication, the Registrar shall give notice thereof to any association representing producers of goods originating from the indicated territory. Any such association may, within three months of the date of publication of the journal containing the notice, file with the Registrar written representations objecting to registration on grounds specified under this Act relating to likelihood of confusion or deceptive similarity. The Registrar shall consider all such objections and provide the applicant with an opportunity to respond in writing. If, after considering the objection and the applicant’s response, the Registrar deems the geographical indication likely to cause dilution of a distinctive character of an earlier trade mark, registration may be refused or modified as provided herein.

An india application for the registration of a trademark shall be accompanied by such particulars as the Registrar deems necessary to identify the applicant, the mark sought to be registered, and the goods or services in relation to which it is used or proposed to be used. The application must specify whether the mark is being used already, and if so, provide details of the date from which its use commenced. Where an india application relates to a collective mark or certification trade mark, further information regarding the constitution and functioning of the association or body proposing registration shall also be submitted. Any alteration to the particulars contained in an india application may only be effected with the Registrar’s consent, provided that such alterations do not substantially affect the nature of the mark or goods/services covered. The Registrar may require any applicant to furnish security for costs under this Act.

An india application for registration of a trademark shall be accompanied by such particulars as the Registrar deems necessary to identify clearly the goods or services in relation to which the trademark is used or proposed to be used. The applicant must provide evidence demonstrating continuous use of the mark within India for at least six months immediately preceding the date of the application, provided that this requirement may be waived under circumstances specified by the Registrar. Further, where the india application relates to a service mark, the applicant shall furnish an affidavit verifying the nature and extent of such services. Any alteration to the details furnished in the initial application requires prior written consent from the Registrar before proceeding with examination.

Any individual or corporate body seeking to secure exclusive rights over a distinctive sign used in connection with goods or services shall file an india application with the Registrar, adhering strictly to the prescribed forms and paying requisite fees as determined by regulations. Failure to submit a complete and accurate application, including all required representations of the mark, will render the application liable for rejection without further notice. Any false representation made within the india application concerning prior use or ownership shall be deemed an offence punishable with monetary penalties and potential criminal prosecution under relevant provisions. The Registrar may require additional documentation to verify authenticity; non-compliance may result in delayed processing or outright refusal of registration.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any proprietor seeking to assign or license their registered trademark, or an india application thereof, shall submit a formal notification to the Registrar within thirty days of the execution of such assignment or licensing agreement. The notification must detail the parties involved, the scope of the assigned rights or licensed usage, and the geographical territory covered by the transfer. Further, any subsequent modification or termination of an existing license agreement relating to a registered trademark shall also be notified to the Registrar in like manner. Provided that, where the assignment is made without consideration, such fact must be explicitly stated within the notification, accompanied by an affidavit verifying its accuracy. The Registrar may require further documentation as deemed necessary to ascertain the validity and completeness of the india application for record purposes.

An application for registration of a trademark shall be deemed invalid if, at the time of filing, the applicant has not been continuously using the mark in relation to the specified goods or services for a period exceeding six months immediately preceding the date of such india application. However, this restriction shall not apply where the non-use is due to import restrictions or other circumstances beyond the applicant’s control, and the applicant demonstrates reasonable diligence to resume use as soon as those circumstances cease. Any party aggrieved by an order rejecting an application may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days of receipt of that order, presenting evidence demonstrating continuous prior use notwithstanding the alleged period of non-use.

Where an india application is refused by the Registrar, either wholly or in part, the applicant shall have the right to appeal against such refusal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The appeal shall lie within sixty days from the date of receipt of the notice of the refusal and shall state the grounds on which the applicant relies. Subject to any directions issued by the Board, the Registrar may require the appellant to submit a memorandum of arguments in support of the appeal.

The Board may, after giving the Registrar an opportunity to be heard, allow the appeal and direct that the india application proceed for registration as if it had been approved initially or may dismiss the appeal. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Board under this Act may further appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such order. The applicant shall remain liable for all applicable fees associated with the processing of their application trade mark throughout the appeals process.

Any applicant seeking an india application relating to a trademark used in connection with crop sciences products, or proposed to be so used, shall furnish a verification confirming the accuracy of particulars contained therein. Failure to do so renders the application liable for rejection without further notice. The Registrar may require amendment of any specification of goods or services if deemed necessary to accurately reflect the intended use. Any false representation made in an india application concerning prior use or reputation of the mark shall be punishable with a fine which may extend to two hundred thousand rupees, and the applicant is also liable for damages to affected parties. The Registrar has discretion to order rectification proceedings where evidence suggests deceptive trade practices.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any proprietor desiring to grant a license relating to a registered trade mark or an india application pending examination shall file with the Registrar a detailed memorandum outlining the scope, duration, and territorial extent of such licensing agreement. This memorandum must specify whether the licensee is exclusive or non-exclusive and detail any royalties payable under the arrangement. Assignment of rights pertaining to a registered trade mark or an india application may be effected only upon prior notification to the Registrar, accompanied by documentation establishing the assignor’s ownership and the assignee's consent. Further, all sums received by the Registrar as fees relating to licenses and assignments shall constitute fund for the promotion of intellectual property awareness amongst small and medium enterprises.

For the purposes of this Act, an india disclosed application means an application for registration of a trademark that has been published under section 59, and wherein the applicant has, prior to such publication, expressly elected to have the application subjected to examination only after its disclosure. Such election shall be deemed conclusive, and the Registrar shall not undertake any preliminary assessment of distinctiveness or other registrability criteria until the period for filing a notice of opposition has expired. An india disclosed application is subject to all procedural requirements applicable to trademark applications as provided herein, notwithstanding the altered sequence of examination steps.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark shall, upon filing an application, disclose to the Registrar any prior use or knowledge of identical or similar marks relating to identical or like goods or services. Such disclosure is intended to facilitate examination under this Act and ensure transparency in the registration process. Failure to make such a disclosure may result in the rejection of the application or subsequent rectification proceedings, subject to considerations of bona fide intention and due diligence on the part of the applicant. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all india disclosed applications for public access, ensuring that interested parties are informed of pending trade mark registrations. Any person aggrieved by an action taken based on a disclosure may appeal as provided herein.

Where an applicant has disclosed an earlier use of a trademark in India, subsequent to the date of filing of the application but prior to the date of advertisement thereof under this Act, the Registrar may, upon receiving evidence demonstrating actual use during that period, grant registration subject to such conditions as he deems fit. Such conditions may include limiting the scope of protection afforded by the registered trade mark to the geographical areas or specific goods and services where the earlier use was demonstrably established. Any party adversely affected by a registration granted under this provision may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of publication of the acceptance of the application, asserting that the disclosure of prior use was misleading or did not accurately reflect the extent of such use. The applicant shall be liable for any damages arising from misrepresentation in the india disclosed application.

An applicant desiring to obtain registration of a trade mark under this Act shall file an India disclosed application with the Registrar, accompanied by the requisite fees as prescribed. The application must specify the trade mark sought to be registered, a clear representation thereof, and a list of goods or services in connection with which the trade mark is used or proposed to be used. Where an applicant has previously filed an identical or similar application relating to the same goods or services, the Registrar may require disclosure of all prior applications and their status. The Registrar shall acknowledge receipt of the India disclosed application within thirty days, and publication for opposition will follow as provided herein. Any person believing they would be prejudiced by registration may file a notice of opposition within the prescribed period.

An applicant desiring to obtain registration of a trade mark under this Act shall, upon filing an application, provide a clear representation of the mark as it is intended to be registered. Such representation may consist of word marks, figurative elements, or combinations thereof, subject to compliance with prescribed guidelines regarding colour and stylization. Where the application incorporates a device previously disclosed in any publication accessible to the public prior to the date of the india disclosed application, the applicant must submit an affidavit attesting to the extent and nature of such prior disclosure. Failure to provide this affidavit, or providing one containing materially false statements, shall render the application liable for rejection as provided herein.

Any applicant submitting an india disclosed application for the registration of a trademark shall, upon discovery of any prior conflicting use by another party within India, immediately notify the Registrar. Failure to provide such notification within thirty days from the date of discovery will render the application liable for summary rejection and forfeiture of all fees paid in respect thereof. The Registrar may, at their discretion, extend this period provided that a written justification demonstrating reasonable cause is submitted alongside an additional penalty fee as determined by regulations. Any party aggrieved by a rejection under this provision may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days; however, such appeal shall be accompanied by a monetary sanction payable to the Government of India.

Where the proprietor of a registered trade mark desires to grant a license or assign the benefit of such registration, including rights arising from an india disclosed application, they may execute a written agreement specifying the scope of permitted use, geographical territory, duration, and any royalty payments. Such agreements shall be recorded with the Registrar within thirty days of execution, provided that the recording is subject to a prescribed fee. The proprietor retains ownership of the trade mark unless explicitly relinquished in the assignment document. Any subsequent modification or termination of the license or assignment must also be formally documented and filed with the Registrar. Failure to do so may render such modifications unenforceable under this Act. The licensee or assignee shall not, without express written consent from the proprietor, alter the registered goods or services associated with the trade mark.

Where an applicant has disclosed an earlier identical or similar trade mark used by another person in India, the Registrar shall provide that person with notice of the india disclosed application. Such notice shall specify the details of the application and invite observations regarding any conflict arising from the prior use. The applicant making the disclosure shall be afforded a reasonable opportunity to respond to these observations, presenting evidence demonstrating either lack of likelihood of confusion or other grounds justifying registration notwithstanding the prior use. Any person aggrieved by the Registrar’s decision following consideration of such observations may appeal to the Appellate Board within three months from the date of that decision, subject to payment of the prescribed fee and compliance with procedural requirements as provided herein.

Where any proprietor of a registered trade mark institutes legal proceedings under this Act against any person for alleged infringement, and it is subsequently determined by the relevant judicial authority that such allegation was without merit or based on demonstrably false representations concerning the nature or origin of goods or services, the proprietor shall be liable to pay costs incurred by the defendant in defending the action. Such costs shall include reasonable legal fees, disbursements, and any other expenses properly incurred. Further, where a proprietor knowingly pursues frivolous or vexatious infringement proceedings, they may also be subject to an order directing them to compensate the defendant for loss of business opportunity arising directly from those proceedings. Any person found guilty of making false claims regarding trade mark infringement with intent to cause financial harm shall be punishable imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years and with a fine extending up to one lakh rupees.

Where a proprietor institutes proceedings under this Act alleging an infringement of his registered trademark, and it is established before the relevant adjudicating authority that the defendant has knowingly used a mark identical or deceptively similar to the plaintiff’s registered trade mark in relation to goods or services for which said registration subsists, then such defendant shall be liable for damages as provided herein. Further, where the infringement constitutes a commercial fraud, or involves wilful deception intended to gain unfair advantage, or causes grievous harm to the reputation of the proprietor's trademark, the court may impose punishable imprisonment for a term not less than six months but which may extend to three years, and with a fine which shall be determined at the discretion of the court. Any employee acting under the direction of such defendant remains subject to similar penalties.

Where a proprietor institutes proceedings alleging an infringement of their registered trademark under this Act and such allegation is contested by the defendant, the court shall afford both parties full opportunity to present evidence pertaining to the similarity between the impugned mark and the plaintiff’s registered mark, considering inter alia the phonetic, visual, and conceptual aspects thereof. Should the court find that the defendant knowingly and wilfully employed a mark deceptively similar to the registered trademark with intent to mislead consumers, such conduct shall be deemed an offence. Upon conviction, the offender shall be subject to punishable imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, and also liable to pay a fine, notwithstanding any appeal filed against the judgment.

The owner of a registered layout design shall be entitled to grant licenses conferring rights to use the protected design, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated within the license agreement. Such agreements may include provisions for royalty payments, duration of exclusivity, and geographical limitations, as deemed appropriate by the licensor. Assignment of ownership or licensing rights under this Act requires registration with the Layout Design Register, detailing the assignor, assignee, and scope of transfer. Any unauthorized reproduction, adaptation, or commercial exploitation of a layout design without proper authorization constitutes an infringement punishable imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or both. Furthermore, any person found guilty of knowingly facilitating such infringement shall also be liable for similar penalties as provided herein.

Where any proprietor of a registered trade mark institutes proceedings under this Act against any person for infringement, and such proceedings are ultimately determined in favour of the proprietor, it shall be permissible for the Court to order that the infringing party undergo punishable imprisonment for a term not exceeding one year, alongside payment of damages as assessed by the Court. Further, where a defendant alleges that the trade mark in question lacks distinctiveness or has become descriptive through common usage, and presents credible evidence supporting such claim, the proprietor shall be obligated to demonstrate the continued recognition of their variety shall registered mark within relevant consumer segments. Any appeal against an order imposing imprisonment may be made to the appellate forum as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, an exclusive licensee is defined as a person to whom copyright in respect of a work has been exclusively assigned under a written agreement, or who is party to a license which confers upon them all rights normally enjoyed by the owner of copyright in that work, subject to any conditions specified therein. Such exclusivity shall extend to all acts permitted under this Act which are not expressly reserved for the assignor or licensor. An exclusive licensee shall be deemed to possess such title and interest as would accrue to an assignee had the copyright been formally assigned. Provided that nothing herein shall prevent the assignor from exercising rights not explicitly excluded by the license agreement.

For the purposes of registration under this Act, an exclusive licensee shall be deemed to possess rights equivalent to those held by the copyright owner in respect of works registered in their name. Where a work is assigned to another party but such assignment includes a grant of an exclusive license, the Registrar may, upon application and subject to verification of the terms of assignment, register the work with both the assignor and the exclusive licensee as joint owners, specifying the nature and extent of the license granted. Any subsequent alteration or transfer of such exclusive license shall be notified to the Registrar within thirty days; failure to do so may render the registration liable for review. The rights conferred upon an exclusive licensee are subject to any prior existing copyright subsisting under this Act.

Where an exclusive licensee is granted rights under this Act in respect of copyright in any work, such licensee shall be entitled to institute proceedings for infringement relating to those rights as if they were the owner of the copyright. Provided that, where the ownership of the copyright remains with a party other than the exclusive licensee, such original owner shall retain the right to grant further licenses or assignments concerning aspects of the work not explicitly covered by the terms of the exclusive license agreement. Any action brought by an exclusive licensee for infringement may seek remedies including injunctions, damages, and delivery up of infringing copies, subject to demonstrating prejudice resulting directly from the alleged infringement. The court shall consider the terms of the underlying copyright agreement when determining the scope of the exclusive licensee’s rights and remedies available under this Act.

Where an exclusive licensee is granted rights under this Act in respect of copyright in any work, such licensee shall be entitled to exercise all powers conferred upon the owner of copyright therein, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated in the license agreement. Any assignment or transfer of right undertaken by the exclusive licensee shall require prior written notification to the assignor, detailing the scope and duration of the proposed transfer. Failure to provide such notification may render the assignee liable for damages as determined by a civil court. The Registrar shall maintain a public record of all licenses creating an exclusive license, accessible upon application and payment of prescribed fees. Any party aggrieved by actions taken by an exclusive licensee concerning the copyrighted work may file a complaint with the relevant jurisdictional authority, outlining the specific instances of alleged infringement or breach of contractual terms.

Where an exclusive licensee is granted rights under this Act pertaining to a copyrighted work, such license shall be deemed contractual in nature and subject to the terms stipulated therein. The licensor shall not, without express written consent from the exclusive licensee, grant further licenses or assignments that would diminish the scope of exclusivity previously conferred. Provided that, any action taken by the licensor which demonstrably prejudices the commercial exploitation of the work by the exclusive licensee may be challenged before a competent civil court. Furthermore, the exclusive licensee shall maintain detailed records pertaining to distribution and sales of the copyrighted work, accessible for inspection upon reasonable notice from the licensor, as provided herein. Failure to comply with these record-keeping requirements shall render the license subject to review and potential termination.

Where an exclusive licensee is granted rights under this Act relating to copyright in any work, such licensee shall be entitled to institute proceedings for infringement as if they were the owner of the copyright. Any act of reproduction, distribution, or adaptation of a work done without the authorization of the exclusive licensee, where such authorization would have been necessary had the copyright owner themselves acted, shall constitute an actionable infringement. The Court may, in determining damages for such infringement, consider the extent to which the licensee has exercised their rights and mitigated any losses suffered as a consequence of the infringing act. Failure by the grantor of the license to provide reasonable assistance to the exclusive licensee in enforcing these rights may render them liable to penalties as provided herein.

Where an exclusive licensee is granted rights under this Act pertaining to copyright in any work, such license shall be deemed an assignment of those specified rights for the duration and geographical scope expressly defined within the licensing agreement. The licensor shall retain no further power to grant conflicting licenses or assignments concerning the same rights during that period, subject to any provisions allowing for sub-licensing as stipulated by contract. Any transfer of ownership in the copyright work subsequent to the granting of an exclusive license shall be void unless it expressly incorporates and affirms the terms of the original license agreement. The exclusive licensee may enforce all rights granted under this Act against infringers, and remedies available to the copyright owner are also available to them. Provided that, termination clauses within licensing agreements shall be governed by principles of fairness and equity as determined by appropriate judicial forums.

Where an exclusive licensee is granted rights under this Act pertaining to copyrighted works, such license shall be deemed a contractual arrangement governed by principles of contract law, subject to the provisions herein relating to copyright infringement. Any dispute arising from the terms or conditions of said license, including but not limited to limitations on distribution territory or duration of exclusivity, may be referred for arbitration as provided under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act. The aggrieved party shall have recourse to judicial review of any arbitral award, specifically concerning questions of law pertaining to the scope of copyright ownership and the validity of the exclusive license itself. Further, a challenge to an exclusive licensee's actions alleging misuse of their rights may be brought before the relevant civil court, provided that such challenge does not constitute an infringement of the underlying copyright.

Where an exclusive licensee has been granted rights under this Act in respect of copyright in a work, any act performed without the license’s consent shall be deemed to constitute infringement. The Registrar may, upon receiving a duly completed international application form relating to such work, issue a certificate confirming the details of the exclusive licensee and the scope of their assigned rights as recorded therein. Failure to provide accurate information on the said form will render the licensee liable for penalties under this Act, including fines up to one million rupees and imprisonment for a term not less than two years. Furthermore, any party claiming damages for infringement must demonstrate prejudice arising directly from the unauthorized act.

Where an exclusive licensee is granted rights under this Act pertaining to copyright in a work, such license shall be deemed a contractual arrangement governed by principles of contract law, notwithstanding any provisions herein. The patentee transferring ownership of underlying technology essential for exercising those licensed rights may not subsequently assert claims that materially impede the exclusive licensee’s ability to exploit said copyright, subject to equitable considerations and bona fide commercial practices. Any dispute arising from actions taken by the patentee which demonstrably frustrate the intended scope of the license shall be referable to arbitration as provided herein, with costs determined at the arbitrator's discretion. The aggrieved party may appeal such an arbitral award to a court exercising ordinary original jurisdiction, demonstrating manifest error or perversity in the decision.

For the purposes of this Act, an exclusive licensee shall be deemed to possess all rights conferred upon the copyright holder in relation to a work, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated within the license agreement. Such license agreement must explicitly grant the licensee the power to enforce copyright against infringers as if they were the original proprietor. Where such license is granted, any action taken by the exclusive licensee under this Act shall be binding upon the grantor of the copyright, provided that the patent means patent relating to the underlying technology has been duly registered and remains in force.

For the purposes of this Act, a “Geographical Indication” means an indication of the origin of goods which is used to identify those goods as having specific qualities, characteristics or reputation, attributable to the geographical location from where they originate. The Geographical Indications Registry shall maintain a public register containing particulars of registered geographical indications and applications for registration thereof. Any person claiming rights in a geographical indication may apply under this Act for its registration, subject to fulfilling all conditions prescribed herein. An application for registration shall include details regarding the territory comprising the geographical area which it identifies, and evidence demonstrating the link between the goods and that origin.

An application for registration of a geographical indication shall be made to the Geographical Indications Registry in the prescribed form and shall contain particulars including the name of the geographical indication as it is proposed to be registered, a map of the area of its origin, details of the products or goods which originate from that area, and a statement of characteristics, qualities, and reputation attributable to the product. The applicant shall also provide evidence demonstrating that the quality, reputation, or other characteristic of the goods originates in the defined geographical area. Any person claiming an interest may oppose registration under this Act within the time specified; such opposition must be filed with the Geographical Indications Registry and state the grounds for objection as provided herein.

Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication shall be entitled to sue in a court of competent jurisdiction for relief relating to infringement under this Act. Such relief may include an injunction restraining any person from using or imitating the geographical indication, or any confusingly similar indicator, in relation to goods or services for which the geographical indication is registered. Furthermore, the proprietor may claim damages sustained by reason of such infringement, subject to limitations as provided herein regarding contributory liability and wilful misconduct on the part of the infringer. The Geographical Indications Registry shall maintain a record of all suits filed relating to registered geographical indications, accessible to the public upon request. Any appeal from an order or decision made under this Act concerning rights conferred by registration with the Geographical Indications Registry may be made to the appellate forum as prescribed.

Applications for registration of a geographical indication shall be made to the Geographical Indications Registry in the prescribed form and accompanied by the requisite fee. The application must clearly describe the goods or services for which the geographical indication is sought, along with details establishing its connection to the territory from which it originates. Any person claiming an interest in opposition to the registration may file a notice of opposition under this Act within the time specified. The Registry shall serve a copy of such notice on the applicant and provide them an opportunity to submit their response as provided herein. Upon receipt of the response, the Registry may proceed with an inquiry into the matter, affording all interested parties a chance to be heard. Decisions made by the Geographical Indications Registry are subject to appeal before the Appellate Board.

An application for registration of a geographical indication shall include particulars specifying the name of the geographical indication as it is proposed to be registered, a map of the area from which the goods originate, and a statement of any prior use of the said indication. The Registrar shall entertain an application only if the applicant satisfies the conditions stipulated under this Act regarding representation and domicile within India. Further, the geographical indication must relate to agricultural products, foodstuffs, wine or spirit, handicraft or manufactured articles as defined herein. Any opposition filed against a pending registration shall be considered by the Registrar based on grounds of deception or misrepresentation, provided that such opposition is lodged within the prescribed timeframe. The Geographical Indications Registry may require further documentation demonstrating continued adherence to quality standards.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the registration of a geographical indication or the revocation thereof, or any other matter provided herein, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. Failure to comply with prescribed procedures during application for registration shall render the application liable for rejection and subsequent penalties as determined by the Geographical Indications Registry. The Central Government may, subject to due process, impose a monetary penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees upon any individual or entity found guilty of using a registered geographical indication without authorization, or engaging in deceptive practices intended to mislead consumers regarding the origin of goods. Such penalties shall be recoverable as arrears of land revenue.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any registered proprietor of a geographical indication may grant non-exclusive licenses conferring the right to use the said indication on goods conforming to the standards as prescribed under this Act. Such license shall specify the territory in which and the period for which the licensee is authorized to use the geographical indication. Further, the registered proprietor may assign their rights relating to the geographical indication, including any pending applications or granted licenses, to another person with the prior approval of the Geographical Indications Registry. The assignee shall be subject to all obligations and liabilities incumbent upon the original registered proprietor as provided herein. Any transfer or assignment undertaken without such approval shall be deemed void. The Central Government may issue guidelines regarding royalty rates for licensing agreements pertaining to geographical indications registered under this Act.

An application for registration of a geographical indication shall be deemed to be refused if the Registrar has reason to believe that any interested party is likely to be misled or deceived regarding the origin of goods due to the use of such name. Any interested party aggrieved by an order of refusal made under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The Appellate Board shall consider whether the Registrar acted reasonably in forming the belief that misleading use occurred, taking into account evidence presented regarding established trade practices and mark use patterns associated with similar names. Decisions of the Geographical Indications Registry are subject to review by the Appellate Board as provided herein.

Any proprietor seeking to enforce rights conferred under this Act against any infringement shall file a suit in the District Court having jurisdiction over the local area where the alleged infringement has occurred or is likely to occur. The court shall have power to grant such remedies as are available under civil procedure code, including injunctions restraining further acts of infringement and orders for delivery up or destruction of goods bearing the protected geographical indication. Provided that a specification patent shall not be granted in respect of any process or method used in the production of goods associated with a registered geographical indication if such use is deemed to dilute the distinctiveness of said indication. Further, where an authorized user acts in violation of the conditions under which their usage was permitted, the Geographical Indications Registry may revoke that authorization and initiate proceedings for damages against them.

For the purposes of this Act, an "Integrated Circuit" shall mean a set of one or more layers comprising active and passive components which have been fixed thereto irreversibly; it includes elements such as interconnections providing electrical connections between said components and insulation materials separating them. An Integrated Circuit may be embodied in semiconductor material, insulating material, ceramic material or any combination thereof. The term "Integrated Circuit" shall not include a layout-design that is solely for the purpose of packaging an Integrated Circuit, nor does it encompass a three-dimensional structure unless such structure incorporates elements as defined herein and functions as a complete Integrated Circuit.

An application for registration of an Integrated Circuit layout-design shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the drawings and documentation relating to the fabrication process, detailing the mask works employed. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further particulars concerning the originality of the design and its conformity with established industry standards, provided that such requirements are reasonable and do not unduly delay the registration process. Where an Integrated Circuit incorporates elements derived from previously registered layout-designs, a statement disclosing these dependencies must be submitted alongside the application. The Registrar shall maintain a register of all applications received under this Act, noting the date of receipt and any objections raised by third parties claiming prior rights in similar designs.

Where any person unlawfully makes, uses, imports, or offers to sell an Integrated Circuit infringing upon the registered layout-design, the owner shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief restraining such acts. Compensation for loss suffered by the owner due to the infringement may be awarded by the competent court, taking into account the extent of damage and unjust enrichment derived from the infringing activity. The amount of compensation shall not exceed a sum equivalent to three times the prevailing market value of the Integrated Circuit at the time of the infringement, or where such value cannot be ascertained, the cost of production plus reasonable royalties. Provided that, in determining damages, the court may consider evidence demonstrating contributory infringement and willful blindness on the part of any party involved under this Act.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, any person alleging infringement of a registered Integrated Circuit layout-design may file a complaint before the Commercial Court having jurisdiction over the place where the alleged infringing act was committed, or where the cause of action arose. The complainant shall specify in the complaint the particulars of the registration certificate of the Integrated Circuit layout-design and details of the alleged infringing activity. Upon receipt of such complaint, the Commercial Court may issue interim orders restraining the defendant from continuing the infringing activity pending disposal of the suit, provided that it is satisfied that irreparable injury would be caused to the complainant if the order is not made. The court shall also have power to direct the defendant to provide an account of sales and profits derived from the alleged infringement. Any party aggrieved by any order passed under this Act may appeal to the appellate forum as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, an Integrated Circuit shall be deemed to be protected if it incorporates original features which reveal the author's intellectual conception and are fixed therein. Protection under this Act shall not extend to any Integrated Circuit that is substantially similar to an earlier Integrated Circuit already registered, unless such similarity arises directly from reverse engineering conducted in compliance with prescribed conditions. The right of layout-design protection conferred by this Act may be assigned or licensed, provided that the terms of assignment or license are documented and readily accessible for inspection as per regulations. Any person desiring to utilize a protected Integrated Circuit for commercial purposes shall obtain prior authorization from the registered proprietor, subject to exceptions outlined herein regarding analysis for defensive purposes.

Any person who, without authorization from the registered proprietor of an Integrated Circuit layout-design, makes, imports, distributes, sells, displays or offers for sale any infringing copy shall be liable to pay damages equivalent to a sum equal to ten times the cost of the infringing act. Where such infringement is committed by an employee or agent, the employer or principal shall also be deemed guilty and subject to similar penalties as provided herein. The Central Government may, upon receiving a complaint from the registered proprietor, issue an injunction restraining any person found to be engaged in activities constituting infringement under this Act. Failure to comply with such an order shall render the offender liable for imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, and a fine that may extend to one million rupees.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder, a registered proprietor of an Integrated Circuit may grant a license conferring specific rights relating to the reproduction, adaptation, or commercial use of their layout design. Such licenses shall be documented in writing and specify the duration, geographical scope, and permitted field of use. Assignment of ownership of an Integrated Circuit layout-design is permissible only through a written instrument executed by the registered proprietor, provided that any such assignment includes a detailed description identifying the specific Integrated Circuit involved. Further, where a license or assignment incorporates confidential information pertaining to manufacturing processes, the assignee or licensee shall be bound by confidentiality agreements as stipulated within the licensing document and subject to remedies available under this Act for breach of contract. The Registrar may require submission of copies of such licenses and assignments for record purposes.

Where any person alleges that another has infringed upon their registered Integrated Circuit layout-design, such allegation shall be made by way of a suit for permanent injunction and damages. The defendant may counter with a claim that the alleged infringement falls within the permissible scope of experimental use, provided that they demonstrate a non-commercial purpose and a lack of unfair competition. Further, it shall be incumbent upon the plaintiff to establish, through expert testimony and documentary evidence, that the defendant’s layout-design substantially replicates protected elements of their registered Integrated Circuit. The court may order an inspection of relevant manufacturing processes subject to reasonable safeguards for confidential information, as provided herein. Appeals against such orders or findings concerning infringement may be made to the High Court within ninety days.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder, an Integrated Circuit shall be deemed to include within its definition any pictorial representation, whether fixed or movable, embodying a design that is substantially similar to a dramatic work. Any person alleging infringement of layout-design rights relating to such an Integrated Circuit may file a complaint with the competent authority specified under this Act, setting forth particulars of the alleged infringement and providing evidence demonstrating unauthorized reproduction or adaptation. The authority shall serve notice upon the accused party, affording them a reasonable opportunity to submit their response within sixty days from the date of service. Upon review of the complaint and the response, if any, the authority may order interim relief including an injunction restraining further acts of infringement pending final determination. Appeals against orders passed by the authority are subject to judicial review as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, a “new invention” shall mean an invention which is not previously known to the public, either by written or oral description or by use or in any other way. An invention shall be deemed new if, at the date of filing of the patent application, it does not involve any element disclosed in the prior art. Prior art includes information that has been made available to the public anywhere in the world, by any means, before the date of filing of the patent application as provided herein. Subject to this, a “new invention” may also include an improvement of an existing process or machine, so long as such improvement results in a technical effect and is not obvious to a person skilled in the art.

An application for registration of a new invention shall be accompanied by a declaration, signed by the applicant or their authorized agent, attesting to the novelty and originality of the claimed subject matter. The declaration must specifically identify each aspect of the invention considered a new invention under this Act. Where an inventor is not the first to file the patent application, the declaration shall also disclose the details of any prior disclosures made regarding the invention, including dates, locations, and recipients. Failure to provide a complete and accurate declaration may render the registration void. The Controller General may require further clarification or documentation pertaining to the inventive step at any stage during examination.

Where any person considers that another has infringed his patent, he may institute proceedings for relief under this Act. Such proceedings shall be commenced within three years from the date on which the infringement is reasonably suspected to have taken place. The remedies available to the patentee include an injunction restraining the infringing party from further acts of infringement and damages sustained by the patentee as a consequence thereof. It is provided that, in determining the amount of damages, due account shall be taken of any benefit accruing to the infringer which does not exceed what is reasonable. For the purposes of establishing novelty, it shall be conclusively presumed that a published document disclosing information relevant to assessing whether an invention constitutes a *new invention* was available to the public prior to the date of filing unless evidence to the contrary is presented by the defendant.

An application for a patent shall be deemed to disclose and take into consideration all prior publications, whether in India or elsewhere, available to the public before the date of filing. The determination of novelty and inventive step under this Act shall proceed upon an assessment of such prior art, considering the totality of the information disclosed therein. An objection may be raised by any person interested in the matter regarding the patentability of a claimed invention based on grounds of lack of novelty or absence of an inventive step. Such objections must be filed within three months from the date of publication of the application under this Act. The Controller shall provide the applicant with an opportunity to respond to such objections, and may require further clarification or experimental data demonstrating the technical advancement constituting a new invention.

An application for a patent shall be deemed to disclose and describe an invention sufficiently if it details the matter worked upon, the process employed, or the result achieved, provided that such disclosure enables a person ordinarily skilled in the relevant field to reproduce the said invention without undue experimentation. For the purposes of determining novelty, any prior publication or use anywhere in the world shall be considered for assessing whether the claimed invention constitutes a *new invention*. An applicant seeking patent protection must demonstrate that the invention is not obvious in view of the existing body of technical knowledge and satisfies the criteria outlined herein regarding industrial applicability. The Controller may require further clarification or experimental data to ascertain compliance with these stipulations, subject to procedural fairness as provided under this Act.

An application for a patent shall be deemed invalid if it is established, through evidence presented before the Controller, that the claimed invention was previously disclosed in a publicly accessible manner more than twelve months prior to the date of filing. Any party aggrieved by a grant of patent may institute civil proceedings seeking revocation, demonstrating under this Act that the subject matter does not constitute a new invention or lacks novelty. Upon finding of invalidity, the Controller shall order forfeiture of the patent and impose a penalty of no less than five hundred thousand rupees payable to the State exchequer. Repeated offences shall attract enhanced penalties and potential criminal prosecution for fraudulent misrepresentation.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any patentee may grant exclusive licenses under the patent, either for the whole term thereof or for part of it, and may also grant assignments of the patent, whether absolute or conditional. Such license or assignment shall be valid only if executed in the prescribed manner and registered with the Controller. Where a license is granted which purports to assign the benefit of the patent, but does not expressly declare that it is an assignment, the Controller may require such declaration to be made before registering the document. The right to grant licenses and assignments relating to a new invention shall vest in the patentee alone, unless otherwise agreed upon through a written contract with the government or any public institution engaged in research and development activities. Any subsequent assignee of a patent shall hold all rights pertaining thereto as if he were the original patentee.

For the purposes of determining novelty under this Act, any disclosure made prior to the date of filing of a patent application shall be disregarded if it is established by the applicant that such disclosure resulted from an act of independent research undertaken solely by the inventor or inventors and without access to information pertaining to the invention. It shall be presumed, absent evidence to the contrary presented by the aggrieved party, that any publication arising directly from such independent research was not intended to disclose the underlying new invention. The Controller may, upon review of documentary evidence and expert testimony, determine whether the claimed inventive step constitutes a genuine technical advance or is merely an obvious modification of existing knowledge, subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

An application for registration of an application registration mark shall be deemed to disclose the nature of the goods or services associated with said mark. Where the Controller is satisfied, upon examination, that the mark as applied for is not registrable under this Act, but that the invention disclosed within the supporting documentation relating to its use constitutes a new invention, the applicant may be directed to amend the application to reflect only the inventive aspects of the process or product. Such amendment shall not prejudice any prior rights held by third parties. The Controller may require further clarification regarding the technical details underpinning the claimed novelty and industrial applicability, provided that such requests are reasonable and do not unduly delay processing.

Where an application for patent relating to a new invention is pending before the Controller, any party aggrieved by a decision of the Controller concerning such application may appeal to the Appellate Board as provided herein. The appellant shall be entitled to seek interim relief from the Appellate Board restraining the Controller from proceeding further with the examination or adjudication of the matter until the disposal of the appeal; subject to just cause shown and upon furnishing security satisfactory to the Appellate Board. Further, where a patent has been granted but is under challenge through an appeal concerning its validity, the grant shall be deemed to be *dies pending proceeding* for all purposes relating to enforcement of the patent against any person other than the appellant until final determination by the Appellate Board; provided that the Controller may, upon application and after hearing affected parties, permit such enforcement.

An application for a patent shall be deemed invalid if it is shown, under this Act, that the claimed invention was previously described in a published layout design commercially exploited within India. The Controller General may, upon receiving an objection from any interested party regarding prior publication of a layout design, direct the applicant to submit evidence demonstrating that the invention satisfies the criteria for a new invention as provided herein. Such evidence shall include, but not be limited to, detailed technical specifications and documentation establishing the novelty and non-obviousness of the claimed subject matter. The objection may be overruled if the applicant demonstrates that the layout design was merely incidental to the commercial exploitation of another product and did not disclose all elements essential to understanding the invention. Failure to comply with this direction shall render the application liable for rejection.

An application for a patent shall be deemed invalid if it is established, beyond reasonable doubt, that the claimed invention was disclosed in a publicly accessible manner prior to the date patent. For purposes of determining novelty, any written description, use, exhibition, or other form of communication relating to the alleged new invention occurring before such date patent will be considered anticipatory disclosure. Provided that, if the applicant can demonstrate diligent efforts were undertaken to secure protection for the invention in a foreign jurisdiction prior to the aforementioned public disclosure, and those efforts were ultimately unsuccessful due to circumstances beyond their reasonable control, the application may proceed subject to further scrutiny by the Controller. The burden of proving such diligence rests entirely upon the applicant.

For the purposes of this Act, “patent of addition” shall mean a subsequent patent granted to a patentee for an invention which is not disclosed in the first mentioned patent, but which is connected therewith, and relates to the subject matter of the original invention. Such patent of addition may be granted only if the invention claimed therein does not involve the same or substantially similar matter as already covered by the said original patent. The grant of a patent of addition shall be subject to the conditions prescribed under this Act for obtaining a patent, provided that the application for such patent clearly indicates its relationship with the earlier patent.

An application for a patent of addition may be filed by any person who is entitled to apply for and obtain a patent under this Act, provided that the invention claimed in such application relates to the subject matter of an existing patent granted to him or her. The applicant shall disclose the connection between the new invention and the invention disclosed in the parent patent, demonstrating how the former builds upon or improves the latter. Further, the claims of the patent of addition must clearly define the inventive step that distinguishes it from the parent patent; otherwise, the application may be rejected. Subject to fulfilling these requirements, a patent of addition shall confer all rights and privileges as are granted under this Act for patents generally.

Where an inventor, having already obtained a patent under this Act, discovers that the invention for which the original patent was granted includes further inventions not claimed in the initial specification, the controller may grant a patent of addition relating to such new matter. The application for a patent of addition shall be filed within three years from the date of grant of the first patent and shall comply with all requirements applicable to an original patent application, subject to any modifications prescribed herein. Any person aggrieved by a decision granting or refusing a patent of addition may appeal under this Act. Further, the rights conferred by a patent of addition are not assignable independently of the original patent unless the controller permits it in writing, provided that such permission is only granted where public interest so warrants and after due consideration of any opposition filed.

An application for a patent of addition may be filed by any person who is entitled to apply for and obtain a patent under this Act, provided that the subject matter of such additional patent relates to the invention claimed in the patent already granted. The applicant shall disclose in his application the particulars of the patent already granted and clearly define the relationship between the inventions claimed in the two patents. Upon receiving an application for a patent of addition, the Controller may require the applicant to furnish further information or clarification regarding the connection between the original invention and the subject matter of the additional patent. The grant of a patent of addition shall not extend to any matter which was disclosed or described in the specification of the parent patent. Any opposition proceedings relating to the patent of addition shall be conducted as provided herein, with due consideration given to the prior art pertaining to both inventions.

An applicant seeking a patent of addition shall demonstrate that the invention for which the additional protection is claimed is not merely an obvious variation of the invention disclosed in the original patent. The application for such a patent must clearly and specifically describe the relationship between the new matter and the subject matter of the prior patent, establishing dependence and novelty as provided herein. Further, the applicant shall satisfy the Controller that the claims defining the additional invention are supported by the description and drawings presented. Subject to compliance with these requirements, and where the Controller is satisfied that the addition does not effectively amount to a new invention distinct from the original subject matter, a patent of addition may be granted for a term extending from the date of grant of the original patent.

Where an invention relates to a method or process, and such method or process is capable of being applied to the manufacture of a substance by a chemical or biochemical process, the Controller may grant a patent of addition for the substance so manufactured, provided that the application for the patent of addition is filed within thirty-six months from the date of first filing of the related application. Any person aggrieved by an order granting or refusing a patent of addition may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. Failure to comply with this provision shall render the appellant liable to a penalty not exceeding one thousand rupees for each day of default, subject to a maximum limit of ten thousand rupees.

Where the subject matter of an invention claimed in a patent of addition relates to improvements made to an invention already patented, or for which a patent application is pending, the patentee shall be entitled to grant licenses and assign such patent of addition as if it were an original patent. Any license granted under this provision may include provisions relating to royalty payments based on sales of both the original invention and the improved invention, subject to regulations prescribed by the Controller. The assignment of a patent of addition shall not affect any rights or obligations arising from the underlying patent or pending application; provided that the assignee shall be bound by all terms and conditions applicable to the original patentee under this Act. Further, where an assignment includes the right to exploit the invention disclosed in both the original patent and the patent of addition, the assignor warrants that they possess full authority to effectuate such transfer as provided herein.

Where an application for a patent of addition is filed, the Controller shall consider whether the invention claimed therein relates to the subject matter of the original patent or constitutes an improvement thereto, and if not, may reject the application. An appeal lies from any order rejecting such an application under this Act, and the Appellate Board shall determine whether the invention in question falls within the scope of section 3, relating to inventive step, considering the prior art as it existed at the date of filing of both the original patent and the application for the patent of addition. The applicant bears the burden of demonstrating a clear nexus between the inventions; failure to do so shall be grounds for dismissal, notwithstanding any argument regarding obviousness presented by the respondent.

For the purposes of this Act, “patent of addition” shall mean a patent granted for an invention which is not itself an invention but includes subject matter disclosed in an earlier patent. Such patent of addition may be granted only if the additional subject matter would, if applied for separately, satisfy the criteria for patentability under this Act. The application for a patent of addition shall specify the original patent and clearly define the relationship between the inventions claimed therein and the invention as defined in the application. An entry register variety arising from research conducted during the prosecution of either the original or subsequent patent may be recorded accordingly.

Where an invention relates to a method or process, and a patentee seeks to claim improvements thereto by way of a patent of addition, such patent shall be subject to stricter scrutiny regarding novelty and inventive step. The Controller may require evidence demonstrating that the claimed improvement significantly enhances the original invention’s utility or functionality; failure to provide satisfactory proof will result in rejection. Any infringement action arising from use of either the primary invention or the patent of addition shall be actionable as a single cause of action, attracting enhanced penalties under this Act. Further, any mark uses registered in connection with products manufactured using processes covered by a patent of addition are deemed infringing if they mislead consumers regarding technological origin and may incur substantial damages.

For the purposes of this Act, "permitted use" with respect to a registered trademark signifies the application of the mark upon goods or services as authorized under this Act. Such authorization may be granted through registration as a registered user, subject to conditions stipulated therein. A permitted use shall not extend beyond the scope of goods or services specified in the registered user’s certificate; any deviation from such specification constitutes unauthorized exploitation and is actionable accordingly. Further, a permitted use does not confer upon the registered user any right to challenge the validity of the trademark itself, as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any proprietor of a registered trade mark may grant a license for permitted use of their trademark to another person, hereinafter referred to as a “registered user.” Such registration as a registered user shall be subject to conditions specified by the Trade Marks Registry and published in the Trade Marks Journal. The application for registration as a registered user must detail the geographical area and goods or services concerning which the permitted use is sought. Further, the proprietor of the trade mark may specify limitations on the quality control measures maintained by the registered user during their period of permitted use. Any alteration to the scope of permitted use requires prior approval from the Trade Marks Registry and notification to all interested parties as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, nothing shall prevent the registration of a trade mark if it is used as honestly intended to describe the quality or other characteristics of any goods or services. Where a proprietor of a registered trade mark has granted consent for another person’s use of the mark, that subsequent user shall be deemed a registered user with rights equivalent to those held by the original proprietor. The proprietor may revoke such consent at any time, provided that reasonable notice is given to the affected party. Upon revocation, the permitted use shall cease immediately and all advertising materials bearing the mark must be withdrawn from circulation within thirty days. Any person continuing such use after this period shall be liable for damages to the registered proprietor. Further, remedies under this Act are available against any act of passing off arising from the continued unauthorized use following consent revocation.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any proprietor of a registered trade mark may grant a license for use thereof, and such license shall be deemed to be a registration of a “permitted use” as provided herein. The application for registration of a permitted use shall be made in Form TM-P and shall specify the goods or services in relation to which the use is authorized, along with the territory within which such use is permissible. Upon receipt of an application, the Trade Marks Registry shall publish a notice thereof in the Trade Marks Journal. Any person may file representations against the registration of the permitted use under this Act, citing grounds for objection relating to likelihood of confusion or dilution of the original mark. The Registrar shall consider any such representations and may require further information from the applicant or objector before making a determination.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, a proprietor of a registered trade mark may grant registration as a registered user to any person who, prior to the date of application for such registration, was using the trade mark, or an identical one, under and in accordance with conditions expressly approved by the proprietor. Such approval shall be evidenced by a written agreement specifying the goods or services in relation to which the use is permitted, the geographical area of such use, and the duration thereof. The registered user shall not, without express consent from the trade mark proprietor, extend the scope of the permitted use beyond that initially agreed upon. Any alteration to the nature of the goods or services used under the registration requires prior notification and approval by the proprietor, failing which the registration may be revoked as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any proprietor of a registered trademark shall be deemed to have assigned exclusively to a registered user the right to apply the trademark for permitted use in accordance with the terms of registration. Any person who, without authorization from the proprietor or the registered user, uses an identical or deceptively similar mark on identical or closely related goods or services to those for which the trademark is registered shall be liable for damages and subject to a penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees. The Intellectual Property Appellate Board may issue injunctions restraining such unauthorized use and order the seizure and destruction of infringing materials. Further, any false representation concerning permitted use constitutes an offence punishable with imprisonment and a fine.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any proprietor of a registered trade mark may grant a license for the permitted use of their trademark to another party, either generally throughout India or limited to a specific territory as defined within the license agreement. Such licenses shall be assignable by the grantor, provided that prior written consent of the licensee is obtained unless the license explicitly states otherwise. Where a license is assigned, all rights and obligations pertaining to the permitted use remain with the assignee. The proprietor may specify conditions regarding quality control or other standards relating to goods or services bearing the trademark under this permitted use, as detailed in the licensing agreement. Any alteration of the registered trade mark during the term of a license shall require the prior consent of both the grantor and the licensee, safeguarding their respective interests as provided herein.

Notwithstanding anything contained herein, the Registrar may, upon application made by any person claiming to be engaged in an activity that utilizes a similar mark to a registered trademark, and demonstrating substantial reliance on prior use predating registration, entertain a request for clarification regarding the scope of permitted use. Such applications shall be accompanied by evidence substantiating the claimant’s continuous and bona fide engagement with the relevant goods or services. The Registrar shall provide an opportunity for the trade mark proprietor to submit objections, which may include arguments asserting impairment of distinctiveness or likelihood of confusion. Any order issued by the Registrar defining permitted use is subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order.

Where an owner of a registered trade mark has granted a license for use of the mark, and such license is subsequently terminated, any continued use of the trade mark by the former licensee shall be deemed an infringement unless such use constitutes a permitted use as defined under this Act. A proprietor may apply to the Registrar seeking clarification regarding whether a particular instance of post-termination usage qualifies as a permitted use; provided that the application must demonstrate reasonable belief that the use falls within an exception or prior contractual agreement. The Registrar shall decide, after affording both the former licensee and the trade mark owner an opportunity for hearing, whether the continued use is permissible. Any party aggrieved by the decision of the Registrar may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board as provided herein.

A trade mark shall be deemed to be distinctive if, in determining trade mark registrability, it possesses inherent distinctiveness or has acquired distinctiveness through use, subject to the provisions of this Act. For the purposes of this determination, ‘inherent distinctiveness’ means that the sign is capable of distinguishing goods or services of one undertaking from those of other undertakings, irrespective of any period of use. A mark consisting exclusively of a word or words having no trade significance shall not be considered inherently distinctive unless it has acquired such distinctiveness through reputation and continuous use as provided herein.

An application for the registration of a trade mark shall be deemed to be allowable subject to satisfying the requirements under this Act and the Regulations framed thereunder. The Registrar may, upon receiving an objection from any person claiming such right or interest as is provided herein, direct that the hearing be held before the Trade Marks Registry. Determining trade marks involves consideration of distinctiveness, acquired through use or inherent nature, and whether it conflicts with existing registered marks or pending applications. Any representation of a mark which does not clearly indicate its intended function shall be deemed descriptive and therefore ineligible for registration unless it has acquired distinctiveness through extensive use. The applicant shall furnish such evidence as the Registrar may require to substantiate claims of prior usage.

A registered trade mark shall confer upon the proprietor thereof the exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered and any other goods or services, provided that such user does not constitute a permitted use under this Act. Any person who, without due cause or consent of the proprietor, uses a trade mark identical or confusingly similar to a registered trade mark shall be liable for damages, including loss of profits and royalties. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint from any interested party, investigate allegations of such infringement and issue injunctions restraining further use of the infringing mark. Determining trade mark distinctiveness shall consider all relevant factors, including acquired reputation and consumer perception. Further, an owner seeking to enforce their rights under this Act must demonstrate that the alleged infringer had knowledge of the registered trade mark.

An application for the registration of a trade mark may be made by any person claiming to be the proprietor of the trade mark and including citizens or bodies corporate residing outside India, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. The Registrar shall examine each application in accordance with the provisions herein relating to distinctiveness and absolute grounds for refusal. Where an applicant demonstrates prior use of a sign within the territory of India, even without formal registration, that applicant may claim recognition trade mark status under this Act. Such recognition shall grant certain rights equivalent to those afforded registered proprietors, provided that evidence of continuous use is submitted periodically as required by the Registrar. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating such prior usage.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person owning a registered trade mark may grant a license to use such trade mark, specifying the goods or services in relation to which the use is permitted, and the geographical area covered by the license. Such licenses may be granted for a term not exceeding the remaining period of protection of the trade mark, provided that the terms of the license are clearly defined within a written agreement executed between the licensor and licensee. Further, any assignment of a registered trade mark shall include an explicit declaration regarding any existing licenses attached to the recognition trade mark, detailing their scope and duration. The assignee shall be deemed to succeed to all rights and obligations under such licenses. Any alteration or modification to these licensed terms requires prior written consent from both the original licensor and the licensee, as provided herein.

An erasure order injunction shall be granted by a competent court where a registered trade mark is found to have been obtained through fraudulent means, including but not limited to misrepresentation concerning the use or reputation of the mark, or suppression of material facts during registration proceedings. Such an injunction may restrain any person from using, advertising, or otherwise exploiting the infringing trade mark and shall include provisions for the erasure of all representations of the mark from public display, subject to a reasoned order specifying the duration and scope of such erasure. The court may also award compensation to aggrieved parties as provided herein.

Where a trade mark is ordered to be erased under this Act, the Registrar may, subject to appeal as provided herein, issue an injunction restraining any person from using, in relation to goods or services identical or similar to those in respect of which the trade mark was registered, any sign that is substantially identical with the mark so erased. Such injunction shall remain in force for a period determined by the court, taking into consideration the extent of public association between the erased mark and the applicant for registration. Provided that, where the erasure order arises from rectification proceedings initiated by the proprietor of an earlier trade mark, the Registrar may grant interim relief pending determination of the appeal against the erasure order injunction.

Where a trade mark is ordered to be erased under this Act, the Intellectual Property Appellate Board may, subject to appeal to the High Court, grant an interim injunction restraining the proprietor of the trade mark from using the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it was registered pending determination of the erasure order. Such injunction shall remain in force until the final disposal of the matter by the appellate board or the high court. Provided that where the use of the trade mark is likely to cause confusion amongst, or detriment to, consumers, the Board may grant a permanent injunction prohibiting such use irrespective of the outcome of the erasure proceedings. The proprietor aggrieved by an erasure order injunction may apply for modification or vacation of the injunction as provided herein.

Where a trade mark is ordered to be erased under this Act, the Intellectual Property Appellate Board may, subject to appeal, issue an interim injunction restraining the defendant from using the impugned sign pending determination of the erasure order. Such injunction shall remain in force for a period not exceeding six months or such further time as the Appellate Board deems appropriate, provided that the plaintiff demonstrates ongoing and substantial likelihood of confusion amongst consumers. Any party violating such interim injunction shall be guilty of contempt of court and liable to a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees and may also face imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year. The Appellate Board may, at any time, modify or discharge this erasure order injunction.

Where a trade mark is ordered to be erased under this Act following a rectification action, the aggrieved party may appeal such erasure order to the Appellate Intellectual Property Tribunal within sixty days from the date of service of the order.
