Any proprietor seeking registration of a geographical indication shall be deemed to hold exclusive rights over the use of such indication for goods corresponding to the description in the application, subject to any prior usage lawfully established under this Act. Where an infringement of these rights is proven before a competent authority, the infringing party may be ordered to cease all infringing activities and account for profits derived therefrom. Furthermore, where a person is convicted of knowingly using a registered geographical indication without authorization, or engaging in deceptive practices intended to mislead consumers regarding the origin of goods, the court convicting such individual may direct a forfeiture directed conviction, whereby any assets acquired through the infringing activity are liable to be seized and appropriated for the benefit of affected producers within the defined geographical area.

Where a proprietor institutes proceedings against any person for infringement of a geographical indication registered under this Act and subsequently obtains a decree establishing such infringement, the Court shall order the infringer to pay damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the registered proprietor. Provided that, where the infringing activity is found to be undertaken with the express intent to deceive or mislead consumers regarding the origin of goods, the Court may direct a forfeiture directed conviction, wherein all profits derived from the infringing sales are ordered to be remitted to a fund established for the benefit of producers within the geographical indication’s territory. Further, subject to appeal under this Act, any order relating to damages or forfeiture is binding on all parties involved in the proceedings and shall be enforceable as per the Code of Civil Procedure. The Registrar may issue guidelines regarding assessment of losses for determining appropriate damage awards.

Where any proprietor institutes proceedings against a person alleging infringement of a geographical indication as provided herein, and such proceedings result in a judgment finding no infringement having occurred, the proprietor shall be liable to pay costs incurred by the alleged infringer. However, where subsequent evidence arises demonstrating that the proprietor knowingly presented false information or engaged in deceptive practices during those initial proceedings, the court may, upon application by the respondent, direct a forfeiture directed conviction of any profits derived from the sale of goods bearing the registered geographical indication since the commencement of the prior litigation. This power shall be exercised judiciously, subject to considerations of proportionality and fairness to both parties, and only after affording the proprietor an opportunity for rebuttal.

Where a registered Geographical Indication is found to be used in relation to goods not conforming to the standards of quality, reputation, or other characteristics as defined in the registration, and such use constitutes an infringement under this Act, the court convicting the offender may, subject to appeal, direct a forfeiture to the Registering Proprietor of any profits derived from that infringing activity. The Registrar, upon receiving a court registrar application detailing the circumstances of such conviction and outlining the proposed forfeiture, shall verify the accuracy of the information presented and notify all interested parties as provided herein. Any party aggrieved by the proposed forfeiture may submit objections within thirty days of the notification. Following consideration of any objections received, the Registrar shall report his findings to the court for final determination regarding the extent of the forfeiture directed conviction.

A *variety registered act* shall be deemed to occur when any person, other than the registered breeder or their authorized agent, undertakes activities relating to the commercial exploitation of a plant variety for which registration has been granted under this Act. Such activities include, but are not limited to, propagation, sale, distribution, and marketing of seeds or planting material derived from the protected variety. The right to prevent a *variety registered act* is subject to limitations as provided herein regarding farmers’ rights to save, re-sow, and exchange seed. Any infringement of these exclusive rights may be actionable under this Act, with remedies including injunctions and damages, as determined by an appropriate forum.

An application for registration as a variety registered act shall be accompanied by detailed documentation pertaining to its lineage, morphological characteristics, and any observed disease resistance. The applicant shall furnish comprehensive data demonstrating distinctness from existing varieties, including tabular comparisons and photographic evidence conforming to standards prescribed by the Authority. Further particulars concerning the method of propagation employed and anticipated yield potential must also be included. Where the variety incorporates traits derived from multiple sources, a full accounting of such contributions is required, subject to verification by the Examining Committee. The applicant shall declare whether any intellectual property rights, including patents or plant breeder’s rights in other jurisdictions, are associated with the registered act.

Subject to other provisions of this Act, any person aggrieved by an order relating to a variety registered act may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appellate Board shall consider all relevant evidence and arguments presented by the appellant and the respondent, including expert testimony where necessary, and may affirm, modify, or reverse the original order. Where the appellate authority finds that a person has acted in contravention of provisions relating to farmers' rights concerning saved seed, they shall be liable for damages as determined by the Board, taking into account the extent of infringement and any profits made thereby. The Central Government may issue guidelines regarding procedures for assessing such damages. Further, an appeal from an order of the Appellate Board lies to the High Court within a period of ninety days.

An application for registration as a variety registered act shall be accompanied by such particulars and documentation concerning the novelty, distinctiveness, stability and uniformity of the variety as the Authority may prescribe. The applicant shall furnish details regarding the method of propagation employed, including whether it is through seeds or vegetative means, and provide samples representative of the variety’s characteristics for examination. Upon receipt of an application, the Authority shall publish a notification inviting objections from any person having knowledge relating to the variety. Any objection received within the prescribed period shall be duly considered by the Examining Committee. The Central Government may, after due inquiry, direct that certain technical data pertaining to the variety remain confidential in the interest of public order or security.

Subject to compliance with all applicable regulations under this Act, any person seeking registration of a plant variety shall submit detailed documentation pertaining to its lineage and morphological characteristics. The application for a variety registered act must include evidence demonstrating that the proposed variety possesses distinctiveness from existing varieties, as determined by established testing procedures. Furthermore, the applicant shall provide an undertaking guaranteeing adherence to bio-containment protocols if genetically modified techniques were employed in the development of the plant variety. Any alteration to the documented characteristics following registration requires prior approval from the Authority and may necessitate a reevaluation of the variety's distinctiveness. The Central Government may, after due inquiry, revoke a certificate of registration if it finds that the applicant acted fraudulently or misrepresented information during the application process.

Any person who, without authorization from the registered owner of a variety registered act, produces, sells, markets, distributes, imports or exports such variety shall be liable to pay damages as determined by the Authority. The amount of damages shall not be less than fifty thousand rupees nor more than two hundred and fifty thousand rupees for each instance of infringement. Further, any person found guilty of contravention under this Act may also face prosecution before a criminal court, where they may be subject to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or both, as deemed appropriate by the court. The Authority shall have power to issue injunctions restraining further acts of infringement.

Subject to appeal to the Appellate Board, any person aggrieved by an order refusing registration of a plant variety under this Act may apply for review within sixty days from the date of communication of such order. The application shall state the grounds on which the applicant challenges the decision and shall be accompanied by all relevant documents substantiating the claim. Upon receipt of such an application, the Authority shall afford the original petitioner an opportunity to file a written response, after which a reasoned order either affirming or reversing the initial determination shall be issued. A successful challenge resulting in registration constitutes a *variety registered act*, entitling the applicant to all rights and privileges as if initially granted registration.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder, a variety registered act shall be deemed valid upon successful completion of the examination process as prescribed. The Authority may, after due inquiry and providing opportunity for hearing to all concerned parties, restore patent rights relating to a plant variety if it is demonstrated that the registration was obtained through fraudulent means or misrepresentation of facts pertaining to its novelty or distinctiveness. Such restoration shall not prejudice the rights of any person who has acquired an interest in the registered variety prior to the order of restoration. Further, the Central Government may issue directions regarding compensation payable by the applicant whose variety is subject to such a restoration patent. The breeder shall comply with all reporting requirements as stipulated under this Act.

Subject to the other provisions of this Act, any holder of a variety registered act shall be entitled to grant licenses for the commercial exploitation of their protected plant variety. Such licenses may be granted on such terms and conditions as the licensing authority deems fit, including royalty rates, duration, and geographical scope. The license agreement shall clearly define the permitted uses of the propagating material derived from the registered variety. Assignment of a variety registered act is permissible with the prior approval of the Central Government, which may impose conditions to ensure continued benefit to farmers and preservation of genetic resources. Further, any binding government undertaking involved in agricultural research or development may enter into non-exclusive licenses under this Act for public service purposes, provided that such use does not unduly prejudice the rights of the registered breeder.

A breeder shall be deemed to have obtained a valid certificate issued breeder when the Plant Variety Protection Authority has formally registered a plant variety in their name, as provided herein. For the purposes of this Act, a "certificate issued breeder" signifies the legal recognition conferred upon an individual or entity demonstrating creativity and expression in developing a new plant variety. The authority may, subject to due process and opportunity for hearing, review any certificate issued breeder if it is established that the claimed novelty was not demonstrable at the time of application, or if the applicant misrepresented essential characteristics of the registered variety.

An application for a certificate shall be accompanied by such particulars and documentation as the Registrar may prescribe, including detailed phenotypic data demonstrating distinctness and stability across generations. The authority may require further testing or analysis to verify these claims prior to proceeding with assessment. Upon satisfactory evaluation of the application and demonstration that the variety is novel, stable, and possesses at least one essential characteristic differentiating it from existing varieties, a certificate issued breeder shall be deemed the owner of the plant variety for the term specified under this Act. This right includes the privilege to produce, propagate, import, export, and sell propagating material of the protected variety, subject to any conditions imposed by the Registrar relating to farmers’ rights and benefit sharing arrangements.

Subject to appeal under this Act, a breeder shall retain exclusive rights pertaining to their registered plant variety for a period as determined by the Authority, provided that such rights may be relinquished or deemed abandoned through non-exercise exceeding ten years from the date of grant. Any person alleging infringement of these rights may institute civil proceedings seeking injunctive relief and damages against any party engaging in unauthorized propagation, sale, or distribution of the protected plant variety. Furthermore, where a certificate issued breeder is found to have misrepresented information concerning the novelty or distinctiveness of their variety during the registration process, the Authority shall have power to issue an order for revocation of said certificate and impose penalties as deemed appropriate. The burden of proving infringement rests upon the claimant, subject to procedural safeguards ensuring fairness to both parties.

Any person aggrieved by an action taken under this Act relating to the issuance or refusal of a certificate issued breeder may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of such action. Failure to comply with prescribed procedures during the application process for a Plant Variety Registration shall render the applicant liable to a penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees, recoverable as arrears of land revenue. The Authority may, upon receiving credible evidence of fraudulent misrepresentation in relation to traits or characteristics claimed by an applicant, initiate proceedings for revocation of any certificate and impose additional penalties up to one million rupees. Repeated violations concerning unauthorized propagation shall attract progressively increasing fines and potential criminal prosecution under this Act.

A breeder shall be deemed to have obtained a certificate issued breeder upon fulfillment of all conditions precedent as prescribed under this Act and subsequent notification. Such a certificate, once granted, confers exclusive rights pertaining to the commercialization of the variety, subject to farmers’ rights as defined herein. The term "breeder" includes any individual, firm, or institution involved in developing a new plant variety, irrespective of their place of business. Any dispute concerning the validity of such a certificate, or the interpretation of the breeder's exclusive rights, may be referred to the Appellate Board for adjudication, as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, a breeder may enter into agreements for the licensing or assignment of rights pertaining to a registered variety. Such agreements shall clearly define the scope of permitted activities, including but not limited to seed production, distribution, and sale, as provided herein. Any licensee obtaining rights under such an agreement shall be bound by conditions stipulated within the license, relating to traceability and benefit sharing with the original breeder. The breeder granting the license or assignment may retain ownership of the registered variety while permitting specific uses by another party. Further, any sub-licensing undertaken by a licensee requires prior written consent from the initial breeder, subject to royalty payments as determined in the primary agreement. This process ensures equitable distribution of benefits derived from the protected plant variety and safeguards the rights of the original registration act breeder.

For the purposes of this Act, "registered user" means a person registered as such under Chapter V, who possesses the exclusive right to use a trade mark in relation to goods or services for which it is registered, subject to any conditions and limitations specified in the registration. An infringement of that exclusive right occurs when an unauthorized party uses an identical or deceptively similar trade mark in connection with goods or services identical or closely related to those for which the registered user holds rights. Where such infringement constitutes a criminal offence under this Act, the offender shall be liable to imprisonment term shall not be less than one year but may extend to five years and also be liable to a fine which shall not be less than fifty thousand rupees.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall include a representation of the marks applied for, along with a statement specifying all goods or services in relation to which the applicant desires to register the trade mark. Where the proposed trade mark comprises a design or device, the application must clearly delineate any elements that are not distinctive and are disclaimed. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further particulars concerning the use of the trade mark prior to the date of application, if such information is deemed necessary for examination under this Act. Any person found guilty of knowingly making a false statement in their application shall be punishable with imprisonment term shall extend to two years and with a fine which may extend to one lakh rupees.

Where any proprietor of a registered trade mark institutes legal proceedings under this Act in respect of an alleged infringement, and fails to substantiate such allegation by clear and convincing evidence, the court may order him to pay costs incurred by the defendant. Further, if it is established that the proprietor acted maliciously or vexatiously in bringing forth said proceedings, the court shall award punitive damages against the proprietor to compensate for loss of business reputation suffered by the defendant. Any person found guilty of knowingly and wilfully using an identical or deceptively similar trade mark without due authorization from the registered proprietor shall be liable to prosecution. In such cases, imprisonment term shall extend up to five years and a fine not less than one lakh rupees may also be imposed, subject to considerations of aggravating factors.

Where any proprietor of a registered trade mark institutes proceedings under this Act against any person for infringement, and such person is convicted thereof, the Court before whom the conviction takes place shall determine whether any order as to damages or injunction is necessary. Any individual found guilty of knowingly making use of an identical or deceptively similar mark in relation to goods or services for which the registered trade mark is protected, without due cause and with intent to deceive or injure the proprietor, shall be liable for prosecution. Upon conviction under this provision, an imprisonment term shall not be less than one year but may extend up to five years, and a fine which shall not be less than seventy-five thousand rupees but may extend to three lakh rupees. The Court may, in its discretion, impose both such imprisonment and fine.

Where a proprietor institutes proceedings for infringement under this Act and obtains a decree against a defendant, the Court may award such damages as it deems fit, taking into consideration the loss suffered by the proprietor, any profits made by the infringer that have not been accounted for, and other relevant factors as provided herein. Further, if the defendant was found to have acted fraudulently or with intent to deceive, or where the infringement has caused substantial damage to the reputation of the trade mark, an imprisonment term shall be imposed upon the offender, ranging from six months to three years, in addition to any monetary penalty determined by the Court. This imprisonment term may be reduced if the defendant demonstrates genuine repentance and undertakes remedial actions as directed by the Court.

Any proprietor or agent who knowingly makes any false representation in connection with the use, ownership, or registration of a trade mark, or who wilfully infringes upon the rights conferred by this Act, shall be liable for damages and subject to prosecution. Where such infringement involves the counterfeiting of goods, or the application to goods of identical or deceptively similar marks, the offender shall, without prejudice to any other penalty provided herein, be punishable with imprisonment term shall not be less than one year but which may extend to five years, and with a fine which shall not be less than seventy-five thousand rupees but which may extend to three lakh rupees. Further, where an offence is committed by a company, the liability shall be on those who were responsible for the conduct of its business.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark shall have the exclusive right to license the use of their trademark for goods or services as defined in the registration, subject to any conditions stipulated within the licensing agreement. Such licenses may be granted freely and without prejudice to the proprietor’s own rights under this Act; however, any assignment of the entire trade mark, including all associated licensed usage, requires prior notification to the Registrar and is conditional upon their approval. Failure to disclose a material alteration in the scope or nature of a license shall render the proprietor liable for damages as determined by a competent court. Where an infringement occurs due to unauthorized use under a terminated license, the infringing party shall be subject to penalties; furthermore, any person convicted of such infringement may face imprisonment term shall not be less than one year and with fine which may extend to five lakh rupees.

Where a proprietor institutes proceedings under this Act alleging infringement of a registered trade mark and the defendant raises an argument asserting that the use of the impugned sign does not cause dilution of distinctiveness or confusion in the mind of the public, the Court shall consider evidence presented by both parties pertaining to consumer perception surveys and market analysis. Should the Court find merit in the defendant’s contention, it may dismiss the infringement claim. However, if the proprietor establishes beyond reasonable doubt that the defendant's actions constitute a deliberate attempt to unfairly capitalize on the reputation associated with the registered trade mark, an imprisonment term shall be imposed upon the offending party, ranging from six months to three years, and they shall also be liable to a fine. An appeal against such conviction lies to the High Court within sixty days.

Where an order adjudicating officer finds, upon review of evidence presented during proceedings under this Act concerning alleged passing off or deceptive trade practices relating to a registered trademark, that the respondent has engaged in conduct wilfully infringing the complainant’s rights, such finding shall be subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. The appellant may submit further documentary proof and testimony not previously considered by the adjudicating officer. Where the infringement is deemed particularly egregious, involving substantial financial loss or demonstrable consumer confusion, the tribunal may recommend to the relevant court that an imprisonment term shall be imposed upon the respondent, alongside any monetary penalties as determined under this Act. Such recommendation is advisory and remains subject to judicial discretion.

For the purposes of this Act, “registry fee paid” means any sum tendered to the Trade Marks Registry in accordance with prescribed rates and regulations, whether for an application for registration, renewal of registration, or other procedural action as provided herein. Such payment shall be deemed complete upon reflection of the credit in the designated government account, irrespective of mode of remittance. The receipt generated following such electronic transfer shall serve as prima facie evidence of registry fee paid. Any dispute concerning the validity of a registry fee paid shall be resolved according to established procedures under this Act and may be subject to review by an appellate authority.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark shall be required to remit a registry fee payment at the time of filing the application, and such payment shall constitute an essential prerequisite for the Registrar’s consideration of the merits of the proposed mark. The amount of the registry fee paid shall be determined in accordance with the prescribed schedule annexed hereto, differentiated according to the class of goods or services associated with the trade mark and the form of application submitted. Provided that, if an applicant elects to file a request for expedited examination, a supplementary processing fee shall also be payable, as detailed within the aforementioned schedule. Failure to remit the requisite registry fee paid will render the application void ab initio, subject to the possibility of reinstatement upon subsequent payment within a period not exceeding six months from the date of notification of non-payment.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Trade Marks Registry relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application for registration, or concerning any matter arising during the consideration thereof, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be filed within sixty days from the date on which the order is communicated to the appellant. The appellate board may allow the appeal and direct the registry to proceed with the application as if it had been originally accepted, or may dismiss the appeal. Where an applicant has failed to pay a prescribed registry fee paid for renewal of registration within the time allowed under this Act, the Registrar shall issue a notice of intention to remove the trade mark from the register. The removal shall not take effect until six months from the date of such notice.

Applications for registration of service marks may be made to the Trade Marks Registry in the prescribed form and accompanied by the requisite registry fee paid as determined under this Act. The Registrar shall, upon receipt of an application and verification of payment of the applicable registry fee paid, proceed with examination thereof. Any deficiency in the amount of the registry fee paid shall render the application deemed not to have been filed until such deficiency is rectified. Failure to rectify any discrepancy concerning the registry fee paid within a period of thirty days from the date of notification by the Registrar will result in rejection of the application. The Trade Marks Registry may, at its discretion, permit payment of outstanding fees in installments, provided that a reasonable interest rate as determined by the Central Government is applied to each installment.

Failure to remit the registry fee paid for the examination of a trade mark application within thirty days from the date specified in the notice issued under this Act shall render the application deemed abandoned, and the Registrar may proceed accordingly without further notification. Any person seeking reinstatement of an application so abandoned must file a petition accompanied by the original registry fee paid, together with a surcharge equivalent to double the prescribed amount. The Intellectual Property Appellate Board shall consider such petitions; however, approval is discretionary and subject to demonstration of good cause for the delay in payment. Repeated failure to adhere to timelines regarding fees may result in penalties as provided herein.

The assignment of trade mark rights, including those arising from applications pending before the Trade Marks Registry, may be effected subject to the provisions herein and with the written consent of the Registrar. Such assignments shall include any benefit derived from the registry fee paid in connection with the original application or subsequent proceedings relating thereto. Where an applicant has assigned their interest in a trade mark application, the assignee shall be deemed to be substituted for the assignor for all purposes under this Act. The registrar may require evidence of such assignment satisfactory to them, and failure to provide such evidence may result in the assignment being deemed invalid. Any person acquiring rights through assignment is bound by any conditions or limitations previously imposed on the trade mark application as determined by the registry fee paid at the time of filing.

The Registrar shall maintain a record of all registry fees paid in connection with trademark applications and renewals, accessible for inspection upon written request to an authorized officer. Any applicant aggrieved by a determination regarding the validity or calculation of a registry fee paid may file an appeal within sixty days from the date of notification of such determination. Such appeals shall be heard by an appellate authority constituted under this Act, which may order a refund of any excess amount paid, subject to just consideration of expenses incurred by the Registrar in processing the original application and subsequent inquiries. The decision of the appellate authority shall be final, provided that it is not challenged further under the provisions relating to judicial review.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark includes representation of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout, the applicant shall be deemed to have acknowledged and accepted that such representation constitutes part of the registered trade mark. Any dispute arising regarding the scope or validity of this inclusion may be referred to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board under this Act. It is provided that failure to remit the registry fee paid at the time of filing the application, or any subsequent prescribed fees relating to the semiconductor integrated circuit layout representation, shall render the application liable for rejection and removal from the register; however, an appeal against such rejection may be made to the Appellate Board within a period of sixty days.

An application for registration of a mark relating to agricultural produce shall be accompanied by evidence satisfactory to the Registry establishing the applicant’s status as a registered breeder or, where applicable, a recognised plant variety protection provider. The Registrar may require further documentation demonstrating continuous cultivation and propagation of the specified agricultural produce. Failure to submit such documentation within the stipulated timeframe will render the application liable for rejection. Any subsequent renewal of registration shall be subject to payment of the prescribed registry fee paid at the time of initial filing; this fee is non-refundable in cases where the mark is subsequently found to be deceptively similar to an earlier mark under this Act.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Trade Marks Registry relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application for registration, or concerning any matter affecting the rights of registrability, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be accompanied by the prescribed fee, which is non-refundable even if the appeal is ultimately dismissed. The registry fee paid in respect of the original application shall not be credited towards the cost of the appeal proceedings. Further, provisions act shall require that any party seeking a stay of action pending an appeal must demonstrate demonstrable and irreparable prejudice should the stay be denied; failure to do so will result in the dismissal of said request. Costs relating to such appeals are at the discretion of the Appellate Board.

For the purpose of this Act, “filed registry fee” means the sum prescribed under regulations framed by the Central Government and required to be remitted at the time of presenting an application for registration of a trade mark, or for any subsequent proceeding requiring formal entry upon the register. This fee is distinct from renewal fees or advertisement costs incurred during examination. The amount constituting the filed registry fee shall be determined based on the class of goods or services covered by the application and may be adjusted periodically as deemed necessary to account for administrative expenses. Failure to remit the correct filed registry fee will render an application voidable, subject to provisions regarding rectification.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark shall remit to the Trade Marks Registry a prescribed filed registry fee at the time of making application. The amount of such fee shall be determined according to the class of goods or services associated with the proposed trade mark, as detailed in the First Schedule. Provided that an applicant may elect to pay a reduced filed registry fee if the application is for registration in respect of agricultural products only, subject to verification by the Registrar regarding the nature of the goods. Failure to remit the requisite filed registry fee shall render the application deemed not to have been made and it may be rejected without further notice. Any alteration to the particulars of an application will necessitate payment of a revised filed registry fee as applicable.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark shall remit a filed registry fee as prescribed under this Act at the time of presentation of the application to the Trade Marks Registry, failing which the application shall be deemed not to have been made. Provided that an applicant who has previously filed an identical or confusingly similar trade mark in respect of related goods or services may, subject to conditions determined by the Registrar, apply for a waiver of all or part of the filed registry fee. Any person aggrieved by the decision of the Registrar regarding such a waiver may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The Trade Marks Registry shall not proceed with examination of an application until evidence of payment of the requisite filed registry fee is received and recorded. Failure to pay this fee constitutes grounds for rejection of the trade mark application.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be accompanied by a filed registry fee as prescribed under this Act; provided that where an applicant elects to file an application electronically, the applicable filed registry fee shall be adjusted as notified by the Registrar from time to time. The amount of the filed registry fee is subject to revision based on prevailing economic conditions and may vary depending upon the class or classes of goods or services for which registration is sought. Failure to remit the prescribed filed registry fee at the time of application will render the application void ab initio. Any deficiency in payment, discovered subsequent to initial processing, shall necessitate a notice issued by the Registrar requiring immediate remittance within thirty days; failing compliance, the application may be deemed abandoned. The Registrar may, upon receiving satisfactory evidence of financial hardship, entertain an appeal for waiver or reduction of the filed registry fee, as provided herein.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark under this Act shall remit a filed registry fee at the time of presentation of the application to the Trade Marks Registry. The amount of such fee shall be determined as per the Schedule appended hereto and may be adjusted by notification published in the Official Gazette, subject to prior approval from the Central Government. Provided that an applicant claiming entitlement to preferential treatment under the provisions relating to small-scale industries or start-ups is eligible for a reduced filed registry fee, as detailed within the aforementioned Schedule. Any application submitted without the requisite filed registry fee shall be deemed invalid and may be rejected by the Registrar. The fees paid are non-refundable except where an appeal against rejection is successful.

Failure to remit the filed registry fee within thirty days from the date of demand shall render the trademark application deemed abandoned, subject to restoration only upon payment of a revival fee equivalent to twice the original amount and submission of an affidavit confirming continued use of the mark for at least six months immediately preceding the application. Any person knowingly submitting a false declaration regarding the timely remittance of the filed registry fee shall be liable to prosecution under relevant provisions of the Indian Penal Code, and further subject to penalties not exceeding fifty thousand rupees imposed by the Controller. The Registrar may, ex officio, initiate proceedings for recovery of unpaid fees as arrears of land revenue.

Any person seeking to assign or license rights pertaining to a trade mark application shall, as part of the assignment deed or licensing agreement, provide a detailed accounting of all sums previously remitted towards the filed registry fee. This disclosure must include dates of payment and specific descriptions corresponding with the services rendered by registered trade mark agents involved in the preparation and filing process. The Registrar may require further clarification regarding these payments if deemed necessary for verification purposes. Furthermore, any subsequent transfer or sub-licensing of such rights is subject to the same requirement of full financial transparency concerning the initial filed registry fee. Failure to provide this information accurately and completely shall render the assignment or license voidable at the option of the assignee or licensee, provided that they demonstrate demonstrable prejudice resulting from the omission.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be accompanied by a filed registry fee as determined under this Act; however, where an applicant disputes the assessment of said fee, claiming it to be manifestly excessive or based on inaccurate information provided during the initial submission, they may appeal to the relevant Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. Such appeals must be made within sixty days from the date of notification of the assessed fee and shall be accompanied by a further sum equivalent to twenty-five percent of the disputed amount. The Tribunal shall consider evidence presented by both the applicant and the Registry, and its decision regarding the filed registry fee shall be final, subject to appeal under the provisions relating to appeals to higher courts as provided herein.

For the purpose of this Act, "filed registry fee" means the sum prescribed under this Act as being due upon the presentation of an application for registration of a trade mark and which remains outstanding pending examination or adjudication thereof; such fee shall be deemed to accrue to the credit of the Trade Marks Fund. The amount constituting the filed registry fee may vary depending on the class of goods or services specified in the application, and the form of representation employed. Where an applicant submits a layout design consisting of distinctive graphical elements alongside their trade mark application, a supplementary filing fee proportionate to the complexity of said layout design shall also be payable as provided herein.

Applications for registration of trade marks may be presented to the Trade Marks Registry at such place or places as the Government may direct. The applicant shall pay, at the time of application, a filed registry fee as prescribed by notification issued under this Act; failure to do so will render the application void ab initio. Such fees are non-refundable even if the application is subsequently rejected for any reason whatsoever. Where an applicant elects to file multiple classes of goods or services in a single application, the filed registry fee shall be adjusted accordingly, as detailed in the First Schedule. The Registrar may require further payment of fees at various stages of processing, including examination and advertisement. It is provided that register patents shall not be affected by any action taken regarding trade mark applications. Any dispute concerning the calculation or validity of these fees may be brought before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

The amount of registry fee for the examination of an application for registration of a trade mark shall be determined based on the class or classes into which the goods or services are classified under the International Classification of Goods and Services, as specified in Schedule 4. Provided that, where an applicant elects to file an application electronically, a discount on the prescribed registry fee may be offered, subject to conditions regarding verification of identity and payment gateway charges as notified by the Trade Marks Registry. The registry fee is non-refundable even if the trade mark application is subsequently rejected or withdrawn under this Act.

Applications for registration of service marks shall be accompanied by a registry fee, calculated as per the prescribed rates detailed in Schedule II appended to this Act. The amount of such fee is non-refundable, subject to provisions relating to withdrawal of applications under this Act. Any alteration or amendment proposed to a registered trade mark, including changes to the list of goods or services, shall also necessitate payment of an additional registry fee. Failure to remit the requisite registry fee within the stipulated timeframe may result in the application being deemed abandoned and removed from the register. The Registrar may, at his discretion, grant exemptions from the prescribed registry fees for certain categories of applicants as notified by the Central Government periodically.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Trade Marks Registry relating to the assessment or recovery of a registry fee may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of that decision. The Board shall, after giving notice to all concerned parties and affording them an opportunity for being heard, pass such orders as it deems fit, which may include setting aside, modifying, or affirming the decision appealed against. Failure to pay a registry fee when due shall render the trademark liable for removal from the register upon application by the Registrar. The Registrar may also serve a notice requiring payment of the outstanding amount within a specified period; default in compliance with such notice will constitute grounds for initiating recovery proceedings under this Act, subject to any limitations prescribed regarding time-barred debts.

Applications for registration of service marks shall be accompanied by a registry fee as determined by notification issued by the Controller General. The amount of said fee varies according to the number of classes of goods or services specified in the application, and is subject to periodic revision under this Act. Any applicant seeking to amend their application after its initial filing must also remit an additional registry fee proportionate to the nature and extent of the amendment. Provided that, if an application is rejected and subsequently reinstated following appeal, a reduced registry fee shall be payable upon re-filing. Failure to pay the prescribed registry fee within the stipulated time period may result in the application being deemed abandoned, as provided herein. The Controller General may, at his discretion, grant exemptions from payment of the registry fee to certain categories of applicants, subject to such conditions as he deems fit.

Applications for registration of service marks shall be accompanied by a registry fee as determined by notification published by the Trade Marks Office from time to time. This fee is non-refundable, subject to exceptions provided herein relating to applications rejected under this Act due to formal deficiencies. Any applicant seeking to avail of expedited examination procedures must pay an additional processing fee, calculated according to scales prescribed in the First Schedule. Failure to remit the full registry fee at the time of application will render the application deemed not filed until such payment is made. The Trade Marks Office may require proof of remittance for any application where doubts arise regarding compliance with these provisions concerning fees and surcharge.

Any applicant seeking registration of a trade mark under this Act shall remit the prescribed registry fee at the time of application. Failure to pay the full registry fee within thirty days from the date of demand by the Registrar will result in the rejection of the application and forfeiture of any provisional fees already paid. The Registrar may, subject to due process, recover outstanding registry fees through attachment of movable or immovable property belonging to the applicant. Repeated default in payment of registry fees relating to multiple trade mark applications shall render the applicant ineligible for further registration proceedings until all arrears are cleared. Any person obstructing the recovery of such fees shall be liable to a penalty as provided herein.

The assignment of trade mark rights, including those arising from pending applications, shall be subject to the payment of a registry fee proportionate to the number of marks included within the assigned portfolio. Any licensee granting sub-licenses relating to registered trade marks must remit a supplementary registry fee reflecting the scope and duration of such sublicense agreements, as determined by regulations framed under this Act. Provided that, where an assignment or license agreement incorporates a reciprocal arrangement involving counter-indemnities for the assignor or licensor, the initial registry fee may be reduced at the Registrar’s discretion, subject to verification of the contractual terms. Further, any transfer of ownership in a trade mark holding company shall necessitate updated registry fees reflecting the new beneficial owner's entitlement and obligations as provided herein. Failure to remit these fees will render the assignment or license voidable.

The amount of registry fee required for the examination of an application for registration of a trade mark shall be determined as per the prescribed schedule; however, any applicant disputing the assessment of such fee may, within thirty days from the date of notification of the assessed amount, file an appeal with the Trade Marks Appellate Tribunal. Provided that the appellant shall deposit twenty-five percent of the disputed registry fee pending the adjudication of the appeal, failing which the appeal shall be deemed withdrawn. Further, where the Registrar deems the deposited sum insufficient to cover administrative costs associated with processing the appeal, a supplementary payment may be demanded, and non-compliance therewith will render the appeal inadmissible as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by any order made under this Act relating to the assessment or recovery of registry fees may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Board shall, after giving notice to all concerned parties and affording them an opportunity for being heard, pass such orders as it deems fit, which shall be binding on the Registrar. Failure to pay any prescribed registry fee within the time specified in a notice issued by the Registrar shall render the trade mark liable for removal from the register. In cases where an alleged offence has been committed involving fraudulent representation concerning the ownership of a registered trade mark and the subsequent evasion of applicable fees, the offender shall be subject to penalties as determined by the Board, without prejudice to any other action that may be taken under this Act.

Any producer failing to remit the prescribed registry fee within thirty days from the date specified on the official demand notice issued under this Act shall be deemed to have committed an offence and is liable, upon conviction, to a fine not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Repeated failure to pay such fees, or attempting to evade payment through fraudulent means, will attract further penalties as determined by the Controller. The Controller may, at his discretion, initiate proceedings for recovery of outstanding registry fees as arrears of land revenue. Any person found assisting a producer in circumventing these fee obligations shall also be subject to similar fines and potential prosecution under this Act.

The assignment of rights pertaining to trade mark applications filed under this Act shall be permitted subject to registration with the Trade Marks Registry and payment of the prescribed registry fee. Any licensee granted usage rights for a registered or pending trademark may, with express written consent from the proprietor, further assign those specific licensing privileges to a third party, provided that such assignment includes a detailed inventory of the licensed goods or services. The registry fee for registering an assignment or sub-license shall be equivalent to twenty percent of the original application patent india filing fee. Failure to declare any subsequent assignments within thirty days will render the assignee liable to penalties as determined by the Registrar. Furthermore, the proprietor retains the right to revoke any improperly registered assignment and reclaim full control over their trademark rights.

A registered geographical indication, as provided herein, signifies that a good’s origin is exclusively linked to a specific geographic area, and such link constitutes an essential factor in determining its quality, reputation or other characteristic. For the purposes of this Act, a geographical indication shall include indications which identify wines, spirits, agricultural products, foodstuffs, handicrafts, and manufactured goods. An application for registration of a registered geographical indication may be opposed by any interested party demonstrating likelihood of confusion with prior trademarks or similar geographical indications already recorded under this Act. The Registrar shall determine eligibility based on established connection to the defined geographic area.

An application for registration as a registered geographical indication may be made by any association of persons or by producers whose interests are represented by an association. Such application shall include particulars specifying the name of the geographical indication sought to be registered, the goods to which it relates, and the area of the territory concerned. The Registrar may require such applicant to furnish further information as he deems necessary for assessing compliance with the provisions herein relating to distinctiveness and reputation. Where the proposed registered geographical indication is deemed descriptive of the characteristics or quality of the goods, the Registrar shall direct the applicant to amend the application or provide evidence demonstrating acquired distinctiveness through use in the relevant territory. The registrar shall publish a notice of the acceptance of the application under this Act.

Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication shall be entitled to institute civil suits for infringement under this Act. Infringement occurs when any person, without authorization from the registered proprietor, makes use of or allows to be used, in connection with goods or services, any sign that falsely suggests that such goods or services originate from the area specified as the agricultural, natural, or manufactured product geographical origin. The remedies available to a registered proprietor upon successful infringement proceedings include an injunction restraining the infringing activity and damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the proprietor. Provided that, in determining damages, due consideration shall be given to the goodwill associated with the registered geographical indication. Further, any goods found to infringe a registered geographical indication may be seized and destroyed as provided herein.

An application for registration as a registered geographical indication may be filed by any association of persons engaged in production or processing of goods, or by collectives, or by cooperatives, provided that such associations, collectives or cooperatives are involved in agriculture, handicrafts, natural resources or other rural industries. The Registrar shall serve notice of the application on interested parties under this Act, and any party who feels aggrieved by the acceptance of an application for registration may within sixty days from the date of publication of the journal containing the notice of the application, file a notice of opposition with the Registrar. Upon receiving such opposition, the Registrar shall give the applicant an opportunity to submit its views in reply. The Registrar may, after considering the opposition and the response of the applicant, either reject the application or proceed with registration as a registered geographical indication if satisfied that the conditions for registration are met.

An eligible good qualifies for registration as a geographical indication where it possesses characteristics attributable essentially to its origin, and such origin is situated within a defined geographical area. The Registrar may require an applicant demonstrating this essential link to provide detailed documentation substantiating the production methods employed and the unique qualities arising from that specific terroir. Further, any association seeking to represent the interests of producers of goods eligible for registration as a registered geographical indication shall submit evidence of widespread recognition amongst those producers and demonstrate its capacity to enforce the conditions of use prescribed under this Act. The Registrar shall reject an application if it finds that use of the proposed name or sign would be misleading regarding the true character or quality of the good.

Any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act relating to the revocation of a registered geographical indication may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. Failure to comply with prescribed procedures during the production and sale of goods indicating a protected registered geographical indication shall constitute an offense, punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine not less than fifty thousand rupees, or both. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, authorize officers to investigate alleged infringements and impose penalties as provided herein. Any false or misleading representation concerning the origin of goods shall be deemed an infringement under this Act and subject to prosecution.

Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication may grant non-exclusive licenses to use the indication in relation to the goods for which it is registered, subject to such terms and conditions as are agreed upon between the parties. Such license agreements shall be documented in writing and duly executed by both licensor and licensee. Further, the right to assign a registered geographical indication or any interest therein may be exercised with the prior written consent of the Registrar, provided that the assignee is demonstrably engaged in production or processing activities relating to the goods specified in the registration. The Registrar shall not unreasonably withhold such consent, but may require assurances regarding continued adherence to quality standards associated with the registered geographical indication. Any transfer without this approval shall be deemed void and unenforceable under this Act.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the revocation of a registered geographical indication may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. Such appeal shall be filed in such form and manner as may be prescribed, and the Board shall follow such procedure as it deems fit for disposal of appeals. The Board may, after giving notice to all parties concerned and affording them an opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify, or reverse the order appealed against. An aggrieved party may further appeal from an order passed by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board to the Supreme Court on a question of law, subject to such conditions as are provided herein.

Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication shall be entitled to institute civil suits against any person or entity infringing upon their exclusive right to use the said indication in connection with goods for which it is registered. Such infringement includes, but is not limited to, the unauthorized application of the registered geographical indication as a trademark or trade name, or its use in a manner likely to cause confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of the goods. The remedies available under this Act shall include an injunction restraining the infringing activity and damages commensurate with the loss suffered by the proprietor. Further, any person seeking to challenge the validity of a registration respect may apply to the relevant authority for rectification, subject to procedural requirements as provided herein.

An application for registration as a registered geographical indication may be made to the Registrar by any association of persons or producers engaged in the production of goods conforming to the quality and characteristics which are unique to that territory. Such an application shall include particulars specifying the name of the geographical indication, the class of goods to which it relates, the area of the originating locality, and a map of the geographical area. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further information or clarification regarding any aspect of the application. Where the registered geographical indication pertains to agricultural products, foodstuffs, or wine, a specification patent shall be included detailing production methods and quality control measures ensuring authenticity. Any interested party may inspect the application and file an opposition under this Act within the prescribed period. The Registrar shall consider all objections received before proceeding with registration.

An eligible good qualifies for registration as a registered geographical indication where its qualities, reputation or other characteristics are essentially attributable to its origin within a defined area. Such an area shall be determined by the Geographical Indications Registry based on documented evidence demonstrating a continuous link between the product and that geographic territory. Provided that any person seeking to apply patent protection relating to a process used in the production of goods conforming to the standards specified for a registered geographical indication must disclose such use within the application, subject to review under this Act. The Registrar may require further verification concerning the authenticity of claims regarding origin and quality before granting registration, ensuring compliance with established protocols as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by an order relating to registered geographical indications may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. Such appeal shall be on grounds that the order is perverse, without sufficient consideration of the evidence, or based on an error of law apparent on the face of the record. Failure to comply with prescribed procedures during registration proceedings shall not preclude enforcement actions against those using falsely indicative signs. The Registrar may, upon receiving credible information, initiate inquiries into matters relating registered geographical indications concerning unauthorized use or imitation. Penalties for infringement, as provided herein, include fines up to five lakhs rupees and imprisonment of up to three years, subject to judicial discretion.

An appeal lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal from any order passed by the Registrar refusing registration of a geographical indication, or revoking its registration. Such an appeal may be made by any person aggrieved by the order, including but not limited to unsuccessful applicants and registered proprietors. The Tribunal shall hear such appeals expeditiously, affording all parties concerned a reasonable opportunity for being heard. Where the grounds of appeal relate to a determination concerning the distinctiveness of the goods or services associated with a registered geographical indication, or challenge the validity of a proprietor layout design incorporated within its branding, the Tribunal may direct the Registrar to reconsider the matter. The decision of the Tribunal shall be final, subject to further appeal under the provisions relating to judicial review.

For the purposes of this Act, a “director” with respect to a cinematograph film shall mean any individual appointed to manage or oversee the production process, including but not limited to creative direction, financial management, and securing necessary permissions. A person shall be deemed a director if they exercise significant control over artistic choices or technical aspects of the film’s creation, irrespective of their formal title under company law. Where multiple individuals share directorial responsibilities, each such individual shall be considered a “director” subject to any agreements made between them regarding copyright ownership as provided herein. This definition extends to associate directors who contribute substantially to the overall direction of the work.

For the purposes of registration under this Act, where a cinematograph film incorporates performances by one or more persons acting as a director, the application for copyright shall specify the name of each such director. The Registrar may require submission of a written consent from each director whose name is included in the application, confirming their participation and acknowledging the inclusion of their directorial contribution within the scope of the claimed copyright. Provided that, if a director’s involvement was solely as a consultant or advisor without exercising creative control over the film's artistic elements, such individual shall not be deemed to be a director for the purposes of this provision. Any alteration to the list of directors after submission of the application shall require prior written approval from the Registrar and may necessitate further declarations.

Where a cinematograph film infringes any copyright under this Act, action may be taken against any individual involved in its creation or distribution. Specifically, where such infringement results from the actions of a *director* of the production company, that director shall be deemed to have committed an act of copyright infringement and is liable for damages as provided herein. The liability of the director shall not preclude the possibility of action being taken against the production company itself, nor limit remedies available to the copyright owner. Further, any person who knowingly aids or abets the infringing actions of a *director*, including but not limited to providing technical assistance or financial support, may also be held liable for contributory infringement. The court shall consider the extent of the director's involvement and authority when determining appropriate compensation and injunctive relief.

Where a cinematograph film incorporates works which are protected under this Act, and the authorship of such incorporation is attributable to the creative direction of a director, the remuneration payable to the director shall be determined by agreement between the producer and the director. Subject to any such agreement, the remuneration shall be commensurate with the scale of production and the extent of the director’s contribution as evidenced in the film's credits. Any dispute arising regarding the determination of such remuneration may be referred to an Arbitrator appointed jointly by the producer and the director. The Arbitrator shall provide a reasoned award within ninety days from the date of appointment, and this award shall be final and binding on both parties. Provided that where the director is also employed under a contract of service with the production house, the terms of such employment shall govern remuneration to the extent they do not conflict with provisions as provided herein.

For the purposes of determining ownership of copyright in cinematograph films, where such film is created under the direction of a director, the said director shall be deemed the author of the work only if the director’s creative contribution transcends mere supervision and demonstrably involves significant artistic decisions pertaining to script adaptation, character development, or musical composition. Provided that, if an agreement exists between the producer and the director specifying allocation of copyright ownership, such agreement shall prevail, subject to the condition that it is executed prior to commencement of principal photography and registered with the designated government authority. Further, where a work incorporates elements created by other individuals under the direction’s guidance, those contributions remain protected under this Act, notwithstanding the director's asserted authorship.

Where a cinematograph film infringes the copyright in any work, and such infringement is attributable to an act or omission by a director during the creation of the film, both the producer and the director shall be jointly and severally liable for damages. Any person demonstrating substantial involvement in the infringing activity may also be held accountable under this Act. Failure to adequately supervise directorial activities relating to copyrightable elements constitutes negligence actionable at law. The Court may order the seizure and destruction of any equipment used in facilitating such infringement, subject to due process. Repeated or willful violations shall attract enhanced penalties, including imprisonment for a term not less than two years, and fines up to five hundred thousand rupees.

Where a copyright subsists in any cinematograph film by virtue of the artistic work of a director, the right to assign or license such copyright shall vest initially with the director. This provision is without prejudice to any agreement entered into prior to the commencement of this Act between the director and the producer of the film. The director may, subject to the terms of any such pre-existing agreement, grant exclusive licenses permitting reproduction, adaptation, publication, distribution, or communication to the public of the cinematograph film, or any part thereof. Any assignment made by a director under this Act shall be in writing and signed by the director as surety for its validity. Provided that where the director is a minor, such assignment shall require the consent of their lawful guardian. The producer may apply to the relevant authority for recognition of an assignment if dispute arises regarding the director’s entitlement.

For the purposes of determining ownership of copyright in cinematograph films, where a film is produced under the direction of an individual designated as “Director”, the question of whether such designation constitutes employment for the purposes of this Act shall be subject to judicial determination based on the terms and conditions of engagement. Provided that, if the Director’s agreement explicitly assigns copyright ownership to the producer or production house, such assignment shall be presumed valid unless evidence is presented demonstrating coercion, fraud, or misrepresentation in obtaining said consent. Any dispute arising regarding the extent of a Director's creative contribution and consequent rights under this Act may be appealed to the relevant High Court, whose decision shall be final and binding on all parties involved, subject to further appeal only on grounds of law.

Where an audiovisual work incorporates elements originating from multiple sources, including literary, dramatic, musical, artistic, and cinematographic works, determination of ownership shall be predicated upon the contribution of each party involved in its creation. For the purposes of this Act, the term "director" signifies the individual exercising primary creative control over the direction and execution of an audiovisual work, irrespective of their formal contractual designation; such authority extends to decisions concerning script adaptation, musical composition selection, and artistic rendering. Any dispute regarding ownership arising from a directorial contribution may be referred to the Controller for adjudication, following established procedures as provided herein. The Controller shall consider evidence pertaining to the extent of the director’s involvement in shaping the work's overall form and content, particularly with regard to elements classifiable under international classification goods relating to artistic expression.

Where a cinematograph film infringes upon copyright under this Act, and such infringement is attributable to an act or omission by a director during the production process, the director shall be held vicariously liable for damages as if they were the principal infringer. This liability extends notwithstanding any contractual agreements limiting responsibility between the producer and the director. Further, where registered draft regulations pertaining to film copyright clearances are demonstrably disregarded by a director in their actions leading to infringement, such disregard constitutes an aggravating factor when determining penalties. Any person failing to report a suspected instance of directorial copyright infringement shall be subject to fines as provided herein; willful concealment may attract enhanced punishment.

For the purposes of this Act, a “director” includes any person appointed by whatever name called who is authorised to exercise all or some of the powers of a director of a company, whether directly or indirectly. A director shall be deemed to have acted for the benefit of the work and its authors; however, where a cinematograph film purports to depict scenes or elements that demonstrably falsifies genuine geographical indications associated with a particular region in India, such depiction shall not constitute an infringement under this Act unless it is established that the director knowingly intended to mislead the public regarding the origin of goods or services.

For the purpose of this Act, an “original work” is defined as a work which has not previously been published under any law in force; provided that works created by government agencies acting through their duly authorized officials are deemed original for the purposes of copyright protection. The appellate board shall have the power to hear and determine appeals against orders passed by Copyright Officers relating to infringement claims, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. Decisions made by the appellate board shall be final and binding, except where a High Court is empowered to review them under this Act. Any party aggrieved by an order of the appellate board may seek redressal through judicial remedy.

Applications for registration of literary works, including computer programs and databases, shall be processed by the Registrar in accordance with the prescribed procedures. An applicant aggrieved by any decision of the Registrar relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application, or concerning objections raised under this Act, may appeal to the appellate board. The appellate board shall consider such appeals within a period not exceeding six months from the date of receipt thereof and shall pass orders in writing accompanied by reasons for the decision. Any party dissatisfied with the order of the appellate board may further appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of communication of the order, subject to just cause shown. The Registrar may require such additional information or documentation as deemed necessary during processing.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed by a Copyright Society under this Act is dissatisfied with such order, he may appeal to the appellate board established as provided herein. The appellate board shall consider all relevant materials placed before it during the original hearing and may, if satisfied that the order was manifestly unjust or erroneous in law, vary or reverse any such order. Any party aggrieved by an order of the appellate board may further appeal to the High Court within whose territorial jurisdiction the cause of action arose, subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder. The appeal shall lie only on a question of law. Costs incidental to the appeal shall be determined by the High Court.

Where an objection is raised before the Controller regarding the originality of any work claimed to be subject matter for copyright under this Act, the aggrieved party may prefer an appeal to the designated Appellate Board. The appeal shall lie within sixty days from the date of communication of the order of the Controller. Such appeal shall be accompanied by a memorandum of grounds specifying the errors apparent on the face of the record and setting out the points of law or fact which the appellant desires the Appellate Board to consider.

The Appellate Board shall give notice to the Controller, who may file its written submissions within thirty days from the date of receipt of such appeal. The Appellate Board may, at its discretion, hear oral arguments from both parties. Any order made by the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, subject to further appeal to the High Court under provisions as provided herein.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act concerning the rectification of entries in a register of copyright or relating to the determination of whether a work is an infringing copy, appeals to the appellate board, such appeal shall be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The appellate board shall give notice to all parties concerned and opportunity for them to present their case, including submission of documentary evidence, subject to compliance with procedural rules as may be prescribed by regulations framed under this Act. Provided that if the appellant can demonstrate reasonable cause for the delay, the appellate board may entertain appeals filed after the expiry of said sixty days. The decision of the appellate board shall be final and binding, provided it does not conflict with any judgment or order of a court.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed by a Copyright Society relating to the collection or distribution of royalties, or concerning disputes arising from licensing agreements as provided herein, desires to appeal against such order, he may prefer an application before the appellate board established under this Act. The appellate board shall consider such applications within ninety days and issue reasoned orders which are final subject only to further appeal to the High Court on a point of law. Failure by a Copyright Society to comply with directions issued by the appellate board shall render its officers liable for penalties not exceeding fifty thousand rupees, recoverable from them jointly and severally.

Where an owner of copyright in any cinematograph film grants a license authorizing reproduction of the work for purposes including but not limited to broadcast, public performance, or distribution through digital means, such license may contain provisions relating to assignment of rights arising under that license. The terms of assignment shall be determined by agreement between the licensor and licensee, subject to limitations imposed regarding moral rights as provided herein. Where no such agreement exists, the appellate board shall determine a reasonable royalty payable to the copyright owner for any subsequent assignments made without their express consent, considering factors including but not limited to the scope of the original license and the commercial value derived from the assignment. Any dispute concerning the validity or enforceability of an assignment under this Act may be referred to the appellate board for adjudication.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act by a Copyright Society appeals to the appellate board, the appeal shall be admitted only if sufficient grounds for challenging the correctness or legality of the order are demonstrated within sixty days of the date of communication of the order. The appellate board may, after affording opportunity for hearing to all concerned parties and considering evidence presented, confirm, vary, or reverse the original order. Provided that where a Copyright Society contests an appeal based on procedural irregularities, the appellate board shall determine whether such irregularity substantially prejudiced the appellant’s case. Any party dissatisfied with the decision of the appellate board may further appeal to the High Court within ninety days, subject to satisfaction of the appellate board regarding the deposit of costs.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to infringement of copyright, including orders concerning damages or injunctions, may appeal to the appellate board. The appellate board shall consider such appeals within ninety days from the date of receipt of the memorandum of appeal and shall issue its reasoned award within a further sixty days. Failure to comply with any condition imposed by the appellate board shall constitute a violation under this Act, attracting penalties as prescribed herein. Assignment rights relating to copyrighted works are subject to review by the appellate board in cases involving disputes over validity or scope, provided that such reviews do not extend to matters already decided by a civil court. The costs of proceedings before the appellate board shall be determined as deemed just and equitable.
