Subject to any agreement entered into prior to the registration of a layout design, the owner of a registered layout design shall be entitled to grant licenses granting rights to utilize the design for commercial purposes. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and the terms thereof shall be determined by the licensor, provided that any assignment of such license requires notification to the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trademarks within thirty days of execution. Where a layout design has been assigned, the assignee shall possess all rights pertaining to licensing as if they were the original owner under this Act. The appellate board shall have jurisdiction to hear and determine disputes concerning the validity or enforceability of licenses granted in relation to registered layout designs, including claims of unfair competition arising from unauthorized use.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Copyright Adjudicating Officer is dissatisfied with such order, he may appeal to the appellate board established under this Act within sixty days from the date of communication of the said order. The appellate board shall consider all submissions made by the appellant and the respondent, and may direct the production of further evidence if deemed necessary for a just determination of the matter. It is provided that an appeal against an order relating to infringement of copyright in any work registered under this Act shall not be entertained unless it is shown that the claimant has diligently pursued remedies available through civil courts concerning unregistered geographical indications associated with the work.

For the purposes of this Act, an “unauthorized digital reproduction” is defined as the creation of a copy of any work protected under this Act without due authorization from the right owner or where such copying constitutes a condition declared unlawful by notification issued by the Controller General. The appellate board shall have power to hear and determine appeals against orders passed by the Copyright Board relating to applications for statutory licenses, objections to assignments of copyright, and requests for rectification of entries in the Register of Copyrights. Decisions of the appellate board shall be final subject only to appeal to the High Court within a period of sixty days from the date of such decision.

An application for registration of a layout design shall include such particulars relating to the author, owner, and proprietor as are prescribed, and shall be accompanied by a representation of the design in the manner specified under this Act. The Layout Design Registrar may require the applicant to submit further information or clarification deemed necessary for proper examination. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall publish it in the Official Gazette. Any person aggrieved by any order made by the appellate board concerning the registration of a layout design may prefer an appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such order; provided that the appellate board shall consider any objections received during the period specified for public notice.

An application to a High Court under this Act shall be deemed to be a court application where such application seeks redressal for alleged infringement of patent rights, or challenges the validity of a granted patent. A court application must specify the grounds upon which it is based, including but not limited to allegations of novelty lacking in an invention, obviousness of the claimed subject matter, or insufficiency of disclosure. The applicant shall further provide particulars of the patent in question and demonstrate standing to bring such a court application. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in the rejection of the application as provided herein.

An applicant seeking registration of a layout plan under this Act shall, within thirty days of the date of filing the application, serve notice upon all persons appearing to have an interest in the land affected by such layout. Such notice shall specify the particulars of the proposed layout and invite objections, if any, from those interested parties. Any person aggrieved by the decision of the Registrar relating to the acceptance or rejection of a layout plan may prefer a court application before the District Court having jurisdiction over the area where the land is situated. The court shall hear such application and pass appropriate orders as it deems fit, subject to the provisions of this Act regarding procedural fairness and natural justice.

Any patentee who alleges that a party has infringed his patent, or is about to infringe it, may institute a court application seeking relief under this Act. Such an application shall specify the acts of infringement alleged and the remedies sought, which may include injunctions restraining the infringing activity and damages sustained by the patentee as a direct result of such infringement. The court shall give notice to the respondent party, affording them reasonable opportunity to file their written statement defending against the allegations. Provided that if the respondent fails to appear or adequately defend, the court may proceed ex parte. Further, where an application for injunction is made, the court shall consider whether a temporary injunction would cause substantial loss to either party pending final determination of the matter. The patentee must demonstrate reasonable prospects of success in establishing infringement.

Any party seeking to challenge a decision rendered under this Act concerning the revocation of a patent, or the grant of an injunction relating to patent infringement, shall make a court application within ninety days from the date of publication of such decision. The court application must be accompanied by a certified copy of the order sought to be challenged and a concise statement of grounds upon which the challenge is based, detailing any errors of law apparent on the face of the record. Provided that, where the party seeking review demonstrates reasonable cause for delay, the Court may condone such delay in its absolute discretion. The Controller shall be served with notice of the court application at least thirty days prior to the hearing, and shall have the opportunity to file a written response. Further, any interested person may also submit observations on the matter before the Court.

Any party seeking to challenge a decision regarding revocation of a patent under this Act shall file a court application within ninety days from the date of publication of the order. Such an application must specify, with particularity, the grounds upon which the revocation is deemed unlawful, and demonstrate that substantial prejudice has resulted directly from the challenged decision. The applicant shall further provide documentary evidence supporting each asserted ground, failing which the court may summarily dismiss the application. Provided that, if the party demonstrates reasonable cause for delay in filing within the stipulated period, the Court may condone such delay at its discretion. The Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trademarks may be impleaded as a necessary party to any such court application.

Any individual demonstrating substantial prejudice resulting from a violation of patent rights as defined under this Act shall be empowered to institute a court application seeking injunctive relief and damages. Such an application must specify the nature of the infringing activity, the period during which it occurred, and the quantifiable losses suffered directly attributable to the infringement. The Controller may, upon receiving notice of such a court application, issue interim orders restricting further acts of alleged infringement pending final adjudication. Provided that any party subject to such an order may appeal to the High Court within thirty days. Failure to comply with a judgment or order issued following a court application concerning patent rights shall render the defaulting party liable for penalties as prescribed herein and may result in criminal prosecution.

Any patentee desiring to grant a license, assign ownership, or otherwise transfer rights pertaining to a patented invention shall make an application before the Controller. Such application shall specify the details of the proposed transaction, including the identity and address of all parties involved, the scope of the rights being transferred, and any royalties or other considerations agreed upon. The Controller may require further documentation substantiating the terms of the agreement and demonstrating that the transfer is consistent with public interest. An applicant seeking to enforce a license granted under this Act may file a court application alleging infringement by a party failing to adhere to the stipulated conditions. This right shall be subject to the provisions regarding limitation periods as provided herein, and any dispute arising from such an application will be adjudicated according to established principles of equity and natural justice.

Any party dissatisfied with a decision rendered under this Act relating to the revocation of a patent, or concerning the validity thereof challenged during opposition proceedings, may institute a court application before the High Court. Such an application shall be made within ninety days from the date of service of the order appealed against, subject to just cause shown for any delay. The High Court shall admit the court application if it determines that the decision in question is demonstrably erroneous in law or fact. Provided that the aggrieved party must demonstrate a substantial prejudice arising directly from the alleged error. The High Court may dismiss the court application if it finds no merit in the arguments presented, and costs may be awarded against the applicant accordingly.

Where a registered proprietor desires to grant a license conferring rights to exploit a patented invention, such license shall be documented in writing and filed with the Controller. The terms of the license, including but not limited to royalty rates, duration, and territorial scope, shall be clearly specified within this documentation. Any subsequent assignment of patent rights, whether partial or complete, must also be registered as provided herein. Persons registered proprietors are obligated to notify the Controller of any such assignments or licenses within thirty days of execution. Failure to do so may result in penalties as determined by the Controller. A court application may be made by any party claiming infringement of a patented invention under license, seeking clarification regarding the scope and validity of said license agreement.

Any party dissatisfied with a decision rendered by the Controller under this Act relating to the grant, revocation, or opposition of a patent may institute a court application before the High Court. Such an application shall be made within ninety days from the date of communication of the order sought to be challenged, subject to justiciability and extension as the High Court deems fit. The applicant must demonstrate that substantial questions of law arise for determination in the court application. Provided that any counter-claim or cross-appeal arising out of the same patent shall be consolidated with the initial application. Further, the Controller’s decision is final unless reversed by the High Court and may be appealed to the Supreme Court on a point of law as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, a "description trade mark" means a sign used to distinguish goods from those of others, which describes characteristics of the goods, their intended purpose, quantity, suitability, value, quality, geographical origin, or mode of manufacture. Such a description shall be registrable as a trade mark only if it is not solely descriptive of the essential features of the goods for which it is used; and further, provided that the applicant demonstrates acquired distinctiveness through extensive use and recognition by consumers over a considerable period. The Registrar may require evidence substantiating such acquired distinctiveness before registration under this Act.

The proprietor of a trade mark shall be entitled to restrain the use of any descriptive words, signs, symbols, marks, letters, numerals, or shapes, sold as a description trade mark, if such use is likely to cause confusion in the minds of the public relating to the goods or services connected with his registered trade mark. Such restraint may include preventing the representation that the goods or services are associated with, approved by, or endorsed by the proprietor. Further, where infringement has occurred, the proprietor shall be entitled to recover damages from the infringing party, calculated as provided herein, taking into account the extent of the damage sustained and any profits made by the infringer as a result of the unlawful use. The remedies available under this Act are without prejudice to any other right or remedy which may be available to the proprietor in law or equity.

The Registrar may, upon application by any registered proprietor of a trade mark, direct that a particular word or words appearing in the description of goods or services associated with another’s registration be expunged from that other registration. Such an application shall specify the grounds for seeking the direction, demonstrating likelihood of confusion arising due to the inclusion of said words within the competing description. The Registrar shall provide the respondent with notice of the application and opportunity to submit a written response, including counter-evidence. Any decision made under this provision is subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Where the applicant demonstrates that the challenged descriptive matter was adopted in good faith after the date of the earlier registration, the Registrar may decline the requested direction. The description trade mark shall be interpreted strictly according to its plain meaning as understood by consumers familiar with the relevant goods or services.

No trade mark shall be registered if, in the opinion of the Registrar, it contains any word or words descriptive of the character or quality of the goods or services with which it is associated, and which are commonly used by traders to describe such goods or services; provided that such a description shall not preclude registration if there is evidence of acquired distinctiveness. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar refusing registration of a *description trade mark* may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Failure to comply with this provision, including use of an unregistered descriptive mark intended to deceive or cause confusion, shall be deemed a violation under this Act and subject to penalties as prescribed herein, including damages recoverable by affected parties.

For the purposes of this Act, a “reference trade mark” means a trade mark registered prior to the date of application for registration of another trade mark, and is used in relation to identical or similar goods or services. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating continuous use of the reference trade mark during the relevant period preceding the filing date of the subsequent trade mark application. Such evidence shall be considered when determining similarity under this Act. A trade mark shall not be deemed deceptively similar by reason only that it contains a reference trade mark, provided that the overall impression created on the mind of the public is distinct and avoids confusion as to origin or sponsorship.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed to include a reference trade mark where the applicant seeks to register a trade mark identical or similar to an earlier registered trade mark, and such earlier trade mark is used in relation to goods or services identical or asynergistically related to those for which registration is sought. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating that the use of the reference trade mark by the proprietor thereof does not create a likelihood of confusion among the public concerning the origin of the goods or services. Provided that, if the applicant demonstrates bona fide intention to use the applied-for trade mark as an authorized user under license from the proprietor of the reference trade mark, registration may be granted subject to such terms and conditions as the Registrar deems appropriate.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark contains a reference trade mark, the Registrar shall consider whether the use of the applicant’s mark is likely to cause confusion among consumers due to similarity between the two marks. The proprietor of the referenced trade mark may file written representations objecting to the registration, detailing the grounds upon which such objection is based and providing evidence substantiating their claims regarding consumer likelihood of confusion. Subject to this, the Registrar shall give notice of any such representation to the applicant and afford them an opportunity to respond in writing. If, following consideration of all submissions and available evidence, the Registrar finds that use of the applied-for mark would likely cause confusion, registration may be refused or modified as deemed appropriate under this Act. The Registrar’s decision shall be final, subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark contains a reference to a previously registered trade mark, the Trade Marks Registry shall examine whether the applicant has sufficient interest in the earlier trade mark. Such interest may include ownership, licensing agreement, or any other contractual arrangement granting rights relating to the said earlier mark. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating this connection and its validity, failing which the application may be rejected.

If the reference trade mark is held by a different legal entity than the applicant, written consent from the owner of the referenced trade mark shall be submitted alongside the application. This consent must explicitly authorize the use of the earlier mark in conjunction with the applied-for trade mark and detail the scope of such authorization. The Registrar may, at any time during the examination process or subsequent to registration, inquire into the continued validity of this consent under this Act.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark contains a reference trade mark, the Registrar shall consider whether the applicant has demonstrated reasonable grounds for believing that the use of the proposed trade mark is unlikely to cause confusion amongst consumers. Such demonstration must include evidence establishing consumer familiarity with both marks and their respective goods or services. The Registrar may require further information from the applicant concerning the nature and extent of such familiarity, including market surveys conducted in accordance with prescribed guidelines. Provided that the reference trade mark is registered under this Act, the Registrar shall not refuse registration solely on the basis of similarity between the two marks unless it is satisfied that there exists a likelihood of dilution or unfair appropriation.

Where any person seeks to register a trade mark identical or confusingly similar to a reference trade mark, the Registrar shall give notice thereof to the proprietor of the reference trade mark. Such proprietor may, within the time specified in the notice, file objections under this Act against the proposed registration. Failure to do so shall be deemed consent to the application for registration and preclude any subsequent challenge regarding similarity. Any objection filed must specify the grounds upon which it is based, including demonstrable evidence of likelihood of confusion or deception. The Registrar may require further submissions from both parties; a penalty of fifty thousand rupees shall apply to any party failing to comply with such directions.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any proprietor of a registered trade mark may grant a license to use their trade mark upon terms and conditions agreed between them and the licensee. Such licenses shall be assignable by the grantor, provided that prior written consent of the Registrar is obtained, and such consent may be withheld if deemed contrary to the public interest or detrimental to the distinctiveness of the trade mark. Where a reference trade mark is used in connection with licensed goods or services, the license agreement must clearly specify the scope of permitted use, including geographical limitations and product categories. Further, any assignment of a license shall include an undertaking by the assignee to abide by all terms stipulated in the original grant. The Registrar may issue directions regarding the form and content of such licenses and assignments as provided herein.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is refused on the ground that it is deceptively similar to a prior existing reference trade mark, the applicant shall have the right to appeal under this Act. The Appellate Board may, upon hearing both parties and considering all relevant evidence including consumer surveys and market analysis, determine whether the use of the applied-for mark would likely cause confusion or mislead consumers regarding the origin or affiliation of the goods or services. Provided that, if the Registrar finds that the reference trade mark has not been used in India for a continuous period exceeding five years, the Appellate Board may allow the application to proceed subject to such conditions as it deems fit to mitigate any potential consumer deception.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is refused under this Act on the ground that it is confusingly similar to a prior reference trade mark, the Registrar shall provide the applicant with a written statement of reasons detailing the specific similarities between the marks and the goods or services in relation to which they are used. Such statement shall include an assessment of the reputation enjoyed by the proprietor of the reference trade mark and any evidence presented regarding consumer perception. The applicant may, within sixty days from the date of receipt of such statement, submit a written response addressing the grounds for refusal. Upon consideration of the applicant’s response, the Registrar may either uphold the initial refusal or direct that the application proceed to registration, subject to conditions as deemed appropriate to mitigate any potential confusion. A denomination variety sub of the reference trade mark shall be treated similarly in this assessment.

Any person who, without due cause and with intent to deceive or falsely represent connection with any goods or services, uses a trade mark identical or confusingly similar to a registered trade mark shall be guilty of an offence under this Act. Such offender shall be liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine which may extend to five hundred thousand rupees, or both. Further, the Court may order the seizure and destruction of goods bearing the infringing trade mark, as well as all materials used in their manufacture. The Registrar may, upon receiving complaint, issue an injunction restraining the defendant from further use of the offending mark, subject to just compensation being paid to the registered proprietor of the registration trade marks.

For the purposes of this Act, a “trade mark proprietor” means any person, whether Indian or foreign citizen, registered as the owner of a trade mark under this Act, or who is otherwise entitled to use a trade mark by virtue of assignment, licence, or other instrument lawfully executed. A trade mark proprietor shall be deemed to include the successors in title and assignees of such proprietor. Where a trade mark is jointly owned, each joint proprietor shall have the right to exercise the rights conferred under this Act relating to the trade mark, subject to any agreement between them as provided herein. Any alteration to the ownership details of a trade mark proprietor must be notified to the Registrar.

An application for the registration of a trade mark shall be deemed abandoned if the applicant fails to file a reply within the time specified by the Registrar under this Act; provided that the Registrar may, at his discretion and upon satisfactory demonstration of excusable delay, extend such time period. Where an objection is raised against an application based on similarity to an earlier registered trade mark, the applicant shall bear the burden of proving that their proposed mark does not create confusion in the minds of the public. The trade mark proprietor shall be entitled to enforce the rights conferred by registration against any person infringing the said mark, subject to any limitations as may be prescribed herein. Any alteration made to a registered trade mark without prior consent from the Registrar shall render the registration liable for cancellation.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person claiming damages for the use of an identical or deceptively similar trade mark shall be entitled to recover from the defendant such sum as represents fair compensation for the loss suffered by the plaintiff as a consequence of the infringement. This includes, but is not limited to, lost profits, damage to reputation, and costs incurred in mitigating the effects of the infringing activity. The trade mark proprietor may also seek an injunction restraining the defendant from further use of the infringing mark or any confusingly similar mark. Where the infringement was committed knowingly, the Court may, as part of its judgment, award punitive damages not exceeding three times the amount of compensation awarded under this Act. Furthermore, a trade mark proprietor shall be entitled to apply for account of profits made by the defendant through the infringing use.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed by any person claiming that the proposed trade mark is likely to be confused with a prior registered trade mark or other earlier right, the Trade Marks Registry shall give notice of the opposition to the applicant and to the proprietor of the prior registered trade mark or other earlier right. The applicant may then file a counterstatement responding to the grounds of opposition as provided herein. Upon receipt of the counterstatement, the Registry shall afford the opponent an opportunity to file a reply thereto.

The Registrar shall proceed to hear and determine the matter in such manner as they deem appropriate, affording both parties a reasonable opportunity to be heard. The decision of the Registrar regarding whether the application should proceed or be refused is final, subject to appeal under this Act. A trade mark proprietor aggrieved by any order made by the Registrar may prefer an appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

A trade mark proprietor seeking assignment of rights under this Act shall submit an application to the Registrar in Form TM-B, accompanied by a certified copy of the instrument effecting the assignment. The Registrar may require further documentation demonstrating due execution and attestation as per prevailing laws relating to transfer of property. Such assignment shall only be valid if it relates to the entire trade mark, or to specific goods or services for which registration exists; partial assignments are expressly prohibited. Further, a proprietor intending to license their registered trade mark must provide an undertaking to the Registrar detailing the scope and duration of such licensing agreement, subject to conditions as may be prescribed by regulations framed under this Act. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all licensed marks and associated agreements.

Any person infringing a registered trade mark shall be liable to pay damages to the trade mark proprietor equivalent to five times the value of the goods or services in relation to which the infringement occurred, or where ascertainment of such value is not possible, an amount determined by the Court as just and reasonable. Further, any individual found guilty of knowingly making false representations concerning the ownership of a registered trade mark shall be subject to imprisonment for a term not less than six months but which may extend to three years, and also liable to a fine which may extend to one hundred thousand rupees. The Registrar may, upon complaint by a trade mark proprietor, issue an injunction restraining any person from engaging in activities detrimental to the distinctiveness or reputation of the registered trade mark.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any trade mark proprietor desiring to grant a license relating to the use of their registered trade marks shall execute a written agreement specifying the goods or services in relation to which the license is granted, the geographical area covered by such license, and the duration of the license. Such agreements may be assigned, either wholly or partially, provided that any subsequent assignee undertakes all obligations imposed upon the original licensee under this Act. The trade mark proprietor shall retain the right to terminate a license agreement if the licensee fails to adhere to the terms stipulated therein, particularly concerning quality control measures as defined by regulations issued under this Act. Further, assignment of licenses requires notification to the Registrar and may be subject to approval where it affects exclusive territories previously granted.

Where an objection is raised against the acceptance of an application for registration of a trade mark on the ground that it conflicts with an earlier trade mark registered under this Act, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to file its written submissions rebutting such grounds. The Registrar may, after considering the objections and the applicant’s response, direct the party raising the objection or the trade mark proprietor to appear before him at a specified time and place for oral arguments. Any order made by the Registrar under this provision is subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Intellectual Property Appellate Board shall hear appeals arising from any decision taken by the Registrar concerning the rights of a trade mark proprietor.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to the rectification of a registered trade mark, or by the refusal of an application for registration, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order sought to be appealed against. The Trade Marks Act provides that in determining whether there has been any misuse of a trade mark, the Board shall take into consideration all relevant circumstances and may grant such relief as it deems just, including an injunction restraining the defendant from using the impugned sign or signs. A trade mark proprietor seeking rectification may also apply to have a registered trade mark expunged if use thereof is no longer honest and has become deceptive. The Registrar’s decisions concerning entries in the patent office register are similarly subject to appeal.

Where an application for the registration of a trade mark is opposed on the ground that the proposed mark lacks distinctive character, the Trade Marks Registry shall give notice of the opposition to the applicant and the proprietor of the earlier trade mark or right relied upon in the notice. The applicant may then file a counter-statement rebutting the grounds of opposition. Upon consideration of the counter-statement and any further submissions made by either party, the Registrar shall determine whether the proposed mark possesses sufficient distinctiveness acquired through use as demonstrated to the satisfaction of the Registry. It is provided that where the application relates to a mark incorporating an element which demonstrates an inventive step in relation to goods or services, the applicant may adduce evidence establishing such inventive character. The trade mark proprietor shall be afforded opportunity for cross-examination during proceedings under this Act.

Where an application for the registration of a trade mark is pending adjudication before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, any subsequent action taken by the trade mark proprietor concerning the subject matter of that application shall be deemed to be without prejudice to the outcome of the proceeding. The Registrar may, upon receiving notification from the Intellectual Property Appellate Board indicating that a dies pending proceeding has been initiated, suspend further processing of any related applications or oppositions until resolution of the original dispute. Further, a trade mark proprietor seeking to rely on prior use in support of an application shall provide documentary evidence demonstrating continuous and uninterrupted usage throughout the pendency period, as determined by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Where any person alleges that another has made use of an identical or deceptively similar trademark in contravention of this Act, and demonstrates a substantial loss of profits attributable thereto, the aggrieved party shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief from the relevant High Court. Such injunction may restrain the infringing activities, including but not limited to advertising campaigns and distribution networks employed by the defendant. The trade mark proprietor seeking such relief must provide evidence establishing prior use and reputation associated with their trademark, irrespective of whether circumstances application advertised were utilized in building that reputation. Failure to comply with a court order under this Act shall render the defaulter liable for compensatory damages, determined at the discretion of the Court, up to an amount not exceeding ten times the loss suffered by the trade mark proprietor.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any trade mark proprietor desiring to grant a license relating to the use of their registered trade mark shall submit an application to the Trade Mark Registrar detailing the scope, duration, and geographical limitations of such license. The Registrar may, after reviewing the application and providing reasonable opportunity for objection from interested parties, record the license as part of the public register pertaining to the trade mark. Assignment of a registered trade mark, or any right associated therewith, including licenses granted under this Act, shall require prior notification to the Trade Mark Registrar and may be subject to conditions imposed by the Registrar to safeguard against unfair competition or dilution of the trade mark’s distinctiveness. Further, a trade mark proprietor granting such a license remains ultimately responsible for ensuring compliance with all provisions of this Act relating to the use of their registered trade mark.

Where an objection is raised against the acceptance of an application for registration of a trade mark on the ground that it conflicts with an earlier right, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to file its written submissions and evidence in response to such objection. The Registrar may, after considering the said submissions and evidence, direct the party holding the earlier right to present their counter-submissions within a prescribed period. Failure by either party to comply with these directions may result in the Registrar’s decision being rendered ex parte. Any aggrieved party dissatisfied with the Registrar's order under this Act relating to conflicting rights may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, provided that such an appeal is filed within sixty days of the date of communication of the order and subject to regulations governing appeals. The trade mark proprietor bears the onus of proving non-infringement in any proceeding.

Where an international registration designating India is opposed under this Act, the evidence presented by the opponent shall be deemed to relate solely to matters affecting distinctiveness within the territory of India and not to any other jurisdiction. Provided that, if the International Bureau notifies the Registrar of a conflict arising from a prior right in another designated country, the Registrar may consider such information relevant for determining registrability in India. The decision of the Registrar regarding the acceptance or rejection of an international registration shall be appealable to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of that decision. Further, any party aggrieved by an order of the Appellate Board concerning an international registration trade mark may prefer an appeal to the Supreme Court under provisions as provided herein.

The proprietor of an Indian trade mark registered under this Act may apply for extension of protection conferred by an international registration designating India, subject to compliance with prescribed formalities. Such application shall be made within five years from the date on which the international registration acquired force in relation to India. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating continued use of the mark internationally during the period since its initial designation of India, as provided herein. Failure to provide satisfactory evidence may result in refusal of extension or limitation of protection. Any person aggrieved by a decision relating to an application for particulars international registration may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of that decision. The Board’s determination shall be final and binding.

Upon receipt of an official communication from the International Bureau concerning an international registration designating India, the Registrar shall diligently record the particulars of such international registration within the Trade Marks Registry. This record shall include, but not be limited to, the mark itself, its representation as filed, the date of filing at origin, and any limitations or restrictions applicable under the law of the originating jurisdiction. The Registrar may require further clarification from the applicant regarding any ambiguity in these particulars before completing the registration.

Any party aggrieved by a decision concerning the recording of particulars international registration may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days of such decision. Provided that, the appeal shall only be maintainable on grounds relating to procedural irregularities or demonstrable errors in the interpretation of foreign law as it pertains to the mark's eligibility for protection under this Act. The Registrar’s determination regarding the completeness and accuracy of the recorded particulars is final subject to any successful appeal.

Any proprietor seeking rectification of a trade mark registered pursuant to an international registration shall provide evidence demonstrating misleading or deceptive use by another party within the territory of India. Failure to submit such compelling evidence, verified under oath and conforming to prescribed forms, will render the application for rectification void ab initio. The Registrar may, at their discretion, require further affidavits or expert testimony to ascertain the veracity of claims made regarding consumer confusion or dilution. Any person found deliberately submitting false information in support of a rectification proceeding relating to particulars international registration shall be liable to a fine not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees and imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years.

The owner of an internationally registered trade mark shall be entitled to grant licenses conferring rights relating to the use of the mark within India, subject to the conditions specified therein. Such licenses may include exclusive or non-exclusive rights and may be assigned freely, provided that any assignment is notified to the Registrar within three months of its execution. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all such assignments as part of the particulars international registration file for each designated mark. Where an internationally registered trade mark incorporates elements already protected under this Act in India, the licensing agreement must explicitly delineate the scope of use permitted that does not infringe upon existing rights. Further, any subsequent modification to the international registration affecting its designation in India shall be notified to all licensees and assignees as provided herein.

Where an application is filed for registration of a trade mark and a notice of opposition is served under this Act, the applicant may, within two months from the date of service of such notice, file with the Registrar a counterstatement rebutting all facts and allegations contained in the notice of opposition. The Registrar shall consider any evidence submitted by either party relating to the distinctiveness or reputation of the trade mark subject to the opposition. Should the Registrar find merit in the applicant’s counterstatement, he may direct that the opposition be set aside. Any person aggrieved by an order setting aside an opposition may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. Failure to comply with this provision shall render the appeal inadmissible and preclude any further remedy as provided herein concerning a *register proposed registered* trade mark.

Application for registration of a trademark may be made by any person claiming ownership or use thereof, subject to compliance with all prescribed formalities. Where a person seeks to register a proposed registered trade mark, such application shall specify in detail the geographical area and the class of goods or services relating to which registration is sought. The Registrar shall examine whether the mark is distinctive in relation to the specified goods or services and not descriptive of them. Further, an examination will be conducted to ascertain if the proposed registered trademark conflicts with any existing trademarks already registered under this Act or pending for registration. Any opposition filed against a register proposed registered trade mark shall be adjudicated according to procedures as provided herein.

Any person seeking to have a mark registered under this Act shall file an application for registration proposing that it be entered on the Register of Trade Marks. Such application must include a representation of the mark and a clear statement of the goods or services in relation to which registration is sought, failing which the application may be rejected outright. Where an objection is raised against a proposed registered trade mark by any interested party, the applicant shall have the opportunity to submit written arguments and evidence within the timeframe prescribed herein. Failure to comply with these procedural requirements will render the application liable for dismissal. Any wilful misrepresentation made in connection with a register proposed registered trademark constitutes a cognizable offence punishable with imprisonment and fine.

Where an application is filed for registration of a trade mark, and objection is raised by any person claiming through prior use or other right under this Act, the Registrar may direct that the applicant furnish such evidence as the Registrar deems appropriate to substantiate the distinctiveness of the proposed registered mark. The objector shall be afforded reasonable opportunity to present counter-evidence and arguments against said submission. Upon consideration of all materials presented, including any expert testimony adduced by either party, the Registrar’s decision regarding whether a register proposed registered trade mark is registrable shall be final, subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The appellant may seek interim relief pending determination of the appeal.

Where an application for registration of a register proposed registered trade mark is opposed under this Act, the applicant shall have the right to file a counter-statement within such time as may be prescribed. The Registrar shall consider both the notice of opposition and the counter-statement, along with any subsequent replies filed by either party, and may direct the parties to appear before him for oral arguments if he deems it necessary for resolving the dispute. Provided that, where the opposing party fails to file a reply within the stipulated period, the Registrar may proceed as if such reply had been received and found unsatisfactory. Any order passed by the Registrar in respect of an opposition shall be final subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order.

For the purposes of this Act, a “register disclosed” means the publication of the trade mark register as provided herein, including particulars of registered trade marks, their proprietors, and dates of registration. Such disclosure shall be deemed complete upon placement of the relevant information in an electronically accessible format on the official website maintained by the Trade Marks Registry. Any person may access and copy any portion of the register disclosed for non-commercial purposes, subject to conditions regarding data integrity as prescribed by regulations. The Registrar shall ensure that the register disclosed is kept up to date and accurately reflects all registrations under this Act.

The Register of Trade Marks shall be maintained in such form as the Controller may prescribe, and shall contain particulars relating to each registered trade mark, including the applicant’s name and address, the goods or services for which registration is sought, the date of application, and any modifications made thereto. Any person intending to search the register for ascertaining whether a proposed trade mark is already registered may inspect the same during office hours. The information contained within the Register of Trade Marks shall be deemed publicly accessible and constitutes a *register disclosed* to all interested parties. Applications for rectification of entries in the register, alleging errors or misrepresentations, may be filed under this Act, subject to procedural requirements as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by an entry appearing in the register disclosed under this Act may, subject to provisions regarding time limits, file a representation before the Registrar. Such representation must specify the grounds upon which the grievance is based and shall be verified by the applicant as provided herein. The Registrar shall consider such representations and may direct that the record be amended or expunged if satisfied that the entry is erroneous or obtained through fraudulent means. Failure to comply with any direction of the Registrar in this regard, or continued use of a trade mark contrary to the register disclosed, constitutes an offence punishable under this Act. The aggrieved party shall have recourse to appeal from any order made by the Registrar concerning such representations before the relevant intellectual property appellate forum.

The Register maintained under this Act shall be open to public inspection during normal business hours, subject to such rules and regulations as may be prescribed. Any person desiring to inspect the Register shall make application in writing to the Registrar for permission to do so, stating therein the specific trade marks or entries sought to be examined. The Registrar may require a fee for each inspection request received. Information pertaining to registered trade marks, including but not limited to the proprietor’s name and address, goods and services for which registration is accorded, and dates of registration and renewal, shall constitute the register disclosed. Any unauthorized reproduction or dissemination of information extracted from the Register without prior written consent of the Registrar shall be deemed a violation under this Act. The registrar may, at his discretion, restrict access to certain sensitive data within the Register, provided that such restriction is duly justified in writing and published on the official website.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is granted and the register disclosed to the public, any subsequent alteration to the particulars of ownership recorded therein shall require prior notification to all parties who have demonstrably relied upon the information contained within said register. Such reliance must be evidenced by documented commercial activity undertaken within six months preceding the proposed alteration, including but not limited to advertising materials or contractual agreements referencing the trade mark as registered. The Registrar may, subject to due process and opportunity for objection from affected parties, permit the amendment if satisfied that it does not prejudice existing rights acquired under this Act. Provided that any such amendment shall be accompanied by a reasoned order detailing the justification for deviation from the initially disclosed register.

Any person aggrieved by an entry appearing in the register disclosed under this Act may, subject to provisions regarding time limits, file a rectification application before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such application shall specify the particulars of the entry sought to be rectified and state the grounds upon which such rectification is claimed. Failure to comply with prescribed forms or payment of requisite fees shall render the application void. The Board may, after affording an opportunity for hearing to all interested parties, direct amendment, deletion, or addition to the register. Any order made by the Board under this provision is final and binding, subject to appeal before a High Court within whose territorial jurisdiction the registered trade mark has its principal place of business; penalties for non-compliance shall apply as provided herein.

Where a trade mark is registered, the proprietor may grant licences for the use of the registered trade mark relating to specified goods or services. Such licences shall be in writing and clearly define the scope of permitted usage, including geographical limitations and duration. The proprietor shall retain the right to terminate any such licence upon providing thirty days’ written notice if the licensee fails to adhere to the terms stipulated therein. Assignment of a registered trade mark, or any rights accruing under this Act, is permissible subject to registration with the Registrar. Any assignment shall include details regarding the licensed use, ensuring continuity for existing licensees. The register disclosed shall reflect all assignments and licences granted, providing public notice of such arrangements and preventing conflicting claims concerning the trade mark’s application.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act, and the grounds of opposition relate solely to the similarity of the applied-for mark to a previously registered trade mark, the Registrar shall provide the applicant and the opponent each with a copy of the register disclosed during the opposition proceedings. The opponent may, within thirty days from the date of receipt of such copy, submit further evidence demonstrating likelihood of confusion arising from the use of the marks as they exist in the public domain. Provided that any submission made after this period shall be deemed inadmissible unless leave is granted by the Registrar for reasons to be recorded in writing. The applicant may then respond to said evidence within a further fifteen days; failure to do so shall be construed as an abandonment of the opposition.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is refused under this Act, the applicant may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeal shall lie within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order of refusal and shall be accompanied by a fee as prescribed. The Board may, after giving notice to all interested parties and affording them an opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify or reverse the decision appealed against. It is provided that any party aggrieved by an order of the Intellectual Property Appellate Board affirming a refusal may further appeal to the Supreme Court within sixty days from the date of such order. The register disclosed under this Act shall be considered conclusive evidence of registration, subject to any successful challenge based on demonstrable misrepresentation or fraudulent use of the mark, including unauthorized mark use.

For the purposes of this Act, a “register disclosed” shall mean the public availability of information pertaining to registered trade marks as displayed on the Trade Marks Registry’s electronic database and accessible by any person. The register disclosed includes, but is not limited to, details concerning the mark itself, the proprietor's name and address, the goods or services for which registration is accorded, and the date of such registration. Further, petition particulars contained within an application for rectification or opposition shall be considered part of the register disclosed, subject to any orders restricting public access as provided herein.

The register disclosed under this Act shall remain accessible for public inspection during normal business hours, subject to regulations as may be prescribed. Any person seeking access shall comply with procedures outlined by the Registrar and pay such fees as determined. Where an application for registration is based on a convention application shall have been made in another country, particulars of that foreign application must be furnished to the Registrar within three months of the date of this Act’s commencement. The applicant shall also provide evidence demonstrating the entitlement to claim priority under the Convention. Any alteration or amendment to the register shall be promptly notified and remain publicly available.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Trade Marks Registry relating to the registration of a trade mark, including but not limited to decisions concerning opposition proceedings or rectification applications, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such decision. The right of appeal shall extend to any matter arising out of an order made under this Act, provided that the aggrieved party demonstrates demonstrable prejudice resulting directly from the Registry’s actions. Furthermore, where a trade mark is registered and subsequently amended by way of a patent of addition covering further goods or services, the register disclosed at registration shall be deemed to reflect such amendment for all purposes relating to infringement proceedings. The Trade Marks Registry may, upon application, correct errors in the register; however, any alteration affecting rights conferred under this Act requires notice to all interested parties.

An application for registration of a trade mark may be refused if it contains matter which, when considered together with the representation of the trade mark, is likely to deceive or cause confusion. Where an applicant has filed an application and paid the requisite fees, the Registrar shall publish particulars of such application in the Trade Marks Journal. Any person alleging that their interests are adversely affected by the acceptance of the application may file a notice of opposition under this Act within the prescribed period. Upon receipt of such opposition, the Registrar shall afford both the applicant and the opponent an opportunity to be heard. The register disclosed publicly shall contain details of all registered trade marks, including the name and address of the business india applicant, and the date of registration.

An application for registration of a trade mark may be made by any person claiming ownership or use thereof, and such application shall contain all particulars specified in the First Schedule. The Registrar shall examine each register proposed in accordance with the provisions under this Act, including verification of distinctiveness and permissible usage. Where an objection is taken to a register proposed on grounds of similarity to existing marks, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity for hearing, subject to payment of the prescribed fee. Further, any person aggrieved by a decision regarding a register proposed may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within a period as provided herein. The Registrar’s determination concerning registrability is final, barring such appeals.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act, the applicant for the register proposed may, within such time as may be prescribed, file a counterstatement responding to the grounds of opposition. Failure to do so shall constitute abandonment of the application. The Registrar shall provide both parties with an opportunity to present evidence and arguments relevant to the validity of the trade mark and the merits of the opposition. Any order made by the Registrar following such consideration may be appealed to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. It is provided that any appeal must specify the grounds upon which it is based, and the appellant shall bear the burden of demonstrating error in the original decision. The applicant’s rights under this Act are subject to any prior conflicting use established before the date of publication of the register proposed.

An application for a register proposed may be made by any person claiming use of a mark as a trade mark, or by any registered proprietor seeking to extend the registration to cover additional goods or services. Such an application shall include a representation of the mark as applied and a list specifying all goods or services in connection with which the applicant claims right to use the mark. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further particulars deemed necessary for proper examination under this Act, including evidence of prior use where claimed. Where the proposed register relates to a collective mark or certification trade mark, the application must also include details regarding the constitution and functioning of the association or body concerned. Objections to a register proposed may be filed by any interested party within the prescribed period, stating reasons for opposition and supported by relevant documentation as provided herein.

An application for a register proposed under this Act shall be deemed incomplete unless it is supported by an affidavit verifying the distinctiveness of the mark as against its use in relation to identical or similar goods or services. The Registrar may require further evidence demonstrating acquired reputation, provided that such requirement does not unduly delay processing. Any representation made within the application concerning prior conflicting marks shall be subject to verification through a search report generated under this Act and submitted alongside the application. Furthermore, where the proposed mark incorporates a geographical indication, consent from the relevant authority administering said indication must be obtained and documented as part of the register proposed. The Registrar may reject the register proposed if any condition precedent is not fulfilled.

Any person seeking to have a register proposed for a mark used in relation to goods or services shall file an application with the Registrar, detailing the specific classes and sub-classes relevant to their intended use. The application must include evidence demonstrating prior honest concurrent usage where applicable, subject to verification by the Registrar. Failure to provide adequate proof of such usage may result in rejection of the register proposed. Any party aggrieved by a decision regarding a register proposed may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days. Deliberate misrepresentation or fraudulent conduct during the application process shall attract penalties as provided herein, including fines and potential criminal prosecution.

Where a trade mark is sought to be registered, and where an existing proprietor desires to grant a license relating thereto, such license may be recorded as part of the register proposed. The application for registration shall specify the full terms of the licensing agreement, including but not limited to the permitted geographical territory, duration, and scope of goods or services covered by the license. Any assignment of rights arising from such a registered trade mark license shall also be notified to the Registrar in writing, accompanied by an affidavit verifying its authenticity. The Registrar may require further documentation as deemed necessary to ascertain compliance with provisions under this Act relating to fair competition and consumer protection. Failure to disclose material terms or conditions within the register proposed will render the licensee liable for penalties as provided herein.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act, the applicant whose register proposed trade mark is subject to opposition may, within such time as may be prescribed, file a counterstatement responding to the grounds of objection raised by the opponent. The Registrar shall consider both the notice of opposition and the counterstatement, along with any subsequent replies filed by either party, and may direct the parties to appear before him for oral arguments if he deems it necessary for resolving disputed issues of fact or law relating to distinctiveness or likelihood of confusion. Any order made by the Registrar after such consideration shall be final subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within a period specified herein.

Where an application is filed for a register proposed under this Act, the Trade Marks Registry shall publish a notice thereof in the Trade Marks Journal. Any person feeling aggrieved by such proposed registration may, within sixty days from the date of publication, file objections with the Registrar, setting forth clearly the grounds upon which such objection is based. The Registrar shall consider all objections received and provide an opportunity for both the applicant and the objector to submit written arguments and counter-arguments. Decisions regarding these registrations are subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. It is provided that the deliberations of the Board concerning matters arising from disputes relating to registration proposals may be viewed by Members of Parliament during sittings of Houses parliament, as per established parliamentary procedure.

For the purposes of this Act, a “composite mark” means a mark consisting of two or more marks which are capable of being treated as separate elements, where one or more of those elements is already registered under this Act or is identifiable as a distinctive mark previously used by another person. The Registrar shall register a composite mark if he is satisfied that the applicant claims the entire mark and does not seek to assert rights only in respect of any particular element thereof. Provided that such registration shall not prejudice any existing right which any other person may have in relation to any element of the composite mark, as provided herein.

The Registrar shall register a geographical indication in Part A of the Register if he is satisfied that the application meets all requirements as provided herein. An applicant seeking registration shall furnish evidence demonstrating use of the good for which the geographical indication is sought by producers within the defined geographic area, and such use must be continuous and substantial. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating this claim before proceeding with registration. Provided that, if the application relates to an agricultural product or a foodstuff, the applicant shall also submit details of the quality, reputation, or other characteristics directly attributable to its origin. The registrar shall register such geographical indications as he deems distinctive and not deceptive under this Act.

Where an application for registration of a trademark is opposed under this Act, and the evidence submitted by the applicant fails adequately to demonstrate acquired distinctiveness in relation to the goods or services specified in the application, the Registrar shall register the mark only if satisfied that use consistent with honest practices has been undertaken prior to the date of publication of the application. Provided that any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar refusing registration on grounds of lack of acquired distinctiveness may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The applicant shall be liable for costs incurred by the appellant if the appeal is unsuccessful, as determined by the Board. Furthermore, failure to comply with procedural requirements during opposition proceedings may render an application ineligible for registration.

An application for registration of a sound mark may be made in the prescribed form, detailing the distinctive elements of the sound and providing an adequate representation thereof through musical notation or verbal description. The Registrar shall register a sound mark if he is satisfied that the representation provided accurately reflects the sound and that it is capable of distinguishing the goods or services of the applicant from those of others under this Act. Where an objection is raised by any person to the acceptance of such an application, the Registrar may direct the applicant to file his written statement of defence within a specified time. The Registrar shall consider all relevant evidence presented by both parties and issue an order either accepting or rejecting the application, providing reasons for the decision. Any party aggrieved by such an order may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board as provided herein.

The Registrar shall register a geographical indication in Part A of the Register of Geographical Indications upon receiving an application that complies with all requirements as provided herein. The applicant must demonstrate, through verifiable data and evidence, that the quality, reputation, or other characteristic of the goods originates from the specified geographical area. Furthermore, the application shall include a map clearly delineating the boundaries of the geographical area, certified by a recognized surveying authority. Any opposition to registration under this Act may be filed within three months from the date of advertisement; however, such opposition must specify grounds for rejection based on deceptive similarity or misrepresentation. The Registrar may require further clarification or documentation before proceeding with registration.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is filed, and the Registrar finds that the use of such trade mark is likely to cause confusion in relation to goods or services offered by another person already using a similar mark, the registrar shall register the mark only subject to limitations as determined by the Registrar. Such limitations will be recorded on the Register and are binding on the applicant. Any party aggrieved by the imposition of these limitations may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of publication of the decision. Failure to comply with the conditions imposed under this Act shall render the registered proprietor liable for damages, including compensation for loss of reputation and goodwill, as provided herein.

The Registrar shall register an assignment of a trade mark where application is made in the prescribed form, supported by a duly executed instrument evidencing the transfer. Such assignment may relate to the entire trade mark or to some specific goods or services for which it is registered, provided that the assignor remains liable under this Act for any pre-existing infringements occurring prior to the date of registration of the assignment. Where a license is granted in respect of a trade mark, the licensee shall be deemed an assignee for the purposes of revocation proceedings initiated by the proprietor, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated within the licensing agreement. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating the validity of any such transfer or license before registration is effected. Any subsequent assignment of rights derived from a prior license requires notification to the Registrar.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act, the Registrar shall register the trade mark in relation to the goods or services specified in the application only after considering all evidence submitted by both the applicant and the opponent. The Registrar may, at any time during the opposition proceedings, require either party to furnish further information or submit additional documents relevant to the dispute. Any order passed by the Registrar determining the merits of an opposition is subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within a period of sixty days from the date of such order. Provided that, if the applicant demonstrates demonstrable prejudice due to any delay in processing the application, the appellate board may condone the delay and entertain the appeal.

For the purposes of this Act, a ‘certified trade mark’ means a trade mark which has been certified as conforming to a particular standard specified in the regulations framed under this Act. The Registrar shall register a certified trade mark upon application made in the prescribed form and accompanied by evidence of conformity with the said standard. An applicant for registration of a certified trade mark must demonstrate that they are authorized by the body responsible for specifying the standard. Further, the validity of such registration is contingent on continued compliance with the specified standard; any deviation may render the registration liable to cancellation. A valid registered proprietor retains rights subject to these provisions.

The Registrar shall register a mark as distinctive where an application is filed under this Act, provided that the applicant demonstrates sufficient use of the mark in relation to the specified goods or services. The period for which such use must be demonstrated shall be determined according to regulations framed by the Central Government. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar refusing registration may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. Further, applications relating to marks associated with proceedings before Parliament during a house parliament session will be afforded priority processing, subject to verification of authenticity and adherence to prescribed timelines. The registrar may require further documentation substantiating claimed use at any stage of the registration process.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is filed under this Act, the registrar shall register the trademark if he is satisfied that it is distinctive in its own right and not confusingly similar to any prior marks. Provided that, where the applicant seeks protection based on use, evidence of such use satisfactory to the Registrar must be submitted within the prescribed timeframe; failure to do so will render the application liable for rejection. Furthermore, an international registration designating India under the Madrid Protocol shall be examined in accordance with these provisions and may be refused if it contravenes any provision as provided herein. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the registrar relating to registration or refusal thereof may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days.

Any individual who knowingly and wilfully applies a sign identical or confusingly similar to a registered trademark to any goods or services, with the intent to deceive or cause confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin, quality, or characteristics thereof, shall be deemed to have committed an act of falsifying trade. Such actions are strictly prohibited under this Act and constitute a civil offence. The proprietor of the trademark may pursue remedies including injunctions preventing further use of the infringing sign, as well as damages commensurate with the loss suffered due to the deceptive practice. Furthermore, repeat offenders shall be subject to enhanced penalties, including imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years and fines up to ten lakhs of rupees, provided that mitigation may be considered based on evidence of good faith.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, no suit for infringement of a registered trademark shall lie unless the trademark is duly registered and the registration is current. The Registrar may, upon application by the proprietor of a registered trademark, issue a notice to any person using a mark identical or confusingly similar to the registered trademark, directing them to cease such use within a specified period. Failure to comply with such direction renders the user liable for damages in a subsequent suit infringement registered under this Act. Provided that, where the defendant demonstrates prior honest concurrent use of the mark before the date of application for registration, relief may be granted as the Court deems just, subject to conditions safeguarding the distinctiveness of the registered trademark and preventing consumer confusion.

Where an owner of a registered trademark reasonably believes that another person is using a sign detrimentally affecting the distinctiveness or reputation of the registered mark, such owner may institute a suit infringement registered under this Act. Provided that, prior to initiating legal proceedings, the owner shall furnish a written representation to the alleged infringer detailing the nature of the suspected infringement and affording them a period of thirty days for response and remediation. Further, if the infringing use is demonstrably unintentional and arises from honest, non-commercial activity, the Court may, subject to considerations of public interest and equitable principles, grant relief proportionate to the harm caused, without necessarily requiring cessation of the activity. The owner shall bear the burden of proving both ownership of the registered mark and the existence of infringement as provided herein.

Any suit infringement registered concerning a trademark as provided herein may only be commenced within the jurisdiction where the defendant resides, carries on business, or has a place of establishment, or where the cause of action arose. The Court shall have power to grant such relief, including injunctions and damages, as it deems just and equitable, subject to the plaintiff demonstrating actual damage resulting from the infringing use. Where the infringement is wilful and for fraudulent purpose, the Court may award punitive damages not exceeding ten times the proven loss or detriment suffered by the proprietor of the trademark. The defendant shall be liable to account for all profits derived from such infringement.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, the proprietor of a registered trade mark may grant exclusive licences relating to the use of the said mark within specified territories or for specific goods or services. Such licence agreement shall clearly define the scope of permitted use, including but not limited to geographical limitations, product categories, and duration. Any assignment of a registered trade mark, whether absolute or partial, shall be recorded in the Register Book as provided herein. Where an exclusive licence is granted, the proprietor retains the right to institute a suit infringement registered relating to any unauthorized use of the trade mark outside the scope of the license agreement. Further, the licensee shall hold the proprietor harmless against claims arising from their use of the mark, unless such claims result directly from acts or omissions attributable to the proprietor.

No suit for infringement of a registered trademark shall lie unless the proprietor has served upon the alleged infringer a notice specifying the nature of the infringement and demanding that the infringing use shall cease within two months. Provided that where the defendant is engaged in industry connected with the trade or business relating to the registered mark, the period specified in the notice may be reduced to one month, subject to judicial review. The proprietor may appeal an order dismissing their suit for infringement under this Act to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such order. Further, any interlocutory orders made during proceedings concerning a suit infringement registered trademark are also subject to appeal as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, “use” in relation to a trade mark shall include not only the application of the mark to goods but also any act which is liable to be associated with the applicant for registration of the trade mark or with the owners of the registered trade mark. An act shall constitute infringement or for passing off referred to in section 13 4 where, subject to the provisions regarding fair use under this Act, a person applies a mark identical or confusingly similar to a registered trade mark in relation to goods or services identical or closely related to those in respect of which the trade mark is registered. Such an act shall be deemed to falsely represent connection with the owner of the registered trade mark.
primary_entity: infringement or for passing off referred to in section 13 4

context: Where a trade mark is registered in accordance with this Act, the registration shall be conclusive evidence of the proprietorship of the trade mark and entitlement to exclusive rights under this Act; provided that such conclusiveness shall not apply where the registration was obtained fraudulently or through misrepresentation. Any person who, without due cause or consent from the proprietor of a registered trade mark, uses a trade mark which is identical or confusingly similar to the said registered trade mark in connection with goods or services for which the trade mark is registered, shall be deemed guilty of infringement or for passing off referred to in section 13 4. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint, investigate any alleged instance of such use and issue directions as he deems appropriate.
