Use registered trade marks shall be deemed to include instances where a similar sign is used in relation to identical or similar goods or services, provided that such use creates confusion amongst consumers regarding the identity of the source. The Registrar may issue directions concerning permissible forms of use under this Act.

The Registrar may, upon application by a registered proprietor seeking to assert their rights under this Act, direct any person making use registered trade mark in relation to goods or services identical or similar to those for which the trade mark is registered, to cease such use. Such direction shall be issued only if the Registrar finds that the continued use registered trade mark constitutes an infringement of the registered proprietor’s exclusive right and causes demonstrable harm to their goodwill or reputation. The application may include evidence demonstrating the extent and nature of the infringing use, as well as any financial losses suffered by the applicant attributable thereto. Provided that, nothing herein shall prevent a person from using a descriptive term solely to accurately describe their goods or services.

The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint from any person alleging interference with their rights under this Act, direct an inquiry to be conducted into the matter. Such inquiry shall ascertain whether the use registered trade mark by another party is causing demonstrable damage to the complainant’s business interests or reputation. The Director General of Trade Marks shall appoint an investigating officer who will record evidence and submit a report within ninety days. If the investigation reveals that the continued use registered trade mark constitutes a violation of equitable considerations, including but not limited to unfair competition or passing off, the Registrar may issue directions restricting such use. These directions are subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The complainant shall bear the cost of the inquiry unless it is determined that the complaint was frivolous or vexatious.

Where any person makes use registered trade mark in a manner that falsely suggests an association with the proprietor thereof, or otherwise creates confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or nature of goods or services, such person shall be liable for damages. The amount of damages shall be determined by the Court, taking into consideration the loss suffered by the proprietor and any profits made by the infringing party as a result of the unauthorized use. Further, where an infringement is established under this Act, the Court may issue an injunction restraining the infringer from continuing such use registered trade mark, provided that the proprietor demonstrates ongoing harm resulting from the deceptive practice. Any appeal against such an order shall be subject to a penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees.

Where an objection is raised against the registration of a trade mark on the ground that it is likely to be confused with a prior registered trade mark, the Registrar may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating honest and continuous use registered trade in relation to the goods or services specified in the application. Such evidence shall include details regarding the extent of sales, advertising expenditure, and market penetration achieved during the period of such use. The proprietor of the earlier registered trade mark may then file a counter-statement disputing the applicant’s claim of honest use, presenting their own evidence to demonstrate that the alleged use is minimal or deceptive. Both parties shall be afforded an opportunity to cross-examine witnesses under this Act and submit written arguments before a decision is rendered by the Registrar.

The registered trade mark ‘SecureFlow’ for software relating to data encryption shall permit use by Bharat Informatics Limited where such use is solely within the context of providing secure government services, and provided that any modification or adaptation of the computer programme incorporating the SecureFlow trade mark is undertaken only by employees of Bharat Informatics Limited possessing appropriate security clearances as determined under extant governmental regulations. Further, such use registered trade mark shall be subject to a periodic audit conducted by an independent auditor appointed by the Controller, confirming adherence to prescribed data handling protocols and non-commercial exploitation. Any distribution or licensing of the modified computer programme outside of government service provision will constitute infringement under this Act.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark shall have the exclusive right to use that trade mark throughout India in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered, and may grant licences permitting such use by third parties. Any licence granted under this Act shall be in writing and specify the territory within which, and the time during which, the licensee is authorized to make use of the registered trade mark. The proprietor may assign any right arising under this Act relating to the use registered trade mark, including any licence agreement, subject to prior approval from the Controller if such assignment involves a foreign entity or concerns goods deemed critical to the security of India. Such approvals shall be granted only after due consideration of national interests and potential economic impact. The proprietor is responsible for ensuring that all licensees adhere to conditions stipulated in their agreements.

For the purposes of this Act, “use registered trade” with respect to a trademark shall mean the employment of the mark in relation to goods or services for which it is registered, or identical thereto, including but not limited to its appearance on labels, packaging, advertising materials, and directly associated with the offering for sale or distribution thereof. Such use shall be deemed continuous where it occurs repeatedly over a period sufficient to indicate an intention to maintain the mark’s presence in the market. A proprietor seeking to demonstrate continued *use registered trade* may submit an affidavit provided under oath detailing such usage, including dates and geographical scope, subject to verification by the Registrar.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, an applicant seeking protection for a plant variety shall propose a denomination for that variety. The proposed denomination must not contain any descriptive or generic terms referring to the plant’s characteristics, origin, or intended use. Furthermore, it shall not resemble any existing denomination already registered under this Act or any similar denomination used in commerce within India, as determined by the Authority. Any alteration of a denomination after registration is permitted only with prior approval from the Authority and following a public notice period of ninety days. The Authority may reject a proposed denomination if it contravenes these stipulations or creates confusion regarding the protected variety’s identity; such rejection shall be communicated in writing to the applicant, detailing the reasons for non-compliance concerning the denomination sub section.

For the purposes of this Act, a “denomination variety sub” shall mean a denomination assigned to a plant variety that has been registered as per the provisions herein and which is further subdivided into distinct lines or varieties exhibiting specific characteristics not readily apparent in the original registration. Such subdivision shall be documented with the Authority, detailing the phenotypic differences and genetic stability of each sub-variety relative to the parent variety. The Authority may require demonstration of continued uniformity within a denomination variety sub through established testing protocols. Any alteration affecting essential characteristics of a registered denomination variety sub requires notification and approval under this Act, subject to guidelines issued by the Central Government.

An application for registration as a denomination variety shall include particulars specifying the botanical name of the plant species concerned, along with details regarding its origin and method of derivation. The Authority may require submission of documentation substantiating the claimed novelty and stability of the proposed denomination. Further, an applicant intending to register a *denomination variety sub* must demonstrate that it possesses characteristics substantially different from existing varieties of the same species, as determined through established testing procedures. Such testing shall be conducted in accordance with guidelines prescribed by the Board. The application shall also state the intended use of the denomination and provide evidence of its suitability for commercial exploitation, subject to fulfilling all requirements under this Act.

Any person who, having knowledge that a denomination is likely to be confused with an existing denomination variety sub for any plant variety, uses such denomination in connection with the marketing or sale of propagating material or seed of any kind shall be liable to pay damages equivalent to three times the value of the infringing material. Further, under this Act, any officer empowered by the Central Government may seize and detain any propagating material bearing an unauthorized denomination variety sub pending investigation. Where a contravention of these provisions is established, the offender shall also be subject to a penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees, recoverable as civil debt. The Authority may issue orders restraining further use of the infringing denomination.

Where a plant breeder or any other person aggrieved by an order passed by the Plant Variety Protection Appellate Authority under this Act, including but not limited to orders concerning the registration or rejection of a denomination variety sub, may prefer an appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such order. The appellate authority shall, before entertaining any appeal, satisfy itself that the appellant has made out a prima facie case involving a substantial question of law. Provided that if the appellant was unable to file the appeal within the stipulated period due to sufficient cause, the High Court may entertain the appeal after hearing arguments from both parties and being satisfied with the reasons for the delay; otherwise, the appeal shall be dismissed.

The Authority may, upon application by a registered plant breeder or farmer, grant a non-exclusive license to utilize a denomination variety sub for propagation or sale, subject to payment of royalties as determined by the Central Government. Such licenses shall be assignable, with prior written consent from the Authority, and any assignment shall be recorded in the Register of Denomination Varieties. Where a licensee exports propagating material containing the protected denomination variety sub under the provisions of the Customs Act 1962, they shall declare such export to the Authority within thirty days of shipment. Failure to do so may result in penalties as prescribed herein. The Central Government may, after due inquiry and providing an opportunity for hearing, revoke a license if the licensee engages in unfair trade practices or breaches the terms stipulated therein. Further, any transfer of rights relating to a denomination variety sub shall be deemed valid only upon registration with the Authority.

An application for registration of a denomination variety shall be accompanied by detailed documentation specifying the lineage of the plant material, including parentage and breeding history. The Registrar may require submission of additional data pertaining to the expression of essential characteristics relevant to maintaining varietal purity. Such information must demonstrate stability across successive generations and adherence to established standards as prescribed under this Act. Further, an applicant proposing a denomination variety sub shall provide evidence demonstrating that the proposed name does not conflict with existing registrations or create confusion amongst farmers regarding plant identity. The Registrar is empowered to reject applications failing to meet these evidentiary requirements, provided that the reasons for rejection are clearly articulated in writing.

Where a Plant Variety Protection Authority determines that a denomination variety sub has been unfairly exploited in contravention of provisions relating to farmers’ rights, it shall order the concerned entity to provide restitution. Such restitution may include compensation for loss of income, costs incurred in defending proceedings under this Act, and damages assessed by the authority based on the extent of the exploitation. An appeal from any order made by the Plant Variety Protection Authority regarding restitution lies to the Appellate Board. The Appellate Board shall consider evidence presented by both the aggrieved party and the entity subject to the order, and may affirm, modify, or reverse the original determination. Provided that, the Appellate Board’s decision is final, subject to further appeal to a High Court under established procedures as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, a denomination variety shall be deemed to have been formally released where it has been distributed to farmers for commercial cultivation in at least three states or three agro-climatic zones within India. Provided that, a variety cultivated solely under contract farming arrangements and not offered for general sale shall be excluded from this calculation. The authority may, subject to guidelines framed by the Board, consider applications for registration of denomination varieties irrespective of whether such release has been accompanied by formal notification as provided herein. Further, any modification or alteration to the released material impacting essential characteristics shall render the original denomination variety ineligible for protection under this Act.

An application for registration of a denomination variety shall be accompanied by a detailed description of the plant variety, including its botanical name, parentage where known, and any relevant distinguishing characteristics. The Authority may require submission of additional data, such as propagation material samples or phenotypic expression reports, to ascertain conformity with the requirements under this Act. Further, an applicant seeking registration must provide evidence demonstrating freedom-to-operate concerning existing intellectual property rights related to the variety. A denomination shall not be registered if it is deemed deceptive or contrary to public order. The Registrar may reject an application if the proposed denomination contains elements that are confusingly similar to a previously registered denomination variety.

Where a denomination variety is registered, the Registrar shall issue a certificate specifying the registrant as the owner of the breeder’s rights in respect of that denomination. Subject to any conditions imposed during registration, the registrant shall be entitled to institute civil proceedings for infringement of those rights and may seek remedies including injunctions, damages, and account of profits derived from the infringing activities. Provided that, where an unauthorized person sells propagating material or harvest bearing a registered denomination variety, the owner may apply to the Authority for appropriate action under this Act. Further, any act of misrepresentation concerning the origin or characteristics of plant material involving a registered denomination variety shall be deemed an infringement and subject to penalties as provided herein. The Registrar may also issue warnings and directions to prevent unfair competition relating to such denominations.

An application for registration of a denomination variety shall be accompanied by a detailed report prepared by an authorized institution, specifying the essential characteristics of the variety and demonstrating its stability and reproducibility across multiple generations. The Authority may require further testing or data submission if it deems the initial report insufficient to ascertain these qualities. Subject to compliance with prescribed guidelines, the Registrar shall publish a notice inviting objections from any person claiming rights or interest in the variety. Any objection received must be substantiated by documentary evidence and submitted within the stipulated timeframe as provided herein. The Authority shall then provide an opportunity for both the applicant and the objector to present their case during a hearing. Following such proceedings, the Authority’s decision regarding registration of the denomination variety shall be final.

A denomination variety shall be eligible for registration subject to compliance with the requirements as provided herein. An application for registration may be filed by any breeder, being either an individual, institution or other legal entity and shall include a detailed description of the plant variety, including its botanical classification, origin, method of production, and expression of essential characteristics. The Authority shall assess whether the denomination proposed is distinct from existing denominations under this Act and does not comprise deceptive or misleading terms. Further, the applicant must demonstrate that the denomination has been consistently used for at least three years prior to the date of application. Any alteration to a registered denomination variety requires prior approval by the Authority, subject to guidelines issued as per rules made thereunder.

Any person who knowingly markets a plant variety using a denomination which falsely suggests that it is a protected denomination variety shall be liable to pay compensation for loss or damage caused to any registered breeder. Such compensation shall be determined by the Authority and may include punitive damages not exceeding five times the value of sales attributable to the infringing use, as provided herein. Further, an officer of the company or individual responsible for the misleading marketing shall face imprisonment extending to two years, or a fine up to one hundred thousand rupees, or both, subject to appeal under this Act. The Authority may also issue a cease and desist order preventing further distribution using the unauthorized denomination variety.

The right to use a denomination variety shall vest initially with the registered breeder or their successors in title, subject to the provisions regarding farmers’ rights as provided herein. Such registration does not confer exclusive ownership but grants a limited license for commercialization and propagation. The registered breeder may grant non-exclusive licenses to third parties under terms approved by the Plant Variety Authority, specifying geographical limitations and permitted uses of the denomination variety. Assignment of these licensing rights is permissible only with prior notification and consent from the Authority, ensuring equitable access for small and marginal farmers. Any sublicensee shall be bound by the original license conditions and may not alter the intended purpose or scope without further authorization. The breeder’s right to enforce actions against infringement of their denomination variety remains subject to demonstrating substantial similarity and consumer confusion.

Where an application for registration of a variety is rejected on the ground that the proposed denomination does not meet the requirements as provided herein, the applicant shall have the right to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeal may be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order of rejection and shall state specifically the grounds upon which the application is considered to be wrongly rejected. The Board may, after affording an opportunity for hearing to both the appellant and the authority that passed the order, confirm, vary or reverse the said order. It is provided that a denomination variety shall not contain any element suggesting traits connected with the variety’s characteristics unless such connection is demonstrably accurate and verifiable through scientific data.

The right to use a denomination variety shall vest initially with the breeder or registrant as recorded in the Register. Provided that, subject to an agreement in writing, such breeder or registrant may grant licenses allowing others to propagate and market plants of the registered denomination variety for commercial purposes. Any assignment of rights under this Act relating to a denomination variety must be executed by a notary public and filed with the Plant Varieties Authority within thirty days of execution; failure to do so shall render the assignment void. Further, where a license is granted incorporating design elements integral to plant presentation or packaging, the licensor retains ownership of those designs and may separately enforce their intellectual property rights therein. The licensee shall not be permitted to sub-license such rights without prior written consent from the original breeder or registrant as provided herein.

An application for registration of a denomination variety shall be accompanied by a detailed description of the plant variety, including its botanical name, parentage where known, and any relevant distinguishing characteristics as determined through established testing procedures. The Authority may require submission of additional data or clarification regarding the applicant’s claim that the variety is new and possesses stability in its expression. Prior to acceptance for examination, the application shall be subject to a preliminary assessment to ascertain compliance with the requirements under this Act concerning essential derivation. Publication of the application will occur within three months of receipt by the Authority, unless the applicant requests deferral due to commercial considerations, provided that such deferral cannot exceed six months and requires written justification. The Registrar shall maintain a publicly accessible register detailing all published applications for denomination varieties.

For the purposes of this Act, “international application” shall mean an application filed under the Patent Cooperation Treaty and designating India as one of the designated States. An international application shall be deemed to relate to a single invention unless it contains a reference disclosing more than one invention; provided that such disclosure does not render the application unpatentable under this Act. The term “designated State” has the meaning assigned to it under the Patent Cooperation Treaty, and includes India where an international search report is available. Applications processed as international applications shall be subject to examination procedures consistent with the provisions herein relating to patentability.

Applications filed under this Act may, subject to the provisions of international treaties and conventions, be claimed as priority from an application previously filed in a convention country or a country designated by the Patent Cooperation Treaty. Where an applicant seeks to claim priority under the Patent Cooperation Treaty, he shall furnish with the application a certified copy of the application initially filed, including any information relating to claims and abstracts. The Controller may require the applicant to submit such further documentation as is necessary to verify compliance with the requirements of the treaty. Such verification shall be conducted without prejudice to the rights of other applicants or patentees under this Act. Information disclosed in an international search report received pursuant to the Patent Cooperation Treaty shall not, by itself, invalidate a patent granted herein.

Where an application for a patent has been filed under this Act, and such application claims priority from an earlier application filed outside India, the Controller may require the applicant to furnish a certified copy of the prior application. Failure to comply with this requirement within the time specified by the Controller shall render the subsequent Indian application liable to be deemed as not having been filed. The rights afforded under the Patent Cooperation Treaty shall apply in respect of international applications designating India, subject to any modifications prescribed herein relating to examination and grant procedures. Any person aggrieved by an order made by the Controller concerning the acceptance or rejection of such a patent application may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of that order. The remedies available under this Act for infringement shall be fully applicable irrespective of whether the patent was obtained directly or through the Patent Cooperation Treaty process.

Applications filed under this Act may be claimed as priority from an application filed in a Convention country, or from an international application filed under the Patent Cooperation Treaty. Where an international application is claimed as priority, the Controller shall require the applicant to furnish a certified copy of the international search report and written opinion, if available, within such time as may be prescribed. The applicant shall also provide particulars regarding any main claims initially filed in the international application. Failure to comply with these requirements will render the Indian application liable for rejection. Any amendment to the claims of an application claiming priority from an international application shall not extend beyond the content disclosed in the initial international application, subject to provisions relating to obviousness and novelty as provided herein. The Controller may require further documentation pertaining to the PCT application at any stage during examination.

Where an application for a patent is filed in India claiming priority from an application filed outside India, and such foreign application has been subjected to international phase processing under the Patent Cooperation Treaty, the Controller shall verify compliance with all applicable provisions relating to priority claims. The applicant shall furnish a certified true copy of the earlier application as part of their documentation, along with proof of filing date accepted by the receiving office designated under the Patent Cooperation Treaty. Failure to provide such evidence within the time prescribed may result in the application being deemed withdrawn. Provided that, if the foreign application undergoes substantive examination in another contracting state before its consideration in India, the Controller may request relevant examination reports from that jurisdiction, subject to reciprocity agreements.

Where an application for a patent is filed under this Act claiming priority from an application made outside India, and such foreign application has been published under the Patent Cooperation Treaty, the Controller may require the applicant to furnish a certified copy of the publication as evidence of the prior art. Failure to provide such documentation within the time specified by the Controller shall render the application liable for rejection. Any person aggrieved by a decision regarding the sufficiency of said publication may appeal to the Appellate Board. The Board’s determination shall be final, subject to further judicial review if it appears that substantial questions of law are involved and penalties for non-compliance with this provision will apply as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, any person claiming an interest in a patent application filed under the Patents Act, 1970, or subsequently designated for examination under the Patent Cooperation Treaty, may grant a license to use the invention disclosed therein. Such licenses shall be assignable, either wholly or partially, subject to registration with the Controller and payment of prescribed fees. The terms of any such assignment shall include details regarding royalties payable to the original applicant or their legal representatives, as determined by mutual agreement or arbitration under this Act. Further provision is made for compulsory licensing where a patentee unreasonably refuses to grant a license relating to an invention required for national security or public health, with appropriate compensation being awarded based on prevailing market rates and taking into account the investment undertaken by the patentee.

Where an application for a patent has been filed under this Act and subsequently enters the stage of examination, the Controller may require the applicant to furnish particulars relating to any corresponding applications made outside India, including those filed under the Patent Cooperation Treaty. Failure to comply with such a requirement shall render the application liable to be refused. Any person aggrieved by an order requiring furnishing of said particulars or by a refusal based on non-compliance may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of that order. The Board’s decision, subject to just considerations, shall be final and binding, provided that the applicant demonstrates good faith in attempting compliance.

Where an application for a patent is filed claiming priority from an application made under the Patent Cooperation Treaty, the Controller may require the applicant to furnish a certified copy of the international search report and written opinion. Failure to comply with such requirement within the time specified shall render the application liable to be refused. An appeal against this decision lies to the Appellate Board. The determination of whether the priority claim is valid, considering discrepancies between the original application and the subsequently filed Indian patent application, remains subject to judicial review. Further, if the mark 'Bharat Chemicals' is found to be a reference trade mark used in connection with similar goods or services as those claimed in the patent, this shall not automatically invalidate the patent but may be considered during any infringement proceedings.

Applications filed under this Act, claiming priority from an application filed outside India, shall be processed in conformity with the Patent Cooperation Treaty. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish copies of correspondence relating to the international search report and written opinion, as well as any subsequent examination reports received under the aforementioned treaty. Further, where an invention is deemed non-obvious by the Controller, but fails to meet requirements for patentability as provided herein, a request for reconsideration shall be entertained only if the applicant demonstrates substantial novelty arising after the initial filing date, subject to section 36e ixd regarding post-grant opposition based on prior publications. The Registrar shall maintain a register of all applications processed under the Patent Cooperation Treaty, accessible for public inspection.

A provisional specification, for the purposes of this Act, constitutes a document submitted with an application for patent that describes the invention in sufficient detail to enable a person skilled in the art to understand it. It may include drawings or diagrams necessary for understanding the invention. A provisional specification need not comply with all the requirements applicable to a complete specification as provided herein; however, it must disclose the matter described therein clearly enough to establish novelty and inventive step at the time of filing. Failure to file a complete specification within the prescribed period following the submission of a provisional specification shall render the application liable for abandonment under this Act.

An applicant seeking protection for an invention may file a patent application with a provisional specification detailing the substance of the invention. Such a provisional specification need not comply with all requirements applicable to a complete specification under this Act; however, it must adequately describe the invention and enable a person skilled in the art to understand its nature. The filing date of the provisional specification shall establish an initial priority date for the invention. An application claiming priority from such a provisional specification must be filed within six months following the date of the provisional specification. Failure to file a complete specification within this stipulated period will render the provisional application lapsed, and any subsequent claim based upon it inadmissible.

Where an applicant files an application for patent protection including a provisional specification disclosing the invention, such provisional specification shall remain in force only for a period of twelve months from the date of its initial filing. Failure to furnish a complete specification within this stipulated timeframe will render the application liable to rejection under this Act. The Controller may, subject to just cause and after affording the applicant an opportunity of being heard, extend this time limit by a further period not exceeding six months. Any person aggrieved by a decision regarding the rejection of an application due to non-compliance with these requirements relating to provisional specifications may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of such order; provided that the appellate board shall consider only questions of law arising out of the interpretation or application of provisions herein.

An applicant seeking patent protection may file an application including a provisional specification in lieu of a complete specification, provided that such provisional specification contains sufficient particulars relating to the invention to enable a person skilled in the art to put the same into practice. The Controller General shall have the power to require, by notification in the Official Gazette, the furnishing of further information or documents concerning any matter mentioned in the provisional specification if deemed necessary for clarity and completeness. Failure to furnish such requested information within the time specified may result in rejection of the application under this Act. A complete specification must be filed within a period not exceeding twelve months from the date of filing the application accompanied by the provisional specification, and shall comply with all requirements prescribed herein regarding form and content.

Where an applicant elects to file a patent application relating to a process or composition for the manufacture of a substance directly usable as a medicine, the provisional specification accompanying such application shall disclose the best method known to the applicant for carrying out the invention. Such disclosure is subject to the requirement that it be sufficient to enable a person skilled in the art to practice the invention without undue experimentation. Provided that, where the provisional specification contains claims relating to uses of the substance, these claims must clearly identify the intended therapeutic application and demonstrate reasonable grounds for believing the substance possesses such activity. Failure to comply with this disclosure standard may result in objections raised during examination under this Act. The applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to amend the provisional specification accordingly.

Where a patent application includes a provisional specification, it shall remain in force only for a period not exceeding twelve months from the initial filing date. Failure to furnish a complete specification within this stipulated timeframe will result in automatic abandonment of the application, precluding any further consideration under this Act. Any person who knowingly files an application containing a false or misleading provisional specification with intent to deceive or gain an undue advantage shall be liable for a penalty not exceeding five thousand rupees and may also face prosecution for offences relating to fraudulent misrepresentation. The Controller may, upon receiving evidence of such deceptive practice, initiate proceedings against the applicant seeking recovery of costs incurred by the office in processing the application.

Where a patent applicant submits an invention described in a provisional specification, and subsequently assigns or licenses the rights to that invention to another party prior to the furnishing of a complete specification, such assignment or license shall be subject to the conditions outlined herein. The assignor retains the right to file a complete specification within the prescribed time limit as provided under this Act; however, any subsequent assignment or further licensing agreement relating to the invention must explicitly acknowledge and incorporate the terms of the original provisional specification’s disclosure. Failure to do so may render such later agreements unenforceable in respect of aspects of the invention not adequately described therein. The Controller shall have the power to determine whether a complete specification sufficiently corresponds to the subject matter disclosed in the initial provisional specification, considering any subsequent assignments or licenses executed.

Where a patent application includes a provisional specification, it shall remain in force only for a period of twelve months from the initial filing date; however, an extension of this period may be granted by the Controller upon demonstration of exceptional circumstances hindering the timely submission of a complete specification. Any party aggrieved by such a grant or refusal may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days of notification of the order. The burden shall lie on the applicant to substantiate the necessity for extension and to prove that due diligence was exercised in preparing the subsequent complete specification. Failure to do so, or demonstrable prejudice to other applicants arising from the extended provisional status, renders the application liable for rejection at the Controller's discretion.

An applicant desiring to file a patent application may choose to initially submit a provisional specification outlining the invention. Such a provisional specification shall disclose the invention in sufficient detail to enable a person skilled in the art to put it into practice. The filing of a provisional specification does not grant any right to priority under this Act, but serves as an initial record establishing a claim date. A party proceeding with a subsequent complete specification must ensure that such complete specification is filed within forty-eight months from the date of the provisional application. Failure to do so will render the original provisional specification void and preclude further action on the invention described therein, subject to any regulations prescribed by the Controller.

Where a patent application includes a provisional specification, the applicant shall ensure that the complete specification filed within the prescribed time incorporates all matters disclosed in the provisional specification. Failure to do so may result in the rejection of the application on grounds of non-compliance with this Act. Furthermore, if the trade description applied for by the applicant in connection with the invention is not accurately reflected and comprehensively detailed within the complete specification, as originally presented in the provisional document, the Controller may issue a notice requiring amendment or clarification. The applicant shall then have opportunity to rectify any deficiencies; however, persistent non-compliance will render the patent liable to revocation under this Act, affording aggrieved parties recourse to appropriate legal remedies.

A provisional specification accompanying an application for patent shall disclose the invention sufficiently to enable a person skilled in the art to put it into practice; provided that such disclosure need not extend to describing all embodiments of the invention. Where a provisional specification is filed, the applicant may subsequently file a complete specification within the period prescribed under this Act from the filed date patent, and such complete specification shall comply with all requirements for specifications as provided herein. Failure to furnish a complete specification within said period will result in the application being considered abandoned; however, the Controller may, subject to conditions determined by him, extend that time if satisfactory reasons are demonstrated.

Where any applicant files an application for patent protection claiming priority from a prior application, and such application includes a provisional specification disclosing the invention as required under this Act, failure to furnish a complete specification within thirty-six months of the date filing application shall render the provisional specification void. Any person aggrieved by such revocation may appeal to the Controller within ninety days, subject to payment of prescribed fees. The Controller may dismiss the appeal or direct the applicant to file the requisite documentation within a further period not exceeding six months; failing compliance, enforcement actions including monetary penalties as provided herein will be initiated against the applicant.

Where an application for patent relating to a process or composition for any article or substance is accompanied by a provisional specification, the applicant shall file a complete specification within a period of twelve months from the date of the initial filing. Failure to comply with this requirement shall render the application liable to be refused. Provided that, where the Controller considers it necessary for the understanding of the invention, he may allow an extension of time not exceeding six months for filing the complete specification, subject to such conditions as he deems fit. Any person aggrieved by a refusal under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The applicant shall be entitled to claim priority from the provisional application’s filing date only if the complete specification discloses the matter disclosed in the accompanied provisional specification.

Where an application for patent relating to a process or composition for any article or substance shall be accompanied by a provisional specification, such provisional specification shall disclose the subject matter in sufficient detail to enable a person skilled in the art to carry out the invention. The applicant shall furnish within six months of the date of filing, a complete specification; failure to do so will render the application liable for rejection under this Act. Provided that, where an examiner considers it necessary for understanding the invention disclosed in the provisional specification, he may require the applicant to submit further clarification or details. An accompanied provisional specification shall not extend beyond thirty pages, inclusive of any drawings and claims. The Controller may, at his discretion, grant extensions of time for filing a complete specification, subject to payment of prescribed fees.

Where an application for patent protection relating to a process or composition for use in agriculture is presented, it shall be accompanied by a provisional specification detailing the method of manufacture and intended agricultural application. The applicant shall furnish data demonstrating efficacy against at least two prevalent pests or diseases common to major Indian crops, as determined by the Controller. Provided that, if the provisional specification does not adequately disclose the scope of protection sought, under this Act, the Controller may require further clarification before proceeding with examination. Furthermore, any claim in the complete specification subsequently filed shall be consistent with the disclosures made within the accompanied provisional specification; otherwise, such claims are deemed invalid and subject to challenge.

Where an application for patent protection is presented with an accompanied provisional specification, the Controller may, upon receiving representations from any interested party disputing the adequacy or completeness of said provisional specification in relation to the claims sought in the subsequent complete specification, direct the applicant to furnish further clarification or amendment. Such direction shall be issued within six months of the filing date of the complete specification. The applicant shall then have a period of three months to respond, failing which the application may be deemed abandoned under this Act. Provided that any such abandonment determination is subject to appeal before an Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal, and the appellant must demonstrate prejudice arising directly from the Controller’s directive.

Where an application for registration of a design is submitted with supporting documentation demonstrating novelty assessment undertaken prior to the filing date, the Controller may require submission of a detailed accompanied provisional specification outlining the inventive features claimed. This specification shall include technical drawings and descriptions sufficient to enable a person skilled in the art to reproduce the design. Failure to provide this specification within six months from the date of request will result in suspension of processing until compliance is achieved. Upon satisfactory review, a certificate registration produced by the Controller shall be deemed conclusive evidence of ownership for a period not exceeding ten years from the filing date, subject to renewal as provided herein.

Where an application for patent protection relating to a process or composition is presented with an accompanied provisional specification, such application shall remain in force only subject to the timely submission of a complete specification. The said complete specification must be furnished within a period not exceeding thirty-six months from the initial date of filing; failure to comply will result in the automatic lapse of the patent application. Furthermore, where a request for priority under a convention or treaty is claimed, the register shall brought up to date reflecting such claims and their validity. Provided that any amendment to the provisional specification shall not be permissible after the expiry of six months from its initial filing.

For the purposes of this Act, a “business india application” means an application filed by any entity engaged primarily in the publication or distribution of newspapers, periodicals, or similar printed materials relating to business, finance, or industry. Such an application may include representations of stylized text, logos, or other visual elements that directly identify the applicant’s publications and are used consistently across multiple editions or platforms. The Registrar shall consider a business india application as distinct from ordinary trade mark applications when assessing distinctiveness under this Act, provided that the applicant demonstrates continuous use for at least three years prior to filing.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark under this Act shall submit a business india application, accompanied by the prescribed fees, to the Registrar. The application must specify the trade mark sought to be registered, a clear representation thereof, and a list of goods or services with which the mark is associated. Where the applicant is not carrying on business or does not have a domicile in India, he shall appoint an agent residing in India to act for him under this Act. Such appointment shall be evidenced by a power of attorney duly executed. The Registrar may require such further information as he deems necessary to ascertain the distinctiveness and registrability of the trade mark. Any alteration made to the business india application after its filing is subject to approval by the Registrar.

Where an applicant files a business india application relating to a trademark that is deemed deceptively similar to an earlier registered trademark, the Registrar shall provide notice thereof to the proprietor of the said earlier trademark. Such proprietor may, within the time specified in the notice, file written representations objecting to the registration of the proposed mark. The Registrar shall consider these representations and any counter-representations filed by the applicant for the business india application, and may require both parties to submit further evidence or appear before him for a hearing. If, after due consideration, the Registrar finds that the use of the applied-for trademark would likely cause confusion among consumers, he shall refuse registration. Any party aggrieved by such refusal may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order.

An applicant seeking registration of a business india application relating to any goods or services shall submit Form TM-B, duly completed and supported by the requisite documentation as specified therein. The application must clearly identify the trade mark sought to be registered, state the class or classes of goods or services with which it is associated according to the prescribed classification system, and provide details regarding the applicant’s entitlement to use the mark under this Act. Where an applicant is a foreign national, they shall furnish proof of their domicile or place of business as may be required by the Registrar. The Registrar may request further information or clarification from the applicant at any stage of the examination process. Any alteration made to the application after its initial filing shall require prior approval from the Registrar and may incur additional fees as determined by regulations framed under this Act.

An applicant seeking registration under this Act shall submit a business india application accompanied by all requisite documentation, including proof of prior use where applicable, as provided herein. The application must clearly identify the goods or services with which the trade mark is associated, conforming to the prescribed classification system. Further, the applicant shall declare that they are the exclusive proprietor of the proposed trade mark and possess the right to apply for its registration. Any alteration to the business india application subsequent to its initial filing requires prior written consent from the Registrar, subject to conditions regarding substantial changes impacting distinctiveness or class coverage. The Registrar may reject an application if it determines that the mark lacks sufficient distinctiveness or conflicts with existing registered trade marks.

Any applicant submitting a business india application relating to a mark used in connection with financial services shall, upon provisional acceptance by the Registrar, furnish evidence demonstrating continuous use of the mark within Indian territory for a period not less than three years immediately preceding the date of such application. Failure to provide satisfactory documentary proof as provided herein will result in automatic rejection of the business india application and forfeiture of any fees already paid. Further, where misleading or fraudulent information is presented concerning prior usage, the applicant shall be liable to pay damages equivalent to ten times the registration fee and may face criminal prosecution under relevant provisions of the Indian Penal Code. The Registrar may also issue a cease and desist order against any infringing use.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any proprietor desiring to grant a license relating to a registered trade mark or an unregistered trademark used in connection with a business india application shall execute a written agreement specifying the scope of such license, including but not limited to territorial limitations, duration, and permitted uses. Such agreements may be assigned by the licensor to its successors in title, provided that prior written consent is obtained from the licensee unless otherwise stipulated within the original licensing agreement. The assignee shall automatically inherit all rights and obligations under the existing license as if it were the original licensor. Further, a business india application relating to a trade mark may be assigned by the applicant or registered proprietor to any person, subject to notification of such assignment to the Registrar within thirty days of its execution. Failure to notify the Registrar shall render the assignee liable for penalties as provided herein.

An application for registration of a trade mark, hereinafter referred to as a business india application, shall be deemed invalid if the applicant has failed to demonstrate continuous use of the mark in commerce within India for a period exceeding five years prior to the date of filing. However, this restriction may be waived by the Registrar upon satisfactory evidence presented that such non-use was due to circumstances beyond the reasonable control of the applicant and did not constitute an abandonment of intent to continue using the trade mark. Any party aggrieved by the decision of the Registrar regarding the validity of a business india application or the waiver of said requirement, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of such order, subject to fulfilling prescribed procedural requirements as provided herein.

Any individual or entity seeking to register a trademark under this Act, and who has demonstrably used such trademark in connection with the conduct of business in India, may file a business india application with the Registrar. Such an application must include detailed particulars regarding the goods or services associated with the mark, its period of prior use, and evidence establishing exclusive right to employ it. Failure to provide accurate information, or representation that a trademark is in use when such use has not occurred, shall constitute a cognizance offence punishable under the relevant provisions of the Indian Penal Code. The Registrar may reject an application if he considers the mark descriptive of the goods or services, or confusingly similar to an existing registered trade mark. Remedies for infringement are available as provided herein, notwithstanding any prior rejection of a business india application.

An applicant seeking registration of a business india application relating to financial consultancy services shall, prior to submission, furnish an affidavit verifying the bona fide intention to utilize the proposed trademark exclusively within the specified sector. Such verification must explicitly detail the intended market penetration strategy and demonstrate non-infringement upon existing registered marks under this Act. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating the applicant’s financial capacity to support the brand's promotion, provided that any clause invention relating to a novel methodology employed in service delivery shall be separately disclosed for assessment of distinctiveness. Failure to comply with these conditions will render the application liable for rejection.

An applicant seeking registration under this Act relating to a business india application, whether already employed or not, shall provide full particulars of the proposed licensee within the application form. Such license may extend to the use of the trade mark for specific geographical territories as determined by the Registrar, subject to conditions regarding quality control and adherence to established standards. The applicant retains ultimate ownership but grants the licensee a non-exclusive right to utilize the mark in accordance with the agreed terms. Assignment of such licenses is permissible, provided that prior written consent from the original applicant is obtained and documented with the Registrar. Where the applicant is based in a convention country section, reciprocal arrangements regarding license recognition may apply as per international agreements ratified by the Government.

Where an objection is raised by any person against a business india application, the applicant shall have the right to submit written representations addressing the grounds of such objection. These representations must be filed within sixty days from the date notice of the objection is served upon the applicant under this Act. The Registrar may, after considering the objections and the applicant’s response, either uphold the objection, requiring amendment or withdrawal of the application, or proceed with examination as if no objection had been raised. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Registrar determining trade mark distinctiveness made pursuant to such consideration may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within a period of three months from the date of receipt of that order.

For the purposes of this Act, “business india situate” means an enterprise incorporated or registered under the laws applicable within India, irrespective of its place of operation. An entity shall be deemed business india situate if its principal place of business is located within Indian territory and it actively engages in commercial activities directed towards the Indian market. This determination shall not preclude a company from also being considered business india situate based on other factors as provided herein. The Registrar may, at his discretion, require further documentation to ascertain whether an applicant qualifies as business india situate for registration purposes.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark under this Act shall furnish proof of business india situate within the territory of India, demonstrating continuous use of the proposed mark in relation to the specified goods or services. Such proof may include, but is not limited to, invoices, advertisements, sales records, and statutory declarations affirming commercial activity. The Registrar may require further documentation as deemed necessary to ascertain authenticity and establish genuine usage. Provided that an applicant who has previously abandoned a similar trade mark shall be subject to enhanced scrutiny regarding the distinctiveness of the current application. Any representation made in support of the application is subject to verification under this Act, and false statements render the applicant liable for penalties as provided herein.

Where any proprietor of a registered trade mark institutes legal proceedings alleging an infringement of that trade mark, the Court may, subject to this Act and the rules made thereunder, grant such relief as it deems just and equitable. This includes, but is not limited to, injunctions restraining the defendant from further infringing acts, damages for past infringements, and delivery up or destruction of goods bearing the infringing trade mark. The measure of damages shall be determined in accordance with principles of fairness and equity, considering factors such as lost profits, unjust enrichment, and the extent of consumer confusion caused by the infringement. Where the infringer is a business india situate outside the territory of India, enforcement proceedings may be initiated under procedures prescribed for extraterritorial jurisdiction.

An application for registration of a trade mark may be refused if, upon investigation, the Registrar is satisfied that the applicant does not possess the requisite reputation or goodwill necessary to substantiate claim of exclusive right to use the mark within India. The Registrar shall provide the applicant an opportunity to present evidence demonstrating such reputation and goodwill, including affidavits from customers, distributors, and other relevant stakeholders attesting to familiarity with the trade mark in connection with the goods or services specified in the application. Where the applicant is a business india situate outside of India, the Registrar may require submission of audited financial statements verifying continuous operation and substantial commercial activity within the territory for a period not less than three years preceding the date of application. Failure to comply with this requirement shall render the application liable for rejection.

Where an applicant seeks registration of a trade mark, it shall be established that the business india situate at the address specified in the application is actively engaged in commercial activities relating to the goods or services indicated in the application. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating such active engagement, including but not limited to audited financial statements and records of sales transactions for the preceding three years. Provided that, a newly formed entity shall submit a business plan outlining projected commercial operations and anticipated revenue streams for a period of five years. Further, where the applicant is a partnership firm, all partners must consent in writing to the trade mark application, subject to compliance with the provisions relating to partnership law.

Any proprietor utilizing a trademark within India who discovers another’s unauthorized use thereof, creating confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or quality of goods or services, shall institute proceedings before the Intellectual Property Disputes Tribunal. Where such infringing activity is demonstrably attributable to a business india situate outside the territory of India, the Registrar may, upon application by the aggrieved proprietor and subject to verification of jurisdictional facts, issue an injunction restraining further use of the mark. Failure to comply with any order issued under this Act shall render the defaulting party liable to a penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees, recoverable as arrears of land revenue. Repeated or willful infringement will attract enhanced penalties and potential criminal prosecution.

Where the proprietor of a registered trade mark desires to grant a license or assign the benefit of such trade mark, he shall execute an instrument in writing specifying the scope and duration of the license or assignment, including any territorial limitations. Such instruments must clearly identify the business india situate that is being granted the right to use the mark, and may stipulate conditions relating to quality control or permitted variations in goods or services offered under the licensed trade mark. The proprietor shall file a certified copy of such instrument with the Registrar within thirty days of its execution. Failure to do so may render the license or assignment voidable at the option of the assignee or licensee. Any subsequent transfer of rights under an existing license or assignment requires prior written consent from the original proprietor, as provided herein.

Where an objection is raised by any person under this Act against the acceptance of an application for registration of a trade mark, such objector may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of receipt of notice of the decision. The Appellate Tribunal shall hear arguments and consider evidence presented by both the applicant and the objector, and may allow or dismiss the appeal as it deems fit. It is provided that in cases where the objection relates to the similarity of the trade mark sought to be registered with an earlier trade mark used by a business india situate outside the territory of India, the Tribunal shall give due consideration to the reputation and goodwill attached to such foreign trade mark.

Where an entity seeks to register a trademark relating to financial services, it must demonstrate that its business india situate is actively engaged in the provision of such services at the time of application. The Registrar may require submission of audited accounts and relevant documentation substantiating this engagement, as provided herein. Failure to comply with these requirements shall render the application liable for rejection. Furthermore, any individual found to be knowingly submitting false or misleading information regarding the location or operational status of a business india situate in support of a trademark registration application is punishable imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, and also liable to fine. This obligation applies irrespective of whether the entity is incorporated within India or operates as a foreign company.

Where an objection is raised by the Registry against the acceptance of a proposed trademark, alleging deceptively similarity to a prior registered trademark or pending application, the applicant shall have the right to submit written arguments rebutting said objection within sixty days from the date of communication. Such arguments must specifically address each ground articulated in the Examiner’s report and may include evidence demonstrating distinctiveness acquired through use, notwithstanding perceived similarities. Further, where the applicant has initiated a patent process relating to goods or services identical or closely related to those associated with the challenged trademark, documentation pertaining to said process may be submitted as supplementary material. The Registrar shall consider all submissions and may affirm, modify, or overrule the objection; any such determination is subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. This provision applies irrespective of whether the business india situate is domestic or foreign.

For the purposes of this Act, a trade mark shall be deemed to have been registered on the date specified as such in the Register of Trade Marks, which date is determined by reference to the earliest priority claim asserted in relation to that trade mark under this Act. Where an application for registration includes multiple representations of the same mark, or where the applicant has previously filed applications relating to similar goods or services, the deemed date registration shall be calculated based on the representation and prior filings considered most representative of the intended scope of protection as determined by the Registrar. This determination is final and binding, subject to appeal under this Act.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is filed under this Act, and such application incorporates by reference any other mark already registered or capable of being registered in India, the date of filing of the original application shall be deemed to be the deemed date registration for the incorporated mark, subject to certain conditions. These conditions include that the proprietor of the original application must also be the proprietor of the referenced mark, or have obtained consent from the proprietor of said mark prior to publication under this Act. Furthermore, any subsequent amendment to the original application affecting the incorporation shall require notification and approval as provided herein. This deemed date registration extends all rights and privileges accruing to a registered trade mark holder.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is filed under this Act, and such application incorporates by reference any other mark already registered or capable of being registered under this Act, the date of registration of the incorporated mark shall be deemed to be the date on which the initial application was filed. This deemed date registration applies irrespective of when the original mark’s registration came into effect, affording protection from that earlier point in time. Any subsequent infringement actions relating to the incorporated mark may be pursued as if the incorporation had been explicitly claimed at the outset. The Registrar shall maintain a record indicating such deemed dates for clarity and transparency. Provided that this provision does not prejudice any rights acquired by third parties prior to the filing date of the initial application, but which are demonstrably relied upon in good faith.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is filed under this Act claiming priority from an earlier application made in a country outside India, the date of filing such foreign application shall be deemed to be the date of filing the Indian application for the purposes of determining seniority and any other right arising under this Act. Provided that, if the Registrar has reason to believe that the claimed priority is not genuine or that the applicant does not possess the necessary legal standing in relation to the earlier application, he may require the applicant to submit such evidence as he deems appropriate to substantiate the claim. The Registrar shall record the deemed date registration prominently on the register of trade marks and provide notice thereof to any party who has previously filed an opposition against the mark. Any subsequent amendment to the trade mark shall not affect the deemed date registration unless approved by the Registrar, subject to such conditions as he may specify.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is filed under this Act relating to goods or services that are identical or confusingly similar to those in respect of which any prior trade mark exists and such prior trade mark was registered before the date on which the applicant acquired rights or reputation in the said trade mark, then for the purposes of determining whether there has been a misrepresentation as provided herein, the date of registration of the prior trade mark shall be deemed the date of registration of the later filed application. This deemed date registration shall apply irrespective of any subsequent amendments to either application and notwithstanding that the applicant may have acted in good faith. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating acquisition of such rights or reputation before proceeding with examination.

For the purposes of this Act, where an application for registration of a trade mark is filed under section 34 relating to use not yet acquired, and such application remains pending for a period exceeding twelve months from the date of filing, it shall be deemed to have been registered as of the date of its original filing. Any person aggrieved by such deemed date registration may institute proceedings before the relevant intellectual property tribunal within six months of notification of the registration under this Act. Failure to initiate such proceedings within that timeframe shall constitute a waiver of any right to challenge the validity of the mark based on grounds relating to non-use prior to the deemed registration date, subject to just exceptions as determined by the tribunal. Penalties for false claims regarding pre-existing use will apply.

Where a trade mark is assigned prior to its registration, and the assignee subsequently files an application for registration under this Act, the date of filing such subsequent application shall be deemed, for the purposes of determining priority between conflicting applications, to be the earlier date of assignment. Provided that, where the assignor’s original application was pending at the time of assignment, and the Registrar has not yet issued a notice of acceptance in respect thereof, the deemed date registration shall extend only to the rights derived from the assigned trade mark as it existed at the point of assignment. Any license granted by the assignor relating to the use of the trade mark prior to the deemed date registration remains valid and enforceable, subject to the terms of such license agreement. The Registrar may require proof of the assignment for verification purposes.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is filed under this Act claiming priority from an earlier application made in a country outside India, the date of filing such foreign application shall be deemed to be the date of filing for the purposes of determining seniority and any right to challenge the distinctiveness of the mark as provided herein. However, it shall not be open to contest that the deemed date registration confers upon the applicant an absolute entitlement free from scrutiny regarding deceptive similarity with earlier marks already registered or applied for in India, particularly where such prior marks were used extensively before the foreign application’s priority date. Any challenge based on pre-existing use may be raised within the prescribed period following advertisement of the mark for opposition.

Where an index registered trade mark is applied for under this Act, and the applicant previously filed an earlier application for registration of an identical mark for identical goods or services, the date of filing of the earlier application shall be deemed the date of filing for the purpose of determining priority and any subsequent claim to damages. Provided that, if the Registrar finds that the earlier application was made with fraudulent intent to impede the applicant’s current application, this deemed date registration shall not apply, and the penalty under subsection (5) may be imposed upon the offending party. Any person aggrieved by such a determination may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days of notification of the order, subject to payment of prescribed fees.

Where a trade mark is assigned or licensed under an agreement entered into prior to the date on which it attains deemed date registration, such assignment or license shall be considered valid notwithstanding any provision to the contrary contained within that agreement. The Registrar may require production of the original agreement for verification purposes and may register a memorandum of such assignment or license as provided herein. Any subsequent assignee or licensee deriving title through a chain of assignments or licenses originating before deemed date registration shall hold their interest subject to the terms initially stipulated in the earliest recorded agreement, unless those terms are demonstrably inconsistent with the rights conferred under this Act. Further, any dispute concerning the validity of such pre-deemed date registration assignment or license may be adjudicated by an instituted district court having jurisdiction over the matter.

For the purposes of this Act, a trade mark shall be deemed to have been registered on the date specified as the deemed date registration in the certificate of registration. This deemed date is significant for determining priority between conflicting applications and for assessing periods of use necessary to establish acquired distinctiveness under this Act. The applicant shall be entitled to exclusive rights over the trade mark as if it had been registered on that deemed date, subject to any prior registrations or pending applications with superior seniority. Any acts performed after the deemed date but before the actual registration date shall be treated as infringements for the purposes of remedies available under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, an indication shall be deemed as claiming geographical origin if it concerns agricultural products, foodstuffs, wines, spirits, beverages, manufactured goods, or handcrafts which have a special quality, reputation, or characteristics attributable essentially to the geographical location where the good originates. Impliedly registration shall occur when such use creates a false or deceptive impression concerning the true origin of the goods, even if no formal application for registration has been filed under this Act. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating a direct and continuous link between the qualities of the good and its specified geographical area, as provided herein. This determination is subject to consideration of consumer perception regarding the indication's association with that location.

An application for the registration of a geographical indication may include a statement specifying the qualities, reputation or other characteristics which are attributed exclusively to the indicated goods. Where an applicant demonstrates a long-standing and continuous association between the specified qualities and the territory identified in their application, registration shall be granted subject to verification by the Geographical Indications Registry that no similar mark exists for identical goods. Further, impliedly registration shall extend protection against any use of the geographical indication which is likely to cause confusion among consumers regarding the origin of the goods. The Registrar may require the applicant to provide further documentation substantiating these claims as provided herein. Any interested party may oppose an application under this Act.

Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication shall be entitled to institute proceedings for relief against any contravention of the rights afforded under this Act. Such proceedings may include claims for damages sustained by reason of the unauthorized use of the geographical indication, including but not limited to loss of profits and damage to reputation. Where an authorized user has been granted a license to make use of a registered geographical indication, the proprietor shall be entitled to enforce the terms of that license as if it were a contract. Further, impliedly registration shall extend to prevent the application of confusingly similar signs or indications in relation to goods with which the registered geographical indication is associated, even where such use does not directly incorporate the protected name. This protection applies irrespective of whether the user had knowledge of the existence of the registration.

An application for registration of a geographical indication relating to agricultural products, foodstuffs, wine, spirit distillates, cereals, spices, natural herbs or medicinal plants shall include particulars specifying the name of the collective body making the application, the area comprising the geographical territory from which the goods originate, and a map of such territory. The Registering Authority may require further clarification regarding the boundaries of the specified area, demanding submission of detailed surveys or other relevant documentation to ascertain authenticity. Where an indication is used by producers within a defined region but not formally registered as a collective body, registration shall be deemed to proceed based on representation from a majority of such producers, subject to verification under this Act. Impliedly registration shall extend protection against all acts of use which are likely to cause confusion amongst the consumers regarding the origin of the goods. The Registrar may issue directions for rectification of the register if evidence suggests improper or misleading claims concerning geographical origin.
