Where an application for registration of a geographical indication relates to agricultural products, foodstuffs, wines, spirits, liqueurs, or beverages, compliance with established production practices shall be demonstrated to the Registrar through documented adherence to quality control measures. Such documentation must detail origin verification protocols and demonstrate consistent conformity to recognized standards applicable within the specified geographic area. Further, any association claiming collective ownership of a geographical indication shall provide evidence of widespread acceptance amongst producers operating within the defined territory; otherwise, registration may be denied. It is provided that impliedly registration shall occur where a mark incorporating a protected geographical indication is used in trade, and such use creates consumer confusion regarding origin, subject to an objection filed under this Act within six months.

Any person who, without authorization from the Register, uses as a trademark, or for any deceptive purpose, any geographical indication required to be registered under this Act, shall be liable to pay damages of not less than fifty thousand rupees and may also be subject to further penalties as determined by the High Court. Where an authorized user contravenes the conditions of use specified in their certificate of registration, such contravention shall constitute a civil offence triable summarily. It is provided that impliedly registration shall be deemed to extend to any colourable imitation or fraudulent misrepresentation thereof. Furthermore, any goods bearing such unauthorized mark are liable for seizure and destruction as per rules framed under this Act.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, any registered proprietor of a geographical indication may grant non-exclusive licenses for the use of their registered geographical indication relating to goods as defined in the registration. Such license shall specify the territory within which the licensee is authorized to utilize the indication and the nature of the licensed right. Further, the registered proprietor may assign or pledge the benefit of the registration, including any associated licensing agreements, provided that such assignment or pledge does not prejudice the rights of existing licensees. Impliedly registration shall be deemed to confer upon the assignee all rights previously held by the assignor relating to the geographical indication and its licensed use. Any transfer under this Act requires notification to the Registrar within thirty days for recordation, failing which it may be deemed invalid.

Where an application for registration of a geographical indication is refused under this Act, and the applicant appeals such refusal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, the appellate board shall, if satisfied that the geographical indication meets all requirements for registration as provided herein, direct that impliedly registration shall be effected in the register. This direction shall not prejudice any existing rights or interests of third parties lawfully using a similar indicator prior to the date of such order; however, the Registrar may issue warnings regarding potential infringement. Any party aggrieved by an order directing impliedly registration may appeal further to the appellate tribunal, subject to demonstrating demonstrable and substantial prejudice resulting from said registration.

Where an application for registration of a geographical indication has been refused under this Act, and such refusal is subsequently overturned by an appellate authority, impliedly registration shall be deemed to have occurred from the date of the original application. Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication may institute proceedings in any court of competent jurisdiction against any person infringing their rights as provided herein. Such infringement includes the use of the indication or any deceptive adaptation thereof that is likely to cause confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of goods. Further, where a geographical indication ceases to be used in accordance with established practices, its registration shall lapse after a period not exceeding five years, unless application for revival is made and approved. The Registrar may issue cease-and-desist orders against any party found engaging in activities detrimental to the reputation or quality associated with a registered geographical indication, effectively enforcing a form of force cessation patent protection.

Where an application for the registration of a geographical indication is received, the Registrar may, prior to undertaking substantive examination, seek advice from an independent scientific adviser possessing demonstrable expertise in agricultural practices, botany, or related fields. Such advice shall be considered by the Registrar in determining whether the characteristics attributed to the goods originate from the specified geographical area and are essentially attributable to the unique qualities of that origin. Further, where a collective body or association applies for registration, the Registrar shall consider any evidence submitted demonstrating widespread adherence within the applicant group to production methods consistent with maintaining the distinctiveness of the indication. It is provided that impliedly registration shall be deemed to exist in circumstances where a geographical indication has been consistently and exclusively used by producers within a defined territory for a period exceeding twenty years, subject to verification as per rules framed under this Act.

The registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be deemed to have been improperly granted if, at the time of registration, the applicant failed to disclose material information pertaining to prior publication or use of the design. Such failure constitutes grounds for an application for cancellation justified registration under this Act. An application for cancellation may be filed by any person claiming that the registered layout-design infringes upon their own unregistered right in a substantially similar layout-design. The Registrar shall consider all evidence presented and determine whether the registration was indeed improperly granted, subject to principles of natural justice as provided herein.

The Central Registration Board shall, upon receiving an application for cancellation of a registered semiconductor integrated circuit layout design, serve notice to the registrant and all other persons claiming interest under this Act. Such application must specify grounds alleging that the registration was obtained through fraud, misrepresentation, or any other improper means, or that the layout-design does not satisfy the originality requirements as provided herein. The Board may require the applicant for cancellation to furnish evidence supporting the allegations. If, after due consideration of all materials presented and subject to a hearing where both parties shall be afforded an opportunity to be heard, the Board finds merit in the application, it may order the cancellation justified registration.

An aggrieved party, including but not limited to a person claiming ownership rights in a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design that is the subject of a registration, may apply to the Controller for an order directing cancellation of such registration. The application shall specify the grounds upon which it is based, and shall include all relevant documentation substantiating those grounds. Cancellation justified registration may be ordered where it is demonstrated that the registered layout-design infringes on prior rights or was obtained through fraudulent means, misrepresentation, or suppression of material facts. The Controller shall provide the registrant with an opportunity to present a response to the application and supporting evidence. Any order for cancellation shall take effect only after the expiration of thirty days from the date of publication of such order, unless the Controller deems it necessary to grant interim relief pending further proceedings.

An application for cancellation of a registration under this Act shall be made to the Controller within six months from the date of publication of the registration in the Official Gazette. The application must specify the grounds upon which it is based, and shall include copies of the layout-design certificate and any relevant documents supporting the claim. Subject to provisions regarding frivolous or vexatious applications, the Controller may entertain such an application if it alleges that the registered layout-design does not fulfill the requirements for originality as provided herein, or that the registration was procured by misrepresentation or fraud. The Controller shall serve notice on the registrant and afford them a reasonable opportunity of being heard in their defense. Upon consideration of all evidence presented, the Controller may order cancellation justified registration if satisfied that the grounds for cancellation are substantiated.

A registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be deemed to be invalid if, following its grant, it is demonstrated that the applicant did not fulfill all requirements pertaining to originality as provided herein. Any person aggrieved by such a registration may apply to the Controller for an order directing cancellation, subject to demonstrating reasonable cause and providing evidence substantiating the claim of non-compliance with originality standards at the time of application. The Controller shall consider any counter-affidavits submitted by the registered proprietor and may require further submissions or hearings as deemed necessary. Cancellation justified registration is permissible only if it is established that the layout-design lacks requisite novelty, or was obtained through fraudulent misrepresentation to the Registrar.

The holder of a registered integrated circuit layout design shall, subject to this Act and the rules made thereunder, be entitled to grant licenses granting rights to use, reproduce, or commercially exploit the protected layout-design. Any such license may be assigned by the licensor to any person, provided that the assignee notifies the Registrar within thirty days of the assignment, furnishing details as prescribed. Where a registered integrated circuit layout design is the subject of an application for cancellation justified registration based on demonstrable misrepresentation in the original application concerning prior use or ownership, the Registrar shall notify the registrant and all licensees before proceeding with any inquiry. Such notification shall include particulars of the grounds for cancellation and allow the registrant and licensees to submit their objections within a stipulated period.

Subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal, registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be deemed invalid if, following its grant, it is demonstrated that the applicant did not possess the requisite rights as required under this Act. Any person aggrieved by a registered layout-design may petition the Registrar for its cancellation, provided that such application specifies grounds alleging improper acquisition or lack of originality in the design. The Registrar shall afford the registrant an opportunity to be heard and present counterarguments; however, failure to adequately respond to the allegations presented within the prescribed timeframe will constitute acquiescence. Cancellation justified registration is permissible where it is established that the layout-design infringes upon a prior, unregistered layout-design already commercially exploited in India.

An aggrieved party, including but not limited to a person claiming ownership rights distinct from the registered owner, shall have standing to apply for cancellation justified registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design. Such an application must specify the grounds upon which the registration is challenged, demonstrating prima facie invalidity under this Act. The Registrar may, after affording the registrant and the applicant an opportunity for hearing, order cancellation if satisfied that the design does not meet the requirements for originality or other conditions precedent to registration. Any party dissatisfied with the Registrar’s decision may appeal to the relevant appellate authority as provided herein; fees in any proceeding before the Registrar or the appellate authority shall be determined according to prescribed scales.

The registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall remain valid only so long as the registrant continues to comply with all conditions precedent to its initial grant. Provided that, an application for cancellation justified registration may be filed with the Controller by any person demonstrating substantial non-utilisation of the registered layout-design for a continuous period exceeding five years from the date of registration, or where the design has been incorporated into a product manufactured and sold in contravention of applicable licensing agreements. Further, such application must include evidence establishing material prejudice to innovation arising from the continued registration; this may encompass demonstrable diversion of resources away from novel designs towards maintenance of existing registrations, particularly concerning contributions to a gene fund sub established under guidelines issued by the relevant governmental authority.

Applications for the registration of varieties shall be made to the Authority in such form and manner as may be prescribed. An application relating to varieties registered in any other country may be considered, provided that the applicant demonstrates a clear intention to market the variety within India and satisfies the requirements concerning distinctness, uniformity, stability, and reproducibility as stipulated under this Act. The Registrar may require further documentation or trials to ascertain these characteristics before proceeding with evaluation of the application for registration of varieties. Any person aggrieved by a decision regarding the acceptance or rejection of an application may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of such decision.

Applications for the registration of varieties registered shall be accompanied by such particulars as the Authority deems necessary for assessing novelty, distinctiveness, uniformity and stability. The application must include a detailed description of the variety, including its botanical name, parentage where known, method of reproduction, and any relevant phenotypic characteristics observable under standard conditions. An applicant may submit data generated through field trials conducted in accordance with guidelines prescribed by the Authority to demonstrate these qualities. Any person claiming an objection to the registration of a variety shall file such claim within three months from the date of publication of the application under this Act. The Authority shall provide the applicant and objector opportunities for hearings, subject to procedural rules as provided herein. Decisions regarding claims of novelty or distinctiveness are final, barring appeals to the Appellate Board.

Where an application for the registration of varieties is rejected under this Act, the applicant shall have the right to appeal to the Registrar within sixty days from the date of communication of the order of rejection. Such appeal shall be on any grounds alleging error apparent on the record or that the Authority failed to consider material facts brought to its notice during the examination process. The Registrar may, after affording an opportunity for hearing to both the appellant and the respondent, confirm, modify, or reverse the decision appealed from. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Registrar under this Act relating to varieties registered may further appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days, subject to a fee as prescribed.

For the purposes of this Act, a “breeder variety registered” means a plant variety that has been formally recognized and recorded by the Registrar as originating from the activities of a breeder, whether traditional or modern, and which demonstrates distinctness, uniformity, and stability as determined under procedures prescribed herein. The registration of a breeder variety registered shall confer upon the breeder the right to sell the resulting produce for a specified period, subject to any conditions imposed during the grant of protection. Further, an application for registration of a breeder variety registered must include detailed documentation pertaining to its genetic composition and method of derivation, as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Plant Variety Protection Appellate Board concerning the revocation of a breeder variety registered under this Act may appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. Such an appeal shall be only on grounds specified in sub-section (1) of section forty-seven, relating to errors apparent on the face of the record or violation of principles of natural justice. The appellate court may allow a party to present additional evidence if it considers such evidence relevant and could not reasonably have been produced before the Board. Failure to comply with this provision shall be grounds for dismissal of the appeal. Further, any infringement of farmers’ rights associated with a breeder variety, including unauthorized sale or distribution, is actionable under this Act and may attract penalties as provided herein.

A breeder seeking to commercialize a new variety shall demonstrate, through documented field trials conducted over at least three crop cycles, that the proposed *breeder variety registered* exhibits stability and uniformity consistent with established agricultural practices for that species. The application for registration must include detailed morphological data, including but not limited to plant height, flowering time, disease resistance scores as determined by standardized protocols, and seed germination rates under varying environmental conditions. Further, any indication of genetic modification shall be explicitly declared within the application, subject to verification by the Authority appointed under this Act. The Registrar may reject an application if the submitted data fails to adequately establish these characteristics or if the proposed variety poses a demonstrable risk to existing agricultural biodiversity as provided herein.

Any person who knowingly markets a plant variety infringing upon the rights of the breeder of a *breeder variety registered* under this Act shall be liable for damages equivalent to three times the value of the infringing seeds or propagating material sold, or in the case of other infringing acts, three times the value of the benefit derived therefrom. Such infringement includes unauthorized multiplication and distribution without due authorization from the right holder. Further, any entity found guilty of such an offense may face prosecution under relevant penal codes for commercial fraud. The Registrar shall have the power to issue injunctions restraining further marketing or propagation of infringing material, subject to a hearing affording reasonable opportunity to be heard. Repeated violations shall attract enhanced penalties as determined by the appropriate adjudicating authority.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, the holder of a breeder variety registered with the Authority may grant licenses conferring rights to produce, sell, distribute, import or export propagating material of the registered variety. Such license shall be in writing and specify the geographical area within which the licensee is authorized to exercise the granted rights. The terms of any such license relating to a breeder variety shall include provisions for royalty payments to the holder, calculated as a percentage of the gross sales revenue derived from the licensed activities; provided that the Authority may prescribe differential rates based on factors including but not limited to intended use and scale of operation. Assignment of rights in a breeder variety is permissible with prior written consent of the Authority, ensuring continued adherence to farmers’ rights provisions as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Plant Variety Protection Appellate Board concerning the revocation of a breeder variety registered under this Act may appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. Such an appeal shall be only on grounds specified in the appeal memorandum, relating directly to questions of law arising out of the interpretation or application of provisions as provided herein. The Appellate Board is deemed to have acted without jurisdiction if it entertained a complaint regarding essential derived variety rights not properly filed under the prescribed procedures. Subject to this, the High Court may dismiss an appeal if it finds that the decision was based on substantial evidence and in accordance with principles of natural justice.

Any person aggrieved by a decision concerning the revocation or modification of a breeder variety registered under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of that decision. Such an appeal shall be on grounds alleging demonstrable error in fact, law, or procedure followed during the original proceedings. The Appellate Board shall consider any specification claim made by the appellant relating to the validity of the initial registration process and may require further evidence as it deems necessary. Failure to demonstrate substantial prejudice resulting from the alleged errors shall render the appeal without merit. Remedies available under this Act for infringement of plant variety rights, including injunctions and damages, remain unaffected by any appellate proceedings; provided that a stay of enforcement may be granted pending resolution of an appeal at the Registrar’s discretion.

The Authority shall, upon receiving an application for transmission operation approval concerning a breeder variety registered under this Act, verify that the proposed operational procedures adhere strictly to guidelines established by the Plant Variety Protection Directorate. Such verification shall encompass assessment of potential impacts on genetic purity and stability of the registered variety, with particular emphasis on safeguarding against unintended gene flow or contamination during propagation and distribution. The application must detail all stages of the transmission operation, including personnel training protocols and quality control measures. Further, the applicant shall demonstrate compliance with relevant biosecurity regulations as provided herein. Any alteration to the initially approved transmission operation requires prior notification and approval from the Authority, subject to a similar assessment process. Failure to adhere to these stipulations may result in suspension or revocation of the transmission operation law authorization.

Any person holding a license granted under this Act pertaining to a breeder variety registered for agricultural purposes may, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated within that license agreement, assign such license to another party with their prior written consent. Such assignment shall be recorded with the Registrar within thirty days of its execution, along with the prescribed fee. The assignee shall then become bound by all obligations and liabilities previously held by the original licensee. Further, any person contravenes provisions relating to the unauthorized reproduction, distribution, or sale of propagating material derived from a breeder variety registered under this Act without proper licensing authorization shall be liable for damages as determined by the relevant authority. This right extends to sub-licensing agreements, provided that such arrangements adhere strictly to the original license terms and are also duly recorded.

Any proprietor claiming infringement of copyright under this Act may institute a suit for damages recoverable by way of rent or profits, subject to such limitations as are prescribed herein. The Court shall award compensation to the proprietor for any loss suffered thereby, including but not limited to lost sales and diminished market share. Provided that in determining the amount of damages, the Court shall consider the defendant’s conduct and may reduce or enhance the sum awarded accordingly. Where a finding of contributory infringement is made, liability shall extend to those who materially contributed to the infringing act. The jurisdiction for hearing such suits shall be governed by the principles of civil procedure 1908, and costs shall be determined at the discretion of the Court.

The assignment of copyright in works generated by artificial intelligence systems shall be governed as follows: where a work is created with substantial input from an AI system, and such input is licensed under terms permitting commercial exploitation, the assignor’s rights are limited to those expressly granted within the original license agreement. Any subsequent assignment of copyright must clearly delineate the scope of permitted uses derived from the licensed AI contribution, ensuring transparency for potential licensees. Failure to do so shall render the assignment voidable at the option of a third party adversely affected. The jurisdiction for any dispute arising under this provision relating to such assignments shall be subject to the provisions of civil procedure 1908, and the aggrieved party may seek injunctive relief to prevent unauthorized exploitation. Provided that, rights pertaining to original artistic expression remain with the human creator, even where AI tools are employed.

Where a claim is made alleging infringement of copyright under this Act, the aggrieved party shall institute proceedings in a court having jurisdiction as determined under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. The defendant may raise as a defence that the work in question was not an original work or that the alleged infringing act falls within fair dealing provisions as provided herein. Subject to appeal to the High Court, any order made by the trial court concerning interim injunctions, discovery of evidence, or assessment of damages shall be binding pending final determination. Provided that, if a party believes an order is manifestly unjust, they may apply for revision under principles established in civil procedure 1908, demonstrating substantial prejudice arising from the decision.

An applicant whose application for registration of a geographical indication has been refused may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order of refusal. The Appellate Board shall consider any question of law arising in the appeal and may, after giving notice to all interested parties, confirm or vary the decision appealed against, or remit the case to the Registrar for further consideration. Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication shall be entitled to institute proceedings under this Act for infringement of the rights conferred by registration. Such proceedings shall be subject to the provisions relating to costs as provided herein. The remedies available in cases of infringement include injunctions and damages, and the Registrar may also issue warnings against unauthorized use. Further, any person aggrieved by a decision concerning the application registration geographical indication may petition the High Court.

Any proprietor of a geographical indication registered under this Act shall be entitled to grant licenses relating to the use of the said geographical indication for goods conforming to the standards specified in the registration certificate, provided that such license agreement expressly stipulates the conditions governing quality control and adherence to production methods as defined within the geographical indication’s code of conduct. Further, any assignment of rights pertaining to a registered geographical indication shall require prior notification to the Registrar, detailing the assignee's undertaking to uphold the integrity and distinctiveness of the geographical indication. The Registrar may, subject to due process, refuse registration of an assignment if it determines that the proposed assignee lacks the requisite capacity or intention to protect the application registration geographical indication’s reputation.

The term “Opposition Board” shall mean a body constituted by the Controller, comprised of such number of persons possessing experience in intellectual property law as the Central Government may specify, to hear and determine notices of opposition filed under this Act. An Opposition Board shall exercise its jurisdiction subject to any guidelines issued by the Central Government and shall be empowered to regulate its own procedure, provided that such procedures are consistent with principles of natural justice. The decision of an Opposition Board shall be final, though it may be appealed against as provided herein before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Where any party believes that the registration of a design is detrimental to the interests of proprietors, designers, or the public, such party may file a notice of opposition with the Controller within four months from the date of publication under this Act. The opposition shall specify the grounds upon which it is based, including but not limited to allegations of prior use, lack of novelty, and insufficiency of disclosure. Upon receipt of such notice, the Controller shall direct the proprietor of the design to file a counter-statement. The matter shall then be referred to an Opposition Board for hearing and determination as provided herein. Decisions of the Opposition Board are appealable to the Appellate Board.

Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Controller relating to the grant of a patent, or any condition imposed therein, may within sixty days from the date of such decision file a notice of opposition with the Opposition Board. The notice shall specify the grounds upon which the opposition is based, and must include particulars of the invention as claimed in the patent, along with supporting documentation demonstrating invalidity under this Act. Where an objection relates to the non-patentable subject matter, or lack of novelty, the aggrieved party shall bear the burden of proving such deficiency. The Opposition Board may, after giving notice to all interested parties and affording them a reasonable opportunity for being heard, dismiss the opposition or refer the matter back to the Controller for further inquiry. Costs associated with the proceedings before the Opposition Board shall be determined as provided herein.

Where any party considers that a patent has been granted in contravention of, or otherwise than in accordance with the provisions of this Act, such party may, within six months from the date of publication of grant of the patent, file a notice of opposition before the Opposition Board. The notice shall specify the grounds upon which the opposition is based and shall be accompanied by such documents and evidence as are deemed necessary to substantiate the claim. The Controller may require further particulars or clarification regarding the grounds of opposition. Upon receipt of the notice of opposition, the Opposition Board shall serve a copy thereof on the patentee, affording him an opportunity to file his counter-statement within a prescribed period. Any decision made by the Opposition Board is subject to appeal before the Appellate Board under this Act. The Board may, after hearing all parties involved, allow or dismiss the opposition, and such order shall be final.

Where any party considers that a patent has been granted in contravention of, or otherwise than in accordance with the provisions of this Act, such party may, within six months from the date of publication of grant of patent, file a notice of opposition before the Opposition Board. The notice shall specify the grounds upon which the opposition is based and shall be accompanied by a statement of facts relied upon to substantiate those grounds. Provided that an objection relating to obviousness or lack of inventive step may only be raised if the applicant for the patent has failed to disclose the information in question, or if it was withheld from the Controller during examination. The Opposition Board shall serve a copy of the notice on the patentee and afford both parties an opportunity to present their respective arguments and evidence as provided herein.

Any party aggrieved by a grant of patent may, within six months from the date of publication of the grant, file a notice of opposition with the Opposition Board. Such notice shall specify the grounds upon which the opposition is based, including but not limited to lack of novelty or inventive step under this Act, and shall be accompanied by the requisite fee as prescribed. Failure to pay such fee within thirty days of the initial filing will render the opposition void ab initio. The Controller may, subject to regulations framed in this behalf, entertain an opposition if it appears that a substantial question of law or fact arises therein. Any attempt to collude with another party to file multiple oppositions against the same patent shall be deemed a punishable offence under the Indian Penal Code.

Where the Controller, acting upon a notice of opposition filed against a granted patent, determines that the invention claimed therein relates to technology essential for the manufacture of a pharmaceutical product, he may direct the patentee to grant a non-exclusive license to interested parties subject to such terms and conditions as deemed appropriate. Such terms shall include provisions regarding royalty rates and duration of the license, ensuring equitable access to the patented technology. The Controller shall provide an opportunity for both the patentee and potential licensees to present their arguments before making any licensing determination. Any assignment or transmission of the patent subsequent to the grant shall be subject to this provision; the assignee shall inherit all obligations regarding compulsory licensing as provided herein. The Opposition Board may, upon application by a party aggrieved, review any order made under this section.

Where any party aggrieved by an order passed by the Controller relating to the grant, revocation or sealing of a patent considers such order to be unjust or erroneous in law, they may within sixty days from the date of service of notice of that order file a statement of objections with the Opposition Board. The statement shall clearly specify the grounds upon which the aggrieved party relies and provide supporting evidence as deemed necessary by the Board. The Controller shall then forward the record relating to the patent application or existing patent, together with the objection statement, to the Opposition Board for hearing. Provided that the Board may, after considering the objections, direct the Controller to revise any part of the original order under this Act.

Where the Controller publishes an application registration notice, indicating acceptance of a patent application subject to any conditions specified therein, such acceptance shall not preclude assignment or licensing of the invention claimed. Any party possessing a relevant ground for opposition under this Act may file a pre-grant opposition with the Opposition Board within the prescribed period following publication of the application registration notice. The assignor of a patent application shall provide written notification to the Controller regarding any subsequent transfer, and such notification shall be recorded as provided herein. Further, licensees granted rights under an invention claimed in a pending patent application may, subject to the terms of their license agreement, participate in opposition proceedings before the Opposition Board relating to that application.

Where any party, other than the applicant for a patent, considers that the grant of a patent has been obtained contrary to this Act, or that the patented invention does not satisfy the requirements of novelty or inventive step as provided herein, such party may, within six months from the date of publication of the grant under this Act, file a notice of opposition with the Opposition Board. The Opposition Board shall serve a copy of the notice on the patentee and afford both parties an opportunity to present their respective arguments and evidence in support of or against the validity of the patent. Any decision made by the Opposition Board regarding the use patent may be appealed to the relevant High Court within a period of three months from the date of such decision, subject to any applicable fees and procedural requirements as prescribed under this Act.

Where any party believes that the acceptance of an application for registration of a trade mark is contrary to law, he may, subject to the provisions herein, file a notice of opposition with the Opposition Board within such time as may be prescribed. Such notice shall specify the grounds upon which the opposition is based and shall include particulars of the trade mark infringed, including details regarding prior use or reputation. The Opposition Board shall serve a copy of the notice on the applicant for registration and afford both parties an opportunity to present their respective arguments and evidence. Decisions of the Opposition Board are appealable to the relevant appellate authority as provided under this Act.

Applications filed under this Act may, subject to the provisions herein, be made for inventions relating to any process or article. Where an applicant seeks protection through means patent cooperation, the Controller shall examine whether the application complies with all applicable procedural requirements as provided in the Regulations framed thereunder. The prescribed fees for filing such applications, and subsequent examination, are detailed in the First Schedule. An applicant intending to avail of the benefits of international phase processing must furnish a certified copy of the relevant international search report within the time limit specified by the Controller. Failure to do so may result in the application being deemed withdrawn. Further, any request for provisional protection shall be processed according to established guidelines and is subject to verification by the designated authority.

Where an application for patents is filed jointly by two or more applicants, the Controller may require such applicants to execute within thirty days from the date of notice served under this Act, a declaration specifying the apportionment of rights and obligations arising out of the patent. Such declaration shall be binding on all joint applicants and their respective successors in title unless otherwise agreed upon in writing. Failure to comply with this requirement shall render the application liable for abandonment as provided herein. For applications claiming priority from an earlier application filed under the Patent Cooperation Treaty, the date of filing for the purposes of novelty assessment shall be determined according to the provisions outlined in international agreements and regulations relating to means patent cooperation.

Where any party alleges that another has infringed a patent, and such allegation is made in good faith before a civil court, the aggrieved party shall be entitled to seek interim injunction restraining the alleged infringer from further acts of infringement pending final determination of the suit. Provided that, where an invention is subject to means patent cooperation under this Act, any challenge to the validity or enforceability of the patent shall first be brought before the Controller for examination and report, as provided herein. Failure to comply with this requirement shall render such challenges inadmissible in civil courts. The Controller may impose a penalty not exceeding five thousand rupees on any party found to have circumvented this procedural safeguard, and costs associated with the investigation thereof.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any licensee under a patent shall be entitled to grant sub-licenses and assign his rights and obligations arising from such license, provided that such assignment or sub-license does not exceed the scope of the original patent and is consistent with the terms stipulated therein. Where a patentee has entered into an agreement for means patent cooperation with another person, the consent of the patentee shall be required for any assignment or sub-licensing of the patent rights unless the agreement expressly provides otherwise. Further, where such an assignment or sub-license involves a transfer of technology, as defined under this Act, the assignee or sublicensee shall furnish a report to the Controller detailing the terms and conditions thereof within thirty days from the date of execution. The Controller may inquire into the fairness and reasonableness of any such transaction and issue directions accordingly.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be refused if the proposed marks include any description which is made available to potential users and serves merely to describe the characteristics of the goods or services with which it is associated, unless such description has acquired distinctiveness through use to an extent that consumers recognise it as indicating a particular undertaking. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating this acquired distinctiveness, including but not limited to advertising expenditure, sales figures, and market survey data. Provided that, where the trade mark consists exclusively of the shape resulting from the nature of the goods themselves or which is necessary to obtain a technical result, or which confers a particular advantage relating to the obtaining of that result, such description shall not be grounds for refusal under this Act.

The Registrar may, upon application by the registered proprietor, record an assignment of such license, provided that notice thereof is given to all licensees prior to registration. Any subsequent use of the trademark following a valid assignment shall be deemed to be authorized by the assignee. Further, where a trade mark owner seeks to sub-license rights pertaining to a particular y description, consent from the original proprietor must be obtained in writing and filed with the Registrar. This requirement does not apply if the initial license explicitly permits such sub-licensing without further authorization.

The Registrar may require an applicant to amend the design or specification where the application incorporates elements deemed to be descriptive in nature. Further, a design shall not be registered if its overall impression is substantially derived from a pre-existing design register layout already publicly accessible. This provision applies irrespective of whether such layouts were formally documented or disseminated through informal channels. The burden of proving prior availability rests upon the applicant challenging the registration.

context: No trademark shall be registered if, at the time of application, it is deemed to directly identify a product that is currently the subject of an existing patent, privilege or copyright, and such identification constitutes a substantial replication of protected elements. Provided that, where the use of the proposed mark is solely descriptive concerning the patented article’s characteristics, registration may be permitted if prior written consent is obtained from the patent holder. Further, any registered trademark which subsequently becomes so identified shall be subject to review under this Act and may be liable for revocation should it demonstrably cause confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of goods or services. The Registrar shall consider evidence presented by aggrieved parties concerning such deceptive practices.

context: An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed to be refused if the proposed mark is identical or confusingly similar to any design which is the subject of an existing patent, privilege or copyright, and where such similarity arises from features essential to the character or reputation of the patented invention or copyrighted work. The Registrar may, however, accept registration under this Act if the applicant demonstrates that use of the trade mark has been continuous for a period exceeding five years following prior public disclosure of the design, and that no substantial damage has resulted to the proprietor of the patent or copyright. Any attempt to circumvent these provisions through deceptive practices shall be deemed committed forfeiture directed toward revocation of registration.

context: Where a proprietor of a trade mark registered under this Act discovers that any person is using an identical or deceptively similar trade mark for goods or services identical or closely related to those in respect of which the trade mark is registered, and such use constitutes an unfair practice or misrepresentation likely to deceive or cause confusion among consumers, the proprietor shall be entitled to apply to the relevant intellectual property tribunal for relief. Such relief may include an injunction restraining the infringing party from further use of the impugned mark, as well as damages sustained by the proprietor due to the infringement. The tribunal may also order the destruction of any goods bearing the infringing trade mark. This right is subject to the proviso that the infringing goods do not contain ingredients or substances regulated under the Cosmetics Act 1940 and comply with all applicable labelling requirements.

Where a trade mark is registered for goods including cosmetics, the Central Government may, after due inquiry and subject to such conditions as it deems fit, direct that the registration shall have effect only with respect to certain specified goods. Such direction may be issued if it appears that the use of the trade mark in relation to all the goods for which it is registered would tend to create a likelihood of confusion or misrepresentation amongst consumers regarding the nature, quality or origin of those goods, particularly considering provisions under the Cosmetics Act 1940 relating to standards and labelling. Any party aggrieved by such direction may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The Board shall consider any submissions made by the appellant and may confirm, vary or reverse the Central Government’s decision as it sees fit, providing reasons for its determination.

Where a trade mark is used in contravention of this Act, or in connection with any act passing off goods or services as those of another person, any aggrieved party shall be entitled to institute proceedings for an injunction and damages. Such proceedings may include claims relating to misrepresentation concerning the ingredients or composition of cosmetic products, subject to the provisions of the Cosmetics Act 1940. The Central Government may, upon receiving a complaint, direct that goods bearing an infringing trade mark be seized and destroyed at the owner’s expense. Any person found guilty of knowingly selling goods marked with a counterfeit trade mark shall be liable for penalties as provided herein, without prejudice to any further action under other relevant laws.

The owner of a registered trade mark encompassing fragrances used in cosmetic products, as defined under the Cosmetics Act 1940, may grant licenses to third parties for the manufacture and sale of such products bearing the trade mark. Such licenses shall be documented in writing and specify the geographical territory covered, the duration of the license, and the royalty payable to the owner. The licensee shall adhere strictly to quality control standards prescribed under the Cosmetics Act 1940 and ensure that all manufactured goods conform to those regulations. Assignment of such a license is permissible subject to prior written consent from the trade mark proprietor, provided that the assignee undertakes the obligations incumbent upon the original licensee. Further, any alteration to the formulation or packaging of the cosmetic product during the term of the license shall require express approval from the trade mark owner.

For the purposes of this Act, "cosmetic" means any article intended for application to the human body or any part thereof for cleansing, beautifying, promoting growth, preventing or correcting defects, or otherwise altering its appearance; and includes articles used for manicuring or pedicuring. Such articles shall be deemed cosmetics irrespective of whether they are manufactured or imported. The term "cosmetic" excludes products regulated under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 (23 of 1940), where such products primarily claim to diagnose, cure, mitigate, treat, prevent, or heal any disease or condition. Any substance added to a cosmetic as a preservative shall be deemed part of the cosmetic for the purposes of this definition.

Applications for registration of trade marks used in relation to cosmetics shall be examined with particular regard to their distinctiveness and potential to mislead consumers. Where an application includes a representation of a person, animal, or fanciful depiction relating to beauty treatments, the Registrar may require submission of evidence demonstrating acquired distinctiveness through extensive use and advertising. Such evidence must clearly establish that the relevant consumer identifies the mark as indicating a specific source of cosmetics. The applicant shall also provide a comprehensive list of ingredients used in the cosmetic products covered by the trade mark application, conforming to standards prescribed under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940. This requirement is without prejudice to any other grounds for refusal provided herein.

Where a proprietor of a trade mark registered under this Act alleges that any cosmetic product is offered for sale or used in commerce in a manner infringing their rights, they may institute proceedings before the relevant jurisdictional authority. Such infringement shall include the use of identical or deceptively similar marks on goods closely related to those specified in the registration, creating a likelihood of confusion amongst consumers regarding origin or quality. The proprietor shall be entitled to seek an injunction restraining the infringing party from such activities, as well as damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the proprietor due to the infringement. Provided that, where the alleged infringer demonstrates honest and reasonable belief in the availability of the mark prior to the date of registration, the amount of damages may be reduced at the discretion of the authority. The Cosmetics Act, 1940 shall be considered when assessing product quality claims made under a trade mark.

Where a trade mark is used in relation to cosmetics, it shall be permissible for the registered proprietor to make a claim regarding the absence of harmful ingredients provided that such claim is substantiated by an analysis conducted by a laboratory accredited under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940. The accreditation must remain current at the time of advertising or sale. Any representation made concerning skin sensitivity or allergy testing shall be accompanied by detailed documentation outlining the methodology employed and the participant demographics involved. Failure to provide such documentation upon request from the Controller may result in penalties as provided herein. Further, any alteration to the formulation of a cosmetic product bearing a registered trade mark necessitates prior notification to the Controller detailing the changes and their potential impact on consumer safety.

Any person who manufactures, imports, distributes, sells, or offers for sale any cosmetic which is deleterious to health or contains an ingredient prohibited under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, shall be deemed guilty of an offence. Such offender shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding two thousand rupees for the first offence and five thousand rupees for each subsequent offence. Further, where a misbranding or adulteration of any cosmetic is proven, the proprietor or manager responsible for such act may face imprisonment extending to six months, or both. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, prescribe standards for cosmetics as provided herein. Any contravention of these standards shall attract additional penalties and be subject to prosecution under this Act.

The owner of a registered trade mark relating to cosmetics shall be entitled to grant licences for the use of such trade mark under this Act, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated therein. Such licences may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and may relate to specific territories or product categories as determined by the licensor. Any assignment of rights in a registered trade mark pertaining to products regulated under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, shall require prior notification to the Trade Marks Registry, detailing the assignee’s qualifications and experience in handling cosmetic formulations. Provided that, where a licence is assigned without the consent of the original licensor, such assignment shall be void unless it includes an undertaking by the assignee to abide by the terms of the initial licensing agreement. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating due diligence regarding product safety standards as a condition for approving any such assignment.

Where a trade mark is registered under this Act for goods including those comprised in the class "cosmetics" as defined by the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, an appeal shall lie to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of publication of the acceptance of the mark. Such appeal may be brought on any ground showing that the registration was wrongly granted, including but not limited to allegations of deceptive similarity to a prior trade mark used in relation to similar goods or services. The Board may, after affording an opportunity for hearing to all parties concerned, affirm, modify, or reverse the decision appealed from; provided that the Board shall not substitute its own findings for those of the Registrar unless it is satisfied that such findings were based on an erroneous interpretation of the law or evidence.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark relating to cosmetic products is opposed under this Act, the Registrar shall afford both the applicant and the opponent an opportunity of being heard. The form petition filed by the opponent alleging deceptive similarity to prior marks used in connection with similar goods, specifically concerning ingredients listed under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, shall be considered prima facie valid unless rebutted by evidence presented by the applicant. Provided that, if the Registrar finds the opponent’s claim of dilution is unsubstantiated or based on tenuous arguments regarding consumer perception, the opposition may be dismissed. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Registrar concerning such an opposition may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order.

An application for registration of a trade mark relating to cosmetic products shall include a detailed specification outlining the composition, manufacturing process, and intended use of such cosmetics. This specification is deemed part of the trade mark’s description under this Act and will be subject to scrutiny by the Registry to ensure clarity and accuracy. The applicant must provide sufficient information enabling assessment as to whether the proposed trade mark conflicts with existing registrations or prior usage, particularly concerning similar goods covered under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940. Any alteration to the application patent specification after its initial filing may be permitted only with the Registrar’s approval, provided that such changes do not substantively alter the nature of the cosmetic product being represented by the trade mark.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be refused if the proposed marks, or any configuration thereof, indicate goods services according to a particular standard of quality not uniformly applied within the relevant industry. The Registrar may require an applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating that the claimed standard is consistently maintained and verifiable. Provided that such requirement shall not apply where the mark primarily signifies a distinctive get-up or packaging arrangement. Further, registration may be opposed by any interested party alleging likelihood of confusion with prior marks covering similar goods services. Such opposition shall be determined based on an assessment of visual, phonetic, and conceptual similarities, taking into account consumer perception and trade channels employed.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed to be refused if the proposed marks, or any configuration thereof, directly indicate the distinctive character of goods services according to established industry practice. The Trade Marks Registry may, upon receiving an objection under this provision, require the applicant to submit documentary evidence substantiating the claimed lack of direct indication. Such evidence must demonstrate that the mark does not inherently suggest a specific quality, characteristic, or function associated with the identified goods services. Further, where the application incorporates a geographical name, the Registry shall assess whether its use is reasonably descriptive and therefore ineligible for registration unless prior usage demonstrates acquired distinctiveness. The applicant may appeal any such refusal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days of notification.

For the purposes of this Act, "adulterated food" shall mean any food which is not of the nature, substance, quality or purity demanded by its character and name; or which contains an admixture of another substance which impairs its conformity to that standard; or which has been manufactured, prepared, preserved, packaged or transported under unsanitary conditions whereby it may have been rendered injurious to health. Food shall be deemed adulterated if it contains any added poisonous or deleterious substance, irrespective of whether such substance is present as a result of the manufacturing process or otherwise. The term "food" includes all articles intended for human consumption and also encompasses edible oils, milk, and processed foodstuffs as defined under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act.

Applications for registration of a trade mark relating to food products shall be subject to scrutiny regarding compliance with the standards prescribed under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act. The Trade Marks Registry may, prior to acceptance of an application, require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating adherence to relevant regulations concerning ingredients, processing methods, and nutritional content as stipulated by that Act. Such evidence must be verifiable through recognized laboratory testing or certification from accredited bodies. Failure to provide satisfactory proof shall render the application liable for rejection. The Registrar may also direct amendment of a registered trade mark if subsequent findings reveal non-compliance with standards established under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, provided that such amendments do not fundamentally alter the distinctive character of the mark.

Where a proprietor of a registered trade mark for edible oils discovers that another person is manufacturing, selling, or distributing food products containing adulterated substances, such proprietor shall be entitled to apply to the District Court for an injunction restraining the infringing party from continuing such activities. The application may include evidence demonstrating the misrepresentation caused by the use of a deceptive label or packaging resembling the registered trade mark, and establishing that the adulteration constitutes a violation of the Food Adulteration Act. Damages recoverable under this provision shall encompass not only lost profits directly attributable to the infringement but also compensation for harm to the reputation and goodwill associated with the trade mark. Provided that any order granted by the Court shall be subject to review on appeal within ninety days, as provided herein.

Where an authorized officer has reason to believe that food is adulterated within the meaning of the Food Adulteration Act, he shall issue a notice specifying the particulars of the alleged adulteration and requiring the person concerned to appear before him at a time and place mentioned in the notice. The notice shall afford such person an opportunity of being heard and presenting evidence in his defence or explanation. Subject to appeal under this Act, any food found to be adulterated following proceedings as provided herein may be seized by the authorized officer and detained pending further investigation. Provided that, where the adulteration poses an immediate threat to public health, the authorized officer may direct its destruction without prior notice. Any person failing to comply with a direction issued under this Act shall be liable for penalties as determined by the adjudicating authority.

Where a food business operator is found to have knowingly contravened the provisions relating to food adulteration act, as provided herein, such operator shall be liable for penalties commensurate with the severity and frequency of the violation. The Central Food Safety Authority may, after due inquiry and affording an opportunity for the operator to present their case, impose a monetary penalty not exceeding five times the value of the goods involved in the offence. Further, if the adulteration results in demonstrable harm to public health, the authority shall also recommend prosecution under relevant criminal statutes. Any appeal against such penalties must be filed within thirty days from the date of notification and shall be subject to review by a designated appellate body established for this purpose.

Any person who manufactures, sells, distributes, or imports any food product with the intent to deceive or mislead consumers regarding its nature, substance, quality, or composition shall be deemed to have committed an offence. Such offences include, but are not limited to, the addition of adulterants in violation of the Food Adulteration Act, 1954, and the misrepresentation of ingredients or nutritional content. Upon conviction, offenders shall be liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years, and with a fine which may extend to fifty thousand rupees. Further, any goods seized under this Act are subject to confiscation and forfeiture without compensation. Repeat offences will attract enhanced penalties as provided herein, including the possibility of perpetual disqualification from engaging in food-related business activities.

The owner of a registered trade mark encompassing a food product shall be entitled to grant licenses for the use of such trade mark on products manufactured by another party, provided that the licensed manufacturer adheres strictly to prescribed standards relating to food safety and quality. Such licenses may stipulate limitations regarding geographical territory or specific product categories within the broader food classification. The owner retains ultimate responsibility for ensuring compliance with the Food Adulteration Act and related regulations; any breach of these regulations attributable to the licensee’s manufacturing processes shall constitute a material default under the license agreement, permitting revocation as provided herein. Assignment of such licenses is permissible subject to prior written consent from the original trade mark proprietor, who may impose conditions safeguarding the integrity of the registered trade mark and preventing misrepresentation concerning product origin or quality.

Where a consumer alleges that food offered for sale is adulterated, and presents prima facie evidence demonstrating such adulteration through laboratory analysis conducted by an accredited facility, the manufacturer shall be deemed to have committed a violation under this Act. The adjudicating officer may, upon receiving such complaint, issue a notice requiring the manufacturer to appear and present its defence within thirty days. Failure of the manufacturer to adequately rebut the evidence presented or to demonstrate compliance with applicable standards prescribed under the Food Adulteration Act shall result in penalties as determined by the officer. Any order passed by the adjudicating officer may be appealed to an appellate authority, subject to a fee as prescribed; and the appellate authority’s decision shall be final, provided that it is not contrary to principles of natural justice.

In this Act, "Assured Produce" means agricultural produce certified by an authorized body under regulations framed for preventing food adulteration act and ensuring adherence to prescribed quality standards. Such certification shall be deemed a representation that the goods conform to those standards. A collective mark may be registered signifying membership in a recognized producers' association dedicated to maintaining Assured Produce protocols, provided that all members comply with the said protocols as verified by the authorized body. The Registrar may require evidence of such compliance prior to registration and periodically thereafter. Misuse or unauthorized application of the collective mark shall constitute an offence under this Act.

The Registrar shall not register a trade mark which, when used in relation to food products, is deemed by the relevant authorities under the Food Adulteration Act to be misleadingly descriptive of the product’s composition or quality. This restriction applies irrespective of any prior use or reputation acquired by the applicant for the trade mark. An application may proceed if the Registrar is satisfied that appropriate safeguards are in place to prevent consumer confusion arising from such a depiction, including but not limited to prominent disclaimers and certification marks. Furthermore, where a food product originates from a registered geographical indication, any proposed trade mark shall clearly differentiate itself from the protected name and characteristics associated with said geographical indication, as provided herein.

Where a registered trade mark is used deceptively to represent that goods are of a particular quality or nature, and such representation constitutes an offence under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, any person aggrieved may institute proceedings for relief including damages. The remedies available shall include an injunction restraining the use of the infringing trade mark, and an order requiring the erasure or alteration of matter making false representations about the nature of the goods. Further, a court may award compensation to the aggrieved party reflecting loss of reputation and goodwill arising from the deceptive practice. Any application for rectification under this Act alleging such deceptive use shall be considered with due regard to evidence demonstrating the misleading effect on consumers. India application shall be entertained irrespective of whether criminal proceedings have been initiated concurrently.

Where a person is found guilty of contravening the provisions relating to food adulteration under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, and such contravention involves the use of a trademark registered under this Act, the Registrar shall be notified immediately by the adjudicating officer. The Registrar may, subject to due process, initiate proceedings for rectification or removal of the trademark from the Register if it is established that the deceptive practice employed in the adulteration has damaged the reputation associated with the name and mark. Any application seeking such rectification must include a certified copy of the order passed by the adjudicating officer under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act. The proprietor of the registered trademark shall be afforded an opportunity to present its case before the Registrar, as provided herein. Failure to comply with this notification requirement may render the adjudicating officer liable for penalties.

Where a person is found guilty of contravening the provisions relating to food adulteration act, as provided herein, such person shall be liable to pay a pecuniary penalty not exceeding five thousand rupees for the first offence and ten thousand rupees for any subsequent offence. Any officer authorised by the Central Government may seize and confiscate any goods which are deemed to have been adulterated or misbranded. The adjudicating authority may, subject to appeal under this Act, order the destruction of such seized goods at the owner’s expense. Further, a specification amended to reflect altered ingredients following regulatory guidance shall not excuse liability if evidence demonstrates deliberate intent to deceive consumers regarding product composition.

An owner seeking to exploit an internationally registered trade mark within India may grant licenses conferring specific rights relating to use of the mark, subject to conditions prescribed under this Act. Such licenses shall be documented and filed with the Registrar prior to commencement of any commercial activity utilizing the international registration’s protections in India. Any assignment of the benefit of an international registration, or a license granted pursuant thereto, requires notification to the Registrar within three months of execution, detailing the assignor, assignee, licensor, and licensee respectively. Failure to provide such notification shall render the assignment or license voidable at the option of any aggrieved party. The Registrar may require further documentation demonstrating due diligence in verifying the identity and legal standing of all parties involved in assignments or licenses concerning international registration India.

For the purposes of this Act, "goods" shall include literary, artistic, scientific, industrial or commercial goods, and services offered to consumers. The register respect goods shall be maintained as per the prescribed forms and procedures; an application for registration may specify a class of goods or services as defined under the International Classification of Goods and Services. Any alteration to the description of goods sought to be registered shall require prior approval from the Registrar. Furthermore, where the applicant’s business is not engaged in trade or manufacture of the specified goods, such fact shall be clearly stated in the application.

The proprietor of a registered trade mark shall, upon proof of actual use of the mark in relation to goods or services for a continuous period of five years following its registration, be entitled to restrain any person from using a sign identical or confusingly similar to the said trade mark in respect of goods or services identical or closely related to those for which the registered trade mark is register respect goods. Such restraint may include an injunction preventing further use and an order requiring the delivery up for destruction of all infringing materials, provided that the proprietor demonstrates demonstrable damage resulting from the unauthorized use. Further, where a proprietor fails to demonstrate such continuous use within the stipulated period, any interested party may apply to have the registration expunged in respect of those goods or services; this application shall be adjudicated according to principles of natural justice and considering all relevant circumstances as provided herein.

An application for the registration of a trade mark shall specify, with as much precision as circumstances permit, the goods or services in respect of which the applicant desires to register the trade mark. The Registrar may require an amendment of the specification of goods or services if he considers it necessary to define them with greater clarity and accuracy. Any person proposing to file an application for registration under this Act shall furnish a certified copy of any prior registration affecting identical or similar marks relating to identical or similar goods or services. Such certification must be verified by an authorized officer. The Registrar may, upon receiving such information, direct the applicant to amend the proposed specification to avoid conflict with existing registrations. Failure to comply with such direction may result in rejection of the application. Registration shall confer on the registered proprietor the exclusive right to use the trade mark register respect goods or services as specified in the registration.

Any proprietor seeking to register a trade mark shall, upon application, specify with particularity the goods or services in respect of which he claims such registration. The Registrar may reject an application if he deems the specified goods or services to be deceptively similar to those already associated with an existing registered trade mark. Failure to maintain the register respect goods for which registration is secured will render the proprietor liable to have their rights revoked, following due notice and opportunity for response as provided herein. Any person demonstrating actual damage resulting from the unauthorized use of a registered trade mark may institute civil proceedings seeking injunctive relief and compensation; penalties shall be determined by the Court based on the severity of the infringement.

The owner of a registered trade mark shall, subject to this Act, be entitled to grant licences allowing others to use the trade mark in relation to goods for which the register respect goods are specified. Such licences may be exclusive or non-exclusive and may be granted for a fixed term or during the subsistence of the registration. Any assignment of the registered trade mark shall include any existing licences relating thereto, unless the assignee expressly declines such inclusion in writing at the time of assignment. Provided that, where a licence is assigned separately from the registered trade mark itself, the assignor remains bound by the terms of the original licensing agreement until the expiry or termination thereof. The Registrar may require evidence of consent from affected licensees prior to registering an assignment which includes their licences, as provided herein.

Subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal, an entry in the Register of Trade Marks may be amended by direction of the Registrar if it appears to him that such amendment is necessary for ensuring greater clarity or accuracy regarding the goods for which registration is sought. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar under this Act relating to the refusal, modification, or removal of a trade mark register respect goods may appeal to the Tribunal within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The Appellate Tribunal shall consider any submissions made by parties and may direct the Registrar to reconsider the matter, or uphold or vary the original decision. Further, an application for revocation of registration may be filed demonstrating non-use exceeding five years, provided that such use is not demonstrably attributable to circumstances beyond the applicant’s control.

An application for the registration of a trade mark shall specify, with as much precision as circumstances permit, the goods or services in respect of which the applicant desires to register the trade mark. The Registrar may require an amendment of the specification of goods or services if he considers it is not accurate enough or does not clearly define the scope of the application. Any person intending to act as a patent agent shall be deemed competent to advise applicants regarding appropriate classification of goods for purposes of registration under this Act. Where objections are raised against the acceptance of an application, the Registrar shall provide the applicant with an opportunity to submit their response in writing and may require a hearing. The register respect goods shall remain open for public inspection during normal business hours.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may be refused if the Registrar has reason to believe that use of the proposed indication is likely to mislead consumers as to the origin of the goods concerned. The applicant shall furnish such evidence as the Registrar deems necessary to substantiate the distinctiveness and reputation associated with the claimed geographical territory. Where an existing registered geographical indication is falsified through the application of a mark or sign, creating a false association with the genuine product, the aggrieved proprietor may apply for rectification under this Act. Such rectification proceedings are subject to provisions regarding evidence and hearings as provided herein. The Registrar shall consider whether the use constitutes a *geographical indication falsified* and infringes upon the exclusive rights granted to the registered proprietor.

Any goods or services a geographical indication where such use is likely to cause confusion as to the origin of the goods or services. (2) Where a proprietor establishes that another has falsified a geographical indication and thereby made misrepresentation concerning the origin of goods, the injured party shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief preventing further acts of falsification and misleading the public. (3) In determining whether an act constitutes geographical indication falsified, due regard shall be had to all relevant circumstances, including the distinctiveness of the indication, the similarity between the use and the registered indication, and any actual or potential confusion likely to arise amongst consumers. (4) Remedies available under this Act for acts of geographical indication falsified may include damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the proprietor, as determined by a civil court.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may be rejected if the Register is satisfied that use of the indication, as proposed in the application, is likely to mislead consumers regarding the origin of the goods.
