Further, where a trade mark is registered in a particular form, its use in a different, substantially altered *mark registered manner* will be deemed an infringement if it creates confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of goods or services.

The proprietor of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to restrain any person from using any mark identical or confusingly similar to their registered mark, provided that such use is made without consent and creates likelihood of confusion among the public regarding the origin of goods or services. Where a registered mark is used in a manner which dilutes its distinctiveness, or unfairly exploits or undermines the reputation associated with the mark, remedies including damages may be awarded by the relevant intellectual property tribunal. Any alteration to the registered mark that affects its *mark registered manner* and creates confusion amongst consumers constitutes infringement under this Act. Further, where an infringing use occurs through false advertising or misleading representations concerning goods or services, enhanced penalties shall apply as provided herein.

The Registrar may, upon application by any person claiming rectification of a registered trade mark, entertain an action for removal of entries on the register if it is demonstrated that the *mark registered manner* has become non-distinctive through reason of subsequent use by other parties. Such applications shall be accompanied by evidence substantiating the alleged loss of distinctiveness, including consumer surveys and market analysis reports submitted in triplicate. The Registrar shall provide a copy of such application and supporting documentation to the proprietor of the trade mark for comment within thirty days of receipt. Any response from the proprietor may include counter-evidence refuting the claim of non-distinctivity. Following consideration of all submissions, the Registrar shall issue an order either rectifying the register or dismissing the application, providing detailed reasons for the decision. Appeals against such orders are permitted to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board as provided herein.

The proprietor of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to institute proceedings for infringement where another person uses a sign identical with, or confusingly similar to, the registered mark, in connection with goods or services. Such use is deemed infringing if it creates a likelihood of confusion on the part of the public as to the origin of the goods or services. The proprietor must demonstrate that the mark has acquired distinctiveness through use following registration; this requirement shall not apply where the mark inherently possesses such distinctiveness. Use in the course of trade, including advertising and promotional activities, is subject to scrutiny under this Act. A finding of infringement requires proof of use in a *mark registered manner* which directly benefits from the reputation attached to the earlier mark.

Any person who, without leave of the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal, uses a mark identical with or deceptively similar to a *mark registered manner* for goods or services specified therein shall be deemed guilty of an offence under this Act. Such offender shall be liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and also be punishable with a fine of not less than fifty thousand rupees but which may extend to two hundred thousand rupees. Further, any goods bearing the infringing mark are subject to seizure and destruction as provided herein. The Registrar *may* issue injunctions restraining such use, and shall do so upon receiving complaint from the registered proprietor demonstrating actual damage or likelihood thereof.

The proprietor of a registered trademark shall retain exclusive rights regarding its use within India, subject to any permitted uses granted under this Act. Any party desiring to utilize a mark registered manner that differs from the proprietor’s established practices must obtain prior written consent. Such consent may be granted on terms and conditions as determined by the grantor, including but not limited to royalty payments and restrictions on geographical scope of use. The grant of such license shall be recorded in the Register of Trade Marks, noting the duration and extent of permitted usage. Further, a proprietor may assign the right to utilize their registered mark, or any part thereof, to another party, provided that such assignment is also duly recorded. Any unauthorized use of a registered trademark, irrespective of intent, constitutes infringement and renders the user liable for damages as provided herein.

The use of a mark shall constitute an offence under this Act if it incorporates elements substantially identical to those comprising a mark registered manner, even where slight alterations are made to distinguish the infringing mark. Provided that, the Registrar may entertain objections to such usage upon demonstration by the registered proprietor that the alteration does not negate the overall impression created by the original mark and that confusion is likely amongst consumers. Further, any party aggrieved by an order of the Registrar relating to deceptive similarity may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order, subject to payment of prescribed fees and demonstrating demonstrable prejudice arising from the Registrar’s decision.

Any proprietor seeking to maintain a mark registered manner shall diligently monitor for instances of unauthorized usage appearing on products or services. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint demonstrating such infringement, issue a notice requiring the alleged infringer to cease and desist from the offending activity. Further, any entity found to be utilizing a trade mark in a way that creates confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or quality of goods or services shall liable penalty as determined by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. This obligation extends to alterations or adaptations of registered marks which, despite modification, retain deceptive similarity and continue to mislead the public concerning their source. The proprietor bears responsibility for ensuring compliance with these provisions under this Act.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Appellate Board sub under this Act relating to rectification of a registered trademark, or concerning the revocation or invalidity of a mark registered manner, may appeal from that order to the High Court within whose territorial jurisdiction the cause of action arose. Such appeal shall be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order to the appellant. The High Court may, after giving notice to all parties concerned and affording them an opportunity of being heard, confirm, vary or reverse the order appealed against, or may dispose of the matter in such a manner as it thinks just and equitable. Costs shall be determined by the High Court in its discretion. Any party dissatisfied with the decision of the High Court may further appeal to the Supreme Court on any question of law arising out of the judgment.

Any person who represents, directly or indirectly, that goods or services are offered under a *mark registered manner* without authorization from the proprietor shall be deemed to have contravened this Act. Such representation includes the display of the mark in a way calculated to create confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or quality of the goods or services. Where an infringement is established, the Court may grant such relief as it deems just and equitable, including injunctions preventing further infringing activity and orders for the delivery up or destruction of all goods bearing the infringing mark. Furthermore, damages shall be awarded to the proprietor of the *trade mark recognised*, reflecting the loss suffered due to the unauthorized use, provided that willful infringement is proven.

Where any person seeks to challenge the validity of a registration granted under this Act, such challenge may only be brought before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within three months from the date of publication of the acceptance of the application for registration. Provided that where the mark incorporates a geographical indication as defined herein, the proprietor proposed registered shall demonstrate due diligence in preventing dilution or misuse of said indication. Any representation made to the public falsely suggesting association with a registered trade mark shall be deemed an infringement and subject to remedies available under this Act. The Board may order the erasure of any registration found to have been obtained through fraudulent means or misrepresentation, and may award damages to aggrieved parties. Further, wilful adoption of an identical or deceptively similar mark after knowledge of the existence of a prior registered trade mark shall attract enhanced penalties as provided herein.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is refused under this Act, the applicant may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be made within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order of refusal. The appellant shall serve a copy of the memorandum of appeal on the Registrar not less than thirty days before the date appointed for hearing the appeal. The Intellectual Property Appellate Board may, after giving notice to all parties concerned and affording them an opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify or reverse the decision appealed from. If the Intellectual Property Appellate Board allows an appeal, it shall direct that the trade mark be registered as originally applied for, or with such modifications as determined by the Board. The proprietor proposed registered may also file a counter-statement to any appeal.

For the purposes of this Act, an affidavit registered proprietor is defined as the individual or entity whose name appears on the Register of Trade Marks as the current and lawful owner of a trade mark, subject to any rights or interests recorded against it. Such proprietor shall be deemed to possess exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to goods or services specified in the registration, provided that this exclusivity is not affected by prior usage or other registered rights under this Act. An affidavit from the registered proprietor verifying the accuracy of information submitted relating to ownership transfer or alteration may be required as evidence for any application processed under this Act.

In any proceeding under this Act concerning rectification of a trade mark register, where an objection is raised against the continued registration based on non-use, the registered proprietor shall be required to submit an affidavit verifying either that use of the trade mark has been duly made in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered, or providing satisfactory explanation for the failure to do so. Such affidavit must detail the circumstances affecting such use and demonstrate reasonable efforts undertaken to re-establish its application. The Registrar may require further evidence supporting the claims within the affidavit. Failure by the registered proprietor to file a compliant affidavit within the time specified shall be deemed conclusive proof of non-use, entitling the objector to rectification as provided herein. Any false statement made in an affidavit registered proprietor submits is subject to penalties under the Indian Penal Code.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act, and the applicant desires to submit evidence in support of his claim, he shall furnish to the Registrar, within the time specified in the notice of opposition, an affidavit verifying the truth and accuracy of such evidence. This affidavit must be sworn before or presented to any officer authorized by law to administer oaths, and a copy thereof shall accompany the documentary proof submitted. The registered proprietor, upon receiving notification of such affidavit, may file with the Registrar within a further period of thirty days a counter-affidavit rebutting the claims made therein. Any challenge to the veracity of an affidavit registered proprietor submits must be brought before the relevant intellectual property tribunal. Failure to comply with these procedural requirements shall render the evidence inadmissible during any subsequent inquiry or hearing as provided herein.

Where any person alleging that their rights have been infringed by use of an identical or deceptively similar trade mark may institute proceedings for damages, they must first serve upon the registered proprietor a notice specifying the nature of the alleged infringement and demanding cessation thereof. Failure to comply with this requirement shall render such proceedings inadmissible before any court in India. The registered proprietor is obliged to file within thirty days of service an affidavit registered proprietor verifying whether the use complained of constitutes a genuine or reasonable user under this Act, and detailing all steps taken to mitigate further infringement. Any false statement made in such an affidavit shall be deemed a cognizable offence punishable with imprisonment and fine.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any registered proprietor may grant a license relating to the use of their trade mark, specifying the goods or services in relation to which such use is permitted. Such licenses shall be assignable along with the ownership of the trade mark, provided that the assignee notifies the Registrar within thirty days of acquiring the right to the license and furnishes an affidavit registered proprietor confirming the transfer and detailing the terms of continued validity of the licensed usage. The Registrar may require further documentation as deemed necessary to verify the authenticity of such assignment. Any subsequent modification or termination of a license shall also be reported to the Registrar in writing, accompanied by an affidavit from both the original licensor and licensee, attesting to the changes. Failure to comply with these notification requirements may render the assignee liable for penalties as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, a “proposed registered proprietor” means an individual or body corporate to whom application for registration of a trade mark has been made and who is reasonably expected to become the registered proprietor upon completion of the examination process and any subsequent appeals. Such expectation shall be determined by the Registrar based on compliance with all relevant provisions under this Act relating to distinctiveness, deceptiveness, and prior rights. The Registrar may require further documentation from an applicant identified as a proposed registered proprietor to ascertain their eligibility and intention to utilize the trade mark in accordance with prescribed guidelines, provided that such requests are reasonable and do not unduly delay the registration process.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act, and where the applicant has filed a counterstatement to the notice of opposition, the Registrar may, upon review of the evidence submitted by both parties, direct that the proceedings be stayed pending resolution of certain disputes concerning ownership or prior use. Such direction shall only be given if the dispute directly impacts the determination of whether the trade mark is distinctive or deceptively similar to an earlier mark. The rights and obligations of a *proposed registered proprietor* in respect of any such stay shall be determined by the Registrar, taking into account the potential prejudice to both the opponent and the applicant, provided that the applicant demonstrates good faith in pursuing registration.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act, and where the applicant has subsequently ceased to exist as a corporate entity, the Registrar may, upon receiving satisfactory evidence of such cessation and identifying a successor in interest or other eligible party, entertain the application further. The proposed registered proprietor, being the successor or otherwise entitled party, shall be deemed to have stepped into the shoes of the original applicant for all purposes relating to the opposition proceedings. Any rights or remedies available to the opponent against the original applicant shall remain applicable against the proposed registered proprietor. Provided that the Registrar may require the proposed registered proprietor to satisfy any conditions precedent which were applicable to the original application, and such conditions must be fulfilled before registration can proceed as provided herein.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act, and where the applicant has indicated that they are acting as an agent for another person who is intended to be the registered proprietor upon successful registration, the Registrar shall serve notice of the opposition on both the applicant and the proposed registered proprietor. The proposed registered proprietor may, within such time as prescribed, file with the Registrar a counterstatement responding to the grounds of opposition. Such counterstatement shall be deemed to be part of the record for consideration during any hearing or inquiry relating to the opposition. Further, the Registrar may require the proposed registered proprietor to furnish evidence demonstrating their ultimate beneficial ownership interest in the trade mark, provided that such requirement is proportionate to the nature and extent of the opposition raised. The applicant shall have the right to cross-examine any witness presented by the proposed registered proprietor at a hearing.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act, and where the applicant has demonstrated satisfactory compliance with all prescribed formalities relating to publication and invitation of objections, the Registrar may, upon review of the opposition record, entertain a request from a proposed registered proprietor seeking intervention as a party. Such intervention shall be permitted only if the proposed registered proprietor demonstrates a clear and demonstrable proprietary interest in the subject trade mark, evidenced by assignment or other legally recognized transfer instruments duly executed and notarized. The Registrar shall require submission of an affidavit verifying the accuracy of all information provided concerning the claimed interest. Further, any such proposed registered proprietor shall abide by the procedural timelines established for existing parties to the opposition proceeding.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act, and where the applicant has subsequently become a proposed registered proprietor following a successful appeal against such opposition, any party aggrieved by the decision granting registration to the proposed registered proprietor may institute proceedings in the High Court within ninety days from the date of publication of that decision. Failure to initiate such proceedings within the stipulated period shall irrevocably bar any subsequent challenge to the registration. The Court may, upon finding merit in the grievance, order rectification of the register and direct deletion of the trade mark entry. Any person found to have acted in bad faith or made false representations during opposition proceedings faces penalties as provided herein.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is pending and a proposed registered proprietor seeks to assign or license the right to use the trade mark, subject to any existing agreements, such assignment or license shall not prejudice the rights of other applicants or prior users. The Registrar may require the proposed registered proprietor to provide evidence demonstrating due diligence in notifying all relevant parties regarding the intended transfer or licensing arrangement. Any agreement for assignment or license must clearly specify the scope and duration of permitted use, and include provisions safeguarding against dilution of the trade mark’s distinctiveness. Further, the proposed registered proprietor shall furnish an undertaking to the Registrar confirming adherence to these stipulations; failure to do so may result in rejection of the application or revocation of registration.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act, and where the applicant has indicated a person as a proposed registered proprietor with whom they intend to enter into an assignment subsequent to registration, the Registrar shall provide notice of such opposition to that proposed registered proprietor. The proposed registered proprietor may, within thirty days from the date of receipt of such notice, file with the Registrar a counter-statement disputing the grounds for opposition and asserting their right to be registered as proprietor. Such counter-statement shall be deemed a written defence under this Act and subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The applicant shall have the opportunity to respond to any assertions made in the proposed registered proprietor’s counter-statement, provided that such response is filed within fifteen days thereafter.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act, and where the applicant has subsequently ceased to carry on business, the Registrar may, upon receiving evidence satisfactory to the Registrar, direct that the proceedings be continued in relation to any proposed registered proprietor who has acquired substantial interests in the trade mark. Such direction shall specify the manner in which the proposed registered proprietor is deemed to have been substituted for the original applicant for the purposes of further consideration of the opposition. The registered user party may submit observations regarding the substitution and its potential impact on existing contractual arrangements relating to the use of the trade mark, provided that such observations are filed within the time prescribed by the Registrar. Any order made under this provision is subject to appeal as provided herein.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark includes a layout design constituting a substantial feature of the goods or services relating to which the trade mark is used, and where such layout design has been created by a person other than the applicant, the proposed registered proprietor shall provide evidence satisfactory to the Registrar demonstrating due diligence in ascertaining the creator’s consent for inclusion and subsequent registration. This requirement applies irrespective of whether the layout design is incorporated as part of the overall trade mark representation or functions as an ornamental element. The Registrar may require further documentation establishing ownership or licensing rights pertaining to the creator layout design, provided that such requests are limited to information reasonably necessary for verification purposes under this Act. Failure to comply with these stipulations shall render the application liable for rejection.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act, and where the applicant has demonstrably engaged in preliminary inventive work relating to goods or services associated with the proposed mark, the Registrar shall provide the opponent with detailed particulars regarding such inventive efforts. The Registrar may require the applicant to submit documentation substantiating claims of prior invention convention participation. Should the opponent dispute the veracity or relevance of this information, a determination shall be made by an independent expert appointed by the Registrar, whose findings are binding subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Furthermore, any person claiming entitlement to the trade mark as a proposed registered proprietor may challenge the validity of such appointment through judicial review.

For the purposes of this Act, a “proposed registered proprietor” means a person who has filed an application for registration of a trade mark under this Act and who is not yet the registered proprietor but to whom the Trade Marks Registry may grant registration subject to any opposition or other proceedings. Where such a proposed registered proprietor utilizes a patented process in the manufacture of goods associated with the trade mark, they shall disclose details of said patented process in their application as provided herein; failure to do so may render the registration liable for revocation under this Act. The Registrar may require further information regarding such processes from any applicant claiming status as a proposed registered proprietor.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act, and where such opposition relates to acquired distinctiveness, the registered proprietor may, within three months from the date of service of the notice of opposition, file with the Registrar a counterstatement affirming that use of the trade mark has been continuous and extensive in relation to the goods or services specified in the application. Such counterstatement shall be accompanied by evidence substantiating such use, including but not limited to sales figures, advertising expenditure, and market survey data. The registered proprietor proposed for registration may also submit a declaration attesting to the bona fide nature of their commercial activities. Failure to file a timely counterstatement shall preclude the registered proprietor from adducing evidence in support of acquired distinctiveness during any subsequent hearing.

Where an application for rectification of a registered trade mark is presented alleging that use by the registered proprietor has been abandoned, the Registrar may require the registered proprietor to furnish evidence demonstrating continued bona fide use of the mark during the relevant period. Such evidence shall include documentary proof of sales, advertising expenditure, or licensing agreements relating to goods or services identifiable with the trade mark. Failure to provide satisfactory evidence within the time specified by the Registrar shall be deemed conclusive against the registered proprietor’s claim of non-abandonment. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar under this Act may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The registered proprietor proposed for rectification has the right to cross-examine witnesses presented by the applicant, subject to procedural safeguards as provided herein.

Where an application for rectification of a registered trade mark is filed alleging that the registered proprietor has failed to use the trade mark in accordance with conditions specified under this Act, the Registrar shall serve notice on the registered proprietor requiring him to show cause why the trade mark should not be expunged from the Register. Such notice shall specify the grounds upon which the application for rectification is based and provide a period of sixty days within which the registered proprietor may submit his response. Failure by the registered proprietor, or any person acting as the registered proprietor proposed, to adequately demonstrate continued use or adherence to stipulated conditions will render him liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees, recoverable as civil debt.

Where the registered proprietor of a trade mark desires to grant a license relating thereto, such license may be granted either for the whole duration of the registration or for a specified period, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated within the licensing agreement. The registered proprietor shall retain ultimate control over the use of the trade mark, even where a license has been issued, and may impose reasonable restrictions on the licensed activities as provided herein. Any assignment of the right to utilize the trade mark under such a license must be notified to the Registrar in writing, along with supporting documentation establishing the transferor’s authority. The registered proprietor proposed for licensing shall ensure that all licensees adhere strictly to the conditions outlined within the agreement and any subsequent amendments approved by the proprietor. Failure to comply may result in termination of the license as determined by the Registrar.

Where an application for rectification of a registered trade mark is presented alleging that the registered proprietor has failed to use the trade mark in accordance with the provisions under this Act, the Registrar shall give notice thereof to the registered proprietor. The registered proprietor proposed may, within the time specified in the notice, file evidence rebutting the allegation and demonstrating genuine use or providing reasons for non-use which satisfy the Registrar. Failure by the registered proprietor to submit such evidence or a satisfactory explanation shall be deemed conclusive against them. Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar relating to rectification may appeal under this Act. The Registrar may impose a penalty, not exceeding one hundred thousand rupees, where any false representation is made in connection with the entered register disclosed.

Where the registered proprietor of a trade mark desires to grant a license for use of the said trade mark, such license may be granted subject to the terms and conditions stipulated therein. The registered proprietor shall retain ownership of the trade mark and any subsequent registrations derived therefrom; however, the licensee shall possess exclusive rights within the scope defined by the licensing agreement as provided herein. Any assignment of this license requires prior written consent from the registered proprietor, which consent may be withheld without providing reasons. Furthermore, should the licensee breach the terms of the license, including unauthorized use beyond the agreed territory or product class, the registered proprietor shall have recourse to seek an injunction sub section restricting such usage and recovering damages as deemed appropriate by a competent court. The registered proprietor proposed assignment must include full details of consideration paid.

For the purposes of this Act, a “registered proprietor proposed” is deemed to include any individual or entity seeking to obtain registration of a trade mark identical or confusingly similar to an existing registered trade mark, subject to demonstrating a demonstrable and lawful interest in such application. The Registrar shall consider all relevant factors pertaining to reputation and goodwill associated with the prior registered trade mark. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar concerning the acceptance or rejection of an application under this definition may appeal to the Authority Appellate Board as provided herein. Such appeals shall be conducted according to prescribed procedures.

An appeal against any decision made under this Act relating to rectification or revocation of registration, or concerning opposition proceedings, shall lie to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. For the purposes of this provision, “dispose th appeal” means the process by which the Tribunal considers arguments presented by all parties and renders a final determination on the merits of the matter. The Tribunal may, subject to any rules made under this Act, require the appellant to furnish security for costs. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Tribunal may further dispose th appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such order, provided that the High Court shall have exclusive jurisdiction in respect of such appeals.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed refused if the Registrar considers that the mark is descriptive of the goods or services with which it seeks to be associated. Any party aggrieved by such refusal, whether applicant or any other person claiming proprietary rights in a similar mark already registered under this Act, may dispose th appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within three months from the date of communication of the refusal order. The tribunal shall give notice to all parties affected by the appeal and afford them an opportunity of being heard. Such disposal shall be subject to the provisions relating to costs as determined by the Tribunal. Provided that a party may, with leave of the Tribunal, file additional evidence in support of their case.

Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to the rectification of a registered trade mark, or concerning the invalidity of a trade mark registration, may dispose th appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. Such appeal must be filed within ninety days from the date of communication of the order sought to be appealed against. The tribunal shall consider all relevant evidence presented by both the appellant and the respondent, including any counter-claims or defenses raised. 

The Registrar shall furnish to the tribunal a complete record of the proceedings before them. Subject to this Act, the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal may allow an appeal if it finds that the decision of the Registrar was erroneous in law or fact. The tribunal may substitute its own decision for that of the Registrar, and may order such remedies as are just and equitable, including but not limited to costs.

Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to the rectification of a trade mark, or concerning any matter arising under this Act where no other right of appeal is specifically provided, may dispose th appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. Such an appeal must be filed within ninety days from the date of communication of the order sought to be appealed against. The appellant shall deposit such fees as are prescribed for appeals before the Tribunal. Provided that, if the aggrieved party can demonstrate reasonable cause for delay, the Tribunal may entertain the appeal notwithstanding the lapse of the stipulated period, subject to its satisfaction regarding the justification for the delay. Further, the Tribunal shall consider any counter-claims filed by other interested parties in relation to the trade mark concerned.

Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to rectification proceedings concerning a registered trade mark may dispose th appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. Such appeal must be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order, subject to an extension not exceeding thirty days where the appellant demonstrates reasonable cause for delay. Failure to comply with this time limit shall render the appeal inadmissible. The Tribunal shall consider evidence presented by both parties and may direct rectification of the trade mark register if it finds grounds for doing so under this Act. Any costs associated with the appeal, including legal representation fees, are at the discretion of the Tribunal and may be imposed on either party.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark shall have the exclusive right to grant licenses relating to the use of that trade mark in connection with specified goods or services, and such license agreements may include provisions for royalty payments as determined by mutual consent between the parties. Any assignment of rights under this Act concerning a trade mark, whether absolute or partial, requires registration with the Trade Marks Registry, subject to payment of prescribed fees. Where a dispute arises regarding the validity or scope of a license agreement, any party aggrieved may dispose th appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board for adjudication and determination of the matter in accordance with principles of natural justice. The Registrar shall maintain a public record of all assignments and licenses pertaining to registered trade marks, accessible upon request.

Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar refusing to register a trade mark, or requiring amendment thereof, may prefer an appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. Such appeal must be filed within sixty days from the date on which the order is received. The appellant shall deposit with the Registry such sum as may be prescribed, failing which the appeal shall stand dismissed. The Tribunal may, after giving notice to all parties concerned and affording them a reasonable opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify, or reverse the decision appealed from. It shall also dispose th appeal expeditiously, considering the balance between public interest and commercial considerations; provided that any subsequent application relating to the same trade mark may be taken into consideration during proceedings.

Any proprietor desiring to dispose th appeal relating to a trade mark registration shall, prior to any assignment or licensing agreement, provide written notice to all registered proprietors claiming rights derived from the same trade mark. Such notice must detail the intended disposition and its potential impact on existing registrations. The Central Trade Marks Registry may, upon receiving such notification, issue a cautionary note for publication in the Trade Marks Journal, advising interested parties of the pending appeal and the proposed transfer or license.

Provided that any assignment made without adherence to this provision shall be voidable at the option of the aggrieved party. Further, where a license is granted, the proprietor retaining ownership of the trade mark registration shall ensure that the licensee complies with all conditions stipulated under this Act relating to quality control and proper use of the registered mark. The Registrar may inquire into any dispute arising from such licensing agreements.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application for registration of a trade mark concerning agricultural products, and particularly those pertaining to genetically modified seeds distributed by the India Department Agriculture, may dispose th appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeal must be filed within ninety days from the date of communication of the said decision. The Board shall give notice to all parties concerned and afford them an opportunity of being heard, both in writing and orally. An appeal will only be entertained if the appellant demonstrates a prima facie case involving substantial injustice arising from the Registrar's order, subject to procedural requirements as provided herein.

An appeal arising from any decision of the Registrar relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application for registration of a trade mark, or concerning rectification proceedings, shall lie before the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal shall hear and dispose th appeal upon such evidence as it deems relevant, affording all parties concerned an opportunity of being heard. Any party intending to challenge a decision made by the Tribunal may further appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of that decision. A required registrar person shall furnish necessary records to the Tribunal for its consideration in adjudicating any appeal under this Act.

Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Trade Marks Registry relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application for registration of a trade mark, or any other matter arising during the consideration thereof, shall have the right to dispose th appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeals may be filed within sixty days from the date on which notice of the decision is served upon the appellant under this Act. The Trade Marks Registry shall furnish to the appellant, along with the notice, a certified copy of the relevant record pertaining to the application or matter in question. Provided that an extension of time not exceeding thirty days may be granted by the Appellate Board for cause shown. The appeal shall state the grounds on which it is based and accompanied by such fees as prescribed.

Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar concerning the rectification or invalidation of a trade mark registered respect of goods or services may dispose th appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. Such appeal must be filed within ninety days from the date of communication of the order, and shall specify the grounds on which it is based. The Tribunal shall give notice to all parties concerned in the matter and afford them an opportunity of being heard, both orally and in writing.

The Registrar may, at any time during the proceedings before the Tribunal, disclose further evidence relevant to the appeal. Any party may apply to the Tribunal for a stay of operation of the order appealed against, pending disposal th appeal, subject to such terms as the Tribunal deems fit. The decision of the Tribunal shall be final and binding, save for an appeal to the High Court under this Act.

Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application for registration of a trade mark, or any other matter arising during the examination of such application, may dispose th appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The Board shall admit appeals only if the appellant deposits before it such fees as may be prescribed. Provided that where the decision relates to a refusal of registration based on absolute grounds under this Act, the Registrar shall provide the applicant with an opportunity to submit his counterstatement. Such counterstatement shall be considered by the Board in disposing th appeal. The Board may, after giving all parties concerned an opportunity of being heard, confirm, vary or reverse the decision appealed from and may also direct the Registrar to exercise any power vested in him under this Act relating to offices patent applications.

An aggrieved party seeking review of a decision rendered concerning rectification proceedings initiated under this Act may file an application for an 112a order appellate with the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. Such application must specify the grounds upon which the original determination is challenged, and shall be accompanied by certified copies of all relevant documents pertaining to the initial adjudication. The Tribunal shall afford both parties a reasonable opportunity to present arguments and evidence in support of their respective positions. Decisions rendered by the Tribunal under this provision are final subject to appeal to the High Court within sixty days.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed refused if the Registrar considers that the proposed mark is likely to be confused with an earlier mark registered under this Act. Any party aggrieved by such refusal order may, subject to provisions regarding time limits, file an 112a order appellate before the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. The tribunal shall give notice to the applicant and any proprietor of a conflicting trade mark and afford them opportunities to present their case. Decisions concerning the distinctiveness of marks or the assessment of likelihood of confusion shall be determined based on evidence presented and principles established under this Act, provided that the tribunal may direct further inquiry as necessary.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Registrar relating to rectification of a registered trade mark, or concerning the invalidity of a registration, may prefer an appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date on which such order is received. The Tribunal shall follow the principles of natural justice and provide both parties with a reasonable opportunity to present their case and offer evidence in support thereof. Subject to this, the Tribunal may affirm, modify, or reverse the order appealed against. An appeal under this Act shall be finally determinable by the Tribunal; however, any party aggrieved by an 112a order appellate decision of the Tribunal may further appeal to the High Court within a period of ninety days from the date of that decision.

Any party aggrieved by any order made by the Registrar relating to rectification of a registered trade mark or concerning proceedings initiated under Chapter X may prefer an application for review before the Appellate Authority. The Appellate Authority shall consist of a judicial officer appointed by the Central Government, possessing expertise in intellectual property law and not below the rank of District Judge. Such applications must be filed within ninety days from the date on account of receiving notification of the order sought to be reviewed.

The applicant shall serve a copy of the application upon all parties involved in the original proceeding at least thirty days prior to the hearing. The Appellate Authority may, after affording an opportunity for hearing to all concerned, confirm, vary or reverse the order appealed from, as it deems fit. An 112a order appellate is final subject to further appeal to the High Court within sixty days of its pronouncement.

Any party aggrieved by an order passed by the Registrar relating to rectification proceedings concerning a registered trade mark, subject to compliance with prescribed timelines, may prefer an 112a order appellate to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. Such appeal shall only be maintainable if the appellant demonstrates that they have first exhausted all available remedies under this Act and has paid such fees as are determined by notification of the Central Government. The Tribunal shall consider any evidence submitted by both parties, provided it is relevant and admissible according to established principles of jurisprudence. Further, the Registrar may, upon request from either party, require submission of further documentation substantiating claims made in the appeal.

Any party aggrieved by an order passed by the Registrar relating to the rectification of a trade mark or concerning damages awarded pursuant to infringement proceedings may prefer an *112a order appellate* to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. Such appeals must be filed within three months from the date on which the order was received, subject to extension not exceeding ninety days if sufficient cause is shown and recorded in writing. The Tribunal shall hear parties de novo and may affirm, reverse or modify the order appealed against. Failure to comply with procedural requirements relating to service of notice under this Act will render an appeal inadmissible. Any costs associated with the appeal shall be determined by the Tribunal as it deems just, considering the conduct of the parties involved.

Any proprietor of a registered trade mark seeking to grant a license or assign their rights therein shall file an application with the Trade Marks Registry, detailing the scope and duration of such license or assignment. The Registrar may, subject to fulfilling prescribed formalities including payment of requisite fees, register the license or assignment as part of the record pertaining to the original trade mark registration. Where disputes arise concerning the terms of a registered license or assignment, any aggrieved party may seek redress through an 112a order appellate process before the designated Appellate Authority. The authority shall consider evidence presented by both parties and issue orders binding on all concerned, ensuring compliance with the provisions of this Act relating to fair trade practices and consumer protection. Further, sub-licensing is permissible provided it aligns with the original license agreement.

Any party aggrieved by an order passed by the Registrar relating to the rectification of a registered trade mark or concerning allegations of passing off, unfair competition, or other deceptive practices detrimental to the distinctiveness or reputation of a trade mark may prefer an 112a order appellate to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. The appeal shall be filed within ninety days from the date of communication of the Registrar’s order. Provided that the Tribunal may entertain appeals lodged after this period if it is satisfied, upon examination of the reasons for delay, that there existed sufficient cause which prevented timely filing. Further, where a commission alleged offence has been reported to the police concerning infringement, the Tribunal shall consider any relevant findings made by the investigating authorities.

Any person aggrieved by a decision concerning the rectification of a registered trade mark, or any other determination made under this Act relating to the validity or infringement thereof, may prefer an 112a order appellate to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. Such appeals shall be filed within ninety days from the date of communication of the relevant order. The Tribunal shall consider all submissions and evidence presented by the appellant and respondent parties, affording both a reasonable opportunity for hearing. Further, where the rectification sought involves claims pertaining to a genetically modified organism’s unique characteristics, as recorded in the National Gene Fund registry, such information shall be deemed highly pertinent during appellate proceedings. Decisions of the Tribunal are final subject to further appeal under the provisions herein.

Any party aggrieved by an order made under this Act relating to rectification of a registered trade mark, or concerning damages awarded for infringement, may prefer an application seeking review before the 112a order appellate authority. Such applications shall be filed within ninety days from the date on which the order was communicated to the applicant. The appellate authority shall consider such applications and may affirm, modify, reverse, or remand the original order for further inquiry as it deems just and equitable.

The appellate authority shall have all the powers of a civil court in respect of matters relating to discovery, admission of evidence, and generally conducting its proceedings. A Judicial Member, possessing expertise in intellectual property law, shall preside over the appellate authority when hearing appeals involving complex technical or legal issues. The decision of the appellate authority shall be final, subject to appeal to the High Court within a further period of sixty days.

Any party aggrieved by an order passed by the Registrar relating to the rectification of a trade mark or concerning proceedings initiated under Chapter X may prefer an 112a order appellate to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. Such appeal shall be made within sixty days from the date on which the order is received, subject to extension as the Tribunal deems fit. The Tribunal shall give notice to all parties involved in the original proceeding and opportunity for them to present their case, including submission of written arguments and oral hearings. Where a trade mark has been used only in relation to goods or services other than those specified in the registered trade mark, such use may be considered as a reference use mark for the purposes of assessing likelihood of confusion during appellate proceedings. The Tribunal’s decision shall be final, provided that it does not contravene any provision under this Act.

Any party aggrieved by an order passed concerning rectification proceedings relating to a registered trade mark, or any other matter subject to review under this Act, may prefer an 112a order appellate before the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. Such appeals shall be filed within ninety days of the date on which the order is received, provided that the Tribunal may entertain appeals lodged after this period if satisfactory cause for delay is demonstrated. Where a trade mark application has been rejected based on grounds similar to those raised in the rectification proceeding, and the appeal results in setting aside the original order, the applicant’s patent application shall be afforded due consideration within six months of the appellate decision. The Tribunal shall give notice to all parties concerned before issuing any final determination.

For the purposes of this Act, “rectification” means an application made to the rectification register court seeking correction or deletion of particulars relating to a registered trade mark. Such applications may be filed by any person claiming interest in the matter and alleging that a trade mark is wrongly registered, or that the registration has become unworkable. The rectification register court shall have power to entertain such applications and determine their merits subject to the provisions herein regarding limitation periods and standing. An application for rectification shall specify the grounds upon which it is based and may include evidence supporting those grounds as provided herein.

An application for rectification of the register may be made to the Rectification Register Court by any person claiming interest in a trade mark or seeking relief under this Act. Such an application shall specify the particulars of the entry sought to be rectified and the grounds upon which such rectification is claimed, including but not limited to allegations of improper acceptance of an earlier trade mark or misleading entries affecting distinctiveness. The Rectification Register Court shall provide notice to the registered proprietor as provided herein and may direct a hearing to consider evidence presented by both parties. Decisions of the Rectification Register Court are subject to appeal under this Act, and such appeals shall be filed within the time prescribed.

Where an entry in the Register of Trade Marks is sought to be rectified, any person claiming title or interest may apply to the Rectification Register Court established under this Act. Such application shall specify the grounds upon which the rectification is claimed, and shall be accompanied by a statement of facts substantiating the claim. The Rectification Register Court shall afford the trade mark proprietor an opportunity to file its response to the application within a prescribed period. Provided that, if the Registrar has already initiated proceedings for removal of the entry from the Register, the Rectification Register Court may decline to entertain the rectification application. Subject to any order made by the High Court under this Act, the Rectification Register Court shall pass such orders as it deems fit, including ordering the correction or deletion of the erroneous particulars in the Register.

An application for rectification of the Register may be made to the Rectification Register Court established under this Act, and shall be in Form TM-R. The applicant shall serve a copy of the application on the Registrar not less than thirty days prior to the date fixed for hearing. The Registrar shall, upon receipt of such application, enter the matter in a register maintained for that purpose, indicating the parties involved and the nature of the rectification sought. Notice of the proposed rectification shall be given by the Registrar to the proprietor of the trade mark concerned, as provided herein. Any party aggrieved by an order made by the Rectification Register Court may appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such order. The court shall hear any counter-statement filed by the proprietor and consider all relevant evidence presented before it.

An application for rectification of the register relating to a registered trademark may be made only by a person claiming rights in respect of an unregistered trade mark, or alleging that any alterations have been made in the particulars of registration without consent. Such application shall comply with prescribed forms and shall specify the grounds upon which it is based, including but not limited to allegations of improper acquisition, fraudulent representation, or misrepresentation. The rectification register court may require the applicant to furnish security for costs if reasonable grounds exist to believe that the application is frivolous or vexatious. Provided that any party aggrieved by an order made under this Act relating to rectification may appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such order.

For the purposes of this Act, a "proceed case registration" shall mean an application for registration of a trade mark which has been examined and found to be acceptable subject to certain modifications or clarifications requested by the Trade Marks Registry. Such applications remain in a state of pending consideration until all required responses are received and assessed by the Registry. A proceed case registration is distinct from an opposed trademark application, wherein third-party objections have been formally raised under this Act. The Registrar may require further documentation relating to such modifications before proceeding with publication for opposition. Failure to respond adequately within the prescribed timeframe shall result in the application being deemed abandoned as provided herein.

An application for proceed case registration relating to a proposed trade mark shall be made in the prescribed form and manner, accompanied by the requisite fee. Such an application must clearly indicate whether the applicant seeks provisional or absolute proceed case registration. Where a notice of opposition is filed against a proceeding case registration, the Registrar may direct that the matter be referred to mediation under this Act; provided that either party may request a hearing before the Registrar if mediation fails to resolve the dispute. The Registrar shall record the outcome of any such referral and may make orders as are deemed appropriate concerning the proceed case registration in question. Further, an applicant whose application for proceed case registration is refused may appeal against such refusal under the provisions herein.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act and a proceed case registration is sought by the applicant, the Registrar shall afford the opponent an opportunity to file their counter-statement within two months from the date of service of notice of the proceed case registration. Failure to comply with this requirement may result in the Registrar deeming the opposition withdrawn. The applicant seeking proceed case registration shall be obligated to demonstrate continued use of the trade mark as it appears on the register, subject to any evidence presented by the opponent challenging such use. Any party aggrieved by a decision relating to a proceed case registration may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of that decision, provided that the grounds for appeal are clearly articulated and supported by relevant documentation.

An application for proceed case registration shall be entertained only if the applicant demonstrates continued use of the mark in commerce for a minimum period of six months immediately preceding the date of the application, subject to exceptions granted under this Act relating to force majeure events. The Registrar may require submission of documentary evidence substantiating such continuous usage, including but not limited to invoices, advertising materials, and sales records. Provided that, if the applicant is unable to furnish satisfactory proof of continued use due to circumstances beyond their reasonable control, the Registrar may grant a temporary extension, not exceeding twelve months, upon payment of prescribed fees. Any challenge to the validity of this proceed case registration shall be adjudicated according to procedures as provided herein and within the timelines specified.

Where an application for registration of a trademark is opposed under this Act and a proceed case registration is sought by the applicant, the Registrar shall give notice thereof to all interested parties. Any party aggrieved by the granting of a proceed case registration may institute proceedings in the Commercial Courts as provided herein, seeking a declaration that the registration is invalid or unenforceable. Failure to comply with the prescribed timelines for filing such proceedings shall be deemed conclusive evidence against the claimant’s right to challenge the validity of the proceeding. The Court may impose a penalty not exceeding five lakhs rupees upon any party found to have acted in bad faith during proceed case registration, obstructing due process and prejudicing the interests of other parties involved.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder, the registered proprietor of a trade mark may grant a license to use the trade mark in relation to specified goods or services. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as determined by the terms of the agreement between the parties. Any assignment of the right to proceed case registration for a trade mark shall include all associated licenses previously granted, unless explicitly excluded within the assignment deed. Further, where a license is assigned alongside the underlying trade mark, the assignee shall become liable to third parties under the terms and conditions of the original licensing agreement. The Registrar may require proof of such assignments and licenses before acknowledging changes in ownership or permitted usage relating to proceed case registration.

Where an application for registration of a trademark is opposed under this Act, and the applicant elects to pursue a proceed case registration, the Registrar shall provide notice to all parties involved in writing, specifying the grounds of opposition and the applicant’s response thereto. The opposing party may then file a counter-statement addressing the applicant's reply within sixty days from the date of such notice. Subject to any order made by the Registrar for an extension of time, failure to file a counter-statement shall be deemed as abandonment of the opposition. Further, if the trademark relates to an invention and patent shall assigned to another entity prior to the application’s filing date, this fact must be disclosed within thirty days of the proceed case registration being initiated; non-disclosure may render the applicant liable for penalties as provided herein. The Registrar shall record all proceedings meticulously.

Where an application for proceed case registration is filed in respect of a distinctive sign used in relation to goods, and any interested person objects on the grounds that the applicant is not entitled produce variety relating to those goods, the Registrar shall give notice of such objection to the applicant. The applicant may then submit counter-statements and evidence rebutting the objections. Failure by the applicant to adequately address the concerns raised regarding entitlement to produce variety will render the proceed case registration application liable for rejection. Any person aggrieved by a decision granting or refusing proceed case registration may appeal under this Act within sixty days of such decision, subject to penalties as provided herein for frivolous or vexatious appeals.

For the purposes of this Act, "goods" with reference to a geographical indication means agricultural products, foodstuffs, wine, spirit, beverages, spices, cereals, textiles, handicrafts and manufactured goods, provided that such goods derive their qualities, reputation or other characteristics substantially from the geographical origin claimed. The term “geographical origin” shall mean identification of the place where the goods originate, irrespective of whether the production takes place therein. An indication which is liable to be used for deceptive purposes, or which falsely suggests a quality or characteristic attributable to a particular geographical location, shall not qualify as a *goods geographical* indication under this Act.

An application for registration of a geographical indication shall be accompanied by a detailed report prepared by an expert committee constituted under this Act, verifying the distinctiveness of the goods and their association with the specified territory. The report must explicitly detail the agricultural practices, traditional processing methods, or unique environmental factors contributing to the quality and characteristics of the goods, demonstrating that these attributes are attributable solely or essentially to the geographical origin. Provided that any alteration in such practices or processes which would affect the qualities or reputation of the goods shall render the registration liable for review. The Registrar may require further clarification regarding the territorial extent claimed within the application concerning the goods geographical indication.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the registration of a goods geographical indication, or by any act of contravention of the provisions concerning protection afforded thereto, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order or occurrence. Such appeal shall be finally determinable by the Board, subject to review by the appellate authority as provided herein. Failure to comply with a cease and desist order issued under this Act shall render the defaulting party liable to pay damages, not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees, recoverable through civil suit. Further, repeat offenders may face prosecution for offences punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or both, in addition to fines as determined by the court.

The registered proprietor of a geographical indication relating to any goods shall be deemed to hold exclusive rights pertaining to the use of such indication for those goods. Any person desiring to utilize the said geographical indication in connection with goods not originating from the territory specified in the registration may apply to the Registrar for permission, subject to payment of prescribed fees and demonstration that their usage will not create confusion or mislead consumers regarding the origin of the goods. Such permission, if granted, shall be limited to a specific scope as determined by the Registrar and may be conditional upon adherence to quality control measures mirroring those associated with the registered geographical indication. Assignment of rights pertaining to licensing agreements under this Act shall require prior notification and approval from the Registrar, ensuring transparency and safeguarding the integrity of the protected goods geographical designation.

An application for registration of a geographical indication shall be deemed invalid if it is shown that the name proposed for registration does not primarily identify goods originating from the specified territory. The Registrar may entertain objections from any interested party alleging that the applicant lacks the requisite connection with the concerned geographical area, provided that such objection is filed within sixty days of publication under this Act. Any decision by the Registrar to reject an application based on lack of connection may be appealed to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Further, a proprietor of a registered goods geographical indication shall not be restricted from using the name in relation to goods manufactured outside the territory unless it is demonstrated that such use causes confusion or dilution of the distinctive character of the indication.

A geographical indication comprised of a name, word, phrase, logo, or any combination thereof shall be registrable under this Act if it relates to goods originating from a specified territory and that territory’s extension, boundary, or location is precisely defined in the application. The applicant must demonstrate that such indication identifies those goods by reason of specific qualities, characteristics, or reputation attributable to the geographical origin. Provided that, the use of the geographical indication shall not be susceptible to prevent others from using similar indications for goods not having any relation with the territory specified, subject to conditions as provided herein.

An application for registration of a geographical indication comprised of “Kanthaloor Moru” shall include detailed particulars regarding the agricultural practices employed within the defined zone of Kanthaloor village, Wayanad district, Kerala. The applicant must demonstrate exclusive linkage between the distinctive qualities of the product – specifically its aroma and texture – and these traditional farming methods. Evidence supporting this connection may be submitted in the form of documented farmer testimonies, scientific analyses confirming unique microbial activity within the soil, and historical records detailing cultivation techniques passed down through generations. Further, the application shall specify the collective body representing the producers entitled to use the geographical indication, provided that such body adheres to quality control measures as prescribed under this Act.

Any proprietor of a geographical indication comprised of Darjeeling tea shall be entitled to institute civil suit for infringement under this Act. Such infringement includes any use of a sign liable to cause confusion as to the origin of the goods, or where such use constitutes an unfair appropriation of the reputation associated with the registered geographical indication. Remedies available to the proprietor include injunctions restraining further infringing acts and damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the proprietor, taking into account the benefit accruing to the infringer. Provided that, in determining damages, due consideration shall be given to any bonafide use prior to registration. The Central Government may, upon receiving a complaint from the registered proprietor, direct any person found to be using the geographical indication deceptively to cease such use and pay compensation for losses incurred.

An application for registration of a geographical indication comprised of “Kashmir Apples” shall be filed with the Registrar in the prescribed form and shall include particulars relating to the growers’ association representing the interests of producers of such goods. The applicant must demonstrate, through documentary evidence and verifiable data, that the quality, reputation, or other characteristics of Kashmir Apples are essentially attributable to the geographical origin within the specified region of Jammu and Kashmir. Any alteration in the name or area of production of the geographical indication requires prior notification to the Registrar, accompanied by supporting affidavits from at least fifty percent of registered proprietors. The Registrar may, after affording an opportunity for hearing to all interested parties, reject the application if it finds that the proposed geographical indication is descriptive of the goods or would likely deceive or cause confusion among consumers.

An application for registration as a geographical indication comprised of “Kanthaloor Pepper” shall include detailed documentation demonstrating continuous production and processing of pepper within the defined geographical boundaries of Kanthaloor village, Malappuram district, Kerala. The applicant must provide evidence substantiating that the unique qualities, including aroma, pungency, and oil content, are attributable to the specific agro-climatic conditions prevailing only in this region. Furthermore, the application shall specify the methods of cultivation, harvesting, processing, and packaging employed by producers within the defined area, conforming to standards prescribed under this Act. Any deviation from these established practices will render the geographical indication ineligible for registration, subject to appeal before an appropriate authority as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the registration of a geographical indication comprised of Darjeeling tea may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. Failure to comply with prescribed quality standards, packaging requirements, or any other condition specified in the registered geographical indication shall constitute an offense and render the offender liable for penalties as provided herein. Further, any unauthorized use of a registered geographical indication by a person not authorized under this Act shall be deemed unfair trade practice and subject to civil suits for damages, with recovery including costs of litigation and compensation for loss of reputation suffered by registered proprietors. The Board may issue injunctions restraining such infringing activities.

Any proprietor of a geographical indication comprised of Alphonso mangoes shall be entitled to grant licenses conferring rights to use the said indication on packaging, labeling, and advertising materials relating to mango products. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as determined by the proprietor, and the terms thereof shall be subject to registration with the Geographical Indications Registry. Assignment of such license agreements is permissible, provided that prior written consent from the original proprietor is obtained and documented within the registry’s records. Further, any entity seeking to sublicense a geographical indication comprised of Alphonso mangoes must demonstrate adherence to quality control standards as prescribed under this Act and maintain traceability throughout its supply chain. The Registrar may issue directions regarding fair trade practices in relation to licensed use, ensuring consumer protection and preventing dilution of the geographical indication’s distinctiveness.

An application for registration of a geographical indication comprised of “Kashmir Apples” shall be deemed invalid if any interested party demonstrates, through verifiable evidence presented before the Geographical Indications Registry, that the use of the said indication by the applicant is likely to cause confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or quality of apples sold. The Registrar may, upon receiving such an objection, issue a notice to both the applicant and the objector, affording each a reasonable opportunity to submit written arguments and counter-arguments. Further, any order passed by the Registrar under this Act concerning the validity of a geographical indication comprised is subject to appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of such order, provided that the appellant deposits before the Board such fees as may be prescribed.

Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication comprised of Alphonso mangoes shall be entitled to grant licenses for use of the said indication under such terms and conditions as they deem fit, provided that any such license may specify the permitted scope of use, including but not limited to packaging materials, promotional activities, and export markets. Assignment of rights in respect of a geographical indication is permissible with prior approval from the Registrar, who shall consider whether the assignee possesses the requisite expertise and commitment to uphold the standards associated with the indication. Failure to comply with the terms of a license agreement or unauthorized use of the registered geographical indication may render an offender liable for prosecution, including innocently punishable imprisonment extending up to six months, in addition to any pecuniary penalties as determined by the relevant court.

Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication prescribed under this Act shall be entitled to institute civil suits for infringement and shall be deemed to be the owner of the exclusive right to use the said geographical indication in relation to goods for which it is registered. Such infringement shall include any unauthorized use or imitation likely to cause confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of the goods. The remedies available to the proprietor upon proof of infringement may include an injunction restraining the infringing party from further use, and damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the proprietor, taking into account the benefit accruing to the infringer. Provided that a registered user of the geographical indication shall also be entitled to enforce these rights subject to any conditions specified in their registration certificate. The Central Government may, upon receiving a complaint, investigate alleged infringements and impose penalties as deemed appropriate.

An application for registration of a geographical indication prescribed under this Act shall be filed with the Registrar in such form and manner as may be specified by regulations. The applicant shall furnish particulars demonstrating exclusive link between the goods and the territory, establishing that the quality, reputation, or other characteristics are attributable to its origin’s unique geographical environment. Where an objection is raised against the application during examination, the Registrar shall issue a notice to the applicant, affording them an opportunity for representation and submission of counter-arguments within a stipulated period. The Registrar may, after considering the objections and the applicant's response, either proceed with registration or reject the application, recording reasons for such decision. Any aggrieved party may appeal against the Registrar’s order under this Act to the Appellate Board.

An application for registration as a geographical indication prescribed under this Act shall include detailed specifications outlining the production methods employed within the defined territory. These specifications must demonstrate adherence to established practices and techniques traditionally utilized in cultivating, processing, or manufacturing the goods. The applicant shall provide documentary evidence substantiating the distinctiveness of the good’s qualities attributable solely to its origin; such evidence may comprise historical records, expert testimonies, or scientific analyses. Provided that the geographical indication does not denote any ingredient or component introduced outside the defined territory after initial production. Further, the application must confirm that the applicant represents a substantial proportion of producers whose interests are directly linked to the continued protection of this geographical indication.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the registration of a geographical indication prescribed, or its revocation, amendment, or cancellation, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. Failure to comply with the provisions regarding proper service of notice shall not invalidate any action taken thereunder. The Appellate Board may, after giving all parties an opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify, or reverse the order appealed against.
