The power to grant interim relief during the pendency of revision shall vest solely with the Controller. Any party aggrieved by any decision made by an adjudicating officer may seek redressal through a revision application, adhering to timelines prescribed under this Act.

An application for registration of a biotechnological invention relating to a genetically modified microorganism shall be accompanied by a detailed description of the biological deposit made under this Act and the accession number assigned thereto. The Controller, upon receiving such an application, may direct the applicant to furnish further particulars or clarification concerning the deposited material, including details regarding viability and stability assessments. Any party aggrieved by a decision relating to the acceptance or rejection of registration based on the examination of the biological deposit may petition the Controller for review. Such petitions shall be examined by an order adjudicating officer appointed specifically for this purpose, whose determination is final subject to appeal under this Act.

Any person dissatisfied with a decision made by an order adjudicating officer concerning rectification of entries in the Register of Patents relating to any fact which was not reflected accurately at the time of registration, may institute proceedings before the Controller seeking review of that order. Such application for review shall specify the grounds upon which it is based and be accompanied by such fees as prescribed under this Act. The Controller shall afford an opportunity to both the applicant and the original respondent to present their respective cases in writing or orally, subject to procedural fairness. If, after considering all evidence presented, the Controller finds that the order adjudicating officer was demonstrably erroneous, he may modify, reverse, or affirm the said order. Costs of these proceedings shall be determined by the Controller at his discretion.

Any party dissatisfied with a decision rendered by an order adjudicating officer concerning rectification proceedings relating to registered trademarks may, within ninety days of communication of such order, file an application for review before the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. The application shall specify the grounds upon which the order is challenged and must be supported by affidavits verifying the material facts presented. Provided that a delay in filing the application may be condoned by the Tribunal if sufficient cause is demonstrated.

The adjudicating officer shall serve a copy of the order, along with notice of the right to appeal, on all parties involved in the rectification proceedings. Further, any interlocutory orders issued during the course of the proceedings are subject to review under this Act upon application made to the Tribunal. The Tribunal may dismiss frivolous applications or those lacking merit, and shall award costs as it deems appropriate.

Where any person considers himself aggrieved by an order passed by an order adjudicating officer relating to infringement of patent rights or revocation of a patent, he may prefer an application for review before the Controller within ninety days from the date on which that order is communicated to him. Such application shall specify the grounds upon which the applicant seeks review and shall be accompanied by such fees as may be prescribed. The Controller may entertain any such application if it appears that there has been a material error of law or fact apparent on the face of the record. Provided that, where the aggrieved party demonstrates reasonable cause for delay, the Controller may condone the delay in filing the review application, subject to satisfaction regarding the merits of the case.

Any person dissatisfied with a decision made by an order adjudicating officer concerning infringement of patent rights or revocation proceedings may institute legal action before the relevant High Court within ninety days from the date such order is communicated to them. Failure to comply with prescribed timelines will render any subsequent challenge inadmissible, subject to exemptions granted solely at the discretion of the court based on demonstrable evidence of excusable delay. The adjudicating officer shall maintain meticulous records pertaining to all proceedings and investigations undertaken, which are accessible for judicial review upon proper application. Penalties for obstructing or misleading an order adjudicating officer during investigation include fines not exceeding five lakhs rupees and potential imprisonment up to two years, as provided herein.

Where the patentee or any other person is granted a license to exploit a patented invention, and such license contains provisions relating to assignment or further licensing rights, the terms of those provisions shall be binding on all subsequent parties subject to the conditions stipulated within the original agreement. Any dispute arising from the interpretation or enforcement of these clauses may be referred to an order adjudicating officer for resolution, who shall consider representations from both licensor and licensee regarding the scope and validity of any purported assignment. Provided that, if a patentee seeks to assign their rights under a license containing such provisions without prior consent obtained as provided herein, the assigning party must notify all affected licensees at least ninety days before the effective date of the assignment. The adjudicating officer may impose penalties for non-compliance with this requirement.

Any party dissatisfied with an order passed by an order adjudicating officer concerning rectification proceedings relating to entries in the safeguards prescribed register may, within sixty days from the date of communication of such order, file an application for review before the Controller. The application shall specify the grounds upon which the order is sought to be reviewed and shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the original order. Provided that where the applicant demonstrates exceptional circumstances preventing timely filing, the Controller may condone the delay. Further, any appeal against an order of the Controller under this provision lies before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within three months from the date of communication of the Controller’s decision, subject to such conditions as are prescribed herein.

An application for rectification of a patent relating to a semiconductor integrated circuit layout design may be made to the Controller if it is alleged that the registered layout design does not satisfy the requirements of novelty or originality as provided herein. The Controller, upon receiving such an application, shall direct the applicant and the registered proprietor to submit their pleadings within specified timeframes. Any party aggrieved by an order adjudicating officer issued in connection with a rectification proceeding may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeals shall be filed within three months from the date of communication of the order, subject to just exceptions.

Any person dissatisfied with a decision made by an order adjudicating officer relating to the registration of a layout plan or building map submitted for approval under this Act may, within thirty days from the date of such order, file an application for review before the designated appellate authority. The application shall specify the grounds upon which the applicant challenges the order and shall be accompanied by all relevant documents supporting the claim. Provided that the appellate authority may, after hearing the concerned parties, confirm, vary or set aside the order of the adjudicating officer. Further, where an order is varied or set aside, the appellate authority may issue an order injunction directing the restoration of the layout plan to its original form, as deemed necessary for compliance with regulations.

An application for rectification of an international registration designating India, where the grounds for rectification relate to matters not concerning patentability but rather to procedural irregularities in the acceptance or publication of the international application, shall be filed before the Controller. Upon receipt of such an application, the Controller may direct that a hearing be held and shall notify the applicant and any designated contracting party under the Madrid Protocol. The Controller shall appoint an order adjudicating officer to examine the evidence presented by both parties and determine whether the grounds for rectification are substantiated. Any party aggrieved by the decision of the order adjudicating officer may appeal to the Appellate Board within three months from the date of communication of that decision, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. The Controller shall ensure due process is followed throughout this procedure.

The Registrar may, upon application made by the applicant for registration of a trademark, direct that any distinctive element appearing in the mark shall be treated separately from the rest of the trade marks and registered accordingly, provided that such direction is deemed to be in the public interest. Any person aggrieved by an order directing separate registration under this Act may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The applicant shall furnish such information as the Registrar may require regarding the use of the trade marks registered separately, including details concerning geographical distribution and sales figures. Where a trademark is registered as part of a series, any subsequent application for registration of similar trademarks in the same series shall be considered subject to existing guidelines pertaining to uniformity. Trade marks registered under this Act are entitled to protection against unauthorized use.

The owner of trade marks registered under this Act shall be entitled to restrain the use of any mark which is identical or confusingly similar to their registered trade mark, and also any false or misleading representation connected with the goods or services for which the trade mark is registered. Such restraint may include actions against parties engaging in passing off, dilution, or unfair competition as provided herein. Where a proprietor establishes that another has made use of a sign without due cause after the date of first registration of their trade marks registered, they shall be entitled to claim damages proportionate to the loss suffered by them and any profits gained by the infringing party. The remedies available under this Act are subject to principles of equitable relief; accordingly, an injunction may be refused if it would operate unreasonably or unfairly.

The proprietor of any trade marks registered under this Act may grant licenses conferring the right to use such trade marks, subject to conditions specified therein and filed with the Registrar. Such licenses shall be assignable, either wholly or partially, provided that notice of assignment is given to the Registrar within three months of the date of transfer. Where a license includes a restriction on territory, goods, or services for which the mark may be used, subsequent assignments of the trade marks registered shall remain subject to those limitations unless expressly modified by written consent from the original proprietor and notification filed with the Registrar. Any person acquiring rights in a trade mark through assignment or sub-license shall be bound by all conditions applicable to the use of the trade marks registered prior to such acquisition. The Registrar may require further documentation demonstrating due diligence regarding the validity of any license granted.

A registered trademark, subject to the provisions herein relating to insolvency proceedings, may be assigned or transmitted by way of license or otherwise, and such assignment or transmission shall vest in the assignee or transferee all rights and privileges of the assignor or transferor as a registered proprietor. For the purposes of this Act, an “assignable transmissible case” exists where the proposed assignment or transmission involves a change in ownership of the entity holding the registration, but does not fundamentally alter the nature of goods or services for which the trademark is used. Provided that any such license shall be in writing and executed as a deed.

The registration of a collective mark may be assigned or transmitted to any person who was a member of the association at the time of the assignment or transmission, or becomes such a member thereafter. Such an assignable transmissible case shall require prior approval from the Registrar, provided that the Registrar may grant such approval only if satisfied that the assignee or transferee is suitably qualified and possesses the requisite experience to maintain the integrity and reputation of the collective mark. Further, any subsequent assignment or transmission by the initial assignee or transferee shall be subject to the same requirements as apply to the original registration under this Act. The Registrar may require submission of detailed documentation demonstrating continued adherence to the association’s governing principles for approval of such transfers.

The right to utilize a registered trademark, including any associated domain name registrations directly related thereto, is an assignable transmissible case subject to the conditions prescribed herein. Any such assignment shall require registration with the Registrar within thirty days of execution, and failure to register will render the assignee’s claim against the proprietor unenforceable. The proprietor may grant licenses relating to the use of the trademark, provided that any such license does not extend to the entire geographical area in which the trademark is registered, unless explicitly stated otherwise in the licensing agreement. Further, an assignment or transmission shall be void if it prejudices the interests of the consumers or unfairly exploits a reputation acquired by the prior proprietor. The Registrar may, upon receiving complaint, investigate and determine whether such prejudice exists, and may refuse registration accordingly.

The right to sue for damages under this Act relating to any registered trade mark shall vest with the assignee or transmittee, provided that such assignment or transmission is formally recorded with the Trade Marks Registry within three months of its execution. Any application for registration of a trade mark may be assigned or transmitted by endorsement in writing on the application form, duly signed by the applicant and the proposed assignee or transmittee, and delivered to the Registrar. The Registrar shall record such assignment or transmission and enter it in the Register of Assignments and Transmissions. An assignable transmissible case arises where the original proprietor has ceased to conduct business under the trade mark and a subsequent party seeks to enforce rights relating thereto; in such instances, evidence of cessation must be submitted alongside the application for recording. The Registrar may require further documentation as deemed necessary to verify the validity of the assignment or transmission.

The right to institute proceedings for infringement under this Act relating to a registered trade mark is an assignable transmissible case, subject to any conditions specified in the instrument effecting such assignment or transmission. Provided that, where an assignment or transmission purports to transfer rights arising from use of a trade mark, the assignee or transferee shall be deemed to have knowledge of all facts known to the assignor or transferor at the time of the assignment or transmission. Any person making default in complying with the provisions of this Act relating to infringement shall be liable for damages, and may also face criminal prosecution under relevant penal statutes. Further, a court may issue injunctions restraining any act of infringement as provided herein.

The right to use a registered trademark, including any associated logos or brand identifiers, may be assigned by the proprietor subject to the provisions outlined herein. Such assignments shall be in writing and executed with the same formality as a transfer of immovable property under applicable contract law. Where a trademark is an assignable transmissible case, the assignee acquires all rights and liabilities of the assignor relating to that mark, including any pending applications or oppositions. The Registrar may require proof of such assignment before registering it on the Register of Trade Marks. Further, a license granted in respect of a registered trade mark shall not be revocable under this Act except with the consent of the licensee, provided that the terms of the license do not contravene any provisions relating to permitted uses or geographical limitations as specified by the proprietor.

The right to sue for damages under this Act relating to any infringement of a registered trade mark shall vest in the assignee or transmittee, whether by way of absolute assignment or otherwise, subject to the terms and conditions of the transfer. Provided that, where an appeal has been filed against a decision concerning the validity of a trade mark prior to its assignability or transmissibility, the subsequent assignee or transmittee shall be bound by such decision until the appeal is finally disposed of, unless the appellate authority deems it just and equitable to allow the assignee or transmittee to raise fresh arguments pertaining specifically to their interest in the case. It is further provided that a claim for damages arising from infringement occurring prior to the assignment or transmission remains with the original proprietor, constituting an assignable transmissible case.

The right to use a registered trade mark is an assignable transmissible case, subject to the conditions prescribed under this Act. Such assignment or transmission may include the entire goodwill associated with the trade mark, or a portion thereof, as agreed between the assigning and assignee parties. Where an application for registration of a trade mark has been filed but not yet granted, the applicant shall be deemed to have transferred their interest upon written notification to the Trade Marks Registry. A fee, being the registry fee specified in Schedule I, shall be payable to the Registry upon recording any such assignment or transmission, provided that this requirement does not apply where the transfer is between related entities as defined herein.

The Registrar may, upon application by the registered proprietor, record an assignment or transmission of a trademark under this Act. Such assignment or transmission shall include any associated goodwill pertaining to the mark and the goods or services for which it is registered. The applicant must provide evidence satisfactory to the Registrar establishing the legal basis of the transfer, including but not limited to duly executed deeds of conveyance and relevant resolutions from governing bodies where applicable. A trademark is an assignable transmissible case and its ownership vests in the assignee or transferee upon registration of the assignment with the Registrar. Any dispute regarding the validity of such assignment shall be referred to the Judicial Member for determination.

An application for registration of a proposed trade mark shall include such particulars relating to the applicant, the goods or services in relation to which the trade mark is sought to be registered, and any claim of prior use as provided herein. The application registrar shall examine each application to ascertain whether the mark fulfils all requirements under this Act and the Regulations made thereunder. Further, the application registrar shall notify the applicant if any deficiency is found, allowing a period not exceeding sixty days for rectification. An amended application, once filed, shall be treated as a fresh application subject to the provisions regarding disclaimer of goods or services.

An applicant seeking registration of a proposed trade mark shall furnish with the application a representation of the marks, being either in colour or monochrome, as the applicant may elect; provided that where the proposed trade mark includes three-dimensional features, the representation shall adequately depict those features. The application registrar shall examine such representation to ascertain whether it complies with the requirements under this Act regarding clarity and faithfulness to the mark as claimed. Further, the application registrar shall record details of any disclaimer accompanying the application relating to particular goods or services. Any alteration made to the representation after its initial filing shall be noted in the register, subject to approval by the application registrar confirming that such change does not fundamentally alter the essential nature of the trade mark.

Where an applicant seeks to register a trade mark containing a geographical indication which is not inherently descriptive of the goods or services with which the trade mark is associated, the application registrar shall issue a notice specifying the geographical indication and inviting any person claiming rights in that indication to file representations against registration. Such representations must be filed within the period specified in the notice, typically two months from the date of publication. The registrar shall consider all representations received and may direct the applicant to amend the trade mark or refuse the application entirely if it appears that registration would unfairly prejudice those claiming such rights. Provided that the applicant demonstrates due cause for non-compliance with a direction issued under this Act, an extension of time may be granted at the registrar’s discretion. The decision of the registrar regarding any representation shall be communicated to all parties involved in writing.

Where the registered proprietor of a trademark desires to assign the entire interest in the mark, including any associated goodwill and pending applications related thereto, they shall submit a formal request to the application registrar for approval of such assignment. This request must detail all parties involved, encompassing both the assignor and assignee, along with a clear description of the rights being transferred. The application registrar may require supporting documentation verifying the identity and legal standing of each party as provided herein.

Further, where a license is granted permitting the use of a registered trademark by another entity, subject to specific conditions outlined in the licensing agreement, the application registrar shall maintain a record of such licenses and their terms. Any subsequent modification or termination of this license must also be formally notified to the registrar for documentation purposes, ensuring transparency and preventing disputes arising from unauthorized usage.

Where an applicant for registration of a trade mark seeks rectification of a registered trade mark based on alleged use by another party, the application registrar shall give notice thereof to the proprietor of the said registered trade mark and afford them an opportunity to file a counterstatement. Such counterstatement must address specifically each ground upon which rectification is sought. The Registrar may, if satisfied that the matter requires specialist expertise, refer the proceedings to a member appointed bench for determination. Provided that any such referral shall not prejudice the rights of either party under this Act. Further, where a proprietor fails to respond to a notice within the prescribed period, the application registrar may proceed ex parte. Any order made by the Registrar or the member appointed bench is subject to appeal as provided herein.

Where an applicant files a basic application for registration of a trade mark, the application registrar shall examine the application in accordance with the provisions herein relating to examination of applications. Provided that, if the registrar finds that the proposed trade mark is deceptively similar or identical to any prior registered trade mark or pending application, he shall issue a notice of concern to the applicant specifying the grounds for such objection. The applicant shall then be afforded an opportunity to file his response and submit counter-arguments within the time stipulated in the notice. Following consideration of the applicant’s reply, the registrar may either proceed with examination of the application or reject it entirely, as he deems appropriate under this Act. Further, the registrar shall maintain a record of all notices of concern issued and responses received pertaining to each trade mark application.

Where an applicant seeks registration of a trade mark containing a geographical indication which is not exclusively associated with a particular goods or services, the application registrar shall require the applicant to furnish a verification from a recognized authority confirming that use of the trade mark will not create confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of the goods or services. Provided that, if the Registrar deems it necessary, he may direct an inquiry into the matter and consider representations from interested parties before making a determination. The registrar shall maintain an index registered trade marks incorporating details of such verifications for public access, subject to restrictions imposed under this Act concerning confidential commercial information.

A geographical indication is an indication identifying goods originating from a specific territory or region, where a quality, reputation, or other characteristic of those goods is essentially attributable to its geographical origin. For the purposes of this Act, such characteristics include natural factors like climate and soil, as well as human factors relating to traditional skills and methods of production. An indication shall not be deemed a geographical indication if it relates to generic names or terms customarily used in describing the kind, quality, or intended purpose of goods. The Central Government may regulate the use of registered geographical indications under this Act to prevent abuse for fraudulent purposes.

Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication shall be entitled to sue for relief including damages or an injunction in respect of any dealings infringing on that registration. Such infringement includes the use of the geographical indication without authorization, or any indication which is likely to cause confusion as to the origin of the goods. The Central Government may, upon receiving a complaint from the registered proprietor, direct any person found to be engaging in such infringing activities to cease and desist therefrom. Further, where an infringer has knowingly made false representations concerning the geographical indications of goods, the Court may award punitive damages exceeding three times the proven loss suffered by the proprietor. The remedies available under this Act are without prejudice to any other right or remedy available to the registered proprietor under any other law for the time being in force.

An application for registration of a geographical indication shall be filed with the Registrar in the prescribed form and manner, accompanied by such fees as may be determined under this Act. The application must clearly describe the goods or services to which the geographical indication relates, specifying the area from which they originate and detailing the qualities, reputation or other characteristics directly attributable to that origin. Prior to registration, the Registrar shall publish a notice of the application in the Official Gazette and on the Registry’s website, inviting objections from any interested party within the period specified therein. Any objection received shall be considered by the Registrar after affording the applicant an opportunity for hearing. The Registrar may register a geographical indication if satisfied that it is entitled to protection under this Act, and shall record particulars of such registration in the Register of Geographical Indications.

The proprietor of a registered geographical indication shall be deemed to hold exclusive rights to use the said indication in relation to goods for which it is registered, subject to any licenses granted under this Act. Any person seeking to utilize a protected geographical indication commercially must apply for a license from the proprietor, outlining the scope and duration of intended usage. The proprietor may grant such licenses on terms and conditions as they deem fit, including royalty payments proportionate to sales generated through the licensed use. Assignment of rights in a registered geographical indication shall require prior approval from the Central Government, ensuring that the assignee possesses the requisite expertise and commitment to uphold the quality standards associated with the protected goods. Further, any transfer or assignment must be recorded with the Geographical Indications Registry as provided herein.

Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication shall be entitled to grant non-exclusive licenses conferring specific rights relating to the use of that indication on goods conforming to the standards as prescribed under this Act. Such licenses may include provisions concerning quality control and packaging requirements, provided that the terms do not unduly restrict competition or innovation. Assignment of a registered geographical indication, including any associated patent rights obtained for processes integral to its production, shall require prior approval from the Central Government. The assignee shall be bound by all conditions and limitations applicable to the assignor under this Act. Any license granted without adherence to these provisions may be revoked as provided herein. Further, sub-licensing is permitted subject to the terms of the original license agreement and with notification to the Geographical Indications Registry.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may be made by any association of persons or producers engaged in the production of goods conforming to the standard of quality and characteristics originating from a defined geographical territory. Such an application shall specify the name of the geographical indication as it is proposed to be registered, a description of the goods, the geographical area from which the goods originate, and particulars of the collective body representing the interests of the producers. The Registrar may require further information or clarification regarding any aspect of the application, including details concerning the expressly impliedly registration process undertaken by the applicant association. An indication shall not be registered if it is deemed deceptive under this Act, or if its use would indicate an origin different from that specified in the application.

A variety shall be deemed to have been registered under this Act when a certificate of registration has been granted by the Authority, specifying the denomination assigned to that variety and the geographical area within which it is protected. For the purposes of this Act, “denomination” means the name given to a variety, subject to the provisions regarding distinctiveness and freedom from conflict with existing trademarks or names under other Acts. An application for registration of a varieties registered act shall include particulars relating to the method of its derivation, any relevant data on its stability and resistance to biotic and abiotic stresses, and details concerning the first location and date of release of the variety.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the grant or refusal of a certificate of registration of a variety, or concerning any other matter decided by the Authority, may appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order to the appellant and shall state specifically the grounds on which the order is sought to be challenged. The Appellate Board may, after giving notice to all parties concerned and affording them an opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify, or reverse the order appealed against. Decisions regarding varieties registered act are final subject only to judicial review under principles of natural justice. Further, any party dissatisfied with a decision of the Appellate Board may petition the Supreme Court on grounds limited to questions of law arising out of that decision.

Where an application for registration of a variety is rejected under this Act, the applicant shall have the right to appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order of rejection and shall state specifically the grounds upon which the applicant relies in challenging the decision. The Appellate Board may, after affording an opportunity for hearing to all concerned parties, confirm, vary or reverse the order appealed against. Any party aggrieved by any order passed by the Appellate Board relating to a varieties registered act may further appeal to the High Court within sixty days of such order, subject to just cause shown. A record of rectification applications and their disposition shall be maintained in a court rectification register for public inspection.

A variety shall be deemed to have been registered as a *varieties registered act* if it has fulfilled all requirements under this Act and the application for registration thereof has been finally disposed of by the Authority. For the purposes of this Act, "registration" includes provisional registration and any subsequent amendment or modification thereto. The central government may, in consultation with the Authority, issue guidelines regarding the procedures to be followed during the examination of applications for registration, ensuring transparency and adherence to principles of natural justice. Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to a varieties registered act may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board as provided herein.

The administering authority shall grant registration to an applicant seeking to establish a registration copyright society upon satisfaction that the applicant fulfils the conditions prescribed under this Act. An application for registration shall be accompanied by a declaration specifying the class or classes of works in respect of which the proposed society intends to operate and the terms of issue of licences relating thereto. The authority may, after giving notice to the applicant and affording him an opportunity of being heard, refuse registration if it is satisfied that the objectives of the proposed society are contrary to public interest or would create a monopoly inconsistent with the principles of fair dealing as provided herein. A registered copyright society shall maintain accounts in accordance with prescribed standards and submit annual reports detailing its activities and financial transactions for review by the administering authority.

Any person found to be collecting or distributing royalties on behalf of authors or other right owners without being duly registered as a registration copyright society under this Act shall be liable for penalties not exceeding five thousand rupees for each instance of infringement. Such unregistered collection constitutes an unlawful trade practice, and aggrieved parties may institute civil proceedings seeking injunctive relief and damages proportionate to the losses incurred due to the unauthorized distribution. Further, any funds collected in violation of these provisions are deemed constructively held in trust for the benefit of the right owners and subject to recovery by appropriate legal authority. The Registrar shall maintain a publicly accessible register of all registered copyright societies, detailing their scope of representation and permitted activities as provided herein.

Any society registered under this Act as a registration copyright society shall be entitled to enforce the provisions relating to royalties and other remuneration payable to authors or owners of copyrights. Subject to the conditions specified herein, a copyright society may grant non-exclusive licences in respect of works for which it has been authorized to collect licensing fees. Any person utilizing copyrighted material without authorization from the relevant registration copyright society shall be liable for damages as determined by civil court proceedings. The provisions act reference relating to fair dealing with literary, dramatic, musical or artistic works shall apply equally to actions undertaken by a copyright society in the course of administering licences. Provided that any dispute regarding the assessment of royalties may be referred to an arbitrator appointed jointly by the authors and the users of copyrighted material.

A patent shall not be granted for any process for producing a substance applied as food, or as an ingredient in food, unless the process results in an invention; provided that this restriction shall not apply to processes relating to the purification of substances. For the purposes of this Act, “invention” with regard to such processes means a new technological method which involves inventive step and is not obvious to a person skilled in the art. Further, any application for a patent under this Act concerning a process for producing food or ingredients thereof shall disclose the nature of the substance produced and its intended use as food.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, a patent shall confer upon the patentee the exclusive right to make, use or sell the patented invention within India. This right extends to preventing others from doing any of these acts without authorization, and includes the right to import the patented article into India. Provided that such exclusive right shall be enforceable against all persons except where an act is done in pursuance of a license granted under this Act or a patent previously granted. Any person aggrieved by an infringement of a patent may institute suit for relief in respect of such infringement in a District Court, and remedies available include injunctions restraining the infringing activity and damages proportionate to the loss suffered. The Controller may also order compensation where appropriate, as provided herein.

An application for a patent shall be accompanied by such particulars as may be prescribed, including details regarding the inventor’s address and nationality, and a concise description of the invention sufficient to enable a person skilled in the art to put it into practice. The Controller General may, at any time during the examination of an application, require the applicant to amend the claims or provide further information relating to the invention; provided that such requirement shall be made only after giving the applicant a reasonable opportunity to respond. Where an objection is taken under this Act against the grant of a patent, the applicant may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. A patent shall not be granted for any process for obtaining a substance directly from natural resources unless such process results in a new compound identified and described therein.

A patent shall not be granted for any process used in or intended for the manufacture of a substance directly employed as food or drink unless such process results in a new product with novel characteristics and properties that significantly alter its existing qualities. The application for a patent under this Act relating to such a process shall disclose, with sufficient clarity and completeness, all details necessary for carrying out the invention; provided that the disclosure does not extend to information which is withheld as confidential trade secrets essential to the operation of the process. Further, any claim in respect of a method or process must be supported by experimental data demonstrating its efficacy and safety for human consumption, subject to verification by an appointed authority.

Any person aggrieved by a notice under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of service of such notice, and the Appellate Board shall consider any question of fact or law arising in relation to the notice. Failure to comply with the prescribed procedures for filing an appeal shall render it inadmissible. Where a patent has been granted in contravention of these provisions, the Controller may, subject to due process, revoke the patent as if it had never been granted and shall order the infringer to pay compensation to all parties demonstrably harmed by the infringing activity. A patent shall be liable for revocation if it is found to have been obtained through fraudulent means or misrepresentation.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder, a patent shall not prevent parties holding valid licenses from exploiting the patented invention in accordance with the terms thereof. Where an assignment of a patent has been effected, the assignee shall be entitled to exercise all rights and powers which the assignor might have exercised as if he were the true owner of the patent; provided that such assignment is registered under this Act within six months of its execution. Any licensee may, subject to any conditions stipulated in the license agreement, grant sub-licenses relating to the licensed invention. The Controller may, upon application by a party claiming an interest in a patent, direct the registration of a license or assignment where it appears that such registration has been unduly delayed. Further, under this Act, failure to register a license within the prescribed period shall render the licensee liable for penalties as determined by the Central Government.

An application for a patent shall not be entertained if it appears that the claimed invention is essentially derived from a process already disclosed in a publicly accessible publication originating outside India, unless the applicant demonstrates, to the satisfaction of the Controller, that substantial inventive effort beyond mere translation or adaptation was undertaken. The burden of proving such inventive effort rests entirely upon the applicant and shall involve submission of detailed technical documentation and expert testimony. Any decision by the Controller regarding the sufficiency of this demonstration may be appealed before an Appellate Board constituted under this Act, subject to a prescribed fee and within a stipulated timeframe; failure to comply with these procedural requirements will render the appeal inadmissible.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, any person claiming title to a patent shall be entitled to grant an exclusive license or licenses under the patent in India, specifying the field of use, duration, and royalty rates. Such license may be granted either wholly or partially, and may include the right to assign or further license the patented invention. Where an amendment claim specification is filed altering the scope of any claim, the Controller shall notify all persons appearing on the public record as having an interest in the patent, providing them with an opportunity to object to the proposed alteration. Any assignment or license granted under this Act shall be recorded in the Patents Office and shall take effect only upon such recording. The licensee shall be bound by the terms of the license agreement and may be subject to revocation if those terms are violated as provided herein.

A patent shall not be granted for any process for manufacturing a pharmaceutical substance unless such process results in the production of a new drug entity as defined under this Act; however, an application for a patent may proceed if the applicant demonstrates to the satisfaction of the Controller that the said process is novel and involves an inventive step beyond what is currently practiced within the industry. Provided that, where it is alleged by any interested party that the claimed process does not meet the criteria outlined herein, such party shall be entitled to file an objection with the Controller, accompanied by a reasoned statement detailing the grounds for their challenge; and further provided that the Controller’s decision on such objections may be appealed before the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. xii shall exempt certain government research institutions from specific procedural requirements relating to patent application fees.

A patent shall be maintainable only if the application for such patent has been filed with the Controller and accompanied by the prescribed fee, and where the term of a patent granted under this Act expires prior to the completion of its full duration as initially determined, an extension of that term may be sought within six months of the expiration date. Such request for renewal shall be made in Form NR-1, duly verified and submitted along with the requisite additional fees calculated according to the prevailing schedule prescribed by the government. The Controller may grant or refuse such extension based on a demonstration that unforeseen circumstances prevented timely application, provided that no appeal lies against an order refusing renewal.

Where any person is found to have made use of a patented invention without leave from the patentee or the exclusive licensee, such person shall be liable for damages. The amount of damages shall be determined by the Controller, taking into account the extent of benefit conferred upon the infringing party and the loss suffered by the patentee. Provided that in cases where the infringement was knowing and willful, the Controller may award exemplary damages not exceeding three times the sum assessed as compensation for the loss suffered by the patentee. Further, any patent shall be liable to be revoked if it is established that the invention was disclosed without authorization by an exclusive licensee acting within the scope of their license. The remedies available under this Act are without prejudice to any other remedy available to the patentee in law or equity.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be refused if the proposed mark, or any element thereof, is used in relation to goods or services in such a manner as to falsely suggest an association with a person or enterprise where no such association exists. This refusal applies even when the use appears innocuous on its face, but serves to mislead consumers regarding the origin, quality, or characteristics of those goods or services. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating that the proposed mark constitutes a purpose falsifying used, particularly if there is an established trade mark already in use relating to similar goods. Such evidence must clearly establish consumer confusion and detrimental impact on the prior user’s reputation, provided that the applicant demonstrates bona fide intention to use the mark legitimately.

Where a registered trade mark is employed in relation to goods or services in such a manner as to falsely suggest an association with another enterprise, or that the goods or services are of a particular quality or origin when they are not, then such use shall be deemed a purpose falsifying used under this Act. Provided that, where the use of the registered trade mark is solely for comparative advertising purposes and complies with conditions regarding honesty, clarity, and fairness as provided herein, it shall not be considered a purpose falsifying use unless it creates demonstrable confusion amongst consumers likely to purchase the goods or services in question. Further, any proprietor seeking relief against such use must demonstrate that they have suffered actual damage attributable to the misleading nature of the application.

Where a person uses a trademark in relation to goods or services in a manner that falsely suggests an association with the owner of the trademark, and such use is intended to mislead the public regarding the nature, quality, or origin of those goods or services, or to otherwise gain an unfair advantage from the reputation of the registered trade mark, it shall be deemed a case of purpose falsifying used. The proprietor of the trade mark may apply to the relevant intellectual property tribunal for relief, including an injunction restraining such use and damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the proprietor as a consequence of that deceptive practice. Any goods bearing such a false representation are subject to seizure and forfeiture under this Act.

Where the registered proprietor of a trade mark desires to grant a license conferring the right to use the trade mark in relation to specified goods or services, such license may be assigned or sub-licensed subject to the provisions herein. Any assignment or sub-licence shall include express terms defining the scope and duration of the permitted usage, as well as any geographical limitations. Where a licensee uses a registered trade mark in a manner that is calculated to deceive the public regarding the nature, quality, or origin of goods or services, constituting what is known as purpose falsifying used, the registered proprietor shall have recourse to remedies available under this Act. Furthermore, such deceptive use may be considered a material breach of the license agreement, entitling the grantor to immediate termination and recovery of damages.

For the purposes of this Act, “international application” shall mean an application for a patentable invention filed in accordance with the procedures established under the Budapest Treaty. Such international applications are deemed to be prior art subject to the provisions relating to grace periods as provided herein. An international application shall be considered to disclose the relevant information at the date of its actual receipt by the International Bureau, irrespective of any subsequent publication or examination thereof. The Controller General may require certified copies of such international applications for inspection and verification purposes. Any reference to a patentable invention within this Act includes inventions claimed in an international application.

Applications for patents relating to inventions made in respect of processes involving microorganisms shall be accompanied by a deposit certificate, issued by an authorized body as specified under this Act. Such certificate must confirm the accession number assigned to the deposited microorganism and details regarding its preservation conditions. Where an applicant elects to utilize the Budapest Treaty on the International Recognition of the Deposited Microorganisms for the purposes of disclosure, the Controller may require submission of a certified copy of the relevant treaty provisions alongside the deposit certificate. The requirements concerning the form and content of such certificates shall be as prescribed by regulations framed under this Act. Failure to provide these documents or discrepancies therein may result in rejection of the application, subject to appeal before an appellate authority.

Where, in proceedings before an Indian court relating to patent revocation under this Act, a party seeks to introduce evidence pertaining to the international application for a patent designating India, such evidence shall be admissible subject to verification as provided herein. The Controller may require that any document submitted pursuant to this provision be accompanied by a certified copy of the relevant communication issued by the International Bureau under the Budapest Treaty on the International Recognition of the Deposited Sequences and Related Information. Failure to provide such certification shall render the document inadmissible, unless the party demonstrates satisfactory reason for non-compliance. Any order made by the Controller regarding admissibility may be appealed before the Appellate Board. The costs associated with obtaining certified copies shall be borne by the party seeking their introduction as evidence.

Applications for patents relating to inventions made in respect of processes utilizing microorganisms shall be examined as provided herein. Where an applicant seeks to claim a microorganism under this Act, they must deposit such microorganism with an internationally recognized depository authority designated under the Budapest Treaty. The Controller may require proof of compliance with the requirements of the Budapest Treaty, including verification of the deposition and viability of the deposited material. Failure to maintain proper records relating to the microorganism’s location and accessibility shall render the patent application liable for rejection. Any alteration or destruction of a deposited microorganism without prior written consent from the Controller is deemed an infringement under this Act. The applicant shall be responsible for all costs associated with maintaining the deposit, subject to any regulations prescribed by the government.

Where an applicant for a patent elects to utilize the provisions of the Budapest Treaty, such election shall be made in writing and filed with the Controller along with the complete specification. The application so filed shall be deemed to comply with all requirements relating to clarity and completeness as provided herein, subject to verification by the Controller that the international search report and written opinion have been duly received from the International Bureau. Further, where an applicant has failed to furnish a certified copy of the international preliminary examination within the prescribed timeframe, the application may be refused. Any modification to the claims following the initial filing under this Act shall not prejudice the rights conferred by the Budapest Treaty, provided that such modifications adhere strictly to established practice.

Where an application for a patent is filed in India claiming priority from an application filed outside India, and such foreign application has been published under the Budapest Treaty on the International Recognition of the Deposited Sequences, the Controller may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating compliance with the treaty’s provisions regarding sequence listing. Failure to provide this documentation within the time specified by the Controller shall render the application liable for rejection. Any person aggrieved by a decision relating to the sufficiency of such evidence may appeal under this Act to the Appellate Board. The penalty for submitting false or misleading information pertaining to Budapest Treaty compliance is a fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, and imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any patentee desiring to grant an exclusive license in respect of a patented invention may execute an instrument of assignment or licensing agreement transferring such rights, provided that such instrument shall clearly define the scope and duration of the license. Where a license is granted under this Act, the licensee shall be entitled to enforce the patent against acts committed by any person without the authorization of the patentee or the licensee. Further, the patentee may retain ownership of the underlying intellectual property while granting a non-exclusive license, but such retention does not preclude assignment under the Budapest Treaty for purposes of international filing. Any transfer of rights relating to an invention shall be recorded in the prescribed manner and deemed effective upon registration.

Where, in proceedings before the Controller under this Act relating to the validity of a patent granted subsequent to an international application designating India, it is alleged that the invention was previously published or otherwise disclosed prior to the priority date claimed, and such publication or disclosure occurred outside India, the applicant shall be afforded opportunity to demonstrate compliance with the Budapest Treaty on the International Recognition of the Deposited Patents. The Controller may require the patent holder to furnish certified copies of documents filed in pursuance of said treaty as evidence. Any party disputing the validity based on prior art shall bear the burden of establishing that the publication or disclosure prejudiced the applicant’s reasonable expectation of obtaining a patent, subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

For the purposes of this Act, “international application” shall mean an application for a patentable invention filed in accordance with the Budapest Treaty and designating India as one of the designated States. Such international applications shall be treated as if they were national applications under this Act, subject to the provisions relating to the examination and grant of patents. A practitioner person registered under this Act may represent applicants filing international applications, provided that such representation is consistent with the regulations governing international patent practice. The Controller General shall maintain a register of international applications received and processed in accordance with the Budapest Treaty.

Where an application for a patent relating to an invention made in, or outside India, is filed under this Act and incorporates by reference material translated from another language, the applicant shall furnish with the application a certified true copy of the original foreign language text. Provided that where such incorporated material has been subjected to copy translation work performed within India, a declaration attesting to the accuracy and completeness of said translation must also be submitted. The Controller may require further verification of any such translations if reasonable doubt exists regarding their fidelity. For purposes of complying with obligations under the Budapest Treaty concerning international applications claiming priority from Indian patent applications, all documentation presented shall adhere strictly to prescribed formats as notified by the Government.

Where an application for a patent is filed in India claiming priority from an application filed outside India, and such foreign application has been subjected to international search under the Budapest Treaty, the Controller may require the applicant to furnish a certified copy of the search report and written opinion. Failure to comply with this requirement within the time specified shall render the application liable for rejection. Any unauthorized reproduction or distribution of said search reports, including their translation into any language, without express permission from the Controller constitutes an infringement under copyright law and is subject to penalties as provided herein. The Controller may impose a fine not exceeding five lakhs rupees upon conviction for such offenses.

For the purposes of this Act, “aggravated infringement” shall mean the use of an identical or deceptively similar mark in relation to goods or services which are identical or closely related to those for which the registered trade mark is used, and where such use is undertaken with the express intent to mislead consumers regarding the origin or nature of the goods or services. Where a person is found guilty of aggravated infringement, they shall be liable to imprisonment for a term not less than six months but which may extend to three years, and also to a fine which shall not be less than fifty thousand rupees. Provided that, where the offence involves commercial gain derived from fraudulent misrepresentation, the offender may be subject to sentence imprisonment for up to five years.

An application for registration of a trademark shall be deemed to be refused if the proposed mark is identical or confusingly similar to an earlier registered trademark used in relation to identical or closely related goods or services, subject to provisions regarding permissible modifications and honest descriptive use. Where any person knowingly makes false statements material to the assessment of registrability under this Act, or wilfully contravenes a direction issued by the Registrar concerning rectification proceedings, they shall be liable for prosecution and may face sentence imprisonment extending to three years, alongside a fine which may extend to rupees five lakhs. Such penalties are without prejudice to any other remedies available as provided herein, including orders for damages and injunctions.

Where a proprietor institutes proceedings under this Act seeking relief from an infringement of their registered trademark and establishes to the satisfaction of the Court that the defendant knowingly and wilfully engaged in activities calculated to deceive or confuse consumers regarding the origin or nature of goods or services, the Court may award damages commensurate with the extent of the loss suffered by the proprietor. Further, where such knowing and wilful conduct is demonstrated, the Court shall have the power to order imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, in addition to any monetary penalties as provided herein. The defendant shall be afforded an opportunity to present evidence mitigating against the imposition of sentence imprisonment. Any person found guilty under this provision may also be subject to a fine not exceeding ten lakh rupees.

Where an individual is convicted under this Act for making a false representation concerning the trademark ownership of another, and such representation is proven to have caused demonstrable financial harm to the aggrieved party, the Court may impose a sentence of imprisonment extending to three years. The prosecution shall be initiated by way of information in writing filed before a Magistrates court or a Court of Sessions, as deemed appropriate by the Public Prosecutor. Any appeal against a conviction under this provision lies to the High Court within sixty days from the date of the judgment. Provided that, where the false representation is made with the intent to deceive and gain an unfair commercial advantage, the Court shall consider aggravating factors in determining the sentence. The offender shall also be liable to pay compensation to the aggrieved party for losses incurred as a result of the misleading representation. It is further provided that habitual offenders may face a term of sentence imprisonment without the option of a fine.

Where an individual is convicted under this Act for knowingly and wilfully making false representations concerning the origin, quality, or characteristics of goods or services with the intent to deceive the public, such conviction shall be subject to a minimum sentence of six months imprisonment. Provided that, if the false representation results in demonstrable financial loss exceeding ten million rupees to any person, the court may impose a sentence of up to three years imprisonment and a fine not less than twenty-five million rupees. Further, where the offence is committed by a company, every director, manager, or secretary thereof shall be deemed guilty of the offence unless they prove that the offence was committed without their knowledge or consent; and such individuals may also face sentence imprisonment as provided herein.

Any person found guilty of knowingly and wilfully using a deceptively similar mark to an existing registered trademark, with intent to defraud or cause confusion amongst consumers, shall be liable for damages as determined by the Court. Further, such offender may also be subject to a penalty not exceeding ten lakhs of rupees. Where the offence is committed for commercial gain or involves large-scale counterfeiting, the Court may impose a sentence imprisonment extending to three years. It is provided that an employee acting under the direction and control of their employer shall not be deemed guilty unless they knowingly participated in the infringing activity. Repeat offenders found violating this provision shall face enhanced penalties including increased fines and a mandatory sentence imprisonment for at least one year.

The registered proprietor of a trademark shall be entitled to grant licenses for the use of their trademark, specifying the geographical area and duration of such license. Any assignment of a trademark, whether absolute or subject to reservations, must be in writing and executed as per the procedures outlined under this Act. Where a licensee acts in violation of the terms stipulated within the granted license, including but not limited to unauthorized alteration of goods bearing the mark or misrepresentation regarding its origin, the registered proprietor shall have recourse to remedies available under civil law. Furthermore, any person found guilty of knowingly facilitating such a breach by providing false information or actively concealing relevant details may be subject to sentence imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and shall also be liable to fine. This provision is without prejudice to other penalties as provided herein.

Where a proprietor institutes proceedings under this Act alleging infringement of a registered trademark and the defendant adduces evidence demonstrating honest, contemporaneous use of a similar mark prior to the plaintiff’s registration, the Court shall consider such evidence in determining whether there exists an actionable confusion likely to deceive or cause error among the public. Provided that, if the proprietor can demonstrate wilful adoption of the defendant's mark with intent to trade on the reputation and goodwill associated with the registered trademark, the Court may dismiss the defendant’s claim of prior use. Any person found guilty of wilfully infringing a trademark in violation of this Act shall be liable for damages as determined by the Court and may also face sentence imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years. The aggrieved party shall have the right to appeal any order made under this Act to the appellate forum established therefor.

Where a proprietor institutes proceedings for infringement under this Act and obtains a decree establishing such infringement, the Court may, subject to provisions regarding contributory infringement, award damages to compensate the proprietor for losses sustained as a result of the infringement. Such damages shall be assessed in accordance with principles of fairness and equity, taking into consideration factors including but not limited to lost profits, royalties, and the extent of the infringer’s gains. Furthermore, where the infringing activity is shown to have been undertaken knowingly or recklessly, the Court may also impose exemplary damages. Any person found guilty of wilfully contravening any provision relating to registered designs, particularly concerning unauthorized reproduction based on a design register layout, shall be liable for sentence imprisonment extending to three years and with fine.

Where a proprietor institutes proceedings alleging an infringement of their registered trade mark and it is established beyond reasonable doubt that the defendant knowingly and wilfully employed an unauthorised use mark identical or deceptively similar to the plaintiff’s mark in connection with goods or services for which the said mark is registered, the Court may, subject to considerations of mitigating circumstances, impose a sentence imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years. This power shall be exercised only where the infringement constitutes a serious commercial crime and demonstrates a deliberate disregard for the rights of the trade mark proprietor. The court shall also consider whether the defendant has acted in good faith or attempted to rectify the infringing use upon being notified of the complaint. Any authorised use mark displayed by the defendant shall not preclude such proceedings, provided that it is demonstrated the infringement was undertaken with malicious intent.

An application for registration of a trade mark relating to goods or services shall include a statement indicating whether the applicant is engaged in industry or commerce in relation to those goods or services. Where an applicant demonstrates that they intend to use the trade mark exclusively for export purposes and do not currently engage in any commercial activity within India, the Registrar may grant provisional registration subject to conditions as provided herein. Such conditions shall include a requirement to file evidence of actual use of the trade mark in international markets within a period of three years from the date of such provisional registration. Failure to comply with this requirement will result in automatic cancellation. The Registrar is empowered to inquire into and determine whether goods are genuinely imported, particularly where there are concerns regarding circumvention of restrictions relating to limits india imported.

For the purposes of this Act, a “registration variety” shall mean a plant variety that has been formally recorded in the Register of Plant Varieties following an application and examination process as provided herein. An applicant seeking registration of a variety shall demonstrate, to the satisfaction of the Authority, that the proposed registration variety is distinct from all other varieties currently registered or publicly available, possesses uniformity for economic production and stability over generations, and exhibits characteristics which are reasonably predictable. The authority may require further testing or documentation to ascertain these qualities before granting registration. A registration variety confers certain rights upon the registrant, subject to limitations as detailed elsewhere under this Act.

An application for registration of a plant variety shall be accompanied by detailed documentation pertaining to the method of its derivation, including specifics regarding any genetic modification undertaken and the lineage tracing back to original parent material. The Registrar may require submission of additional data demonstrating stability and uniformity of characteristics across successive generations, particularly where the claimed novelty arises from hybridization techniques. Any applicant seeking registration as a *registration variety* must provide evidence substantiating that the distinctiveness criteria outlined in Schedule B have been met; failure to do so shall render the application liable for rejection. Further, documentation relating to geographical location and cultivation practices employed during evaluation periods must be included, provided that such information does not compromise trade secrets.

Where a person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to the grant, refusal, or revocation of registration of a *registration variety* has no other adequate remedy, they may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such decision. The Appellate Board shall consider any question of fact or law arising in the appeal and may confirm, vary, or reverse the order appealed against. Any party to an appeal before the Appellate Board who intends to raise a new ground not previously raised before the Registrar must do so with reasonable diligence and subject to the satisfaction of the Board that there was sufficient cause for such delay. The decision of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, provided that any question relating to the interpretation or application of this Act may be referred to the High Court.

An application for registration of a *registration variety* shall be made to the Authority in Form A, accompanied by such documentation as the Authority may prescribe, including detailed phenotypic data demonstrating distinctness and stability across multiple generations. The applicant shall furnish evidence substantiating the genetic uniformity of the variety, where applicable, and indicating its resistance or susceptibility to prevalent pests and diseases within relevant agro-climatic zones. Provided that an application relating to a farmers' variety need only include information pertaining to its traditional cultivation practices and geographical distribution. The Authority may require further clarification or additional data from the applicant at any stage of the examination process. Any technical report submitted by the Examining Officer shall be considered confidential until publication under this Act, subject to review by the Appellate Board upon request.

An application for registration of a plant variety shall be accompanied by detailed documentation pertaining to the method of propagation, including specific instructions regarding seed treatment and nursery practices where applicable. The applicant must demonstrate that the proposed denomination conforms with guidelines established under this Act concerning distinctiveness, uniformity, and stability. Further, evidence substantiating the novelty of the registration variety relative to existing varieties shall be submitted in a form acceptable to the Authority. Provided that if the application relates to a farmers' variety, the documentation may be simplified as determined by the Registrar; however, verification of essential characteristics remains mandatory. The applicant warrants compliance with all relevant provisions concerning benefit-sharing arrangements and traceability protocols.

Any person found to have knowingly made a false statement in their application for registration of a variety, or who has wilfully failed to comply with the conditions stipulated under this Act regarding the maintenance of records pertaining to a registered variety, shall be liable to pay a pecuniary penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees. Furthermore, any entity engaged in the commercial exploitation of a registered variety without authorization from the registrant, as provided herein, is subject to an additional penalty equivalent to ten times the aggregate royalties that would have been payable had proper licensing occurred. The Authority may also order the seizure and destruction of propagating material derived from such unauthorized exploitation. Repeated offences shall attract enhanced penalties and potential revocation of the registration variety.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, the holder of a registration variety may grant licenses conferring rights to exploit the registered variety for specific purposes, including but not limited to propagation, sale, and distribution. Such licenses shall be documented in writing and may be exclusive or non-exclusive as determined by the licensor. Assignment of ownership of a registration variety is permissible, provided that prior consent of the Controller General is obtained, demonstrating adherence to principles of benefit sharing with any affected farmers’ varieties. Any assignment agreement must clearly delineate the scope of rights transferred and include provisions for royalty payments where applicable. Further, sub-licensing may be granted by the initial licensee with the approval of the registration holder, ensuring continued compliance with conditions stipulated under this Act regarding protection of plant variety rights.

An appeal lies to the Appellate Board against any order passed by the Registrar refusing registration of a variety, or revoking such registration, provided that the application for appeal is made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The Board may, subject to this Act and after giving all parties an opportunity of being heard, confirm, vary, or reverse the order appealed against. Any party aggrieved by any decision of the Appellate Board may further appeal to the High Court within a period of ninety days from the date of such decision; however, the High Court shall only entertain appeals based on questions of law arising out of interpretation of provisions relating to distinctness and stability in determining eligibility for registration variety.

An application for registration of a plant variety may be made by any person claiming rights in the variety, subject to compliance with the requirements as provided herein. Such application shall include particulars concerning the designation of the variety, its source, and the method of its derivation, along with detailed phenotypic data conforming to the guidelines published by the Authority. The Registrar shall register a plant variety only if it is deemed distinct, uniform, and stable, following established procedures for conducting necessary trials and observations. Further, registration may be refused if the applicant fails to disclose information relevant to assessing the novelty of the registration variety or if the claimed rights are demonstrably invalid. An application seeking registration make international shall be processed in accordance with reciprocal agreements entered into by the Central Government.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person holding a valid registration for a plant variety may grant a license conferring rights to use propagating material derived from such registered variety. Such licenses shall specify the geographical area and duration of the granted right, as well as royalty rates payable by the licensee to the licensor. The Registrar may be notified if a dispute arises regarding the terms or validity of any such license agreement. Further, where an infringement action is initiated under this Act concerning a registered variety, the plaintiff forthwith ceased all activities constituting the alleged infringement upon written notice from the defendant demonstrating reasonable grounds for believing that the plant material in question does not originate from the registered variety. Assignment of rights relating to a registration variety requires prior approval from the Registrar and must be recorded as per prescribed procedures.

Where an objection is raised by any person against the grant of registration for a particular plant variety, the Registrar shall provide both the applicant and the objector with an opportunity to present their respective arguments in writing and be heard, subject to such reasonable time limits as may be prescribed by regulations framed under this Act. The decision regarding whether or not to proceed with the application for registration variety shall be based on a careful consideration of all evidence presented, including any expert testimony relating to the distinctness, uniformity, and stability of the plant variety in question. Further, if the objection pertains to the provision of services related to the propagation or marketing of the registered variety, the Registrar may require both parties to submit detailed accounts of such activities for verification.

For the purposes of this Act, a “registration variety” shall mean a plant variety that has been formally recorded in the Register of Plant Varieties and granted protection under this Act, subject to the conditions stipulated therein.
