For the purposes section 41, “essentially derived variety” with reference to a plant variety shall mean a variety that is not protected under this Act but has been selected and raised from an initial variety, where such selection and raising have resulted in characteristics which are clearly identifiable as being attributable to the initial variety; provided that the characteristics result only from successive selections over generations and do not involve any genetic modification. The Authority may determine whether a variety qualifies as essentially derived under this definition, taking into consideration factors including morphological similarity and reproductive compatibility with the initial variety, as provided herein.

Applications for registration of plant varieties shall be accompanied by a detailed description conforming to the format prescribed under this Act and including particulars regarding its origin, method of derivation, expression of traits, and stability data. The Authority may require submission of additional documentation demonstrating genetic uniformity and distinctiveness, particularly where the variety is claimed as essentially derived from an existing variety. For the purposes section 41, evidence relating to farmers' rights concerning traditional knowledge associated with the plant variety shall be considered during examination. Provided that such evidence is verifiable through recognized institutions or community protocols. The Registrar may reject an application if it determines that the information provided is insufficient or misleading regarding the aforementioned aspects of the plant variety’s characteristics and lineage.

Where a person alleges infringement of plant variety rights under this Act, such person shall be entitled to seek remedies including, but not limited to, an injunction restraining further acts of infringement and damages sustained by reason of the said infringement. The Tribunal may, upon finding that infringement has occurred, order the infringer to account for profits made from the infringing activity, subject to limitations as provided herein regarding undue hardship. Further, any person aggrieved by a decision relating to plant variety rights may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days of such decision. For the purposes section 41, an act shall be deemed to constitute infringement if it involves the commercial exploitation of a registered variety without authorization from the Registrar or where such exploitation is in contravention of the conditions stipulated therein.

Applications made under this Act for the grant of Plant Variety Rights shall be examined by the Authority in accordance with prescribed procedures. The Registrar shall, upon receipt of an application, issue a notification inviting objections from any person having a substantial interest in the variety or claiming to possess relevant knowledge. Objections received within the stipulated period shall be forwarded to the Applicant and the Applicant shall have opportunity for rebuttal. Subject to compliance with all requirements as provided herein, the Authority may grant Plant Variety Rights upon satisfaction that the variety is distinct, uniform, and stable. The Registrar shall record the decision of the Authority and publish it in the Official Gazette. For the purposes section 41, any appeal arising from a decision under this Act shall lie to the Appellate Board within sixty days of such decision.

The Authority shall, in determining eligibility for benefit under this Act concerning farmers’ rights, consider whether the applicant has demonstrably conserved indigenous varieties or contributed to their preservation. Provided that, such contribution must be evidenced by records maintained by recognized agricultural institutions or community-based organizations, and verified as per guidelines issued by the Central Government. Further, any application seeking recognition of farmer's rights shall include a declaration affirming adherence to principles of sustainable agriculture, avoiding practices detrimental to biodiversity. The Authority may require submission of soil samples and crop yield data to ascertain compliance with these standards. For the purposes section 41, the determination of ‘substantial contribution’ will be based on quantitative assessments as detailed in the regulations framed under this Act.

Any person found to have made use of an unregistered plant variety in contravention of the conditions stipulated under this Act shall be liable to pay a compensatory fee, determined by the Authority based on the extent and nature of the infringement. The Authority may also order the seizure and destruction of propagating material derived from such unauthorized utilization, subject to due process. Further, any commercial entity engaging in the marketing or distribution of plants incorporating an unregistered variety, knowing that it infringes upon the rights holder’s exclusivity as provided herein, shall face penalties including fines not exceeding five lakhs rupees and potential prohibition from future dealings under this Act. For the purposes section 41, such actions constitute unfair trade practices detrimental to innovation.

Any person holding a Plant Variety Rights authorization shall be permitted to grant licenses in respect of the commercial use of such variety, subject to conditions as may be prescribed. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive and may cover activities including, but not limited to, seed production, propagation material sales, and importation for commercial purposes. The grantor of a license under this Act shall provide full disclosure of the terms and conditions thereof to the Registrar of Plant Varieties. Assignment of Plant Variety Rights, including any associated licenses, requires prior notification and approval from the Registrar, demonstrating that the assignee is competent to exercise the rights transferred. For the purposes section 41, any such assignment shall be deemed valid only upon registration with the Registrar within ninety days of execution.

Where a person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the revocation of protection granted to a plant variety, or concerning the grant of compulsory license, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The Appellate Board shall hear appeals arising under this Act and may pass such orders as it deems fit, subject to just cause shown for delay in preferring the appeal. Any order passed by the Appellate Board shall be final; however, a further writ petition challenging the decision may be filed before the High Court only on grounds involving principles of natural justice or jurisdictional error. For the purposes section 41, the definition of "just cause" shall include demonstrable prejudice resulting from procedural irregularities.

The Authority shall, when determining whether a plant variety is essentially derived from an existing variety under this Act, give due regard to the details furnished in the application patent specification submitted by the applicant. Such specifications must clearly delineate the process of derivation and any modifications introduced, including but not limited to alterations in genetic material or propagation techniques. The Authority may require further documentation or experimental data to ascertain the veracity of claims made within the specification regarding essential derivation. Provided that, if the applicant fails to provide satisfactory evidence as per the requirements of the Authority, the application shall be deemed invalid. For the purposes section 41, the burden of proof concerning essential derivation rests entirely upon the applicant seeking registration of the new variety and any challenge to this assertion will be adjudicated according to established principles of natural justice.

Where an objection is raised by the Trade Marks Registry against the acceptance of an application for registration, asserting that the proposed trade marks, when used in relation to the goods services description specified in the application, would likely cause confusion amongst the public, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to submit a written response addressing such objections. The Registrar may require the applicant to attend an oral hearing to further clarify their position. Following consideration of the objection and any submissions made by the applicant, the Registrar’s decision shall be communicated in writing. Any party aggrieved by this decision may prefer an appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The appeal period is deemed to commence from the day following the date of such communication.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark includes a specification of goods or services, that specification shall be deemed to define the scope of protection afforded by the registered trade mark. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Trade Mark Registrar regarding the accuracy or appropriateness of such description may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days. Failure to comply with this provision renders the applicant liable for penalties as provided herein, including but not limited to fines and rejection of the application. The Registrar shall have power to issue directions requiring amendment of a goods services description if it is found to be misleading or unduly broad in scope, subject to affording the applicant an opportunity of being heard.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed refused if the proposed marks are identical with an earlier registered trade mark or a trade mark applied for under this Act and used as specified therein, unless the applicant demonstrates honest concurrent use. The Registrar may, however, accept such an application provided that he is satisfied that the essential attributes of distinctiveness are not diluted by the existence of the prior registration. Any person aggrieved by a decision refusing registration may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. Further, any alteration made to a registered trade mark shall be recorded in the Register and deemed part of the original registration India, subject to compliance with prescribed forms and fees.

Subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal, an application for registration shall be deemed refused if the Trade Marks Registry fails to issue a notice under this Act within six months from the date of filing. Any proprietor of a registered trade mark may institute suit in the District Court claiming damages sustained by reason of the use by any person without due cause of a trade mark identical or similar to the distinctive characters of the registered trade mark, provided that such use creates confusion or is likely to do so in the minds of the public. The remedies available under this Act shall include an injunction restraining the infringing activities and recovery of costs incidental to the litigation. Further, any person aggrieved by an order made by the Registrar may appeal as provided herein; however, no suit for passing off shall be maintainable where registration india has been refused or revoked.

An application for registration shall be made in the prescribed form and shall contain such information as may be required by the Regulations framed under this Act relating to the applicant’s identity, address for service, representation of the trade mark, a list of goods or services associated with the trade mark, and the class or classes according to the International Classification of Goods and Services. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further particulars concerning the application, provided that such requirement is reasonable and does not unduly delay the processing thereof. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall acknowledge its receipt and assign it a serial number. An official fee, as determined by notification published in the Official Gazette, shall be payable with the application; failure to pay this fee will result in the application being deemed withdrawn. The applicant’s entitlement to registration India will be assessed according to established procedures.

An application for registration shall be deemed to be refused if the proposed trade mark contains exclusively generic words relating to the goods or services with which it seeks association, unless the applicant demonstrates acquired distinctiveness through extensive use prior to the date of application. Further, an objection may be raised by any person claiming a prior right under this Act, provided that such claim is substantiated by documentary evidence establishing continuous and exclusive use for a period exceeding five years immediately preceding the filing date of the trade mark application. The Registrar shall consider all submitted documentation and hear representations from both the applicant and objector before rendering a decision regarding registration india. Any appeal against such a decision may be made to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days.

Any person who, without due cause and with intent to deceive, uses a trade mark identical or confusingly similar to a registered trademark in India shall be guilty of an offence. Such offender shall be liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, and also be liable to a fine extending to one million rupees. Further, the infringing goods shall be subject to seizure and destruction as provided herein. Where the infringement involves counterfeiting, the penalty shall be doubled. The owner of the registration shall have the right to apply to the relevant court for an injunction restraining the infringing activity and seeking damages for losses suffered due to the unauthorized use impacting their registration India.

The owner of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to grant licenses conferring specific rights relating to the use of the mark within India, provided that such license agreement clearly defines the geographical area and the goods or services for which the right to use is granted. Any assignment of the registration itself, whether partial or complete, must be executed in the prescribed form and registered with the Registrar, subject to payment of the requisite fee as determined under this Act. Furthermore, a licensee may, with prior written consent from the trade mark owner, sub-license rights pertaining to their assigned territory and goods; however, such sub-licensing shall not extend beyond the scope originally granted by the primary license agreement. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating the validity of any assignment or sub-licensing arrangement before proceeding with registration. This process ensures transparency in matters concerning registration India and protects the interests of all parties involved.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed abandoned if the applicant fails to respond to a notice issued by the Registrar requiring clarification or amendment within the period specified therein, provided that the Registrar may, at his discretion and for reasons recorded in writing, extend such period. Upon receipt of an application requesting surrender of a registered trade mark, the Registrar shall publish a notification in the Trade Marks Journal inviting objections from interested parties. Any objection received within the prescribed time limit shall be considered by the Registrar who may, after affording the applicant an opportunity to be heard, either allow or reject the request for surrender. The registration india shall cease to have effect upon the date specified in the order of the Registrar allowing the surrender, and such cessation shall be recorded accordingly under this Act.

Where an application for registration india is opposed under this Act, and the evidence submitted by either the applicant or the opponent relates to matters not arising on the face of the application, the Registrar shall issue a notice to both parties inviting them to submit written arguments within a prescribed period. Provided that such notice may be issued electronically where permitted under regulations framed in accordance with this Act. Any party aggrieved by the manner issuing notice, or by any decision taken by the Registrar based upon evidence not arising on the face of the application, shall have the right to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of that decision; and the Board may, after affording an opportunity for hearing, confirm, reverse, or modify the said decision.

Where any person is convicted of an offence under this Act involving the use of a false trademark, or the making or application of a false mark, such conviction shall carry with it a sentence imprisonment term. The sentence imprisonment term shall be determined by the Court considering factors including the duration and scale of the infringing activity, the extent of consumer deception caused thereby, and any demonstrable financial loss suffered by the registered proprietor. Provided that in cases where the offence is committed for commercial gain or involves significant premeditation, the sentence imprisonment term may extend to five years, and a fine not exceeding five lakh rupees shall also be imposed.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed to be refused if the proposed marks include representations likely to falsely suggest an association with any person engaged in the production or supply of goods or services. Where such refusal is contested by the applicant and the matter proceeds to hearing before the Registrar, the burden of proving that no such false suggestion exists lies upon the applicant. Any individual found guilty of knowingly making a false representation during proceedings relating to trade mark registration, including submitting fabricated documents or providing wilfully misleading testimony, shall be liable for a sentence imprisonment term extending up to three years and may also be subject to a fine. This provision is without prejudice to any other penalties provided under this Act.

Where any proprietor of a registered trade mark institutes legal proceedings alleging an infringement of his rights under this Act, and it is established that the defendant knowingly and wilfully engaged in activities calculated to deceive or mislead consumers regarding the origin or nature of goods offered for sale, the Court may, as part of its judgment, order the imposition of costs upon the defendant reflective of the claimant’s reasonable legal expenses. Furthermore, where such infringement involves the counterfeiting of a registered trade mark, and the offender has been previously convicted under this Act for similar offences, he shall be liable to sentence imprisonment term which shall not be less than one year but may extend to five years, in addition to a fine exceeding two lakh rupees. The Court shall also consider any evidence demonstrating significant financial gain derived from the infringing activity when determining the appropriate penalty.

Where an individual is convicted under this Act for making a false representation concerning the nature, quality, or geographical origin of goods, or for falsely applying a mark identical or confusingly similar to a registered trade mark, the Court may impose a sentence imprisonment term extending to three years, and shall also be liable to pay a fine which shall not be less than fifty thousand rupees. The prosecution of such offences shall be initiated by written complaint preferred by an officer authorized under this Act, or by any person claiming to be aggrieved by the offence. Provided that, where the false representation is made for the purpose of gaining an undue advantage over competitors, the Court may enhance the sentence imprisonment term and fine as it deems fit, subject to guidelines issued by the Central Government from time to time. The offender shall also be liable to pay costs in respect of the proceedings.

Where an individual is convicted under this Act for making a false representation concerning the origin, quality, or characteristics of goods, and such representation is made with fraudulent intent to deceive consumers, the Court may impose a sentence imprisonment term extending to three years. This shall be without prejudice to any other punishment provided herein, including fines commensurate with the scale of the deceptive practice. Further, if the false representation results in demonstrable financial loss to another party, the Court shall consider such loss as an aggravating factor when determining the appropriate sentence imprisonment term. Provided that a first-time offender demonstrating genuine remorse and verifiable steps towards rectifying their actions may be considered for leniency under this provision.

Where any proprietor of a registered trade mark institutes legal proceedings under this Act, and it is subsequently determined by the relevant judicial authority that such proceedings were manifestly frivolous or vexatious, or undertaken with the primary intent to harass or obstruct another party’s lawful activities, then the court may order the proprietor to pay damages to the aggrieved party. Furthermore, any individual found guilty of knowingly making false representations concerning the ownership of a trade mark, intending to deceive or mislead the public, shall be punishable with sentence imprisonment term which may extend to five years and with a fine not exceeding one million rupees. Such conviction may also result in disqualification from registering marks under this Act for a period as determined by the court.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark shall have the exclusive right to license the use of their mark, either in its exact form or with permitted variations as detailed within the licensing agreement. Such licenses may be granted for specific goods or services, or across all categories covered by the registration, subject to conditions stipulated therein relating to quality control and adherence to brand guidelines. Assignment of a trade mark, including any associated licensed rights, requires prior written consent from the Controller, who shall consider whether such assignment prejudices the interests of consumers or dilutes the distinctiveness of the mark. Any individual found to be utilizing a registered trade mark in contravention of an existing license agreement, or without proper authorization following an assignment, shall be guilty of an offence and may face a sentence imprisonment term extending up to two years, alongside substantial pecuniary penalties.

Where a proprietor institutes proceedings under this Act alleging an infringement of their registered trademark and the defendant adduces evidence demonstrating honest, contemporaneous belief regarding the validity of their use, notwithstanding any prior communication from the complainant, the Court may consider such belief as a mitigating factor in determining appropriate remedies. However, where the defendant’s actions demonstrably involve wilful disregard for established legal precedent concerning similar marks or are undertaken with the express intent to deceive consumers, the Court shall be empowered to impose a sentence imprisonment term not exceeding three years, alongside any other penalties provided herein. The aggrieved party retains the right to appeal any such determination regarding mitigating factors or sentencing to the appellate forum as prescribed under the relevant procedural law.

Where an individual is convicted under this Act for making a false representation concerning the ownership of a registered trademark, or for knowingly dealing with counterfeit goods infringing upon such registration, the Court may impose a sentence imprisonment term extending to three years. Such conviction shall be predicated on evidence demonstrating deliberate intent to deceive and cause financial harm to the proprietor of the mark. The prosecution must demonstrate that the accused acted without reasonable excuse, failing which, leniency may be considered. An assignee of a registered trademark, upon notification by the Registrar, shall be deemed to have standing to initiate proceedings for infringement or other violations as if they were the original registrant. Any appeal against such conviction and sentence imprisonment term shall lie before the High Court within ninety days from the date of judgment. The court may order forfeiture of assets derived from the infringing activity.

Where an application for the registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act, and such opposition is ultimately unsuccessful, the applicant shall, upon compliance with all prescribed conditions relating to payment of fees and submission of requisite documentation, be entitled to proceed with registration. However, any registered trade mark may be subject to cancellation if it is shown that its registration was obtained through fraud or misrepresentation, or that subsequent use constitutes a violation of public interest as determined by the relevant authority. In cases where such fraudulent activity is proven beyond reasonable doubt, the offender shall be liable for sentence imprisonment term extending up to two years and also be required to undertake the procedure cancelling registration.

Where any proprietor of a registered trade mark institutes proceedings against an infringer alleging damages, the aggrieved party shall be entitled to recover from the defendant such sum as the Court deems reasonable, taking into account the loss suffered by the proprietor and the benefit gained by the infringer. However, in cases where the infringement involves the unauthorized reproduction or distribution of works subject to copyright and managed by a registration copyright society, the Court may, notwithstanding any other provision under this Act, impose an additional penalty of sentence imprisonment term not exceeding one year. An appeal lies from such decision to the appellate forum within sixty days of the order; provided that the defendant may demonstrate mitigating circumstances affecting the assessment of damages or the imposition of custodial sentencing.

Where any user party proceeding against an accused for an offence under this Act alleges that such person has knowingly or fraudulently used a trademark identical or deceptively similar to a registered trade mark, and it is established beyond reasonable doubt that the accused intended to gain unfair advantage or mislead consumers, then such offender shall be liable to sentence imprisonment term which shall not be less than one year but may extend to three years. Further, where the offence involves counterfeiting, the sentence imprisonment term shall not be less than five years and may extend to seven years, subject to any mitigating circumstances presented before the court.

Where rectification proceedings are initiated against a registered trade mark alleging dilution due to use of an identical or confusingly similar sign by another person, the Registrar may direct such person to cease using the impugned sign. Any order directing cessation of use under this Act shall be enforceable as if it were a decree of a civil court. Further, where a party fails to comply with an order made under this Act, they shall be liable for damages sustained by the registered proprietor of the trade mark as a consequence of such non-compliance. The amount of damages shall be determined based on principles of fairness and equity, considering factors including lost sales and reputational harm. Provided that, any appeal against an order directing cessation of use must be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order; otherwise, the proceeding shall liable to dismissal.

Where an appeal lies from any order passed by the Registrar relating to rectification of a trade mark, or concerning opposition proceedings, the Appellate Board may, at any stage of the hearing, direct that any person who is demonstrably affected by the outcome of such appeal be joined as a party. Notice of such direction shall be served upon all parties already before the Appellate Board and upon the newly joined party in accordance with the rules framed under this Act. Further, where evidence is adduced before the Appellate Board which relates to matters beyond the scope of the original order appealed from, the Board may direct that such evidence be considered only if it directly impacts the substantive issues raised in the appeal. Any person who fails to comply with a direction issued by the Appellate Board shall be deemed to have wilfully obstructed the proceedings and consequently, any proceeding shall liable to dismissal or other appropriate action as determined by the Board.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed by any person claiming such right or interest as is specified under this Act, the Registrar may direct that the opposition proceed as a hearing. Any party to such a hearing who fails to appear at the time appointed and has notice of the hearing shall be deemed to have abandoned their opposition, and the proceeding shall liable to continue in absentia. Provided that, where any party demonstrates reasonable cause for non-appearance, the Registrar may, subject to just considerations, allow them to file written submissions within a stipulated period. Further, an appeal shall lie from any order made by the Registrar under this provision, to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

For the purposes of this Act, "invention" means a new and useful art, process, manufacture or composition of matter; provided that it is patentable under this Act. An invention shall not include discoveries of scientific principles, merely the properties of living things, nor any method for treating diseases in human beings or animals unless such methods are formulated using novel techniques and compositions. The term "application" means a request made to the Controller for the grant of a patent, containing all particulars as may be prescribed; subject to which the applicant seeks to obtain exclusive rights under this Patents Act 1970.

For the purposes of this Act, an “alleged offence” shall mean any act or omission constituting a violation of provisions relating to registered trademarks, including but not limited to passing off, dilution, or use as a trademark without due cause. An alleged offence may be predicated on actions taken by any person, whether acting alone or in concert with others, and subject to the principles of vicarious liability as provided herein. Where an individual is charged with an alleged offence, it shall be presumed that such individual had knowledge of the facts constituting the violation unless proven otherwise. The determination of whether a particular act constitutes an alleged offence shall be made considering the totality of circumstances.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed to disclose an alleged offence if it contains any representation likely to cause confusion with respect to goods or services offered under existing registered trade marks. The Registrar may, upon receiving information pertaining to such an alleged offence, issue a notice to the applicant requiring them to submit a written response within thirty days, detailing measures taken to mitigate potential infringement. Failure to respond adequately or demonstrating wilful disregard for established rights as provided herein shall render the application liable for rejection. Any person aggrieved by the Registrar’s decision may appeal under this Act to the relevant intellectual property tribunal, subject to payment of prescribed fees and adherence to procedural guidelines.

Where a proprietor institutes proceedings alleging an offence against another person under this Act, such proceedings shall be deemed to be civil suits for the purposes of limitation. The remedy available to the proprietor shall include damages proportionate to the loss suffered by reason of the alleged offence, and may encompass injunctive relief preventing further acts infringing upon registered trade marks. Provided that, in determining the quantum of damages, the Tribunal shall consider any evidence presented demonstrating reasonable belief on the part of the defendant that their actions did not constitute an infringement. Further, a proprietor seeking remedies under this Act must demonstrate demonstrable prejudice resulting directly from the alleged offence; otherwise, claims for exemplary or punitive damages shall be disallowed. The defendant may offer proof mitigating the severity of the alleged offence, subject to scrutiny by the Tribunal as provided herein.

Where an information regarding a potential infringement of registered trademarks is received by the Registrar, such information shall be treated as a report concerning an alleged offence. The Registrar may, after providing notice to the informant specifying the nature of the reported transgression and affording them an opportunity for clarification, forward the report along with all accompanying documentation to the appropriate police authority having jurisdiction over the territory where the suspected infringement occurred. Such forwarding shall be accompanied by a recommendation that investigation be initiated under this Act. The police authority is then obligated to register a First Information Report and proceed with inquiry as provided herein. Provided that, the Registrar may decline to forward a report if it appears manifestly frivolous or vexatious, recording reasons for such declination.

Where a proprietor institutes proceedings alleging an offence relating to the use of any trade mark contrary to the provisions of this Act, such proceedings shall be deemed to have been initiated only if the proprietor furnishes to the Registrar, within thirty days of the institution of those proceedings, a certified copy of the plaint or equivalent document detailing the particulars of the alleged offence. The Registrar may, upon receipt of said documentation and after affording the respondent an opportunity for representation, issue a notice requiring the proprietor to demonstrate reasonable grounds exist for pursuing the claim. Failure to satisfy the Registrar regarding such grounds within sixty days shall result in the proceedings being deemed abandoned without prejudice to any other remedies available under this Act.

Where any proprietor alleges an offence has been committed by another person relating to a registered trademark, such allegation shall be made before the Intellectual Property Enforcement Tribunal. The Tribunal may, upon receiving such allegation, issue summons requiring the alleged offender to appear and submit a written statement of defence within thirty days. Failure to comply with the summons shall render the individual liable for penalties as provided herein. Further, where the proprietor demonstrates demonstrable financial loss attributable directly to the actions constituting the alleged offence, the Tribunal may order recovery of damages proportionate to said loss, subject to limitations prescribed by regulations framed under this Act. The Tribunal shall have power to impose interim injunctions restraining further infringing activity pending final determination.

Where the registered proprietor of a trade mark desires to grant a license conferring the right to apply the mark to goods or services, such license shall be documented in writing and executed by both parties. The agreement may stipulate territorial limitations, duration, quality control measures, and permitted modifications to the licensed application process. Assignment of rights under this Act relating to a registered trade mark is permissible only with the prior written consent of the Registrar, who may require demonstration that the assignee possesses sufficient resources and expertise to maintain the distinctiveness of the mark. Failure to comply with these conditions shall constitute an *alleged offence* punishable as provided herein. Any subsequent transfer or sub-licensing requires notification to the Registrar within thirty days, subject to a prescribed fee.

Where a proprietor institutes proceedings alleging an offence against another party under this Act, the respondent shall be afforded full opportunity to present evidence rebutting the allegations. The Tribunal may, upon review of the submitted materials and any oral arguments presented by both parties, determine whether a prima facie case exists demonstrating commission of the alleged offence. Provided that, if the proprietor fails to establish, with reasonable certainty, that the use or adoption of the mark in question creates a likelihood of confusion on the minds of the relevant public, the Tribunal shall dismiss the proceedings without further inquiry. Further, any order issued by the Tribunal may be appealed to the appellate body within sixty days from the date of such order, subject to prescribed procedures.

For the purposes of this Act, an “alleged offence” shall mean any act or omission constituting a violation of provisions relating to registered trademarks, including but not limited to infringement, passing off, or false representation. An alleged offence may be investigated by such officers as are authorized under this Act. It is provided that where it is established that a trade mark exists and the use thereof by another party creates confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of goods or services, such usage shall constitute an alleged offence, subject to considerations of fair dealing and permitted uses as defined herein.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed on the ground that the mark is deceptively similar to a prior mark already registered under this Act, and the applicant demonstrates that following notification of the opposition, the plaintiff forthwith ceased using the impugned mark in relation to the goods or services specified in their application, the Intellectual Property Appellate Board may direct the Registrar to consider whether the continued use of the prior mark creates an unreasonable likelihood of confusion amongst consumers. The determination of whether an alleged offence has occurred shall be based on a comprehensive assessment of all relevant factors, including but not limited to, the similarity of the marks, the relatedness of the goods or services, and the evidence presented by both parties as provided herein.

Where any proprietor alleges an offence relating to the use of a registered trade mark without their consent, they may institute civil proceedings against the alleged offender seeking injunctive relief and damages. The proprietor shall provide evidence demonstrating reasonable grounds for believing that the use in question constitutes an infringement under this Act. Provided that, where the proprietor has granted an exclusive licence concerning the specific goods or services affected by the alleged offence, the licensee may also pursue such remedies as if they were the proprietor, subject to any terms and conditions stipulated within the licensing agreement. The Court shall consider factors including the extent of confusion likely to be caused to the public, the defendant’s state of mind, and any deliberate attempts to pass off goods or services as those of the proprietor in determining appropriate compensation for damages.

Where an investigation into a suspected infringement of registered trademarks is initiated by the Registrar, any Government undertaking involved in the production or distribution of goods bearing the allegedly infringing mark shall be notified forthwith. The notification shall detail the nature of the alleged offence and provide copies of all relevant documentation pertaining to the trademark registration and the evidence supporting the claim of infringement. Upon receipt of such notification, the Government undertaking is obliged to furnish a report within thirty days outlining its assessment of the matter and detailing any remedial actions taken or proposed. Failure to submit this report may result in penalties as provided herein. The Registrar shall have the power to conduct on-site inspections of premises belonging to the Government undertaking if deemed necessary for the purpose of ascertaining compliance with the provisions under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, an entry register document shall mean any record maintained by the Registrar relating to the examination of a trade mark application, including but not limited to correspondence between the applicant and the Registry, reports from investigating officers appointed under this Act, preliminary objections raised during examination, and decisions rendered by the Registrar concerning registrability. An entry register document is deemed conclusive evidence of facts stated therein, subject to any appeal or revision as provided herein. Any person seeking access to an entry register document shall apply in writing, and such access may be granted at the discretion of the Registrar, considering privacy concerns and trade secrets.

The Registering Authority shall maintain an Entry Register Document pertaining to each trademark application filed under this Act. This Entry Register Document shall record particulars of the applicant, the goods or services for which registration is sought, and the proposed trade mark representation. Further, it will include details regarding any prior conflicting marks notified to the Registrar and any observations received from interested parties during examination. The document may also contain records relating to requests for rectification made by third parties, including supporting evidence submitted as part of such requests. Any amendment or modification to the trademark application shall be duly noted within the relevant Entry Register Document, ensuring a complete audit trail is preserved. Access to these documents shall be subject to restrictions as provided herein and in accordance with established privacy protocols.

An aggrieved party seeking remedies under this Act may apply to the relevant High Court demonstrating demonstrable prejudice arising from an entry appearing in the Entry Register. Such application shall be accompanied by a sworn statement detailing the nature of the misleading impression created by the erroneous or incomplete information contained within the Entry Register document, and quantifying the resultant damages suffered. The court may order the rectification of any inaccurate entries upon being satisfied that such inaccuracies have caused, or are likely to cause, confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or character of goods or services. Further, the court shall possess jurisdiction to award compensation for losses incurred as a direct consequence of reliance placed on information presented in the Entry Register document, provided that the applicant proves reasonable diligence in verifying the accuracy of such information was not exercised.

The Registering Officer shall maintain an entry register document pertaining to each trade mark application received under this Act. This entry register document shall record particulars of the application including the date of receipt, applicant details, representation of marks, and classification of goods or services. The Registrar may, upon written request from any interested party demonstrating a legitimate need for access, permit inspection of the entry register document subject to conditions deemed necessary by the Registrar to protect confidentiality and prevent unauthorized reproduction. Any extract from the entry register document shall be certified as true by an officer authorized by the Registrar. Such certification shall be prima facie evidence of the contents of the entry register document. The Registrar is empowered to prescribe a fee for inspection and provision of extracts, as provided herein. Failure to adhere to prescribed procedures regarding access or reproduction may result in penalties under this Act.

An applicant seeking inclusion of a mark in the entry register document shall submit Form TM-J along with the prescribed fee. Such form must contain particulars including the trade mark applied for, the owner’s name and address, and a clear representation of the mark as it is to be registered. The Registrar may require further information or clarification regarding any aspect of the application if deemed necessary for proper examination. Inclusion in the entry register document does not confer any right upon the applicant beyond notification of their intention to use the trade mark. Any person claiming an interest in opposition to such inclusion must file a notice of opposition within sixty days from the date of publication of the entry register document, as provided herein. The Registrar shall consider all submissions and determine whether the application warrants inclusion.

Any person who knowingly makes false statements or submits fraudulent documents relating to an entry appearing in the Entry Register shall be liable to a penalty of not less than fifty thousand rupees but which may extend to two hundred and fifty thousand rupees, and such person shall also be subject to prosecution under relevant provisions of the Indian Penal Code. The Registrar may, at any time, initiate proceedings for rectification of the register if it comes to their notice that an entry has been secured through misrepresentation or suppression of material facts. Further, any proprietor whose trade mark is adversely affected by a false entry in the Entry Register shall have the right to seek injunctive relief and damages as provided herein. The Registrar shall maintain strict confidentiality regarding information contained within the Entry Register document.

The Register shall maintain an entry register document detailing all assignments and licenses granted concerning trademarks registered under this Act. Any proprietor desiring to grant a license of their trademark may execute a formal instrument specifying the scope, duration, and territory of such license, which must be filed with the Registrar for recording. Such recorded licenses shall create assignable interests, permitting the licensee or subsequent assignee to enforce the terms of the license against the grantor or any successor in title. Further, an assignment of a trademark, whether absolute or partial, shall only be valid if formally executed and registered as provided herein. The entry register document relating to such assignments and licenses shall be deemed public record, accessible for inspection subject to applicable privacy regulations. Any alteration or revocation of a license must also be recorded in the entry register document to maintain clarity regarding rights and obligations.

The Register shall maintain an entry register document pertaining to each application filed under this Act, recording particulars of any notifications received regarding proposed amendments or objections raised against said applications. Any party aggrieved by a notation entered within the entry register document may, subject to prescribed timelines, file an appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, demonstrating how the recorded information demonstrably misrepresents facts presented during examination proceedings. The Board shall consider such appeals and issue orders directing rectification of entries where it finds that errors or omissions have occurred, provided that the appellant substantiates their claim with documentary evidence and testimony. Further, any decision by the Board regarding an entry register document is appealable to the High Court on grounds of law alone.

The Register shall maintain an entry register document pertaining to each trademark application examined under this Act, recording particulars of objections received from third parties and responses submitted by the applicant. Any party aggrieved by a decision regarding inclusion or exclusion of information within such entry register document may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days of communication of that decision. The Board shall consider whether the information in question accurately reflects the indication sought to be protected, and whether its presence or absence prejudices the rights of any other person under this Act. Subject to just cause shown, appeals against decisions concerning entries made regarding prior use claims will be entertained only if they demonstrate demonstrable prejudice resulting from the entry’s inaccuracy.

An entry register document, as defined herein, shall mean a record maintained by the Trade Marks Registry pertaining to applications for registration of trade marks, including but not limited to particulars of the applicant, representation of the mark, statement of goods or services, and any subsequent amendments or notations relating thereto. Such documents are deemed public records subject to restrictions imposed under this Act regarding confidential information. The Registrar may, upon request from a copyright societies registrar acting on behalf of its members, provide certified copies of entries in an entry register document for purposes directly related to the administration of copyright.

A registered breeder variety shall mean a plant variety that has been formally protected under this Act and is recorded in the Register of Plant Varieties. For the purposes of this definition, “registered” signifies that the applicant has fulfilled all requirements for registration as provided herein, including demonstrating novelty, distinctiveness, uniformity, and stability. An application for the grant of protection to a registered breeder variety shall include details pertaining to the genetic composition of the plant, its method of reproduction, and any relevant data concerning its expression potential under diverse environmental conditions. Subject to appeal, the Registrar may refuse registration if it is determined that the claimed characteristics do not meet these criteria.

An application for registration of a plant variety as a registered breeder variety shall include particulars specifying the denomination proposed for the variety and a detailed description conforming to the guidelines issued by the Authority, including its essential characteristics relevant for identification. The applicant shall furnish documentation demonstrating that the variety is substantially uniform, stable, and distinct from other varieties currently available or previously registered under this Act. Further, an assessment fee, as prescribed, must accompany the application. Provided that if the Registrar determines that the proposed denomination is deceptive or contrary to public interest, they may reject it and direct the applicant to propose an alternative. The Authority shall maintain a publicly accessible register of all registered breeder varieties.

Any person aggrieved by an order relating to the revocation or modification of a registration for a registered breeder variety may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of that order. Such appeal shall lie only on grounds specified in the memorandum of appeal, detailing the errors of law or fact apparent on the face of the record. The Appellate Board may, after giving all parties an opportunity of being heard, confirm, vary, or reverse the order appealed against and may also direct the Registrar to grant such remedies as it deems just, including compensation for loss suffered due to the impugned decision. Provided that any claim for compensation shall be substantiated with appropriate documentation and evidence demonstrating a causal link between the challenged action and the alleged damages, subject to limitations prescribed under this Act.

An application for registration of a plant variety as a registered breeder variety shall include particulars specifying the denomination proposed for the variety, a detailed description of the morphological and physiological characteristics of the variety, including its reaction to biotic and abiotic stresses, and information regarding its origin and method of derivation. The Authority may require the applicant to provide further data or clarification concerning any aspect of the application. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall publish a notification inviting objections from any person having knowledge of the proposed registered breeder variety. Any objection received shall be forwarded to the applicant for his response, which shall then be considered by the Registrar before proceeding with examination. The Registrar may reject the application if it is found that the denomination conflicts with an existing one or does not comply with prescribed guidelines.

A registered breeder variety shall remain protected for a period not exceeding fifteen years from the date of registration, provided that this period may be extended where the applicant demonstrates to the satisfaction of the Authority that propagation of the variety is challenging due to its inherent characteristics or specific environmental requirements. The right to sell propagating material of a registered breeder variety is granted exclusively to the registered breeder, subject to any license agreements entered into as per provisions relating to benefit-sharing. Any person desiring to utilize the registered breeder variety for research purposes may apply to the Authority for authorization, and such authorization shall be conditional upon adherence to prescribed protocols ensuring non-commercial exploitation of resultant material. Further, compulsory licensing may be granted under this Act if deemed necessary in the public interest.

Any person aggrieved by an order relating to the grant, refusal, modification or revocation of registration of a registered breeder variety may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of that order. Failure to comply with prescribed conditions for maintaining a registered breeder variety shall render the registrant liable to pay compensation as determined by the Board, not exceeding five times the annual royalty fees collected during the period of non-compliance. Furthermore, any act of unauthorized propagation or sale of a protected registered breeder variety, discovered through inspection carried out under this Act, constitutes an offense punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and a fine as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, a registered breeder shall have the exclusive right to authorize or assign licenses relating to the commercial exploitation of their registered breeder variety. Such authorization or assignment may encompass rights pertaining to seed production, sale, distribution, import, export, and any other activity involving the multiplication or propagation of the protected plant material. Any license granted by the registered breeder shall be in writing and clearly define the scope of permitted activities, geographical limitations, and duration. The registered breeder may impose reasonable royalty fees for such licenses, as determined through mutual agreement with the licensee. Provided that, a farmer who has obtained seeds of a registered breeder variety may continue to save and replant seed from their harvested produce, but shall not be entitled to sell or distribute such saved seed without prior authorization from the registered breeder.

Where a person aggrieved by any decision made under this Act relating to the grant, revocation, or modification of registration of a registered breeder variety has reason to believe that the decision was manifestly unjust, arbitrary, or in violation of principles of natural justice, such person may appeal to the Appellate Board. The appellate authority shall consider whether the original decision was supported by adequate evidence and reasoned argument, taking into account any relevant precedents established under this Act or other applicable legislation concerning intellectual property rights. Provided that an appeal does not lie against a decision relating solely to procedural matters unless it is shown that such procedural irregularity has resulted in demonstrable prejudice to the appellant’s case. The Board may confirm, vary, or reverse the original decision as it deems fit.

An applicant seeking registration of a plant variety shall furnish particulars relating to the method and means employed for the creation and maintenance of the germplasm of the variety, including details regarding any novel genetic modification undertaken. The application must also specify the denomination proposed for the registered breeder variety, ensuring it complies with guidelines issued by the Authority; failure to adhere to these guidelines may result in rejection. Where a plant variety has been developed through techniques involving patent shall dated processes, documentation substantiating the validity of such patents is required as an annexure to the application. The Registrar may request further information or clarification at any stage during examination and processing under this Act.

Any person aggrieved by a decision relating to the grant, refusal, modification, or revocation of registration of a registered breeder variety may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of that decision. Such an appeal shall lie irrespective of whether the decision concerns the validity of any claim made in respect of novelty, distinctiveness, stability, or uniformity required for registration under this Act. The Appellate Board may, while hearing appeals, direct the Registrar to undertake further examination into any matter relevant to the determination of rights concerning a registered breeder variety. Further, where data pertaining to a registered breeder variety is temporarily stored as transient incidental storage during digital transmission, that storage shall not be deemed an infringement of breeders’ rights as provided herein.

An amendment specification relating to a registered breeder variety shall be submitted to the Authority in Form-D, accompanied by a fee as determined under this Act. The application must detail the proposed alterations to the phenotypic characteristics previously recorded during examination and registration, providing justification for such modification based on observed field performance or subsequent scientific analysis. Where the amendment concerns traits impacting essential derivation or distinctiveness, an expert’s report substantiating the continued compliance with the criteria for a registered breeder variety is mandatory. The Authority may require further trials or data submission to assess the impact of the proposed changes. Any alteration approved under this process shall be recorded in the Register of Plant Varieties and publicly notified as per the prescribed procedure.

Subject to compliance with the novelty criteria as provided herein, the registrar shall register a plant variety as a registered breeder variety if the applicant demonstrates, through documentation and field trials conducted according to established protocols, that the variety possesses distinct characteristics substantially uniform and stable across generations. The application for registration must include detailed morphological descriptions, genetic analysis reports confirming lineage, and evidence of deposit with an approved gene bank. Provided that the variety does not contain any genetically modified material beyond tolerance levels permitted under extant regulations, the registrar may require further testing to ascertain its conformity with national biodiversity objectives. Any challenge to a proposed registered breeder variety shall be addressed through established dispute resolution mechanisms as outlined under this Act.

Any person aggrieved by a decision relating to the grant, revocation, or amendment of registration of a registered breeder variety shall have the right to appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. Failure to comply with prescribed conditions for maintaining a registered breeder variety may result in suspension or cancellation of such registration under this Act. Furthermore, any entity utilizing a registered breeder variety without authorization from the registered breeder, or engaging in acts likely to prejudice the rights conferred herein, shall be liable to pay damages as determined by the Board. A collective mark shall be eligible for registration if it represents an association of breeders protecting their respective registered breeder varieties.

For the purposes of this Act, a “registered breeder” shall mean the person who has been recognized as the breeder of a plant variety under this Act and whose name is entered in the Register of Plant Varieties. A registered breeder shall possess the rights as provided herein, including but not limited to the right to produce and sell propagating material of the protected variety, subject to any conditions stipulated during registration. Any person claiming to be a registered breeder shall provide evidence satisfactory to the Registrar demonstrating their entitlement under this Act, and may appeal decisions regarding recognition to the Plant Variety Protection Appellate Board. The rights of a registered breeder are assignable as provided herein.

An application for registration as a registered breeder shall include particulars relating to the duration of breeding and maintenance of genetic purity of the plant variety, along with details regarding any novel traits exhibited. The Authority may require submission of documentation demonstrating adherence to established protocols for maintaining distinctiveness during multiplication processes. Further, an applicant claiming rights as a registered breeder must provide evidence substantiating their contribution towards the development of the plant variety, including records pertaining to selection and hybridization procedures undertaken. Subject to verification by the Examining Committee, registration shall confer upon the registered breeder exclusive rights concerning the commercialization of the protected variety, provided that farmers’ rights are not prejudiced under this Act.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the revocation of registration, the imposition of any condition restricting the sale, offering for sale, distribution or importation of a plant variety, or concerning infringement of registered breeder’s rights may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appellate Board shall consider all relevant materials and hear submissions from both the aggrieved party and the Authority whose decision is being appealed. Subject to just considerations, the Appellate Board may affirm, reverse, or modify the order appealed against, or remand the matter for reconsideration. Failure to comply with any condition imposed by the Authority relating to benefit sharing with traditional rural communities shall render a registered breeder liable to penalties as provided herein.

An application for registration as a registered breeder shall be made in the form specified under this Act and accompanied by the requisite fee. The application must detail the applicant’s qualifications, including demonstrable experience in plant breeding techniques and adherence to ethical research practices. Upon receipt of an application, the Authority may direct the applicant to submit further documentation or attend a hearing to clarify any ambiguities regarding their expertise. If the Authority determines that the applicant possesses the necessary competence and good faith, they shall proceed with examination of the merits of the proposed registration. The Registrar shall publish a notice inviting objections from interested parties within sixty days of publication of the application. Any objection received shall be considered by the Authority, who may require further evidence or argument from both the applicant and the objector before rendering a decision.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, a registered breeder shall be entitled to perform acts including multiplication, sale, distribution and import of propagating material of the plant variety for commercial purposes. Such entitlement is conditional upon adherence to the prescribed quality standards as determined by the Central Government from time to time; failure to comply with these standards may result in suspension or revocation of registration. The registered breeder shall also be obligated to provide relevant documentation pertaining to lineage, genetic purity and field performance data upon request from the Plant Variety Protection Authority. Further, any modification to the plant variety subsequent to its registration, undertaken without prior written consent from the Plant Variety Protection Authority, will render the registered breeder liable for penalties as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the revocation of registration, imposition of any penalty, or seizure of propagating material shall have the right to appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. Failure to comply with conditions stipulated during registration may render a registered breeder liable for damages sustained by affected farmers and other breeders. The Authority may, upon receiving complaints regarding unauthorized exploitation of plant variety protection rights, issue notices requiring production of records and impose fines not exceeding five lakhs rupees per instance of infringement. Furthermore, any act constituting wilful misrepresentation concerning the identity or characteristics of a protected variety shall be deemed an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, a registered breeder shall have the exclusive right to authorize or prohibit the making, selling, importing, or exporting of propagative material of their protected plant variety. Any person desiring to utilize such propagative material for commercial purposes other than those expressly permitted under this Act must obtain a license from the registered breeder, specifying the terms and conditions governing such utilization. The registered breeder may grant licenses on non-exclusive or exclusive bases, and may stipulate royalty payments as compensation for the use of their protected variety. Assignment of rights in a plant variety registration shall include the right to grant such licenses, provided that the assignee notifies the Authority within thirty days of the assignment. Further, any license granted prior to an assignment shall remain valid unless expressly terminated by the registered breeder or successor.

Subject to appeal to the Appellate Board, a claim that a registered breeder has acted contrary to the conditions stipulated under this Act regarding the commercial exploitation of a plant variety shall be investigated by the Authority. The Authority shall provide the registered breeder with an opportunity for representation and may require submission of documentary evidence substantiating the allegation. If, following such investigation, the Authority determines that the registered breeder has indeed violated these conditions, it may issue a warning or impose penalties as provided herein. Any decision of the Authority under this provision is subject to review by the Appellate Board upon appeal filed within sixty days, and the burden shall be on the appellant to demonstrate material error in the findings of the Authority.

Where a registered breeder institutes proceedings under this Act seeking remedies for infringement of plant variety protection rights, the relevant adjudicating authority shall grant such relief as is equitable and just, including but not limited to injunctions restraining further acts of infringement, damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the registered breeder, and costs incidental to the litigation. An applicant patent relating to a method or process involving a protected variety may be challenged on grounds that it constitutes an unauthorized use or exploitation of such variety, subject to demonstrating substantial novelty and inventive step beyond the inherent characteristics of the registered plant variety. The adjudicating authority may order the destruction of infringing material and grant interim relief pending final determination of the matter, provided that sufficient cause is shown by the registered breeder.

Where a person aggrieved by any entry relating to registration, or non-registration, of a plant variety under this Act believes that such entry is erroneous, they may apply to the Registrar for direct notice rectification. Such application shall state the grounds upon which it is based and shall be accompanied by all relevant documents supporting the claim. The Registrar shall serve notice of the application on the registered breeder or the applicant whose registration is contested, affording them a reasonable opportunity to submit their response within the prescribed time limit. Upon consideration of the application and any responses received, the Registrar may direct rectification of the erroneous entry, subject to ensuring that such action does not prejudice the rights of any other person under this Act. A registered breeder shall be deemed to have sufficient interest in maintaining the accuracy of records pertaining to their plant variety.

Where a plant variety is deemed eligible for registration under this Act, and an application for registration is filed by any person claiming to be the registered breeder, the Authority shall assess compliance with all relevant provisions pertaining to novelty, distinctiveness, stability, and uniformity. The applicant must provide detailed documentation substantiating their claim as registered breeder, including records of derivation and selection processes undertaken. Further, prior public disclosure of the variety shall disqualify registration unless such disclosure is deemed to have occurred under conditions of good faith and without commercial exploitation. Any denomination variety shall be subject to review by the Authority for potential conflict with existing denominations, ensuring clarity and preventing consumer confusion as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, a registered breeder shall have the exclusive right to authorise others to propagate or sell propagating material of the plant variety for commercial purposes. Such authorisation shall be granted through a written license agreement specifying royalty rates, duration, and geographical scope. The registered breeder may assign their rights under this Act to any person, including another breeder or research institution, by way of an instrument in writing duly executed. Any international registration opposed under the International Union for the Protection of New Varieties of Plants shall not affect existing licenses granted prior to notification of such opposition, provided that the terms of those licenses are consistent with the objectives of promoting farmer’s rights and ensuring access to plant genetic resources for research. The registered breeder may also grant non-exclusive licenses on terms deemed equitable by the Controller.

For the purposes of this Act, “Controller General Patents” means the officer appointed by the Central Government to exercise the powers and discharge the duties conferred upon him under this Act relating to the examination of patent applications and grant of patents. The Controller General Patents shall be assisted by such officers as the Central Government deems necessary. Decisions made by the Controller General Patents are subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, provided that appeals may only be filed on grounds specified in regulations framed for this purpose. The functions of the Controller General Patents include maintaining records pertaining to patent applications and granted patents.

An applicant seeking registration of a design shall, upon filing the application, remit the prescribed fee to the Controller General Patents. The particulars of such remittance, including the date and amount paid, shall be recorded in the register maintained by the office of the Controller General Patents. Any request for amendment or alteration to the design details after initial registration may be entertained only with the prior approval of the Controller General Patents, subject to payment of a stipulated additional fee as determined by the Central Government. The applicant shall furnish all necessary documentation substantiating the novelty and originality of the design. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in rejection of the application or cancellation of the registration under this Act.

The Controller General Patents shall, upon receipt of a request for rectification of a patent from any interested party, issue notice to the patentee and other parties appearing on record. Such request must specify the grounds upon which the rectification is sought, detailing particulars relating to the invention or the claims as originally granted. The Controller General may require the requester to furnish further information or clarification regarding the basis for the claim of invalidity or error. An opportunity shall be afforded to the patentee and other interested parties to file their response within a prescribed period, after which the Controller General will consider all submissions presented. Decisions concerning rectification are subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board as provided herein. The Controller General’s determination regarding the validity of any claim is final, barring further appeals under this Act.

The Controller General Patents shall, upon receipt of a request for rectification of a patent granted under this Act, examine the same and may direct that such alterations be made as are necessary to ensure compliance with the provisions herein. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Controller General Patents relating to the rectification of a patent may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The request for rectification must specify the grounds upon which it is based and shall be accompanied by all relevant documents substantiating the claims made therein. Provided that, any alteration directed by the Controller General Patents shall not extend to the substance of the invention as originally claimed in the patent application.

Any person aggrieved by any order passed under this Act relating to the revocation, sealing, or destruction of goods infringing patent rights may appeal to the Controller General Patents within sixty days from the date of such order. Such appeal shall be accompanied by a memorandum of grounds and an appropriate fee as prescribed. Failure to comply with these procedural requirements will render the appeal inadmissible. The Controller General Patents shall afford the appellant and the respondent an opportunity for being heard, and may, after considering the evidence presented, confirm, vary or reverse the original order. Any party dissatisfied with the decision of the Controller General Patents may further appeal to the High Court within a period of ninety days from the date of that decision, subject to imposition of costs as deemed appropriate by the court.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any patentee may grant a license to use or exercise the patented invention under the terms and conditions specified therein, such license being assignable by the patentee subject to registration with the Controller General Patents. Where an assignment or license is registered, the particulars thereof shall be recorded in the Register of Patents and Deeds. The Controller General Patents may, upon application made by any interested party, inquire into the reasonableness of royalty rates stipulated within a license agreement relating to a patented invention, considering factors such as the prevailing market conditions and the extent of exploitation of the patent. Any person acquiring an interest in a patent through assignment or sub-license shall be deemed to succeed to all rights, privileges and obligations of the assignor or licensor, provided that prior written consent from the Controller General Patents is obtained.

The appeal against any decision rendered by the Controller General Patents relating to the grant, revocation or sealing of a patent shall be made within sixty days from the date of communication of such decision. Provided that where the appellant was prevented by act of God, public emergency or other cause beyond his control from filing an appeal within the said period, the Board may entertain the appeal if sufficient cause is shown for the delay. The Board may, subject to just considerations and after affording opportunity of being heard to all concerned parties, allow such delayed appeal. Any order made by the Board under this Act shall be final. Further, the Controller General Patents may, at his discretion, require a party seeking review of a decision to furnish security for costs.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks under this Act, including orders relating to revocation, opposition proceedings, or compulsory licensing, desires to appeal, he shall file an appeal with the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Board may, after giving notice to all parties concerned and affording them a reasonable opportunity for being heard, affirm, modify, or reverse the order appealed against. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Intellectual Property Appellate Board may further appeal to the High Court within three months from the date of the order. During any house parliament session dedicated to reviewing intellectual property legislation, the government shall provide regular updates on pending appeals before the Appellate Board and the High Court concerning decisions made by the Controller General Patents.

The power to determine disputes arising from the rejection of a patent application, or subsequent revocation proceedings, shall vest with the Controller General Patents, acting in accordance with principles of natural justice. Any party aggrieved by an order passed under this Act may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board; provided that such appeals must be filed within sixty days of the date of communication of the order and accompanied by a fee as prescribed.
