Where any goods are knowingly offered or exposed for sale, or deceptively represented to be of a particular kind or quality, by the use of a false trade description, the offender shall be liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, and also to a fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees. Such representation includes any statement or affirmation concerning the geographical origin of the goods. Further, where such offence is committed by a company, every director, manager, secretary, or other officer thereof shall be deemed guilty of the offence and liable for punishment as if he were an individual. The court may order seizure of the misrepresented goods, provided that reasonable opportunity to defend has been afforded to the accused.

Where any individual or entity holds exclusive rights pertaining to a product’s distinctive character and utilizes a specific trade description in connection with its sale or offering, that right holder may grant a license permitting another party to employ said trade description for similar goods or services. Such licenses shall be documented in writing and specify the scope of permitted use, including geographical limitations and duration. The licensor retains ownership of the underlying trade mark rights and may assign those rights, along with any associated licenses, to a successor entity subject to adherence to conditions stipulated under this Act concerning prior consent from licensees. Any assignment or license granted subsequent to the initial registration shall be recorded as per prescribed procedures. Furthermore, a licensee may, with written permission from the licensor, sub-license certain aspects of the permitted trade description usage, provided that such sub-licensing does not contravene the terms of the original agreement.

Where any person, in connection with the supply or offer for supply of goods or services, uses a false trade description, subject to exceptions provided herein relating to artistic impression and parody, such person shall be guilty of an offence. The term "trade description" includes any statement or indication which is likely to mislead consumers as to the nature, quality, characteristics, origin, quantity, suitability, or other relevant attribute of those goods or services. An appeal against a conviction under this provision may be made to the High Court within sixty days from the date of the order of the lower court. It shall be presumed, pending contrary evidence, that a trade description is false if it contains a representation which is demonstrably inaccurate and likely to cause commercial harm.

Where any goods are knowingly offered or exposed for sale, or deceptively represented as possessing particular qualities, such representation shall constitute a false trade description. Any person who makes use of a false trade description under this Act is liable to prosecution and may be subject to pecuniary penalties as determined by the relevant adjudicating authority. Further, where a trade mark has been registered, any subsequent use of a sign or words identical or confusingly similar thereto, which incorporates such false trade description, shall constitute an infringement actionable at the suit of the registered proprietor. Impliedly registration shall not preclude remedies available under this Act for misrepresentation relating to the nature of goods or services offered. The aggrieved party may seek injunctive relief and damages as provided herein.

Where any person, whether acting alone or colluding with others, offers for sale, exposes for sale, uses, or advertises goods or services under a false trade description, such person shall be deemed to have committed an offence. A false trade description includes any statement likely to deceive the public concerning the quality, nature, properties, characteristics, quantity, origin, or suitability of those goods or services. The term "trade description" encompasses not only words but also symbols, marks, and images. Any employee acting under the direction of another shall be considered an agent for that purpose, and the principal may be held liable as a commission offence attributable to the actions of their subordinate. Investigations into alleged false trade descriptions shall be conducted by officers authorized under this Act. Evidence obtained during such investigations is admissible subject to procedural safeguards provided herein.

Where any person uses an incorrect or false trade description in connection with goods or services offered for sale, and such use is likely to deceive or cause confusion amongst the public, that person shall be liable to prosecution under this Act. An appeal against a finding of misleading use lies to the Appellate Intellectual Property Tribunal. The Registrar may, upon receiving credible evidence of such deceptive practice, issue a notice requiring the party concerned to cease the offending activity and submit an explanation within thirty days. Failure to comply with such a notice shall be deemed conclusive proof of intent to mislead, subject to the right of appeal as provided herein. The India Registrar retains discretion in determining whether a trade description is indeed false or misleading.

For the purposes of this Act, “certification mark” means a sign used to signify that any goods or services meet certain defined standards, characteristics, quality, or conditions; and the provisions act shall apply to certification marks in manner similar to those applicable to trade marks, subject to such modifications as may be prescribed. A certification mark shall not, however, indicate an attribute of the person providing the certification but rather a guarantee concerning the certified goods or services. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating adherence to these standards before registration is granted and may revoke a certification mark if those standards are no longer maintained.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall include a representation of the marks applied for, and a list specifying goods or services in relation to which the applicant desires to register the trade mark. The Registrar may require the applicant to amend the representation if it is not clear enough for identification purposes. Further, an applicant seeking registration under this Act shall furnish such documentary evidence as the Registrar deems necessary to establish ownership of the proposed trade mark, including details regarding prior use or assignment. Where a trade mark comprises a word or words which do not indicate any particular characteristic relating to the goods or services, the provisions act shall require that the application explicitly state the intended meaning within the context of the applicant’s business.

Where any proprietor of a registered trade mark institutes proceedings for infringement under this Act, and it is shown that the defendant has made use of a sign identical or confusingly similar to the registered trade mark in relation to goods or services not identical with those in respect of which the trade mark is registered, but which are essentially connected therewith, the provisions act shall apply as if the use had been in relation to identical goods or services. The Court may grant such remedy or remedies as it deems just and equitable, including an injunction restraining the defendant from further infringing use, damages for past infringement, and delivery up of all infringing materials. Provided that where the proprietor has failed to exercise due diligence in adopting and maintaining the trade mark, the Court may reduce or refuse relief accordingly. The plaintiff shall be entitled to costs proportionate to the extent of the infringement proven.

Applications for registration of service marks shall be examined in accordance with the procedures prescribed under this Act, and any observations arising during examination shall be communicated to the applicant within a period not exceeding six months from the date of filing. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further particulars or documentary evidence relating to the use of the mark in relation to the specified services, provided that such requirement is reasonable and proportionate to the information sought. Any appeal against an order passed by the Registrar refusing registration shall lie before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The provisions act shall govern all proceedings before the Board concerning service mark applications, and decisions rendered by the Board are final subject to further appeals as provided herein.

Where any proprietor of a registered trade mark seeks to alter the representation of that trade mark, such alteration shall not be permissible without prior approval obtained under this Act. The application for such approval must specify the nature and extent of the proposed modification, accompanied by representations demonstrating its continued distinctiveness following the change. Provided that an alteration does not affect the essential characteristics or connotations associated with the registered trade mark, it may be approved. Furthermore, any proprietor seeking to amend their trade mark shall provide evidence confirming that consumers are likely to recognise the altered representation as denoting the same goods or services previously indicated under this Act. The provisions act shall govern all applications for alteration and subsequent registration thereof.

Any proprietor utilizing a registered trade mark in connection with goods or services shall be liable for damages sustained by any party demonstrating that such utilization has resulted in confusion, misrepresentation, or dilution of goodwill associated with a similar mark already lawfully used. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint and after affording the alleged infringer an opportunity to be heard, issue an injunction restraining further infringing use, subject to considerations of proportionality between the harm suffered and the remedial action ordered. Further, any person found guilty of knowingly making false representations concerning the ownership or registration of a trade mark shall face penalties as provided herein, including imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years and fines up to one million rupees. The provisions act shall extend to cover online platforms facilitating infringing activities.

The provisions act shall govern assignments and licenses of registered trade marks, enabling flexibility in commercial exploitation. Any proprietor may assign their exclusive right to use a registered trade mark, either wholly or in relation to specific goods or services, by instrument in writing. Such assignment shall be recorded in the Register upon application made by the assignee, subject to payment of prescribed fees. Furthermore, proprietors may grant non-exclusive licenses permitting others to utilize the trade mark for specified purposes and territories; these licenses also require registration as assignments under this Act to be enforceable against third parties. A license granted prior to the commencement of this provision shall remain valid unless revoked by express written notice from the licensor. Any subsequent dealings with a licensed trade mark are subject to the terms stipulated in the registered license agreement.

Where any question arises regarding the distinctiveness of a trade mark, the Registrar may direct that such question be determined by way of hearing. Any party aggrieved by an order made under this Act directing a determination of distinctiveness may appeal against such order to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication thereof. The Appellate Board shall consider evidence submitted by all parties and may, subject to just considerations, substitute its own decision for that of the Registrar. It is provided that any party seeking to challenge the validity of a trade mark based on lack of distinctiveness must demonstrate demonstrable consumer confusion arising directly from the use of the impugned mark; otherwise, the provisions act shall not apply.

The provisions act shall extend to claims made concerning deceptive similarity between registered trade marks, even where such similarity arises solely through alterations in colouration or font style. An appeal lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board against any order determining that a mark is deceptively similar, provided that the appellant demonstrates demonstrable prejudice resulting from the registration of the impugned mark. Further, registration shall apply equally to marks used in connection with services and goods, notwithstanding variations in presentation across different media. The burden of proving deceptive similarity rests upon the complainant; however, where the allegedly infringing mark incorporates a dominant element of the registered trade mark, such presumption may be rebutted only by clear and convincing evidence demonstrating lack of consumer confusion.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall include a representation of the marks applied for and a list specifying goods or services in relation to which the applicant desires that the trade mark be registered. The Registrar may, upon receiving such an application, direct the applicant to amend the statement of goods or services if he considers them to be too wide or otherwise objectionable under this Act. Where the description of any invention far claimed within a representation includes elements not exclusively indicative of a particular good or service, the Registrar shall require clarification from the applicant detailing the scope of protection sought. The provisions act shall govern the examination process and determination of distinctiveness as per established guidelines.

For the purposes of this Act, a "provisions act" is defined as any legislative instrument enacted by the Parliament or State Legislature that supplements, amends, clarifies, or otherwise affects the operation of provisions contained herein. Such a provisions act shall be deemed to have effect only to the extent that it expressly states its intention to modify, interpret, or expand upon existing obligations and entitlements under this Act. Nothing in this definition shall permit a provisions act to contradict any fundamental principle established as provided herein relating to trademark registration or infringement. A provisions act may specify procedures for implementation of changes introduced thereby.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall include a representation of the marks applied for, and may also include a statement of disclaimer relating to any element of the marks. Where the Registrar considers that any part of the proposed trade mark is not distinctive in relation to the goods or services specified in the application, he may require the applicant to furnish a statement indicating which portion of the mark is disclaimed. Such disclaimers shall be recorded in the Register and shall have effect as if they had been included in the original application. The provisions act relating to acceptance of an application for registration shall apply equally where a disclaimer has been filed, provided that the remaining portions of the mark are capable of distinguishing the goods or services.

Where any proprietor of a registered trade mark institutes legal proceedings for infringement under this Act, and it is shown that the defendant has made use of a sign identical or confusingly similar to the registered trade mark in relation to goods or services not identical with those in respect of which the trade mark is registered, but which are essentially connected therewith, the remedies available shall include an injunction restraining the defendant from such use. This restraint may extend to preventing any representation likely to be held to constitute a violation of the provisions act relating to unfair competition. The Court may also order the recovery of damages sustained by the proprietor as a consequence of the infringement, calculated in such manner as the Court deems just and equitable, taking into account factors including lost profits and the defendant’s gains derived from the infringing activity. Provided that any claim for damages shall be substantiated with reasonable evidence.

Applications for registration of marks incorporating geographical indications shall be examined in accordance with the procedures prescribed under this Act, provided that the Registrar may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating use of the mark within the territory associated with the indication. Such evidence must satisfy the Registrar as to the continued and authentic connection between the goods or services and the specified geographical origin. The provisions act relating to opposition proceedings shall apply mutatis mutandis to applications for registration involving geographical indications, allowing interested parties to challenge the validity of such registrations based on grounds including misrepresentation of origin or likelihood of confusion. Further, any alteration to a registered mark incorporating a geographical indication requires prior approval from the Registrar, ensuring preservation of its distinctive character and integrity as a designation of origin.

Where any registered trade mark is used exclusively for the export of goods, the proprietor shall not be deemed to have used such trade mark in India unless and until the goods are imported into India; provided that this condition does not apply where the use occurs outside India by a licensee authorized under this Act. The provisions act relating to importation shall be interpreted strictly according to prevailing customs regulations. Furthermore, any entity claiming entitlement to use a registered trade mark based on prior assignment must provide documented evidence of such transfer, conforming to standards prescribed by the Trade Marks Registry. Failure to comply with these evidentiary requirements will render the claim invalid and subject to cancellation proceedings as provided herein.

Any proprietor seeking rectification of a registered trade mark under this Act shall file an application with the relevant intellectual property office, specifying the grounds for such rectification and supported by affidavits verifying the material facts. Failure to comply with prescribed forms and timelines as provided herein will render the application liable for dismissal without further notice. Where a false or deceptive representation is made in connection with goods or services, utilizing a trade mark identical or confusingly similar to a registered mark, the proprietor shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief and damages commensurate with the loss suffered. The provisions act relating to consumer deception are particularly stringent; any wilful infringement will attract enhanced penalties, including imprisonment of up to three years.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark may, by instrument in writing, grant exclusive licences under this Act relating to specific geographical territories or particular goods or services for which the trade mark is registered. Such licences shall be subject to such terms and conditions as are agreed upon between the grantor and licensee, provided that the licence agreement expressly reserves the right of the proprietor to revoke the licence upon written notice if the licensee fails to use the trade mark diligently within the licensed territory or in respect of the licensed goods or services. Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall be deemed to include any existing licences granted under this Act relating thereto, unless the assignment instrument specifically excludes such licences and provides for their continued validity as provisions acting on behalf of the assignor. The assignee shall be bound by all terms and conditions applicable to those provisions.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark may, by instrument in writing and subject to such terms and conditions as they deem fit, grant a license to use the trade mark for specific goods or services. Such licenses shall be assignable, either wholly or partially, provided that any assignment is notified to the Registrar within thirty days of its execution. The provisions act relating to sub-licensing are governed by regulations framed under this Act and published in the Official Gazette; these will detail requirements regarding territorial limitations and duration. A manufactured notification specifying the precise scope of permitted use shall accompany every license agreement, and copies thereof must be filed with the Registrar within fourteen days of the grant. Any alteration to a licensed trade mark requires prior written consent from the proprietor and subsequent registration as a variation under this Act.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall include such particulars relating to the applicant, the goods or services in relation to which the trade mark is proposed to be registered, and any claim to priority under this Act, as may be prescribed. Where an application relates to more than one class of goods or services, each class shall be separately specified within the application. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further information relating to the use of the trade mark in relation to any of the goods or services specified therein, provided that such requirement is reasonable and proportionate to the scope of the registration sought. Any alteration to an application after its initial filing shall be subject to approval by the Registrar, ensuring compliance with the provisions act governing amendments. Application registration shall be deemed conclusive evidence of proprietorship unless otherwise proven.

Where any proprietor of a registered trade mark institutes legal proceedings for infringement under this Act, and it is established that such proprietor has failed to exercise reasonable diligence in monitoring the use of identical or confusingly similar marks, the Court may, subject to appeal, impose a penalty not exceeding two per centum of the turnover attributable to the infringing goods or services. This inquiry imposing penalty shall be conducted independently of any determination regarding damages recoverable by the trade mark proprietor. The provisions act relating to limitation periods for bringing such proceedings remain unaffected by this obligation on proprietors. Further, where an injunction is granted restraining infringement, the Court may order the infringer to undertake corrective advertising at their expense to mitigate consumer confusion arising from the infringing use.

An application for registration of a certification trade mark shall be examined in accordance with the procedures prescribed under this Act, subject to the provisions relating specifically to such marks. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating adherence to defined standards and practices relevant to the goods or services certified by the proposed mark. Such standards must be verifiable and operated impartially, ensuring equitable treatment of all users. Certification trade marks shall not indicate any attribute of the registered proprietor but rather a quality guaranteed under a prescribed certification scheme. The Registrar may reject an application if it appears that the certification process lacks transparency or is susceptible to abuse. Any interested party may file objections concerning the validity of the proposed standards, provided that such objections are filed within the stipulated period as provided herein.

The Registrar shall consider an application for rectification of a registered trade mark, as provided herein, with particular regard to the distinctiveness of the mark and its association with the applicant’s goods or services. For the purposes of this consideration, the Registrar may take into account evidence demonstrating that, following registration, the use of the mark by others has caused confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of those goods or services. The Registrar shall also consider whether any relevant consumer surveys have been submitted as evidence and their methodological soundness. Further, the Registrar shall consider any arguments presented concerning dilution of the trade mark’s reputation.

In determining whether an application for trademark registration should proceed, the Registrar shall consider any evidence submitted by the applicant demonstrating acquired distinctiveness relating to the goods or services specified in the application. This assessment will take into account the period during which the mark has been used in India and the extent of recognition amongst the relevant consumer base. The Registrar may require further clarification or supporting documentation from the applicant if the initial submission is deemed insufficient to establish acquired distinctiveness, provided that such requests are reasonable and do not unduly delay the processing of the application. Further, the Registrar shall consider any opposition filed under this Act in relation to the mark’s similarity to existing trademarks.

Where an objection is raised by any person claiming an interest in a trade mark, or by the Trade Marks Registry, against the acceptance of an application for registration, the Registrar shall consider the grounds of such objection and afford the applicant an opportunity to submit their response. The Registrar may require both the objector and the applicant to furnish further information or documents relevant to the determination of the objection. Subject to this, the decision of the Registrar regarding the validity of the objection shall be final, provided that any party aggrieved by such decision may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within a period of sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The applicant’s right to registration shall not arise until all objections have been resolved and the trade mark is formally registered as provided herein.

In determining an application for registration of a geographical indication, the Registrar shall consider any evidence submitted by the applicant demonstrating that the quality, reputation or other characteristic of the goods originates from the asserted geographical origin. The Registrar may require the applicant to provide further particulars regarding the local producers and their traditional practices relating to the production of the indicated goods, provided that such requirements are reasonable and do not unduly burden the application process. Where an objection is raised by any interested party concerning the distinctiveness of a proposed geographical indication, the Registrar shall consider all submissions from both the applicant and the objector before making a determination. The Registrar’s decision in this regard shall be final, subject to appeal under this Act. Any evidence presented must adhere strictly to the prescribed format as detailed in the Trade Marks Rules.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed, the Registrar shall consider the notice of opposition and any counter-statement filed by the applicant. The Registrar may require both parties to submit further information or documentary evidence relevant to the grounds of opposition as provided herein. Subject to compliance with regulations pertaining to procedural fairness, the Registrar shall afford each party a reasonable opportunity to present their case in writing and, if requested, in person. Provided that any representation made by either party is supported by verifiable documentation, the Registrar’s determination regarding distinctiveness or deceptive similarity shall be based solely on the information presented and applicable precedents under this Act. The Registrar shall record reasons for any decision rendered concerning the validity of the opposition.

Where an objection is raised against a proposed trade mark under this Act, the Registrar shall consider the grounds of such objection and any counter-statement filed by the applicant. The Registrar may direct a hearing if either party requests it or deems it necessary for due consideration of the matter. Any order made following such a hearing shall be final subject to appeal under Chapter VIII. Failure to comply with directions issued by the Registrar concerning hearings, including attendance or submission of evidence, will render the party liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. The Registrar's decision regarding the registrability of a mark is binding and enforcement actions may be initiated against infringers without further notice.

Where a trade mark has been assigned or licensed, and an application for rectification of that trade mark is made, the Registrar shall consider any evidence submitted by the assignor or licensee demonstrating continued use of the mark subsequent to the assignment or license agreement. Such consideration will include assessment of whether the ongoing usage materially impacts the distinctiveness of the mark as originally registered. The Registrar may require further clarification from either the assignee or licensor regarding the scope and duration of their respective rights, particularly where conflicting claims arise concerning permitted uses. Provided that the assignor or licensee can establish a legitimate interest in maintaining the integrity of the trade mark’s reputation, they shall be afforded an opportunity to present arguments against rectification. The Registrar is not bound by any contractual limitations contained within the assignment or license agreement itself.

In determining whether a proposed trade mark is distinctive, and subject to any evidence presented by interested parties, the Registrar shall consider objections raised concerning alleged descriptiveness or lack of inherent distinctiveness. The applicant bears the onus of demonstrating that the mark, when used in relation to the specified goods or services, reasonably distinguishes them from those of other traders. Where an objection is based on prior use establishing acquired distinctiveness, the Registrar may require the applicant to submit evidence substantiating such usage, including but not limited to sales figures, advertising expenditure, and consumer surveys. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar under this Act may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of that decision.

Where an objection is raised by any person claiming an interest in a trade mark, or by the Trade Marks Registry, against the acceptance of an application for registration, the Registrar shall consider such objection and afford the applicant and the objector an opportunity of being heard. The Registrar may require parties to submit written arguments and evidence within prescribed time limits; failure to comply with these requirements may render submissions inadmissible. In determining whether a trade mark is distinctive, the Registrar shall give due weight to any evidence demonstrating consumer recognition or association, provided that such evidence is verifiable and relevant. For purposes of assessing *trade mark identity*, the Registrar will consider not only identical marks but also those which are similar in concept and visual appearance, taking into account the overall impression created on the mind of the average consumer. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board as provided herein.

The Registrar shall consider an application for trademark registration, subject to compliance with the provisions of this Act, and shall determine whether the mark as shown in the application is distinctive in its registered form. For purposes of such consideration, the Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further particulars relating to the use of the mark or any prior applications concerning similar marks. An application deemed ready for examination under this Act will be accompanied by an application registration notice, which shall specify the date on which objections, if any, are invited from interested parties as provided herein.

Upon receipt of an application for trademark registration, or upon receiving a communication regarding an opposed mark, the Registrar shall consider whether the proposed mark conflicts with any existing registered trademarks or pending applications, taking into account not only identicality but also similarity in concept and appearance that might cause confusion amongst consumers. The Registrar may require further clarification from the applicant concerning the nature of the goods or services for which registration is sought, particularly where such description appears ambiguous or lacks specificity. Where a trademark has been transmitted by assignment or otherwise, the Registrar shall verify the validity of such transmission under this Act and ensure proper documentation reflecting the change in ownership is filed. Provided that the Registrar deems the application to be compliant with all relevant provisions as provided herein, registration may proceed.

In determining whether a trade mark is distinctive, the Registrar shall consider any evidence demonstrating that the sign, though initially lacking inherent distinctiveness, has acquired such distinctiveness through the efforts of the applicant in promoting and advertising the goods or services associated with it. This assessment shall include an evaluation of the duration and geographical extent of those promotional activities, alongside a consideration of consumer perception as established by market surveys or other relevant data. The Registrar may refuse registration if satisfied that the mark’s acquired distinctiveness is solely attributable to factors unrelated to the applicant's commercial undertakings. Furthermore, where the trade mark incorporates elements derived from an invention far claimed in a patent application, the Registrar shall be particularly vigilant regarding potential consumer confusion and the impact on prior users.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark includes proposed amendments to the description of goods or services, the Registrar shall consider such application and may require the applicant to submit amendment specification documents detailing the precise nature and scope of the intended modifications. These documents must clearly articulate how the amended list conforms with accepted commercial practices and avoids ambiguity that could mislead consumers regarding the origin or characteristics of the goods or services. The Registrar is further empowered to request clarification from the applicant concerning any aspect of these amendments, particularly where they relate to classifications under the International Classification of Goods and Services. Subject to compliance with all relevant provisions under this Act, and provided that the amended list does not conflict with existing registered trade marks, the Registrar may proceed with processing the application.

For the purposes of this Act, "imported goods" shall mean any goods brought into India from outside India by sea, land or air, and includes goods which have been unloaded from a vessel or aircraft at an Indian port or aerodrome but are still under customs control as provided under the Customs Act 1962. Goods so imported shall be deemed to bear the mark of the proprietor unless it is established that such goods were genuinely traded in their country of origin and not for the purpose of defrauding any person under this Act, or otherwise infringing rights vested herein. Any alteration made to imported goods after entry into India may render them liable to seizure as per regulations prescribed therein.

An application for registration of a trade mark may include a representation in clear terms indicating that the applicant seeks to register the trade mark as distinctive apart from any acquired reputation or get-up of earlier trade marks. Where the Central Government considers it necessary for the protection of registered trade marks, and subject to regulations framed by the Trade Marks Registry, goods imported under the Customs Act 1962 may be detained at ports of entry if they bear a mark identical or confusingly similar to a registered trade mark. The Registrar shall provide an opportunity to the proprietor of the registered trade mark to submit their objections within a prescribed period. Any decision regarding such detention shall be recorded in writing and made available for public inspection.

Where any imported goods are suspected of being counterfeit or deceptively misdescribed in relation to a registered trade mark, an officer of customs shall immediately notify the Registrar. The Registrar may, upon receipt of such notification and after affording the proprietor of the trade mark an opportunity to be heard, issue instructions to the Customs authorities regarding the disposition of the goods. Such instructions may direct that the goods be seized and detained pending further investigation or examination. Where the imported goods are determined to be in violation of this Act, they shall be subject to confiscation under the provisions of the Customs Act 1962. The proprietor of the trade mark shall be entitled to recover from the importer any costs incurred by the Registrar in connection with the examination and disposition of the goods, provided that the importer is found to have acted in bad faith or with knowledge of the infringing nature of the goods.

Where any imported goods are suspected of infringing a registered trade mark, an officer authorized under this Act may, subject to compliance with regulations prescribed by the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs, detain such goods pending verification of their origin and intended destination. The owner of the registered trade mark shall be notified promptly of such detention, providing details regarding the consignment and the basis for suspicion of infringement. Provided that, if the imported goods are accompanied by a valid certificate of origin issued under the auspices of an international agreement to which India is a party, the officer may require further documentation demonstrating compliance with applicable provisions of the Customs Act 1962 before releasing the goods. Any determination regarding infringement shall be made in accordance with procedures established herein.

Any person importing goods, or having custody of goods, suspected to be counterfeit marks infringing registered trade marks shall, upon demand by an authorized officer, produce documentary evidence relating to the origin, ownership and transaction history of those goods. Failure to comply with such a demand shall render that person liable for penalties as provided herein, including but not limited to fines up to five times the value of the suspected infringing goods. Where imported goods are seized under this Act or under the Customs Act 1962, they may be detained pending determination of their authenticity and ownership. Any proprietor of a registered trade mark aggrieved by such seizure may apply for an expeditious hearing before the relevant adjudicating authority to challenge the seizure and seek release of the goods.

The owner of a registered trademark may grant a license permitting the use of their mark in relation to specified goods or services, subject to conditions stipulated within the licensing agreement. Such licenses shall be assignable, provided that any assignment is notified to the Registrar of Trade Marks in the prescribed manner and accompanied by the requisite fee. Where the licensed goods are imported, the importer shall comply with all applicable provisions under the Customs Act 1962 relating to declaration of trademarks and payment of duties. Any subsequent assignee of a trademark license retains the rights and obligations as if they were the original licensor, subject to any modifications agreed upon in writing by both parties. The Registrar may require production of documentation substantiating the chain of title for such assignments.

Where any goods are seized pursuant to a seizure warrant issued under this Act, or otherwise detained in connection with an investigation relating to infringement of a registered trade mark, the owner of the goods shall be afforded reasonable opportunity to demonstrate that such goods were lawfully imported into India and comply with all applicable provisions of the Customs Act 1962. Provided that, if the seized goods are determined by the Adjudicating Officer to have been imported in violation of any regulation under the aforementioned Customs Act, or otherwise represent counterfeit trade mark articles, they shall be subject to confiscation as per the procedures outlined herein and may also be liable for further penalties as deemed appropriate. Any party aggrieved by such a determination may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days.

Where a trade mark is affixed to any imported goods, or the packaging thereof, and such affixation constitutes an infringement of another’s registered trade mark as provided herein, the owner of the infringed trade mark shall be entitled to apply to the Customs Authority to detain the infringing goods. The Customs Authority may, subject to due process, seize and hold such goods pending determination by the relevant intellectual property tribunal. Further, where imported goods bear translated printed copies of a protected design or trade mark without authorization from the registered proprietor, these shall also be deemed actionable under this Act. Any person importing goods in violation of these provisions is liable for damages equivalent to three times the assessed value of the infringing material and may face prosecution under the Customs Act 1962.

Where any sound recording, including but not limited to musical scores or dialogue extracted from a film sound track, is imported into India, such goods shall be deemed subject to examination and assessment under this Act. Provided that if the importer declares the goods as intended solely for non-commercial exhibition within India, and furnishes an affidavit confirming compliance with conditions prescribed by the Central Government, then provisional clearance may be granted pending final determination of duties. Further, any imported sound recording which is determined to bear a registered trade mark shall be subject to seizure if it is established that such importation constitutes infringement under this Act or contravenes provisions of the Customs Act 1962 relating to prohibited imports.

For the purposes of this Act, “imported goods” shall mean any goods brought into India from outside its territory, whether by sea, air, land or post, and includes goods declared under the Customs Act. The term "declared value" in relation to imported goods signifies the valuation assigned to those goods for duty assessment as recorded in the relevant customs declaration form; provided that such declared value shall be subject to verification and adjustment by appropriate authorities under this Act. Any alteration or falsification of a customs declaration concerning imported goods with intent to deceive, constitutes an offence triable under the Customs Act and may render the declarant liable to penalties as prescribed herein.

An application for registration of a trade mark may include a representation of any goods or articles made from the materials indicated in the trade mark, provided that such representation does not mislead consumers regarding the nature or quality of the goods. Where a trade mark is sought to be registered in relation to goods imported into India, the Registrar shall require evidence satisfactory to him demonstrating compliance with relevant provisions under this Act and the Customs Act, 1962. Such evidence may include import documentation, declarations from importers, and verification reports obtained by the Registrar. The registrar may refuse registration if he believes that the mark is likely to be confused with marks already registered or applied for in relation to imported goods subject to customs duties.

Where any proprietor institutes proceedings against a person alleged to have infringed a registered trade mark, it shall be lawful for such person to counter-claim that the goods or services in respect of which the trade mark is registered are classifiable under headings specified in the Schedule to the Customs Act, and that the registration was improperly granted due to misclassification. Such counter-claim may seek revocation of the said trade mark registration. The proprietor shall bear the burden of proving proper classification at the time of application for registration. Provided that a finding of improper classification shall not, by itself, invalidate any other registered trade marks held by the proprietor. Further, where goods are seized under the Customs Act and suspected to be counterfeit, the investigating officer may request production of documentation relating to the alleged infringing mark as evidence.

Where any goods are seized under the Customs Act, 1962, and it is determined that such seizure relates to goods infringing a registered trade mark, the Investigating Officer shall immediately notify the Registrar of Trade Marks. The Registrar may, upon receipt of such notification, furnish copies of relevant documents pertaining to the registered trade mark to the appropriate authority conducting proceedings under the Customs Act. Any decision regarding confiscation of goods seized pursuant to this process shall be subject to review by a designated officer appointed by the Central Government, who shall possess expertise in both customs law and intellectual property rights. The said officer may require further investigation or documentation as deemed necessary before rendering a determination. Appeals against such decisions under this Act are governed by the procedures prescribed herein and shall be filed within sixty days of the date of notification of the order.

Where any goods are seized pursuant to a seizure notice issued under the Customs Act, 1962, and such goods bear a mark identical or deceptively similar to a registered trade mark, the adjudicating officer shall provide written intimation to the proprietor of the said trade mark. Such intimation shall detail the particulars of the seized goods, the date and place of seizure, and the reasons for suspicion of infringement as provided herein. The proprietor may, within thirty days from receipt of such intimation, submit a written representation outlining their claim of ownership and detailing any demonstrable consumer confusion arising from the use of the mark on the imported goods. Subject to compliance with prescribed procedures, the adjudicating officer shall consider this representation before determining whether confiscation proceedings are warranted.

Where any imported goods are suspected of being counterfeit or deceptively marked, officers authorized under the Customs Act shall detain such goods pending verification of their authenticity and ownership. Any person importing goods bearing a trade mark identical or confusingly similar to a registered trade mark shall be deemed guilty of an offence against this Act. The Central Government may, upon receiving information regarding suspected infringement, direct customs officials to seize any infringing goods found within ports of entry. Failure to comply with such directions constitutes a punishable offence and renders the importer liable for penalties as provided herein, including forfeiture of the imported goods and imposition of fines not exceeding ten times the value of the infringing trade mark.

The owner of a registered trade mark, intending to grant a license relating to importation of goods subject to the provisions of the Customs Act, may execute an assignment or a non-exclusive license agreement allowing another party to act as their authorized importer. Such authorization shall be in writing and clearly specify the scope of permitted imports, including but not limited to product categories and geographical origins. The licensor retains the right to audit the licensee’s import records to ensure compliance with applicable regulations under this Act and relevant customs procedures. Any sub-licensing is prohibited without prior written consent from the original trade mark owner. Provided that the licensee adheres strictly to the terms of the license agreement, including payment of royalties as stipulated therein, the licensor shall indemnify the licensee against any claims arising from infringement related to importation activities conducted pursuant to this authorization.

Where any goods are seized by an officer authorized under the Customs Act, 1962, and it is determined that such seizure relates to a registered trade mark or a deceptively similar representation thereof, the owner of the trade mark shall be notified in writing within thirty days of the seizure. The proprietor may, subject to appeal before the Appellate Authority as provided herein, challenge the determination of infringement relating to imported goods. Any order made under this Act concerning seized goods is further subject to judicial review by a High Court if it appears that the Customs officer acted without due process or exceeded their authority in interpreting provisions pertaining to trade mark rights. The aggrieved party may petition for relief within ninety days of notification.

Where any goods are seized by an officer authorised under the Customs Act, 1962, suspicion arising from a potential infringement of a registered trade mark, such seizure shall be deemed provisional pending assessment and determination as provided herein. The owner of the registered trade mark may, within thirty days of notification of the seizure, file a claim with the adjudicating authority asserting their rights and specifying the nature of the alleged infringement. Should the adjudicating authority find that the imported goods bear a sign identical or confusingly similar to the registered trade mark, they shall order forfeiture of those goods. A date claim shall be considered invalid if it is not accompanied by evidence demonstrating reasonable grounds for believing an infringement has occurred. The owner may further seek damages under this Act proportionate to the loss suffered due to the infringing import.

Where any goods are seized by an officer authorized under the Customs Act, 1962, and it is alleged that such seizure relates to counterfeit or deceptively similar goods infringing a registered trademark as defined under this Act, the investigating officer shall provide the trademark proprietor with a copy of the certificate registration produced at the time of import. The proprietor may, within thirty days from the date of receipt of such copy, file an objection to the release of the seized goods. Such objection shall be accompanied by an affidavit verifying the grounds for alleging infringement and detailing the specific marks affected. Failure to provide the certificate registration or a timely objection does not preclude subsequent legal action under this Act but may render any appeal against seizure less favorably considered.

A user party proceeding, as contemplated under this Act, refers to an instance where a person who is neither the proprietor of a trade mark nor an applicant for registration thereof, but who possesses a license or otherwise has permission to use the trade mark, becomes involved in legal proceedings relating to that trade mark. Such involvement shall occur when the interests of the user party are directly affected by matters under consideration within the proceeding, including, but not limited to, claims of infringement or challenges to validity. The Registrar may, at any stage of a proceeding, determine whether a particular individual qualifies as a user party and is entitled to participate, provided that such determination shall be made in accordance with principles of natural justice.

A user party proceeding may be instituted by any person claiming rights in respect of an alleged infringement of a registered trade mark, provided that such person has given notice to the proprietor of the trade mark and to all other known users of the mark. The Registrar shall, upon receiving such application, determine whether the applicant is indeed a person with a substantial interest in the matter. Further, any party affected by the outcome of a user party proceeding may appeal against an order made by the Registrar under this Act to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. It shall be the duty of the appellant to demonstrate prejudice arising from the decision being appealed. The Registrar may require such parties to furnish security for costs as deemed appropriate.

Where a user party proceeding is initiated concerning infringement of a registered trade mark, the owner of the trade mark shall have the right to seek injunctive relief against all parties engaged in the infringing activity. Such injunction may restrain acts specified under this Act as constituting infringement, and may further require the infringer to recall or destroy any goods bearing the impugned trade mark. Provided that, where an allegation of bad faith is raised by a defendant, the owner shall bear the burden of proving such bad faith by clear and convincing evidence. Further, if it is demonstrated that the user party proceeding has been initiated without reasonable cause, the court may award costs against the plaintiff, including compensation for losses incurred by the defendant in defending the action. The remedies available under this Act are subject to principles of equity and fairness as determined by the relevant judicial forum.

Where a user party proceeding is initiated concerning the validity of a trade mark registration, the Registrar shall serve notice thereof upon all persons appearing on the register as registered users of the said trade mark. Such notice shall specify the grounds alleged in respect of invalidity and provide a period of ninety days from the date of service within which any interested party may file written submissions in response. The Registrar may, at his discretion, extend this period by a further thirty days upon application made before the expiry of the initial ninety-day period, provided that such application demonstrates reasonable cause for extension. Any registered user who receives notice under this provision shall be deemed to have special interest and may participate fully in the proceeding, presenting evidence and arguments as they deem relevant. The Registrar is empowered to direct any party to provide further information or clarification as necessary to facilitate a just determination of the matter.

A user party proceeding relating to rectification of a trade mark registration may be initiated by any person claiming an interest therein, subject to demonstrating reasonable grounds for believing that the mark is being used contrary to this Act. Such a claim must specify with particularity the nature and extent of the alleged misuse and provide supporting documentation as evidence thereof. The Registrar shall serve notice upon the registered proprietor, affording them opportunity to file a counter-statement within the prescribed timeframe. Further, where the user party proceeding involves allegations of dilution or tarnishment of reputation, the claimant shall be required to quantify the damages suffered, provided that such quantification is demonstrably linked to the alleged infringing activity. The Registrar may, at any stage, require further clarification from either party.

Any user party proceeding initiated against a proprietor alleging infringement of a registered trade mark shall require prior written notification served upon all registered users entitled to use the mark under license. Failure to provide such notification shall render the initiating party liable to pay compensatory damages, determined at the discretion of the adjudicating officer, not exceeding ten thousand rupees for each instance of non-compliance. Further, any order granted in favour of the proprietor based on a proceeding where proper user party notification was omitted may be subject to review and modification. The proprietor shall provide evidence demonstrating actual prejudice arising from the lack of notification; otherwise, remedies are restricted to injunctive relief and costs.

A user party proceeding relating to the enforcement of a trade mark may be initiated by the proprietor of the trade mark or by a registered user duly authorized under this Act. Where a license agreement grants rights to use a protected trade mark, such assignment of usage rights shall remain valid notwithstanding any subsequent alteration in ownership of the trade mark itself, provided that the original terms of the license are adhered to and no detrimental impact on the distinctiveness of the trade mark results from the continued use. Any transfer or disposal of a registered user’s entitlement to use a trade mark requires prior written consent from the proprietor, such consent not to be unreasonably withheld. Failure to obtain this consent shall render any subsequent action taken by the transferee void and subject to penalties as provided herein.

Where a third party opposes the registration of a trade mark, or seeks revocation of a registered trade mark under this Act, and such opposition or application for revocation is based on grounds relating to acquired distinctiveness, any user party proceeding in relation to that trade mark who has demonstrably relied upon representations made by the applicant or proprietor concerning the scope or nature of use shall be deemed to have a substantial interest in the outcome of the proceedings. The Registrar may, at the request of such user party, direct that they be joined as a co-respondent in the matter. Provided that any order directing joinder shall not prejudice the rights of appeal available under this Act to either the applicant or the proprietor. Further, the Tribunal may, upon application by a user party, grant interim relief pending determination of their participation.

Where a user party proceeding is initiated concerning the validity of a trade mark registration, the Registrar shall provide written notice to all parties appearing on the register as proprietors of identical or confusingly similar marks. Such notice shall detail the grounds upon which the challenge has been raised and afford each proprietor a period of sixty days from the date of such notice within which to file their response. Further, where the trade mark in question is an unregistered trade mark used by another party prior to the application for registration, evidence of such prior use must be submitted alongside the validity challenge. The Registrar may, at his discretion, require further documentation or clarification from any proprietor before proceeding with the hearing.

Where a user party proceeding is instituted alleging infringement of a registered trade mark, the Registrar may, subject to appeal under this Act, issue an injunction restraining the defendant from further acts of representation or use which constitute such alleged infringement. Provided that, in determining whether an act constitutes infringement, due consideration shall be given to any fair dealing undertaken by the defendant. Any party aggrieved by an order made during a user party proceeding may seek redress through appropriate legal channels. Furthermore, failure to comply with an injunction issued under this Act shall render the infringer liable to penalties as provided herein and subject to further design registry exercise review.

Where a user party proceeding is instituted concerning an alleged infringement of a trade mark, and such infringement demonstrably arises from modifications implemented following a patent addition relating to the goods or services for which the trade mark is registered, the Registrar may, sua sponte or upon application by any interested party, direct that the patent holder be joined as a necessary party in the said proceeding. This direction shall not prejudice the rights of either the trade mark proprietor or the patentee, and both parties shall be afforded full opportunity to present evidence and argument under this Act. Any order made pursuant to this provision may be appealed before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order, subject to any conditions prescribed herein.

A user party proceeding relating to rectification of a trade mark shall include any application filed by a person alleging that the registration of a trade mark is invalid or ought to be amended. For the purposes of this Act, an application entitled breeder means an application made by an individual who has demonstrably contributed to the development and propagation of a plant variety claimed as distinctive in the trade mark. Such an applicant shall be deemed a user party proceeding if they demonstrate ongoing commercial use of the registered trade mark in connection with said plant variety. Provided that this status does not confer any right to challenge the underlying validity of the plant variety protection itself, but only its registration as a trade mark.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark shall be entitled to institute proceedings for infringement under this Act in respect of any use of an identical or confusingly similar mark which is produced limits india. Where such infringement involves the passing off of goods as those of the registered proprietor, the remedies available include damages sustained by the proprietor, and further account of profits made by the infringing party. The Court may also grant an injunction restraining the defendant from continuing to use the infringing trade mark or any confusingly similar representation in relation to the impugned goods or services. Provided that, a finding of infringement shall not preclude a claim for passing off where the elements of deception and misrepresentation are independently established. Any order made under this Act may be enforced as if it were a decree of the Court.

The registration of a trade mark relating to goods manufactured or produced beyond the limits of India shall require evidence satisfactory to the Registrar that the applicant is duly authorized to use the trade mark in relation to those goods. Provided that, where the applicant is not the proprietor of the trade mark, such authorization must be evidenced by a power of attorney or other instrument executed in accordance with applicable law and duly authenticated. The Registrar may, at any time, require the deposition of an affidavit verifying the continued existence of this authorization. Failure to comply with these requirements shall render the registration liable for cancellation under this Act. Any alteration in the manufacturing process affecting the distinctive character of goods produced limits India necessitates notification to the Registrar within thirty days.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark relating to goods manufactured or produced beyond the limits of India may grant licenses for the use of that trade mark in respect of those goods within India. Such licenses shall specify the territory within which the licensee is authorized to manufacture, produce, import, distribute, sell, or otherwise deal with the licensed goods. The proprietor retains full ownership and control over the trade mark, subject to the terms stipulated in the license agreement. Any assignment of a registered trade mark relating to goods produced limits India must explicitly include provisions concerning any existing licenses granted under this Act, ensuring that such licenses remain valid and enforceable unless expressly terminated by mutual consent or as otherwise provided herein. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating compliance with these conditions prior to registration of an assignment.

The Registrar shall, upon receiving a request for international registration designating India, examine whether the mark is permissible under this Act and consistent with principles of natural justice. Where an objection arises concerning descriptiveness or conflict with prior rights, the applicant shall be afforded opportunity to submit representations. Failure to comply with such directions may result in rejection of the application. The Registrar may also require proof of due compliance with the provisions of the Budapest Treaty relating to the international registration. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar regarding the acceptance or refusal of an international mark produced limits india shall have recourse to appeal under this Act, subject to penalties for frivolous claims and costs awarded at the discretion of the Appellate Board.

For the purposes of this Act, a “reference geographical indication” means an indication which identifies goods originating from a specific area and is subject to conditions relating to the production, processing, or preparation of those goods, but which has not been registered as a geographical indication under this Act. Such reference geographical indications shall be deemed to possess characteristics attributable exclusively to the origin within that area. The use of a reference geographical indication shall not confer any right upon any person other than those who have acquired rights in respect of a registered geographical indication for identical or similar goods, provided that such use does not mislead consumers as to the true origin of the goods.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may include particulars relating to the agricultural area, its boundaries and natural conditions contributing to the qualities or characteristics of goods specified in the application. Subject to the provisions under this Act, an applicant shall furnish evidence demonstrating that the alleged reference geographical indication is exclusively associated with the territory named therein at the time of filing the application. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating such exclusive association, including historical records and demonstrable links between producers within the defined area and the reputation or qualities of the goods. Provided that any prior use of a similar name or mark shall not preclude registration if it can be demonstrated that there is no likelihood of confusion with registered geographical indications.

Any person alleging an infringement of a registered geographical indication may file a suit in the competent civil court seeking remedies including, but not limited to, injunctions restraining the use of the geographical indication or any confusingly similar indicator, and damages for losses suffered by the registrant as a consequence of such infringement. Subject to appeal under this Act, the court shall determine whether the defendant’s use constitutes an unfair advantage or misappropria­tion, considering factors such as consumer deception and dilution of the distinctive character of the registered geographical indication. Where a suit is filed alleging infringement of a reference geographical indication, the court may order the destruction of goods bearing the infringing indicator. The remedies available under this Act shall be without prejudice to any other rights or remedies available to the registrant under general principles of law.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may include particulars relating to the history, traditions and cultural heritage associated with the agricultural product or good concerned. Subject to the provisions under this Act, an officer authorized by the Registrar shall give notice of the receipt of such application to interested parties, specifying the geographical indication in question and inviting objections within two months from the date of publication of the notice. Any objection received shall be forwarded to the applicant for a reply, after which the Registrar may afford both parties an opportunity of being heard. Where the geographical indication sought to be registered is a *reference geographical indication*, the Registrar shall consider whether its use would likely cause confusion or misrepresentation among consumers. The Registrar’s decision on any objection shall be recorded in writing and made available for public inspection.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may be refused if the proposed name does not exclusively indicate the origin of the goods and is deemed descriptive of such goods, subject to an assessment that the distinctive character has been acquired through continued use. Where a geographical indication is already registered under this Act, any subsequent application proposing a substantially similar designation shall be rejected unless it can be demonstrated that there exists no likelihood of confusion arising with the existing reference geographical indication. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating adherence to established production practices and quality control measures as stipulated by a recognized producers’ association representing the interests of those engaged in producing goods corresponding to the proposed geographical indication, provided that such association is duly constituted under applicable law.

Any person who, without authorization from the Register, uses a registered geographical indication in contravention of this Act shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall be assessed at an amount not less than ten thousand rupees and not exceeding one million rupees per instance of infringement, as determined by the Geographical Indications Registry. Where the use is fraudulent or intended to cause a likelihood of confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of goods, the Register may also order seizure and destruction of infringing materials. The Register shall have the power to issue injunctions restraining any person from using a reference geographical indication in a manner prejudicial to the interests of the registered proprietor. Failure to comply with an order issued under this Act will attract penalties as provided herein.

The owner of a registered geographical indication may grant non-exclusive licenses authorizing specific uses of the indication relating to goods matching the description in the registration. Such licenses shall specify the duration, scope, and territorial extent of permitted activities, including but not limited to production, processing, packaging, distribution, and sale. Any assignment or transfer of ownership of a registered geographical indication requires prior approval from the Registrar, subject to publication for public objection under this Act. The Registrar may grant such approval if satisfied that the proposed assignee is suitable and possesses the requisite expertise to protect the interests associated with the reference geographical indication. Further, any licensee seeking to sub-license rights granted under this Act shall obtain written consent from the owner of the registered geographical indication, provided that such consent cannot be unreasonably withheld.

Where an objection is raised under this Act against the registration of a proposed geographical indication, alleging that it conflicts with pre-existing rights relating to trademarks or other forms of intellectual property, the Examining Officer shall provide the applicant and the objector each with an opportunity for written submissions and rejoinders. The Registrar may, after considering such submissions, direct the amendment of the application or proceed with registration as provided herein. Any party aggrieved by such direction may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. For the purposes of determining distinctiveness, a reference geographical indication shall be treated as lacking inherent distinctiveness unless evidence is presented demonstrating acquired reputation through extensive use and consumer recognition in the relevant market.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the registration of a geographical indication, including orders concerning revocation or amendment, may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of such order. Failure to comply with prescribed conditions for continued protection of a reference geographical indication shall render the registered proprietor liable to prosecution and penalties as provided herein. The Registrar may, suo moto or upon complaint, initiate inquiries into alleged violations of this Act concerning deceptive practices relating to geographical indications. Such investigations are deemed summary proceedings subject to judicial review under law. Penalties for fraudulent use or misrepresentation shall include fines up to five lakhs rupees and imprisonment extending to three years.

Where an objection is raised under this Act against the registration of a proposed geographical indication on the ground that it conflicts with an earlier registered trademark, or any right in a patented article, the Registrar may direct the applicant to amend the proposed indication so as not to cause such conflict, provided that the Trademark Registry or patent holder demonstrates demonstrable and ongoing commercial confusion arising directly from the similarity. The applicant shall be afforded a reasonable opportunity to present its case against such direction. Any party aggrieved by the Registrar’s decision under this provision may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days of the date of communication of the order, subject to payment of prescribed fees; the Appellate Board's determination shall be final. A reference geographical indication is deemed to conflict where it creates a likelihood of association with an existing trademark or patented article.

For the purposes of this Act, a “reference geographical indication” means an indication which is used in relation to goods for which a geographical indication is registered under this Act and which serves to identify those goods as originating from the territory specified in the registration of that geographical indication. Such reference shall not create any right or entitlement in respect of the registered geographical indication itself, but may be considered by a court section rectifying instances where such use constitutes unfair competition or misrepresentation affecting the interests of the registered proprietor. Provided that nothing herein shall prevent the legitimate and descriptive use of a reference geographical indication to describe characteristics of the goods.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may include particulars relating to the quality, reputation, or other characteristic of goods which are attributable to the origin of such goods. Subject to the provisions under this Act, the Geographical Indications Registry shall consider an applicant’s claim regarding the distinctiveness of the proposed geographical indication based on documented evidence demonstrating its association with the specified territory. Where the application relates to a reference geographical indication already recognized internationally, the Registrar may require additional documentation substantiating continued exclusive linkage between the goods and their origin within India, ensuring security india explanation is adequately addressed. Provided that such documentation demonstrates ongoing adherence to established production standards, registration shall be granted.

Any authorized user of a registered geographical indication shall be entitled to institute civil proceedings for infringement under this Act. Such infringement includes any act which, without due cause, uses a geographically misleading indication likely to deceive the public concerning the origin of goods and prejudice the interests of the registered proprietor. The remedies available in such suits include injunctions restraining further acts of infringement, damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the proprietor, and the delivery up or destruction of infringing goods as the Court deems fit. Provided that, nothing herein shall prevent a person from using a geographical indication which functions solely to describe the characteristics of the goods indicating their regional origin, but not in a way that constitutes a representation likely to mislead consumers regarding the true origin. The use of a trade mark incorporating elements of a reference geographical indication is subject to these restrictions.

Any authorized user utilizing a registered Geographical Indication in connection with goods conforming to the standards of quality and characteristics prescribed under this Act shall be entitled to restrain any party from making false indications that such goods originate from, or are produced in, the geographical territory associated with the indication. This right extends to preventing the use of similar names, marks, or symbols likely to cause confusion as to the origin of the goods. Where a registered Geographical Indication is subject to reference use geographical by an authorized user outside the defined area, such use shall not infringe upon the rights of the registration holder provided that it is demonstrably incidental and does not mislead consumers regarding the product's provenance. Remedies for infringement may include damages proportionate to the loss suffered and injunctions preventing further unauthorized use.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may include a statement specifying the extent of the territory to which the applicant claims protection under this Act, subject to the provisions regarding reference use geographical indications. Where an applicant seeks to limit the scope of protection afforded by registration to a specific area within the defined geographical unit, such limitation shall be clearly delineated in the application and supported by verifiable documentation demonstrating the distinct characteristics attributable solely to that restricted territory. The Geographical Indications Registry may require further evidence establishing the connection between the quality or other characteristic of the goods and the specified reference use geographical area. Failure to provide satisfactory evidence may result in rejection of the application or limitation of protection as determined by the Registrar. Any subsequent alteration of this defined area requires a separate application and approval process, as provided herein.

The Registering Authority may permit reference use of a registered geographical indication where such use is solely for descriptive purposes and does not suggest that the goods originate from the area associated with the indication. Such permission shall be granted only if the applicant demonstrates, through verifiable documentation, that the proposed use accurately reflects an inherent quality or characteristic of the goods, irrespective of their actual place of production.
