Where an aggrieved party alleges that a patent has been granted in contravention of this Act, and demonstrates to the satisfaction of the Controller that the specification does disclose matter which renders the claimed invention obvious at the time of filing, the Controller may, subject to due process, order rectification of the patent. Such rectification shall involve amendment of the claims to exclude the disclosed matter or, where such exclusion is not possible without substantially altering the nature of the invention, revocation of the patent in its entirety. The aggrieved party shall be entitled to recover from the patentee costs incurred in pursuing such proceedings, provided that the Controller finds the claim of obviousness to be well-founded and supported by credible evidence. Further, any use of a patented article infringing on amended or revoked claims will constitute an actionable wrong, subject to remedies available under this Act, including injunctions and damages, taking into account relevant mark regulations concerning consumer confusion.

Where an inventor elects to license rights pertaining to a patentable invention under this Act, and such invention’s specification does disclose all essential elements required for its practice, the licensing agreement shall clearly delineate the scope of permitted use. The licensee may, subject to the terms agreed upon, manufacture, use, or sell the patented invention within the territory specified in the license. Provided that any assignment of patent rights relating to a registered certification trade mark associated with the invention requires prior written consent from the Controller, confirming that such assignment does not dilute the distinctiveness or reputation of the certified product. Furthermore, sub-licensing is permissible only with the express authorization of the patent holder and shall be documented in writing. The patent holder retains the right to terminate the license agreement if the licensee fails to adhere to its terms, particularly concerning quality control measures relevant to any registered certification trade mark involved.

In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires,— (a) “well known trade mark”, in relation to any goods or services, means a mark which has acquired distinctiveness through association with goods or services provided by the proprietor and is widely recognized by section of the public likely to use those goods or services; such recognition shall be assessed having regard to duration, geographical extent, and reputation enjoyed by the mark. A mark may be deemed well known even if it is not registered in India, provided that its fame extends to India through importation, advertising, publicity, or other means. The Registrar shall consider evidence relating to consumer perception when determining whether a trade mark qualifies as “well known”.

context: For the purposes of this Act, “well known trade mark”, in relation to any goods or services, means a trade mark which has acquired distinctiveness through association with the goods or services and whose reputation is such that use by an unauthorized person would likely create confusion amongst consumers. The Registrar may determine whether a mark is well known based on factors including duration of use, geographical extent of the mark’s use, advertising expenditure, market share, recognition in different segments of society, and evidence of actual deception. A commission offence shall be committed where any person knowingly makes false representations concerning the distinctiveness or reputation of a trade mark to the Registrar as provided herein.

context: For the purposes of this Act, a “use mark relation” exists between two trademarks where one trademark has been used in relation to goods or services and that use creates a likelihood of confusion among the public regarding the origin or nature of those goods or services with respect to the other trademark. Such a relation shall be determined considering all relevant factors including, but not limited to, the similarity of the marks, the relatedness of the goods or services, and the conditions under which the trademarks are used in the marketplace. A use mark relation does not arise merely from contemporaneous use; it requires an element of consumer perception that links the two marks.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed on the ground that it is deceptively similar to a prior mark, the Registrar shall consider whether there exists a use mark relation between the applied-for mark and the earlier mark. For the purposes of determining such a relation, the Registrar may examine evidence demonstrating actual use of the earlier mark in connection with identical or closely related goods or services. The applicant for registration shall be afforded an opportunity to rebut any evidence presented by the opponent establishing this use mark relation. Provided that the mere existence of a prior mark does not automatically preclude registration; demonstrable lack of consumer confusion, notwithstanding similarity, may warrant allowing the application as provided herein.

Where the proprietor of a registered trademark, having used the mark in India for a continuous period of not less than five years, becomes aware that another person is using a sign identical or deceptively similar to the said mark in relation to goods or services not identical with but similar to those for which the registration is granted, the proprietor shall be entitled to apply to the Intellectual Property Tribunal for relief. Such relief may include an injunction restraining the infringing party from further use of the impugned sign and recovery of damages sustained by the proprietor as a consequence of the infringement. The determination of the *use mark relation* between the registered trademark and the infringing sign will consider, amongst other factors, the reputation and distinctiveness of the registered mark and the likelihood of confusion among consumers. Provided that, any such application shall be accompanied by an affidavit verifying the continuous use of the mark and the extent of damages suffered.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed on the ground that it is identical or confusingly similar to a prior mark used in relation to identical or similar goods or services, the Hearing Officer shall direct both the applicant and the opponent to submit their respective evidence pertaining to the use mark relation. Such evidence may include affidavits from proprietors, distributors, retailers, and consumers attesting to the extent and duration of such use. The Registrar may, at any stage of the proceedings, call upon either party to provide further clarification or documentation regarding the claimed use. Evidence submitted shall be deemed admissible subject to verification under this Act concerning its authenticity and relevance. Failure to adequately demonstrate a continuous and substantial use mark relation for a period exceeding five years prior to the date of the application may result in the opposition being dismissed, provided that the applicant demonstrates bona fide intention to use the mark.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is refused under this Act on the ground that it is deceptively similar to a prior mark, the Registrar shall consider whether there exists a use mark relation between the applied-for mark and the earlier mark. For determining such relation, the applicant must demonstrate continuous and substantial use of the mark in India for at least three years immediately preceding the date of application, provided that this period may be extended if the applicant establishes exceptional circumstances hindering prior use. The Registrar shall further assess whether said use has created confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or quality of goods or services offered under either mark. Evidence presented by third parties asserting such consumer confusion shall be given due weight in the assessment process.

Where any person institutes proceedings under this Act alleging infringement of a registered trade mark, and it is shown that the defendant has used a sign identical or similar to the plaintiff’s mark in relation to goods or services not identical with those for which the plaintiff's mark is registered, but such use constitutes a *use mark relation* whereby consumer confusion is likely to arise, the Court shall order an injunction restraining the defendant from any further use of the infringing sign. Such injunction may extend to all similar signs calculated to cause a likelihood of confusion. Furthermore, the plaintiff shall be entitled to recover damages sustained by him as a result of the infringement, or account for profits made by the defendant, whichever is higher, subject to such limitations as are provided herein regarding contributory infringement.

Where the registered proprietor of a trade mark, hereinafter referred to as the “licensor,” grants a license to another person, hereinafter referred to as the “licensee,” permitting the use of the said trade mark for specific goods or services, such license shall be assignable by the licensee subject to the prior written consent of the licensor. Provided that any assignment made without such consent shall be deemed void and unenforceable. The licensor may stipulate conditions within the license agreement regarding quality control measures relating to the licensed goods or services; failure to adhere to these conditions constitutes a breach of the license. Furthermore, where a use mark relation exists between a registered trade mark and another sign employed by a third party prior to registration, the proprietor shall be obligated to disclose this information in any assignment documentation submitted under this Act.

Where an objection is raised under this Act against the registration of a proposed trade mark on the ground that it is identical or confusingly similar to a prior registered trade mark, and the applicant demonstrates continuous use of the mark in relation to the goods or services for which registration is sought, notwithstanding such similarity, the Registrar may permit registration if satisfied that there exists a demonstrable *use mark relation* between the two marks. Such satisfaction shall be predicated upon evidence establishing that the public associates the proposed trade mark with the earlier registered mark due to factors including but not limited to common descriptive elements or shared promotional activities. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Registrar under this provision may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days, subject to payment of prescribed fees.

For the purposes of this Act, a “use mark relation” exists where a proprietor demonstrates continuous and demonstrable utilization of an identical or deceptively similar mark upon goods or services not covered by their registration, but which are related to those specified within the register. Such use shall be considered in determining whether there is likelihood of confusion under this Act. The demonstration of such use must include evidence establishing the geographical scope and duration of said usage. Further, any application for rectification based on a claim of improper use shall be subject to regulations concerning registration common regulations as provided herein.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is refused under this Act, and the applicant has previously used the mark, the Registrar may, if satisfied that the use was made bona fide and without intention to deceive or injure any other person, allow the registration subject to such limitations and conditions as he deems appropriate. Such conditions may include restricting the goods or services in relation to which the trade mark is registered, or requiring a disclaimer of certain rights claimed under this Act. The existence of a use mark relation does not, however, automatically entitle the applicant to registration; it remains subject to all other provisions herein relating to distinctiveness and potential conflict with prior marks. The registered proprietor shall be responsible for ensuring continued compliance with any such imposed limitations or conditions.

Where any proprietor of a registered trademark institutes proceedings under this Act for infringement, and it is established that the defendant has made use of an identical or deceptively similar mark in relation to identical or closely related goods or services, the Court may grant such remedy as it deems fit, including but not limited to an injunction restraining the defendant from further infringing the said trade mark. The proprietor shall be entitled to claim damages sustained by reason of the infringement, calculated on the basis of the defendant’s profits attributable to the infringing use, or where those cannot be ascertained with reasonable certainty, such sum as the Court may consider appropriate. Provided that in determining damages, the Court shall take into account any losses suffered by the defendant directly resulting from the proprietor's actions taken to protect their goods services act. The Court may also order delivery up or destruction of the infringing materials.

Where an application for registration of a trademark is refused under this Act, the applicant shall have the right to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeal may only be filed within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order of refusal. The appellant must demonstrate that the grounds for refusal are without merit and do not prevent registration in accordance with established principles concerning goods services act. Provided that, if the trademark contains a geographical indication defining a specific region or origin, the Appellate Board shall consider evidence establishing consumer recognition of such association. Further, any appeal challenging a finding regarding deceptively similar trademarks must include expert testimony substantiating the assessment.

For the purposes of this Act, “use” with reference to a trademark shall include not only the application of the mark on goods but also any act by which the sign is brought to the knowledge of the public as an indication of a connexion between the goods and services and a person undertaking trade under that mark. Such use includes, but is not limited to, representation of the mark in connection with the offering for sale, exposure for sale, or importation of such goods or services. The Registrar may prescribe conditions regarding the manner of *mark use* where it appears necessary to prevent dilution of distinctiveness. Provided that, use in the course of advertising shall be deemed a form of use under this Act.

The Registrar may require an applicant for registration of a proposed trade mark to furnish evidence demonstrating the extent and nature of the *mark use* undertaken prior to the date of application. Such evidence shall include, but not be limited to, invoices relating to sales, advertising materials distributed, and specimens illustrating the manner in which the mark is affixed to goods or packaging thereof. Where the applicant claims user as a potential trade mark, the period of such use shall be calculated from the earliest date of any such *mark use*. The Registrar may consider evidence submitted by third parties challenging the genuineness or extent of claimed *mark use*, provided that such challenges are filed within the prescribed timeframe and accompanied by supporting documentation. Any determination regarding the validity of *mark use* evidence is subject to appeal under this Act.

Where the registered proprietor of a trade mark institutes proceedings for infringement under this Act, it shall be incumbent upon the defendant to demonstrate that the alleged infringing use constitutes fair dealing. Such demonstration requires proof that the *mark use* was solely for the purpose of criticism or review and that no undue advantage was taken of the reputation or goodwill associated with the registered trade mark. The proprietor may seek an injunction restraining further acts of infringement, as well as damages to compensate for losses suffered directly attributable to the defendant’s actions. Provided that the court finds the infringing use has caused dilution of distinctiveness, it may award additional compensation reflecting such harm. Further, any party found guilty of intentional and substantial infringement shall be liable to pay enhanced damages, subject to considerations of proportionality and public interest.

The Registrar may, upon receiving an application for registration of a trade mark, direct the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating consistent and substantial *mark use* in accordance with the prescribed conditions. Such evidence shall include documentary proof detailing the manner and extent of such use across various media, including but not limited to packaging, advertising materials, and online platforms. The Registrar may require further clarification regarding the geographic scope of this mark use if it appears ambiguous or incomplete. Failure to provide satisfactory evidence as directed within the stipulated timeframe shall render the application liable for rejection under this Act. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar concerning the sufficiency of mark use evidence may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, subject to the procedural requirements outlined herein and payment of the prescribed fee.

The proprietor of a registered trade mark shall, subject to compliance with prescribed regulations, be entitled to institute proceedings for infringement where there is demonstrable evidence of unauthorized application of an identical or deceptively similar mark upon goods or services. Such application constitutes *mark use* and may include, but is not limited to, display on packaging, advertising materials, or directly affixed to the goods themselves. The Registrar may require submission of detailed records documenting the extent and duration of such use as proof of infringement. Provided that the proprietor can establish a likelihood of confusion amongst relevant consumers, remedies including injunctions and damages shall be available. Further, any alteration to the registered mark following registration, which affects its distinctiveness, is subject to review under this Act.

Where any person makes use of a trade mark identical or confusingly similar to a registered trade mark in contravention of this Act, without the consent of the proprietor of the registered trade mark, such person shall be liable for damages. The amount of damages shall be determined having regard to the loss suffered by the proprietor as a result of the infringing *mark use*, and may include an assessment of profits made by the infringer attributable to the infringement. Further, any goods so bearing the infringing mark are deemed to be falsely marked and subject to seizure and destruction at the expense of the offender. Repeated or flagrant instances of such unauthorized *mark use* shall attract enhanced penalties as determined under this Act, without prejudice to criminal proceedings.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any registered proprietor of a trademark may grant a license to use the mark for specific goods or services, defining the geographical area and duration of such license. Such licenses shall be assignable, subject to registration with the Registrar within thirty days of the assignment. Where a license is granted, the licensee shall be deemed to be using the trademark in relation to the licensed goods or services for the purposes of determining infringement under this Act. The registered proprietor may impose conditions on the use of the mark by the licensee, provided that such conditions do not contravene any other provision of this Act and are clearly stated within the license agreement. Any subsequent assignment of the registered trademark shall include a record of all existing licenses and their terms as provided herein. The continued mark use by a licensee shall be contingent upon adherence to these stipulated conditions.

Where an objection is raised before the Trade Marks Registry alleging that the applicant’s proposed mark, or any element thereof, conflicts with matter already registered under this Act, or capable of being registered, the Registrar shall provide the opponent with a reasoned statement detailing the grounds for such conflict. The applicant shall then be afforded a reasonable opportunity to rebut the objection and present counter-arguments demonstrating the absence of likelihood of confusion or deception amongst consumers. Evidence pertaining to the extent and nature of *mark use* by both parties may be submitted, including but not limited to advertising materials, sales figures, and consumer surveys. Any determination made by the Registrar shall be subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, provided that such appeal is filed within a period specified herein.

For the purposes of this Act, “mark use” shall mean the application of a registered trademark to goods or their packaging, or the presentation of a service under that mark. Such application may include, but is not limited to, affixing, imprinting, embroidering, painting, or otherwise incorporating the mark onto the relevant item. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating continuous and substantial mark use following an application registration, particularly where objections have been raised concerning distinctiveness or deceptively similar marks. Any alteration of a registered trademark after its initial registration shall be deemed a new mark use subject to further scrutiny under this Act.

The Registrar may, upon application and subject to the provisions herein, register a proposed trade mark if he is satisfied that the applicant has established continuous *mark use* in accordance with prescribed guidelines. Such use shall demonstrate bona fide commercial exploitation of the mark within the territory of India for at least three years preceding the date of application, or as otherwise permitted under this Act. Evidence of such use may include invoices, sales records, advertising materials and other documentation demonstrating consumer recognition. Failure to adequately establish *mark use* may result in refusal of registration. Where a registered trade mark is used in a manner contrary to honest practices in industrial competition, or which constitutes an act of passing off, the Registrar shall consider any objections raised by interested parties.

Where any proprietor institutes proceedings alleging an infringement of their registered trademark, and it is demonstrated before a Bench that the respondent has used a sign identical or confusingly similar to the said mark, the Court shall grant such remedy as it deems just and equitable. This includes, but is not limited to, perpetual injunction restraining further use of the infringing sign, and an order for accounts of profits derived from the unauthorized *mark use*. The proprietor may also seek damages proportionate to the loss suffered due to the infringement, subject to considerations of bad faith on the part of either party. Further, where the respondent has made false representations concerning their association with the trademark owner, the Court may award punitive damages as a deterrent against similar conduct. Any order for delivery up or destruction of infringing materials shall be enforceable by appropriate processes under this Act.

A trade mark consists of a sign having the capability of distinguishing the goods or services of one undertaking from those of other undertakings. Such signs include, but are not limited to, words, letters, numerals, shapes, configurations, patterns, monograms, three-dimensional objects, colour arrangements, and any combination thereof. Provided that such signs are capable of being represented graphically, they shall be eligible for registration as a trade mark under this Act. The representation may be in the form of a drawing, photograph or other visual means. Subject to certain conditions specified herein, sounds, smells, tastes, and gestures may also constitute a trade mark.

A trade mark shall be deemed registrable under this Act if it is capable of distinguishing the applicant’s goods or services from those of others and does not consist exclusively of a sign which describes those goods or services. Where an application for registration includes a device, the description thereof shall clearly indicate the elements of the device that are claimed as distinctive. The Registrar may require the applicant to amend the representation of a mark if it is deemed unclear or fails to accurately reflect the applied-for trade mark. Provided that any amendment does not alter the character of the trade mark, such alteration shall be permissible. A trade mark consists of words, letters, symbols, shapes, and colours used to identify goods or services.

A trade mark shall be deemed to consist of a sign capable of representing words, including invented words, letters, numerals, shapes, configurations, patterns, monograms, three-dimensional objects, colour arrangements, or any combination thereof. Provided that such signs are graphically representable and may distinguish the goods or services of one undertaking from those of other undertakings. Any proprietor seeking relief under this Act for infringement shall demonstrate a likelihood of confusion arising amongst the relevant public due to the use of an identical or similar sign in relation to identical or similar goods or services. Further, where a trade mark consists exclusively of signs serving solely to indicate the geographical origin of the goods, such a mark is not registrable unless it has acquired distinctiveness through use. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating this acquired distinctiveness prior to registration.

A trade mark shall be deemed to consist essentially of a label, ticket, device, signature, or any other mark of identification used in relation to the sale of any goods or services. Where an application for registration is filed and it is alleged that the proposed trade mark consists of a geographical indication as defined under this Act, the Registrar may require the applicant to furnish evidence establishing their connection with the territory named in the indication, and demonstrating that use of the mark will not mislead consumers regarding the origin of the goods or services. Any party opposing such an application may present counter-evidence challenging these claims. The Registrar shall consider all submitted documentation and hear any interested parties before rendering a decision as provided herein. Further, a trade mark consisting of shapes of articles may be registered if it has acquired distinctiveness through use.

A registered trade mark shall be deemed personal property and may be assigned or licensed by the proprietor subject to such terms and conditions as are agreed upon between the parties. Where a license is granted, the licensee shall possess the right to use the trade mark in relation to specified goods or services for a defined period, provided that the licensing agreement explicitly states whether it is exclusive or non-exclusive. Any assignment of a registered trade mark requires registration with the Registrar and takes effect only upon such registration. The proprietor may also grant security interests over their trade marks, permitting another party to claim rights in the trade mark as collateral for a debt. A trade mark consists of a word, name, symbol, device, or any combination thereof. Further, sub-licensing is permissible provided it aligns with the original licensing agreement’s stipulations and does not contravene this Act.

A trade mark shall be deemed to consist not only of a word, name, symbol, device, or any combination thereof, but also of any colour or configuration of goods or their packaging, provided that such colour or configuration is capable of distinguishing them from the goods or services of others. An appeal against a determination under this Act concerning whether a proposed trade mark consists exclusively of signs which are common to the trade may be made to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The Board shall, in hearing such an appeal, consider whether the applicant has demonstrated acquired distinctiveness through extensive use and recognition by consumers, subject to the provisions regarding unfair competition as provided herein.

The Registrar shall not register any mark under this Act if it contains solely marks indications customary in the relevant trade or industry and serving merely to indicate such characteristics as the nature, quality, mode of manufacture, or intended purpose of the goods or services. Provided that a sign or combination of signs may nevertheless be registered if, through association with the goods or services, it has acquired distinctiveness by the time of application for registration. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating such acquired distinctiveness, and shall consider any opposition filed under this Act relating to the customary nature of the mark applied for. Further, marks which are geographically descriptive of the origin of goods shall be subject to similar scrutiny as provided herein.

The Registrar shall not register any mark under this Act if it contains merely marks indications customary in the particular trade or locality where the goods or services are supplied. Such marks indications, when used, do not reasonably distinguish the goods or services from those of other traders. Provided that the Board may, upon application by an interested party and after affording due opportunity for hearing, allow registration if satisfied that the mark has acquired distinctiveness through use subsequent to its first entry into commerce. The applicant shall bear the burden of proving such acquired distinctiveness. Any objection raised under this provision must be filed within three months from the date of advertisement of the trademark application. The Registrar may require further evidence or clarification as deemed necessary during the examination process, and any decision made by the Registrar is subject to appeal before the Appellate Board.

A mark shall not be registered as a trade mark under this Act if it contains any indication likely to deceive consumers regarding the nature, quality or geographical origin of goods or services. Where a sign functions primarily as an indication customary in the relevant trade, and its use is prevalent and understood by those familiar with such trade practices, registration may proceed provided that evidence demonstrating non-distinctiveness has not been presented. The Registrar shall consider any submissions from interested parties regarding the customary nature of a mark and whether it serves solely to describe goods or services. Further, an application for registration shall be refused if the proposed mark comprises exclusively marks indications customary in relation to the goods or services concerned, unless the applicant demonstrates acquired distinctiveness through extensive use over a significant period.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, any proprietor of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to grant a license conferring upon the licensee the right to use the said trade mark in relation to specified goods or services for a defined period. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as determined by the licensor, and the terms thereof shall be documented in writing. Where a proprietor seeks to assign their registered trade mark, including any associated goodwill arising from its usage, consent of the Registrar shall be obtained prior to such assignment taking effect. Marks indications customary to designate goods may be licensed without requiring specific permission from the owner provided that such use does not create confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or quality of those goods and is consistent with established trade practices. Any transfer of rights relating to marks indications customary must adhere to principles of fair dealing as outlined herein.

An application for registration of a mark shall include a representation of the mark and a list specifying the goods or services with which the mark is associated. The Registrar may require an applicant to amend the marks indications included in their application if they are deemed offensive, deceptive, or contrary to law. Where the proposed mark comprises a combination of elements, including words, devices, or three-dimensional shapes, the representation shall clearly depict all such components as intended for use. An applicant seeking registration under this Act must provide evidence demonstrating distinctiveness acquired through the use of the mark in trade, provided that such use has been continuous and substantial. The Registrar may object to an application if it considers the proposed marks indications to be generic or descriptive of the goods or services.

A proprietor shall be entitled to institute proceedings for infringement of a registered trade mark under this Act where there is use by any person in the course of trade likely to cause confusion to the public, or denote that the goods or services are connected in the trade with him. Such use includes the application of a mark identical or similar to the registered marks as marks indications, whether precise or approximate, and whether adopted in relation to identical or similar goods or services. Provided that, where the defendant proves that he has used the mark honestly and for the purpose of describing the characteristics of his goods or services, or indicating their geographical origin, relief may be granted subject to such terms and conditions as the Court deems just. The remedies available include an injunction restraining further infringement and damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the proprietor.

Marks used as indications of geographical origin shall be admissible for registration subject to provisions regarding deceptive practices. An application for registration of a mark indicating geographical origin must specify the actual place or region from which the goods originate and provide detailed particulars establishing such origin. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating that the asserted geographical connection is verifiable and not misleading to consumers. Any person claiming rights in relation to a registered geographical indication may, under this Act, institute proceedings before the relevant intellectual property tribunal for infringement or passing off. Such claims shall be considered based on whether the use of the mark creates confusion regarding the goods’ origin. The Registrar may, upon receiving objections from interested parties, conduct hearings and determine the validity of such marks indications.

The proprietor of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to grant licences conferring rights to use such mark upon specified goods or services, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated in the licence agreement. Such agreements may include provisions for royalty payments, duration of the licence, and geographical limitations on usage. Further, under this Act, a proprietor may assign their entire interest in a registered trade mark, including all associated rights and privileges, to another party by way of deed or other instrument in writing. Any such assignment shall be recorded with the Trade Marks Registry as provided herein. The use of marks indications that are confusingly similar to an existing registered mark, even under a valid licence or assignment, is prohibited unless expressly permitted through a co-existence agreement approved by the Registrar.

The use of any mark, whether registered under this Act or not, in relation to goods or services identical or similar to those for which registration has been obtained by another person, and calculated to create confusion or deception among the public as to the identity of the origin of such goods or services, shall constitute infringement. Where a proprietor of a trade mark establishes that use of an impugned mark is likely to cause dilution of distinctiveness of their registered marks, they may apply for an injunction restraining such use. Any alteration to the registered form of a mark, or any colourable imitation thereof, without leave of the relevant authority, shall also be deemed infringement. The proprietor shall be entitled to claim damages proportionate to the loss suffered by them as a result of the infringement, and further, account of profits made by the infringer may be awarded. Marks indications used in a manner contrary to honest practices in industrial property are prohibited under this Act.

A mark shall be considered registrable as a trademark only if it is capable of distinguishing the goods or services of the applicant from those of others and does not consist exclusively of marks indications that describe essential characteristics of the goods. Provided that, marks indicating the geographical origin of goods are permissible for registration subject to compliance with prescribed conditions regarding accuracy and absence of misleading implications concerning such origin. Further, a mark shall not be registered if its use or application is contrary to accepted principles of morality or public order. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating acquired distinctiveness where an initial assessment suggests a lack thereof, particularly in relation to goods that are widely distributed.

A mark shall be deemed to be capable of being a trademark if it is used to represent or distinguish goods or services offered by any person and includes any sign, symbol, device, letter, numeral, shape, configuration, colour or arrangement of colours, or any combination thereof. For the purposes of this Act, marks indications serve primarily to identify and associate specific goods or services with a particular undertaking. Nothing in this provision shall prevent a mark from being registered if it has acquired distinctiveness through use subsequent to its first use in trade or otherwise as provided herein. The Registrar may require proof of such use during examination of the application.

An application for registration of a mark shall be deemed to be made in bad faith if it is filed with intent to deceive or cause confusion amongst consumers regarding the source or nature of the goods or services. The Registrar may require an applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating acquired distinctiveness where the applied-for mark possesses no inherent distinctive character, provided that such evidence substantiates consumer recognition and association with the applicant’s goods or services. Marks indications serve primarily to identify and distinguish goods from those of others; consequently, a refusal of registration shall be issued if the proposed mark is descriptive of the essential characteristics of the goods for which it is sought, or if its use would unfairly prejudice existing trade mark proprietors.

An application for registration of a mark shall be deemed to be made in accordance with this Act if it contains a clear representation of the mark sought to be registered and a list specifying all the goods or services in relation to which the applicant desires that the mark should be registered. The Registrar may, upon receiving an application, direct the applicant to amend the representation of the mark or the specification of goods or services where such amendment is necessary to conform to the provisions herein. Where a mark contains elements adopted from existing marks already registered under this Act, the applicant shall provide evidence demonstrating that use of the applied-for mark will not cause confusion amongst consumers. Marks indications serve primarily to identify and distinguish goods or services; therefore, any mark which is likely to be confused with an earlier mark shall be rejected. The Registrar may require further information from the applicant at any stage of the examination process.

A mark shall be registrable under this Act if it is capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one undertaking from those of other undertakings. Provided that a mark may still be registered even if it has initially acquired its distinctive character solely by reason of the fact that it has been continuously used in India, subject to compliance with prescribed conditions regarding duration and extent of such use. Marks indications serve primarily to identify and differentiate goods or services within the marketplace; therefore, any representation which is liable to be confused with a prior mark already registered shall not be registrable. Furthermore, marks consisting exclusively of shapes resulting from the nature of the goods themselves are ineligible for registration unless they indicate specific quality characteristics.

Any individual or enterprise employing a mark identical or confusingly similar to a registered trade mark, with the intent to unfairly exploit the reputation and goodwill associated therewith, shall be liable for damages. Such liability extends to instances where the infringing use creates a likelihood of confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or sponsorship of goods or services. The Registrar may, upon complaint, issue an injunction restraining further acts of infringement, subject to due process and opportunity for the defendant to present their case. Failure to comply with such an order shall constitute contempt of court and render the defaulter liable to a fine not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees, or imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or both, as provided herein. Marks indications serve solely to identify goods and services and are not permissible for deceptive advertising purposes.

The owner of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to grant licenses conferring specific rights relating to the use of their mark upon third parties. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and may specify geographical limitations or restrictions on the goods or services in relation to which the license is granted. Assignment of a trade mark, or any interest therein, including such licenses, shall require registration with the Trade Marks Registry, subject to payment of prescribed fees. Any person acquiring an assignment under this Act shall be deemed the new proprietor for all purposes. Where a license agreement includes provisions concerning quality control measures relating to goods bearing the marks indications serve to identify their origin or characteristics, these provisions shall be binding on both licensor and licensee. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating compliance with such quality control standards.

Where an objection is raised under this Act against the registration of a proposed trade mark on the ground that it conflicts with an earlier mark, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to file a counter-statement rebutting such objection. The Registrar may, after giving notice to both parties and affording them a hearing, determine whether the use of the impugned mark is likely to cause confusion or deception as to the origin of goods or services. Provided that, if either party disputes the findings of the Registrar, an appeal lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. It is established that marks indications serve to identify and distinguish goods; therefore, similarity in appearance or sound shall be a material consideration in such determinations.

The registered mark, “Evergreen Spices,” shall be deemed a valuable asset subject to assignment and licensing as provided herein. Any proprietor desiring to grant a license for use of the said mark upon any product other than those specifically detailed in their specification claim relating to culinary herbs and related seasonings must submit an application to the Controller detailing the scope of such permitted usage, including geographical territories and duration. The Controller may approve or reject such applications based on considerations of consumer protection and potential dilution of the Evergreen Spices brand identity. Marks indications serve to identify goods; therefore, any sublicensee shall adhere strictly to the terms stipulated in the primary license agreement and as further defined by the Controller’s approval. Failure to comply with these conditions will render the sublicense liable for damages and revocation of their usage rights under this Act.

For the purposes identifying goods, a “good” shall include any commodity, article, manufacture, or composition which is bought, sold, or bartered. The term "services" includes the rendition of an act or performance relating to any trade, business, calling, profession, or occupation. A representation concerning goods or services shall be deemed to propose a mark even if it does not contain elements that are capable of graphical depiction under this Act. Provided that, where a geographical indication is used in relation to goods indicating the origin of those goods, such use shall not constitute an unfair competition unless it deceives consumers as to the true source thereof.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall include a clear representation of the marks applied for and a list of goods or services in relation to which it is sought. The Statement of Goods and Services must specify with sufficient clarity the nature of those goods or services, ensuring that the description facilitates consumer understanding and avoids ambiguity. Where the applicant seeks to register a trade mark for multiple classes of goods or services, each class shall be distinctly identified within the application. Registration may be refused if the marks applied for, when used in relation to the specified goods, are descriptive solely of the characteristics of those goods. The purposes identifying goods must be clearly articulated and substantiated by the applicant.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark shall be entitled to restrain the use of any sign which is identical or confusingly similar to the said trade mark in relation to goods or services, provided that such use creates a likelihood of confusion on the part of the public and causes damage to the reputation or goodwill associated with the trade mark. Where a person uses a trade mark in a manner contrary to honest practices in industrial or commercial matters, or takes unfair advantage of, or is detrimental to, the distinctive character or repute of the registered trade mark, remedies shall be available under this Act. The purposes identifying goods shall not excuse conduct that dilutes the distinctiveness of a mark enjoyed by another. Any party aggrieved may institute proceedings seeking an injunction and damages for infringement as provided herein.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark includes a representation of goods which are not exclusively those comprised in class 25, the Registrar may require the applicant to amend the specification of goods to exclude such representations. Such amendment shall be made only if the Registrar is satisfied that the original representation was included inadvertently or due to a misunderstanding of the classification system as provided herein. The Registrar shall provide written reasons for any requirement to amend the application. An appeal against this determination may be filed under this Act within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. For the purposes identifying goods, an applicant must demonstrate a genuine connection between the trade mark and the specified goods; failure to do so will render the application liable to rejection.

A trade mark shall be eligible for registration if, upon application, it is demonstrated that its primary function is to serve purposes identifying goods. The Registrar may require evidence substantiating this claim, including but not limited to market research data and consumer surveys indicating a direct association between the mark and the specified goods. Provided that the applicant demonstrates exclusive use of the trade mark in relation to those goods for a continuous period exceeding three years immediately preceding the date of application, such demonstration shall be considered conclusive evidence of its suitability under this Act. However, registration may be refused if it is established that the mark’s adoption was primarily intended to confuse or mislead consumers regarding the origin or quality of the goods.

No trade mark shall be registered if, at the time of application, use thereof by any person in relation to goods or services is the sole means of identifying those goods or services and such use has been continuous for a period exceeding five years from the commencement of this Act. Provided that where an applicant can demonstrate prior honest non-infringing use solely for purposes identifying goods, the Registrar may, subject to conditions as deemed appropriate, allow registration if it is established that any subsequent conflicting mark would likely cause confusion amongst consumers. Any person employing a trade mark in violation of these provisions shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakhs rupees and further damages proportionate to lost sales.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark shall have the exclusive right to grant licenses permitting the use of their trade mark for purposes identifying goods, subject to the conditions stipulated in the license agreement. Such agreements may specify the geographical area within which the licensee is authorized to utilize the trade mark and the specific classes of goods covered by the license. A license granted under this Act shall be assignable along with the underlying trade mark registration, provided that notice of such assignment is filed with the Registrar within thirty days of the transfer. Any subsequent use of the trade mark by the assignee shall be deemed to be authorized by the original proprietor until such time as the assignment is formally registered. The Registrar may require proof of consent from the original proprietor before registering an assignment involving a license agreement.

Where an objection is taken under this Act against the registration of a trade mark on the ground that it is descriptive of the goods or services for which it is sought to be registered, the Registrar may allow the registration if he is satisfied that, by reason of its use and reputation, the mark has acquired distinctiveness applicable to those goods. Such acquisition shall not preclude an appeal against the decision of the Registrar permitting such registration, wherein the appellant may demonstrate that the purported acquired distinctiveness is attributable solely to extensive advertising campaigns undertaken by the applicant and does not genuinely reflect consumer perception concerning purposes identifying goods. The burden of proving this lies upon the appellant, subject to a rebuttable presumption in favour of the applicant’s claim.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark shall have the exclusive right to license the use of that trade mark for purposes identifying goods or services, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated in the licensing agreement. Such agreements may grant non-exclusive rights allowing multiple licensees to utilize the mark concurrently within defined geographical territories or product categories. Further, any assignment of a registered trade mark shall include all associated licenses previously granted, unless expressly excluded by written consent from both the assignor and assignee. Where a licensee utilizes a trade mark in a manner inconsistent with the terms of their license, or engages in activities that demonstrably dilute the distinctiveness of the mark, the proprietor may initiate proceedings under this Act to have such use deemed falsify trade and seek injunctive relief.

For the purposes identifying goods, a ‘generic name’ shall mean a term which, at the time of application for registration, is commonly used in relation to a class of goods and has no trade significance. A term shall not be deemed to have trade significance merely by reason of its frequent use in normal descriptive speech. The Registrar may, upon receiving an objection under this Act regarding the generic nature of a proposed mark, require the applicant to submit evidence demonstrating acquired distinctiveness through extensive use. An entry register maintained for record purposes shall note any such objections and supporting documentation received concerning a mark’s potential genericity.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall include a clear representation of the marks applied for and a list specifying the goods or services with which the mark is proposed to be associated. The Registrar may require an applicant to amend the description of goods or services if he considers it too wide or vague, ensuring clarity in identifying goods. Such amendments shall not alter the essence of the application. Where the trade mark includes non-distinctive elements, the applicant must demonstrate acquired distinctiveness through use, providing evidence of reputation and consumer recognition relating to the purposes identifying goods. The registered proprietor shall possess exclusive rights to use the trade mark in relation to the specified goods or services, subject to any limitations imposed during registration.

Where any dispute arises concerning the validity of a trade mark registration based on its relation to a Contract ing State or a Contracting Organisation, the aggrieved party shall have the right to appeal under this Act to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. Such an appeal may only be entertained if it is demonstrated that the purported connection lacks genuine commercial substance and constitutes an attempt to circumvent the provisions regarding domicile or establishment requirements. The Tribunal shall consider evidence pertaining to the operational activities, personnel, and financial resources of the entity claiming relation, provided that the burden of proving lack of genuine connection rests upon the appellant. Any order made by the Tribunal may be further appealed to the High Court within ninety days.
primary_entity: ation to a Contract ing State or a Contracting Organisation

context: For the purposes of this Act, “real and effective industrial or commercial establishment” means an undertaking possessing tangible assets, including but not limited to land, buildings, machinery, and equipment, utilized for the manufacture of goods or provision of services directly related to the trade mark in question; provided that such undertaking demonstrates continuous operational activity and employs a minimum number of personnel as may be prescribed by regulations framed under this Act. An entity maintaining only a registered office or a postal address shall not, without further demonstration of substantial commercial operations, be considered to possess a real and effective industrial or commercial establishment as defined herein.
primary_entity: “real and effective industrial or commercial establishment

context: Where an objection is raised under this Act against the registration of a trade mark on the ground that it is deceptively similar to any prior registered trade mark or any other identifiable trade mark, the Trade Marks Registry shall give notice thereof to the applicant for registration and to the proprietor of the earlier trade mark. The applicant may then file its counter-statement within the time specified in the notice, setting out reasons why the objection should not be sustained. In determining whether a trade mark is deceptively similar, the Registry shall consider all relevant factors including the similarity of the marks, the goods or services for which the respective trade marks are used, and the likelihood of confusion on the part of the public. For the purposes of establishing a “real and effective industrial or commercial establishment”, an applicant must demonstrate continuous activity directly related to the use of the mark in commerce.
primary_entity: “real and effective industrial or commercial establishment

context: Where any proprietor institutes proceedings for infringement under this Act, it shall be incumbent upon such proprietor to demonstrate beyond reasonable doubt the existence of a “real and effective industrial or commercial establishment” in India relating to the trade mark in question at the time of the alleged infringement. Failure to provide satisfactory evidence establishing said connection may result in the dismissal of the suit with costs. Provided that, where the defendant asserts that the use of the impugned sign does not cause damage to the proprietor’s interests, the onus shall be upon the defendant to substantiate this claim. Any party found to have knowingly presented false or misleading information regarding their industrial or commercial establishment shall be liable for penalties as provided herein.
primary_entity: “real and effective industrial or commercial establishment

context: For the purposes of this Act, an international registration basic to an earlier trade mark shall mean a designation made under the Madrid Protocol wherein the applicant seeks protection for their trade mark in India, and such designation incorporates by reference the list of goods or services specified in the initial application for the international registration. The earlier trade mark is deemed to be the trade mark upon which the subsequent international registration is based. An international registration basic to an earlier trade mark shall not affect any rights acquired under this Act prior to the date of its extension to India, provided that such rights were duly established.

An international registration shall be deemed to be based on an earlier trade mark registered in India if the applicant for such international registration has previously filed an application for the same marks in respect of identical goods or services under this Act. The Trade Marks Registry may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating the priority date of the earlier Indian registration, including certified copies of the register entry and any relevant correspondence exchanged with the registry. Where multiple designations include India within an international registration, the provisions relating to opposition shall apply as if the international registration were a trade mark application filed directly in India on the date of its designation. Any person aggrieved by the acceptance of an international registration designating India may institute proceedings under this Act against the proprietor of the earlier Indian trade mark. The Registrar shall have the power to order rectification of the register, provided that such rectification is consistent with the principles governing international registration basic.

An international registration shall have effect only to the extent that the mark is registrable under the law of the designated country, subject to any limitations specified by that country’s legislation concerning the scope of protection afforded. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating compliance with all applicable regulatory requirements in each designated territory prior to recording an international registration basic to a trade mark registered in India. Such evidence shall include, but is not limited to, declarations from authorized representatives confirming registrability and any necessary translations of the mark or application. Failure to provide satisfactory evidence as provided herein may result in refusal to record the international registration basic.

An international registration shall have effect only to the extent that the mark is registrable under the laws of the designated country and any refusal by the receiving office to accept the designation shall be deemed conclusive evidence for the purposes of enforcement proceedings under this Act. Where an international registration designating India is subsequently opposed, the Registrar may require the applicant to furnish proof of use of the trade mark in India as a condition precedent to registration, subject to such reasonable extensions as the Registrar deems fit. Any person aggrieved by a decision relating to an international registration basic application may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order and shall be liable for costs determined by the Board.

The owner of a trade mark registered under this Act shall be entitled to apply for an international registration designating India, provided that such application is based on a prior registration of the trade mark in the country or origin of the applicant. Any assignment or license of the trade mark, whether absolute or subject to conditions, shall be deemed valid only if recorded with the Trade Marks Registry within three months from the date of execution; failure to do so renders the assignee or licensee liable to proceedings as if they were an infringer. Further, a subsequent international registration basic upon such prior Indian registration may be assigned freely, subject to any restrictions contained in the original assignment document relating to the initial domestic trade mark. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all assignments and licenses pertaining to internationally registered marks.

Where an applicant seeks to avail himself of the benefits of international registration under this Act, he shall file with the Registrar Form TM-R, accompanied by a certified copy of the international registration certificate issued by the International Bureau and details of the designating countries including India. The Registrar may require such further documentation as is necessary to establish the priority date and entitlement to claim an international registration basic to an earlier application filed in another jurisdiction. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar regarding the acceptance or rejection of an application for international registration, or concerning the validity thereof, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of such decision; provided that the Board shall not be bound by any observation made during the hearing and may substitute its own observations.

The owner of an international registration designating India under this Act shall be entitled to grant licenses relating to the use of the trade mark for any goods or services specified in the register, subject to such terms and conditions as are agreed upon between the licensor and licensee. Such license agreements may include provisions for assignment of the right to utilize the mark within India, provided that the assignor retains ultimate ownership of the international registration itself. Where an international registration basic to an Indian trade mark is subsequently surrendered or cancelled in a designated country outside of India, this shall not automatically affect the validity of the designation relating to India unless such surrender or cancellation arises from a decision concerning registrability under this Act. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating compliance with the Budapest Treaty International system for recording international marks.

For the purposes of this Act, a “business basic application” shall mean an application for registration of a trade mark filed by a person who, at the time of filing, possesses no prior demonstrable use of the mark in relation to any goods or services within the territory of India, and whose intention is solely to secure exclusive rights in the mark through registration under this Act. Such an applicant shall be deemed to have knowledge of all prior relevant trade marks and shall be subject to a higher standard of scrutiny regarding distinctiveness assessment as provided herein. A business basic application does not preclude subsequent demonstration of use affecting entitlement.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed to include a business basic application where the applicant demonstrates a bona fide intention to use the mark in relation to the goods or services specified therein. Such demonstration may take the form of prior use, however limited, or evidence of concrete steps taken towards bringing the mark into use within a reasonable period. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating this business basic application and may reject the same if satisfied that the applicant has not genuinely intended to apply the trade mark as claimed. An appeal against such rejection lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, subject to conditions regarding timelines for filing appeals and supporting affidavits.

Where any person makes a business basic application for registration of a trade mark, the Trade Marks Registry shall examine whether the proposed marks are distinctive in their respective goods or services and not descriptive of those goods or services. If, upon examination, the Registrar finds that the use of the mark would likely to cause confusion amongst the public, or otherwise infringe any pre-existing rights under this Act, the application may be rejected. Any party claiming such prior rights shall have standing to object to the business basic application and present evidence substantiating their claim. The applicant shall then be afforded an opportunity to respond to said objections and submit counter-evidence. Failure to adequately address these concerns may result in the rejection of the trade mark application, subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed to include a business basic application where the applicant demonstrates, through documentary evidence satisfactory to the Registrar, that they have used the proposed trade mark in connection with the specified goods or services within the territory of India for a period not less than six months immediately preceding the date of filing. Such use shall constitute honest commercial practice and must not be deceptive or misleading to the public regarding the nature, quality, or geographical origin of those goods or services. The Registrar may require further particulars concerning such prior use, including details of sales figures and marketing activities. Provided that, if the applicant is unable to provide complete documentation relating to the business basic application, they shall be afforded an opportunity for a hearing before a decision is made regarding acceptance or rejection of the trade mark.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed to constitute a business basic application where the applicant demonstrates continuous and verifiable engagement with the goods or services specified in the application for a period not less than six months immediately preceding the date of filing. Such engagement must manifest through documented commercial activities, including but not limited to sales records, advertising expenditures, and contractual agreements relating directly to those goods or services. Provided that, where the applicant is a start-up entity as defined under applicable government regulations, this requirement may be relaxed subject to submission of an incubation certificate from a recognized body. The Registrar may require further evidence substantiating the claimed commercial activities at any stage during examination and opposition proceedings; failure to provide such evidence shall render the application liable for rejection.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark shall file a business basic application only if such applicant possesses demonstrable and continuous engagement with the goods or services indicated in the applied-for trade mark within the territory of India; provided that this requirement does not apply to applicants who are foreign nationals demonstrating prior use of the mark outside India. Any person aggrieved by a decision rejecting a business basic application may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, subject to payment of prescribed fees and demonstration of prejudice arising from the rejection. Failure to comply with these provisions renders the applicant liable for penalties as provided herein, including but not limited to fines and costs associated with proceedings.

Where the Registrar receives a business basic application for registration of a trade mark relating to goods or services provided by an enterprise engaged in the manufacture or supply of pharmaceuticals, the applicant shall provide evidence demonstrating a licensing agreement with a pharmaceutical research institution. This requirement is waived only if the applicant can demonstrate prior use of the proposed trade mark for at least five years preceding the date of application. Any subsequent assignment of the trade mark, or any right derived therefrom, must include an irrevocable undertaking by the assignee to maintain adherence to Good Manufacturing Practices as stipulated under this Act. The Registrar may require periodic audits to verify compliance with such undertakings. Failure to comply shall render the registration liable for revocation.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed to include a business basic application where the applicant demonstrates a bona fide intention to use the mark in relation to specified goods or services within the territory of India; however, this presumption is rebuttable should the Registrar, upon receiving an objection from any interested party, find that the applicant has failed to establish such genuine intent through documentary evidence and testimony. The burden of proving lack of genuine intent rests with the objector, subject to a proviso that the applicant may be called upon to provide further clarification regarding their commercial activities. Any appeal against a decision denying registration based on this provision shall lie before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Where a trade mark is subject to a business basic application filed by an Indian national or citizen residing outside India, the applicant shall provide evidence satisfactory to the Registrar demonstrating continued engagement with commercial activities within India relevant to the goods or services specified in the application. Such evidence may include, but is not limited to, documented sales transactions, service agreements, or licensing arrangements. The Registrar may require further clarification regarding the nature and extent of such engagement at any time during the examination process. Furthermore, where a business basic applicant intends to assign their rights under this Act, they shall notify the Registrar within thirty days of the assignment’s execution, providing details of the assignee and the scope of the assigned rights as provided herein. Failure to comply with this notification requirement may render the assignment voidable.

Where any party aggrieved by the rejection of a business basic application for registration of a trade mark alleges that such rejection was effected without due consideration being given to the distinctiveness arising from the novel design elements incorporated within the mark, the Registrar shall, upon review, consider whether the applicant has demonstrated sufficient acquired distinctiveness through extensive use and marketing efforts. The aggrieved party may submit evidence pertaining to sales figures, advertising expenditure, consumer surveys, and market research data to substantiate their claim. Provided that the Registrar is satisfied that the rejection was manifestly erroneous in failing to appreciate this acquired distinctiveness, the application shall be deemed to have been conditionally approved, subject to a further hearing where both parties may present arguments under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, “registration common regulations” shall mean the procedures and conditions governing the acceptance and processing of applications for registration of trademarks by multiple applicants seeking identical or deceptively similar marks in relation to identical or closely related goods or services. Such regulations are established to ensure equitable consideration under this Act and prevent undue delay caused by conflicting claims. An application may be held pending if it is determined that another application, filed prior thereto, raises a substantial conflict; provided that the Registrar shall provide both applicants with written notice of such pendency and an opportunity to submit representations.

An applicant shall furnish such particulars concerning the trade mark as are required under this Act, including a representation of the marks and a statement of goods or services with which the mark is associated. The Registrar may, upon receiving an application, direct the applicant to amend the representation or clarify the description if they appear deficient or ambiguous. Where multiple applications are filed for identical trade marks in respect of identical goods or services, the Registrar shall determine priority according to established regulations and principles of registration common regulations. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to acceptance or refusal of an application may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The applicant must also provide evidence of use of the mark in India if required as provided herein.

An owner of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to institute proceedings against any person infringing their rights under this Act, seeking an injunction restraining the infringing activity and damages commensurate with the loss suffered by the proprietor. Such remedies are available irrespective of whether the infringement is wilful or negligent, provided that the proprietor demonstrates reasonable diligence in monitoring use of identical or deceptively similar marks within the relevant class of goods or services. Further, where a trade mark has acquired distinctiveness through association with the owner’s goods or services, any use which creates a likelihood of confusion on the part of the public shall constitute infringement. The provisions relating to registration common regulations apply equally to foreign registered trade marks seeking extension of protection within India, and such proprietors are subject to similar remedies for infringement as domestic owners.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark shall file an application with the Registrar in such form and manner as may be prescribed. The application must specify the goods or services in relation to which the trade mark is sought to be registered, classified according to the International Classification of Goods and Services. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall acknowledge its receipt and assign it a serial number. The Registrar may require the applicant to submit further information or clarification regarding any aspect of the application. Where an objection arises under this Act concerning the distinctiveness or deceptiveness of the mark, or any other ground for refusal, the Registrar shall issue a notice of concern to the applicant. The applicant shall then have opportunity to file a reply addressing the concerns raised. These registration common regulations are intended to ensure fairness and transparency in the trade mark examination process.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark shall furnish with the application a representation of the marks applied for, conforming to prescribed standards regarding clarity and reproducibility; provided that where the trade mark comprises three colours or more, the applicant must submit specimens demonstrating the arrangement and relative placement of each colour within the mark. Further, an applicant intending to claim priority under this Act must file a certified copy of the earlier application within ninety days from the date of filing the subsequent application. The Registrar may require such further information as is deemed necessary for assessing compliance with these regulations concerning registration common regulations, including evidence demonstrating use of the trade mark in India if the applicant has not previously used it commercially.

Any proprietor seeking registration of a trade mark shall diligently maintain its distinctiveness and reputation following grant; failure to do so constitutes grounds for revocation under this Act. The Registrar may, upon receiving complaint from any interested party demonstrating material damage resulting from use contrary to accepted regulations concerning registration common regulations, initiate proceedings for rectification of the register. Such complaints must be substantiated with documentary evidence establishing ongoing misrepresentation or dilution of brand identity. Any person found guilty of knowingly employing a deceptively similar mark shall face penalties including fines up to five hundred thousand rupees and imprisonment extending to three years; repeat offences will attract enhanced sanctions as provided herein.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark shall be entitled to grant licences conferring the right to use the trade mark for specific goods or services, subject to such terms and conditions as are agreed upon between the proprietor and the licensee; provided that any such licence agreement must clearly define the geographical territory within which the licensed rights may be exercised. Furthermore, the registered proprietor may assign the entire interest in the trade mark, including all associated licensing agreements, to another party, with the approval of the Trade Marks Registry. Such assignment shall not prejudice existing rights of licensees unless expressly agreed upon in writing. The provisions relating to registration common regulations apply equally to licences and assignments, ensuring transparency and adherence to established protocols under this Act.

Where any proprietor seeks to register a trade mark identical or confusingly similar to an earlier registered trade mark under this Act, the Trade Marks Registry shall give notice thereof to the proprietor of the earlier trade mark and afford them an opportunity to file representations against such registration. Such representations must be supported by evidence demonstrating likelihood of confusion arising from the proposed registration; failure to provide adequate substantiation may result in the representation being deemed frivolous. The Registrar may, after considering all submissions, direct that the application for registration proceed notwithstanding the objection, or dismiss it entirely.
