The right to challenge decisions regarding claims purposes is afforded to all parties affected under this Act through appropriate appellate mechanisms.

Applications filed under this Act relating to plant varieties shall be examined by the Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers’ Rights Authority, acting in accordance with principles of established crop sciences. The Authority may require applicants to furnish further particulars or documentation demonstrating compliance with eligibility criteria as provided herein. Claims purposes for registration must clearly delineate the novelty and distinctiveness of the variety, substantiated by data derived from field trials conducted under standardized protocols. Any challenge to a granted claim shall be referred to an Adjudicating Officer appointed by the Central Government, whose decision is final subject to appeal before the Appellate Board. The Authority shall maintain a publicly accessible register detailing all registered varieties and associated claims purposes, including information on breeder’s rights and farmers' privileges.

An application for registration shall be accompanied by a detailed statement specifying the characteristics of the variety and its essential derivation, including parentage where known. The Authority shall examine such an application to ascertain whether the claims made therein are supported by adequate documentation and experimental data demonstrating distinctness, uniformity, and stability. Where the applicant seeks protection based on novelty arising from genetic modification, the application must include a comprehensive report detailing the methodology employed and its impact on the variety’s traits. The Authority may require further clarification or supplementary information to verify the accuracy of the registration claims purposes. Any person aggrieved by a decision regarding an application may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days of receipt of notification thereof, subject to fulfilling prescribed procedural requirements as provided herein.

The Authority shall entertain appeals against orders rejecting an application for registration under this Act within sixty days from the date of communication of such order to the applicant. Provided that, if the rejection is based on novelty or uniformity considerations relating to essential derived characteristics, the appellant may submit further documentary evidence demonstrating compliance with the requirements as provided herein. The Appellate Board shall allow a counter-claimant, who alleges infringement of their rights during examination of registration claims purposes, to present arguments and supporting data within thirty days of notification. Any order passed by the Appellate Board is final subject to revision if it appears that any substantial question of law has arisen which was not previously decided.

An application for registration claiming a variety shall be examined by the Authority in accordance with the procedures as provided herein. The applicant shall furnish such particulars relating to the expression of the distinctive characteristics of the variety and its essential derivation as the Authority may require. Subject to fulfilling all requirements under this Act, the Authority may direct the publication of the application for registration in the Official Gazette. Objections, if any, received within the prescribed period following such publication shall be considered by the Authority, affording the applicant an opportunity of being heard. The examination process shall include a comparative assessment against existing varieties to ascertain novelty and distinctiveness. Patent shall examined similarly with regard to prior art disclosures. The decision of the Authority regarding registration claims purposes is final subject to appeal under this Act.

For the purposes of defining “breeder’s exemption” as provided herein, a farmer shall be deemed to have exercised breeder's exemption if, subject to conditions prescribed under this Act, they are engaged in activities relating to the propagation and sale of plant variety material derived from seeds obtained by them. Such activities include multiplication of seeds for self-consumption or distribution amongst other farmers, and may extend to commercial sales where the farmer has not entered into a legally binding agreement restricting such actions. The term "derived" shall mean originating from a protected variety through subsequent generations, retaining substantially similar characteristics as defined under section 41 clause (b).

Applications for compulsory licensing under this Act shall be made to the Controller, in such form and manner as may be prescribed. The application must specify the reasons for requiring a compulsory license, demonstrating that the plant variety concerned is not available to farmers in sufficient quantity or at a reasonable price. Further, the applicant shall provide evidence of attempts made to negotiate with the right holder, detailing the offers presented and the responses received.

The Controller may grant a compulsory license if satisfied that all reasonable efforts have been made to obtain authorization from the right holder on mutually acceptable terms. Decisions regarding such applications are subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The provisions of section 41 clause (b) dictate that any conditions imposed by the Controller in granting a compulsory license shall include stipulations ensuring equitable compensation to the plant variety right holder, proportionate to the exploitation of the protected variety.

Where a Plant Variety Protection Committee finds, upon review under this Act, that an application for compulsory licensing is demonstrably linked to circumstances involving unreasonable denial of authorization by the Registrar, it shall proceed according to section 41 clause (b). Such determination requires evidence establishing that the applicant diligently pursued all avenues for obtaining necessary approvals and licenses prior to submission. The Committee may grant a compulsory license only if it is satisfied that the public interest demands such action, considering factors including the accessibility of the protected variety to small and marginal farmers and its contribution to food security. Provided that any conditions imposed under this clause shall be proportionate to the nature of the denial and designed to promote innovation within the plant breeding sector.

Any person found guilty of contravening the provisions relating to benefit sharing under this Act, including unauthorized commercialization of plant varieties registered hereunder, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakhs rupees for the first offence. Subsequent offences may attract penalties up to ten lakhs rupees and imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years. The Authority established as provided herein may issue cease and desist orders directing any infringing party to immediately halt activities violating farmers’ rights or intellectual property protections. Further, damages equivalent to thrice the value of profits derived from such unauthorized use shall be recoverable. This applies particularly where infringement occurs in direct disregard of stipulations outlined under section 41 clause (b), concerning geographical indications.

Any person holding a Plant Variety Rights authorization shall be entitled to grant licenses in respect of the rights conferred under this Act, subject to such terms and conditions as are deemed fit by the Registrar. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and may relate to any right granted, including but not limited to the commercialization, propagation, or importation of propagating material derived from the variety. Assignment of Plant Variety Rights authorizations shall require prior approval of the Registrar and must specify the scope of rights being transferred. Where a license is assigned as part of a larger transaction involving other intellectual property, the Registrar may review the terms to ensure they do not unduly restrict access to the plant variety under section 41 clause (b). The assignee shall be bound by any conditions previously imposed on the authorization holder.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the grant, revocation, or amendment of protection of a plant variety, or concerning infringement proceedings initiated pursuant thereto, may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appellant shall specify in the memorandum of appeal the orders against which the appeal is taken and the grounds on which it is based; provided that failure to comply with this requirement shall not be a bar to the appeal if the Appellate Board considers that sufficient cause exists for condoning the delay or non-compliance. Decisions of the Appellate Board concerning matters arising under section 41 clause (b), specifically regarding evidence presented in relation to farmers’ rights, are final subject only to further review by the Supreme Court on a point of law.

For the purposes of defining “essentially derived variety” under this Act, a plant variety shall be deemed to satisfy the criteria outlined herein if it is clearly distinguishable from the original variety based on established characteristics and exhibits traits demonstrably linked to genetic material originating from that initial stock. The determination of such linkage shall consider the provenance records maintained by registered breeders and any accompanying documentation pertaining to breeding strategies employed. A “package” of agricultural practices, including but not limited to irrigation techniques and fertilizer application schedules, used during evaluation shall be documented as relevant context for assessing phenotypic stability. This definition applies specifically in relation to section 41 clause (b).

The Authority shall maintain an index of registered plant varieties, accessible for public inspection subject to reasonable restrictions as provided herein. An application for inclusion in said index shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the registration certificate and a detailed description conforming to the format prescribed under this Act. The Registrar may refuse entry if the information submitted is deemed insufficient or inaccurate, providing the applicant an opportunity for rectification. Further, any proprietor seeking to associate an index registered trade name with their variety must submit proof of exclusive use and demonstrate that such association does not mislead regarding the plant’s characteristics or origin. This process operates without prejudice to the provisions concerning infringement under this Act, particularly as they relate to section 41 clause (b).

Subject to the conditions outlined herein, an order granting protection under this Act relating to a plant variety shall remain valid only so long as the registered holder continues to comply with the obligations stipulated in Schedule V. Such compliance includes, but is not limited to, maintaining accurate records of breeding and propagation activities, providing access for reasonable testing purposes as determined by the Plant Varieties Protection Appellate Authority, and adhering to any restrictions imposed concerning farmer’s rights relating to saved seed. Failure to satisfy these conditions, demonstrated through documented non-compliance or a substantiated complaint filed under section 41 clause (b), shall render the registered holder vulnerable to an application for order cancellation initiated by the Central Government or any aggrieved party.

An application for registration of a utility model shall be deemed to include a declaration by the applicant specifying the field of use for which the utility model is intended, and such declaration shall be binding on the applicant during subsequent proceedings. Where an alleged infringer utilizes a registered utility model without authorization, the proprietor may initiate civil action seeking injunctive relief and damages; however, subject to this Act, any claim for infringement must be predicated upon demonstrable commercial exploitation of the utility model by the defendant. It is provided that the right to commence such proceedings shall vest only after the registration certificate has been issued and the prescribed annual renewal fees have been duly paid. Further, a finding of invalidity under this Act shall automatically extinguish all rights pertaining to proceedings infringement patent.

Where a person aggrieved by an entry on the register, or by any order made in relation thereto, desires to seek rectification, he shall apply to the Controller for that purpose; such application shall specify the particulars of the entry sought to be rectified and the grounds upon which it is alleged to be erroneous. The Controller may entertain such application only if notice of the intended application has been served on the patentee or other person whose interest is affected by the proposed rectification, as provided herein. Any party aggrieved by an order made by the Controller under this Act relating to a notice rectify register may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order; and the Board shall have power to entertain appeals against any decision or direction of the Controller.

Where the author of an invention, having previously assigned their rights therein, subsequently seeks to rectify the register relating to a patent granted to another party, such application shall be accompanied by evidence demonstrating both the original assignment and the grounds for rectification. The Controller may, upon receiving such an application, issue notice to the registered patentee, affording them an opportunity to submit objections under this Act. Should the Controller find merit in the author’s claim, they may order the variation of the register to reflect the true ownership or interest in the invention, provided that any such alteration does not prejudice existing licensees or assignees acting in good faith and without notice rectify register of the original assignment. The Controller shall ensure due consideration is given to the impact on third parties who have relied upon the published patent information.

A person claiming infringement of a trade mark shall be deemed a party proceeding notwithstanding the pendency of an application for registration of an identical mark in respect of goods or services similar to those for which the trade mark is registered. Such a claimant may, subject to conditions prescribed herein, seek interim relief restraining the alleged infringer from further use of the impugned sign. Provided that where the applicant’s rights are contested under this Act, the determination of validity shall not preclude any subsequent action by a party proceeding in respect of infringement. The Registrar may, upon application, direct service of process on any such person.

An application for registration of a trade mark may be opposed by any person claiming use of a similar mark under this Act or having knowledge of such use; provided that where an applicant has demonstrably and continuously used a mark in commerce prior to the date of publication of the trade mark, and another party proceeds notwithstanding said prior use to file an application for registration, the earlier user shall be entitled to submit evidence substantiating their claim. The Registrar may require such party proceeding notwithstanding the existing usage to furnish affidavits verifying the extent and duration of their claimed use. Further, any person aggrieved by a decision regarding opposition or rectification proceedings relating to a trade mark may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board as provided herein.

A proprietor of a trade mark aggrieved by any act or omission constituting infringement may institute suit for damages and an injunction as provided herein; however, where a defendant in such a suit claims that their use of the sign does not infringe the registered trade mark, they shall be entitled to demonstrate bona fide acquisition of a corresponding right under this Act. Further, notwithstanding any order made by a court or tribunal regarding interim relief or permanent restraint, a party proceeding notwithstanding an injunction may apply for modification or vacation thereof, demonstrating substantial compliance with the terms of the original order and proving that continued operation is essential for their livelihood. The proprietor shall be entitled to claim damages proportionate to the extent of actual loss suffered due to such continuing use; provided that contributory infringement shall be actionable only where the infringer knew, or had reasonable grounds to know, of the registered trade mark.

A person aggrieved by an order passed by the Registrar relating to rectification of a trade mark may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of such order. The appeal shall lie on a question of fact or law, and the Board may entertain the appeal notwithstanding that the applicant for rectification has subsequently withdrawn their application or failed to pursue the matter diligently. Further, where an appeal is preferred by any party proceeding notwithstanding a prior settlement agreement reached between the parties concerning the subject trade mark, the Appellate Board shall consider all relevant aspects of the settlement including its terms and duration. The Registrar may require such party to furnish security for costs as deemed appropriate before admitting the appeal. Any order passed by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board shall be final subject to further appeal under this Act.

A person seeking relief under this Act concerning infringement of a trade mark may, subject to compliance with prescribed forms and fees, continue proceedings notwithstanding that an appeal has been filed against an order granting interim injunction or otherwise restraining such person from utilizing the trade mark. Provided that where a party proceeding notwithstanding an interlocutory order demonstrates to the satisfaction of the relevant authority that the continued operation of the order is causing demonstrable and irreparable harm, the authority may, upon application by the affected party, modify or stay the effect of the original order pending final determination of the appeal. Such modification shall be subject to conditions as deemed appropriate to safeguard the interests of all parties involved in the underlying dispute.

Where a proprietor of a trade mark institutes proceedings for infringement, and such proceedings are stayed pending determination of an earlier conflicting application or registration, the proprietor shall remain entitled to pursue remedies against any party proceeding notwithstanding the stay. This right includes, but is not limited to, seeking interim injunctions and damages relating to acts committed during the period of the stay. Provided that, where a subsequent registration is granted following resolution of the conflict, the proprietor’s claim for damages shall be assessed with due consideration to the reasonable costs incurred by the infringing party in reliance on the conflicting application or registration prior to its revocation or amendment. The Tribunal may order compensation against any such party found to have acted in bad faith during this period.

A proprietor seeking to assign or license rights in a registered trade mark may, subject to the provisions of this Act and the regulations framed thereunder, grant such assignment or licence to any person without requiring prior approval from the Registrar. Where an application for registration of a trade mark is pending, and a party proceeding notwithstanding a notice served under section 86 has initiated proceedings challenging the validity of the proposed mark, the applicant shall be deemed to have consented to the inclusion of that party as a necessary participant in any subsequent inquiry relating to the registrability of the mark. Any such assignment or licence shall remain valid until the expiry of its term, or until revoked by the proprietor, provided that the terms and conditions are consistent with the fundamental principles governing trade mark law as established under this Act.

Notwithstanding any order passed by the Registrar concerning rectification proceedings initiated against a trade mark registration, any person aggrieved by such an order may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of service of notice of the order. The Board shall hear parties and consider all relevant evidence presented, subject to the provisions governing appeals under this Act. Where the appellant is a party proceeding notwithstanding having previously filed an application for registration of a similar mark, the Board may require them to demonstrate distinctiveness acquired through use subsequent to the earlier registration. Failure to comply with such a requirement shall be grounds for dismissal of the appeal.

A person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to the acceptance or refusal of registration of a trade mark may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board; provided that where an application for registration has been refused and the reasons for such refusal are recorded in the omission register, the appellant shall demonstrate, with reasonable diligence, that the grounds for refusal were either factually incorrect or legally unsustainable. Further, notwithstanding anything contained herein, a party proceeding notwithstanding a prior notice of opposition may continue to pursue their application if they submit an affidavit confirming diligent attempts at amicable resolution and detailing the nature of those efforts to the satisfaction of the Registrar. The Registrar shall maintain records pertaining to such affidavits.

A trade proprietor registered under this Act may institute proceedings relating to the infringement of their registered trade mark notwithstanding that such proprietor has assigned the entire interest in the trade mark to another party. Provided that, where an assignment has taken place, the assignee shall be deemed to be the sole person entitled to maintain any action or other proceeding for damages or for injunctions relating to the infringement thereof. Further, a party proceeding notwithstanding any prior notice of such assignment shall be subject to the same limitations and conditions as if they were the original registered proprietor. This provision applies irrespective of whether the assignee has notified third parties of their ownership.

A person seeking relief relating to rectification of a registered trade mark shall file an application with the relevant intellectual property office, provided that such application specifies clearly the particulars of the registration sought to be rectified and the grounds upon which it is claimed that the registration is erroneous or ought to be amended. Where any party proceeding in respect of such an application alleges fraud relating to the acquisition or use of the trade mark, they shall provide supporting evidence demonstrating a material misrepresentation made during the registration process. Further, any party proceeding shall be entitled to cross-examine witnesses presented by another party as provided herein.

Where an appeal lies from any order passed by the Registrar relating to rectification of a trade mark, notice of such appeal shall be served upon all parties who were parties to the original proceeding before the Registrar. Any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act may prefer an appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. Provided that where the order relates to refusal of registration, the applicant shall have the right to present his case again before the Registrar following notice of such opportunity. Further, a party proceeding shall be entitled to file cross-objections in any rectification proceeding, subject to the conditions prescribed herein and as provided for under the rules framed by the Government. The Intellectual Property Appellate Board may, after hearing all parties concerned, confirm, vary or reverse the order appealed against.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order; provided that the Appellate Board may, if it is satisfied that there was reasonable cause for the delay, entertain an appeal lodged after the expiry of the said period. Where a party proceeding shall seek leave to appeal to the Supreme Court against any order passed by the Appellate Board, such application must be made within ninety days from the date of communication of the order of the Appellate Board. Further, where an appeal is preferred under this Act, all parties concerned shall be served with notice of the proceedings and given a reasonable opportunity to present their case as provided herein.

Any party proceeding against another concerning alleged infringement of a registered trade mark shall file an affidavit verifying the particulars of the infringing goods or services and detailing the extent of damages suffered as a direct consequence of such infringement. Provided that, failure to submit this affidavit within thirty days from the date of institution of the suit will render the claim unsustainable under this Act. Further, where rectification proceedings are initiated, any party proceeding shall be obligated to provide documentary evidence substantiating claims of dilution or tarnishment of reputation. The Tribunal may, subject to just considerations, impose a penalty not exceeding five lakhs rupees upon any party failing to comply with these disclosure requirements.

Any proprietor desiring to grant a license concerning the use of their registered trade mark may execute an assignment agreement transferring such rights, subject to the conditions stipulated therein. A party proceeding shall notify the Trade Marks Registry within thirty days of any such licensing arrangement or assignment, providing details of the licensee or assignee and the scope of permitted usage. Further, where a license is granted for a specific territory, the proprietor remains responsible for ensuring that the use by the licensee does not infringe upon existing rights held by others under this Act. Any subsequent transfer of ownership of the business undertaking to which the trade mark relates shall be deemed notification to the Trade Marks Registry and will require no further action from the previous proprietor provided that all records are updated accordingly.

Where a rectification action is filed alleging misuse of a registered trade mark, and the respondent claims such use is authorised by contract or license, the Registrar shall issue notice to all parties involved in said contractual agreement. Any party proceeding shall demonstrate, through admissible evidence, that the alleged authorisation was validly executed and continues in force at the time of the rectification application. Provided that, if the respondent fails to substantiate this claim with a legally binding document, the rectification action may proceed on its merits without further consideration of the purported authorisation. Further, any party aggrieved by an order made under this Act relating to such contractual authorisation may appeal to the relevant appellate authority within sixty days from the date of communication of that order.

Where a notice of opposition is served upon an applicant for registration of a trade mark, and such applicant subsequently institutes proceedings seeking declaratory relief against the opponent alleging undue delay or lack of bona fide intention on the part of the opponent in pursuing said opposition, any party proceeding shall be entitled to adduce evidence pertaining to the timeliness and good faith of their actions. The Registrar shall, upon receiving an application for a direction regarding such alleged delay, unconditionally registrar shall afford both parties an opportunity for cross-examination and submission of written arguments. Any order made by the Registrar under this Act concerning the continuation or dismissal of opposition proceedings is subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

For the purposes of this Patents Act, “invention” means a new and useful art, process, manufacture, or composition of matter; provided that it is not obvious to a person skilled in the art. An invention shall be deemed to include any improvement of an existing invention. The term "skilled in the art" refers to a person possessing ordinary knowledge and skill within the relevant field at the date of filing the patent application. Further, an invention which is frivolous or contrary to law or morality shall not be considered an invention under this Act. Any process for producing a substance that falls within the definition of “pharmaceutical” as defined elsewhere herein, may also constitute an invention.

An application for registration of a patent shall include particulars specifying the invention, its claims, and details regarding the applicant’s entitlement to file. The prescribed fee for filing an application under this Patents Act is subject to adjustments determined by the Central Government from time to time, based on factors including the nature of the invention and the applicant's status as a small entity or otherwise. Where an applicant has previously published particulars concerning the invention outside India, such publication shall be disclosed in the application. The Controller may require further information or clarification regarding any aspect of the patent application before proceeding with examination. Any alteration to the claims after the initial filing must be accompanied by a statement explaining the changes and their impact on the novelty of the invention.

An application for a patent shall include particulars specifying the invention, its claims, and the class into which it is classified under this Act. The applicant shall furnish proof satisfactory to the Controller that they are the true and first inventor of the claimed subject matter. Where an invention relates to a process for producing a substance or article, the application may also claim the substance or article produced by that process, provided that such claim complies with the requirements regarding enablement as provided herein. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish further information or clarification concerning any aspect of the invention described in the application. Any person aggrieved by an order made under this Patents Act may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order, subject to payment of prescribed fees.

Subject to the provisions of this Patents Act, 1970, any person claiming title to an invention which is the subject matter of a patent application may grant licenses under that application to other parties, either wholly or partially, and such license agreement shall be in writing and specify the scope of rights granted. Assignment of patent rights, including all or any part of the patent, the benefit of the application, or the patent itself, may also be effected by written instrument, and registration of such assignment with the Controller is mandatory for it to be deemed valid against third parties. Further, where a license or assignment includes provisions relating to royalties or other considerations, these shall be clearly articulated within the agreement. The Central Government may, under this Act, prescribe conditions governing the transfer of patent rights to ensure equitable access and prevent anti-competitive practices related to patented technologies.

Any person who, knowing or having reason to believe that any invention has been patented under this Patents Act, reproduces, distributes, imports into India, or offers to sell for sale any article comprising the substance of the said invention, without authorization from the patentee, shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall be assessed at three times the proven loss suffered by the patentee as a direct result of the infringing act. Further, where an infringement involves a broadcast work stating the patented process or device, the penalty may be increased to five times the proven loss, considering the wider dissemination and potential commercial exploitation facilitated by such broadcasting. The Central Government may, upon receiving a complaint, issue interim injunctions restraining further acts of infringement pending final adjudication.

Any person who, knowing or having reason to believe that any invention has been patented under this Patents Act, without authorization from the patentee, makes, uses, sells, or offers to sell, for sale, or imports the patented article, shall be deemed to have infringed the patent and is liable for damages. Such damages may include compensation equivalent to the lost profits derived from the infringing activity, as determined by the High Court. Further, where such infringement constitutes a wilful violation of the rights conferred by the patent, the court may also award punitive damages not exceeding three times the amount of compensation awarded. The aggrieved party shall have the right to seek an injunction restraining the infringer from continuing the infringing conduct, subject to principles of equity and natural justice. Criminal prosecution under relevant provisions of the Indian Penal Code may be initiated for acts of counterfeiting or fraudulent representation relating to patented inventions.

For the purposes of this Act, “designated territory” means any territory specified in Schedule I; (b) "foreign applicant" means an applicant who is not resident of India; (c) “convention country” means a country or a territory which is a 6referred convention country as notified by the Central Government from time to time in the Official Gazette, and such notification may be amended or withdrawn as deemed necessary; (d) An application for patent shall be deemed to be a convention application if it contains an express reference to an earlier corresponding application made in a convention country. The benefit of priority under this Act shall only accrue where the particulars of the earlier application are furnished as provided herein.

An application claiming priority from a convention application shall be deemed to be a convention application if it is filed within twelve months from the date of filing of the said convention application. For the purpose of determining whether an applicant is entitled to claim priority under this Act, the term "convention country" means any country which is a member of the World Trade Organization as on the date of commencement of this Act or any other country notified by the Central Government in the Official Gazette as a 6referred convention country. The benefit of claiming priority shall not be available if the applicant has already claimed such benefit under this Act for the same invention. Provided that, where an application has been published prior to the expiry of the twelve-month period, the Controller may, subject to just cause, allow the claim for priority.

Where, upon revocation of a patent under this Act, the aggrieved party demonstrates that such revocation was predicated on misrepresentation made by the patentee concerning the novelty or inventive step of the invention, and where such misrepresentation arose from information originating within a 6referred convention country, the Controller may order the patentee to pay compensation. Such compensation shall be determined considering the losses suffered by the aggrieved party, including but not limited to lost profits, costs incurred in challenging the validity of the patent, and reasonable legal expenses. The amount awarded as compensation is subject to an upper limit equivalent to three times the annual fees paid by the patentee during the term of the patent. Further, any appeal against this order may be made to the Appellate Board within a period of ninety days from the date of communication of the Controller’s decision.

For the purposes of this Act, a “6referred convention country” shall be deemed to include any nation that has acceded to the Paris Convention for the Protection of Industrial Property and which is designated by the Central Government through notification in the Official Gazette. Applications filed in a 6referred convention country by persons residing or having domicile therein shall be treated as convention applications under this Act, subject to the provisions regarding priority claims. The determination of whether a nation qualifies as a 6referred convention country may be reviewed periodically by the Controller and reported to the Central Government annually. Any dispute arising concerning the status of a particular country as a 6referred convention country shall be resolved at the discretion of the Controller, whose decision is final and binding. Further, an application claiming priority from a convention application shall be examined in accordance with the established procedures outlined herein.

For the purposes of this Act, a patent shall be deemed to be derived from a corresponding application filed in a 6referred convention country if the applicant establishes, through documentary evidence satisfactory to the Controller, that the present application relates to an invention disclosed in the earlier application and that such earlier application was filed on or before the date specified as the priority date for the current application. Provided that, where the invention has been modified from that originally disclosed in the convention country application, the modifications shall be considered permissible only if they do not depart significantly from the subject matter of the original disclosure and are consistent with the principles of innovation as understood under this Act. The Controller may require further declarations or submissions to verify compliance with these conditions.

Any person importing into India any product manufactured using a patented invention shall be deemed to have contravened this Act, subject to the provisions regarding experimental use and research. Where such importation is found to infringe a patent granted under this Act or corresponding to a patent in a 6referred convention country, the Controller may order seizure of the imported goods. The owner of the patent shall be entitled to seek damages equivalent to the aggregate value of the infringing imports, plus an additional penalty not exceeding five per centum of such value. Failure to comply with any order issued under this Act regarding seizure or destruction of infringing products will render the offender liable for a further fine and imprisonment up to one year.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any patentee or assignee may grant exclusive licences under the patent, and such licence shall be irrevocable without the consent in writing of the licensee. Where a patent has been assigned, the assignee shall have all rights which the patentee might have had under this Act. The power to assign or license a patent shall extend to include the right to grant licenses relating to inventions claimed in a corresponding application for patents filed in a 6referred convention country. Provided that any such assignment or licence granted prior to the publication of the patent, if it contains terms which restrict the exploitation of the patented invention within India, may be challenged under provisions pertaining to anti-competitive practices as determined by relevant regulatory authorities. The Controller may require evidence demonstrating compliance with these conditions before registering an assignment or license relating to a 6referred convention country.

Where, upon review under this Act, the Controller finds that a patent application claims an invention disclosed in a corresponding application filed in a 6referred convention country, and such disclosure contains matter not present in the original Indian application, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to amend the claims to conform with the originally filed specification. However, any amendment so made shall only be permissible if it does not substantially alter the nature of the invention as claimed initially. The Controller may, after hearing arguments from both the patent holder and any interested party objecting to the amendment, determine whether such alteration has occurred. This determination is subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, provided that the appellant demonstrates prejudice resulting from the Controller’s decision.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person claiming assignment of the right to make and sell a patentable invention derived from an application filed in a 6referred convention country may apply for a license under this Act. Such application shall specify the details of the original convention application, including the applicant’s name, filing date, and assigned priority number. The Controller may grant such license if satisfied that the assignment was made in good faith and complies with all applicable regulations regarding mark relation goods associated with the invention. Further, the licensee shall be obligated to disclose full particulars of the consideration paid or to be paid for the right granted under the license. Any modification or sub-license granted by the licensee shall also require prior approval from the Controller, ensuring continued adherence to the principles outlined herein.

Where, upon examination under this Act, it appears that the invention claimed in a patent application is anticipated by prior art existing in a 6referred convention country, the Controller may grant the patent only if the applicant demonstrates that the said prior art was not reasonably discoverable by a person skilled in the relevant field within India at the time of the application’s filing. The burden of proving such reasonable non-discoverability shall rest entirely upon the applicant. Failure to satisfy this requirement will result in the rejection of the patent claim or, if already granted, may be grounds for revocation under procedures as provided herein. This provision is without prejudice to any remedies available to aggrieved parties, including the right to appeal decisions before houses parliament. The Controller’s decision on discoverability shall be final subject to judicial review.

For the purposes of this Act, “patented process” shall mean any method or series of acts described in a claim of a patent, wherein such method or series of acts are novel and involve an inventive step as provided herein. A patented process includes, but is not limited to, industrial processes for manufacturing substances, compositions, or products; methods for treating materials to alter their properties; and techniques employed in agricultural production. Subject to the provisions relating to compulsory licenses under this Act, the use of a patented process shall be restricted unless authorized by the patentee. Any activity constituting an infringement of a patented process shall be actionable as per the remedies available under this Act.

The Register shall maintain a publicly accessible record of all processes submitted for registration as patented processes, detailing the applicant’s name, address for service, and the nature of the claimed invention. Any person aggrieved by the acceptance of a registered patented process may file an appeal with the Controller within sixty days from the date of publication of the acceptance in the Patent Journal. Such appeals shall be accompanied by a statement of grounds and any supporting documentation deemed relevant to the assessment of novelty and inventive step as provided herein. The Register may, subject to due process, refuse registration if it determines that the claimed patented process is contrary to public order or morality. An applicant seeking registration of a patented process must disclose all prior art known to them at the time of filing.

Where any person, having notice of a patent granted under this Act, without authorization from the patentee, uses or imports for sale or distribution within India a patented process, the patentee shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief against such infringing party. Such injunction may restrain not only the direct use of the patented process but also acts likely to result in its infringement. Provided that where the alleged infringer demonstrates prior use of the patented process as a matter of right under section 107, or has obtained an authorization from another person possessing rights relating to the invention, this remedy shall be subject to such limitations as are deemed just and equitable by the High Court. The patentee may also claim damages proportionate to the loss suffered due to the infringement, calculated on the basis of the infringer’s profits derived from the unauthorized use.

Where an application relates to a patented process, the Controller may, prior to grant, require the applicant to disclose any biological material required for the implementation of the invention, provided that such disclosure does not compromise trade secrets or confidential information. The applicant shall furnish this disclosure in a manner prescribed by the regulations framed under this Act and may be subject to a confidentiality agreement as determined by the Controller. Any party aggrieved by the requirement to disclose biological material may file an appeal before the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. Further, if the disclosed material is not readily available or accessible, the Controller shall provide reasonable opportunity for the applicant to demonstrate alternative means of implementation. The provisions relating to examination and sealing of applications shall apply mutatis mutandis to applications involving patented processes.

Where a patented process involves the use of one or more biological materials, including but not limited to microorganisms, plant cells, or animal tissues, such process shall be deemed to be subject to review under this Act if it results in the production of an article intended for use as food, feed, drug, or cosmetic. Provided that, where the biological material is rendered incapable of reproduction at the time of its use in the patented process, a determination regarding patentability shall consider whether the inventive step contributes significantly to the advancement of technology and is not merely the application of known techniques. Further, any modification to the patented process which alters the intended outcome or functionality of the final product must be disclosed accurately in supporting documentation submitted under this Act.

Any person aggrieved by the grant of a patent for a patented process may, subject to conditions prescribed herein, institute rectification proceedings before the Controller within one year from the date of publication of the grant. Such proceedings shall be limited to demonstrating that the claimed patented process does not involve an inventive step or is obvious in view of prior art available to the public prior to the filing date of the patent application. Failure to demonstrate such lack of novelty or inventiveness shall render the aggrieved party liable for costs, including reasonable attorney’s fees as determined by the Controller. Furthermore, any infringement of a patented process established through rectification proceedings will be deemed null and void ab initio.

Where a patented process involves the use of a substance, whether existing or newly discovered, the owner of the patent shall be entitled to grant licenses for the utilization of such process, subject to the conditions specified therein. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and the terms thereof, including royalty rates and duration, shall be determined by mutual agreement between the patent owner and the licensee. Assignment of a patented process is permissible under this Act, provided that the assignee undertakes all obligations and liabilities associated with ownership. Further, any subsequent license granted relating to the assigned patented process shall remain valid unless expressly revoked by the assignor in writing, notifying both the assignee and the relevant Controller. The Controller may intervene where disputes arise concerning licensing terms or assignment validity, as provided herein.

Where a claim extends to a patented process, the Controller may, upon review initiated by any interested party demonstrating substantial prejudice arising from the enforcement of such patent, entertain objections relating solely to the novelty and inventive step of that process. Such review shall be conducted expeditiously, with both the patentee and the objector afforded equal opportunity to present evidence and arguments pertaining directly to these aspects. The burden of proving a lack of novelty or an absence of inventive step shall rest upon the objector; however, the patentee shall be obligated to provide full disclosure of all data relied upon in establishing the validity of the patented process. Decisions rendered under this provision are subject to appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of notification.

Where an application relates to a patented process, the Controller may, upon receiving a written request from any person interested, direct the applicant to furnish such further information as the Controller deems necessary for assessing the novelty and inventive step involved. Such direction shall be accompanied by a statement of reasons. The applicant shall have a period of ninety days from the date of receipt of the said direction to comply therewith, which may be extended by the Controller for a further period not exceeding thirty days if satisfactory cause is shown. Any appeal against an order directing furnishing of information under this provision lies to the Appellate Board. In determining whether a patented process satisfies the requirements of novelty and inventive step, a Technical Member shall be included in the composition of the Board hearing such appeals.

Any individual acting as a patent agent shall be deemed to have committed an offence if, having knowledge of any material fact likely to influence the grant of a patent or the determination of its validity, he wilfully conceals such fact from the Controller or attempts to mislead the Controller regarding it. Such offences are punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and with a fine which shall not be less than fifty thousand rupees but may extend to two hundred thousand rupees. Furthermore, any person who knowingly aids or abets an act patent agent in the commission of such an offence shall also be deemed guilty of that offence and subject to similar penalties as provided herein. The Controller may, upon receiving credible information regarding a violation under this Act, initiate proceedings against the accused individual without prejudice to other remedies available under law.

The Controller shall maintain a comprehensive register of all inventions for which patent applications have been filed under this Act, distinguishing between pending applications and granted patents. Such register shall be deemed public record and accessible for inspection by any person subject to the payment of such fees as may be prescribed. The particulars recorded in the register shall include the name and address of the applicant, the title of the invention, the date of filing the application, and details pertaining to any subsequent amendments or objections raised during examination. Any modification to these particulars requires formal notification and registration within the register. Further, the Controller may, upon request by a patent holder, record assignments or licenses relating to patents; such recording shall confer constructive notice as provided herein. The accurate means register patents is crucial for maintaining transparency and facilitating due diligence in matters of intellectual property.

Where any person aggrieved by a decision made under this Act relating to the registration of a patent, or the revocation thereof, or any other matter arising in connection with proceedings before the Controller, may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such decision; and the Appellate Board shall have the power to entertain appeals against orders passed by the Controller. Provided that an appeal under this Act shall be admitted only if the appellant deposits with the Appellate Board such sum as may be prescribed. The Controller may, at any time, require the Registrar to amend the register to correct any clerical error or oversight; and the amended means register patents accordingly. Any person who fraudulently makes a false statement in his application for registration of a patent shall be liable to prosecution under section 134.

Any person aggrieved by any entry in the register relating to the registration of a patent shall have the right to appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date on which such entry was made; provided that the Appellate Board may, subject to conditions as prescribed herein, entertain appeals filed after the expiry of the said period if satisfactory reasons are tendered for the delay. Failure to comply with the provisions regarding notification prior to registration shall render the patent holder liable to a penalty not exceeding one hundred thousand rupees, and further action under this Act relating to infringement may be stayed pending resolution of the appeal. The Controller General shall maintain an updated means register patents accessible to the public, subject to restrictions as determined by regulations framed under this Act.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any patentee may grant a license to use the patented invention under conditions specified in the license agreement, which shall be binding on all parties involved. Such licenses may be exclusive, non-exclusive, or partial, as determined by the patentee. Assignment of patents, including rights pertaining to such licenses, may occur through a registered instrument executed before a notary public, and details thereof shall be recorded in the register of patents maintained under this Act. The Controller General may, upon application and subject to due process, facilitate the registration of assignments and record amendments to license agreements relating to inventions already means register patents. Any person acquiring an interest in a patent through assignment or license is deemed to be the substitute for the original patentee for all purposes as provided herein.

An applicant seeking to have an invention registered shall submit Form XP with the Controller, detailing the particulars of any prior publication or disclosure relating to the subject matter of the application. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish further information concerning such disclosures and their dates. Where a relevant entry register pertaining to the application exists, its contents shall be considered in assessing compliance with the novelty requirements under this Act. Failure to accurately disclose all prior publications as required will render the patent liable for revocation upon opposition. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Controller regarding the disclosure obligations may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such decision, subject to prescribed procedures. The register means register patents and shall be maintained in accordance with regulations framed under this Act.

The Controller shall, upon granting a patent and entering it on the means register patents, publish a registration notice in the Official Gazette specifying the patent number, title of the invention, name of the patentee, and date of grant. Any party aggrieved by the entry or omission relating to any matter recorded in the register may, subject to conditions as provided herein, institute proceedings before the Controller seeking rectification within six months from the date of such publication. Failure to comply with this timeframe shall permanently bar any claim for correction. The Controller may impose a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees on any person found to have made a false statement or suppressed material facts in connection with an application or proceeding under this Act, and further action may be taken as deemed appropriate by the relevant authorities.

For the purposes clause invention, an invention shall be considered non-obvious if it does not involve any element which would have rendered the said invention obvious to a person skilled in the art; provided that such assessment shall take into account technical knowledge and expertise readily available or ascertainable under this Act. An invention shall also be deemed non-obvious where it incorporates elements already known in the relevant field, but combines them in an unexpected manner resulting in a technical effect not anticipated by those skilled in the art. The determination of obviousness shall be based on the totality of the circumstances and considering all prior publications available to the public.

For the purposes clause invention, an application for registration as a patent shall be deemed to disclose sufficiently the nature and manner of manufacture of the claimed invention if the description clearly enables any person skilled in the art to produce the invention without undue experimentation, subject to the requirement that such enablement extends to all essential components and processes. Provided that, where the invention relates to a method or process applicable to a range of substances, the application shall specify at least one representative substance for illustrative purposes. Furthermore, an applicant may submit supplementary documentation demonstrating operational parameters; however, this submission does not supersede the fundamental obligation to provide complete disclosure as provided herein. The Controller General may require further clarification regarding the scope of the invention if ambiguities arise during examination.

For the purposes clause invention, an application for a patent shall be deemed to disclose the matter necessary for carrying out the invention unless such disclosure is withheld under conditions prescribed herein. The Controller may require the applicant, prior to proceeding with examination, to furnish further particulars relating to the claimed invention if he considers that the description is insufficient to enable a person skilled in the art to carry it into effect. Such requirement shall be accompanied by a reasoned statement specifying the deficiencies perceived and outlining the information sought. Failure to comply within the stipulated period may result in rejection of the application, subject to an opportunity for appeal before the Appellate Board. The applicant shall also provide evidence demonstrating working of the patented invention in India within three years from the grant of patent, as provided herein.

For the purposes clause invention, an application for a patent shall be deemed to fail to disclose the matter necessary for understanding the invention unless it clearly and completely describes the method and manner in which the claimed invention may be made or used. Provided that, where the invention is in relation to a process for producing a substance controlled under any existing law, the application must also specify the safeguards incorporated to prevent diversion of such substance to prohibited uses. Furthermore, an invention shall not be considered non-obvious merely because it incorporates elements previously known individually, unless it demonstrates a synergistic effect resulting from their combination as provided herein. Subject to this, the controller may require further clarification if the description is ambiguous or lacks sufficient detail for skilled persons in the art.

For the purposes clause invention, an application for patent shall be deemed invalid if it is established that the claimed invention was previously used commercially in India without authorization, and such use constitutes exploitation under this Act. Any person demonstrating such unauthorized commercial use prior to the date of filing of the patent application may petition the Controller for revocation of the patent. The burden of proof regarding said unauthorized use shall rest upon the petitioner. Provided that, if the invention relates to a method of agricultural or horticultural practice, the Controller may disregard minor or casual uses not impacting market competitiveness. Failure to comply with these provisions renders the applicant liable to penalties as provided herein and subject to civil action for damages.

For the purposes clause invention, an application for a patent shall be deemed invalid under this Act if it is demonstrated to the satisfaction of the Controller that the claimed subject matter was previously disclosed in a publicly accessible publication originating outside India, provided that such disclosure did not constitute prior teaching as understood within established principles of inventive step. The burden of proving such previous disclosure and its impact on novelty shall rest upon the applicant challenging the validity of the patent. Further, any appeal against an order determining invalidity based on this provision may only be entertained if the appellant establishes a clear nexus between the disclosed information and the specific elements comprising the invention as claimed; otherwise, the appeal shall stand dismissed.

For the purposes clause invention, an act constituting an alleged offence under this Act shall be deemed to include the unauthorized manufacture, use, or sale of any article embodying a patented invention if it is established that the accused had knowledge, or reasonably ought to have had knowledge, of the existence of such patent. Provided that, where the infringement involves a process, the accused’s actions shall be considered in relation to the products derived from that process. Any person found guilty of an offence as provided herein shall be liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and with fine which shall not be less than ten thousand rupees and may extend to fifty thousand rupees; or both. The Court may, subject to appeal, order seizure and forfeiture of the infringing goods.

For the purposes clause invention, an application for a patent shall be deemed invalid if it is demonstrated to the Controller, through documentary evidence and testimony, that the claimed invention was previously employed in any commercial activity within India, notwithstanding its non-disclosure to the public. Provided that, such demonstration must establish that the use constituted exploitation of the invention and not merely incidental operation. The burden of proving prior use shall rest upon the applicant challenging the patent’s validity. Further, where a registered trademark is affixed to goods manufactured utilizing the challenged process, the evidence presented must also address any deceptive or misleading implications arising from such mark use. Appeals against decisions under this provision may be made to the Appellate Board as provided herein.

For the purposes clause invention, an application for registration as a Plant Variety Protection shall be deemed to disclose all characteristics relating to the expression of the essential features of the variety, including its stability and distinctiveness, subject to any modifications arising from subsequent cultivation. The Registrar may require further documentation pertaining to the genetic composition and lineage of the plant material if concerns are raised regarding its novelty or conformity with established agricultural practices. Applications submitted by entities claiming farmers’ rights shall be processed expeditiously through the Farmers Rights Authority, ensuring due consideration is given to traditional knowledge and customary usage patterns. Provided that any prior public disclosure occurring before the filing date shall not invalidate the application unless it demonstrates a clear intention to commercially exploit the variety.

Application for registration of a biological entity shall be accompanied by a detailed report specifying the method of isolation and characterization of said entity, including particulars regarding its genetic makeup and metabolic pathways. The Controller General may require submission of additional data demonstrating stability and reproducibility of the biological entity across multiple generations or experimental conditions. Further, an applicant seeking to secure a patent act relating to a genetically modified organism must provide evidence substantiating that the modification does not unduly prejudice public health or environmental safety, as determined by guidelines issued by the relevant regulatory authority. The application shall also include a declaration affirming adherence to bio-containment protocols and ethical considerations during experimentation.

An application for a patent act shall not be entertained if it discloses an invention that constitutes an obvious modification of existing technology, unless the applicant demonstrates to the satisfaction of the Controller that such modification results in significant advancement in the field and possesses unexpected technical effects. Further, where the claimed invention relates to a method of agricultural practice, the applicant must provide detailed documentation substantiating that the process is novel and non-obvious, taking into consideration traditional knowledge and practices prevalent within the relevant geographical region. The Controller may require an expert assessment regarding the impact on biodiversity if the invention involves genetic modification or utilization of biological resources. Any infringement proceedings shall be subject to a preliminary determination concerning patent validity.

Where an application for a patent act relates to a method of treatment or diagnosis practised as medicine, the Controller may require the applicant to furnish such documentary evidence as he deems necessary to demonstrate that the invention possesses inventive step and industrial applicability. Any party aggrieved by any decision made under this provision relating to the requirement of documentary evidence may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The Appellate Board shall consider all relevant materials presented by the appellant and respondent, and its determination shall be final, subject to further review only on a petition to the Supreme Court based solely on grounds of law.

An application shall be deemed to be filed on the date on which it is received by the Controller or his representative. For the purposes of this Act, an application relating to a process for producing a substance shall include an application relating to the use of that substance. An applicant may be required to furnish such particulars concerning the invention as the Controller deems necessary for the purpose of examination under this Act. Where an application is filed jointly by two or more applicants, they shall be deemed to have taken steps jointly for the prosecution of the application india and any communication relating thereto shall be sent to one of them.

An applicant seeking registration of a patent under this Act shall furnish with the application a statement in English and Hindi specifying the claims supported by the description. The Controller may require the applicant to amend any claim if it is unclear or ambiguous; such amendment shall be made within the time specified, subject to the provisions regarding novelty and inventive step. Where an invention relates to a process for producing a substance defined by its chemical composition, the application shall clearly disclose how to obtain the substance. Any prior publication or public knowledge concerning the invention before the date of filing the *application india* will be considered in assessing patentability as provided herein.

An applicant seeking entry of an *application* relating to a process by which a substance is changed is required to furnish a certified copy of any corresponding *application india* filed in a convention country, provided that such corresponding application was filed within twelve months preceding the date of the request for entry. The Controller may require the applicant to submit further particulars or amendments deemed necessary to ensure clarity and compliance with the prescribed formalities under this Act. Failure to comply with these requirements shall render the *application* liable for rejection. Where an invention relates to a method for using a biological process, the applicant must demonstrate that the process is not contrary to public morality and ethics as provided herein.

An applicant seeking patent protection under this Act shall have the right to assign or license the rights pertaining to their pending *application india* to any person, firm, or company, subject to the provisions regarding royalty and conditions as may be stipulated within the agreement. Such assignments or licenses shall require registration with the Controller of Patents, and failure to register an assignment shall render it void unless otherwise proven by clear and convincing evidence before a competent judicial authority. The Controller may, upon receiving a complaint from any aggrieved party, investigate the terms of any such license and determine whether they are manifestly prejudicial to the public interest or contrary to the principles of fair competition. Any subsequent transfer of rights derived from an initial assignment shall also be subject to registration requirements as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, “invention” shall mean a new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or any improvement thereof, that is patentable under this Act. An invention shall be deemed to include agricultural or horticultural processes; however, such processes relating solely to the treatment of plants or animals are excluded from consideration as inventions unless they involve a method for producing a new plant or animal. A person shall be entitled to apply for a granted new patent if he has made the invention and in respect of which no prior publication exists anywhere in the world. The right to apply is subject to conditions regarding originality and non-obviousness, as provided herein.

Where an application for a patent has been granted new patent and subsequently challenged under this Act, the Controller may, upon receiving evidence demonstrating invalidity due to prior publication or use, issue an order revoking the patent. Such revocation shall be without prejudice to any rights already accrued by third parties acting in good faith based on the existence of the patent. The aggrieved party, including the patent holder and any claimant impacted by the revocation, may appeal such an order before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within a period of sixty days from the date of communication of the order. Further, where infringement proceedings are pending at the time of revocation, the Court shall determine the validity of the claims in light of the revoked patent’s status and any consequential remedies available to the parties involved as provided herein.

An application for a patent may be filed in the prescribed form with the Controller, setting forth the particulars of the invention and specifying the claims supported by proper specification. The applicant shall furnish such documents, statements, or declarations as are required under this Act to substantiate the novelty and inventive step of the claimed invention. Upon receipt of the application, the Controller shall assign an official number and date thereof and send a copy of the acknowledgement to the applicant. Where the Controller considers that the invention is not novel or does not involve sufficient inventive step, he may communicate these objections to the applicant, affording him an opportunity for response. If, following such response, the Controller remains satisfied that the invention fulfills the requirements under this Act, a patent shall be granted new patent and published in the Patent Journal.

Any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act relating to revocation of a patent may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The Appellate Board shall consider only questions of law arising out of the decision appealed against and may affirm, reverse, or modify the order appealed from, subject to such inquiry as it deems necessary. Where an infringement action is instituted following a patent having been granted new patent, any interlocutory orders passed by the trial court shall be appealable directly to the High Court. Failure to comply with an injunction issued under this Act shall render the defaulter liable for compensatory damages as determined by the Court and may also attract imprisonment for a term not exceeding one year.

Where an application for a patent has been granted new patent and subsequently challenged under this Act on grounds of novelty or inventive step, the Controller may, upon receiving written representations from interested parties disputing the validity of said patent, direct the patentee to submit counter-representations within a period not exceeding ninety days. Failure by the patentee to respond as directed shall be deemed an abandonment of the challenge proceedings and the matter shall stand dismissed. Provided that, any party aggrieved by such direction may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final subject to further review under principles of natural justice and judicial precedent as provided herein.

Where an application for a patent has been filed and subsequently examined under this Act, and where the Controller finds that the invention is novel, involves an inventive step, and is capable of industrial application, a new patent shall be granted to the applicant. The grant of such patent shall confer upon the patentee exclusive rights within India relating to the subject matter of the invention for a term as provided herein. Provided that any trade mark registered in accordance with the Trade Marks Act, 1999, which is identical or confusingly similar to a feature claimed in the granted new patent, may be considered during post-grant opposition proceedings. The Controller shall publish particulars of the granted patent in the Patent Journal for public information and awareness.

Where an invention relates to a process for producing a substance intended for use, or produced in the course of, a particular medical, dental, or veterinary treatment, the Controller may, subject to conditions specified therein, permit the applicant to extend the term of protection granted under this Act. Such permission shall be predicated upon demonstration that the invention possesses technical merit and involves inventive step beyond established practice within the relevant field. The court permits patent extension where it is satisfied that the delay in obtaining regulatory approval for marketing was not reasonably foreseeable at the date of filing the application, provided that such delay does not prejudice public interest.

Where an aggrieved party demonstrates to the satisfaction of the Controller that a patent has been granted in error due to material misrepresentation made by the applicant during the examination process, the Controller may refer the matter to the High Court for determination. The High Court shall have exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine such references, and its decision shall be final and binding. Subject to appeal under this Act, the court permits patent revocation if it finds that the representation was indeed material and induced reliance by the Controller. Further, any party adversely affected by a finding of the High Court may petition for costs incurred in pursuing the reference, as provided herein. The applicant whose patent is subject to such proceedings shall be liable to compensate the aggrieved party for demonstrable losses arising from the challenged validity, if the court so directs.

Where an application for a patent has been rejected by the Controller under this Act, and the applicant desires to challenge said rejection, he may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The Board shall give notice to the Controller requiring him to submit his reasons for such rejection within a period not exceeding sixty days from the date of service of the notice. Upon hearing the appellant and the Controller, and considering all relevant evidence presented, the Board may allow the appeal and direct that the patent be granted as originally applied for, or may modify the application and direct that a patent be granted according to such modification, or may dismiss the appeal. The court permits patent grant only after due consideration of the Board’s findings, subject to any legal challenge brought before it under established procedures as provided herein.

Where the Controller, upon receiving an objection relating to the patentability of an invention under this Act, determines that the objection raises substantial questions regarding the scope and validity of a pending application, he may permit the patent holder or applicant to enter into a licensing arrangement with any third party. Such permission shall be granted subject to conditions deemed necessary by the Controller to ensure fair competition and prevent abuse of market position. The terms of such license agreement, including royalty rates and duration, shall be disclosed to the Controller for record. Further, where an assignment of patent rights is made pursuant to a court order or as part of a settlement agreement relating to infringement proceedings, the court permits patent transfer may include provisions regarding ongoing obligations concerning maintenance fees or related intellectual property assets.

A patent granted new shall confer upon the patentee exclusive right to make, use and sell the patented invention for the term specified herein, subject to the provisions regarding compulsory licenses. For the purposes of this Act, a “patent granted new” is defined as a patent which has been examined and certified by the Controller as meeting all requirements under this Act, including novelty, inventive step, and industrial applicability; provided that such certification does not preclude challenges to the validity of the patent under any other provision of law.
