A registration notice is defined as a written communication submitted to the Trade Marks Registry under this Act, expressing objection to the proposed registration of a trade mark application. Such a notice must specify the grounds upon which the opposition is based, including but not limited to prior conflicting marks or deceptive similarity. The applicant for registration shall be afforded an opportunity to respond to the registration notice as provided herein. Failure to comply with the prescribed form and fee requirements when submitting a registration notice may render it invalid. Any person aggrieved by a decision relating to a registration notice may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

The Registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for registration of a trade mark, publish a preliminary acceptance in the Trade Marks Journal, indicating the goods or services with which the trade mark is proposed to be associated. Any person possessing a right or interest may, subject to this Act and within the prescribed period following publication of the registration notice, file a counterstatement opposing the application. The Registrar shall consider any such counterstatement and provide the applicant with an opportunity for response as provided herein. Further, where a trade mark is deceptively similar to an earlier mark, the opposition proceedings may be initiated based on evidence demonstrating likelihood of confusion amongst consumers. The Registrar’s decision regarding acceptance or rejection of the registration notice shall be final, subject to appeal under this Act.

Where an application for the registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act, any interested person may file a counter-statement within such time as may be prescribed, responding to the grounds of opposition. The Registrar shall, upon receipt of a valid counter-statement, proceed with the inquiry into the merits of the opposition. Failure by an opponent to comply with the requirements of filing a timely and properly constituted notice of opposition shall render the opposition void. Any person aggrieved by a decision regarding a registration notice may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such decision. The Board’s determination shall be final, subject to further appeal under the provisions relating to appeals to higher courts.

Upon receipt of an application for registration of a trade mark, the Registrar shall publish a preliminary acceptance in the Trade Marks Journal, specifying the trade mark, its class, and the date of filing. Any person may, within three months from the date of such publication, file with the Registrar a written opposition to the proposed registration, stating clearly the grounds upon which it is based and supported by affidavits verifying the facts alleged. The Registrar shall serve a copy of the notice of opposition on the applicant for registration, who may then submit a counterstatement in response within two months from the date of service. Where an opposition is founded solely on use prior to the filing date, evidence of such prior use must be furnished with the initial notice. Failure to comply with these procedural requirements regarding the *registration notice* shall render the opposition invalid, as provided herein.

The Registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for registration of a trade mark, publish a preliminary acceptance in the Trade Marks Journal, accompanied by a statement indicating the date on which objection may be lodged. Any person possessing a legitimate interest subject to this Act may, within four weeks from the date of such publication, file a notice of opposition with the Registrar, specifying the grounds for opposing registration and providing supporting documentation as prescribed herein. The Registrar shall promptly acknowledge receipt of the notice of opposition and transmit a copy thereof to the applicant for registration. Failure to comply with the stipulated format or payment of the requisite fee renders the registration notice invalid. Further, any subsequent amendment to the grounds stated in the initial notice requires prior consent from the Registrar.

Any proprietor seeking to rely upon a registration notice published under this Act shall file an affidavit verifying the accuracy of the information contained therein with the Registrar within thirty days of publication. Failure to do so renders the registration notice void ab initio and subjects the proprietor to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees, recoverable as arrears of land revenue. Any party aggrieved by the contents of a registration notice may petition the Intellectual Property Appellate Board for review, provided such petition is filed within sixty days of its publication and accompanied by a fee determined by notification. The Board’s decision shall be final, subject to appeal under this Act. Deliberate misrepresentation in a registration notice constitutes an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years.

Where the Registrar publishes a registration notice concerning a trade mark, any existing proprietor of a similar mark used in relation to identical or similar goods or services may, subject to this Act, grant a license to use the registered trade mark under specified conditions. Such licenses shall be recorded with the Registrar upon payment of the prescribed fee and shall detail the scope of permitted usage, including geographical limitations and duration. The proprietor granting such a license may assign the right to grant further licenses pertaining to that specific aspect of the registration notice, provided that any assignee undertakes to adhere to the original conditions stipulated within the initial license agreement. Any alteration or modification to these conditions requires prior written consent from the Registrar, ensuring continued compliance with provisions relating to fair trade practices and consumer protection as provided herein.

Any party aggrieved by the acceptance or rejection of an application for registration of a trade mark may, subject to provisions regarding time limits as provided herein, file an appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. Such appeal shall specify the grounds upon which it is based, including but not limited to errors apparent on the face of the record pertaining to the publication of a registration notice. The Registrar shall, within thirty days of receiving such appeal, transmit all relevant documents and records to the Tribunal for consideration. It shall be open to the applicant whose application was affected by the decision under appeal to present counter-arguments and evidence, provided that any such submissions are filed within fifteen days from service of the appellant’s grounds.

Any proprietor of a registered certification trade mark shall, upon application by any interested party demonstrating demonstrable prejudice resulting from non-compliance with the conditions of registration, furnish to that party a detailed accounting of all fees collected under this Act relating to the certification process. Failure to provide such an accounting within thirty days shall render the proprietor liable to a penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees and subject to further action by the relevant adjudicating authority. The Registrar may, upon receiving credible evidence of systematic failure to issue timely registration notices to certified users, initiate proceedings against the proprietor for breach of conditions. Such breaches may result in suspension or revocation of the certification trade mark registration.

Where a trade mark is registered under this Act, the Registrar shall publish a registration notice in such manner as may be prescribed, including electronic dissemination through the Trade Marks Registry website. Any proprietor of an existing trade mark identical or confusingly similar to the registered mark may, within three months of the publication of the registration notice, file with the Registrar a request for rectification seeking invalidation of the registration. Such requests shall specify the grounds upon which the opposition is based and provide supporting documentation as required by regulations framed under this Act. Furthermore, any collective management organization acting as a registration copyright society administering rights in literary or artistic works incorporated within goods bearing the registered trade mark may apply to the Registrar for assignment of sub-licensing powers relating to those copyrighted elements, subject to conditions prescribed herein.

The Registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for registration of a trade mark, publish a registration notice in the Trade Marks Journal, specifying the goods or services associated with the mark and inviting any interested party to file a counterstatement. Such notice shall remain published for a period not less than three months. Any person claiming prior right to use a similar mark may, within the stipulated timeframe as provided herein, submit a detailed counterstatement outlining their claim and supporting documentation. Failure to do so within that time will be deemed conclusive evidence against such claim, and the aforesaid committed forfeiture of any rights they might otherwise have asserted under this Act concerning the contested trade mark.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act, the Registrar shall issue a registration notice to the applicant and each opponent specifying the particulars of the trade mark and the grounds of opposition. The manner issuing such registration notices shall be as prescribed by regulations framed under this Act; provided that the Registrar may, at his discretion, permit service by electronic means where both parties consent or where such electronic service is otherwise permissible under applicable law. Failure to comply with the prescribed manner does not invalidate the notice itself but may affect the enforceability of any subsequent orders against a party claiming lack of due notice. Any aggrieved party may petition the Intellectual Property Appellate Board if they demonstrate prejudice arising from irregularities in the issuance of the registration notice, subject to just cause shown.

The Registrar may, upon receiving an application for registration of a proposed trade mark, direct that the hearing of the application be conducted before the Trade Marks Registry if reasonable grounds exist to believe that the applicant’s claim to priority or earlier rights is disputed by any interested party. Such direction shall specify the date, time and place for the hearing, providing at least thirty days' notice to all parties appearing on the register as opposers or claimants. The applicant shall be obligated to present documentary evidence substantiating their asserted prior use of the mark, if applicable. Failure to appear at the appointed hearing may result in the application being deemed abandoned, subject to reconsideration by the Registrar. Any person aggrieved by a decision made under this Act relating to uses registered trade marks may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such decision.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, no person shall utilize a registered trade mark except with the consent of the proprietor, provided that such utilization complies fully with established guidelines regarding fair competition. The Registrar may, upon application by an aggrieved party demonstrating actual damage resulting from unauthorized uses registered trade marks, issue an order restraining further use where the infringing activity creates confusion amongst consumers concerning the origin or quality of goods or services. Such orders shall specify the precise nature of the prohibited activities and may include requirements for corrective advertising to mitigate any existing consumer deception. Any subsequent violation of a restraint order issued under this Act will be deemed a continuing offence, subject to penalties as provided herein.

Any person who, without leave of the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal, uses a registered trade mark in connection with goods or services for which it is not registered, shall be liable to pay damages of an amount determined by the High Court. Such damages may include loss of profits sustained by the proprietor of the registered trade mark and any but not limited to costs incurred by the proprietor in taking action under this Act. Further, where a false or misleading representation concerning the use, quality, or origin of goods or services is made in connection with the uses registered trade marks, the offender shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and with a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees.

The proprietor of a registered trade mark shall have the exclusive right to prevent, subject to this Act, the use of any mark identical or similar as to be likely to cause confusion with their registered trade mark. Any proprietor may grant licences permitting others to uses registered trade marks owned by them, specifying the goods or services in relation to which such use is authorized and defining the territorial extent of such authorization. Such licenses may be assigned or sub-licensed, provided that any assignment or sub-licence shall be recorded with the Trade Marks Registry. Where a proprietor has entered into an agreement for the uses registered trade mark, they are bound by the terms thereof unless otherwise permitted under this Act. Further, where consent is given for a particular use of a registered trade mark, such consent does not constitute a perpetual right and remains subject to revocation at the discretion of the proprietor.

Subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal, no person shall be found to have made unlawful uses registered trade marks unless it is demonstrated that the defendant’s adoption of a sign creates a likelihood of confusion on the part of the public to the detriment of the proprietor. Provided that such demonstration considers not only the similarity of the signs themselves but also factors including the nature of the goods or services, the channels of trade and the state of information of the relevant consumers. It shall be a defence for the defendant to prove prior honest concurrent use of an identical mark in relation to similar goods, provided that such use did not create confusion at the time of registration. The Tribunal may order damages as appropriate.

Where a trade mark is registered in India and subsequently subject to an international registration application filed under the means madrid agreement, the proprietor shall be entitled to enforce the rights conferred by such Indian registration against any person infringing the said trade mark within the territory of India. Any act constituting infringement, occurring after the date of publication of the international registration designating India, shall be actionable as if the international registration had been directly registered in India. Provided that, where an opposition is filed under this Act against the designation of India in an international registration, the proprietor’s rights are subject to the outcome of such opposition proceedings and may be suspended pending their resolution. Furthermore, remedies available for trade mark infringement under this Act shall apply equally to infringements arising from international registrations, subject to any procedural modifications deemed necessary by the relevant intellectual property authority.

For the purposes of this Act, where a trade mark is designated for protection in India through an international application filed under the means madrid agreement, the designation shall be deemed to constitute a separate application relating only to India. Such application is subject to all requirements and procedures applicable under this Act to applications for registration as if it were an initial application made directly within India. The Registrar may require the deposit of any prescribed fees associated with such international designations. Provided that, where an international registration extends protection to India, subsequent amendments or renewals shall be processed in accordance with regulations pertaining to extensions of existing registrations and subject to compliance with all relevant provisions regarding distinctiveness and non-use.

Where a trade mark is registered in India and subsequently subject to an international application designating India, as facilitated by the means madrid agreement, any challenge to the validity of that registration may be brought before the relevant intellectual property forum within three months from the date of publication of such designation. Failure to initiate proceedings within this stipulated timeframe shall preclude subsequent legal recourse regarding the designated trade mark’s enforceability. The Registrar shall, upon receiving notice of a challenge under this provision, promptly issue summons to all interested parties and may order interim relief pending final determination. Any party found to have acted in bad faith or deliberately obstructed enforcement procedures will be liable for compensatory damages as determined by the forum.

Where a trade mark is registered in India and subsequently subject to an international application designating India, as facilitated by the means madrid agreement, any challenge to the validity of the registration arising from grounds available under this Act shall be deemed to have been raised upon the filing of a notice of opposition within the prescribed period. Provided that such notice must specifically identify the designated trade mark and articulate the relevant statutory ground for invalidity pertaining to prior use or confusing similarity. The Registrar may, at his discretion, require the applicant for extension of protection to furnish evidence demonstrating continued use in India since the initial registration. Any appeal against an order passed by the Registrar concerning international registrations shall lie to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Where a trade mark is registered in India and subsequently extended through the means madrid agreement to a designated contracting party, any infringement occurring within that designated territory shall be actionable under this Act as if the trade mark were originally registered therein. The owner of such an internationally protected trade mark may institute proceedings for relief against acts of adaptation or use contrary to law, including those relating to layout design vested in another person, irrespective of whether the original registration was challenged or revoked within India. Further, remedies available under this Act concerning damages, injunctions, and account of profits shall apply equally to infringements committed abroad through such extensions. The Registrar may, upon application by an aggrieved party, issue directions for seizure and destruction of goods bearing infringing marks extended via the Madrid system.

For the purposes of this Act, "international trademark" means a trade mark registered through an application extended under the Madrid Protocol international system for the registration of marks. Such an international trademark shall be deemed to confer rights only in respect of those Contracting Parties designated in the international registration, subject to any limitations or conditions as may be prescribed by the regulations of that designated territory. An applicant seeking extension of protection via the Madrid Protocol must satisfy all requirements under this Act applicable to a domestic application, provided that priority date considerations shall be determined according to the rules established within the aforementioned protocol.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark shall, in addition to fulfilling requirements as provided herein regarding distinctiveness and acceptable matter, indicate whether the application is intended to claim priority from an earlier trade mark application filed in a designated Contracting Party under the Madrid Protocol International system. Such indication must be made at the time of filing the application or within such period as may be prescribed by regulations framed under this Act. The Trade Marks Registry shall maintain a separate record of applications claiming priority under the aforementioned protocol, noting the date and reference number of the earlier application. Failure to accurately disclose details concerning the priority claim may render the registration vulnerable to challenge during opposition proceedings, subject to judicial review.

Where a trade mark is registered in India and subsequently extended through the mechanism of the Madrid Protocol International, the proprietor shall be entitled to enforce the rights conferred by such registration against any person infringing the same within the territory of India. Any act constituting infringement under this Act shall render the infringer liable for damages, including but not limited to lost profits, reasonable royalties, and costs incurred in protecting the trade mark’s validity. Provided that, where an opposition is filed against an international registration extension, the rights afforded by the Indian registration shall remain subject to the outcome of such opposition proceedings. Further, any party aggrieved by a decision relating to the acceptance or rejection of an international registration extension may appeal to the relevant appellate authority as provided herein.

Where a trade mark is registered in India and subsequently extended through the mechanism of the Madrid Protocol International, the proprietor shall be entitled to enforce the rights conferred by such registration against any person infringing the said trade mark within the territory of India. Any party seeking relief for infringement must demonstrate that the challenged use or activity falls within the scope of protection afforded under this Act and relates directly to the internationally registered trade mark as extended. Furthermore, a claim predicated on an international registration shall not preclude reliance upon prior conflicting rights existing in India, irrespective of the date of filing of the initial application. The remedies available for infringement, including injunctions and damages, are subject to principles governing patent litigation concerning novelty and inventive step, ensuring equitable balance between proprietors and potential infringers.

Applications for registration of a trade mark may be filed in accordance with the provisions of this Act, and shall include an indication, where applicable, that the application is intended to seek extension of protection under the Madrid Protocol international system. The Trade Marks Registry shall maintain a register of such applications, separate from the principal Register, detailing the basic designation and any priority claims asserted therein. Any representation or reproduction of registered trade marks for purposes of reprography, including but not limited to photocopying or digital scanning, undertaken in connection with an international application is subject to the same limitations as apply to similar acts concerning domestic registrations under this Act. The Registrar may require applicants seeking protection through the Madrid Protocol to furnish such documentation and declarations verifying entitlement and use as deemed necessary for examination purposes. Failure to comply with these requirements shall render the application liable for rejection.

For the purposes of this Act, "international trademark" means a trademark registered through an application made under the Protocol Madrid Agreement concerning the International Registration of Marks. Such registration shall confer upon its proprietor the rights that he would have been entitled to had an identical mark been registered directly in India under this Act, subject to any limitations or conditions specified therein. An international trademark shall be deemed to be registered in India from the date on which the relevant international registration extends protection to India, as notified by the Registrar. The provisions relating to rectification proceedings and opposition may apply to international trademarks as provided herein.

An applicant seeking designation of India in an international application filed under the Protocol Madrid Agreement shall furnish, along with the request for registration, a certified true copy of the international registration certificate issued by the International Bureau. The Registrar may require such further particulars or declarations as are necessary to ascertain compliance with the provisions of this Act and the regulations framed thereunder. Where an international mark is designated in India, the priority date for determining rights shall be that of the earlier application from which the international application originated, subject to any conflicting prior registrations under this Act. The applicant shall also provide a translation of the mark into Devanagari script where the mark is not wholly comprised of letters or numerals.

Where a trade mark is registered internationally through the application of the Protocol Madrid Agreement, and such international registration designates India, the rights afforded to the proprietor shall be subject to the provisions of this Act as if the international registration were an initial registration under this Act. Any person aggrieved by any act or omission relating to the designation of India in an international registration may institute proceedings before the relevant intellectual property tribunal seeking remedies including injunctions and damages, provided that such grievance arises from a violation of rights conferred under this Act or any other law for the time being in force. The proprietor of an internationally registered trade mark shall be liable to render accounts of profits derived from use of the mark in India if such use is determined to infringe upon prior conflicting rights established within Indian territory, as provided herein.

Where an applicant seeks designation of India in an international application filed under the Protocol Madrid Agreement, such application shall be examined for compliance with all applicable provisions relating to registrability as if it were a domestic trade mark application. The Registrar may require the deposit of any prescribed fee within three months from the date of receipt of the international application at the International Bureau, provided that failure to comply with this requirement shall render the designation ineffectual. Further, an indication of refusal issued by the International Bureau concerning India’s designation shall be binding on the Registrar unless a reasoned objection is formally submitted by the applicant within sixty days from notification under this Act.

Any person who, without due cause and with intent to deceive, uses a trade mark identical or confusingly similar to an international registration extending to India under the protocol madrid agreement shall be guilty of an offence. Such offender shall be liable for damages equivalent to three times the value of the goods or services in relation to which the infringement occurred, as determined by the Intellectual Property Disputes Tribunal. Further, any proprietor of a registered trade mark who knowingly makes false statements regarding the status of an international registration under this Act may face prosecution and penalties including imprisonment for a term not exceeding five years, and a fine which shall extend to one million rupees. The Registrar may issue injunctions restraining such deceptive practices as provided herein.

The owner of a trade mark registered in India may, subject to this Act and the regulations framed thereunder, grant a license conferring the right to use the trade mark exclusively for specific goods or services within a defined territory. Such licenses shall be assignable, either wholly or partially, provided that any such assignment is recorded with the Trade Marks Registry and takes effect only upon such recording. Where an international application designating India has been received by the Receiving Office under the Protocol Madrid Agreement, the owner’s consent to any subsequent assignments or licenses relating to the designated goods or services shall be deemed necessary for validity against third parties within Indian jurisdiction unless expressly waived in writing. Further, a licensee may freely assign their rights derived from a license granted under this Act, but such assignment does not extend to the underlying trade mark ownership itself as provided herein.

Where a trade mark is designated for registration in India through an international application filed under the Protocol Madrid Agreement, and an objection is raised by the Trade Marks Registry based on grounds similar to those which could have been taken if the application had been filed directly with the Registry, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity of being heard. Such hearing may be conducted either orally or in writing, as the Registrar deems fit. The decision rendered following such hearing shall be final, subject to appeal under this Act to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within a period of sixty days from the date of communication of said decision. Any party aggrieved by the order of the Appellate Board may further appeal to the High Court on grounds specified herein.

Where a trade mark is registered in India and subsequently subject to an international application filed under the Protocol Madrid Agreement, extending protection to designated Contracting Parties, any challenge to the validity of the Indian registration shall be deemed to affect the corresponding international registration to the extent of such extension. The Registrar may, upon receiving notice from any interested party alleging that the trade mark’s use in a designated country is contrary to law or public order, and causing confusion amongst consumers, initiate proceedings for revocation. Such proceedings shall apply geographical indications where the challenged use incorporates or alludes to those indications. Further, remedies available under this Act for passing off actions relating to the Indian registration shall also be enforceable against infringers operating within a designated Contracting Party benefiting from the extended protection, subject to reciprocity agreements.

Where a trade mark is designated for India in pursuance of the Protocol Madrid Agreement, and the designation is accepted by the Trade Marks Registry, any subsequent application for registration of an identical mark for identical goods or services shall be deemed to have been filed on the date accorded patent under the Patents Act. Any party aggrieved by such acceptance may institute proceedings before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within ninety days from the publication of the acceptance in the Trade Marks Journal. Failure to comply with this provision will render any subsequent action void and subject the offending applicant to a penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees, recoverable as a debt owed to the Union. The Registrar shall have power to issue injunctions restraining acts contrary to these provisions.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark shall, in addition to fulfilling requirements as provided herein, submit evidence demonstrating adherence to an agreement means madrid protocol concerning the international registration of marks. Such evidence must clearly articulate the designated Contracting Parties included within the scope of the international registration and specify any limitations or disclaimers applied during the application process. The Registrar may request further clarification regarding the applicant’s compliance with the aforementioned agreement, including details pertaining to translation requirements for elements of the mark not originally in English or Hindi. Failure to adequately substantiate adherence to an agreement means madrid will render the application liable for rejection, subject to appeal before the Appellate Board.

Where a proprietor seeks to register a trade mark in India based on an earlier trade mark registered or applied for in respect of identical or similar goods or services, and such registration or application is obtained through an *agreement means madrid*, the Registrar shall issue a notice to any interested party claiming rights under that prior registration or application. Such notice shall detail the pending application and provide a period not exceeding sixty days within which objection may be filed. Failure to comply with this provision will render the applicant liable for penalties as provided herein, including but not limited to fines up to one hundred thousand rupees. Any successful objection shall require the Registrar to refuse registration unless the applicant demonstrates sufficient cause mitigating against infringement.

Where a trade mark owner, being a party to an agreement means madrid, desires to assign or license the right to use such registered trade mark in relation to any goods or services for which it is registered, such assignment or licence shall be recorded with the Trade Marks Registry. The Registrar may require such documentation as deemed necessary to verify the authenticity of the agreement and the identity of all parties involved. Any subsequent transfer of rights arising from a licensed agreement means madrid shall also be subject to registration under this Act. Provided that, where an agreement means madrid involves a security interest in the trade mark, the terms thereof shall be clearly defined within the recorded documentation. The Registrar may refuse registration if the proposed assignment or licence is deemed prejudicial to the interests of consumers or unfairly restricts competition within the relevant market.

Where a proprietor seeks to register a trade mark in India based on an earlier trade mark registered or applied for in respect of identical or similar goods or services, and such registration or application is founded upon an *agreement means madrid*, the Registrar shall give notice thereof to the applicant for the conflicting mark. Such notice shall specify the grounds relied upon by the proprietor, detailing any likelihood of confusion arising from the similarity between the marks and the identity or resemblance of the goods or services. The recipient of such notice may file a counter-statement within the prescribed period, disputing the claim and presenting evidence to demonstrate absence of deception or misrepresentation. Any dispute concerning the validity of the *agreement means madrid* itself shall be subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, as provided herein.

Where a trade mark proprietor seeks to designate India as part of an international application, such designation shall be treated for all purposes under this Act as if it were an initial application filed directly with the Trade Marks Registry. The Registrar may require further particulars or modifications to the representation or description of the trade mark as presented in the international application to ensure compliance with Indian requirements. An agreement means madrid system protocol and is binding upon both parties, subject to any subsequent revocation under this Act. The application date shall be deemed to be the filing date of the international application, provided that any priority claim asserted therein is duly substantiated. Any fees payable relating to the designation shall be determined according to prevailing regulations as provided herein.

Where a proprietor of a trade mark, having entered into an agreement means madrid concerning the use of their trade mark in relation to cinematograph film production and distribution within India, subsequently institutes proceedings for infringement under this Act, the court shall consider whether the defendant’s actions constitute a breach of that agreement. Any party seeking relief based on such a contractual violation must demonstrate clear evidence of the agreement's existence and its material terms. Failure to do so will result in dismissal of the claim without prejudice to any other remedies available under contract law. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint regarding unauthorized use stemming from an alleged breach, issue summons requiring parties to submit relevant documentation; wilful non-compliance shall attract penalties as provided herein.

An international registration shall be deemed to have resulted in a resulting international registration when an application for registration of a trade mark is made under this Act relating to any goods or services identical to those specified in the international registration, and such application incorporates by reference the earlier international registration. For the purposes of determining priority under this Act, the date of filing of the international registration shall be taken into account as if it were the date of filing of the trade mark application made under this Act. Nothing in this section shall prevent an applicant from making any alteration to the goods or services specified in the Indian application beyond those included in the resulting international registration.

An international registration shall have effect subject to any limitations and conditions specified therein, and for the purposes of determining entitlement under this Act, the applicant for such registration shall be deemed to be the proprietor of the trade mark in India in relation to the territory of India as designated in the international application. Where an international registration extends to India, any subsequent application filed in India relating to goods or services identical or similar to those covered by the resulting international registration shall be treated as if it were a later date of filing for the purposes of priority and earlier rights. The Registrar may require evidence of compliance with the provisions governing international registrations before accepting any application claiming benefit from such a registration, provided that this requirement does not prejudice the applicant’s right to seek remedies under this Act.

Upon an international registration resulting from an earlier Indian trade mark application, any person aggrieved by the use of a sign identical or similar to the registered trade mark, and likely to be confused with it, may institute legal proceedings for infringement under this Act as if the international registration were a domestic registration. The remedies available shall include injunctions restraining further infringing acts, damages sustained by the proprietor of the trade mark, and delivery up or destruction of goods bearing the infringing sign. Provided that where an opposition is filed against the acceptance of the Indian application forming the basis of the resulting international registration, the provisions relating to rectification proceedings under this Act shall apply mutatis mutandis to challenge the validity of the international registration itself. Further, any counterclaim arising from such rectification proceedings shall be dealt with according to established procedures.

An international registration resulting from an earlier trade mark shall have effect subject to the provisions of this Act and any relevant rules made thereunder. The Trade Marks Registry may, upon receipt of a request for extension of time under section 126, grant such extension where it is satisfied that the applicant has diligently prosecuted the application for international registration and that there are reasonable grounds for believing that the international registration will proceed to completion. Where an objection is raised against an application for resulting international registration based on any ground specified in this Act, the procedure prescribed under Chapter VI shall apply mutatis mutandis. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registry relating to a request for extension or regarding objections may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such decision. The Registrar shall maintain a register of international registrations and resulting international registration available for public inspection.

An international registration resulting from an earlier trade mark shall have effect subject to compliance with the provisions relating to territorial extent under this Act. Where a refusal of registration is recorded against an applicant in India subsequent to the date of application for an international registration, the Registrar may require the deposit of a sum sufficient to cover the costs incurred by the office in investigating the matter. Such requirement shall be communicated in writing and the amount so deposited shall be deemed part of the official fees payable under this Act. The proprietor of the resulting international registration shall remain responsible for ensuring continued compliance with all applicable regulations pertaining to trade mark usage and renewal as provided herein.

Where an international registration extends to India and is subject to a subsequent application for registration under this Act, any infringement occurring before the date of that Indian registration shall be actionable as if the resulting international registration had existed from its inception. The Registrar may, upon receiving complaint from any person aggrieved by such infringement, issue summons to the alleged infringer requiring them to appear and show cause why they should not be restrained from further infringing the trade mark. Failure to comply with such summons or a finding of infringement shall render the infringer liable to pay damages, costs, and in cases of wilful infringement, a penalty not exceeding five lakhs rupees for each instance of contravention.

Where an international registration is based on a trade mark registered in India, and such resulting international registration covers goods or services for which the Indian trade mark owner desires to grant a license or assign rights, the licensee or assignee shall be deemed to hold only those rights pertaining directly to the territory of India as specified within the international registration. Such licenses and assignments may be recorded with the Trade Marks Registry upon payment of the prescribed fee, provided that the original proprietor of the Indian trade mark provides written consent for such recording. Further, any subsequent assignment or license granted by the licensee or assignee shall require similar consent from both the original proprietor and the holder of the international registration. The Registrar may request further documentation to verify the authenticity of these consents as deemed necessary.

Where an international registration extends to India pursuant to the provisions relating to resulting international registrations, and a conflicting mark is subsequently applied for or registered under this Act, any party aggrieved by such application or registration may institute proceedings before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such proceedings shall be limited to demonstrating that the earlier resulting international registration was validly extended and that the subsequent application or registration constitutes a violation of its rights. The Board may, upon consideration of evidence presented, order the cancellation of the conflicting mark or restrain its use, provided that such order does not prejudice the continued validity of the existing resulting international registration as determined under this Act.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and the regulations framed thereunder, any proprietor of a trade mark who has obtained an international registration designating India shall have the right to grant a license conferring the exclusive privilege to use the registered trade mark within the territory of India. Such licenses may be granted for a reasonable period, not exceeding twenty years from the date of initial designation in the international registration, and may be assignable subject to conditions prescribed by the Registrar. Where an assignment of the trade mark or any such license occurs, the resulting international registration shall vest with the assignee, provided that the Assignee acknowledges and adheres to all obligations previously undertaken by the Assignor under this Act concerning the said international registration. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating due diligence in ensuring continued compliance with Indian law following any such assignment.

An international registration shall have effect subject to any limitations or conditions specified therein and shall confer upon the proprietor the rights which accrue under this Act as if the trade mark were registered in India with that date of application for registration. For the purposes of determining entitlement to remedies for infringement, a resulting international registration shall be deemed to be a registered trade mark within the meaning of this Act. Where an international registration includes denominations relating to agricultural produce or other products, denomination variety shall be considered as part of the indication and afforded protection accordingly, provided that such use does not create confusion among consumers.

For the purposes of this Act, “international registration protection” shall mean the benefit derived from an international registration made under the Madrid Protocol, wherein a trade mark registered in India is extended to designated contracting states. Such extension is subject to any limitations or conditions prescribed by the laws of those states and as provided herein. Producers intending to avail themselves of such international registration protection must demonstrate that their goods or services conform to relevant quality standards applicable within each designated territory. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating this conformity prior to granting extensions, provided that the trade mark remains eligible for renewal under this Act.

An applicant desiring to avail of the benefits of india international registration in respect of a trade mark shall file Form TM-IR with the prescribed fee. Such application may be made only if the trade mark is registered or formally applied for in the country of origin. The Registrar shall publish particulars of the india international registration application, including details of the original registration and any limitations of protection sought. Any person claiming to be interested may, subject to this Act, file a notice of opposition within the period specified herein. Where an opposition is filed, it shall be dealt with in accordance with the procedures applicable to applications for registration under this Act, provided that the Registrar may require evidence demonstrating continued use of the trade mark in the country of origin.

An owner seeking to extend the protection conferred by an earlier trade mark to India through an india international registration shall be entitled to apply to the Registrar for entry of the international registration on the Register of Trade Marks. Such application must be accompanied by a certified true copy of the international registration certificate and any statement of designation of India contained therein. The Registrar may, upon receiving such application, direct that the international registration be treated as if it were an application for registration under this Act, subject to the provisions relating to examination and acceptance. Any person aggrieved by the entry of an international registration on the Register may file a notice of opposition within the prescribed period, provided that the grounds of opposition shall be limited to those specified in section 29. The Registrar shall afford all parties a reasonable opportunity to present their case during any such proceedings.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark under this Act may elect to extend the protection conferred by an india international registration to India, subject to compliance with the provisions herein. Such election shall be made within six months from the date on which the International Bureau sends notice that the international registration is deemed to have effect in India, as per the Madrid Protocol. The Registrar shall publish a notice of such extension in the Trade Marks Journal. Any person may file a post-grant opposition against the extended registration within four months of the publication date. The grounds for opposition shall be those available under this Act relating to acquired distinctiveness and deceptively similar marks. The applicant shall furnish any prescribed fee as determined by notification issued from time to time. Failure to comply with these procedures will render the india international registration unenforceable in India.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark through an india international registration shall furnish to the Registry a certified true copy of the international application form, together with the statement of designation specifying India as one of the designated territories. Such application is subject to examination under this Act as if it were an original application for registration and may be refused if any ground for refusal exists under section 9 or section 11. Provided that where the International Bureau has already carried out an examination of absolute grounds for refusal, the Registry shall consider such findings but retains discretion to conduct further investigation if deemed necessary. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating use of the mark in India prior to grant of registration, as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by any act or omission in contravention of this Act relating to an india international registration may institute proceedings before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board seeking appropriate relief, including but not limited to damages, injunctions, and account of profits. The Board shall have power to award costs as it deems just. Where a trade mark is registered under an india international registration, any use of an identical or deceptively similar mark in relation to goods or services for which the registration is valid shall be deemed a violation subject to penalties prescribed herein. Further, wilful infringement may attract enhanced fines and imprisonment up to three years, as determined by the Board based on the extent of commercial detriment caused.

Where an owner of a trade mark seeks to obtain india international registration designating India, and such designation involves territory where another person is already registered or has applied for registration of an identical or similar mark, the owner may enter into a licensing agreement with that other person. Such agreement shall specify the scope of permitted use within the designated territory, including but not limited to goods and services as defined in the existing or pending registration. The Registrar may require submission of such licensing agreement prior to acceptance of the india international registration designation, provided that the terms do not contravene any provisions under this Act relating to dilution or unfair competition. Any assignment of rights arising from such a license shall be subject to the same requirements as apply to assignments of trade mark ownership generally, and must be notified to the Registrar for recordation.

Where an applicant seeks to avail themselves of the provisions relating to india international registration under this Act, they shall file Form TM-IR together with the prescribed fee. The Registrar may, upon examination, direct that any mark included in such application be refused registration if it conflicts with a prior registered trade mark or pending application as provided herein. Any party aggrieved by such direction of refusal may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. It shall be open for the appellant to demonstrate, during the appellate proceedings, that the Registrar’s assessment of conflict was erroneous and did not adequately consider relevant distinguishing characteristics.

An international registration designating India shall be deemed to constitute an application for registration of the marks specified therein in respect of the goods or services for which such designation was made, subject to compliance with all requirements under this Act applicable to applications filed on or after the date of such designation. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish further particulars relating to the international registration, including details of earlier trade mark registrations or pending applications relied upon in support thereof. Any representation appearing on the register resulting from an india international registration shall be subject to the same rights and limitations as if it were a trade mark registered directly under this Act.

An applicant seeking India International Registration in respect of goods or services may apply to the Registry for entry of the international registration onto the Register of Trade Marks, subject to compliance with the provisions herein. Such application shall be accompanied by a certified true copy of the international registration document as issued by the Contracting Party’s office responsible for international registrations. The Registrar shall examine the application and may require the applicant to furnish further information or documentation relating to the goods or services specified in the international registration.

Provided that, if an interested party demonstrates substantial local investment and use related to a similar mark, they may apply to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board for a compulsory licence permitting parallel importation of goods bearing the internationally registered trade mark, subject to conditions determined by the Board considering public interest and equitable compensation. The Registrar shall publish a notice of acceptance or rejection within three months from the date of filing of the application.

Where an international registration designating India is subject to an opposition under this Act, the opponent shall serve a copy of the Notice of Opposition on the applicant for international registration within the prescribed period. The applicant may file a counterstatement in response to the opposition, as provided herein, and such counterstatement shall be accompanied by any evidence relied upon in support thereof. Failure to comply with these procedural requirements regarding service and filing may render the opposition vulnerable to challenge under this Act. If an objection is raised concerning acquired distinctiveness of the mark within India, the Registrar shall consider all relevant evidence presented by both parties. The applicant for international registration retains the right to appeal any decision made by the Registrar relating to such an international registration opposed.

Where an international registration designating India is subject to an opposition, the Registrar shall give notice thereof to the applicant for the international registration in accordance with the prescribed manner. The notice shall specify the grounds of opposition and the name and address of the opponent. Subject to any direction by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, the Registrar may require the opponent to furnish security for costs as provided herein. Any party aggrieved by an order made under this Act relating to an international registration opposed may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The International Bureau shall be notified of any opposition filed and of any subsequent orders affecting the status of the international registration, in accordance with the Convention establishing the Agreement on Trade Marks.

Where an international registration designating India is subject to an opposition under this Act, the grounds for such opposition shall be limited to those which could have been raised had the application for registration constituted an original application filed in India. The opponent shall serve notice of the opposition on the applicant within the time prescribed herein, and the applicant may file a counterstatement responding to the particulars of the objection. Failure by the applicant to file a timely counterstatement shall not, however, preclude the Board from considering arguments raised during the hearing. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Registrar relating to such international registration opposed may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of that order, subject to any applicable fees and conditions as provided herein.

Where an international registration designating India is refused in whole or in part, any party aggrieved by the refusal may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the notice of the refusal. Such an appeal shall be finally determinable by the Board. The Board may, after affording opportunity for a hearing to all parties concerned, confirm, modify, or reverse the decision appealed against and may direct the Registrar to proceed with registration as if the international registration had been initially filed in India. Further, any person who has suffered damage by reason of any act or omission done in contravention of this Act relating to an international registration case shall be entitled to sue for damages in a suit in the appropriate court.

An international registration designating India shall be treated as an application for registration under this Act; provided that the applicant shall furnish to the Registrar a certified copy of the international application form and any subsequent amendments or designations. The Registrar may require the applicant to provide such further information relating to the goods or services for which registration is sought as are necessary for the proper examination of the application. Where an objection is raised against an international registration, the procedure applicable shall be that prescribed for opposition proceedings under this Act, with the International Bureau being notified accordingly. The Registrar shall afford any interested party a reasonable opportunity to file evidence in support of or opposing the designation of India within the international registration case. Decisions rendered by the Registrar concerning such designations are appealable as provided herein.

Where an international registration designating India is refused in whole or in part, the applicant may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the refusal order. Such appeal shall be filed in the prescribed manner and accompanied by a fee as determined under this Act. The Board may, after giving notice to all interested parties and affording them an opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify or reverse the decision appealed against. Any party aggrieved by any order passed by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board relating to an international registration case may further appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such order, subject to just cause shown.

An international registration designating India may be subject to examination in accordance with the procedures applicable to applications for registration under this Act, provided that any prior conflicting trade mark registered in India shall be given due consideration. The Registrar shall provide an opportunity to the applicant and the proprietor of any potentially conflicting mark to submit their respective arguments and evidence. Where an appeal is filed against a decision refusing registration or limiting the scope of protection granted through an international registration case, the prescribed appeal fee accompanied by the requisite documentation must be remitted within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. Failure to comply with this requirement shall render the appeal void ab initio.

Where an assignment or transmission of a registered trademark is disputed under this Act, the aggrieved party may file an objection with the Registrar within three months from the date of publication of the proposed registration of title. Such objection shall specify the grounds upon which it is based, including but not limited to allegations of fraud, misrepresentation, or lack of consent from the original proprietor. The Registrar shall provide the assignee or transmittee with a reasonable opportunity to respond to the objection and present evidence in their favour. Following consideration of all submissions, the Registrar’s decision regarding the validity of the assignment transmission registered shall be final, subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days.

Subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal, an objection filed under this Act against a proposed registration of a trade mark may be based on any ground demonstrating that the applicant lacks sufficient distinctiveness for the relevant goods or services. The Registrar shall consider such objections in accordance with principles of natural justice and provide the applicant with an opportunity to submit written arguments and evidence rebutting the grounds raised. If, following this process, the Registrar determines that the objection is meritorious, he may refuse registration; however, such a determination is subject to review by the Tribunal upon appeal from any party aggrieved. The registrar register title shall be conclusive evidence of ownership unless proven otherwise through fraud or misrepresentation.

An applicant seeking registration of a geographical indication shall file an application with the Registrar in the prescribed form, accompanied by the requisite fee. The application must specify the name of the geographical indication as it is proposed to be registered, a description of the products for which the indication seeks protection, and the area of its origin. Upon receipt of such application, the Registrar may direct the applicant to rectify any defects or ambiguities therein.

The Registrar shall publish particulars of the application in the Trade Marks Journal and invite objections from interested parties within the time specified under this Act. Any person alleging that the registration of the geographical indication would be contrary to law or prejudicial to the public interest may file an objection. The Registrar shall consider all such objections and, after affording the applicant and objector an opportunity of being heard, determine whether the application should proceed for registration in the registrar register title.

For the purposes of this Act, an “application register proprietor” means a person whose name is entered upon the Register of Trade Marks as the proprietor of a trade mark solely by virtue of being the applicant for registration thereof, prior to the grant of such registration. Such entry shall not confer any right or title to the trade mark other than that which arises from the subsequent grant of registration under this Act. An application register proprietor may, subject to prescribed conditions and as provided herein, assign or transmit their interest in the pending application. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all assignments and transmissions affecting an application register proprietor’s rights.

An application for registration of a trade mark may be refused by the Registrar if he considers that the proposed marks are likely to be confused with any registered trade marks under this Act. Upon such refusal, the applicant shall have the right to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Where an application is accepted and registered, the person whose name appears on the register as the proprietor of the trade mark shall be entitled to enforce the rights conferred by registration against all persons infringing or likely to infringe that trade mark. The Registrar may, upon receiving a request in writing from any interested party, require the applicant to furnish further information relating to the use of the trade mark. Any alteration to details recorded concerning an application register proprietor must be notified to the Registrar within thirty days.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is refused under this Act, the applicant may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The Board shall hear such appeals expeditiously and may allow the appeal, set aside the refusal, or direct the Registrar to reconsider the matter in accordance with any observations made by the Board. Upon successful appeal and subsequent registration, the appellant shall be registered as an *application register proprietor* for the trade mark, subject to compliance with all prescribed conditions. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Intellectual Property Appellate Board relating to such refusal may further appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of that decision. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all proprietors and their respective rights as provided herein.

An application for registration of a trade mark may be made by any person claiming to be the owner of the intended trade mark, and where such an applicant is not the originator of the trade mark, he shall furnish along with the application evidence of his right to make the application. Upon receipt of an application meeting the requirements as provided herein, the Registrar shall record the particulars thereof in the Trade Marks Journal. Any person may file a notice of opposition under this Act within the prescribed period from the date of such publication. If an opposition is filed and determined against the applicant, the Registrar shall refuse to register the trade mark. However, if the application proceeds unchallenged or any opposition is resolved in favour of the applicant, he shall be entered as the *application register proprietor* for the goods or services specified in the application, subject to such limitations and conditions as may be imposed by the Registrar.

An application for registration of a trade mark may be refused by the Registrar if it contains any disclaimers required under this Act. Where an applicant is recorded as the proprietor of a trade mark upon initial registration, subsequent alterations to ownership details shall necessitate notification to the Registrar within thirty days of such change. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating the transfer or assignment and shall verify compliance with prescribed forms and fees. Failure to provide satisfactory evidence, or non-compliance with procedural requirements as provided herein, will result in temporary suspension of the application register proprietor’s rights until rectification is achieved. Any person aggrieved by such a decision may appeal under this Act.

Any person seeking to challenge the entry of a name in the application register relating to a trademark shall file an opposition within four months from the date of publication of the said application. Failure to do so shall render such objection unenforceable under this Act. The Registrar may, upon receiving a timely and duly supported opposition, issue a notice to both the applicant and the opponent, affording them opportunities for reasoned submissions. Where the Registrar determines that the entry of a name as an *application register proprietor* is detrimental to existing rights or contrary to public interest, he shall refuse registration, and any subsequent attempt by the applicant shall be subject to enhanced scrutiny and penalties for frivolous claims.

Where a registered trade mark is subject to a licensing agreement granting rights to use the mark for specific goods or services, the application register proprietor may, with the written consent of the registered proprietor, assign such license agreement, together with the associated right to continue using the trade mark as per the terms thereof, to any third party. Such assignment shall be recorded in the Register upon submission of a prescribed form and payment of the requisite fee. Provided that, where the original licensing agreement contains restrictions on assignment, those restrictions shall remain binding on the assignee. Further, an application register proprietor intending to sub-license rights granted under the primary license must obtain prior written approval from both the registered proprietor and the initial licensee, as provided herein. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating compliance with these conditions before registering any such transfer or sub-licensing arrangement.

Where an objection is raised against the acceptance of an application for registration of a trademark under this Act, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to submit its response within sixty days from the date of service of the notice of objection. The Registrar may, after considering the response submitted by the applicant and any counter-statement filed by the objector, either accept the application or reject it entirely. Any party aggrieved by such decision of the Registrar relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application register proprietor may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within a period of three months from the date of communication of the order. The Appellate Board shall hear arguments and evidence presented by both parties before passing any judgment.

Where an application for registration of a trademark is refused under this Act, the applicant may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Upon such an appeal, the Board shall consider whether the refusal was justified based on the grounds presented by the Registrar, including but not limited to conflicts with existing trademarks or deceptive similarity. The Board’s decision shall be final and binding, subject to further appeal to a High Court. Any person aggrieved by any action taken by the Registrar concerning an application register proprietor may also institute proceedings in a court of competent jurisdiction for redressal of grievances. A court shall cognizance only of matters directly related to the validity or infringement of registered trademarks as provided herein.

An application for registration of a trade mark may be refused by the Registrar if it contains any disclaimers required under this Act; provided that such refusal shall not prejudice any subsequent application filed by the applicant incorporating the same mark but omitting the disclaimer. Where an application register proprietor seeks to alter the particulars relating to ownership or address appearing in the Register, they shall submit a request in the prescribed form and along with the requisite fee. The Registrar may require verification of the information provided, subject to satisfying themselves that the proposed alteration does not contravene any provisions of this Act or the Marks Act 1999. Any such alteration shall be recorded in the Register and notified as per regulations framed by the Government.

An application register proprietor desiring to grant a license concerning their registered trademark may execute an agreement specifying the scope of use permitted under such license. Such agreements shall be filed with the Registrar within thirty days of execution, providing details of the licensee’s identity and the geographical territory covered by the license. The Registrar shall record these licenses in a supplementary register maintained for that purpose. Further, where the application register proprietor fails to utilize the trademark continuously for a period exceeding five years following the grant of such a license, any interested party may apply to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board for a compulsory licence under this Act, subject to demonstrating substantial prejudice resulting from the non-use. The Registrar shall provide notice to the applicant register proprietor prior to any determination by the Board.

A permitted register trade mark is defined as a trade mark that has been entered upon the Register under this Act and remains so until removed therefrom or subject to an order for rectification. For the purposes of determining entitlement to relief in proceedings concerning a permitted register trade mark, such registration shall be deemed to confer upon the registered proprietor exclusive rights within India relating to the goods or services specified in the register. A trade mark may be considered for inclusion on the permitted register if it is distinctive in its nature and capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one undertaking from those of other undertakings as provided herein.

An applicant shall be deemed eligible for a permitted register trade where the proposed mark possesses distinctive character arising solely from the use made of it in relation to the goods or services as specified in the application. Such eligibility is subject to the condition that the applicant demonstrates, through verifiable documentation, continuous and substantial usage of the mark within India for a period not less than three years immediately preceding the date of the application. The Registrar may require further evidence substantiating this usage if deemed necessary. Provided that, where the goods or services are of a nature requiring a longer period to establish distinctiveness, the Registrar may extend this requirement up to five years. Any opposition filed under this Act shall be considered only after assessment of such demonstrated use.

The proprietor of a permitted register trade mark shall be entitled to sue for and recover damages in respect of any infringement thereof. Where an infringement has occurred, the Court may grant such relief as it deems just and equitable, including but not limited to injunctions restraining further acts of infringement, delivery up or destruction of infringing goods, accounts of profits made from the infringement, and costs of the action. It is provided that a proprietor seeking remedies for infringement shall demonstrate reasonable efforts have been undertaken to notify the alleged infringer of the existence of the registered trade mark prior to commencement of legal proceedings; failure to do so may be considered in assessing damages awarded. Any person who knowingly imports or exposes for sale infringing goods shall be liable to additional penalties as determined by the Court, subject to principles of fairness and proportionality.

A trade mark shall be eligible for registration as a permitted register trade where the applicant demonstrates prior use of an identical or deceptively similar mark in relation to goods or services. Such demonstration requires submission of documentary evidence, including but not limited to invoices, advertising materials, and sales records, spanning a period of at least three years immediately preceding the date of application. The Registrar may require further verification through affidavits from distributors or consumers. Registration as a permitted register trade is conditional upon the applicant’s continued compliance with quality control standards relevant to the goods or services specified in the application, as determined by the appropriate regulatory authority under this Act. Failure to maintain such standards shall render the registration liable for review and potential revocation.

Any proprietor seeking registration of a proposed trade mark shall be deemed to have consented to its use by another party where such use is demonstrably established prior to the date of application and relates to identical or similar goods or services. The Registrar may, upon receiving evidence of such prior usage, grant a permitted register trade mark subject to conditions as he deems fit, including but not limited to limitations on geographical scope and duration. Failure by the proprietor of a permitted register trade mark to diligently enforce its rights against the established prior user shall constitute an abandonment, rendering them liable for damages and injunctive relief under this Act. Any challenge to the validity of a permitted register trade mark may be brought before the relevant judicial forum within one year from its publication in the Trade Marks Journal.

The owner of a permitted register trade mark shall be entitled to grant licences conferring the right to use the trade mark in relation to specified goods or services, subject to such terms and conditions as may be agreed between the licensor and licensee. Such licences may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and may extend to specific territories; provided that any assignment of a permitted register trade mark shall include all rights under any existing licence relating thereto unless expressly excluded in writing. Further, where a license is granted, the owner shall provide the Registrar with a certified copy of the licensing agreement within thirty days of its execution. Any subsequent modification or renewal of such licences must also be reported to the Registrar in like manner. The Registrar may require disclosure of financial considerations pertaining to any assignment or licence as provided herein.

Subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal, an objection may be raised against the acceptance of an application for registration of a trade mark by any person claiming an interest in a similar trade mark already registered under this Act. Such objection shall specify the grounds upon which it is based and must demonstrate likelihood of confusion or deception arising from the proposed permitted register trade. The Registrar shall provide the applicant with an opportunity to file a counter-statement addressing the objections raised, and both parties may submit evidence and arguments in support of their respective positions. A decision by the Registrar following such consideration may be challenged before the Tribunal within three months of its communication, asserting errors of law or fact.

Any proprietor of a permitted register trade mark shall be liable for damages in respect of any infringement occurring after the publication of notice of such registration under this Act. Where a notice opposition applicant has filed an objection to the acceptance of an application for registration, and that objection is subsequently determined in favour of the applicant, the Registrar may order the proprietor whose trade mark was the subject of the objection to pay compensation to the notice opposition applicant representing costs incurred in relation to such proceedings. Failure to comply with any order made under this Act regarding damages or compensation shall constitute a cognizable offence punishable with imprisonment and a fine.
