An appeal lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal from any order adjudicating officer passed under this Act relating to the determination of infringement or validity of a registered layout-design, or concerning any other matter provided for under this Act. Such an appeal shall be filed within sixty days from the date on which the concerned party is served with notice of the order. The Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal may, at its discretion, entertain appeals filed after the expiry of the said period if satisfactory reasons are tendered for the delay. An applicant aggrieved by any decision or direction issued by the Tribunal in a proceeding appellate may further appeal to the Supreme Court on a question of law. The Tribunal shall give notice to all parties concerned and provide them an opportunity to be heard before passing any order.

For civil court purposes relating to infringement actions under this Act, “layout-design” means a three-dimensional representation of the integrated circuit’s structure, expressed in terms of the arrangement of layers and interconnections as deposited on or within a semiconductor material; provided that such representation does not include features which are necessary to achieve mechanical functionality. The term "integrated circuit" shall have the meaning assigned thereto under this Act. A layout-design is deemed to be infringed if any person, without authorization, makes a layout-design that infringes the exclusive right of the registered proprietor as provided herein. Such determination shall be made irrespective of whether the infringing layout-design incorporates all elements of the original design.

For civil court purposes relating to infringement proceedings under this Act, a certificate issued by the Controller upon registration of a layout-design shall be prima facie evidence that the applicant is the owner of the registered integrated circuit layout-design and that the design is valid and has not been previously registered. Any person claiming ownership of an unregistered layout-design may apply to the Controller for determination of title, provided that such application shall specify details regarding prior use or publication of the design. The Controller may require submission of documentation substantiating the claim, including records pertaining to creation, modification, and commercial exploitation of the integrated circuit layout-design. Such determinations are subject to appeal as provided herein.

Where a person institutes proceedings alleging an infringement of layout-design rights under this Act, the remedies available shall be those prescribed herein and may include injunctions restraining further acts of infringement, damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the registered proprietor, and delivery up or destruction of infringing goods. The Court determining such infringement shall have regard to any measures taken by the registered proprietor to maintain the confidentiality of the layout-design prior to registration. For civil court purposes, a finding of infringement constitutes prima facie evidence of the validity of the registered layout-design. Provided that, in assessing damages, the Court may consider any profits made by the infringer attributable to the infringing activity, even if those profits are not directly related to the sale or use of the infringing integrated circuit.

Where a claim for infringement of layout-design rights is brought before civil court purposes, the claimant shall demonstrate that the alleged infringing integrated circuit possesses a substantial similarity to the registered layout-design, considering both the overall impression and any relevant distinguishing features. Such determination shall be made subject to an assessment of whether the defendant had access to the registered layout-design prior to the creation of the allegedly infringing design. Provided that, if the defendant proves that the alleged infringement arose independently without copying or having access, the claim shall not succeed. Furthermore, evidence presented regarding manufacturing processes and technical documentation may be considered by the court in ascertaining substantial similarity as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act may appeal to a High Court within whose territorial jurisdiction the cause of action arose, subject to such fees as may be prescribed. Such appeals shall lie only on grounds specified in the appeal memorandum and relating directly to matters of law or fact determinative of the right to protection afforded herein. The High Court may, while hearing an appeal, require any party to produce further evidence, and its decision thereon shall be final, provided that it does not contravene any provision of this Act. For civil court purposes, the jurisdiction of a High Court under this Act shall extend to all matters concerning infringement or violation of layout-design rights as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person holding a valid layout-design registration relating to a semiconductor integrated circuit may grant licenses conferring rights to use or exploit such registered layout design, either wholly or partially, for commercial purposes. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive and shall specify the duration, geographical scope, and field of application of the granted right. Assignment of layout designs, including those subject to existing licenses, is permissible with the written consent of all relevant licensees, provided that such assignment does not prejudice any rights already vested in them under this Act. For civil court purposes, disputes arising from licensing agreements or assignments shall be adjudicated according to principles of equity and fairness, considering the reasonable expectations of both licensors and licensees at the time of contract formation. The Registrar may issue guidelines regarding standard license terms for certain categories of integrated circuits.

Subject to appeal to the High Court, any determination made by a civil court purposes relating to infringement of layout-design rights under this Act shall be final until modified or reversed in appeal. Provided that an aggrieved party may challenge such determination on grounds including but not limited to errors of law apparent on the face of the record, misdirection in assessing substantial similarity, or failure to consider relevant evidence presented during the original proceedings. The High Court may, while hearing an appeal, require further discovery or examination of witnesses as it deems necessary for just resolution. Further, any order passed by a civil court concerning interim injunctions or other conservatory measures shall be subject to similar appellate review and scrutiny under this Act.

For civil court purposes relating to claims arising under this Act, a certificate issued by the Register of Layout-Designs confirming registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be prima facie evidence of the validity of that design and ownership thereof, subject to the provisions herein. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Register regarding the acceptance or rejection of an application for registration may appeal to the designated appellate body as notified by the Controller. The appellate body shall consider such appeals based on the records submitted and may direct the Register to reconsider any aspect of the registration process. Further, the appellate body’s determination concerning originality and freedom from prior publication shall be binding, notwithstanding any conflicting opinions previously expressed by the Copyrights Appellate Board.

Any infringement of layout-design rights under this Act shall be actionable as a civil wrong, and without prejudice to any other remedies available, an aggrieved party may institute proceedings for damages in a court of competent jurisdiction. Such damages shall include compensation for loss resulting from the infringement, including but not limited to lost profits, reasonable royalties, and costs associated with investigating the infringement. The recovery of punitive or exemplary damages is prohibited. For civil court purposes relating to the determination of infringement, evidence pertaining to the layout-design’s originality and skill involved in its creation shall be admissible. Where an integrated circuit layout-design is protected under this Act and also by international treaty means Budapest, such protection shall not be affected by any conflicting provisions in domestic law.

A judicial proceeding relating to infringement of a registered layout-design shall be deemed to include any civil suit filed in a court not subordinate to the High Court, or any reference made under this Act for determination of questions of fact or law. For the purposes of such proceedings, “court” means a District Court or a High Court exercising ordinary original jurisdiction. The term "infringement" shall mean the unauthorized making, importing, selling by way of trade or hire, or offering to sell any layout-design that is substantially similar to the registered layout-design, subject to considerations of fair use as provided herein. Any party may appeal from an order made in a judicial proceeding under this Act to the High Court.

An application for registration of a layout-design relating to an integrated circuit shall be deemed refused if the Registrar considers that any judicial proceeding concerning the validity of the layout-design is pending in a court or tribunal within India, provided that the applicant may submit an affidavit stating that such proceedings are settled amicably and do not prejudice the interests of registered proprietors. The registrar shall record particulars of any such settlement. Further, where a layout-design incorporates elements previously registered under this Act, the application shall clearly identify those incorporated elements and demonstrate that the overall design constitutes an original work subject to assessment during examination. Any challenge to registration based on prior publication may be raised within sixty days from the date of advertisement as provided herein.

Where a judicial proceeding is instituted under this Act alleging infringement of a registered layout-design, the Tribunal may, subject to appeal before the High Court, grant such remedies as it deems just and equitable, including permanent or interim injunctions restraining further acts of infringement. Compensation for loss suffered by the registrant due to the infringing activity shall be determined based on evidence presented, considering factors such as the extent of damage caused, the infringer’s profits attributable to the infringement, and reasonable costs incurred in bringing the action. The Tribunal may also order the delivery up or destruction of infringing layouts-designs or materials relating thereto. Provided that any order for damages shall not preclude the registrant from seeking further remedies under other laws pertaining to contractual obligations or unfair trade practices.

Where a judicial proceeding is instituted under this Act concerning infringement of layout-design rights, the District Court shall be seized of such proceeding unless the parties agree otherwise in writing, or where the High Court has exercised jurisdiction pursuant to an appeal. Any party aggrieved by an order made by the District Court may prefer an appeal to the concerned High Court within sixty days from the date of communication of the order, subject to any conditions prescribed regarding delay. The High Court shall hear appeals de novo. Evidence adduced before the District Court shall be available to the High Court and further evidence may be adduced at the discretion of the High Court. Costs associated with a judicial proceeding shall be determined by the court exercising jurisdiction, taking into account the complexity of the matter and the conduct of the parties involved. The presiding officer of the District Court shall record reasons for every decision made in relation to any such proceedings.

Where a judicial proceeding is instituted under this Act concerning alleged infringement of a registered layout-design, the proprietor shall provide evidence demonstrating reasonable grounds for believing that an act of copying has occurred. Such evidence must be presented to the relevant court within ninety days of the discovery of the infringing activity, as provided herein. The court may require further documentation substantiating the claim, including records of design registration and comparative analyses of the layout-design in question. Failure to submit adequate proof within the stipulated timeframe shall render the proprietor ineligible for injunctive relief or damages relating to that specific allegation. Any counterclaims asserting validity challenges to the registered layout-design must be filed concurrently with the initial proceeding.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act may prefer an appeal from such order to the Commercial Court having jurisdiction over the matter, subject to a penalty not exceeding five thousand rupees for frivolous or vexatious appeals. Such appeal shall be admitted only if the appellant demonstrates demonstrable prejudice resulting directly from the order appealed against. The Commercial Court shall hear and dispose of any judicial proceeding arising under this Act within six months from the date it is instituted; failure to do so may result in a fine, as determined by the presiding officer, levied upon the court administration. Costs associated with such proceedings shall be borne by the defaulting party, provided that the appellate authority may order otherwise where equity dictates.

Where a judicial proceeding concerning infringement of a registered layout-design involves a claim for damages or an injunction relating to a licensed integrated circuit layout-design, the licensor may, subject to any prior agreement between the parties, assign the right to pursue such remedies to another entity. Such assignment shall be recorded with the Controller and shall become effective upon notification to the infringing party. The assignee shall stand in the place of the original licensor for all purposes relating to the judicial proceeding and shall be bound by any terms or conditions previously agreed upon between the licensor and licensee. Provided that, where an assignment is made subsequent to a judgment being rendered, the judgment shall remain binding on the assignee with respect to matters already adjudicated. The Controller may prescribe fees for recording such assignments as provided herein.

Where a judicial proceeding is instituted under this Act alleging infringement of a registered layout-design, the Tribunal may, subject to appeal before the High Court, order interim relief pending final determination, provided that such order specifies the terms thereof and the period for which it shall remain in effect. The respondent in any such proceeding shall be afforded an opportunity to present evidence rebutting the claim of infringement, and the Tribunal shall consider all submissions made by both parties before rendering a decision. Further, any party aggrieved by an order passed under this Act may appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of communication of that order; provided that the appellate court may dismiss an appeal if it finds the appeal frivolous or vexatious.

An application for registration of a layout-design relating to an integrated circuit shall be deemed invalid if it is found that the design incorporates elements substantially derived from a previously registered layout-design, unless the applicant demonstrates due diligence in ascertaining the absence of prior registration and provides evidence of payable notice having been served upon the owner of the earlier design. Any judicial proceeding challenging the validity of such registration must specify the allegedly infringing elements and demonstrate their substantial similarity to the pre-existing layout-design. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating claims of due diligence, including records of searches conducted under this Act and correspondence related to the payable notice. Failure to comply with these requirements shall prejudice the applicant’s position in the judicial proceeding.

Where a judicial proceeding is instituted under this Act concerning an allegation of infringement of a registered layout-design, the Intellectual Property Disputes Tribunal shall determine the matter in accordance with principles of natural justice. Evidence presented before the Tribunal shall be admissible subject to the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (Act V of 1908). The Tribunal may, at its discretion, permit inspection of the layout-design register and any documentation pertaining to a registered distinct denomination variety associated with the layout-design. Parties involved in such proceedings shall be served notice as prescribed by regulations framed under this Act. Any order passed by the Intellectual Property Disputes Tribunal relating to interim relief or damages shall be appealable to the High Court within ninety days from the date of the order, provided that the High Court may require security for costs.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any proprietor of a registered layout-design relating to a semiconductor integrated circuit may grant licenses conferring rights to use, exploit, or reproduce such design, either in whole or in part, within India or concerning products manufactured and sold in published India. Such licenses shall be assignable in accordance with standard commercial practice, provided that the terms of assignment are clearly documented and registered with the Controller General of Patents, Designs, and Trademarks. Any judicial proceeding regarding the validity or scope of such a license shall require prior notification to the relevant layout-design proprietor, affording them an opportunity to present their interests. Further, any subsequent assignment of rights derived from a licensed design shall be subject to the original licensing agreement’s conditions as provided herein. The Controller may issue guidelines concerning acceptable forms of documentation for assignments and licenses under this Act.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Registrar relating to the registration or rejection of a plant variety, or concerning farmers’ rights, may prefer an appeal to the authority. The authority shall admit such appeal only if it is demonstrated that substantial injustice has resulted from the decision under appeal. The authority registrar case shall be heard expeditiously, and the appellant shall bear the burden of proving the grounds for their claim. Decisions made by the authority are final subject to further review by a judicial forum as provided herein. Any party failing to comply with procedural requirements relating to appeals may have their petition dismissed. The authority may grant such remedies as it deems just, including but not limited to directing the registrar to reconsider an earlier decision or awarding compensation for losses incurred.

An application for registration of a plant variety shall include a detailed report verifying its distinctness, uniformity, and stability, as determined through rigorous field trials conducted in accordance with guidelines prescribed by the Central Government. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish additional data or conduct further tests if reasonable doubt exists regarding the veracity of the initial findings. Should any objection be raised against the registration by an interested party, the matter shall be referred to the authority for adjudication. The authority registrar case determination shall consider evidence presented by both the applicant and the objector, prioritizing information demonstrating adherence to established protocols concerning genetic purity and lineage tracing. Any decision made by the authority is subject to appeal before a designated appellate body.

A registration issued act, in relation to a plant variety, shall be deemed to occur when an action undertaken by the registered holder directly impacts the rights conferred under this Act and is brought to the attention of the Registrar. Such actions may include, but are not limited to, unauthorized sale for commercial purposes, offering for cultivation without proper authorization, or making representations misleading regarding the genetic composition of the variety. The Registrar shall provide an opportunity for the alleged wrongdoer to be heard before determining whether a registration issued act has occurred and what remedial measures, as provided herein, should be implemented.

An application for registration of a plant variety shall be accompanied by detailed documentation pertaining to its genetic composition, lineage, and distinctive characteristics as determined through rigorous testing procedures prescribed under this Act. Upon receipt of the application, the Registrar may initiate an examination process involving expert assessors to ascertain whether the plant variety meets the criteria for novelty, distinctiveness, uniformity, and stability. If, following such assessment, the Registrar is satisfied that the applicant has fulfilled all requirements, a registration issued act shall be executed, granting exclusive rights pertaining to the commercialization of the registered plant variety for a period not exceeding fifteen years from the date of application. Provided that any challenge to this registration may be brought before the Appellate Board within six months of publication in the Official Gazette.

Any breeder who has obtained a registration issued act for a plant variety shall be liable to pay compensation to any farmer, community, or other entity demonstrably suffering loss as a direct result of the registered breeder’s actions in enforcing their rights under this Act. Such enforcement may include, but is not limited to, restrictions on seed saving and replanting practices. The amount of compensation shall be determined by the relevant forum considering factors such as the extent of the economic hardship suffered, the reasonableness of the breeder's conduct, and any demonstrable benefit derived from the plant variety’s commercialization. Provided that a farmer establishes prior use or cultivation of the variety, subject to conditions prescribed herein, they may claim exemption from restrictions imposed by the registration issued act, without prejudice to their rights under other applicable laws.

An application for the grant of registration as a Plant Variety shall be accompanied by such particulars, including details regarding the expression of essential characteristics and distinctive features, as may be prescribed. Upon receipt of an application, the Authority shall publish a notice indicating the intention to grant registration, inviting objections from any interested person within a period specified under this Act. Any objection received shall be communicated to the applicant, who shall have opportunity for rebuttal. Following consideration of all submissions, the Authority may proceed with or decline the registration request. A registration issued act confers upon the registrant exclusive rights in relation to the commercialization of the variety, subject to limitations regarding farmers' rights and on-farm conservation and use. The Registrar shall maintain a publicly accessible register detailing granted registrations and any subsequent modifications.

An application for a registration issued act concerning a plant variety shall be deemed complete upon submission of all requisite documentation, including but not limited to, detailed morphological data, genetic purity reports verified by an authorized laboratory, and evidence demonstrating stability across three successive generations. The Authority may require further information or clarification at any stage prior to granting the registration. Subject to compliance with prescribed guidelines regarding geographical indication protection, a breeder shall be entitled to claim rights pertaining to the plant variety only if it is demonstrably novel, distinct, uniform, and stable. Provided that the applicant furnishes an undertaking to share propagating material with research institutions as stipulated under this Act, the Authority may proceed with assessment of the application’s merits.

Any breeder who, having obtained a registration issued act for a plant variety, knowingly markets or distributes seeds or other propagating material that does not conform to the characteristics specified in the registration certificate shall be liable to pay a penalty of not less than fifty thousand rupees and may also face revocation of the registration. Further, any person found to have made false representations during the application process leading to the grant of such an act is subject to a fine extending up to one hundred thousand rupees and imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years. The Registrar shall issue notices prior to imposing penalties, providing opportunity for explanation as provided herein. Repeated offenses will attract enhanced penalties and potential prohibition from applying for future registrations under this Act.

Any holder of a registration issued act in respect of a plant variety shall be entitled to grant exclusive licenses conferring rights to produce, propagate, sell, import, and export propagating material of the registered variety, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated in the license agreement. Such agreements may include royalty payments, duration limitations, and territorial restrictions as mutually agreed upon by the licensor and licensee. Further, a registration holder may assign their right to a registration issued act to any other person or entity, provided that such assignment is recorded with the Registrar within thirty days of execution. The assignee shall then be deemed the successor in title for all purposes under this Act. Any transfer or license granted without proper recording shall be voidable at the option of the original registrant.

Any breeder or farmer aggrieved by a decision relating to the grant, refusal, revocation, or modification of a registration issued act concerning a plant variety may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The appeal shall be filed in the prescribed form and manner, accompanied by a fee as determined under this Act. Provided that the Appellate Board may entertain appeals received after the expiry of the said period if satisfactory reasons for the delay are submitted, subject to its discretion. The Board shall give notice to all parties concerned and afford them an opportunity of being heard. Any order made by the Appellate Board shall be final, but the aggrieved party may challenge such order in a court of law on grounds specified under this Act.

An applicant seeking a registration issued act concerning a plant variety shall submit a petition in Form A, duly completed and verified as provided herein, along with the requisite fee prescribed under this Act. The Registrar may require further information or clarification regarding any aspect of the application detailed within the form petition, including but not limited to documentation pertaining to the distinctiveness and stability of the plant variety. Subject to compliance with all applicable regulations concerning experimental record keeping, an applicant demonstrating adherence to established protocols for field trials shall be deemed to have satisfied initial requirements. Provided that the Registrar is satisfied that the information submitted accurately reflects the characteristics of the plant variety, the application may proceed to examination.

Where an application for registration of a plant variety is rejected, or a registration issued act is deemed invalid by the Authority following inquiry, the applicant may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The Appellate Board shall consider any question of fact or law arising in relation to the rejection or invalidation and may affirm, reverse, or modify the order appealed against. Provided that, if the plant variety is deemed essential for food security or rural livelihoods, the Authority may grant a compulsory licence under this Act, subject to conditions as determined by the Central Government; such determination shall be reviewable by the Appellate Board on grounds of proportionality and public interest.

Where any person is found to be engaging in activities that are detrimental to the integrity of a registered plant variety, including but not limited to unauthorized multiplication and commercialization, the Board may issue an order injunction sub. This order shall specify the nature of the prohibited activity and its geographical scope, subject to considerations of public interest and farmer’s rights as provided herein. Any party aggrieved by such an order may appeal to the Appellate Board within a period of sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The Appellate Board shall consider all relevant evidence before affirming, modifying or reversing the original order injunction sub.

Where a person is found to have engaged in activities contravening the rights granted to a plant breeder under this Act, the Board may, subject to appeal before an appropriate judicial forum, issue an order injunction sub. This power extends to preventing further acts of infringement and compelling the cessation of ongoing unlawful practices relating to the commercial exploitation of protected varieties. Provided that any application for such an order must demonstrate reasonable grounds for believing that irreparable harm will be caused unless interim relief is granted. The Board shall consider representations from all parties involved before issuing any injunction, ensuring procedural fairness. Further, damages may be awarded to the plant breeder as compensation for losses sustained due to the infringement, calculated in accordance with principles of equity and justice, as provided herein.

Where the Authority determines that any person is engaging in activities which are likely to cause substantial and irreparable injury to the interests of a plant breeder or farmer, it may apply to the District Court for an order injunction sub. The application shall specify the nature of the activity and the manner in which such injury is being caused or is likely to be caused. Upon receiving such an application, the District Court may grant an interlocutory order restraining the person from continuing such activities pending final determination by the Authority.

The court shall give notice to the affected party and provide them with a reasonable opportunity to present their case under this Act. Any order granted under sub-section (1) shall be subject to review by the Appellate Board within thirty days of its issuance. The Authority may, after due inquiry and providing an opportunity for hearing, modify or set aside any such interlocutory order.

Where a Plant Variety Protection Authority determines that a person has engaged in activities contravening provisions relating to farmers’ rights concerning saved seed, it may issue an order directing such person to cease and desist from the offending conduct. Subject to compliance with due process as provided herein, any aggrieved party may apply to a competent court for an injunction restraining the enforcement of said order. Such application shall be accompanied by evidence demonstrating substantial prejudice resulting from the Plant Variety Protection Authority’s determination. The court may grant a temporary or permanent injunction, or such other relief as it deems just and equitable, provided that the applicant demonstrates a reasonable likelihood of success on the merits. An order injunction sub judice shall not prevent the authority from undertaking further investigations.

Any person found to be engaging in activities that contravene a Plant Variety Protection Order shall be liable to pay compensation as determined by the Authority. Such compensation shall account for losses incurred by the registered plant variety holder due to unauthorized propagation, sale, or distribution. Further, upon receiving a complaint duly substantiated with evidence, the Tribunal may issue an order injunction sub judice against any individual or entity demonstrably infringing upon the rights conferred under this Act. This power extends to preventing actions that undermine the exclusivity granted to the registrant and includes measures to restrain future acts of infringement. Failure to comply with such orders shall attract penalties as provided herein, including fines and potential imprisonment.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, a Plant Variety Protection Agreement entered into between a breeder and a licensee shall clearly define the scope of rights granted, including geographical limitations and permitted uses relating to propagated material. The agreement may stipulate royalty payments based on sales or cultivation area, provided that such terms are equitable and do not unduly restrict farmers’ access to saved seed. Any assignment of Plant Variety Protection rights requires registration with the Authority, detailing the consideration paid and any continuing obligations of the assignor. Furthermore, a court may issue an order injunction sub in cases where unauthorized propagation or commercialization occurs, violating the terms of a registered agreement or infringing on protected breeder's rights as provided herein.

Where any person alleges that another has contravened any provision of this Act relating to registration, designation, or licensing of plant varieties, such allegation may be brought before the relevant authority. The authority shall provide both parties with an opportunity for a hearing and shall record its findings in writing. Any party aggrieved by the decision of the authority may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days of the date of that decision. Pending determination of any such appeal, the appellate board may issue an order injunction sub-judice restraining the respondent from continuing the action complained of, subject to just cause shown and after hearing arguments from both sides. The appellant shall be required to furnish security as determined by the Appellate Board.

Any person found to be engaging in activities that are detrimental to the interests of registered plant varieties, including but not limited to unauthorized multiplication, distribution, or sale, shall be liable for penalties as provided herein. Where such activity constitutes a clear and present danger to the integrity of a protected variety, the Authority may issue an order injunction sub judice against the offending party pending final determination of the matter. Impliedly registration shall not preclude enforcement action against those who knowingly contribute to or benefit from these detrimental activities. Further, any entity found guilty of such offenses is liable to pay compensation for losses incurred by the registered breeder, subject to judicial assessment and as determined under this Act.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, a Plant Variety Protection Agreement entered into between a breeder and another party shall be deemed valid, provided that such agreement explicitly defines the scope of rights granted concerning the commercialization, propagation, and research relating to the protected plant variety. The licensee may assign their rights under the agreement to an affiliate or successor company with prior written consent from the grantor, which consent shall not be unreasonably withheld. Further, any party seeking a license to utilize the protected variety for crop sciences research purposes must disclose all intended methodologies and anticipated outcomes to the Plant Variety Protection Authority. A court of competent jurisdiction may issue an order injunction sub in cases of breach of contract concerning licensing terms or unauthorized propagation, as provided herein.

An application for registration of a Plant Variety shall be accompanied by detailed documentation pertaining to the expression of characteristics and essential derivation. Where the Applicant claims novelty based on the integration of an Integrated Circuit within a plant propagation system utilized during breeding, such circuit’s design specifications must be submitted as Annexure B. The Authority may require further clarification regarding the method of integration and its impact on varietal stability. Subject to compliance with these requirements, the application shall proceed for examination. An order injunction sub judice relating to any claim of prior disclosure concerning a Plant Variety registration shall immediately suspend processing under this Act until resolution by an appropriate judicial forum.

For the purposes of this Act, “literary work” shall include any creation in tangible form expressing original thought, irrespective of its medium. This definition extends to computer programs, tables, compilations, and databases, provided that such works demonstrate intellectual effort sufficient for originality as determined under this Act. A literary work may encompass musical scores or lyrics if they are fixed permanently in a readable notation. The determination of whether a work qualifies as a literary work shall be subject to the consideration of its substantial character and not merely its form or purpose. Works produced by artificial intelligence alone, without demonstrable human authorship, do not qualify as literary works under this Act.

For the purposes of registration under this Act, a “literary work” shall be deemed to include unpublished manuscripts submitted for evaluation by publishing houses, provided that such submission is accompanied by a declaration from the author affirming their intention to publish the work within a period not exceeding five years from the date of application. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating the claim of authorship and the nature of the manuscript’s submission process. Where an applicant seeks registration for a literary work jointly authored, all co-authors shall be required to consent in writing to the application and share equally in the copyright accruing under this Act, subject to any contractual agreements between them duly filed with the Registrar. The refusal of registration may be appealed before the designated appellate authority as provided herein.

Where a literary work has been published without proper authorization, and the owner thereof subsequently discovers an infringing reproduction disseminated commercially, the owner shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief restraining further distribution. Such injunction may extend to all forms of public display or communication where the infringement is readily apparent. Provided that, in determining whether an act constitutes infringement under this Act, due consideration shall be given to the extent to which the alleged infringer demonstrably altered the original literary work. The owner may also claim damages proportionate to the loss suffered as a direct result of the unauthorized reproduction and commercial exploitation; these damages shall include lost profits reasonably foreseeable. Further, where wilful infringement is established, aggravated damages up to five times the actual damages awarded may be imposed by the relevant judicial authority.

For the purposes of this Act, a “literary work” shall include computer programs, source code, and object code thereof, irrespective of whether such works are fixed in a tangible medium. The right of the author to control all reproductions of their literary work extends to the creation of derivative works based upon the original, subject to limitations as provided herein regarding fair dealing for research or private study. Any person desiring to undertake an adaptation of a protected literary work shall first obtain written authorization from the owner of copyright in that work. Such authorization may be granted on such terms and conditions as the authorizing party deems fit, including stipulations concerning royalty payments and duration of the license. Failure to secure prior authorization constitutes infringement under this Act, and proceedings for redressal of grievances relating to alleged infringements shall be initiated before the relevant High Court jurisdictionally vested with cognizance of matters pertaining to intellectual property.

Where a literary work is comprised substantially of elements originally derived from traditional cultural expressions belonging to indigenous communities, and such derivation occurs without prior informed consent as provided herein, the author shall be deemed to hold copyright subject to conditions. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating due diligence in ascertaining the provenance of said elements before registration of copyright is granted. Further, any commercial exploitation of the literary work utilizing these traditional cultural expressions requires a prominent acknowledgement of the source community and a declaration detailing measures undertaken to ensure equitable benefit-sharing with that community. Failure to comply with this requirement shall render the copyright liable to revocation under this Act.

Any person who, without authorization from the owner of copyright in a literary work, reproduces the work for sale or distribution, or exhibits it in public, shall be liable to prosecution under this Act. Where such unauthorized reproduction is committed with the intention to gain financial advantage or to cause loss to the copyright owner, the court may impose a penalty not exceeding ten times the amount that would have been payable had the acts been carried out with due authorization. Further, any person found guilty of infringing upon the exclusive rights pertaining to a literary work as provided herein shall be subject to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and a fine which may extend to two hundred thousand rupees.

Where the copyright subsists in a literary work created under contract for services, the right to grant licenses and assign such copyright shall vest initially in the party commissioning the work, provided that the agreement expressly stipulates the terms governing subsequent exploitation. Such agreements may delineate specific rights granted to the creator, including but not limited to reproduction, distribution, public performance, and adaptation of the literary work. Further, where an assignment of copyright is made, it shall be deemed a conveyance of all rights therein unless the instrument of assignment specifically reserves certain privileges for the assignor. The assignee shall have full authority to sub-license the literary work subject to any limitations outlined in the original contractual agreement or subsequent assignments. Any royalties derived from such licensing activities shall be distributed as per the terms agreed upon between the parties involved, reflecting their respective contributions and negotiated percentages.

Where a claim is made that a particular compilation constitutes a literary work, and such claim is contested on the grounds that the selection, arrangement, and presentation of the material within the compilation are not original, the burden shall lie upon the claimant to demonstrate, by clear and convincing evidence, the exercise of intellectual labour sufficient to warrant copyright protection. Provided that, in determining originality, regard shall be had to whether the choices made in compiling the work reflect a distinctive creative approach or merely represent a mechanical or predictable process. Any party aggrieved by a decision regarding the originality of a literary work may appeal to the relevant High Court, subject to such conditions as are prescribed under this Act concerning timelines and costs.

Where the copyright in a literary work is vested in an organization registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1960, and such organization has entered into an agreement with its members for the purpose of exploiting that copyright, the organization shall be deemed to be the first owner of the copyright therein. Provided that any member who contributed substantially towards the creation of the literary work may, subject to the terms of the aforementioned agreement, apply to a judicial proceeding seeking recognition of their individual rights in respect of such contribution. The organization may grant licenses or assign the entire copyright or portions thereof relating to the literary work to third parties as it deems fit, provided that such assignment includes provisions ensuring equitable remuneration for contributing members, proportionate to their involvement in its creation.

For the purposes of registration under this Act, a “literary work” shall include any compilation of data presented in a structured format intended for electronic processing, provided that such compilation demonstrates originality in selection, arrangement, and presentation. The Registrar may require submission of metadata detailing the creation process and authorship attribution for all works falling within this definition. Where the literary work incorporates elements originating from a Contracting Party to a relevant international convention, the applicant shall provide an affidavit confirming due diligence regarding compliance with applicable foreign copyright laws. Any subsequent modification or derivative work based on such registered material remains subject to these provisions, requiring separate registration if it constitutes a substantial adaptation of the original literary work.

Where a literary work is reproduced without authorization, and such reproduction constitutes a substantial copying of an alphabetical index classification system integral to the original work’s organization and accessibility, the owner of copyright therein shall be entitled to injunctive relief preventing further acts of reproduction. This right exists subject to the proviso that the alleged infringing copy demonstrates a clear and demonstrable commercial purpose distinct from any legitimate scholarly or research endeavor. Furthermore, damages may be awarded to compensate for loss suffered by the copyright holder as a result of the unauthorized reproduction; such damages shall not exceed an amount equivalent to the reasonable cost of licensing the literary work had authorization been sought prior to the infringing act. The court may also order the delivery up of all copies made in violation of this Act, provided that their destruction is deemed necessary to prevent further infringement.

For the purposes of this Act, "copy" with respect to any work shall mean and include any mere reproduction of the work in any medium whatsoever, including but not limited to, the making of copies of a work, by photocopying or similar processes. Such copy shall be deemed an infringing reproduction where it is made without authorization from the owner of copyright under this Act, provided that such authorization may be granted expressly or impliedly. A digital file containing identical data as the original work shall also constitute a copy for the purposes of determining infringement. The term "similar processes" includes any technological means resulting in a substantially similar reproduction of the protected elements of the work.
primary_entity: making of copies of a work, by photocopying or similar

context: Where the owner of copyright in any work desires to facilitate wider dissemination and accessibility thereof, they may elect to register a declaration specifying permissible methods for the making of copies of a work, by photocopying or similar processes. Such registration shall be deemed conclusive evidence that the declared practices do not constitute an infringement of copyright, subject to conditions outlined in the application. The applicant must detail the scope of permitted reproduction, including quantity limitations and intended distribution channels. Provided that the declaration explicitly addresses any associated fees payable for each copy made, and ensures equitable compensation to right holders, the Registrar may grant registration. Any subsequent alteration to the declared practices requires a fresh application and approval under this Act.
primary_entity: making of copies of a work, by photocopying or similar

context: Where the making of copies of a work, by photocopying or similar processes, is undertaken for commercial purposes without authorization from the owner of copyright, such act shall constitute an infringement under this Act. The right to prevent unauthorized copying extends to all forms of reproduction, including but not limited to digital reproductions and scans. Any person found guilty of infringing copyright in this manner may be liable to pay damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the copyright owner as a consequence of the infringement. Provided that, where the infringement is proven to have been committed due to ignorance of the existence of copyright, the court may reduce the amount of damages awarded, subject to considerations of fairness and equity. Further, remedies for injunctive relief are available to copyright owners seeking to restrain ongoing acts of unauthorized reproduction.
primary_entity: making of copies of a work, by photocopying or similar

context: Where the owner of copyright in a literary or dramatic work grants a license permitting the making of copies of a work, by photocopying or similar means, such license may be assigned to a third party subject to the terms and conditions stipulated therein. The assignor shall retain the right to audit records pertaining to royalties derived from the licensed reproduction activities for a period not exceeding three years following the assignment date, provided that reasonable notice is given prior to any such audit. Any subsequent assignments of this license shall require express written consent from the original copyright owner unless the initial license agreement explicitly waives this requirement. The licensee may sub-license the right to make copies only with the prior approval of the assignor, and such approvals shall not be unreasonably withheld. Further, any modifications to the licensed work are prohibited without explicit authorization from the copyright holder as provided herein.
primary_entity: making of copies of a work, by photocopying or similar

context: Where the making of copies of a work, by photocopying or similar means, is undertaken for purposes deemed to be educational and non-commercial, such action shall not constitute an infringement under this Act provided that the number of copies made is limited to the demonstrable needs of the institution undertaking said copying. However, any aggrieved party may challenge the assertion of ‘educational’ or ‘non-commercial’ purpose before a court of competent jurisdiction, demonstrating undue commercial gain or systematic dissemination beyond reasonable institutional use. The burden of proving such legitimacy shall rest upon the entity claiming exemption. Further, where copies are distributed for remuneration, even if ostensibly within an educational context, this provision shall not apply and proceedings may be initiated as provided herein.
primary_entity: making of copies of a work, by photocopying or similar

context: For the purposes of this Act, "copy" with respect to any work shall include the making of copies of a work, by photocopying or similar processes, whether such process is undertaken for commercial gain or otherwise. A copy so made shall be deemed an infringing reproduction if it reproduces substantial portions of the original work. The right to control the making of such copies vests in the owner of copyright under this Act. Provided that, where a registered breeder of plant varieties has secured intellectual property rights relating to a particular botanical illustration depicting said variety, permission for photocopying or similar reproduction must be obtained from the breeder prior to dissemination.
primary_entity: making of copies of a work, by photocopying or similar

context: For the purposes of this Act, "film sound recording" means a series of related sounds exclusively made during and directly resulting from the filming process, fixed in a tangible medium, and intended to accompany a cinematographic work. A film sound recording shall include both synchronized dialogue and ambient sound captured during principal photography, but excludes separately recorded musical scores or voiceovers added post-production unless such addition is integral to the narrative and demonstrably part of the original artistic conception. The rights conferred under this Act in respect of a film sound recording are vested in the producer of the cinematographic work, subject to any agreement as provided herein regarding ownership transfer.

For the purposes of registration under this Act, a film sound recording shall be deemed to include all sounds exclusively fixed in relation to a cinematographic work, irrespective of whether such sounds form an integral part of the visual elements or are supplementary thereto. The application for registration concerning a film sound recording must specify the year of its creation and identify the producer responsible for its initial fixation. Where a film sound recording incorporates pre-existing musical works, the applicant shall provide details regarding any necessary licenses obtained to utilize such copyrighted material. Registration of a film sound recording does not confer exclusive rights over the underlying cinematographic work itself, but rather pertains solely to the unique sonic elements captured and preserved as described herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, copyright in a film sound recording shall vest initially in the producer of the film. The owner of such copyright shall be entitled to control the reproduction, distribution, adaptation, and public exhibition of the film sound recording. Any person who without due authorization infringes upon these rights may be liable for damages sustained by the copyright holder. Provided that, where a film sound recording incorporates pre-existing musical works, the copyright in those underlying works remains with their respective owners and shall not be transferred by virtue of the producer’s ownership of the film sound recording. Further, any unauthorized use of a film sound recording for commercial purposes constitutes an infringement under this Act and is subject to remedies as provided herein, including injunctions and account of profits.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, a film sound recording shall be deemed an artistic work and protected under this Act. The ownership of such a film sound recording shall vest in the producer unless otherwise agreed upon in writing between the producer and the composer or lyricist involved in its creation. Any person desiring to utilize a film sound recording for commercial purposes, including but not limited to public performance, broadcasting, or mechanical reproduction, shall be required to obtain prior written permission from the owner of copyright therein. Applications for such permissions may be submitted to the designated Copyright Society established under this Act, and the Society shall process these applications in accordance with prescribed procedures. Provided that, where a film sound recording incorporates pre-existing musical works, the rights pertaining to those underlying works remain separate and require distinct authorization as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, a film sound recording shall be deemed an artistic work and protected under this Act for sixty years from the year following the year in which the work is first published. Provided that, where such film sound recording incorporates pre-existing musical works or literary works, copyright therein shall remain with the owners as determined under existing law. The owner of copyright in a film sound recording shall be entitled to control the reproduction, distribution, and communication to the public of the said recording. Any person desiring to make use of a film sound recording for commercial purposes must obtain prior authorization from the copyright holder, and such authorization may be subject to royalty payments as negotiated between the parties or determined by an adjudicating officer.

Any person who, without authorization from the owner of the film sound recording, reproduces such recording in any form, including but not limited to digital formats for distribution or public display, shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall be assessed at a minimum of ten times the cost of procuring or producing such infringing copy, or rupees one lakh, whichever is greater. Where the infringement is committed by an employee acting within the scope of his employment, the employer shall also be deemed guilty and subject to penalties as provided herein. Further, any equipment used in the commission of this offence may be seized by authorized officers. The owner of a film sound recording may apply to the relevant judicial authority for an injunction restraining further acts of infringement.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any producer of a film sound recording shall be entitled to grant licenses for the reproduction, distribution, and public exhibition of such recordings. Such licenses may be granted in whole or in part, and may specify conditions regarding territory, duration, and manner of use. Assignment of rights relating to a film sound recording is permissible only through a registered agreement executed before the Registrar of Copyrights, containing details of both assignor and assignee, including their addresses for service of notices. Where a license is granted under this Act, the producer shall provide reasonable information regarding the terms and conditions thereof to any person seeking access to such information, provided that such request does not compromise trade secrets or confidential business practices. Any subsequent transfer of rights relating to a film sound recording requires similar registration as an assignment.

Notwithstanding anything contained herein, the ownership of copyright in a film sound recording shall vest initially in the producer of the film. Provided that, where such film sound recording incorporates substantial elements of pre-existing musical works or literary compositions, the rights holders of those incorporated works may, subject to contractual agreements executed prior to the commencement of the film’s production, challenge this ownership determination before a court of competent jurisdiction. Such challenges must be predicated upon demonstrable evidence establishing the originality and significant contribution of the pre-existing work to the overall character of the film sound recording. The burden of proving such substantiality rests with the claimant; failure to do so shall preclude any further recourse under this Act regarding copyright infringement claims related to the film sound recording.

Where a film sound recording has been commercially released without authorization, and the owner of copyright in such film sound recording demonstrates to the satisfaction of the Appellate Board that substantial commercial damage has resulted from the unauthorized release, the Appellate Board may order the cessation of further distribution or communication to the public. Such orders shall be accompanied by an assessment of damages payable by the infringer, calculated based on prevailing market rates for similar recordings and taking into account any demonstrable loss of revenue suffered by the copyright owner. Provided that, if the infringer demonstrates good faith reliance upon a written representation from a person appearing to have authority to grant permission, the Appellate Board may reduce the assessed damages proportionally. The right to apply under this provision shall lapse two years after the date of first commercial release without authorization.

Any person who, without the written authorization of the owner of the film sound recording and the producer of the work, reproduces such film sound recording in any form, or by any means, shall be liable to pay as damages an amount equivalent to fifty per cent of the reasonable cost of obtaining the necessary rights for such reproduction, or ten times the number of copies made or intended to be made, whichever is greater. Where a contravention of this provision occurs with the knowledge or consent of an officer of a company, that officer shall also be liable jointly and severally with the company. The owner may apply to the relevant court for interlocutory orders restraining any acts infringing upon their rights under this Act, provided that such application is made within six months from the date of becoming aware of the infringement.

For the purposes of this Act, "film sound" means sounds exclusively fixed in relation to a cinematographic work and which are capable of reproduction, including musical scores, dialogue, ambient noise, and effects recorded during or after the filming process. Film sound shall be deemed an integral part of the cinematograph film for copyright subsistence; however, it may also exist independently as a separate copyrighted work if such separation is demonstrably intended by the producer. The rights in film sound are subject to any contractual agreements between the producers and those involved in its creation, provided that such agreements do not contravene the principles of fairness under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, registration of film sound shall be deemed conclusive evidence of ownership of copyright therein, subject to the provisions regarding joint authorship. An application for such registration may be made by the producer of the film or any person duly authorized by him in writing. The application shall specify the title of the film, the name and address of the applicant, and a detailed description of the film sound recording, including its duration and technical specifications. Provided that where the film sound incorporates pre-existing musical works, the application must also identify those works and their respective owners. Any alteration to the registered film sound subsequent to registration shall require notification to the Copyright Office.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, copyright in film sound shall vest initially in the producer of the cinematographic work. Any infringement of such copyright shall render the infringing party liable for damages, calculated at the option of the copyright owner as either the reasonable royalty that would have been payable had the use been authorised or the actual loss suffered by the copyright owner as a consequence of the infringement. Provided that, in determining such damages, due account shall be taken of any benefit accruing to the infringer which is not reflected in the amount of those damages. The right to sue for and recover damages for contributory infringement relating to film sound remains with the producer. Further, remedies available under this Act may be pursued by assignment holders or licensees of the copyright therein.

The owner of copyright in any film sound shall be entitled to exercise all rights conferred under this Act as if the film sound were an artistic work. Where a film incorporates pre-existing musical works, the copyright subsisting in such musical works shall not prejudice the copyright in the film sound itself; provided that the producer of the film shall ensure that adequate remuneration is paid to the owners of those incorporated musical works, as determined by the relevant collecting society registered under this Act. Any person desiring to utilize a portion of a protected film sound for commercial purposes must obtain prior written permission from the owner of copyright therein. Failure to secure such authorization will render the user liable to prosecution and subject to penalties as provided herein. The Registrar shall maintain a public register detailing licenses granted concerning film sound usage, accessible upon application by any interested party.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, copyright in film sound shall vest initially in the producer of the cinematograph film. Provided that where the film sound is generated wholly or substantially by means other than direct recording of voices or performances, copyright therein shall vest in the person by whom such generation was commissioned, unless otherwise agreed upon in writing with the party commissioning the work. The rights conferred under this Act are not assignable except with prior written consent from all performers whose voices or performances are incorporated within the film sound. Any reproduction or communication to the public of film sound without authorization shall be deemed a violation and subject to remedies as provided herein, irrespective of whether such action infringes upon any underlying musical composition.

Any person who, without authorization from the owner of copyright in the film sound, reproduces, distributes, exhibits, or performs the said film sound to the public shall be deemed guilty of an offence. Such infringement is actionable at law and subject to penalties as provided herein. Where the infringing act involves the commercial exploitation of the film sound for financial gain, the court may impose a fine not exceeding ten times the actual damages suffered by the copyright owner or one million rupees, whichever is greater. Further, any equipment used in the commission of such an offence relating to film sound shall be liable to seizure and forfeiture. The right holder may also seek injunctive relief to restrain further acts of infringement.

The owner of copyright in film sound, being the producer of the cinematographic work, shall be entitled to grant licenses granting rights to reproduce the said film sound in any medium, including but not limited to audio recordings and musical scores. Such licenses may specify the duration, geographical scope, and permitted uses of the reproduced film sound, subject to reasonable royalty payments as determined under this Act. Assignment of copyright in film sound is permissible by way of a registered agreement, clearly identifying the assignor and assignee and detailing the extent of rights transferred. Provided that any license granted prior to assignment shall remain valid and enforceable against the assignee. Further, where a license has been exclusively assigned, the original producer retains the right to audit royalty accounts for a period of three years following the termination of the agreement. The grant or assignment is deemed invalid if it contravenes provisions relating to fair dealing.

Notwithstanding anything contained under this Act relating to the ownership of copyright in cinematographic films, where the film sound exclusively comprises musical works and literary works created independently of the filming process, the author or authors of such works shall be deemed the first owners of copyright therein. This determination is subject to the condition that the producers demonstrate, through documented evidence presented before an adjudicating officer appointed by the Central Government, that they were not party to any agreement assigning said rights prior to the commencement of film production. Any dispute arising from this provision may be appealed to a High Court within whose territorial jurisdiction the cause of action arose, provided such appeal is made within ninety days of the order of the adjudicating officer.

Where the unauthorized reproduction of film sound infringes upon copyright under this Act, the owner of the copyright shall be entitled to injunctive relief preventing further acts of infringement. Damages recoverable in such cases shall be assessed based on demonstrable financial loss suffered by the copyright holder, or a sum not less than fifty thousand rupees and not exceeding two hundred thousand rupees, whichever is greater, as determined by the relevant adjudicating officer. Provided that, if the infringing reproduction incorporates elements of layout design registered under the Designs Act, 2000, additional damages may be awarded to account for the dilution of goodwill associated with the registered design. The court may also order the destruction of all infringing copies of the film sound and any materials used in their creation. Any person found guilty of contributory infringement shall be subject to similar remedies as provided herein.

Any person infringing the exclusive right of the registration proprietor in respect of film sound shall be liable to prosecution under this Act. Such infringement includes unauthorized reproduction, distribution, adaptation, and public exhibition of the said film sound. Where an infringement is committed by an employee or agent acting within the scope of their employment, the employer or principal shall also be deemed guilty of the offence and subject to penalties as provided herein. The Court may order seizure and destruction of infringing copies of the film sound, along with any equipment used in its unlawful production. Repeated or commercial scale infringements will attract enhanced fines and imprisonment terms, as determined by the presiding officer. Failure to comply with a cease-and-desist order issued under this Act shall constitute contempt of court.

The owner of copyright in film sound, being the producer of the cinematographic work, shall be entitled to grant licenses granting rights to reproduce the said film sound in various media. Such licenses may specify the duration, geographical scope, and permitted uses, including but not limited to synchronization with other works or incorporation into audio-visual productions. Assignment of copyright in film sound is permissible, provided that a formal instrument executed as per prescribed procedures is registered with the designated Copyright Office. Where an error appears in any registered assignment document relating to film sound ownership or licensing terms, the Registrar may issue an error amendment notice to the concerned parties, affording them opportunity for objection before rectification. Any subsequent license granted shall be subject to the corrected record. The producer’s rights under this Act are not assignable without prior consent of the original composer and lyricist, unless otherwise agreed in writing.

Where any work has been infringed by the unauthorized reproduction or distribution thereof, the owner of copyright in such work shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief restraining further acts of infringement. For the purposes of determining ownership under this Act, a *recording means person* who undertakes the technical direction and control of the sound recording process shall be deemed the primary author, unless evidence demonstrates otherwise through contractual agreements or demonstrable creative contribution beyond mere technical execution. Any individual participating in the creation of a sound recording, but not fulfilling the criteria for authorship as defined herein, may claim rights incidental to their participation, subject to limitations imposed by this Act regarding remedies available. Provided that such claims must be substantiated with documentary evidence establishing the nature and extent of said participation. The right to claim damages shall remain solely with the primary author or duly authorized assignee.

For the purposes of this Act, "recording means person" shall include any individual directly involved in the capture, manipulation, or preservation of an audio-visual work, irrespective of their contractual relationship with the copyright owner. This definition encompasses, but is not limited to, camera operators, sound engineers, editors, and individuals responsible for digital archiving processes. Any such recording means person who contributes substantially to the creation of a cinematograph film shall be deemed to possess certain rights as provided herein, subject to the terms of any agreement entered into with the producer. The Registrar may, upon application by a recording means person, issue a certificate recognizing their contribution and outlining the scope of their permissible actions relating to the work. Such applications must detail the nature of involvement and provide supporting documentation verifying participation in the creation process.

For the purposes of this Act, where any sound recording, cinematographic film, or other artistic work is produced by means of an apparatus operated and controlled by a person, that person shall be deemed to be the ‘recording means person’ in relation to such production. Provided that, if the operation and control of said apparatus are undertaken under the direction and supervision of another individual, then the directing individual may also be considered a recording means person, subject to demonstrating substantial creative contribution beyond mere instruction. Further, where multiple persons jointly operate and control an apparatus, the determination of who constitutes a ‘recording means person’ shall be resolved based on their respective roles in the production process, as evidenced by written agreements or other verifiable documentation. This provision applies irrespective of whether such person is employed or engaged under contract.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any individual engaged in the creation of an audio recording shall be deemed a "recording means person" and possesses exclusive rights pertaining to the reproduction and distribution of said recording. These rights may be assigned or licensed to other parties through written agreements specifying the scope and duration of such authorization. Provided that, where a recording means person licenses their copyright for commercial use, they shall retain the right to determine the manner in which the work is presented and distributed, ensuring its integrity remains consistent with the original artistic intent. Further, any subsequent assignment or licensing agreement must clearly identify the initial recording means person as the originator of the recorded material, acknowledging their intellectual property rights under this Act. Such assignments are irrevocable except by mutual consent.

For the purposes of determining ownership under this Act, a "recording means person" shall be deemed to have acted as an agent of the work’s creator where such recording was undertaken pursuant to a contractual agreement explicitly assigning copyright. However, it is provided that if the contract fails to clearly delineate the scope of assignment and expressly address moral rights, the recording means person may challenge the validity of said assignment in proceedings before the relevant judicial authority. Such challenges shall be predicated on demonstrable evidence indicating a lack of free consent or an imbalance in bargaining power between parties. Further, where ambiguity exists regarding the intent of the contractual agreement, the burden of proof lies with the claimant asserting complete ownership. This provision is subject to any applicable principles of equity and fairness as determined by the court.

Where any unauthorized recording means person infringes upon the copyright in a work, such person shall be liable to pay an account of profits derived from the infringing act, together with damages assessed by the Controller. The assessment of damages may take into consideration not only the retail price of copies made without authorization but also any loss suffered by the owner of the copyright as a direct result of the infringement. Further, where such unauthorized recording means person has acted fraudulently or recklessly in making the infringing copy, the Controller may award exemplary damages to deter similar conduct. An application patent shall not be granted for a method of circumventing technological protection measures employed by the copyright holder to prevent unauthorized access to works. Remedies available under this Act are without prejudice to any other remedies that may be available to the copyright owner in law or equity.

For the purposes of this Act, a "recording means person" is defined as an individual directly involved in the creation and capture of audio-visual works, including but not limited to cinematographers, sound engineers, editors responsible for initial recording, and individuals designated by the producer to oversee the technical aspects of the recording process. The name of such a recording means person shall be permanently affixed to copies of the work made available to the public, subject to any modifications approved in writing by the individual concerned or their legally appointed representative. Any alteration or removal of this designation without explicit consent constitutes an infringement under this Act. Further, where a recording means person contributes significantly to the artistic merit of a work, they may apply for recognition as a co-author, provided that such application is made within six months from the date of first publication and accompanied by supporting documentation demonstrating their substantial contribution. The Registrar shall consider these applications in accordance with procedures prescribed herein.

Where a recording means a person engaged in the creation of an audio-visual work, such person shall be deemed to possess all rights pertaining to authorship under this Act, subject to any agreement executed prior to the commencement of the recording process. Provided that, if such recording is undertaken on behalf of and at the express direction of a registered user party, the terms of engagement between the recording means person and the said registered user party shall govern the allocation of royalties and other benefits arising from the commercial exploitation of the work. Any assignment of copyright in respect of the recorded work must be executed in writing and duly notarized to be valid under this Act. Further, a recording means person may elect to retain ownership of their copyright, licensing usage rights to others as they deem fit, provided that such licenses are transparently documented.

Any person making a recording of a cinematographic work shall be deemed to be an author thereof and subject to this Act, shall possess all rights accruing to the original author. Where such recording is made by an employee in the course of their employment, the employer shall be considered the ‘recording means person’ for the purposes of ownership, unless otherwise agreed in writing with the employee.
