Any unauthorized reproduction or distribution of a work recorded in violation of these provisions shall incur a penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees and may result in imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years. Furthermore, any registered layout design incorporated into such recording, used without authorization, will attract additional penalties as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, "makes performance photograph" means a photographic work that is created during the course of a live performance and which captures elements substantially representing such performance. Such a photograph shall be deemed an artistic work and subject to copyright under this Act. The creation of a makes performance photograph does not, however, grant any right to the performer in respect of their performance itself; provided that the photographer’s rights are derived solely from the photographic work created. This definition applies irrespective of whether the performance is recorded for broadcast or other purposes as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, a "makes performance photograph" shall be defined as a photographic work which records a live performance, whether musical, theatrical, cinematographic, or otherwise, and is created by capturing images during said performance. Such photographs are considered works of authorship subject to protection under this Act, provided that the copyright therein vests initially in the photographer who undertook the creation of the photograph. The right to make copies of a makes performance photograph shall be restricted where such reproduction would infringe upon the performer’s rights as defined herein; however, fair dealing provisions relating to criticism and review may apply subject to judicial interpretation. Assignment of copyright in a makes performance photograph requires registration with the Copyright Office for validity against third parties.

For the purposes of this Act, a "makes performance photograph" shall be defined as a photographic work that is created during the execution of a live performance by one or more performers and which captures an essential aspect of said performance. The right to make a makes performance photograph shall vest in the performer whose performance is captured, subject to any contractual agreement executed prior to the commencement of the performance explicitly granting such rights to another party. Any person desiring to create a makes performance photograph shall obtain written consent from the relevant performing artist or their authorized representative, detailing the scope and duration of permitted usage. Failure to secure such consent will render the photographic work infringing under this Act. The Registrar shall maintain a public record of all consents granted relating to makes performance photographs for transparency and dispute resolution purposes.

Where a photograph is made as a result of a performance, the performer shall have an exclusive right to authorize or prohibit the making of such photograph. This authorization extends to all subsequent reproductions, communications to the public, and any other acts restricted under this Act. Provided that, where the photograph is made incidentally during a performance intended primarily for another purpose, such as news reporting or artistic documentation, the performer’s rights shall be limited to preventing commercial exploitation without explicit consent. Further, if the making of the photograph constitutes fair dealing with the original performance, as determined by considerations of public interest and originality, this restriction may not apply. The right conferred herein is subject to any contractual agreements entered into prior to the creation of the makes performance photograph.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, where a photograph is made as a result of a performance by an artist, the copyright therein shall vest initially in the performer. However, such performer may, by instrument in writing, assign or license the said copyright, or any part thereof, to any person, including but not limited to photographic studios or commercial entities engaged in image reproduction. Any assignment or license granted under this Act shall be void unless it is registered with the designated authority as provided herein and specifies the duration of the assigned rights. Further, where a photograph constitutes an artistic work incorporating elements of the performance, the copyright owner shall be deemed to hold exclusive rights for making such photographs available for public display or commercial use. The performer retains the right to receive equitable remuneration from any exploitation of their likeness captured in the makes performance photograph.

For the purposes of this Act, "makes performance photograph" means a photographic work which is created during the course of a live performance and records aspects substantially relating to that performance. Such a photograph shall be deemed an artistic work independently existing from the performance itself, subject to the performer’s rights as provided herein. The creation of a makes performance photograph does not, however, grant any right to reproduce or distribute the underlying performance; such rights remain with the performers involved. Any dispute arising concerning ownership or usage relating to a makes performance photograph may be adjudicated in accordance with established case proceeding sections.

For the purposes of this Act, “territorial extent” shall mean the geographical area over which a patent is enforceable, and such extent is determined by the jurisdiction of the relevant High Court. An appeal under this Act from any order passed by the Controller may be made to the High Court within whose territorial jurisdiction the respondent resides or carries on business, or at the option of the appellant, to the High Court of Delhi. Subject to provisions regarding interim orders, proceedings in appeals before a High Court shall be conducted as if they were original suits instituted in that court under its code of civil procedure. Provided that the High Court may, for reasons to be recorded, entertain an appeal notwithstanding lack of territorial jurisdiction.

Applications for registration of designs relating to integrated circuits may be filed jointly by two or more applicants, provided that the respective rights and liabilities of each applicant are clearly defined within the application. Upon receipt of an application, the Designs Registry shall publish a notice indicating acceptance for examination. Any interested party may, subject to conditions as prescribed herein, file a written objection to the registration within a period of three months from the date of such publication. The Designs Registrar may require the submission of further documentation or clarification regarding the novelty and originality of the design. Decisions concerning objections shall be made by a judge of the High Court, whose determination is final.

Where any party aggrieved by an order passed under this Act concerning revocation of patent rights, or relating to infringement proceedings, is dissatisfied with the decision of the Controller, such party shall have the right to appeal to the High Court. The appeal may be made on grounds that the Controller’s decision was manifestly unjust, based on an error apparent on the face of the record, or resulted from a failure to consider material evidence presented during the proceedings. Provided that the appeal must be filed within ninety days from the date of communication of the order appealed against. Further, the High Court may, subject to just considerations and principles of natural justice, entertain appeals where it is demonstrated that the Controller exceeded their jurisdiction in making the original determination. The costs of such an appeal shall be determined by the High Court as deemed appropriate.

Appeals arising from any order passed by the Controller under this Act shall lie to the High Court within whose territorial jurisdiction the defendant’s dwelling place is situated. The High Court shall have power to entertain such appeals notwithstanding any other provision of law relating to limitation, and may admit an appeal if it appears to the court that the decision in question involves a substantial question of law or is otherwise fit for determination by it. Provided that no appeal shall be entertained unless the appellant has deposited with the High Court such sum as determined by the Controller, representing costs incurred by the respondent. The High Court may, after hearing the parties, dismiss the appeal, reverse the order appealed from, or substitute its own order in lieu thereof. Any party aggrieved by an order of the High Court under this Act may further appeal to the Supreme Court on such grounds and manner as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Controller relating to the grant, revocation or sealing of a patent may appeal to the appropriate High Court within sixty days from the date of such order. Provided that where the order relates to a compulsory license, the appellant shall demonstrate substantial detriment resulting directly from the operation of the order. The High Court may, if it deems fit, require the appellant to furnish security for costs and other expenses incurred by the respondent in defending the appeal. Further, the High Court shall not entertain any appeal under this Act unless the prescribed fee has been duly paid, and all conditions precedent to the appeal have been satisfied as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to revocation of patent, rectification of register, or any other matter where a right has been conferred or denied may appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such order. The High Court shall admit the appeal if it appears to be for the purpose of securing justice and may entertain an appeal despite delay, provided that sufficient cause is shown for the delay. Failure to comply with the prescribed time limit shall not preclude a party from approaching the High Court under Article 226 or 227 of the Constitution; however, any costs incurred due to such delay will be determined by the High Court. Enforcement of remedies granted by the High Court shall be subject to the provisions regarding injunctions and specific performance as provided herein.

Where the patentee of a registered invention desires to grant a license conferring rights to use, manufacture, or sell the patented invention, such license shall be assignable by the patentee subject to the provisions herein. Any assignment or license granted prior to registration shall require notification to the Controller within thirty days of its execution and shall be recorded in the Register of Patents. The terms of any license agreement may specify royalties payable to the patentee, which shall be determined at the discretion of the parties involved provided that such royalty rates are not manifestly excessive. Further, a licensee may sub-license rights under the primary license with the prior written consent of the patentee. Disputes concerning the validity or enforceability of assignments and licenses relating to patents shall be subject to adjudication by the appropriate High Court.

Where an appeal is brought before a High Court against any order passed by the Controller relating to the grant, revocation or sealing of a patent, the High Court may, subject to the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder, entertain such appeal without regard to the pecuniary jurisdiction of the High Court. Provided that the appellant shall deposit with the High Court such sum as the Central Government may prescribe by notification in the Official Gazette, representing costs incurred by the respondent in defending the appeal. The High Court shall have power to grant any relief or redress which it deems just and equitable under this Act, including but not limited to affirming, modifying, reversing or remanding the order appealed from. Any party aggrieved by an order of the High Court may further appeal to the Supreme Court as provided herein.

Where an application for a patent relates to a process for producing a substance directly usable as a medicine, and such process includes one or more steps performed solely by means of enzymes produced by microorganisms, the Controller may require the applicant to furnish particulars relating to the conditions under which the microorganism is cultivated and maintained. Further, any subsequent patent addition shall be deemed invalid if it incorporates elements disclosed in an earlier application that was not published prior to the date of filing of said later application. The High Court shall have exclusive jurisdiction to determine disputes arising from such claims regarding validity, subject to compliance with procedural requirements as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to revocation of patent, sealing of premises, or any other enforcement action may appeal to the relevant High Court within sixty days from the date of such order. Provided that the High Court may entertain appeals filed after the expiry of said period if the appellant satisfies the court that they had sufficient cause for not preferring the appeal within the prescribed time. Failure to comply with a mandatory injunction issued by a High Court in relation to patent infringement shall render the defaulter liable to a penalty, which may extend to ten times the damages awarded or such higher amount as the High Court deems just and equitable, considering the nature of the violation and the impact on the patent holder’s commercial interests. The application patent period is not relevant when determining penalties for willful infringement.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder, the right to exploit a patent shall vest in the assignee or licensee thereof, and such exploitation may include the manufacture, use, sale, offer for sale, or importation of the patented invention. Where a license is granted under this Act, the licensing agreement shall clearly define the scope of the licensed rights, including but not limited to geographical limitations and field of use restrictions. Any assignment or license relating to a patent shall be recorded in the Patents Office within three months from the date of such assignment or license; failure to do so may render the assignment or license voidable. Furthermore, where the patented invention incorporates elements derived from a well-known trade mark, any exploitation undertaken by the assignee or licensee must not create confusion among consumers and shall respect the rights of the proprietor of that trade mark. Disputes concerning the validity of such assignments or licenses may be referred to a High Court for adjudication.

An appeal lies from any order passed by the Controller relating to the acceptance or rejection of a basic application, or concerning any matter arising during the examination thereof, to the relevant High Court within sixty days from the date of communication of such order. Provided that where an order is made against which an appeal would lie under this Act, and the order relates also to some other matter in respect of which no appeal lies, the applicant may appeal only on the ground(s) relating to the matters as to which an appeal does lie. The High Court shall have power to entertain such appeals notwithstanding any technical objection concerning the maintainability thereof, subject to just cause shown. Further, the decision of the High Court shall be final, save for further appeal to the Supreme Court under provisions governing appeals from High Courts.

The Register of Geographical Indications shall maintain a record of all registered geographical indications and any applications pending registration. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application for registration, or the revocation or amendment of a registered geographical indication, may appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The Register shall be open to public inspection during normal business hours, subject to any reasonable restrictions imposed by the Registrar to protect confidential information. Furthermore, evidence presented in proceedings before the High Court concerning alleged falsification of a registered geographical indication’s origin or characteristics may include expert testimony regarding agricultural practices and local production methods which demonstrably falsifies genuine geographical provenance.

For the purposes of this Act, a “patent india claim” shall be construed as a statement defining the scope of protection sought for an invention. Such a claim must be clear, concise and supported by the description contained within the patent specification; otherwise it may be deemed invalid under this Act. A patent india claim shall particularly define the matter for which protection is sought, distinguishing it from prior art disclosures. It is provided that claims incorporating essential elements derived directly from existing processes or apparatuses shall be subject to stricter scrutiny during examination. The interpretation of a patent india claim shall take into account the entire specification and any drawings accompanying it.

An application for a patent shall include particulars verifying the novelty and inventive step of the invention, alongside details regarding its first filing date and place. The Registrar may require submission of certified copies of prior publications or registrations relevant to assessing the validity of a patent india claim. Such claims must clearly define the scope of protection sought and be supported by the description contained within the complete specification. Where an applicant seeks to amend any claim after the initial publication of the application, such amendment shall not broaden the scope beyond what was originally disclosed. The Controller may reject a patent if it is determined that the claimed invention lacks unity of invention as provided herein.

Where, upon revocation of a patent under this Act, any person aggrieved by the decision granting the patent may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. Such an appeal shall be on grounds that the invention was not novel or involved inventive step, or that the claim in the patent was improperly construed as lacking unity of invention. The Appellate Board may, after affording all parties a reasonable opportunity for being heard, confirm, modify, or reverse the decision appealed from. Further, where infringement proceedings are pending and a patent is revoked during those proceedings, any injunction granted prior to revocation shall lapse immediately, subject to just satisfaction for losses incurred by the claimant. Any person who has been restrained by an injunction under this Act may seek compensation from the patentee. The interpretation of a *patent india claim* shall be guided by principles of fair and reasonable construction.

An application for a patent shall be deemed to contain claims unless the applicant explicitly states otherwise in writing, and such statement shall be considered part of the formal record. The determination of novelty and inventive step under this Act shall be assessed solely on the basis of the matter disclosed in the claims as presented at the time of grant. Where an objection is raised regarding the clarity or precision of a patent india claim, the Controller may direct the applicant to amend the claim within a prescribed period, subject to the condition that such amendment does not broaden the scope of protection sought. Any amended claim shall be accompanied by a reasoned explanation justifying the alteration and demonstrating its conformity with established legal principles. The Board constituted under this Act may review decisions concerning claim interpretation if it is satisfied that there exists an error apparent on the face of the record or that substantial injustice has occurred.

An application for a patent shall be deemed to disclose and fairly describe the invention sufficiently for enabling a person skilled in the art to make and use it, provided that the description includes all essential elements necessary for carrying out the invention. Claims appended to such an application defining the scope of protection sought are subject to scrutiny regarding their clarity and precision; any claim which is ambiguous or lacks support within the specification shall be rejected. Furthermore, a patent india claim must particularly point out and distinctly describe the matter claimed, ensuring that it does not extend beyond the disclosure contained in the complete specification as originally filed. Any alteration of the invention after the date of filing, unless adequately disclosed therein, will invalidate subsequent claims relating to such modifications.

Any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appellate Board shall, after giving notice to all parties concerned, hear the appeal and may pass such orders as it deems fit, subject to the provisions herein. Failure to comply with a cease and desist order issued pursuant to an infringement action constitutes a criminal offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both, at the discretion of the Court. The determination of validity of a patent india claim shall be conclusive against all parties to the proceedings; provided that any party demonstrating fraud in obtaining the patent may pursue remedies as provided under this Act.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any patentee may grant a license to use the patented invention under this Act, and such license shall be assignable by way of absolute or conditional assignment, either wholly or partially. The terms and conditions of any such license, including royalty rates and duration, shall be determined at the discretion of the patentee, provided that any assignment made without the prior written consent of the Controller shall be deemed invalid. Where a patent has been assigned, the assignee shall have all rights to grant licenses as if he were the original patentee. Further, a license granted under this Act may include provisions for sub-licensing, allowing the licensee to permit others to utilize the patented invention within specified territories or fields of use, consistent with the scope of the *patent india claim* and subject to any restrictions stipulated by the patentee.

The Controller may, upon receiving notice of an objection under this Act from any person interested, direct the patent applicant to furnish such further information or particulars relating to the invention as he deems necessary for the purpose of determining whether the invention is novel and involves inventive step. Such direction shall be accompanied by a statement specifying the grounds on which the objection is based; and the applicant shall have a period of ninety days from the date of receipt of such direction to comply, subject to extensions granted under this Act. Failure to furnish the required information within the stipulated time may result in the rejection of the patent application. The validity of any patent granted shall be open to challenge on the grounds that the claim lacks clarity or does not satisfy the requirements for a valid patent india claim.

For the purposes of this Act, a “patent india claim” shall be construed as a statement defining the scope of protection sought for an invention, delineating the subject matter for which exclusive rights are requested. Such a claim must be clear, concise and supported by the description in the patent specification; otherwise, it may be deemed invalid under this Act. The interpretation of a patent india claim shall take into account the entire disclosure of the patent document and any prior art considered during examination. Further, acquiring restrict imposed through an improperly drafted or overly broad claim shall not be enforced if such restriction unduly impedes innovation in related fields.

An application for a patent shall be deemed to be lacking novelty if the matter disclosed in the patent, or any part thereof, is disclosed in a document laid before or published in India’s official gazette under this Act; provided that such disclosure does not anticipate the invention as a whole. The determination of novelty shall consider the entirety of the specification and claims presented by the applicant. A *patent india claim* relating to a patented process may be amended only if the amendment maintains consistency with the original disclosure and does not introduce subject matter which extends beyond the scope of the initial application. Further, any prior use or knowledge impacting the assessment of inventive step shall be documented in the gazette for consideration during examination.

Where, upon revocation of a patent under this Act, any person aggrieved by the decision granting the patent may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. Such an appeal shall be on grounds that the patent was improperly granted, including but not limited to errors in interpreting the novelty or inventive step requirements as defined herein. The Board may, after affording all parties a reasonable opportunity for being heard, confirm, vary, or reverse the decision appealed from. Further, if a *patent india claim* is found invalid upon appeal, any person who has derived benefit from the patent’s existence shall be liable to compensate the aggrieved party for losses demonstrably incurred as a direct result of the patent's enforcement; such compensation will consider the reasonable royalties that would have been payable had a license existed. The *claim complete specification* is crucial in determining scope and validity during these proceedings.

For the purposes of this Act, an invention shall be deemed to lack novelty if it was disclosed to the public prior to the date of filing of the patent application, whether by written or oral description, by use, or in any other way. This disclosure must have enabled a person skilled in the art to produce and operate the claimed invention without undue experimentation. However, information obtained during an exhibition expressly for the purpose of applying for a patent shall not be considered prior art under this Act, provided that adequate records of the exhibition were maintained as evidence. The burden of proving lack of novelty rests upon the party alleging it.

An application for registration of a design shall be deemed invalid under this Act if the design lacks novelty, being identical or substantially similar to a design already registered or publicly known prior to the date of filing. For the purposes of determining novelty, any disclosure made by the applicant or their successors in interest, whether through written publications, oral descriptions, use, or exhibition, shall be considered as anticipatory of the filing date provided that such disclosure occurred before the priority date claimed, if any. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating a clear distinction between the design sought to be registered and prior art designs. Failure to satisfy this requirement may result in rejection of the application.

Where an application for a patent has been refused solely on the ground that the claimed invention lacks novelty, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to present evidence demonstrating that the prior art disclosure did not reasonably inform the skilled person. Such evidence may include expert testimony and comparative analysis of the claimed invention against the cited document. The Controller may, after considering such evidence, reconsider the assessment of novelty. If, following reconsideration, the Controller finds that the application does indeed disclose matter which would have prevented the grant of a patent under this Act, then the applicant shall be deemed to have failed to establish sufficient grounds for granting the patent. Any party aggrieved by such determination may appeal to the Appellate Board as provided herein.

An application for a patent shall be deemed invalid if it is determined that the claimed invention lacks novelty. The determination of novelty shall be assessed based upon prior publications, public uses, and knowledge available to the public before the date of filing of the patent application as provided herein. Where an objection regarding lack of novelty is raised by a person during the examination process, the applicant shall have the opportunity to submit documentary evidence or written arguments demonstrating that the claimed invention possesses the requisite inventive step sufficient to overcome said objection. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish translations of any foreign language documents submitted in support of the application. Further, an appeal against a decision finding lack of novelty may be made before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within three months from the date of communication of such decision.

An invention shall be considered non-patentable under this Act if it lacks novelty. For the purposes of determining novelty, an invention shall not be deemed new if there exists prior public knowledge, whether in documentary form or otherwise, relating to the said invention; provided that such prior public knowledge must have been available to the applicant for a patent as on the date of filing of the patent application or priority date, whichever is earlier. Where the prior public knowledge comprises an advertisement, exhibition, or use which involves the matter disclosed in the invention, it shall be deemed to have been made available to the public irrespective of whether such advertisement, exhibition, or use was known to any person. Subject to this, a disclosure made by the applicant before the filing date shall not affect novelty if it meets conditions as provided herein.

An invention shall be considered not novel if it was disclosed to the public prior to the date of filing of the patent application, whether through written or oral description, exhibition, use, or otherwise. Provided that this lack of novelty may be overcome where such disclosure occurred no earlier than six months preceding the filing date and resulted from an express written communication made by the applicant or their successor in title. Any party demonstrating a prior public knowledge establishing a deficiency in novelty shall be entitled to file an objection with the Controller, accompanied by supporting documentation. Failure to provide adequate evidence of prior publication may result in penalties as determined under this Act, including fines and potential invalidation of any patent subsequently granted based on the challenged invention.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, where a patent has been granted for an invention incorporating elements derived from a previously patented process, the patentee shall be obligated to offer a non-exclusive license to utilize said incorporated elements. This obligation arises when the novelty of the subsequent invention is demonstrably dependent on the earlier patent’s disclosure. The licensing fee shall be determined by the Controller based on factors including the extent of reliance and the commercial value derived from the combined technologies, provided that such fees are just and reasonable. Assignment of this license may occur with the consent of the Controller, ensuring continued adherence to the terms stipulated herein. Any attempt to circumvent these provisions through contrived modifications designed solely to avoid licensing obligations shall be deemed an act contrary to public interest under this Act.

Notwithstanding anything contained herein, an objection regarding the lack of novelty under this Act shall not be deemed valid where the applicant demonstrates, through documented evidence presented before the Controller, that prior public knowledge or use was actively suppressed by a third party with demonstrable intent to hinder the applicant’s commercial exploitation of the invention. Such suppression must be proven to have occurred within the twelve-month period preceding the date of filing of the patent application. The burden of proving such active suppression shall rest entirely upon the applicant, and any finding against them on this ground is subject to appeal before a High Court. Provided that, mere coincidence of prior disclosure does not constitute actionable suppression as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, where a patent has been granted incorporating an amendment specification relating to a claimed invention, the patentee shall be deemed to have assigned all rights pertaining to the novelty of the amended claims to any licensee duly authorized under a written agreement. Provided that such assignment is explicitly documented within the licensing agreement itself, detailing the scope and duration of the license concerning said novelty. Further, where an application for compulsory license is filed against a patent incorporating an amendment specification, the Controller may consider the terms of any existing licensing agreements as relevant in determining whether the invention is available to be worked on a commercial scale within India. The patentee shall provide full disclosure regarding such assignments and licenses upon request by the Controller.

An invention shall be considered not novel if it was disclosed to the public prior to the date of filing of the patent application, whether by written or oral description, use, exhibition, or otherwise. However, this determination shall be subject to a reasoned assessment considering any subsequent attempts at commercial exploitation that were demonstrably unsuccessful and did not constitute an enabling disclosure under this Act. The Controller may, upon appeal from an objection based on lack of novelty, direct that the prior publication was insufficient to preclude patentability if it is established that the applicant had no reasonable means of ascertaining the contents thereof. Threatened infringement trade arising from reliance on such a determination shall be considered in assessing the merits of any challenge under this Act.

For the purposes of determining novelty under this Act, an invention shall be considered not novel if it forms part of prior publication anywhere in the world, whether by written description, drawings, oral disclosure, use, exhibition, or otherwise. This determination shall take into account any information disclosed in an international application form filed under the Patent Cooperation Treaty, provided that such form was published within twelve months preceding the date of filing of the patent application in India. Further, if a translation is included with the international application, the translated version also constitutes prior publication for assessing novelty as provided herein.

Where an application for a patent has been refused solely on the ground that the claimed invention lacks novelty, and subsequent evidence demonstrates that the prior art disclosure was rendered ineffective due to alterations introduced by an issued breeder who subsequently disseminated those altered materials without knowledge of the pending patent application, the Controller may, subject to just terms and conditions, order the restoration of the application for further consideration. Such terms shall include compensation to the applicant reflecting demonstrable commercial prejudice suffered as a result of the unauthorized dissemination. The determination of “just terms” shall consider the extent of the breeder’s contribution to the loss of novelty and any benefit derived therefrom. Provided that this remedy is only available where the applicant can prove, with reasonable certainty, that the alteration directly impacted the assessment of novelty under this Act.

An application for a patent shall be deemed invalid under this Act if it is established that the claimed invention was not novel at the date of filing. The determination of novelty shall consider whether the invention has been disclosed to the public anywhere in the world by means of written description, use, or otherwise. Where a user party proceeding against an applicant alleges lack of novelty, they must submit evidence demonstrating such prior disclosure and specifying the details thereof. The Controller may require the user party to furnish further particulars regarding the alleged prior art. Any document submitted as evidence shall be deemed admissible subject to verification of its authenticity by the Controller. An applicant aggrieved by a determination of non-novelty may appeal to the Appellate Board, provided that such an appeal is made within the prescribed time limit and accompanied by the requisite fee.

For the purposes of this Act, “renewal” shall mean the payment of a prescribed fee to maintain a patent in force for successive periods of twenty years from the date of application. The renewal fee must be paid within three months preceding the expiration of the current term or within six months where an extension is granted under this Act. Failure to pay the renewal fee as provided herein will result in the patent ceasing to have effect, unless a request for dispensation from penalty has been made and approved by the Controller. Any application for such dispensation shall be accompanied by reasonable justification for the delay in payment.

Where an application for patent has been granted and the term of protection is nearing expiry, it shall be incumbent upon the patentee to initiate proceedings for renewal prior to the lapse of the said term. The prescribed fee for such renewal shall be remitted electronically through the designated portal, accompanied by a declaration confirming continued ownership and entitlement to the patent. Failure to submit this declaration may result in rejection of the renewal application. Under this Act, any person aggrieved by an order rejecting a renewal request may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of such order. Provided that the Controller may, upon satisfactory demonstration of compelling circumstances, entertain applications for renewal received after the expiry of the prescribed period, subject to payment of additional fees as determined by regulations framed under this Act.

Where a patent has lapsed due to non-payment of the prescribed renewal fee, any person aggrieved may petition the Controller for its restoration. Such petition shall be made within six months from the date on which the lapse occurred and must demonstrate reasonable grounds for the failure to pay said fee. The Controller may, subject to just cause shown, grant leave for the patentee to apply for a continuation of the patent, effectively enabling renewal. This application shall include payment of all outstanding renewal fees together with any applicable late payment penalties as determined under this Act. Provided that the Controller may require an additional hearing if the restoration would prejudice the public interest or affect existing rights derived from the expired patent. The decision of the Controller regarding such petitions is final, subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

The application for renewal of a patent shall be made to the Controller not less than three months before the date of its expiry and may be accompanied by such documents and fees as are prescribed. Upon receipt of an application for renewal, the Controller shall issue notice to any person appearing likely to object to the grant of the renewal, affording them an opportunity to submit their objections in writing within a period specified therein. The patentee shall furnish proof of payment of the prescribed fee along with the application; failure to do so will render the application void. Where an objection is received, the Controller may hold a hearing and consider any evidence presented by the patentee and the objector before making a determination regarding the renewal. If the Controller deems it necessary, he may require the patentee to submit further information or clarification concerning the invention's continued utility. The grant of renewal shall revive the patent as if it had not expired, subject to all limitations and conditions applicable at the time of its original grant.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, a patent shall remain in force for a term of twenty years from the date of application for patents, or such lesser period as specified in the regulations. The renewal fee for the first ten years following the grant of the patent shall be remitted within six months of the expiry of the initial term; failure to remit said fee prior to the expiration of that six-month window will render the patent liable to lapse. Subsequent renewals may be effected, provided that each such renewal is accompanied by a statement confirming continued compliance with all applicable conditions under this Act pertaining to working and manufacture. Any application for renewal shall be considered only if the prescribed forms are duly completed and submitted along with the requisite fee.

Where a patent has lapsed due to non-payment of the prescribed renewal fee, any person aggrieved may institute proceedings before the relevant High Court seeking restoration of the patent. Such application shall be made within six months from the date on which the lapse occurred and must demonstrate reasonable cause for the failure to pay said fee. The Controller may, subject to satisfying himself that the applicant has a prima facie case, grant leave to file such an application. Failure to comply with any condition imposed by the Controller in granting such leave shall render the application liable to dismissal without further hearing. Any person found to have knowingly and willfully obstructed or hindered the renewal process shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years.

Where a patent is subject to renewal under this Act, any licensee or assignee may, prior to the expiration of the term for which the renewal fee remains unpaid, apply to the Controller for permission to pay such fee on behalf of the patentee. Such application shall specify the grounds upon which the applicant claims entitlement to effect the renewal and provide evidence satisfactory to the Controller demonstrating a legally recognized interest in the patent, including but not limited to an assignment or license agreement duly registered under this Act. The Controller may grant or refuse such permission at his discretion, provided that any objection by the patentee shall be considered. If permission is granted, the applicant shall pay all applicable renewal fees and charges within the time stipulated by the Controller. Failure to do so will render the patent liable for lapse, as if no application had been made.

Where an application for renewal of a patent has been rejected under this Act, the applicant may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. Such appeal shall be accompanied by a fee as prescribed and shall state specifically the grounds on which the order is challenged. The Appellate Board may, after giving notice to the Controller and affording him an opportunity of being heard, confirm or vary the order appealed against, or remit the matter for reconsideration. Any party aggrieved by any decision of the Appellate Board under this provision may further appeal to the High Court within sixty days, subject to such conditions as are provided herein regarding costs. The continued validity of the patent remains in abeyance pending final determination of the appeal.

Where a patent has lapsed due to non-payment of the prescribed renewal fee, an application for revival may be made within six months from the date of such lapse, subject to payment of all overdue fees and any default surcharge as determined under this Act. The Controller shall consider such application only if it is accompanied by an affidavit explaining the reasons for the failure to pay the renewal fee in a timely manner. Any party aggrieved by the decision of the Controller regarding the revival application may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order, and the relevant entry register pertaining to the patent shall be admissible as evidence during such proceedings. Provided that the Appellate Board may dismiss an appeal if it finds the grounds thereof to be frivolous or vexatious.

Where an application for renewal of a patent has been filed under this Act, the Registrar shall record the particulars of such renewal in the Register of Patents and Patented Documents. The fee payable for renewal shall be as prescribed by the First Schedule. Provided that where the applicant for renewal is an exclusive licensee of the patent, they may, subject to conditions determined by the Controller, file the application on behalf of the patentee. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Controller regarding the acceptance or rejection of a renewal application may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of such decision. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all applications for renewal and related correspondence accessible for public inspection, subject to reasonable restrictions as determined by regulations framed under this Act.

Where a patent has lapsed due to non-payment of the prescribed renewal fee, any person aggrieved by such lapse may petition the Controller for restoration of the patent. The Controller shall entertain such petitions only if they are made within six months from the date on which the patent ceased to have effect and accompanied by evidence demonstrating reasonable grounds for the failure to pay the renewal fee. Upon being satisfied that there is sufficient cause, the Controller may direct that the patent be deemed to be in force as if it had not lapsed, subject to a fresh payment of all overdue fees with interest at such rate as may be prescribed under this Act. The register patents shall reflect any restoration order issued by the Controller and include details of the date of revival and any conditions imposed.

Where a patentee fails, without reasonable justification, to work the patented invention within India, or where the patented invention is not readily available to the public at a price that is reasonable and equitable, the Central Government may, subject to the provisions of this Act, grant a compulsory licence. An application for such a compulsory licence shall be made to the Controller, who shall give notice to the patentee and provide them an opportunity to present their objections. The patentee shall be entitled to receive adequate remuneration, determined in accordance with guidelines framed by the Central Government, taking into account the nature of the invention, the extent of its working, and the investment undertaken by the patentee. Any person granted a compulsory licence under this Act shall not manufacture or import the patented article for sale within India without prior authorization from the Controller.

Where an aggrieved party, demonstrating substantial prejudice arising from the non-working on the territory of India of a patent granted under this Act, files a petition with the Controller alleging failure to meet stipulated timelines or conditions as provided herein, the Controller shall afford the patentee an opportunity for reasoned response. Such response may include evidence substantiating diligent efforts towards working the patented invention within India. The Controller may, after considering all submissions and relevant circumstances, grant a compulsory licence subject to terms and conditions deemed just and equitable, including payment of adequate remuneration determined by principles established under this Act. Any order made by the Controller shall be appealable before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Applications for registration of designs relating to integrated circuits shall be examined in accordance with the prescribed procedure. Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board within a period of sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The Board shall follow such procedures as are provided herein when hearing appeals, and its decision shall be final. Further, any party dissatisfied with the decision of the Appellate Board may seek redress through proceedings act before the High Court. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further particulars or amendments deemed necessary for clarity and compliance with this Act’s provisions concerning design registration.

Where any party aggrieved by an order made under this Act is dissatisfied, such party shall have the right to appeal from that order to the Appellate Board. The appeal shall be filed within a period of sixty days from the date of service of the order appealed against and shall state specifically the grounds on which the order is sought to be challenged. Upon receipt of an appeal, the Appellate Board may entertain the same only if it is satisfied that the appellant has worked out sufficient remedies available under this Act prior to seeking appellate relief. The Board shall have power to affirm, modify, or reverse the order appealed against and may grant such further relief as it deems just and equitable in the circumstances of the case. Any party dissatisfied with an order of the Appellate Board may prefer an appeal to the High Court within a period of ninety days from the date of that order; these proceedings act as the final recourse available under this Act.

Where an objection is taken by any person against the grant of patent, or against the validity of a patent granted, such person shall be entitled to institute proceedings acting through an authorized representative for seeking redressal thereof. The Controller may, upon receiving notice of such proceedings and after affording opportunity of being heard to all interested parties, direct the institution of mediation in accordance with principles established by the Central Government. Provided that where the objection relates to a matter of fact which could have been raised during the examination or opposition process, it shall not be entertained unless sufficient cause is shown for the failure to do so at an earlier stage. The Controller may require any party to furnish security, as deemed appropriate, to ensure compliance with orders made under this Act and to cover costs incurred by other parties in relation to such proceedings acting.

Where an interested party seeks to challenge the validity of a patent granted under this Act, such proceedings act shall be instituted within six months from the date of publication of the grant. The Controller may, upon receipt of notice of such challenge, direct that the matter be heard expeditiously and may prescribe timelines for filing pleadings and submissions by all parties involved. Provided that any party seeking to introduce evidence relating to prior use or public knowledge shall furnish a detailed inventory of such evidence at least thirty days before the scheduled hearing. Further, where the patentee fails to appear or adequately represent themselves during these proceedings act, the Controller may proceed ex parte. The Controller’s decision in respect of validity shall be final subject to appeal under this Act.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to rectification, revocation or infringement of a patent shall have the right to appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appellate Board may, after giving notice to the appellant and respondent, hear arguments and examine evidence relevant to the appeal, subject to such procedures as it deems fit. Failure to comply with the prescribed timelines for filing an appeal shall render the appeal inadmissible. Further, any party found to have instituted frivolous or vexatious proceedings act before the Appellate Board may be liable to pay costs, including compensation for loss of time and expenses incurred by the other parties involved in the litigation.

Where an invention relates to a process for producing a substance, any person claiming title to the patent or possessing a license to exercise the patented process shall be deemed to hold an implied license to use such process for the manufacture of that substance, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated in the assignment agreement or licensing contract. This provision applies irrespective of whether the substance is itself claimed as part of the invention. Any proceedings act undertaken by a licensee relating to infringement of the patent by another party shall be considered an exercise of rights granted under this implied license, provided that such proceedings do not contradict any restrictions outlined within the original contractual agreement. The Controller may issue directions regarding the scope and validity of these implied licenses in cases where disputes arise concerning their interpretation or application, ensuring equitable access to patented technologies while respecting legitimate commercial interests.

Where an objection is raised to the grant of patent under this Act, the Controller may, after giving notice to the applicant and the objector, direct that the proceedings act be conducted as a hearing. Such hearing shall afford both parties an opportunity to present oral arguments and submit further evidence relevant to the objection. The Controller shall record reasons for any decision made on the basis of such hearing. Any party aggrieved by any order or direction passed in the proceedings act may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of that order, subject to just cause shown for delay. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final and binding, provided that it does not conflict with any other provision under this Act.

Where any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act relating to the revocation or surrender of a patent, or concerning the validity of a claim within a patent, institutes proceedings challenging such order or validity, the Controller shall provide notice to all parties who appeared in the original proceeding and to any other party registered as having a substantial interest in the patent. Such aggrieved person may seek remedies including but not limited to damages for infringement occurring between the date of the challenged order and the final determination of the proceedings act. The Controller shall ensure that the register said layout is updated to reflect the outcome of such proceedings, whether affirming or altering the original decision. Further, any party dissatisfied with the findings in these proceedings may appeal to the High Court within a period prescribed under this Act, subject to payment of fees as determined by regulations framed hereunder.

Where an objection is raised against the grant of a patent relating to a pharmaceutical product, the Controller shall provide notice to the applicant and any interested party as per the prescribed form, affording them a period of sixty days from the date of such notice for filing their respective responses. The proceedings act initiated by either the applicant or an interested party may include submission of documentary evidence, expert testimony, and counter-arguments pertaining to the validity of the patent claim. Further, where the subject matter of the patent application relates to an invention claimed in a prior international application filed under the Protocol Madrid Agreement concerning the International Registration of Marks, the Controller shall require disclosure of relevant details regarding such international registration. The Controller may, at any stage during these proceedings, direct parties to attend conferences for clarification or settlement attempts. Decisions rendered by the Controller are subject to appeal before the Appellate Board.

For the purposes of this Act, “goods” includes merchandise contemplated for sale or hire, and services offered to the public, whether by way of trade, business, profession, or occupation; provided that where goods are classified under the International Classification of Goods for the Purposes of the Registration of Trade Marks, a reference in any provision of this Act to goods shall be deemed to include such classification. The term "service" includes activities relating to the supply of accommodation, transport, communication, entertainment, and the distribution or transmission of information; subject to the provisions act reference concerning financial services as defined by the Banking Regulation Act.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall include particulars identifying the applicant and stating whether the applicant is an individual or a body corporate; provided that where the applicant is a partnership, the application shall state the names and addresses of all the partners. The Registrar may require such further information as he deems necessary to ascertain the identity and status of the applicant. Where an earlier trade mark exists which is identical or nearly so with any element of the proposed trade mark, the Registrar shall issue directions concerning the provisions act reference relating to distinctiveness. Such directions are binding on the applicant for the purposes of proceeding with the application under this Act. The Trade Marks Registry maintains records accessible to the public.

Where an owner of a registered trade mark institutes legal proceedings under this Act against any person alleging infringement of their rights, and it appears to the Court that the defendant has used a sign identical or confusingly similar to the plaintiff’s registered trade mark in relation to goods or services not covered by the registration, the Court may, subject to provisions act reference regarding costs, grant such relief as it deems just. This includes an injunction restraining the defendant from further infringing use, and may also order the delivery up of all goods bearing the infringing sign for destruction, or disposal as the Court directs. Furthermore, where damages have not been adequately assessed, the Court may award compensatory damages to the plaintiff representing their losses attributable to the infringement. The provisions act reference concerning limitation periods shall apply to such claims.

An application for registration of a trademark shall contain a clear representation of the mark applied for and a list of goods or services associated with it. The Registrar may require the applicant to specify the manner in which the mark is used or proposed to be used, particularly where the mark incorporates descriptive elements. Where an earlier trademark exists relating to identical or similar goods or services, the application shall include a statement addressing any potential conflict and demonstrating due consideration of relevant provisions act reference concerning prior rights. The Registrar may direct the applicant to amend the representation of the mark if it is deemed unclear or improperly presented. Any objection raised by a third party under this Act must be accompanied by supporting documentation establishing their claim, as provided herein.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark includes a device comprising one or more letters which are commonly used in ordinary language, the Registrar shall not refuse the registration solely on the ground that those letters do not possess distinctive character when applied to the goods or services specified in the application. Provided that such refusal may be made if it is established that, prior to the date of application, use of the device by another person in relation to identical or similar goods or services has resulted in a reputation among the relevant section of the public. The Registrar shall give due regard to any provisions act reference relating to acquired distinctiveness and consider whether such use would create confusion amongst consumers. Further, an appeal against this decision lies under this Act.

Any person who, having knowledge of registered trade marks used in relation to goods or services, uses an identical mark or a mark which is deceptively similar to a registered trade mark in connection with goods or services identical or closely resembling those in relation to which the trade mark is registered, shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall be determined by the relevant court, taking into account the loss suffered by the proprietor of the registered trade mark and any profits made by the infringing party. The provisions act reference regarding assessment of damages shall apply as provided herein. Further, where an infringement has occurred, the Court may order the seizure and destruction of goods bearing the infringing mark or packaging thereof, subject to due process.

Where the registered proprietor of a trade mark desires to grant a license conferring the right to use the trade mark exclusively or non-exclusively, he shall execute an assignment agreement detailing the scope and duration of such permission. This agreement must specify the goods or services in relation to which the licensee is authorized to employ the trade mark, subject to conditions as may be prescribed by the Registrar. Any subsequent transfer of ownership of the licensed business shall not automatically invalidate the license, provided that the assignee notifies the registered proprietor within thirty days and consents to a review of the licensing terms under this Act. The registered proprietor retains the right to terminate the license if material breaches occur, referencing the specific clauses violated in written notice. Further provisions act reference regarding royalty payments and audit rights are detailed in Schedule B annexed hereto.

Where an appeal under this Act is preferred against any decision or order made by the Registrar, the Appellate Board shall hear appeals arising with respect to refusals of registration, revocation of registrations, rectification proceedings, and directions relating to trade mark usage. The Board may, acting upon evidence adduced before it, confirm, vary, or reverse the decision appealed from; provided that the Board is not bound by any observation made during hearings before the Registrar. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Appellate Board may further appeal to the High Court within ninety days of such order, subject to provisions act reference regarding costs and procedure applicable in appeals to the High Court.

For the purposes of this Act, “false trade description” means any representation, whether in words, figures, marks, symbols, or other forms, concerning the quality, characteristics, quantity, origin, mode of manufacture, or intended purpose of goods or services. A false trade description shall be deemed to include a statement which is likely to deceive the public as to the nature, substance, qualities, or properties of such goods or services. Nothing in this definition shall apply to descriptions relating solely to packaging or presentation where those aspects do not materially affect the consumer's perception of the goods themselves; provided that any such description complies with regulations issued under this Act.

An application for registration of a trademark shall be deemed refused if the proposed marks contain a false trade description relating to the nature, quality, characteristics, geographical origin, production method, or other qualities of the goods or services in connection with which it is used. The Registrar may require an applicant to furnish evidence establishing the genuineness of any claim made within the application that might constitute a false trade description; failure to provide such satisfactory evidence shall result in rejection. Where the use of a trademark incorporates information susceptible to interpretation as a false trade description, the proprietor shall be obligated to rectify or withdraw such misleading representation under this Act. Any person aggrieved by an action taken concerning a false trade description may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Where any person applies a false trade description to any goods or services offered for sale, or represents that goods or services are of a particular quality, standard, grade, composition, quantity, or characteristic when they are not so, such person shall be liable to prosecution under this Act. Any proprietor of a registered trademark may institute legal proceedings against another who engages in such deceptive practices, seeking an injunction restraining the offending party from further use of the false trade description and damages commensurate with the loss suffered by the plaintiff due to the misleading representation. The court may also order the destruction or removal of any goods bearing the false trade description, provided that this remedy shall not prejudice the right of the proprietor to claim compensation for past infringements. Further, a conviction under this provision may result in imprisonment and/or a fine as determined by the Court.

Where any person applies a mark used in relation to goods or services, or uses such mark in connection with the offer for sale or supply of goods or services, and makes therein a false trade description, he shall be deemed guilty of an offence under this Act. A false trade description includes statements regarding the geographical origin of goods, the manufacturing process employed, or the quality characteristics possessed by those goods or services. Any consumer who believes they have been misled by such a false trade description may file a complaint with the Registrar for Trade Marks, detailing the particulars of the misleading representation and any resulting loss suffered. The Registrar shall investigate the complaint and may require the person alleged to have made the false trade description to submit evidence refuting the claim. If found substantiated, penalties as provided herein shall apply, including fines and potential injunctions preventing further use of the offending mark.

Where any person applies a mark to goods or renders services in such a manner as to indicate that those goods or services are of a particular quality, origin, or have acquired a particular characteristic, he shall be deemed to have used the mark in relation to those goods or services. Provided that if the application of the mark is deceptive and likely to mislead the public regarding the nature, quality, or geographical origin of the goods or services, it constitutes a false trade description under this Act. Any person who knowingly makes a false trade description shall be liable for damages. Furthermore, where a false trade description is used in connection with the sale or supply of any goods or provision of any services, such action may constitute an offence punishable as provided herein.

Where any person applies a false trade description to goods or offers for sale or hires out goods so marked, he shall be guilty of an offence and liable on conviction to imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years, or with fine, or both. The expression "false trade description" includes any representation likely to deceive the public concerning the nature, quality or geographical origin of such goods. Further, where a false trade description is used in connection with services offered, the offender shall be subject to similar penalties as provided herein. Any officer authorised by the Central Government may seize and detain goods bearing a false trade description pending investigation, and any person aggrieved may seek redress through civil remedies for damages suffered.

Where a proprietor of a registered trademark grants a license to use such mark, and incorporates within the terms thereof provisions relating to quality control measures for goods bearing the mark, any assignment of that license shall be subject to the condition that the assignee undertakes to maintain those same quality control standards as were stipulated in the original licensing agreement. Failure to adhere to these conditions may result in a revocation of the assigned license by the grantor. Furthermore, where an entity knowingly uses a false trade description relating to goods or services offered under a licensed trademark, representing them as originating from, or being approved by, the proprietor without due authorization, such actions shall be deemed a violation under this Act and render the offending party liable for damages. The proprietor may also seek injunctive relief to prevent further misrepresentation.

Where any person, either fraudulently or negligently, applies a false trade description to any goods or services offered for sale, or in connection with the supply or advertising thereof, such person shall be liable to prosecution under this Act. The term "false trade description" includes not only statements directly concerning the nature, quality, quantity, origin, or suitability of those goods or services but also representations that create a false impression as to any of these aspects. Any aggrieved party, including competitors and consumer protection agencies, may institute proceedings seeking an injunction restraining further use of the offending description and damages commensurate with the loss suffered. Appeals against orders made under this provision shall lie to the Appellate Tribunal established for intellectual property disputes, subject to judicial review by the High Court.

Where any person applies a mark used in relation to goods or services in such a manner as to mislead the public as to the nature, quality or geographical origin of those goods or services, or as to the mode of manufacture or other production characteristics thereof, such action shall constitute a false trade description under this Act. Provided that, where the use of a mark is solely for descriptive purposes and does not claim any affiliation with or endorsement by another entity, it shall be presumed not to amount to a false trade description unless proven otherwise. Further, nothing in this provision shall apply to marks which have ceased to be registered and are beyond their expiry term patent, provided that the use continues without intent to deceive and is demonstrably consistent with prior established usage.

For the purposes of this Act, “false trade description” means any representation relating to goods or services sold or offered for sale, including but not limited to their quality, quantity, origin, characteristics, ingredients, properties, suitability for a particular purpose, or the time or place when they were made or acquired. A false trade description shall be deemed misleading if it is likely to deceive or cause confusion in the minds of purchasers or consumers as to the nature, substance, qualities or value of such goods or services. Where two or more persons have used an identical or similar mark in relation to goods or services, priority date shall be determined according to principles established under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, a trade mark shall be defined as a mark capable of being represented graphically and which is used or proposed to be used, in connection with goods or services to identify them as those of a particular undertaking. Such marks may include words, names, symbols, numerals, shapes, configurations, patterns, monograms, letters, signatures, domain names, colour arrangements, or any combination thereof. A trade mark shall not extend to geographical indications signifying the origin of goods unless such indication is used in accordance with conditions as provided herein and does not falsely represent the product's qualities. The Registrar may require proof of use of a proposed trade mark under this Act.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed refused if the proposed trade mark, when used in relation to the goods or services for which it is sought to be registered, conflicts with any existing prior right. Such conflict may arise from similarity to an earlier trade mark, whether registered or not, and where such earlier trade mark is used in connection with identical or similar goods or services. The Registrar shall consider evidence presented by the applicant demonstrating that there exists no likelihood of confusion on account of a phonetic or visual resemblance between the applied-for trade mark and any prior right. Provided that, an application may proceed notwithstanding such conflict if the Registrar deems the earlier right to be weak or inactive under this Act.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark shall be entitled, subject to any rights acquired prior to registration as provided herein, to restrain the use in India of any trade mark which is identical or deceptively similar to the registered trade mark in relation to goods or services for which the trade mark is registered. Such restraint may include an injunction preventing the adoption of a confusingly similar trade mark and an order requiring the erasure of all marks bearing the infringing sign from packaging, advertising material, and business premises. Further, where damage has been proven as a direct result of the infringement, the proprietor shall be entitled to claim damages proportionate to the loss suffered; provided that wilful infringement may attract enhanced penalties as determined by the relevant adjudicating authority. The remedies available under this Act are without prejudice to any other right or remedy available to the registered proprietor in law.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed to be refused if, upon examination, it appears that the proposed trade mark is descriptive of the goods or services with which it seeks association. The Registrar may, however, accept such an application if the applicant demonstrates acquired distinctiveness through extensive use and consumer recognition prior to the date of the application. Evidence presented in support of this demonstration shall include market research data, sales figures, and advertising expenditure relating directly to the trade mark's usage. Any person aggrieved by a refusal order may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of that order. The Board’s decision is final subject to further appeal under this Act. Consideration shall be given to whether the use has created an appreciable association in the minds of consumers.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be refused if, upon examination, it contains any disclaimers required by this Act. Such refusal may be reviewed by the relevant Intellectual Property Office tribunal upon written submission from the applicant demonstrating compliance with all prescribed procedural requirements and providing evidence substantiating the distinctiveness of the proposed trade mark in relation to the specified goods or services. The Registrar shall consider whether use of the trade mark, as presented in the application, would create confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of those goods or services. Any representation made within an application that proves false under oath may render the applicant liable for penalties as provided herein.

Any individual or enterprise employing a registered trade mark in relation to goods or services, without authorization from the proprietor thereof, shall be liable for damages as determined by the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. Such damages may include compensation for loss of profits sustained by the proprietor and any other incidental damage resulting from the infringing use. Further, where an infringement is established, the Court may order the apprehension of the infringing goods and materials of any kind used in making such goods, and their destruction as provided herein. The proprietor shall have the right to apply to a civil court for injunction restraining further acts of infringement, subject to demonstrating reasonable prospects of success.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark shall be entitled to grant licenses conferring rights to use the trade mark for specific goods or services, subject to conditions stipulated in the license agreement. Such agreements may include restrictions on geographical territory, duration of usage, and quality control measures relating to the licensed products or services. Assignment of a trade mark, or any part thereof, requires execution of a formal instrument verified before a notary public, and registration of such assignment with the Trade Marks Registry as provided herein. A licensee may further assign their rights under the license agreement, but only with prior written consent from the registered proprietor, unless otherwise expressly permitted within the original licensing terms. Any unauthorized use or reproduction of a trade mark without proper authorization constitutes an infringement, actionable under this Act.

The Registrar may, upon receiving an objection under this Act from any interested party to the registration of a proposed trade mark, direct the applicant to submit further particulars regarding the goods or services in relation to which the trade mark is sought. Such direction shall be accompanied by a statement outlining the grounds for the objection and the specific information required. The applicant may then file a written response addressing each point raised within thirty days of the receipt of the Registrar’s direction, failing which the application shall stand rejected. Any party aggrieved by such rejection or by any decision made under this Act concerning the similarity of trade marks may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark includes a representation that the applicant is the proprietor of the trade mark by virtue of being a director of a company, the Registrar shall require the applicant to furnish satisfactory evidence confirming such directorship. Such evidence must include a certified copy of the certificate of incorporation and any subsequent resolutions relating to the appointment or change in status of the director. The Registrar may, at his discretion, request further documentation substantiating the authority of the director to act on behalf of the company concerning trade mark matters. Failure to provide such evidence within the stipulated timeframe shall render the application liable for rejection under this Act, provided that a written explanation for the delay is not submitted and deemed acceptable by the Registrar.
