The owner of a registered trade mark shall, subject to any conditions specified in the registration certificate, be entitled to grant licenses conferring specific rights relating to the use of the trademark for goods or services as defined therein. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive and shall clearly delineate the geographical territory covered by the permitted usage. Assignment of a trade mark, including all associated goodwill and unregistered trade marks used in connection therewith, requires execution of a formal instrument witnessed as per prescribed procedures under this Act. Any subsequent transfer or sub-licensing must adhere to similar formalities, ensuring transparency regarding the original grant’s scope and limitations. Provided that, where an unregistered trade mark has been consistently employed prior to registration, any license granted shall not prejudice existing rights acquired through such prior use by third parties.

Where an objection is raised under this Act against the registration of a proposed trade mark, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to file a written response addressing the grounds for said objection. Should the Registrar uphold the objection following consideration of the applicant’s reply, the applicant may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The Board shall hear appeals and may allow or dismiss them, as it deems fit, providing reasons in writing. Any party aggrieved by an order passed by the Board may further seek redressal through a petition under appropriate law. It is provided that any appeal must specify the grounds upon which it is based and demonstrate prejudice arising from the decision sought appealed.

For the purposes of this Act, a “trade mark” shall mean a mark capable of being represented graphically and which is used or proposed to be used, in relation to goods or services, including sounds, smells, tastes or any combination thereof, for the purpose of distinguishing the goods or services of one undertaking from those of others. Such marks may include words, names, symbols, devices, letters, numerals, shapes, configurations, patterns, or combinations thereof. The owner of a registered trade mark shall be liable to pay a copyright society fee as determined by the central government, provided that such fee is proportionate to the usage and commercial exploitation of the mark under this Act.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed complete upon submission of the prescribed form, accompanied by the requisite fee and representation of the mark. The Trade Marks Registry may, at any time prior to acceptance, require the applicant to amend the description of goods or services associated with the trade mark to conform to the International Classification of Goods and Services. Where an application relates to a design, the design registry shall maintain a record of such applications separate from other trade mark filings. The Registrar may refuse registration if he considers that the proposed trade mark is generic for the goods or services indicated, or conflicts with any existing rights as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, a mark shall be deemed to lack distinctive character if, by its very nature, it directly signifies the common name or characteristics of goods or services with which it associates. This determination shall consider whether the sign functions solely to describe those qualities and does not indicate origin. However, a mark that initially lacks distinctiveness may acquire such character through consistent use over time, provided that such use has resulted in the relevant consuming public perceiving the mark as an indication of origin rather than merely descriptive information. The limitations on registrability under this Act apply equally irrespective of whether the mark is inherently distinctive or subsequently acquires distinctiveness.

The Registrar may, upon application by any proprietor of a registered trade mark, extend the period of registration thereof for further periods of ten years each, subject to payment of the prescribed fees. Such extension shall be granted only if the applicant demonstrates continued use of the trade mark in relation to the goods or services specified in the register during the immediately preceding five-year period. However, this requirement is not applicable where the non-use can be attributed directly to actions taken by a third party without the proprietor’s consent. The limitations on extending registration apply equally if the applicant has entered into a licensing agreement affecting the mark's use, as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, the registered proprietor of a trade mark shall be entitled to restrain the use of any representation in relation to goods or services which is identical or confusingly similar to the said trade mark, provided that such use constitutes infringement under this Act. However, no remedy shall be granted where the alleged infringing use falls within specifically permitted limitations relating to descriptive use for indicating the character or quality of goods, or for honest comparison of goods with those of another. Further, a proprietor may not enforce their rights in relation to a trade mark if they have acquiesced in the defendant’s conduct, or if the defendant had prior knowledge and reasonable grounds to believe that the use was permissible under this Act. Any order restraining such use shall be subject to equitable considerations.

The Registrar may, upon application by any interested party demonstrating substantial and ongoing disuse of a registered trade mark for a period exceeding three years immediately preceding the date of such application, grant leave to another person to utilize a confusingly similar sign in relation to goods or services not identical with those for which the trade mark is registered. Such permission shall be conditional upon the applicant proving that the continued registration of the original trade mark impedes their own legitimate commercial activities and that any resulting consumer confusion will be demonstrably minimal. The Registrar may impose such limitations on the permitted use as are deemed necessary to protect the distinctiveness of the earlier trade mark, provided that these limitations do not render the authorized use commercially unviable.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark shall be liable for penalties under this Act if, despite reasonable efforts to prevent it, the use of an identical or deceptively similar sign in relation to identical or similar goods or services creates confusion among the public. This liability shall extend to instances where such use is undertaken by a party lacking consent and demonstrably exploits the reputation associated with the registered trade mark. However, limitations on enforcement may arise if the infringing use falls within the scope of fair dealing for purposes of criticism or review, provided that such use is accompanied by an acknowledgement of the source and does not prejudice the distinctive character or repute of the trade mark as provided herein. Any wilful infringement shall attract enhanced penalties.

Where the proprietor of a registered trade mark desires to permit the use of their mark by another party for specific goods or services, they may grant a license under this Act. Such licenses shall be in writing and clearly define the scope of permitted usage, including geographical limitations and duration. The licensee shall be deemed a limited user of the trade mark and subject to the terms stipulated within the licensing agreement. Assignment of such licenses is permissible, provided that the assignee adheres to all conditions originally set forth by the proprietor. Any alteration to the goods or services for which the license applies requires prior written consent from the original proprietor. This provision recognizes limitations on proprietary rights where a trade mark has been licensed and assigned, ensuring continued protection for the registered owner while facilitating commercial flexibility.

The Registrar shall, upon receiving an objection under this Act from any interested party regarding the registration of a proposed trade mark, afford the applicant an opportunity to present arguments in support thereof. Such objections may be predicated on grounds that the mark lacks distinctiveness, is descriptive of the goods or services with which it seeks association, or otherwise infringes existing rights. The Registrar’s decision shall be final subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within a period of sixty days from the date of such order. It is provided that any party aggrieved by an appellate board determination may further appeal to the High Court, asserting limitations on the scope of permissible challenges based solely on prior unregistered use.

Notwithstanding anything contained herein, registration of a trade mark encompassing or comprising a representation of genetic material, including but not limited to sequences catalogued within a national gene fund sub-registry, shall be subject to limitations where such representation demonstrably describes a naturally occurring biological process. An appeal against refusal of registration based on this provision may be made to the relevant intellectual property appellate tribunal, and the burden of proving that the representation lacks inventive character or is purely descriptive of said natural process shall lie upon the applicant. The tribunal shall consider evidence presented by both the Registrar and any interested party demonstrating potential confusion arising from such registration, provided that a claim of prior use may be asserted under this Act.

Notwithstanding anything contained herein, a registered trade mark shall be subject to limitations regarding its exclusive right to prevent the use of a sign by any person where such use occurs in relation to goods or services not identical with those for which the registration is made and does not create confusion among the public. This limitation applies even if the registry fee paid upon initial application was substantial, provided that the subsequent use falls within the scope of fair dealing as determined under this Act. The Registrar may, at the request of an interested party, review such a determination concerning limitations based on evidence presented demonstrating actual consumer deception or likelihood thereof.

The proprietor of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to restrain the use of any sign which is identical or confusingly similar to the said mark in relation to goods or services for which it is registered, provided that this right shall be subject to limitations where the alleged infringing use occurs incidentally through the indication of the geographical origin of goods. Such incidental use may be permitted if it accurately describes the place of manufacture and does not falsely suggest any connection with the proprietor. Further, a specification of goods or services in a trade mark registration shall be construed strictly against the applicant; any ambiguity arising from the wording will be resolved in favour of limiting the scope of protection afforded to the registered mark. Any party aggrieved may seek remedies under this Act for infringement.

Where any trade mark is found to be identical to a prior registered trade mark in respect of identical or similar goods or services, such registration shall be deemed invalid upon application by an aggrieved party. Any person claiming damage as a result of the registration of a trade mark identical to their own existing right may institute civil proceedings for recovery of damages, including loss of profits and costs incurred in challenging the infringing registration. The Registrar may, sua sponte or upon complaint, order rectification of the register removing such offending entry. Failure to comply with an order under this Act shall render the defaulting party liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakhs rupees, recoverable as arrears of land revenue, without prejudice to any other remedy available under this Act.

Where the owner of a registered trade mark grants a license permitting the use of their mark, such license may be assigned to any person, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated in the original agreement. Provided that, where a licensed user subsequently seeks to register a trade mark identical to the registered mark for goods or services similar to those for which the registration is already subsisting, the application shall be refused if it is established that such registration would likely cause confusion amongst consumers. Further, any assignment of a license under this Act shall require notification to the Registrar within thirty days of the transfer, detailing both the assignor and assignee. The Registrar may request further documentation as deemed necessary to verify the validity of the assignment. This provision applies irrespective of whether the original trade mark registration was obtained prior to or subsequent to the granting of the initial license.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark shall furnish with the application a representation of the marks applied for, clearly indicating the features of the mark; provided that where the mark comprises three colours any one of which is not distinctive, the applicant shall submit a statement explaining why each colour is necessary to identify the goods or services. The Registrar may, at any time during the examination of an application, require the applicant to amend the representation if it is deficient in clarity or does not accurately reflect the trade mark as proposed for registration. Failure to comply with such requirement within the prescribed period shall render the application liable to rejection. Further, the Registrar india registrar require applicants to submit certified true copies of prior registrations where use has been claimed under this Act.

Where a trade mark is opposed under this Act, and the grounds of opposition relate solely to acquired distinctiveness within India, the Registrar shall provide the applicant with an opportunity to file a written response addressing each ground raised by the opponent. Should the opponent fail to substantiate any ground of opposition with documentary evidence or other credible proof as determined by the Registrar, the Registrar may direct that such unsubstantiated ground be disregarded for the purposes of determining the merits of the opposition. Furthermore, in instances where an opponent resides outside India and fails to comply with a direction issued under this Act regarding the filing of documents or attendance at hearings, the india registrar require them to furnish security for costs within thirty days; failure to do so shall render the opposition vulnerable to dismissal.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark shall furnish with the application a certified copy of any prior registration or pending application relating to the same goods or services in any country outside India. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar may direct the applicant to amend the representation of the trade mark if it is deemed unclear or improperly rendered for examination purposes. The Registrar shall provide the applicant with a reasoned explanation for such direction and allow a period of thirty days for compliance. Failure to comply with this direction within the stipulated timeframe will result in the application being deemed withdrawn. Further, where an objection is raised under this Act concerning similarity to an earlier trade mark, the India registrar require that the applicant submit evidence demonstrating distinctiveness or acquired reputation sufficient to overcome said objection.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark shall furnish with the application a verified statement attesting to the exclusive use of the proposed trade mark in relation to the goods or services specified in the application, provided that such verification is supported by documentary evidence acceptable to the Registrar. The Registrar may, at any time and without assigning reasons, require the applicant to provide further documentation substantiating the claim of exclusive use, including but not limited to affidavits from distributors, sales records, and advertising materials. Failure to comply with such a requirement within the period specified by the Registrar shall render the application liable for rejection under this Act. The India registrar require adherence to these evidentiary standards to ensure transparency in trade mark registration proceedings.

Where a trade mark owner desires to grant a license conferring exclusive rights relating to specific goods or services associated with a registered trade mark, such license shall be recorded with the Registrar prior to its operation. The recording shall include details of the licensed territory and the duration of the license. Further, any assignment of a registered trade mark, or of the benefit of any application for registration, including assignments incorporating licenses, must also be formally documented with the Registrar. The India registrar require that such documentation clearly identifies both the assignor and assignee, along with a precise description of the rights being transferred. Provided that, where an assignment includes a continuing security interest, this shall be explicitly stated in the recorded document. Failure to record these transactions as provided herein will render them unenforceable against third parties.

Where an objection is raised against the registration of a proposed trade mark under this Act, the applicant shall have the right to file a reply within sixty days from the date of service of the notice of objection. The Registrar shall consider both the objection and the reply before proceeding further; provided that if the applicant fails to submit a satisfactory reply within the stipulated period, the Registrar may proceed ex parte and determine the matter based solely on the grounds articulated in the objection. Furthermore, any party aggrieved by an order passed by the Registrar concerning the acceptance or rejection of a trade mark application may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board; however, the India registrar require that such appeals be accompanied by a security deposit commensurate with the potential damages claimed, as determined by the Board.

For the purposes of this Act, “basic registration” shall mean the initial entry of a mark onto the Register of Trade Marks, signifying its protection under this Act. A basic registration confers upon the proprietor exclusive rights to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered, subject to any prior conflicting rights as provided herein. An application for basic registration must include a representation of the trade mark and a list of goods or services with which the mark is associated. The Registrar may refuse a basic registration if the mark lacks distinctiveness or is otherwise objectionable under this Act.

An applicant shall file an application for basic registration of a trade mark with the Registrar in such form as may be prescribed, specifying goods or services, classified according to the International Classification of Goods and Services for the Purposes of the Registration of Marks, in respect of which he seeks to register the trade mark. The application shall include a representation of the trade mark as applied for, and where it comprises a device, a description of the colours used therein. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further particulars or amend the application to conform to the requirements of this Act. Basic registration confers upon the proprietor the exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services specified at the time of registration throughout India.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark shall have the exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered, and any other person shall be prohibited from using a sign identical or confusingly similar to the said trade mark in connection with such goods or services. Any party infringing upon this exclusive right may institute legal proceedings under this Act seeking an injunction restraining the infringing use, as well as damages commensurate with the loss suffered by the proprietor due to the infringement. The grant of basic registration shall not prejudice any rights in a trade mark previously used by another person; however, such prior use does not constitute grounds for revocation of the registered trade mark. Provided that the Registrar may order correction of errors or omissions appearing on the register relating to a basic registration.

An applicant seeking basic registration of a trade mark shall file an application with the Registrar in such form as may be prescribed. The application must specify the trade marks proposed to be registered and clearly state the goods or services, or both, in relation to which the trade mark is to be used. Where the applicant is not residing in India, he shall appoint an agent resident in India to act on his behalf under this Act. The Registrar may require such further information as he deems necessary for the proper examination of the application and determination of its merits. Any representation accompanying the application must conform to the guidelines issued by the Trade Marks Registry. An applicant is deemed to have notice of any prior conflicting trade mark registrations upon filing, subject to a search conducted under this Act.

An applicant seeking basic registration of a trade mark shall submit an application to the Registrar in the prescribed form, accompanied by the requisite fee. The application must specify the goods or services with which the trade mark is associated, classified according to the International Schedule of Classes of Goods and Services. Provided that, if the applicant desires to include colour as a feature of the mark, such indication shall be clearly stated within the application, along with a representation thereof. Further, the Registrar may reject an application if he has reason to believe that the proposed trade mark is descriptive of the goods or services, or conflicts with existing rights under this Act. The applicant must demonstrate distinctiveness and non-deceptiveness as provided herein.

Any proprietor seeking basic registration of a trade mark shall file an application with the Registrar in the prescribed form and manner, providing details including but not limited to the representation of the mark, goods or services associated therewith, and the applicant’s address for service. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in rejection of the application. Where any person believes that registration has been improperly granted, they may institute proceedings under this Act seeking rectification of the register, subject to demonstrating demonstrable prejudice arising from the continued validity of said registration. The Registrar shall have power to impose a penalty where an applicant makes a false statement material to the grant of basic registration.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark shall be entitled to grant licenses conferring rights to use the mark for specific goods or services, subject to any limitations stipulated within the license agreement and consistent with the integrity of the basic registration. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as determined by the proprietor, and may include provisions relating to quality control and territory restrictions. Assignment of a trade mark, including all associated rights and obligations arising from its basic registration, is permissible through a written instrument executed by the registered proprietor and duly notified to the Registrar. Any subsequent licensee shall be bound by the terms of the original license agreement and any amendments thereto, provided that such amendments do not prejudice the interests of third parties who have acquired rights under the trade mark. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating the validity and scope of any assignment or license granted as provided herein.

Where any person desires to obtain registration of a trade mark under this Act, he shall make an application for basic registration in the prescribed form, accompanied by the requisite fee. Such application shall specify the goods or services with which the trade mark is associated and claim priority from a prior application made in a convention country, provided that the applicant satisfies the Registrar that the said prior application is still in force. The Registrar may require further evidence to establish the validity of such claim and may reject it if he deems the foreign application not genuinely intended to secure the rights claimed. Any aggrieved party disputing the acceptance of an application for basic registration may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within a period of sixty days from the date of receipt of the order.

An applicant seeking basic registration of a trade mark shall furnish particulars relating to the goods or services with which the mark is associated, classifying them according to the International Classification of Goods and Services. Where the trade mark incorporates or comprises a new variety of plant, the application must include a declaration affirming that the applicant possesses the necessary breeding certificate issued by an authorized body as per established guidelines. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating this claim, including details regarding propagation methods and genetic stability. Any alteration to the goods or services listed shall be subject to approval under this Act, ensuring continued compliance with classification standards. Failure to provide accurate information at the time of application may render the registration vulnerable to cancellation.

Any proprietor seeking basic registration of a trade mark shall file an application with the Trade Marks Registry, accompanied by the prescribed fee. Failure to comply with the requirements for filing, including providing accurate representations regarding prior use or confusing similarity to existing marks, renders the application liable for rejection and forfeiture of any fees paid. Where a geographical indication is claimed as part of a proposed trade mark, the Registrar may require evidence demonstrating its origin and reputation within the specified territory, subject to verification by the Geographical Indications Registry. Any person aggrieved by a decision regarding registration or refusal may appeal under this Act; however, such appeals shall be accompanied by an additional penalty proportionate to the delay in filing.

For the purposes of this Act, “Common Regulations” shall mean the rules governing the use of trade marks by authorized users within a collective mark or certification mark scheme, and these regulations shall be documented in writing and made available for public inspection at the registered office of the owners of the respective marks. Such Common Regulations may specify permitted alterations to the representation of the mark, limitations on goods or services eligible for association with the mark, and procedures for ensuring adherence to quality standards where applicable. Any deviation from these Common Regulations shall constitute an infringement under this Act, provided that such deviation is demonstrably prejudicial to the distinctiveness or reputation of the mark.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark shall furnish with the application a representation of the marks applied for, being either in colour or monochrome, and such representation shall comply with the requirements prescribed under this Act regarding clarity and faithfulness to the proposed use. Where the trade mark includes three-dimensional characteristics, photographs or other visual depictions may be submitted as an alternative to a formal drawing, provided that these accurately reflect the essential features of the mark. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish additional representations if deemed necessary for proper examination. These Common Regulations regarding representation apply equally to collective marks and certification trade marks, ensuring uniformity in registration procedures across all categories.

Where any proprietor of a registered trade mark institutes legal proceedings alleging an infringement of his rights under this Act, he shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief restraining the defendant from further infringing acts, and also to claim damages sustained by him as a direct consequence of such infringement. The measure of damages shall be determined having regard to all relevant circumstances, including but not limited to, the extent of the loss suffered by the proprietor, the profits made by the infringer attributable to the infringing activity, and any other factor deemed just and equitable by the adjudicating authority. Subject to appeal to a higher judicial forum, decisions regarding damages are final. Common Regulations governing trade mark disputes shall apply uniformly across all jurisdictions within the Union, ensuring consistent application of remedies for infringement. Provided that, in cases involving wilful infringement, enhanced damages may be awarded.

The Registrar shall maintain Common Regulations for the registration and management of collective marks, ensuring uniformity across all registrars under this Act. Any proprietor seeking to amend the regulations pertaining to their collective mark must submit a request in writing, detailing the proposed changes and providing justification for their necessity. The application shall be published in the Trade Marks Journal for a period of two months, during which any interested party may file objections with the Registrar. Objections received will be considered by the Registrar, who may require further clarification or modification of the proposed regulations. Approval of amendments is subject to ensuring they do not conflict with the provisions of this Act and that the continued use of the collective mark remains consistent with its original purpose as defined during registration. The Registrar’s decision on such matters shall be final, appealable only before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Where a trade mark is registered under this Act for goods or services of one class, the proprietor shall not, without authorization from the Controller, use such trade mark in relation to goods or services belonging to a different class unless such use complies with the Common Regulations established by the Trade Marks Registry. These Common Regulations detail permissible cross-class usage predicated upon demonstrating no likelihood of confusion amongst consumers and ensuring that the distinctiveness of the registered trade mark is not diminished. Further, any advertising material utilizing the trade mark across classes must clearly indicate the different nature of goods or services being offered, as provided herein. The Controller may require submission of market research data to ascertain consumer perception before granting authorization under these conditions.

Any proprietor utilizing a trade mark in connection with goods or services shall be subject to Common Regulations pertaining to fair competition and consumer protection, as provided herein. Failure to adhere to these regulations, including but not limited to deceptive advertising practices employing registered marks, will constitute an offense punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, and with a fine which may extend to fifty thousand rupees. Furthermore, any person found in violation of Common Regulations shall be liable to pay damages to the proprietor of the trade mark, determined by the relevant adjudicating authority. The Registrar may, suo moto or upon complaint, initiate investigations into alleged infringements under this Act and issue cease-and-desist orders as deemed necessary.

The Registrar shall maintain a register of assignments and licenses relating to registered trade marks, accessible for public inspection upon payment of prescribed fees. Any person claiming title to a trade mark by way of assignment or license under this Act may apply to the Registrar for entry of such assignment or license in the said register. Such application shall contain particulars as specified herein, including details of the assignor or licensor, assignee or licensee, and the extent of rights transferred. The Common Regulations governing licenses granted prior to the amendment of section 59 shall remain valid until their expiry or modification by mutual agreement between the parties involved; provided that such regulations do not contravene any provisions relating to fair trade practices as may be prescribed under this Act. Further, a license may be assigned subject to conditions stipulated in the original licensing agreement.

Where any proprietor of a registered trade mark alleges that any other person has contravened this Act in relation to his trade mark, such allegation shall be substantiated by evidence demonstrating reasonable grounds for belief and affording particulars of the alleged infringement. The Registrar may, upon receiving such an allegation, issue notice to the party accused of contravention, providing them opportunity to submit a written response within thirty days. Failure to respond or a response deemed unsatisfactory by the Registrar shall not preclude further proceedings under this Act. Disputes arising from interpretations of ‘use in commerce’ as applied to registered marks are subject to Common Regulations and may be referred for arbitration as provided herein. The outcome of such arbitration shall be binding, save where appeal is made within sixty days to the relevant High Court.

Where any proprietor of a trade mark institutes proceedings for infringement under this Act, the remedies available to such proprietor shall include an injunction restraining the defendant from further infringing acts and an account of profits made by the defendant as a result of the infringement, subject to just terms being awarded where the use of the trade mark was in good faith. Furthermore, damages may be awarded against the infringer, not exceeding a sum determined by the Court based on factors including the loss suffered or likely to suffer by the proprietor and any profits of the infringing party that have been unduly obtained. The application of Common Regulations regarding parallel imports shall be governed by principles of exhaustion of rights; however, patent shall assigned where such assignment is demonstrably linked to the initial trade mark registration.

The Registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for registration of a trade mark, examine whether the proposed marks conform to the requirements of this Act and the Regulations framed thereunder. Where any objection arises during examination concerning similarity between the applied-for mark and prior registered trademarks or pending applications, the Registrar may direct the applicant to submit further particulars or representations in support of their claim that the marks do not create a likelihood of confusion. Such directions shall be accompanied by a reasoned statement outlining the grounds for concern. The Common Regulations governing trade mark examination procedures are binding on all applicants and officers of the Registry. An assignee of a trade mark, having provided notice to the Registrar as prescribed herein, shall be substituted as the registered proprietor with effect from the date specified in such notice.

Where any proprietor registers index names relating to goods or services under this Act, such registration shall not preclude the use of an identical or similar index name by another person where such use is solely for descriptive purposes and does not create confusion among consumers regarding the origin or quality of those goods or services. Common Regulations pertaining to the display and arrangement of goods in retail establishments shall apply equally to proprietors of registered trade marks as they do to all other vendors, provided that any signage employed complies with guidelines issued by the Controller General under this Act. The Registrar may require submission of detailed inventories listing index names registered alongside corresponding product categories prior to renewal of registration.

The owner of a registered layout design shall be entitled to grant licenses conferring rights to use the protected design, subject to the terms stipulated within such license agreement and consistent with the principles of Common Regulations governing trade mark usage. Any assignment of ownership or licensing rights relating to a registered layout design must be executed in writing and attested by at least one witness competent to testify under this Act. Such assignments shall include details regarding the specific design, the duration of the assigned rights, and any restrictions placed upon the assignee’s use thereof. Further, an owner may create blanket licenses permitting multiple users within defined categories, provided that a comprehensive register of licensees is maintained alongside the layout design registry. The Registrar may require submission of these license agreements for inspection to ensure compliance with prevailing Common Regulations.

For the purposes of this Act, a “Contracting Party” shall mean any person who enters into a written agreement with the Registrar for the provision of services relating to trade mark registration, renewal, or opposition proceedings. Such an agreement shall clearly define the scope of services undertaken and the remuneration payable under this Act. A Contracting Party may be an individual, partnership, company, or other legal entity duly registered as per applicable law. Provided that a Contracting Party shall not include any person acting solely as an employee or agent of another party unless such employee or agent is expressly named in the agreement with the Registrar and consents to being designated as a Contracting Party.

Where an applicant seeks to register a trade mark relating to goods or services, such applicant shall furnish particulars regarding the prior use, if any, of the proposed trade mark or a mark identical therewith in relation to those goods or services. The Registrar may require the applicant to provide evidence substantiating such prior use, including documentary proof and declarations from witnesses familiar with the commercial activities involved. For the purposes of this Act, a Contracting Party intending to file an application shall be deemed to have sufficient standing irrespective of whether the mark has been previously used within India. Provided that, if the Registrar deems the submitted evidence insufficient or misleading, the application may be rejected or subject to limitations as provided herein.

Where a proprietor institutes proceedings for infringement under this Act, the court shall determine whether the defendant was a Contracting Party at the time of the alleged infringing act. For the purposes of such determination, a Contracting Party includes any individual or corporate body who has entered into a written agreement with the proprietor specifying terms and conditions governing the use of the trade mark in question. The court may consider evidence demonstrating that the defendant’s actions were undertaken pursuant to, or in reliance upon, representations made by or on behalf of the proprietor, provided that such reliance was reasonable under the circumstances. Further, any damages awarded shall be adjusted to reflect any benefit derived by the defendant from their status as a Contracting Party and subsequent breach of contractual obligations. The court may also order an account of profits obtained by the defendant attributable to the infringement.

Where any agreement relating to the use of registered trade marks is entered into between the owner of the mark and a Contracting Party, such agreement shall specify the territorial extent of the rights granted and the duration for which those rights are assigned. The Registrar may require production of a certified copy of said agreement as evidence in proceedings concerning infringement or rectification under this Act. A Contracting Party who fails to comply with the terms of an agreement relating to a trade mark shall be liable to damages, recoverable at the suit of the owner of the mark. Further, any assignment of rights granted pursuant to such an agreement must be registered within three months of its execution; failure to do so will render the assignment void against subsequent assignees. The Registrar is empowered to issue directions regarding the form and content of agreements entered into by a Contracting Party concerning trade marks.

A Contracting Party seeking to utilize a registered trade mark for promotional purposes relating to financial services shall submit a detailed proposal to the Trade Marks Registry at least thirty days prior to commencement of such promotion. This proposal must specify the exact nature of the promotional activities, including but not limited to advertising mediums and target audience demographics. The Registry may require further clarification or modification of the proposed plan if it deems that the use of the trade mark is likely to cause confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or quality of the financial services offered. Provided that the proposal complies with all applicable regulations under this Act, and does not contain any misleading or deceptive representations, approval shall be deemed automatic unless a written objection is received within fifteen days from the date of submission.

Where any infringement of a registered trade mark occurs through an act committed by a Contracting Party acting under a contract for services relating to the use or adaptation of the trade mark, the proprietor shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief against both the infringing party and the Contracting Party who facilitated such infringement. The remedy available to the proprietor may include damages proportionate to the loss suffered as a result of the infringement, taking into account any benefit accruing to the Contracting Party from the unauthorized use. Provided that the Contracting Party demonstrates reasonable diligence in ensuring compliance with this Act, liability shall be mitigated accordingly; however, wilful blindness to infringing activity will preclude such mitigation and render the Contracting Party fully liable for all resultant damages.

Where a Trade Mark owner desires to grant a license for use of their registered trade mark, such license shall be documented in writing and executed by both the Trade Mark owner and the proposed Contracting Party. The license agreement must clearly specify the goods or services relating to which the right to use is granted, the geographical territory covered by the license, and the duration of the license period. Further, it shall detail any restrictions imposed on the manner of use, including quality control measures that the Contracting Party must adhere to, as provided herein. Assignment of a trade mark license requires prior written consent from the Trade Mark owner unless the original agreement expressly permits assignment without such consent. Any subsequent transfer or encumbrance affecting the rights granted under this license shall be void unless approved by the Trade Mark owner in writing.

Where any dispute arises concerning whether a party qualifies as a Contracting Party under this Act, such determination shall be subject to appeal before the relevant Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. The Registrar’s initial assessment regarding a party's status as a Contracting Party is deemed prima facie correct and binding unless proven otherwise through substantial evidence presented during proceedings. A challenge to the designation of a Contracting Party may only be initiated within ninety days from the date of notification of registration or refusal, as provided herein. Further, any assertion that a purported Contracting Party lacks genuine commercial activity related to the trade mark shall necessitate presentation of documentary proof demonstrating such deficiency; failure to do so will result in dismissal of the appeal.

Where a Contracting Party seeks to enforce a registered trade mark against an alleged infringer who has obtained protection for a patent invention relating to goods identical or similar to those for which the trade mark is registered, the Registrar shall provide notice to the patent holder of record. Such notice shall specify the nature of the infringement allegation and detail the remedies sought by the Contracting Party. The patent holder may, within sixty days from the date of such notice, file with the Registrar a written response addressing the alleged infringement and asserting any defenses available under this Act or applicable law concerning the validity or scope of either the trade mark or the patent invention. Failure to respond within the stipulated period shall be deemed consent to the proceedings before the Registrar. The Registrar may, at its discretion, require both parties to attend a hearing to resolve disputed issues relating to the interaction between the registered trade mark and the patent invention.

A Contracting Party seeking to utilize a trade mark registered under this Act shall furnish a detailed declaration affirming compliance with all applicable regulations pertaining to goods or services associated with said mark. This declaration must specify the manufacturing processes employed and the quality control measures implemented to ensure consistency with the representations made during initial registration. The marks registry established for the purpose of maintaining records of registered trademarks may, at any time, require further documentation substantiating these claims, including but not limited to audit reports and consumer satisfaction surveys. Failure to provide such documentation within the timeframe stipulated by the Registry shall render the Contracting Party liable to penalties as provided herein.

Where a Contracting Party holds exclusive rights to a registered trade mark encompassing pharmaceutical products, such party may, by written agreement, grant a license permitting another entity to manufacture, distribute, and sell those products within a defined territorial jurisdiction. This license shall specify the duration of the permitted use and any royalty payments due to the original Contracting Party. Assignment of these licensing rights is permissible, subject to prior notification being provided to the Trade Marks Registry at least thirty days before the effective date of such assignment. Further, any sub-licensing undertaken by the licensee requires express consent from the initial Contracting Party, failing which it shall be deemed a breach of contract and actionable under this Act. The original owner retains ultimate control over quality standards for the pharmaceutical products manufactured under license.

Where any Contracting Party alleges that another party has failed to comply with the terms of a licensing agreement relating to a registered trade mark, such allegation shall be substantiated by submission of a duly completed form petition to the relevant Intellectual Property Disputes Tribunal. The petition must specify the material breach and provide documentary evidence demonstrating the existence and terms of the agreement. Subject to appeal under this Act, the Tribunal’s determination regarding the validity of the alleged breach is final. Provided that, if the Contracting Party contesting the finding presents compelling evidence indicating procedural irregularity in the form petition's preparation or submission, the Tribunal may review its initial decision. Any party aggrieved by an order made under this provision may file an appeal within sixty days.

For the purposes of this Act, a “Contracting Party” shall mean any individual, firm, company, society, association or other body corporate duly registered under the laws applicable to its place of incorporation or formation and who has entered into a written agreement with the Trade Marks Registry for the use of a registered trade mark. Such Contracting Party shall be deemed the licensee in respect of the agreed usage rights. A registered user shall not, without express written consent from the Contracting Party, engage in activities that infringe upon the scope of the license granted under this Act, as provided herein. Any dispute arising regarding the actions of a registered user shall be subject to resolution through arbitration.

For the purposes of this Act, a “Contracting State” shall mean any state which has acceded to the Multilateral Convention on the Recognition and Enforcement of Trade Marks and has notified the International Bureau that it designates India for the purpose of registration under this Act. Such designation shall confer upon trade mark owners the right to seek remedies within Indian jurisdiction relating to registered marks in the designated Contracting State, subject to any limitations expressly provided therein. The term “Contracting State” includes any territory for which a Contracting State is responsible, as may be determined by international agreement and notified under this Act.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark shall furnish with the application a declaration specifying whether the mark is being used in relation to any goods or services. Where an applicant is located in a Contracting State and claims priority from an earlier application made in that Contracting State, they must submit as evidence a certified copy of the prior application, duly authenticated by the appropriate authority within that Contracting State. The Registrar may require such further documentation as necessary to verify the authenticity of this claim and establish the date of the earlier application. This requirement applies irrespective of whether the goods or services are identical to those specified in the prior application; provided that the applicant demonstrates a genuine connection between themselves and the Contracting State, as determined under this Act.

Where any proprietor of a registered trade mark institutes proceedings for infringement under this Act in India against a person carrying on business or residing in a Contracting State, the Central Government shall, upon application by the proprietor and after due consideration of the facts presented, determine whether such person is deemed to be carrying on business or resident solely for the purpose of those proceedings. Such determination shall be binding on Indian courts unless it is demonstrated that the activities within the Contracting State are demonstrably contrived to evade the provisions of this Act. The proprietor may seek remedies available under this Act notwithstanding any finding that the alleged infringer lacks substantial commercial presence in India, provided that the infringing activity directly impacts the goodwill associated with the trade mark within India. Any order made by a court shall be communicated to the relevant authority in the Contracting State for enforcement purposes as deemed appropriate.

Where any proceeding under this Act relates to an alleged infringement occurring within the territory of a Contracting State, the Central Government shall, upon request from the Registrar, furnish all relevant documentation pertaining to the registration and use of the trade mark in question. Such documentation includes, but is not limited to, copies of registration certificates, evidence of advertising expenditures, and declarations regarding the extent of commercial operations. The Registrar may, subject to due process, serve notices and issue summonses relating to such proceedings upon parties located within the Contracting State through diplomatic channels or other internationally recognised methods as determined by the Central Government. Any order made under this Act concerning a trade mark infringement in a Contracting State shall be binding on all persons within that state’s jurisdiction, provided that reciprocal arrangements exist between India and the relevant Contracting State.

Where a trademark registration is sought relating to goods or services intended for supply within a Contracting State, the Registrar shall require evidence demonstrating compliance with all applicable regulatory standards prescribed by that Contracting State’s governing authority. Such evidence must be submitted in a form acceptable to the Registrar and verified by an accredited certification body recognized under this Act. Provided that the trademark owner undertakes to maintain such compliance throughout the duration of the registration, and subject to any reciprocal arrangements established between India and the Contracting State concerning enforcement mechanisms, the application shall proceed for examination. Failure to provide satisfactory evidence or a subsequent breach of regulatory standards within the Contracting State may result in rectification proceedings as provided herein.

Where any infringement of a registered trade mark occurs within the territory of a Contracting State, an aggrieved proprietor shall have the right to institute legal proceedings for remedies available under this Act, subject to compliance with the procedural laws of that Contracting State relating to service and jurisdiction. Provided that such proceedings are deemed to be in pursuit of redress for actions violating rights conferred by Indian law. Any party failing to comply with orders issued by a court or tribunal concerning trade mark infringement within a Contracting State shall be liable to pay compensatory damages, as determined by the presiding officer, not exceeding five million rupees. Furthermore, wilful and repeated contravention may attract penalties including imprisonment of up to three years.

Where the owner of a registered trade mark desires to grant a license conferring the right to use the trade mark within the territory of a Contracting State, such license shall be recorded with the Trade Marks Registry, provided that the application for recording specifies the geographical limits of such usage and the goods or services in relation to which the right is granted. Any assignment of a registered trade mark, or of any license recorded under this Act, to a person established within a Contracting State shall require prior notification to the Registrar, who may request further information regarding the assignee’s commercial activities as provided herein. The owner shall ensure that all sub-licenses are similarly documented and adhere to the terms initially stipulated in the primary licensing agreement. Failure to comply with these requirements may render the license or assignment voidable at the instance of any aggrieved party.

Where any dispute arises concerning whether a territory constitutes a Contracting State for the purposes of this Act, such determination shall be subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. The Registrar’s initial assessment regarding the territorial extent of trademark protection granted under this Act is deemed prima facie correct; however, this presumption may be challenged by any aggrieved party demonstrating demonstrable evidence to the contrary. Further, a challenge predicated on the assertion that a territory's legal framework fundamentally diverges from principles recognized as essential for maintaining reciprocal trade relations shall be entertained. The burden of proof regarding such divergence rests entirely upon the appellant and must be substantiated with documentary evidence admissible under the Evidence Act.

Where a trade mark registration subsists in India and an application for the same or a similar trade mark is filed in a Contracting State, the Registrar shall, upon receiving notification from the Trade Marks Office of that Contracting State, conduct such inquiry as he deems necessary to ascertain whether the use of the foreign trade mark has created confusion amongst consumers within the territory of India. This determination shall be made irrespective of any distinct denomination variety employed by the applicant in either jurisdiction. Provided that, if the notified application relates to goods or services identical with those for which registration is already granted in India, the Registrar may require the Indian proprietor to submit evidence demonstrating continued and substantial use of the trade mark within India.

Where a trade mark proprietor licenses the use of their registered trade mark within a Contracting State, such license shall constitute a contractual arrangement governed by Indian law, and any breach thereof may render the licensor entitled to injunctive relief under this Act. The terms governing the royalty payable for such licensed usage must be clearly stipulated in writing; failure to do so shall be deemed evidence of an intent to circumvent provisions relating to fair trade practices. Any person found to have wilfully infringed a registered trade mark, acting on behalf of or in conjunction with a Contracting State’s entity without proper authorization, shall be subject to penalties as provided herein, including but not limited to fines and damages proportionate to the extent of commercial detriment caused.

Where a dispute arises concerning the validity of a trade mark registration based on an alleged contractual obligation entered into by a party operating within a Contracting State, the Intellectual Property Appellate Board shall consider whether the form filed patent pertaining to the underlying technology demonstrably substantiates the claim that the applicant possessed the requisite intention to use the mark as at the date of application. It is provided that such determination shall not be binding if it is demonstrated that the contractual obligation was procured by misrepresentation or undue influence, and that the applicant did not reasonably foresee the potential impact on existing trade mark proprietors within India. The Board may require production of all relevant correspondence relating to the contract and the form filed patent before rendering a decision.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark shall furnish particulars regarding the goods or services with which the mark is associated, classifying them according to the International Classification of Goods and Services. Where an application relates to goods or services in respect of which a prior conflicting trade mark exists within a Contracting State, the Registrar may require the applicant to demonstrate due diligence in ascertaining the availability of the proposed mark. Failure to comply with such a requirement shall render the applicant vulnerable to appeal forfeiture; that is, any subsequent challenge to the registration based on lack of due inquiry will be deemed inadmissible. The provisions relating to geographical indications as provided herein apply equally to applications originating from a Contracting State.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, registration of a trademark confers upon the registered proprietor exclusive rights to use the trademark in relation to goods or services for which it is registered and to prevent others from using a mark that is identical or confusingly similar. Such exclusive rights extend to representation of the trademark in any form, including but not limited to its graphical depiction or textual presentation. The right to obtain relief against infringement shall be available only to a proprietor holding valid registration under this Act; however, nothing herein prevents an unregistered user from claiming common law rights where applicable and as provided herein.

Application for registration of a trade mark may be made by any person claiming to be the proprietor of the said trade mark, subject to the provisions regarding joint ownership under this Act. Where an application is filed relating to a trade mark comprising a geographical indication defining and indicating the origin of goods, the applicant shall furnish such documentary evidence as may be prescribed demonstrating use of the mark in relation to those goods within the specified territory. The Registrar may require further information or clarification from the applicant concerning their entitlement to claim exclusive rights in the proposed trade mark. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to an application for registration may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any proprietor of a registered trade mark shall possess exclusive rights to the use of the said mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered. Such exclusive right extends to preventing the use by any person of a sign identical or confusingly similar to the registered trade mark in connection with identical or similar goods or services, and also in such manner as may cause dilution of the distinctiveness of the mark. Any infringement of these exclusive rights shall render the infringing party liable for damages, including loss of profits sustained by the proprietor, and any other relief as deemed appropriate by the relevant intellectual property tribunal. Further, the proprietor may apply to restrain the defendant from continuing such infringing activity, provided that evidence of actual damage or likelihood thereof is presented.

The Registrar may, upon application made by the registered proprietor of a trademark, enter into the Register of Trade Marks a memorandum indicating that the exclusive rights conferred under this Act are subject to a license granted by him. Such license shall be recorded with particulars thereof and shall be binding on any subsequent proprietor or licensee. An objection to the entry of such memorandum may be filed within sixty days from the date of publication of the application in the Trade Marks Journal, and the Registrar shall consider any objections received before making a determination. The applicant shall provide evidence demonstrating the scope and duration of the license agreement. Provided that, where the license is non-exclusive, the Registrar may require additional undertakings to ensure continued compliance with provisions relating to honest practices in trade. Any alteration or revocation of such license requires prior notice to all interested parties as provided herein.

The proprietor of a registered trade mark shall possess exclusive rights to use the mark exclusively in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered, subject to compliance with prescribed advertising guidelines. Any person desiring to utilize a substantially identical mark relating to similar goods or services must first obtain written consent from the registered proprietor, provided that such consent is not granted unconditionally and explicitly outlines permitted usage parameters. Failure to secure prior authorization constitutes an infringement under this Act and renders the infringing party liable for damages commensurate with lost profits and demonstrable reputational harm. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint demonstrating ongoing unauthorized use, issue a cease-and-desist order pending judicial determination of exclusive rights.

The use of any trademark identical or deceptively similar to a registered trademark for goods or services identical or closely related to those specified in the registration shall constitute infringement under this Act. Any person who, without due cause, applies for registration of a trade mark that is likely to be confused with an earlier mark already on the register shall be liable to prosecution and penalties as provided herein. The exclusive rights conferred by registration are further protected against passing off actions initiated by aggrieved proprietors. Where infringement occurs, the proprietor may seek injunctions restraining the infringing activities and damages commensurate with the loss suffered, subject to limitations determined by the relevant adjudicating authority. Repeated or willful infringements shall attract enhanced penalties and potential criminal prosecution.

The owner of a registered trade mark may grant licenses conferring exclusive rights to use the mark for specific goods or services, subject to the conditions stipulated within the license agreement. Such licenses shall be in writing and may be assigned to any person or entity with the prior written consent of the original proprietor, provided that such assignment does not contravene any restrictive covenants contained within the initial licensing arrangement. Further, a license granted under this Act may include provisions relating to quality control measures for goods bearing the trade mark, ensuring consistency with the reputation associated therewith. Any attempt to assign a license without obtaining the requisite consent shall be deemed void and unenforceable against the proprietor of the registered trade mark, as provided herein. The assignee of a licensed right shall hold such rights subject to the terms governing the original grant.

The use of a sign for goods or services shall give rise to exclusive rights under this Act, subject to any conditions specified therein. Provided that, where an objection is raised by a third party challenging the validity of such exclusive rights on grounds of prior honest usage, the Trade Marks Registry may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating continuous and uninfringing application of the mark throughout the territory in question. Any aggrieved party disputing this determination may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. Further, the Tribunal shall consider whether the alleged prior usage genuinely predates registration and constitutes a reasonable expectation of continued use by the claimant, failing which the exclusive rights remain valid as provided herein.

Where an objection is raised to the registration of a proposed trademark by a person claiming prior common law right relating to the use of that sign, the Registrar may require such claimant to furnish evidence establishing the extent and duration of such prior use. The applicant shall have the opportunity to file a counter-statement responding to the evidence presented. Upon consideration of both submissions, the Registrar’s decision regarding whether the proposed trademark infringes upon the existing common law right shall be final, subject to appeal under this Act. Further, where a registered breeder demonstrates that their unique breeding line is identifiable by a specific mark, they are entitled to exclusive rights concerning its commercial application and may pursue remedies against unauthorized use.

For the purposes of this Act, a “colour mark” shall be deemed to include any shade or hue applied to goods or their packaging in such a manner as to serve as an identifier and distinguish them from those of others. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating acquired distinctiveness where registration is opposed on grounds that the colour lacks inherent distinctiveness; provided that such requirement shall not apply if the applicant demonstrates widespread recognition of the colour mark through substantial use prior to application. Under this Act, any representation used as a trade mark, including a colour mark, shall be capable of being separately registered irrespective of its constituent elements, following provisions act relating to composite marks.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed to be refused if the proposed marks consist exclusively of geographical indications defining places or regions where the goods originate, subject to any indication that such origin has become generally descriptive of the goods. The Registrar may, following provisions act relating to acceptance and publication, require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating acquired distinctiveness in relation to the trade mark within a period not exceeding six months from the date of notification of the refusal. Such evidence shall include documentary proof of extensive use in commerce and consumer recognition. Provided that, where the geographical indication is protected under another Act, the Registrar may consider such protection as satisfying the evidentiary requirements, as provided herein.

Where a trade mark is registered in contravention of the provisions of this Act, any person claiming an interest which would be affected by the revocation of the registration may give notice to the Registrar requesting that the matter be referred to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board for determination. The Registrar shall, following provisions act upon receiving such notice and after affording the trade mark proprietor an opportunity of being heard, refer the matter to the Board. The Board shall determine whether the registered trade mark was indeed registered in contravention of this Act and may, if it finds that to be the case, direct the revocation of the registration. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Intellectual Property Appellate Board under this section may appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such order.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed to be refused if the Registrar considers that the proposed trade mark is descriptive of the goods or services with which it seeks association, subject to the provisions relating to acquired distinctiveness. The applicant shall have the right to appeal such refusal under this Act within sixty days from the date of communication of the refusal order. Further, where a trade mark is registered following provisions act in relation to prior use, the Registrar may require the registration proprietor to submit evidence establishing continued use of the mark for a period not exceeding five years from the date of registration. Failure to comply with such a requirement shall render the trade mark vulnerable to expungement upon application by an interested party. The Registrar’s decision on any appeal under this Act is final, provided that it is subject to review by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is refused under this Act, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to submit representations in writing addressing the grounds of refusal, provided that such representations must be filed within sixty days from the date of receipt of the refusal notice. The Registrar may, after considering the representations and any counter-submissions made by the opposing party, either uphold the initial refusal or proceed with registration subject to such modifications as deemed necessary to ensure compliance with provisions relating to descriptiveness and distinctiveness. Following provisions act where the trade mark contains a geographical indication that is protected under another Act, the Registrar shall consult with the relevant authority administering that other Act before making any decision regarding registration.

Any person who, following provisions act in contravention of this Act or any rules made thereunder, makes, uses, imports, exports, distributes, sells, offers to sell, or knowingly deals with goods or services marked with a false trade mark shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to five years and with a fine which may extend to ten lakh rupees. Where an offence involves the use of a registered trade mark in relation to goods or services identical or similar to those in respect of which the trade mark is registered, such person shall also be liable to pay damages equivalent to three times the value of the infringing goods or services sold. Repeated offences may attract enhanced penalties as determined by the adjudicating officer.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark shall be entitled to grant licenses conferring the right to use such trade mark in relation to specified goods or services, subject to any conditions stipulated therein and recorded at the time of registration. Any assignment of a trade mark, whether absolute or partial, including assignments of the benefit of application for registration, shall require prior written consent from the Controller, provided that such consent may be withheld only on grounds demonstrably prejudicial to consumer interest or fair competition. Where a license is granted under this Act, the licensee shall be deemed an agent of the registered proprietor and bound by their obligations relating to the trade mark’s use. Following provisions act in accordance with principles of good faith and transparency, ensuring that sub-licensees are fully informed of any limitations or restrictions imposed on the primary license agreement.

Where an appeal is made under this Act against a decision of the Registrar refusing registration of a trade mark, or revoking it, the Appellate Board shall admit such appeal within sixty days from the date of communication of the order to the appellant, provided that the Registrar may extend this period where satisfied that there were sufficient cause preventing the timely institution of the appeal. The Board shall hear any party aggrieved by the decision of the Registrar and may, following provisions act as it deems fit, confirm, vary or reverse the said decision. Any party to the proceedings before the Appellate Board may petition for a review of its order within thirty days thereafter, subject to such conditions as are prescribed herein regarding costs and preliminary objections.

For the purposes of this Act, a “plant variety” shall mean any species or lower taxonomic rank such as cultivars and lines that is capable of reproduction through or from seed or vegetative material. The term "distinctiveness" when applied to a plant variety means that it exhibits characteristics which differentiate it from other varieties available in the public domain; provided that these characteristics are stable and heritable. A “registered breeder” shall be deemed to include any person who has been granted rights under this Act relating to a particular plant variety, or their legal representative. Following provisions act upon applications for registration where the claimed distinctiveness is demonstrably lacking, subject to appeals before an appellate tribunal as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, a “certification mark” shall apply certification to goods or services in relation to which such quality, origin, material, mode of manufacture, workmanship, or other characteristics are defined and specified under regulations framed by the Registrar; provided that such specifications shall be verifiable through inspection or testing procedures as may be prescribed. The owner of a certification mark shall not be restricted from using any trade mark distinguishing their own goods or services, notwithstanding the use of the certification mark. Any representation used in connection with a certification mark shall conform to the standards established under this Act and shall accurately reflect the characteristics certified.

An application for registration of a certification trade mark shall be made to the Registrar in the prescribed form and shall contain such particulars as are required under this Act. The applicant shall specify the goods or services in relation to which the certificate relates, and indicate clearly the conditions and standards that must be met by those goods or services to qualify for certification. Registration of a certification trade mark shall not prejudice any right acquired under this Act prior to the date of such registration. Further, an owner of a registered certification trade mark may require any person using or proposing to use a sign identical or deceptively similar to the certified mark to furnish evidence demonstrating compliance with the prescribed standards. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint, investigate whether the conditions are being adhered to and shall apply certification as provided herein.

Where a registered trade mark is used in connection with goods or services that are certified by an organization authorized under this Act, the owner of the trade mark shall be liable for damages sustained by any person who has been misled as to the quality, origin, or characteristics of those goods or services. Such liability may extend to consequential losses directly attributable to the misleading use, provided that the claimant demonstrates reasonable reliance on the certification mark and quantifiable harm resulting therefrom. The organization issuing the certification shall also be deemed jointly responsible for such damages if it fails to adequately monitor adherence to the standards underlying the certification scheme. Any action brought under this provision shall be subject to a limitation period of three years from the date of discovery of the misleading use, as provided herein. This right shall apply certification and does not preclude other remedies available under this Act.

The Registrar shall apply certification marks in accordance with the provisions herein relating to registration, subject to the conditions stipulated by the relevant standards body. Any applicant seeking registration of a certification mark must demonstrate that they have entered into a legally binding agreement with the designated standards body, outlining their responsibilities and obligations regarding adherence to established quality benchmarks. The Registrar may require periodic audits to verify continued compliance with these benchmarks; failure to provide satisfactory evidence of such compliance shall render the certification mark liable for cancellation under this Act. Further, any use of the certification mark by a licensee must be demonstrably consistent with the specifications detailed in the agreement and approved by the standards body as provided herein.

Where an objection is raised to the registration of a certification trade mark alleging that it conflicts with any prior right or is otherwise deceptive, the Registrar shall provide the applicant with a reasoned opportunity for rebuttal and may require submission of documentary evidence substantiating the conformity of goods or services certified under the mark to prescribed standards. Any party aggrieved by such determination may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The Board’s decision shall be final, subject to further appeal to the appellate court as provided herein. It is clarified that this process shall apply certification trade marks irrespective of whether they incorporate a geographical indication or other protected designation.
