The Controller may, subject to satisfaction that the applicant has diligently pursued the patent and suffered no prejudice to any interested party as a consequence of the lapse, grant a restoration patent for the unexpired term remaining at the date of application. Any person aggrieved by an order granting or refusing a restoration patent may appeal under this Act. Failure to comply with procedural requirements shall render the application liable for dismissal without further notice.

Where a patent has lapsed due to non-compliance with any provision relating to post-grant opposition under this Act, and the applicant for restoration demonstrates that the grounds for such opposition were demonstrably unfounded or based on misinformation not readily available during the original examination process, the Controller may grant a restoration patent. Such restoration shall revive the patent as if it had never lapsed, subject to the condition that the patentee provides assurance of adequate compensation to any party who demonstrated reasonable cause for the initial opposition. This compensation shall be determined by an arbitration panel appointed under this Act and may include royalties payable on future sales derived from the patented invention. The assignment or licensing of rights pertaining to a restored patent shall be governed by the same principles as apply to original patents, provided that existing license agreements are subject to review for fairness concerning the aggrieved party.

Where a patent has lapsed due to non-compliance with any provision relating to post-grant opposition under this Act, an application for restoration may be made to the Controller within six months from the date on which the order revoking the patent became final. Such application shall state the grounds upon which the applicant contends that the decision against him was erroneous and warrants reconsideration. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish such evidence as he deems necessary to substantiate these claims, and shall provide the opponent with an opportunity to file a counter-affidavit. Any order granting or refusing a restoration patent is subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, provided that the appellant demonstrates demonstrable prejudice resulting from the initial decision.

An application for a restoration patent may be made to the Controller within six months from the date on which the patent ceased to have effect; provided that the applicant shall satisfy the Controller that there were reasonable grounds for failing to pay the renewal fee and that the invention is still in respect of which the patent was granted continues to be in use or has been prepared for use. The application shall include a statement setting out the circumstances giving rise to the failure to pay the renewal fee, along with supporting documentation as may be required by the Controller. Upon receiving such an application, the Controller shall give notice thereof to any person who publishes or requests to be heard under this Act. Any registration copyright society claiming interest in the invention may also submit objections. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish further information and conduct hearings before deciding on the restoration patent request.

Where a patent has lapsed due to non-compliance with any provision relating to post-grant opposition under this Act, an application for restoration may be made to the Controller within six months from the date on which the said decision became final. Such application shall state the grounds upon which the applicant relies to demonstrate sufficient cause for the revival of the patent and shall be accompanied by the prescribed fee. The Controller may grant a restoration patent if satisfied that the failure to comply was unintentional, or attributable to circumstances beyond the reasonable control of the patentee; provided that any copy translation work undertaken during the period of lapse shall not be considered as grounds against restoration. The applicant must also demonstrate continued novelty and inventive step as required under this Act.

Application for registration of a proposed trade mark may be made in the prescribed form and manner, subject to fulfilling all requirements as provided herein. Upon receipt of an application, the Trade Marks Registry shall examine whether the mark is distinctive within the meaning of this Act and capable of distinguishing the goods or services of the applicant from those of others. If any objection arises during examination, notice thereof shall be given to the applicant who may submit his response. Following consideration of such response, the Registrar may proceed with registration or reject the application. Further, proceedings prosecution shall continue notwithstanding any challenge raised by a third party regarding the similarity of the mark to an earlier trade mark already registered.

Where a registered trademark proprietor institutes proceedings against any person alleging infringement under this Act, and the defendant asserts as a defense that the mark has been used in relation to identical or similar goods by another person without consent prior to the date of application for registration, the Registrar may be called upon to determine the extent and validity of such prior use. The Registrar shall, after giving notice to all parties concerned and affording them an opportunity to be heard, make a finding as to whether the alleged prior use constitutes a relevant earlier mark. Further, any party aggrieved by the decision of the Registrar concerning the priority date may appeal to the Appellate Board. It is provided that proceedings prosecution shall continue before the civil court notwithstanding any such determination made by the Registrar or order passed by the Appellate Board, subject to the outcome of any subsequent judicial review.

Where an appeal arises from any order passed by the Registrar under this Act, the Appellate Board may, at any stage of the proceedings, require the appellant or respondent to produce additional documents or evidence as it deems necessary for a proper determination of the matter. The Board shall give each party reasonable opportunity to inspect such documents and cross-examine witnesses presented. Any party aggrieved by an order made by the Appellate Board may further appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of communication of the order, and such appeal shall be on grounds specified in the Act. In proceedings prosecution shall be stayed pending determination of the appeal unless the appellate court otherwise directs. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all evidence adduced before the Appellate Board and make it available for inspection by any party to the appeal upon payment of prescribed fees.

Where an application for rectification of a registered trademark is filed under this Act, and the applicant alleges non-use of the mark by the proprietor, proceedings prosecution shall be stayed pending determination of the issue of use. Provided that the Registrar may, upon review of the circumstances, direct the continuation of such proceedings if it appears that undue delay or prejudice to other interested parties would result from a stay. The application for rectification must specify the period during which the mark has not been used and provide evidence supporting this claim. Further, the proprietor shall be afforded an opportunity to demonstrate continued use of the trademark through advertising, sales, or licensing agreements. Failure to adequately respond may impact the outcome as provided herein.

Where an appeal lies under this Act against any order passed by the Registrar refusing to accept an application for registration of a trade mark, or revoking a registered trade mark, the appellate authority may, subject to such conditions as it deems fit, direct that the proceedings prosecution shall be continued before the Registrar. Provided that if the appellant fails to comply with the directions of the appellate authority regarding security or furnishing further information, the appeal shall stand dismissed. The Registrar shall then resume the original proceeding and make a fresh determination based on the record and any additional evidence considered by the appellate authority. Any party aggrieved by such fresh determination may prefer further appeals as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, "fair use" with respect to a registered trade mark shall exempt person from liability for infringement where such use is solely for the purpose of criticism or review and is accompanied by a reproduction of sufficient portions of the original work as are necessary for affording due understanding of the fair use being claimed. Provided that, such exemption shall not extend to uses which create a likelihood of confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or endorsement of goods or services. Further, any person claiming exemption under this Act must provide evidence demonstrating the transformative nature of their use and its non-commercial character, as provided herein.

An application for registration of a trade mark may include a representation of any goods or services which the applicant seeks to associate with the trade mark, and where such representation incorporates elements that are commonly used in advertising or promotional materials, the Registrar may require submission of supplementary documentation detailing the origin and intended use of those elements. Provided that the applicant demonstrates due diligence in ascertaining the veracity of claims made within said documentation, the Registrar shall exempt person from liability for unintentional misrepresentation contained therein, subject to a review process initiated by any interested party alleging deliberate falsification. Furthermore, an appeal against such exemption may be filed before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Where an aggrieved party demonstrates that the use of a registered trade mark by another infringes upon their exclusive right to employ the same for identical or similar goods or services, and where such infringement has resulted in demonstrable dilution of distinctiveness or irreparable harm to reputation, the Registrar may order cessation of the infringing activity. Further, the Registrar shall exempt person who demonstrably relied upon the defendant’s prior use of a mark in good faith from liability for damages relating to that usage, provided that such reliance was reasonable and did not involve an intent to deceive consumers. This exemption is subject to a determination by the relevant civil court regarding the extent of permissible continued use. The aggrieved party shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief and account of profits derived from the infringing activity as provided herein.

The Registrar may, upon application made by an aggrieved party and after affording the trade mark owner an opportunity of being heard, direct that a specified geographical indication used in relation to goods, notwithstanding its similarity to an earlier registered trade mark, shall exempt person engaged solely in the production or processing of those goods within the territory traditionally associated with the geographical indication from any action for infringement under this Act. Such direction shall be subject to the condition that the applicant demonstrates continued and substantial connection between the goods and the origin indicated, and provides evidence satisfactory to the Registrar confirming adherence to established practices and quality standards specific to that geographic region. The Registrar’s decision may be appealed before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within a period of sixty days from the date of communication of the order.

Where an infringement of a registered trade mark is established under this Act, the Tribunal may order the infringer to recall all goods bearing the infringing mark from any marketplace, warehouse, or retail outlet within India. Further, the Registrar shall publish a notice of the judgment and order in the Trade Marks Journal, at the cost of the defendant. Any person who knowingly imports, distributes, or exposes for sale goods infringing a registered trade mark shall be liable to pay damages equivalent to three times the value of the infringing goods seized, subject to a minimum penalty of one hundred thousand rupees. This provision shall exempt persons acting under bonafide contract from liability where the infringement was unknowingly facilitated by a supplier.

Where the registered proprietor of a trade mark has granted an exclusive license under this Act conferring upon the licensee the right to apply for and obtain registration of a related trade mark, and where such related trade mark is subsequently registered, the proprietor shall exempt person acting solely as agents or distributors for the licensee from any liability arising from use of the related trade mark in connection with authorized distribution activities. Provided that, this exemption shall not extend to instances of wilful infringement occurring after written notice has been served upon both the proprietor and the licensee detailing the nature of such infringement. Furthermore, assignment of a registered trade mark or any right granted therein, including exclusive licenses, must be executed in the prescribed manner and duly recorded with the Registrar; failure to do so shall render the assignee’s rights unenforceable against third parties.

The Registrar may, upon application sub section, grant a non-exclusive license to utilize a registered trade mark for the purposes of research and development relating to pharmaceutical formulations, provided that the applicant demonstrates a clear public interest benefit arising from such utilization. Such license shall be granted subject to conditions as deemed appropriate by the Registrar, including limitations on commercial exploitation beyond preliminary testing phases. Further, any entity receiving such a license shall undertake to disclose all findings derived from the licensed trade mark usage in peer-reviewed scientific publications within a stipulated timeframe. The Registrar shall exempt person engaged solely in academic research and non-profit activities from payment of fees associated with obtaining this type of license. This provision does not preclude the registered proprietor’s right to pursue legal remedies against any misuse beyond the scope of the granted license.

The Registrar may, upon application by an eligible entity engaged primarily in the provision of financial services, and subject to verification of their operational scope as determined under this Act, grant a certificate of registration for a services trade mark denoting a secure payment gateway. Such registration shall be valid for a period of ten years from the date of publication and is renewable indefinitely upon fulfillment of prescribed renewal fees. The Registrar shall exempt person involved in the initial assessment process of such applications from liability regarding unintentional errors arising from reliance on publicly available data, provided that reasonable due diligence was exercised. Any challenge to this registration must be filed within ninety days of its publication, as provided herein.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act, and the applicant demonstrates that the grounds for opposition are demonstrably frivolous or vexatious, the Registrar may, subject to due process, grant summary judgment in favour of the applicant. Such a finding shall exempt person from any further proceedings relating to the specific objection deemed frivolous, without prejudice to other valid objections raised by the opponent. Further, where a form filed patent is presented as evidence supporting the distinctiveness of a trade mark, and it is established that such patent was obtained through fraudulent means or misrepresentation, the Registrar may order its exclusion from consideration. The applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to rebut this evidence before a final determination is made; provided that any costs incurred by the opponent in presenting said evidence shall be borne by them.

An application for registration of a layout design may be filed by the creator of the layout design or by any person authorized by him to make such an application. The applicant shall furnish particulars relating to the layout design, including its title and a concise description of its function. Where the layout design incorporates elements which are commonplace or readily accessible, the applicant must demonstrate that the overall arrangement constitutes original authorship. Registration shall confer upon the registered creator exclusive rights to exploit the layout design commercially for a period as provided herein. Any person seeking to utilize a registered creators layout designs without authorization may be subject to remedies available under this Act.

Where a creator establishes that the reproduction or importation for commercial purposes of a protected layout design has occurred without authorization, such creator shall be entitled to injunctive relief preventing further acts of infringement. The remedies available under this Act are without prejudice to any other remedy available to the creator in law or equity. Compensation for loss and damage sustained by the creator as a result of the infringing act may be awarded by the relevant court, taking into consideration factors including but not limited to the flagracy of the infringement and the commercial value of the creators layout designs. Any person found guilty of knowingly assisting or inducing an infringement shall also be liable for damages. The right to seek remedies accrues from the date of first commercial exploitation of the protected layout design.

An application for registration of a layout design may be filed by the creator of the layout design or by any person authorized by him in writing. The applicant shall furnish with the application a representation of the layout design in such form as the Controller may prescribe, along with a statement specifying the name and address of the creator. Where an application relates to a layout design that incorporates elements which are commonplace or readily accessible, the applicant shall submit a detailed justification demonstrating originality of the overall arrangement. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish further information or clarification regarding the layout design’s novelty and inventive step. Upon receipt of such information, the Controller shall consider whether the claimed layout design qualifies as an original creation under this Act. Any interested party may file objections to the registration of a creators layout designs within a period specified by notification in the Official Gazette.

A creator claiming protection under this Act for their layout designs shall submit detailed technical specifications alongside the application form, demonstrating adherence to established industry standards regarding circuit functionality and component placement. The Registrar may reject an application if it is determined that the submitted design incorporates elements substantially derived from previously registered layout designs or publicly available documentation without demonstrable original contribution. Furthermore, any applicant asserting novelty must provide a sworn affidavit confirming absence of prior publication or commercial use of the claimed creators layout designs anywhere in the world within the preceding twelve months. This requirement shall not apply if such prior activity was undertaken with explicit written consent from the rightful owner of the underlying intellectual property.

Any person who knowingly makes, uses, imports, or offers to sell any product containing a copied creators layout designs without the authorization of the owner shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall include compensation for loss of profits and reasonable royalty fees as determined by the relevant adjudicating officer. Further, where an infringement is established, the court may order the destruction of the infringing products and materials used in their manufacture. The owner of a creators layout designs shall have the right to apply to the civil court for an injunction restraining further acts of infringement, subject to demonstrating reasonable prospects of success. Penalties under this Act are without prejudice to any other action that may be brought against the infringer.

Where an appeal lies against a determination made under this Act regarding the originality of a creators layout designs, the Appellate Authority shall consider whether the alleged copying constitutes substantial similarity, taking into account both the overall impression and any distinctive features. The appellant shall bear the burden of demonstrating that the finding of the original determining authority was erroneous; however, the respondent may present evidence to rebut such claims. It is provided that a determination regarding infringement shall not be invalidated solely on grounds of minor procedural irregularities. Further, the Appellate Authority may order discovery of relevant documents if it deems necessary for just resolution of the dispute and subject to reasonable restrictions as prescribed by regulations.

Where an application for registration of a creators layout designs is opposed on the ground that the layout design incorporates elements derived from geographical indication goods originating in Darjeeling and falsely suggests such origin or quality, the applicant shall be required to demonstrate, through verifiable documentation, that the incorporation does not constitute misleading representation. The Registrar may, after affording the applicant an opportunity for hearing, direct the amendment of the layout designs to remove the offending elements or reject the application entirely if the applicant fails to satisfy the Registrar regarding the absence of such misrepresentation. Any party aggrieved by this decision may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of communication of the order, subject to further provisions under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, "creation provided layout" means a three-dimensional representation of an integrated circuit, embodied in a mask or master from which copies may be made, and shall include any original features of such representation relating to its shape, configuration, topography or other technological aspects. A creation provided layout is deemed to have been created at the time when it is first recorded in a tangible form, subject to the provisions regarding joint ownership as provided herein. The term "integrated circuit" includes semiconductor devices irrespective of their complexity and function, and any element or combination thereof which performs an electronic function.

An application for registration of a layout-design shall accompany a certified copy of the original documentation establishing creation provided layout, detailing the date of first manufacture of an integrated circuit embodying the design and the name and address of the person responsible for such manufacture. The Registrar may require further evidence demonstrating the originality of the layout-design, particularly where similarities exist with previously registered designs or published works. Any alteration to the layout-design after the date of first manufacture shall invalidate any subsequent claim under this Act relating to that altered design. Subject to the provisions regarding prior publication elsewhere, an applicant shall disclose all details pertaining to the development and refinement process undertaken in arriving at the final layout-design.

Where the proprietor of a layout-design establishes that another person has reproduced the integrated circuit layout-design in contravention of this Act, the aggrieved party may institute civil proceedings for redress. Such reproduction shall be deemed an infringement unless the alleged infringer proves to the satisfaction of the court that the creation provided layout was independently created without access to or knowledge of the registered layout-design. The remedies available under this Act include injunctions restraining further acts of infringement and damages, calculated as a sum equivalent to the reasonable royalty which the proprietor would have been willing to pay for the right to use the infringing layout-design, or in cases where such willingness cannot be ascertained, an amount not exceeding three times the value of the goods or services sold using the infringing layout-design. Costs incidental to such proceedings shall be determined by the court.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design may be filed with the Controller under this Act in such form and manner as the Central Government prescribes. The applicant shall furnish particulars relating to the creation provided layout, including its title, date of first commercial exploitation, if any, and the name and address of the creator. Where the application relates to a layout-design which incorporates elements previously disclosed, the applicant must provide a statement detailing such prior disclosures and their dates. The Controller may require the applicant to submit further documentation or information deemed necessary for assessing originality and novelty. Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Controller under this Act may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The Board shall dispose of such appeals expeditiously, as provided herein.

A layout-design shall be deemed to have been created if the arrangement of elements comprising such layout-design reflects the intellectual effort and skill of an individual or team in producing a unique configuration, subject to the condition that said arrangement is not substantially similar to any existing layout-design already registered under this Act. The Registrar may require submission of detailed technical specifications demonstrating the novelty of the creation provided layout, including but not limited to, descriptions of masking techniques employed and variations from prior art. Furthermore, where a layout-design incorporates elements derived from previously published sources, it shall be incumbent upon the applicant to provide documented evidence establishing independent creation of the overall arrangement. Any attempt to circumvent these requirements may render the application liable for rejection as provided herein.

Any person who, without authorization from the registered proprietor, makes, imports, sells, or offers to sell, distributes, hires or displays any product containing a layout-design infringing the copyright in such layout-design shall be deemed guilty of an offence under this Act. Such infringement includes the reproduction of the creation provided layout in whole or in part, whether temporary or permanent, and whether by means of printing, lithography, photography, electronic scanning, or otherwise. The registered proprietor may institute civil proceedings for damages sustained as a result of the infringement, subject to limitations prescribed herein regarding contributory infringement. Penalties for repeat offences shall be doubled, and any goods found infringing the layout-design are liable to seizure and destruction as provided herein.

The owner of a creation provided layout may grant licenses conferring the right to utilize the layout-design for specific purposes, including but not limited to manufacture of semiconductor devices incorporating the said layout. Such licenses shall be documented in writing and may be exclusive or non-exclusive as determined by the licensor. Assignment of ownership rights under this Act relating to a creation provided layout is permissible subject to registration with the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trademarks. Any assignment shall include details regarding the consideration paid, if any, and the scope of rights transferred. Further, where an assignment or license involves sub-licensing, the original owner retains the right to audit the utilization of the creation provided layout to ensure compliance with the terms stipulated therein, as provided herein. The Controller General may issue guidelines pertaining to standardization of licensing agreements.

Where an objection is raised to the registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design alleging lack of originality, the applicant shall submit evidence demonstrating the creation provided layout and its substantial differences from any prior published work. Such evidence may include design documentation, technical specifications, and testimony from personnel involved in the layout’s development. The Controller may require further clarification or expert assessment to determine whether the alleged differences constitute a sufficient degree of originality as required under this Act. An aggrieved party disputing the Controller's finding may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days of the order; provided that the appellate board’s decision shall be final, subject to judicial review on grounds limited to errors apparent on the record.

For the purposes of this Act, "creation provided layout" means an original three-dimensional spatial arrangement of elements forming part of a semiconductor integrated circuit, irrespective of the function or purpose of those elements. Such creation shall be deemed to exist when it is first fixed in any form and recorded in a tangible medium. The determination of originality in a creation provided layout may be subject to review under case proceeding sections where allegations of substantial similarity to an existing layout are made. This definition extends to include variations and modifications thereof, provided that such alterations do not fundamentally alter the overall spatial arrangement constituting the original creation as provided herein.

Where the Controller determines, upon receiving an objection under this Act, that a person has infringed upon the exclusive rights conferred by registration of a layout-design, or is likely to do so, he may, subject to due process and affording opportunity for hearing to all concerned parties, issue an order directing such person to cease the infringing activity. The determination of infringement shall be based on evidence demonstrating unauthorized reproduction of the registered creation provided layout. Any party aggrieved by an order issued under this provision may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. Further, where a violation of the rights conferred by registration is imminent, the Controller may, ex parte and upon such terms as he deems fit, grant temporary relief in the form of an injunction sub section restraining the infringing activity pending final determination of the matter.

Any person who knowingly makes, uses, imports, or offers to sell any product containing a layout-design infringing a registered creation provided layout shall be liable to pay damages of an amount determined by the Intellectual Property Enforcement Tribunal. Such damages may include compensation equivalent to lost profits attributable to the infringement and reasonable attorney's fees. Where multiple varieties registered under this Act are involved in the infringement, liability shall extend to each proprietor of those varieties. Further, any infringing product seized pursuant to a warrant issued under this Act shall be subject to confiscation and disposal as determined by the adjudicating officer. Repeated or flagrant violations may result in imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, without prejudice to other penalties as provided herein.

The Appellate Board constituted under this Act shall consist of a Chairperson and two other members, each possessing expertise in intellectual property law, semiconductor technology, or commercial matters. The Chairperson shall be a retired Judge of a High Court or a person holding or having held the office of a District Judge. Members may be appointed from amongst legal professionals with at least ten years’ experience practicing before courts or tribunals and engineers or scientists with substantial experience relevant to integrated circuit design. The Board shall have the power to entertain appeals arising from orders passed by the Registrar under this Act, as provided herein, and shall follow principles of natural justice in its proceedings.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be deemed refused if the Registrar considers that the design incorporates elements substantially derived from an earlier unregistered layout-design. Any applicant aggrieved by such refusal may, within sixty days from the date of communication of the order refusing registration, prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board. The appeal shall specify the orders against which the appeal is taken and the grounds on which it is based. The Appellate Board may, after giving notice to the Registrar and opportunity for them to be heard, confirm the refusal or direct the Registrar to register the layout-design subject to such modifications as the Board deems fit. Decisions of the Appellate Board are final and binding under this Act.

An aggrieved party alleging infringement of a registered semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall have the right to appeal from an order passed by the Registrar under this Act. Such appeals shall be made to the Appellate Board within sixty days of the date of communication of the order. The Board may, after giving notice to all concerned and affording them an opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify, or reverse the order appealed against. Any party dissatisfied with the decision of the Appellate Board may further appeal to the High Court within a period of ninety days from the date of such decision. The Appellate Board shall have the same powers as vested in a civil court for granting relief including injunctions and damages, subject to provisions regarding costs as provided herein.

An appeal from an order passed by the Registrar under this Act shall lie to the Appellate Board. The Appellate Board shall consist of a Chairperson and two other members appointed by the Central Government, being persons having experience in intellectual property law or technology. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Registrar may, within sixty days from the date of receipt of such order, file an appeal with the Appellate Board in the prescribed form and manner, accompanied by such fees as may be determined. The Appellate Board shall give notice to all parties concerned and hold a hearing where both sides are afforded opportunity to present their case. The decision of the Appellate Board shall be final, subject to further appeal to the High Court only on grounds specified under this Act relating to jurisdiction or other substantial questions of law.

An appeal shall lie to the Appellate Board from any order passed by the Registrar under this Act relating to the registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design, or concerning rectification of register entries. The aggrieved party may prefer an appeal within sixty days from the date of communication of the order; provided that the Board may entertain appeals filed after the expiry of such period if satisfactory reasons are tendered for the delay. Subject to compliance with prescribed procedural requirements, including payment of stipulated fees, the Appellate Board shall consider evidence submitted by both parties and issue orders as it deems fit, which shall be binding on the Registrar. The Board’s decision concerning infringement claims may also be appealed further under the provisions relating to judicial review.

Any party aggrieved by an order passed under this Act may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appellate Board shall consist of a Chairperson and two other members, each being a person having experience in intellectual property law or technology. Appeals shall be heard expeditiously, and the Board may, while hearing appeals, require parties to produce evidence or submit further information relevant to the dispute. Failure to comply with any direction issued by the Appellate Board may render a party liable for penalties as determined by the Board, not exceeding fifty thousand rupees per instance of non-compliance. The decisions of the Appellate Board are final and binding, subject to revision only by the High Court on a point of law.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, an owner of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design may grant a license to utilize such layout-design, including the right to manufacture integrated circuits incorporating it, upon terms and conditions as they deem fit. Such licenses shall be assignable, either in whole or in part, provided that any assignment is registered with the Registrar within three months of its execution. Where an owner has granted a non-exclusive license, subsequent assignments or further licensing agreements shall not prejudice the rights of existing licensees under this Act. The Appellate Board may entertain appeals against orders passed by the Registrar relating to the registration of such licenses and assignments, including disputes concerning the validity or scope of any licensed utilization. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Appellate Board may appeal to the High Court within sixty days.

An appeal lies to the Appellate Board from any order passed by the Registrar under this Act concerning the registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design. Such an appeal may be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order, provided that the Appellant shall deposit with the Board such fees as may be prescribed. The Board shall consider all relevant evidence presented by both the Appellant and the Respondent, which includes the Registrar. Decisions regarding infringement claims are also subject to review under this process. The Board’s decision shall be final, subject to further appeal only to the High Court on a limited ground of law.

An appeal from an order passed by the Registrar under this Act shall lie to the Appellate Board. The Appellate Board shall consist of a Chairperson and two other members to be appointed by the Central Government, having expertise in intellectual property law or related fields. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Registrar may, within sixty days from the date of communication of the order, file an appeal with the Appellate Board in the form specified herein. The appeal shall state the orders against which the appeal is made and the grounds on which it is based.

The Appellate Board may, while hearing appeals, require the production of any documents or evidence as it deems necessary. Any indication that a layout-design infringes another’s rights shall be considered by the board during appellate proceedings. The decision of the Appellate Board shall be final subject to further appeal to the High Court under such conditions as are provided herein.

Any party aggrieved by an order passed under this Act may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appellate Board shall consist of a Chairperson and two other members appointed by the Central Government, possessing expertise in intellectual property law or semiconductor technology. Appeals shall be heard expeditiously, and the Board may, subject to provisions relating to natural justice, dismiss frivolous appeals with costs. Failure to comply with prescribed procedures during appeal proceedings may result in dismissal. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final, but it may award compensation for demonstrable financial loss arising from an incorrect enforcement action.

An applicant seeking registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall furnish with the application a detailed description specifying all aspects of the design’s functionality and intended use. The Registrar may require further clarification regarding the nature of the invention or its relation to existing prior art. Where the layout-design incorporates elements derived from previously registered designs, an explicit declaration outlining such india relates use must be included, detailing the extent and purpose of integration. Failure to provide this information accurately shall render the application liable for rejection under this Act. The Registrar is empowered to request supplementary documentation demonstrating compliance with these disclosure requirements before proceeding with examination.

The Controller shall, upon receiving an application for compulsory license relating to a registered integrated circuit layout design, serve notice on the owner of the layout design specifying the grounds upon which the application is based and providing a period of ninety days from the date of such service within which the owner may file its response. Such response shall be considered by the Controller in determining whether the conditions for granting a compulsory license have been met as provided herein. The grant of a compulsory license under this Act shall be subject to the requirement that the application demonstrates that the use sought is primarily for the purpose of serving the public interest, and that the owner has failed to satisfy reasonable demands concerning the manufacture of integrated circuits incorporating the layout design; specifically, india relates use must be demonstrably necessary. The Controller may require further information from both the applicant and the owner during the proceedings.

The owner of an integrated circuit layout-design may grant a license conferring the right to use such design for specific purposes, subject to conditions stipulated in the licensing agreement. Such licenses shall be assignable, provided that any assignment is recorded with the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trademarks within three months of its execution. Where a licensee utilizes the licensed layout-design for manufacturing integrated circuits, they shall ensure that their use does not infringe upon any existing registered layout-designs in India. Further, the owner may assign the entire interest in a layout-design, including all rights pertaining to it under this Act, to another party; such assignment also requires registration with the Controller General. The terms of any license or assignment relating to india relates use shall be governed by contract law principles as applicable within India.

Where an allegation is made that use of a registered integrated circuit layout-design has occurred in relation to a product manufactured or imported for sale within India, such allegation shall be deemed substantiated only upon presentation of prima facie evidence demonstrating substantial similarity between the alleged infringing layout-design and the registered design. The respondent may then challenge this finding by presenting counter-evidence establishing that the use was solely incidental to the functioning of the product and did not involve reproduction or adaptation of the protected elements, as provided herein. Any appeal against a determination regarding india relates use shall lie before the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of notification of the order, subject to payment of prescribed fees.

Any person found to be engaging in commercial exploitation of a registered semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design without authorization from the registered proprietor shall be liable for damages as determined by the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. Such damages shall include compensation for loss of profits and reasonable royalties attributable to the infringing use, calculated on a basis that does not unduly burden the infringer but provides just remuneration to the owner. Where the registered proprietor is deceased or has become incapacitated, their legal representative shall be empowered to initiate proceedings under this Act and recover such damages. Further, any entity facilitating or knowingly participating in such unauthorized india relates use may face penalties as provided herein, subject to due process and opportunity for a hearing.

Where an application is filed under this Act for registration of a plant variety, the Registrar shall examine whether the applicant has furnished all information as required by the regulations framed thereunder. The registrar case shall be deemed to include any objection raised by any person regarding the novelty or distinctiveness of the plant variety claimed in the application. Further, the Registrar may require the applicant to submit additional data demonstrating genetic uniformity and stability, provided that such requirement is reasonable and proportionate to the scope of the claim. Any decision made by the Registrar concerning the acceptance or rejection of an application shall be communicated in writing to the applicant and all interested parties as prescribed.

An application for registration of a plant variety shall include particulars as prescribed, including details regarding its lineage, method of propagation, and any unique morphological characteristics. The Registrar case shall be examined to ascertain compliance with these requirements and verification of distinctness, uniformity, and stability. Should the Registrar find that an applicant has failed to disclose material information or misrepresented facts concerning the plant variety’s origin, they may direct the rejection of the application. Further, if evidence emerges after registration indicating a fraudulent misrepresentation, the Registrar shall initiate proceedings for revocation under this Act. The Board constituted by the Central Government may hear appeals against decisions made by the Registrar in relation to these matters.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Registrar relating to the grant or refusal of Plant Variety Rights, or concerning revocation proceedings, seeks redressal, such person shall have the right to appeal. The appeal shall be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order to the appellant. Upon receipt of an appeal, the Registrar case shall proceed with due diligence to examine all relevant records and submissions presented by both the appellant and any respondent party. Any technical or scientific evidence submitted must be accompanied by a certificate verifying its authenticity and methodology. The Appellate Board may, after affording parties a reasonable opportunity for hearing, affirm, modify, or reverse the order of the Registrar. Costs associated with the appeal shall be determined at the discretion of the Appellate Board as provided herein.

Where an application is filed under this Act for compulsory licensing of a plant variety, the Registrar case shall be referred to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board for determination. The applicant shall furnish with the application all relevant information regarding the nature of the invention, the working of the patented plant variety in India and the circumstances which have led to the application being made. Further, the Registrar may require the applicant to provide additional documentation substantiating claims of reasonable non-infringement or undue delay in exploitation. The Board shall give notice to the registered owner of the plant variety and afford them an opportunity to be heard. Decisions of the Intellectual Property Appellate Board are final subject to appeal under this Act.

Where an application for registration of a plant variety is deemed to be refused under this Act, the applicant shall have the right to prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order of refusal and shall state specifically the grounds on which the order is contested. The Registrar case shall then proceed with due consideration given to the points of law and fact raised in the memorandum of appeal, and all relevant documents submitted by the appellant. Further, the Registrar may require the appellant to provide additional information or clarification regarding the claimed novelty or distinctiveness of the plant variety. Provided that the Appellate Board finds merit in the appeal, it shall direct the Registrar to reconsider the application in accordance with its directions.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Registrar in relation to the registration or refusal of registration of a plant variety shall have recourse to appeal under this Act. The Registrar case shall be deemed to include decisions pertaining to infringement notices and revocation proceedings, and any failure to comply with a direction issued by the Registrar regarding reporting of unauthorized multiplication or sale of protected varieties will attract penalties as prescribed herein. Further, where an infringer fails to remit the assessed damages within thirty days of notification, the Registrar may initiate recovery proceedings through designated enforcement officers. Such officers shall be empowered to seize infringing material and impose fines not exceeding five times the value of the illegally obtained benefit, subject to judicial review.

Where a Plant Variety Protection Agreement includes provisions relating to the licensing or assignment of rights in respect of a registered plant variety, such agreement shall be deemed valid subject to compliance with the conditions prescribed under this Act. The Registrar case shall consider any challenge to the validity of such licensing terms based on allegations of undue restraint of trade or exploitation of farmers’ rights. Provided that, where an initial licensee subsequently seeks to assign their rights further, notification of such assignment must be submitted to the Registrar within thirty days, accompanied by a declaration confirming adherence to the original agreement's stipulations regarding royalty rates and benefit-sharing arrangements. Any modification to these terms requires prior approval from the Registrar, ensuring continued equitable access for farmers utilizing propagating material derived from the protected variety.

Where an application for registration of a plant variety is rejected by the Registrar, such rejection shall be accompanied by written reasons specifying the grounds upon which it is based. The applicant aggrieved by any such decision may, within sixty days from the date of receipt of the notice of rejection, prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board. Upon receiving such an appeal, the Appellate Board shall give notice to the Registrar and opportunity for both parties to present their case. It shall be open to the Registrar to submit counter-arguments and evidence in support of the original decision. The Appellate Board’s determination shall be final, subject to further appeal under this Act. A registrar case shall be handled with due regard to principles of natural justice.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, any person holding a Plant Variety Registration shall be entitled to grant licenses in respect of the registered variety, specifying the rights granted, duration, and geographical area covered by such license. Such licenses may include rights relating to propagation material, seed production, or cultivation practices associated with the plant variety. The registrar case shall involve notification of all assignments and licenses to the public through publication on the official website within thirty days of execution. Further, any application for a Plant Variety Registration made subsequent to an assignment or license agreement must disclose details of such agreements as part of the registrar application process. Provided that, no license granted shall diminish the farmers' rights guaranteed under this Act concerning the use and conservation of plant varieties.

An application for registration of a plant variety shall include particulars as prescribed, including details regarding its lineage, expression potential, and stability across diverse agro-climatic zones. Where an objection is raised by any person against the grant of registration, such objector may file a representation before the Registrar. The registrar case shall be examined in accordance with established procedures, affording both the applicant and the objector opportunities for argument and submission of evidence. Any party aggrieved by an order passed by the Registrar relating to the registration process may appeal to the court having jurisdiction, subject to limitations on time as provided herein. Further, the Registrar is empowered to request supplementary information from applicants to ensure comprehensive assessment under this Act.

An applicant seeking to register copyrights shall submit a duly completed application, accompanied by the requisite fee, detailing particulars pertaining to the work and identifying the claimant as the author, composer, proprietor, or assignee. For works generated through artificial intelligence processes, the application must explicitly state the nature of such involvement and identify any human contributors significantly involved in shaping the final form of the copyrighted material. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating ownership claims where ambiguity exists; failure to provide this information within the stipulated timeframe shall render the application liable for rejection as provided herein.

Any person claiming to be the author, owner, or assignee of copyright in a literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic work may apply to the Registrar of Copyrights for registration of such copyright. The application shall be accompanied by a statement of ownership and a copy of the work, or an abridged version thereof as the Registrar deems appropriate. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar may require further information or clarification regarding the details provided therein. An applicant seeking to register copyrights relating to cinematograph films shall also furnish a synopsis of the film’s plot. The Registrar shall publish a notification indicating that an application for registration has been received and invite objections from any person claiming an interest in the work. Subject to such objections being resolved, the copyright shall be registered as provided herein.

Any person claiming copyright in a literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic work shall be eligible to register copyrights therein under this Act. An application for registration may be made by the author, owner of the copyright, or an authorized agent acting on their behalf; provided that where the work has been published, the applicant must demonstrate ownership through assignment or license agreement duly executed and recorded. The prescribed fee shall accompany each application, and failure to remit said fee will render the application invalid. Furthermore, the applicant shall provide a certified copy of the work’s publication details, if applicable, alongside a statement confirming its originality and compliance with provisions relating to moral rights as provided herein.

Any person claiming an infringed copyright shall furnish to the designated Intellectual Property Enforcement Authority a sworn affidavit detailing the nature of the infringement, including but not limited to unauthorized reproduction, distribution, or adaptation of the copyrighted work. Failure to provide this affidavit within thirty days of discovering the alleged infringement will preclude such claimant from seeking injunctive relief under this Act. The authority may, after providing reasonable opportunity for hearing, issue an order restraining further acts of copyright violation and directing the destruction of infringing materials. Any party failing to comply with a lawful order issued by the Intellectual Property Enforcement Authority shall be liable to a fine not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees or imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or both. It is incumbent upon applicants to diligently register copyrights as provided herein.

The owner of copyright in a literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic work may grant licenses granting rights to reproduce, distribute, perform, or communicate the work to the public, subject to the terms and conditions specified therein. Such licenses shall be assignable by way of written agreement, and registration of such assignment with the Registrar of Copyrights is deemed conclusive evidence thereof against third parties. Where a copyright owner desires to register copyrights in multiple works simultaneously, a single application may be submitted, provided that each work is clearly identified and accompanied by the requisite fee for each individual registration. Any person acquiring an interest in a copyrighted work through such assignment or license shall be entitled to enforce the terms of the agreement as if they were the original copyright owner, subject to any limitations expressly stated within the licensing documentation. The Registrar may require further declarations regarding ownership and chain of title during the process of registering copyrights.

Any person claiming ownership of copyright in a literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic work may apply to register copyrights therein with the Office of the Registrar, submitting evidence satisfactory to the Registrar establishing prima facie validity of the claim. Such application shall be accompanied by the requisite fee and such particulars as are prescribed under this Act. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further documentation substantiating ownership, including deeds of assignment or testamentary instruments. An aggrieved party disputing the registration may within sixty days from the date of publication of notice thereof in the Official Gazette file an appeal with the Controller, detailing grounds for objection and submitting supporting evidence. The Controller’s decision on such appeals shall be final, subject to further judicial review under law.

Any person claiming to be the author, owner, or assignee of copyright in a literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic work may apply to register copyrights therein with the Registrar. Such application shall contain such particulars as are prescribed and shall be accompanied by the requisite fee. Where an applicant for registration is based outside India, they may designate an agent within India authorized to receive communications relating to the application under this Act. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further information or documentation deemed necessary to verify ownership and authenticity of the work. For works created abroad but subsequently imported into India, compliance with provisions of the Budapest Treaty on the Allocation of Responsibilities in Respect of Certain Deposits Made Under the Berne Convention for the Protection of Literary and Artistic Works shall be a condition precedent to registration.

For the purposes of this Act, a “layout design” means any arrangement of elements, including electrical or mechanical devices, recorded in three dimensions, intended to create an integrated circuit. The term "element" includes active and passive electronic components and interconnections. A layout design shall not include features solely for achieving artistic expression. Where an application for registration is filed, the design registry shall examine whether the layout design contains any elements that are substantially similar to a previously registered layout design or a published work. Subject to appeal under this Act, the design registry’s decision on such similarity shall be final.

An application for registration of a layout-design shall include a representation of the integrated circuit in a form specified by the regulations. The Registrar shall examine each application to ascertain whether the layout-design is original and not contrary to public order or morality. Where an applicant has failed to comply with any requirement under this Act, the Registrar may afford him an opportunity to remedy such failure within a prescribed time. If the layout-design incorporates elements already registered, the design registry shall record that fact in the register. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, prescribe the fees for various proceedings before the design registry and specify conditions relating to the examination of applications.

Where a proprietor alleges that any person has contravened section 10 or section 12 under this Act, the proprietor shall have recourse to civil remedies available under the general law. Any infringement of layout-design rights as provided herein shall entitle the proprietor to seek damages equivalent to the loss suffered by him, or where ascertainment is not possible, a sum determined reasonably and equitably. Furthermore, subject to any order made by the relevant judicial authority, the proprietor may apply for an injunction restraining the infringing party from further acts of infringement. The design registry shall maintain records of all registered layout-designs and related information accessible only to authorized personnel or upon court order. Any false representation regarding registration status constitutes a civil offense, punishable with monetary penalties as determined by the Central Government.

An application for registration of a layout-design shall be made to the design registry in the prescribed form and accompanied by the requisite fee. The applicant shall furnish such particulars relating to the layout-design as are required under this Act, including details regarding its creation and any prior disclosures. Upon receipt of an application, the design registry shall verify that it complies with the formal requirements as provided herein. If the application is found deficient in any respect, the design registry may call upon the applicant to rectify such deficiencies within a specified period. The design registry shall maintain a record of all applications received and their respective status. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the design registry relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application may appeal to the designated appellate authority as provided under this Act, subject to prescribed timelines.

An application for registration of a layout-design shall include a representation of the integrated circuit in a form specified by the regulations. The Registrar shall examine whether the layout-design is original and not substantially similar to any prior published matter; provided that such examination shall not extend to assessing the merits of the underlying technology incorporated within the design. If, upon review, the Registrar determines that the application meets all requirements under this Act and the rules made thereunder, the design registry shall proceed with registration. The applicant shall furnish such additional information or clarification as the Registrar may require for proper assessment. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar concerning an application may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to the refusal of registration of a layout-design or the revocation of registration thereof, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such an appeal shall be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order and shall state specifically the grounds on which the appeal is based. Failure to comply with this provision will render the appeal inadmissible. The design registry shall maintain a record of all applications for registration, granted registrations, and revocations, accessible for public inspection subject to reasonable restrictions as provided herein. Any wilful falsification of information in an application may attract penalties under this Act, including fines up to one lakh rupees and imprisonment.

The owner of a registered integrated circuit layout-design shall be entitled to grant licenses conferring rights to utilize the design, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated in the license agreement. Such agreements may include provisions relating to royalty payments, duration of use, and geographical limitations, as deemed appropriate by the parties involved. Assignment of ownership or licensing rights under this Act requires registration with the design registry shall be completed within ninety days from the date of such assignment; failure to do so renders the assignee liable for penalties as provided herein. Any subsequent transfer of a license already assigned must also be registered in like manner. The Central Government may, by notification, prescribe guidelines regarding fair licensing practices and prevent anti-competitive conduct relating to integrated circuit layout-designs.

Where an application for registration of a layout-design is rejected under this Act, the applicant may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. Such appeal shall only be entertained if the requisite fee has been paid and the grounds of appeal are clearly specified, demonstrating a substantial error in the interpretation or application of the provisions relating to novelty or originality as provided herein. The Tribunal may, after affording an opportunity for hearing to both parties, confirm, reverse, or modify the order appealed against. Any party aggrieved by any decision of the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal may further appeal to the Supreme Court on a question of law, subject to the conditions and limitations prescribed under this Act; it is provided that the design registry shall not be bound by any prior determination made in respect of a similar layout-design.

A design registry shall maintain a register of geographical indications in respect of goods or services originating from specific territories within India. The register shall contain particulars including the name of the geographical indication, the territory it identifies, the class of goods or services to which it relates, and the proprietor thereof. An application for registration as a geographical indication may be filed by any association of persons or producers engaged in producing goods or rendering services with that geographical origin; provided that such an applicant shall demonstrate control over the qualities defining the defendant geographical indication.

Where a person believes that any design is being infringed under this Act, they may institute civil proceedings in the competent court seeking an injunction restraining the infringing party from further acts of infringement. The design registry shall maintain a publicly accessible record of all registered designs and related information, including details of any oppositions or rectifications. Any interested party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to the acceptance or rejection of a produced registrar application may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Furthermore, where an infringing act has occurred, the court may award damages equivalent to the reasonable royalties that would have been payable had the design owner licensed the design to the infringer, subject to considerations of bad faith and proportionality as provided herein.

An act patent shall confer upon the patentee the exclusive right to make, use and sell the patented invention for a term extending from the date of filing of the application. This right is subject to any compulsory license granted under this Act or as provided herein. The scope of an act patent shall be defined by the claims contained therein, which must clearly define the matter claimed. Further, an act patent shall not extend to any invention already available to the public before the date of filing of the application, unless such availability was due to the acts of the applicant. Any alteration to a patented process may also affect the validity of the act patent.

An applicant seeking registration of a design shall furnish such particulars concerning priority as are prescribed; provided that where the application relates to designs comprised in more than one article class, the applicant shall specify each class and indicate the basis for claiming priority in relation to each. The Controller may require the applicant to submit certified copies of any documents relied upon in support of the claim of priority. Where a patent is granted based on an earlier filed application under this Act, the publication of such grant shall include details of the prior application’s filing date and country. Every act patent shall be deemed to be registered from the date of its acceptance unless otherwise specified by the Controller.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to revocation of a patent, opposition to a patent, or the grant of a compulsory license, has suffered damage as a consequence thereof, that person may institute a suit for damages against the party responsible for the order. Such suits shall be governed by the principles of tort law and subject to any limitations on liability prescribed herein. The amount recoverable in such a suit shall not exceed an assessment determined by the High Court, taking into account factors including the nature and extent of the damage suffered, the conduct of the parties involved, and any relevant considerations relating to public interest. It is provided that no act patent shall be invalidated solely based on evidence presented after the initial grant unless it demonstrates a clear and substantial impact on the validity criteria as defined under this Act.

An act patent shall confer upon the patentee the exclusive right to make, use and sell the patented invention for a term extending from the date of filing of the application. The Controller may, at any time within six months from the date of publication of the grant of the patent, receive objections from any person interested in the subject matter of the invention. Such an objection shall be preferred in writing and shall specify the grounds on which it is based, including but not limited to novelty or inventive step. The Controller shall give notice of the objection to the applicant and afford him an opportunity of being heard under this Act. If, after considering the objections and the response of the applicant, the Controller deems them to be well-founded, he may require modification of the claims of the patent. Any person aggrieved by any order made by the Controller relating to a patent may appeal to the Appellate Board.

An act patent shall confer upon the patentee the exclusive right to make, use and sell the patented invention for a term extending from the date of filing of the application. Provided that such right shall be subject to any compulsory license granted under this Act or as may be prescribed by rules made in consultation with the Controller General. The patentee shall furnish an annual statement to the Patents Office detailing the extent to which the patented invention has been manufactured in India, and also specify the reasons for any shortfall against the projected manufacture. Failure to comply with these reporting requirements may result in revocation of the act patent under provisions relating to non-working. Any person aggrieved by a decision concerning the grant or refusal of an act patent may appeal to the Appellate Board.

Any person aggrieved by any order made under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order; provided that the Appellate Board may, if it considers necessary, require the appellant to furnish security for costs. Failure to comply with a direction issued by the Controller regarding the rectification of a patent shall be deemed an offence and subject the defaulting party to a penalty not exceeding one lakh rupees, recoverable as arrears of land revenue. Further, any false representation made in relation to the invention claimed in an application for a patent shall render the applicant liable to prosecution under Indian Penal Code; it is provided that no act patent shall confer rights beyond those specifically defined herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder, a patent holder may grant licenses relating to the patented invention, either wholly or partially, for specific territories or fields of use. Such license agreements shall clearly define the scope of rights granted, including but not limited to, manufacturing, selling, importing, or using the invention. An act patent shall be assignable by way of absolute transfer or mortgage, and any such assignment shall be recorded in the prescribed manner. Where an assignment includes a security interest, the assignee may enforce the right against the assignor and third parties subject to applicable insolvency laws. Further, where a license is granted under this Act, the terms thereof shall not restrict the patent holder’s ability to grant further licenses or assignments relating to the same invention, provided that such subsequent actions do not conflict with existing contractual obligations as provided herein.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the revocation of a patent, or concerning the validity of a patent, appeals against such order to the Appellate Board, the Board may, after giving notice to all concerned parties and affording them a reasonable opportunity for being heard, confirm, modify, or reverse the order appealed from. It shall be open to any party affected by an order of the Appellate Board to further appeal to the Supreme Court on a question of law arising out of the decision of the Appellate Board. An act patent shall not be deemed invalid solely based upon evidence presented after the grant of the patent unless such evidence demonstrates fraudulent misrepresentation or wilful suppression of material facts, and any indication of such fraud must be substantiated with documentary proof.

An act patent shall confer upon the patentee the exclusive right to make, use and sell the patented invention for a term extending from the date of grant until ten years from the date of filing of the application. This right is subject to limitations as provided herein regarding compulsory licenses and revocation. Where an applicant has previously sought protection for the same invention under an international registration prescribed by the Patent Cooperation Treaty or any other convention administered by the World Intellectual Property Organization, the priority date shall be determined in accordance with the rules governing such international applications. The patentee may assign his interest in the patent to any person, either wholly or partially.

An act patent shall remain in force for a term of twenty years from the date of filing of the application, subject to any earlier termination as provided herein. Basic registration of the invention is a prerequisite for the grant of a patent under this Act and must be evidenced by a certificate issued by the designated authority. An applicant seeking a patent shall disclose the best method known to them for performing the invention; failure to do so may render the patent liable to revocation. The Controller, upon receiving an objection from any person interested, may require the applicant to submit further information or clarification regarding the novelty and inventive step of the claimed invention. Any alteration made to the specification after the date of grant shall be permissible only with the approval of the Controller.

An act patent shall be deemed invalid if it is found, upon examination or through subsequent challenge, that the invention was not novel at the time of filing the application. Novelty, for the purposes of this Act, requires that there exists no identical prior publication or use anywhere in the world disclosing all elements constituting the claimed invention. However, a disclosure made during an exhibition accessible to the public shall not be considered prior art provided that such disclosure was accompanied by a written and signed declaration stating that it was for the purpose of exhibiting only. The burden of proving lack of novelty rests upon the party alleging invalidity under this Act.

An application for a patent shall be accompanied by a statement specifying the class or classes to which the invention relates and a full description of the invention, including all drawings necessary to understand it. The Controller General may require the applicant to furnish further particulars concerning the nature and scope of the claimed invention, provided that such requirements are reasonable and do not unduly delay the registration process. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall assign an official filing date and record the details in the prescribed register. Any person claiming inventorship under this Act must provide documentation substantiating their contribution to the conception of the act patent. The Controller may reject an application if it is found to be deficient in clarity or completeness as per guidelines issued by the Central Government.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, where an act patent has been granted, any person aggrieved by a decision or order made under this Act relating to the grant, revocation, or infringement of such patent may appeal to the Appellate Board. The Appellate Board shall have the power to entertain appeals arising from orders passed by the Controller relating to compulsory licenses and to pass such orders as it deems fit, including setting aside or modifying any such order. Further, a party aggrieved by an order of the Appellate Board may prefer an appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The High Court shall have similar powers and jurisdiction in respect of appeals under this Act as it has in relation to suits relating to tortious infringement of patent rights, provided that costs may be awarded at the discretion of the court.

An application for a patent shall be deemed to disclose the information which was not known prior to the date of filing or priority date, subject to exceptions provided herein. The Controller may, upon receiving an objection from any person interested, direct the applicant to amend the claims to define the invention more clearly and precisely. Where such amendment is made, a fresh notice shall be published as if the application were first filed with the amended claims. Any person aggrieved by the order of the Controller under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order.
