The Trade Marks Registrar shall provide copies of records relating to the proceedings before him to the appellant upon request and payment of prescribed fees.

Applications for registration of service marks relating to financial services shall be examined by the Trade Marks Registrar with particular regard to whether such mark indicates, directly or indirectly, the cost of services, the interest rate applicable to any transaction, or any other financial condition. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further particulars regarding the nature and extent of the services rendered under the proposed trade mark, including details of pricing structures and contractual terms. Where an application includes a representation that the service is ancillary to another service, the Registrar shall consider whether this relationship exists and if so, whether the primary service is clearly identifiable. Any party may submit objections to an application within the prescribed period, detailing grounds for opposition based on deception or misrepresentation under this Act. The Trade Marks Registrar shall provide all parties with a reasonable opportunity to be heard before making any determination.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be refused by the Trade Marks Registrar if the statement of goods or services included therein is not classified according to the International Schedule of Classes of Goods and Services. Provided that, where an applicant demonstrates diligent effort to ascertain the correct classification under this Act, but inadvertently omits or misstates a class, the Registrar may permit amendment prior to publication for opposition. Furthermore, any representation accompanying the trade mark shall conform to prescribed guidelines regarding colour usage and font size; failure to comply will result in rejection of the application. The applicant must also provide evidence of intended use of the trade mark within India, unless claiming right to continue use from a previous registration under this Act or an earlier foreign registration.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Trade Marks Registrar relating to the acceptance or refusal of registration of a mark, or the rectification of the register under this Act, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeals shall be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. Failure to file an appeal within the prescribed time shall render the appellant estopped from challenging the validity of the decision. The Registrar shall, upon receiving notice of any such appeal, transmit all relevant records pertaining to the matter to the Appellate Board without delay. Any party failing to comply with procedural requirements as provided herein may be subject to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees, and the appeal may be dismissed summarily.

The Trade Marks Act provides that any person holding a license to use a registered trade mark under an assignment or other agreement may, subject to the terms thereof, apply to the Trade Marks Registrar for permission to enter into a further sub-license relating to the same goods or services. Such application shall specify the proposed scope of the sub-license and identify the intended sublicensee. The Trade Marks Registrar may, after giving notice to the assignee and any other interested parties as provided herein, grant or refuse such permission, acting reasonably and considering the impact on the distinctiveness of the trade mark. Further, where a registered trade mark has been assigned, the assignee shall notify the Trade Marks Registrar within thirty days of the assignment; failure to do so may render subsequent sub-licensing agreements voidable. The registrar retains discretion to require undertakings from any party involved in such licensing arrangements.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act, the applicant shall have the right to file a counterstatement within such time and manner as may be prescribed. The Trade Marks Registrar shall consider both the notice of opposition and the counterstatement, along with any subsequent submissions by either party, and shall afford them a reasonable opportunity to present their arguments in writing or orally. Any decision made by the Trade Marks Registrar regarding the merits of an opposition may be appealed to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such decision. Provided that, if the appellant fails to deposit the prescribed fee within the stipulated time, the appeal shall be deemed withdrawn and the order of the Trade Marks Registrar shall remain in effect.

For the purposes of this Act, the term "trade marks registrar" means the officer appointed by the Central Government to perform the functions specified herein and shall exercise such powers as are conferred upon him or her under this Act. The trade marks registrar shall be responsible for receiving applications for registration of trade marks, examining those applications in accordance with prescribed procedures, and making determinations regarding their acceptance or rejection. Decisions made by the trade marks registrar concerning registered trade marks are subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board as provided herein. Further, the Registrar may require applicants to furnish such documentation as is necessary to substantiate claims relating to distinctiveness.

Applications for registration of service marks relating to financial services shall be examined by the Trade Marks Registrar in accordance with procedures prescribed under this Act, and such examination shall prioritize assessment of distinctiveness based on acquired reputation within the Indian territory. The Registrar may require an applicant to furnish further particulars or documentary evidence demonstrating the nature of the services rendered and their geographical scope. Any omission from the Omission Register discovered after the expiry of the period specified for filing notices under section 59, but prior to publication of the Acceptance Journal, shall be rectified by the Registrar upon receipt of a written request accompanied by supporting documentation establishing the error. The applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to submit representations regarding any proposed rectification before it is implemented. Decisions concerning entries in the Omission Register are subject to appeal as provided herein.

An application for registration of a trade mark may be refused by the Trade Marks Registrar if he is satisfied that the proposed trade mark, or any element thereof, would likely cause confusion amongst consumers relating to goods or services offered under existing registered marks. Provided that such refusal is accompanied by a reasoned order detailing the specific grounds for objection and referencing comparable prior registrations, the applicant shall have standing to appeal said decision. The appeal must be filed within sixty days from the date of service of the Registrar’s order. Further, the appellant shall pay the prescribed fee at the time of filing the appeal; failure to do so will render the appeal void. Any party aggrieved by an appellate determination may seek further review under the manner applying appellate as provided herein.

Any person seeking to file an application for registration of a trade mark shall engage a registered patent agent unless that person is themselves a practicing advocate or holds a degree in law from a recognized university. Failure to comply with this provision renders the application void ab initio, and any fees paid are forfeit to the Trade Marks Registry. The Trade Marks Registrar may, at their discretion, require evidence of continued engagement of the registered patent agent throughout the proceedings. Any false representation regarding compliance with these requirements shall be deemed a cognizable offence, punishable with imprisonment for a term not less than six months and a fine extending up to one hundred thousand rupees. Further, any party found guilty of such misrepresentation is liable for damages as provided herein.

Where an application for the registration of a mark is refused under this Act, the applicant may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. Such appeal shall be finally determined by the Board, and its decision shall be binding on all parties concerned. The Registrar may, upon receiving an application for registration containing a representation of a mark that includes three-dimensional characteristics, require the applicant to furnish a specimen demonstrating such characteristics in relation to the goods or services with which the mark is associated. Marks registered accordance with the provisions herein are entitled to protection against use by any person without due cause and consent from the proprietor. The Registrar shall maintain a register of all marks registered in accordance with this Act, available for public inspection.

Where any person institutes proceedings under this Act seeking relief for infringement of a registered trade mark, it shall be conclusively presumed that the defendant’s use of a sign or representation is likely to cause confusion amongst the public unless the defendant proves otherwise. The proprietor of a registered trade mark may seek an injunction restraining the infringing activities and further damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the plaintiff. It is provided that where a registered trade mark has been used in commerce for a continuous period exceeding five years, it shall be deemed to have acquired distinctiveness within the territory of India. Marks registered accordance with this Act are entitled to protection against all forms of unfair competition and passing off. The remedies available under this Act may also include delivery up of infringing goods or materials.

Applications for the registration of service marks may be made by any person claiming to use, or proposing to use, the mark in relation to services. Such applications shall specify the class or classes of services with which the mark is associated and provide evidence of such intended use, or proposed use, as provided herein. The Registrar may require further particulars regarding the nature of the services and the applicant’s connection therewith. Where an application relates to a mark that is identical or confusingly similar to marks registered accordance with this Act, the Registrar shall issue a notice to the proprietor of the existing registration, affording them an opportunity to file representations against the proposed registration. Any such representations must be submitted within the time specified in the notice and will be considered during examination. The applicant may then submit replies to these representations.

Where an application for the registration of a mark is refused under this Act, the applicant may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within three months from the date of receipt of the order of refusal. Such appeal shall be accompanied by a fee as prescribed; provided that the Board may, in its discretion, entertain appeals filed after the expiry of the said period if satisfactory reasons are shown for the delay. The Board shall hear parties and evidence adduced and make such orders as it deems fit, including setting aside or modifying the order of refusal. Any party aggrieved by an order made by the Board under this Act may appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of that order; marks registered accordance with section 27 shall be subject to review upon application by any interested person.

The proprietor of a mark registered accordance with this Act may grant licenses permitting the use of their registered trademark for specific goods or services, subject to conditions stipulated within the license agreement. Such licenses shall be assignable, either wholly or partially, provided that any such assignment is notified to the Registrar in the prescribed manner and accompanied by the requisite fee. Further, a proprietor intending to assign the entire registration of a mark may do so with the consent of the assignee, recorded as per rules framed under this Act. Any license granted shall clearly define the geographical territory covered and the duration for which such use is permitted; failure to adhere to these limitations constitutes infringement. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating ongoing compliance with licensing terms, and may investigate complaints regarding unauthorized usage or breaches of contractual obligations relating to marks registered accordance.

For the purposes of this Act, “advertised acceptance” means a public notification published by the Registrar concerning an application for registration of a trade mark, indicating that such application has been accepted, either unconditionally or subject to specified limitations or modifications. The advertisement shall include particulars identifying the applicant and the goods or services in relation to which the trade mark is sought, along with any conditions imposed under this Act. Any party may file a post-acceptance opposition against a trade mark following an advertised acceptance, as provided herein. Such oppositions must be filed within the prescribed period from the date of such advertisement.

An applicant seeking registration of a mark under this Act shall furnish an affidavit verifying the distinctiveness and non-deceptiveness of the proposed trade mark. Where the Registrar is satisfied with the application’s compliance with all relevant provisions, he or she may publish the acceptance thereof in the Trade Marks Journal. Any party believing they possess prior rights relating to the advertised acceptance of a mark may within four months from such publication file a notification of opposition. Such notifications shall be accompanied by a statement of grounds and supporting evidence as provided herein. The Registrar shall provide an opportunity for both parties to present arguments, subject to procedural guidelines established under this Act, before determining the validity of the registration.

Where a proprietor of a registered trade mark institutes proceedings against another alleging infringement under this Act, and such other party offers an acceptance of liability for damages arising from the alleged infringing activity, but expressly disclaims any admission of guilt or responsibility regarding the underlying validity or distinctiveness of the registered trade mark, that offer shall be deemed to constitute an advertised acceptance. Such advertised acceptance does not preclude the proprietor from pursuing remedies available under this Act, including injunctive relief and account of profits. However, the amount of damages awarded may be reduced proportionately to the extent the court finds that the offered sum reasonably compensates for the demonstrable financial prejudice suffered by the proprietor as a direct result of the infringing activity, subject to considerations of fairness and equity. Further, any such advertised acceptance shall not create an estoppel against subsequent challenges to the validity of the trade mark.

Where an applicant seeks rectification of a registered trade mark based on acquired distinctiveness, and the Registrar deems such evidence sufficient for preliminary consideration, notice of the application shall be published in the Trade Marks Journal. Any party claiming an interest in the registered trade mark may, within sixty days from the date of publication, file with the Registrar a written counter-statement opposing the rectification. The applicant shall then have fourteen days to respond to the counter-statement filed. If the Registrar finds that the applicant has demonstrated acquired distinctiveness through extensive advertising and consumer recognition, he or she may proceed to consider the application further. An advertised acceptance of this finding by the respondent shall be deemed conclusive for purposes of procedural finality, subject to appeal under this Act.

Where a trade mark is advertised under this Act following an initial acceptance, any person claiming rights in relation to the proposed trade mark shall have standing to submit objections provided such objection is lodged within the period specified in the official gazette. Any communication from the applicant or any other party indicating agreement with the terms of advertisement, or otherwise demonstrating acquiescence to the advertised acceptance, shall not be construed as a waiver of right to subsequently raise an objection. Further, where an advertised acceptance explicitly references prior use by another entity, such reference shall constitute notice to the applicant of potential conflict and may preclude subsequent claims regarding earlier identical or deceptively similar usage. The Registrar shall consider all submitted objections in accordance with procedures prescribed herein.

Where a trade mark is registered and subsequent use thereof by another party constitutes an unfair advantage derived from association with the registered trade mark, and such use is demonstrably communicated through advertising or other promotional materials constituting what amounts to an advertised acceptance of the registered trade mark’s goodwill, any proprietor of the registered trade mark may institute proceedings before the relevant jurisdictional authority. Such proceedings shall be directed towards seeking injunctive relief preventing further unauthorized use and recovery of damages commensurate with the detriment suffered by the proprietor as a direct consequence of the infringing activity. Failure to comply with an order issued under this Act concerning advertised acceptance shall attract penalties, including fines not exceeding ten lakhs of rupees and imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years.

Where a proprietor of a registered trade mark grants a license for use of the mark under this Act, such license shall be deemed an assignment unless explicitly stated otherwise within the licensing agreement. Any subsequent transfer or disposal of the licensed undertaking by the licensee shall require prior written consent from the grantor, provided that such consent shall not be unreasonably withheld. Furthermore, where the proprietor advertises acceptance of a trade mark application to a third party through any medium, including but not limited to publication in a journal or online platform, it shall constitute an irrevocable offer subject to the terms and conditions stipulated therein. The recipient of such advertised acceptance may accept the offer by fulfilling the prescribed formalities as detailed within the advertisement itself.

Where a trade mark is registered following an advertised acceptance, and a challenge to said registration is subsequently filed under this Act by a person claiming proprietary right or interest in relation to the impugned mark, the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal shall consider whether the advertisement of acceptance adequately informed such claimant of the conditions precedent to registration. It shall be presumed that any representation made during proceedings relating to an advertised acceptance was bona fide unless proven otherwise before the Tribunal. Further, a finding that the advertised acceptance failed to accurately reflect the scope of the mark’s intended use shall not, by itself, invalidate the registration; however, it may limit the registered rights as provided herein.

Where an applicant seeks registration of a variety under the Varieties Registry established under this Act, and tenders a fee as prescribed, the Registrar shall examine whether the proposed name distinguishes the variety from existing varieties listed therein. Should the Registrar determine that the proposed name constitutes an advertised acceptance of another registered variety, creating a likelihood of confusion amongst growers or consumers, the applicant shall be afforded opportunity to submit counter-arguments demonstrating absence of such deceptive similarity. The Registrar may then require modification of the proposed name, subject to compliance with regulations regarding phonetic resemblance and visual appearance as provided herein. Failure to adequately address this concern will result in rejection of the application.

Where a trade mark is advertised acceptance under this Act, and an interested party files objections within the period specified, such objections shall be deemed duly filed irrespective of whether they are transmitted electronically or through postal services, provided that proof of dispatch by registered post with acknowledgment due is furnished. Failure to furnish such proof shall render the objection inadmissible. Any person found to have knowingly misrepresented facts in their objection, or acted in collusion to undermine the advertised acceptance process, shall be liable for a penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees and may face prosecution under relevant provisions concerning offenses against security of India.

Where a trade mark is sought to be registered and an advertisement of acceptance has been published under this Act, any person claiming an interest adversely affected by such registration shall have standing to appeal against the decision relating to said advertisement. Such appeal must be filed within sixty days from the date of publication of the advertised acceptance, failing which it shall be deemed time-barred. The appellant shall bear the burden of demonstrating prejudice arising directly from the published acceptance and its subsequent impact on their existing rights. Further, any challenge based upon prior use shall date filing to the earliest demonstrable instance of such use, subject to verification by the relevant intellectual property authority.

For the purposes of this Act, an “invention disclosure” is deemed to be filed on the date the first written record pertaining to the invention is received by the designated authority. Where a joint application for patent registration is submitted by multiple applicants claiming common inventive conception, the *application date shall* be determined as the date of filing by the first applicant to submit a complete and compliant disclosure. This determination is subject to verification through records maintained by the receiving office; provided that any subsequent co-applicant may provide supplementary documentation substantiating their contribution to the inventive step. The authority may request further clarification regarding the sequence of filings under this Act.

An application for registration of a mark shall be deemed to be filed on the date the prescribed fee is remitted, provided that where an applicant submits multiple representations relating to the same mark within a period of six months, the application date shall be determined by reference to the earliest such representation received by the Registrar. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further particulars or documentary evidence substantiating the claim of use of the mark in relation to any goods or services specified in the application. Where an amendment is made to the list of goods or services following the initial filing, the application date shall remain unchanged unless such amendment substantially alters the character of the mark. The Registrar may entertain objections relating to clarity and precision of description under this Act.

An application for registration of a mark shall be deemed to have been made on the date it is received by the Registry. Where an applicant files multiple applications relating to identical goods or services using substantially similar marks, the application with the earliest application date shall take precedence in examination and adjudication. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further particulars or documentary evidence supporting the claim of use of the mark, particularly where the mark has not been previously registered under this Act. Provided that, if an applicant seeks to amend the description of goods or services following the initial filing, the application date shall remain unchanged unless such amendment fundamentally alters the nature of the mark itself. The Registrar may, at any time, require a further search fee to be paid where the examination process reveals complexities requiring additional investigation.

Where an application is made under this Act for registration of a mark by transmitting it from outside India to the Trade Marks Registry in Mumbai, the application shall be treated as if it were filed within India. The date of filing such an application shall be deemed to be the date on which the application was received at the designated post office in the foreign country and dispatched by registered or certified mail. Provided that, if the applicant fails to provide proof of dispatch via registered or certified mail, the application date shall be considered as the date upon which it is physically received by the Registry. Further, any deficiency in the prescribed fee accompanying such an application may be remedied within a period specified by the Registrar; failing compliance, the application will stand rejected.

An application for registration of a mark shall be deemed to have been filed on the date it is received by the Trade Marks Registry, provided that where an applicant subsequently files another application relating to the same goods or services and disclosing the earlier application date, the later application’s application date shall be taken as the date of the subsequent filing. Any person aggrieved by a decision regarding the application date may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of that decision. Failure to comply with this provision will render such an appeal inadmissible. The Registrar may, at any time, require proof substantiating the claimed application date and impose penalties for false statements made in connection therewith.

Where a trade mark application is assigned or licensed, subject to any terms stipulated within the assignment deed or license agreement, the assignor or licensor shall retain the right to utilize the mark for their own purposes provided that such utilization does not create confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of goods or services. An application date shall be deemed to relate to the initial filing by the original applicant irrespective of subsequent assignments or licenses granted concerning said trade mark. Further, any modification to the list of goods or services covered within an application following assignment requires consent from both the assignee and the Registrar. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating consumer understanding regarding the change in ownership or licensing arrangement. This requirement is intended to safeguard against misleading representations under this Act.

Where an application for registration of a mark is filed under this Act, the determination of priority between competing applications shall be predicated upon the respective application dates. For the purposes of establishing prior use and subsequent claim to ownership, it is provided that the *application date shall* be conclusively deemed to be the date on which the formal request for examination is received by the Registry, subject to any evidence presented demonstrating a clear error in recording such receipt. Any party disputing the recorded application date may petition the Intellectual Property Appellate Board with supporting documentation; however, such petitions must be filed within three months of notification of acceptance and are subject to costs as determined by the Board. The Registrar’s decision on priority is appealable to the Appellate Board.

Where an application is filed for registration of a mark under this Act, the application date shall be deemed to be the date on which the specification filed proceeded through the prescribed formalities. Provided that, if the applicant has previously filed an identical or similar mark relating to goods or services identical or similar to those specified in the current application, the Registrar may require submission of documentary evidence demonstrating prior use and reputation, and the application date shall then be adjusted accordingly. Further, where a request for amendment of the specification is made after the initial filing, such amendment must not substantially alter the character of the mark; otherwise, a fresh application date shall be assigned to the amended document as provided herein.

Where an application date shall be considered to establish priority under this Act, any subsequent use of a similar mark by another party shall constitute infringement. The owner of a registered trade mark may institute proceedings for relief against such infringement, and it is provided that where the defendant has been demonstrably aware of the plaintiff’s prior registration and continuing use, the plaintiff forthwith ceased all advertising or promotional activities featuring the impugned mark upon receiving notice of the impending action. Failure to comply with this provision shall be deemed a mitigating factor in assessing damages recoverable under this Act. The Registrar may, ex officio, initiate investigations into suspected instances of wilful infringement and impose penalties as determined appropriate.

An application trade mark, as defined herein, is a representation indicating an intention to apply for the registration of a trademark under this Act. Such an application shall contain particulars identifying the applicant and specifying the goods or services in relation to which the proposed trademark is to be used. The representation may include devices, words, or other marks capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one undertaking from those of others. An application trade mark confers no right upon the applicant prior to registration; however, it does provide a period of provisional protection subject to certain conditions as provided herein.

An application trade mark shall be deemed to be registered upon the date specified in the certificate of registration. Where an objection is raised against a proposed trade mark under this Act, the applicant may amend the marks or statement of goods and services to overcome said objection, provided that such amendment does not fundamentally alter the identity of the mark. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further particulars relating to the use of the trade mark in relation to the specified goods or services as part of the examination process. Upon successful completion of examination and any subsequent opposition proceedings, a certificate of registration shall be issued, conferring upon the registered proprietor exclusive rights within India. Any person aggrieved by a decision regarding an application may appeal under this Act.

An application trade mark shall confer upon the applicant exclusive rights to use the mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered, subject to any prior conflicting rights. Any person aggrieved by the acceptance of an application may institute proceedings under this Act seeking a declaration that the mark does not qualify for registration. Such proceedings must be brought within four months from the date of publication of advertisement of the acceptance. The Registrar shall consider evidence presented by all parties and may, after affording them an opportunity to be heard, determine whether the applicant’s application should proceed or be refused. Further, if a registered trade mark is subsequently used in a manner contrary to honest practices in industrial competition, remedies including injunctions and damages are available as provided herein.

An application trade mark shall be deemed to be refused if the Registrar considers that it is contrary to declared public policy or morality. The Registrar may, prior to refusal, afford the applicant an opportunity for their representation regarding such considerations and shall record the reasons for any decision made under this Act. Where a proposed trade mark contains a geographical indication which is protected under another enactment, the Registrar shall require evidence from the applicant demonstrating due cause for use of said indication in connection with the goods or services specified in the application. Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar relating to the acceptance or refusal of an application may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within a period of sixty days from the date of communication of that order, as provided herein.

An application trade mark shall be deemed to be refused if the proposed mark is identical or confusingly similar to a prior registered trade mark used in relation to identical or closely related goods or services, subject to any conditions that may be prescribed. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish such documentary evidence as demonstrates due and reasonable use of the mark in relation to the specified goods or services if there exists a conflicting earlier right. Provided that, an application shall not be refused solely on the basis of prior honest concurrent use where the applicant can demonstrate continuous use for a period exceeding five years immediately preceding the date of filing, and such use was without any intention to deceive or trade off the reputation of the proprietor of the earlier registered mark.

An application trade mark shall be deemed to infringe this Act if, following its publication under section 59, any person knowingly uses a sign identical or confusingly similar to the applied-for mark in relation to goods or services for which the mark is registered, with the intent to gain an unfair commercial advantage or to exploit the reputation of the proprietor. Such infringement shall be actionable at the suit of the applicant and may result in damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the applicant, not exceeding five per cent of the infringer’s turnover attributable to the infringing use. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint, issue an injunction restraining the infringing activity and order the seizure and destruction of goods bearing the mark, provided that due process is followed as prescribed herein.

Subject to any agreement entered into prior to the filing of an application trade mark, the registered proprietor may grant a license to use the trademark for specific goods or services. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as determined by the terms of the agreement and subject to conditions stipulated therein relating to quality control and permitted geographical territories. An assignment of the entire undertaking or a substantial part thereof shall include an automatic transfer of all pending applications trade mark related thereto, provided that the assignor provides written notification to the Registrar within thirty days of such assignment. The assignee may elect to continue the application as their own, or request its cancellation; failing either action, the application lapses after sixty days. Any sub-license granted under a primary license shall be subject to the terms and conditions of that initial agreement, as provided herein.

Where an application trade mark is refused under this Act, the applicant may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within three months from the date of receipt of the order of refusal. Such appeal shall be on grounds that the refusal was erroneous in law or fact and that the Registrar failed to consider material evidence submitted by the applicant during examination. The Board may, after affording an opportunity for hearing to both the applicant and the Registrar, confirm, modify, or reverse the decision appealed from. Any party aggrieved by any order of the Intellectual Property Appellate Board under this provision may further appeal to the Supreme Court within sixty days, subject to satisfaction of the conditions prescribed herein regarding deposit of security.

An application trade mark shall be deemed to be refused if the evidence of use filed by the applicant, as required under this Act, fails adequately to demonstrate continuous performance of the mark in relation to the goods or services specified in the application for a period of at least three years from the date of registration. Provided that, where the Registrar considers it necessary due to exceptional circumstances affecting the trade, such as unforeseen regulatory changes impacting market conditions, the applicant may be granted an opportunity to submit further evidence substantiating continued performance within a time frame determined by the Registrar. The Registrar shall record reasons for any refusal and provide notice thereof to the applicant, allowing them fifteen days to respond with arguments against the finding.

Subject to the provisions relating to distinctiveness, any registered trade mark owner may grant a license conferring rights to use their application trade mark for specific goods or services, provided that such license is documented in writing and specifies the geographical area of permitted usage. Such licenses shall be assignable alongside the underlying trade mark ownership, subject to prior notification to the Registrar and approval if the assignee’s activities could reasonably affect existing licensees. Furthermore, where a patent of addition relating to a product bearing the registered trade mark has been granted to another party, that party may seek a non-exclusive license from the trade mark owner for use consistent with the patented invention, as provided herein. Any assignment or licensing agreement shall be deemed invalid if it contravenes any conditions stipulated under this Act regarding fair competition and consumer protection.

Where an application trade mark is refused under this Act on grounds relating to distinctiveness, the applicant may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the refusal order and shall state specifically the grounds upon which the applicant relies in challenging the decision. The Board may, after affording an opportunity for hearing to both the applicant and the Registrar, confirm the refusal or direct registration of the trade mark, subject to such modifications as it deems fit. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Intellectual Property Appellate Board relating to India rights concerning a refused application may further appeal to the High Court within ninety days from the date of that order.

Subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal, an application for rectification of a registered trademark may be made by any person claiming interest alleging that such registration is invalid or ought to be amended or expunged. Such applications shall be filed in the prescribed form and accompanied by the requisite fee. The Registrar shall serve notice on the registered proprietor, affording them an opportunity to file their counterstatement within a stipulated period as provided herein. Upon receipt of the counterstatement, the Registrar may direct the presentation of such evidence as they deem necessary for determining the dispute. Where the application relates to newly acquired distinctiveness, the applicant must demonstrate use consistent with building consumer recognition. The registered proprietors trade shall be considered in light of all submitted documentation and arguments.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person who, without due cause or consent from the registered proprietor, uses a registered trade mark identical or confusingly similar to that of another in connection with goods or services shall be deemed guilty of an offence and liable to a penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees. Such use includes, but is not limited to, applying the mark to labels, packaging, advertising materials, and offering goods or services under the deceptive guise of association with the registered proprietor. Further, any person found in violation may be ordered by the relevant adjudicating authority to cease such infringing activity immediately and account for all profits derived therefrom. The registered proprietors trade shall be vigorously defended against such unauthorized exploitation.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, a registered proprietor may grant licenses relating to the use of their registered trademark, specifying the goods or services for which such use is permitted and the geographical area covered by the license. Such licenses shall be assignable, either in whole or in part, subject to prior registration with the Trade Marks Registry and publication thereof as provided herein. Any subsequent registered proprietor acquiring rights through assignment shall be deemed a continuing assignee of any existing licenses granted by the previous proprietor. The terms of such licenses may include royalty payments and restrictions on quality control measures relating to the goods or services bearing the trademark, ensuring consistent consumer perception. Furthermore, the registered proprietors trade mark rights are not diminished by the granting of a license unless explicitly stated within the licensing agreement itself.

Subject to any rights previously existing, the registration of a trademark shall confer upon the proprietors trade marks the exclusive right to use the mark throughout India in connection with the goods or services for which it is registered. Any person desiring to institute proceedings alleging infringement under this Act may give notice of such intention to the proprietor of the trademark, specifying the acts complained of and demanding that they cease; provided that failure to provide such notice shall not bar any subsequent action unless the court deems it just and equitable in the circumstances. The proprietor may also seek damages for actual losses suffered by him as a consequence of the infringing activity, subject to proof of causation and reasonable foreseeability. Further, remedies available include injunctions restraining further infringement and delivery up or destruction of goods bearing the mark.

An application for registration of a trademark shall be refused if it contains only such features as may serve to distinguish the goods or services of one undertaking from those of others, but is descriptive in its character and has been used in relation to those goods or services prior to the date of the application by another person. Where an objection is taken under this provision, the applicant shall be afforded a reasonable opportunity to demonstrate acquired distinctiveness through extensive use. The Registrar may require the applicant to submit evidence substantiating such use, including but not limited to market surveys and sales figures. Upon review of the submitted documentation, the Registrar shall determine whether sufficient proof of acquired distinctiveness exists. If satisfied, the application may proceed; otherwise it will be rejected as provided herein. Proprietors trade marks are subject to periodic renewal under this Act.

Subject to any other provision of this Act, a proprietor of a trademark shall be entitled to institute proceedings for recovery of damages sustained by reason of the infringement thereof. Such damages may include loss of profits resulting from the sale of goods or services bearing an infringing mark, as well as the costs and expenses incurred in protecting the proprietors trade marks against unauthorized use. Further, where an infringer has employed a transmissible use layout substantially identical to that associated with the registered trademark, the Court may grant an injunction restraining the infringer from further utilizing such layout, even if the overall impression differs. The proprietor shall be deemed to have suffered damage regardless of whether actual monetary loss can be precisely ascertained; consequential damages are recoverable as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, a “valid registered proprietor” shall be deemed to be the person whose name appears as such on the Register of Trade Marks, subject to any rectification proceedings pending under this Act and not finally determined. Where a trade mark is registered jointly by two or more persons, each joint registered proprietor shall be considered a valid registered proprietor with respect to the rights conferred herein. The exclusive right afforded to a valid registered proprietor extends to preventing the use of an identical or confusingly similar mark on identical or closely related goods or services, provided that such use is likely to cause confusion in the minds of the public or indicate that the goods or services originate from the registered proprietor or a person connected with him.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, an application for registration of a proposed trade mark shall be refused if it contains any matter which, while not directly infringing upon an existing registered trade mark, is otherwise contrary to law or morality. Where a trade mark is accepted and certified for registration, the Registrar shall record particulars thereof in the Register of Trade Marks, including the date of application, the applicant’s address for service, and the goods or services for which the registration is sought. The right to use a registered trade mark as indicated in the register shall vest solely with the *valid registered proprietor* and may be enforced against any person using a similar mark in relation to identical or closely related goods or services without due cause. Any alteration of the particulars relating to a registered trade mark requires prior approval from the Registrar.

Subject to any rights subsisting in another person under prior registration or use, a valid registered proprietor shall be entitled to institute proceedings for infringement against any party employing a sign identical or confusingly similar to the registered trademark, even where such use occurs without direct commercial competition. Any representation made falsely as to the origin, nature, quality or characteristics of goods or services offered by another person constitutes an actionable misrepresentation under this Act and may be restrained by injunction. The remedies available to a valid registered proprietor include damages sustained by reason of the infringement, seizure of infringing materials, and account of profits derived from the unauthorized use. Provided that the proprietor has diligently prosecuted their trademark rights, they shall also be entitled to seek Anton Pillar orders where there is evidence of threatened or actual infringement causing immediate and irreparable harm.

Subject to appeal under this Act, a determination regarding entitlement to rectification of a registered trademark shall be made within six months from the date of receipt of the application by the relevant Intellectual Property Office. Where an application for rectification is filed alleging that a trade mark has become devoid of distinctiveness through use by a third party, the office shall provide the *valid registered proprietor* with an opportunity to submit a written response and supporting documentation demonstrating continued distinctiveness. Failure by the registered proprietor to respond within thirty days of notification may be considered as evidence against their claim. The Intellectual Property Office may, after considering all submissions, direct rectification or dismiss the application, providing reasoned findings in its order. Any party aggrieved by such an order may further appeal under this Act.

Subject to compliance with all applicable regulations pertaining to domain name registration, a person claiming to be a valid registered proprietor of a trademark shall be deemed to possess such right only if they have consistently maintained their registration through timely renewal fees as stipulated under this Act and have not received notice of rectification proceedings initiated by any third party. Furthermore, the exclusive rights afforded to a valid registered proprietor are contingent upon adherence to prescribed standards of trade practice; any demonstrable misrepresentation or deceptive conduct in connection with the use of the trademark may render such rights susceptible to challenge and revocation as provided herein. The Registrar shall maintain records confirming compliance with these conditions.

Subject to appeal under Chapter VIII, any person who, knowing that a particular trade mark is registered in the name of a valid registered proprietor, uses such trade mark or a deceptive imitation thereof in connection with the offering for sale, supply or exposure for sale of goods or services shall be guilty of an offence and liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine which may extend to fifty thousand rupees, or both. Further, where infringement occurs through false representation that the infringing goods or services are connected with the registered trade mark, the offender shall also be liable to pay damages as determined by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The Court may order seizure and destruction of the infringing goods and materials used in their production.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, a valid registered proprietor shall be entitled to grant licences for the use of their registered trademark, either exclusively or non-exclusively, and may stipulate conditions relating to quality control, territorial limitations, and permitted goods or services in such licence agreements. Any assignment of the registered trademark, whether absolute or conditional, shall require prior written consent from the Controller General, provided that such consent shall not be unreasonably withheld. Further, a registered proprietor intending to assign their rights may offer a royalty-bearing sublicence to third parties as part of a commercial arrangement, subject to fulfilling all obligations under this Act concerning trademark usage and enforcement. The validity of any licence or assignment is contingent upon compliance with the prescribed forms and fees, as provided herein.

Subject to appeal to the Appellate Board, a person shall be deemed a valid registered proprietor of a trademark where registration has been granted following due process under this Act, and such registration remains unchallenged through an application for rectification based on grounds specified herein. However, if an objection is raised alleging that the mark conflicts with an earlier trade mark or is descriptive of the goods or services, the burden shall lie upon the registered proprietor to demonstrate continued validity and distinctiveness. The Board may, in considering any appeal, direct a further inquiry into questions of fact relating to use, reputation, or consumer perception, provided that such direction does not unduly delay proceedings. Any order made by the Appellate Board is final, subject to further appeal to the Supreme Court on grounds of law only.

For the purposes of this Act, a valid registered proprietor shall be deemed to possess such title to the trademark as is evidenced by the certificate of registration issued under this Act, subject to any rectification proceedings pending before the relevant intellectual property forum. Where an application for registration has been accepted and published in accordance with the prescribed procedures, the shall established registry shall maintain a record thereof, accessible to the public upon payment of the requisite fee. Any person claiming rights as a registered proprietor must demonstrate that such claim is not vitiated by fraud or misrepresentation during the examination process.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, where a person has been duly registered as a valid registered proprietor of a trademark, that proprietor shall be entitled to institute proceedings for recovery of damages sustained by reason of the infringement thereof. Such proceedings may be brought against any party making use of an identical or confusingly similar name in relation to goods or services identical or closely resembling those for which the trade mark is registered. The remedies available under this Act include, but are not limited to, injunctions restraining further acts of infringement and an account of profits made as a result of such infringing activities. Provided that, any defence based on prior use of a name shall be considered only if evidence establishing continuous and honest use predating the date of registration is presented. The proprietor’s rights are subject to limitations imposed by other laws for the time being in force.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, an application for registration of a layout design consisting of visual elements relating to the packaging of a consumer product shall be refused if the said design is substantially similar to a previously registered layout design or one which has been published prior to the date of filing. Where multiple applicants claim rights in respect of the same layout design, priority shall be determined based on the earliest date of application filed under this Act. The Registrar may require any applicant claiming to be a valid registered proprietor to furnish such evidence as is deemed necessary to substantiate their ownership and entitlement. Any challenge to the validity of a registration concerning a layout design must be brought before the relevant intellectual property tribunal within five years from the date of publication of the registration.

Subject to appeal under Chapter X, any person who, knowing that a particular trade mark is registered in the name of a valid registered proprietor, uses such trade mark or a deceptive imitation thereof in connection with goods or services shall be guilty of an offence and liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or both. Further, where a holder licence patent relating to a process incorporates a protected trademark without express authorization from the registered proprietor, such use constitutes infringement subject to remedies as provided herein. The Court may also order the seizure and destruction of goods bearing the infringing mark, and impose costs reflective of the damages suffered by the proprietor.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person claiming rights in a proposed trade mark may apply for registration thereof as provided herein. An application shall specify the goods or services with which the trade mark is intended to be associated and shall include such particulars as are required under this Act. Where an applicant has previously filed an application for the same trade mark relating to identical or similar goods or services, the Registrar may require disclosure of all prior applications. The registration of a trade mark shall confer upon the persons registered proprietors exclusive rights within the territory of India in relation to the goods and services specified in the register. Such rights are subject to any limitations or conditions noted on the register.

Subject to any rights previously existing, a person registered as proprietor of a trade mark shall be entitled to institute proceedings against any person or persons infringing that trade mark. Such proceedings may include claims for damages sustained by the proprietor as a direct result of the infringement, calculated without regard to any profits made by the infringer. The right to sue for relief under this Act is further subject to the condition that the registered proprietor has not consented to the use of the trade mark by another party; such consent shall constitute an express abandonment of rights against that user. Further remedies available to persons registered proprietors include injunctions restraining future acts of infringement and, where applicable, delivery up or destruction of infringing goods. The Registrar may also order rectification of the register if it appears that a registration has been obtained through fraudulent means.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark has been refused under this Act, the applicant may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order of refusal. Such appeal shall be filed in the prescribed form and accompanied by such fee as may be determined by the Central Government. The Board shall give notice to all persons registered proprietors who are likely to be affected by the decision on the appeal, affording them an opportunity of being heard. Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board under this Act may further appeal to the Supreme Court within sixty days from the date of such order. Decisions of the Board shall be final subject to any appeal made as provided herein. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, prescribe the manner in which appeals are to be filed and heard.

Subject to compliance with prescribed procedures, a person shall be deemed a registered proprietor upon successful entry of their mark onto the Register of Trade Marks. Such registration confers upon the registered proprietor the exclusive right to employ the trademark within the territorial limits of India, pertaining solely to the class of goods or services for which registration was secured. Provided that, any alteration to the list of goods or services specified in the application shall require subsequent notification and approval by the Registrar. Furthermore, a registered proprietor may institute proceedings relating to infringement only if they have diligently pursued remedies through alternative dispute resolution mechanisms as provided herein, failing which their claim shall be deemed inadmissible. The rights afforded to persons registered proprietors are subject to any prior conflicting usage established under this Act.

Any person registered as a proprietor of a trademark shall be entitled to institute proceedings for recovery of damages sustained by reason of the institution of an infringing use of the said trademark, subject to proof that such use has caused actual and demonstrable harm. Where any infringement occurs after notice has been given to the persons registered proprietors, the amount of damages recoverable shall include reasonable royalties which the infringer would have paid had they obtained a license from the proprietor. Failure to provide such notice prior to initiating legal action will preclude recovery for lost profits exceeding ten percent of the claimed damages. The Central Government may, upon application by an aggrieved party, issue injunctions against continued infringing activity as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, a registered proprietor may grant licences conferring specific rights relating to their registered trademark, including but not limited to the right to use the mark for particular goods or services, within defined geographical territories, and for specified durations. Such licences shall be in writing and clearly delineate the scope of permitted usage, royalty structures, and termination clauses. Assignment of a trademark registration is permissible with the prior written consent of the Controller, provided that such assignment does not prejudice existing licensees’ rights as established under this Act. Further, any subsequent registered proprietor shall be bound by all previous licences and assignments relating to the mark, unless expressly modified through mutual agreement documented in writing and approved by the Controller. Persons registered proprietors are obligated to inform the Controller of any changes concerning their trademark ownership or licensing arrangements within thirty days.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act, and such opposition is ultimately unsuccessful following decision by the relevant intellectual property tribunal, the applicant shall be deemed to have acquired rights equivalent to those of persons registered proprietors from the date of publication of the advertisement of the application. Provided that, if any subsequent proprietor claims prior use of an identical or confusingly similar mark, they may appeal the finding of such equivalence to the High Court within ninety days of notification of the tribunal’s order. The burden of proving such prior use and demonstrating resultant consumer confusion shall rest entirely upon the appellant, subject to a review of the original opposition record by the court.

Subject to appeal under this Act, a person registered proprietor of a trademark shall be entitled to restrain the use of any representation or sign which is identical or confusingly similar to his registered trademark if such use constitutes infringement as defined herein. Provided that, where an international registration designating India has been extended to cover goods or services, the rights afforded to the persons registered proprietors under this Act shall include the right to apply to a High Court for appropriate remedies against any act of adaptation or alteration of the mark which would otherwise constitute infringement. Further, such proprietor may seek damages and injunctions as provided herein in cases where deceptive practices are employed to mislead the public regarding the origin or quality of goods or services offered under an infringing trademark. The remedies available shall be without prejudice to any other rights or actions accruing to the registered proprietor.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, a registration referred fact concerning ownership of a trademark shall not preclude a person demonstrating prior honest use of an identical or confusingly similar mark from seeking equitable relief as determined by the relevant intellectual property tribunal. Where persons registered proprietors elect to grant a license for the use of their trademarks, such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive and shall specify the geographical territory and goods or services covered thereby. Any assignment of trademark rights, including partial assignments relating to specific licensed uses, must be executed in writing and attested as provided herein. Further, any sublicense granted under an existing license agreement shall require the express written consent of the registered proprietor, failing which it is deemed void. The registered proprietor retains full authority over enforcement actions related to their mark, even concerning activities undertaken by licensees.

For the purposes of this Act, a “trade proprietor registered” shall be deemed to include any individual, partnership, company, or other body corporate duly incorporated and possessing valid registration of a trademark under this Act in respect of specified goods or services. Such trade proprietor registered shall be entitled to institute proceedings for infringement as provided herein, subject to the limitations prescribed regarding concurrent use and territorial scope. The rights conferred upon a trade proprietor registered are not absolute but are circumscribed by principles of fair dealing and public interest, and may be relinquished through abandonment as defined under this Act. Any assignment or transmission of such registration shall adhere to procedures outlined elsewhere.

A trade proprietor registered under this Act shall be entitled to exclusive rights over the representation of the trademark for which registration is granted, encompassing all forms and variations thereof that create an identical or confusingly similar impression. Such entitlement extends to preventing the use of any sign by others in connection with goods or services identical or similar to those for which the trade proprietor’s mark is registered, subject to limitations as provided herein regarding descriptive use. The Registrar may, upon application by a trade proprietor, record particulars relating to assignment or transmission of rights under this Act, including details of the assignor and assignee. Further, any alteration to the registered trademark shall require prior approval from the Registrar and be recorded in the Register of Trade Marks.

Where any person shall infringe a registered trade mark, subject to the provisions regarding fair use under this Act, such infringement shall constitute a cause for civil suit in the competent court. The trade proprietor registered may seek an injunction restraining the defendant from continuing such infringing activity and further may claim damages proportionate to the loss suffered by reason of the infringement. Provided that where the infringement is deemed to be negligent, enhanced damages may be awarded at the discretion of the court. Further, any goods manufactured or sold bearing a false or deceptive representation identical or similar to the registered trade mark shall be liable for seizure and destruction as provided herein. The trade proprietor registered also has the right to demand an account of profits made by the infringer from such infringing activities.

The Trade Marks Act provides that an application for registration of a trade mark shall be refused if it is deemed deceptive under this Act. Where a trade proprietor registered a trade mark in respect of particular goods or services, and another person subsequently seeks to register a similar trade mark in relation to identical or closely related goods or services, the Registrar may direct the applicant to amend their application to avoid likelihood of confusion with the earlier registered trade mark. Such direction shall be accompanied by written reasons. Any party aggrieved by such direction may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The Trade Marks Registry shall maintain a record of all applications, registrations and amendments as provided herein, accessible for public inspection subject to applicable regulations concerning confidentiality.

A trade proprietor registered under this Act shall be entitled to institute proceedings for infringement of their registered trade mark against any person using identical or confusingly similar marks in relation to goods or services. Such entitlement is subject to the condition that the infringing use occurs within the territory of India, or directed at consumers within India, and has caused demonstrable damage to the reputation or goodwill associated with the registered trade mark. Provided that, where a trade proprietor has not used their registered trade mark continuously for a period exceeding five years, they may be denied relief under this Act if another person has demonstrably established use of an identical or similar mark acquired in good faith and without intent to deceive. Further, any proceedings shall comply with the procedural requirements as provided herein.

Any person who, without due cause and after receiving notice from the Trade Marks Registry, continues to use a trade mark identical or deceptively similar to a registered trade mark shall be guilty of an offence. Such offender shall be liable for damages sustained by the trade proprietor registered as a consequence of the infringing use, calculated in such manner as may be prescribed. Further, repeated contravention of this provision may result in imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years and a fine which may extend to ten lakhs of rupees. The Trade Marks Registry shall have power to issue injunctions restraining any person from engaging in activities that constitute infringement under this Act, provided that the trade proprietor registered demonstrates demonstrable consumer confusion.

A trade proprietor registered under this Act shall be entitled to grant licenses for the use of their registered trademark, specifying the geographical area and range of goods or services covered by such license. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as determined by the trade proprietor at the time of granting. Any assignment of a registered trademark shall include all associated licenses unless explicitly stated otherwise in the assignment deed. A licensee may further sub-license their rights subject to the terms and conditions stipulated within the original licensing agreement with the trade proprietor; however, such sub-licensing cannot contradict any limitations imposed by the Act or previous agreements. The trade proprietor retains the right to terminate a license if the licensee fails to adhere to the agreed upon usage guidelines as provided herein.

Where an objection is raised under this Act against the registration of a proposed trade mark on the ground that it conflicts with an earlier trade mark, the Registrar shall provide both the applicant and the proprietor of the earlier trade mark with an opportunity to submit their respective representations and evidence. The Registrar may, after considering such submissions, direct that the applicant amend the proposed trade mark to mitigate or remove the conflict, or proceed with registration as originally applied for. If either party disputes this decision, they shall have the right to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within a period of sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The determination of the Board shall be final, subject to further appeal under the provisions relating to appeals to higher courts. A trade proprietor registered prior to any conflicting application retains priority rights as provided herein.

Where an application for registration is made in respect of a trade mark used in connection with pharmaceutical products, the Trade Marks Registry shall require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating prior use of the mark within India. Such evidence may include, but is not limited to, invoices, advertisements, and sales records pertaining to the relevant goods. The Registrar may, at his discretion, request further documentation or conduct a hearing to ascertain the veracity of the claimed usage. A trade proprietor registered under this Act shall be deemed to have exclusive rights over the representation of their mark within the territory of India, subject to any prior conflicting registrations or demonstrable use by another party. Any challenge to the validity of such registration may be brought before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board as provided herein.

A trade proprietor registered under this Act shall be entitled to institute proceedings for relief against any person who, without due cause and with intent to deceive, falsely represents that his goods or services are associated with such proprietor. Such representation includes the use of a mark identical or confusingly similar to the registered trade mark, or any false designation of origin which constitutes a geographical indication falsified in relation to the goods or services for which the trade mark is registered. Provided that, where the alleged infringement occurs through an authorized dealer acting within the scope of their contractual relationship with a distributor, the proprietor shall first exhaust all remedies available under the terms of such contract before pursuing legal action as provided herein. The Court may grant such relief as it deems just and equitable to prevent further infringements.

Where any person knowingly and wilfully infringes a registered trade mark, or falsely represents connection with a trade proprietor registered under this Act, such person shall be liable for damages. The amount of damages shall be determined by considering the loss suffered by the trade proprietor as a consequence of the infringement, taking into account factors including but not limited to the extent of the false representation and any profits made by the infringer. Provided that, if the prosecutor gave information leading directly to the apprehension and conviction of an offender under this Act, the court may award additional compensation to the trade proprietor reflecting such contribution. Any order for damages shall be enforceable as a decree of a civil court.

A trade proprietor registered under this Act shall be entitled to grant licences relating to the use of their registered trademark, subject to such terms and conditions as are agreed upon between the proprietor and the licensee. Such licences may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and may cover specific goods, services, or territories, as determined by the agreement. The trade proprietor retains full ownership of the trademark and any licence granted does not constitute a transfer of title. Assignment of the registered trademark shall include assignment of all existing licences pertaining to that mark, provided that the assignee undertakes the obligations of the assignor under those licences. Any modification or termination of a licence requires written consent from both the trade proprietor and the licensee, as provided herein. The proprietor may revoke a licence if the licensee fails to comply with the terms stipulated therein.

Where an appeal is made under this Act against any order passed by the Registrar relating to rectification of a trade mark, the Appellate Board shall hear and dispose of such appeal within six months from the date of its receipt. The Board may, after giving all parties concerned an opportunity of being heard, confirm, vary or reverse the order appealed against. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Appellate Board may further appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of that order. It is provided that in cases involving wilful infringement and fraudulent misrepresentation concerning a trade proprietor registered mark, the court may impose a sentence imprisonment term not exceeding three years alongside any monetary penalty as deemed appropriate.

Where, in determining whether a trade mark is distinctive, reference is made to the context otherwise requires,— (h) “international application” means an application for registration of a trade mark filed with the Office under the Madrid Protocol and designating India as a designated Contracting Party. An appeal against a refusal to register based on a prior conflicting international application shall be maintainable before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, provided that the appellant demonstrates diligent examination of the design registry pertaining to the earlier mark. The Board may direct the Registrar to reconsider the matter if it finds that the Registrar failed to adequately consider evidence submitted regarding acquired distinctiveness or use in commerce predating the filing date of the international application.

For the purposes of this Act, “designated territory” means India, and where a trade mark is registered in a foreign country and application has been made for its extension to India, such extension shall be deemed to be registration india designated. The term "foreign registry" includes any registry maintained by a competent authority outside India responsible for registering trade marks, and the Registrar may request information from such foreign registries concerning pending applications or registrations relating to marks that are identical or deceptively similar to those applied for or registered under this Act. Any official communication received from a foreign registry shall be treated as evidence, subject to challenge under procedures prescribed herein.

An application for the registration of a trade mark shall be deemed refused if the proposed marks include representations or words which directly associate it with the Indian Standards Institution unless prior approval has been obtained from that institution. The registrar may, upon review and subject to payment of prescribed fees, accept such an application provided that the applicant demonstrates due diligence in ensuring compliance with relevant standards and regulations pertaining to quality assurance. Further, where a trade mark is sought for registration india designated as part of an international registration, the registrar shall verify the status of said international registration and any conflicting applications or registrations existing within India. Any challenge to such designation must be filed within the timeframe prescribed under this Act.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be refused if it contains exclusively geographical indications as defined under this Act and which are currently registered or have previously been registered. Provided that, an applicant may proceed with their application if they can demonstrate to the satisfaction of the Registrar that use of the geographical indication is generic in India, or that such use does not falsely suggest any connection with the place indicated. The Registrar shall maintain a publicly accessible register detailing all trade marks granted registration india designated as part of international registrations, including dates of initial designation and subsequent modifications thereto. Any alteration to details pertaining to a registered mark, particularly concerning its geographical scope, must be reported to the Registrar within thirty days for verification and recordation.

Any person aggrieved by a decision relating to the acceptance or refusal of an application for registration india designated under this Act may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. Failure to comply with prescribed forms and fees during such an appeal shall render it void ab initio. The Board, after affording opportunity of being heard to all parties concerned, may confirm, modify, or reverse the decision appealed against. Any act done in contravention of this Act or any rule made thereunder shall be deemed a civil offence and subject to penalties as provided herein, including imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and fines up to one million rupees.

The owner of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to grant licenses conferring rights to use the trade mark for goods or services as defined under this Act. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and the terms thereof shall be governed by contractual agreement between the licensor and licensee. Assignment of the right to registration India designated is permissible, subject to prior written consent from the Registrar, which consent shall not be unreasonably withheld. Any assignment shall include a detailed description of the trade mark, the goods or services in relation to which the assignment relates, and the duration of the assigned rights. Further, any sub-license granted under a primary license must adhere to the original terms stipulated by the licensor, provided that such terms do not contravene provisions relating to fair competition as established herein. The Registrar may require periodic reporting on licensed usage to ensure compliance with conditions set forth in the registration.
