The remedies available include injunctions preventing further misuse and orders for accounts of profits derived from such infringing activity.

For the purposes of this Act, “permitted use” with respect to a registered trade mark means any application or incorporation of the mark in relation to goods or services for which the mark is registered, undertaken by a person who has obtained prior written consent from the proprietor of the trade mark, subject to conditions specified therein. Such conditions may relate to quality control measures, geographical limitations on distribution, or restrictions regarding advertising materials employed. The regulations governing the granting and revocation of such consents shall be prescribed by the Trade Marks Registry. Any permitted use that contravenes these regulations is deemed an infringement under this Act, provided that the proprietor has not waived their rights in writing.

Applications for registration of a trade mark shall be accompanied by such particulars as may be prescribed, including a representation of the mark and a list specifying all goods or services in relation to which the applicant desires to register the trade mark. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further information concerning the use of the mark prior to the date of application, particularly where the mark incorporates descriptive terms or has been previously utilized in a manner that necessitates clarification under this Act. Regulations made by the Authority shall govern the procedures for filing and processing these applications, including timelines for response to objections raised by the Registrar or third parties. Any alteration to the list of goods or services after the initial application is filed requires prior approval from the Registrar, subject to prescribed fees.

Where any proprietor of a registered trade mark alleges that any other person is making use or proposing to make use of a mark which is identical or confusingly similar to his registered trade mark, and such use constitutes an infringement under this Act, he may apply to the relevant High Court for relief. The application shall specify the acts of infringement complained of, and the remedies sought, including but not limited to injunctions restraining the infringing activities and damages sustained by reason thereof. Provided that, in determining the amount of damages, the Court shall take into account any benefit accruing to the defendant or loss suffered by the plaintiff due to the alleged infringement. The proprietor shall be entitled to apply for discovery of documents relevant to establishing the extent of such use and associated profits. These regulations governing applications for relief are subject to judicial review as provided herein.

Applications for registration of a trade mark involving colour marks shall be examined by the Registrar, and such examination shall include assessment of distinctiveness acquired through use subsequent to the date of application. The applicant shall furnish evidence demonstrating exclusive use of the colour mark within India for a continuous period not less than three years preceding the date of the request for such demonstration. Failure to provide satisfactory evidence as required under this Act may result in rejection of the application. Any person aggrieved by a decision regarding the distinctiveness assessment made by the Registrar may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, provided that the appeal is filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The regulations governing appeals and procedures for hearings shall be as prescribed by the government.

The use of a trademark, including any colour or configuration thereof, shall be subject to compliance with such conditions as may be prescribed. Any proprietor seeking to utilize a registered trade mark in connection with goods or services not identical to those for which it is registered must obtain prior approval from the Controller. Such approval shall only be granted if the proposed use does not create confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of the goods or services. The regulations pertaining to applications for such approvals will detail required documentation, including but not limited to, market research demonstrating non-infringement and a declaration affirming adherence to ethical advertising standards. Failure to adhere to these regulations may result in penalties as provided herein.

Any proprietor utilizing a trade mark in connection with goods or services shall, within three months from the date such utilization commences, furnish a statement of such utilization to the Registrar, specifying the manner and extent thereof. Failure to comply with this provision renders the proprietor liable for a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees, and may be subject to further penalties of ten thousand rupees for each subsequent month of non-compliance. The Registrar shall publish notice of any such failure in the Trade Marks Journal. Any person aggrieved by a statement submitted under these regulations may file an objection with the Registrar within sixty days, detailing grounds for dispute; the Registrar’s determination on objections is final.

Where the proprietor of a registered trade mark, intending to grant a license for use of the mark, desires to assign the right to collect royalties arising from such licensed use, he shall submit a declaration to the Registrar detailing the terms and conditions governing both the license and the assignment. This declaration must specify the duration of the license, the geographical territory covered, and the nature of the goods or services in relation to which the mark may be used under the license. The Registrar may require further clarification regarding any aspect of these regulations before registering the assignment. Provided that the assignment is consistent with the terms initially stipulated within the licensing agreement, it shall be deemed valid. Any subsequent alteration to the license’s scope requires prior notification and approval from the Registrar, ensuring continued compliance as provided herein.

The Registrar shall, upon receiving a complaint alleging non-compliance with the regulations pertaining to the use of registered trade marks in relation to goods or services, serve notice on the complainant and the alleged infringer. The notice shall specify the particulars of the complaint and provide both parties an opportunity for written submissions within thirty days from the date of service. Following this period, the Registrar may proceed ex parte if a party fails to respond, subject to providing reasons for such decision in writing. Any party aggrieved by any order or direction made under these regulations may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days; provided that the Appellate Board shall consider only questions of law arising out of the order and not matters of mere evidence.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark includes a representation of an invention, or contains matter which may amount to an invention, the Registrar may require the applicant to furnish proof that such invention is capable of industrial application and does not infringe any existing patent of addition. Such proof shall be submitted within the time specified by the Registrar, failing which the application shall stand rejected. The regulations governing the assessment of said proof shall be published in the Official Gazette. Any person aggrieved by a decision under these regulations may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of such decision. Compliance with the prescribed format for submission of evidence is mandatory, and any deviation therefrom will render the submission invalid.

For the purposes of this Act, "prescribed form" means a form specified by notification in the Official Gazette and published by the Registrar; such notification may prescribe different forms for different classes of trade marks or for different purposes under this Act. The power to issue such notifications shall include the authority to effect modifications to existing prescribed forms, and any such modification shall take effect from the date specified therein. Regulations issued under this Act relating to examination procedures, including those concerning evidence submitted in opposition proceedings, may be subject to periodic review; these draft regulations modification processes will adhere to principles of transparency and public consultation as provided herein.

The Trade Marks Rules, as amended, shall govern the process for submitting and evaluating proposed modifications to existing trade mark regulations. Any entity seeking a draft regulations modification must submit a detailed proposal outlining the specific alterations sought, along with a justification demonstrating that such changes are necessary to ensure clarity or operational efficiency under this Act. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating the need for the modification, including impact assessments and consultations with relevant stakeholders. Subject to compliance with prescribed forms and fees, the Registrar shall publish the draft regulations modification for public comment. Objections received during the public consultation period will be considered before a final determination is made regarding approval or rejection of the proposed changes.

The owner of a registered trade mark shall, subject to the provisions herein, be entitled to grant licenses conferring specific rights relating to the use of their trade mark on any person, firm or company. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive and shall clearly define the geographical area and goods or services in relation to which the licensee is authorized to utilize the mark. Any assignment of a registered trade mark, or of any license granted thereunder, requires prior written consent from the Registrar, provided that such consent shall not be unreasonably withheld. Further, where a draft regulations modification concerning permitted uses of a licensed trade mark is proposed by either the owner or the licensee, notification must be submitted to the Registrar for review and approval before implementation. This ensures continued protection of the registered mark’s distinctiveness as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, "registered certify goods" means goods which conform to a defined standard and are certified as such by an authorized certification trade mark owner. Such conformity shall be demonstrated through adherence to specifications prescribed under this Act and documented in a certificate issued by the certification trade mark owner. The term “certification trade mark” refers to a trade mark defining registered certify goods according to specified standards. Any person utilizing a certification trade mark for purposes other than certifying goods as provided herein, or falsely representing goods as certified, shall be deemed to have contravened this Act and subject to penalties.

An applicant seeking registration of a certify goods trade mark shall furnish with the application a detailed specification of the goods or services in relation to which certification is proposed, and such specification shall be deemed to define the scope of certification under this Act. The Registrar may require further particulars regarding the standards of quality, characteristics, or other attributes that the certified goods must possess, provided that these criteria are objectively verifiable and do not relate to trade marks themselves. Any person claiming rights in relation to a registered certify goods trade mark may apply to the Registrar for rectification if it is used in a manner contrary to honest practices in industrial competition. The registrar shall consider any opposition filed against registration of such marks based on likelihood of confusion with existing marks.

The owner of a registered certify goods trade mark shall be entitled to restrain any person from using, in connection with goods or services, signs or symbols identical or deceptively similar to the certified marks if such use misrepresents those goods or services as being certified by him. Such restraint may extend to all means of advertising and marketing. Further, where a proprietor of a registered certify goods trade mark proves that any person has made false representations concerning the certification, he shall be entitled to seek damages for losses suffered thereby. The remedies available under this Act include injunctions and account of profits derived from the infringing use. Nothing in these provisions shall prevent the use of a certified mark by or on behalf of the certifying authority itself.

Where an applicant seeks registration as a certifier of goods under this Act, they shall demonstrate to the Registrar their adherence to specified quality standards and operational procedures. The application must include detailed documentation outlining the certification process, including inspection protocols, testing methodologies, and conformity assessment criteria. Certification marks granted pursuant to this Act are restricted to denoting that the certified goods conform to the applicant’s defined standards, as evidenced in the register. Any alteration to these standards requires prior notification and approval from the Registrar. The holder of a registered certify goods mark shall maintain records pertaining to each batch of certified goods, available for inspection by authorized officials. Failure to comply with these conditions may result in suspension or revocation of the certification mark.

Any person employing the registered certify goods mark in connection with goods not conforming to the standards specified in the regulations governing its registration shall be deemed guilty of an offence under this Act. Such offender shall be liable for a penalty of fifty thousand rupees, and where the offence is a continuing one, a further daily penalty of ten thousand rupees shall accrue until compliance is secured. The owner of the registered certify goods mark may institute civil proceedings to restrain any such infringing use and recover damages sustained by reason thereof. Further, upon conviction, the Court may order the destruction or disposal of goods bearing the offending mark as it deems fit. This power extends even where the infringement occurs through an agent acting under express or implied authority.

The owner of a registered certify goods trade mark shall be entitled to grant licenses conferring the right to apply the mark to goods meeting the prescribed standards. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and may be assigned along with the underlying business undertaking subject to prior notification to the Registrar. Any assignment of a license shall be in writing and executed by both licensor and licensee. The Registrar may require proof of such assignment before acknowledging its validity under this Act. Further, where a license is granted for the manufacture or sale of certified goods, the licensee shall be deemed an agent of the trade mark proprietor for purposes relating to quality control and compliance with certification regulations as provided herein. Any alteration to the scope of licensed activities requires consent from the registered owner.

The owner of a registered certify goods mark shall be entitled to grant licenses conferring the right to affix such mark upon goods meeting the prescribed standards. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive and may extend to the use of associated designs incorporated into the packaging or presentation of the certified goods, subject to conditions specified in the license agreement. Any assignment of a registered certify goods mark shall include all rights pertaining to any existing licenses attached thereto; provided that such assignment is executed in the prescribed manner and duly notified to the Registrar. The Registrar may require disclosure of license terms during examination of an application for registration or upon request from an interested party, ensuring transparency and preventing anti-competitive practices relating to certified goods. Further, sub-licensing shall be permitted only with prior written consent from the original owner under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, "registered certify goods" means goods certified as conforming to a particular standard, quality, or characteristic by an authorized user under a certification trade mark. Such certification shall be evidenced by a certificate issued in the prescribed form and affixed to the certified goods. The authorized user may surrender its registration of a certification trade mark if it ceases to function as an authorized user, provided that such surrender does not prejudice any rights acquired by bona fide purchasers prior to notice of the intended surrender. Any person claiming entitlement to use a certification trade mark shall be subject to the provisions relating to registrability under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, "certification trade mark" means a trade mark which identifies goods as conforming to a particular standard and which is used by any person other than the registered proprietor for certifying that the goods so identified conform to his prescribed standard; such standards shall be defined in regulations framed under this Act. An application for registration of a certification trade mark shall specify the geographical area or areas in relation to which the applicant claims to control the use of the proposed mark. The Registrar may, subject to any conditions specified therein, accept an application for register certification if satisfied that the applicant fulfills all requirements as provided herein.

An applicant seeking registration of a certification trade mark shall furnish such particulars as are prescribed, including details regarding the authority controlling the quality and characteristics certified. The Registrar may require further information to ascertain compliance with these requirements and may reject the application if the applicant fails to provide it within the stipulated timeframe. Upon acceptance of an application for register certification, the Registrar shall record the name of the applicant and a description of the goods or services in relation to which the certification applies. Any alteration to the registered mark or the regulations governing its use requires prior approval from the Registrar, obtained through a formal request submitted as provided herein. The Registrar may refuse registration if he considers that the proposed mark is deceptive or contrary to public interest.

Where an applicant obtains registration of a trade mark under this Act as a certification trade mark, the Registrar shall issue a certificate of registration in the prescribed form. The holder of such registration shall be entitled to use the distinctive device specified therein and may institute proceedings for infringement against any person using or authorizing the use of a sign identical or deceptively similar to the certified trade mark in connection with goods or services covered by the certification. Any proprietor whose rights are adversely affected by the grant of registration as a certification trade mark may apply to the Registrar for rectification, subject to demonstrating material prejudice resulting from the registration. The Registrar shall consider such applications and may order cancellation or modification of the register certification if it is found to be obtained through misrepresentation or contrary to the provisions herein.

An applicant seeking registration of a certification trade mark shall submit with the application a detailed description of the characteristics, quality, or other attributes which the goods or services certified under the mark must possess to qualify for certification. The Registrar may require further particulars regarding the standards and procedures employed in assessing conformity to these requirements. Upon receipt of the application and after affording due opportunity to interested parties to object, the Registrar shall determine whether the applicant is a suitable body for administering the proposed register certification scheme. A certificate of registration shall be deemed to have effect from the date of filing the application, subject to any subsequent amendments or modifications approved by the Registrar. The date patent shall not affect the validity of existing agreements relating to quality assurance prior to this Act’s commencement.

The Registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for notification of assent to a proposed alteration of a registered trade mark, conduct such inquiries as are deemed necessary to ascertain whether the proposed change is permissible under this Act and consistent with existing registrations. The applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to present arguments against any objections raised by third parties or identified during the Registrar’s inquiry process. Should any interested party challenge the validity of the application or raise concerns regarding potential confusion arising from the altered mark, the registrar shall appear before a designated Trade Marks Settlement Officer for mediation and conciliation. The officer's recommendations are advisory; however, the Registrar must provide reasoned justification should they deviate from such advice.

Where, upon receiving an objection under this Act regarding the deceptively similarity of a proposed trade mark to an existing one, the applicant fails to submit a satisfactory response within the prescribed time limit, or if the evidence presented by the applicant is deemed insufficient to overcome the grounds for opposition, the Registrar shall appear and be heard before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The Board’s determination on such matters shall be final, subject to appeal to the High Court only on questions of law. Further, any party aggrieved by a decision of the Intellectual Property Appellate Board may seek redress through appropriate legal proceedings, provided that such proceedings are initiated within ninety days from the date of communication of the order. The Registrar’s appearance is without prejudice to his right to submit further evidence or arguments at any stage of the proceedings as deemed necessary.

Where, upon receipt of an objection under this Act, the applicant fails to submit a satisfactory reply within the time prescribed, or if the applicant defaults in appearance at any hearing appointed by the Registrar, the Registrar shall proceed to consider the objection ex parte. The Registrar may, after giving due notice to all interested parties as provided herein, direct that such default be treated as abandonment of the application. Any party aggrieved by a direction issued under this provision may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. Should any question arise regarding the interpretation of the grounds for objection or the propriety of an ex parte determination, the Registrar shall appear and present arguments on behalf of the Trade Marks Registry. The decision of the Appellate Board shall be final, subject to appeal under the relevant provisions governing appeals from orders of that body.

Where an objection is taken by any person against the acceptance of an application for registration of a trademark, and such objection raises a question of fact requiring determination beyond that which may be resolved through documentary evidence alone, the applicant shall provide to the Registrar within thirty days of notification of the objection, all relevant supporting documentation. The Registrar may, at his discretion, direct a hearing wherein both the objector and the applicant may present oral arguments and further evidence. In such instances, the registrar shall appear, either personally or through an authorized representative, to adjudicate upon the submitted materials. Provided that any party failing to comply with these procedural requirements will have their submissions deemed inadmissible; subject to the Registrar’s power to extend deadlines where exceptional circumstances are demonstrated.

Where, upon receiving an objection under this Act, the applicant fails to submit a reasoned response within the prescribed period, or where such response demonstrably does not address all material aspects of the objection, the Registrar shall appear before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board and present arguments substantiating the initial refusal. Failure by the Registrar to diligently pursue enforcement actions as provided herein regarding trade mark infringement will render them liable for penalties determined by the Board, proportionate to the demonstrable harm suffered by the aggrieved party. Any order issued by the Board concerning such appearances or penalties shall be final, subject only to appeal to the High Court on grounds of legal error. The Registrar’s appearance is deemed essential for ensuring procedural fairness and upholding the integrity of the register.

Where the registered proprietor of a trademark desires to grant a license conferring exclusive rights to use the trademark within a defined geographical territory or for specific goods or services, such license agreement shall be recorded with the Trade Marks Registry. The recording shall include details of the licensor, licensee, the scope of the licensed rights, and the duration of the license. Upon application by either party to the license agreement, the Registrar shall appear and provide a certificate confirming the existence and terms of the registered license, which may be presented as evidence in any legal proceedings relating to the trademark. Provided that, assignment of such recorded licenses is permissible subject to prior notification to the Registry and approval based on compliance with regulations concerning fair trade practices and consumer protection under this Act.

Where an objection is taken by any person against the acceptance of an application for registration of a trademark, and such objection relates to distinctiveness or deceptively similarity under this Act, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to file a written response within sixty days from the date of service of notice of the objection. Should the Registrar consider the response unsatisfactory or fail to adequately address the grounds raised in the objection, he may direct further submissions and counter-submissions between the objector and the applicant. In any such proceedings before the Registrar, the registrar shall appear, either personally or through an authorized representative, to present arguments on behalf of the Trade Marks Registry. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days.

Where an objection is taken by the Examiner under this Act against the acceptance of an application for registration of a services trade mark, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to submit their response within the time specified in the notice of examination. Should the applicant fail to respond or the response received does not adequately address the grounds of objection, the Registrar may proceed with further investigation and may direct the publication of the trademark for opposition. In any proceeding arising from such a direction, the registrar shall appear on behalf of the Trade Marks Registry and present arguments pertaining to the maintainability of the registration. The applicant retains the right to be heard in person or through an authorized representative.

Where, upon receiving an objection under this Act, the applicant fails to submit a satisfactory reply within the prescribed period, or if the applicant’s representation is deemed insufficient by the Examining Officer, the registrar shall appear before the Trade Marks Registry Appellate Board at the time and place specified in the notice of hearing. The Board's decision regarding the validity of the objection shall be final, subject to appeal to the High Court within a stipulated timeframe as provided herein. Further, any party aggrieved by an order made under this Act concerning the design shall extent of protection afforded to a registered trade mark may seek redressal through the Appellate Board. The Registrar is empowered to issue directions for rectification of the register if it appears that a trade mark has been improperly registered or used in contravention of these provisions and to award compensation where applicable.

Where, upon receipt of an objection under this Act, the objector fails to file a counter-statement within the prescribed period, or if the applicant and the objector fail to reach a settlement through mediation as provided herein, the Registrar shall appear before such officer designated by him for further consideration. The Registrar may, at his discretion, direct both parties to submit written arguments pertaining specifically to the grounds of objection raised. Decisions rendered under this process are final subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal.

Furthermore, any material submitted during these proceedings, including but not limited to design specifications and marketing materials, shall be deemed confidential and protected from unauthorized dissemination; such protection extends also to works incorporated within those submissions, conditions subject copyright as per prevailing legislation. The Registrar’s determination regarding the admissibility of evidence is conclusive.

Where, upon receiving objection under this Act, the applicant fails to submit a satisfactory response within the prescribed period, or neglects to appear before the Registrar at the appointed hearing date, the Registrar shall appear and present arguments substantiating the grounds for opposition. Failure by the objector to attend such hearing without just cause, as determined solely by the Registrar, will result in automatic dismissal of their objection. Furthermore, registration shall cease if it is subsequently proven that the registered trade mark was obtained through fraudulent misrepresentation or wilful suppression of material facts during the application process. Any party aggrieved by a decision under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days, subject to payment of prescribed fees and demonstrating demonstrable prejudice.

Where the registered proprietor of a trademark desires to grant a license conferring exclusive rights to use the trademark within a defined geographical territory or for specific goods and services, such proprietor shall submit a form petition to the Trade Marks Registry. This petition must detail the scope of the licensed rights, including any limitations on usage and duration of the license. The Registrar shall appear before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board if any party objects to the proposed licensing arrangement, citing concerns regarding dilution or unfair competition. Provided that the registered proprietor affirms their continued responsibility for ensuring compliance with trademark law by the licensee, the Trade Marks Registry may approve the assignment or sub-license of these rights subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all approved licenses and assignments on the public register.

For the purposes of this Act, a ‘distinctive representation’ includes any symbol, logo, numeral, or combination thereof, used to identify goods or services and distinguish them from those of others. The registrar statement shall be binding upon all parties involved in opposition proceedings unless revised by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board under appeal. Where an application for registration is refused on the grounds that the proposed trade mark is descriptive, the registrar statement may indicate reasons for such refusal, provided that these reasons are specific and relate directly to the inherent nature of the goods or services specified in the application. Any challenge to a registrar statement must be made within sixty days.

The applicant shall furnish such documentary evidence as the Registrar may require to substantiate the claim of use and reputation, particularly where the applied-for mark incorporates a geographical indication. The Registrar shall consider all submissions made by interested parties during the opposition period and any subsequent examination proceedings. Further, registrar statement shall be recorded in the register detailing the reasons for acceptance or rejection of the application, including observations on distinctiveness and potential consumer confusion. Any party aggrieved by such registrar statement may prefer an appeal under this Act within a prescribed time limit. The Registrar is empowered to direct the applicant to amend the representation of the mark if it deems the initial depiction inaccurate or misleading, provided that such amendment does not substantially alter the essential nature of the trade mark.

Where an objection is taken by the Registrar against the acceptance of an application for registration of a trademark under this Act, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to submit their response within sixty days from the date of communication of such objection. If the applicant fails to respond or the response submitted does not adequately address the concerns raised, the Registrar may proceed with the examination of the mark and determine whether it is registrable. The registrar statement shall clearly articulate the grounds for refusal, citing relevant provisions under this Act pertaining to deceptiveness, similarity to existing marks, or generic character. Any party aggrieved by a decision made pursuant to such registrar statement may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within three months from the date of communication of the order.

Where an objection is taken by the Registrar under this Act against the acceptance of an application for registration of a trademark, and such objection relates to similarity with an earlier mark, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to submit their written response within sixty days from the date of communication of the objection. The Registrar shall consider any such response received, together with the original application and all documents filed in support thereof. Following consideration, the registrar statement shall indicate whether the objection is withdrawn or maintained, providing detailed reasoning for the determination made. Provided that if the applicant fails to submit a written response within the stipulated timeframe, the registrar statement shall be conclusive evidence of abandonment of the application.

Where an objection is taken by the Registrar against the acceptance of an application for registration of a trademark under this Act, and such objection relates to deceptiveness or likelihood of confusion with prior marks, the applicant shall be afforded opportunity for written response. Following consideration of the applicant’s reply, the Registrar may proceed with the examination of the mark. The Registrar statement shall constitute conclusive evidence regarding the grounds for said objection, subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of such statement. Failure to pursue an appeal within this timeframe will preclude any further recourse under this Act and render the applicant’s application liable for rejection without further notice. Any party aggrieved by a decision based on the Registrar's statement may also be subject to penalties as provided herein.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark shall be entitled to grant a license conferring the right to use the trade mark, subject to such terms and conditions as are agreed upon between the parties, provided that any such license agreement must specify the geographical area within which the licensee is permitted to utilize the mark. Further, where an assignment of a registered trade mark includes a continuing security interest in respect of the licensed rights, the assignee shall notify the Registrar within thirty days of the assignment, detailing the nature and extent of the security interest granted. The registrar statement shall indicate whether such notification has been received and recorded, and any subsequent transfer or release of that security interest must also be reported to the Registrar for recordation as provided herein. Failure to comply with these reporting requirements may render the security interest unenforceable against third parties.

Where an objection is taken by the Registrar under this Act against an application for registration of a trademark, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to submit written representations addressing the grounds of said objection. Such representations must be filed within sixty days from the date of dispatch of the notice containing the objection. The registrar statement shall then be considered in conjunction with the original application and any prior art documents presented. If, following review of these submissions, the Registrar remains unconvinced that the trademark is registrable, a reasoned decision will be recorded. This decision may consider whether the applicant can demonstrate they are the true and first inventor of the mark’s distinctive elements, provided that such demonstration satisfies the requirements as provided herein.

Where a registered trade mark has been assigned, and the assignee seeks to grant a non-exclusive license over specified goods or services included within the scope of that registration, the registrar statement shall reflect such licensing arrangement upon receipt of a duly executed instrument evidencing the assignment and detailing the terms of the license. This instrument must clearly identify both the assignor, assignee, and licensee, alongside a precise description of the licensed rights. Provided that the Registrar is satisfied with the veracity of this documentation and its compliance with regulations under this Act, he shall record the license in the register. Further, should any dispute arise regarding the validity or scope of such a license, the court directs registrar to maintain records pertaining to all submitted instruments and related correspondence for evidentiary purposes during judicial proceedings.

The Registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for registration of a geographical indication, conduct such inquiries as may be deemed necessary under this Act to ascertain the authenticity and continued use of the indication. The applicant shall furnish all requisite documentation substantiating the connection between the goods or services and the specified geographical origin, including evidence of traditional knowledge and production methods. Should any objection arise regarding the distinctiveness of the proposed geographical indication, the Registrar shall right to request further clarification from the applicant, inviting submissions and counter-evidence as deemed appropriate. The decision of the Registrar concerning such objections shall be final, subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Where, upon receiving an objection under this Act, the applicant fails to submit satisfactory evidence demonstrating acquired distinctiveness within the prescribed timeframe, the Registrar shall right to direct the removal of the mark from consideration for registration. This direction is without prejudice to any subsequent application for similar marks, provided that such applications demonstrate a genuine and substantial use of the mark in commerce following the initial rejection. Further, if an aggrieved party demonstrates through verifiable documentary evidence that the Registrar’s decision was demonstrably influenced by improper considerations or procedural irregularities, they may petition the Intellectual Property Appellate Board for review. The Board shall have the power to quash the Registrar's order and remit the matter for reconsideration as provided herein, ensuring due process is observed in subsequent proceedings.

The Registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for extension of time under this Act, serve notice thereof upon all parties appearing on the register as proprietors or registered users of the trademark concerned. Such notice shall specify the grounds relied upon by the applicant and invite objections from any interested party within sixty days from the date of such service. Where no objection is received within the stipulated period, or where all objections are withdrawn, the Registrar may proceed to consider the application on its merits. The Registrar shall right to require the submission of further documentation deemed necessary for a proper assessment of the request, and may grant, refuse, or conditionally extend the time as he deems appropriate, recording his reasons in writing. Any party aggrieved by such decision may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order.

The Registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for amendment of a registered trademark, verify that such proposed amendment does not alter the character or essential features of the goods or services specified in the original registration. The applicant must demonstrate, through documentary evidence satisfactory to the Registrar, that the intended alteration is necessitated by changes in product nomenclature or packaging consistent with evolving market conditions and does not mislead consumers regarding the origin or quality of the trademarked goods. Further, the Registrar shall right to reject an amendment application if it finds that the proposed change would result in a conflict with any prior rights existing under this Act. Any appeal against such rejection must be filed within sixty days from the date of notification of the order.

Where, upon receiving an objection under this Act, the applicant fails to submit a satisfactory reply within the time prescribed, or if the evidence submitted by the applicant does not adequately address the grounds raised in the objection, the registrar shall right to proceed with the examination of the application as though no such objection had been filed. Any party aggrieved by any decision of the Registrar relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application for registration may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of that decision. Failure to comply with this provision shall render the appeal inadmissible, and the registrar retains full authority to impose penalties as provided herein for frivolous or vexatious appeals.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark shall be entitled to grant licenses conferring rights to use the trade mark, subject to such terms and conditions as are specified in the license agreement. Any assignment of a trade mark, or of any interest in a trade mark, including a license, shall require notification to the Registrar within thirty days of the execution thereof. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all assignments and licenses registered under this Act, accessible for public inspection upon payment of prescribed fees. Further, where a licensee seeks to assign their rights derived from a license agreement, they may apply to the Registrar for registration of such assignment, provided that the original trade mark proprietor has consented in writing to the proposed sub-licensee’s acquisition of those rights. The registrar shall right to refuse registration if the application is incomplete or contains information inconsistent with existing records.

The Registrar shall, upon receiving an objection under this Act from any person aggrieved by a proposed trademark, provide such objector with a reasoned statement detailing the grounds for opposition and affording them opportunity to submit written arguments within sixty days. The applicant may then file a rejoinder addressing these objections, also within sixty days. Following consideration of all submissions, the Registrar shall right to determine whether the trademark is deceptively similar to any existing mark or conflicts with section 9, provided that such determination shall be based solely on the documentary evidence presented and without regard to oral testimony. Any party dissatisfied with the Registrar's decision may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within a period of three months from the date of the order.

For the purposes of this Act, “distinctiveness” with respect to a proposed trade mark shall be determined considering its inherent ability to distinguish goods or services and, where applicable, its acquired distinctiveness through use. The registrar considers whether a sign is capable of distinguishing goods or services from those of others; provided that, in determining distinctiveness, the registrar may take into account factors such as the perception of the relevant consumer class, including their knowledge of trade marks and practices within the industry. Further, the registrar shall be guided by established principles concerning deceptive similarity when assessing whether a mark is distinctive.

Upon receipt of an application for registration of a proposed trade mark, the Registrar shall examine whether the mark is distinctive and not deceptive as provided herein. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further information or clarification regarding the goods or services with which the trade mark is associated, and may also request documentary evidence substantiating the claimed use of the mark in commerce. Should any objection arise under this Act concerning prior conflicting rights or other grounds for refusal, the Registrar shall issue a notice thereof to the applicant, affording them an opportunity to file a counterstatement. The registrar considers all such submissions before making a determination regarding acceptance or rejection of the application, and may direct the holding of hearings as deemed necessary to resolve any disputed issues.

Where an objection is taken by the Registrar under this Act against the acceptance of an application for registration of a trademark, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to submit their reply within sixty days from the date of service of the notice of the objection. Should the applicant fail to respond within that period, or if the response does not adequately address the grounds raised by the Registrar, the Registrar may proceed with the examination of the application as if no response had been received. The Registrar considers all evidence and arguments presented by both parties before making a determination regarding whether the trademark is registrable. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar concerning registration or refusal may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days, provided that such an appeal shall not operate as a stay of the Registrar's order unless otherwise directed.

Upon receipt of an opposition notice under this Act, the Registrar shall give directions regarding its processing and determination. The Registrar may, at his discretion, require the parties involved to submit further documentary evidence or attend hearings to clarify their respective positions concerning the registrability of the trademark in question. Should any ambiguity arise during consideration of such evidence, the Registrar shall provide both parties with a reasonable opportunity for rebuttal. The Registrar considers all submissions and arguments presented before making a decision on the opposition. A notice detailing the Registrar’s findings and the rationale behind them will be served upon each party. Any request for an extension of time to file documents or attend hearings must be made in writing, subject to approval by the Registrar.

Where the registered proprietor of a trade mark desires to grant a license conferring the right to apply a trademark, or assign the entire ownership of such trade mark, to another party, they shall submit a formal notification to the Registrar. This notification must detail the scope and duration of the proposed license, or specify the terms of assignment including any royalties payable under the agreement. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating the consent of all relevant stakeholders involved in the transaction, particularly where the trade mark relates to goods or services subject to specific regulatory approvals. Upon receipt of this notification, the Registrar considers whether the proposed arrangement complies with the provisions relating to permissible use and dilution as provided herein. Any third party may object to the assignment within a period specified by the Registrar.

For the purposes of this Act, a “Registrar Statement” means a written communication issued by the Registrar concerning an application for registration or relating to a registered trademark. Such statement shall be binding upon the applicant or proprietor only to the extent that it explicitly addresses a procedural matter under this Act, or clarifies the interpretation of any provision herein pertaining to distinctiveness or deceptively similarity. A Registrar Statement does not constitute a determination on the merits of an application unless expressly so stated therein; provided that such express statement shall be subject to appeal as provided herein.

The Registrar, while considering an application for registration of a trade mark, may require the applicant to submit further particulars or documentary evidence substantiating the claim of use as required under this Act. Upon receipt of such information, the Registrar shall issue a written statement detailing any deficiencies observed in relation to the claimed distinctiveness or acquired reputation of the proposed mark. This registrar statement will be served upon the applicant and made available for public inspection at the Trade Marks Registry. The applicant shall then have a period of ninety days from the date of service within which to respond, either by amending the application or providing additional evidence as deemed necessary by the Registrar. Failure to adequately address the concerns raised in the registrar statement may result in rejection of the application.

Where, upon review of an objection filed under this Act against the acceptance of a proposed trademark, the Registrar finds that the grounds for opposition are not substantiated by evidence or legal precedent, the Registrar shall issue a statement affirming the initial acceptance. Such a registrar statement shall be binding on all parties involved in the proceedings unless appealed within sixty days from its publication in the Trade Marks Journal. Failure to appeal within this period will constitute acquiescence to the decision and bar any subsequent challenge to the trademark’s registration based on the original objection. The aggrieved party, having received such a registrar statement, may pursue remedies available under general law for misrepresentation or fraudulent inducement arising directly from the initial acceptance of the mark.

The Registrar shall, upon receipt of an objection under this Act, provide notice thereof to the applicant and the interested parties as provided herein. Such notice shall specify the grounds of the objection with sufficient particularity to enable the applicant and interested parties to formulate a response. Following consideration of any submissions made by the applicant or interested parties, the Registrar may proceed to issue a *Registrar statement* detailing the findings on which the decision regarding the application is based. This statement shall be recorded in the register and shall include reasons for accepting or rejecting arguments presented. The Registrar’s determination, as reflected in the Registrar statement, shall be final subject only to appeal under this Act. Any party aggrieved by a decision made following issuance of a Registrar statement may file an appeal within the prescribed time limit.

The Registrar shall, upon receipt of an objection under this Act, provide written notice to the applicant and the objector detailing the grounds for opposition. Such notice shall include a summary of the relevant provisions considered in formulating the objection. The Registrar may, after affording both parties a reasonable opportunity to submit their respective arguments and evidence within a stipulated timeframe as provided herein, issue a *Registrar statement* outlining findings on material facts and applicable legal principles. This statement is binding upon the Registrar for subsequent decision-making regarding the application unless substantial new evidence emerges demonstrating an error in the initial assessment. The applicant shall have the right to request clarification of any term used within the Registrar’s statement, subject to limitations as prescribed by regulations.

The Registrar shall, upon receiving an objection under this Act, issue a written statement detailing the grounds for such objection and specifying the relevant provisions relied upon. Any party aggrieved by the contents of the registrar’s statement may file a reply within sixty days from the date of its receipt, accompanied by any supporting evidence. Failure to file such a reply within the stipulated time shall be deemed an abandonment of the application, subject to the Registrar's discretion to grant extensions in cases of demonstrable hardship. The Registrar may, after considering the objection and any subsequent reply, proceed with or reject the registration application. Any deliberate misrepresentation made in connection with a registrar statement constitutes a punishable offence under this Act, attracting penalties as prescribed herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, and without prejudice to any existing agreements, the registered proprietor of a trademark may grant a license to use the said trademark relating to specified goods or services. Such licenses shall be assignable, either in whole or in part, along with the underlying rights granted by registration, provided that prior written consent is obtained from the Registrar for any such assignment. The Registrar’s statement regarding the acceptance of an assignment or license shall be conclusive evidence thereof, unless proven to be erroneous through due process under this Act. Any party seeking to challenge a registrar statement must provide demonstrable proof of material misrepresentation at the time of its issuance. Furthermore, sub-licensing is permitted, but requires notification to the registered proprietor and may be subject to conditions imposed by them as provided herein.

Where, following examination under this Act, the Registrar finds reasonable grounds to believe that a registered trade mark, utilized by an export concerned pharmaceutical company, is being used in a manner contrary to accepted standards of fair competition or creates confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or quality of goods, the Registrar shall issue a statement outlining these concerns. Such statement may be published in such manner as the Registrar deems appropriate and shall serve as prima facie evidence of infringement for the purposes of subsequent legal proceedings. Any party failing to comply with directions issued pursuant to a registrar statement shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees, and repeat offenders may face further penalties or revocation of registration.

A described trade mark shall mean a mark comprising exclusively of words and phrases indicating geographical origin, or denoting characteristics relating to the quality, properties, features, composition, quantity, size or shape of goods or services, or that have become associated with a particular enterprise or group of enterprises. Provided that such words and phrases are not distinctive in relation to the goods or services for which they are used; and further provided that the use of such described trade mark shall not be deemed to constitute passing off under this Act. The Registrar may require proof of the factual basis underlying any claim made in a described trade mark, as provided herein.

An application for registration of a described trade mark shall be refused if the representation of the marks is not clear and precise, enabling the competent authority to determine the extent of the protection sought. The applicant may submit further representations or explanations to clarify the description, subject to the condition that such clarifications do not fundamentally alter the essence of the applied-for mark. Where a described trade mark incorporates elements already registered as distinct trade marks under this Act, the application shall specify clearly how the combination creates a new and distinctive representation. The Registrar may require the applicant to provide detailed technical specifications illustrating the configuration of any three-dimensional or non-linear element forming part of the described trade mark.

The registered proprietor of a described trade mark shall be entitled to restrain the use of any representation in relation to goods or services that is identical or confusingly similar to their mark, provided that such use is made without consent. This right extends to preventing the application of a sign likely to be used as a trade name or for descriptive purposes if it creates confusion among consumers regarding the origin or characteristics of the goods or services. Further, where infringement has occurred, the proprietor may seek damages equivalent to the loss suffered by them due to the infringing activity, or in cases of flagrant disregard for their rights, an enhanced sum not exceeding ten times the actual damage. The remedies available under this Act are without prejudice to any other right or remedy which a party may have against the infringer.

A registered proprietor shall be entitled to institute proceedings for infringement under this Act against any person who, without the leave of the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, uses a sign identical or confusingly similar to the *described trade mark* in relation to goods or services identical or closely related to those in respect of which the registration is made. Such proceedings may be commenced in the High Court having jurisdiction over the place where the alleged infringement occurs, or where the defendant resides or carries on business. The Board shall consider applications for leave based upon factors including the bona fide nature of the use and any demonstrable consumer confusion arising therefrom. Evidence presented to the Appellate Board is admissible under this Act as evidence before the High Court in subsequent proceedings relating to the same matter. The Registrar may, following a complaint received from an aggrieved party, issue directions concerning cease and desist orders pending judicial determination.

A registered *described trade mark* shall be deemed to retain its distinctiveness where, following registration, the proprietor demonstrates continuous use of said mark across all relevant classes of goods and services as specified in the register. Such demonstration requires submission of annual affidavits attesting to such continued application, verifiable through inspection records maintained by the Registrar. Provided that, if an objection is raised regarding non-use during any period exceeding five years, the proprietor shall be obligated to provide substantive evidence substantiating ongoing commercial exploitation or a compelling justification for cessation. Failure to comply with this requirement may result in removal of the mark from the register under this Act and forfeiture of associated rights. The Registrar may require further documentation as deemed necessary to ascertain compliance.

Any individual or entity employing a described trade mark in connection with goods or services shall be liable to prosecution if such use is calculated to cause confusion amongst the public and results in dilution of the distinctive character of the registered trade mark. Where an infringement occurs, the owner may apply to the relevant court for an injunction restraining further infringing activity and for damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the proprietor as a consequence of the unauthorized use. Furthermore, any goods bearing the infringing described trade mark are subject to seizure and destruction at the expense of the offender, without prejudice to criminal proceedings initiated under this Act. Repeated or flagrant violations shall attract enhanced penalties, including imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, the registered proprietor of a described trade mark may grant licenses conferring specific rights relating to the use thereof. Such licenses shall clearly delineate the geographical area, the goods or services in relation to which the licensee is authorized to apply the described trade mark, and the duration of the license. Assignment of a described trade mark, or any interest therein, requires registration with the Registrar, provided that such assignment does not contradict the terms of any existing license agreement. Further, where a license has been granted, subsequent assignments shall be subject to the consent of the licensee unless the original license expressly provides otherwise. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating compliance with licensing conditions as part of an examination process under this Act.

Where an objection is taken under this Act against the registration of a proposed described trade mark on the ground that it does not distinguish the goods or services of the applicant from those of others, the Registrar shall give notice thereof to the applicant and all interested parties. Any interested party may, within such time as may be prescribed, file with the Registrar written representations either supporting or opposing the registration, stating the grounds upon which they are founded. The Registrar shall consider any such representations received and may afford the applicant and other interested parties an opportunity for oral hearing. An order of the Registrar refusing registration may be appealed to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within a period of sixty days from the date of receipt of that order.

An application for registration of a described trade mark shall be refused if the proposed marks are so similar as to likely cause confusion or misrepresentation concerning the identity of the applicant or connect with any goods or services in relation to which the applicant has previously used the mark. The Registrar may require an applicant to furnish such further particulars, documents and specimens relating to the use of the trade mark as he deems necessary for the purpose of determining whether the application is complete. Where a patent shall be granted for an invention incorporating elements identifiable within a registered described trade mark, the grant does not prejudice existing rights under this Act. The Registrar may extend the time allowed for filing documents provided that the applicant satisfies him that sufficient cause exists for such extension.

A registered described trade mark shall be deemed to retain its distinctiveness if, following registration, continuous use thereof has not occurred within the territory of India. Provided that, non-use attributable to conditions prevailing in the market, such as import restrictions or extraordinary economic circumstances, shall not constitute abandonment under this Act. The Registrar may, upon application by a registered proprietor demonstrating reasonable grounds for believing that another person is using an identical or confusingly similar mark, initiate inquiries concerning potential infringement. In any proceeding before the Registrar, the chairperson shall be responsible for ensuring procedural fairness and adherence to timelines as provided herein. Any finding of deceptive trade practices relating to a described trade mark may result in damages being awarded.

A consumer shall have recourse under this Act where it is established that another has engaged in conduct constituting a trade mark falsified. Such falsification occurs when an individual reproduces, adapts, or imitates a registered trade mark in relation to goods or services, creating likelihood of confusion amongst purchasers and prejudicing the reputation associated with the original mark. The proprietor of the trade mark shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief preventing further acts of falsification, as well as damages commensurate with the financial loss suffered due to the deceptive use. Provided that, where the infringing conduct is demonstrably unintentional or undertaken in good faith without knowledge of the registered trade mark, a court may exercise discretion in mitigating remedies. The proprietor must demonstrate reasonable grounds for believing that the actions constitute a trade mark falsified and have caused demonstrable harm.

A trademark shall be considered falsified where an individual reproduces, imitates, or adopts a mark identical or confusingly similar to a registered trademark in connection with goods or services. This applies irrespective of whether the reproduction is exact or involves minor alterations intended to create a deceptive impression regarding the origin or quality of those goods or services. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint from any person aggrieved by such falsification, issue a notice requiring the alleged infringer to appear and present their defense within a stipulated period. Failure to respond adequately to the notice shall be construed as an admission of guilt, permitting the Registrar to proceed ex parte. Any proprietor demonstrating that another’s use constitutes a trade mark falsified may seek injunctive relief and damages under this Act, subject to procedural safeguards ensuring due process for all parties involved.

Where the registered proprietor of a trade mark desires to grant a license for use of their trade mark, they may execute an assignment agreement specifying the permitted scope of application and geographic territory. Such licenses are transferable subject to conditions stipulated within the original registration or subsequent amendments filed under this Act. However, any alteration or modification to a registered trade mark, whether intended or unintentional, which results in a trade mark falsified as defined herein, shall render the responsible party liable for damages. This liability extends to those who reproduce or apply a falsified trade mark without express written consent from the proprietor, even if acting under a purportedly valid license agreement. The proprietor retains the right to terminate any license where evidence of such falsification is presented and deemed substantiated by an adjudicating authority.

A trade mark shall be considered falsified where an individual reproduces a mark identical or nearly so to a registered trade mark in relation to goods or services identical or closely resembling those for which the registration subsists. Such reproduction is deemed a falsification irrespective of intent to deceive, provided that it creates a likelihood of confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of the goods or services. The Registrar shall maintain a public record of all instances where a complaint alleging trade mark falsification has been filed and forwarded to the relevant civil court registry for adjudication. Any party aggrieved by an action constituting a trade mark falsified may initiate proceedings as provided herein, seeking injunctive relief and damages.

A geographical indication plaintiff alleging infringement under this Act shall demonstrate that the defendant has employed a sign which is identical or confusingly similar to the registered geographical indication “Kashmir Apples”, and that such use creates a likelihood of association with the genuine article. Where a trade mark falsified incorporates elements of a protected geographical indication, the proprietor of the geographical indication may pursue remedies as if the falsification directly infringed upon their exclusive rights. The defendant shall be required to prove reasonable grounds for believing that the use of the sign did not constitute a trade mark falsified or an attempt to mislead consumers regarding the origin of the goods. This requirement applies irrespective of whether the defendant is engaged in commercial activity within the geographical limits associated with “Kashmir Apples”.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be refused if the proposed mark, or any element thereof, is likely to be confused with an earlier registered trade mark, or a trade mark applied for in respect of identical or similar goods or services. Where an applicant has knowingly and wilfully adopted a mark that incorporates elements intended to falsely represent association with another entity possessing a pre-existing trade mark, such action shall constitute falsify trade mark under this Act. The Registrar may require the applicant to submit evidence demonstrating due diligence undertaken prior to application, including searches of existing registrations and pending applications. Failure to provide satisfactory evidence may result in refusal or revocation of registration, subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

A registered trade mark owner shall have recourse under this Act where another party intentionally utilizes a sign in commerce that creates a likelihood of confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of goods or services. Such utilization constitutes falsify trade mark if the infringing sign incorporates elements substantially identical to the distinctive characters of the registered mark, or combines those elements with other signs in a manner which produces such confusion. Provided that, where the use is solely for descriptive purposes relating to the characteristics of the goods or services and does not suggest any trade connection with the proprietor, it shall not be deemed an act of falsify trade mark as provided herein. Further, this provision applies irrespective of whether the infringing party had knowledge of the existence of the registered trade mark.

Any entity seeking to utilize a registered trade mark relating to pharmaceutical products for manufacturing, distribution, or promotional purposes shall obtain prior written consent from the trade mark proprietor. Such consent may be granted subject to conditions stipulated by the proprietor, including but not limited to restrictions on geographical territory, product categories within the pharmaceutical sector, and duration of usage. Failure to secure such authorization constitutes an act of falsify trade mark under this Act. The proprietor retains the right to assign or license their trade mark rights pertaining to pharmaceuticals to another party, provided that any subsequent assignee or licensee adheres strictly to the original conditions of consent. Any modification to the licensed use requires further written agreement from both the initial proprietor and the current licensee.

Where a registered trade mark is used in relation to goods or services in such a manner as to create a likelihood of confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or nature of those goods or services, and that use incorporates or imitates any element of another existing trade mark, it shall be deemed that the later mark falsifies genuine trade marks already established within the relevant class of goods. Provided that, where the proprietor of the earlier trade mark has demonstrably failed to exercise a continuous right to prevent such use for a period exceeding five years, the subsequent user may be permitted to continue their application subject to conditions determined by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. This permission shall not extend to instances where the falsification is intentional and undertaken with the primary purpose of unfairly benefiting from the reputation associated with the earlier mark.

Where a registered trade mark is employed in a manner that a consumer reasonably believes it originates from the proprietor of the mark, and such use constitutes a mark falsifies genuine, the Registrar may, subject to due process, issue an order restraining further application of said mark. This restraint shall be conditional upon demonstrable evidence presented by the aggrieved proprietor establishing actual or likely confusion amongst consumers. Furthermore, provided that the infringing use also incorporates elements demonstrably derived from a pending patent application relating to similar goods or services, the Registrar may direct the applicant for the patent shall entered into negotiations with the trade mark proprietor regarding equitable resolution of both intellectual property rights.

A trade mark shall be deemed to be falsified where an individual applies a sign, including words, letters, numerals, shapes, configurations, patterns or other marks, in relation to goods or services which creates a likelihood of confusion among consumers as to the origin, quality, characteristics, or intended purpose of those goods or services. For the purposes of this Act, "falsifies genuine trade" includes any modification, addition, subtraction, or distortion of an existing registered trade mark that results in misrepresentation concerning its ownership or affiliation with another entity. This applies irrespective of whether such actions are undertaken for commercial gain or other motives, subject to considerations of honest practices in industrial or commercial matters.

Where any person, through the use of a sign identical or confusingly similar to a registered trade mark, misrepresents the origin, nature, quality, characteristics, or geographical indication of goods or services, and thereby falsifies genuine trade enjoyed by the proprietor of that trade mark, such person shall be liable for damages. The amount of damages shall be determined based on the extent of financial loss suffered by the proprietor as a direct consequence of the deceptive practice, taking into consideration factors including lost sales, diminished reputation, and costs incurred in mitigating the harm caused. Further, under this Act, any goods bearing the infringing mark may be seized and destroyed at the expense of the offending party, provided that due process is followed to allow for representation before an adjudicating officer. The proprietor shall also be entitled to seek injunctive relief to restrain further acts of falsification.

A registered trade mark owner may institute proceedings in the District Court alleging that another party has falsified their genuine trade mark through the use of confusingly similar packaging for related goods. The court shall consider evidence presented by both parties regarding consumer perception and likelihood of confusion. Where a finding is made that such falsification has occurred, the defendant shall be liable to pay damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the registered proprietor, taking into account any benefit accruing to the defendant as a result of the infringing activity. Further, the court may issue an injunction restraining the defendant from continuing the practice which falsifies genuine trade and order the destruction or disposal of goods bearing the offending mark, subject to regulations prescribed under this Act concerning hazardous materials. The Registrar shall be notified of such orders for record.

A registered trade mark owner shall institute proceedings under this Act if another party’s use of a sign, symbol, or phrase creates a likelihood of confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or nature of goods or services. Such use constitutes falsifies genuine trade where the infringing application is made in relation to identical or similar goods or services to those for which the registered trade mark is used. Provided that, if the proprietor demonstrates that the infringing party had knowledge of the existence of the registered trade mark at the time of adoption and first use, the burden shall shift to the infringing party to prove absence of intent to deceive. Further, any alteration made to a genuine trade mark with the intention to mislead or create an erroneous association with the registered owner is deemed a falsification under this Act.

Any individual or entity that knowingly and wilfully employs a sign, symbol, name, or device in commerce which materially falsifies genuine trade marks registered under this Act shall be liable for damages. Such actions include, but are not limited to, the reproduction, imitation, or adoption of a mark so closely resembling a registered mark as to create confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or quality of goods or services. The proprietor of the registered trade mark may apply to the relevant intellectual property enforcement authority seeking an injunction restraining such infringing activity and claiming compensation for losses incurred due to the deceptive practice. Penalties, including fines and imprisonment, shall be imposed subject to considerations of aggravating factors as determined by the court.

A registered trade mark owner may grant a license to use their trade mark upon such terms and conditions as they deem fit, including but not limited to limitations on geographical territory, range of goods or services, and duration. Such licenses shall be assignable subject to prior notification to the Registrar and approval which shall not be unreasonably withheld. Where a licensee’s activities, undertaken pursuant to a valid license, demonstrably falsifies genuine trade marks belonging to other proprietors through deceptive packaging or advertising, the registered proprietor granting the license shall remain primarily liable under this Act, notwithstanding any contractual agreements between themselves and the licensee. Further, the Registrar may, upon receiving complaint, investigate instances where assignment of a trade mark license appears intended to circumvent restrictions imposed by the original registration, and may require further undertakings from the assignee.

Where an appeal is brought under this Act concerning a determination that a mark falsifies genuine trade, the Appellate Authority shall consider whether the respondent’s use of the impugned sign creates a likelihood of confusion amongst the relevant consuming public. It shall be presumed that such likelihood exists if the signs are identical and the goods or services are closely related; provided that this presumption may be rebutted by evidence demonstrating a clear distinction in channels of trade, consumer perception, or other factors as determined appropriate by the Authority. The respondent shall bear the onus of proving any such rebuttal.
