Further, the Appellate Authority may consider whether the use constitutes passing off under principles of common law, subject to the provisions herein relating to trade mark rights.

Where an individual, through the reproduction and distribution of artistic works incorporating a registered trademark, creates a representation that materially falsifies genuine trade, such actions constitute an infringement under this Act. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint from the registered proprietor, issue an injunction restraining further dissemination of the infringing material. Provided that, the complainant must demonstrate clear evidence of consumer confusion arising directly from the deceptive similarity between the artistic work and the protected trademark. Further, any claim of copyright violation relating to the underlying artwork shall be considered separately and will not automatically constitute a finding of trade mark falsification; however, such findings may be relevant in assessing damages. An appeal against an order issued under this provision lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal.

For the purposes of this Act, a “composite mark” means a mark comprising at least one element which is capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one undertaking from those of other undertakings and at least one other element which is not so distinctive. Where a composite mark includes elements that are separately registrable as trade marks, such elements shall be deemed to be registered individually under this Act, subject to any conditions specified in the registration certificate. A proprietor of a mark containing a *mark separately registered* within a larger design may seek rectification regarding only the portion constituting the separately registered mark, provided that such rectification does not prejudice the rights of other proprietors.

An application for the registration of a trade mark shall be refused if the proposed mark is deemed descriptive of the goods or services with which it is associated, subject to the applicant demonstrating acquired distinctiveness through established use. Where a composite mark includes elements capable of independent registration, and one or more such elements are already registered as a *mark separately registered* under this Act, the Registrar may grant registration for the remaining portions of the composite mark only if satisfied that the existing registrations do not prejudice the interests of the proprietor of those earlier marks. Further, any alteration to a trade mark after registration shall require prior approval from the Registrar and will be deemed invalid if it affects elements registered separately.

Where a trade mark is registered in relation to goods or services of one class, and subsequently applied for registration in relation to goods or services of another class, the Registrar may grant such subsequent registration subject to proof that the earlier registration does not create an unreasonable likelihood of confusion or misrepresentation as to the identity of the source of the respective goods or services. Any proprietor aggrieved by a decision under this Act relating to the refusal or acceptance of a mark separately registered may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of such decision. Further, any person who, without consent, uses a trade mark identical or confusingly similar to a mark separately registered shall be liable for damages sustained by the proprietor of the mark.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark includes a depiction of a composite mark, and a portion thereof is capable of distinguishing goods or services of one undertaking from those of another, the Trade Marks Registry may accept such application provided that the applicant specifies, in their application, which elements of the composite mark are claimed as a *mark separately registered*. The Registrar shall then record these distinct portions within the register. Any subsequent application incorporating any element of a previously registered mark separately registered shall be examined to ascertain whether it is likely to cause confusion or misrepresentation amongst consumers. Further, where an owner seeks to extend protection under this Act to a mark separately registered, they must file a request detailing the specific goods and services for which such extension is sought, subject to fulfilling all procedural requirements as provided herein.

Where an application for the registration of a trade mark includes depictions of multiple elements, and one or more of those elements are eligible for separate registration under this Act as a distinct trade mark, the Registrar shall permit such element or elements to be filed for registration as a mark separately registered, provided that the applicant demonstrates clear intention to pursue such separate registration at the time of initial application. The request for separation must specify the precise depiction constituting the proposed mark separately registered and its intended use, consistent with the overall trade mark’s representation. Further, any subsequent amendment to the main trade mark shall not affect the validity of a mark separately registered unless that amendment fundamentally alters the distinctive character of the separately registered element.

Where a proprietor seeks to enforce rights under this Act relating to a mark, and such mark comprises elements which are also marks separately registered in the name of another person, the proprietor shall be deemed to have waived any right to restrain use of those specifically marked elements unless it is demonstrated that the infringing use directly impacts the distinctiveness or reputation of the proprietor’s overall trade mark. Any party demonstrating wilful and intentional exploitation of a mark separately registered by another for unfair gain shall be liable to pay damages equivalent to three times the value of the infringing goods or services, subject to judicial review. Furthermore, such offending parties may face criminal prosecution under provisions relating to fraudulent impersonation as provided herein.

Where a proprietor elects to have a mark separately registered under this Act, and such registration has been completed, the proprietor shall retain exclusive rights pertaining solely to the elements comprising said mark as individually delineated in the certificate of registration. Assignment of the parent trademark shall not automatically extend to the mark separately registered unless expressly stated within the assignment documentation. Any license granted by the proprietor relating to the use of the main trade mark may be extended to cover the use of the mark separately registered, provided that such extension is clearly articulated and documented in writing, specifying the permitted scope of usage and duration. Further, sub-licensing of the mark separately registered shall require prior written consent from the original proprietor, subject to conditions as they deem fit.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark includes a representation of a composite mark wherein one or more elements are capable of distinguishing the goods or services of another person, and such element has been previously registered as a mark separately registered, the Registrar may direct the applicant to disclaim any right to the exclusive use of that pre-existing mark within the composite mark. Such direction shall not prejudice the applicant’s claim to registration of the remaining elements of the trade mark application, provided that the overall mark possesses distinctiveness. Any party aggrieved by such a direction may appeal under this Act to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The Registrar's determination regarding separability and prior registration shall be final unless overturned on appeal.

Where an application for the registration of a trade mark includes depictions of elements capable of separate registration under this Act, and such elements are not explicitly disclaimed by the applicant during examination proceedings, the Registrar shall afford the applicant opportunity to elect whether each element shall be treated as part of the composite mark or pursued as a mark separately registered. Should the applicant fail to make such an election within the prescribed timeframe, the application shall stand rejected in respect of any un-elected elements. Recognition trade marks, where eligible for registration, may also be considered for separate registration subject to compliance with all applicable provisions regarding distinctiveness and non-infringement as provided herein.

Any person who, without due cause and subject to the provisions regarding fair use under this Act, applies a false trademark identical or deceptively similar to a mark separately registered by another party shall be guilty of an offence. Such offender shall be liable for damages equivalent to three times the value of goods or services sold using the infringing mark, as determined by the Intellectual Property Enforcement Tribunal. Furthermore, repeated violations may result in imprisonment for a term not exceeding five years and a fine which may extend up to one million rupees. The Registrar may, upon complaint, issue an injunction restraining any person from further use of such trade marks registered or otherwise.

Where a trade mark is registered in the name of a company, and any element thereof is also registered *mark separately registered*, the proprietor may, subject to an agreement in writing, grant a license to use the entire trade mark or any particular goods or services associated with that mark. Such licenses shall be assignable by the grantor, provided that the assignee complies with all conditions precedent to the original registration and subsequent licensing agreements. Further, a company may, through board resolution duly recorded in its minutes, irrevocably assign the right to use a *mark separately registered* element of its composite trade mark to another entity, including an individual or partnership, as it deems fit. Any such assignment shall be notified to the Trade Marks Registry within thirty days and shall become effective upon registration thereof.

Where a trade mark comprises distinctive elements which are capable of separate registration and are so registered, such elements shall be deemed marks separately registered for the purposes of this Act. The owner of a trade mark may use any one or more of these marks separately registered, provided that the trade description manner in which they are used does not falsely represent to the public that the goods or services originate from an unrelated source. Any alteration to a mark separately registered shall not affect its continued registration unless such alteration substantially changes the distinctive character of the element itself as it was originally registered.

The Registrar shall maintain a comprehensive supervision registrar index, accessible to the public during normal office hours, detailing all trademarks registered under this Act and those applications currently undergoing examination. Any party aggrieved by an entry or omission within said index may, subject to procedural guidelines as provided herein, petition the Registrar for rectification. Such petitions must specify the nature of the error and provide supporting documentation demonstrating grounds for correction. The Registrar shall consider such petitions expeditiously and issue a reasoned order either rectifying the index or dismissing the claim. Failure to comply with the prescribed timelines in processing rectification requests may render the Registrar liable for compensatory damages, as determined by an appropriate adjudicating authority. Further, any deliberate falsification of information submitted for inclusion within the supervision registrar index constitutes a cognizable offence and is subject to penalties as stipulated under this Act.

The Registrar shall maintain a comprehensive and publicly accessible index of all trademarks registered under this Act, detailing proprietor information and goods/services classifications. Any party aggrieved by an inaccuracy or omission in the supervision registrar index may file a complaint with the Registrar within sixty days of the date of publication of the relevant section of the index. Upon receiving such a complaint, the Registrar shall investigate expeditiously and issue a reasoned order within thirty days; failure to do so will constitute prima facie evidence of negligence. Deliberate falsification or manipulation of entries in the supervision registrar index is punishable with imprisonment for a term not less than two years, but which may extend to five years, and with a fine which shall not be less than fifty thousand rupees.

The Registrar shall maintain a comprehensive supervision registrar index detailing all assignments and licenses relating to registered trademarks, including those arising from collective or certification marks. Any assignment or license granted under this Act shall be recorded in the said index within thirty days of its execution by submitting a prescribed form along with the requisite fee. The Registrar may, upon receiving such documentation, require further clarification or supporting evidence deemed necessary for verification. Failure to register an assignment or license as provided herein will render it unenforceable against third parties unless demonstrable prejudice is shown. Furthermore, any subsequent modification or termination of a registered license shall also be recorded in the supervision registrar index promptly and according to prescribed procedures. The Registrar’s determination regarding the validity of such recordings is final, subject to appeal under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, “index names proprietors” shall mean a publicly accessible register maintained by the Registrar, detailing the individuals or entities legally recognized as owners of trademarks registered under this Act. This register shall include full legal names, addresses for service, and dates of proprietorship commencement. Any alteration in ownership, including assignment or transmission, must be formally recorded to maintain accuracy within the index names proprietors. The Registrar may require supporting documentation verifying such changes. Information contained herein is subject to correction procedures as provided herein, ensuring fairness to all parties concerned with trademark rights.

Where a proprietor of a trade mark seeks to assign or license their rights under this Act, they shall provide notice of such transaction to the Registrar within thirty days of its execution. Failure to do so may render the assignment or licence unenforceable against third parties who have not received actual notice. The Registrar shall maintain an index names proprietors affected by assignments and licences recorded under this Act, accessible for public inspection upon payment of a prescribed fee. Any person aggrieved by an entry in such index may apply to the Registrar for its correction or deletion, subject to demonstrating material error or misrepresentation. The Registrar’s decision on such applications is final, provided that it is not open to appeal under any other provision of this Act.

The Registrar shall maintain a comprehensive register detailing all index names proprietors associated with registered trademarks, accessible for public inspection during normal office hours subject to payment of prescribed fees. Applications concerning changes in proprietorship, including alterations to index names, must be submitted in Form TM-P and accompanied by an affidavit verifying the accuracy of information provided. The Registrar may require further documentation as deemed necessary to establish legal entitlement under this Act. Any objection to a proposed change in an index name proprietor shall be notified to all interested parties within thirty days of receipt by the Registrar, affording them opportunity for representation before a decision is rendered. Decisions regarding index names proprietors are appealable to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order.

The Registrar shall maintain a comprehensive register detailing all index names proprietors associated with registered trademarks, ensuring accuracy and accessibility to interested parties. Any alteration in proprietorship affecting an index name proprietor requires notification to the Registrar within thirty days, accompanied by supporting documentation demonstrating legal transfer or assignment. Failure to comply with this provision may result in temporary suspension of trademark rights until rectification is confirmed. Furthermore, any third party possessing a demonstrable interest in a registered trademark shall be afforded reasonable opportunity to review and contest entries concerning index names proprietors under this Act. The Registrar may, upon receiving credible evidence of inaccuracies or irregularities, initiate investigations and mandate corrective actions as deemed necessary for maintaining the integrity of the register.

Any person who, without due cause or reasonable excuse, knowingly uses a mark identical or confusingly similar to a registered trade mark, or any mark which is likely to be confused with such registered trade mark, shall be liable for damages as determined by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint from an aggrieved proprietor, issue a notice requiring the offending party to cease such use and submit evidence of compliance within thirty days. Failure to comply with such notice shall render the offender subject to further penalties including but not limited to fines up to one million rupees and potential injunctions preventing continued infringement. The index names proprietors are deemed vital for enforcement proceedings under this Act.

The Registrar shall maintain a comprehensive register detailing the assignment and licensing of rights pertaining to registered trademarks, including provisions for collective mark schemes. Any proprietor seeking to assign or license their trademark, or any portion thereof, to another party shall file a formal notice with the Registrar within thirty days of such transaction. This notice must specify the precise index names proprietors involved in the transfer, the scope of the assigned rights, and the duration of any licensing agreement. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating the validity of the assignment or license, as deemed necessary. Failure to comply with these notification requirements shall render the assignment or license unenforceable against third parties unless registered within a period of six months from the date of execution. Further provisions relating to sub-licensing are detailed under this Act.

Notwithstanding anything contained herein, a proprietor seeking to challenge the entry of a name within the index names proprietors shall serve notice upon the Registrar and the individual whose name is so listed, specifying the grounds for objection with particularity. The Registrar may, after affording both parties an opportunity for hearing and presentation of evidence, direct the removal or amendment of such entry if it is established that the inclusion was erroneous or based on information demonstrably false. An aggrieved party dissatisfied with the Registrar’s decision under this Act may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within a period of sixty days from the date of communication of the order; provided that any appeal shall be accompanied by a deposit of such fees as may be prescribed.

The Registrar shall maintain a comprehensive index, accessible to the public upon payment of prescribed fees, detailing the names of all *index names proprietors* registered under this Act. Any proprietor desiring to grant a license for use of their trade mark, or assign their rights therein, must file a memorandum with the Registrar outlining the scope and duration of such permission. This memorandum shall clearly describe the *described trade mark*, including any variations permitted under the license or assignment. The Registrar may require further clarification or documentation as deemed necessary to ascertain the validity and enforceability of the proposed arrangement. Such licenses and assignments are subject to review by the Registrar, who shall ensure they do not contravene any provisions of this Act regarding unfair competition or consumer deception. A copy of each filed memorandum shall be added to the relevant index within thirty days.

Where the proprietor of a trade mark reasonably believes that another person is using an identical or confusingly similar trade mark in relation to goods or services identical or closely related to those for which the registration is made, and such use constitutes infringement under this Act, the proprietor shall be entitled to institute proceedings for relief. Such relief may include an injunction restraining the infringing party from further use of the impugned mark, as well as damages sustained by the proprietor due to the infringement. The amount of damages shall be determined having regard to factors including the extent of the infringement and any loss of profits suffered. Provided that where the infringing activity was committed unknowingly or with a genuine belief in the right to use the mark, the court may reduce the amount of damages awarded. Further, the proprietor may seek an account of profits made by the infringer as a result of their unauthorized exploitation thereof protection trade marks.

An application for registration of a design act relating to an integrated circuit layout shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the drawings or photographic representations clearly depicting the said design. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further particulars concerning the design, including details regarding its functionality and intended use, provided that such requirements are reasonable and do not unduly burden the application process. Where the applicant is an entity incorporated outside India, they shall designate a person resident in India as their agent for all purposes under this Act. The Registrar shall register the design act upon satisfaction that it meets the criteria of originality and novelty as defined herein, and shall issue a certificate of registration accordingly.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to the grant or refusal of registration of a layout-design or any other matter arising under this Act may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order appealed against, and shall state specifically the grounds on which the appeal is based. The Appellate Board may allow or dismiss the appeal, or may substitute the decision appealed against with a different decision. Where a layout-design has been copied in contravention of this Act, the owner of the design shall be entitled to seek remedies including damages, injunctions and delivery up of infringing copies. Compensation for infringement shall be determined having regard to the loss suffered by the owner as well as the profit made by the infringer. The right conferred by registration under this Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Act is subject to any prior use or publication.

An application for registration of a design act relating to an integrated circuit layout shall be filed with the Office, in the prescribed form and manner. The applicant shall furnish particulars specifying the nature of the design, including drawings or photographs clearly illustrating the features of the layout. Upon receipt of such application, the Registrar may require further information or clarification deemed necessary for proper examination under this Act. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application may prefer an appeal to the Controller within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The Controller shall give notice to all parties concerned and afford them an opportunity of being heard before passing any order on such appeal, provided that the findings of the Controller shall be final.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, a person claiming ownership of a registered semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be entitled to exclusive rights comprising technological protection and subject to compliance with prescribed standards. Such entitlement arises upon successful registration and continued adherence to renewal timelines as provided herein. The right to apply for registration of a design act is conditional upon demonstrating that the layout-design is original, not previously published anywhere in the world, and does not contain elements solely derived from existing prior art. Furthermore, any modification or adaptation of a registered layout-design shall require explicit consent from the proprietor unless such alteration falls within permissible fair use guidelines as determined by the relevant adjudicating authority. The Controller may issue directions regarding compliance with these conditions.

Any person who, without due authorization from the registered proprietor of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design, makes, imports, sells, or offers to sell any product in which the design is applied or embodied, shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall be determined by the Court, taking into consideration the loss of profits suffered by the proprietor and reasonable royalty that such infringer would have paid had they obtained a license under this Act. The Court may also issue an injunction restraining the infringing party from further acts of infringement, subject to conditions as it deems fit. Repeated or willful infringements shall attract enhanced penalties, including imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, and fines which may extend to ten times the value of goods produced or sold infringing the design act.

The right in a registered design act shall vest initially with the registrant, who may grant licenses conferring specific rights relating to the exploitation of the layout-design. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and may stipulate limitations on geographical territory or field of use, subject to the terms being clearly defined within the license agreement. Assignment of the registered design act is permissible, provided that such assignment is recorded with the Controller of Layout-Designs. Any subsequent licensee shall hold rights as per the original grant, but cannot further assign those rights without explicit consent from the initial registrant unless otherwise stipulated in their licensing contract. The Controller may require evidence demonstrating a genuine commercial intention behind any proposed license or assignment to ensure protection against frivolous claims and maintain the integrity of registered designs.

Where a claim for protection of a design act is contested upon grounds of prior publication, the claimant shall bear the onus of demonstrating that such publication did not reasonably disclose all features of the layout-design necessary to enable a person skilled in the art to reproduce the integrated circuit. Provided that, where the alleged prior publication occurred outside India, the burden shifts to the respondent alleging prior publication to establish the date and circumstances of said disclosure. Any appeal against an order determining validity under this Act may be made within sixty days from the date of such order, subject to a stay application being filed concurrently with the memorandum of appeal; failure to do so shall render the appeal non-joinder. The Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal may, in its discretion, permit late filing where good cause is demonstrated.

A registered design shall relate to the shape, configuration, pattern or ornament applied to an article; provided that it does not include features solely for utility or functionality. For the purposes of this Act, "article" means any three-dimensional object having aesthetic appeal and susceptible of being manufactured by any industrial process or craft. An application for registration of a design shall disclose full particulars as to its shape, colour, and construction; furthermore, it must clearly demonstrate that the registered design is novel and possesses individual character when applied to the article. The Controller may require further information under this Act concerning the nature of the design.

An application for registration of a registered design shall be accompanied by such information as may be prescribed, including detailed representations in the form of drawings or photographs clearly illustrating the features of the design and its intended use. The Controller General may require amendments to the application if he considers them necessary for clarity or precision, provided that such amendments do not alter the identity of the registered design sought to be protected. Upon acceptance of the application, a certified copy of the accepted design shall be published in the Design Journal. Any person aggrieved by a decision relating to registration or rejection may appeal under this Act to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of that decision.

The proprietor of a registered design shall be entitled to sue for relief in respect of any infringement of his exclusive right under this Act. Such infringement includes unauthorized making or imitation of the registered design where it is used for the purposes of trade or export. Where an infringement has occurred, the Controller may grant such remedies as are equitable and just, including injunctions restraining further acts of infringement and orders requiring the delivery up to the proprietor of all infringing articles in his possession or under his control. Compensation for loss suffered by the proprietor due to the infringement shall be determined by the Court, taking into account factors such as the extent of the damage caused and any profits made by the infringer. Provided that, a design shall not be deemed infringed if it falls within the scope of an exception provided herein.

An application for registration of a registered design shall include particulars specifying the article in respect of which the design is claimed, a statement showing whether the design relates to any trade mark or service mark used in relation to the goods or services, and representations of the design in the form of drawings or photographs as the Controller may direct. The applicant shall furnish such documentary evidence as the Controller deems necessary to establish ownership or right to apply for registration. Where an application contains more than one design, each design shall be treated separately for the purposes of examination and registration under this Act. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Controller relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of such decision. The Board’s determination shall be final subject to further appeals as provided herein.

An application for registration of a design shall be refused if the proposed design is not new or does not involve an aesthetic feature; provided that information which has been disclosed to the public by any means before the date of filing of the application, subject to certain conditions as provided herein, shall not preclude registration. The Controller may require the applicant to amend the design drawings and specifications to clearly define the features claimed as original. A registered design confers upon the proprietor exclusive right to apply or import the design in relation to articles falling within the class specification indicated in the register. Any person infringing a registered design shall be liable for damages, subject to limitations regarding proportionality of compensation awarded under this Act.

Any proprietor of a registered design shall be deemed to be the owner thereof for all purposes under this Act; provided that where a registered design has been infringed, the proprietor may institute suit for damages recoverable by way of injunction and monetary compensation against any person who without permission has made, sold, offered for sale, or in any other manner dealt with an article embodying the design. The Controller shall, upon receiving complaint from aggrieved party, issue notice to alleged infringer requiring them to appear before him and present their defence; failure to comply may result in ex parte proceedings and a finding of infringement. Any order made under this Act is subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days.

The owner of a registered design shall be entitled to grant licenses conferring rights to exploit the design in relation to articles within the scope of the design, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated in the license agreement. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as determined by the proprietor; provided that any exclusive license granted shall be recorded with the Controller upon application and payment of a prescribed fee. Assignment of the registered design or any such license is permissible, and must also be formally documented with the Controller to be considered valid against third parties claiming rights under this Act. The assignee shall automatically step into the shoes of the assignor regarding all existing rights and obligations pertaining to the registered design. Any subsequent transfer or further licensing undertaken by the assignee shall adhere to these provisions as provided herein, ensuring transparency and clarity in ownership transitions.

Where an appeal is brought under this Act from a decision of the Controller refusing registration of a design, the Appellate Board may, subject to any conditions it deems fit to impose, allow the appeal and direct that the design be registered, or may dismiss the appeal; and in allowing or dismissing such appeal, the Board shall have regard only to the grounds specified in the notice of appeal. Any party aggrieved by an order passed by the Appellate Board under this Act may further appeal to the High Court within whose territorial jurisdiction the appellate authority is situated, but only on a question of law. The validity of a registered design may be challenged before the Controller based on prior use or publication, provided that such challenge is made within one year from the date of registration and demonstrates substantial similarity to an existing article.

Any proprietor desiring to institute a suit for infringement of a registered design shall first serve upon the alleged infringer a notice in writing specifying the nature of the infringement and demanding that such infringement be discontinued, and if the infringement continues after the expiration of two months from the date of service of such notice, the proprietor may institute such suit. Provided that, where an application for registration of a design has been filed, and the applicant has obtained an application registration mark in respect thereof, the provisions relating to damages for pre-registration use shall apply as if the design were registered on the date of the first use by the alleged infringer after publication of the application registration mark. Further, any person found to have infringed a registered design shall be liable to pay such compensation as the Court deems fit, taking into account the loss suffered by the proprietor and the profits made by the infringing party.

Any proprietor of a registered design shall be liable for damages sustained by any person through infringement of that design under this Act. Such damages shall include compensation for loss of profits attributable to the infringing activity, and where the infringement was wilful, may extend to an enhanced amount as determined by the Controller. The filing specification matter relating to a registered design is deemed conclusive evidence of the features claimed therein unless proven otherwise before a court or tribunal. Any party seeking to challenge the validity of a registered design based on discrepancies between the filed specification and the actual design shall bear the burden of demonstrating such inconsistency with clear and convincing evidence, subject to penalties for frivolous claims as provided herein.

The owner of a registered design shall be entitled to grant licenses conferring rights to exploit the design commercially, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated in the license agreement; provided that such agreements must clearly define the scope of permitted use, including but not limited to manufacture, sale, import, or distribution of articles incorporating the design. Any assignment of the registered design, whether absolute or partial, shall require registration with the Controller of Designs and shall be deemed invalid unless so recorded. Where a license is granted under this Act relating to a design that has been subject to international registration prescribed by the Regulations for Administration of Designs, the terms of such license shall explicitly address any conflicting rights arising from the international registration. The owner may also assign the right to collect royalties pertaining to licenses granted as provided herein.

An appeal lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal under this Act if any party aggrieved by an order passed by the Registrar relating to the revocation or amendment of a registered design considers that order to be contrary to law or based on erroneous findings of fact. The Tribunal shall, after giving notice to all parties involved and affording them opportunities for being heard, determine the matter arising on appeal; provided that the Tribunal may dismiss the appeal if it finds that the appellant has not made out a prima facie case demonstrating substantial injustice resulting from the Registrar’s decision. Further, where the design in question incorporates elements originating within a Contracting Party, the provisions regarding novelty assessment shall be interpreted consistently with international obligations as agreed upon by the Government.

For the purposes of this Act, a "design" shall mean any visual feature, pattern, configuration, composition of lines or colours or shape, whether two dimensional or three dimensional, applied to an article by means of an industrial process or which is intrinsically present on the article. A design shall not include a trade mark under this Act as defined in the Trade Marks Act, 1999, nor shall it include any property mark used to indicate origin. The term "article" includes any three-dimensional object or surface relief and relates to the aesthetic characteristics of the shape and configuration; however, features solely for utility purposes are excluded from consideration under this design sub section.

An application for registration of a design shall include particulars as prescribed, including detailed representations demonstrating the aesthetic characteristics claimed. The applicant may submit additional views or sketches illustrating aspects not readily apparent in the principal design representation, subject to approval by the Controller. Registration under this Act confers exclusive rights to use and apply the registered design, provided that such use does not conflict with existing prior usage. Any alteration to the registered design after its initial registration requires a formal request for modification, assessed according to established procedures. The design sub section dictates that subsequent applications relating to substantially identical designs shall be rejected unless demonstrating significant inventive novelty over previously published works.

Where a registered proprietor institutes an action claiming infringement of his design, it shall be presumed that the design was valid and had been infringed unless the defendant proves otherwise, subject to the provisions regarding novelty as provided herein. The Court may grant such relief as it deems fit, including permanent or interim injunctions restraining the infringing party from further exploitation of the impugned design, alongside damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the registered proprietor. In determining the amount of damages, consideration shall be given to the defendant’s profits attributable to the infringement and the reasonable royalty that would have been payable had the defendant obtained a license under this Act. The Court may also order delivery up or destruction of infringing goods, dies, printing blocks, and other materials used in making such goods, provided that the registered proprietor demonstrates genuine commercial harm. Any appeal from an order made under this design sub section shall lie to the High Court.

An application for registration of a design shall contain particulars as prescribed, including a clear and accurate representation of the design. The Controller may require an applicant to amend any such representation if it is deemed deficient in clarity or accuracy, providing written reasons for the requirement. Where an amendment is necessitated due to a deficiency relating to the aesthetic characteristics of the design itself, the application shall be considered as one made originally with the amended representation. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Controller regarding the acceptance or rejection of a design under this Act may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of such decision. The determination of novelty and originality concerning a design sub section is subject to examination by the Controller, who shall consider prior published designs and existing works.

An application for registration of a design shall include particulars specifying the article in relation to which the design is applied, and such article must be solely ornamental or primarily intended for use as an article of decoration. The Controller may require the applicant to amend the design to ensure its distinctiveness under this Act. Where a design incorporates features dictated by technical function or process, it shall not be registrable unless those features are combined with elements that contribute significantly to aesthetic appeal. Registration of a design sub section relating to prior publishing requires disclosure of all instances where the design or substantially similar designs have been publicly revealed before the application’s filing date, subject to exceptions as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act may appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such order, provided that the Appellate Board shall consider any application for extension of time made in writing with reasons satisfactory to the court. Where a design registration is revoked or suspended due to infringement, the proprietor shall be liable to pay damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the aggrieved party, as determined by the Controller. Failure to comply with an injunction order issued under this Act regarding unauthorized copying of a registered design shall attract penalties including fines not exceeding two hundred thousand rupees and imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years. The provisions relating to design sub section registration are subject to judicial review.

The registered proprietor of a design shall, subject to the provisions herein, have the exclusive right to exploit commercially the design as recorded in the Register. Such exploitation may include, but is not limited to, manufacture, import, sale, offering for sale, or hire of articles incorporating the design. A registered proprietor desiring to grant a license relating to the design sub section shall execute an agreement specifying the scope and duration of such license, including any royalties payable. The licensee shall be bound by the terms of the license agreement and may not assign the right to exploit the design further without express written consent from the original registered proprietor. Any assignment of the entire design, or a substantial part thereof, requires notification to the Controller within thirty days, accompanied by prescribed fees. Failure to notify shall render the assignee liable for penalties as provided herein.

An appeal lies to the High Court within a period of sixty days from the date of receipt of the order sought to be appealed against, provided that the Appellate Board may, if it is satisfied that the appellant was prevented by sufficient cause from filing the appeal within the said time, allow it to be filed within such extended time as it thinks just. The determination of whether a design is registered or not shall be final subject only to an appeal under this Act. Any party aggrieved by any order made by the Appellate Board may further appeal to the High Court on grounds specified in the pleadings and supported by affidavits, concerning the interpretation of provisions relating to design sub section registration and novelty assessment. The Central Government may intervene in any such appeal with leave of the court.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to the registration of a design, including decisions concerning the validity of a registered design or the rectification of the register, shall have the right to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeals must be filed within ninety days from the date of communication of the order appealed against. Failure to comply with this time limit shall render the appeal inadmissible. The Registrar may, subject to any directions issued by the Board, impose a penalty for making false statements or suppressing material facts in connection with an application for registration or regarding a permitted register trade mark. Any infringement of design sub section rights is actionable under this Act and will be dealt with summarily.

Where an objection is raised by any person claiming through assignment or succession against a registered design, alleging that the design lacks novelty or originality as defined under this Act, such objection shall be deemed to constitute grounds for appeal. The Appellate Board may, upon hearing both the proprietor of the design and the objector, determine whether the design in question satisfies the requirements for registration. Provided that, if the objector demonstrates that identical or substantially similar designs were imported into India prior to the date of application for registration, and such importation occurred in violation of the Customs Act 1962, this shall be considered a material factor in assessing novelty. The Board’s decision on appeals relating to design sub section matters shall be final.

Where an infringement of layout-design rights has been established under this Act, the proprietor shall be entitled to seek remedies including, but not limited to, injunctions restraining further acts of infringement and damages commensurate with the loss suffered. The Court may also order the delivery up or destruction of infringing integrated circuits, layouts, or any materials used in their manufacture. In cases where the infringer has knowingly and willfully engaged in persistent and widespread unauthorized reproduction or adaptation of a registered layout-design, the Court may direct forfeiture directed of all assets derived from such infringement, including profits realized and equipment utilized in the unlawful activity. This power of forfeiture is without prejudice to any other remedies available under this Act or at law, provided that due process considerations are observed throughout proceedings.

Where an integrated circuit layout-design has been determined to infringe under this Act, and where the proprietor demonstrates substantial financial loss directly attributable to such infringement, the Court may direct forfeiture of assets utilized in the infringing activity. Such assets shall include, but are not limited to, manufacturing equipment, storage media containing unauthorized copies, and any proceeds derived from the commercial exploitation of the layout-design. Provided that, before a direction for forfeiture is issued, the infringer shall be afforded an opportunity to present evidence demonstrating legitimate use or ownership of the contested assets. Further, forfeiture directed will only occur if the Court finds that the infringing party knowingly engaged in activities violating the provisions herein and failed to comply with cease and desist orders previously served.

Where an integrated circuit layout-design incorporates elements derived from a protected film sound recording, and such incorporation constitutes a substantial reproduction without due authorization, the owner of the copyright in the film sound recording shall have the right to demand assignment of the relevant layout-design rights. This assignment shall be executed within ninety days of written notification served upon the assignee, detailing the infringing elements and their provenance. Failure to comply with this demand will render the assignor liable for forfeiture directed of the integrated circuit layout-design, which may then be licensed by the copyright holder under terms deemed equitable by a designated adjudicating officer. Any sub-licensees deriving rights through such assignment are bound by the original licensing conditions as stipulated in the forfeited layout-design documentation and shall remain subject to this Act.

The court registrar, in exercising powers conferred under this Act, shall be deemed a judicial officer within local limits for all purposes relating to the discharge of his duties. The court registrar may require any party or person concerned with an application or proceeding before him to furnish such information and documentation as is reasonably necessary for the proper determination thereof. Provided that, where the court registrar receives conflicting evidence concerning the distinctiveness of a geographical indication, he shall record reasons in writing for accepting one piece of evidence over another. The court registrar's decisions are subject to appeal under this Act.

Applications for registration of a geographical indication shall be submitted to the court registrar in the prescribed form, accompanied by particulars specifying the name and address of the applicant, the description of the goods or services for which the geographical indication is sought, and a map accurately depicting the territorial limits of the geographical area. The court registrar may require the applicant to furnish further information or clarification regarding any aspect of the application, provided that such requirements are reasonable and do not unduly delay the registration process. Upon receipt of an application, the court registrar shall issue an acknowledgment containing a date of receipt. Any objections received under this Act concerning the distinctiveness or reputation of the geographical indication must be promptly communicated to both the applicant and the relevant authorities for consideration.

Any proprietor seeking rectification of a registered geographical indication shall file an application with the court registrar, setting forth the grounds upon which such rectification is claimed and supported by affidavits. The court registrar may require the applicant to provide further particulars or clarification regarding the claims made in the application. Failure to comply with such requirements within the time specified may result in the rejection of the application. Upon receiving a valid application for rectification, the court registrar shall notify the registered proprietor of the geographical indication and afford them an opportunity to file their response under this Act. The court registrar’s decision on any rectification proceedings is subject to appeal to the relevant High Court within sixty days from the date of such decision. Any order made by the court registrar may be enforced as if it were a decree of that High Court.

Applications for registration of geographical indications shall be filed with the court registrar in the prescribed form and accompanied by all requisite documentation demonstrating distinctiveness and origin. The court registrar is empowered to scrutinize applications for completeness and adherence to procedural requirements under this Act. Any deficiency identified during examination may be communicated to the applicant, who shall have a period of ninety days from the date of such communication to rectify the same. Failure to address deficiencies within that timeframe will result in rejection of the application by the court registrar. Objections received from interested parties regarding the proposed geographical indication must be promptly forwarded to the relevant authority for consideration and adjudication. The court registrar maintains records pertaining to all applications, registrations, and oppositions as provided herein, accessible subject to applicable privacy regulations.

Applications for registration of a geographical indication shall be examined by the court registrar to ascertain compliance with the provisions relating to distinctiveness and reputation. The registrar may require the applicant to submit further documentation demonstrating exclusive use or prior established reputation within the defined territory, provided that such requests are limited to information reasonably necessary for assessment under this Act. Any objection raised against an application must be served upon the applicant within sixty days of publication in the Geographical Indications Journal; failure to do so shall render the objection inadmissible. The court registrar is empowered to conduct hearings and consider oral arguments from both proponents and opponents, ensuring a fair opportunity for all parties to present their case as provided herein.

Any proprietor seeking rectification of a registered geographical indication shall file an application with the court registrar, specifying the particulars of the alleged error or omission and supported by affidavits. Failure to comply with prescribed forms or pay requisite fees at the time of filing renders the application void ab initio. The court registrar may summarily reject any application demonstrably frivolous or vexatious, providing written reasons for such rejection which shall be communicated to the applicant within thirty days. Any person aggrieved by an order of the court registrar rejecting an application may appeal to the Appellate Board under this Act within sixty days from the date of communication of that order; penalties for non-compliance with timelines are as provided herein.

The owner of a registered geographical indication shall be entitled to grant non-exclusive licenses conferring the right to use the indication on goods conforming to the standards of quality and characteristics prescribed for that indication, provided that any such license agreement specifies the territory in which the licensee is authorized to operate. Assignment of rights under a registered geographical indication may occur with the consent of the Registrar, who shall consider whether the assignee possesses the requisite expertise and commitment to uphold the reputation and distinctiveness associated with the indication. Further, where an assignment involves transfer of control over production or processing related to the indicated goods, the Registrar may require submission of a detailed business plan demonstrating continued adherence to established quality protocols. The court registrar is empowered to review license terms for fairness and compliance with this Act.

An appeal lies to the Appellate Board from any order passed by the court registrar refusing registration of an indication or revoking a registered geographical indication, provided that the appeal is filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The Registrar may entertain an application for rectification of a register on grounds including newly discovered facts demonstrating consumer confusion arising from use of a similar sign, but such applications are subject to review by the court registrar before being referred to the Appellate Board. Any party aggrieved by an interlocutory order passed by the court registrar in proceedings relating to registration or revocation may appeal under this Act to the Appellate Board within thirty days, and the appellate authority shall determine whether the order was demonstrably erroneous.

The owner of a registered geographical indication shall be entitled to grant licenses relating to the use of the said indication, and such license may be exclusive or non-exclusive, perpetual or for a limited duration, subject to terms and conditions approved by the court registrar. Any assignment of rights in respect of a registered geographical indication, including any right to sublicense, shall require prior notification to the Registrar and registration with him, provided that the Registrar may refuse registration if he deems the proposed assignee not suitable to protect the interests connected with the indication. Further, where marks registered associated with a geographical indication are also assigned, the assignment documentation must explicitly detail the relationship between the geographical indication and such marks, ensuring continued protection under this Act. The court registrar shall maintain a record of all licenses and assignments for public inspection.

An appeal lies to the Appellate Board against any order passed by the court registrar refusing registration of a geographical indication, or revoking its registration. Such an appeal shall be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order to the applicant or registered proprietor, as the case may be. The Appellate Board may, after giving notice to all parties concerned and affording them an opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify, or reverse the order appealed against. Where a geographical indication is opposed under this Act, the court registrar shall provide both the interested party and the applicant with a reasonable opportunity to present their case. The layout design registrar may be called upon by the court registrar to furnish technical expertise in matters pertaining to distinctive signs.

For the purposes of this Act, a “court registrar” means an officer appointed by the Central Government and assigned specific duties relating to the registration process for Geographical Indications, including but not limited to receiving applications, conducting preliminary examinations, maintaining records pertaining to registered Geographical Indications, and issuing certificates of registration as provided herein. The court registrar shall be responsible for ensuring compliance with all procedural requirements under this Act and may request further information from applicants or other interested parties to facilitate the determination of eligibility for registration of a Geographical Indication. Decisions of the court registrar are subject to appeal before the Appellate Board.

Applications for registration of geographical indications shall be filed with the court registrar in the prescribed form and accompanied by such fees as may be determined. The registrar is empowered to require the applicant to submit further particulars or clarifications regarding the application, including detailed descriptions of the production methods employed within the defined geographical area. Any interested party may, within sixty days from the date of publication of a notice under this Act, file an opposition to the registration. Such oppositions shall be adjudicated by the court registrar after providing all parties with an opportunity for hearing and presentation of evidence. The registrar’s decision on any such opposition is final, subject to appeal before the Appellate Board. Consideration may be given to whether integrated circuits layout designs used in production processes are integral to the geographical indication's character.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder, the registered proprietor of a geographical indication may grant exclusive licenses relating to the use of such indication in connection with goods for which it is registered. Such license shall specify the territory within which and the time during which the licensee is authorized to use the geographical indication, and the conditions under which such use is permitted. The registered proprietor shall be entitled to receive royalties or other consideration from the licensee as agreed upon between them, provided that any assignment of a geographical indication or of rights granted by license requires prior approval of the Registrar. Further, where the Government intends to utilize a protected geographical indication for public purposes, it shall obtain a binding government license from the registered proprietor, compensating them fairly and in advance for such use, as determined through an arbitration process established under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, "transmission operation" with respect to a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design means the involuntary transfer of rights in such layout-design arising from events such as succession by inheritance, dissolution of a partnership, or similar occurrences not involving an express agreement. Such transmission shall vest in the legal heirs or successors as determined under applicable laws relating to property and succession. Provided that, where the original owner is a body corporate, the transmission operation shall be governed by its articles of association and relevant provisions concerning winding up or liquidation. This definition applies irrespective of whether such transfer is explicitly documented as a "transmission" under this Act.

For the purposes of registration under this Act, a "transmission operation" relating to a layout-design right shall include any transfer of ownership or interest in the registered layout-design occurring by way of inheritance, gift, will, or other legal mechanism. Such transmission operations are subject to disclosure requirements as provided herein, necessitating the filing of Form LD-T within thirty days of the effective date of such transfer with the Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Registry. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating the legitimacy and validity of the transmission operation, including but not limited to certified copies of relevant legal instruments. Failure to comply with these disclosure requirements shall render the transmitted layout-design vulnerable to challenge regarding its ownership status.

Where a registered layout-design is infringed by the unauthorized transmission operation of an integrated circuit, the owner shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief restraining further acts of infringement. Such injunction may include orders preventing the manufacture, import, sale, offer for sale, or distribution of infringing integrated circuits. Provided that, in determining whether an act constitutes infringement under this Act, due consideration shall be given to any evidence demonstrating a lack of commercial exploitation by the alleged infringer following the transmission operation. The owner may also claim damages equivalent to the reasonable royalty which would have been payable had the layout-design been validly licensed, or where such amount cannot be ascertained, the net profit made from the infringing acts. Subject to limitations prescribed under this Act, recovery of costs incurred in pursuing legal remedies is permitted.

The Registrar may, upon receiving an application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design, direct that a notice specifying the particulars of the design and the name and address of the applicant be served on any person claiming right in the design under this Act. Any such transmission operation shall be deemed to be a communication of intent regarding potential infringement. The Registrar shall provide an opportunity for interested parties to file objections within sixty days from the date of publication of the notice, as provided herein. Objections may relate to novelty, originality, or prior use affecting the validity of the layout-design. Where an objection is filed, the Registrar shall afford the applicant a reasonable opportunity to respond in writing and present evidence supporting their claim. The decision regarding the registration shall be recorded by the Registrar and communicated to all parties involved within ninety days from the conclusion of the hearing.

Where a registered layout-design is utilized in the manufacture of integrated circuits for commercial purposes, and such utilization involves a process of automated testing wherein signals are routed through designated pathways within the circuit, the operator conducting said transmission operation shall ensure that all parameters governing signal integrity remain consistent with specifications outlined during initial registration. Any deviation from these established parameters, demonstrable through documented quality control procedures, necessitates immediate notification to the Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Registry and a detailed report outlining corrective measures undertaken. Failure to adhere to this requirement may result in penalties as provided herein, subject to verification by authorized inspectors appointed under this Act. The operator shall maintain records pertaining to all transmission operations for a period of not less than seven years.

Any person who, without authorization from the registered proprietor, undertakes or facilitates a transmission operation involving a protected layout design for the purpose of commercial exploitation shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall be determined by the Controller and may include compensation for loss of profits, reasonable royalty fees that the infringer would have paid had they obtained a license, and in cases of wilful infringement, punitive damages not exceeding three times the amount of actual damages established. The registered proprietor may also apply to the civil court for an injunction restraining further acts of infringement as provided herein. Where the infringing transmission operation involves the reproduction or adaptation of the layout design, the Controller shall consider such factors when assessing the quantum of compensation.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, the right to authorize a transmission operation in respect of a registered layout-design may be granted by the owner through an irrevocable license agreement. Such agreements shall clearly specify the scope of permitted transmissions, including but not limited to reproduction, modification, and commercial use, as determined by the licensor. The licensee may further assign this right to transmit operations, provided that such assignment is recorded with the Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Registry within thirty days of its execution. Any subsequent transmission operation undertaken without prior written consent from the original layout-design owner shall be deemed a violation under this Act and subject to penalties as prescribed herein. The licensor retains the power to audit the licensee’s compliance with the terms of the license agreement concerning permitted transmissions.

Where a registered layout-design is exploited without authorization through a process involving the unauthorized transmission operation of data relating thereto, the owner may institute proceedings before the relevant judicial forum seeking injunctive relief and damages. Such proceedings are subject to the condition that the claimant demonstrates reasonable efforts were undertaken to prevent the initial dissemination of the infringing information. It shall be presumed, absent contrary evidence presented by the alleged infringer, that any commercial use of a layout-design incorporating elements substantially similar to those protected under this Act, occurring within five years of its registration, constitutes unauthorized exploitation unless it can be shown that such use was independently developed or derived from publicly available sources. The burden of proving independent development rests entirely upon the defendant.

Where a registered layout-design is utilized in the manufacture of an integrated circuit, and such utilization involves a transmission operation resulting from reverse engineering undertaken solely for the purpose of analyzing the functionality or performance characteristics of the said integrated circuit, that use shall not constitute infringement provided that the analysis does not involve reproduction of any protected element of the layout-design. Further, if the resultant information is subsequently employed to create an integrated circuit incorporating elements substantially similar to those found in the registered layout-design, and such similarity demonstrably derives from the aforementioned reverse engineering process, then a determination regarding potential infringement shall be made considering whether the effect registered trade mark associated with the original design has been unfairly exploited.

Any person found to have, without authorization, engaged in the commercial exploitation of a registered layout-design by means of a prohibited transmission operation shall be liable to pay damages equivalent to a sum not exceeding five per centum of the total sales of the infringing integrated circuits. Such damages may be increased up to ten per centum where the infringement is proven to have been committed wilfully and with knowledge of the registered layout-design’s protected status. Further, an aggrieved proprietor shall retain the right to seek injunctive relief preventing further transmission operations or assignable transmissible cases related to the infringing layout-design. The Registrar may issue a cease and desist order under this Act upon receiving a complaint demonstrating such infringement; failure to comply will result in penalties as provided herein.

Where an integrated circuit layout-design is transmitted by operation of law due to inheritance or succession, the right holder’s successors shall be deemed to possess all rights and privileges previously vested in the original owner. Disputes arising concerning the validity of such transmission may be referred to the relevant judicial forum for determination, subject to the provisions herein regarding limitation periods. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, establish guidelines pertaining to the evidentiary standards required to substantiate claims of lawful transmission. Any party aggrieved by a decision relating to the transmission operation may appeal to the appellate authority as provided under this Act, within sixty days from the date of communication of the order, and the appellate authority’s determination shall be final.

An application for registration of a layout-design relating to a semiconductor integrated circuit may be filed by the first owner of the layout-design or, where the ownership has been transferred, by the assignee of such owner. The Registrar shall require particulars concerning the applicant and details pertaining to the creation date and initial location of reduction of the layout-design to practice. Where an application incorporates elements previously disclosed, the applicant must provide a detailed statement outlining the nature and extent of prior publication. For the purposes of this Act, “transmission means transmission” by any documented method including electronic file transfer or physical delivery of storage media, irrespective of whether such transmission constitutes a sale or other commercial transaction. The Registrar may request further documentation to verify ownership claims as provided herein.

Where an infringement of layout-design rights has occurred, the owner may institute civil proceedings for damages and seek injunctive relief against the infringing party. Such remedies are subject to the principle that actual damage suffered by the owner must be proven, unless the infringer deliberately copied the registered layout-design, in which case presumed damages as determined by the Court shall apply. For the purposes of determining infringement, any act involving the reproduction, adaptation, or commercial exploitation of a protected layout-design constitutes an infringing activity. It is clarified that “transmission means transmission” and includes the unauthorized transfer of layout-designs through digital media, physical storage devices, or any other technological means. The Court may also order the delivery up or destruction of goods manufactured using the infringing layout-design, as provided herein.

Where an integrated circuit layout-design is transmitted by way of assignment, the Assignor shall provide written notice of such transmission to the Registrar within thirty days of the date of execution of the assignment deed. Such notice shall include particulars relating to the assignor and assignee, a copy of the assignment deed duly executed, and details regarding any prior transmissions affecting the layout-design. The Registrar may require further documentation as deemed necessary for verification purposes. Failure to provide such notice within the stipulated timeframe will render the Assignor liable to a monetary penalty, determined by the Controller. For the avoidance of doubt, *transmission means transmission* whether it occurs through a formal deed or any other legally recognized method of transfer. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all transmissions and make them available for public inspection subject to restrictions as may be prescribed under this Act concerning trade secrets.

For the purposes of this Act, where an integrated circuit layout design is transmitted by way of digital signal or electronic medium, such transmission means transmission irrespective of whether it involves physical movement of storage media. The right holder shall have standing to pursue remedies under this Act if a person copies or does any act restricted under this Act relating to a layout design that was communicated to them through such a transmission. Provided that, the communication must be for a lawful purpose and not in violation of any contractual agreement restricting access. Further, where an unauthorized copy is made following such transmission, the onus shall lie on the recipient to demonstrate due diligence in preventing further dissemination if they were unaware of the infringing activity at the time of initial receipt as provided herein.

Any person found to have reproduced an integrated circuit layout design in violation of this Act shall be liable for damages, calculated at the option of the aggrieved party, either on a compensatory basis reflecting lost profits or reasonable royalties, whichever is higher. Where such reproduction involves commercial exploitation, a further penalty may be imposed, not exceeding five times the value of the infringing goods or services. For the purposes of determining infringement, “transmission means transmission” by any electronic medium, including but not limited to digital broadcasting and internet distribution, shall be deemed an act of unauthorized copying. The Central Government may, subject to due process, issue directives for seizure of infringing materials and suspension of business operations engaged in such unlawful activities as provided herein.

The registered owner of a layout-design may, subject to this Act and the regulations made thereunder, grant licenses permitting the use or exploitation of their design. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and may specify particular fields of application for the licensed technology. An assignment of rights in a layout-design shall include all rights pertaining thereto, including but not limited to the right to manufacture integrated circuits incorporating the design. Where a license is granted under this Act, the terms thereof shall be binding on both the grantor and grantee, and any dispute arising from such terms may be referred for arbitration as provided herein. For the purposes of this section, “transmission means transmission” by way of assignment or otherwise, including through testamentary disposition or operation of law, shall vest full ownership in the transferee.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design relating to a transmission operation law arising from inheritance shall include, alongside the prescribed drawings and specifications, a detailed genealogy chart tracing ownership lineage back three generations. Such charts are subject to verification by the Registry through official records and may be challenged by any interested party within thirty days of publication in the Official Gazette. The Registrar shall have the power to require further documentation or clarification regarding the transmission operation law if reasonable doubt exists concerning the validity of the claimed inheritance. Failure to provide satisfactory evidence as provided herein will result in rejection of the application, without prejudice to subsequent re-application with corrected information and supporting affidavits.

Where an integrated circuit layout design is transmitted by operation of law due to the death of the registered proprietor, the right in that layout design shall vest in their legal heirs or successors as determined under applicable inheritance laws. Provided that, if such transmission occurs prior to the expiry of any contractual period restricting exploitation rights granted under this Act, the terms of said contract shall remain binding on the legal heirs or successors. Any person claiming title through transmission operation law may apply to the Controller for registration as proprietor, submitting evidence of succession and a copy of the relevant testamentary or intestate succession document. The Controller may require such further documentation as deemed necessary to establish rightful claim. Failure to comply with these requirements shall render the application void. Remedies for infringement remain available to the legal heirs or successors in the same manner as if they were the original registered proprietor.

The Registrar may, upon receiving an application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout design alleging infringement under this Act, direct the alleged infringer to submit within sixty days a written response detailing their defense.
