This obligation extends to instances involving wilful misrepresentation concerning the trademark's ownership.

Any proprietor who, having knowledge of an infringement of patent rights, fails to initiate reasonable steps within ninety days as provided herein to restrain such infringement, shall be deemed to have contributed to the unlawful exploitation of the patented invention. Such proprietor shall liable penalty proportionate to the damages suffered by the aggrieved party, not exceeding five per centum of the aggregate sales of the patented article during the period of infringement. Further, where a false representation is made in an application for patent or in any document filed under this Act, and such misrepresentation causes demonstrable prejudice to another person’s legitimate business interests, the applicant shall liable penalty up to two times the cost incurred by the prejudiced party in rectifying the harm caused.

Where the patentee grants a license relating to an invention, whether exclusive or non-exclusive, assignable either wholly or partially, such license agreement shall specify the royalty rate payable by the licensee to the patentee, as determined through negotiation and documented in writing. Any subsequent modification of this royalty rate requires mutual consent and must be recorded in an addendum signed by both parties. Furthermore, where a licensee sub-licenses the patented invention under the terms granted by the primary license, they shall ensure that such sub-license adheres to the principles of fair use and equitable distribution of benefits. Failure to comply with these provisions, including unauthorized alteration of royalty structures or restrictive sub-licensing practices, shall liable penalty not exceeding two lakhs rupees, recoverable from the defaulting party. The Controller may issue directives for rectification if deemed necessary under this Act.

Where an aggrieved party contests the revocation of a patent granted under this Act before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, such contestation must be filed within ninety days from the date of publication of the order of revocation. The Board shall afford all parties concerned a reasonable opportunity for being heard and may require production of evidence as it deems necessary to determine the validity of the revocation. Any party dissatisfied with the decision of the Intellectual Property Appellate Board may appeal to the High Court within sixty days of that decision. It is provided that if any person, through fraudulent misrepresentation or wilful suppression of material facts, obtains a patent, he shall liable penalty which may extend to three times the cost of administration incurred by the Controller.

Where an applicant for registration of a patent elects to avail of the provisions relating to india international registration as contemplated under this Act, and subsequently withdraws such election prior to the grant of the patent, the Controller may direct that the fees paid towards the international registration shall not be refunded. Any person who, having knowledge of proceedings pending before the Controller concerning the validity or infringement of a patent, makes any false representation intended to influence the outcome of those proceedings, shall liable penalty which may extend to two hundred thousand rupees and imprisonment for a term not less than six months but which may extend to three years. An appeal against an order made under this provision lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order.

Any proprietor seeking rectification of a registered geographical indication may apply to the Geographical Indications Registry, and such application shall specify the particulars of the registration sought to be rectified and the grounds upon which it is claimed that rectification is necessary. The Registry shall give notice of the application to the applicant and any other interested parties as identified under this Act, affording them an opportunity to submit objections or counter-claims. Following consideration of all submissions, the Registrar may order such modifications to the register as are deemed appropriate, subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Furthermore, the Central Government shall cause to be placed before both Houses of Parliament once a year a parliament year report detailing instances where rectification orders have been issued and outlining any challenges encountered in their implementation, including assessments of impact on producers.

The Registering Authority, upon receiving an application for registration of a geographical indication, shall forward the same to the Standing Committee constituted under subsection (3) of section 14. The Committee shall examine the application and any objections received in accordance with the provisions herein relating to public notice and opposition proceedings. Following such examination, the Committee shall submit its findings and recommendations, including observations on distinctiveness and reputation as may be relevant, to the Registrar within a period not exceeding six months from the date of receipt of the application by the Standing Committee. The Registrar shall consider the report of the Standing Committee and any further submissions made by the applicant or objector. A comprehensive parliament year report detailing the number of applications received, registrations granted, oppositions filed, and decisions rendered under this Act will be laid before both Houses of Parliament annually.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any registered Geographical Indication owner may grant exclusive licenses relating to the use of the indication for specific goods or services within defined territories, provided that such license agreements shall clearly state the scope and duration of the permitted usage. Any assignment of a registered Geographical Indication shall require prior approval from the Registrar, who may demand evidence demonstrating due diligence in protecting the distinctiveness of the indication following transfer. The Registrar shall maintain a public register detailing all licenses and assignments executed under this Act, accessible for inspection during office hours. Furthermore, the Central Government shall cause to be placed before both Houses of Parliament once a year a parliament year report outlining the number of licenses granted, assignments approved, and any disputes arising concerning unauthorized use or infringement related to registered Geographical Indications.

Notwithstanding anything contained herein, any aggrieved party alleging improper consideration of an application for registration of a geographical indication may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of publication of the decision in the Geographical Indications Journal. Such appeals shall be based solely on demonstrable errors of law apparent on the face of the record and shall not involve relitigation of factual disputes previously determined by the Registrar. The Intellectual Property Appellate Board, after affording an opportunity for hearing to both the applicant and any opposition party, may affirm, reverse, or modify the decision appealed from. A further appeal lies to the High Court, but only on a question of law arising out of the order of the Appellate Board, as detailed in the parliament year report submitted annually by the Controller General.

Any person found, upon investigation conducted pursuant to an inspection authorized under this Act, to have made use of any registered geographical indication in contravention of the provisions herein, shall be liable for damages equivalent to three times the value of the goods or services sold bearing the infringing mark, or where such value cannot be ascertained, one million rupees. Furthermore, proceedings initiated by the Register may result in a conviction and imprisonment term shall extend up to five years, subject to judicial discretion considering the severity and repetition of the offense. The Parliament year report detailing instances of infringement and enforcement actions undertaken will include particulars of each prosecution and any penalties imposed.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any registered Geographical Indication owner may grant exclusive licenses relating to the use of the indication in connection with goods for which it is registered, provided that such license shall be documented in writing and specify the territory and duration of the granted rights. Any assignment of a registered Geographical Indication, including by way of mortgage or pledge, shall also be recorded as per the prescribed manner. Further, any licensee or assignee may sub-license or assign their respective rights subject to the terms stipulated in the original license or assignment agreement. The Central Government shall cause to be placed before both Houses of Parliament once a year a parliament year report detailing all licenses and assignments granted relating to registered Geographical Indications, including particulars of the parties involved and the scope of such authorizations; patent means patent as defined under the Patents Act, 1970, will be considered in assessing potential conflicts.

Where an objection is raised against the registration of a geographical indication, and such objection challenges the distinctiveness of the goods associated with the proposed indication based on prior use or established reputation, the Registrar shall decide the matter after affording both the applicant and the objector a reasonable opportunity for being heard, including submission of documentary evidence. The decision of the Registrar concerning said distinctiveness may be appealed to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. Furthermore, the Central Government shall cause to be placed before both Houses of Parliament once a year a parliament year report detailing the number of such objections received, the decisions rendered by the Registrar, and any appeals filed against those decisions.

An affidavit submitted under this Act shall be deemed a written statement and is admissible as evidence without proof of the executioner’s signature, provided that the deponent affirms its contents before an authorized officer. The affiant shall state their full name, place of residence, and occupation in the opening paragraph. Any document or record referred to within the affidavit may be exhibited thereto, clearly marked for identification purposes. Should any material fact relevant to the proceedings come to light after the filing of an evidence affidavit, a supplementary affidavit may be submitted correcting or clarifying such information as provided herein.

In proceedings before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board relating to rectification applications under this Act, a party seeking to introduce documentary evidence shall file with the Board an indexed list of all documents intended to be relied upon. Each document so listed may be accompanied by an affidavit affirming its authenticity and relevance to the issues in dispute. The Board may, at its discretion, require such affiant to appear for oral examination regarding the contents of the affidavit or the veracity of the statements contained therein. Provided that if a party disputes the genuineness of any document submitted as evidence affidavit, the Board shall direct the filing party to produce the original document for inspection and verification. Failure to comply with this direction may result in the rejection of the challenged documentary evidence. The Board’s decision on admissibility of such evidence shall be final subject to appeal under this Act.

Where a patentee desires to assign their interest in a granted patent, or to grant an exclusive license under that patent, such assignment or license shall be recorded with the Controller. The instrument effecting the transfer must specify the full name and address of both the assignor and assignee, or licensor and licensee, as applicable, and clearly define the scope of the rights being transferred. To substantiate the claims made in the assignment or license agreement, a duly sworn affidavit from the patentee, or their authorized representative, shall be submitted to the Controller. This affidavit must attest to the authenticity of the document and confirm that the transfer is executed freely and without coercion. Failure to provide a satisfactory evidence affidavit may render the recorded assignment or license voidable under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, “lease patented article” means the grant of a right to hold possession and use an apparatus or substance for a specified period, where such apparatus or substance is itself the subject matter of a patent under this Act. Such lease shall not extend beyond the term of the patent relating to the leased item. A contract providing for the hire-purchase of a patented article may be considered a lease patented article if it incorporates an option granting the hirer the right to purchase the apparatus at the termination of the hire period, subject to fulfilling stipulated conditions as provided herein.

Where a patent has been granted for an invention relating to machinery or apparatus, and such machinery or apparatus is let on lease, the lessee shall be deemed to have taken a non-exclusive license under this Act to use the patented article for the purpose specified in the lease agreement. Provided that, any modification of the leased article by the lessee beyond what is reasonably necessary for its intended operation as defined within the patent specification shall require prior written consent from the patentee. The Registrar may, upon application by either the lessor or lessee, investigate and determine whether the terms of the lease patented article infringe upon the rights granted under this Act, particularly concerning restrictions on further manufacture or sale. Such investigations are subject to payment of prescribed fees as determined by the Controller General.

Where a patentee grants a lease of a patented article, the terms and conditions governing such lease shall be subject to the provisions of this Act. Any stipulation within the lease agreement restricting use or repair of the leased article beyond that reasonably necessary for its intended function, provided that such restriction does not directly relate to the preservation of the patent’s novelty or inventive step, may be deemed an unreasonable restraint of trade under this Act and is accordingly void. The Controller shall have jurisdiction to determine whether a condition within a lease patented article constitutes an unreasonable restraint. Applications relating to disputes concerning the validity of conditions imposed on leases may be filed with the Controller in the prescribed manner. Parties aggrieved by any determination made under these provisions may appeal to the Appellate Board as provided herein, subject to payment of the requisite fee.

Any person who leases a patented article without the authorization of the patentee, or their duly authorized representative, shall be deemed guilty of an offence under this Act. Such offence is punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and with a fine which shall not be less than fifty thousand rupees, and may extend to two hundred thousand rupees. Further, any agreement entered into for the lease patented article in contravention of these provisions shall be voidable at the option of the patentee. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, prescribe procedures for determining damages recoverable from a lessee found guilty of such infringement, provided that the assessment considers lost profits and reasonable royalty.

Where a patentee grants a lease of a patented article, such lease shall be deemed an assignment for the duration specified therein unless the agreement expressly states otherwise. Any subsequent transfer of rights relating to that leased article, whether by way of further assignment or through operation of law, shall require the prior written consent of the original patentee, provided that such consent may be withheld only on grounds demonstrably impacting the validity or enforceability of the primary patent. The terms and conditions governing the lease, including royalty payments and permitted uses, are subject to review under this Act if they appear manifestly restrictive of competition within the relevant market. A lessee obtaining a lease patented article shall not be restricted from independently improving upon the leased technology, but any resulting inventions derived directly from such improvements must be jointly disclosed with the patentee.

Where a patentee grants a lease of a patented article, such lease shall be deemed to incorporate, subject to this Act, all rights pertaining to the use and exploitation of the invention as defined within the granted patent. Any dispute arising concerning the scope of permissible activities under such a lease, or regarding whether conditions imposed by the patentee unduly restrict the lessee’s lawful commercial practices, may be referred for arbitration as provided herein. The arbitrator shall consider evidence presented demonstrating both the intent of the parties at the time of the lease agreement and any subsequent modifications thereof. It is further stipulated that challenges to the validity of a lease patented article agreement are subject to appeal before the relevant appellate authority, following established procedures under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, a “lease patented article” shall mean the temporary right granted to another person to possess and utilize an invention for a specified period, where such possession and utilization are directly enabled by the patent covering that invention. Such lease shall not constitute transfer of ownership under this Act. The lessee’s rights shall be strictly limited to those expressly defined within the lease agreement, subject to any restrictions imposed by the terms of the patent itself. Further, prior to offering a lease patented article for commercial use, the applicant or patentee shall fulfill all registrar prescribed requirements pertaining to documentation and reporting as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, "proprietor certification trade mark" means a trade mark registered as such under regulations prescribed herein, denoting that the certified products or services conform to a particular standard, specification, characteristic, quality, or other attribute, and which is used by persons authorized by the proprietor of the trade mark. Such authorization shall be granted in writing and specify the conditions for use. The proprietor certification trade mark may include representations signifying adherence to such standards as are defined by the proprietor. Any person using a proprietor certification trade mark without express written consent from the registered proprietor, or failing to comply with the stipulated conditions, shall be deemed to have contravened this Act.

An application for registration of a proprietor certification trade mark shall be made to the Registrar in the prescribed form and shall include particulars relating to the standards established by the applicant for ensuring that the goods certified there under conform to those standards. The applicant must demonstrate, as part of the application, their capacity to consistently monitor and enforce adherence to these standards amongst producers utilizing the proposed certification trade mark. Further, the registrar may require submission of detailed operational manuals outlining quality control procedures. Registration shall be granted only if the Registrar is satisfied that the applicant possesses adequate resources for maintaining the integrity of the certification process and ensuring consumer confidence in goods bearing the proprietor certification trade mark.

Any proprietor issuing certificates bearing a proprietor certification trade mark shall maintain accurate records detailing the standards for conformity and processes followed in assessing adherence thereto. Failure to do so constitutes a violation under this Act and renders the proprietor liable to penalties as prescribed herein, including but not limited to fines up to five hundred thousand rupees and suspension of certificate issuance privileges. Any person knowingly using goods or services certified under a proprietor certification trade mark that fail to meet the declared standards shall be deemed guilty of an offence and subject to imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or both. The Registrar may, upon receiving credible evidence of such non-compliance, initiate investigations and impose corrective measures as provided herein.

The proprietor of a proprietor certification trade mark shall be entitled to grant licenses conferring the right to use such trade mark upon applicants meeting standards prescribed by regulations made under this Act. Such licenses may be granted for specific territories and limited periods, subject to conditions relating to quality control and adherence to the proprietor’s established guidelines. Assignment of these licensing rights is permissible only with the prior written consent of the proprietor, which shall not be unreasonably withheld. Any licensee desiring to transfer their right to use the certification trade mark must apply to the proprietor for approval, providing full details of the proposed assignee and demonstrating their compliance with relevant standards. The proprietor may impose additional conditions on any such assignment deemed necessary to protect the integrity of the certification trade mark and prevent dilution of its reputation.

Subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal, an application for registration as a proprietor of certification trade mark shall be refused if the applicant does not demonstrate sufficient control over the quality and characteristics of the goods or services certified. Provided that, where such control is exercised through a contractual arrangement with relevant bodies, the Registrar may require evidence establishing the enforceability of those contracts under Indian law. Any party aggrieved by a decision to refuse registration may appeal within sixty days, presenting arguments demonstrating compliance with the requirements for proprietor certification trade mark eligibility as provided herein. The Appellate Tribunal shall consider whether the applicant’s proposed certification scheme adequately safeguards consumer interests and prevents misleading representations concerning certified goods.

Where a proprietor certification trade mark is registered, the proprietor shall possess the sole and exclusive right to control the quality and characteristics of goods bearing that mark, and no person other than the proprietor or with their express written consent shall apply the mark to any goods. Any use of the proprietor’s certification trade mark without authorization constitutes an infringement under this Act and renders the infringing party liable for damages, including but not limited to lost profits, royalties, and costs incurred in rectifying the misrepresentation. The Registrar may, upon complaint by the proprietor or any aggrieved party, issue injunctions restraining further acts of infringement. A trade mark recognised as distinctive through prior use shall not preclude registration as a proprietor certification trade mark if it meets all other requirements under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, “proprietor certification” means the use of a mark by an individual or body who has been granted exclusive right to certify that goods or services meet specified standards, and who is registered as such under this Act. Such proprietor shall be entitled to prevent the use of their certification trade mark by any person not authorised by them in writing, provided that the use by the unauthorized party indicates a representation that the certified goods or services conform to the standards defined by the proprietor. The proprietor may specify conditions for continued certification and may revoke such right if those conditions are not met.

Any person seeking to utilize a proprietor certification mark shall first obtain explicit written authorization from the registered proprietor, detailing the precise scope and limitations of such usage. Failure to adhere strictly to these prescribed parameters constitutes an infringement under this Act. The proprietor may pursue civil remedies including damages proportionate to the lost profits suffered by them as a direct result of unauthorized use. Furthermore, any entity found guilty of deceptive certification shall be liable to pay a penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees and subject to prosecution for offences punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years. The proprietor retains the right to immediately seek an injunction preventing further infringing activities.

The proprietor of a proprietor certification trade mark may grant licenses authorizing specific persons to apply the mark to goods conforming to the standards established by the proprietor, provided that such license agreements explicitly state the terms and conditions governing the use of the mark. Any assignment of the proprietor certification trade mark or any interest therein shall be deemed invalid unless it is accompanied by a comprehensive transfer of all documentation relating to the certified standards and quality control procedures maintained by the proprietor. Further, sub-licensees operating under such licenses are bound by the original terms stipulated in the primary license agreement and remain subject to the oversight of the proprietor regarding adherence to prescribed specifications. The proprietor shall retain the right to terminate any license or assignment if there is a material breach of the conditions as provided herein.

Where an application for registration as a proprietor of certification is opposed, the Appellate Board may, upon review of the record and hearing arguments from both the applicant and the opponent, determine whether the proposed certification mark conforms to the standards prescribed under this Act and adequately safeguards consumer interests. It shall be open to any party aggrieved by an order of the Appellate Board refusing registration to appeal to the High Court within sixty days of such order, on grounds limited to errors apparent on the record or questions of law arising out of the interpretation or application of provisions relating to proprietor certification. The High Court may confirm, reverse, or modify the order appealed from, and direct a re-hearing before the Appellate Board as it deems fit, provided that any decision regarding the inherent distinctiveness of the mark remains within the exclusive jurisdiction of the Appellate Board.

Where a proprietor certification trade mark is registered, the proprietor shall be entitled to institute proceedings for infringement against any person using a sign which is identical or confusingly similar to the certified trade mark in relation to goods or services for which it is registered. Such remedies may include an injunction restraining the infringing use and damages commensurate with the loss suffered by the proprietor as a consequence of the infringement, subject to considerations of fair use. Furthermore, any layout design registered under the Designs Act that incorporates elements of the proprietor certification trade mark shall be deemed protected against unauthorized reproduction or application in connection with goods or services covered by the certification. Provided that, nothing herein shall prevent the use of such designs where they are incidental and do not create a likelihood of confusion among consumers regarding the origin or quality of the goods.

The proprietor of a proprietor certification trade mark shall maintain detailed records pertaining to all certified goods, including origin, processing methods, and quality control measures employed by the producers whose goods bear the mark. Such records are accessible for inspection by the Registrar upon request, provided that reasonable notice is given to the proprietor. Any alteration in the standards or procedures governing the proprietor certification process must be notified to all registered users of the trade mark at least sixty days prior to their implementation. Failure to provide such notification shall render any subsequent challenge to the validity of the certification trade mark more readily admissible under this Act. The Registrar may, after due inquiry and subject to principles of natural justice, issue directions regarding the format and content of these records. Further, a proprietor seeking to amend the scope or definition of certified goods must notify all affected producers prior to any formal application.

For the purposes of this Act, “misleading indication” with respect to goods or services means any statement or representation which is likely to create confusion in the minds of the public as to the nature, quality, origin, characteristics, or suitability of such goods or services. Such misleading indications include, but are not limited to, representations concerning the geographical origin of goods where such origin has a reputation extending beyond the place of origin. Any person who makes any false representation under this Act shall be deemed guilty of an offence and shall cognizance offence by a court; provided that the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, specify further categories of misleading indications.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed refused if the proposed mark is identical or confusingly similar to any existing mark already registered under this Act in relation to identical goods or services, subject to provisions regarding permissible disclaimers. Any person aggrieved by such refusal may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the refusal order. Where a false or misleading representation is made in an application for registration concerning the character, distinctiveness, reputation or substantial use of the trade mark, it shall constitute an offence and shall cognizance offence punishable with imprisonment and fine as provided herein. The Registrar may require submission of further documentation to verify claims regarding prior usage.

Any proprietor aggrieved by an act of deceptive trademark use or unfair competition may institute civil proceedings for recovery of damages sustained as a direct result of such infringement. Such proceedings shall be governed by principles of equity and fairness, considering the extent of confusion created in the minds of consumers and the resultant loss to goodwill. Further, where a false designation, misrepresentation, or any other deceptive practice is employed with intent to pass off goods or services as those of another, it shall constitute an offence under this Act. No court shall cognizance offence relating to such deceptive practices except on complaint made by the Registrar, or an authorised officer acting on behalf of the proprietor. Provided that a certificate from the Registrar detailing the infringing activity is deemed sufficient prima facie evidence for initiating proceedings.

Where a proprietor institutes proceedings for infringement of a trade mark under this Act, and it is demonstrated to the satisfaction of the Court that the defendant has used any name, mark or sign which is identical or confusingly similar to the registered trade mark in relation to goods or services identical or closely related to those in respect of which the trade mark is registered, such use shall be deemed a violation. Further, where it is established that the infringing activity was undertaken with the intent to deceive or cause confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or quality of the goods or services offered, such act shall cognizance offence punishable under this Act. The Court may also order the defendant to provide an account of profits derived from the infringing use, provided that a full and accurate accounting is presented.

Any person found to be using a deceptively similar mark or trade name with intent to defraud or cause confusion amongst consumers shall be liable for damages as determined by the Court. Such use, whether in advertising, packaging, or distribution, constitutes an offence under this Act and may result in injunctions preventing further infringing activity. The proprietor of the registered trademark may initiate civil proceedings seeking recovery of losses incurred due to the infringement. Furthermore, any contravention of these provisions shall cognizance offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both, as deemed appropriate by the Court. This penalty applies irrespective of whether profit was realised from the deceptive practice.

The owner of a trade mark, or any person duly authorised by them in writing, may grant a license conferring specific rights relating to the use of the trade mark for particular goods or services. Such licenses shall be assignable subject to the terms and conditions stipulated within the licensing agreement itself, and provided that such assignment is notified to the Registrar within thirty days of its execution. Any subsequent transfer or sub-licensing of these rights requires prior written consent from the original licensor, failing which it shall constitute a breach of contract. Where a false or misleading representation concerning the ownership of a trade mark or the existence of a license is made in connection with any goods or services, such act shall cognizance offence punishable under this Act. The Registrar may issue directions to prevent unfair exploitation of licensed rights.

Where a proprietor institutes proceedings for infringement under this Act, and such proceedings are withdrawn without prejudice to any other right or remedy available to him, the aggrieved party may subsequently initiate fresh proceedings based upon the same acts or omissions. However, where an order of injunction is obtained restraining the defendant from certain conduct, subsequent actions predicated solely on that restrained behaviour shall be deemed repetitive litigation. Any wilful infringement of a registered trade mark, constituting a fraud or deception intended to cause confusion amongst consumers, shall cognizance offence and may attract enhanced penalties as determined by the adjudicating authority. The decision of the adjudicating authority is subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, provided that such appeals must be filed within ninety days from the date of the order.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed abandoned if the applicant fails to provide documentary evidence, as may be prescribed, substantiating the use of the mark in relation to the goods or services specified in the application within six months from the date of request under this Act. Where such failure occurs, and the Registrar is satisfied that the applicant has not diligently pursued the registration, the Registrar shall direct the abandonment of the application. Any person aggrieved by an order directing abandonment may appeal to the Appellate Board as provided herein. It is further stipulated that any act constituting a false representation in connection with the use or adoption of a trade mark shall cognizance offence and commission offence shall be dealt with under this Act, subject to penal provisions.

Any person found to be using a trademark identical or confusingly similar to a mark already registered in respect of specified goods or services, without due leave and license from the proprietor thereof, shall be deemed guilty of an offence under this Act. Such offence may be reported to the appropriate police station by any aggrieved party or authorised representative of the Registrar of Trade Marks. Upon receiving such report, the officer-in-charge of the police station shall initiate investigation as per established procedures. The court before which a prosecution is brought for any such offence shall cognizance offence only upon written complaint filed by the Registrar or an officer duly authorized in writing to act on their behalf. Further proceedings may be initiated concerning counterfeit goods seized under these provisions, adhering to principles outlined within the Budapest Treaty International framework regarding enforcement of intellectual property rights.

Any person found to be using a trademark identical or deceptively similar to a mark already registered in respect of specified goods or services, without due leave and license from the proprietor thereof, shall be deemed guilty of an offence. Such use includes, but is not limited to, affixing, applying, or exhibiting such trademark upon any goods, their containers, packaging, labels, or advertisements relating thereto. Further, where such infringing activity involves the unauthorized transmission of digital representations of the registered mark across a network for commercial purposes, the severity of the offence shall be enhanced. No court shall cognizance offence under this Act except on a written complaint filed by the proprietor of the trademark or their duly authorised representative; provided that the Registrar may initiate proceedings where such infringement demonstrably prejudices public interest.

Any person found to be using a trademark identical or confusingly similar to a registered trademark without due license or consent shall cognizance offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, and with a fine which may extend to five hundred thousand rupees. Where such use is determined by the Controller to constitute an act of unfair competition impacting demonstrable industrial application of the mark’s proprietor's goods or services, the penalty shall be doubled. Further, any director, manager, secretary, or other officer in default of this Act, being responsible for the offence, shall also be deemed guilty and liable to punishment as if he were the person actually committing such act. Recovery of damages may be pursued under provisions relating to civil remedies.

The owner of a trade mark, or any person duly authorised by them in writing, may grant a non-exclusive license to use the trade mark for specific goods or services within India. Such licenses shall be assignable subject to prior written consent from the Trade Marks Registry, and such consent shall not be unreasonably withheld. Any assignment or sub-license granted without this consent will render the assignee liable under this Act. Further provision is made that a licensee may further license the trade mark rights granted to them, provided they notify the original owner of said sub-licensing arrangement in writing within thirty days. Failure to do so shall be deemed an offence and shall cognizance offence before a Magistrates court. It is understood that citizens India have a right to fair dealing regarding licensed goods and services.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed refused if the proposed marks incorporate or closely resemble emblems denoting government authority, subject to provisions allowing use with explicit permission. Any person aggrieved by such refusal may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the refusal order. Further, where an applicant knowingly submits false information regarding prior trade mark usage or ownership during registration proceedings, that constitutes a cognizance offence under this Act and is punishable with imprisonment and fine as provided herein. The Registrar shall maintain records detailing all applications, refusals, and appeals concerning government emblems.

Where an individual is found to have used a trademark identical or confusingly similar to a registered trade mark in relation to goods or services for which registration has been made, without due cause and with intent to deceive the public or gain unfair advantage, such act shall constitute an offence under this Act. The Trade Marks Registry may, upon receiving information indicating the commission of such an offence, file a complaint before a Magistrates Court detailing the particulars of the alleged infringement and specifying the relief sought. No court shall take cognizance of such an offence otherwise than on a written complaint filed by the Registrar or any officer duly authorised in writing for this purpose. Provided that the complainant shall serve notice upon the accused at least thirty days prior to filing the complaint, indicating the nature of the allegations. The Court may require further evidence as it deems necessary during proceedings related to this cognizance offence.

Where a proprietor institutes proceedings for infringement under this Act, and such proceedings are withdrawn or discontinued without the matter being decided on its merits, the Court may, subject to compliance with prescribed procedures, direct the proprietor to pay costs commensurate with the time expended by the defendant in defending the suit. Further, where an alleged infringer fails to comply with a direction issued under this Act pertaining to the destruction of infringing goods, or removal of false trade marks, such failure shall constitute a cognizance offence triable as per provisions relating to disobedience of court orders. Any police officer may arrest without warrant any person reasonably suspected of committing such an offence, provided that prior written intimation is given to the proprietor.

Any person found to be using a deceptively similar mark or trade description with intent to mislead the public and cause damage to the reputation of the proprietor shall be deemed guilty of an offence. Such offence is a cognizance offence, and no court shall take cognizance thereof except on a written complaint made by the registered proprietor or their authorised agent. The Court may impose a penalty not exceeding five thousand rupees for each day during which the infringing use continues after conviction. Further, the Court shall order the infringer to recall and destroy all goods bearing the infringing mark at their expense. Failure to comply with this order will result in an additional daily fine of one thousand rupees until compliance is achieved, as provided herein.

The owner of a trade mark, or any person duly authorised by them in writing, may grant a non-exclusive licence to use the trade mark for specific goods or services, subject to conditions stipulated within the agreement. Such licences shall be assignable alongside the underlying trade mark ownership, provided that prior written notification is given to all existing licensees of record. Any assignment or licensing arrangement affecting registered trade marks must include a detailed inventory of associated goodwill and reputation attributable to the mark. Failure to disclose material terms relating to such assignments constitutes a cognizance offence, punishable as per provisions outlined herein. The Registrar may require submission of these arrangements for public inspection, ensuring transparency within the marketplace. Further, any alteration to licensed usage beyond the scope initially defined requires prior consent from both the trade mark owner and all other licensees.

Where a proprietor or any person authorised by the proprietor discovers that any goods or services are being offered in trade with likely deception arising from use of identical or confusingly similar marks, they may institute proceedings for infringement. Such proceedings shall be brought before a District Court having jurisdiction over the area where the infringing act occurred or where the cause of action arose. The court shall have power to grant such remedies as it deems just and equitable, including injunctions restraining further acts of infringement, damages reflecting lost profits and costs incurred by the proprietor, and delivery up or destruction of infringing materials. Any wilful contravention of an order made under this Act constitutes a cognizance offence punishable with imprisonment and fine, subject to appeal to the High Court.

The owner of a trade mark, or any person claiming through him, may grant a license permitting transmissible use of their layout embodying the mark for specific goods or services, subject to conditions stipulated in the licensing agreement. Such licenses shall be assignable, either wholly or partially, along with the underlying right to the trade mark, provided that notice of such assignment is registered with the Trade Marks Registry within thirty days. Any subsequent assignee assumes all rights and obligations pertaining to the original license. Failure to register an assignment constitutes a cognizance offence, punishable as per provisions under this Act relating to false representation. The Registrar may issue directions regarding the form and content of licensing agreements concerning transmissible use layouts to ensure clarity and prevent disputes. This power extends to prescribing standard terms where deemed necessary for consumer protection.

The Registrar shall maintain a publicly accessible register of registered works pertaining to artistic works, including architectural designs and photographic works. Any person claiming ownership of copyright in any such work recorded in the Register may serve notice upon another alleging unauthorized reproduction or adaptation. Such notice shall specify the nature of the alleged infringement and provide particulars of the copyrighted work as listed within the Register. Failure to respond adequately to this notice within thirty days, demonstrating lawful authorization or a lack of infringement, shall constitute infringement copyright under this Act. Provided that, where an architectural design is reproduced for purposes solely connected with the construction, demolition, repair or alteration of a building, it shall not be deemed an act of infringement.

Where an adaptation of a work is made without authorization from the copyright owner, and such adaptation substantially reproduces the original work’s protected elements, including but not limited to its plot, characters, dialogue, and overall structure, it shall constitute infringement of copyright under this Act. Provided that, where the adaptation incorporates sufficient originality in its expression or treatment so as to create a demonstrably new aesthetic impact distinct from the underlying work, such use may be permissible subject to consideration of whether the adaptation unfairly prejudices or detracts from any potential market for the original work. Further, if the alleged infringing activity is undertaken solely for non-commercial educational purposes and involves minimal reproduction, it shall not automatically constitute infringement copyright, provided that proper acknowledgement is given to the author and owner of the original work.

The right to assign copyright in any musical work shall extend to the grant of exclusive licenses permitting reproduction and public performance, subject to the condition that such license specifies the territory within which it operates and the duration for which it is valid. Where an assignment or license purports to transfer rights beyond those actually held by the assignor, such purported transfer shall be deemed invalid only to the extent of the excess. Any person who, without authorization or in violation of the terms of a license granted under this Act, undertakes acts restricted under this Act shall constitute infringement copyright. An aggrieved party may apply to the relevant High Court for redressal, and the manner applying appellate shall follow established judicial procedures as provided herein.

The reproduction of any work in a derivative form shall not constitute infringement where such derivative form is created by the adaptation of a pre-existing work already lawfully made available to the public. For the purposes of this provision, ‘adaptation’ means the expression of the original work in another medium, including but not limited to translation, dramatization, incantation or musical arrangement. It shall be understood that alterations merely intended for commercial exploitation without substantial modification of the underlying creative elements do not fall within this exemption. Nothing herein shall permit the reproduction of any copyrighted photograph unless permission is obtained from the photographer, as provided herein.

Where an artistic work is registered under this Act, and the Registrar has issued a certificate of registration confirming such registration, any unauthorized reproduction, distribution, public display, or adaptation of that work without the authorization of the owner of copyright shall constitute infringement. Provided that, where a work has been published with the prior permission of the copyright holder but no formal registration was undertaken, subsequent commercial exploitation mirroring the registered elements may also be deemed to infringe upon the rights vested in the claimant. The determination of whether such exploitation constitutes infringement will consider the extent of similarity between the original and the reproduced work, taking into account the date of publication and any evidence presented regarding ownership claims as provided herein.

Where an act is done without obtaining the requisite license under this Act, and that act involves the reproduction of a substantial portion of a copyrighted work, such act shall constitute infringement. The owner of copyright may, subject to provisions regarding fair use and transformative works as provided herein, institute legal proceedings seeking injunctive relief against any person found to be engaged in acts infringing upon their exclusive rights. Damages recoverable in an action for copyright infringement shall include reasonable compensation to the copyright owner for any detriment suffered by him by reason of such infringement, not less than a sum determined by the Court and not exceeding five times the amount of damages assessed. Further, where wilful infringement is established, enhanced damages may be awarded as deemed just by the court.

Where an aggrieved party alleges that another has engaged in acts contrary to the exclusive rights granted under this Act, such party shall institute proceedings before the relevant High Court. The plaint shall specify, with particularity, the work claimed to be infringed, the nature of the infringing act, and the details of any damages or losses sustained as a direct consequence thereof. Notice of such action must first be served upon the alleged infringer, affording them a reasonable opportunity to respond to the allegations made within thirty days from the date of service. Failure to provide such notice shall render the proceedings vulnerable to challenge. The Court may, subject to just considerations, grant interim relief pending final determination. It is established that acts involving substantial reproduction or adaptation of copyrighted material without authorization shall constitute infringement.

Where an adaptation of a work is made without authorization from the owner of copyright therein, and such adaptation substantially reproduces elements of the original work which are protected under this Act, then that act shall constitute infringement. Provided that, where the adaptation incorporates only minor alterations to the original work, and those alterations do not create a new expression or convey a different meaning than that originally intended by the author, it shall be presumed that such alteration does not amount to substantial reproduction unless proven otherwise before an adjudicating authority. Furthermore, if the alleged infringer demonstrates good faith belief that they possessed valid authorization at the time of the adaptation’s creation, the burden shall shift to the copyright owner to establish lack of consent.

Any unauthorized adaptation of a cinematograph film, whether by way of translation, duplication, or alteration, without due authorization from the owner of copyright therein shall constitute infringement. Where such infringement is committed with the intent to create an undue advantage or cause substantial loss to the copyright holder, the court may impose a penalty not exceeding ten times the reasonable licensing fee that would have been payable had the adaptation been made under license. Further, any person found guilty of commercial-scale reproduction for distribution shall be liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and with fine which may extend to one million rupees. This provision is without prejudice to any other remedies available to the copyright owner as provided herein.

The right to assign copyright in any musical work shall extend to the grant of a license permitting the mechanical reproduction thereof, provided that such license specifies the duration and geographical scope of the permitted reproductions. Any assignment made under this Act may be further assigned or licensed by the assignee, subject to the terms initially stipulated in the original assignment agreement. Where an exclusive license is granted for the distribution of a literary work, subsequent assignments of copyright shall be deemed void unless expressly authorized by the grantor of such initial license. To constitute infringement of copyright in respect of a computer program, it shall be necessary to demonstrate unauthorized reproduction or adaptation beyond that permitted under this Act’s provisions relating to fair use and reverse engineering for interoperability purposes. The owner of copyright may also grant licenses allowing public performance rights.

The reproduction of any work in a digital format shall not constitute infringement under this Act if such reproduction was undertaken solely for the purpose of archival preservation by an entity recognized as a public library, provided that the said entity demonstrates adherence to established protocols designed to prevent unauthorized distribution. However, where it is demonstrated that the reproduction facilitated access to the copyrighted work beyond the scope of legitimate research or educational activities, or was commercially exploited without due authorization from the copyright owner, such actions shall be deemed actionable under this Act. Any aggrieved party may appeal a determination regarding infringement to the relevant High Court, presenting evidence substantiating their claim and challenging the findings of any preliminary assessment.

The unauthorized reproduction or distribution of any registered design, where such reproduction is substantially similar to the protected design as recorded in the design registry and used without due license, shall constitute infringement under this Act. Any person found guilty of such infringement may be liable to pay damages equivalent to a percentage of the profits earned by the infringer from the infringing activity, or failing that, an amount determined by the Court to be just and reasonable. Further, where the infringement is proven to have been committed with intent to deceive or cause confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of goods, enhanced penalties, including imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, may be imposed as provided herein.

The reproduction of any photograph shall be deemed to constitute infringement where such reproduction is undertaken without due authorization from the owner of copyright therein. For the purposes of this Act, "photograph" includes any digital representation thereof, and extends to derivative works created by alteration or manipulation of the original image, subject to reasonable considerations regarding transformative use. An act of copying a photograph for commercial gain, or distribution beyond private circulation, shall be presumed to constitute infringement unless proven otherwise. Nothing herein shall prevent the fair dealing with a photograph for criticism or review, provided that such dealing is accompanied by proper acknowledgement of the copyright owner.

A section patent shall confer upon the patentee exclusive right to make, use and sell the patented invention for the term specified herein. For the purposes of this Act, an invention shall be deemed to be granted a section patent if it relates to a method or process for producing a substance applied in an agricultural, horticultural, piscicultural, pastoral or industrial process or product. Provided that such method or process does not involve the use of any biological agent including microorganisms, viruses, cell lines and recombinant DNA techniques. The right conferred by a section patent shall be subject to compulsory licensing as provided herein.

An application for a section patent may be filed with the Controller in the prescribed form and manner, detailing the invention claimed and its supporting documentation. The applicant shall furnish particulars relating to priority, if any, claimed under this Act. Where an inventor is not the applicant, the application must explicitly state the relationship between the inventor and the applicant, along with a written assignment of rights duly executed. The Controller may require further information or clarification regarding the invention’s novelty or non-obviousness, and failure to comply within the stipulated time shall render the application liable for rejection. Any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act relating to registration of a patent may appeal to the Appellate Board.

Where a person aggrieved by an order made under this Act relating to the grant, revocation or infringement of a section patent has suffered material loss or injury as a consequence thereof, such person may institute proceedings in the High Court. The High Court shall have jurisdiction to entertain these proceedings and may issue such writ, direction or order as it deems just and equitable, subject to the limitations prescribed under this Act regarding judicial review of technical decisions. Any party seeking remedies under this provision must demonstrate that the impugned decision was demonstrably erroneous in law and resulted in quantifiable damages. The Court may award compensation for losses incurred, including but not limited to lost profits and costs associated with defending or prosecuting the patent. Provided that any order made by the High Court shall be subject to appeal before the Supreme Court as provided herein.

An application for a section patent may be filed with the Controller in the prescribed form and manner, setting forth the particulars of the invention and, as far as possible, claiming the matter which the applicant regards as his invention. The applicant shall furnish such documents, drawings and information as are necessary to enable the Controller to ascertain the nature of the invention claimed. Upon receipt of an application, the Controller may require the applicant to submit further details or clarifications regarding the claims made therein. An official search report relating to prior art shall be generated and provided to the applicant for their consideration. The applicant shall have a period of six months from the date of said report to amend the patent specification if deemed necessary. Failure to respond within this timeframe may result in abandonment of the application under this Act.

An application for a section patent shall be deemed invalid if it does not disclose the matter in a manner sufficiently clear and complete for a person skilled in the art to put the invention into practice; provided that such lack of clarity or completeness is demonstrably attributable to deficiencies in the original disclosure and not arising from subsequent interpretation. The Controller may, upon receiving an objection under this Act regarding novelty, require the applicant to furnish further particulars substantiating the inventive step claimed within the patent application. Such particulars shall be submitted within a period as determined by the Controller, failing which the application is liable for rejection. Any modification made to the invention after the date of filing the application shall not be incorporated unless expressly disclosed in the original specification and supported by documentary evidence.

Any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act relating to a section patent may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appellate Board shall consider only questions of law arising out of the order appealed against and may confirm, reverse, or modify the order, or remit the case to the Controller for further consideration as it deems fit. Failure to comply with the prescribed time limit for appeal shall be a ground for dismissal; however, the Board may entertain an appeal delayed beyond that period if satisfactory explanation for the delay is furnished. Any party dissatisfied with the decision of the Appellate Board may petition to the Supreme Court under Article 136 of the Constitution. The Controller may impose penalties for wilful violation of provisions relating to patent applications and revocation proceedings.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, the holder of a section patent may grant licenses relating to the patented invention, either wholly or partially, in India or elsewhere. Such license may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and may be granted for a specified period or perpetually, as determined by the patentee. Any assignment of a patent shall include all rights and privileges which the assignee may exercise under this Act, including the right to grant licenses. Where a license is assigned along with the patent, the terms thereof shall be deemed part of the assignment unless expressly stated otherwise. The Controller may require disclosure of any agreements relating to licensing or assignment if he deems it necessary for ensuring fair practices and preventing abuse of intellectual property rights under this Act.

The grant of a section patent shall be deemed invalid if it is demonstrated, on appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, that the invention was previously known or used in India, notwithstanding the absence of publication under this Act. The burden of proving such prior knowledge or use rests upon the appellant and must be substantiated by documentary evidence or credible testimony; failure to meet this evidentiary threshold shall result in dismissal of the appeal. Provided that, where the respondent demonstrates reasonable grounds to believe that the appellant’s claim is based on information obtained in breach of confidence, the Board may direct further inquiry into the matter. The decision of the Intellectual Property Appellate Board concerning such appeals shall be final, subject to challenge before a High Court only on limited grounds as provided herein.

The holder of a section patent may grant exclusive licenses in respect of the patented invention, either wholly or partially and for the entire term thereof, or for a specified period. Such license shall be assignable under this Act, and a certificate purporting to be an assignment or license, when signed by the patentee or their duly authorized representative, shall be admissible as prima facie evidence of the validity of such assignment or license. Where an exclusive license is granted, the licensee shall have the right to sue for infringement of the patent, subject to any conditions specified in the license agreement. Further, a non-exclusive license may be granted without prejudice to the rights of the patentee to exploit the invention themselves. Any transfer of a section patent or associated licenses requires registration with the Controller and is only valid upon such registration as provided herein.

An application for a section patent may be filed in India by any person claiming to be the inventor of the invention, or by any person authorized to make the application on behalf of an inventor, including legal representatives of deceased inventors. Where an applicant has previously made an international registration sub designating India, the application shall incorporate such prior designation and the documents presented for examination under this Act shall include a copy of the international search report and written opinion, if available. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish further information or clarification regarding the invention claimed, including details pertaining to the derivation of the invention from existing knowledge. Any request for amendment to the patent application must be supported by evidence demonstrating novelty and inventive step as provided herein.

For the purposes of ensuring impartiality in proceedings concerning inventions relating to biotechnology and pharmaceutical processes, under this Act, where a dispute arises regarding the technical soundness or novelty assessment of an invention, the Controller may, subject to regulations framed by the Central Government, appoint independent scientific experts. Such appointed individuals shall possess demonstrable expertise within the relevant field of science or technology and be free from any conflicting interests as determined by the Controller. The Controller shall provide these independent scientific advisors with access to all pertinent documentation presented during examination proceedings, provided that confidentiality obligations are observed as prescribed herein.

For the purposes of facilitating efficient examination and adjudication under this Act, the Controller may, at his discretion and subject to guidelines framed by the Central Government, appoint independent scientific advisors. Such appointment shall be made where complex technical aspects of an invention are involved, or when clarification is required regarding prior art references cited in opposition proceedings. The Controller shall maintain a panel of qualified individuals possessing relevant expertise for this purpose. Any party aggrieved by the appointment or conduct of such advisor may file representations with the Controller, who shall consider them and take appropriate action as provided herein. Further, the costs associated with the services of any appointed independent scientific advisor shall be borne equally by the parties unless otherwise determined by the Controller.

Where an objection is raised during examination under this Act concerning the novelty or inventive step of an invention, the Controller may, acting on his own motion or at the request of any interested party, appoint independent scientific experts to advise upon technical matters arising in connection with such objection. The appointment shall be made in writing and specify the scope of inquiry for the expert(s), which shall not extend beyond the issues directly relevant to assessing novelty and inventive step as defined under this Act. Such appointed individuals must possess demonstrable expertise within the relevant field of technology, free from any conflict of interest that could reasonably compromise their impartiality. The Controller shall provide the expert(s) with all pertinent documentation relating to the invention and the objection raised. Their report shall be submitted to the Controller within a timeframe as may be specified in the appointment order.

Where a patent is challenged on grounds of novelty or inventive step, the Controller shall, subject to appeal under this Act, have power to appoint independent scientific experts to examine and report upon the technical aspects of the invention in dispute. Such appointment shall be made where the Controller deems that specialized knowledge beyond that possessed by the presiding officer is necessary for a just determination of the matter. Failure to comply with any direction issued by an appointed expert may render a party liable to penalties as determined by the Controller, not exceeding one hundred thousand rupees. The costs associated with engaging such experts shall be borne equally by the patentee and the challenger, unless otherwise directed by the Controller.

Where a dispute arises concerning the novelty or inventive step of an invention claimed in a patent application or relating to the validity of a granted patent, the Controller may, sua sponte or upon application by any interested party, appoint independent scientific experts. Such appointment shall be made where the technical subject matter is complex and requires specialized knowledge beyond that readily available within the Controller’s office. The appointed expert's report shall not be binding on the Controller but must be considered in reaching a decision. Any party aggrieved by the selection or conduct of an independently appointed scientific advisor may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, provided that such appeal is filed within sixty days of the publication of the Controller’s order.

For the purposes of ensuring impartiality in examination proceedings under this Act, the Controller shall have power to appoint independent scientific advisors where questions of technical merit arise that require specialized expertise beyond the Controller’s own understanding. Such appointments shall be made subject to regulations framed by the Central Government prescribing qualifications, remuneration and terms of engagement for these advisors. The Controller may direct any such advisor to investigate specific aspects of an invention's novelty or inventive step, and their reports shall be considered alongside other evidence presented during examination. Mark regulations pertaining to certification schemes relating to biotechnological inventions shall also inform the selection criteria for appointed scientific advisors.

For the purposes of ensuring impartiality in proceedings concerning the validity or infringement of patents relating to pharmaceutical formulations, the Controller shall have the power to appoint independent scientific advisors. Such appointments may be made sua sponte or upon application by any party involved in a dispute under this Act. The Controller shall specify the qualifications and scope of work for each appointed advisor, ensuring expertise relevant to the patented article in question. An advisor so appointed shall submit a written report detailing their findings and opinions to the Controller within a timeframe as determined by him. Any party aggrieved by the findings of an independent scientific advisor may challenge them before the Controller, subject to such procedures as are prescribed herein.

Where an application for patent is examined under this Act, the Controller shall, if he considers it necessary for the proper determination of novelty, inventive step, or other matters relating to the invention, appoint independent scientific experts. Such appointment shall be made in writing and specify the scope of inquiry and report expected from the appointed expert. The Controller may request the expert’s opinion on any technical aspect relevant to the assessment of patentability as provided herein. A register maintained by the Controller shall record details of all such appointments, including the names of the experts, their qualifications, and the subject matter of their reports. Any party aggrieved by a report submitted under this Act may submit written objections within thirty days from the date of its communication. The Controller shall consider these objections before making any decision based on the expert’s opinion.

For the purposes of this Act, an “independent scientific adviser” means a person possessing qualifications and experience in a relevant field of science or technology, appointed by the Controller to provide expert guidance on matters relating to patentability, novelty, inventive step, and undue preference. Such an individual shall not be employed by any applicant for patents or possess a significant financial interest in such application. The Controller may determine the terms and conditions of engagement of an independent scientific adviser, provided that their remuneration is commensurate with their expertise and time commitment. An opinion rendered by an independent scientific adviser under this Act shall be advisory to the Controller and not binding.

An applicant seeking registration of a patent relating to a process for producing a novel pharmaceutical compound shall be required to disclose, in the prescribed form, details regarding all individuals who have provided scientific advice during the development and refinement of said process. Such disclosure must include the name, qualifications, and nature of services rendered by each such individual. Where an independent scientific adviser has been engaged to evaluate aspects of the invention’s novelty or non-obviousness, a declaration from that adviser confirming their impartiality and absence of any vested interest in the applicant's enterprise shall be submitted alongside the patent application. Failure to comply with these disclosure requirements may render the patent registration liable for revocation under this Act.

Where an applicant seeks to obtain a patent for an invention relating to a process by which a substance is produced, and where that process involves complex scientific principles, the Controller may, at his discretion, require the assistance of an independent scientific adviser. Such an adviser shall be appointed from a panel maintained by the Patents Office, comprising individuals possessing demonstrable expertise in the relevant field. The costs associated with the engagement of this independent scientific adviser shall be borne equally by the applicant and the patent office, subject to regulations prescribed by the Central Government. Any party aggrieved by the appointment or findings of an independent scientific adviser may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days of the order being made, provided that such appeal does not operate as a stay on any subsequent proceedings under this Act.

Where in proceedings relating to the validity of a patent, or concerning allegations of infringement under this Act, a matter of significant technical complexity arises, the Controller may, sua sponte or upon application by any party, direct the appointment of an independent scientific adviser. The selection of such an adviser shall be made from a panel maintained by the Patents Office, comprising individuals possessing demonstrable expertise in the relevant field of technology. Any person appointed as an independent scientific adviser shall submit a written report to the Controller detailing their findings and opinions on the technical aspects of the matter under consideration. This report shall be accompanied by a declaration confirming impartiality and absence of any conflicting interest. The Controller shall consider the report, but is not bound by its conclusions; provided that reasons for departing from such recommendations must be recorded in writing. An independent scientific adviser appointed under this provision shall be entitled to remuneration as determined by the Patents Office.

Where an invention relates to a process for producing a substance intended for use in or in connection with pharmaceuticals, the Controller may, at his discretion, require the applicant to furnish detailed information regarding clinical trial data and manufacturing protocols. Such requirement shall be deemed necessary where the claimed invention incorporates elements derived from traditional knowledge, as evidenced by documented usage prior to the filing date of the patent application. Furthermore, if any question arises concerning the novelty or inventive step of such an invention, the Controller may appoint an independent scientific adviser possessing expertise in pharmacology and related disciplines. The appointed individual shall provide a written report detailing their assessment, subject to confidentiality obligations under this Act.

Where, in proceedings relating to revocation or validity of a patent, a substantial question of scientific or technical complexity arises, the Controller may, subject to regulations framed under this Act, direct the appointment of an independent scientific adviser. The costs associated with such an adviser shall be borne by the petitioner or respondent as determined by the Controller. Failure to comply with directions issued by the appointed independent scientific adviser, including providing requested documentation or appearing for examination, shall constitute contempt of court and render the party liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Any person found to have misrepresented their qualifications in order to serve as an independent scientific adviser is subject to prosecution under relevant provisions concerning false evidence.

Where a patent holder desires to exploit an invention commercially through a licensee, and such exploitation necessitates access to technical data or advice pertaining to the patented process, the patent holder shall be obligated to provide reasonable facilities for consultation with an independent scientific adviser appointed by the licensee. The appointment of such an adviser requires prior written consent from the patent holder, provided that the scope of the adviser’s remit is clearly defined within the licensing agreement and does not extend beyond matters directly relevant to the licensed technology. Further, any assignment or transfer of a patent shall be deemed to include all rights pertaining to existing licenses granted under this Act, subject to the terms stipulated therein regarding continued access for an independent scientific adviser. The patent holder may charge reasonable fees for such facilities, as agreed upon in writing with the licensee.

Where, in proceedings concerning the validity of a patent or relating to infringement under this Act, a dispute arises regarding the technical expertise required to determine novelty or inventive step, the Controller may, sua sponte or upon application by any interested party, appoint an independent scientific adviser. Such appointment shall be made after providing all parties with reasonable notice and opportunity to object to the proposed appointee’s qualifications or potential bias. The report of the independent scientific adviser is advisory only and does not bind the Controller; however, any challenge to the impartiality or competence of such an adviser may be raised by appeal before a High Court. Provided that the Controller shall record reasons for departing from any recommendation made by an independent scientific adviser.
