The Controller may require further information or clarification as deemed necessary before rendering a decision.

Where a published work is translated into another language, the translator shall be deemed the author of the translation insofar as the arrangement and expression of such translation are original. Provided that, where the translation reproduces without alteration any substantial portion of the original work, copyright therein shall extend only to the translations of those portions which constitute original literary effort. The owner of copyright in the original work shall have the right to grant or withhold permission for the publication work translation. Any person seeking authorization to publish a translation must provide evidence demonstrating due diligence in attempting to ascertain the current copyright holder. Failure to comply with this requirement may render such publication an infringement under this Act.

Where a published work has been translated into another language without authorization from the owner of copyright therein, such unauthorized translation shall be deemed an infringement under this Act. Any individual engaging in the reproduction, distribution, public display, or performance of such infringing translation is liable to prosecution and subject to penalties as provided herein. The court may impose fines not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees and imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years. Further, any person found guilty of knowingly assisting in the creation or dissemination of an unauthorized publication work translation shall be deemed complicit and similarly penalized, subject to considerations of mitigating circumstances presented before the adjudicating authority.

Where the copyright subsists in a published work, any individual or body corporate engaged primarily in the business of publishing may apply for authorization to undertake a publication work translation. Such application shall specify the original work, the proposed language of translation, and the intended territory of distribution. The owner of the copyright in the original work may grant such authorization unconditionally or subject to terms and conditions regarding royalties and other remuneration as they deem fit. Provided that where an initial authorization is granted, subsequent authorizations for similar translations shall be offered to previous licensees at rates not exceeding those previously agreed upon, unless a compelling reason demonstrably justifying a higher rate is presented. Any assignment of rights relating to publication work translation under this Act shall require registration with the designated authority and shall be deemed invalid if unregistered.

Where a published work is translated into another language, such translation shall be deemed an original literary work subject to the conditions prescribed herein. The translator shall possess exclusive rights in respect of the translation, notwithstanding that the underlying work remains protected under this Act. Any person desiring to reproduce, distribute, or adapt such a publication work translation without authorization from the copyright owner of the translation shall be considered guilty of an accused offence and may face penalties as provided for under this Act. Provided that, where the original work is in the public domain, permission from the author of the original work is not required for the creation of the translation; however, rights pertaining to the translation itself remain with the translator.

For the purposes of this Act, "Darjeeling Tea" means tea produced exclusively in the defined geographical area consisting of specified hillsides and valleys within the Darjeeling district of West Bengal, as notified by the Register; such production being subject to adherence to traditional processing methods including orthodox or green leaf processing. The term “defined geographical area” shall include any subsequent modifications thereto as provided herein. Any use of the word "Darjeeling" in connection with tea not meeting these provisions shall be deemed an infringement under this Act, and may result in penalties as determined by the relevant authorities. This definition is without prejudice to other provisions relating to quality standards for registered geographical indications.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may be filed with the Registrar in such form and manner as may be prescribed, including particulars relating to the name of the geographical indication sought to be registered, the goods or services to which it relates, the area of entitlement, and the history and characteristics of the product or service. The applicant shall furnish evidence that the said indications are essentially attributable to the geographical origin of the goods or services. Further provisions concerning the examination of applications stipulate that the Registrar may require the applicant to submit additional information or clarification regarding any aspect of the application. Any interested party may, within sixty days from the date of publication of a notice under this Act, file an opposition to the registration.

Any proprietor seeking rectification of a registered geographical indication may file an application with the Registrar, setting forth the facts and grounds upon which such rectification is claimed. The Registrar shall afford every interested party an opportunity of being heard in opposition to the application, and after considering all evidence presented, may grant or refuse the rectification sought. Where rectification is granted, the provisions relating to the registered geographical indication shall have effect as if the rectified register had been originally drawn up in that form.

Further, any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act concerning the revocation or amendment of a registration may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final and binding, subject to provisions for judicial review as provided herein. Any false or misleading indication that falsely suggests goods originate from a registered geographical indication constitutes an infringement actionable under this Act.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may be filed with the Registrar in such form and manner as may be prescribed, including particulars relating to the name of the geographical indication sought to be registered, the goods or services for which it is used, and the area of its origin. The applicant shall furnish evidence establishing that the quality, reputation, or other characteristic of the goods or services originates from the geographical territory specified in the application. Where an objection is raised by any person against the registration of a geographical indication under this Act, the Registrar shall give notice to the applicant and afford both parties an opportunity of being heard. The Registrar may, after considering the objections and the response of the applicant, either proceed with the consideration of the application or reject it entirely. These provisions relating to procedure are without prejudice to any other power vested in the Registrar to regulate the conduct of proceedings.

An application for registration as a geographical indication shall contain particulars specifying the name of the agricultural product or good, its essential qualities and characteristics derived from its origin, the defined geographical area constituting such origin, the production methods employed, and the history and traditions relating to its establishment. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further information deemed necessary for assessing compliance with these provisions. Any association representing producers of goods conforming to the standards specified in the application shall be eligible to file on behalf of its members, provided that a majority of such producers consent in writing. Further, any alteration to production methods or quality characteristics after registration will require prior approval from the Registrar, subject to guidelines issued under this Act concerning continued adherence to established norms.

Any person who, without due cause and after being notified by the Register, continues to use a protected geographical indication in contravention of the provisions relating to registration shall be liable for damages equivalent to three times the value of the goods sold under that mark during the period of infringement, recoverable as a civil debt. Further, such offender may also face prosecution under this Act and shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees, or both, at the discretion of the court. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, issue directions regarding enforcement measures against infringements as provided herein.

Any proprietor seeking to grant a license relating to the use of an indication registered under this Act shall, in the application for such license, specify the geographical area within which the licensed party is authorized to utilize the indication and clearly delineate the goods or services to which the authorization pertains. Such licenses may be granted on exclusive or non-exclusive terms as determined by the proprietor, subject to the condition that the terms of use are consistent with maintaining the quality and reputation associated with the registered geographical indication. Further provisions relating to assignment of rights in a registered geographical indication stipulate that any assignment shall include not only the right to utilize the indication but also all privileges afforded under this Act pertaining to its protection. The assignee shall be deemed subject to all prior licenses and encumbrances existing at the time of assignment, provided that written consent from the original proprietor is obtained for any subsequent sub-licensing activities.

The Registrar may entertain an application for registration of a geographical indication only if the applicant demonstrates exclusive use of the name by a defined group of producers within the specified territory; however, any person aggrieved by such determination under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The provisions relating to the assessment of prior usage shall be interpreted strictly in favour of protecting established geographical indications, provided that evidence presented by an objecting party substantiating a reasonable belief of consumer confusion due to similarity with an existing mark will necessitate further consideration. Further, the Board may require additional documentary proof regarding production methods and quality control measures before upholding any claim concerning continued exclusivity.

For the purposes of determining original jurisdiction under this Act, a "district court having jurisdiction" shall be deemed to possess such jurisdiction over any matter relating to the alleged unauthorized reproduction, distribution, or public performance of cinematograph films. This determination shall apply irrespective of the place where the alleged infringement occurred, provided that the cause of action arose within the territorial limits of India. Subject to appeal to the High Court as provided herein, no other court shall entertain suits concerning claims arising from the exploitation of artistic works incorporated within a cinematograph film. The term "cinematograph film" includes any work in which images are moving and capable of being shown on a screen.

Registration of musical works shall be deemed conclusive evidence of ownership, subject to proof demonstrating fraudulent intent at the time of registration. An applicant seeking registration of a sound recording may also register any underlying musical work incorporated therein, provided that such application specifies the nature and extent of the claimed copyright. Where disputes arise concerning the authenticity of a registered work or the validity of an asserted claim under this Act, proceedings shall be initiated in a district court having jurisdiction over the place where the applicant’s principal place of business is situated. The Court may order inspection of original manuscripts, recordings, or other relevant materials to determine rightful ownership and resolve any ambiguities as provided herein.

Where an aggrieved party alleges that their copyright has been infringed through unauthorized reproduction, distribution, or public performance of a literary work, they may institute legal proceedings to seek redress under this Act. Subject to provisions regarding limitation periods, any such action must be commenced within three years from the date the infringement is reasonably ascertainable. The plaintiff shall be entitled to claim damages proportionate to the loss suffered by them as a direct result of the infringing activity, or where actual damage is difficult to quantify, a sum not exceeding ten per cent of the reasonable cost of production and sale of the work. Furthermore, the court may grant an injunction restraining the defendant from further acts of infringement, provided that such relief is demonstrably necessary to prevent irreparable harm. Any suit arising under this Act shall be brought before a district court having jurisdiction over the place where the cause of action arose.

Any action seeking damages or injunctive relief pertaining to allegations of unauthorized reproduction, distribution, public performance, or adaptation of cinematograph films shall be filed exclusively within the civil courts. The determination of territorial jurisdiction under this Act shall be governed by the principles established under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, as amended. Provided that, where a copyright owner demonstrates reasonable grounds to believe that an infringement extends beyond the geographical limits of a single district, they may elect to initiate proceedings in any district court having jurisdiction over at least one location where such infringement occurred or is reasonably believed to have occurred. The plaintiff shall be required to submit an affidavit detailing the basis for asserting jurisdiction across multiple districts. Failure to do so may result in dismissal of the action without prejudice.

Where an action alleging copyright infringement is initiated under this Act, jurisdiction shall vest solely in a district court having jurisdiction over the place where the alleged infringing act occurred, or where the cause of action arose. Provided that, if the defendant has a place of business within the local limits of another such district court, suit may also be brought therein. Further provided that, for determining purposes under this subsection, an act of communication to the public shall be deemed to have occurred at each location from which said communication originates and at each location where it is received. Subject to compliance with prescribed rules regarding service of summons, a defendant’s failure to maintain a registered address shall not preclude jurisdiction in any district court as provided herein.

Any person found to have knowingly reproduced, distributed, or publicly displayed any copyrighted work without authorization shall be liable for damages as determined by the Court. Such damages may include actual loss suffered by the copyright owner and a sum not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees, awarded at the discretion of the Court. Further, where an infringement is established, the Court may order the seizure and destruction of infringing copies and materials used in their creation. The institution of proceedings under this Act shall be exclusively within the jurisdiction of a district court having jurisdiction over the place where the infringement occurred or where the cause of action arose. Repeated offenses shall attract enhanced penalties as determined by the presiding officer, subject to principles of natural justice.

Any assignment of copyright in a musical work, or any adaptation thereof, shall be deemed to include the right to grant non-exclusive licenses for public performance and mechanical reproduction, unless such exclusion is expressly stated within the instrument effecting the assignment. Provided that, where an assignment relates to multiple works, the licensor may stipulate conditions restricting the scope of permitted performances and reproductions relating to each work individually. Further, any subsequent transfer of rights under a copyright shall be subject to the terms and conditions of the original assignment, as recorded with the competent authority. Suits concerning disputes arising from such assignments or licenses shall be brought before a district court having jurisdiction over the place where the alleged infringement occurred, or where the defendant resides or carries on business. The right to enforce these provisions is vested in any person demonstrably prejudiced by a breach thereof.

Subject to appeal to the appellate jurisdiction under this Act, no civil suit alleging copyright infringement concerning a musical work shall lie in any court other than a district court having jurisdiction over the territory within which the defendant resides or carries on business, or where the cause of action arose. Provided that, if the defendant has places of business in multiple districts, the plaintiff may initiate proceedings in any such district court. The determination of whether a particular district court possesses such jurisdiction shall be subject to review by the High Court upon petition demonstrating demonstrable prejudice resulting from the chosen forum. Further, an aggrieved party may challenge the jurisdictional competence of a district court through interlocutory application pending trial, should it be reasonably asserted that venue was improperly selected.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, any person claiming that copyright in a work has been infringed may institute a suit for redressal of such infringement in a district court having jurisdiction over the place where the alleged infringement occurred, or where the cause of action arose. Where the defendant has places of business in multiple districts, suits relating to copyright infringement may be filed in any district court within whose territorial limits one or more of those places of business are located. The determination of jurisdiction shall be subject to appeal as provided herein. Further, for works initially published abroad and subsequently registered under the provisions governing international agreements such as the Patent Cooperation Treaty, the jurisdictional framework outlined above shall apply irrespective of the place of first publication. Costs associated with litigation shall be determined according to established principles of equity and fairness.

Any person found to have reproduced, distributed, or publicly displayed any copyrighted work without due authorization shall be liable for damages as determined by the Court. Such damages shall not be less than five times the actual loss suffered by the copyright owner and may extend up to ten times such amount where the infringement is deemed willful. Further, subject to provisions regarding fair dealing, a proprietor of registered trade marks used in connection with copyrighted material shall have standing to bring an action for contributory infringement. The district court having jurisdiction shall be empowered to issue injunctions restraining further acts of copyright violation and may order the destruction of infringing copies. Penalties under this Act are without prejudice to any other penalties provided elsewhere.

Any assignment of copyright in a musical work, including but not limited to rights pertaining to public performance and mechanical reproduction, shall require endorsement by the assignor unless such assignment is executed before a Notary Public attesting to their identity and confirming voluntary consent. Where an assignment is made without proper endorsement or notarization, any party proceeding against the assignee for breach of contract may petition the district court having jurisdiction to declare the assignment voidable at the option of the original copyright holder. Further, sub-licensing rights granted under a valid assignment are transferable subject to the terms stipulated within the initial agreement and provided that such transfer does not diminish the assignor’s share of royalties as determined by the Comptroller. The Registrar shall maintain a public record of all assignments and sub-licenses registered under this Act.

Where an action is brought alleging unauthorized reproduction or adaptation of a copyright design, and the defendant’s place of business or residence is situated within the territorial limits of multiple districts, the plaintiff may elect to initiate proceedings in any district court having jurisdiction over such defendant. Provided that, if the defendant contests the jurisdictional basis for venue under this Act, the court shall determine whether it possesses subject matter and personal jurisdiction as provided herein. Further, an appeal from any order or decree made by a district court having jurisdiction concerning copyright design infringement may be made to the High Court within whose territorial jurisdiction the district court is situated, subject to such conditions regarding costs as the High Court may prescribe.

For the purposes of this Act, in relation to an invention, “prior use” shall mean a documented and verifiable demonstration of public exploitation of a process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter occurring within the territory of India prior to the date of filing of the patent application claiming such invention. Such documentation must include credible evidence establishing both the availability of the invention to the public and its practical implementation. Prior use shall not be imputed solely from circumstantial evidence or promotional material; it requires substantive proof of operational deployment. Provided that, any prior use made under conditions of confidence, or for experimental purposes only, shall not constitute prior use as defined herein.

For the purposes of registration under this Act, an invention shall be deemed to relate to an invention if it incorporates novel and non-obvious features distinguishing it from prior art. The Controller may require further clarification regarding the technical aspects of such an invention during examination proceedings, particularly concerning its application or utility as claimed in the patent specification. Subject to compliance with prescribed formalities, including payment of requisite fees, a request for registration shall be processed irrespective of whether the invention is capable of industrial application. Provided that the description clearly and accurately defines the scope of protection sought, any modification or alteration subsequent to the initial filing date shall not invalidate the registration if it remains consistent in relation to an invention as originally disclosed.

Where, in relation to an invention, a patent has been granted but is subsequently revoked by order of the Controller under this Act, any person who prior to the date of grant had possessed knowledge or used the invention shall be liable for damages sustained as a direct result of the patentee’s actions during the period of enforceability. Such damages shall include, but not be limited to, lost profits reasonably attributable to the infringing activity and compensation for costs incurred in adapting processes or equipment. Provided that, if the revocation is determined to have been caused by an error on the part of the Controller, the patentee may seek redress through appropriate legal proceedings against the Controller for any losses suffered due to the wrongful revocation. Further, a party seeking such damages must demonstrate clear and convincing evidence of reliance upon the validity of the patent in question.

For the purposes of determining novelty, inventive step, and obviousness under this Act, an assessment shall be made as to whether the prior art discloses or renders obvious the claimed invention in relation to an invention. The Controller may, at any time during the examination of a patent application, require the applicant to furnish such further information or particulars relating to the specification or claims as he considers necessary for the purpose of determining compliance with the provisions herein. Such requirement shall be accompanied by a statement specifying the grounds on which it is based and providing a reasonable opportunity for the applicant to respond in writing. The response submitted by the applicant may include arguments, evidence, or amendments to the application. Any amendment proposed shall not alter the nature of the invention as originally claimed, subject to provisions regarding minor modifications. Failure to comply with such requirement within the prescribed period may result in the rejection of the patent application.

For the purposes of determining novelty, prior publication shall be deemed to include any disclosure by any means, whether in India or elsewhere, relating to an invention, provided that such disclosure was available in a form in which it could be carried out by a person skilled in the art. Where an application for patents is filed disclosing matter not contained in the specification as originally filed, but which forms, with the said specification, a complete description of the invention, the patent shall be granted only for the portion of the invention disclosed in the original specification, subject to compliance with all other requirements under this Act. In relation to an invention, any modification or adaptation thereof that does not involve an inventive step shall not be considered a separate invention.

Where, in relation to an invention, it is established before the Controller that a person has knowingly and wilfully made, used, sold, or imported any patented article without authorization from the patentee, such person shall be liable for damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the patentee. The amount of damages may include lost profits reasonably attributable to the infringing activity, together with interest at a rate determined under this Act. Further, where an infringement is proven, the Controller may order the destruction of the infringing goods and materials used in their manufacture. Any appeal against such orders shall be made within ninety days from the date of notification, subject to penalties for delay as provided herein.

Where, in relation to an invention, a patentee desires to grant a license conferring specific rights pertaining to the exploitation of the patented process or product, such license may be assigned wholly or partially to any person, firm, or company, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated within the agreement. Provided that any assignment shall require registration with the Controller, and failure to register shall render the assignee’s rights unenforceable against third parties claiming prior use or similar inventions. The patentee shall provide a detailed statement of the licensed territory and scope of exclusivity granted under this Act. Further, where an invention is jointly owned, the consent of all joint owners shall be required for any assignment or license agreement relating to that invention. Any subsequent transfer of such rights must also adhere to these stipulations as provided herein.

For the purposes of determining novelty, as provided herein, an invention shall be considered to lack novelty if it is disclosed in a document available to the public before the priority date claimed, subject to the proviso that such disclosure does not necessarily preclude the grant of a patent. Where a claim extends to a matter which differs from the prior art disclosure, and the extent of said difference is disputed by an interested party during examination or opposition proceedings, the Controller may require the applicant to demonstrate, through clear and concise argumentation, how such difference constitutes a contribution over the existing body of knowledge. The burden of proof in relation to an invention shall rest upon the applicant to establish that the aforementioned contribution warrants patentability, failing which the application may be rejected.

Where, in relation to an invention, it is found that the claimed subject matter incorporates elements derived from a breeder variety registered under this Act, and such incorporation constitutes a substantial reproduction or adaptation without due authorization from the registering authority, then any patent granted shall be deemed invalid. Further, the Controller may, upon receiving credible evidence of such infringement, issue a cease-and-desist order directing the patentee to refrain from manufacturing, using, or offering for sale the infringing product. Failure to comply with this order shall render the patentee liable to penalties as provided herein and subject to recovery of damages proportionate to the extent of commercial exploitation.

Where a patentee, in relation to an invention, desires to grant a license conferring exclusive rights within India, such license shall be recorded with the Controller. The application for recording shall specify the scope of exclusivity granted, the territory covered by the license, and the royalty rate payable under the terms thereof. Any subsequent assignment or transfer of such license, whether in whole or in part, shall also require recording as provided herein. Failure to amend register shall render the licensee’s rights unenforceable against third parties claiming prior use based on publicly available information. The Controller may, upon application by any interested party and after due notice to the patentee and licensee, inquire into the reasonableness of royalty rates stipulated within a recorded license agreement.

Where, in relation to an invention, a claim is made alleging novelty has been compromised by prior publication occurring subsequent to the date of filing but prior to the grant of patent, the Controller shall provide the applicant with a reasoned written statement detailing the specific publications relied upon and their asserted relevance. The applicant may then submit a counter-statement disputing said assertion, accompanied by documentary evidence substantiating the claim that the publication did not impact the inventive step or novelty as understood under this Act. Subject to an appeal being filed within sixty days of the Controller’s determination, any patent granted shall be deemed invalid if it is established, on review, that the prior publication demonstrably anticipated all elements of the invention; provided that such anticipation does not preclude a patent addition regarding improvements made after the date of the initial publication.

For the purposes of this Act, “in relation to an invention” includes consideration of whether the claimed subject matter is novel and non-obvious, taking into account any prior publication or use anywhere in the world. The determination shall be made considering the entirety of the specification as originally filed, including drawings and claims. Further, a permitted register trade mark, if incorporated within the invention’s description or claim, does not, by virtue of its registration alone, preclude patentability; provided that the inventive step relates to the underlying technical contribution and is not merely ornamental or indicative of the registered trade mark.

An application for registration of a biological material shall be accompanied by a detailed inventory specifying the source, method of acquisition, and any modifications undertaken. The Controller may require submission of documentation demonstrating compliance with relevant bio-safety guidelines as provided herein. Where the applicant seeks to claim protection based on an invention utilizing a microorganism, such organism must be deposited in an internationally recognized depository authority, adhering to the procedures outlined under this Act. For applications referencing international agreements, “treaty means Budapest” and any amendments or protocols thereto shall be deemed incorporated for the purpose of interpreting registration requirements concerning microbial deposits and access conditions.

Where, upon proof satisfactory to the Controller that an act relating to the patent has been performed in a country where reciprocal rights are not granted to persons having the nationality of India, the interests of the Indian patentee have been prejudiced, the Controller may grant such remedies as appear equitable, including but not limited to injunctive relief and compensation for losses directly attributable to the infringing activity. Such prejudice shall be determined considering the scale and nature of the infringement, the commercial impact on the patent holder’s market share, and any demonstrable attempts at trade misrepresentation. For the purposes of this Act, “treaty means Budapest” refers specifically to the Budapest Treaty on the International Recognition of the Deposits of Microorganisms, and its provisions relating to microbial deposits shall be deemed binding upon all parties involved in patent proceedings. The Controller may require evidence demonstrating reasonable efforts made to mitigate damages prior to awarding compensation.

Applications for patents shall be filed in the prescribed form, accompanied by a declaration under oath or affirmation specifying the invention and its claimed novelty. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish further particulars concerning the invention if deemed necessary for examination. Where an application incorporates information derived from published documents, the applicant must provide a comprehensive list of such references. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Controller relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application may appeal to the Appellate Board. The term "treaty means Budapest" shall be interpreted as referring exclusively to the Budapest Treaty on the International Recognition of the Deposits of Microorganisms, and any amendments thereto ratified by India. Further, the provisions regarding provisional applications apply equally to those seeking international protection under this treaty.

Where an application for a patent relating to a pharmaceutical substance is filed, the Controller shall require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating compliance with Good Manufacturing Practices as prescribed under regulations issued by the Central Government. Such evidence must be current and verifiable through independent audits conducted within the preceding three years. Provided that, if the invention relates to a process for producing such a substance, documentation pertaining to quality control measures implemented throughout the production chain shall also be submitted. Further, where an applicant seeks patent protection under this Act in relation to biological material deposited pursuant to the Budapest Treaty means budapest, the deposition must adhere strictly to the requirements outlined therein and remain accessible for inspection as provided herein.

Any person who, having obtained the grant of a patent in contravention of this Act, knowingly and wilfully manufactures, uses, imports, or offers to sell any patented invention shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, and with a fine which may extend to fifty thousand rupees. Further, where such manufacture, use, import, or offer constitutes a commercial activity undertaken for the purpose of profit, the offender shall also be liable to pay compensation equivalent to five times the lost profits suffered by the patentee as determined under this Act. For the purposes of determining said compensation, any act of infringement occurring after the commencement of proceedings before an appropriate forum shall be deemed relevant. “treaty means Budapest” is defined for clarity and consistency with international obligations.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any patentee may grant exclusive licences under the patent and such licence shall be irrevocable unless expressly stated otherwise in the terms thereof. Where a patent has been assigned or an exclusive licence granted, the right to exercise any prerogative vested in the patentee shall vest concurrently in the assignee or licensee, as applicable. An assignment or exclusive licence relating to a patent may be made by way of instrument in writing and executed by or on behalf of the assignor or licensor, and such instrument shall be admissible as evidence under this Act. The International Bureau, acting under the Budapest Treaty means budapest, shall maintain records of assignments and licences for public inspection, subject to any confidentiality agreements entered into pursuant to regulations framed thereunder. Further, a licensee may sub-license rights granted under an exclusive licence, provided that such sub-licence does not contradict the terms of the original agreement.

Where, in proceedings before the Controller under this Act relating to the revocation of a patent for non-obviousness, evidence is presented demonstrating a substantial similarity between the claimed invention and prior art publications originating outside India, the burden shall lie upon the patentee to demonstrate that such foreign publications did not reasonably inform any person skilled in the relevant art at the time of the patent’s grant. Provided that, if the Controller finds that the said publications were disseminated through official gazettes or other publicly accessible channels within India, the presumption shall be against the patentee unless rebutted by affirmative evidence. For the purposes of this section, “treaty means Budapest” and any reference to a publication's dissemination includes its availability via electronic databases as may be prescribed. Any appeal arising from such determination is subject to review based on demonstrable error of law.

Any person who, having made an application for registration of a patent under this Act, knowingly makes a false statement or withholds material information in relation to any particular concerning the invention, shall be punishable with imprisonment which may extend to three years and with a fine extending to one hundred thousand rupees. Further, such applicant shall be deemed guilty of an offence cognizable under this Act and liable to arrest without warrant. Where an application incorporates by reference matter protected by copyright, the Registrar may require the submission of evidence demonstrating proper authorization for use of that material; failure to comply will result in rejection. The term "treaty means Budapest" applies specifically regarding international filings made pursuant to the Budapest Treaty. Any unauthorized use of a pending application registration mark is subject to penalties as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, “true and first inventor” means the individual who conceived of the inventive concept without reference to prior public knowledge or disclosure, and who demonstrated diligent effort towards reducing the same to practice; provided that where an application for a patent discloses that the invention was derived from research conducted by an institution funded by the government, the determination of true and first inventor shall consider contributions made by personnel employed by such institution. An individual claiming to be the true and first inventor shall satisfy the Controller as to their entitlement under this Act, subject to the provisions relating to joint inventions as provided herein.

For the purposes of registration under this Act, where an application for patent relating to an inventive step discloses that it has been derived from a prior disclosure made by another party, the Controller shall require the applicant to demonstrate, through documentary evidence and testimony, that they are indeed the true and first inventor of the subject matter claimed. Such demonstration must establish that the applicant conceived of the invention independently or contributed significantly to its development beyond merely implementing the earlier disclosure. The burden of proving this lies entirely upon the applicant. Provided that, if the Controller is satisfied that the prior disclosure was made without the knowledge or consent of the applicant, and that the applicant has diligently pursued the inventive step, registration may proceed subject to such conditions as the Controller deems appropriate.

Where any question arises as to who is the true and first inventor of an invention, the Controller may determine the matter after affording all parties interested a reasonable opportunity for being heard, and his determination shall be final subject to appeal under this Act. For the purpose of such inquiry, the Controller may consider evidence relating to the conception of the invention, documentary proof establishing priority, and testimony from expert witnesses. It is provided that any party claiming to be the true and first inventor must demonstrate a substantial contribution to the inventive concept, beyond mere translation or adaptation of existing technology. Failure to do so shall render such claim invalid. The Controller may also order rectification of the register if it appears that an incorrect determination has been made regarding inventorship, ensuring equitable redress for all parties aggrieved by erroneous entries.

Where any question arises as to who is the true and first inventor of an invention, the Controller may require such evidence as he deems appropriate to determine said status, including but not limited to declarations from individuals involved in the conception and development of the invention, documentation relating to laboratory notebooks or design records, and testimony regarding the circumstances surrounding the initial disclosure of the inventive concept. The burden of establishing entitlement to be regarded as the true and first inventor shall rest upon the applicant for a patent. Subject to appeal under this Act, the Controller's determination on such matters is final. Further, any party aggrieved by a decision made concerning inventorship may petition the Controller within ninety days from the date of communication of that decision. The Controller may, after affording an opportunity for hearing, revise any prior order if it appears necessary in the interests of justice or to ensure proper application of this Act.

Where an application for a patent relates to an invention developed jointly by two or more persons, the determination of who constitutes the true and first inventor shall be undertaken in accordance with principles of equitable contribution; provided that if it can be demonstrated, through documented evidence including but not limited to laboratory notebooks, correspondence, and assignment agreements, that one person conceived of a substantial aspect of the invention independently and without direct contribution from others, such person may be considered the true and first inventor notwithstanding joint development. Further, where an applicant claims priority based on an earlier application filed outside India, the evidence establishing said priority shall satisfy the Controller as to the date and circumstances under which the invention was conceived and diligently pursued.

Where any question arises as to who is the true and first inventor of a claimed invention, the Controller may, subject to appeal under this Act, determine such question based on evidence presented by all interested parties; provided that in determining priority, the Controller shall consider not only documentary proof establishing the date of invention but also testimony regarding diligent efforts undertaken towards reduction to practice. Any person aggrieved by an order of the Controller concerning inventorship may further petition the Intellectual Property Appellate Board for review, and failure to comply with a Board order shall render such party liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. The determination of inventorship is binding on all parties involved in any proceeding under this Act.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any patentee desiring to grant a license relating to a patented invention shall execute an assignment or register a license agreement with the Controller, specifying the scope and duration thereof. Such agreements may include conditions pertaining to field of use, quantity limitations, or exclusive rights granted to the licensee, provided that such conditions are reasonable and do not unduly restrain trade. Where a patent has been assigned, the assignee shall be deemed the holder of the patent for all purposes under this Act. The determination of who is considered the true and first inventor remains paramount in establishing ownership and entitlement to assign or license rights. Any transfer of interest in a patent, whether by assignment or otherwise, requires notification to the Controller within three months of its execution; failure to do so may render such transfer voidable.

Where any question arises as to who is the true and first inventor of an invention claimed in an application for patents, the Controller may require such party claiming priority under this Act to submit proof establishing their claim, including but not limited to documentary evidence demonstrating conception and reduction to practice prior to any other person. Such proof shall be assessed by the Controller considering all relevant circumstances, subject to the proviso that a mere declaration of inventorship submitted by an applicant or assignee shall not, of itself, constitute sufficient proof. Any party aggrieved by the Controller’s determination may appeal under this Act within sixty days from the date of communication of the order, and the Appellate Board shall consider any evidence presented demonstrating error in the initial assessment.

Where any question arises as to who is the true and first inventor of an invention claimed in an application for patents, the Controller may hold such inquiry as he deems necessary, affording all parties concerned an opportunity of being heard. The determination of inventorship shall be based on evidence presented before the Controller, including but not limited to affidavits from individuals claiming inventive contribution and documentary proof establishing priority of conception or reduction to practice. Subject to this, a person other than the applicant may be declared as the true and first inventor, provided that such declaration is made within three months of the grant of patent to the original applicant. In cases where an invention has been assigned, the assignee shall be deemed to have derived title from the assignor and any determination regarding inventorship shall affect the rights of both parties accordingly. The Controller’s decision on matters of inventorship shall be final, subject to appeal under this Act.

An application filed patent shall be deemed to include a formal request submitted to the Controller seeking grant of exclusive rights for an invention as described in the specification annexed thereto. Such an application must contain particulars relating to the applicant, the inventor, and the priority claim, if any, subject to the requirements regarding novelty and non-obviousness under this Act. The term “specification” shall mean a full description of the invention, enabling a person skilled in the art to make and use it; provided that such specification is accompanied by claims defining the scope of protection sought for the application filed patent.

An application filed patent relating to a process for producing a novel pharmaceutical intermediate shall include detailed specifications outlining the methodology employed, including but not limited to reaction conditions, purification techniques, and yield percentages. The Controller General may require submission of additional data demonstrating reproducibility and scalability of said process under this Act. Where an applicant seeks to claim protection for a method of use, such claims must be supported by experimental evidence substantiating efficacy and safety as provided herein. Any alteration to the originally described process post-filing shall necessitate amendment of the patent application and may impact the grant date. The applicant is responsible for ensuring compliance with all relevant regulatory guidelines pertaining to pharmaceutical manufacturing.

Where an application filed patent has been rejected under this Act, the applicant may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order of rejection. Such appeal shall state the grounds on which it is based and shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the order appealed against. The Appellate Board may entertain any appeal if it is satisfied that the appellant has deposited with it such fees as may be prescribed. Failure to deposit the requisite fee within the stipulated time shall render the appeal incompetent. The Board, after affording an opportunity for hearing to both sides, may allow or dismiss the appeal, and its decision shall be final subject to further appeals under this Act. Any party aggrieved by any order of the Appellate Board may seek redressal as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by a decision refusing an application filed patent may appeal to the Appellate Intellectual Property Tribunal within sixty days from the date of communication of the order; provided that the Appellant shall deposit with the Registry, at the time of filing the memorandum of appeal, such sum as may be prescribed. Failure to comply with this provision will render the appeal inadmissible. The Tribunal shall hear appeals expeditiously and its decision is final subject to further appeal under the writ jurisdiction of the High Court. Any party failing to abide by an order or direction of the Tribunal shall be liable for a penalty not exceeding one hundred thousand rupees, recoverable as civil debt.

Where an application filed patent relates to an invention for which patent rights are already held by another party, the Controller may, subject to conditions prescribed herein, grant permission for a limited license of the patented technology. Such permission shall not prejudice the validity of the existing patent but allows for specified use within India as determined by the Controller. The applicant seeking such licensing permission must demonstrate compelling reasons for its necessity and provide details regarding proposed royalty rates and duration of the license. Any assignment of rights arising from this permitted license shall be subject to prior approval from the Controller, ensuring equitable distribution of benefits derived from the technology. Further, any subsequent application filed patent based on improvements to the licensed invention requires notification to the original patent holder.

Where an application filed patent is challenged on the grounds of lacking novelty under this Act, the Controller may require the petitioner to submit evidence substantiating their claim. Such evidence shall include, but not be limited to, prior publications or publicly available products demonstrating identical subject matter. The applicant for the patent shall then have a period of ninety days from the date of receipt of such requirement to file a counter-statement rebutting the petitioner’s assertions and presenting arguments in support of the novelty claim. Failure to respond within this timeframe shall be deemed an admission of the lack of novelty, subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The Board's decision shall be final, provided that it is not challenged further under revision.

An application filed patent for an invention relating to a novel pharmaceutical composition shall include with it a detailed register of all prior disclosures made by the applicant concerning the subject matter of the claimed invention, including but not limited to presentations at scientific conferences, publications in peer-reviewed journals, and public demonstrations. Such register shall be deemed part of the record pertaining to the application. Where an applicant has previously filed an application relating to a similar invention, they shall explicitly state this fact within the current application and provide details regarding the status of the earlier filing. A party proceeding shall have the right to request access to this disclosure register subject to reasonable restrictions as provided herein.

A provisional specification shall disclose the substance of the invention claimed therein with sufficient particularity as to enable a person skilled in the art to carry out the invention. For the purposes of this Act, a "provisional specification claim" refers to any assertion of subject matter contained within a provisional specification that defines the scope of protection sought for an invention. Such claims are not independently examinable and do not confer any right or privilege under this Act beyond those arising from the complete specification subsequently filed. The disclosure required in a provisional specification claim shall be commensurate with the level of detail necessary to support subsequent prosecution of the corresponding application, subject to limitations imposed by regulations framed thereunder.

An applicant seeking to register an invention may file a provisional specification disclosing the substance of the invention; such filing shall be deemed registration for a period not exceeding twelve months from the date of the provisional application. The provisional specification must contain a clear and concise description sufficient to enable a person skilled in the art to practice the invention, and it is permissible to include preliminary experimental data supporting the claimed functionality. A provisional specification may incorporate one or more provisional specification claims defining the scope of protection sought, provided that these claims are supported by the disclosure within the provisional document itself. Failure to adequately support such claims under this Act shall render them invalid upon subsequent examination of a complete application.

Where an applicant files a provisional specification disclosing the invention for which patent protection is sought, any subsequent complete specification shall be deemed to derive its priority from the date of filing of that provisional application. Subject to this, if the complete specification contains claims diverging materially from the disclosure within the provisional specification, the Controller may require the applicant to amend such claims to align with the originally disclosed matter. Failure to comply with such a direction shall render the claims invalid and unenforceable against any party acquiring rights under this Act prior to the date of the complete specification’s publication. The remedies available for infringement relating to a provisional specification claim are limited to those arising from the complete specification, provided that the original disclosure remains demonstrably present within it.

Where an applicant files a provisional specification disclosing the invention for which patent protection is sought, such specification may include a provisional specification claim relating to a particular aspect or feature of the invention. The acceptance of a provisional specification shall not be construed as an indication that the claimed subject matter is novel or non-obvious under this Act. Upon filing a complete specification within the prescribed time limit following the provisional application, the applicant shall clearly indicate the relationship between the claims in the complete specification and the disclosures made in the earlier provisional specification claim. Failure to do so may result in objections being raised during examination of the patent application. The Controller may require the applicant to amend or clarify any such indication if it is deemed insufficient for establishing a clear link as provided herein.

A provisional specification shall disclose the substance of the invention sufficiently to enable a person skilled in the art to put it into practice; provided that such disclosure need not extend to describing all embodiments or variations thereof. Where an applicant files a complete specification within twelve months from the date of filing a provisional specification, the claim contained therein relating to any matter not disclosed in the provisional specification shall be deemed invalid under this Act. Further, if the provisional specification fails to adequately describe the invention’s subject matter, rendering it impossible for a skilled person to reasonably reproduce the claimed process or apparatus, then subsequent claims referencing that omitted detail are ineligible for patent protection as provided herein. The Controller may require further clarification regarding the scope of a provisional specification claim.

Where an applicant files a provisional specification claiming priority from a previously filed application in another country, such claim shall be deemed valid only if the prescribed forms are duly executed and submitted to the Controller within three months of the initial filing date abroad. Failure to comply with this provision will render the provisional specification invalid and subject the applicant to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees for each instance of non-compliance. Any party demonstrating demonstrable prejudice due to reliance on an improperly validated provisional specification claim may petition the Intellectual Property Appellate Board for injunctive relief and damages, as provided herein. The Controller shall have the power to issue directions regarding rectification of deficiencies in such filings.

Any person owning an interest in a patent application filed with a provisional specification may grant a license to utilize the information disclosed within that provisional specification, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated in the licensing agreement. Such licenses shall be assignable, either wholly or partially, provided that any subsequent assignee assumes all obligations and liabilities arising under the original license. Where a provisional specification contains a claim relating to an invention, the scope of such claim is deemed for the purposes of assignment only to encompass the matter explicitly disclosed within the provisional specification itself; this limitation applies irrespective of later amendments in a complete application. Further, any transfer or assignment of ownership of a patent application shall be recorded with the Controller and shall include details pertaining to all prior licenses granted based on the provisional specification claim.

The Controller may, upon review of an objection raised against a patent application during examination, entertain arguments pertaining to the adequacy of disclosure within a provisional specification, even if such arguments were not initially presented. This shall apply particularly where the claimed invention’s novelty or inventive step is challenged based on prior art disclosed subsequent to the filing date of the provisional specification but before the publication of the complete specification. It is provided that any challenge concerning the scope of a provisional specification claim must be demonstrably linked to a deficiency in enabling the skilled person to practice the invention as described therein, and not merely reflect differences in interpretation. The applicant shall have the right to rebut such objections with supplementary documentation; however, the Controller’s determination remains final subject to appeal under this Act.

Where, upon revocation of a patent under this Act, any person claiming title to the invention has suffered damage by reason of acts done during the term of the patent which but for the existence of the patent would have infringed a right vested in that person, such person may sue for damages against the patentee. The measure of damages shall be determined having regard to the benefit accruing to the claimant from the use of the invention as if the patent had never been granted. It is provided that an objection to the validity of the specification claimed claim may be raised by any interested party in proceedings before the Controller, and such objection shall be deemed to be a ground for revocation. The burden of proving the existence of such damage rests upon the claimant, subject to provisions regarding estoppel as provided herein.

Where, upon examination, it appears to the Controller that an invention does not satisfy the requirements of novelty and inventive step under this Act, the Controller shall issue a communication to the applicant specifying the grounds on which the objection is based. The applicant may, within six months from the date of such communication, file a reply addressing each ground raised by the Controller. Such reply shall include arguments and evidence demonstrating compliance with the provisions relating to patentability.

The complete specification accompanying the application shall clearly define the scope of the invention as delineated in the claims. Any amendment to the claims proposed during examination must be supported by the disclosure contained within the original specification claimed claim, and may only relate to clarifying the description or correcting minor errors. The Controller may require further clarification regarding the interpretation of any term used in the claims if ambiguity is perceived.

An application for a patent shall be deemed to be lacking novelty if the matter disclosed in the specification, including the *specification claimed claim*, is identical or practically identical to information which has already been made available to the public before the date of filing. Provided that such lack of novelty shall not invalidate the application where the disclosure arose from an exhibition solely for domestic arts, agriculture or science purposes and did not involve a written description available to the public. Further, if the invention relates to a process for producing a substance controlled under any Act, the *specification claimed claim* must clearly articulate measures taken to prevent circumvention of such controls. The Controller may require further clarification regarding these preventative measures prior to proceeding with examination.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appellate Board shall, after giving notice to all concerned parties, hear appeals and dispose of the same as expeditiously as possible. Where any patent has been granted in respect of a specification claimed invention, and it is shown that the said invention was not adequately described or does not disclose the manner in which to make or use the invention, an application for revocation may be filed. Such applications shall be adjudicated with due regard to the clarity and completeness of the specification claimed claim as presented at the time of grant. Failure to comply with procedural requirements regarding notice shall render the appeal liable to dismissal.

An application for patent shall be deemed to be lacking novelty if the matter disclosed in the specification, including the specification claimed claim, is identical or nearly identical to information available to the public before the date of filing of the India application. Provided that such lack of novelty shall not be established by reference to any publication made prior to the commencement of the proceedings unless such publication was made under circumstances involving a breach of confidence owed by the applicant to another person. Furthermore, where an invention is disclosed in a specification claimed claim but is not fully described, and it appears to a person skilled in the art that the said invention could be carried out only by means of the matter so undisclosed, the application shall not be considered lacking novelty.

For the purposes of this Act, an “ii india document” shall mean any publication, whether printed, written, lithographed or mechanically reproduced, originating within the territory of India and disseminated therein, irrespective of its format or medium. Such dissemination may occur through physical distribution, electronic transmission, or any other means by which it becomes reasonably accessible to the public within India. An ii india document shall be deemed to disclose information for the purposes of novelty assessment under this Act regardless of whether such publication was made with the permission of the inventor or owner of the intellectual property rights pertaining thereto; provided that a mere reference to an invention in an ii india document shall not, by itself, constitute disclosure.

An application for registration of a design shall be deemed to be incomplete if it does not include a clear and concise statement identifying all prior published works relevant to the novelty assessment. Such identification must encompass any existing *ii india document* pertaining to similar ornamental or aesthetic features, irrespective of whether such documents are formally registered or publicly accessible. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish further details regarding the provenance and content of these referenced materials, subject to maintaining confidentiality where appropriate. Failure to adequately disclose relevant prior art as determined by the Controller shall render the application liable for rejection, provided that a reasonable opportunity is afforded to rectify any deficiencies. This requirement applies equally to applications filed jointly or severally.

Where, following the grant of a patent under this Act, it is demonstrated to the Controller, through presentation of verifiable *ii india document* and supporting affidavits, that the patented invention was commercially exploited by an unauthorized party within India without the consent of the patentee, the Controller may order such infringing entity to pay damages proportionate to the profits derived from said exploitation. Such damages shall be calculated considering the reasonable royalty which would have been payable had a license been granted to the patentee. Further, the Controller may, subject to due process and opportunity for both parties to present their case, issue an injunction restraining the infringer from further commercialization of the invention. The patentee shall bear the burden of proving unauthorized exploitation and resultant profits; provided that the Controller may consider evidence demonstrating a pattern of similar activity in determining reasonable royalty.

An application for a patent shall be deemed to disclose the best and most complete method of performing the invention known to the applicant on the date of filing, subject to any modifications or improvements made subsequent thereto and incorporated into the patent as granted. Where an inventor has previously published details pertaining to an *ii india document* relating to the claimed invention in a journal accessible to the public within India, the Controller may require submission of certified copies demonstrating the publication’s dissemination and date of release. Such publications shall be assessed for their impact on novelty and inventive step as provided herein. The applicant shall furnish an affidavit verifying the accuracy of all information presented concerning prior publication. Failure to comply with this requirement may result in rejection of the application, or a condition imposed regarding patentability. Any challenge to the validity of the patent based on such prior disclosure must be filed within six months of grant.

An application for a patent shall be deemed to disclose and fairly represent the state of knowledge relating to the invention if it incorporates, or makes reference to, any ii india document pertaining to prior art. Such incorporation or reference shall not invalidate the patent where the applicant demonstrates that the information contained within the referenced document was not reasonably accessible to, nor relied upon by, a person skilled in the relevant field at the time of filing. Further, if an invention is patented and subsequently determined to be wholly anticipated by information disclosed in a ii india document published prior to the filing date, the patent may be revoked under this Act only if the Controller finds that the applicant acted with intent to deceive or mislead.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appellate Board shall, after giving notice to all parties concerned, hear the appeal and may pass such orders as it thinks fit, subject to the provisions of this Act. Failure to comply with any direction issued by the Appellate Board constitutes an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both. Where infringement of patent rights is established, the Court may grant injunctions restraining the infringing party and order delivery up of the patented article or substance in question; furthermore, damages shall be assessed according to principles outlined herein, considering any ii india document demonstrating reasonable royalty rates.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any patentee may grant a license to use the patented invention under this Act, either wholly or partially, and such license shall be assignable. The terms and conditions of such licenses, including royalty rates and duration, shall be determined by agreement between the parties; provided that where no agreement can be reached, the Controller may, upon application by either party, determine a fair and reasonable rate considering prevailing industry standards and the nature of the ii india document pertaining to the invention. Assignment of a patent or license under this Act requires registration with the Controller and shall only take effect on such registration. Further, any transfer of rights relating to a patented invention must disclose all relevant details concerning prior licenses granted, ensuring transparency and preventing conflicting claims regarding ownership and usage permissions.

Where an application for patent relating to an invention described in a ii india document is filed, and it is alleged by the Controller that the said invention was anticipated or obvious due to prior publication within such document, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to present evidence rebutting this assertion. The burden of proving anticipation or obviousness rests upon the Controller, subject to the provision that the mere existence of a ii india document does not automatically invalidate a patent claim. Any determination made by the Controller regarding the relevance and impact of the cited ii india document may be appealed before the Appellate Board, with the appeal being decided based on established principles of statutory interpretation and consideration of expert testimony concerning technical disclosure.

An application for a patent shall contain a clear and concise description of the invention, disclosing the manner and method of performing it, sufficient to enable a person skilled in the art to put the same into practice. The description shall include any *ii india document* which forms part of the invention or is necessary for its understanding. Where an inventor has previously published details relating to the invention, including through use trade mark applications or promotional materials, such prior publication shall be disclosed in a statement annexed to the application, specifying the nature and date of the disclosure. Failure to disclose relevant prior publications may render the patent liable to revocation under this Act. The Controller General may require further information regarding any aspect of the invention’s description or its relationship to existing knowledge as provided herein. Any such request shall be complied with within a period specified by the Controller.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The Appellate Board shall, after giving notice to all concerned parties, hear appeals and may pass such orders as it deems fit, subject to the provisions herein. Failure to comply with a direction issued by the Trade Mark Registrar concerning rectification proceedings or the cessation of use of a mark that constitutes infringement shall attract a penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees, recoverable as civil debt. Repeated contravention may result in further penalties and potential criminal prosecution under relevant sections of the Indian Penal Code. The Registrar’s decision regarding an ii india document is final, barring appeal to the Appellate Board.

A patent application is deemed to be filed on the date the prescribed fees are remitted and the formal requirements under this Act are satisfied. For the purposes of determining priority under this Act, a patent application shall be considered as disclosing the invention from the date it was first described in a publication anywhere in the world; provided that such disclosure does not constitute prior art unless the same is cited or derived from a source publicly available before the date of filing of the patent application. An applicant may include provisional specifications with a patent application, detailing aspects of the invention not fully elaborated within the main specification.

An applicant seeking entry of a patent application into the Register shall furnish with the request, a certified copy of the priority document, if the claimed invention relates to a matter in respect of which an application for protection has been filed earlier. The Controller may require the applicant to submit further particulars or clarifications regarding the subject matter disclosed within the patent application, and such requirements shall be complied with within the time specified by him. Failure to provide the requested information may result in the rejection of the patent application. Where a request for registration is accompanied by an incorrect statement of fact material to the acceptance of the invention, the applicant shall be liable to penalty as determined under this Act. The Register shall record details pertaining to each patent application filed.

Where a patent application is refused under this Act, the applicant shall have the right to appeal against such refusal before the Appellate Board. The Board shall consider all evidence presented by the applicant and the Controller, and may direct that further information be furnished or an inquiry held. If the Board allows the appeal, it shall direct the Controller to proceed with the examination of the patent application as if the refusal had not been made. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Appellate Board may prefer an appeal from such order to the Supreme Court within sixty days from the date of that order. The applicant’s remedies are subject to any conditions imposed by the Board regarding costs and timelines for compliance with directions issued under this Act.

An applicant seeking a patent application shall furnish with the request, particulars as to priority if the invention is claimed as an improvement on or modification of an existing technology. The prescribed fee for such a request shall be remitted at the time of filing and may be subject to revision by notification in the Official Gazette. Where the Controller considers that the information provided regarding priority is insufficient or unclear, he may require the applicant to submit further particulars within a specified period. Failure to comply with this requirement shall render the patent application liable for rejection under this Act. The Controller may also direct the applicant to amend any claim where it appears ambiguous or does not clearly define the scope of protection sought. Any such direction must be accompanied by a reasoned explanation, and the applicant shall have an opportunity to respond before a final determination is made regarding the validity of the patent application.

An applicant submitting a patent application relating to a process for producing a substance covered by an existing pharmaceutical product shall disclose, with sufficient particularity under this Act, the nature and extent of any modifications made to the established process. Such disclosure must include details pertaining to reaction conditions, catalysts employed, and purification methods utilized, ensuring reproducibility by persons skilled in the art. Failure to provide adequate information as provided herein may render the patent application liable for rejection. Further, where the claimed invention incorporates elements derived from prior publications or publicly accessible data, a statement of provenance shall accompany the patent application, detailing the source material used. The Controller may require additional clarification if ambiguities exist regarding compliance with these stipulations.

Any person found to have knowingly made a false statement or representation in a patent application before the Controller shall be liable for a penalty not exceeding two hundred thousand rupees, and further subject to prosecution under relevant provisions of the Indian Penal Code. The Controller may, at any time during the examination of a patent application, require the applicant to furnish such additional information or particulars as he deems necessary for determining whether the invention is novel and involves an inventive step. Failure to comply with such a requirement within the prescribed period shall render the patent application liable for rejection. Any appeal against an order refusing a patent application may be made to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of that order, subject to payment of the prescribed fee.

Where a patent application relates to an invention which incorporates technology licensed or assigned to the applicant prior to the date of filing, the Controller may require evidence demonstrating the validity and scope of such license or assignment. The licensee or assignee shall be deemed to have standing to participate in proceedings relating to the patent application, including but not limited to objections under this Act concerning novelty or inventive step. Any subsequent transfer or assignment of rights arising from a granted patent shall be subject to the terms and conditions of the original license or assignment agreement, as recorded with the Patents Office.
