The Controller shall consider representations made by interested parties concerning the impact of acquiring restrict upon public health, safety, or national security during proceedings under this provision. Any person aggrieved by an order issued under these provisions may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within a period of sixty days from the date of such order.

Any person who, without authorization under this Act or the rules made thereunder, directly or indirectly acquires restrict over a patented invention shall be deemed guilty of an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and with a fine which may extend to ten lakhs rupees. Where such acquisition is made by a company, every director of that company shall be liable to be proceeded against as if he were the person who committed the offence. Further, any goods infringing a patent and obtained through unauthorized acquiring restrict are deemed forfeited to the Central Government. The government may order their disposal in such manner as it deems fit, after due process is followed, including notification to affected parties.

Where a patentee grants a license conferring the right to make, use, or sell a patented invention in India, such license may be assigned or further licensed by the licensee with the prior written consent of the patentee. Provided that, where the assignment or further license is made without such consent, it shall be void unless the patentee subsequently ratifies the transaction in writing. The patentee shall not unreasonably withhold such consent; and an application for consent may specify a royalty to be paid by the assignee or further licensee as consideration for the grant of permission. Any person acquiring restrict rights under an assignment or further license made in contravention of this provision shall be deemed a trespasser, subject to remedies available under civil law. The patentee retains the right to terminate any such unauthorized assignment or further license upon providing reasonable notice.

Where a patent is granted for an invention relating to a process for producing a substance controlled under this Act, the Controller may, subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal, direct that the patentee shall, prior to commencing commercial exploitation of the said process, enter into an agreement with such entities as the Central Government specifies, ensuring non-discriminatory access to the produced substance. This direction may be imposed where it is demonstrated that the invention significantly impedes research or development in a field of national importance. The patentee shall have the right to challenge this imposition on grounds of manifest arbitrariness or lack of reasoned justification; however, any such challenge does not preclude the Central Government from subsequently issuing further directives concerning acquiring restrict relating to similar inventions.

An application for the registration of a trade mark may include representation of the marks shape goods, provided that such representation accurately reflects the three-dimensional configuration of the article. The Registrar shall refuse registration if he considers that the marks shape goods is primarily functional in nature and serves solely to achieve a technical result or to ensure the efficient performance of its intended purpose. Further, an application may be rejected where the marks shape goods lacks distinctiveness and does not reasonably distinguish the applicant’s goods from those of other traders. The Registrar may require the applicant to submit further documentation demonstrating that the marks shape goods possesses the requisite characteristics for registration as provided herein.

The proprietor of a registered trade mark relating to the marks shape goods may institute proceedings in the Commercial Courts for relief against any person who, without leave, applies a false or deceptive indication concerning the trading name, origin, quality, characteristics, geographical indications, or other particulars of any goods sold or offered for sale under that trade mark. Such an application shall be deemed to constitute infringement under this Act if it is likely to cause confusion in the minds of the public as to the identity of the goods, their ownership, or their source. The Court may grant such remedies as are provided herein, including injunctions restraining further infringing activity and ordering the destruction of infringing materials. It is provided that a mark’s shape shall not be registrable if it primarily serves merely to describe the nature of the goods.

The Registrar may refuse registration of a trade mark if it consists exclusively of the marks shape goods, provided that such shape serves solely to indicate the characteristics of the goods, such as their nature, quality, quantity, intended purpose, value, geographical origin, or other similar attributes. Where an application for registration includes a representation of the marks shape goods, the description accompanying the mark shall clearly and unambiguously define the essential features contributing to its distinctive character. Any challenge to the registrability of a trade mark based on this ground may be raised by any interested party within three months from the date of publication under this Act. The Registrar shall consider evidence presented by both the applicant and the challenger, including expert testimony regarding functionality and consumer perception. A decision made by the Registrar concerning the marks shape goods is appealable to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

The Registrar may refuse registration of a mark if it consists exclusively of the marks shape goods, provided that such shape is dictated solely by factors relating to the characteristics of the product itself. Where a proprietor seeks to register a three-dimensional configuration as a trade mark representing the marks shape goods, they shall demonstrate that the said shape signifies distinctiveness in relation to the specified goods or services. Any person aggrieved by a decision under this Act concerning the registrability of a mark based on its shape may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such decision. Failure to comply with these provisions renders the proprietor liable for penalties as provided herein, including but not limited to fines and injunctions against use.

The proprietor of a registered trade mark relating to the marks shape of goods may grant a license conferring upon the licensee the right to use such mark in connection with specified goods or services, subject to terms and conditions as agreed between them and recorded in writing. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and the proprietor shall retain ownership of the trade mark unless expressly assigned otherwise. An assignment of the registered trade mark, including any associated licensing agreements, requires registration under this Act and is deemed effective only upon such registration. Where a license agreement includes provisions for sub-licensing, the original proprietor’s consent, obtained in writing, shall be mandatory. Further, any alteration to the marks shape goods depicted on the registered trade mark following assignment necessitates notification to the Registrar within three months, accompanied by supporting documentation demonstrating continued distinctiveness.

The Registrar may refuse registration of a trade mark if it contains as a dominant feature the shape of goods, but such refusal shall only apply where that shape is dictated solely by factors including packaging efficiency, manufacturing processes, or aesthetic considerations intrinsic to the product's function. An appeal against this decision lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the Registrar’s order. Provided that, if the applicant demonstrates a distinctiveness acquired through extensive use and consumer recognition subsequent to initial sale, the refusal may be reconsidered subject to evidence establishing such acquired distinctiveness outweighs any deceptive effect arising from the marks shape goods. The burden of proving this lies with the appellant.

The Registrar may refuse registration of a mark if it consists exclusively of the marks shape goods, provided that such shape serves solely to indicate the characteristics of the goods, such as their form, size, weight, material, or function. Where an application for trade mark registration includes a claim based on the marks shape goods, the Chairperson shall direct the Registrar to conduct a comparative assessment against prior registered designs and existing market presence. Any proprietor demonstrating deceptive similarity between their goods and those bearing a similar shape may petition the Intellectual Property Appellate Board for injunctive relief and damages. Failure to comply with such orders shall render the offending party liable to penalties as provided herein, including fines not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees and imprisonment of up to two years.

A trade mark shall not be registrable if it exclusively consists of the shape of goods, provided that such shape is wholly determined by factors such as the nature of the goods themselves, their intended function, or requirements for handling or preservation. For the avoidance of doubt, shapes dictated solely by manufacturing processes or packaging considerations are excluded from protection under this Act. The determination of whether a shape possesses distinctive character shall be assessed considering consumer perception and recognition in relation to the relevant goods or services. A shape which is primarily functional and offers no non-functional advantage shall not qualify as a trade marks shape for registration purposes, subject to any demonstrable acquired distinctiveness.

The Registrar may refuse registration of a trade mark if it contains exclusively or predominantly the shape of goods that are primarily functional, provided that such shape is dictated solely by factors relating to durability, safety requirements, or aesthetic considerations inherent in the nature of the goods. Where an application incorporates a three-dimensional shape, the applicant shall furnish detailed specifications outlining the precise dimensions and material composition thereof. Further, if the applied-for trade mark comprises a distinctive shape, it must be demonstrated that acquired distinctiveness has been established through extensive use and consumer recognition, supported by documentary evidence such as market surveys or sales figures. The Registrar may require further clarification regarding the trade marks shape to ascertain its eligibility for registration under this Act.

The Registrar may, upon application by any proprietor of a registered trade mark, direct that the shape of specified goods be considered as part of the distinctive character of such trade mark. Such direction shall only be granted if the applicant demonstrates, through evidence presented during proceedings under this Act, that the shape in question signifies a substantial and unique association with the goods and has acquired distinctiveness through reputation or recognition earned by the proprietor’s use thereof. The application must include detailed technical specifications delineating the precise trade marks shape, including dimensions and material composition where relevant. Any party may object to the direction being granted, submitting counter-evidence demonstrating that the shape is primarily functional or descriptive of the goods, thereby precluding its registration as a trade mark shape.

The Registrar may refuse registration of a trade marks application if the applied-for mark consists exclusively of the shape of a product and that shape is wholly dictated by factors including functional considerations, manufacturing processes, or packaging requirements. Provided that, where the applicant can demonstrate acquired distinctiveness through extensive use and consumer recognition of the said shape as identifying their goods, registration may be granted subject to conditions imposed by the Registrar. Such conditions shall ensure continued clarity regarding the origin of the goods and prevent confusion amongst consumers. The trade marks shape must not also deceive or mislead consumers concerning the nature, quality, or geographical origin of the goods. Further, any representation of a trade marks shape in advertising material shall comply with guidelines issued under this Act.

The use of any shape as a trade marks shall be permissible only if it demonstrably and exclusively identifies the goods or services with the proprietor thereof, and does not solely serve to indicate the nature, quality, or geographical origin of such goods or services. Provided that, shapes which are primarily functional in character, or which are dictated by manufacturing processes essential for achieving a particular utility, shall be deemed ineligible for registration as trade marks. Any person aggrieved by the registration of a shape as a trade mark may institute proceedings before the relevant intellectual property tribunal seeking rectification of the register, and shall be entitled to damages if it is proven that such registration has caused demonstrable financial harm. The proprietor of a registered trade marks shape shall be liable for penalties under this Act in cases of unauthorized use or imitation thereof.

The proprietor of a registered trade mark relating to any goods may grant a license conferring upon the licensee the right to use such trade mark in relation to those goods, or in relation to specified goods that are similar to those for which the trade mark is registered, subject to terms and conditions as agreed between them and recorded in writing. Such licenses shall be assignable by the proprietor, provided that any assignment of a license requires notification to the licensee within thirty days of the assignment’s execution. Further, where a trade marks shape is used under a license agreement, the licensee may sub-license such right to use, but only with the prior written consent of the original proprietor, and subject to conditions mirroring those stipulated in the primary licensing arrangement as provided herein. The proprietor retains full ownership of the trade mark shape regardless of any licensed or assigned usage.

The Registrar may refuse registration of a trade marks application if it is demonstrated that the applied-for shape possesses no distinctive character and serves solely to identify the product’s features, provided that the applicant establishes a demonstrable secondary meaning acquired through extensive use. An appeal against such refusal lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. Further, where an objection is raised concerning deceptive similarity between the applied-for trade marks shape and existing goods or services, the applicant shall bear the burden of proving non-similarity, subject to a review by the Board considering consumer perception and potential confusion. The decision of the Appellate Board shall be final, save for further appeal to the High Court on grounds of law only.

The Registrar may entertain an application for registration of a trademark in respect of goods or services, notwithstanding that the applied-for trademark includes a shape, provided that such shape does not fall within the descriptions specified as unregistrable under this Act. Where the applicant seeks to benefit from an international registration referred to in Chapter V, the Registrar shall examine whether the designation extends to India and if so, proceed with examination according to the established procedures for domestic applications. The determination of registrability concerning a trademark’s shape shall be subject to consideration of consumer perception and distinctiveness, taking into account all relevant circumstances as presented during opposition proceedings or other challenges. Any representation of the applied-for trade marks shape must accurately reflect its essential features, and any alteration thereof may render the application liable for rejection.

The Registrar may refuse to register any proposed trade marks if he considers that the shape of the goods, though distinctive, is wholly dictated by factors such as packaging efficiency, manufacturing considerations, or aesthetic appeal inherent to the product’s function. Subject to this provision, an application for registration shall be deemed invalid if the mark incorporates a three-dimensional shape which falsely suggests a connection with any existing goods or services. The applicant shall provide detailed specifications and supporting documentation demonstrating that the trade marks shape possesses acquired distinctiveness through extensive use and consumer recognition, as provided herein. Furthermore, it shall register proposed trade marks only upon satisfaction that the mark does not conflict with prior rights under this Act.

The owner of a registered trade marks shall have the exclusive right to use and authorize others to use the said trade marks in relation to the goods or services for which the registration is granted. Any person desiring to assign or license the use of a trade mark, whether registered or applied for, must submit a formal application to the Registrar, detailing the scope of such assignment or licensing agreement. The register shall brought up-to-date with particulars of every assignment and licence recorded, including the names and addresses of both the assignor/licensor and assignee/licensee. Such assignments and licences may be granted subject to conditions as deemed appropriate by the Registrar, ensuring fair competition and preventing abuse of intellectual property rights. Provided that any trade marks shape incorporated into packaging or product design requires explicit consent from the original proprietor for subsequent commercial exploitation.

For the purposes of this Act, "international trademark" means a trademark registered through an application originating in India and extended under the provisions of the Madrid Agreement Concerning the International Registration of Marks. Such international trademarks shall be deemed to have effect only as to the Contracting Parties designated in the international registration, subject to any limitations or conditions specified therein. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating compliance with the requirements of the Madrid Agreement before proceeding with an examination or acceptance of an application for extension of protection. Any opposition proceedings relating to an international trademark shall be conducted under rules consistent with those applicable to applications filed directly under this Act.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark shall, in addition to fulfilling requirements as provided herein regarding distinctiveness and acceptable matter, provide evidence demonstrating compliance with Article 3(2)(d) of the Madrid Agreement concerning the international Registration of Marks. Such evidence must include a certified copy of the basic application or registered trade mark upon which the international registration is based, translated into English if originally in another language. The Registrar may require further documentation to ascertain the status and validity of said basic application or registration, including details regarding any oppositions or cancellations filed against it under the laws of the designating country. Failure to submit satisfactory evidence shall render the international mark vulnerable to rejection during examination.

Where a trade mark is registered in India and subsequently extended through the process afforded by the Madrid Agreement concerning the International Registration of Marks, any infringement occurring within India relating to that internationally protected mark shall be actionable under this Act as if the international registration were an independent Indian registration. The owner of such an internationally registered trade mark may institute proceedings for relief against acts of representation or use which are likely to cause confusion with their mark, subject to the provisions regarding territoriality and priority established herein. Further, any counterclaim arising from actions taken by a defendant alleging invalidity of the international registration shall be adjudicated according to the principles governing opposition proceedings under this Act, considering both Indian law and the requirements for maintaining an international registration. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating compliance with the Madrid Agreement’s procedural rules in such cases.

Applications for designation of India as a designated territory in respect of marks registered internationally under the Madrid Agreement concerning the Registration of Marks shall be filed with the Trade Marks Registry within thirty days from the date on which the International Bureau transmits the request for registration to the Office. The Registrar may, after giving notice to the applicant and opportunity of being heard, refuse registration if he considers that the mark is descriptive of the goods or services in relation to which it is sought to be registered, or otherwise fails to comply with the requirements as provided herein. Any objection raised against an international application shall be determined by the Registrar according to the procedures applicable to oppositions under this Act, subject to any modifications necessary due to the nature of international registration. The applicant shall furnish such documentary evidence and information as the Registrar may require to substantiate the claim for registration.

An applicant seeking designation of India within an international application filed under the Madrid Agreement shall, upon examination by the Receiving Office and subsequent transmission to the Trade Marks Registry, be subject to the same procedural requirements as would apply to a domestic trade mark application. The Registrar may require the submission of translations of any marks or designations not in English or Hindi, certified by a translator accredited under this Act. Further, where an international registration designates India, the extent of protection conferred shall correspond precisely with the goods and services for which the mark is registered within India, as specified in the International Registration. Any opposition to such designation must be filed within four months from the date of publication of the international registration in the Trade Marks Journal.

Where a trade mark is registered in India and subsequently subject to an international application designating India, as facilitated by the Madrid Agreement concerning the International Registration of Marks, any challenge to the registrability of that trade mark under this Act shall be deemed a violation punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, and with a fine which may extend to fifty thousand rupees. Furthermore, where such a violation is proven to have resulted in demonstrable financial loss to a third party due to confusion or misrepresentation arising from the challenged registration, aggravated penalties, as determined by the relevant court, shall apply. The Registrar may, sua sponte or upon complaint, initiate proceedings against any person found guilty of contravening these provisions, and such proceedings shall be conducted expeditiously.

The owner of a trade mark registered in India may, subject to fulfilling all conditions as provided herein, extend the protection afforded by such registration through an international application under the Madrid Agreement concerning the International Registration of Marks. Such extension shall be deemed a license granted to the applicant’s designated representative for the purpose of managing and prosecuting the international registration within specified territories. Any assignment of the underlying Indian trade mark registration prior to the completion of the international registration process shall require notification to the Trade Marks Registry, accompanied by evidence demonstrating continued consent from the assignor regarding the extension application. Further, any subsequent transfer or licensing agreement concerning the internationally registered mark must explicitly address the rights and obligations pertaining to the original Indian registration, ensuring compliance with provisions relating to territorial scope and duration as determined under this Act.

Where a trade mark is registered in India and subsequently subject to an international application designating India, as facilitated by the Madrid Agreement concerning the International Registration of Marks, any challenge to the registrability of such designated trade mark shall be entertained only if it arises within three months from the date of publication of the international registration under this Act. Such challenges must specifically allege a violation of existing law relating to trademarks, including but not limited to those pertaining to descriptiveness or likelihood of confusion with prior registrations. Failure to demonstrate a clear and demonstrable prejudice resulting from the designated mark’s registration will render any appeal frivolous and unsustainable. The Registrar may, at his discretion, require evidence substantiating such claims before proceeding with an examination.

An application for designation of India in an international application filed under the Madrid Agreement shall be examined as if it were an application for registration of a trade mark in India, subject to the provisions herein relating to relative grounds for refusal. The Trade Marks Registry may require the applicant to furnish such information or documents as are necessary to ascertain whether the marks indicated in the international application comply with Indian law and practice concerning clarity, distinctiveness, and acceptability of marks indications. Where an international registration extends to India, it shall be deemed to be registered in the Register of Trade Marks maintained under this Act, and the International Bureau shall be notified accordingly by the Registry. Any opposition proceedings relating to such extended registrations shall be conducted as provided herein, with the Registrar having jurisdiction over all matters arising during those proceedings.

Where a trade mark is registered in India and subsequently extended through an application filed under the Madrid Agreement concerning the International Registration of Marks, the registered proprietor shall be deemed to hold such registration for the territory of India subject to any modifications made as provided herein. Any alteration to the layout of the goods or services specification appearing on the original Indian registration, following extension under the Madrid Agreement, requires prior notification to the Trade Marks Registry and may necessitate further examination. Failure to provide timely notification regarding alterations in registered proprietor layout shall render the extended registration liable for revocation by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Penalties for such non-compliance will be as prescribed; repeated offences invite substantial monetary fines and potential injunctions preventing continued use of the mark.

The owner of a trade mark registered in India, seeking to benefit from the provisions of the Madrid Agreement concerning the international registration of marks, shall be permitted to effectuate an assignment or license of their Indian trade mark rights prior to and during the pendency of an international application. Such assignments and licenses may include, but are not limited to, exclusive rights relating to specific goods or services as defined in the original registration. Where a claim specification amendment is subsequently required for the international registration, reflecting changes to the list of goods or services initially specified, the owner shall provide such amended details to the Registrar within three months, and this may impact existing assignments and licenses proportionally. The Registrar may require further documentation demonstrating continued consent from assignees regarding any modifications impacting their designated territories.

Where a trade mark is registered in India and subsequently subject to an international application designating India, as facilitated by the Madrid Agreement concerning the International Registration of Marks, any objection raised against such designation shall be adjudicated solely before the relevant intellectual property tribunal. The Registrar may, upon receiving notice of opposition from any interested party claiming prior rights relating to identical or similar trade goods services, issue a provisional refusal. Such refusal is subject to appeal to the tribunal within three months of notification. Failure to pursue an appeal within this timeframe shall constitute abandonment of the objection and render the international registration provisionally accepted for India. The burden of proving priority lies entirely with the applicant seeking extension under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, "international trademark" means a trademark registered through an application filed in India designating one or more countries which are Contracting Parties to the Madrid Protocol. Such designation shall be construed as an election by the applicant to seek protection for the mark within those designated territories, subject to any limitations or conditions specified in the regulations framed under this Act. An international trademark shall enjoy the same rights and remedies as a trademark registered directly under this Act, provided that the requirements of Article 34 of the Madrid Protocol are satisfied regarding priority claims. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating compliance with these provisions as deemed necessary.

An applicant seeking to obtain protection for a trade mark in India through the Madrid Protocol shall file a request for extension of protection with the Trade Marks Registry, accompanied by a certified copy of the international registration and the prescribed fee. Such request must specify the goods or services in respect of which protection is sought, ensuring these correspond to those listed in the international registration unless an amendment is included within the request itself. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further particulars or documentary evidence as deemed necessary to verify compliance with the provisions under this Act relating to registrability and distinctiveness. Any opposition to the extension shall be treated as an opposition under this Act, subject to such modifications as are required by the Madrid Protocol.

An applicant whose trademark is refused registration under this Act may, within sixty days of the date of communication of the refusal order, appeal to the Appellate Board. Where such an appeal concerns a mark sought for international registration through the Madrid Protocol, the Board shall consider whether the refusal was based on grounds available under the law of India or those permissible under Article 6(4) of said Protocol. The applicant shall bear the burden of demonstrating that the challenged ground does not apply in India. Failure to satisfy the Appellate Board may result in dismissal of the appeal and forfeiture of any fees paid. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Appellate Board concerning an international registration extension may further appeal to the High Court within ninety days, subject to satisfying the conditions for appeals under this Act.

An applicant seeking to avail of the benefits of the Madrid Protocol shall file with the Registrar a certified copy of an international application, accompanied by a declaration specifying the Contracting Parties in respect of which protection is sought. The Registrar may require such further particulars or documents as are necessary for determining compliance with the requirements under this Act and the Regulations implementing the Madrid Protocol. Where an international registration extends to India, the mark shall be deemed to be registered in the Register of Trade Marks maintained by the Registrar subject to any limitations specified in the international registration. Any opposition that may arise concerning such extension shall be adjudicated according to procedures as provided herein for oppositions to applications for registration under this Act. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all extensions of protection resulting from an international registration, accessible for public inspection.

An applicant seeking designation of India in an international application filed under the Madrid Protocol shall, prior to acceptance by the International Bureau, ensure that the mark is registrable under this Act as if the application were made directly in India. Such determination shall be subject to verification by the Trade Marks Registry and may require submission of additional documentation demonstrating compliance with all applicable provisions relating to distinctiveness and permissible representation of the trade mark. Where an international registration extends to India, it shall enjoy the same rights and remedies as a registered trade mark under this Act, provided that any conflicting prior registrations or applications existing at the time of extension shall be considered in accordance with established principles of relative grounds for refusal.

Where a trade mark is registered in India and subsequently subject to an international application filed under the Madrid Protocol, the Registrar shall maintain a record of such extension of protection. Any party demonstrating substantial prejudice arising from reliance upon the continued validity of a trade mark registration extended through the Madrid Protocol may petition the Intellectual Property Appellate Board for review. Such petitions must be accompanied by evidence establishing the nature and extent of the prejudice suffered. Failure to provide adequate substantiating documentation shall result in automatic dismissal of the petition, without further hearing. The Registrar may, upon receiving notification of a cancellation or limitation of protection under the Madrid Protocol, initiate inquiries as provided herein.

The Registrar may, upon receiving a request and subject to payment of the prescribed fee, grant permission for the assignment or licensing of rights arising from an international registration under the Madrid Protocol. Such assignments or licenses shall be in writing and executed in accordance with procedures as provided herein relating to the transfer of trade mark ownership. The assignor or licensor retains all rights not explicitly transferred or licensed through the documented agreement. Any subsequent assignee or licensee may further assign or license those rights, again subject to Registrarial approval and applicable fees. This provision applies equally to extensions of protection resulting from an international registration. Furthermore, any party seeking to enforce the terms of such assignment or license shall provide evidence satisfactory to the Registrar demonstrating compliance with these stipulations.

Where a trade mark is registered in India and subsequently subject to an international application filed under the Madrid Protocol, designating India as a designated Contracting Party, any opposition proceedings initiated prior to the date of effectuation of such designation shall be deemed to continue with full force and effect. The Registrar may, upon receiving notification from the International Bureau regarding the extension of protection, entertain objections based solely on grounds available under this Act at the time of original registration, notwithstanding any subsequent changes in law or practice relating to international registrations. Any party aggrieved by a decision concerning an internationally registered trade mark’s effectuation may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such decision, subject to payment of prescribed fees and demonstrating prejudice arising directly from the order appealed against.

An applicant seeking to obtain the benefit of international registration of a trade mark under the Madrid Protocol shall, prior to effecting such extension, provide evidence satisfactory to the Registrar that the mark is registrable in India as if the application were made directly under this Act. Such evidence must demonstrate compliance with all applicable provisions relating to distinctiveness and permissible representation of marks. Further, where an international registration designates India, the purposes identifying goods or services listed therein shall be construed strictly in accordance with the classification established by the Registrar for the purposes of this Act. The Registrar may require further clarification regarding such purposes if they are deemed ambiguous or potentially misleading to consumers.

Where an applicant seeks to obtain the benefit of international registration in India pursuant to the Madrid Protocol, such application shall be deemed to be an application for registration under this Act. Any challenge to the registrability of a mark arising from an international application may be brought before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within ninety days of the date on which particulars of the application are advertised as provided herein. Failure to comply with this timeframe shall preclude any subsequent legal recourse against the Registrar’s decision concerning said mark. The Registrar, in considering such challenges, shall give due weight to prior conflicting applications or marks existing in India, irrespective of the circumstances application advertised internationally. Penalties for frivolous claims under this provision shall be as prescribed.

The owner of a trade mark registered in India, seeking to benefit from the protections afforded by the Madrid Protocol, shall be permitted to grant a license conferring rights relating to the use and exploitation of that trade mark within designated territories. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as determined by the licensor, provided that the terms are clearly defined within the licensing agreement and filed with the Trade Marks Registry. Further, where an international registration incorporates a designation for India based on an earlier Indian application, any subsequent assignment of rights in the underlying patent addition relating to the trade mark shall be deemed to include assignment of the corresponding trade mark registration itself, subject to notification to the Controller. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating due diligence in ensuring compliance with applicable laws within each designated territory where the licensed trade mark is utilized.

For the purposes of this Act, "international trademark" means a trade mark registered through an application based on an international registration granted under the Madrid Protocol. An applicant seeking to obtain protection for a trade mark in India by way of such an international registration shall be deemed to have made an application for registration under this Act. Such an application is subject to examination as if it were an initial application filed directly with the Trade Marks Registry, provided that the prescribed application fee accompanied by the requisite documentation relating to the international registration must be remitted at the time of filing. The Registrar may require further particulars or modifications to ensure compliance with Indian trade mark law.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark shall, upon filing the application in India, be eligible to file an international application designating India, provided that such designation is made within thirty months from the date of the initial filing. Where a user party proceeding with an extension of protection under the Madrid Protocol designates India, the Trade Marks Registry shall examine the request for extension as if it were an application for registration in India, considering any conflicting marks already registered or applied for. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish such documentary evidence substantiating the use of the mark internationally as is deemed necessary. Any opposition to the international registration arising from a designation of India shall be dealt with under procedures similar to those applicable to oppositions against applications filed directly in India.

An application for extension of protection of a trade mark internationally shall be filed with the Trade Marks Registry within six months from the date on which the international registration is refused or cancelled, subject to provisions regarding extensions granted under this Act. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish such documentary evidence as demonstrates continued use of the mark in relation to the goods or services specified in the international registration, provided that failure to do so shall render the application liable for rejection. Any objection raised against an extension application shall be adjudicated according to procedures prescribed herein, and the applicant shall have the right to present arguments and counter-evidence. The Registrar’s decision on such objections is final, subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Regulations international registration are governed by these provisions.

Where an objection is taken against the acceptance of a proposed trade mark under this Act, the applicant may file his response within such time as may be prescribed. Following consideration of the response and any counter-submissions made by the Trade Marks Registry, the Registrar shall determine whether the grounds for objection persist. If the Registrar finds that the objection remains valid, he may direct that the application not proceed to registration. However, if the applicant demonstrates a substantial acquired reputation in relation to the goods or services indicated in the application, notwithstanding the initial objection, the matter shall be referred to an examining officer who will assess whether the register shall brought into effect. The Registrar’s decision on such referral is final.

Where a registered trade mark is used in relation to goods or services other than those for which it is registered, and such use is likely to cause confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or nature of those goods or services, any person aggrieved may apply to the High Court. The application shall specify the particulars of the infringing user and the manner in which the infringement has been committed. Upon hearing all parties, the High Court may grant such relief as it deems just and equitable, including an injunction restraining further use of the trade mark. Further, where a registered trade mark is found to be deceptively similar to a prior unregistered mark used by another party, the register shall brought before the court for review of its validity. This provision applies irrespective of whether damages have been claimed under this Act.

Where an objection is raised by the Trade Marks Registry against the acceptance of a proposed trade mark, the applicant may submit their reply and evidence within such time as prescribed. Upon receipt of the applicant’s response, the Registrar shall consider the same in light of the grounds for opposition initially presented. If, after due consideration, the Registrar deems the objection to be substantiated, notice thereof shall be served upon the applicant. The applicant then has a right to appeal against this decision before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Further, where an application is refused and no appeal is filed, or where an appeal fails, the register shall brought into effect only after the lapse of ninety days from the date of communication of the order of refusal or appellate determination, as applicable.

Where an applicant seeks to amend a registered trade mark, such application shall be accompanied by a reasoned statement detailing the proposed alterations and their justification. The Registrar may require further clarification if the rationale is deemed insufficient or ambiguous. Any alteration sought must not conflict with existing rights under this Act, nor mislead consumers as to the nature of goods or services offered. Further, any amendment affecting the representation of the trade mark shall be subject to public notice for a period of three months. Following such notice, objections may be filed by interested parties. The register shall brought up to date reflecting all approved amendments within sixty days of their finalization, provided that no valid objection remains unresolved.

Where a registered trade mark is used in contravention of this Act, and such use causes confusion amongst the public as to the origin of goods or services, any person aggrieved may apply to the Commercial Court for an injunction. The application shall specify the nature of the infringement and the remedies sought. Upon receiving such an application, the Court shall issue notice to the defendant, affording them a reasonable opportunity to respond. Failure by the defendant to appear or adequately defend against the allegations will result in ex parte proceedings. Any person whose name appears on the register shall be deemed to have standing to bring such action under this Act. The register shall brought before the court as prima facie evidence of ownership and validity, subject to challenge based on fraud or misrepresentation.

Where a registered trade mark is subject to an assignment, or where a license is granted relating to the use of a registered trade mark, the assignee or licensee may apply to the Registrar for entry of such assignment or license in the Register. The application shall specify the details of the assignor or licensor, the assignee or licensee, and the extent of the rights transferred or licensed. Upon receiving an application under this Act, the Registrar shall bring the matter to the attention of the registered proprietor, who may file objections within a prescribed period. Any objection received shall be considered by the Registrar before proceeding with the entry. The register shall brought up to date reflecting such assignments and licenses as are deemed appropriate following due process. Further, any subsequent transfer or revocation of an assignment or license shall also be recorded in the Register.

Where an objection is raised against a proposed trade mark, and such objection relates to similarity with existing registered marks, the applicant may submit counter-statements and evidence demonstrating distinctiveness. Following consideration of these submissions, the Registrar shall bring the matter before the Trade Marks Registry for further deliberation. If, after this process, the Registrar remains unconvinced that the proposed mark does not conflict with a previously registered trade mark, the application shall be refused. It is provided that an applicant may pursue registration of separate trade marks encompassing variations of a core design or name, subject to satisfying the requirements under this Act concerning distinctiveness and non-deceptiveness. The register shall brought up to date reflecting any such decisions promptly.

Where an objection is taken against the registration of a trade mark under this Act, the applicant may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Upon such appeal, the Board shall direct the Registrar to reconsider the matter and issue further directions as it deems fit. The Registrar shall then proceed to determine whether the grounds for objection are substantiated, considering all evidence presented by both the applicant and the objector. If, following reconsideration, the Registrar remains of the opinion that the trade mark should not be registered, notice thereof shall be given to the applicant, affording him an opportunity to submit further representations. Subsequently, the register shall brought into effect only upon satisfaction that the trade mark does not conflict with existing rights or is otherwise registrable as provided herein. A specification patent relating to the goods and services listed in the application will be reviewed concurrently.

Where a registered trade mark is used in relation to goods or services not covered by the period of registration, the proprietor shall be liable for damages. Any person aggrieved by the use of a trade mark contrary to the provisions of this Act may institute proceedings in the manner provided herein seeking an injunction restraining such use and claiming compensation for losses sustained. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint regarding misuse of a registered mark, issue directions requiring the proprietor to amend their internal mark regulations referred to in their registration documentation. Failure to comply with such directions shall render the proprietor liable to penalties as determined under this Act. Further, any deliberate or reckless adoption of marks confusingly similar to existing registrations, despite notice of those registrations, will be deemed a violation entitling the registered owner to seek account of profits derived from the infringing use.

Any proprietor seeking registration of a service mark relating to financial services shall submit detailed regulations governing its application. These mark regulations referred to herein must explicitly outline procedures for ensuring quality control amongst authorized users and mechanisms for preventing dilution of brand identity. Failure to provide comprehensive regulations, or subsequent amendment thereof without prior approval from the Registrar, constitutes an offense punishable with a fine not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Further, any unauthorized use of the service mark by a person not adhering to the prescribed regulations shall render them liable for damages, subject to judicial determination, and may be restrained under this Act. The Registrar may, at any time, require amendment or clarification of these regulations.

Subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal, a registered trade mark owner seeking to alter their mark’s regulations shall provide prior notice to all licensees under this Act. Such notice must detail the proposed changes and their anticipated impact on existing agreements. Failure to provide adequate notice, or where the alterations demonstrably prejudice a licensee's established commercial interests, may render the amended regulations unenforceable against that licensee. The Registrar may, upon receiving representations from aggrieved parties, direct the trade mark owner to modify the altered regulations to mitigate such prejudice. Any dispute concerning the validity of these mark regulations referred shall be resolved through arbitration as per the provisions outlined in the Arbitration and Conciliation Act.

Any proprietor seeking to register a service mark relating to financial services shall provide detailed regulations governing permissible usage by authorized agents. These mark regulations referred must explicitly define acceptable promotional materials and client communications. Failure to adhere to these prescribed standards constitutes infringement under this Act, entitling aggrieved parties to seek injunctive relief and damages. The Registrar may, upon receiving credible evidence of misuse or deceptive practices, issue a warning notice to the proprietor. Further, any proprietor electing to benefit from the Madrid Protocol International system for obtaining international registration shall ensure their domestic mark regulations are consistent with applicable treaty obligations. Such inconsistencies will render the international registration vulnerable to cancellation and expose the proprietor to liability for misrepresentation.

Where a person is charged with an offence under this Act relating to the use of a trade mark and the accused pleads registration, the Court shall consider the validity of the said registration. For the purposes of this sub-section, “pleads registration” means that the accused expressly raises as a defence the assertion that the registered trade mark was improperly registered or is otherwise invalid. The court may require the proprietor of the trade mark to provide evidence supporting the registration’s validity. Subject to any order made by the Court, such evidence shall be considered only for the purpose of determining whether the charge should proceed; provided that a separate action regarding the validity of the registration remains unaffected as provided herein.

Where a person is charged with an offence under this Act relating to the use of a mark identical or confusingly similar to a registered trade mark and the accused pleads registration, the court may direct that the validity of the said registration be determined as part of the proceedings. Provided that such direction shall only be given if the accused demonstrates a reasonable basis for challenging the registration’s validity, supported by evidence demonstrating conflicting prior use or other grounds under this Act. The Registrar shall then furnish to the Court all relevant records pertaining to the registration within thirty days. Further, any party aggrieved by the determination of validity may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board as provided herein.

Where a person is charged with an offence under this Act relating to the use of a trade mark and accused pleads registration, the Court may direct that the validity of the said registration be determined as part of the proceedings. Provided that such direction shall only be given if the accused demonstrates a reasonable basis for challenging the registration’s legitimacy, supported by evidence indicating potential defects in the application or subsequent conduct undermining its enforceability. The court shall not stay the main trial solely on account of this determination; however, any finding concerning the validity of the trade mark registration shall be binding upon all parties to the proceedings and may be appealed separately under the provisions relating to appeals from decrees. Further, costs associated with determining the registration’s validity shall be borne by the party who successfully challenges or defends it, as determined by the Court.

Where a person is charged with an offence under this Act relating to the use of a trade mark and accused pleads registration, the Court may direct that the validity of the said registration be determined as part of the proceedings. Such direction shall be given only if the accused demonstrates a reasonable basis for challenging the registration’s validity, supported by documentary evidence filed prior to commencement of trial. The Court shall provide the registered proprietor with an opportunity to file its response within thirty days from the date of such direction. Any determination made regarding the validity of the trade mark registration shall be final and binding only for the purposes of that particular prosecution. Further, this determination shall not prejudice any other proceedings concerning the same or similar matters under this Act or otherwise. The Court may, at any stage, set aside its earlier direction if it finds that the challenge to registration is frivolous or vexatious.

Where a person is charged with an offence under this Act relating to the use of a trade mark and accused pleads registration, the Court may require the accused to furnish, within thirty days from the date of such pleading, evidence demonstrating the validity of the alleged registration. Such evidence shall include a certified copy of the registration certificate issued by the Registrar and any documents relied upon by the accused in support of their claim that the trade mark is lawfully registered. Provided that if the accused fails to provide the required documentation within the stipulated timeframe, the Court may proceed with the trial as if no such defence had been raised. The Registrar shall be obliged to furnish copies of registration certificates upon a written request from the Court and payment of prescribed fees.

Where a person is charged with an offence under this Act relating to the use of a trade mark and the accused pleads registration, the prosecution shall bear the burden of proving the validity of the said registration. Provided that, if the accused successfully establishes material inconsistencies in the record of opposition or examination proceedings before the Trade Marks Registry, the court may direct the prosecution to produce such records for further scrutiny. Failure to do so shall render the trade mark registration liable to be presumed valid for the purposes of the trial. Any person aggrieved by an order directing production of records may appeal under this Act within sixty days from the date of such order; and penalties for wilful obstruction of justice in relation to these proceedings shall apply as provided herein.

Where a person is charged with an offence under this Act relating to the use of a trade mark and accused pleads registration, the prosecution shall be obliged to provide evidence demonstrating the validity and subsistence of the said registration. Provided that, if the accused demonstrates to the satisfaction of the court that a contractual agreement exists permitting their use of the impugned mark, irrespective of its registered status, the court may stay proceedings pending resolution of the contractual dispute. Further, any assignment or license granted in respect of a trade mark shall be deemed valid only when duly recorded with the prescribed Trade Marks Registry and such recording shall create an estoppel against all persons claiming under the original registration. The Registrar may, upon application by any interested party, investigate the veracity of any claimed assignment or license and issue appropriate directions as provided herein.

Where a person is charged with an offence under this Act relating to the use of a trade mark and accused pleads registration, the Court may direct that the validity of the said registration be determined as preliminary issue. Provided that such direction shall only be given if the accused demonstrates a reasonable basis for challenging the registration’s subsistence. The Registrar shall then file an affidavit verifying the record pertaining to the registration. Subject to any order made by the court, the proceedings before the Court shall remain stayed pending determination of the validity issue. Any party aggrieved by an order determining such validity may appeal under this Act within sixty days from the date of that order.

Where a person is charged with an offence under this Act relating to the use of a trade mark and accused pleads registration, the Court may direct that the validity of the registration be determined as part of the proceedings. The Registrar shall, upon receiving such direction from the Court, investigate the grounds for challenging the registration and submit a report within sixty days detailing its findings concerning the distinctiveness, deceptive similarity, or other invalidity arguments raised by the accused. This report shall include any evidence considered relevant to the validity determination. Provided that the Registrar may extend this period with prior approval of the Court if further investigation is deemed necessary. The Court shall consider the Registrar's report and any counter-evidence submitted before making a finding on the registration’s validity, subject to its own independent assessment of all presented material.

Where a person is charged with an offence under this Act relating to the use of a trade mark and the accused pleads registration of the said trade mark, the Court may direct that the validity of such registration be determined as part of the proceedings. Provided that, if the accused demonstrates reasonable grounds for believing that the registered proprietor has obtained the registration through fraudulent means or misrepresentation, the Court shall order an inquiry into the circumstances surrounding the registration. Upon completion of such inquiry and finding that the registration was indeed procured by fraud, it shall be deemed falsify trade, notwithstanding any prior legal action regarding the mark's validity. The aggrieved party may appeal against this determination to the appellate authority within sixty days.

For the purpose of facilitating efficient adjudication relating to rectification proceedings, the court provided registrar shall be deemed a judicial officer. The court provided registrar has power to regulate their own procedure, subject to the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, as applied by notification issued by the Central Government. Any party aggrieved by an order passed by the court provided registrar may appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such order. The Registrar shall record reasons for every decision rendered and make available copies thereof upon application made under this Act.

Where an appeal is brought before the Appellate Tribunal against any decision or order passed by the court provided registrar relating to the rectification of a registered trade mark, the appellant shall serve upon the other party notice of such appeal at least sixty days prior to the date fixed for hearing. The Appellate Tribunal may, after giving all parties affected an opportunity of being heard, confirm, vary, or reverse any decision or order so passed, and may substitute its own decision or order in place thereof. Any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act by the court provided registrar relating to the acceptance or refusal of a trade mark application, or the registration of a trade mark, may appeal to the Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of such order. The Tribunal shall have power to grant any relief which it deems just and equitable in relation to the subject matter of the appeal, including but not limited to injunctive relief against infringement.

Applications for registration of service marks shall be examined by the Registrar in accordance with the provisions relating to trade mark applications generally, provided that the applicant shall furnish such documentary evidence as demonstrates the rendering of services and geographical area covered. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar concerning the acceptance or rejection of an application may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The Registrar may, at any time, require an applicant to provide further information or clarification regarding the nature of the services for which registration is sought. Upon receipt of such request, the applicant shall comply within thirty days; failure to do so may result in the refusal of the application. Decisions made by the court provided registrar are final and binding subject only to appeal as described herein.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the court acting as the registrar concerning the rectification of a registered trade mark shall have the right to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeals must be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order, and failure to do so shall render the appeal inadmissible. The court provided registrar may, upon receiving evidence of fraudulent use or misrepresentation relating to a trade mark, issue an injunction restraining such conduct. Any party violating this restraint is liable to a penalty not exceeding one hundred thousand rupees for each instance of infringement, recoverable as civil debt. Repeated offences shall attract enhanced penalties and potential criminal prosecution under the Indian Penal Code.

A registered user party, as defined herein, is a person duly registered under this Act as having exclusive right to use a trade mark in relation to particular goods or services for which the proprietor of the trade mark is also registered. Such registration may occur with the consent of the proprietor and subject to any conditions specified therein. A registered user party shall be entitled to institute proceedings relating to infringement of the trade mark, provided that such proceedings are brought on behalf of and for the benefit of the proprietor. The rights conferred upon a registered user party extend only to the goods or services as defined in their registration certificate and do not encompass any other aspect of the proprietor's trade mark ownership.

A registered user party seeking to extend the territorial scope of their registration shall file an application with the Registrar within three months from the date on which the trade mark is initially registered in another territory. Such application must specify the original territory of registration and clearly delineate the proposed new territory, demonstrating a genuine use of the mark within the initial jurisdiction for at least two years preceding the application. The Registrar may require further evidence substantiating this continuous usage and establishing that no confusing similarity exists between the existing and prospective markets. Provided that the applicant satisfies these conditions as provided herein, the registration shall be extended to the new territory subject to any opposition filed by interested parties within a period of sixty days from the date of publication of the application.

A registered user party seeking relief against infringement of a trade mark shall have the right to institute an action in a court of competent jurisdiction, subject to the provisions regarding limitation periods as provided herein. Such action may include claims for damages sustained by reason of the infringing use, including but not limited to lost profits and reasonable royalties. The measure of damages shall be determined taking into account the extent of the infringement and any willful misconduct on the part of the infringer. Provided that, where the registered user party can demonstrate a substantial investment made in promoting or improving the trade mark after its registration, enhanced damages may be awarded at the discretion of the court. Further, the registered user party is entitled to seek an injunction restraining the infringing activity, and may apply for interim relief pending determination of the suit.

Subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal, an application by a registered user party seeking leave to institute proceedings relating to revocation of a trade mark may be entertained only if such application is filed within six months from the date on which the applicant received notice of the institution of the rectification proceeding. The Registrar shall serve a copy of such application upon the proprietor of the trade mark and any other interested parties as identified by the registered user party, providing them with a period of thirty days to file their response. Failure by the Registrar to provide timely notification shall not invalidate subsequent orders made under this Act. A registered user party may also apply for intervention in rectification proceedings initiated by another party, provided that they demonstrate a material interest and potential prejudice resulting from the outcome of those proceedings.

A registered user party seeking to challenge a rectification action initiated against the proprietor of the trade mark shall file an application with the relevant intellectual property authority within thirty days from the date of service of notice of the action upon the proprietor. Such application must clearly demonstrate that the registered user’s interests are materially affected by the outcome of the rectification proceedings and specify the grounds upon which they rely to oppose the proposed alteration or deletion of the trade mark registration. The intellectual property authority may, after affording both the proprietor and the registered user party an opportunity for hearing, determine whether the application is admissible. An inadmissible application shall be deemed withdrawn without further notice.

Where a registered user party institutes proceedings seeking relief against an infringement of a trade mark, such proceedings shall be deemed civil suits within the meaning of Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. The proprietor of the trade mark shall be obligated to actively participate in and diligently prosecute any action brought by a registered user; failure to do so may result in summary judgment against the proprietor for costs incurred by the registered user. Any wilful or negligent abandonment of such proceedings by the proprietor without reasonable cause, as determined by the relevant court, will render them liable to pay damages to the registered user party equivalent to three times the actual losses suffered. Further, any attempt to obstruct a registered user’s enforcement actions shall constitute contempt of court and be subject to appropriate penalties.

A registered user party may grant licenses relating to the use of the trade mark as specified in the registration, subject to the conditions that such license does not conflict with the exclusive right conferred upon the proprietor and is recorded within thirty days of its execution with the Trade Marks Registry. Any assignment or pledge of the benefit of a license granted by a registered user party shall also be recorded in like manner, provided that the assignee or pledgee undertakes to observe all terms and conditions stipulated in the original license agreement. The Registrar may require such further information as is deemed necessary to ascertain compliance with these provisions. Failure to record any assignment or pledge within the prescribed timeframe shall render the same void against the proprietor of the trade mark and subsequent registered user parties.

Where a dispute arises concerning the use of a trade mark by a registered user party, and such use is alleged to constitute infringement under this Act, the aggrieved party may institute proceedings against both the proprietor of the trade mark and the registered user. Provided that, where the registered user demonstrates, through evidence presented before an adjudicating officer, that they were acting in good faith and without knowledge of any claim of right by the proprietor, the officer may apportion liability between them. Further, a decision concerning the validity or extent of a registered user’s rights shall be appealable to the relevant appellate authority within sixty days from the date of such decision. The appellate authority shall consider whether due process was followed in determining the registered user party's entitlement.

A registered user party, having lawfully obtained consent for use of a trade mark as provided herein, shall be deemed an aggrieved party if another person uses a confusingly similar mark. Such infringement constitutes a violation punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and with a fine which shall not be less than fifty thousand rupees. Further, where the infringing mark incorporates or imitates genera species specified within the registered trade mark’s description of goods, the penalty shall be doubled. The Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal may, upon receiving complaint, issue injunctions restraining further use of the infringing mark and order recovery of damages sustained by the registered user party.

Where a registered user party challenges the validity of a mark registered trade before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, such challenge may only be brought if the registered user has demonstrably suffered material prejudice as a direct consequence of the registration. Provided that, where the proprietor of the mark contests the standing of the registered user to bring such a challenge, the burden shall lie upon the registered user to establish their entitlement under this Act. Further, any order made by the Appellate Board affirming the validity of the mark against the challenge of a registered user party is subject to appeal to the High Court within ninety days from the date of that order, provided that the appellant demonstrates special cause for delay where such period has lapsed.

Where a registered user party seeks to enforce the rights conferred by registration of a trade mark against infringement, such action may be brought in the name of the proprietor of the trade mark. Provided that, where such registered user has suffered damage as a result of the infringing activity, they shall be entitled to claim compensation for such damage independently of any claim made by the proprietor. Further, a registered user party is empowered to grant licences relating to the use of the trade mark within the scope of their permitted use, and may demand royalty from licensees subject to conditions prescribed under this Act. Any dispute concerning the amount or validity of such royalty shall be resolved through arbitration as provided herein, with both parties bound by the arbitrator's decision.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall include a representation of the marks applied for by way of label, device, or otherwise as may be prescribed; and where such application relates to three-dimensional objects, colours, sounds, or other marks which are not capable of being represented graphically, the applicant shall furnish such description as is sufficient for the purpose of identification. The Registrar may require the applicant to amend the representation or description if it is deemed deficient in clarity or precision. Any party opposing an application under this Act shall be liable costs unless the opposition is found to be frivolous or vexatious; provided that the Tribunal, upon review of the circumstances, may order a contribution towards costs from any successful applicant where undue delay or obstruction has been employed.

Where a proprietor institutes proceedings alleging the infringement of a registered trade mark, and such proceedings are ultimately dismissed on the ground that the proprietor has failed to establish a reputation commensurate with the distinctiveness claimed for the mark, or that the alleged infringing use does not constitute an actionable form of unfair competition as provided herein, the court may order the proprietor to pay liable costs unless it is satisfied that there existed reasonable grounds for believing that an infringement had occurred. The determination of whether reasonable grounds existed shall take into account any evidence presented by the defendant demonstrating a genuine belief in the validity and enforceability of the trade mark right. Further, where such dismissal results from the proprietor’s deliberate misrepresentation of facts or concealment of material information, the court may award costs to the defendant reflecting the extent of their prejudice.

Where a rectification action is brought before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board alleging an error apparent on the face of the register relating to a trade mark, the Board may, after affording all parties concerned an opportunity of being heard, direct such amendment as it deems fit. The Board shall record the reasons for its decision and transmit the amended register to the Registrar for implementation. In any rectification proceeding, a party who has incurred costs in relation to the action is generally entitled to recover those costs from the opposing party; however, a party shall not be liable costs unless they acted without reasonable cause or failed to comply with procedural requirements as provided herein. The Board may, on application, order discovery of documents relevant to the rectification action. Any appeal from an order of the Board concerning costs is subject to review under this Act.

Where a proprietor institutes proceedings alleging infringement of a registered trade mark, and such proceedings are ultimately determined against the proprietor or are withdrawn by them without order as to costs, the court may order that the proprietor shall be liable for costs incurred by the defendant in defending the action. This liability extends to reasonable legal fees, disbursements, and any other expenses properly incurred in resisting the claim. Provided that, where the proprietor can demonstrate a genuine and plausible belief in the existence of infringement at the time of initiating proceedings, and acted reasonably in pursuing those proceedings, the court may exercise discretion in assessing the amount of costs recoverable; however, they shall remain liable costs unless such reasonableness is clearly established to the satisfaction of the court.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is refused under this Act, the Registrar may require the applicant to furnish, along with the application or at any subsequent stage prior to acceptance, a detailed manufactured notification specifying the precise geographical location and production methods employed in relation to the goods or services associated with the proposed trade mark. Such manufactured notification shall be deemed an integral part of the registration process and failure to comply with this requirement may result in rejection of the application. The Registrar shall maintain a public record of all such notifications, accessible for inspection by any interested party. Provided that, where the applicant demonstrates reasonable cause preventing full compliance, the Registrar may grant a temporary extension, subject to conditions as deemed appropriate.

Where a trade mark is registered under this Act, the proprietor shall be entitled to institute proceedings for infringement against any person who, without authorization, applies a manufactured notification specifying the trademark or a confusingly similar representation in connection with goods or services identical or similar to those in respect of which the trade mark is registered. Such manufactured notifications shall be deemed to be acts of false representation under this Act, and the proprietor may seek an injunction restraining the use of such notifications, together with damages for any loss suffered by reason of the infringement. Provided that a genuine user defense may be raised if the unauthorized application of the manufactured notification was made prior to the date of registration and constitutes honest descriptive use relating to the characteristics of the goods or services.

Where a trade mark is registered in accordance with this Act, the Registrar may, upon application by any interested party and after affording due opportunity for hearing, direct that a manufactured notification specifying the geographical origin of goods bearing the trade mark be affixed to such goods or their packaging.
