Such direction shall not be issued unless it is demonstrated that use of the trade mark creates confusion amongst consumers regarding the actual place of manufacture. Any party aggrieved by an order made under this Act relating to a manufactured notification may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order, subject to such conditions as are prescribed herein. The Board’s decision shall be final.

For the purposes of this Act, “India-produced goods” shall mean any goods manufactured, processed, assembled or otherwise produced wholly or partly within the territory of India. Where such goods are subsequently exported and re-imported into India, they shall continue to be considered as India-produced goods unless substantial transformation has occurred outside India, determined according to regulations framed under this Act. Goods initially imported into India and then subjected to minimal processing or alteration within India shall not, by virtue of that processing alone, qualify as India-produced goods; the determination of “substantial transformation” shall consider factors including labour content and value addition. The Registrar may issue guidelines clarifying application of these principles concerning "imported india produced" articles.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall include a statement indicating whether the goods or services in relation to which the trade mark is sought to be registered are primarily manufactured, produced, or rendered within India, or if they are imported into India. Where an applicant seeks to register a trade mark for goods that are initially conceived and designed outside India but subsequently manufactured or produced within India, such application shall clearly state this fact under oath by the applicant. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating the “imported india produced” nature of these goods, including evidence of design origin and manufacturing processes employed in India. Failure to provide satisfactory evidence as provided herein may result in rejection of the application or subsequent amendment of the register.

Where any goods manufactured or produced in India bear a trade mark identical or deceptively similar to an earlier registered trade mark for goods of the same class, and those goods were originally imported into India prior to the date of registration of the said earlier trade mark, then such importation shall be deemed an infringement under this Act. Provided that, where the importer demonstrates good faith reliance on a valid license agreement executed before the relevant date, permitting use of the mark for *imported India produced* goods, no penalty shall apply; however, continued importation without such license constitutes actionable misrepresentation. Any person infringing as provided herein shall be liable to pay damages equivalent to three times the value of the infringing goods and may also face imprisonment extending to three years.

Where a proprietor of a registered trade mark, hereinafter referred to as the “licensor,” desires to grant a license relating to goods wholly or partly manufactured, processed, or assembled in India using imported raw materials, such license shall be assignable subject to conditions stipulated by the licensor. The assignment may include rights pertaining to the use of distinctive signs and associated goodwill derived from the original registration. Provided that any sub-licensee operating under this arrangement shall clearly indicate on all goods bearing the trade mark, a statement confirming they are “imported India produced” items, as determined by the Registrar. Further, the licensor may stipulate limitations regarding geographical scope or specific product categories covered within the license agreement. Any alteration to these conditions requires prior written consent from both parties and notification to the Trade Marks Registry.

Where a trade mark is registered under this Act in respect of goods manufactured or produced outside India but subsequently imported and sold within India, the proprietor shall be entitled to enforce the rights conferred by registration against any person who, without due cause, uses an identical or confusingly similar trade mark in relation to like goods which are also *imported India produced* and offered for sale within Indian territory. Any such infringement may be restrained by injunction as provided herein. The Central Government, acting through the Patent Office central, shall have power to issue directions regarding the verification of origin claims made in connection with imported goods bearing registered trade marks, including requiring documentary evidence substantiating that the goods were indeed manufactured or produced outside India at the time of registration. Failure to comply with such directions may render the proprietor liable for penalties and potential revocation of their trademark rights.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall include a statement specifying the goods or services in relation to which the trade mark is sought to be registered. Where the Registrar considers that any of the specified goods are required to be associated with particular characteristics under this Act, the applicant may be directed to amend the description of such goods to accurately reflect those characteristics. The Registrar shall publish particulars of the application in the Official Gazette, including a representation of the mark and a list of the goods for which registration is sought; it being understood that publication in the gazette require goods to be clearly defined. Any person may oppose the registration on grounds specified herein.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is accepted, the Trade Marks Registry shall direct that the acceptance be published in the Official Gazette. Such publication shall include particulars of the trade marks and list of goods or services in relation to which the trade mark has been accepted. Any person may, within three months from the date of such publication, give notice of opposition to the registration under this Act. The Registry shall consider any opposition received and provide an opportunity for all parties concerned to be heard. If, after due consideration, the Registrar is satisfied that no grounds for objection exist, or that those grounds are not sufficient to warrant refusal, he may proceed with the registration. It is provided that goods specified in the application must correspond with classes as defined under the International Classification of Goods and Services. The gazette require goods be accurately reflected in the register.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark used in relation to goods shall, upon application by any person seeking to use an identical or confusingly similar mark for goods corresponding to those specified in the registration, and subject to satisfying the Intellectual Property Appellate Board that such use would not constitute unfair competition, grant a license permitting the use of the trade mark. Such license may be granted on terms and conditions as the Board deems appropriate, including limitations regarding geographical area, duration, or specific product categories. The proprietor shall require publication of any assignment or sub-license of the trade mark in the Official Gazette, detailing the scope of goods covered by such assignment or sub-license. Failure to comply with this requirement shall render the assignment or sub-license void against subsequent proprietors and third parties claiming under them; it is imperative that all transactions relating to a registered trade mark are properly reflected in the gazette require goods.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is accepted, the Trade Marks Registry shall direct that the acceptance be published in the Official Gazette. Any person considering himself aggrieved by such publication or by the acceptance of the trade mark may, within four weeks from the date of such publication, file a notice of opposition with the Registrar, setting forth particulars of the grounds on which he bases his objection. The Registrar shall give reasonable opportunity to both the applicant and the opponent to be heard under this Act. It is provided that where the goods or services specified in the application are not clearly defined, the gazette require goods specification may be challenged as unduly broad. The decision of the Registrar shall be final, subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is accepted, the Trade Marks Registry shall direct that the acceptance be published in the Official Gazette. Such publication shall include particulars of the goods or services in respect of which the trade mark has been accepted and any disclaimer contained in the application. Any person considering himself aggrieved by such acceptance may, subject to provisions regarding time limits, file a representation with the Registrar against the registration of the trade mark as published in the gazette require goods. The Registrar shall consider all representations received and may direct that the trade marks deemed to be registered be amended or refused accordingly. Notice of any such direction shall also be published in the Official Gazette for public information. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar under this Act may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Where a person, by any means whatsoever, represents that goods or services are affiliated with a particular enterprise, or endorsed or approved by such enterprise, without its express consent, shall be deemed to have made false representations for the purposes of this Act. Such representation is actionable irrespective of whether it causes actual confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or quality of the goods or services in question. Provided that, where the representation is made in good faith and without any intention to deceive, and relates solely to the characteristics of the goods or services themselves, it shall not be considered a violation under this Act, subject to conditions as provided herein.

Where a person, by representing any goods or services as being used with the approval of another, or as being in relation to such goods or services, without his consent, applies for registration of a trade mark under this Act, the Board may, subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal, refuse the application if it finds that such representation is likely to cause confusion in the minds of the public. Provided that where the owner of the goodwill has subsequently given consent, or otherwise acquiesced in the use of his name or mark by the applicant, registration shall be permissible as provided herein. The Board may require the applicant to submit evidence demonstrating a lack of likelihood of confusion before proceeding with consideration of the application.

Where a person, by falsely representing that goods or services are affiliated with, connected to, or endorsed by another person, induces, or has induced, any member of the public to believe such representation, and thereby causes damage to the reputation or goodwill associated with the other person’s brand, that other person shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief. Provided that the false representation was made in the course of trade, and the damage is reasonably attributable to the misrepresentation. Further, a court may order compensation for losses suffered by the aggrieved party, including but not limited to lost profits, diminution in value of their brand, and costs incurred in mitigating the harm caused. The remedies available under this Act are without prejudice to any other right or remedy which may be available to the aggrieved person under any other law for the time being in force.

Where a person, by falsely representing that goods or services are affiliated with, connected to, or endorsed by another person, induces, or has induced, any member of the public to believe such representation, and thereby gains an unfair advantage or causes detriment to the claimant, then the Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint duly verified before him, issue directions for rectification. Such directions shall include, but not be limited to, orders restraining the continuance of the false representation and mandating corrective advertising measures as deemed appropriate by the Registrar. The complainant shall bear the burden of proving the falsity of the representation and its detrimental effect. Provided that any order issued under this provision is subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within a period of sixty days from the date of such order. Further, the claimant may seek interim relief pending determination of the matter.

Where a person, by representing any goods or services as being used in connection with a trademark that is identical or confusingly similar to a mark already registered under this Act in respect of particular goods or services, induces, or attempts to induce, consumers to believe that those goods or services originate from the proprietor of the earlier trade mark, such person shall be deemed to have engaged in unfair competition. Provided that where the representation made is demonstrably accurate and concerns bona fide characteristics of the goods or services, this provision shall not apply. Furthermore, a consumer who reasonably believes the representation made may file a complaint with the relevant adjudicating authority as provided herein. Any order issued under this Act concerning such representations shall be subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Where a person, by knowingly and wilfully representing goods or services as being connected with any trade mark already registered in India, or falsely suggesting an association therewith, induces confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or quality of those goods or services, such person shall be deemed to have committed an offence under this Act. Any proprietor of a registered trade mark aggrieved by such misrepresentation may apply to the relevant High Court for an injunction restraining the offending party from continuing such conduct and seeking damages commensurate with the loss suffered due to the deceptive practice. Failure to comply with any order issued pursuant to these provisions shall render the offender liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakhs rupees, and further subject to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years.

Where a person, by way of assignment or sub-licence, transfers rights in a registered trade mark, such transfer shall be deemed to include all associated intellectual property relating directly to the goods or services for which the trade mark is registered, unless explicitly excluded within the instrument of transfer. Any licensee operating under a valid licence agreement may, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated therein, further sub-licence those rights pertaining solely to the scope granted in their initial license, provided that such sub-licence does not contradict or diminish the original trade mark owner’s control over core brand elements. The assignee shall be bound by any prior agreements concerning quality control measures associated with the licensed goods or services. Further, a trade mark owner may grant a non-exclusive licence to another party for use in specific geographical territories, as provided herein.

Where a person, by engaging in deceptive soliciting practices directed towards clients associated with an established trademark owner, induces those clients to terminate their existing contractual relationships and enter into new agreements for substantially similar services, such actions shall constitute grounds for injunctive relief. Provided that, the aggrieved party must demonstrate a likelihood of confusion amongst consumers arising from these solicitations, coupled with evidence of demonstrable financial prejudice suffered as a direct consequence thereof. It is further provided that any appeal against an order restraining such soliciting activities may only be pursued upon establishing that the respondent’s conduct falls demonstrably short of constituting unfair competition under this Act and does not involve passing off.

Where a person, by entering into an agreement for the use of a registered trade mark, grants a license conferring the right to apply for entry in the Entry Register relating to a particular variety of goods or services, such license shall be deemed a registrable assignment under this Act. Provided that any subsequent transfer of rights arising from such licensed application requires prior written consent from the original proprietor of the trade mark and notification to the Trade Marks Registry. The licensee may, subject to the terms of the initial agreement, further assign these prospective registration rights relating to the entry register variety, but shall remain bound by the obligations imposed upon them under this Act concerning proper use and quality control of the goods or services bearing the licensed trade mark. Any alteration to the scope of the registered trade mark after the grant of license will require renegotiation of terms between proprietor and licensee, as provided herein.

Where a person, by representing goods or services as being used in association with a trademark that has been previously applied for but not yet registered, creates confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or nature of those goods or services, such representation shall constitute an actionable deceptive practice under this Act. Provided that, where the applicant for registration can demonstrate reasonable grounds to believe that the misleading use was initiated subsequent to the date accorded patent protection on a related invention, the aggrieved party may appeal the finding of deception to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Further, it is stipulated that any order issued by the Board shall be subject to review by the relevant High Court within ninety days of notification.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed to be improperly filed if the applicant’s address for communication, as specified therein, does not conform to the standards prescribed by the Registrar. The Registrar may, at any time, require an applicant or registered proprietor to furnish further information relating to the ownership or use of a trade mark under this Act. Where a person seeks to act on behalf of another in proceedings before the Registrar, such person shall be required to file a power of attorney duly executed and stamped as per prevailing regulations. The registrar person acting for any entity must provide proof of authorization satisfactory to the Registrar. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in rejection of the application or other appropriate action as provided herein.

Where an application for registration of a trademark is rejected under this Act, the applicant shall have the right to appeal to the Registrar within sixty days from the date of receipt of the rejection order. The Registrar may, upon receiving such an appeal and after affording the appellant an opportunity of being heard, either confirm or reverse the decision of the initial examining officer. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar under this process may further petition the Intellectual Property Appellate Board for review. It is provided that any representation made to the *Registrar person act* during these proceedings shall be considered without prejudice to the rights and remedies available to other parties concerned, including those claiming prior use or similar rights in respect of the trademark.

Where an application for registration of a trademark is filed with the Registrar, such application shall be examined to ascertain compliance with the provisions under this Act. The Registrar may, at any time during examination, require the applicant to submit further particulars or amendments deemed necessary for clarity and accuracy. Any objection raised by the Registrar concerning distinctiveness or other grounds specified herein must be communicated in writing to the applicant within a period of six months from the date of filing. Failure to respond adequately to such objections within the prescribed timeframe shall render the application liable for rejection. The *Registrar person act* allows the Registrar, or any officer authorised by them, to conduct hearings and inspections as deemed necessary to verify information provided in the application.

Where an application for registration of a trademark is refused under this Act, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to submit written representations and evidence rebutting the grounds for refusal. The Registrar may, after considering such submissions, either uphold the initial refusal or direct that the application proceed to examination. Any party aggrieved by any decision of the Registrar relating to the acceptance or rejection of a trademark application, or concerning the rectification of the Register, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The Registrar shall provide reasons in writing for any such decision and the appeal process is as provided herein; however, the *Registrar person act* does not preclude informal resolution through mediation.

Where an application for registration of a trademark is refused under this Act, the applicant shall have the right to appeal against such refusal. The Registrar person act shall be recorded and made available for inspection by any interested party within thirty days of the order being passed. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Registrar may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board, provided that the appeal is filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the said order. The Appellate Board shall consider all relevant evidence presented before it and may affirm, modify, or reverse the decision of the Registrar. Further, any interlocutory order made by the Registrar or the Appellate Board may be challenged under this Act through a writ petition in the High Court.

For the purposes of this Act, "Darjeeling Tea" means tea produced exclusively in the Darjeeling district and having specific characteristics attributable to the terroir of that region, including but not limited to altitude, slope, rainfall, and soil composition; provided that such characteristics are demonstrably distinct from teas produced elsewhere. The central government shall determine, by notification in the Official Gazette, the precise geographical boundaries constituting the territory of production for Darjeeling Tea, subject to periodic review as may be necessary. Any use of the term "Darjeeling Tea" on goods not conforming to these criteria is prohibited under this Act and constitutes an infringement.

An application for registration of a geographical indication, accompanied by prescribed forms and fees, may be filed with the Registrar, specifying the name of the geographical indication as it is proposed to be registered, particulars of the agricultural products, natural products, manufactured goods or handicraft goods for which the geographical indication is used, and details of authorized users. The central government shall, after giving opportunity to all interested parties to make their representations, determine whether the geographical indication satisfies the conditions laid down under this Act. Provided that, if any objection is raised against the registration, the Registrar may refer the matter to the central government for further consideration and decision. The applicant shall furnish such documentary evidence as the Registrar deems necessary to substantiate the claim of distinctiveness associated with the geographical indication.

Any proprietor seeking rectification of a registered geographical indication may apply to the appropriate forum as provided herein, detailing the grounds upon which such rectification is sought and supported by relevant evidence demonstrating misrepresentation, fraud, or any other action contrary to the interests of the registered proprietors or consumers. The central government shall, upon receiving complaints regarding unfair competition arising from the use of a geographically indicative term identical or deceptively similar to a protected indication, initiate an inquiry into the matter. Any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act may appeal to such authority as is prescribed, subject to limitations on time and scope as detailed in the regulations. The central government shall also have the power to issue directions for the seizure and disposal of goods infringing upon registered geographical indications, ensuring due process and opportunity for hearing before any action is taken.

Applications for registration of geographical indications, duly completed in the prescribed form and accompanied by the requisite fee, shall be submitted to the Registrar. The Registrar may require the applicant to submit further information or clarification regarding the application, including particulars relating to the quality and characteristics of the goods for which the geographical indication is sought, and the area of production concerned. Upon receipt of such an application, the Registrar shall publish a notice thereof in the Geographical Indications Journal. Any person feeling aggrieved by the publication may, within the time specified therein, file objections with the Registrar, stating clearly the grounds upon which such objection is based. The central government shall determine the procedure for dealing with objections received and for affording interested parties an opportunity to be heard. Following due consideration of any objections, the Registrar shall proceed as provided herein.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may be filed with the Registrar, subject to compliance with the prescribed forms and fees as determined by notification in the Official Gazette. The applicant shall provide detailed particulars regarding the quality and characteristics of the goods associated with the proposed geographical indication, including verifiable data demonstrating their unique origin and reputation. Provided that, if the Central Government is satisfied that the use of a geographical indication as applied for is contrary to public order or morality, it may refuse registration. Further, the Registrar shall issue an examination report outlining any objections received under this Act, which the applicant must address within the stipulated timeframe. The central government shall establish guidelines regarding permissible alterations to production methods impacting the distinctiveness of registered goods.

Any proprietor seeking rectification of a registered geographical indication, alleging inter alia that use by an authorized user constitutes unfair competition and damages the reputation of the indication, shall apply to the Central Government in the prescribed form accompanied by the requisite fee. The central government shall, after affording opportunity for hearing to all interested parties including the alleged infringer and any other persons claiming rights under the geographical indication, determine whether such use is detrimental to the distinctiveness or reputation of the registered indication. If the central government finds that the use does indeed constitute unfair competition, it may direct cessation of the infringing activity and impose a penalty not exceeding five lakhs rupees for each instance of violation. Further, repeated contravention shall render the offender liable to prosecution under this Act.

Any proprietor of a geographical indication seeking to grant a license for use of such indication, whether exclusive or non-exclusive, shall submit an application in the prescribed form to the central government, detailing the scope and duration of the proposed license, as well as royalty rates and any restrictions on permitted uses. The central government may, after providing opportunity for hearing to all interested parties including potential licensees and objectors, approve or reject such application. Where a geographical indication has been assigned by transfer, the assignee shall be deemed the proprietor for the purposes of granting licenses under this Act. Further, the central government shall ensure that any license granted includes provisions safeguarding the quality and reputation associated with the registered geographical indication, preventing its use in connection with goods not conforming to established standards.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Registrar relating to the registration, amendment, revocation or refusal of registration of a geographical indication institutes an appeal under this Act, the Appellate Board shall hear and dispose of such appeals within six months from the date of receipt of the appeal. The central government shall, upon receiving representations concerning alleged misuse of a registered geographical indication, direct the Registrar to investigate whether any unfair competition or deceptive practices are being employed that infringe upon the rights conferred by registration. Provided that, if the Registrar finds merit in such allegations and determines that infringement has occurred, he may issue directions for rectification of trade practices as deemed necessary; however, any party disputing these findings may appeal to the Appellate Board within thirty days.

Where an application for registration of a geographical indication is refused, the applicant shall have the right to appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order of refusal; provided that such appeal must demonstrate demonstrable prejudice arising directly from any error apparent on the face of the record relating to compliance with sub-section (2) regarding prior use. The central government shall, upon receiving a substantiated complaint alleging deceptive use of a registered geographical indication in relation to goods not conforming to the established standards as defined under this Act, initiate an inquiry and may direct seizure of such infringing products if it is determined that the use constitutes unfair competition. Furthermore, any technological process essential for maintaining quality characteristics which are intrinsically linked to the geographical indication shall be afforded protection analogous to a patent, subject to conditions prescribed by regulations.

Any proprietor seeking rectification of a registered geographical indication, alleging that entry of a particular good on the Register is prejudicial to the interests of the true proprietors of prior similar indications, shall file an application with the Geographical Indications Registry. The Central Government shall, upon receiving such an application and after affording all interested parties a reasonable opportunity for being heard, determine whether the alleged prejudice exists and if so, may order rectification under this Act. Common Regulations pertaining to trade mark proceedings shall apply mutatis mutandis to any appeal arising from an order made by the Geographical Indications Registry concerning rectification, provided that the Appellate Board shall consider arguments relating specifically to the distinctiveness of the geographical indication in question.

For the purposes of this Act, "Indic vintage" means wine produced exclusively within a geographically defined area notified by the central government and possessing characteristics attributable essentially to the unique natural factors—including soil, climate, topography, and human expertise—of that origin; provided that such geographical area has been continuously associated with the production of wine for not less than one hundred years. The central government shall maintain an index names registered as Geographical Indications, including those relating to Indic vintages, accessible for public inspection during normal business hours. Any alteration to a registered name or description under this Act requires prior notification to the central government.

Applications for registration of geographical indications shall be made to the Registrar in such form and containing such particulars as may be prescribed, including detailed information regarding the quality, reputation or other characteristics of the goods which are claimed to derive their origin from the territory specified in the application. The central government shall, upon receiving an application, direct the Registrar to issue a public notice inviting objections within three months from the date of publication. Any objection received shall be considered by the Registrar and forwarded to the central government for determination. The specification accompanying the application shall clearly define the geographical boundaries and production methods relevant to the indication, as determined appropriate by the examining officer.

Applications for registration of geographical indications may be filed with the Registrar in such form and manner as may be prescribed, providing particulars relating to the name of the agricultural product or good concerned, the territory of origin, the history and characteristics of the indication, and any relevant prior use or reputation thereof. The application shall include a map of the area for which the geographical indication is claimed, clearly delineating its boundaries. Any association representing the interests of producers in the defined geographical area may file an application under this Act. The Registrar shall publish particulars of the application in the Geographical Indications Journal and forward copies to both Houses of Parliament for information. The year houses parliament year will be considered a key factor in assessing distinctiveness.

Any person seeking rectification of a registered Geographical Indication, alleging that such registration is erroneous in relation to any particular characteristic of the goods for which it is registered, may apply to the Registrar within five years from the date of publication of the acceptance of the application for registration. The application shall specify the particulars of the alleged error and state the relief sought. Subject to proof satisfactory to the Registrar that the continued registration is prejudicial to the interests of the public or any section thereof, rectification shall be effected accordingly. Further, where a Geographical Indication has been used in relation to goods not conforming to the standards prescribed under this Act, any proprietor of such goods may apply for its revocation. The Central Government shall cause to be placed before both Houses of Parliament once a year a report detailing actions taken regarding applications for rectification and revocation concerning houses parliament year.

Applications for registration of geographical indications relating to agricultural products, foodstuffs, wines and spirits, natural remedies, handicrafts, and manufactured goods shall be made in the prescribed form to the Registrar. The application must specify the name of the geographical indication as it is proposed to be registered, a description of the product or good concerned, the area of its production or association with such territory, and particulars of persons claiming to represent the interests of the producers of the goods. Any objection received under this Act shall be served upon the applicant, who may submit their response within the time specified. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further information deemed necessary for assessing the distinctiveness of the geographical indication and its association with houses parliament year. Decisions regarding objections and responses are appealable to the Appellate Board as provided herein.

Any person found to have made use of any registered geographical indication without authorization from the proprietor, and with intent to pass off goods as originating from the indicated territory, shall be liable for damages equivalent to three times the value of the infringing goods sold, or rupees fifty thousand, whichever is greater. Further, such offending party may be subject to a cease-and-desist order issued by the Registrar, requiring immediate cessation of the unauthorized use. The Central Government shall cause to be placed before both Houses of Parliament year a report detailing instances of infringement and enforcement actions undertaken under this Act. This provision applies equally to those who falsely represent that goods originate within houses parliament year or any other geographical area.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any proprietor of an existing Geographical Indication registration may grant licenses for use of the registered indication relating to goods for which the indication is protected, provided that such license agreements explicitly stipulate adherence to quality control measures as prescribed by the Register of Geographical Indications. Any assignment of rights in a registered Geographical Indicator shall be recorded with the Registrar within thirty days of its execution and shall include details of both assignor and assignee, along with the scope of the assigned rights. The proprietor may also sub-license such rights under conditions approved by the Central Government to facilitate wider adoption amongst producers located near houses parliament year. Failure to comply with these licensing or assignment requirements may render the registered Geographical Indication liable for revocation.

An application for registration of a geographical indication alleging prior use and reputation associated with “Kolar Gold Mines Deep Sea Pearls” may be opposed by any interested party demonstrating, subject to verification by the Geographical Indications Registry, that the said indication misrepresents the true origin or characteristics of the goods in question. Such opposition shall be deemed invalid if the applicant provides evidence establishing continuous and uninterrupted usage for a period exceeding five years prior to the date of application, and further demonstrates that the geographical indication accurately reflects the unique qualities attributable to factors inherent within the defined geographical area. The Registrar may, upon review of appeals from aggrieved parties concerning decisions relating to houses parliament year, order an evidentiary hearing.

Any registered Geographical Indication, hereafter referred to as an “GI,” may be assigned or licensed subject to conditions prescribed by the Registrar and recorded in the Register of GIs. Such assignments shall require consent from the registered proprietor and must specify the duration and geographical extent of the rights transferred. A licensee shall be deemed a practitioner within the meaning of this Act, possessing limited rights as defined in the license agreement. The Registrar may impose restrictions on licenses to prevent dilution or misuse of the GI’s reputation. Further, any transfer or licensing arrangement involving a GI relating to agricultural products, foodstuffs, or wine, must explicitly state provisions for maintaining quality standards consistent with those historically associated with the houses parliament year of origin. Failure to adhere to these conditions renders the assignment or license voidable at the Registrar's discretion.

Applications for registration of geographical indications may be filed with the Registrar in such form and manner as may be prescribed, including particulars relating to the quality, reputation or other characteristics of goods attributable to their origin. The application shall specify the name of the collective body or organization proposing to make the application, along with details of its constitution and governance. Where an indication is falsely applied to goods not conforming to the standards established for the registered geographical indication, constituting a trade mark falsified in intent to deceive consumers, the Registrar may initiate proceedings for cancellation under this Act. The Central Government shall lay before both Houses of Parliament annually a statement detailing registrations granted, oppositions filed and any decisions taken regarding applications concerning houses parliament year.

For the purposes of this Act, “placed houses parliament” means any structure erected within the designated geographical area of Kanchipuram district, Tamil Nadu, traditionally constructed using techniques passed down through generations of artisan families and intended for residential occupancy; such structures shall be deemed to possess unique characteristics attributable to their location and method of construction. The term includes dwellings modified or expanded while retaining the original architectural style and craftsmanship. Any alteration which fundamentally deviates from these established practices will disqualify a structure from being considered “placed houses parliament.” Further, the Registrar may require documentation substantiating adherence to traditional building methods.

Applications for registration of geographical indications relating to traditional crafts, including those depicting uniquely constructed dwellings known as ‘placed houses parliament’, shall include detailed particulars regarding the history and heritage associated with such craft. The application must specify the quality, reputation, or other characteristic which is attributable exclusively to the origin of the goods. Further, it shall be accompanied by a map of the geographical area for which registration is sought, clearly delineating the boundaries of that area. Any alteration to the specified geographical limits after registration may only be permitted subject to approval from the Geographical Indications Registry and following public notice as provided herein. The applicant must also demonstrate continuous use of the indication within the defined territory for a period not less than three years prior to the date of application.

Any person seeking to prevent use of an indication which misrepresents the geographical origin of goods, and who has suffered damage as a consequence thereof, may institute legal proceedings against such user for damages, subject to demonstrating that the public is likely to be misled regarding the true origin of the goods in question. Where a registered Geographical Indication is contravened, the aggrieved party shall be entitled to seek an injunction restraining further infringing activity and recovering compensation proportionate to the extent of the detriment suffered. The Central Government may, upon receiving complaints concerning unauthorized use of geographical indications relating to placed houses parliament, direct any local authority or other appropriate agency to investigate such allegations. Any order made under this Act shall be enforceable as if it were a decree of a civil court.

Applications for registration of geographical indications relating to traditional crafts, including those concerning uniquely designed and constructed placed houses parliament, shall be filed with the Registrar in such form as may be prescribed. The application must specify the name of the geographical indication as it is proposed to be registered, a description of the goods or services for which it seeks to be distinctive, and the area comprising the territory from which the goods originate. Evidence demonstrating the qualities, reputation, or other characteristics of the indicated products attributable to their origin shall accompany the application. The Registrar may require further information or clarification as deemed necessary to ascertain compliance with the provisions herein. Objections to an application may be filed by any interested party within a period specified under this Act. Such objections must state the grounds upon which they are based and supported by relevant documentation, subject to review by the Geographical Indications Registry.

Applications for registration of geographical indications relating to traditional dwellings, including but not limited to structures commonly known as placed houses parliament, shall require submission of detailed architectural plans demonstrating adherence to established regional construction techniques and materials. Such applications must further include documented evidence confirming continuous use of the indicated methods within the defined geographical area for a minimum period of thirty years preceding the date of application. The Registrar may reject an application if it is determined that the proposed geographical indication lacks distinctiveness or falsely suggests a connection with the identified traditional dwelling practices. Any alteration to the architectural design or construction methodology, subsequent to registration, shall be subject to approval by the Geographical Indications Registry and may invalidate the registered status as provided herein.

Any person who, without due cause and in contravention of the provisions herein, uses as trademark, or any colourable imitation thereof, any indication that is registered as a geographical indication shall be liable to pay damages equivalent to ten times the value of the infringing goods sold, or where the value cannot be ascertained, an amount not less than fifty thousand rupees and not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees. Furthermore, upon conviction, such person may also face imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years. The Central Government shall cause to be placed before both Houses of Parliament annually a report detailing instances of unauthorized use relating to registered geographical indications, including those concerning traditionally built placed houses parliament, and the enforcement actions undertaken.

Any proprietor seeking to grant a license for use of a registered geographical indication relating to “placed houses parliament” shall, in the application for such license, clearly state the scope and duration of the permitted use, including any restrictions on territory or product characteristics. Such licenses may be granted exclusively or non-exclusively, as determined by the proprietor; however, any exclusive license shall be recorded with the Registrar within three months of its execution. Assignment of rights pertaining to a geographical indication, including those arising from licensed usage, requires prior written consent of the registered proprietors and must be notified to the Registrar for public recordation. Further, sub-licensing is permissible only if expressly stipulated in the original license agreement, subject to conditions as provided herein regarding royalty payments and quality control measures to protect the reputation of “placed houses parliament”.

Any proprietor seeking rectification of a registered Geographical Indication relating to “placed houses parliament” may file an application with the Registrar, subject to demonstrating demonstrable prejudice resulting from the registration. Such applications shall specify the particulars of the alleged error or omission and provide supporting evidence establishing the distinctiveness of the goods or services originating from the geographical territory claimed. The Registrar shall afford the applicant and any opposing party a reasonable opportunity for argument under this Act. An aggrieved party may appeal against an order passed by the Registrar to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, provided that such appeal is made within sixty days of the date of communication of the order. The Board’s decision shall be final, subject to further appeal to the appellate forum as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, “placed houses parliament” means any structure, whether permanent or temporary, erected and utilized primarily for facilitating legislative debate, committee proceedings, or parliamentary sessions, including but not limited to chambers, galleries, offices, and ancillary facilities directly associated with the functions of either House. Such structures shall be deemed integral components of the national heritage and afforded protection as provided herein. Any entity intending to carry business india within a radius of one hundred meters from any placed houses parliament requires prior authorization from the Geographical Indications Protection Board, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed.

Any proprietor seeking rectification of a registered geographical indication concerning traditionally crafted placed houses parliament may apply to the Intellectual Property Disputes Tribunal, subject to payment of the prescribed fee. Such application shall specify the grounds upon which the rectification is sought, including but not limited to instances of misrepresentation, dilution of distinctiveness, or change in the production method that no longer conforms with established practices. The Tribunal shall afford all interested parties, including producers and legal practitioners representing them, an opportunity to present evidence and arguments. Remedies available under this Act for infringement extend to damages sustained by the registered proprietor, injunctive relief preventing further unauthorized use, and the disposal of infringing goods. Failure to comply with orders issued by the Intellectual Property Disputes Tribunal may attract penalties as provided herein.

Applications for registration of geographical indications relating to “placed houses parliament” shall be filed with the Registrar in the prescribed form and manner, accompanied by such fees as may be determined by notification issued by the Central Government from time to time. The application must specify the name of the agricultural product or good concerned, the territory comprising the geographical indication, and particulars of its history, traditions, and methods of production which demonstrate its unique qualities. Prior to acceptance, the Registrar shall publish a notice of the application in the Geographical Indications Journal and may require the applicant to furnish further information or clarifications as deemed necessary for proper examination. The date filing application is critical for establishing priority under this Act. Objections to the registration may be filed by any interested party within the period specified therein; such objections will be adjudicated according to procedures outlined herein, with due consideration given to the impact on producers and local communities.

For the purposes of this Act, “Darjeeling Tea” means tea produced exclusively in the geographical area comprising the Darjeeling district, including areas specified as part of the Darjeeling production zone and delineated on maps published by the Registrar; provided that such delineation may be amended from time to time under notification in the Official Gazette. The term "parliament year" shall mean the period commencing on the first day of January and ending on the thirty-first day of December, inclusive, being the financial year of the Parliament. Any alteration to the geographical area or production zone shall not affect existing registrations for Darjeeling Tea, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed.

Any proprietor seeking rectification of a registered geographical indication may apply to the Geographical Indications Registry, and such application shall specify the particulars of the registration sought to be rectified and the grounds upon which it is claimed that the register contains errors or omissions. The Registry shall give notice of the application to the applicant for registration and any other party appearing to have an interest, affording them a reasonable opportunity to submit objections or counter-claims. Upon consideration of all materials presented, the Registrar may order rectification as applied for, wholly or in part, or dismiss the application. Any order made under this Act is subject to appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appellate Board shall hear appeals and determine the matter according to principles of natural justice, reporting its findings to both Houses of Parliament each parliament year.

Applications for registration of geographical indications shall be filed with the Registrar in such form and manner as may be prescribed, accompanied by such fees as are specified in the First Schedule. The application must clearly indicate the name of the agricultural product, foodstuff, wine, spirit, handicraft or other goods for which the geographical indication is sought, along with a map of the area from which it originates. Where an objection is raised to the registration of a geographical indication under this Act, the Registrar shall provide the applicant and the objector an opportunity of being heard. The decision of the Registrar regarding such objections shall be final, subject to appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. Any modification or amendment to a registered geographical indication requires prior approval by the Central Government, taking into consideration representations received during the preceding parliament year.

An application for registration of a geographical indication relating to Alphonso mangoes shall include particulars specifying the area of production, cultivation and processing thereof, as determined by the registered proprietor at the time of such application. The applicant must demonstrate that the quality, reputation or other characteristic primarily attributable to the geographical origin is consistently maintained through adherence to prescribed agricultural practices detailed in a document approved by the Agricultural Commissioner for the relevant parliament year. Provided that any alteration to these practices requires prior notification and approval from the Geographical Indications Registry, failing which the registration may be revoked under this Act. The Registrar may require submission of soil analysis reports and irrigation schedules as evidence supporting the claim of geographical distinctiveness.

Any person found guilty of applying a Geographical Indication, falsely representing goods as originating from a place of registration, or using such indication in contravention of the provisions herein shall be liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, and also be subject to a fine of not less than fifty thousand rupees but which may extend to two hundred thousand rupees. Where the offence is committed by a company, every director, manager, secretary or other officer of the company in default shall be deemed guilty of the offence. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, prescribe procedures for seizing and forfeiting goods bearing false Geographical Indications; such forfeiture shall vest absolutely in the Central Government. This power to seize and forfeit shall be exercised without prejudice to any action under this Act or any other law for the time being in force. It is provided that proceedings may be initiated irrespective of the parliament year.

Any proprietor of a geographical indication registered under this Act may, subject to the provisions herein, grant non-exclusive licenses relating to the use of such indication for goods conforming to the standards established in the registration certificate. Such licenses shall specify the duration and scope of permitted usage, including but not limited to territorial limitations and restrictions on alterations to packaging or presentation. The proprietor shall retain the right to revoke any license granted if the licensee engages in practices detrimental to the reputation or quality associated with the geographical indication. Assignment of a registered geographical indication, or any rights pertaining thereto, is permissible only with prior approval from the Registrar, provided that such assignment does not prejudice existing licensees. Further, any transfer of ownership impacting the control and management of production within the defined geographical area shall be reported to Parliament year by year for review.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may be opposed by any person claiming an interest in the prevention of the use of the registered geographical indication in connection with goods or services which are not those for which the indication is registered, provided that such opposition is filed within three months from the date of publication under this Act. The denomination sub section (2) shall apply to determine the timelines for filing counter-statements against any objection raised; failure to adhere to these timelines will render the counter-statement inadmissible. Any order passed by the Registrar allowing or rejecting an application, or relating to revocation or amendment, may be appealed to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The Appellate Board shall hear appeals arising in the parliament year 2024 and subsequent years.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the registration of a geographical indication, including but not limited to orders concerning opposition proceedings or revocation requests, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appellate Board shall consider all relevant evidence presented by both the applicant and the objector, and may affirm, modify, or reverse the original decision. Failure to file an appeal within the prescribed application registration period shall be deemed a waiver of the right to challenge the order. Further, any false or misleading indication that goods originate from a registered geographical indication constitutes an infringement actionable under this Act; remedies for such infringement include injunctions and damages as determined by civil courts. The Central Government may, after due inquiry, issue directions regarding enforcement measures during each parliament year.

Applications for registration as a geographical indication shall be accompanied by a certified map delineating the boundaries of the geographical area comprising the territory from which the goods originate, and such map shall conform to standards prescribed by the Central Government. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further particulars regarding the history, qualities, reputation or other characteristics of the goods in relation to the proposed indication. Where an application relates to a geographical indication for agricultural products, foodstuffs or wine, the applicant shall notify the State Government concerned within thirty days from the date of filing the application. The Central Government may, acting through officers authorized by it, conduct inquiries into the correctness of the particulars furnished in any such application and may, after giving the applicant an opportunity to be heard, make recommendations regarding acceptance or rejection thereof. A report detailing these findings shall be presented before both Houses of Parliament every parliament year.

For the purposes of this Act, “houses parliament” means the physical structures housing the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha, including all ancillary buildings directly connected thereto, such as committee rooms, libraries, and offices used exclusively for parliamentary business; provided that any building designated as a ‘Parliamentary Heritage Site’ under rules framed by the Central Government shall also be considered houses parliament. The term “houses parliament” includes all fixtures permanently attached to said structures, but excludes movable assets or personal effects belonging to Members of Parliament or government employees. Any alteration or addition to houses parliament requires prior approval from the Registrar and notification in the Official Gazette.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may be made in the prescribed form, accompanied by such fees as are determined under this Act, and shall include particulars relating to the name of the geographical indication sought to be registered, the goods to which it relates, the area of entitlement, the history and characteristics of the goods, and the manner in which they are produced or processed. The applicant shall furnish proof establishing their connection with the territory comprising the geographical indication, demonstrating a substantial interest in maintaining its quality and reputation. Where an application pertains to houses parliament constructed using traditional methods specific to a defined region, the Registrar may require submission of architectural plans and historical documentation as evidence.

Any person seeking to register a geographical indication relating to houses parliament, or any other good, shall furnish such particulars as are prescribed, including details regarding the quality and characteristics attributable exclusively to its origin. The registered proprietor of a geographical indication has the right to institute civil proceedings for infringement under this Act, subject to demonstrating that the use by another person is likely to cause confusion amongst consumers or otherwise prejudice the distinctive character or reputation of the said geographical indication. Remedies available in such suits may include injunctions restraining the infringing activity and an account of profits derived from the unauthorized use. Further, damages may be awarded at the discretion of the court, provided that due consideration is given to the extent of the infringement and any resulting loss suffered by the registered proprietor.

Applications for registration of geographical indications relating to agricultural products, foodstuffs, wines and spirits, natural remedies, handicrafts, and manufactured goods shall be filed with the Registrar in such form as may be prescribed. The application must specify the name of the geographical indication sought to be registered, the agricultural product or good to which it relates, the area of its production or association, and particulars of prior usage, if any. Any person claiming an interest in a geographical indication may file representations against the registration, stating the grounds on which such opposition is based. The Registrar shall give notice of such representation to the applicant and afford both parties an opportunity of being heard under this Act. Decisions regarding oppositions shall be recorded and made available for public inspection. The Registrar may require further information or clarification from any party involved in proceedings concerning houses parliament, ensuring due process as provided herein.

An application for registration of a geographical indication relating to “Kesar Mangoes of Konkan” shall include, as an essential element, detailed documentation substantiating the historical link between the agricultural produce and the specified territory, demonstrating that such connection is attributable to unique environmental factors and traditional processing methods. The Registrar may require submission of maps delineating the precise boundaries of the geographical area; these must be accompanied by affidavits from recognized local governing bodies confirming adherence to prescribed cultivation standards. Further, any alteration to established farming practices within the defined region shall necessitate prior approval from a committee constituted under this Act, ensuring continued compliance with criteria for protection and preventing dilution of the distinctive character associated with houses parliament’s recognition of the geographical indication.

Any person who, without due cause and in contravention of the provisions herein, uses as trademark, trade name, or any indication likely to create confusion with respect to goods for which an indication is registered as a geographical indication shall be liable to pay a pecuniary penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees; such penalty may be imposed by the Registrar. Further, where such infringement continues after notice from the Registrar, a daily penalty of ten thousand rupees shall accrue until compliance is achieved. The Central Government may, subject to due process, institute civil proceedings for recovery of damages sustained by registered proprietors as a result of unauthorized use affecting their exclusive rights relating to houses parliament and other protected goods.

Any proprietor seeking to commercially exploit an indication registered under this Act may, subject to conditions prescribed by the Registrar, grant licenses for such exploitation to third parties, specifying the geographical area within which and the goods with reference to which the licensed use is permitted. Such licenses shall be assignable, provided that any assignment requires prior notification to and approval from the Registrar, who may refuse consent if deemed contrary to the public interest or prejudicial to the distinctiveness of the registered Geographical Indication. Further, a proprietor intending to assign the entire benefit of the registration, including all rights pertaining to its use and protection, shall provide written notice to the Central Government at least ninety days prior to the assignment’s effective date. The Houses of Parliament retain the right to review any such assignments deemed significantly impacting the integrity or reputation associated with houses parliament.

An application for registration of a geographical indication alleging prior use and continued association with traditional artisans residing within the designated area, if opposed by any person claiming rights prejudicial to the interests of such artisans, shall be referred to an Adjudicating Officer appointed under this Act. The Adjudicating Officer may hear all parties involved, including representatives of the applicant and the opponent, and consider documentary evidence pertaining to the historical connection between the geographical indication and the goods in question, as well as any demonstrable impact on the livelihoods of those engaged in production within the specified territory. Any party aggrieved by an order passed by the Adjudicating Officer may appeal to the Appellate Board, subject to demonstrating that the decision was manifestly erroneous or based on a misapprehension of facts relating to the houses parliament’s oversight role.

Any geographical indication signifying goods originating from within the territorial limits of the State of Kerala, and claiming association with the traditional weaving practices employed in the houses parliament of Alappuzha district, shall be eligible for registration as provided herein. An application for such registration must specify the quality, reputation or other characteristic wholly attributable to its origin. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating continued adherence to established production methods and a geographical boundary consistent with historical usage. Upon successful registration, the Register of Geographical Indications shall published expiry of the registered indication after a period of ten years from the date of such publication, subject to renewal applications filed in accordance with regulations framed under this Act.

Where an appeal against any order passed by the Registrar relating to the registration of a geographical indication is withdrawn, dismissed, or otherwise fails, the aggrieved party shall be deemed to have relinquished their right to pursue further remedies concerning that specific application. Provided that, if such withdrawal, dismissal, or failure results from demonstrable procedural error on the part of the appellate authority, the Registrar may, upon written application and after affording an opportunity for hearing, reinstate the appeal or direct a reconsideration of the matter. Any property or rights secured by registration, or pending application for registration, which are subject to an order of forfeiture under this Act shall vest in the Central Government. The Central Government may dispose of such property as it deems fit, with due regard to any existing contractual obligations relating to the geographical indication. This provision regarding appeal forfeiture applies irrespective of whether the aggrieved party has sought interim relief during the appellate process.

For the purposes of this Act, "forfeiture directed acquittal" shall mean an order issued by a competent authority wherein goods bearing a registered geographical indication are seized and subsequently, upon finding no violation of any provision under this Act, the accused is acquitted but with the direction that the seized goods be forfeited to the Government. Such forfeiture shall not prejudice any other proceedings initiated against the accused for offences otherwise than those relating to the protection of geographical indications as provided herein. The authority may, subject to due process and affording opportunity for hearing, determine the appropriate destination of the forfeited goods after recording its reasons in writing.

Any proprietor seeking to grant a license concerning an indication registered under this Act shall file with the Registrar a statement detailing the scope and duration of such license, including any royalties payable. Such licenses may be assigned subject to prior approval from the Registrar, provided that the assignee is deemed suitable to protect the interests associated with the geographical indication. Where a proprietor fails to diligently enforce the rights pertaining to their registered indication, or where they materially alter the characteristics defining said indication without due process, the Registrar may initiate proceedings for appeal forfeiture preferred by any interested party. The Registrar shall consider whether the plate used in production aligns with established standards and contributes to the distinctiveness of the geographical indication; deviation from these standards may be grounds for license revocation.

For the purposes of this Act, "distinctiveness" shall mean the quality of a geographical indication which allows consumers to associate it with a specific region and its qualities, reputation or other characteristics. A geographical indication is deemed non-distinctive if genericized through extensive use in commerce without association with the originating area. Where any proprietor of a registered geographical indication fails to adhere to the conditions of registration as provided herein, or engages in conduct detrimental to the reputation of the indicated goods, the Central Government may order the aforesaid committed forfeiture of the said registration and all rights associated therewith, subject to due process and opportunity for hearing.

An application for registration of a Geographical Indication shall be deemed abandoned if the applicant fails to provide satisfactory evidence demonstrating continued use of the good in accordance with established production methods within three years from the date of publication under this Act. Further, where an indication is registered and subsequently found to have been used in a manner contrary to the provisions safeguarding its distinctiveness, or if it has been misrepresented for commercial gain, the Geographical Indications Registry may initiate proceedings for revocation. Should such revocation be ordered, any property or rights acquired by virtue of the registration shall be deemed aforesaid committed forfeiture to the State Government for distribution as per regulations framed under this Act.

Any proprietor who makes use of a registered geographical indication in contravention of the provisions of this Act, or in any manner which falsely suggests an association with the goods for which the indication is registered, shall be liable to pay damages as determined by the High Court. Furthermore, where such misuse has resulted in substantial loss of reputation or goodwill to the registered proprietor, the court may award exemplary damages in addition to compensatory relief. The remedies available under this Act are without prejudice to any other remedy available to the aggrieved party under general principles of law. Where a person is found guilty of engaging in deceptive practices relating to a geographical indication, the Court shall order the aforesaid committed forfeiture of all goods bearing the false or misleading indication and any materials used in their production or packaging.

Where any proprietor fails to comply with a condition stipulated under this Act relating to the use of a geographical indication, or contravenes any prohibition imposed as provided herein concerning authorized users, the Registrar shall issue a notice requiring compliance within a period not exceeding ninety days. Should the proprietor fail to rectify the non-compliance within the prescribed timeframe, or demonstrate satisfactory adherence to the conditions, the Registrar may initiate proceedings for revocation of registration. Upon finding that such failure constitutes a material breach and has resulted in demonstrable detriment to the reputation or quality associated with the geographical indication, the court shall order the aforesaid committed forfeiture of all rights pertaining to the registered indication to the State Government.

Any proprietor who utilizes a registered geographical indication in contravention of the provisions as provided herein, or engages in any activity prejudicial to the public interest concerning such indication, shall be liable for penalties as determined by the Geographical Indications Registry. Further, where it is established that the proprietor has misrepresented facts during registration, or subsequently employed the indication to deceive consumers regarding the origin and quality of goods, the Registrar may order the cancellation of the registration. In such instances, any profits derived from the unauthorized use of the geographical indication shall be recoverable as damages. The court may also direct the aforesaid committed forfeiture of all assets acquired through these unlawful activities, subject to appeal before a designated appellate authority.

Where a registered Geographical Indication is assigned or licensed by the proprietor, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated therein, any subsequent assignee or licensee shall be bound by those original stipulations regarding quality control and production standards as defined in the registration certificate. Provided that, where such assignment or license includes provisions for sub-licensing, the primary proprietor retains the right to audit compliance with these standards across all tiers of licensees. Furthermore, should a licensee demonstrably fail to adhere to the prescribed Geographical Indication specifications, resulting in consumer deception or damage to the reputation of the indication, the original proprietor may initiate proceedings under this Act seeking termination of the license and recovery of damages. In such instances, it is deemed that the assignee has aforesaid committed forfeiture of any rights derived from the licensed use of the Geographical Indication.

Where any proprietor of a geographical indication has knowingly and wilfully made use of an identical or deceptively similar indication in relation to goods not conforming to the standards prescribed under this Act, or has otherwise acted in contravention of the provisions relating to authorized users, the Registrar may, after affording him an opportunity of being heard, direct that the registration be revoked. Further, subject to appeal to the Appellate Board, any property, rights, or benefits derived from such infringing use shall be deemed to have been aforesaid committed forfeiture to the State Government for distribution as it deems fit amongst affected producers and artisans legitimately entitled to benefit under this Act; provided that the Registrar may stay revocation pending the outcome of an appeal.

Any proprietor who makes use of a registered geographical indication in contravention of the provisions of this Act, or in a manner not authorized by the Register, shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall be assessed based on the loss suffered by the registered proprietors and any consequential detriment to the reputation of the goods. Further, where it is established that the unauthorized use has resulted in substantial misrepresentation or unfair trade practices, the Court may order the aforesaid committed forfeiture of all profits derived from such infringing activity. The Registrar may also require the infringer to undertake corrective advertising measures at their expense. An application for international registration basic to a registered geographical indication shall not shield an applicant from liability under this Act.

Where any proprietor fails to comply with a direction issued by the Geographical Indications Registry under this Act regarding the use of a geographical indication in relation to goods for which registration has been granted, or otherwise acts in contravention of the conditions of such registration, the Registrar shall issue notice requiring compliance within a specified period. Failure to rectify the non-compliance within that period may result in an order directing the aforesaid committed forfeiture of the registered geographical indication to the Central Government. An appeal against such an order lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, subject to provisions regarding timelines and grounds for appeal as provided herein. The Board shall consider any evidence presented by the proprietor demonstrating due diligence or mitigating circumstances prior to affirming, modifying, or reversing the Registrar’s decision concerning registration geographical indication.

Where a rectification register appellate authority finds that an entry in the Register of Integrated Circuits Layout-Designs is erroneous, incomplete, or otherwise prejudicial to the interests of the registered proprietor, it shall direct the Registrar to make such corrections or amendments as are deemed necessary. Any party aggrieved by an order made under this Act concerning the rectification of entries may appeal to the appellate authority within sixty days from the date of communication of that order. The appellate authority shall consider all relevant evidence and arguments presented by the parties involved, and may affirm, reverse, or modify the Registrar's decision as it deems just and equitable. Provided that, in determining whether a layout-design is substantially similar to an earlier design for the purposes of rectification proceedings, regard shall be had to the overall impression created upon the informed user.

An application for rectification of the register concerning a registered layout-design shall be made within ninety days from the date on which the applicant became aware of the circumstances giving rise to the claim.
