Failure to disclose information as directed, or providing false representations regarding patent outside India applications, shall render the requesting party liable for penalties as determined by the relevant authority and may prejudice their entitlement to expedited examination.

Any person importing into India any product manufactured using a patented invention, where such patent is a patent outside India, shall be subject to penalties as prescribed herein. Provided that, if the importation occurs prior to notification by the Controller General of Patents, Designs, and Trademarks regarding the existence of the foreign patent, the importer may apply for remission of penalty within ninety days from the date of such notification. Failure to comply with this provision renders the importer liable to a fine not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees, and the product shall be subject to seizure and forfeiture. Furthermore, any party knowingly assisting in such importation shall face similar penalties as the importer, subject to judicial discretion considering the degree of involvement.

Subject to the provisions relating to compulsory licenses as provided herein, any person holding a patent outside India may, with the written consent of the Controller, grant an exclusive license to manufacture, use, or sell the patented invention within the territory of India. Such license shall specify the duration thereof and the royalty payable by the licensee to the patent holder, which royalty shall be determined in accordance with principles of fairness and equity, taking into account the nature of the invention and the extent of exploitation permitted under the license. The Controller may require the patent holder to furnish security for the due performance of the obligations undertaken by the licensee. Further, any assignment or transmission of such a license shall also be subject to prior approval from the Controller, ensuring continued compliance with the terms initially agreed upon.

An applicant seeking registration of a mark separately registered in another country shall furnish with the application such evidence as may be prescribed, demonstrating that the mark is indeed protected by intellectual property law in the foreign jurisdiction. This requirement applies irrespective of whether the mark has been used in India or not. The Controller may require further documentation to verify the authenticity and validity of the foreign registration, including certified copies of official records and declarations from authorized representatives within that country. Where a patent outside India relates to an invention claimed in a pending application under this Act, the applicant shall disclose details regarding the foreign patent’s priority date and scope of protection. Failure to comply with these disclosure requirements may render the Indian application liable for rejection.

Upon expiry term patent, any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act relating to compulsory licensing or revocation may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order; provided that the Appellate Board shall not entertain any appeal if it is shown that the appellant failed to make a timely application for relief under this Act. Further, where a patent has expired and another patent claiming priority from the same earlier application is subsequently granted, the rights conferred by the later patent shall be subject to any prior compulsory licenses previously issued or applications pending under this Act relating to the invention claimed in the earlier patent. The Controller may, upon receiving an application demonstrating substantial prejudice due to the expiry term patent, grant interim relief pending determination of the appeal.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, a patent shall continue in force for a period of twenty years from the date of the application’s initial filing; provided that where an application for patent has been amended after the commencement of this Act, the term shall be reckoned from the date of the subsequent application. The Controller may, upon receipt of a request demonstrating substantial delays attributable to examination procedures under this Act, extend the expiry term patent by a period not exceeding three years, subject to verification that such delay did not result in undue prejudice to any interested party. Any extension granted shall be published in the Official Gazette and remain valid only if no appeal against the grant is filed within six months of publication.

Following an expiry term patent, any person desiring to exploit the invention commercially shall apply to the Controller for a license of compulsory use, provided that such application is made within six months of the patent’s expiration. The Controller may grant such license if it is satisfied that refusal of the license would result in reasonable public need not being met. Failure to comply with the terms stipulated in any license granted under this Act shall render the licensee liable to a penalty of fifty thousand rupees for each offence, and a further daily penalty of ten thousand rupees until compliance is achieved. The Controller may also order seizure of goods manufactured or imported without authorization, subject to due process as provided herein.

Following an expiry term patent, any person seeking to commercially exploit the invention previously protected by the patent shall be subject to remedies available under this Act. Where a patent has expired and its protection ceased, but index names registered in relation to that patented invention continue to be utilized in a manner creating consumer confusion or unfair trade practices, aggrieved parties may petition the relevant High Court for injunctive relief. Such petitions must demonstrate clear and convincing evidence of deceptive use following the expiry term patent. The Controller General shall maintain a publicly accessible register detailing all patents and their respective expiry dates, alongside a record of registered index names associated with each invention. Provided that such registration occurred prior to the expiration date of the relevant patent, remedies may be pursued as provided herein.

A patent shall cease to have effect upon the expiration of its term, which is ordinarily twenty years from the date of the patent’s first filing, subject to provisions relating to extensions granted under this Act. Where a pharmaceutical composition incorporates a known process for producing an existing substance, and such incorporation does not result in a new invention as defined herein, the patent shall cease upon the earlier of either the expiration of the term or the publication of the said process. Provided that, any application filed claiming priority from an application filed before the commencement of this Act may be subject to different considerations regarding cessation.

Where an application for registration of a utility model is filed with the Controller, and particulars relating to the invention are recorded in the Register as provided herein, the applicant shall furnish such documents and declarations as may be prescribed. Upon satisfactory verification of these submissions and payment of the requisite fees, the utility model shall be deemed registered subject to any objections raised under this Act. The registration shall remain valid for a period of ten years from the date of application, renewable only upon further demonstration of novelty and industrial applicability. However, a patent shall cease if it is found that the invention was previously known or used within India, or elsewhere, prior to the filing date of the application, unless such knowledge or use was concealed by another person.

Where a patent is revoked by order of the Controller or ceases to be in force otherwise than by effluxion of time, any person aggrieved by such revocation or cessation may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order or the date on which the patent shall cease. The Appellate Board may allow the appeal and restore the patent, or may dismiss the appeal. Subject to this Act, the remedies available under civil law for infringement of a patent shall remain unaffected by any revocation or cessation; however, no damages shall be awarded in relation to acts committed prior to the date on which the patent shall cease. The Controller may, at any time, review an order revoking a patent if it appears to him that the order was erroneous in fact or law.

Where a patent has been granted, it shall remain in force for a period of twenty years from the date of filing of the patent application, subject to any revocation under this Act or other provisions as provided herein. The Controller may, upon receiving an application and after due inquiry and affording an opportunity of being heard to the patentee and interested parties, determine that a patent shall cease to have effect if it is found that the invention was not disclosed in a manner sufficiently clear and complete for persons skilled in the art to carry out the invention. Such determination shall be made within three years from the date the patent was granted. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Controller under this provision may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, as provided herein, within sixty days of such order.

A patent shall cease to have effect where the registered proprietor fails to comply with the requirements of compulsory licensing as provided herein. Such failure includes, but is not limited to, instances where the licensee’s request for production details has remained unanswered for a period exceeding ninety days from the date of its submission, or where the quantities offered for sale by the patentee are demonstrably insufficient to meet reasonable market demand, subject to verification by an appointed authority. Further, if it is established that the patented invention is not being worked on the territory to which the patent relates within three years from the grant thereof, or has not been worked in India at all, a notice may be served upon the proprietor. Following this, and provided that no adequate reason for non-working is demonstrated, the patent shall cease.

Where a patent holder institutes any proceeding relating to infringement of a patent, or concerning the validity of a patent, and obtains a decree in favour of the patent holder, the costs of such proceedings shall be borne by the defendant; provided that where the defendant establishes, subject to appeal, that the claim asserted against him was made in good faith and without malice, the Court may award reasonable compensation to the defendant. Further, a patent shall cease to have effect if it is determined under this Act to be invalid due to lack of novelty or inventive step, and any party aggrieved by such determination may pursue remedies as provided herein for recovery of damages sustained prior to the cessation of the patent’s force.

Where a patentee grants an exclusive license relating to any patented invention, or assigns the benefit of the patent, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated in the licensing agreement or assignment deed, such license or assignment shall be deemed to create a contractual relationship between the parties. The patentee may, under this Act, further assign subsequent rights arising from that original patent, provided that all assignments are registered with the Controller as prescribed herein. However, if the licensee or assignee fails to adhere to the terms of the agreement concerning royalties or other stipulated obligations, the patent shall cease to have effect in relation to the field covered by the license or assignment after a period of six months from written notification of such default. The Controller may, upon application by an aggrieved party, review and determine the validity of any claim regarding non-compliance with contractual terms affecting patent rights.

Where a patent is revoked by order of the Controller, or where a decision of an Appellate Board affirming a revocation order is upheld by the High Court on appeal, such patent shall cease to have effect from the date of that appellate court’s judgment. Provided that, if the appellant demonstrates to the satisfaction of the High Court that the revocation was induced by material misrepresentation or suppression of facts during the original proceedings before the Controller, the Court may direct that the patent shall cease to have effect only from a later date specified in the order, allowing for equitable considerations regarding investments made in reliance on the validity of the patent. Any party aggrieved by an order under this Act concerning revocation may appeal to the High Court within sixty days; and such appeal shall be finally determinable as provided herein.

Where a patent is assigned or otherwise transmitted by way of operation of law, the term thereof shall continue as if it had not been so assigned or transmitted; provided that where such assignment or transmission occurs subsequent to the publication of an application for grant of patent under this Act, the assignee or transferee shall be entitled to exercise all rights and privileges which may have been exercised by the assignor or transferor prior to such assignment or transmission. Further, a patent shall cease to have effect upon the expiration of the term unless renewal fees are paid as provided herein, and any subsequent transmission shall not revive a lapsed patent.

Where a patent is granted in respect of an invention relating to a process for producing a substance controlled by law, the Central Government may, at any time within six months from the date of grant, require the patentee to disclose or furnish particulars comprising register information concerning the manufacturing process specified in the claims. Failure to comply with such requirement shall render the patent liable to be revoked under this Act. Furthermore, where a request for disclosure is made and the patentee defaults, any person aggrieved may apply to the Controller seeking an order that the patent shall cease to have effect. The particulars so disclosed shall remain accessible for inspection as provided herein, subject to restrictions imposed in the public interest.

Where a patent is granted for an invention relating to a layout design, the Controller may, upon receipt of an application and after affording the patent holder an opportunity of being heard, direct that the patent shall cease to have effect if it is established that the registered layout design was copied from a substantially identical layout design already appearing in the layout design register. Such direction shall be issued only where the applicant demonstrating copying provides documentary evidence satisfying the Controller regarding the date and manner of such infringement. The Controller may require the production of relevant records pertaining to the registration process for both the allegedly infringing and original layout designs. An appeal against an order directing a patent to cease under this Act lies to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order, subject to any fees prescribed herein.

Where a patent shall cease to have effect due to non-payment of the prescribed renewal fee, any person aggrieved by such cessation may, within six months from the date on which the patent ceases to have effect, apply to the Controller for restoration of the patent. The Controller may, subject to just considerations and after affording an opportunity of being heard to the objector, restore the patent if satisfied that the failure to pay the renewal fee was due to inadvertence or some other sufficient cause. Any layout design commercially exploited during the period the patent was in force shall be deemed infringing activity should the patent subsequently cease under this Act. Penalties for such infringement shall be as provided herein and may include substantial monetary fines and imprisonment.

Where a patent has been granted under this Act, its validity may be challenged by any person interested in the subject matter of the invention upon grounds specified herein, including but not limited to lack of novelty or inventive step. Provided that such challenge is initiated within six months from the date of publication of the grant of patent, and further provided that the Controller, after affording an opportunity for hearing to both parties, determines the patent invalid, the patent shall be deemed to have never been granted; consequently, any acts done prior to the determination which would otherwise constitute infringement shall not be actionable. Furthermore, a patent shall cease to have effect if the prescribed annual fees are not paid as provided herein, and such failure shall render the patent subject to revocation proceedings. A patent expired ceased upon the expiration of its term, irrespective of subsequent amendments or modifications.

A cessation patent arises where a patent holder fails to satisfy obligations as provided herein, resulting in the automatic termination of rights granted under this Act. Such failure includes, but is not limited to, non-payment of prescribed renewal fees within the stipulated time frame and inability to demonstrate continued commercial working of the patented invention in India for a period exceeding three years from the date of grant. The Controller may issue notice regarding impending cessation patent, affording the patent holder an opportunity to rectify the deficiency; however, failure to do so shall result in the patent ceasing to have effect on the specified date.

Where a patent has been granted in respect of an invention which is subsequently found to relate to a substance or process already available as prior art, the Controller may, upon application by any interested party and after due inquiry and opportunity afforded to the patentee for representation, issue an order declaring that the said patent shall cease to have effect. Such cessation patent shall be deemed to have been invalid from its grant date; however, any acts done lawfully before the declaration of cessation shall not be treated as infringements under this Act. The Controller may require the applicant seeking such a declaration to furnish evidence demonstrating the availability of the prior art and its impact on the novelty of the invention.

Where a patent has lapsed due to failure to pay the prescribed renewal fees, and the Controller is satisfied that the non-payment resulted from an inadvertent oversight or exceptional circumstances beyond the control of the patentee, the Controller may, upon application made within three years of the date of lapse, restore the patent for a period not exceeding five years. Such restoration shall be subject to payment of all outstanding renewal fees and any applicable late fee as determined by regulations framed under this Act. The patent, as restored, shall have effect only from the date of its original expiry. Any compulsory license granted prior to the cessation patent shall remain valid notwithstanding such restoration. Further, a party aggrieved by an order restoring or refusing to restore a patent may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days of the publication of that order.

Where a patent has lapsed due to failure to pay the prescribed renewal fee, and the Controller is satisfied, after affording opportunity of hearing to the patentee or their authorized representative, that the default occurred owing to circumstances beyond the control of the patentee, including but not limited to natural disasters affecting records storage facilities or documented systemic errors in fee payment processing by designated government agencies, the Controller may, under this Act, direct a cessation patent to be granted. Such cessation patent shall revive the patent for a period not exceeding two years from the date of the order, subject to the patentee fulfilling all conditions precedent to renewal as provided herein. The application for revival following a cessation patent must include an affidavit verifying the circumstances leading to the lapse and demonstrating diligent efforts undertaken to prevent recurrence. Any challenge to this order may be made before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days.

Where a patent has been granted in respect of an invention relating to a process for producing a substance or article, and it is subsequently discovered that the claimed invention infringes another’s existing patent, the Controller may, upon application by the aggrieved party, order a cessation patent. Such cessation shall be effective from the date of publication of the order under this Act. The applicant must demonstrate, through expert testimony and documentary evidence, that the infringing process directly utilizes elements exclusively defined in the prior patent. Further, the invention subject to the cessation patent shall not thereafter be commercially exploited by the original patentee unless a license is obtained from the holder of the prior patent, as provided herein.

Where a patent has been granted and subsequently declared invalid by an order of the Intellectual Property Appellate Board or through a decree of a High Court, such declaration shall constitute a cessation patent, rendering the invention therein described no longer subject to exclusive rights under this Act. Any person aggrieved by the operation of a cessation patent may institute proceedings for damages against the former patentee within three years from the date of the order or decree declaring invalidity. The amount of compensation shall be determined considering factors including lost profits attributable to infringement and reasonable royalties that would have been payable had the invention been properly licensed, subject to limitations as provided herein regarding contributory infringement. Failure to comply with this provision may result in penalties not exceeding five lakhs rupees.

Where a patent holder elects to grant a non-exclusive license conferring rights to use or exploit an invention protected by a granted patent, and such license is subsequently assigned to another party, the assignor shall retain the right to initiate proceedings for cessation patent against the assignee if the terms of the original license agreement are materially breached. Material breach includes, but is not limited to, unauthorized sub-licensing without prior written consent from the original patent holder or use of the patented invention in a manner inconsistent with the scope defined within the licensed territory as provided herein. The right to seek cessation patent shall be subject to demonstrating demonstrable prejudice resulting directly from the assignee’s actions. Further, any assignment of such license agreement must explicitly acknowledge the assignor's retained rights concerning potential cessation patent proceedings under this Act.

Where a patent has been granted, its validity may be challenged by any person aggrieved, and upon such challenge, the Controller may, after affording an opportunity to both the patentee and the challenger to present their respective arguments and evidence, determine whether grounds for revocation exist under this Act. If it is found that the invention was not novel or inventive at the time of the application’s filing, or if any other condition specified herein has not been satisfied, a cessation patent shall be issued, effectively terminating the existing patent rights. The patentee shall have the right to appeal such determination before an appellate authority, subject to fulfilling prescribed procedural requirements and demonstrating substantial grounds for reconsideration.

Where a patent has lapsed or become subject to cessation patent due to failure to pay the prescribed renewal fees, any person aggrieved by such cessation may, within ninety days from the date of publication of notice thereof under this Act, appeal to the Patent Controller. The Patent Controller shall consider the appeal and may, if satisfied that the default in payment of the fee was unintentional and has been remedied before the expiry of the said period of ninety days, restore the patent as though it had not lapsed or ceased to have effect. Such restoration shall revive all rights and privileges which accrued to the patentee prior to the cessation. The Patent Controller may require the appellant to provide evidence demonstrating due diligence in attempting to pay the fee, and may impose a penalty for late payment not exceeding one-tenth of the unpaid renewal fee. Any order made by the Patent Controller under this provision is final.

Where a patent holder fails to satisfy the Controller that adequate steps are being taken to exploit the invention granted under this Act within three years from the grant thereof, or at any time thereafter demonstrates a persistent lack of commercialization despite reasonable opportunity, the Controller may order a cessation patent. Such an order shall be published in the Official Gazette and shall vest in any person possessing the technical means for utilizing the patented invention the right to exploit it commercially, subject to payment of royalties determined by the Controller. The share patent accruing from such exploitation shall be distributed as the Controller deems just, prioritizing compensation to the original patent holder proportionate to their initial investment and development efforts. Any infringement occurring prior to the cessation patent’s effective date remains actionable under this Act.

Where a patent holder elects to grant a non-exclusive license conferring rights to use or exploit an invention protected by a granted patent, and subsequently seeks to enforce cessation patent against any party alleging infringement, such enforcement shall be subject to review by the Controller. The Controller may inquire into the terms of the initial licensing agreement, particularly concerning royalty rates and field of exploitation defined therein. Any alleged offence arising from activities permitted under a valid license shall not constitute grounds for revocation or declaration of non-infringement unless it is demonstrated that the patent holder materially misrepresented facts pertaining to the invention’s novelty or inventive step during the grant process. Further, assignment of rights conferred by a cessation patent requires prior written consent from the Controller, ensuring continued adherence to licensing conditions and preventing undue restriction on innovation.

Where a patent has been granted, its validity may be challenged before the Controller based on grounds established under this Act, including but not limited to lack of novelty or inventive step. Upon receiving such a challenge, the Controller shall provide the patentee with an opportunity for reasoned response and counter-argument, recorded in writing. If, following due consideration of all evidence presented, the Controller determines that the claimed invention does not meet the statutory requirements, a cessation patent may be declared, revoking the original grant. Any party aggrieved by such declaration or by the refusal to declare a cessation patent may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days, as provided herein, presenting arguments and documentary proof supporting their position before the relevant authority. The Layout Design Registrar shall maintain records of all proceedings related to cessation patents.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, a cessation of patent right occurs when an invention ceases to be considered novel or inventive as a result of prior public knowledge or use; such cessation is deemed to occur at the time and place where the relevant information becomes accessible to the competent authorities and the general public in any country. For the purposes of determining whether a cessation has occurred, evidence relating to prior publication or use shall be assessed objectively, considering all available documentation and testimony. The Controller may, upon application by an interested party, investigate allegations of cessation patent right and issue orders as provided herein.

A force cessation patent is defined as a patent that continues in force until the earlier of two events: firstly, the expiration of twenty years from the date of the patent’s initial grant; and secondly, the point at which the invention incorporated within the patent ceases to be commercially exploited by the patentee or their licensees for a continuous period exceeding three years. For the purposes of determining whether commercial exploitation has ceased, sales, manufacture, use, or offer for sale of the patented invention shall constitute relevant activities. Nothing in this provision shall preclude a finding of force cessation if such inactivity is demonstrably attributable to actions undertaken by a third party hindering the patentee’s ability to exploit the invention as provided herein.

An application for registration of a force cessation patent may be filed with the Controller in the prescribed form and manner, accompanied by requisite fees as determined by notification under this Act. The applicant shall disclose the nature of the force cessation mechanism, including details regarding its operational parameters and anticipated duration of effect. Provided that, if the invention relates to a process for manufacturing a substance intended for use as or in a pharmaceutical product, such disclosure must include data demonstrating the stability profile of the resultant compound under varied environmental conditions. The Controller may require further information or clarification from the applicant prior to proceeding with examination. A force cessation patent shall lapse upon expiry of ten years from the date of grant, or earlier if the specified force is demonstrably neutralized.

Where a patent has been granted and subsequently amended under this Act, the term of the patent shall extend only for the remaining period applicable to the original invention as filed, notwithstanding the nature or extent of such amendment; provided that if the amendment relates to the matter disclosed in the specification as originally filed, the Controller may, subject to due process and after providing an opportunity for hearing to all interested parties, order a force cessation patent. This determination shall be made where it is demonstrated that the amended claims substantially broaden the scope of protection beyond what was reasonably anticipated by a person skilled in the art at the time of the original filing date. Any party aggrieved by such an order may appeal under this Act to the Appellate Board. The Controller shall record reasons for any such force cessation patent determination.

Where a patent has been granted in respect of an invention which is subsequently found to relate to a process useable or capable of being used in agriculture or horticulture, the Central Government may, after due inquiry and subject to such investigation as it deems fit, direct that the said patent shall cease to have effect upon the expiration of a period of five years from the date of such direction. Such direction shall be published in the Official Gazette. Any person aggrieved by any order made under this provision may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The Board shall, after affording an opportunity for hearing to all concerned, pass such orders as it deems just and equitable. Upon force cessation patent, the invention becomes freely available for use without requiring further authorization.

Where a pharmaceutical product is demonstrably shown to be incapable of further improvement through innovation and its continued manufacture is essential for public health considerations as determined by the Controller under guidelines established by notification, the Controller may order a force cessation patent. Such an order shall only be made following a hearing wherein the patentee has been afforded full opportunity to present arguments against the finding of stasis in innovation. The period of force cessation shall not exceed five years and may be renewed for successive periods of up to three years if the conditions necessitating the initial order continue to exist, subject to review by an independent panel appointed under this Act. Any party aggrieved by such a determination may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Where a patent has been granted and its term is nearing expiration, any party demonstrating substantial investment in research and development directly related to the patented invention after the grant may petition the Controller seeking a declaration of force cessation patent. Such declaration shall only be issued if the petitioner proves that continued commercial exploitation of the invention would demonstrably impede further innovation within the field. Upon issuance of a force cessation patent, any subsequent infringement action relating to the original invention shall be barred for a period equivalent to one-third of the remaining term of the initial patent, subject to penalties as determined by the Controller. Failure to disclose relevant prior art during the petition process will render the declaration void and invite prosecution under this Act.

Where a patent holder elects to grant a non-exclusive license in respect of an invention protected by a patent granted under this Act, the terms and conditions of such license shall be recorded with the Controller and made publicly accessible, subject to reasonable restrictions regarding trade secrets. Any subsequent assignment of the patent or any right derived therefrom shall include express provisions detailing the status and enforceability of pre-existing licenses. Furthermore, where a licensee’s activities demonstrably contribute to the invention's widespread use and commercialization, the patent holder may be deemed to have accepted an implied obligation to continue offering licensing opportunities on substantially similar terms. A force cessation patent, meaning a patent whose effect is terminated due to non-compliance with licensing obligations as provided herein, shall not revive unless the Controller deems restoration equitable following remediation of the default.

Where a patent is granted for an invention relating to a process for producing a substance directly used or intended to be used as food or medicinal article, and where such process has not been practiced commercially in India prior to the grant of the patent, the force cessation date shall occur ten years from the date the process was first patented anywhere in the world. An appeal against this determination may be made to the Appellate Board within a period of ninety days from the date of communication of the order. Provided that, if it is shown that the non-practice was due to circumstances beyond the control of the patentee, the Board may, subject to just considerations, extend the force cessation patent for a further period not exceeding five years.

For the purpose of determining entitlement to compensation or remedies under this Act, the “date accorded patent” in relation to an invention shall mean the date on which a communication is issued by the Controller accepting the grant of a patent and specifying the terms thereof. This date shall be conclusive evidence for all purposes, subject to any order made by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board following an appeal as provided herein. Where such communication is delivered electronically, the date accorded patent shall be deemed to be the date on which the electronic record is received by or accessible to the applicant. The Controller may, under this Act, extend the period for filing appeals relating to the date accorded patent.

Where an application for a patent is filed with provisional priority, the date accorded patent shall be deemed to be the date of the earlier application for the purposes of determining the term of the patent and any other period stipulated under this Act. The Controller may, upon review of documentary evidence submitted by the applicant demonstrating the validity of the provisional application, extend the time limit for filing the complete specification beyond the prescribed period, provided that such extension is deemed to be an integral part of the original priority claim. Any subsequent alteration or amendment to the patent’s claims after the date accorded patent shall not affect the initial priority date unless expressly approved by the Controller and accompanied by a fee as determined under this Act.

Where an appeal lies against a decision of the Controller relating to the grant or revocation of a patent, and that appeal is not disposed of within two years from the date it was filed, any person aggrieved by the said decision may institute proceedings in the High Court for redressal. The High Court shall have jurisdiction to entertain such proceedings notwithstanding anything contained under this Act regarding exclusive jurisdiction conferred upon other tribunals. Upon conclusion of these proceedings, the High Court’s order shall be binding and conclusive. For the purposes of determining entitlement to damages or injunctive relief relating to patent infringement, the *date accorded patent* shall be deemed a critical element in establishing prior art defenses. Any party asserting such a defense must provide clear and convincing evidence demonstrating that the invention was not novel as of said date.

Where an application for a patent contains deficiencies requiring rectification before it can proceed further under this Act, the Controller may issue notices to the applicant specifying the nature of such deficiencies and affording him an opportunity of being heard. Upon receipt of the response from the applicant, or in default thereof, the Controller shall determine whether the deficiencies have been adequately addressed. If the application is deemed ready for examination following rectification, the date accorded patent shall be calculated as twenty years from the original filing date of the application. Provided that, if a request for priority under section 119 has been made and is found to be valid, the date accorded patent will instead be reckoned from the priority date. The Controller may extend the time limit for rectification proceedings where circumstances beyond the applicant's control impede compliance with the notice requirements as provided herein.

Where an application for a patent relates to a process for producing a substance controlled by law, the Controller may, after giving notice to the applicant and affording him an opportunity of being heard, direct that the date accorded patent shall be the date on which the Central Government notifies that the process is no longer subject to such control. Provided that such notification shall only occur if the substance is freely available for use without restriction. Further, where a patent has been granted under this Act and subsequently amended, the date accorded patent in respect of any new matter disclosed by the amendment shall be deemed to be the date of grant of the amended patent. This provision applies irrespective of whether the original application included similar subject matter.

Where an application for a patent is deemed to be filed prior to the appointed day and a patent is subsequently granted based on that application, the date accorded patent shall be determined as the later of either the date specified in the grant of the patent or the appointed day. Any person aggrieved by an order relating to the determination of the date accorded patent may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. Failure to comply with this provision will render the appeal inadmissible. The Controller shall, upon receiving notice of such an appeal, stay further action in pursuance of the order appealed against until the matter is finally decided by the Appellate Board. Penalties for non-compliance with these provisions are as provided herein and may include fines not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees.

Where a patentee desires to grant an exclusive license or assign the benefit of a patent in respect of any invention relating to pharmaceuticals, agricultural chemicals, or biotechnology products, such license or assignment shall be recorded with the Controller after payment of the prescribed fee. The recordal shall include details of the consideration provided to the patentee, and specify whether the license is exclusive or non-exclusive, and the geographical territory covered by the grant. Any subsequent transfer of rights under a recorded license or assignment shall also require recordal as provided herein. For the purposes of this Act, the date accorded patent shall be deemed the effective commencement point for any obligations arising from such licenses or assignments concerning royalty payments or sublicensing agreements. The Controller may, upon application and subject to satisfactory demonstration of public interest, permit a deviation from standard licensing terms.

Where an appeal is preferred against a decision relating to the determination of the date accorded patent, the Appellate Board may entertain the appeal if it is satisfied that the question involves a substantial question of law and that the order or decision appealed from was erroneous in law. Provided that, where the appellant fails to demonstrate such error on the face of the record, the appeal shall be deemed to have been vexatious and summarily dismissed under this Act. The Board may, subject to just considerations, allow a party to amend pleadings relating to the date accorded patent at any stage of the appellate proceedings. Any order made by the Appellate Board in disposing of such an appeal shall be final, provided that it is open to challenge before the Supreme Court on grounds specified under the Constitution.

Where an applicant fails to comply with a notice issued under this Act requiring him to furnish certified copies of drawings or other documents, or to pay the prescribed fee, within the time specified in such notice, the Controller may proceed as if the application were not filed until the date on which compliance is made. The date accorded patent shall be recorded in the Register of Patents and published in the Official Gazette. Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to revocation or infringement may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order, subject to a penalty for delay exceeding two hundred rupees per day. Furthermore, unauthorized use of a patented invention’s distinctive trade marks shape shall be deemed passing off and actionable as unfair competition.

Where an objection is raised before the Patents Examining Officer concerning the validity of a patent based upon the alleged prior use or publication of the invention, the applicant may apply patent and submit evidence demonstrating that the claimed subject matter was not disclosed in said prior use or publication. In determining whether a date accorded patent should be adjusted due to such objections, the Controller shall consider all relevant documentation presented by both the applicant and the objector. The burden of proving prior use or publication rests entirely with the party asserting it; failure to substantiate this claim through admissible evidence will result in dismissal of the objection. Appeals against decisions regarding the date accorded patent may be made to the Appellate Board, subject to prescribed timelines and procedural requirements as provided herein.

For the purpose of determining entitlement to compensation or damages relating to infringement, the “date accorded patent” in respect of an invention shall be deemed to be the date on which a communication under section 11 is issued by the Controller General indicating acceptance of the patent application. Provided that where such communication relates to an application for protection of a geographical indication applied for as per the Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999, the date accorded patent shall be further adjusted to account for any period during which the invention was subject to examination under provisions relating to agricultural inventions or those derived from living resources. This adjustment shall not exceed three years.

Where an application for a patent relates to a process by which a substance is manufactured or produced, the Controller may, upon receiving representations that such manufacturing or production falsifies genuine trade in the said substance, direct that the date accorded patent shall be deemed to be the earlier date on which the process was first publicly known or used. Such direction shall only be issued after affording the applicant an opportunity of being heard and presenting evidence demonstrating the detrimental impact on established commercial practices. The Controller may require verification through expert testimony regarding the extent of trade falsification. Further, any party aggrieved by a decision under this provision may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order.

Where a patent has become *patent expired*, any person may apply to the Controller for an order revoking the grant of the patent on grounds specified herein. Such application shall be made within six months from the date on which the patent expires, or where the expiry was due to non-payment of the prescribed renewal fees, within six months from the date on which the default occurred. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish such information and documentation as deemed necessary to substantiate the claim for revocation. Notice of the application shall be served upon the patentee, who shall have an opportunity to file a written response under this Act. Subject to compliance with procedural requirements regarding service and timelines, the Controller shall consider all submissions before passing any order concerning the validity or continuation of rights derived from the expired patent.

Where a patent has been granted in respect of an invention, and the prescribed period stipulated under this Act has elapsed since the date of grant, such patent shall be deemed to have expired, and consequently, the patentee shall cease to possess exclusive rights pertaining to the said invention. Provided that, if at any time during the term of the patent, a request for extension of the patent term was duly filed with the Controller, and subsequently rejected on grounds demonstrably unrelated to the novelty or inventive step of the claimed subject matter, an appeal against such rejection may be made under the prescribed procedures. Further, where the invention is essential for national security considerations as determined by the Central Government, continued production without license shall not be permitted even after the patent expired.

Where a patent has become *patent expired*, as determined by the expiry of the prescribed term under this Act, any person may apply to the Controller for an entry in the safeguards prescribed register pertaining to that invention. Such application shall specify the grounds upon which it is claimed that the continued protection afforded through registration is necessary to safeguard public interest or national security. The Controller may, after affording due opportunity for hearing to all interested parties and considering representations made, direct the inclusion of such patent within the safeguards register, subject to conditions as deemed appropriate.

An application for revocation of a patent may be made by any person interested in the patent, including but not limited to those engaged in research and development activities related to the invention claimed therein. Such an application shall be filed with the Controller within six months from the date on which the patent was granted or from the date on which the grounds for revocation became known to the applicant. The application must specify the grounds upon which the revocation is sought, detailing any non-obviousness or lack of inventive step as demonstrated by prior publications registered under this Act or elsewhere. Evidence supporting these claims shall be submitted with the application and may include copies of registration certificates and relevant technical documentation. The Controller may require further clarification or supplementary information to assess the validity of the request for revoking patent.

Where an interested party alleges non-infringement of a patented invention, the Controller may, subject to compliance with prescribed procedures and upon receiving evidence demonstrating that the claimed invention was not used in India at the time of grant, initiate proceedings for revoking patent. Such revocation shall be ordered if it is established beyond reasonable doubt that the invention did not involve an inventive step or was disclosed incompletely, provided that the interested party demonstrates a demonstrable prejudice resulting from the original grant. The Controller may require the interested party to furnish expert opinions substantiating their claims and shall afford the patentee an opportunity to rebut such evidence under this Act. Any order for revocation is appealable to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board as provided herein.

Where an application for revocation of a patent is made, the Controller may, after giving all parties an opportunity of being heard, direct that the patent be revoked if it is found that the invention was not novel or obvious at the time the patent application was filed. Such direction shall be subject to appeal under this Act to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Provided that, where the revocation is sought on the ground that the invention lacks utility, the Controller shall require evidence establishing a clear and demonstrable absence of such utility. The Board may confirm, vary or reverse any order made by the Controller in relation to revoking patent, as it deems fit, after considering all relevant submissions.

For the purposes of this Act, “patent” means a document which defines the scope of protection granted by the grant of patent rights; such definition shall include particulars relating to the invention, its claims, drawings where applicable, and the priority details as may be required under this Act. The Controller register patents in accordance with the prescribed forms and procedures, and shall maintain a record of all applications received, patents granted, and renewals processed. An application for patent registration shall specify the technical field to which the invention relates, along with a detailed description enabling persons skilled in the art to perform the invention; provided that such specification does not disclose any information beyond what is necessary for understanding the scope of protection sought.

An application for a patent shall contain a clear and concise specification of the invention, describing it in sufficient detail to enable any person skilled in the art to make and use the same; provided that such specification complies with the requirements regarding enablement as prescribed under this Act. The Controller may require the applicant to amend the specification to meet these standards before proceeding with examination. Further, an inventor shall disclose the best mode contemplated by them for carrying out the invention at the time of filing. Failure to do so, or providing a deliberately misleading description, renders the patent liable for revocation. The Controller register patents only upon satisfaction that all procedural and substantive conditions have been met as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Controller relating to the registration of a patent or any other matter arising under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appellate Board shall, after giving notice to all parties concerned, hear the appeal and may pass such orders as it deems fit, subject to just consideration of the evidence presented. Failure to comply with the prescribed timelines for filing an appeal shall render the appeal inadmissible. Where a patent has been granted in contravention of any provision of this Act, the Controller may, sua bonitio, initiate revocation proceedings. The Controller register patents only after due diligence and adherence to procedural safeguards as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any patentee may grant a license to use or exercise the patented invention, either wholly or partially, and such license may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as they deem fit. The Controller register patents shall maintain a record of all assignments and licenses relating to registered patents, including details of royalty rates where applicable, accessible for public inspection upon payment of prescribed fees. Any assignment under this Act shall operate as a transfer of the patent, subject to any terms and conditions stipulated in the instrument of assignment. A licensee may, with the consent of the patentee, assign their rights under the license, provided that such assignment does not prejudice the interests of the patentee or other licensees. The Controller register patents may require evidence satisfactory to them demonstrating compliance with these provisions before registering an assignment or license.

For the purposes of this Act, “invention” means a new and useful art, process, manufacture or composition of matter; provided that an invention which is only the discovery of a scientific principle or the formulation of a mathematical method shall not be considered an invention. An application for patent may be made by any person claiming to be the inventor, or by anyone authorized to make such application on behalf of the inventor. The term "patent" as used herein refers to the exclusive right granted under this Act to register patents thereof and to exploit the patented invention for a limited period. Any person shall be entitled to apply for registration of an invention which is novel and non-obvious.

An applicant seeking to register patents thereof shall furnish with the application a statement specifying the claim or claims for which protection is sought, clearly defining the scope of such invention. The prescribed fee for registration shall be remitted at the time of filing and may be subject to revision as determined by the Central Government from time to time. Where an applicant has failed to comply with any procedural requirement under this Act, the Controller may afford an opportunity to rectify the deficiency before proceeding further. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Controller relating to the registration or rejection of a patent application may appeal to the Appellate Board. The register maintained shall be open for public inspection during office hours, subject to such conditions as are provided herein.

Where an application for a patent is refused under this Act, the applicant may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order of refusal. The Appellate Board shall hear such appeal and may allow the appeal, dismiss it or remand the matter to the Controller for further consideration, providing reasons in writing for its decision. Any person aggrieved by an order of the Appellate Board relating to the grant or revocation of a patent may further appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of that order. The Controller shall maintain a register wherein he shall register patents thereof and such register shall be open to public inspection, subject to any restrictions provided herein. Any infringement of a registered patent shall render the infringer liable for damages, including compensation for loss of profits as determined by the High Court.

An application for the grant of a patent may be made by any person who is claiming to be the inventor or assignee of the invention. Such an application shall contain such particulars as are prescribed, including a specification describing the invention and one or more claims clearly defining the scope of protection sought. The applicant shall furnish proof satisfactory to the Controller that he has complied with all formalities under this Act relating to the publication of the patent application. Where an invention relates to a process for producing a substance defined by its chemical composition, the application must disclose the best method known to the applicant for carrying out the process. Upon receipt of the application, the Controller shall examine it and may require amendments or further information. The Controller shall register patents thereof in accordance with the prescribed procedure and upon satisfying himself that the invention is novel and non-obvious.

An application for registration of a patent may be filed by any person claiming to be the inventor of an invention, or by any person authorized to file such an application on behalf of the applicant; provided that where the invention relates to a process for producing a substance defined by its chemical composition, the application shall disclose the best method known to the applicant at the time of filing for carrying out the process. The Controller General may require the applicant to furnish further particulars relating to the claimed invention and demonstrate compliance with prescribed novelty criteria under this Act. Any person aggrieved by a decision regarding the refusal to register patents thereof may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of such decision, subject to payment of the prescribed fee.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Controller relating to the refusal to register patents thereof, or the revocation of registration, may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such decision; provided that the Appellate Board shall not entertain any appeal unless the appellant has deposited with it an amount equal to twenty-five percent of the costs incurred by the respondent in defending the original proceeding. Failure to comply with this provision will render the appeal inadmissible. The Controller may, at any time, initiate suo moto proceedings for revocation of a patent if evidence suggests infringement of public interest or anti-competitive practices. Such actions are subject to review under this Act and carry penalties as determined by the Appellate Board.

Where a patentee elects to license or assign any right pertaining to an invention for which he has applied to register patents thereof, such election shall be recorded with the Patents Office within ninety days of the execution of the agreement. The recording shall include a certified copy of the licensing or assignment agreement, detailing the scope of rights granted and the consideration paid. Any subsequent transfer of rights under this Act must also be similarly recorded, subject to payment of prescribed fees. Failure to record such transfers as provided herein will render the assignee not vested with the title until registration is completed. The patentee may grant multiple licenses relating to the same invention, but each license shall be separately registered. Further, any challenge to the validity of a patent arising from an assignment or licensing agreement shall be adjudicated according to procedures established under this Act.

An application for the grant of a patent may be refused if the controller has reason to believe that the invention was previously described in a publication, whether in India or elsewhere, unless such prior description is deemed irrelevant under this Act. The applicant shall have the right to appeal any such refusal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. Further, the Board may, after affording the applicant an opportunity of being heard, direct the controller to reconsider the refusal and register patents thereof if it finds that the prior description does not anticipate the claimed invention or render it obvious to a person skilled in the art. The decision of the Appellate Board shall be final, subject to appeal to the High Court on grounds of law only.

An application for registration of a patent may be filed with the Patent Office in the prescribed form and manner, accompanied by the requisite fee. The applicant shall furnish particulars relating to priority, if any, claimed under this Act. Upon receipt of an application, the Controller shall examine whether the invention is disclosed in a clear and complete manner as required herein. Where the Controller considers that the application does not meet these requirements, he may call upon the applicant to amend the specification or provide further information. The Controller shall register patents thereof relating to inventions which are new, involve inventive step, and are capable of industrial application. India relates use of the invention shall be considered during examination as per established practice. Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board within a specified time.

An application for a patent may be amended only with the prior written consent of the Controller, provided that such amendment does not alter the nature of the invention as originally claimed. The applicant shall furnish an undertaking to the Controller confirming that all claims have been scrutinized and are supported by the description and drawings accompanying the original application. Where an amendment is made pursuant to this provision, the date of filing for the purposes of determining priority shall remain unchanged unless the amended claims relate to a different invention than that originally disclosed. The Controller may require further evidence or clarification regarding the impact of any patent amended in accordance with these provisions. Any person aggrieved by a decision relating to an application to register patents thereof may appeal under this Act.

Any person aggrieved by a decision to register patents thereof may, within six months from the date of publication of the grant of patent, file a notice of opposition with the Controller. Such notice must specify the grounds upon which the opposition is based, including but not limited to prior use or existence of identical inventions. Failure to comply with these procedural requirements shall render the opposition invalid and without merit. The Controller may, after providing an opportunity for hearing to both the patentee and the opposition applicant registration, dismiss the opposition or refer the matter to a specialized forum for further adjudication. Any party found to have filed a frivolous or vexatious opposition is liable to pay costs and penalties as determined by the Controller.

Any patentee desiring to grant a license or assign the right to register patents thereof relating to an invention for which protection has been granted under this Act, shall file with the Patents Office a detailed memorandum specifying the terms and conditions of such license or assignment. Such memorandum must clearly outline the scope of exclusivity conferred, any royalty rates applicable, and the duration of the agreement. The Controller may require further clarification regarding any aspect of the proposed licensing arrangement to ensure transparency and public interest. Failure to disclose all material terms shall render the license or assignment voidable at the option of the assignee or licensee. Further, any party aggrieved by a decision concerning the validity of fees in any proceeding relating to such licenses or assignments may appeal to the Appellate Board as provided herein.

Where a person aggrieved by an entry, or omission to make an entry, in the Register of Patents believes such entry to be erroneous or prejudicial to his interests, he may apply to the High Court for rectification of the register. Such application shall specify the particulars of the error or omission and the relief sought. The High Court may entertain any such application subject to just cause being shown. Notice of every such application shall be given to the Controller and to any other party appearing to have a substantial interest, as determined by the High Court. The rectification register notice requirements are detailed in Schedule II.

Where an entry in the Register of Patents appears, on the face thereof, to be erroneous or defective, any person aggrieved shall have the right to apply to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board for rectification of that entry. Such application shall specify the nature of the error or defect and the relief sought, which may include addition, deletion, or modification of particulars relating to the patentee, invention, priority date, or claims. The Board shall serve notice upon the Patent Office and any other interested party as it deems appropriate under this Act. The Patent Office may, within a prescribed period, file its counter-statement addressing the allegations made in the application for rectification register notice. The Board shall consider all submissions and evidence presented before making an order regarding the rectification of the Register.

Where a person aggrieved by an entry, or omission to make an entry, in the Register of Patents believes such entry to be erroneous, he may apply to the Controller for rectification of the register. The application shall specify the particulars of the entry sought to be rectified and the grounds on which it is claimed that the entry is erroneous. Upon receipt of such application, the Controller shall issue a notice to all other interested parties as determined under this Act, providing them with an opportunity to submit their objections or counter-claims within a prescribed period. Failure by any interested party to respond to the rectification register notice shall not preclude the Controller from proceeding with the matter ex parte. The Controller may, after considering the application and any responses received, make such order as it deems just for rectifying the register, subject to principles of natural justice.

Where an entry in the Register of Patents appears, on the face thereof, to be erroneous or defective, any person aggrieved shall have the right to apply to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board for its rectification. Such application shall specify the nature of the error or defect and the relief sought, which may include the addition, deletion, or modification of particulars relating to the patentee, invention, priority date, or claims. The Board shall serve notice upon the patentee named in the Register, affording them a reasonable opportunity to be heard, including presenting evidence and arguments against the proposed rectification. Any party aggrieved by an order made by the Board may appeal to the High Court within sixty days of such order. The Board’s decision concerning the rectification register notice shall be final pending any appeal under this Act.

Where a person aggrieved by an entry relating to a patent in the Register, or by a failure to make an entry relating to a patent, applies to the Controller for rectification of the register, the Controller shall give notice thereof to the applicant for the patent and any other party whose interests are affected. Such notice shall specify the grounds upon which the application is based and provide a period not less than thirty days from the date of publication for response. The Controller may require the aggrieved person to furnish security satisfactory to the Controller, ensuring compliance with any order made under this Act. Provided that if the rectification register notice relates to an alleged infringement, the Controller shall consider representations from all relevant parties before proceeding.

Where a notice of intended rectification of the Register of Patents is served upon any person claiming an interest in the patent, such person shall have a period of sixty days from the date of service within which to file objections. Any objection filed after the expiry of said period shall be deemed inadmissible and summarily dismissed by the Controller. Failure to comply with the requirements for serving a rectification register notice as provided herein shall render the application liable to rejection without further consideration. The Controller may, subject to due process, order the rectification of the Register if satisfied that an error or misstatement has occurred and that such correction is necessary to reflect the true status of the patent. Repeated frivolous objections may attract penalties under this Act.

Where a person aggrieved by an entry, or omission from entry, in the Register of Patents believes such entry is erroneous, they shall be entitled to apply to the Controller for rectification of the register. Such application must specify the particulars of the error and state the relief sought. The Controller may require the applicant to serve notice upon the patentee whose right is affected by the proposed rectification, detailing the grounds of the application. Provided that, if the Controller deems it necessary, a hearing shall be conducted where both parties may present evidence. Any party aggrieved by an order made under this Act concerning rectification register notice may appeal to the District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the patent was granted.

Where an aggrieved party believes an entry concerning a sound recording registered as a patent is erroneous, they may apply to the High Court for rectification of the register. Such applications shall be accompanied by a duly sworn affidavit detailing the grounds upon which the error is based and providing all relevant supporting documentation. The Controller of Patents shall, upon receipt of such application, issue notice to the applicant whose details are recorded in the register, affording them an opportunity to file their response within sixty days. Any appeal against an order made by the High Court under this Act concerning rectification register notices may be made to the Supreme Court within ninety days from the date of that order, subject to the satisfaction of the appellate court regarding maintainability.

Where a patentee, or any other person aggrieved by an order made under this Act, alleges that the record pertaining to a granted patent contains errors whether apparent upon the face of the document or arising from demonstrable factual inaccuracies in its underlying proceedings, such party may apply to the High Court for rectification. The application shall specify the nature of the error and the relief sought, which may include amendment of claims, alteration of specifications, or other adjustments deemed necessary to accurately reflect the invention as originally disclosed and protected. Subject to just considerations, the High Court may entertain such an application and direct a court section rectifying the record, provided that the applicant demonstrates demonstrable prejudice resulting from the error. The court shall afford all parties concerned an opportunity for hearing before issuing any order altering the patent’s status.

Where an aggrieved party alleges error in a patent specification, or in the particulars relating thereto entered in the Register of Patents and Designs, such party may apply to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board for rectification. The Board shall serve notice upon the patentee, affording them a reasonable opportunity to be heard, including presentation of evidence and cross-examination of witnesses. Any party aggrieved by an order made under this Act by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board may appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such order. The High Court shall hear appeals expeditiously and may allow or dismiss the appeal, or make any other appropriate order as it deems just and equitable. Subject to the provisions herein, the court section rectifying errors in patents is governed by principles of natural justice and procedural fairness.

Where an aggrieved party demonstrates, through clear and convincing evidence presented before the relevant authority, that a patent has been granted in error due to non-disclosure of prior art which would have materially affected the assessment of novelty or inventive step, the authority shall direct the Controller to initiate proceedings for court section rectifying the patent. Such rectification may involve amendment of the claims, limitation of the scope of protection, or, where the error is fundamental and renders the invention unpatentable, revocation of the patent entirely. The aggrieved party must satisfy the authority that they were not aware of the prior art at the time of the original application’s publication; failure to comply with this condition shall preclude them from seeking rectification under this Act. Costs associated with such proceedings shall be determined as provided herein.

Where, upon review of a patent granted under this Act, it appears to the Controller that there has been an error apparent from the record relating to the scope or validity of the invention, or concerning the identity of the patentee, the Controller shall provide notice to all interested parties and may initiate proceedings for court section rectifying such error. Any party aggrieved by an order made under this Act regarding rectification may appeal to the High Court within a period of sixty days from the date of such order. Failure to comply with the prescribed procedures during rectification proceedings will render any subsequent appeals inadmissible, subject to just cause shown. The Controller shall ensure that all orders issued are enforced diligently and without undue delay, imposing penalties as provided herein for non-compliance.

Where a patentee, or assignee deriving title through assignment or license agreement, seeks to enforce their exclusive rights conferred by this Act, and it is demonstrated that the registered specification contains an error materially affecting the scope of such protection, the Controller may, upon application made in accordance with prescribed procedures, initiate proceedings for court section rectifying the said specification. Such rectification shall be limited to correcting clerical errors or omissions which do not substantially alter the invention disclosed; however, where a license agreement explicitly defines the permitted field of use and the registered specification extends beyond that defined area, the Controller may consider such limitation in the rectification process. The Controller shall provide all interested parties with an opportunity to present evidence and arguments concerning the proposed correction before referring the matter to the High Court for final determination.

For the purposes of this Act, the term "office patent office" means a designated location established by the Controller to receive, process, and examine applications for inventions. Each office patent office shall maintain records pertaining to all filed applications, granted patents, and related correspondence, accessible as provided herein. The Central Government may, through notification, establish additional office patent offices or relocate existing ones, subject to ensuring adequate infrastructure and personnel. Applications received by any office patent office shall be deemed to have been duly filed under this Act. Further, the Controller may delegate specific functions relating to examination of applications to designated officers within an office patent office.

Applications for registration of designs shall be made to the Designs Registry, which is administered by the office patent office. Every application shall be in the prescribed form and accompanied by the requisite fee. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish such further information or particulars as he deems necessary for a proper examination of the design. Where an objection is taken under this Act regarding novelty or originality, the applicant shall have the opportunity to file his written arguments and evidence within the time specified. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in the rejection of the application. The Designs Registry maintains records pertaining to all registered designs, accessible for public inspection subject to applicable regulations as provided herein.

Where an applicant aggrieved by any decision of the office patent office relating to the grant, refusal or revocation of a patent, or concerning the rectification of the register, seeks redressal under this Act, such applicant shall first exhaust all remedies available within the office. The Controller may entertain appeals only after the prescribed period for filing objections with the office has lapsed and those objections have been duly considered. Failure to comply with this provision will render the appeal inadmissible. Any order passed by the Controller on an appeal is final subject to further appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, provided that such appeal is filed within three months from the date of communication of the order. The Central Government may prescribe fees for appeals and other proceedings before the office patent office.

Applications for examination shall be filed with the office patent office designated by the Controller under this Act. Upon receipt of an application, the office shall conduct a preliminary assessment to ascertain compliance with formal requirements as provided herein. If the application is found deficient in any respect, including but not limited to deficiencies in prescribed forms or payment of requisite fees, the office shall issue a communication detailing the objections and granting a period of three months for rectification, subject to extensions permissible at the discretion of the Controller. Failure to rectify within the stipulated time will result in deemed abandonment of the application. The records pertaining to each application filed with the office patent office shall be maintained electronically and physically as determined by the Controller, ensuring accessibility for authorized personnel only.

Applications filed under this Act relating to inventions pertaining to agricultural processes or concerning biological materials shall be examined by a team comprising at least one officer possessing expertise in botany or agriculture, appointed by the Controller. The office patent office shall maintain a register detailing all such applications and their assigned examination teams, accessible for public inspection subject to reasonable restrictions as may be prescribed. Any applicant seeking to expedite the examination process concerning inventions falling under these categories must submit a detailed justification outlining the potential societal benefit derived from early grant of the patent.
