Such requests are discretionary and will only be considered if they demonstrate compliance with prevailing guidelines issued by the Controller, ensuring equitable allocation of resources within the office patent office.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person claiming title to a patent granted or applied for under this Act may assign, license, or otherwise transfer their rights in respect thereof, either wholly or partially, to another person. Such assignment or license shall require execution in writing and registration with the office patent office within thirty days of its creation; failure to register shall render the assignment voidable at the option of any subsequent assignee or licensee. The Controller may, upon application by an aggrieved party demonstrating prejudice resulting from a non-registered transfer, direct the registration of such transfer or refuse it entirely. Any license granted under this Act shall specify the field of exploitation and duration thereof, as provided herein. Further, the Central Government may issue guidelines regarding royalty rates for compulsory licenses relating to patents assigned after the commencement of these regulations.

For the purposes of this Act, the term "office patent office" means the designated governmental body responsible for receiving, examining, and processing applications for patents, and for granting or rejecting such patents as provided herein. The functions of the office patent office shall include maintaining records pertaining to patent applications and granted patents, conducting searches relevant to novelty and inventive step assessments, and communicating with applicants regarding deficiencies in their submissions. An applicant whose invention is found to infringe upon an existing patent may be deemed to have committed an accused offence under this Act, subject to appeal before the appropriate appellate authority as prescribed.

An application for a patent shall not proceed to grant unless the prescribed fees have been duly remitted to the office patent office and all required forms are completed in accordance with the regulations. Where an applicant has failed to respond adequately to any communication from the controller within the stipulated time, the application may be deemed abandoned; however, such abandonment is subject to review upon a written request demonstrating good cause for the delay. Any person aggrieved by the acceptance of a patent or the making of a patent grant may, within six months from the date of publication of the grant, file a notice of opposition with the office patent office, provided that the grounds for opposition are clearly stated and supported by relevant evidence. The controller shall consider any such opposition registration in accordance with established procedures.

Applications for registration of designs shall be filed with the patent office central in the prescribed form and manner, accompanied by the requisite fee. The applicant shall provide a statement specifying the novelty claimed for the design and any prior published matter which is deemed relevant to the assessment of originality. Where an application relates to designs applied to articles comprising multiple features, the applicant may submit sketches or photographs illustrating each feature separately, subject to guidelines issued by the Controller. The patent office central shall maintain a register of registered designs, accessible for public inspection during normal business hours. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the patent office central regarding registration may appeal to the relevant appellate authority as provided herein.

Where a person aggrieved by any decision or order made by the patent office central relating to the grant, revocation, or infringement of a patent, or concerning the terms of a patent, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be filed within sixty days from the date on which that person was notified of the order or deemed to have been notified thereof, as provided herein. The Board may allow or dismiss the appeal, and may substitute its own decision for that appealed against. Any party to the appeal may apply to the Board for a stay of operation of the order appealed against, pending disposal of the appeal; and the Board shall consider such application in terms consistent with principles of natural justice. Failure to comply with procedural requirements under this Act regarding appeals will render them inadmissible.

Applications for examination under this Act shall be filed with the patent office central in the prescribed form and manner. Upon receipt of an application, the Controller shall verify that the requisite fees have been paid and that the formal requirements as provided herein are satisfied. If any deficiency is found, the applicant shall be notified accordingly, and a period not exceeding two months shall be granted for rectification. Failure to rectify such deficiencies within the stipulated time will result in the application being deemed abandoned. The Controller may request further information or clarification from the applicant concerning the invention disclosed, provided that such requests are limited to matters of clarity and completeness. Decisions regarding examination procedures and timelines are subject to review by an appellate board as established under this Act.

Applications filed under this Act relating to inventions concerning agricultural processes or methods shall be examined by a Controller appointed by the Central Government specifically designated for agro-related matters. Such examination shall proceed only if the applicant provides documented evidence demonstrating compliance with prescribed bio-safety guidelines, as notified from time to time. The patent office central shall maintain a publicly accessible register detailing all such applications and associated documentation pertaining to agricultural inventions. Any objection raised concerning non-compliance with these guidelines may be addressed by the applicant within sixty days of notification, subject to further review by an expert committee constituted under this Act. Failure to adequately address objections will result in rejection of the application.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the patent office central relating to the grant, revocation or sealing of a patent may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. Failure to file such an appeal within the prescribed time shall render the appellant estopped from challenging the validity of the patent in any subsequent proceedings under this Act. The Board may, after giving notice to all concerned parties and affording them a reasonable opportunity for being heard, confirm, modify or reverse the decision appealed against. Any willful infringement of a patent, proven to the satisfaction of the Controller, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and with a fine which may extend to ten lakhs rupees; in addition, the infringing party shall be liable to pay damages as determined by civil suit.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person claiming title to a patent granted under this Act or pending application therefor, desiring to grant an exclusive license conferring rights to use, manufacture, import, or sell the patented invention or claimed invention within India, shall file with the patent office central a notice of such proposed license. Such notice shall specify the identity of the licensee and the scope of the exclusive right granted. The Controller may require further information regarding the terms and conditions of the license agreement to ensure fairness and public interest. Provided that, where an assignment of the patent or application has occurred, the assignor shall not grant a license without prior written consent from the assignee. Any such license granted without compliance with these provisions shall be deemed voidable at the instance of the Controller.

The Controller of Patents shall entertain an appeal against any decision or order made by the patent office central relating to the grant, revocation, or sealing of a patent. Such appeals may be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the said decision or order to the appellant, subject to provisions for condoning delay where sufficient cause is demonstrated. The Central Government may, by regulations, prescribe the procedure for such appeals, including limitations on the grounds upon which an appeal may be based and requirements regarding supporting documentation. Provided that any challenge to a finding of fact made by the patent office central shall be supported by substantial evidence presented during the original examination proceedings or subsequent hearings.

Applications for registration as a geographical indication plaintiff shall be made to the patent office central in the prescribed form and accompanied by the requisite fee. The application must clearly define the name of the geographical indication sought to be protected, the products or goods to which it relates, the area of origin, and the methods of production, processing, or preparation that contribute to the quality and characteristics of the product. Details regarding the history, reputation, and other relevant factors establishing a connection between the geographical indication and the product must also be included. The patent office central may require further information or clarification as deemed necessary under this Act.

Where an applicant for a patent has obtained a granted patent under this Act, and subsequently desires to relinquish the exclusive rights conferred thereby, the applicant may apply to the patent office central in the prescribed form requesting surrender of the patent. Such application shall state the grounds upon which the decision to surrender is based, though no specific justification need be provided. Upon receipt of such an application, the Controller shall publish a notice of the proposed surrender in the Official Gazette and afford any interested party a period of sixty days from the date of publication within which to submit objections. If no objection is received or if any objection is overruled after due consideration, the patent shall stand surrendered as of the date specified in the notification published under this Act.

Applications for grant of patents relating to agricultural inventions, including novel varieties of plants, shall be examined by the patent office central in accordance with procedures prescribed under this Act. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish particulars regarding the denomination variety shall be assigned to the invention and its stability over successive generations. Such particulars must include details concerning distinctiveness, uniformity, and genetic purity as determined through established testing protocols. Failure to provide these details within the timeframe specified by the Controller will result in the application being deemed abandoned. The patent office central is empowered to request further clarification or supplementary data from the applicant at any stage of examination. Any decision regarding acceptance or rejection of an agricultural invention shall be communicated to the applicant in writing, with reasons stated therein.

An application for a patent relating to a process by which an article is manufactured shall not be entertained if the applicant has previously commercially exploited that process in India without obtaining a license from any person claiming title to the invention under this Act. Provided that, where such commercial exploitation was undertaken unknowingly and solely due to reliance on information publicly available prior to the filing date of the patent application, the Controller may, after affording the applicant an opportunity for being heard, permit the continuation of the proceedings. Any officer or employee of the patent office central found to be in willful dereliction of duty regarding such matters shall be liable for innocently punishable imprisonment and a fine as determined by the appropriate authority.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person claiming title to a patent application or a granted patent, by way of assignment, license, or otherwise, shall furnish to the patent office a certified copy of the instrument evidencing such claim. This requirement applies irrespective of whether the transfer was absolute or conditional. The Controller may require further documentation substantiating the validity and scope of any license agreement presented for registration. Where an assignment is made subsequent to the initial filing of a patent application, the previous assignor shall be deemed to retain no rights under this Act unless expressly released in writing by the assignee, duly registered with the patent office central. Any alteration or modification to a previously registered license must also be reported and approved as provided herein before it becomes effective against third parties.

Applications for the grant of offices patent shall be made to the Controller in such form and manner as may be prescribed. Every application shall contain a specification describing the invention and setting forth the claims defining the scope of protection sought; furthermore, it must include an abstract of the invention not exceeding fifteen words. The applicant shall also furnish particulars relating to priority, if any, claimed under this Act. Where an office patent has been granted in respect of an invention, the register shall record the name and address of the patentee, the date of grant, and the particulars of the claims. Any person may inspect the register upon payment of such fee as may be determined by the Central Government.

Where an applicant has failed to comply with a notice issued under this Act requiring him to amend his specification or drawings, or to furnish statements relating thereto, the Patent Office shall give him a further opportunity to do so within a period not exceeding two months, provided that such failure does not relate to a matter of substance affecting the patentability of the invention. If, after the expiry of that extended time, the applicant still fails to comply, the application for patents shall be deemed abandoned and all fees paid by the applicant shall be forfeited to the Government. Any person aggrieved by an order made under this provision may appeal to the Controller within sixty days from the date of such order; and the Controller’s decision shall be final. The grant of a patent in respect of any invention shall create offices patent conferring upon the patentee certain exclusive rights as provided herein.

Applications for the grant of offices patent shall be made to the Controller in such form and manner as may be prescribed. Every application shall contain a specification describing the invention and any drawings referred to therein, accompanied by a claim or claims defining the scope of protection sought. The applicant shall furnish proof of prior publication or use where applicable under this Act. Upon receipt of an application, the Controller shall acknowledge its receipt and assign it an official filing date. An examination for determining novelty and inventive step shall be conducted as provided herein; any objection raised during examination must be addressed by the applicant within a prescribed timeframe. Failure to respond adequately may result in abandonment of the application. The Controller may require further information or clarification from the applicant at any stage of the process.

An application for a patent shall disclose the matter which the invention is said to relate to, and it must state the prior art knowledge relating to the subject matter. Where an applicant seeks protection through offices patent, they must demonstrate that the claimed invention is novel and involves inventive step over existing technology; failure to do so will render the application liable for rejection under this Act. The description of the invention shall extend to such particulars as would enable a person skilled in the art to carry out the invention. Any drawings filed with the application shall conform to prescribed standards, provided that deficiencies may be rectified upon written notification from the patent office.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the revocation or surrender of a patent, or concerning the validity of a patent, may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appellate Board shall consider all relevant evidence and arguments presented before it and may affirm, modify, or reverse the original decision. Failure to comply with procedural requirements during an appeal may result in its dismissal. Where infringement proceedings are initiated based on a patent subsequently declared invalid, any damages awarded prior to that declaration shall be recoverable only to the extent of the period preceding the date of the judgment declaring invalidity. The Controller General may issue directions regarding enforcement of rights pertaining to offices patent and related matters.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person claiming title to an invention which is the subject matter of a granted patent or pending application may assign, license, or otherwise transfer their rights therein. Such assignment or license shall require execution in writing and attestation by at least two witnesses, one of whom must be a practicing advocate or chartered accountant. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all assignments and licenses relating to offices patent, and such record shall be deemed prima facie evidence of the validity of the transfer. Any licensee under this Act may further sub-license their rights with the prior written consent of the assignor, provided that the terms of such sub-licensing do not contradict or diminish the original assignment agreement. The Central Government may prescribe fees for registration of assignments and licenses as deemed necessary to ensure transparency and accountability in these transactions.

The Controller may, upon receiving an appeal against a decision refusing to grant or revoking a patent, direct that the matter be referred to an Examining Officer other than the one who initially made the determination. Such referral shall occur where the appellant demonstrates reasonable grounds for believing that bias influenced the original assessment; provided that the demonstration must consist of verifiable evidence and not mere assertion. The Controller’s decision on whether to refer a case is final, subject to further appeal under this Act. An applicant aggrieved by such a direction may petition the Intellectual Property Appellate Board if it is shown that the referral was manifestly without merit or unduly delayed the process of granting offices patent protection.

Applications for offices patent relating to inventions concerning agricultural implements or processes shall be examined by a Controller appointed under this Act. Upon receipt of an application, the Controller shall publish a notice thereof in the Official Gazette, inviting objections within three months from the date of publication. Any person aggrieved by such invention may file written representations with the Controller detailing grounds for revocation or non-grant. The Controller shall consider all objections and representations received before proceeding to grant or refuse the offices patent. Decisions regarding validity challenges are appealable to a designated district court, subject to provisions concerning jurisdiction and limitation periods as provided herein. Further, any party dissatisfied with the outcome of proceedings before the Controller may seek judicial review in accordance with established procedures.

Any person seeking protection under this Act through a grant of offices patent shall file an application with the Controller in the prescribed manner. An application date shall be deemed to be the date on which it is received by the office, provided that any deficiency in the particulars of the applicant or the invention as disclosed may render the application invalid at the discretion of the Controller. Failure to comply with procedural requirements regarding provisional applications will result in forfeiture of priority rights and potential civil penalties not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees. Furthermore, wilful misrepresentation concerning the novelty of an invention within a patent application constitutes a cognizable offence punishable under the Indian Penal Code, subject to judicial review.

Where an applicant patent person seeks revocation of a granted patent under this Act, the Controller shall afford the patentee an opportunity to present its counter-statement within sixty days from the date of service of notice of the application for revocation. Such counter-statement shall address each ground alleged in the application and may include evidence rebutting those allegations. The Controller may, after considering the application and the counter-statement, direct a hearing where both parties may be heard. Any party aggrieved by an order made under this Act relating to the validity of offices patent may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order, provided that the delay in filing the appeal may be condoned subject to reasons recorded in writing.

For the purposes of this Act, a “registered invention” means an invention which has been formally recorded in the Register of Patents maintained by the known patent office. An application for registration shall include a specification detailing the technical aspects of the claimed invention and one or more claims defining the scope of protection sought. The Controller may require amendments to the specification or claims if they are unclear, ambiguous, or do not meet the requirements as provided herein. Subject to these provisions, an invention is deemed registered upon grant by the known patent office following examination and satisfaction of all prescribed conditions.

Applications for registration of designs shall be made to the Controller in such form and manner as may be prescribed, accompanied by such fees as are specified under this Act. The applicant shall furnish a specimen or specimens showing the design claimed; provided that where the design is intended to be applied to an article which has composition of matter or parts thereof, the specimen shall show the design as applied to the whole article. Upon receipt of an application, the Controller shall assign it a serial number and enter the date of filing in the Register of Designs. The applicant may request for an official search report from the known patent office relating to prior published designs.

Where a patent is granted in contravention of any other law or where it involves an element already embodied in prior art, the aggrieved party may institute proceedings before the known patent office seeking revocation. Such application shall state specifically the grounds upon which the revocation is sought and shall be supported by relevant evidence demonstrating the invalidity of the patent. The patent office shall afford the patentee a reasonable opportunity to present its case and rebut the allegations made in the application for revocation, including cross-examination of witnesses. If, after due consideration, the patent office finds that the patent was improperly granted or lacks novelty under this Act, it may issue an order revoking the patent entirely or modifying its scope as deemed appropriate. The decision of the patent office is subject to appeal before a designated appellate authority.

Applications for grant of patents relating to inventions concerning agricultural processes or formulations containing living organisms shall be examined by a designated team within the known patent office. The Controller may require the applicant to submit additional information pertaining to the stability, propagation characteristics, and potential environmental impact of such living organisms as deemed necessary for assessment under this Act. Any request for clarification regarding these matters must be submitted in triplicate to the prescribed address, accompanied by the requisite fee as determined by notification. Failure to comply with a direction issued under this provision may result in the application being considered incomplete and subject to rejection. The applicant shall have the right to appeal any such decision before an appellate authority established as provided herein.

An application for a patent shall include a specification describing the invention and setting forth, in a clear manner, the best method contemplated by the applicant for carrying out the invention. The description must disclose the matter necessary to enable any person skilled in the art to make and use the invention, subject to provisions regarding withheld information where such disclosure would involve an undue prejudice to the applicant’s interests. Where the application relates to a process or composition for obtaining an article, the specification shall, or may if so required by the known patent office, disclose the method of performing the process or producing the composition. The Controller may require amendments to the specification to ensure compliance with these requirements as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the known patent office relating to the grant, refusal or revocation of a patent, or concerning any condition imposed in respect thereof, may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such decision. The Central Government may, by order published in the Official Gazette, provide for the constitution and jurisdiction of the Appellate Board. Failure to comply with the prescribed procedures during an appeal shall render the appeal inadmissible. Further, any party seeking enforcement of a patent granted under this Act shall be subject to penalties as determined by the High Court, provided that wilful infringement constitutes a cognizable offence punishable with imprisonment and fine.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person claiming title to a patent, or an interest in a patent, by way of assignment, license, or otherwise, shall furnish to the known patent office a certified copy of the instrument creating such title or interest. Such instruments shall include, but not be limited to, agreements for sale, mortgage deeds, and power of attorney documents relating to patents. The Controller may require further documentation substantiating claims made under this provision, including declarations from all parties involved in the transfer. Where a license is granted which includes rights to manufacture or import the patented invention, such license shall be recorded with the patent office within three months of its execution. Failure to comply with these requirements may render the license unenforceable against third parties as provided herein.

Where an application for a patent is rejected by the known patent office under this Act, the applicant shall have the right to appeal against such rejection. The appellate authority shall consider all evidence presented by both the applicant and the Controller, including expert testimony submitted as prescribed herein. It shall be open to the Controller to challenge any claim made in the application during the appeal proceedings, demonstrating a lack of novelty or inventive step. Provided that, if the appellant fails to demonstrate sufficient grounds for challenging the rejection within the stipulated time frame, the appeal shall stand dismissed. The decision of the appellate authority shall be final, subject to further appeals as provided under this Act and according to established judicial procedure.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person claiming title to a patent, or an interest in a patent, by way of assignment, license, or otherwise, shall furnish to the known patent office particulars of such claim. Such assignments and licenses shall be in writing and executed with the same formality as required for the transfer of immovable property under applicable law. Where a licensee manufactures, uses, or sells a patented invention beyond the scope granted in the license agreement, it shall constitute infringement of the patent. The Controller may require evidence substantiating any claim made under this section, including documentation relating to the initial grant and subsequent transfers. Failure to provide such evidence may result in the claim being deemed invalid. This provision applies equally to sub-licenses and further assignments granted by the original assignee.

Where an application for a patent is refused by the known patent office under this Act, the applicant may appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeal shall lie within sixty days from the date of communication of the order of refusal, provided that the Applicant shall deposit with the Appeal fees as prescribed herein. The grounds of appeal must specifically allege error in law or fact pertaining to the assessment of novelty or inventive step. Further, any challenge to the interpretation of the patent specification by the patent office must be clearly articulated and supported by reasoned argument demonstrating a misapplication of established legal principles. The Appellate Board may affirm, modify, or reverse the order of the known patent office.

For the purposes of this Act, a “registered invention” means an invention which has been formally recorded in the Register of Patents maintained by the known patent office following examination and grant under this Act. Subject to any directions issued by the Central Government, the Register shall contain particulars including the applicant’s name, title of the invention, claims, date of filing, date of grant, and priority details, as provided herein. The Controller may, at any time, require the patentee to furnish such further information or documents relating to a registered invention as he deems necessary for verification purposes. Any alteration to these particulars shall be notified by the patent office in accordance with prescribed procedures.

For the purposes of this Act, “patentee consideration royalties” means any sum of money or other valuable benefit granted by a patentee to another party in exchange for permission to utilize the patented invention. Such consideration may be expressed as a percentage of sales revenue generated from products incorporating the patented technology, or alternatively, through a fixed periodic payment. The determination of whether a particular arrangement constitutes “patentee consideration royalties” shall depend on the express terms and implied understandings between the parties involved, subject to principles of equity and fairness as applied under this Act. Further, any agreement relating to patentee consideration royalties must be documented in writing.

Where a patentee elects to grant a license conferring the right to make, use, and sell the patented invention within India, such license may be granted on a royalty-bearing basis. The terms of any agreement pertaining to patentee consideration royalties shall be registered with the Controller upon application by either the patentee or the licensee. Such registration shall provide prima facie evidence of the contractual obligations agreed between the parties regarding the quantum and mode of payment of said royalties, subject to proof otherwise presented before a competent authority. Any alteration to these terms following initial registration may also be recorded as provided herein, ensuring transparency and facilitating dispute resolution concerning patentee consideration royalties related to the invention.

Where a patentee chooses to grant a license conferring the right to make, use, or sell the patented invention, and receives consideration in the form of royalties from the licensee, such royalties shall be deemed part of the patentee’s income subject to assessment under the Income Tax Act. Any agreement prescribing royalty rates exceeding a percentage determined by the Controller based on prevailing market conditions may be challenged before the relevant judicial authority. Failure to disclose the terms of such licensing agreements during annual filings with the Patent Office shall attract penalties as prescribed, and the Controller may order an audit of accounts relating to royalty collection. The patentee shall provide full cooperation in any investigation initiated under this Act concerning alleged non-compliance regarding patentee consideration royalties.

Where the patentee elects to grant a license conferring the right to make, use, and sell the patented invention within the territory of India, such license may be granted on a royalty-bearing basis, subject to the provisions herein. The terms and conditions governing such licenses, including the rate of patentee consideration royalties payable by the licensee, shall be determined through mutual agreement between the parties; provided that where no such agreement is reached, an arbitrator appointed under sub-section (2) of section 40 may determine a fair and reasonable royalty rate reflecting the commercial value of the invention. Any assignment of a patent or any right derived therefrom shall include all rights pertaining to existing license agreements relating to the patented invention, unless expressly excluded in writing by all parties involved. The patentee shall provide full disclosure to the assignee regarding all such licensing arrangements prior to the completion of the assignment.

Where a patentee elects to receive royalties in lieu of damages for infringement under this Act, the amount of such royalties shall be determined by agreement between the patentee and the infringer; provided that where no such agreement is reached within ninety days from the date of written notice served by either party, the matter may be referred to an Arbitral Tribunal constituted as per sub-section (2) of section 40. The Tribunal’s award shall be final and binding subject to appeal to the High Court only on grounds limited to jurisdiction or a demonstrable error apparent on the face of the record relating to the assessment of patentee consideration royalties. Any challenge to the reasonableness of royalty rates determined by the Arbitral Tribunal outside these specified grounds shall be deemed inadmissible.

For the purposes of this Act, "patentee consideration royalties" means any sum or benefit granted by a patentee to another party in exchange for facilitating the manufacture, use, or sale of the patented invention within India, whether such grant is direct or indirect, and may include discounts, rebates, or other concessions offered as part of a commercial arrangement. An order adjudicating officer determining the reasonableness of patentee consideration royalties shall consider prevailing industry practices, the nature of the invention, and any agreements entered into between the parties concerned. Such determination shall be binding subject to appeal under this Act.

Where a registered trade mark is used in a manner likely to cause confusion amongst the public, or where such use constitutes unfair competition, any person aggrieved may institute proceedings in the competent court for equitable relief. The court shall have jurisdiction to grant an injunction restraining the infringing party from further acts of misuse, and may order the defendant to account for profits derived from the unauthorized application of the trade mark. Further, under this Act, where it is demonstrated that the infringement has caused demonstrable damage to the reputation or goodwill associated with the registered trade mark, the court shall compelled court to award compensatory damages sufficient to redress the harm suffered by the proprietor. This remedy applies irrespective of whether the defendant acted in good faith or was aware of the existence of the prior registration, provided that the elements of confusion and/or unfair competition are established.

Where a registered trade mark is used in contravention of the rights conferred by registration, and such use causes or is likely to cause confusion amongst the public, or dilution of the distinctiveness of the said trade mark, any person aggrieved may institute proceedings in the District Court claiming relief as provided herein. The court shall give notice to the defendant under this Act at least thirty days prior to the commencement of the hearing. Further, where the defendant alleges that the use is fair dealing for the purposes of criticism or review, the burden of proving such fairness shall lie upon the defendant. Any party seeking an injunction restraining the use of a trade mark shall compelled court to consider whether damages would afford adequate relief in lieu of injunctive relief.

Where a registered trade mark is used in relation to goods or services other than those for which it is registered, and such use creates confusion amongst the public regarding the origin, quality, or characteristics of those goods or services, any person aggrieved may institute proceedings under this Act seeking an injunction restraining such infringing use. Provided that, where the alleged infringer demonstrates honest belief that the use does not constitute infringement, the court may grant a declaration clarifying the permissible scope of the registered trade mark. Further, if it is established that the infringing use has been employed in good faith and without intent to deceive, the court shall compelled court to consider mitigating factors before issuing any order restricting such usage, balancing the interests of the proprietor with those of the public.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark, desiring to grant a license for use of their mark within the territory of India, may execute an assignment agreement specifying the permitted scope and duration of such usage. Such agreements shall be in writing and clearly delineate the goods or services relating to which the license is granted, as well as any geographical limitations applying thereto. Where a dispute arises concerning the validity or enforceability of a licensing arrangement, the aggrieved party shall compelled court to determine whether the terms adhere to principles of fair trade practice and do not unfairly prejudice the interests of consumers. Further provision is made that sub-licensing is permissible only with express written consent from the registered proprietor, unless otherwise stipulated within the original assignment agreement. Any alteration or modification to a granted license requires notification to the Registrar of Trade Marks for record purposes.

Any person who knowingly represents that goods or services are registered under this Act when they are not so registered shall be guilty of an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. Further, any individual found to have employed counterfeit marks upon goods offered for sale, or in the course of trade, without due cause and subject to provisions regarding fair use as provided herein, shall face penalties equivalent to ten times the value of the infringing goods, recoverable by way of damages from affected citizens India rights holders. The Registrar may issue injunctions preventing further acts of infringement where such actions demonstrably mislead consumers or constitute unfair competition. Repeated violations will result in prosecution under relevant criminal law provisions and potential revocation of any existing registrations held by the offender.

The owner of a registered trademark shall be entitled to grant licenses conferring specific rights relating to the use of the mark within or outside of India. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and the terms thereof shall be governed by contract law as provided herein. Any assignment of a registered trade mark, including assignments arising from license agreements, requires registration with the Trade Marks Registry and is only effective upon such registration. Where a licensee subsequently becomes entitled to use the trademark under this Act, their rights are subject to the original agreement's terms concerning duration and geographical scope. Citizens India rights relating to trademarks include the ability to freely enter into licensing arrangements and assign ownership, provided that all required formalities are fulfilled as stipulated by the Trade Marks Registry. The Registrar may require disclosure of beneficial owners in any assignment or license agreement involving foreign entities.

Any person claiming damages for the use of a registered trademark without consent shall be entitled to recover from the defendant such sum as the Court deems fit, having regard to the loss suffered by the claimant, but not exceeding five times the value of the goods or services in relation to which the infringement occurred. The Court may also award interest on such sum at such rate as it considers appropriate. Where the infringing use is found to have been made for the purpose of securing an unfair advantage or to deceive or confuse the public, the Court shall grant an injunction restraining the defendant from further infringing acts. It is provided that this remedy shall be available only to citizens India and those registered in India under this Act. Further, any order granted under these provisions may be enforced as if it were a decree of the High Court.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any proprietor of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to institute proceedings for infringement thereof against any person using or proposing to use a sign identical or confusingly similar to the said trade mark in relation to goods or services. Such remedies may include an injunction restraining the defendant from further infringing acts, and damages sustained by the plaintiff as a consequence of the infringement. The measure of damages shall be determined having regard to all relevant circumstances, including but not limited to, the extent of the damage suffered, the profits made by the infringer, and the need to deter similar infringements in the future. Further, where an infringing use is found to have resulted in dilution of distinctiveness of the registered trade mark, enhanced damages may be awarded. The rights respect registration conferred under this Act are paramount and shall be vigorously defended against any unauthorized exploitation.

The owner of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to grant licenses conferring the right to use the trade mark for specific goods or services, subject to any conditions stipulated therein. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and the terms thereof shall be governed by contract law principles as provided herein. Assignment of rights in a registered trade mark, including the benefit of any license agreement, requires registration with the Trade Marks Registry, and such assignment shall only take effect upon completion of that process. Any person acquiring an interest in a trade mark through assignment or sub-license may enforce the rights respect registration associated with that mark against infringers, provided they comply with the requirements for standing under this Act. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating the validity of any license or assignment before registering it.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark shall be entitled to grant licenses conferring specific rights relating to the use of the mark within defined territories or for particular goods or services. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and the terms thereof shall be subject to this Act. Any assignment of a trade mark, whether absolute or conditional, requires registration with the Trade Marks Registry to be deemed valid against third parties; failure to register an assignment shall render it unenforceable in respect of any subsequent infringement proceedings. Where a licensee utilizes a registered trade mark in a manner that falsely suggests an affiliation or endorsement not authorized by the proprietor, such conduct constitutes used falsifying trade and is actionable under this Act. The rights respect registration remain paramount, and all sub-licenses must adhere to the original license agreement’s stipulations.

For the purposes of this Act, a “copyright design” is defined as an aesthetic pattern or composition applied to an article by means of any industrial process and relating only to the appearance of the article, its lines, colours, shapes, or textures. A copyright design shall not include features which are solely for the purpose of obtaining utility or functionality; however, such functional elements may be considered if they contribute significantly to the overall aesthetic impression. An application for registration of a design incorporating a copyright design shall disclose whether it is intended to claim protection based on both design and copyright aspects, subject to the provisions relating to originality as provided herein.

Upon application for registration of a design, the Controller may require the applicant to furnish such documentary evidence as he deems necessary to establish ownership and originality of the proposed design. Where an applicant claims copyright design rights relating to a pattern or composition applied to any article by an industrial process, they shall submit detailed specifications outlining the manufacturing method employed, including materials used and dimensions achieved. The Controller may reject an application if it appears that the design incorporates elements already disclosed in prior publications, unless such disclosure was made with the consent of the copyright design owner. Any alteration to a registered design subsequent to its initial registration requires notification to the Controller within three months, detailing the changes and their impact on the original aesthetic features.

The proprietor of a registered copyright design shall be entitled to sue for and recover damages suffered by him by reason of an infringement of his design. Such damages may include loss of profits resulting from the infringing use, as well as any expenditure reasonably incurred by the proprietor in taking action against the infringer. Where an injunction restraining the defendant from further infringing the design has been granted, the measure of damages shall be such sum as the Court deems just and proportionate to the harm suffered, subject to the principle that the plaintiff must demonstrate a causal link between the infringement and his loss. The Court may also award costs in favour of the prevailing party under this Act. Provided that any claim for damages arising from copyright design infringement must be brought within three years from the date of discovery of the infringement.

An application for registration of a copyright design shall be accompanied by such information as the Controller may require regarding the applicant and the proprietor of any trade mark or other right claimed in relation to the design. The Registrar may, upon receiving an application, direct that certain features of the design be altered or omitted if they are deemed to conflict with existing registered designs or trademarks. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar under this Act may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The Controller shall consider any such appeal and issue an appropriate order, which is final subject to further appeal to the High Court. Where a design incorporates elements already disclosed in prior publications, the applicant must provide detailed justification demonstrating originality as provided herein.

Where an application for registration of a design includes or refers to any literary work, musical work, artistic work other than a design, or cinematograph film, which is not original and does not form an integral part of the design, such work shall be deemed to be separately protected under this Act as copyright design. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish proof of ownership or license relating to any such copyrighted material included in the application; failure to provide satisfactory evidence shall render the application liable for rejection. Further, where a registered design incorporates elements subject to copyright design belonging to another person, the proprietor’s rights are conditional upon obtaining prior written consent from the copyright holder, and such consent must be recorded with the Registrar.

Any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act may appeal to the Commercial Court within sixty days from the date of such order. Where a design is copied and reproduced for commercial purposes without authorization, constituting infringement of copyright design rights as provided herein, the proprietor of the registered design shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief restraining further acts of reproduction or exploitation. Furthermore, damages equivalent to a reasonable royalty that could have been charged for the use of the design, or in cases of willful infringement, three times the amount of proven damage, may be awarded. The Court may also order the destruction of infringing articles and materials used in their production. Failure to comply with such orders shall render the offender liable to further penalties as determined by the Court.

The proprietor of a copyright design may grant licenses conferring specific rights relating to the application and exploitation of the design, subject to the terms stipulated within the license agreement. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as determined by the proprietor, and shall clearly define the geographical territory covered by the granted rights. Assignment of the copyright design, including all associated rights under this Act, is permissible through a written instrument executed in accordance with prescribed procedures. Any assignment shall vest complete ownership in the assignee, extinguishing the previous proprietor’s entitlement to utilize or enforce the design. Provided that, where an assignment relates only to particular aspects of the design's application, the assignor retains all rights not explicitly transferred. The terms of any license or assignment are binding and enforceable as per general principles of contract law.

Where an appeal under this Act is preferred against any decision or order made by the Controller relating to the revocation of a registered design, or concerning the validity of a copyright design, the Appellate Board shall consider whether the Controller erred in law or fact. The appellant shall be required to demonstrate that the decision was manifestly unjust or unreasonable, considering all relevant evidence presented during the original proceedings. Furthermore, any party aggrieved by an order made by the Appellate Board may appeal further to the High Court within a period of sixty days from the date of such order, provided that the grounds for appeal are limited to questions of law arising out of this Act.

Any person who, without the consent of the proprietor of a registered design or any other person by law authorized to grant such consent, makes, sells, offers to sell, displays for sale, hires or otherwise uses any article which is a copy of the registered design or so nearly resembles it as to be likely to deceive the public shall be deemed to have infringed the design. Such infringement includes not only direct reproduction but also adaptation that substantially recreates the aesthetic characteristics protected by the copyright design. A proprietor seeking remedy for such infringement may apply to the relevant court for an injunction restraining the infringing activity and damages proportionate to the loss suffered, considering any patent application previously filed relating to the underlying functionality of the article. The court shall have discretion to award costs as it deems just.

Any person who, without the consent of the proprietor of a registered design, applies any process or uses any means for the manufacture, sale, hire or exhibition of an article which is a copy of that design, or so nearly resembling it as to deceive the eye, shall be deemed guilty of an offence under this Act. Such infringement includes unauthorized reproduction or adaptation of a copyright design, irrespective of whether such reproduction constitutes a new invention. The penalty for first conviction shall be imprisonment for a term not exceeding one year, or with fine which may extend to fifty thousand rupees, or both; and for subsequent convictions, the penalties shall be doubled as provided herein. Any proprietor aggrieved by an infringement may seek redress through civil proceedings, including injunctions and damages.

The owner of a copyright design may grant licenses permitting the reproduction and application of their registered design on articles, subject to conditions specified within the license agreement. Such licenses shall be assignable by the owner in writing, including assignment as part of any larger transfer of intellectual property rights held by that person or entity. Any transmission of such a license, whether through sale, gift, or other means, must clearly indicate the scope and duration of the permitted reproduction and application. Further, where a design is licensed for use on articles intended for export from India, the licensee shall provide an annual declaration to the Controller confirming compliance with the terms of the license agreement as provided herein. The owner retains the right to terminate any license if the licensee engages in activities that are detrimental to the reputation or commercial value of the copyright design.

For the purposes of this Act, "tea" with reference to a geographical indication means Camellia sinensis (L.) O. Kuntze, or any variety or hybrid thereof, cultivated for its leaves or buds and processed for infusions; and “Darjeeling tea” shall mean tea exclusively produced in specified areas within the Darjeeling district, including but not limited to areas situated at an elevation of not less than two thousand feet above sea level, as notified by the Central Government. The Registrar may register said geographical indication if satisfied that it is used to identify goods originating from such area and possesses qualities or characteristics attributable exclusively to the influence of the environment, including natural factors and human craftsmanship.

An eligible geographical indication, upon submission of a complete application containing all prescribed particulars, shall be examined by the Registrar to ascertain its compliance with the requirements under this Act. If the Registrar is satisfied that the geographical indication satisfies the criteria for distinctiveness and reputation as associated with the goods or services specified in the application, he may proceed to register said geographical indication. The applicant shall furnish such documentary evidence substantiating the origin of the goods and their connection to the defined geographical area as the Registrar deems necessary. Any person claiming an interest in a pending application may file opposition within the stipulated period, provided that grounds for objection are clearly articulated. Following registration, the Register of Geographical Indications shall be updated accordingly.

Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication shall be entitled to institute civil proceedings for infringement under this Act, subject to demonstrating that use of an identical or confusingly similar indicator is likely to cause dilution of the distinctiveness of the registered geographical indication. Such remedies may include injunctions restraining the infringing party from further use of the mark, and damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the proprietor as a result of the infringement. The Registrar shall maintain a publicly accessible register detailing all successful actions taken against infringers, including particulars of the order passed and any penalties imposed. Further, where an application is refused registration, or a geographical indication is removed from the register, the applicant or former proprietor may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days of communication of the decision. The power to register said geographical indication vests solely with the Registrar.

An application to register said geographical indication may be made by any association of persons or producer group being owners of the said geographical indication, or authorised users thereof. The application shall contain a statement of such particulars concerning the geographical indication as are required to be furnished under this Act, including but not limited to its name and origin. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall issue a notification for public inspection, specifying the geographical indication sought to be registered and inviting objections from any person or organisation claiming interest in the matter. Any objection received shall be communicated to the applicant, who may submit their response within the time prescribed. The Registrar shall consider all submissions before determining whether to accept or reject the application, provided that the Registrar may require further information or clarification as deemed necessary.

An application to register said geographical indication may be filed by any association of persons or producers engaged in the production of goods conforming to the standard of quality, reputation or other characteristics attributed to that geographical origin, or by collectives representing such producers. The applicant must demonstrate exclusive use of the name as indicative of a specific agricultural product, foodstuff, wine, spirit, handicraft or manufactured good originating from the defined geographical area. Prior to registration, the Registrar shall publish a notice inviting objections concerning deceptive similarity with prior marks under this Act. Registration shall be refused if the application is deemed to mislead consumers regarding the true origin of the goods, provided that any existing use shall not preclude registration if it does not create confusion.

Any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act relating to the registration or protection of a geographical indication may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. Failure to register said geographical indication as provided herein does not absolve any producer, packer, bottler, distributor, or seller from civil liability for misleading the public regarding the origin of goods. Where an authorized user contravenes a condition relating to use of the registered geographical indication, the Registrar may issue a warning and, upon repeated or flagrant violation, may revoke the authorization. Penalties for falsely representing goods as originating from a geographically indicated area shall be imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both, as deemed appropriate by the court.

Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication may grant non-exclusive licenses to use the said geographical indication in connection with goods for which it is register said geographical. Such licenses shall be documented in writing and specify the scope of permitted use, including territorial limitations and duration. The license agreement must also stipulate royalties payable to the proprietor, calculated as a percentage of net sales derived from the licensed products. Assignment of rights relating to a registered geographical indication requires prior approval of the Registrar, who may condition such assignment on ensuring continued adherence to quality standards associated with the indication. Further, any subsequent assignee shall be bound by all terms and conditions previously agreed upon between the original proprietor and licensee. The Registrar may require periodic audits to verify compliance with licensing agreements and protect the integrity of the registered geographical indication.

An aggrieved party seeking to challenge a decision regarding the registration of a geographical indication may file an appeal with the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. Such appeal shall be limited to questions of fact arising out of decisions made by the Registrar concerning the distinctiveness or reputation associated with the goods for which the application seeks to register said geographical indication. The Central Government may, at its discretion, direct that any question of law arising in connection with an appeal under this Act be referred to the Supreme Court for determination. Any party dissatisfied with the decision of the Tribunal may further appeal to the Supreme Court on a point of law, subject to fulfilling requirements as provided herein.

An application to register said geographical indication relating to Alphonso mangoes may be filed by any association of persons or producer group being residents of the Taluka of Devgad, Maharashtra, provided that such association or group demonstrates continuous and exclusive use of the name “Alphonso” in connection with mangoes originating from within the defined geographical boundaries for a period not less than five years immediately preceding the date of application. The Registrar shall require evidence establishing adherence to quality standards as prescribed by the Agricultural Produce (Grading and Packing) Order, and verification that any breeder registered variety utilized in cultivation maintains genetic purity consistent with traditional practices. Failure to comply with these conditions will render the application liable for rejection under this Act.

Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication may grant exclusive licences conferring upon the licensee the right to use the said indication in connection with goods identical to those for which the registration is granted, subject to such terms and conditions as are agreed between them; provided that any such licence shall be registrable under this Act and shall specify the territory within which the licensee’s rights are conferred. Further, where an unregistered geographical indication has been used in commerce without authorization from the registered proprietor, and resulting damages have been sustained by the latter, a civil suit for recovery of those damages may be instituted against the infringing party, notwithstanding that the indication is not registered. Assignment of rights under this Act, including any such right to recover damages infringement unregistered, shall require prior notification to the Registrar.

Where a registered Geographical Indication has been infringed and the infringer is not a registered proprietor, the aggrieved party may institute proceedings seeking damages proportionate to the loss suffered, subject to demonstrating reasonable diligence in discovering the infringing activity. Provided that, if the alleged infringement occurs prior to registration but subsequent to public notice under this Act, the assessment of damages shall consider any reliance placed by consumers upon the indication as signifying origin and quality attributable to the registered geographical area. The Registrar may, at the request of an interested party, investigate complaints regarding such unregistered use and issue directions for its cessation; however, these directions do not confer a right to claim damages infringement unregistered under this Act independently. Appeals against any order made by the Registrar concerning such investigations shall lie to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

An application for registration of a layout-design for a semiconductor integrated circuit shall be made to the Registrar in the prescribed form and accompanied by the requisite fee. The applicant shall furnish particulars relating to the design, including its title, relevant views, and a description of the functions performed by the integrated circuit. Where an application relates to a layout-design that incorporates elements previously registered under this Act, the applicant must disclose such prior registration details. The Registrar may require further information or modifications to ensure clarity and compliance with the requirements as provided herein. Any person claiming rights in a design shall be deemed to have knowledge of designs already registered; consequently, subsequent applications incorporating substantially similar features are subject to scrutiny regarding originality under the Design Act 2000.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, a person shall not manufacture, import, or sell any layout-design that infringes upon the exclusive right of another person in the design. An infringement occurs where a substantially similar layout-design is created, without authorization, and such creation constitutes an adaptation of the original work. The determination of substantial similarity shall consider the overall impression of the layout-design, taking into account its component elements and their arrangement. Where a licensee manufactures a layout-design in accordance with the terms of the license, such manufacture shall not constitute infringement under this Act. However, any subsequent assignment or modification of that licensed design requires explicit consent from the original registrant of the Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Act 2000.

Any person who, without authorization from the registered proprietor of a layout-design or a related layout-design, makes, imports, distributes, sells, hires or displays a product which infringes the said layout-design shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall be determined by the relevant adjudicating officer and may include compensation equivalent to the reasonable royalty that would have been payable had the infringing party obtained a license from the proprietor. Further, where an infringement is established under this Act, the Court may order the destruction of the infringing products and materials used in their manufacture. The Central Government may, through notification, prescribe penalties for contravention of these provisions, subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. This applies specifically to matters concerning the Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Act 2000.

Where a person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act concerning infringement of a registered Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout-Design is dissatisfied with the decision of the relevant authority, that person may appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of communication of the said order. The appellate court shall have the power to entertain appeals arising out of any direction issued or order made by an adjudicating officer relating to damages for infringement under this Act, provided that the aggrieved party demonstrates a substantial question of law is involved. Any appeal filed without demonstrating such a legal point may be dismissed summarily. Further, the High Court may, subject to just considerations and principles of natural justice, review any findings regarding originality in a registered design as per the Design Act 2000.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, a person shall be entitled to claim creator layout rights in respect of an integrated circuit layout-design if that person is the first to file for registration under this Act and demonstrates, through documented evidence, substantial contribution towards its creation. Such contribution includes, but is not limited to, conceptualization, drafting, or significant modification of existing designs. Where multiple persons jointly claim creator layout rights, the Register shall require a written agreement specifying the respective contributions and profit-sharing arrangements amongst them; failure to provide such an agreement may result in rejection of the application. Any person infringing upon the registered layout-design of a claiming creator layout shall be liable for damages as provided herein, calculated based on lost profits or unjust enrichment, whichever is higher.

An application for registration alleging a claim as the creator layout shall contain a detailed statement specifying the nature and extent of the applicant’s contribution to the creation of the integrated circuit, including particulars of any prior art considered and demonstrating originality under this Act. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish further documentation substantiating the asserted authorship, such as design records, technical specifications, or correspondence relating to the layout-design's development. Where multiple individuals are listed as creators on an application, each shall attest to their individual contribution and acknowledge the contributions of others. Any challenge to a claim as the creator layout may be brought before the Controller within three months from the date of publication of the acceptance for registration. The applicant bears the burden of proving, through admissible evidence, that they are indeed entitled to claiming creator layout status as provided herein.

An applicant seeking registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall, in the application, explicitly declare the individual(s) who claim creator layout status for the design. Such declaration must identify each claimant by full legal name and current registered address, accompanied by documentary evidence substantiating their direct contribution to the creation of the layout-design. Where multiple individuals are identified as claiming creator layout, they shall jointly submit a written statement affirming their agreement regarding ownership and exploitation rights pertaining to the registered design, as provided herein. The Registrar may reject the application if the declaration is incomplete or contains conflicting claims concerning authorship. Any subsequent alteration to the claimed creator layout after submission requires prior written consent from all initially declared claimants.

No person shall assert a claim as the sole creator layout unless they can demonstrate, to the satisfaction of the Controller, exclusive contribution towards the conception and reduction to practice of the integrated circuit. Any individual falsely claiming creator layout with intent to deceive or gain an undue advantage shall be liable for a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees, recoverable by way of civil suit. Furthermore, where such false claim is made in connection with commercial activity, the offender may also face proceedings under relevant provisions relating to unfair competition. The Controller may, upon receiving credible evidence of a fraudulent creator layout assertion, issue an order restraining further dissemination or exploitation of the design and direct rectification of any misleading representations.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person claiming creator layout of a semiconductor integrated circuit may grant a license conferring upon the licensee the right to use, exploit, and reproduce the said layout-design for specific purposes. Such licenses shall be documented in writing and executed by both licensor and licensee, clearly outlining the scope, duration, and territorial extent of the granted rights. The licensor retains full ownership of the claiming creator layout unless expressly transferred through a separate assignment agreement. Any assignment of such rights must adhere to the formalities prescribed under this Act and shall be registered with the designated authority. Provided that, where an employee creates a layout-design within the scope of their employment, the employer shall be deemed the claimant for the purposes of licensing or assigning those rights, unless otherwise agreed in writing.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, a person shall be entitled to claim creator layout status for an integrated circuit layout-design if they demonstrate, through documented evidence and testimony, that they conceived and substantially reduced the layout-design into tangible form. However, where multiple individuals or entities jointly assert claiming creator layout status, the burden shall lie upon each claimant to establish their individual contribution exceeding de minimis levels; failure to do so may result in a finding of lack of entitlement. Any dispute regarding the validity of such claims may be referred to an Arbitral Tribunal constituted under this Act, whose decision shall be final and binding, subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal on grounds limited to legal error apparent on the face of the record.

An application for registration as a claiming creator layout shall include, alongside the prescribed fee, a detailed schematic representation conforming to Schedule A and an exhaustive list of contributors involved in its conception. The applicant must provide evidence demonstrating their direct involvement in the creation process, satisfactory to the Controller. Where a layout-design incorporates elements previously disclosed or utilized under a reference use mark, the application shall explicitly identify such elements and detail the nature of the permitted usage as documented within the original licensing agreement. Failure to adequately disclose this information may render the registration liable for cancellation. The applicant warrants that they possess exclusive rights over the claimed layout design, subject to any prior agreements or encumbrances disclosed herein.

For the purposes of this Act, "layout design vested" means a layout design in respect of which the right to apply for registration is held by any person other than the first owner of that layout design. Such vesting may arise from assignment, testamentary succession, or operation of law, and shall be evidenced by an instrument duly executed and registered under applicable laws. The transferor of a layout design shall provide notice of such transfer to the Office within thirty days of execution; failure to do so renders the transfer voidable at the option of the original owner. A layout design vested shall continue to enjoy protection as provided herein, subject to any conditions stipulated in the instrument effecting the vesting.

An application for registration of a layout design shall accompany an affirmation by the applicant verifying ownership and detailing the circumstances under which the layout design was first conceived and reduced to form. Where a layout design is created by an employee during the course of their employment, the right to apply for registration shall vest in the employer, provided that the terms of employment explicitly assign such rights. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating the applicant’s claim to the layout design vested, including records of development, internal memoranda relating to the design process, and evidence of commercial exploitation. Any prior publication or disclosure of the layout design before registration shall be disclosed in the application, subject to a waiver obtainable under conditions prescribed herein.

Where a person infringes a layout design vested under this Act, the proprietor shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief restraining the infringing party from further acts of infringement. Such injunction may include orders prohibiting the manufacture, import, sale, offer for sale, and distribution of integrated circuits incorporating the infringing layout design. Further, damages equivalent to the reasonable royalty that the infringer would have paid had they obtained a license from the proprietor, or in cases where actual damages are difficult to ascertain, the profits made by the infringer as a result of the infringement, shall be recoverable. The proprietor may also claim compensation for losses directly attributable to the infringement, subject to demonstrating such losses with reasonable certainty. Provided that, any order granted under this Act is without prejudice to any other remedies available to the proprietor under general principles of law.

Where a person claims ownership of a layout design, the Registrar may require submission of documentary evidence demonstrating the circumstances under which the layout design was created and the extent of contribution by each individual involved. Such evidence shall include, but not be limited to, records pertaining to employment contracts, consultancy agreements, or joint venture arrangements relevant to the creation process. The determination of ownership rests solely with the Registrar, who shall consider all submitted documentation and any oral testimony presented during proceedings. Where a layout design is found to be derived from an earlier work, the rights vested in the original creator shall remain paramount, subject to provisions regarding fair use and derivative works as provided herein. Any dispute concerning the layout design vested shall be resolved through arbitration conducted under the auspices of the Intellectual Property Facilitation Council.

Any person who, having knowledge of a layout design vested in another person, without consent makes, imports, manufactures, distributes, sells, hires or offers for sale any integrated circuit embodying that layout design shall be liable to pay damages. Such damages shall be determined by the relevant adjudicating officer and may include compensation equivalent to the reasonable royalty which the infringer would have been willing to pay. Further, where an infringement occurs through import, the importer shall also be deemed guilty of such infringement and subject to penalties as provided herein. The Central Government may, by notification, prescribe a minimum penalty for each instance of infringement found under this Act.

Where a dispute arises concerning the validity of a claim asserting layout design vested, the Intellectual Property Disputes Tribunal shall hear and determine the matter subject to appeal to the High Court. The claimant alleging infringement shall bear the burden of proving, on a balance of probabilities, that the challenged layout-design incorporates protected elements substantially similar to the registered layout-design. Provided that, if the respondent demonstrates prior use of an analogous design within the territory of India, the Tribunal may consider such use in assessing the degree of similarity and potential infringement under this Act. The determination of whether a layout-design is ‘substantially similar’ shall be guided by principles of fair competition and technological advancement as provided herein.

Where a person alleges that another has engaged, or is likely to engage, in an act constituting infringement of layout design vested under this Act, such person may institute proceedings before the relevant Commercial Court having jurisdiction over the matter.
