Where the assignment was executed with a Contracting State, the Controller shall prioritize considerations of international trade obligations in any determination regarding extended exploitation rights.

Where a patent is assigned or licensed under this Act by a sole proprietor, partnership, or individual, the assignee or licensee shall be subject to the same obligations and liabilities as would have been borne by the assignor or licensor had they continued to hold the patent. In relation to a firm, any assignment or license granted by the partners acting for the firm shall be deemed valid only if it is executed by all such partners or their duly authorized representatives. Provided that, where a license is granted exclusively to one party, the firm shall not subsequently grant a conflicting license without obtaining the express written consent of the original licensee. Further, any agreement concerning royalty payments arising from such assignment or license shall be binding on the firm and its successors in title. The Intellectual Property Appellate Board may entertain appeals against orders pertaining to disputes regarding these assignments and licenses as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, “partnership” shall mean an association of persons formed for the purpose of carrying on a business as a firm, whether incorporated or unincorporated, and includes a co-operative society registered under any law for the time being in force; and where reference is made to a firm, it shall be construed as including not only the partnership itself but also any person who is, or has been, a partner in relation to that firm. The term "partner" when used in relation to a firm includes an individual admitted as a partner, subject to provisions under this Act regarding liability and representation. Parliament may by notification amend the definition of “partnership” for specific regulatory purposes.

A trademark shall be deemed to be “used” in relation to goods if it is affixed to the goods or appears on the packaging thereof, or is applied in connection with an offer for sale, or exposure for sale, or advertising of such goods. For the purposes of this definition, use in the course of trade includes offering services which relate to those goods. The expression “used” also encompasses instances where a trademark is used in relation to specified services as provided herein, and shall include, but not be limited to, activities undertaken for the purpose of making known the connection between the trademark and the person using it. Provided that use in the electronic environment, including on websites or digital platforms, shall similarly constitute “trade mark used”.

The Registrar may accept an application for registration of a trade mark if he considers that the proposed trade mark is distinctive in its intended class and is capable of distinguishing the goods or services of the applicant from those of others. However, an application shall be refused if the representation of the trade mark includes any element which directly suggests the nature, quality or geographical origin of such goods or services. Where a trade mark is sought to be registered in relation to particular goods or services, evidence of the *trade mark used* in connection with those goods or services may be required by the Registrar as proof of its existence and reputation. The applicant shall furnish such evidence within the time specified under this Act.

Where any person has made use of a registered trade mark without authorization from the proprietor, and such use constitutes an infringement under this Act, the proprietor may institute proceedings for recovery of damages. Such damages shall include loss suffered by the proprietor as a direct result of the infringing use, together with any profits made by the infringer attributable to the unauthorized exploitation of the trademark. The Court may also grant an injunction restraining the person from further using the registered trade mark or any confusingly similar representation. It is provided that in determining the amount of damages, the Court shall consider factors including the extent of the infringement and the goodwill associated with the registered *trade mark used*. Any order for account of profits shall be subject to a deduction for any sums which the infringer duly paid to the proprietor as royalties or license fees.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark proceeds to final hearing, the Registrar may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating continuous use of the applied-for mark within India. Such evidence must pertain to the period commencing from the date of first use as claimed in the application and continuing up to the date of the hearing. The Registrar shall consider any submissions made by interested parties regarding the extent or nature of such use, provided these are supported by documentary proof or affidavits verified according to prescribed procedures. Failure to adequately demonstrate a *trade mark used* will constitute grounds for refusal of registration. Further, where an objection is raised concerning non-use, the applicant may be called upon to rebut this challenge with satisfactory evidence of ongoing commercial exploitation under this Act.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed on the ground that the mark is deceptively similar to a prior *trade mark used* by another person, the Registrar shall give notice of the opposition to the applicant and the opponent. The opponent shall furnish evidence demonstrating continuous use of the earlier trade mark in India for at least three years immediately preceding the date of the application under consideration, provided that such use was not abandoned or discontinued with an intention to avoid registration. Further, it shall be established that the public is likely to associate the goods or services offered under the later trade mark with those previously offered under the earlier *trade mark used*. The applicant may submit counter-evidence refuting this association and demonstrating a lack of confusion among consumers.

Where any person utilizes a registered trade mark in contravention of the conditions specified under this Act, or employs it in a manner that creates confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or quality of goods or services, such person shall be liable for damages. The amount of damages shall be determined by the relevant adjudicating authority, taking into consideration factors including but not limited to the extent of the infringement, the profits derived from the unauthorized use, and the loss suffered by the registered proprietor. Any party aggrieved may institute civil proceedings seeking an injunction restraining further acts of infringement and claiming compensation for losses incurred. The term “trade mark used” includes any display or application of the trade mark on goods or their packaging, or in connection with services offered to the public.

Where a proprietor of a registered trade mark grants a license for use of the trade mark under this Act, such license may be assigned by the licensee subject to the prior written consent of the grantor, provided that any assignment without such consent shall be deemed void. The grantor may stipulate conditions within the license agreement regarding quality control measures relating to goods or services bearing the *trade mark used* and may reserve the right to terminate the license in instances of non-compliance with these stipulated standards. Further, a licensee seeking to assign their rights under a trade mark license shall provide the grantor with detailed information pertaining to the proposed assignee, including their business activities and reputation. The grantor shall have thirty days from receipt of this notification to either consent or withhold consent to the assignment, providing written justification for any refusal.

Where an objection is taken under this Act against the registration of a trade mark on the ground that it is deceptively similar to a prior *trade mark used* by another person, the Registrar may require both parties to submit evidence relating to the existence and extent of such use. The party claiming priority through earlier use shall bear the burden of demonstrating continuous and substantial adoption of the mark in commerce. It shall be open to the other party to challenge this claim by presenting evidence indicating a lack of recognition or consumer confusion arising from the alleged prior *trade mark used*. Decisions regarding deceptive similarity, as provided herein, are subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, whose determination shall be final and binding, barring appeals on grounds of law.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark includes a representation of a plant variety, the Registrar may require the applicant to provide evidence demonstrating that the breeder entry relating to said plant variety has been recorded under the Plant Varieties and Farmers’ Rights Protection Act. Such evidence shall include a certified copy of the record from the relevant authority maintaining records pertaining to plant varieties. The trade mark used in connection with goods or services derived from, or containing, such plant variety shall not be registered if the applicant fails to comply with this requirement within the time specified by the Registrar. Provided that, where compliance is demonstrably delayed due to administrative processes of the Plant Varieties and Farmers’ Rights Protection Act, the Registrar may extend the timeframe as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, "certified trade mark" means a trade mark which satisfies the conditions specified under this Act and has been registered as such. A certified trade mark shall denote that the goods or services in relation to which it is used conform to a particular standard, specification, or characteristic as defined by the registering proprietor and approved by the Registrar. The use of a certified trade mark shall be restricted to those goods or services meeting the prescribed criteria; any deviation from such standards may render the user liable for actions under this Act. Further, the registered certify mark confers upon the proprietor exclusive rights subject to limitations imposed herein.

Where an applicant seeks registration of a proposed trade mark as a certified trade mark, such application shall be accompanied by evidence demonstrating compliance with prescribed quality standards and adherence to specified production processes. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating these claims, including audit reports from accredited certification bodies. Registration as a certified trade mark is conditional upon continued conformity with the initially declared standards; any material deviation or failure to maintain requisite levels of quality shall render the registration liable for cancellation under this Act. Further, the proprietor of a registered certify trade mark must submit annual declarations confirming ongoing compliance and may be subject to periodic inspections by officers authorized by the Registrar.

Any person employing a registered certify trade mark in relation to goods or services shall be liable to prosecution under this Act if such employment constitutes an unfair representation likely to deceive or cause confusion among consumers regarding the origin, quality, or characteristics of those goods or services. Where a false or misleading statement is made concerning the nature, quantity, or production method of goods bearing a registered certify trade mark, the offender shall be subject to a penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees and may also face imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years. The proprietor of the certified trade mark shall have standing to bring an action for damages arising from such infringement as provided herein.

The owner of a registered certify trade mark shall be entitled to grant licences conferring the right to use the mark upon such terms and conditions as they deem fit, provided that every such licence shall be in writing and specify the goods or services in relation to which the licensee is authorised to use the mark. Any assignment of the registered certify trade mark, whether absolute or subject to reservations, requires prior notification to the Registrar, who may object thereto if it appears that the proposed assignee lacks the requisite reputation or quality standards necessary for maintaining the integrity of the certification scheme as provided herein. Further, a licensee under such a grant shall be bound by the terms and conditions stipulated in the original registration certificate and any subsequent amendments thereof, failing which the owner may revoke the licence. The Registrar may also require periodic audits to ensure compliance with these obligations.

Where a registered certify trade mark is infringed, the owner shall be entitled to seek remedies under this Act as if the infringement were of an ordinary trade mark. Any person who, without due cause or consent, uses a registered certify trade mark in relation to goods or services for which the mark is registered, or any identical or confusingly similar representation thereof, shall be deemed guilty of infringement and liable to damages. The owner may also apply to the relevant court for an injunction restraining the infringing conduct, provided that such restraint is necessary to protect the distinctiveness of the certified goods or services. Further, where a person has falsely represented that their goods or services are certified under a registered certify trade mark, they shall be subject to penalties as prescribed herein. The register patents shall remain accessible for public inspection and verification of certification status.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark shall file an application with the Registrar in the prescribed manner and form. The application must contain a clear representation of the trade mark and a list specifying all goods or services for which registration is sought, classified according to the International Classification of Goods and Services. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall examine it to ascertain whether it complies with the requirements of this Act. If any defects are found, the Registrar may intimate them to the applicant for rectification. The Registrar may also require the applicant to furnish further information or clarification concerning the trade mark or its intended use. A registrar application presented under this Act is subject to scrutiny regarding distinctiveness and potential conflicts with existing registered marks.

Where an application for registration of a trademark is refused under this Act, the applicant shall be entitled to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeal may be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order of refusal and must specify the grounds upon which it is based. The Intellectual Property Appellate Board shall afford the Registrar an opportunity to present its reasons for the refusal and allow both parties to submit written arguments and evidence.

The Registrar, in considering any such appeal relating to a registrar application pr ocedure, may direct that the matter be heard by a Bench constituted as provided herein. If the Intellectual Property Appellate Board finds merit in the applicant’s case, it shall set aside the refusal and direct the Registrar to proceed with registration; otherwise, the order of refusal shall stand affirmed. The decision of the Intellectual Property Appellate Board is final subject to appeal under the relevant provisions.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark shall file an application with the Registrar in the prescribed manner and form. The application must contain a clear representation of the trade mark as it is intended to be used, along with a list specifying all goods or services with which the trade mark is associated. Upon receipt of such an application, the Registrar shall acknowledge its receipt and assign it a filing date.

The Registrar may, at any time, require the applicant to furnish further information or clarification regarding the application or the details provided therein. Any objection to the acceptance of the application arising from examination under this Act shall be communicated to the applicant in writing, providing an opportunity for response within the stipulated period as provided herein. Failure to respond adequately may result in rejection of the *registrar application pr*ocessing. The Registrar’s decision on any such objections is final and binding subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

An application for registration of a trademark, filed under this Act, shall be deemed incomplete if it does not include a clear representation of the mark as applied and intended to be used. The Registrar may require an applicant to furnish further particulars or documentary evidence demonstrating distinctiveness, particularly where the proposed mark comprises commonplace words or phrases. Any alteration made to the mark after the initial application is filed shall necessitate a fresh filing, subject to compliance with all applicable requirements. Furthermore, if the Registrar finds that the trademark description lacks clarity regarding the goods or services for which registration is sought, he may direct the applicant to amend it accordingly. The registrar application process will be deemed abandoned if the applicant fails to respond within sixty days of such direction.

Any person making an application in the prescribed manner seeking rectification of a registered trademark shall be subject to penalties as provided herein if such application contains false representations concerning prior use or reputation. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish evidence substantiating claims made within the application, and failure to comply with this requirement will result in rejection of the application and imposition of a fine not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Further, any party demonstrating that rectification was sought maliciously or for an unlawful purpose shall be liable to pay damages to the registered proprietor as determined by a civil court. The Registrar’s decision regarding a registrar application pr is final, subject to appeal under this Act.

An applicant seeking registration of a trademark under this Act may, subject to fulfilling all procedural requirements as provided herein, grant a license conferring specific rights relating to the use of the mark. Such licenses shall be registrable as assignments if they include provisions for royalty payments and duration, and explicitly state the geographical territory covered by the permitted usage. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all registered licenses alongside the primary trademark registration. Any subsequent assignment of the trademark, whether partial or complete, must disclose any existing license agreements to the Registrar at the time of application. Failure to do so may render the assignee jointly liable for obligations under those pre-existing license arrangements. The Registrar’s decision regarding the validity of a registrar application pr esented concerning an assignment is final and binding.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed abandoned if the applicant fails to attend personally, or by an authorized representative, at the hearing appointed under this Act. The Registrar may, however, upon review of the circumstances and subject to satisfaction that good cause exists, permit the applicant’s absence and proceed with the examination of the application. Where a trade mark is opposed, any person interested shall be entitled to file evidence in support of or opposing the registration. Such a ‘person interested’ includes, but is not limited to, proprietors of earlier marks, and those claiming rights through assignment or succession. The Registrar may require such persons to furnish security for costs incurred by other parties involved in the proceedings relating to the registrar application pr oceeding.

Any person making an application for registration of a trademark shall be deemed guilty of an offence if, at the time of filing, the proposed trademark is demonstrably identical or confusingly similar to a previously registered mark used in relation to identical or closely related goods or services. Such an applicant shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees and may also face prosecution for wilful infringement under this Act. Further, any registration granted based on a fraudulent or misleading application for the registrar application pr is voidable at the instance of any aggrieved party. The Registrar may, sua sponte or upon complaint, initiate proceedings to cancel such a mark. Application registration mark procedures shall be strictly adhered to in all instances.

Proceedings before the High Court concerning disputes arising under this Act shall be governed by the principles of natural justice, and every party involved shall have the right to present evidence and arguments. For the purposes of determining jurisdiction, proceedings before the High Court in which the relief sought includes an injunction restraining the use of a trade mark or damages for passing off shall be deemed civil suits subject to the provisions regarding costs as determined by the court. The Intellectual Property Appellate Board may submit observations on matters of law arising during such proceedings, but its submissions are advisory and do not bind the High Court.
primary_entity: proceedings before the High Court in which the relief sought

context: An applicant aggrieved by a refusal under this Act may, subject to provisions regarding time limits and procedural requirements as provided herein, institute proceedings before the High Court seeking relief. Such proceedings shall be maintainable where the applicant contends that the refusal was unwarranted or based upon an incorrect interpretation of the law relating to distinctiveness or deceptive similarity. The High Court may, in considering such a challenge, direct the Registrar to reconsider the application and provide reasons for any subsequent decision. Further, proceedings before the High Court in which the relief sought includes a declaration regarding the validity of a registered trade mark shall be governed by principles of natural justice and subject to judicial review.
primary_entity: proceedings before the High Court in which the relief sought

context: Where, upon hearing arguments and considering evidence presented by parties involved in proceedings before the High Court in which the relief sought includes an injunction restraining the use of a registered trade mark or the recovery of damages for infringement, the High Court finds that the respondent has engaged in conduct constituting detrimental passing off, it shall be entitled to award such remedies as are just and equitable. These remedies may include, but are not limited to, compensatory damages calculated to account for lost profits and unjust enrichment, punitive damages where the infringing activity was undertaken with knowledge of the registered trade mark’s distinctiveness and reputation, and an order requiring the destruction or recall of goods bearing the infringing mark. Subject to principles of fairness and proportionality, the High Court may also grant a perpetual injunction preventing further acts of passing off.
primary_entity: proceedings before the High Court in which the relief sought

context: Where, following a decision by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, an aggrieved party institutes proceedings before the High Court in which the relief sought involves the enforcement of any right conferred under this Act or challenges the validity of any registered trademark, such proceedings shall be conducted in accordance with the principles of natural justice. The High Court may, subject to compliance with procedural requirements as provided herein, grant such remedies as it deems just and equitable, including but not limited to injunctions, damages, and account of profits. Provided that a party seeking interim relief must demonstrate an irretrievable injury if the relief is denied. Further, any order made by the High Court shall be subject to appeal under the provisions governing appeals from orders of civil courts.
primary_entity: proceedings before the High Court in which the relief sought

context: Where, upon investigation under this Act, the Controller finds that any person has made use of a deceptive trade mark or falsely represented connection with goods or services offered by the registered proprietor, the Controller may initiate proceedings to recover damages. Such recovery shall include compensation for loss sustained by the proprietor and profits made by the infringing party as determined by the Court. Further, the Controller may apply to the High Court seeking an injunction restraining the offending party from continuing such deceptive practices. Proceedings before the High Court in which the relief sought includes a mandatory injunction against continued use of the mark shall be expedited. Any failure to comply with an order issued under this Act will render the offender liable for further penalties and imprisonment.
primary_entity: proceedings before the High Court in which the relief sought

context: Where the registered proprietor of a trade mark, hereinafter referred to as the “licensor,” grants a license to use such trade mark, or assigns the same, subject to conditions relating to quality control and permitted geographical territory, the licensor shall retain the right to inspect records pertaining to the licensee’s or assignee's compliance with those stipulated conditions. Such inspection may be conducted at reasonable times and upon providing advance notice, as provided herein. Any dispute arising from the interpretation of these conditions or the scope of permissible use shall be resolved through arbitration, unless either party elects to pursue proceedings before the High Court in which the relief sought includes a declaration regarding the validity of the license agreement or assignment contract. The Registrar may issue directions concerning the form and content of such licenses and assignments to ensure transparency and protect consumer interests.
primary_entity: proceedings before the High Court in which the relief sought

context: For the purposes of this Act, a “trade description applied” shall mean the representation, whether by means of words, figures, marks, signs, or otherwise, that is directly affixed to, printed upon, or in any way connected with goods offered for sale or provided as services. This includes, but is not limited to, labels, tags, wrappers, containers, and accompanying literature. A trade description applied shall be deemed false if it contains information which, whether true or untrue, is likely to mislead the public regarding the nature, quality, characteristics, origin, or suitability of those goods or services. Provided that such misleading representation must materially affect a consumer's decision-making process as provided herein.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall include a statement specifying all goods or services in relation to which the applicant desires to register the trade mark, classified according to the International Classification of Goods and Services. Where the applicant seeks to register a trade mark incorporating a geographical indication as part of the proposed trade description applied to the goods or services, such application must be accompanied by an affidavit verifying that the applicant is authorized to use the said geographical indication in accordance with applicable regulations. The Registrar may require further information regarding the applicant’s entitlement to utilize the geographical indication if reasonable doubt arises concerning their authorization. Any alteration to the list of goods or services after filing shall necessitate a formal amendment request, subject to approval by the Registrar.

Where a proprietor institutes proceedings under this Act alleging that another person has made misrepresentation concerning the nature, quality, origin, characteristics or suitability of goods or services, the Court may grant such relief as it deems just and equitable. This includes an injunction restraining the defendant from continuing to use the offending representation, and ordering the destruction or removal of any materials bearing the false trade description applied. The proprietor shall be entitled to claim damages sustained by them as a direct result of the misrepresentation, calculated in such manner as the Court considers appropriate, taking into account lost profits and harm to reputation. Provided that, if the defendant proves they acted in good faith and had no knowledge or reasonable grounds for believing the representation was false, the Court may reduce or deny damages accordingly. The proprietor must demonstrate a causal link between the misleading trade description applied and the alleged detriment suffered.

Where a proprietor seeks to register a trade mark, and the application includes a proposed trade description applied to the goods or services specified therein, the Registrar shall examine whether such description conforms to established standards of accuracy and clarity. Any objection raised by an interested party concerning the veracity or misleading nature of the trade description applied must be submitted in writing within three months from the date of advertisement under this Act. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish supporting documentation substantiating the claims made within the proposed trade description, including but not limited to technical specifications and certification records. Failure to provide such documentation within the stipulated timeframe shall render the application liable for rejection. Further, any alteration to the trade description applied after the initial filing requires prior approval from the Registrar, subject to a fee as prescribed.

Where a person, through false representation, uses a *trade description applied* to goods offered for sale or provided as services, intending to deceive the public regarding their nature, quality, quantity, origin, or other characteristics, such person shall be guilty of an offence. This offense is punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and with a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees, but which may extend to two hundred thousand rupees. Further, any goods in respect of which the false representation was made are liable to seizure and forfeiture. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, specify authorities empowered to investigate offenses under this Act and exercise powers relating to search and arrest as provided herein.

Where a proprietor of a registered trademark elects to permit another party to utilize their trade description applied to specific classes of goods or services, such permission shall constitute a license granted under this Act. The licensee may, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated in the licensing agreement, manufacture, offer for sale, sell, or otherwise deal with those goods or services bearing the trademark. Provided that any assignment of rights relating to the trade description applied shall require prior written consent from the original proprietor, and such consent may be withheld at their sole discretion. Further, a licensee intending to assign their rights under the license must notify the proprietor in writing at least sixty days before completing the proposed assignment, allowing for objection based on grounds reasonably related to maintaining the integrity of the trademark. The proprietor retains the right to terminate the license upon material breach by the licensee.

Where a proprietor seeks to register a mark, and such mark incorporates a *trade description* applied by the applicant, the Registrar shall examine whether the use of that description conforms with standards established under this Act. The application may be rejected if the Registrar is satisfied that the inclusion of the *mark trade description* creates confusion likely to mislead the public regarding the nature, quality or geographical origin of goods or services. Any party claiming an interest in opposition to registration may submit evidence demonstrating such misleading potential. Further, the Registrar shall provide a reasonable opportunity for the applicant to present counter-evidence and arguments. The decision of the Registrar concerning the propriety of the *trade description applied* is subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. This process ensures adherence to principles safeguarding consumer interests and maintaining integrity within the trade mark registry.

Where a proprietor of a registered trademark desires to grant a license permitting the use of their trade description applied to particular goods or services, such license shall be documented and entered into the Register of Trade Marks. The entry register document relating to such licenses must specify the precise scope of permitted usage, including geographical limitations and duration. Any subsequent assignment of rights pertaining to this licensed application may only occur with the prior written consent of the proprietor, recorded as a separate entry in the aforementioned register. Provided that the assignee undertakes to adhere strictly to the terms initially stipulated within the original license agreement. Further, any alteration or modification of the goods or services covered by the trade description applied requires notification to and approval from the Registrar before such changes become effective under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, "applies goods" shall mean the use of a mark upon goods in such a manner as to indicate, directly or indirectly, a connection between the goods and the owner of the mark. This includes, but is not limited to, affixing the mark by way of imprint, label, plate, tag, embroidery, painting, or otherwise; provided that the application shall be considered deceptive if it is likely to cause confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or nature of those goods. The use of a mark on packaging associated with the goods also constitutes applying goods as defined herein.

Where an application for registration of a trademark is refused under this Act, the applicant may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. Such appeal shall be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order of refusal and shall state specifically the grounds on which the applicant relies. The Registrar may, prior to any hearing before the Tribunal, require the appellant to submit a concise statement of the points they intend to raise in support of their appeal, along with supporting documentation.

The Trademark Registry shall provide copies of all relevant records pertaining to the application and refusal to the appellant upon request and payment of prescribed fees. An applicant who applies goods bearing a trademark identical or confusingly similar to an earlier mark may be required to demonstrate distinctiveness acquired through use subsequent to the date of first use of the earlier mark, as provided herein. The Tribunal shall consider all evidence presented and may allow the appeal if satisfied that the refusal was unwarranted.

Where a proprietor seeks to register a mark under this Act, it shall be a condition precedent that the applicant demonstrates genuine use of the mark in relation to the specified goods or services. Such demonstration requires evidence establishing continuous and substantial commercial exploitation within the territory of India for a period not less than six months preceding the date of application, provided that exceptions may apply where registration is sought based on prior honest intent to use. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating such use, including invoices, advertising materials, or sales records. Failure to adequately demonstrate how the mark applies goods shall render the application liable for rejection, subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Where a proprietor institutes proceedings under this Act alleging an infringement of their registered trademark, and it is established that the defendant applies goods with a sign identical or confusingly similar to the plaintiff’s mark, the Court shall order such remedies as are just and equitable. These may include permanent injunction restraining the defendant from further applying the infringing sign to any goods or services, and directing the destruction of all materials bearing the offending mark. Furthermore, damages equivalent to the loss suffered by the proprietor, or a sum not exceeding five per centum of the defendant’s turnover attributable to the infringement, whichever is higher, shall be awarded. The Court may also order the recovery of costs incurred by the plaintiff in bringing the action.

Where a proprietor institutes proceedings alleging an infringement under this Act, and the defendant contends that the impugned use does not constitute an application of the mark to goods, the Tribunal shall determine whether such use creates a likelihood of confusion on the minds of the relevant public regarding the origin or nature of those goods. It shall be presumed that any representation of the trade mark, even if altered or adapted, applies goods unless the defendant proves, by clear and convincing evidence, that the representation serves solely an honest descriptive purpose unrelated to identifying the source of the goods. The proprietor may adduce evidence demonstrating actual confusion among consumers as corroborative of their claim; however, such evidence shall not be conclusive.

Where an international registration designating India is extended under this Act, the Registrar shall examine whether the application for extension meets the requirements as provided herein. The applicant shall furnish such documentary evidence substantiating the use of the mark in relation to the goods or services specified in the international registration as the Registrar may require. Failure to demonstrate satisfactory use will result in a notice being issued under this Act, providing an opportunity for the applicant to submit further information within a prescribed period. If the mark applies goods that are identical or closely resemble those for which earlier registrations exist in India, the Registrar shall consider any evidence of likelihood of confusion presented by existing proprietors. The Registrar may require translation of documents submitted as part of the international registration process.

For the purposes of this Act, a “trade description manner” shall be construed as encompassing the mode and form in which a representation concerning the nature, quality, characteristics, quantity, origin, or suitability for a particular purpose of goods or services is presented. This includes, but is not limited to, visual depictions, textual descriptions, audio statements, and any combination thereof. A trade description manner shall be deemed deceptive if it contains false information or omits material facts which are likely to create a misleading impression in the minds of consumers as provided herein. Nothing in this definition shall preclude the application of other relevant provisions under this Act relating to unfair practices.

An application for registration of a trade mark may include a specification of the manner in which the trade marks appear on the goods or their packaging. Such specification shall describe the colours used, the materials employed, and any particular features distinguishing the trade mark’s presentation. The Registrar may require amendments to this description if it is deemed unclear, ambiguous, or fails to accurately reflect the applied-for trade mark. Further, a trade description manner specified in an application shall be consistent with representations made elsewhere within the application documents concerning the goods or services for which registration is sought. Any alteration to the registered trade mark’s appearance subsequent to registration must adhere to this initial specification, subject to approval by the Registrar.

Where a proprietor institutes proceedings under this Act alleging an infringement of their registered trademark, it shall be sufficient cause for relief if it is demonstrated that the defendant has used a false trade description in connection with goods or services. Such a false trade description includes any representation, whether by words, figures, marks, signs, or otherwise, falsely indicating the nature, quality, origin, characteristics, or suitability of those goods or services. The proprietor may seek an injunction restraining the infringing use, as well as damages sustained by reason of the infringement, subject to limitations imposed under this Act concerning contributory infringements. Further, the court may order the delivery up of all goods bearing the false trade description manner and materials used in their manufacture for destruction.

Where a proprietor seeks registration of a trade mark incorporating a descriptive term, the Registrar shall require evidence demonstrating that, at the time of application, such term was widely accepted by the relevant consumer base as an indication of origin or quality. This requirement applies particularly when the proposed trade mark incorporates a *trade description manner* relating to the characteristics, properties, or intended use of the goods or services. The proprietor must submit affidavits from industry experts and documented market research confirming this widespread acceptance. Failure to provide satisfactory evidence shall constitute grounds for refusal under this Act. An appeal against such a decision may be made to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days of the order’s communication. The Board's determination shall be final, subject to further judicial review on limited grounds as provided herein.

Where a proprietor seeks registration of a trade mark encompassing a descriptive term relating to the character or quality of goods or services, such application shall be accompanied by evidence demonstrating acquired distinctiveness. This evidence must satisfy the Registrar that, as a result of the applicant’s activities in marketing and promoting the goods or services under the proposed trade mark, a substantial portion of the relevant public recognizes the trade mark as an indicator of origin, not merely a descriptive feature. The *trade description manner* in which the goods or services are presented to consumers shall be considered by the Registrar when assessing this acquired distinctiveness; representations utilizing solely the descriptive element will not suffice. Provided that the applicant fails to submit adequate evidence, the application may be rejected.

Where a registered trade mark is used in a manner that misrepresents the nature, quality, or origin of goods or services, and such use constitutes a false trade description, an appeal may be filed before the relevant Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. The Registrar shall investigate complaints regarding deceptive practices concerning the trade description manner employed by any person, including but not limited to alterations to packaging or misleading advertising campaigns. It is provided that the aggrieved party must demonstrate demonstrable consumer confusion arising directly from the challenged use. Further, a finding of deceptive intent shall be presumed where the similarity between the registered mark and the impugned representation creates an immediate likelihood of association in the minds of ordinary consumers.

Where a proprietor utilizes a trade description manner in advertising goods or services, such description shall be deemed accurate and not misleading only if it conforms to established industry standards as recognized by the relevant sectoral authority. Provided that, where ambiguity exists regarding said standards, a member appointed bench of the Intellectual Property Appellate Board may determine the prevailing practice for purposes of this section. Further, any alteration to the trade description manner after registration shall require prior approval from the Registrar, and such approval will be granted only if it is demonstrated that the change does not materially affect the distinctive character or reputation associated with the mark under this Act. Failure to comply with these conditions renders the proprietor liable for penalties as provided herein.

Any individual found to falsely apply goods with a registered trademark, or a mark readily identifiable as such, shall be liable for damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the trademark owner and any consequential financial detriment. Such application includes affixing, imprinting, embroidering, painting, or in any other manner representing the trademark upon any article whatsoever offered for sale, or exposed for hire or reward. The Court may order seizure and destruction of goods so marked, as provided herein. Further, a first offence shall attract a minimum penalty of fifty thousand rupees, escalating to one hundred thousand rupees for subsequent violations. This liability extends where the false application is intended to deceive or likely to cause confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or quality of those goods.

Where the owner of a registered trademark grants a license permitting the use of such trademark upon specific goods, and subsequently assigns the entire undertaking relating to those goods to another party, any subsequent application of the trademark by the assignee shall be deemed valid only if accompanied by an express endorsement from the original licensor. This provision is subject to the condition that the licensing agreement explicitly outlines the scope of permissible use and transferability. Furthermore, a person shall be deemed to falsely apply goods bearing a registered trade mark where they utilize the mark in connection with goods not covered under any existing license or assignment, without obtaining prior written consent from both the trademark proprietor and the assignor, provided that such usage creates a likelihood of confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of the goods.

Any individual or entity found to falsely apply goods bearing a registered trademark in a manner calculated to deceive or likely to cause confusion amongst consumers shall be liable for damages as determined by the relevant adjudicating authority. Such liability extends to instances where the infringing application exploits the reputation and goodwill associated with the genuine mark, irrespective of intent. Further, any copyright society collecting royalties on behalf of creators may pursue civil remedies against those engaging in such false applications, recovering lost licensing fees and punitive damages not exceeding ten times the value of goods affected. Repeated or egregious violations shall attract enhanced penalties including imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and fines up to one million rupees, as provided herein.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is refused under this Act on the ground that it conflicts with a prior registered trade mark, and the applicant subsequently uses a sign in commerce which incorporates elements of both the applied-for mark and the earlier conflicting mark, such use shall be deemed falsify trade if it creates a likelihood of confusion among consumers regarding the origin or affiliation of goods or services. Provided that, where the use is solely for descriptive purposes relating to the characteristics of the goods or services and does not function as a trade mark in itself, this provision shall not apply. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating consumer perception to determine whether such a likelihood exists, subject to principles of natural justice.

Where a registered trade mark is used in a manner that creates a false or misleading impression concerning the nature, quality, origin, characteristics, or suitability for their intended purpose of goods or services, the owner shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief under this Act. Such use shall be deemed falsify trade if it exploits the reputation and goodwill associated with the registered mark, regardless of whether the defendant intends to deceive consumers. The proprietor may also claim damages proportionate to the loss suffered by them as a consequence of such deceptive conduct. Provided that, nothing in this section shall prevent the fair description or accurate representation of goods or services offered for sale. Further, any person found guilty of falsify trade is liable to prosecution and penalties as provided herein.

Where an individual, through the use of a sign identical or confusingly similar to a registered trademark, induces consumer confusion regarding the origin, quality, or characteristics of goods or services, such actions shall constitute a deemed falsify trade. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint from any aggrieved party demonstrating reasonable likelihood of deception amongst consumers, initiate inquiries under this Act. Such inquiries will involve notice to the alleged infringer and an opportunity for them to present their defense. If, following due process and consideration of all evidence presented, the Registrar finds that a deemed falsify trade has occurred, they may issue an order directing the cessation of the infringing activity and potentially award damages commensurate with the loss suffered by the trademark proprietor. The aggrieved party shall have recourse to appeal any such decision before the relevant appellate authority as provided herein.

Where an advertisement prominently features a representation concerning the qualities or characteristics of goods or services, and such representation is demonstrably false or misleading, it shall be considered an act of deemed falsify trade under this Act. This determination is subject to review by the relevant adjudicating authority, which may consider evidence presented by both the complainant and the respondent regarding the veracity of the claim. Provided that, a finding of deemed falsify trade does not automatically imply intent to deceive; negligence in substantiating claims may be sufficient grounds for adjudication. Any party aggrieved by such an order may appeal to the appellate forum as provided herein, presenting arguments challenging the factual basis or legal reasoning underlying the original decision.

Where the registered proprietor of a trade mark grants a license conferring rights to use the mark in relation to specified goods or services, such license may include a provision permitting the assignment of those licensed rights to a third party. Provided that any assignment shall be made in writing and duly executed by both the licensor and assignee, and registered with the Trade Marks Registry as provided herein. Further, where an authorized user, acting under a contract assigning trade mark usage rights, subsequently engages in activities which demonstrably undermine the distinctiveness of the mark or create confusion amongst consumers, it shall be deemed falsify trade, irrespective of whether such actions were explicitly prohibited within the assignment agreement. A party proceeding with the unauthorized use of a licensed trade mark following termination of the license agreement may face legal action for damages and injunctive relief.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act on the ground that the proposed mark, if registered, would likely cause confusion in the minds of the public with respect to any existing marks, and where such opposition alleges that the applicant’s use or intended use of the mark constitutes a deemed falsify trade, the Appellate Board may, upon hearing both parties, determine whether the alleged deceptive similarity is substantial enough to warrant refusal of registration. It shall be open to the applicant to demonstrate through evidence of actual consumer perception that no such confusion exists, notwithstanding any formal similarities between the marks. The Board’s decision on an india application regarding this matter shall be final, subject to appeal before the High Court within a period of sixty days from the date of the order.

A trademark, once registered under this Act, shall remain valid for a period of ten years from the date of registration, and is renewable indefinitely in successive periods of ten years each, subject to payment of the prescribed fees. The right conferred by registration is deemed falsify trade if any person, knowing that a similar mark is already registered in relation to identical or closely related goods or services, adopts or uses such a mark with intent to deceive or cause confusion amongst consumers. Such adoption shall be considered a violation, and the proprietor of the registered trademark may seek injunctive relief and damages as provided herein. The right to a registered trade mark is freely transmissible, whether by way of assignment or operation of law, subject to any conditions stipulated in the instrument of transfer.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is refused under this Act, and such refusal is based on grounds relating to prior use or reputation of an identical or similar mark by another party, the Registrar shall provide notice thereof to the claimant alleging prior rights. The notice shall specify the particulars of the alleged prior use and any evidence submitted in support thereof. Upon receipt of such notice, the applicant may submit a written response refuting the claims and presenting counter-evidence. If, following consideration of all submissions, the Registrar remains satisfied that the existence of prior use or reputation would likely cause confusion amongst consumers, the trade mark shall be deemed falsify trade if its adoption unfairly capitalizes upon the established goodwill associated with the earlier mark. Any transfer assignment vice relating to rights claimed in opposition proceedings shall be subject to approval by the Registrar and filed within thirty days of such assignment.

For the purposes of this Act, "effect registered trade" means the visual representation of a registered trade mark as it appears on any goods or their packaging, including but not limited to labels, cartons, and promotional materials. The depiction shall accurately reflect the form of the mark as entered in the Register of Trade Marks; provided that minor variations necessitated by the nature of the goods or packaging are permissible, subject to ensuring there is no likelihood of confusion amongst consumers. Any alteration which misrepresents the registered trade mark or its distinctive character constitutes an "effect registered trade" violation under this Act and may be subject to remedies as provided herein.

Where any person has made use of a registered trade mark in contravention of the rights conferred by registration, and such use has resulted in damage to the reputation or goodwill associated with the registered trade mark, the owner shall be entitled to seek damages from the offending party. The amount of damages shall be determined having regard to all relevant circumstances, including but not limited to, the extent of the infringing use, the loss of profits suffered by the owner as a direct result of the infringement, and any other financial detriment incurred. Further, where the infringing activity constitutes an act of unfair competition under this Act, enhanced damages may be awarded at the discretion of the Court. The remedies available to the registered proprietor shall include an injunction restraining further use of the mark, and an order requiring the defendant to account for profits derived from the sale of goods or services bearing the effect registered trade mark.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is refused under this Act, the applicant may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be filed within three months from the date of communication of the order of refusal and shall state specifically the grounds on which the applicant relies. The Board may, after giving notice to all interested parties and affording them an opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify or reverse the decision appealed against. Any party aggrieved by any order passed by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board under this Act may appeal to the Supreme Court within sixty days from the date of such order. Consideration shall be given to whether the use of a sign creates confusion in relation to goods or services for which an earlier registered trade mark exists, and the effect registered trade marks have on consumer perception.

Any person who, knowing that a particular trade mark has been registered in India, uses such trade mark or any colourable imitation thereof in relation to goods or services for which registration has been made, shall be guilty of an offence. Such use includes applying the mark as a device or brand upon or in connection with any goods or services, or in any manner likely to cause confusion among the public regarding the origin or nature of those goods or services. Where the effect registered trade mark is employed deceptively, the offender shall be liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and also to a fine. The Court may, in determining the appropriate penalty, consider the extent of the deceptive use and any resulting damage to the reputation of the proprietor.

The owner of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to grant exclusive licences in respect of any goods or services for which the trade mark is registered, and such licence may be granted for a term not exceeding the remaining period of protection of the registration. Any assignment of the registered trade mark, or of the benefit of any registered trade mark, shall include all rights relating to use of the effect registered trade mark, unless the assignment expressly provides otherwise. Where an exclusive licence is granted, the licensee shall be deemed to be the proprietor for the purposes of suing for infringement only with respect to the goods or services specified in the licence agreement. The Registrar may require evidence of such licences and assignments to be filed, as provided herein, and may refuse registration if the terms are considered unduly restrictive.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is refused under this Act, the applicant may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. Such appeal shall be filed within three months from the date of communication of the order of refusal and shall state specifically the grounds on which the applicant relies. The Tribunal may allow or dismiss the appeal, or make such other order as it deems fit, provided that any decision altering the effect registered trade mark status granted to a prior user shall only be made after affording them an opportunity for hearing. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal may further appeal to the Supreme Court within sixty days from the date of that order.

For the purposes of this Act, “effect registered trade” means the visual representation of a registered trade mark as it appears on the register maintained under this Act, including any alterations or additions made thereto pursuant to lawful authority. The depiction shall accurately reflect the particulars specified in the provisional specification completed at the time of application for registration, and may include details concerning colour, material, or other distinctive features explicitly described therein. Any subsequent modification to the registered trade mark, subject to provisions regarding rectification proceedings, will be recorded as a new “effect registered trade” replacing the prior depiction.

Where any person, without due cause and subject to the provisions regarding fair use under this Act, applies a false trademark identical or confusingly similar to a registered trade mark in relation to goods or services for which the registration subsists, such person shall be liable for damages. The amount of damages shall be determined by considering the extent of the effect registered trade mark has suffered due to the infringing application and any profits made by the infringer attributable to the false trademark. Further, an aggrieved proprietor may apply to the relevant intellectual property tribunal for an injunction restraining the continuance of the infringing activity, provided that such application is made within three years from the date of first knowledge of the infringement. Application registration shall not preclude remedies available under this Act against acts of passing off or unfair competition.

For the purposes of this Act, “distinctiveness” with respect to a proposed trade mark shall be assessed considering its inherent ability to distinguish goods or services and the acquired distinctiveness it may possess through use. A trade mark shall not be deemed deceptively similar to an earlier mark under this Act if both marks relate to dissimilar goods or services, provided that such dissimilarity is clearly demonstrable to the satisfaction of the Registrar. The right conferred by registration of a trade mark shall include the exclusive right to use the mark throughout India in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered and to prevent use of an identical or confusingly similar mark by others who do not have consent, thereby protecting the mark registered respect.

An application for registration of a proposed trade mark shall be refused if the mark, when considered in relation to the goods or services with which it is associated, is deemed descriptive under this Act. However, an applicant may overcome such refusal by demonstrating acquired distinctiveness through extensive use and consumer recognition, provided that evidence substantiating such recognition is presented before the Registrar. The registration of a trade mark shall confer upon the registered proprietor the exclusive right to use the mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered; this right extends to preventing others from using any identical or confusingly similar mark. A mark registered respect of particular goods may be subject to limitation as to colour or other features, as determined by the Registrar.

The proprietor of a mark registered respect of goods or services shall be entitled to restrain the use of any representation which is likely to deceive or confuse the public as to the existence of an association, connection or affiliation between such proprietor and any person using it in relation to those goods or services. This right extends to preventing the application of identical or similar marks to goods or services that are identical or closely related to those for which the mark registered respect is used, where such use creates a likelihood of confusion. Provided that, nothing herein shall prevent the use of a trade description honestly applied in relation to those goods or services. Further, any person infringing under this Act may be ordered by the relevant authority to account for profits made from the infringement and to pay damages as deemed appropriate.

The Registrar may, upon application by the proprietor of a mark registered respect of goods or services, and after due notice to all interested parties as provided herein, direct the removal of any false or misleading statement appearing on any goods or their packaging. Such direction shall be binding if the statement creates a likelihood of confusion with another trade mark registered under this Act, or otherwise misrepresents the nature, quality, or origin of those goods. The proprietor seeking such direction must demonstrate that the infringing representation is being made without consent and causes demonstrable harm to the distinctiveness of their registered mark. Any party aggrieved by the Registrar’s order may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within a period of sixty days from the date of communication of the order.

Any person who, without due cause and with intent to deceive or injure, uses a trademark identical or confusingly similar to a mark registered respect of goods or services, shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall include not only direct pecuniary loss but also consequential losses reasonably foreseeable as a result of the infringing use. Where the infringement is established, the Court may order an injunction restraining the defendant from further acts of infringement and may require the destruction or disposal of any goods bearing the infringing mark. Furthermore, repeated or flagrant infringements may attract enhanced penalties, including imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, as provided herein.

The owner of a mark registered respect of goods or services may grant licenses conferring the right to use the mark exclusively within a defined geographical territory, provided that such license agreement specifies the duration and scope of permitted usage. Any assignment of the mark shall include all rights and obligations pertaining to prior licenses granted under this Act; furthermore, the assignor remains liable for any breach of those licensing agreements occurring before the date of assignment. Where a licensee uses the mark in a manner inconsistent with the terms of the license, the owner may pursue remedies available under contract law, without prejudice to their right to initiate proceedings concerning trademark infringement. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all assignments and licenses relating to marks registered respect of goods or services, accessible for public inspection upon payment of prescribed fees.

Where an appeal lies against a decision of the Registrar refusing registration of a proposed trade mark, the Appellate Board may allow such appeal if it finds that the Registrar erred in interpreting the provisions relating to distinctiveness, or failed to consider material evidence presented by the applicant. The Board shall not be bound by any finding arrived at by the Registrar but may affirm, reverse, or modify the decision appealed from. It is provided that a mark registered respect of goods or services shall not be deemed invalid solely on the grounds that it is descriptive of those goods or services if, through use in trade subsequent to registration, it has acquired distinctiveness indicating its association exclusively with the applicant. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Appellate Board may further appeal to the High Court.

For the purposes of this Act, “licensed user” means any person who has obtained from the owner of a registered trade mark permission to use such mark under a licence agreement, and includes a broadcasting organisation shall be deemed a licensed user where it uses a mark in respect of broadcasts relating to goods or services for which the mark is registered. A mark registered respect of particular goods or services shall not be deemed to be registered in relation to any other goods or services unless specifically indicated as such on the register, provided that use of the mark in association with related goods may constitute registration under this Act subject to conditions prescribed herein.

For the purposes of this Act, “distinctiveness” with respect to a proposed trade mark shall be determined by considering its inherent capacity to distinguish goods or services of one undertaking from those of others, and whether, when used in relation to those goods or services, it has acquired secondary meaning in the relevant market. A trade mark shall be deemed deceptively similar to an earlier registered trade mark if, due to their similarity, a substantial likelihood exists that the relevant consuming public will associate the later mark with the prior one, leading to confusion or damage to the reputation of the respect registered trade mark. This assessment shall take into account all relevant factors including visual appearance, phonetic resemblance and conceptual similarities.

An application for registration of a proposed trade mark shall be refused if the marks applied for, or any combination thereof, are identical or confusingly similar to an earlier registered trade mark used in relation to identical or closely related goods or services. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish such information as he deems necessary to ascertain the distinctiveness of the proposed trade mark and its potential impact on existing rights. Where a trade mark is sought to be registered which includes respect registered trade marks, the application shall include details regarding any licensing agreements pertaining to those underlying marks. Further, the Registrar may direct that certain disclaimers are incorporated into the register concerning elements of the applied-for mark if they lack inherent distinctiveness.

The proprietor of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to an injunction restraining the use by any person of a sign identical or confusingly similar to the registered trade mark in relation to goods or services identical or closely related to those in respect of which the registered trade mark is registered, provided that such use constitutes infringement under this Act. Further, where damage has been caused to the proprietor by reason of the infringing use, he shall be entitled to claim damages from the infringer, subject to limitations as may be prescribed by rules made under this Act. The Court may also order the delivery up or destruction of goods bearing the infringing sign, and any materials used in making such goods. Any false representation concerning respect registered trade marks shall be deemed a civil wrong actionable at the suit of the aggrieved party.

An application for registration of a proposed trade mark shall be refused if the marks applied for, taken as a whole or in combination, are deemed descriptive of the goods or services with which they seek to be associated. The Registrar may require an applicant to furnish such further information and documentary proof as he deems necessary to ascertain whether the requirements of this Act have been fulfilled. Where any objection is raised by a third party against the registration of a trade mark, the objector shall file a written statement setting out the grounds for their opposition. Such objections must be addressed in writing by the applicant within the time specified under this Act. The Registrar shall provide both parties with an opportunity to present arguments and evidence relating to respect registered trade marks. Decisions regarding oppositions will be made based on the merits of the case, as provided herein.

Any proprietor seeking to utilize a registered trade mark in connection with goods or services shall ensure such use does not create confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of those goods or services. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint demonstrating demonstrable misrepresentation concerning respect registered trade marks, initiate an inquiry into whether the said usage constitutes unfair competition under this Act. Provided that, any entity claiming infringement must demonstrate actual damage resulting from the unauthorized application of the mark. Further, where the proprietor has demonstrably altered the character or quality of the goods bearing the registered trade mark, such alteration shall be deemed a material change and may invalidate subsequent claims regarding identical usage.

The owner of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to grant licenses conferring rights to use the respect registered trade mark in relation to specified goods or services. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and the terms thereof shall be determined at the discretion of the grantor, subject to any conditions stipulated under this Act regarding fair competition. Any assignment of a registered trade mark, whether partial or complete, including assignments relating to licensed use, requires registration with the Trade Marks Registry, and such registration shall be deemed conclusive evidence of the transfer of rights as provided herein. Further, where a license is assigned, the assignee shall possess all the same rights and obligations pertaining to the original licensee, subject to any limitations expressly stated in the original licensing agreement. The Registrar may require submission of detailed documentation substantiating the scope and duration of such licenses or assignments.

An appeal lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal from any order passed by the Registrar under this Act refusing registration of a proposed trade mark, provided that the appellant demonstrates demonstrable prejudice resulting directly from the refusal. The Tribunal may entertain such an appeal if it is satisfied that the grounds presented challenge the Registrar’s interpretation of distinctiveness or likelihood of confusion as applied to the relevant goods or services. Further, any party aggrieved by a decision of the Tribunal affirming respect registered trade marks may petition the Supreme Court on a question of law arising out of the order. The Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal shall give notice to all parties before issuing any such determination and may direct further evidence be submitted as it deems necessary for just resolution.

An application for the registration of a trade mark shall include a provisional specification claim detailing the goods and services in relation to which the applicant seeks protection. Such a claim must be clear, concise, and reasonably specific, reflecting the intended scope of exclusive rights sought under this Act. The Trade Marks Registry may require further clarification or amendment of the provisional specification claim if it is deemed ambiguous or overly broad. Failure to adequately define the goods and services at the time of application may prejudice the applicant’s ability to assert respect registered trade marks in subsequent enforcement proceedings. Any alteration to the goods and services listed within a provisional specification claim after its initial submission shall be subject to review by the Registry, which may require supporting documentation demonstrating continued relevance and distinctiveness.

The owner of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to grant licenses conferring rights to use the mark in relation to specified goods or services. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and the terms thereof shall be governed by contract law as applicable. Any assignment of the registered trade mark, or any license granted under this Act, requires registration with the Trade Marks Registry, subject to a prescribed fee. The Registrar may refuse registration of an assignment or license if it appears that the proposed assignee or licensee has no locus standi to claim respect registered trade in the mark, particularly where such claims are predicated upon overlapping patent India claims relating to processes utilized in manufacturing goods bearing the mark. Further, any sub-license granted shall also be registrable and subject to similar scrutiny as provided herein.

An application for registration of a trademark shall be deemed refused if, upon investigation, it appears that the mark bears a substantial similarity to an earlier registered trademark or a well-known trademark used in relation to identical or similar goods or services. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating distinctiveness acquired through use subsequent to the date of the earlier registration. Where any person alleges that another has infringed upon a registered trade mark, and initiates proceedings before a court, the accused offence section shall apply; it is incumbent on the defendant to demonstrate reasonable grounds for believing their use did not constitute infringement, considering factors such as consumer perception and potential confusion. Provided that this does not preclude fair dealing or descriptive use under this Act.

Any proprietor who discovers that any person has contravened section 51 of this Act shall be entitled to institute appropriate proceedings for damages and seek an injunction restraining further infringement. Where a person is found, upon investigation by the Registrar or through civil suit, to have used a mark identical or confusingly similar to a registered trade mark without due cause, they shall be liable to pay compensation reflecting lost profits attributable to the infringing use, as determined by the Court. Further, such an accused offence section will trigger a mandatory review of all related registrations held by the infringer and may result in their cancellation if found to have been obtained through fraudulent means or misrepresentation. The Registrar may also impose a penalty not exceeding five lakhs of rupees for each day the infringing activity continues.

For the purposes of this Act, an “accused offence” shall mean any act or omission constituting a violation of section 27, section 29, section 30, or section 51, as provided herein. Where such an accused offence is alleged to have been committed by a corporate entity, the responsibility for the said offence shall be deemed to lie upon the directors, managers, and other officers of the corporation who were directly involved in the decision-making process leading to the infringement. Nothing in this definition shall preclude the imposition of liability on any individual or entity beyond those specifically identified as being part of that decision-making process, subject to demonstrating their direct participation in the accused offence.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed refused if, upon investigation, it appears that the applicant has knowingly adopted a mark identical or confusingly similar to an existing registered trade mark used in relation to goods or services identical or closely related to those for which registration is sought. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating due diligence exercised in ascertaining prior registrations and usage. Where such failure constitutes an *accused offence*, the proprietor of the earlier trade mark shall be entitled to seek remedies under this Act, including but not limited to damages and injunctive relief. Provided that, a good faith belief by the applicant regarding non-infringement shall be considered as a mitigating factor during proceedings.
