Where an application for registration of a utility model is granted under this Act, the Controller may specify conditions regarding the manufacture, use, or exploitation of the registered utility model, provided that such conditions are reasonable and do not unduly restrain competition. Any condition declared unlawful by order of the Intellectual Property Appellate Board shall be deemed null and void from the date of such order; however, registration remains valid subject to any modifications directed by the Board. The applicant for registration shall furnish an affidavit verifying compliance with all specified conditions at the time of renewal application. Failure to adhere to a lawful condition may result in suspension or revocation of the utility model’s registration as provided herein.

Where an invention is granted patent protection under this Act and a condition attached to the grant restricts competition in a manner deemed detrimental to public interest, the Controller may, following due inquiry and notice to the patentee, declare such condition unlawful. Any party aggrieved by a declaration made under this provision may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days of receipt of notification of the order. The Board shall consider representations from all interested parties before affirming, reversing or modifying the Controller’s determination. Further, where a condition declared unlawful involves an unreasonable tying arrangement for a complementary product, the patentee shall be liable to pay damages proportionate to the loss suffered by affected licensees and consumers. This liability is without prejudice to any other remedies available under contract law.

Where an application for patent is granted subject to a condition imposed under this Act, and such condition relates to the use of the invention in respect of any particular field, the Controller may, upon receiving a representation from any person aggrieved by the imposition of that condition, direct the revision thereof. Such direction shall be accompanied by notice served upon the patentee, affording them an opportunity to make representations against the proposed modification or removal of the condition. The Controller shall consider all submissions received and issue an order either confirming, modifying, or revoking the imposed condition. A condition declared unlawful under this Act due to its discriminatory effect on competition may be subject to immediate revocation without prior notice to the patentee if it is deemed a matter of urgency affecting public interest. Appeals against orders issued by the Controller concerning conditions shall lie before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Where an application for patent is granted subject to a condition requiring the licensee to manufacture in India a quantity equivalent to twelve per centum of the total production, and such manufacturing obligation is not fulfilled within three years from the date of grant, the Controller may issue a notice to the patentee. The notice shall specify the shortfall in manufactured quantities and provide thirty days for compliance or submission of reasons for non-compliance. Failure to adequately address this deficiency, as determined by the Controller, constitutes a condition declared unlawful under this Act. Further, if it is demonstrated that the imposed manufacturing requirement was intended to create an undue restraint on trade or unfairly prejudice competition within India, the patent may be liable for revocation upon application made by any interested party.

Where any patent is granted subject to a condition declared unlawful under this Act, and such condition relates to the manufacture, use, or disposal of the patented invention in a manner that restricts competition or creates an undue burden on other persons seeking to engage in similar activities, the Controller may, upon application by an aggrieved party, issue an order declaring the patent revoked to the extent necessary to remove the unlawful condition. Any person found to have violated such an order shall be liable to pay damages equivalent to three times the lost profits reasonably attributable to the infringement, and further subject to imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years. The Central Government may also initiate proceedings under the Competition Act for anti-competitive practices arising from the enforcement of the patent.

Where an invention is granted patent protection under this Act and a condition imposed as part of the terms of grant relates to the utilization of the patented invention for purposes deemed beneficial to public health or national security, such condition shall be considered a condition declared unlawful if it demonstrably restricts competition within the relevant market. This determination may be challenged by any aggrieved party through appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. Provided that, the appellant must demonstrate with clear and convincing evidence that the imposed condition operates as an unreasonable restraint of trade or creates a monopolistic advantage contrary to the principles enshrined in this Act. The burden of proof regarding such unlawfulness shall rest upon the appellant.

Where any patent is granted subject to a condition declared unlawful under this Act, and such condition relates to the manufacture, use, or disposal of the patented invention, any person infringing upon the rights conferred by the patent shall be liable for damages proportionate to the extent of such infringement. The Controller may, acting on complaint from an aggrieved party, issue an injunction restraining further acts of infringement where it is established that the unlawful condition has been imposed as a barrier to competition or to unduly restrict access to the patented invention. Further, any entity found to have wilfully induced infringement in violation of this provision shall be subject to enhanced penalties as determined by the Controller, considering the impact on public interest and technological advancement.

Where an application for registration of a geographical indication is opposed on the ground that its use would be contrary to morality or public order, or would otherwise constitute a condition declared unlawful under this Act, the Appellate Board shall hear and determine such opposition. The Board may, after affording the applicant and the opponent a reasonable opportunity of being heard, dismiss the opposition if it finds that the alleged unlawfulness is unsubstantiated; however, should the Board find merit in the objection raised by the geographical indication plaintiff, registration shall be refused or, where already granted, revoked. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Appellate Board may appeal to the High Court within a period of sixty days from the date of such order.

For the purposes of this Act, "goods" includes not only commodities but also raw materials, manufactured articles, and services offered to consumers. A “trade mark” is defined as a mark capable of distinguishing goods of one undertaking from those of other undertakings and may include words, names, symbols, or any combination thereof. The term "service mark" shall be construed as a trade mark used to identify and distinguish the provision of services. Any representation which does not fulfil the requirements for registration as a trade mark under this Act is deemed not to be a trade marks act 1999, irrespective of its usage in commerce or perception by consumers.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall contain such particulars as are necessary for identifying the trade mark and clearly defining the goods or services in relation to which it is used or proposed to be used. The applicant shall furnish along with the application, a representation of the trade marks being sought for registration, conforming to the requirements prescribed under this Act. Where the trade mark includes a device or logo, a specimen showing the use of the trade mark on goods or their packaging shall also be submitted. Any alteration made to an already registered *marks act 1999* after its initial acceptance is subject to approval by the Registrar and may require further examination as provided herein.

Where an owner of a registered trade mark institutes legal proceedings under this Act concerning infringement or breach of contract relating to the trade mark, the court may, subject to the provisions herein, grant such relief as it deems just and equitable. This includes, but is not limited to, injunctions restraining further acts of infringement, damages for past infringements, and an account of profits made by the infringer. The measure of damages shall be determined having regard to the loss suffered by the owner as a result of the infringement, or where that cannot be ascertained, the profit made by the infringing party. Further, any contract relating to a trade mark which contains terms inconsistent with this Marks Act 1999 shall be deemed void to the extent of such inconsistency.

An application for registration of a trademark under this Act shall contain a clear representation of the mark applied for. Such representation must comply with the prescribed standards regarding colour or three-dimensional features, provided that where the mark includes devices or colours, the applicant shall furnish a description of such devices or colours as are essential to identify the mark. The Registrar may require amendments to an application if it appears deficient in clarity or fails to adequately describe the elements constituting the trademark. Further, any proposed trademark which is deemed deceptive under this Act, or likely to cause confusion with existing registered marks, shall be subject to objection and potential rejection by the Registrar. This determination shall consider prevailing consumer understanding and industry practices relating to trademarks act 1999.

Any person who, having knowledge of registered marks under this Act, makes use of an identical mark or a mark which is deceptively similar to a registered mark in connection with goods or services for which the registration has been made, shall be liable to pay damages. Such damages shall be assessed by the Commercial Court and may include compensation for loss of profits, dilution of goodwill, and any other consequential losses suffered by the proprietor of the trade marks. Further, where an infringement is established, the court may order the infringer to account for all profits derived from the infringing use, subject to a statutory cap as determined by the Central Government. The Registrar shall also be empowered to issue injunctions against continued deceptive practices relating to the Marks Act 1999.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark under this Act may grant a license to use the trade mark to another person, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated in the licensing agreement. Such agreements shall clearly define the scope of permitted usage, geographical limitations, and duration of the license. The grantor retains ownership of the trade marks act 1999 and any subsequent registrations derived therefrom; however, the licensee may assign their rights under the license to a third party with prior written consent from the grantor, provided that such assignment does not prejudice existing obligations or alter the fundamental nature of the licensed use. Further, where a trade mark is subject to multiple licenses, priority among licensees shall be determined by the date upon which the respective licensing agreements were executed and registered with the competent authority as prescribed herein.

For the purposes of this Act, "description means trade" shall include any representation, indication, or suggestion relating to the nature, quality, characteristics, origin, quantity, or intended purpose of goods or services. Such a description is deemed misleading if it deceives or is likely to deceive the public regarding the identity of the source of the goods or services. A depiction employing fanciful imagery, provided that such imagery directly and unambiguously conveys information about the aforementioned attributes, shall also be considered within this definition. This understanding applies irrespective of whether the representation is expressed in words, symbols, marks, figures, shapes, colours, sounds, or any combination thereof, as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, "description means trade" shall include any visual representation, symbol, letter, word, phrase, numeral, shape, configuration, colour, or combination thereof adopted by a proprietor for distinguishing their goods or services from those of others. Such description may incorporate elements suggestive of the nature, quality, or characteristics of the goods or services, provided that such suggestion does not directly and unequivocally identify the goods or services themselves. The Registrar shall consider applications for registration of trade marks containing descriptive matter only if the applicant demonstrates acquired distinctiveness through extensive use and consumer recognition, as evidenced by market surveys and sales figures. Any alteration to a registered description means trade without the consent of the proprietor shall be deemed an infringement under this Act.

Where an owner of a registered trade mark institutes proceedings under this Act for infringement, and establishes that the defendant has used in connection with goods or services a sign containing a false trade description, the Court may grant such remedy or remedies as it deems just and equitable. For the purposes of determining whether a sign contains a false trade description, “description means trade” and shall include any indication which is likely to be understood by consumers as an attribute of the goods or services, including their geographical origin, mode of manufacture, quality, or intended purpose. The Court may also order the defendant to account for profits made from the infringing use, subject to limitations imposed under this Act regarding calculation of damages. Further, any false trade description used in contravention of these provisions shall be deemed a misrepresentation actionable at law and the remedies available for such misrepresentation shall apply accordingly.

For the purposes of this Act, “description means trade” shall be interpreted to encompass any representation, explicit or implied, concerning the nature, quality, characteristics, origin, or suitability for a particular purpose of goods or services offered for sale. Such representations are deemed to constitute a trade description when they directly relate to commercial activities and influence consumer perception regarding the value or utility of those goods or services. The Registrar may require any person utilizing such a representation to provide documentary evidence substantiating its accuracy, subject to due process and affording an opportunity for hearing. Failure to comply with this requirement shall render the individual liable to penalties as provided herein. Any trade description found to be false or misleading, whether intentionally or negligently employed, is actionable under this Act and may result in civil remedies available to aggrieved parties.

For the purposes of this Act, "description means trade" shall be interpreted to encompass all representations made concerning the nature, quality, characteristics, origin, and suitability for a particular purpose of goods or services offered for sale. Such representations, whether expressed verbally, graphically, or through any other medium, are deemed descriptions within the meaning of this Act if they create an impression in the mind of the consumer regarding the identity or attributes of those goods or services. Provided that, a representation shall not be considered a description unless it is likely to induce purchasers to believe them concerning the origin or production process of the goods. Any alteration made to such representations with intent to deceive consumers shall also be subject to penalties as provided herein.

Where any person applies a false trade description to any goods or services offered for sale, or makes use of any false representation in connection with the sale thereof, such person shall be deemed guilty of an offence under this Act. For the purposes of this provision, “description means trade” and includes any indication which is likely to mislead as to the nature, quality, characteristics, origin, suitability or other aspect of the goods or services. Any infringement of this section shall attract a penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees, and in the case of a second or subsequent offence, not less than one million rupees. Furthermore, where an offence occurs repeatedly, the court may order the seizure and destruction of the infringing goods.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any proprietor of a registered trade mark may grant a license to use such trade mark in relation to specified goods or services. Such licenses shall be assignable, either wholly or partially, along with the underlying rights pertaining thereto, provided that the assignee obtains registration of the assignment under this Act within six months from the date of transfer. Where a license is granted for a term less than the unexpired period of the trade mark registration, the licensee may, subject to fulfilling all conditions precedent as stipulated in the license agreement, sub-license the right to use the trade mark. For the purposes of this Act, “description means trade” and includes any representation or indication used to distinguish goods from those of others. Any transfer of a sub-license shall be deemed an assignment requiring registration.

For the purposes of this Act, “description means trade” shall be interpreted liberally and with due regard to consumer perception; provided that, where an entity utilizes a visual representation purporting to indicate the origin, quality, or characteristics of goods, such representation constitutes a description within the meaning of this Act even if lacking explicit textual claims. An appeal against any order determining whether a particular depiction qualifies as a misleading trade description may be made to the Appellate Intellectual Property Tribunal; however, such appeal shall only be entertained where it is demonstrated that the original determination was manifestly arbitrary or based on an erroneous interpretation of established legal principles concerning deceptive advertising practices and consumer detriment.

Where an objection is raised under this Act against the registration of a proposed trade mark on the ground that the said mark consists exclusively of a descriptive term, the Registrar shall give notice thereof to the applicant and any interested party. Such interested party may, within the time specified in the notice, file with the Registrar written representations explaining why the objection should prevail. The Registrar shall consider such representations and the response, if any, from the applicant, and may require both parties to submit further documentary evidence or attend a hearing. For the purposes of this Act, a “description means trade” where it directly conveys the nature, quality, characteristics, or intended purpose of goods or services, irrespective of its literal accuracy. The Registrar’s decision shall be published in the Official Gazette.

For the purposes of this Act, “description means trade” shall be interpreted liberally to encompass all representations concerning the nature, quality, characteristics, origin, and suitability for a particular purpose of goods or services offered for sale. Any depiction, symbol, name, model, or other mark employed in relation to such goods or services, whether registered or not, is deemed part of this description. This definition extends to include claims made regarding the manufacturing process or materials used, provided that these relate directly to consumer perception and purchasing decisions. Furthermore, a representation concerning a patented article shall be considered a trade description under this Act if it falsely suggests an association with the patent holder or implies superior quality derived from patent protection.

For the purposes of this Act, “trade description” means an affirmation, statement, or indication, whether in words, figures, symbols, marks, labels, designs, illustrations, or any other form whatsoever, which is used to describe the nature, quality, characteristics, quantity, origin, ingredients, properties, capabilities, style, grade, condition, or suitability for a particular purpose of goods or services. A trade description shall be deemed to include representations relating to the geographical origin of goods; and where a trade description denotes that goods are manufactured in a specific region, such designation must accurately reflect the place of manufacture as provided herein.

Where any person applies a trade description to goods or provides services in such a manner as to mislead the public concerning the nature, quality or origin of those goods or services, such person shall be deemed to have committed an offence under this Act. For the purposes of this provision, *trade description denotes* particulars relating to the goods or services, including their quantity, size, weight, characteristics, suitability for a particular purpose, value and mode of manufacture or packaging. Any individual found guilty of employing a false trade description shall be liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with a fine which may extend to fifty thousand rupees, or both. Furthermore, any goods bearing such misleading descriptions are subject to seizure and forfeiture as provided herein.

Where a proprietor of a registered trademark, hereinafter referred to as the “licensor”, elects to grant a license for the use of their mark, such license may be assigned to any person, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated in the original licensing agreement. The licensor shall retain the right to specify the geographical area within which the licensee or assignee may utilize the trade description associated with the registered trademark. Furthermore, the licensor may impose restrictions on the quality control measures employed by the licensee or assignee to ensure consistency with the reputation of the mark. Any subsequent assignment of a license requires notification to the Registrar within thirty days, accompanied by prescribed fees. The Registrar shall publish notice of such assignment for public inspection. This provision applies where the trade description denotes origin or intended purpose of goods and services.

Where a registered trade mark is used in relation to goods or services other than those for which it is registered, any person aggrieved may file a complaint before the appropriate forum as provided herein. Such complaints must specify the nature and extent of the alleged misuse and demonstrate resultant damage to the reputation or goodwill associated with the registered trade mark. The Registrar shall, upon receiving such a complaint, issue notice to the respondent and afford them an opportunity to be heard. Following due deliberation, the Registrar may order the cessation of the infringing use, subject to just considerations and equitable remedies. Any determination made by the Registrar regarding the scope of permissible usage or the assessment of damages shall be determined registrar accordance with principles of fairness and proportionality, ensuring adequate protection for both the proprietor and the public interest.

The application for registration of a trade mark, if accompanied by any representation of the trade mark, shall be examined by the Registrar to ascertain whether the mark is capable of distinguishing the goods or services of the applicant from those of others. Where an objection arises under this Act concerning the distinctiveness of a proposed trade mark, the Registrar shall issue a notice specifying the grounds for such objection and afford the applicant an opportunity to submit their response in writing within the prescribed time. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further information or documents relevant to the assessment of the application. Any decision made by the Registrar concerning the acceptance or rejection of an application, or regarding any procedural matter arising under this Act, shall be determined registrar accordance with principles of natural justice and documented for record.

Any person who, without due cause and after written notice from the Trade Marks Registry specifying the grounds for objection, continues to use a trade mark identical or deceptively similar to a registered trade mark in respect of goods or services for which the registration is valid shall be liable to pay a penalty of not less than fifty thousand rupees and may also be ordered to deliver up for destruction all infringing materials. The amount of such penalty may be increased by an additional ten thousand rupees for each day during which the infringement persists following a final warning issued by the Registrar. Determination of whether due cause exists shall be determined registrar accordance with principles of fair trade and consumer protection, as provided herein.

The owner of a registered trade mark shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, be entitled to grant licences for the use of the said trade mark, and may assign the entire interest in the registration, including any associated goodwill. Any such licence agreement shall clearly specify the geographical area within which the licensee is permitted to utilize the trade mark, as well as the specific goods or services to which the usage pertains. Further, a license granted under this Act shall be revocable by the owner upon written notice of default in performance of contractual obligations, provided that such notice allows for a period of thirty days for rectification. The determination of whether a licensee’s activities constitute permissible use, or an infringement of the registered trade mark rights, shall be determined registrar accordance with established principles of fair competition and consumer protection as provided herein.

The determination of whether a mark is deceptively similar to an earlier mark shall be undertaken by the Registrar, acting as provided herein. For the purposes of this assessment, the Registrar shall consider all relevant factors including, but not limited to, the visual appearance, phonetic similarity, and conceptual meaning of the marks in question. The Registrar may require parties to submit evidence or arguments relating to consumer perception. A reasonable period shall be afforded to each party to respond to submissions made by the other. Decisions regarding deceptiveness shall be determined registrar accordance with principles of fairness and equity as established under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, “distinctiveness” with respect to a trade mark means the capability of distinguishing goods or services of one undertaking from those of other undertakings. A trade mark shall be deemed distinctive if, before registration, it is capable of distinguishing such goods or services as made or rendered by the applicant; and in determining distinctiveness, regard shall be had to all relevant circumstances, including acquired reputation. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating acquired reputation where a trade mark is initially considered descriptive. Decisions regarding distinctiveness shall be made by the registrar accordance with established principles of intellectual property law.

The application for registration of a trade mark shall contain such particulars as may be prescribed, including a representation of the marks applied for and a list of goods or services associated therewith. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall examine it to ascertain whether it complies with the requirements of this Act. If the Registrar finds that the applicant has not furnished the requisite information or that the form is incomplete, he may require the applicant to submit such further particulars as are necessary for proper examination. The decision of the Registrar in respect of acceptance or rejection of an application shall be final, subject to appeal under this Act. Further, the registrar accordance with established practice may issue directions regarding procedural aspects of registration and renewals.

Applications for registration of service marks shall be examined in relation to their distinctiveness, considering whether, through use prior to the date of application, the mark has become reasonably associated with a particular service. The Registrar may require an applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating such acquired distinctiveness, and the form and manner of presentation of this evidence shall be as prescribed by regulations framed under this Act. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall record particulars thereof in a register maintained for that purpose, noting the filing date and any priority claims asserted. Objections raised by third parties to the acceptance of an application must be addressed according to procedures outlined herein; the applicant shall have opportunity to respond to such objections in writing. The decision of the Registrar concerning the registrability of a mark is final, subject to appeal under this Act. Decisions made by the registrar accordance with established practice are binding on all parties involved.

The owner of a registered trade mark shall, subject to this Act, be entitled to grant licences for the use of the trade mark and may assign the entire interest in the trade mark to any person, either wholly or partially, and such licence or assignment shall be recorded in the Register. Any application for recording a licence shall specify the geographical area within which and the goods or services in relation to which the licensee is authorised to use the trade mark, and the duration of the licence. The Registrar may require such supporting documentation as he deems necessary to verify the authenticity of any proposed assignment or licence agreement. Further, where an application for recording a licence is made, the applicant shall provide proof that all parties involved have consented to the terms outlined therein. The registrar accordance with these provisions ensures transparency and facilitates orderly transfer of trade mark rights.

The Trade Marks Act provides that an application for registration of a trade mark may be refused if, upon review, it is deemed deceptively similar to any prior mark already registered under this Act. Any party aggrieved by such a refusal order issued by the Registrar shall have the right to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The Appellate Board shall hear arguments and consider evidence presented by both the applicant and the Registrar, and may affirm, reverse, or modify the Registrar’s decision. Decisions of the Appellate Board regarding the interpretation of this Act concerning registrar accordance are final, subject to further appeal to the High Court on a point of law only.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person claiming rights in a trade mark registered prior to the commencement of this section may enter into an assignment agreement for the benefit of another party, provided that such agreement explicitly acknowledges the continued validity of the original registration. The Registrar shall maintain a public register detailing all assignments and licenses granted concerning trademarks under this Act, accessible upon application and payment of the prescribed fee. Further, where a provisional specification claim is made regarding a mark’s distinctiveness during an assignment process, the registrar accordance with established procedures will require submission of supporting documentation demonstrating acquired reputation within the relevant territory. Any subsequent transfer or sub-license shall be subject to similar disclosure requirements, ensuring transparency and facilitating orderly trade practices relating to registered trademarks.

For the purposes of facilitating searches and ensuring clarity in trademark examination, an alphabetical index classification of goods and services shall be maintained by the Trade Marks Registry. This index classifies goods and services according to their nature and intended use, as provided herein. The Registrar may update this alphabetical index periodically to reflect changes in commercial practices and emerging categories of goods or services. Any applicant seeking registration under this Act shall ensure that the specified goods or services are accurately represented within the existing classification system; however, the Registry’s determination regarding appropriate placement within the alphabetical index classification is final, subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Applications for registration of a trade mark shall, upon receipt, be examined to ascertain whether the proposed marks are capable of distinguishing the applicant’s goods or services from those of others. The Registrar shall maintain and publish an alphabetical index classification of goods and services as per the International Classification of Goods and Services, ensuring clarity in identifying relevant categories for trademark examination. Any applicant seeking registration under this Act may submit a reasoned representation regarding the appropriate classification of their goods or services if they believe the existing alphabetical index does not accurately reflect their offerings; provided that such representation shall be accompanied by supporting documentation demonstrating the nature of those goods or services. The Registrar’s determination on classification is final, subject to appeal as provided herein.

Any proprietor seeking to enforce a registered trade mark shall, upon proof of prior use consistent with the class designation appearing in the alphabetical index classification, be entitled to injunctive relief against any party employing a sign confusingly similar to their mark within that designated class. Provided that such prior use must have been continuous and uninterrupted for a period not less than three years immediately preceding the date of infringement. Further, where an applicant demonstrates bad faith adoption of a trade mark by another, relying on the alphabetical index classification as a deceptive tactic, damages may be awarded to compensate for losses suffered due to dilution or misrepresentation. The Registrar shall maintain a publicly accessible record detailing all classifications and any subsequent amendments made under this Act, ensuring transparency in the application of these remedies.

The Trade Marks Registry shall maintain a comprehensive alphabetical index classification of goods and services for the purposes of examination under this Act. This index, accessible to all applicants and stakeholders, will facilitate efficient assessment of trademark applications against existing registered marks and pending applications within similar classes. The Registrar may, from time to time, revise and update the alphabetical index classification to reflect evolving commercial practices and technological advancements, provided that such revisions are published for public comment prior to implementation. Any party aggrieved by a classification assigned under this Act may file an appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, subject to the procedural requirements as provided herein. The Registrar’s determination regarding the appropriate class of goods or services shall be binding pending any appellate review and is deemed quasi-judicial in nature.

The Trade Marks Registry shall maintain a current alphabetical index classification of goods and services for the purposes of examination under this Act. This index shall be regularly updated to reflect evolving commercial practices and technological advancements, provided that any amendment to the existing classifications requires prior consultation with relevant trade associations. Applicants seeking registration shall ensure their specified goods or services align precisely with entries in the published alphabetical index; deviations require a detailed justification submitted alongside the application. The Registrar may reject an application if the proposed classification is deemed inappropriate based on established criteria and prevailing industry standards, subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. This process ensures consistency and clarity in trademark examination procedures as provided herein.

Any proprietor of a trade mark registered under this Act may, subject to an application approved by the Controller, grant a non-exclusive license relating to the use of their trade mark within a specific alphabetical index classification. Such licenses shall clearly define the scope of permitted goods and services as categorized within that particular class, preventing any ambiguity regarding authorized usage. The licensee shall be obligated to maintain quality standards consistent with those associated with the registered trade mark, failing which the proprietor may revoke the license. Assignment of rights pertaining to such licensed use is permissible, provided that the assignee undertakes to adhere to all terms and conditions stipulated in the original licensing agreement as recorded with the Registrar. Further, any subsequent assignment shall be notified to the Controller within thirty days for record.

The Trade Marks Registry shall maintain an alphabetical index classification of goods and services for the purposes of examination under this Act, reflecting the Nice Classification as modified by regulations. Any party aggrieved by a determination made by the Registrar concerning the placement or omission of any goods or service within said alphabetical index may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of notification of such determination. The Appellate Board shall consider evidence presented by both the appellant and the Registry, including arguments pertaining to the descriptive nature of terms used in classification. Provided that the Registrar’s initial decision is presumed correct unless proven otherwise through substantial documentary evidence.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Trade Marks Registry relating to the assignment or rectification of a trade mark, or concerning its placement within the alphabetical index classification of goods and services, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such an appeal shall be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order sought to be appealed against. The Board may, after affording all parties concerned an opportunity of being heard, confirm, vary, or reverse the decision appealed from. Further, if the Board finds that a trade mark has been wrongly classified under the alphabetical index classification due to misrepresentation by any person, it shall direct rectification accordingly and award such costs as it deems just. The Trade Marks Registry shall comply with any order made by the Appellate Board within thirty days.

The Trade Marks Registry shall maintain a comprehensive alphabetical index classification of goods and services for the purpose of facilitating searches and examinations relating to trade mark applications. Any party aggrieved by an assignment of goods or services within this index, particularly where such assignment appears to unfairly prejudice existing registered marks, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The Registrar is empowered to revise the alphabetical index classification periodically, provided that any changes are published at least sixty days prior to their effective date and do not contradict principles established under the Patents Act 1970 regarding inventive step. Failure to adhere to this prescribed process shall render such revisions voidable and subject to penalties as determined by the relevant adjudicating authority.

The Trade Marks Registry shall maintain an alphabetical index classification of goods and services for the purposes of examination under this Act, and any challenge to the assigned class designation may be raised before the Appellate Intellectual Property Tribunal. Provided that, where a mark incorporates elements relating to integrated circuits layout, the Registrar shall consider whether such features necessitate a more specific or nuanced classification beyond those typically associated with computer software or electronic devices. The burden of demonstrating the appropriateness of an alternative classification rests upon the applicant; however, decisions regarding class assignment are subject to judicial review on grounds of manifest arbitrariness. Further appeals concerning interpretations of this alphabetical index classification may be made as provided herein.

The registration of a trade mark for services shall be permissible only if the services fall within classes as defined in Schedule A. Applications relating to services specified alphabetically under that schedule will be examined according to their order of appearance, subject to any priority claims or earlier applications filed under this Act. Where an applicant seeks to register a trade mark covering multiple classes of services, each class shall be considered individually for distinctiveness and compliance with the provisions herein. The Registrar may require further clarification regarding the nature of the services claimed if they are ambiguous or not clearly defined within the alphabetical listing. Provided that any representation made in the application concerning the scope of services is deemed material to the assessment of registrability.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark used in relation to services specified alphabetically within Class 35, relating to business administration, office functions and management consultancy, shall be entitled to relief against any person who, without their consent, applies for registration of an identical or deceptively similar trade mark for services falling within the same alphabetical sub-section. Such relief may include an injunction restraining the applicant from proceeding with the application and requiring them to account for profits derived from any use of a confusingly similar sign prior to the grant of registration. Provided that where the Registrar considers the alleged infringement to be trivial, they may direct the registered proprietor to satisfy the court that damage has been or is likely to be caused by the applicant’s actions. The remedies available under this Act shall not preclude claims for damages as provided herein.

The Board shall maintain a register detailing all registered service marks, arranged alphabetically according to the nature of the services specified. Applications for registration of service marks shall be examined to ascertain compliance with the provisions relating to distinctiveness and deceptively similar matter. Where an application pertains to multiple classes of goods or services, the applicant must clearly delineate each class in their statement of services. The Board may require further clarification regarding the precise nature of any service listed if it is deemed ambiguous or insufficiently defined. Any objection raised by a third party concerning the classification of services shall be considered during the examination process and addressed according to established procedures as provided herein. Services specified alphabetically within a single class will be prioritized for assessment, subject to the overall order of application receipt.

The registration of a trade mark for financial services shall be conditional upon adherence to the prescribed schedule of services specified alphabetically within Class 36. Applications pertaining to services not explicitly listed must include a detailed justification, demonstrating clear alignment with existing classifications and avoiding ambiguity. The Registrar may require submission of supplementary documentation outlining the nature and scope of such services before proceeding with examination. Provided that the applicant demonstrates genuine use of the mark in relation to the claimed services within five years from the date of registration, as evidenced by verifiable records, failure to do so shall render the trade mark liable for removal under this Act. Any alteration to the list of services specified alphabetically requires prior approval from the Registrar and a public notice period.

Any person employing a service mark in relation to services specified alphabetically within Class 35, relating to business administration, office functions, and management consultancy, shall be liable for damages if such use creates confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or nature of the services offered. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint demonstrating demonstrable misrepresentation or unfair competition arising from such employment, issue an injunction restraining further use. Failure to comply with such an order shall constitute a cognizable offence, punishable with imprisonment and a fine as determined by the adjudicating officer. This provision applies irrespective of whether registration of the mark has been secured under this Act; however, remedies available to registered proprietors are not prejudiced.

The owner of a registered trade mark for services specified alphabetically relating to financial advisory services may, subject to fulfilling conditions as provided herein, grant a non-exclusive license permitting another party to use the mark in connection with those services. Such licenses shall be documented by deed and filed with the Registrar within thirty days of execution. The licensee under this Act shall not alter the registered trade mark without prior written consent from the owner, nor may they offer or advertise services that are materially different from those for which the trade mark is registered. Assignment of such a license requires notification to the Registrar and approval as per the procedures outlined in relation to assignments generally under this Act. The original owner retains the right to terminate any license agreement if the licensee engages in activities detrimental to the reputation of the trade mark.

The registration of a trade mark for financial advisory services shall be deemed invalid if, following an examination under this Act, it is demonstrated that the applied-for mark incorporates a listing of services specified alphabetically within class thirty-five which directly replicates or substantially approximates a previously registered mark. An appeal against such a determination ma y be made to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the Registrar’s decision. Provided that, in assessing substantial similarity, due consideration shall be given to the overall impression created on the relevant public and any potential for confusion arising therefrom. The burden of proving prior registration and demonstrating such deceptive similarity rests entirely upon the applicant challenging the validity of the trade mark.

Where a proprietor of a registered trade mark for services specified alphabetically utilizes said registration to engage in unfair competition, misrepresentation, or dilution of another’s established goodwill, the High Court may, upon application by an aggrieved party, order the immediate forfeiture of all materials bearing the infringing mark. Such materials shall include, but not be limited to, advertising matter, packaging, promotional goods, and any digital content employed for commercial purposes. The proprietor shall be liable to render accounts of profits derived from such infringing use, which shall be paid over to the aggrieved party as compensation. Failure to comply with a court directed forfeiture order shall constitute contempt of court and attract severe penalties as provided herein.

The owner of a registered trade mark for financial advisory services, specifically listed alphabetically as “Investment Planning,” may grant a license to another entity permitting the use of said mark for related services such as “Portfolio Management” and “Retirement Solutions.” Such licenses shall be in writing and clearly define the geographical territory within which the licensee is authorized to utilize the registered trade mark. The owner retains full control over quality assurance standards applicable to all services rendered under license, and may terminate the license agreement upon demonstrable failure to maintain these standards. Further, any assignment of a licensed right relating to services specified alphabetically shall require prior written consent from the original proprietor, ensuring continued protection against unauthorized use and facilitating the acquiring restrict of trade mark rights within the financial sector.

The Trade Marks Registry shall maintain an alphabetical index of goods and services, reflecting classifications as understood for purposes of examination under this Act. This index is to be updated periodically, not less than once every two years, and notice of such updates shall be published in the Official Gazette. Any party aggrieved by a classification appearing within the alphabetical index may file an objection with the Registrar within sixty days of the publication of the relevant update. The Registrar shall consider all objections received and issue a reasoned order, which may include amendment or deletion of entries. Decisions regarding the accuracy and appropriateness of entries in the alphabetical index goods are final subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Applications for registration shall be examined with reference to this index; however, deviation from an entry is permissible provided that such deviation does not mislead consumers as to the nature of the goods or services.

The proprietor of a trade mark relating to alphabetical index goods shall ensure that any alterations made to such goods, as reflected within the official Trade Marks Journal, are accurately and promptly updated on all promotional materials. Provided that where the alteration involves a change in class designation under the Nice Classification, the proprietor must submit a revised form TM-M detailing the amended description of goods for Registrar’s approval prior to public dissemination. Failure to comply with this requirement shall render the proprietor liable to administrative action, including but not limited to, a direction to rectify misleading representations and potential imposition of penalties as provided herein. The Registrar may, at his discretion, require submission of supporting documentation substantiating the nature and extent of the goods alteration.

The use of an alphabetical index of goods, as maintained by the Trade Marks Registry, shall not preclude a proprietor from seeking registration of a trade mark encompassing goods not explicitly listed therein. However, any objection raised during examination regarding the descriptiveness or classification of such goods, based on their absence within the current alphabetical index, may be contested before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The Board’s determination concerning whether the goods fall legitimately under a class represented in the index shall be final, subject to appeal to the High Court only on grounds of legal error apparent on the face of the record. Provided that such an appeal must be filed within ninety days from the date of the Board's order and demonstrate demonstrable prejudice arising directly from the decision concerning the alphabetical index goods.

Where a registered trade mark is used in relation to goods or services, or as a geographical indication, and any other person seeks to challenge the validity of such registration on the ground that it conflicts with prior rights, the aggrieved party shall be entitled to file an application for rectification before the Registrar. Such application must specify the nature of the conflicting right claimed and provide evidence substantiating the claim. The Registrar may, after affording the trade mark proprietor a reasonable opportunity to respond to the allegations, direct rectification if satisfied that the registration was obtained fraudulently or is otherwise invalid under this Act. Further, any order for rectification shall be subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. In all cases where the validity of a registered trade mark shall determined registrar’s decision will be final and binding, pending judicial review.

A trade mark application is deemed to be filed when it is delivered at the Trade Marks Registry, accompanied by the requisite fee as prescribed under this Act. For the purposes of processing a trade mark application, the applicant shall furnish such particulars relating to the goods or services in respect of which the trade mark is sought, as are required for classification under the International Classification of Goods and Services. An application may be refused if it contains any matter that is likely to deceive the public concerning the nature, quality or geographical origin of the goods or services. The Registrar shall record all particulars of a trade mark application in the prescribed manner.

An application for the registration of a trade mark shall be deemed to be finally refused if the Registrar considers that the proposed trade mark is likely to cause confusion with an earlier registered trade mark or any other similar mark used in relation to identical or similar goods or services, subject to the provisions regarding honest concurrent use. The applicant may submit evidence and arguments rebutting such a finding of likelihood of confusion; provided that this submission shall be made within the time specified under this Act and after due notice is given by the Registrar. Further, where an application for registration includes a device, the description accompanying the trade mark application shall clearly define the elements comprising said device. The Registrar may require clarification or amendment to such descriptions as he deems necessary.

Where an application for a trade mark is refused under this Act, the applicant shall have the right to appeal against such refusal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeal may be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order of refusal and shall state specifically the grounds on which the applicant relies in challenging the decision. The Board shall give notice to the Registrar of Trade Marks and afford him an opportunity to submit his objections to the appeal. If, after considering the appeal and any submissions received, the Board finds that the trade mark application was wrongly refused, it may direct the Registrar to proceed with registration as if the refusal had not been made; provided that such direction shall be subject to compliance with all other requirements under this Act. The applicant shall bear the costs of the appeal unless the Board determines otherwise.

An application for the registration of a trade mark shall be accompanied by a declaration as to the goods or services with which the trade mark is proposed to be associated, specifying each class according to the International Classification of Goods and Services. The Registrar may require an applicant to amend such declaration if it appears that the goods or services are not clearly defined or do not fall within the scope of any recognised classification. Further, a trade mark application shall include particulars relating to the use, if any, of the trade mark prior to the date of the application, and details of any previous applications for registration in respect of the same mark. The Registrar may refuse registration where it is shown that the applicant has failed to comply with these procedural requirements as provided herein. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to a trade mark application may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

An application for a trade mark shall be deemed invalid if the applicant is not the true owner of the trade mark sought to be registered, subject to demonstrating prior use or assignment as provided herein. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish evidence establishing ownership, including but not limited to documentation relating to incorporation, partnership agreements, or contractual assignments. Further, a trade mark application shall be refused if it contains any matter which, in the opinion of the Registrar, is likely to offend religious susceptibilities or ethnic sentiments within India. Provided that such refusal may be appealed under this Act before the relevant intellectual property appellate tribunal. The applicant must also declare compliance with all applicable advertising codes and regulations as they pertain to trade mark usage.

An application for a trade mark shall be deemed abandoned if the applicant fails to file the requisite documentary evidence as prescribed by the Regulations within six months from the date of request made by the Trade Marks Registry, or where such failure continues for a further period of three months following a second request. Any person aggrieved by an order directing abandonment may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days of receipt of the order; provided that the Appellant shall deposit with the Board a sum equivalent to twenty-five percent of the prescribed fee for late filing, or such higher amount as the Board deems just under this Act. Failure to comply with this provision will render the appeal inadmissible. The Trade Marks Registry may, at any time, initiate prosecution proceedings against an applicant found to have made false statements in their trade mark application.

An application for a trade mark relating to goods or services connected with an existing business carried on by another person shall be deemed to include an implied assignment of any right, title, or interest the applicant possesses in respect of similar marks previously used or applied for, but not registered under this Act. Such assignment shall extend to all territories where the other person conducts such business, provided that a written agreement detailing the scope and duration of the license is filed with the Registrar at the time of the trade mark application. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating the applicant’s claim to ownership or usage rights prior to acceptance of the application. This provision shall not apply where the applicant demonstrates good faith reliance on advice from a registered trade mark attorney, and the assignment is executed in accordance with prescribed forms.

An application for a trade mark shall be deemed to be refused if the Examining Officer is satisfied that the proposed mark is deceptively similar to an earlier registered trade mark or a pending trade mark application, and such similarity would likely cause confusion among the public as to the origin of goods or services. The applicant may, within two months from the date of communication of the refusal order, file an appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board against such decision. Provided that, if the appellant fails to demonstrate clear evidence distinguishing the mark from the cited earlier trade mark, the appeal shall be dismissed. Further, the Board may direct the Registrar to reconsider the application subject to revised grounds for objection being presented by the Examining Officer.

For the purposes of this Act, a “trade mark application” includes any document presented to the Trade Marks Registry for examination and potential registration of a trade mark, whether filed electronically or in physical form, and shall contain such particulars as are prescribed by the First Schedule. A person submitting a trade mark application under this Act is deemed a "recording means person" for all purposes relating to acknowledgement of receipt and communication regarding the progress of said application. Any alteration to a trade mark application after its initial presentation must be made in accordance with regulations framed hereunder, provided that such alterations do not fundamentally change the nature of the applied-for trade mark.

For the purposes of this Act, "use" with reference to a trade mark means not only sale but also the display of the trade mark on any goods or their packaging, or on any containers for those goods, and includes offering for sale or distributing such goods. The term “mark uses registered” shall be deemed to include instances where a proprietor permits another person to use its registered trade mark under a license agreement, provided that such agreement is in writing and specifies the scope and duration of the permitted usage. Any alteration or modification of the registered mark which affects its distinctive character will be considered an unauthorized use as provided herein.

Where any person makes default in complying with an injunction issued under this Act, the Court may, subject to appeal, order such person to pay by way of damages to the registered proprietor such sum not exceeding twenty-five thousand rupees for each day during which the default continues. The right to apply for rectification of a registered trade mark shall be available to any person claiming rights in relation to the mark or that the registration of the mark is rectifiable under this Act, provided that an application for rectification based solely on acquired distinctiveness may only be made after five years from the date of registration. Any proprietor who discovers that another has used a registered mark without consent shall have recourse to remedies available as provided herein, including seeking an order restraining further use and claiming damages proportionate to the loss suffered. The owner’s right to prevent others from using their mark is predicated on demonstrating unauthorized mark uses registered by competitors.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act, the Registrar may, at any time during the pendency of the opposition proceedings, require both the applicant and the opponent to submit documentary evidence affirming their respective claims. Such evidence shall be submitted within such period as the Registrar specifies by order, and failure to comply with that order may result in the Registrar’s decision against the defaulting party. The Registrar is empowered to examine any person under oath or affirmation regarding matters arising during opposition proceedings. Further, a proprietor of a registered trade mark shall be deemed to have knowledge of earlier marks relevant to their application, irrespective of whether those marks were previously brought to their attention. Any use of a *mark* by another party without authorization from the registered proprietor constitutes an actionable infringement if it is determined that such *mark uses registered* trademarks in a manner causing confusion amongst consumers.

The proprietor of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to restrain the use of any mark identical or confusingly similar to their registered mark, provided that such restraint is sought within three years from the date of first appearance of the infringing mark in commerce. Use of a *mark* by another person shall not constitute infringement under this Act if such use falls within the definition of *permitted use*, as determined according to guidelines published by the Controller General. Further, any entity demonstrating prior honest concurrent use of a similar mark before the date of registration may continue such use subject to conditions prescribed herein regarding distinctiveness and consumer clarity. The proprietor must demonstrate actual damage or likelihood thereof resulting from the unauthorized *mark uses registered* in order to succeed in an action for infringement.

Where any person makes use of a registered mark without authorization from the proprietor, and such use creates confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or quality of the goods or services offered under that unauthorized mark, then such person shall be deemed guilty of an offence. The penalty for this offence shall be imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, and with a fine which shall not be less than fifty thousand rupees. Further, any goods bearing the infringing mark are liable to seizure and destruction as provided herein. Nothing in this section shall prevent civil remedies available under this Act, including an injunction restraining further use of the mark. The proprietor is entitled to recover damages suffered due to the unauthorized *mark uses registered*.

Where an appeal lies under this Act against any decision relating to the revocation of a registration, the Appellate Board may, subject to the provisions herein, confirm, reverse or modify the order appealed from. It shall be open for the appellant to demonstrate that the registered trade mark has not been used in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered during the period of five years preceding the date of the application for revocation; and further, that such non-use was unintentional and without reasonable cause. The Board may require the proprietor of the mark uses registered to provide evidence substantiating continued use, failing which the appeal shall be dismissed. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Appellate Board may prefer a further appeal to the Supreme Court.

For the purposes of this Act, "mark uses registered" shall mean the application of a mark by any person who has obtained registration thereof under this Act, or by an authorized user as defined herein. Such usage includes, but is not limited to, display on goods, packaging, advertising materials, and providing services bearing the mark. The right to prevent others from using identical or deceptively similar marks arises immediately upon such registered mark uses. Provided that, where a person believes their prior use predates registration, they may apply to the relevant authority for consideration of equitable relief, relating plaintiff forthwith to the date of first bona fide usage.

A proprietor shall be entitled to register a proposed trade mark if it is distinctive in its nature and is used in connection with the goods or services for which registration is sought. The Registrar may require evidence of the *mark uses registered* in India, including details of advertising campaigns, sales figures, and distribution networks demonstrating such use. Where a geographical indication is claimed as part of a trade mark, the applicant must provide documentation establishing its long-standing association with specific goods originating from that region; this association shall be considered during examination. Further, any person seeking to register a trade mark incorporating an existing *indication use geographical* name must satisfy the Registrar that their proposed registration will not create confusion or mislead consumers regarding the origin of the goods.

For the purposes of this Act, “use” in relation to a trade mark includes not only the application of the mark upon goods but also any act whereby the sign is reproduced, including its appearance on packaging, labels, or associated documents. The term "trade mark uses" shall extend to acts undertaken for the purpose of advertising, promoting, or otherwise bringing goods or services to the attention of the public. Use may occur directly by the trade mark proprietor or indirectly through authorized users, subject to any conditions stipulated in a licensing agreement. A use is deemed deceptive if it creates confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or characteristics of the goods or services.

The Registrar may require an applicant seeking registration of a proposed trade mark to furnish evidence demonstrating permissible trade mark uses relating to specified goods or services. Such evidence shall include, but not be limited to, invoices documenting sales, advertising materials disseminated within the Indian territory, and contracts establishing commercial relationships utilizing the mark. Where the application relates to colour marks or non-traditional trade marks, additional proof of consistent and widespread use demonstrating consumer recognition may be demanded. The Registrar’s determination regarding sufficient evidence is final, subject to appeal under this Act. Failure to provide satisfactory documentation as requested shall constitute grounds for rejection of the application, provided that the applicant may subsequently reapply with appropriate supporting materials.

The proprietor of a registered trade mark shall have the right to restrain any person from using, or continuing to use, any trade mark identical or confusingly similar to their own mark where such use constitutes an infringement under this Act. This right extends to preventing the application of a mark to goods or services specified in the registration, or to goods or services which are essentially connected with those specified. The proprietor may also seek damages for losses suffered as a direct result of the infringing trade mark uses, including but not limited to loss of profits and damage to reputation. Provided that, where the use is demonstrably fair and does not create confusion amongst consumers, such use shall be considered permissible and not actionable as infringement. Any person aggrieved by an act of infringement may apply to the relevant judicial authority for relief as provided herein.

The Registrar may, upon receiving an application for rectification of a registered trade mark alleging improper acquisition or use thereof, direct the proprietor of the trade mark to submit its submissions within sixty days from the date of service of notice. Such notice shall specify the grounds on which the rectification is sought and detail any evidence supporting the claim. Where the Registrar finds that the continued registration of the trade mark prejudices the interests of other persons by reason of dilution or non-use, an inquiry into the extent of such prejudice may be initiated. The proprietor shall then be afforded a further opportunity to demonstrate legitimate *trade mark uses* within the preceding three years. Failure to adequately substantiate these uses will render the trade mark vulnerable to partial or complete removal from the register, as provided herein. Any party aggrieved by the Registrar’s order may appeal under this Act to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

The proprietor of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to restrain any person from using any trademark in relation to goods or services, where such use constitutes an unfair trade practice. Such restraint may be sought if the use is without due cause and creates confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or quality of the goods or services offered. The term "trade mark uses" includes not only direct application of the mark upon goods but also its display in advertising materials and packaging, provided that such display is integral to offering those goods or services for sale. Further, use by a licensee under a contractual agreement shall be considered a trade mark use subject to the terms stipulated within that license. Any alteration or modification of a registered trademark during trade mark uses must not dilute the distinctiveness of the original mark.

Any person who, without leave of the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal, applies a false trademark, or any fraudulent device resembling a trademark, upon any goods, or uses such false trademark or device in connection with the offering for sale, disposal or hire of any goods, shall be guilty of an offence and liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, and also liable to a fine. Such use includes the display of a trade mark in a manner likely to cause confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or quality of the goods. The owner of a registered trademark may apply to the relevant High Court seeking an injunction restraining such infringing uses, subject to demonstrating actual damage resulting from the unauthorized trade mark uses.

The proprietor of a registered trade mark shall retain exclusive rights pertaining to its use; however, permission for specific trade mark uses may be granted through licensing agreements executed in writing. Such licenses shall clearly define the scope of permitted activities, including but not limited to, manufacturing, distribution, and advertising relating to goods or services specified within the license. Assignment of a registered trade mark, or any right pertaining thereto, requires registration with the relevant Trade Marks Registry and is only valid upon such registration. A licensee may further sub-license rights granted under this Act, provided that such sub-licensing does not exceed the scope of the original agreement and is subject to approval by the proprietor. Any unauthorized trade mark uses shall be actionable as infringement, irrespective of any prior consent or purported assignment.

The Registrar may, upon receiving an objection from any person claiming a proprietary interest in a mark alleging that the use of a proposed trade mark constitutes unfair competition, direct the applicant to provide evidence demonstrating bona fide commercial application. Such evidence shall include detailed particulars regarding advertising expenditure, sales figures, and distribution networks employed during the period of alleged use. The burden of proof rests upon the applicant to establish that the continued trade mark uses do not create confusion amongst consumers or otherwise prejudice existing proprietors. An appeal against this direction lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order, subject to a stay application being filed concurrently.

The proprietor of a registered trademark shall possess exclusive rights to prevent the use of any sign, including words, names, symbols, devices, or combinations thereof, that is identical or confusingly similar to their mark, provided that such use occurs in connection with goods or services identical or closely related to those for which the registration subsists. Any breeder who, without due authorization from the proprietor, applies a trademarked brand name or logo to seeds or plant material derived from protected varieties shall be deemed to have engaged in infringing trade mark uses. The remedies available to the registered proprietor include an injunction restraining further acts of infringement and damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the proprietor as a consequence of the unauthorized use. Further, any goods bearing the infringing trademark may be seized and destroyed under procedures prescribed herein.

The Registrar may, upon application by any person aggrieved by a refusal to register a geographical indication, direct the hearing of an appeal against such refusal. Any party seeking to challenge the validity of a registration based on improper trade mark uses shall file a notice of opposition with the Registrar within four months from the date of advertisement under this Act. The opposition may be founded on any ground that the trademark is devoid of distinctive character or misdescriptive, or that its use constitutes passing off or unfair competition. Where an application for registration includes a reference to a geographical register, the Registrar shall verify the accuracy and completeness of such information with the relevant authority maintaining the included register geographical indication. The applicant shall be deemed to have knowledge of all matters contained therein.

The proprietor of a registered trade mark shall have the exclusive right to apply for and obtain licences granting third parties permission to make specified uses of the trade mark, subject to conditions stipulated within the licence agreement. Such licences may cover any aspect of commercial exploitation relating to goods or services associated with the registered mark, including but not limited to distribution, advertising, and promotional activities. An application for a licence shall be deemed valid only if it clearly defines the scope of permitted trade mark uses, geographical limitations, and duration of the authorisation. The proprietor may assign such licences to another party, provided that prior written consent is obtained from the licensee. Any subsequent assignment shall be recorded with the Trade Marks Registry as provided herein. Further, any alteration to the terms of a licence requires mutual agreement between the proprietor and the licensee.

For the purposes of this Act, "infringed advertising trade" shall mean a situation where a person uses a sign, whether registered or not, in connection with goods or services, and such use creates a likelihood of confusion amongst the public regarding the origin or sponsorship of those goods or services. This determination shall consider the overall impression created by the advertisement, encompassing its visual elements, textual content, and accompanying sounds. The mere appearance of similarity between advertising material is insufficient; there must be demonstrable evidence that consumers are likely to believe that the advertised goods or services originate from, or are associated with, a different undertaking than the registered proprietor.

An advertising trade mark shall be deemed infringed where any person, without authorization from the proprietor of the trade mark, reproduces or imitates a distinctive element of an advertisement featuring a registered trade mark, with the intention to create confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or sponsorship of goods or services. Such infringement includes the unauthorized use of slogans, imagery, or jingles inextricably linked to the advertised product and which contribute significantly to its public recognition as associated with the registered trade mark. The proprietor may apply for relief against such infringed advertising trade, including an injunction restraining further reproduction and damages commensurate with the loss suffered due to the deceptive marketing practices employed. Provided that this provision shall not restrict fair use or parody under this Act.

Where an advertising campaign prominently features a registered trade mark, and that campaign’s distinctive elements, including slogans, imagery, and overall presentation, are substantially copied or imitated by another party for the promotion of competing goods or services, such appropriation shall constitute infringed advertising trade.
