The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint from the registered proprietor alleging such infringement, issue a notice to the alleged infringer requiring them to submit their response within thirty days. Failure to respond adequately or demonstrating lack of due diligence in preventing the infringing advertising campaign will be considered as evidence against the alleged infringer under this Act. Any order issued by the Registrar regarding infringed advertising trade is subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, provided that such appeals must be filed within sixty days from the date of the order.

Where an advertising campaign prominently features a registered trade mark, and subsequent use by another party replicates substantial elements of that campaign’s visual presentation, layout, and promotional messaging, such replication shall constitute infringement of advertising trade. This determination is subject to consideration of whether the replicating advertisement creates confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or sponsorship of the goods or services being advertised. Provided that the registered proprietor can demonstrate a direct causal link between exposure to the infringing advertisement and demonstrable consumer detriment, relief may be granted under this Act. Further, any use which dilutes the distinctiveness of the trade mark, even absent evidence of confusion, is actionable as infringed advertising trade if it exploits the reputation associated with the earlier mark.

Any person who utilizes advertising material featuring an infringed advertising trade mark shall be deemed guilty of an offence under this Act. Such utilization includes, but is not limited to, the display of the infringing advertisement on any medium, whether physical or digital, and the distribution thereof through any channel. The penalty for such offence shall be a fine which may extend to five hundred thousand rupees, and imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years. Repeated contravention shall attract enhanced penalties as determined by the adjudicating officer. Further, the proprietor of the registered trade mark is entitled to seek an injunction restraining further use of the infringing advertising material, subject to demonstrating actual damage or likelihood thereof.

The owner of a registered advertising trademark shall have the exclusive right to grant licenses for its use in promotional materials and marketing campaigns. Such licenses may specify the geographic territory, duration, and permitted scope of application of the advertisement featuring the trade mark. Any assignment of rights under this Act relating to an infringed advertising trade must be executed in writing and attested by at least two witnesses, one of whom shall be a practicing advocate. Further, where a license is granted for use of a registered trademark in connection with digital marketing activities, including but not limited to social media campaigns and search engine optimization, the licensor may stipulate conditions regarding data collection and user privacy, provided that such stipulations are consistent with applicable data protection laws. The licensee shall be liable to the owner for any damages arising from unauthorized modifications or misuse of the advertising trade mark beyond the scope of the granted license.

Where an advertising campaign prominently features a trade mark, and that campaign has been demonstrably adopted by another party for promotional purposes relating to similar goods, a finding of infringement may arise. The Registrar shall consider whether the adoption constitutes an attempt to pass off the other party’s services or products as those associated with the registered proprietor. However, it is provided that such a determination requires clear and convincing evidence establishing consumer confusion, prejudice, or dilution of the distinctive character of the trade mark. An appeal against this finding lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal, subject to demonstrating demonstrable prejudice resulting from the Registrar’s decision regarding infringed advertising trade.

Where an advertising campaign prominently features a registered trade mark, and that campaign has demonstrably generated goodwill for the proprietor, unauthorized reproduction or adaptation of substantial elements of said advertising shall constitute infringement of the advertising trade. This right extends to instances where the infringing advertisement creates confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or sponsorship of goods or services. The remedies available under this Act in cases of infringed advertising trade include an injunction restraining further use of the infringing material and damages, calculated to compensate for lost sales and harm to reputation. Genera species specified within a registered mark shall not limit the scope of protection afforded to its advertising trade; any depiction that exploits the distinctive character of the mark is actionable.

Where an advertising campaign prominently features a registered trade mark, and that campaign’s visual elements, slogans, or overall presentation are substantially copied by another party for promotional purposes relating to similar goods or services, such appropriation shall constitute infringed advertising trade. This determination is subject to the condition that the original advertisement possesses distinctiveness sufficient to warrant protection under this Act. For clarity, an invention means invention as defined in the Patents Act and does not automatically preclude a finding of infringement where the copied elements are primarily related to branding and consumer recognition. Provided that the infringing use creates a likelihood of confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or endorsement of the goods or services, remedies may be sought as provided herein.

For the purpose of register purposes legal, a “composite mark” means a mark consisting of at least one element which identifies goods or services and at least one further element which serves merely as a device or decoration; provided that such device or decoration does not independently indicate any quality of those goods or services. A composite mark shall be deemed to be registrable only if the identifying element is distinctive, irrespective of whether the decorative element possesses distinctiveness. Further, an application for registration of a composite mark may include a representation showing the elements intended to be registered as a whole and also representations showing each such element separately, subject to guidelines prescribed by the Registrar.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be refused if the proposed marks are identical to a previously registered trade mark in respect of identical goods or services, unless the owner of the earlier trade mark consents to the subsequent application proceeding. For purposes of determining identity under this Act, regard shall be had not only to the visual appearance of the signs but also to their phonetic similarity and conceptual relevance. Where an applicant seeks registration of a composite trade mark, the assessment for distinctiveness shall consider the entirety of the mark as applied for, subject to the provisions regarding arrangement of elements. The Registrar may require further particulars or clarification from any applicant concerning the goods or services for which registration is sought, particularly where such specification appears ambiguous or unclear for register purposes legal.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be refused if the proposed marks are identical to a prior registered trade mark in respect of identical goods or services, unless the owner of the earlier trade mark consents to the use of the later mark. Where an applicant demonstrates honest concurrent use of a sign identical or similar to a pre-existing registered trade mark for at least five years immediately preceding the date of the application, registration may be granted subject to limitations as provided herein regarding the scope of protection afforded to the prior proprietor. Any person aggrieved by a refusal under this Act may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The remedies available to a proprietor whose rights are infringed include damages and an injunction preventing further infringing activity; such relief shall be awarded at the discretion of the court, taking into account the nature and extent of the infringement and any loss suffered. For register purposes legal clarity is paramount.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be refused if the proposed marks contain only such signs as are capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one undertaking from those of other undertakings. Where an applicant seeks to register a device comprising words and figurative elements, the Registrar may require that the representation of the device submitted for registration clearly indicate the relationship between the word and figurative components. The examination process shall include verification against existing registered trade marks and pending applications as provided herein. For purposes of determining similarity under this Act, regard shall be had to the visual, phonetic, and conceptual similarities between signs. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to registration or refusal may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The applicant shall furnish such documentary evidence substantiating their claim for register purposes legal as the Board deems necessary.

Any person who, without due cause and with intent to deceive, applies for registration of a trade mark identical or confusingly similar to an existing registered trade mark shall be liable to pay a penalty not exceeding two hundred thousand rupees. Such application shall be deemed a violation under this Act and the Registrar may summarily reject it. Further, any proprietor of a registered trade mark who knowingly makes false statements in relation to prior use for register purposes legal or other material facts during an opposition proceeding or subsequent rectification action faces imprisonment extending to three years, alongside a fine which may extend to five hundred thousand rupees. The Central Government may, by notification, increase these penalties as deemed necessary to safeguard consumer interests and prevent fraudulent trade mark practices.

The owner of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to grant licenses conferring rights in relation to the use of the mark for specific goods or services. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as determined by the terms agreed between the parties and recorded in writing. Any assignment of the registered trade mark, or any license granted thereunder, shall require notification to the Registrar within thirty days of execution, accompanied by prescribed fees. The Registrar shall maintain a public record of all such assignments and licenses for register purposes legal clarity. Further, where a license is assigned without the consent of the original owner, the assignee’s rights shall be subject to the terms of the initial licensing agreement. This provision applies irrespective of whether the goods or services are identical or similar to those specified in the registration.

The Registrar may, upon receiving a notice of opposition to an application for registration of a trade mark, direct that the hearing be conducted before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board or, in its absence, designate an officer of the Trade Marks Registry to preside over such proceedings. Any party aggrieved by any order made under this Act relating to the refusal of registration, acceptance of a disclaimer, or the rectification of the register purposes legal shall have the right to appeal from that order to the Appellate Board, subject to payment of the prescribed fee and within the time stipulated herein. The Appellate Board may confirm, vary, or reverse the order appealed against, and may substitute its own order in place thereof. Further appeals concerning decisions of the Appellate Board are permissible before the Supreme Court on grounds specified under this Act.

The owner of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to grant licenses conferring rights to use the trade mark in respect of specified goods or services. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as determined by the terms agreed between the parties and recorded in writing. Any assignment of the registered trade mark, or any license granted thereunder, shall require notification to the Registrar within thirty days of execution, accompanied by the prescribed fee. The Registrar may request further documentation substantiating the validity of such assignment or license. Where a licensee acts in breach of the terms of their registration respect article, the owner of the trade mark shall be entitled to pursue remedies as provided herein for infringement. This right extends to sub-licensees acting under the authority of the primary license holder.

The use of a registered trade mark in relation to goods or services identical or similar to those for which registration is sought shall not be restricted solely on the grounds that such use constitutes honest description of the qualities, characteristics, or intended purpose of the goods or services. However, any party aggrieved by an action alleging infringement under this Act may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board if it is demonstrated that the registered trade mark’s distinctiveness has been unfairly diminished through said descriptive use. The Board shall consider whether the continued registration respect article has been maintained and balance the interests of the proprietor with those of consumers, providing reasons for its decision which are final subject to further appeal to the appellate court.

The owner of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to grant licenses conferring rights to use the trade mark in respect of specified goods or services, and such license may be exclusive or non-exclusive as determined by the terms thereof. Any assignment of the registration itself under this Act shall include all associated licensed rights unless expressly excluded within the instrument of transfer. Where a patent agent acts on behalf of a licensor to negotiate or execute a trade mark licensing agreement, they are deemed to act with the authority of the owner and any obligations undertaken by the agent bind the owner as if directly executed. The registration respect article shall be upheld in all instances where licensed use is consistent with the character and reputation of the registered trade mark; however, sub-licensing is permissible subject to conditions stipulated within the primary license agreement.

The right to exclusive use conferred by registration respect article shall not be absolute and may be challenged upon demonstration of prior honest concurrent usage, subject to a balancing exercise considering consumer confusion. An appeal lies from an order determining such prior usage, where the appellant establishes that the alleged prior user’s activities were demonstrably limited in geographical scope or class of goods, and did not create a likelihood of distortion of trade channels. Further, any claim of registration respect article is subject to limitations imposed by fair dealing principles relating to reporting of current events or criticism; however, such use must be accompanied by due acknowledgement of the registered mark. The Intellectual Property Appellate Board may review findings concerning the scope of permissible usage under these limitations.

The Registrar may, upon application and subject to fulfilling all requirements as provided herein, register a geographical indication in respect of goods or services originating from a specific territory where the quality, reputation, or other characteristic is essentially attributable to its origin. Such registration shall confer on the registered proprietor exclusive rights to use the geographical indication relating to those specified goods or services within India. The right of registration under this Act does not preclude any person from using a name or description which is honestly and exclusively used by them in relation to their own goods, provided that such use does not constitute a representation likely to mislead the public regarding the origin of those goods. Any challenge to the validity of registration respect article shall be made within the prescribed period.

For the purposes of this Act, the term "International Bureau" means the International Bureau of the World Intellectual Property Organization, and references to the International Bureau shall be construed as references to that body acting in its capacity under the Madrid Protocol. Any communication required or permitted to be sent to the Trade Marks Registry may, subject to any rules made by the Registrar, be transmitted electronically to the International Bureau for onward transmission. The Registrar shall cooperate with the International Bureau in matters relating to international registration of trade marks as provided herein and shall furnish such information as it deems necessary for the proper functioning of the system under the Madrid Protocol.

An applicant intending to seek international registration of a trade mark shall file a request for recording the certified copy of the Indian trade mark register with the Registrar, provided that such request is accompanied by the prescribed fee. The Registrar may, upon verification of the authenticity of the certificate and compliance with all applicable provisions under this Act, record the said request in a separate Register maintained for the purpose of international registrations. Any alteration to the particulars of a registered trade mark shall be notified to the International Bureau within thirty days from the date on which such alteration is recorded in the Indian register. Failure to notify the International Bureau as provided herein may render the applicant liable to penalties, subject to appeal before an appellate authority.

Where a trade mark is registered in India and subsequently extended through an international registration process administered by the International Bureau, the proprietor shall be entitled to enforce the rights conferred under this Act as if the international registration had been directly effected in India. Any person seeking to challenge the validity of such an internationally protected trade mark may institute proceedings before the relevant intellectual property tribunal, subject to demonstrating a lack of use within the territory of India for a continuous period exceeding five years following the date of extension. The proprietor shall be deemed to have knowledge of any conflicting prior rights existing in India at the time of application for international registration and shall remain liable for any damages arising from infringement occurring before such extension.

Applications filed in India for the purpose of seeking benefits under the Madrid Protocol shall be processed initially by the Trade Marks Registry, which will transmit the international application to the International Bureau. The Registrar may, at any time, require the applicant to furnish further information or documentation relating to the goods and services specified in the list appended to the international application, provided that such requirement is consistent with the provisions of the Madrid Protocol and this Act. Upon receipt of the international application from the Trade Marks Registry, the International Bureau shall perform its functions as prescribed by the Regulations under the Madrid Protocol. Any communication received from the International Bureau concerning an international registration or application shall be promptly forwarded by the International Bureau to the Registrar, who shall then notify the applicant accordingly. The Registrar’s decisions regarding procedural matters relating to international applications are subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

An applicant seeking designation of India in an international application filed with the International Bureau shall, within four months from the date of receipt of the request for designation by the Office, furnish a certified true copy of the international application and any subsequent amendments. Failure to comply with this requirement will result in the application being deemed not to have been filed with respect to India. The Trade Marks Registry may, subject to due process and after providing an opportunity for hearing, extend this period where satisfactory cause is demonstrated. Any fees payable under this Act relating to the international registration shall be remitted as provided herein, calculated according to prevailing regulations determined by the Government.

Any person who, without due cause and with intent to deceive, uses a trade mark identical or confusingly similar to a registered trade mark in respect of goods or services for which the registration is effective shall be liable to pay damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the proprietor of the trade mark. Such damages may include lost profits, costs incurred in combating the infringing use, and an additional sum not exceeding ten per centum of the defendant’s turnover attributable to the infringement. Furthermore, where an international application designating India is refused or deemed to be withdrawn, the Registrar shall promptly notify the International Bureau accordingly, and any subsequent attempts at registration through that avenue will be subject to enhanced scrutiny under this Act.

The owner of a trade mark registered in India may, subject to payment of prescribed fees and provided that such assignment or license does not contravene any provision under this Act, grant an exclusive license relating to the use of the trade mark for specific goods or services within the territory of another Contracting Party. Any such exclusive license shall be deemed an assignment for the purposes of revocation proceedings; however, the registered proprietor retains ultimate ownership and responsibility concerning opposition or rectification actions. Where a trade mark owner has filed an international application through the International Bureau, any subsequent assignment or licensing agreement relating to that international registration must be notified to both the Indian Registry and the International Bureau within thirty days of execution. Failure to do so may render such assignments voidable at the discretion of either body.

Where a trade mark is registered in India and subsequently extended through an international application, as provided herein, any objection raised by a person claiming to be interested in relation to registrability under this Act shall be entertained only if such objection is filed within three months from the date of publication of the international registration details. The Registrar may, after giving notice to the applicant for extension and opportunity of being heard, refuse to extend the protection afforded by the Indian registration if he finds that the grounds of opposition existed at the time of the original registration but were not previously raised. Appeals against such a refusal shall lie to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, subject to the provisions regarding limitation periods applicable under this Act concerning appeals before said Board. The International Bureau shall be notified of any such appeal and its outcome.

The owner of a registered trade mark may, subject to this Act and the regulations framed thereunder, grant exclusive licences allowing for reproduction or adaptation of the mark in connection with goods or services specified in the licence. Such licences shall be assignable, either wholly or in part, provided that any such assignment is notified to the Trade Marks Registry within thirty days of its execution. Where a trade mark owner has granted an exclusive license permitting export of goods bearing the mark, and where circumstances arise preventing the licensee from fulfilling their obligations due to unforeseen events impacting production capacity, the Registrar may, upon application by the licensee, authorize a compulsory licence export enabling continued supply to international markets. The International Bureau shall be notified of any such authorization within fourteen days. Any fees associated with this process will be determined as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, the term "International Bureau" means the General Division of the World Intellectual Property Organization and includes any successor body designated under the Madrid Protocol. An application for registration of a trade mark may be made in accordance with the provisions of the Madrid Protocol, subject to such conditions as are prescribed herein relating to translation and representation of the mark. The trade proprietor registered under this Act shall be deemed the applicant for the purposes of an international application filed through the International Bureau, provided that all required fees have been duly paid.

Where a trade mark is registered in India and subsequently subject to an international registration through the International Bureau, the rights conferred by the Indian registration shall remain paramount within the territory of India. Any challenge to the validity of such a trade mark, whether arising from pre-existing prior use or other grounds available under this Act, may be brought before the relevant judicial forum as if the international registration had not been undertaken. Further, an application for rectification concerning an internationally registered trade mark shall be admissible only after exhaustion of all remedies available directly with the International Bureau and its decisions pertaining to that specific international registration. It is provided that any claim for damages resulting from infringement occurring prior to the date of publication of the international registration in India shall be adjudicated according to Indian law, irrespective of any provisions within the Madrid Protocol. International registration shall not prejudice existing rights acquired under this Act.

An international application form, as used within this Act, means a document submitted to the International Bureau of the World Intellectual Property Organization in accordance with the Madrid Protocol, seeking extension of protection of a registered trade mark beyond the territory of India. Such a form shall contain prescribed particulars relating to the basic trade mark registration, including but not limited to the date of registration, the goods or services for which it is registered, and the applicant’s details. The international application form must be accompanied by the requisite fee as determined under this Act and may include a designation of additional countries where protection is sought, subject to any limitations imposed by those jurisdictions.

An applicant intending to seek protection for a trade mark in any designated contracting country under the Madrid Protocol shall file an international application form with the Trade Marks Registry, accompanied by the prescribed fee and a copy of the basic trade mark registration certificate. The international application form must accurately reflect the details contained within the original Indian trade mark registration, including but not limited to the representation of the mark, any claims of colour or three-dimensional features, and the list of goods or services for which protection is sought. It shall be the duty of the applicant to ensure that the information provided on the international application form corresponds precisely with the particulars recorded in the Register of Trade Marks. Any discrepancies discovered during examination may result in rejection of the international registration.

An applicant seeking to avail themselves of the Madrid Protocol system shall file an international application form within six months from the date of publication of their Indian trademark in the Trade Marks Journal, provided that such filing is made in respect of goods or services identical to those for which registration exists under this Act. Failure to adhere to this timeframe will render the international registration ineffective as against third parties who have acquired rights prior to notification under Article 34 of the Protocol. Any alteration to the list of goods and services specified in the international application form after its initial submission shall be deemed a material change, requiring fresh publication and potentially impacting priority claims. The Registrar may, at any time, require an applicant to furnish further particulars relating to the international registration or to demonstrate continued use of the mark internationally.

An international application form submitted under this Act shall be in such form as the Registrar deems appropriate, consistent with the requirements of the Madrid Protocol and any subsequent amendments thereto. The applicant shall complete all fields on the international application form accurately and truthfully, providing details regarding the trade mark, its goods or services, and the country or countries for which protection is sought. Failure to disclose material information in the international application form may render the application liable to rejection. Where an earlier trade mark registration exists in India relating to any of the goods or services specified in the international application, a statement confirming such prior registration shall be included with the form. The Registrar may request further documentation or clarification from the applicant concerning the details provided on the international application form before proceeding with examination.

An applicant intending to file an international application form in pursuance of the Madrid Protocol shall ensure compliance with all stipulated requirements as provided herein. The application must be accompanied by a certified true copy of the Indian registration certificate, or where applicable, evidence of pending application under this Act. Furthermore, the prescribed fee, calculated according to prevailing regulations, is payable at the time of submission. Any discrepancy between the marks designated for international protection and those registered in India shall render the international application liable for rejection. The Registrar may require additional documentation substantiating the applicant’s entitlement to file an international application form if reasonable doubt arises concerning their compliance with these provisions.

An international application form filed under this Act shall be accompanied by a certified true copy of the Indian registration certificate, and failure to provide such documentation constitutes grounds for immediate rejection without further notice. Any party discovering a false or misleading statement within an international application form submitted concerning prior use or rights in India may institute civil proceedings seeking injunctive relief and damages commensurate with the financial harm suffered as a direct result of the misrepresentation. The Registrar shall have the power to issue warrants for the seizure of any materials used in the preparation or dissemination of fraudulent international application forms, subject to judicial oversight. Penalties for knowingly submitting an incomplete or inaccurate form extend to imprisonment for up to three years and fines not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees.

An international application form submitted pursuant to this Act shall be deemed a record of assignment only if it explicitly identifies the assignor and assignee, along with a clear description of the rights being transferred relating to the underlying trademark. Such assignments are subject to registration under this Act to be considered valid against third parties; failure to register an assignment documented within the international application form will render the transfer unenforceable. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating the validity of any such assignment, including but not limited to corporate resolutions or power-of-attorney documents. Any licensee granting sublicences based on rights detailed in an international application form must provide a written notification to both the assignor and assignee within thirty days of the sublicense agreement’s execution. This provision applies irrespective of whether the trademark is already registered under this Act.

An international application form filed pursuant to this Act shall be deemed a representation of the applicant’s exclusive claim to the specified goods or services within the territories designated therein, subject to any conflicting prior rights established under the laws of those jurisdictions. Any party disputing the validity of such an international registration may initiate proceedings before the relevant intellectual property authority demonstrating a likelihood of confusion arising from the earlier use of an identical or similar mark for identical or similar goods or services. The applicant shall bear the burden of proving that the designation of territories in the international application form was made in good faith and without intent to deceive or mislead any potential consumer, provided that evidence of reasonable inquiry into existing registrations is presented.

An international application form, as used herein, shall be a document submitted to the International Bureau of the World Intellectual Property Organization in accordance with the Madrid Protocol, seeking to designate India for the purpose of obtaining protection for a trade mark. The said form must contain particulars relating to the applicant, the trade mark sought to be protected, and the goods or services associated therewith, as prescribed by regulations governing international applications. Where an earlier trade mark has been used in India under a reference use mark, such usage shall be disclosed within the international application form, subject to verification by the Trade Marks Registry.

An applicant seeking to avail themselves of the Madrid Protocol concerning the International Registration of Marks shall, upon filing an international application form, provide a detailed specification outlining the goods and services in relation to which protection is sought. This specification must accurately reflect the description contained within the original trade mark registration under this Act. The term "specification invention meaning" as used herein refers to a clear and unambiguous delineation of the commercial scope claimed by the applicant. Failure to adhere to these requirements may result in rejection of the international application or subsequent limitations on protection afforded abroad, subject to any procedural remedies available under the regulations governing international trade mark registration.

An international application form filed pursuant to this Act shall be accompanied by a certified true copy of the Indian registration certificate, or where such certificate has not been issued, evidence of prior use in India satisfactory to the Registrar. The Registrar may require any applicant submitting an international application form to furnish further documentation demonstrating compliance with applicable treaty obligations and regulations; failure to do so within thirty days shall render the application liable for rejection. Where a trade mark registered following an international application is subsequently found to infringe upon existing rights, or where evidence emerges of fraudulent misrepresentation in the initial application process, the High Court may order court directed forfeiture of the registration, subject to due process and opportunity for the registrant to be heard. The Registrar shall maintain a register of all international applications received, accessible for public inspection as provided herein.

An international application form filed pursuant to this Act shall contain a declaration verifying the accuracy and completeness of all information provided therein, including details pertaining to the goods or services in respect of which the trade mark is sought to be registered. Such declaration must explicitly state whether the applicant intends to avail of priority rights under Article 18 of the Paris Convention. Where the application relates to an importation patented pharmaceutical product, the form shall also specify the country where the patent was initially granted and its expiration date. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating claims made within the international application form, provided that such requests are reasonable and do not unduly delay processing. Failure to comply with these requirements renders the application liable for rejection.

Any individual or corporate body seeking to avail themselves of the Madrid Protocol system shall be required to submit a duly completed international application form, as prescribed by the regulations governing such applications, alongside proof of underlying national registration in India. Failure to accurately complete and file the international application form, including providing verifiable details regarding marks indications relating to goods and services, will render the application liable for rejection without further notice. Any subsequent attempt to rectify deficiencies after initial filing shall be deemed a fresh application subject to all applicable fees and timelines under this Act. Deliberate misrepresentation or fraudulent information provided within the international application form constitutes an offence punishable with fines not less than fifty thousand rupees and imprisonment up to two years.

An effected international registration shall mean an international registration made under the Madrid Protocol which has formally extended to effect its legal protection within India, subject to any limitations specified during that extension process. For the purposes of this Act, an effected international registration shall be deemed to be a single trade mark registration for all goods and services in respect of which protection is sought and obtained through such extension. Any opposition or revocation proceedings under this Act relating to an effected international registration shall be construed as pertaining to the entirety of the registered mark, notwithstanding any partial refusal or limitation initially encountered during examination abroad.

An effected international registration shall have effect subject to any limitations or restrictions contained therein and shall confer upon the proprietor the same rights and remedies as if it were a registered trade mark under this Act, but only in relation to the territory of India and for the goods or services specified in the international registration. Provided that where an international registration includes designations for more than one country, including India, any subsequent amendment affecting the designation of India shall be treated as an effected international registration from the date of its effectuation under the International Convention. The Registrar may require evidence to satisfy him regarding the status and extent of such effected international registration before accepting it for record purposes. Any opposition proceedings relating to an effected international registration shall be conducted in accordance with procedures prescribed herein.

Where an effected international registration is extended to India under this Act, the proprietor shall be entitled to enforce the rights afforded by such registration against any person infringing the trade mark as registered. Such enforcement may be pursued through remedies available under this Act for infringement, including but not limited to damages, injunctions, and delivery up of infringing goods. Provided that, in determining whether an act constitutes infringement, the relevant territory shall be deemed to be India, irrespective of where the initial international registration was effected. Further, any counterclaim brought by a defendant alleging prior use or other grounds for invalidity of the trade mark as registered shall be subject to the same procedures and limitations applicable to counterclaims under this Act relating to domestic registrations. The proprietor’s rights are not diminished by virtue of the international nature of the original registration.

An effected international registration shall become entitled to protection in India upon the filing of a request with the Registrar within six months from the date on which the International Bureau sends out the notification mentioned under Article 2(3) of the Madrid Protocol. Such request shall be accompanied by a certified true copy of the international registration certificate and the representative’s address for service in India, as provided herein. The Registrar may require such further information or documentation as is deemed necessary to verify the authenticity of the documents submitted. Upon verification, the effected international registration shall be entered on the Register subject to any limitations specified in the request. Any opposition to the registration may be filed within four months from the date of publication of the acceptance of the effected international registration under this Act.

An effected international registration shall become entitled to protection in India upon fulfillment of conditions precedent as provided herein. Such fulfillment requires that the applicant furnish a certified true copy of the international registration certificate, duly authenticated by the International Bureau, within six months from the date notification under Regulation 64 of the Madrid Protocol is received by the Trade Marks Registry. The Registry may, subject to compliance with prescribed forms and payment of requisite fees, record the effected international registration as an Indian trade mark. However, this recording shall not prejudice any prior conflicting rights existing in India at the time of such recording, and the applicant remains responsible for addressing any oppositions arising under this Act.

Where an effected international registration is opposed under this Act, the Registrar shall give notice of the opposition to the International Bureau and shall afford the proprietor of the trade mark concerned a reasonable opportunity to present its case. Failure by the proprietor to respond within the time specified may be deemed abandonment of the application for registration in India. Any person aggrieved by an order made by the Registrar concerning an effected international registration may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, subject to payment of prescribed fees and filing of security for costs. The Board’s decision shall be final, but is open to challenge under revision before a High Court if it involves a question of law as provided herein. Penalties for wilful violation of this provision shall apply as determined by the court.

Where an effected international registration is assigned or otherwise transferred to a successor in title, such assignment shall be deemed to include any pending applications for extension of protection under this Act relating to the marks registered thereby. The Registrar may require evidence satisfactory to him demonstrating the due execution and validity of any such transfer before registering it as affecting the rights pertaining to the effected international registration within India. Provided that a licensee granted prior to the assignment or transfer shall continue to be entitled to exercise the rights conferred by their license, subject to the terms thereof and without prejudice to the successor’s ownership of the mark. Any subsequent assignments of the effected international registration shall require notification to the Registrar, along with supporting documentation as prescribed in the regulations framed under this Act.

Where an effected international registration is opposed under this Act, the Registrar shall give notice of the opposition to the International Bureau and shall afford the proprietor of the trade mark a reasonable opportunity to submit its observations on the grounds of opposition. The proprietor may, within such time as prescribed, file with the Registrar counter-statements responding to the particulars of the opposition. Subject to any appeal under this Act, the Registrar’s decision in respect of an effected international registration shall be final and binding; provided that if a party aggrieved by such decision alleges material error or substantial injustice, they may prefer an appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The Board may allow such appeal and direct the Registrar to reconsider any matter decided therein.

An effected international registration shall become entitled to protection in India upon notification by the International Bureau to the Trade Marks Registry, provided that such notification specifies the contracting country which designated India. The Registrar may, subject to compliance with prescribed procedures, accept and record the effected international registration as if it were a domestic trade mark registration. Where an applicant or proprietor is unable to be personally present for any proceedings relating to an effected international registration, they may appoint a legal representative duly authorised in writing to act on their behalf; such representation shall be deemed sufficient compliance with requirements of personal appearance. The protection afforded by the effected international registration shall be limited to the goods and services listed therein at the date of its effectuation.

Where an effected international registration is opposed under this Act, the Registrar shall give notice thereof to the applicant for such registration and to the owner of the earlier trade mark, if any, as provided herein. Any party aggrieved by a decision relating to such opposition may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. Further, where the layout design connected with the goods or services specified in an effected international registration infringes upon registered designs under the Designs Act, the owner of the infringed design shall be entitled to seek remedies as if the infringement had occurred in India. Failure to comply with these provisions will render the infringing party liable for damages and costs.

Where an effected international registration extends to India and includes pharmaceutical products, the proprietor shall have the power to grant exclusive licenses relating to the use of the trade mark within Indian territory. Such license may be granted for the entire duration of the registration or for a specified period thereof, as determined by the proprietor. Any assignment of the registered trade mark under this Act shall include any existing licenses previously granted in relation to it, unless expressly excluded in writing and agreed upon by all relevant parties. The assignee shall become liable to perform all obligations undertaken by the assignor relating to such licenses. Further, a license granted prior to an assignment may continue in effect as if it had not been assigned, subject to any terms stipulated within the original licensing agreement or subsequent amendments approved by the proprietor.

An effected international registration shall mean an international registration brought into force pursuant to the Madrid Protocol, and which extends to India under this Act. For the purposes of determining entitlement to seek rectification or revocation, an effected international registration shall be deemed to be a registered trade mark as against any person by whom representation has been made in accordance with the provisions herein. Where such effected international registration incorporates a design registered layout for goods, the proprietor’s rights extend only to that specific visual presentation and do not encompass the underlying functional aspects of the product. Subject to this, the application process shall mirror those applicable to domestic trade mark registrations.

An effected international registration shall have effect subject to any limitations or restrictions contained therein and notwithstanding anything to the contrary in this Act. Where an effected international registration designates India, the trade mark shall be deemed registered as from the date of its international registration, provided that a copy of such international registration is filed with the Trade Marks Registry within six months thereafter. The Registrar may require the deposit of security for the due observance of any conditions applicable to the effects of the international registration. Any person claiming rights under an effected international registration may apply to have the trade mark entered on the register of secured interests, as provided herein, and such entry shall confer upon them priority in respect of that effect registered trade mark.

Where an international registration designating India is subject to a final refusal by the Registry, any party aggrieved by such decision may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. Failure to comply with this timeframe shall render the appeal inadmissible. The Registrar shall be empowered to impose a penalty of one thousand rupees for each day of delay in processing an international registration final determination request, provided that the total penalty shall not exceed fifty thousand rupees. Any person found to have made false representations concerning the status or validity of an international registration before the Registry is liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and a fine.

Where an international registration designating India is extended under this Act, and such designation incorporates marks already registered in India, the proprietor shall be deemed to have granted a non-exclusive license to any person holding a conflicting prior mark. This license permits use of the internationally registered trade mark subject to reasonable royalties determined by arbitration as provided herein. Assignment of rights arising from an international registration shall include assignment of this implied license, with the assignee bound by the same royalty obligations. Further, where an international registration final and designating India is subsequently abandoned or expires, any person previously granted a license under this provision may continue use of the mark for a period not exceeding two years, provided they offer evidence of reliance on the licensed usage during that time.

Where an international registration designating India is opposed under this Act, and such opposition proceeds to a final determination by the relevant intellectual property tribunal, the Registrar shall provide notice thereof to each person registered proprietor appearing on the record of the International Bureau as having an interest in the mark. Any party aggrieved by a decision relating to the acceptance or rejection of an international registration final concerning goods or services for which India is designated may appeal to the appellate body within sixty days from the date of such order, subject to payment of the prescribed fee and demonstrating demonstrable prejudice arising directly from the impugned decision. The appellate body shall hear appeals regarding the validity of the designation and any related claims made by persons registered proprietors.

An international trade mark registration shall remain valid for such period as is prescribed by the law under which it was initially registered, subject to renewal provisions applicable therein. Where an extension of protection is sought following the expiry of the initial term and prior to the commencement of proceedings under this Act relating to infringement, the applicant must demonstrate continued use of the trade mark in accordance with the relevant international regulations. The validity of such extended protection shall be assessed based on the laws governing international registrations, including provisions pertaining to *years international registration* and any applicable grace periods for non-use.

An international trade mark shall continue to enjoy protection in India for such period as is prescribed by the relevant international treaty and subject to compliance with the provisions relating to renewal under this Act. Where an international registration extends to India, the proprietor may apply for extension of the term of that registration beyond the initial ten-year period, provided that such application is made within the prescribed timeframe following the expiry date indicated on the register of international trade marks. The right to seek further extensions shall be contingent upon payment of the requisite fees as determined by the Trade Marks Registry and adherence to all procedural requirements outlined herein. Failure to comply with these stipulations may result in lapse of protection, even during the period of years international registration.

The proprietor of an international trade mark registration shall be entitled to institute proceedings for infringement under this Act as if the international registration were a registered trade mark in India. Provided that, where an international registration is renewed and remains in force, the right to extend such renewal internationally shall not prejudice any rights acquired by a person in India prior to the date of such extension. Further, upon expiry or cancellation of an international registration, the proprietor may apply for registration of the same trade mark in India, subject to the provisions relating to earlier marks. The period of validity of any subsequent Indian registration obtained under this provision shall be calculated from the date of that new registration and not from the original date of international registration. A proprietor seeking extension of an international registration shall maintain records demonstrating compliance with renewal requirements for a minimum of ten years after the final termination of such international registration, including details regarding *years international registration*.

An international trade mark registration shall remain valid for such period as is prescribed by the law under which it was initially registered, subject to renewal procedures consistent with that foreign jurisdiction. Where an applicant seeks to extend the protection conferred by an international registration within India, they must file a request for extension before the expiry of the initial ten-year term following recordal under this Act. The Trade Marks Registry may require submission of documentary evidence demonstrating continued use of the mark in connection with the goods or services specified in the international registration, as provided herein. Failure to demonstrate such use may result in refusal of the extension request. Importantly, for purposes of maintaining an international registration’s validity within India, the concept of *years international registration* applies; extensions are governed by the initial term and subsequent renewal cycles under the originating national law.

An international trade mark registration shall remain valid for such period as is prescribed by the law governing the initial registration, subject to compliance with conditions stipulated herein. Renewal fees relating to an international registration must be paid within the time limits specified under this Act and any failure to do so will result in lapse of protection afforded thereby. Where an applicant seeks to extend the term of an international trade mark registration beyond the initially granted period, such extension shall only be permissible if all renewal requirements have been fulfilled without exception. The validity of continued international registration is contingent upon maintaining active registrations for designated territories and a minimum duration of ten years from the date of initial grant; any territory where protection ceases will impact overall years international registration.

Where an international trade mark is registered under this Act, and renewal fees are duly paid for successive ten-year periods, the proprietor shall remain entitled to enforce the exclusive rights afforded by such registration within India. However, failure to renew said fees within the prescribed timeframe will render the registration vulnerable to challenge by any aggrieved party. Any person utilizing a similar mark without authorization following such lapse shall be deemed guilty of trade mark infringement and subject to penalties as provided herein. Furthermore, an international registration’s validity in India is contingent upon maintaining compliance with all applicable provisions under this Act; specifically, concerning requirements for demonstrating continued use and the maintenance of *years international registration* beyond the initial ten-year term.

The owner of an international trade mark registration extending to India shall have the option to grant a license conferring specific rights relating to the use and exploitation of the mark within Indian territory. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as determined by the licensor, and are subject to conditions regarding quality control and permitted geographical areas specified in the licensing agreement. Assignment of the international registration, or any portion thereof pertaining to India, requires prior written consent from the Registrar, provided that such consent shall not be unreasonably withheld. Further, where an international registration maintains its validity for a period exceeding ten years, the owner must file a renewal application under this Act to continue protection in India; failure to do so will render the mark vulnerable to challenge regarding distinctiveness and prevent further licensing activities. The term "years international registration" refers specifically to the duration of ongoing legal effect granted by Indian law.

Where an international trade mark registration is extended to India under this Act, and such extension remains valid for a period exceeding ten years from the date of initial Indian registration, any party aggrieved by the decision granting or maintaining such extension may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days of the publication of that decision in the Trade Marks Journal. Provided that an appeal lies notwithstanding that the international trade mark registration incorporates goods or services not identical to those previously registered in India, unless it can be demonstrated that the difference is immaterial and does not prejudice the interests of consumers. The Board shall consider whether the continued validity of the extension infringes upon existing Indian registrations, particularly concerning similar marks used for related goods; and may order revocation after a period of five years international registration if such infringement is established.

The owner of an international trade mark registration shall have the option to grant a license conferring specific rights relating to the use and exploitation of the mark within India. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and their terms regarding royalty payments and duration are subject to contractual agreement between parties. Where the initial basic application for the trade mark was filed in India, any assignment of the international registration shall require notification to the Trade Marks Registry, accompanied by prescribed documentation verifying consent from all prior licensees. Further, under this Act, a licensee may apply to extend the term of the international registration’s protection within India, provided that such extension does not exceed the remaining years international registration period and is consistent with the original basic application's scope.

Where an international trade mark registration is extended to India under this Act, the period for which such extension remains valid shall not exceed ten years from the date of such extension. An application for renewal of the international registration may be filed with the Registrar person within a period of six months preceding the expiration of the said ten-year period; provided that any delay in filing such an application beyond this stipulated timeframe is subject to payment of prescribed fees and may, at the discretion of the Registrar, permit continued validity. Any party aggrieved by a decision regarding the renewal or non-renewal of an international registration’s extension may appeal under this Act within sixty days from the date of communication of that decision. The duration of years international registration is thus subject to timely application and potential appeals.

Where a trade mark is registered internationally under the Madrid Protocol and such international registration incorporates a designation of India, the proprietor shall maintain the validity of that registration for so long as the underlying Indian registration remains in force. However, where an article patented incorporating the trade mark is subsequently withdrawn from sale within India or ceases to be manufactured therein, the proprietor may apply to the Registrar for a modification of the international registration’s scope relating to those specific goods. Failure to do so within six months of such cessation shall constitute grounds for revocation under this Act. The period of protection afforded by an international registration remains subject to the same renewal requirements as would apply to a domestic Indian trade mark, and any lapse in renewal will impact years international registration status accordingly.

For the purposes of this Act, “international registration keeping” means the process by which a trade mark proprietor maintains the effect of an international registration designating India, subject to compliance with prescribed procedures and payment of requisite fees. An international registration shall be deemed kept in force only when the Registrar confirms its continued validity following examination under this Act. Failure to respond to an official action within the stipulated time may result in partial or complete cancellation of the designation for India. The proprietor shall furnish such information as the Registrar deems necessary regarding changes affecting the ownership or status of the trade mark internationally.

An international registration shall have effect only in relation to Contracting Parties designated in the declaration of designation filed with the International Bureau under the Madrid Protocol. Where an indication is registered as a trade mark in India and subsequently, the proprietor seeks to maintain that registration through international registration keeping, they must file renewal forms within the prescribed time limits as provided herein. Failure to do so shall render the Indian registration subject to removal from the register. The Registrar may, upon receiving notification of any limitation or amendment affecting the protection afforded by an international registration, issue a public notice accordingly. Any person aggrieved by such action may appeal under this Act.

The proprietor of an international registration shall be entitled to request that the International Bureau transmit a notice of extension of protection to the competent authority in India, provided that such request is made within six months of the date on which the international registration would otherwise expire. Upon receipt of this notice, and subject to verification by the Registrar that all prescribed fees have been duly paid, the trade mark shall be deemed registered in India for a further period as specified in the notice. Any person aggrieved by a decision relating to an extension of protection under this Act may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such decision. The proprietor’s rights and remedies concerning international registration keeping are subject to any conflicting prior registrations existing under this Act at the time of deemed registration.

An international registration shall have effect only to the extent that declarations of extension of protection have been received from the Contracting Parties specified in the application. Upon receipt of a declaration of extension of protection, the Trade Marks Registry shall record particulars thereof and publish such recording in the Trade Marks Journal. Any person may inspect these records during office hours. The Registrar may require any declarant to furnish further information or documentation relating to the declaration, provided that such requirement is reasonable and proportionate to the verification sought. Failure by a declarant to comply with a request for information within the time specified shall be deemed abandonment of the declaration. Where an international registration ceases to have effect in respect of any Contracting Party, the Registrar shall maintain a record indicating the date upon which this occurred. The Trade Marks Registry is not liable for errors or omissions in published particulars relating to international registration keeping.

The Registrar shall, upon receiving a request for international registration keeping from an applicant who is entitled to seek such protection under this Act, examine whether the mark is eligible for continuation and if so, record the extension. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar regarding the acceptance or rejection of an application for international registration keeping may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of that decision. The Board shall hear appeals arising under this provision and may allow such time as it deems fit for parties to file documents and present arguments, subject to just considerations. Further, a party demonstrating prejudice due to delay in hearing shall be entitled to appropriate relief as determined by the Appellate Board.

The Registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for renewal of a trade mark registered internationally under this Act, verify whether the international registration remains valid and enforceable in each designated contracting country. Where an international registration expires in any such country, the effect on the Indian registration shall be determined as provided herein. The renewal fee for an international trade mark shall be payable at the time of application for renewal, subject to provisions regarding late payment penalties. An international registration is deemed to expire ten years from the date of its initial registration, or from the date of any subsequent revival, unless renewed under this Act. Any alteration affecting registrability may impact expiry years internationally and necessitate further examination.

The renewal of a trade mark registered internationally shall be subject to compliance with the provisions relating to domestic renewals under this Act. Where an international registration incorporates a designation for India, and the corresponding Indian trade mark registration expires, the international registration shall continue in force only insofar as it relates to goods or services for which protection was afforded by the expired Indian registration. Further, any subsequent renewal of the international registration affecting India must adhere to the prescribed timelines applicable to renewals of domestic registrations; failure to do so will result in deemed abandonment of that portion of the international mark pertaining specifically to India. The expiry years internationally are governed by the terms of the Madrid Protocol and as provided herein.

The Registrar shall, upon receiving a request from an international trade mark proprietor seeking renewal of their international registration extending to India, examine whether the underlying national registrations remain valid and enforceable. Provided that, where any such national registration has expired, the renewal application may proceed only if the proprietor demonstrates diligent efforts were undertaken to reinstate said registration within a reasonable period following its expiry years internationally. Any party aggrieved by a decision refusing or granting such renewal may appeal under this Act to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days of the order’s communication. The Tribunal shall consider whether the failure to maintain national registrations constitutes wilful neglect, impacting the integrity of international trade mark protection as provided herein.

Where a trade mark is registered internationally under the Madrid Protocol and subsequently ceases to have effect in one or more designated Contracting Parties, the registration shall remain valid in India subject to compliance with conditions as provided herein. The expiry years international of such a registration are determined by the laws of the Contracting Party where the initial refusal or cancellation occurred, and this determination is binding for Indian purposes. Renewal fees for the trade mark may be required upon application, calculated according to prevailing regulations. Further, if the registered proprietor fails to demonstrate continued use of the trade mark in India within a reasonable period following any such cessation, the registration shall be subject to review under this Act.

Registration shall cease to have effect under this Act if the registered proprietor fails to submit renewal fees within the prescribed time and period, provided that a notice has been previously served upon the proprietor indicating impending lapse. The Registrar may extend such time as deemed appropriate, subject to conditions regarding payment of additional charges reflecting the delayed submission. Further, where a trade mark is subsequently used in contravention of any condition specified during registration, or if it becomes deceptive and misleads consumers concerning the nature, quality, or origin of goods or services, the registered proprietor shall be liable for penalties as provided herein.

Where an application for registration of a trademark is granted and entered on the Register of Trade Marks, the proprietor shall be entitled to exclusive rights pertaining to the use of the mark in relation to the goods or services specified in the register. However, registration shall cease to have effect under this Act if the Registrar receives notice from any interested person alleging non-use of the trademark for a continuous period exceeding five years following its registration. Such notice must be accompanied by an affidavit verifying the grounds for the allegation and detailing the circumstances contributing to the lack of use. The Registrar may, after affording the proprietor an opportunity to be heard, direct that the mark be removed from the register; provided that such direction shall not prejudice any rights acquired by any person prior to the date of removal.

Where a registered trade mark is used contrary to the provisions of this Act, or the conditions under which it was registered, and such use causes damage to any other person, that person may institute proceedings for damages. The Intellectual Property Appellate Board shall have power to award compensation commensurate with the loss suffered, taking into account factors including duration of infringing use and extent of commercial harm. Further, upon a finding of persistent or egregious misuse, the Registrar may initiate an inquiry as to whether registration shall cease. Such inquiry will consider evidence demonstrating abandonment of the trade mark by its proprietor, or other conduct undermining the distinctiveness afforded by the registered rights. The proprietor shall be given opportunity to present arguments against such cessation.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is granted under this Act, and subsequent to that grant, the registered proprietor fails to file the renewal form required as provided herein within the prescribed time limit, notice of which has been duly served upon them by the Registrar, the Registrar shall issue a public notice indicating the impending cessation of registration. The said notice shall specify the trade mark number, the goods or services for which it is registered, and the date on which registration shall cease to have effect. Any party may, within sixty days from the date of publication of such notice, file an application with the Registrar requesting a reconsideration of the decision to allow registration to lapse. Such application must be accompanied by an affidavit explaining the reasons for the delay in renewal. Upon consideration, the Registrar may, if satisfied, reinstate the registration subject to payment of any applicable fees and penalties.

Registration shall cease to have effect where the registered proprietor fails to file renewal forms within the prescribed period and after the expiry of the grace period granted under this Act. Provided that, if upon an application made by the registered proprietor within six months from the date of default, it is demonstrated to the satisfaction of the Registrar that satisfactory cause existed for the failure to renew on time, the Registrar may, subject to such terms and conditions as deemed fit, restore the registration. Further, any alteration to the goods or services listed in relation to a trade mark following registration shall require notification to the Registrar within three months; non-compliance with this requirement may render the registered trade mark vulnerable to revocation proceedings initiated by interested parties.

Where an owner fails to submit renewal fees within the prescribed period, or within such extended time as may be permitted under this Act, registration shall cease to have effect; however, the Registrar may, upon application made within six months from the date of cessation and subject to payment of all outstanding dues plus a surcharge not exceeding fifty percent of the said dues, restore the trade mark to the register. Any person aggrieved by such restoration or refusal thereof may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days. Failure to comply with this provision shall constitute an offence punishable with monetary penalties as provided herein. The Registrar is empowered to issue directions for enforcement of these provisions and may impose further penalties for wilful non-compliance.

Where the registered proprietor of a trademark grants a license conferring exclusive rights to use the mark for specific goods or services, such license agreement shall clearly delineate the scope and duration of the permitted usage. Any assignment of the registered trademark, whether partial or complete, must be executed in the prescribed manner under this Act and duly recorded with the Registrar. Furthermore, where a licensee subsequently acquires the right to assign their sub-licensees’ rights, they shall notify the registered proprietor within thirty days of such transfer. It is provided that registration shall cease if the registered proprietor fails to provide evidence, as may be required by the Registrar, demonstrating continued use of the trademark in accordance with the terms of any license or assignment granted, for a continuous period exceeding five years following the date of initial registration.

Where an objection is raised under this Act against the registration of a proposed trade mark, and the applicant fails to submit satisfactory evidence demonstrating acquired distinctiveness within the period prescribed by the Registrar, the Registrar shall notify the objector of such failure. The objector may then, within thirty days from the date of notification, petition the Intellectual Property Appellate Board requesting that the application be deemed abandoned. Provided that, if the applicant subsequently submits compelling evidence rebutting the grounds for abandonment, the Board may direct the Registrar to reconsider the application. Furthermore, registration shall cease to have effect where a registered proprietor fails to respond adequately to a rectification action initiated by an aggrieved party within the stipulated timeframe, as provided herein.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark shall file a registrar application prescribed by this Act in Form TM-A, accompanied by the requisite fee. The Registrar may require further information from an applicant if deemed necessary for assessing distinctiveness and compliance with provisions regarding deceptive similarity. Failure to respond adequately within the time specified under this Act will result in the registrar application being refused. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to the acceptance or rejection of a trade mark shall have the right to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, provided that such an appeal must be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The remedies available on appeal include orders for reconsideration and direction to the Registrar to perform its duties as provided herein.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark shall submit a completed registrar application prescribed by these regulations and accompanied by the requisite fee, payable to the Controller. The registrar application must contain a clear representation of the mark as it is intended to be used, alongside a detailed description sufficient for identification purposes. Further, the application shall specify the goods or services with which the trade mark is associated, classified according to the International Schedule of Products and Services. Provided that an applicant demonstrates good faith in their assertion of ownership rights, the registrar may request supplementary documentation substantiating such claim. Any alteration made to a registrar application after its initial filing requires express written consent from the Registrar, subject to conditions deemed necessary for maintaining procedural fairness.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark under this Act shall, upon submission of a complete registrar application prescribed by these regulations, be deemed to grant a non-exclusive license to any party demonstrating prior use of an identical or deceptively similar mark within the territory of India. This license is transferable and assignable subject to approval from the Registrar, who may require demonstration of continued beneficial ownership and ongoing quality control measures relating to the licensed goods or services. Provided that such assignment does not prejudice existing rights holders as determined by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.
