It shall be presumed, unless rebutted by evidence presented by the proprietor, that any alteration in the prescribed standards for certification constitutes a breach of those conditions. The proprietor may adduce testimony to demonstrate adherence to revised protocols approved by the relevant sectoral authority; however, such approval does not preclude scrutiny regarding consumer deception as provided herein. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Tribunal may appeal further to the Supreme Court.

The proprietor of a use certification trade mark shall be entitled to institute proceedings for relief from acts of adaptation, application, or importation contrary to the provisions of this Act. Any person seeking to oppose the registration of a proposed certification trade mark may submit evidence demonstrating that the mark falsely suggests an association with a person not authorized by the applicant, or that its use would be detrimental to consumers. The Opposition Board shall consider such evidence and may direct rejection of the application if it finds merit in the objection. Further, where infringement is established, remedies available include injunctions restraining further infringing acts, damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the proprietor, and the delivery up for destruction of goods bearing the infringing mark, subject to any orders made under this Act concerning disposal.

A proprietor seeking registration as a user of a use certification trade mark relating to agricultural produce shall furnish, with the application, proof satisfactory to the Registrar that the applicant is a society registered under the Societies Registration Act and possesses the requisite infrastructure for ensuring adherence to specified quality standards. The Registrar may require the applicant to provide detailed protocols outlining inspection procedures and testing methodologies employed in verifying compliance with these standards. Further, prior to registration, payable notice shall be served upon all known producers of the relevant agricultural produce within a radius of fifty kilometers from the proposed certification mark’s area of operation, affording them an opportunity to submit objections under this Act. The Registrar may reject the application if substantial objections are received and remain unresolved following due consideration.

Any proprietor of a use certification trade mark shall be liable for damages sustained by any party prejudiced thereby, owing to the proprietor’s failure to adhere strictly to the conditions and regulations governing the application of the mark. Such prejudice includes, but is not limited to, misrepresentation concerning the quality or origin of goods bearing the certification trade mark. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint duly supported by evidence of such non-compliance, initiate inquiries and impose penalties as provided herein, including suspension of registration. Further, any party aggrieved by an action taken under this Act relating to the registration sub section of a use certification trade mark may appeal to the relevant appellate authority within sixty days.

An appeal, as provided herein, shall lie to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board from any order passed by the Registrar relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application for registration of a trade mark. For the purposes of this Act, “th appeal specified” means that where an appeal is admitted against an order of the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, and subsequently challenged before the High Court, the time limit for preferring such further appeal shall be calculated from the date on which the judgment or order of the Intellectual Property Appellate Board is communicated to the appellant. Subject to any procedural requirements under this Act, a party may seek clarification regarding the scope of an order made in relation to a trade mark application.

An application for registration of a trade mark, once rejected by the Trade Marks Registry, may be subject to review through an appeal process as provided herein. Where a first appeal is decided in favour of the applicant and the Registrar’s initial decision is overturned, any subsequent party aggrieved by that appellate order shall have the right to file a further appeal. Such th appeal specified must be lodged within sixty days from the date of communication of the original appellate order to the appellant. The grounds for this second appeal shall be limited to matters of law and not involve re-examination of facts already determined in the earlier proceedings. Any documentation supporting the claim for registration must be submitted contemporaneously with the filing of the th appeal specified.

Where a party aggrieved by the determination of the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal considers the decision unjust, they may institute an appeal to the High Court. Such appeal must be filed within ninety days from the date on which the order sought to be appealed against is communicated to the appellant; failure to adhere to this timeframe shall render the appeal inadmissible. The High Court shall consider all relevant evidence presented by both parties and may affirm, reverse, or modify the Tribunal’s decision. Further, if the High Court finds that the original determination was manifestly erroneous in law, it may direct a rehearing before the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal with specific instructions regarding the issues to be reconsidered. A th appeal specified within this process is permissible only where fresh substantial questions of law arise which were not previously addressed by either the Tribunal or the High Court.

An appeal arising from any interlocutory order passed by the Appellate Board, concerning rectification proceedings relating to registered trade marks, may be filed in the High Court within sixty days from the date of communication of such order. The High Court shall admit an appeal only if it is satisfied that the order complained of is without jurisdiction or exceeds the powers conferred upon the Appellate Board under this Act. Further appeals against a decision of the High Court on any matter arising under this Act are permissible, but the th appeal specified must be accompanied by a certificate from the High Court certifying that the case involves a substantial question of law. The Registrar shall serve notice to all parties affected by the interlocutory order before transmitting records to the High Court. Provided that an extension of time for filing such appeal may be granted in circumstances deemed appropriate by the High Court.

Where a party seeks redressal concerning a rectification proceeding initiated under this Act, and having exhausted remedies before the Registrar, may pursue an appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal, such appeal shall only be entertained where the grounds for appeal are clearly articulated in writing. Provided that, if the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal determines that the order of the Registrar was manifestly erroneous or resulted from a failure to consider material evidence presented during the original proceeding, it may entertain an appeal notwithstanding delay exceeding six months from the date of the decision appealed against. Further, where the delay is attributable solely to force majeure events duly substantiated with documentary proof, the Tribunal may, at its discretion, permit the appeal; however, any th appeal specified must be accompanied by a reasoned justification for the lateness.

Where any party dissatisfied with the outcome of proceedings before the Registrar concerning the rectification of a registered trade mark, or relating to passing off actions initiated under this Act, elects to pursue further recourse, such party may file an appeal to the Appellate Tribunal. The Appellate Tribunal shall consider all evidence presented and arguments advanced by both the appellant and the respondent. It is provided that any subsequent th appeal specified in these proceedings must clearly articulate grounds demonstrating material error of law or fact in the decision appealed from; failure to do so will result in dismissal. Furthermore, the appellate authority may direct a rehearing before the Registrar if it deems such action necessary for a just resolution of the dispute, subject to procedural fairness and natural justice principles as provided herein.

An appeal lies from any order passed by the Appellate Board under this Act, subject to the provisions herein regarding timelines and procedural requirements. The High Court may, at its discretion, entertain an appeal notwithstanding the delay in its presentation, provided that the appellant satisfies the Court that there were sufficient reasons for such delay and that it was just and equitable to do so. Where a record of proceedings before the Appellate Board is not available, the Board shall, as far as practicable, cause such record to be reconstructed from any recording means person who may have been present during the hearing. The appeal shall specify clearly the order or decision sought to be challenged and the grounds upon which it is based. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in the dismissal of the appeal. Any party aggrieved by an interim order passed during consideration of a th appeal specified may seek redress through appropriate legal channels as provided herein.

Where a determination regarding deceptively similar marks has been made by the Appellate Board, any party aggrieved by that determination may institute an appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The High Court shall consider only such grounds as were specifically raised in the memorandum of appeal and which relate directly to errors apparent on the face of the record. It is provided that a second appeal lies only with special leave of the High Court, granted where substantial questions of law involving interpretation of this Act are involved. Further, the trade mark proprietor shall be deemed to have waived any objection to the maintainability of an appeal if they do not raise it within thirty days of the filing of the appeal itself. A th appeal specified under these provisions requires prior leave from the Supreme Court.

An offence under this Act relating to the use of any trademark falsely represented as or as being connected with goods or services in respect of which another person has the exclusive right, or the application of any false trademark to goods or their packaging, shall be deemed a cognizance offence basis. No court shall take cognizance of such an offence except on a written complaint made by the Registrar or an officer duly authorised for this purpose. Provided that where the use of the trademark is alleged to have been made with fraudulent intent, the court may proceed upon its own motion without any formal complaint being lodged. The Registrar may, subject to conditions specified therein, authorise any person to make such a written complaint.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed abandoned if the applicant fails to provide the requisite documentary evidence substantiating prior customary use within the stipulated timeframe as provided herein. Where such failure occurs, and it is determined that the claimed prior use constitutes a recognizable infringement upon an existing registered mark, the Registrar may initiate proceedings under this Act. No court shall take cognizance of any offence relating to fraudulent representation of prior use in an application for registration except on complaint made by the Registrar or an authorised officer. This cognizance offence basis applies irrespective of whether the applicant acted with knowledge or intent to deceive. The Registrar is empowered to issue directions concerning rectification of such applications.

Where a proprietor institutes proceedings for infringement of a trade mark under this Act, no civil court shall take cognizance of such proceeding except with the prior permission of the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Provided that where the alleged infringement involves an act constituting a criminal offence as defined in the Indian Penal Code, 1860, or any other law for the time being in force, the aggrieved proprietor may also institute proceedings before a court competent to try such offences. The Board shall, upon receiving information of such concurrent proceedings, issue directions regarding coordination between the civil and criminal forums to avoid conflicting orders. Any order passed by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board under this Act is final subject to appeal to the appellate forum as provided herein. This cognizance offence basis applies irrespective of any other remedy sought by the proprietor.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to rectification proceedings may appeal to the Appellate Board. The Appellate Board shall dispose of such appeals expeditiously and its decision shall be final, subject to further appeal to the High Court only on a point of law. Where any offence has been committed involving the use of a trademark contrary to the provisions herein, no court shall take cognizance of such offence except on a complaint made by an authorized officer appointed under this Act or by the Registrar. This principle establishes a strict cognizance offence basis for prosecuting trademark infringements. The complainant shall furnish all relevant documents and information pertaining to the alleged infringement. Failure to do so may result in the dismissal of the complaint. Further, any investigation undertaken pursuant to such a complaint shall be conducted strictly in accordance with established procedures as provided herein.

Where a person is found to be using a trademark identical or confusingly similar to a mark already registered in respect of goods or services, and such use constitutes a violation of this Act, any aggrieved party may file a complaint with the appropriate jurisdictional authority. Such complaints shall detail the infringing activity, including dates, locations, and specific representations made to consumers. The adjudicating officer shall investigate the matter and determine whether an offence has been committed under this Act. No court shall take cognizance of such an offence except on a written complaint filed by the Registrar or an authorised officer, establishing prima facie evidence of infringement. This cognizance offence basis applies irrespective of any subsequent civil remedies sought by the aggrieved party.

Where a proprietor alleges infringement of a trade mark registered under this Act, and presents prima facie evidence demonstrating such infringement, the Intellectual Property Appellate Board may direct the respondent to appear and adduce counter-evidence. Subject to appeal to the High Court, any order made by the Appellate Board concerning the admissibility or relevance of said evidence shall be final until reversed. It is provided that no court shall take cognizance of an offence relating to trade mark infringement based solely on a proprietor’s assertion without supporting documentation filed with the Registrar; this constitutes a cognizance offence basis. Further, any party aggrieved by a decision regarding evidentiary matters may appeal within sixty days as provided herein.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark shall be empowered to grant licences conferring the right to use the trade mark for specific goods or services, provided that such licence is documented in writing and filed with the Registrar. Any assignment of a trade mark, whether partial or complete, including assignments of rights granted by way of licence, requires prior notification and registration under this Act to be deemed valid against third parties. The registrar shall power to scrutinize any proposed licensing agreement for compliance with equitable terms and conditions, particularly concerning royalty rates and duration of the grant. Further, a proprietor may assign the benefit of any registered trade mark to another party, subject to the payment of prescribed fees and adherence to stipulated procedures as provided herein. Such assignments are irrevocable except by consent of the assignee and registration with the Registrar.

Where a trade mark application is opposed under this Act, and any party to such opposition proceedings dies pending the resolution thereof, the matter shall proceed notwithstanding such death. For the purposes of this provision, “dies pending proceeding” means the occurrence of death while the opposition remains unresolved by decision or withdrawal. The Registrar may, at his discretion, require evidence demonstrating the transmission of the deceased’s legal interest in maintaining the opposition. Provided that, if all parties to an opposition die pending proceeding, the Registrar shall direct the matter be closed and no further action taken concerning the opposed trade mark application.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is pending before the Registry and the applicant dies during the pendency thereof, the proceedings shall continue as though the applicant were living. Provided that, where such death occurs prior to the grant of registration, the Registrar may, upon receiving satisfactory evidence demonstrating transmission of interest in accordance with applicable laws governing succession, allow the successor-in-interest to be substituted for the deceased applicant. This substitution shall not prejudice any rights accrued to third parties under this Act. The Registrar is empowered to require such documentation as he deems necessary to verify the claim of succession and may reject the application if the evidence is deemed insufficient or if continuation of the proceedings would be manifestly unjust. A dies pending proceeding, in this context, refers specifically to applications still under examination by the Registry.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is pending before the Trade Marks Registry and the applicant dies during the pendency thereof, the proceedings shall continue as though the applicant were living. Provided that, where such death occurs prior to the grant of registration, the Registrar may, upon receiving satisfactory evidence demonstrating the transmission of all rights and interests in the application from the deceased applicant’s estate or legal representatives, allow a successor-in-interest to be substituted as the applicant for the purposes of pursuing the trade mark application. The Registrar shall not be obligated to entertain such substitution if it appears that the succession is contested or otherwise uncertain. Further, any appeal filed under this Act by the original applicant will abate *dies pending proceeding* upon their death unless continued by a duly authorized successor.

Where an application for rectification of a registered trade mark is pending before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board and the applicant dies during such pendency, the Board shall proceed with the matter subject to the provisions relating to succession under this Act. Provided that, if the death occurs prior to the final determination of objections raised by the Registrar or any interested party, the Board may require proof satisfactory to it of transmission of the applicant’s interest before further proceedings are entertained. The Board shall give notice of such death to all parties involved in the rectification proceeding and afford them an opportunity to submit evidence regarding the succession claim. Failure to provide adequate documentation establishing a valid successor will result in the application being deemed abandoned, *dies pending proceeding*, and the matter closed accordingly.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is pending adjudication under this Act and the applicant dies, the proceedings shall not abate but may continue against the estate of the deceased applicant. Provided that, within six months from the date of the death of the applicant, a duly authorized representative acting on behalf of the estate must file with the Trade Marks Registry an affidavit confirming their authority to proceed in place of the deceased and detailing the manner in which they intend to pursue the application. Failure to comply with this requirement shall result in the application being deemed abandoned. The Registrar may, at his discretion, require further documentation substantiating the representative’s claim, particularly where multiple parties assert conflicting claims as successors in interest; such a situation constitutes *dies pending proceeding* and requires diligent assessment by the Registry.

Where a trade mark application is pending adjudication under this Act, and the applicant dies during such pendency, the estate of the deceased shall be deemed to continue the said application. The Intellectual Property Office may, upon receipt of a duly authenticated transmission document indicating assignment or bequest of the trade mark rights, permit substitution of the deceased applicant with their legal representative or assignee. Provided that any such substitution must occur within six months from the date of death of the original applicant; failing which, the application shall be deemed to be abandoned. Further, where an appeal is pending before a relevant appellate authority and the appellant dies during the proceedings, the appeal will continue *dies pending proceeding*, allowing for substitution as described above.

Where an appeal lies under this Act against any decision rendered by the Registrar, and the appellant dies pending the determination of such appeal, the appeal shall abate. Provided that, where a trade mark application has been opposed, and the opposition proceeding remains unresolved at the time of the applicant’s death, the estate of the deceased applicant may continue the opposition as if the applicant were living, subject to furnishing satisfactory evidence of representation. Further, in cases involving a counterclaim or cross-examination relating to deceptively similar marks, the appeal shall not abate but will proceed with the substituted party, representing the interests of the deceased appellant. This provision regarding *dies pending proceeding* applies equally where the respondent in an appeal meets their demise before final adjudication.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark relating to “Kashmir Apples,” a geographical indication prescribed under this Act, is opposed, and the opponent dies pending the opposition proceedings, the Registrar shall proceed with the matter notwithstanding such death. Provided that, the applicant or any other interested party may, within sixty days from the date of notice of the death, notify the Registrar of their intention to continue the proceeding. If no such notification is received, or if multiple notifications are received and the Registrar determines a dispute exists regarding representation of interests, the opposition shall be deemed to abate *dies pending proceeding*. The Registrar may require evidence of authority to act on behalf of any continuing party before further action is taken.

A suit relating to the alleged infringement of a registered trademark may be filed only before the Commercial Court established under this Act, provided that such Commercial Court exercises jurisdiction within the local limits of the place where the defendant resides or carries on business. For the purposes of determining jurisdiction, “carrying on business” includes offering goods or services through any form of advertisement or solicitation. The term "court suit infringement" shall be deemed to encompass any action alleging unauthorized use of a mark identical or confusingly similar to a registered trademark, irrespective of whether such use is for commercial gain or otherwise affects the distinctiveness of the mark.

An action concerning the alleged infringement of a trademark registration may only be commenced before the Commercial Court established under this Act, provided that such Court has territorial jurisdiction over the defendant's place of business. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all pending and disposed-of suits relating to registered trademarks, including details of the marks involved and the nature of the alleged infringement. Further, any party seeking relief against an act of court suit infringement must demonstrate demonstrable similarity between the impugned mark and the registered trademark, considering not only visual appearance but also phonetic resemblance and conceptual meaning. The Court shall have power to grant such remedies as are deemed appropriate under this Act, including injunctions and damages.

Where an owner of a registered trademark reasonably believes that another person is engaging in activities likely to cause confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin, quality, or nature of goods or services, and such activities constitute a court suit infringement under this Act, the owner may institute legal proceedings seeking equitable relief. Such relief shall include, but not be limited to, an injunction restraining the infringing party from further use of the mark or confusingly similar marks, as well as damages sustained by the trademark owner due to the infringement. Provided that, in determining the amount of damages, the court shall consider any profits made by the infringer attributable to the infringing activities and any losses suffered by the plaintiff directly resulting from such infringement. The court may also order the delivery up or destruction of goods bearing the infringing mark as provided herein.

Where an aggrieved party alleges infringement of a registered design under this Act, such suit shall be maintainable only within the local limits of the jurisdiction where the defendant carries on business, or has a place of establishment, or resides, or where cause of action arose. Provided that, if the plaintiff is unable to ascertain with reasonable diligence the location of any such defendant, the suit may be instituted in the court having jurisdiction over the place where the goods incorporating the design are manufactured or sold. Further provided that, for the purposes of determining jurisdiction, a display of goods online through an electronic medium shall constitute carrying on business. The Court shall have power to grant all remedies available under this Act, including injunctions and damages, in any suit relating to court suit infringement.

Where an aggrieved party believes that their registered design has been infringed upon through unauthorized manufacture, import, or sale, they may institute a suit for infringement before the High Court. Such suits shall be actionable irrespective of whether the infringing activity was undertaken with knowledge of the registration. The defendant in any such action is liable to pay damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the plaintiff, and furthermore, subject to judicial discretion, may be ordered to surrender goods bearing the infringing design for destruction. Costs associated with rectifying the infringement, including advertising expenses aimed at correcting public perception, shall also be recoverable under this Act. A finding of court suit infringement constitutes a civil remedy available to registered proprietors.

Where the proprietor of a registered trademark grants a license conferring the right to apply the trademark to goods or services, such license may be assigned subject to the terms and conditions stipulated therein. Any assignment shall require registration with the Trade Marks Registry within three months of execution, failing which it shall be deemed void. Further, where an assignee commences proceedings relating to court suit infringement of the registered trademark, they shall provide evidence of their valid assignment and the original proprietor’s consent, as provided herein. The proprietor retains the right to terminate any license agreement if the licensee engages in activities detrimental to the reputation or distinctiveness of the mark. This termination does not prejudice the assignee's existing rights under a properly recorded assignment, but limits its scope to the period prior to notification of termination.

Where a proprietor alleges infringement of their registered trademark, such suit may only be brought before the High Court having jurisdiction over the territorial extent where the alleged infringement occurs, subject to appeal to the Supreme Court as provided herein. The defendant shall have the right to challenge the jurisdictional basis of the suit and request transfer to a subordinate court if they demonstrate compelling reasons for doing so, which determination rests solely with the High Court. Further, any counterclaim asserting validity or ownership challenges against the registered trademark itself must be raised within the same proceeding; failure to do so will preclude such claims in subsequent litigation concerning this trademark. A finding of court suit infringement shall not prejudice other remedies available under this Act.

Where an action alleging court suit infringement of a registered trademark is brought before a High Court, the plaint shall specify the details of the infringing use, including but not limited to the goods or services involved and the geographical area where such infringement occurs. The defendant may, within thirty days from the date of service of summons, file with the High Court a counter-claim asserting validity of their own mark or challenging the plaintiff’s registered trademark. Should the defendant claim entitlement to use a similar mark based on an entitled assignment transmission from a prior rights holder, they must produce documentary evidence substantiating such transfer and its effective date. The High Court shall afford both parties reasonable opportunity for argument and presentation of evidence as provided herein. Any order restraining or preventing infringement shall be subject to conditions regarding damages and costs determined by the court.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark has been refused under this Act, and the applicant appeals against such refusal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, subsequent use of a substantially identical mark by another party during the pendency of that appeal shall not constitute actionable infringement. Provided that, if the appeal is dismissed or deemed to have been withdrawn, any suit for court suit infringement arising from such subsequent use may be instituted as provided herein, subject to conditions regarding demonstrable consumer confusion and bad faith on the part of the infringing user. Further, where a basic application has been filed in a convention country, the Registrar shall consider evidence pertaining to prior use demonstrating likelihood of confusion before determining whether an infringement action is permissible.

For the purposes of this Act, "threatened infringement trade" shall mean conduct engaged in by any party whereby such party communicates, directly or indirectly, to another party that such other party’s use of a sign, whether identical or similar to a registered trademark, is likely to result in legal action under this Act. Such communication may be made through written notices, public statements, or other means reasonably calculated to induce apprehension of litigation. Nothing herein shall prevent legitimate enforcement activities undertaken by the owner of a trade mark; however, such actions must not constitute an unreasonable restraint on trade or competition as provided herein.

Where any individual engages in conduct creating a reasonable apprehension within another that their trade mark rights are being or will be infringed, such apprehension constituting threatened infringement trade, the injured party shall have recourse to remedies as provided herein. This right applies irrespective of whether the threatening party is currently the proprietor or registered user of the mark in question. The aggrieved person may institute proceedings seeking an injunction restraining the continuation of such threatening conduct and claiming damages sustained directly attributable to the threat. Further, a court may order the publication of an apology and retraction by the individual engaging in the threatened infringement trade, at their expense, if deemed necessary to mitigate harm caused to the reputation or goodwill associated with the affected trade mark.

Where any individual or entity engages in conduct that constitutes threatened infringement trade concerning a trademark registered under this Act, and such conduct includes representations, either express or implied, to restrain another from using a similar mark or engaging in activities likely to cause confusion amongst consumers, an aggrieved party may institute proceedings before the relevant intellectual property tribunal. Such proceedings shall be initiated within six months of the date upon which the threatened infringement trade first occurred. The tribunal may, after affording all parties concerned an opportunity for hearing and presenting evidence, determine whether the conduct constitutes a threat of infringement as provided herein. If the tribunal finds that such threats exist, it may issue orders restraining the offending party from continuing with the threatening behaviour and directing them to retract any misleading representations made.

Where any entity engages in conduct reasonably calculated to deter another from utilizing a mark identical or confusingly similar to a registered trade mark, and such conduct constitutes threatened infringement trade, the party so deterred may institute proceedings before the relevant intellectual property tribunal. Such deterrence shall include, but not be limited to, explicit warnings regarding potential legal action, demands for cessation of use, or the imposition of contractual restrictions designed to limit the availability of similar marks. Provided that the entity engaging in such conduct possesses demonstrable knowledge of the registered trade mark and its associated goods or services, and further provided that the actions taken are disproportionate to any legitimate commercial interest, a finding of threatened infringement trade may be made.

Any enterprise engaging in conduct intended to deter another from utilizing a trade mark, even absent actual infringement, shall be deemed to engage in threatened infringement trade. Such actions include, but are not limited to, the dissemination of notices asserting ownership and prohibiting use without consent, coupled with explicit warnings of legal action. Where an aggrieved party demonstrates that such conduct has created a reasonable apprehension of legal proceedings, they may apply to the relevant intellectual property tribunal for injunctive relief and compensation. The tribunal shall consider the proportionality of any remedy granted, balancing the need to protect trade mark rights against the potential stifling of legitimate business activities. Damages awarded under this provision shall be determined as provided herein, taking into account lost profits and reasonable legal costs incurred.

Any entity possessing a valid license relating to a trade mark shall, upon written application to the owner of record, be entitled to assign such license, including any associated rights pertaining to threatened infringement trade, subject to approval by the Controller. Such assignment shall not prejudice existing contractual obligations between the licensor and third parties. The Controller may grant or refuse such assignment based on considerations of public interest and equitable distribution of intellectual property benefits. Where a licensee proposes to sub-license its rights, including those relating to preventing actions for threatened infringement trade, prior consent from the owner must be obtained, unless specifically exempted under this Act. Failure to secure requisite consents shall render any subsequent enforcement action voidable. The Controller may impose conditions on assignments and sub-licenses as deemed necessary to ensure fair competition within relevant market sectors.

Where any party initiates correspondence or undertakes actions indicating an intention to pursue legal remedies against another for threatened infringement trade in respect of a trademark registered under this Act, such communication shall be deemed actionable. Provided that, the aggrieved party may institute proceedings before the relevant intellectual property forum seeking injunctive relief and damages. The respondent shall bear the burden of demonstrating reasonable grounds for asserting the alleged infringement. Further, any order restraining actions based on threatened infringement trade shall be subject to review upon a subsequent demonstration by the respondent of material changes in circumstances rendering such restraint unjust or inequitable; appeals against orders made under this provision may be filed as provided herein.

Where any party believes that another’s actions constitute threatened infringement trade in respect of a trademark registered under this Act, such party may file a complaint before the Intellectual Property Disputes Tribunal. The complaint shall specify the nature of the threatened action and provide detailed particulars of the conduct giving rise to the apprehension of infringement. Where the alleged infringing activity involves replication or substantial imitation of a design incorporated within the trade mark, the Tribunal shall consider the distinctiveness of both the trade mark as a whole and the design element in determining whether a likelihood of confusion exists. The respondent shall be afforded an opportunity to present its defence, including evidence demonstrating that no infringement is intended or likely. The Tribunal may issue interim orders restraining further actions pending final determination, subject to just terms being agreed upon.

The owner of a registered trademark shall have the right to grant licenses conferring specific rights to use the mark in relation to particular goods or services. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as determined by the terms stipulated within the license agreement. Assignment of such licensing rights is permissible, subject to adherence to procedures prescribed under this Act and notification to the Trade Marks Registry. Where a licensee engages in activities exceeding the scope of granted rights, or where unauthorized use occurs through an assignee, the trademark owner shall be entitled to initiate a proceeding infringement trade action against the infringing party. Further, any agreement transferring licensing rights must clearly delineate the duration and geographical extent of such transfer, preventing ambiguity and ensuring clarity for all stakeholders involved.

An application for registration of a trademark shall include a representation of the mark and a statement indicating the goods or services in relation to which the mark is sought to be registered. Where the Registrar considers that any action proceeding infringement may arise from the use of a proposed trade mark, he may require the applicant to amend the description of such goods or services to avoid conflict with existing registrations. The Registrar shall give notice of such requirement to the applicant and an opportunity for them to submit representations against it. Subject to these representations, the Registrar’s decision is final. An appeal from this decision lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Provided that any alteration made under this provision does not substantially affect the identity of the mark, the registration shall proceed as if the original application had been filed with the amended description.

Where any individual believes that an action proceeding for infringement has been initiated against them without due cause, they may institute proceedings in the District Court having jurisdiction over the territory where the defendant resides or carries on business. Such a petition shall specify the grounds upon which it is based, detailing the alleged lack of merit in the claim and providing supporting documentation as evidence. The court may, subject to just considerations, issue an injunction restraining further action proceeding infringement if satisfied that the initial legal process was manifestly vexatious or without reasonable foundation. It is provided that any party seeking such relief shall bear the burden of demonstrating a clear and present threat of unwarranted litigation. Furthermore, costs associated with these counter-proceedings may be awarded at the discretion of the court, taking into account the conduct of both parties throughout the matter.

Where any proprietor of a registered trademark reasonably believes that another party’s use of a sign constitutes an action proceeding infringement under this Act, they shall provide written notice to the alleged infringer detailing the specific infringing activities and outlining the basis for such belief. Such notice must specify the elements constituting the claimed infringement, including but not limited to similarity of signs, identity or relatedness of goods or services, and likelihood of confusion amongst relevant consumers. The proprietor may, subject to fulfilling all procedural requirements as provided herein, seek an injunction restraining the infringing use. Provided that, any such action proceeding infringement must be initiated within three years from the date of the initial notice, failing which the claim shall be deemed time-barred.

Any party claiming damages resulting from an action proceeding infringement of a registered trade mark shall file a suit within three years from the date of discovery of such infringement. The plaint shall specify with particularity the acts constituting the alleged infringement, the territorial extent thereof, and the quantifiable losses suffered by the claimant as a direct consequence of said actions. Failure to provide adequate documentary evidence substantiating these claimed damages may result in dismissal of the suit without further notice. Where the defendant is found liable for contributory infringement, they shall be jointly and severally responsible for all damages awarded. The Court may also order the destruction of infringing goods or materials as it deems fit, provided that such orders are executed under judicial supervision.

The owner of a registered trademark shall have the right to grant licenses conferring specific rights to use the mark in relation to particular goods or services. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as determined by the terms stipulated within the license agreement. Any assignment of the registered trademark, or any portion thereof including associated goodwill, requires prior registration with the relevant Trade Marks Registry and shall be deemed invalid if such registration is not completed within ninety days. Where a licensee acts outside the scope of their granted rights, or in violation of the conditions specified in the license agreement, an action proceeding infringement may be initiated by the trademark owner against the licensee. The right to assign sub-licenses remains with the original licensor unless expressly prohibited under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, a “registrar person” shall mean any individual employed within the Trade Marks Registry and designated by the Registrar to perform specific functions relating to the examination of applications for registration, the hearing of opposition proceedings, and the maintenance of the Register of Trade Marks. A registrar person may exercise such powers and discharge such duties as are delegated to them under this Act or as directed by the Registrar. The designation of a registrar person shall be recorded in writing and publicly accessible on the Registry’s website. Provided that any decision taken by a registrar person is subject to review by the Registrar, and may be appealed against as provided herein.

An application for registration of a trademark shall be deemed to be improperly filed if the particulars furnished relating to the applicant do not accurately reflect their identity as recorded under relevant government documentation. The Registrar may, at any time prior to acceptance of an application, require the applicant to furnish such further information or submit such documents as are necessary to verify the correctness of the details provided. Where the applicant is a body corporate, the application must specify the registration number assigned to it by the appropriate regulatory authority. Any individual acting on behalf of another in submitting an application shall be deemed a *registrar person* for the purposes of this Act and subject to all obligations imposed upon such individuals.

Applications for registration of service marks shall be examined in accordance with the provisions relating to applications for registration of trademarks, subject to any modifications specified herein. Where an application contains particulars which are incomplete or ambiguous, the Registrar may require the applicant to submit further information or clarification within a prescribed time period. Any such requirement shall be communicated by written notice served on the applicant. Failure to comply with such a notice may result in the rejection of the application. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all communications relating to an application and make it available for inspection as provided herein. A *registrar person* acting under this Act is empowered to issue notices, demand documents, and conduct hearings concerning any matter arising during examination or opposition proceedings.

Any application for registration of a trademark shall be accompanied by such particulars and documents as are required under this Act. The Registrar may, at any time, require an applicant to furnish further information or submit additional documentation deemed necessary for proper examination of the application. Failure to comply with such requirements within the prescribed period shall render the application liable for rejection. Where the applicant is a body corporate, the application must be signed by a duly authorised officer who possesses the authority to bind the corporation; otherwise, the application will not be processed. The *Registrar person* appointed under this Act shall verify all submitted documents and attest to their authenticity before proceeding with further action as provided herein.

Any application filed under this Act shall be deemed improperly presented if it fails to include the prescribed fee and contains any material misstatement of fact. Where an applicant, or their authorised representative, contravenes these provisions, the Registrar may reject the application outright without further notice. Any person attempting to circumvent established procedures for engaging a *registrar person* to file on behalf of another shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees and subsequent offences may attract imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months. Failure to comply with directions issued by the Registrar regarding presentation of documents constitutes an offence, punishable as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and the regulations made thereunder, any proprietor of a registered trademark may grant a license to use such trademark to another person, either for a specific territory or otherwise, and such license shall be assignable under this Act in the same manner as the right to sue for infringement of the trademark. Where a license is granted, the licensee shall be deemed to be subject to the obligations imposed upon the proprietor regarding quality control and permitted uses of the mark, as stipulated within the licensing agreement. The Registrar person may, at the request of any party claiming an interest in a trademark or licensed use thereof, investigate whether the terms of such license have been adhered to, and may issue directions for compliance. Any assignment of a trademark license shall be registered with the Registrar, and failure to register shall render the assignee subject to all prior encumbrances.

Where an application for registration of a trademark is rejected under this Act, the applicant shall have the right to appeal to the Appellate Board. The Registrar may, at any time, require the appellant to furnish such further particulars and documents as the Registrar deems necessary for proper adjudication of the appeal. Failure to comply with such requisition within the prescribed period shall render the appeal liable to dismissal. Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Appellate Board relating to a decision made by the Registrar concerning the acceptance or rejection of a trademark application may, subject to limitations provided herein, prefer an appeal to the High Court. The determination of whether a *Registrar Person* acted reasonably in exercising their discretion shall be reviewed on record.

An application for registration of a trade mark under this Act shall be deemed to include an indication, where applicable, that the applicant seeks protection through international registration prescribed by the Regulations concerning the Registration of Trade Marks. The Registrar person is empowered to require further particulars from any applicant seeking such extended protection, including evidence demonstrating compliance with relevant treaty obligations and designated territory requirements. Failure to provide these particulars within the time specified by the Registrar shall render the application liable for rejection. Any representation made in an international registration application concerning ownership or entitlement shall be subject to verification as provided herein, and may be challenged under procedures consistent with this Act.

Where any proprietor institutes proceedings under this Act seeking rectification of a registration for layout-design, the Registrar shall, upon receiving notice thereof from such proprietor, issue a direction to the respondent requiring them to appear and answer the claim. Failure by the respondent to file a written response within the time specified in the direction may be taken as an admission of the facts alleged in the complaint, subject to the right of the respondent to subsequently challenge any order made based on such deemed admission. Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Registrar under this Act concerning layout-design registration or rectification proceedings may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The registrar person shall ensure that all notices are served as per the prescribed manner, and a copy is also displayed prominently at the registered office of the respondent.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is received by the Registrar, the Registrar shall examine such application under this Act and may require the applicant to submit further information or clarification regarding any aspect of the proposed trade mark or its intended use. Any communication required to be sent to the applicant relating to the examination process shall be deemed duly served if dispatched by registered post to the address specified in the application, or to a subsequent address notified to the Registrar. Should the Registrar deem it necessary to conduct a hearing concerning an objection raised during examination, notice of such hearing shall be given to the applicant at least thirty days prior to the appointed date. The Registrar person may, at any time, request information from a trade marks proprietor regarding the use and extent of their registered trade mark.

The Registrar may, upon application and subject to payment of the prescribed fee, grant permission for the assignment or licensing of any pending trademark application. Such applications shall be accompanied by a duly executed instrument specifying the assignor, assignee, licensor, and licensee, along with a detailed description of the rights being transferred or licensed. Where a trademark application is assigned, the Registrar person shall record such assignment and notify the applicant accordingly. Any subsequent dealing, including further assignments or sub-licences, requires fresh notification to the Registrar. The original applicant retains responsibility for ensuring compliance with all procedural requirements under this Act until the registration of the mark, provided that any respect filing application related to a licensed mark must explicitly acknowledge the licensor’s interest.

For the purposes of this Act, a “required registrar person” shall mean any individual or body corporate obligated to perform an action before the Registrar under this Act. Such obligation arises where the performance of that act is explicitly mandated by regulations promulgated thereunder or deemed necessary for the proper administration of trade mark registration proceedings. A required registrar person may delegate their authority to another, provided such delegation adheres strictly to the prescribed procedures and maintains a clear chain of accountability. The individual so delegated must possess the requisite qualifications as determined by the Registrar, ensuring due diligence in all interactions with the Registry.

Where any application for registration of a trademark is filed with the Registrar, and such application requires verification under this Act by a designated individual, that verification may be undertaken instead by a *required registrar person* duly authorised on behalf of the applicant. This authorisation shall be in writing and submitted alongside the application or at the time of subsequent amendment. The required registrar person must possess demonstrable experience in trade mark matters and provide confirmation of their appointment as per prescribed guidelines. Further, where any communication relating to an opposed trademark is addressed to the applicant, such communication may be forwarded by a *required registrar person* acting on behalf of the applicant, subject to providing proof of authority.

Where any application for rectification of a registered trademark is filed under this Act, the Registrar shall serve notice of such application on the proprietor of the trademark. The proprietor may, within the time specified in the notice, file with the Registrar counter-statement to the application. If the proprietor fails to file a counter-statement within that period, the Registrar may proceed ex parte and determine the matter based solely upon the applicant’s case. Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar made under this Act relating to rectification proceedings may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. However, such appeal shall not operate as a stay of the operation of the order unless the Board directs otherwise. Where any act, other than the making of an affidavit, is required to be done before the *required registrar person*, it may be performed by an authorised representative.

Where any application for registration of a trademark, or any document required under this Act to be filed with the Registrar, is tendered by an applicant through an authorised representative, such representative shall be deemed a *required registrar person* for the purposes of that filing. The authorisation must be in writing and submitted contemporaneously with the relevant documentation; failure to provide adequate written authority will render the application void. Any communication from the Registrar regarding the application or proceeding shall be directed to the registered proprietor unless otherwise specified within the authorization document. A *required registrar person* may, subject to any conditions prescribed by the rules made under this Act, represent multiple applicants simultaneously. The Registrar is not bound to inquire into the validity of an authorisation beyond its apparent authenticity and compliance with the prescribed form.

Where any application for registration of a trademark is rejected under this Act, and such rejection incorporates findings of fact pertaining to distinctiveness or deceptive similarity, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to submit written representations addressing each finding. The Registrar may, upon review of these submissions and any counter-representations filed by the trade mark examiner, either uphold the original rejection or direct that a hearing be convened. Any person required under this Act to furnish information or documents relating to a trademark application shall do so within the time specified in the notice served by the Registrar. Failure to comply with such directions may result in the application being deemed abandoned. The *required registrar person* is empowered to extend these timelines where good cause is demonstrated, as provided herein.

Where any application for registration, opposition notice, request for rectification, or other document required under this Act to be filed with or presented to the Registrar is tendered by an individual, that individual shall be deemed the *required registrar person* for purposes of service and jurisdiction. Failure to tender such documents personally will not invalidate proceedings unless demonstrable prejudice arises from the deviation. Any party seeking to act on behalf of a registered proprietor or applicant must provide prior written authorisation, subject to verification by the Registrar. False or misleading authorisations shall be deemed a cognizable offence, punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years and a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees.

Where a proprietor seeks to assign the benefit of any registered trademark, or any pending application for registration thereof, such assignment shall be executed in writing and delivered to the Registrar within thirty days of the date of execution. The instrument of assignment must specify both the assignor and assignee with sufficient particularity to identify them as persons appearing on the Register or who are otherwise a required registrar person seeking entry upon it. Further, any subsequent transfer of such assignment, whether by way of further assignment or other means, shall be subject to similar requirements regarding written execution and timely delivery to the Registrar. The Registrar may require verification of identity and address of both assignor and assignee before registering the assignment. Provided that a registered trademark is assigned in accordance with these provisions, the rights accruing from such registration shall pass to the assignee.

Where an application for registration of a trademark is opposed under this Act, and the applicant fails to submit a counterstatement within the time specified, the Registrar shall proceed with consideration of the opposition. However, any party aggrieved by such action may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order directing further proceedings. It is provided that where an individual or entity seeks to represent another in submitting documents or attending hearings relating to a trademark application or opposition, they must be a registered required registrar person as defined under this Act and possess the qualifications prescribed therein. Failure to comply with these requirements renders such representation invalid, subject to review by the Appellate Board on appeal.

Where any proprietor desires to grant a license relating to the use of their registered trademark, they may execute an instrument of assignment or licensing agreement specifying the permitted geographical area, goods, and services for which such use is authorized. Such instruments shall be filed with the Registrar within thirty days of execution, accompanied by the prescribed fee. The Registrar shall maintain a public record of all licenses so filed, detailing the original proprietor, licensee, and scope of the granted rights. A person acting outside the terms of a validly registered license, or without authorization from the required registrar person, shall constitute infringement under this Act. Further, any assignment made subsequent to the grant of a license must clearly delineate which rights are assigned and which remain with the original proprietor, subject to their existing licensing arrangements.

Where an application for registration of a new variety of seed potato is opposed under this Act, the Registrar shall give notice thereof to the applicant and the opponent. The applicant may, within such time as may be specified therein, file with the Registrar a counter-statement replying to the grounds of opposition. Upon receiving the counter-statement, the Registrar shall afford the opponent an opportunity to file a rejoinder thereto. Any party aggrieved by any decision of the required registrar person relating to the acceptance or rejection of a new variety application may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such decision; provided that the Board may entertain appeals filed after the said period if satisfactory reasons are tendered for the delay.

For the purposes of this Act, “prescribed form” means a form specified in the First Schedule or a form approved by the Controller and published electronically on the official website maintained for the purpose of administering this Act; provided that any alteration to a prescribed form shall be notified in the Official Gazette at least thirty days prior to its effective date. The use of a mark, whether identical or similar to a registered trade mark, in connection with goods or services, shall constitute an infringement under this Act only when such use is not carried out in the authorised prescribed manner as determined by regulations framed by the Government; and where such regulations prescribe specific conditions for fair dealing, those conditions shall be deemed relevant in assessing infringement.

An application for registration of a mark shall include a representation of the mark and a statement specifying the goods or services in relation to which the mark is proposed to be registered. Where the mark contains a pictorial element or three-dimensional shape, the applicant may submit a specimen demonstrating its features as used in connection with the specified goods or services; such specimens are subject to verification under this Act. The Registrar shall prescribe the manner in which such representations and specimens must be submitted, provided that any alteration made to the mark after the initial application is filed requires notification to the Registrar and approval granted in the authorised prescribed manner. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in rejection of the application.

Any proprietor seeking to institute proceedings under this Act for infringement shall provide evidence demonstrating that the use of the impugned mark has resulted in demonstrable confusion amongst the relevant consuming public. Such evidence need not be conclusive but must indicate a likelihood of such confusion, considering all surrounding circumstances and the inherent distinctiveness of the registered trade mark. Where the defendant demonstrates prior honest concurrent usage of a similar sign, the proprietor shall be required to prove that continued use by the defendant is causing demonstrable damage to the reputation or goodwill associated with the registered trade mark. The Registrar may, upon application from any party aggrieved, order an injunction restraining the infringing activity, provided that such restraint is exercised in a manner proportionate to the harm suffered and in accordance with the authorised prescribed manner.

The Registrar shall prescribe the form and content of applications for registration of service marks relating to financial services. Such applications must be accompanied by an affidavit verifying the accuracy of the particulars furnished therein and confirming that the applicant is duly authorised to use the proposed mark in connection with the specified services. The application, once submitted, shall not be processed until all prescribed fees have been remitted through the designated electronic payment gateway or as otherwise directed by notification issued by the Registrar. Any alteration to the service description or class of goods and services indicated in the initial application requires prior approval from the Registrar obtained in the authorised prescribed manner, subject to a further fee being paid. The Registrar may require additional documentation demonstrating ongoing compliance with regulatory requirements applicable to financial institutions.

The use of any mark identical to or confusingly similar to a registered trade mark shall be permitted only where such use occurs in relation to goods or services that are demonstrably dissimilar to those for which the trade mark is registered. Provided that, prior to utilising said mark, an application must be submitted to the Controller detailing the intended usage and demonstrating reasonable efforts to ascertain existing registrations under this Act. The Controller may require further clarification regarding the nature of the dissimilarity and its potential impact on consumer perception. Any subsequent use deviating from the particulars outlined in the approved application shall constitute a violation. Furthermore, any promotional material relating to such use must be disseminated in the authorised prescribed manner as detailed within the guidelines issued by the Trade Marks Registry.

Any proprietor utilising a trademark in connection with goods or services shall ensure such utilisation adheres strictly to the colours, devices, and configurations officially registered under this Act. Failure to display a trademark in the authorised prescribed manner constitutes an infringement, actionable at law. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint from any interested party demonstrating demonstrable consumer confusion arising from non-compliance, issue a notice requiring rectification within thirty days. Persistent deviation from the registered form, despite such notice, renders the proprietor liable to penalties not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees and further subject to injunction proceedings as provided herein. Any alteration impacting distinctiveness may also invite revocation proceedings.

The owner of a registered trademark shall be entitled to grant licences granting rights to use the mark for specific goods or services, subject to conditions stipulated within the licence agreement. Such licences may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and the terms thereof shall bind all subsequent assignees of the trademark unless expressly modified by written consent from the licensor. Any use of a registered trademark under a licence granted pursuant to this Act must occur in the authorised prescribed manner as defined within the licensing agreement itself, including limitations on geographical territory and class of goods or services covered. Provided that, where a licensee sub-licences the mark, such sub-licence shall not extend rights beyond those initially conferred by the primary licence. The Registrar may inquire into any dispute concerning the scope or validity of a sub-licence agreement, but shall only act upon written complaint from an aggrieved party.

The use of a mark identical to or confusingly similar to a trademark already registered for goods or services shall be deemed an infringement under this Act, provided that the proprietor of the earlier trademark has not materially altered the character or reputation of those goods or services. An appeal against a determination by the Registrar regarding such similarity may be made to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. It is further stipulated that any entity utilising a mark in an unauthorised prescribed manner, despite receiving written notice specifying the grounds for objection, shall be liable for damages as assessed by the Tribunal; this liability extends even if no actual confusion has been demonstrated to have arisen amongst consumers.

The proprietor of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to institute proceedings for infringement where there has been use of any layout-design which is substantially similar to or used as a substitute for the distinctive elements of the said trade mark. Such use shall constitute an infringement only if it is employed in connection with goods or services identical or closely resembling those for which the trade mark is registered, and without the express written consent of the proprietor. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint alleging such infringement, direct any person found to be using a layout-design in the authorised prescribed manner that they cease such use within a period not exceeding ninety days, provided that the respondent demonstrates reasonable grounds for continued application under this Act.

Any proprietor desiring to grant a license for use of their registered trademark shall execute an assignment agreement conforming to the form specified in Schedule B. Such agreements must clearly delineate the goods and services for which the licensee is authorised to utilise the mark, and specify the geographical territory covered by the licence. The proprietor may, subject to this Act, assign such rights to a third person, provided that any subsequent assignee shall be bound by the terms of the original license agreement. A person operating under a license granted in the authorised prescribed manner shall not, without express written consent from the grantor, alter or misrepresent the nature of the goods or services associated with the trademark. The proprietor retains the right to terminate the licence upon material breach of contract by the licensee, as determined by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

For the purposes of this Act, an “act fee paid” shall be deemed to have occurred when the prescribed amount for any action undertaken by or submitted to the Trade Marks Registry, whether relating to application, renewal, amendment, rectification, or other procedural matter, has been received into government revenue. An act fee paid is conclusive evidence that the relevant action has been formally initiated within the framework of this Act, subject to any subsequent order passed under appeal. The Registrar may, at his discretion, accept payment via electronic modes as prescribed; however, physical receipt of funds constitutes an act fee paid irrespective of the method employed.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark shall remit a prescribed application fee to the Trade Marks Registry at the time of filing the application. This fee is non-refundable, subject to provisions relating to restoration of lapsed registrations. Any subsequent request for amendment or alteration to the proposed marks after initial examination requires payment of an additional act fee paid by the applicant. The Registrar may entertain any representation or communication received from an applicant only upon receipt of the relevant prescribed fee. Failure to remit such fees within the stipulated time period as provided herein shall render the application liable for rejection, without prejudice to the applicant’s right to re-file a fresh application and pay the requisite charges anew.

Where any person institutes proceedings under this Act seeking relief for infringement of a registered trade mark, and such person has previously paid an act fee relating to the application for registration of the said trade mark, they shall be entitled to claim from the infringing party compensation proportionate to the expenses reasonably incurred in bringing those proceedings. Such expenses shall include, but not be limited to, legal fees, expert witness charges, and costs associated with gathering evidence demonstrating infringement. Provided that, a claimant seeking such compensation must demonstrate a direct causal link between the act fee paid and the subsequent need for litigation. Further, the amount of compensation awarded shall be subject to review by the relevant adjudicating authority to ensure fairness and proportionality, considering the nature and extent of the infringing activity.

Applications for registration of service marks may be made to the Registrar in the prescribed form and accompanied by the requisite act fee paid at the rate specified in Schedule I, subject to any exemptions or reductions as determined by notification issued under this Act. The Registrar shall verify that the application complies with all applicable provisions and that the act fee paid is accurate; failure to comply may result in rejection of the application. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar regarding the sufficiency of an application or the validity of an act fee paid may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The Registrar shall maintain records of all fees received and provide for their secure storage, ensuring transparency in financial transactions related to trademark registration processes as provided herein.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be accompanied by an act fee paid to the Trade Marks Registry, and such fee shall be non-refundable irrespective of whether the application proceeds to examination or opposition. The Registrar may entertain any application only upon confirmation that the requisite act fee has been remitted through the prescribed electronic channels or via demand draft payable at [City Name]. Provided that, in cases where an applicant demonstrates financial hardship certified by a recognized chartered accountant, the Trade Marks Registry may, at its discretion and after due verification of documentation, waive a portion of the act fee. Any appeal against such waiver decision shall be subject to review under this Act.

Any person who, having applied for registration of a trade mark and having paid the prescribed act fee, subsequently fails to comply with any requirement under this Act or makes default in providing information as directed by the Registrar, shall be deemed to have abandoned the application. The Registrar may, upon receiving written complaint from any aggrieved party alleging such abandonment, issue notice to the applicant affording an opportunity of being heard. Failure to satisfy the Registrar that the application has not been abandoned within the stipulated period will result in automatic rejection and forfeiture of the act fee paid. Any attempt to circumvent this provision through fraudulent means shall be punishable with a fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees.

The assignment of rights pertaining to registered trade marks shall be permissible subject to the conditions outlined herein. Any individual or entity holding ownership of a registered trade mark may, by way of a written instrument executed as per prescribed formalities, assign the entire interest and title therein to another party. Such assignment shall include, but not be limited to, the right to use, license, and enforce the said trade mark. Where an act fee paid for the initial registration or subsequent renewal of a trade mark has been remitted by the assigning party, the assignee shall be deemed liable for any outstanding fees accruing prior to the effective date of assignment, as determined by the Registrar. Furthermore, licenses granted under this Act relating to the assigned trade mark remain valid unless expressly revoked by the new owner within six months from the date of registration of the assignment.

The Registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for registration of a trade mark and the requisite act fee paid, proceed to examine whether the proposed marks are distinctive and comply with the provisions relating to acceptable representations. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar refusing registration based on examination under this Act may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of such decision. The appellate board shall consider any evidence submitted regarding the payment or non-payment of the act fee and its impact on the validity of the refusal, provided that failure to pay the prescribed act fee prior to the commencement of proceedings before the Board may be grounds for dismissal of the appeal as provided herein.

Any person who, having made an application for registration of a trade mark and having paid the requisite act fee, subsequently fails to comply with any direction issued by the Trade Marks Registry under this Act relating to the submission of documentary evidence or other information, shall be deemed to have abandoned the application. The Registrar may, upon receiving satisfactory proof that such non-compliance was unintentional and due to circumstances beyond the applicant’s reasonable control, grant a reprieve, but only after levying a penalty not exceeding twice the original act fee paid. Producers who deliberately obstruct investigations into suspected trade mark infringement, or fail to provide requested information regarding their production processes, are liable for fines as provided herein.

The Registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for registration of a trade mark and the requisite act fee paid, conduct an examination to ascertain whether the proposed mark conflicts with any existing registered trade marks or pending applications. An appeal against such determination may be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the refusal order, subject to payment of the prescribed appellate fee. The Appellate Authority shall consider whether the applicant has demonstrated a clear distinction between their mark and any prior registration, particularly where the applied-for mark shares similarities with a distinguishable registered layout already in use for unrelated goods or services. Any decision by the Appellate Authority is final, save for further appeal to the High Court.

For the purpose of this Act, an “act fee paid” shall be deemed to have occurred when funds equivalent to the prescribed amount for any action undertaken by or before the Registrar are received into the Consolidated Fund of India, irrespective of the mode of payment. This includes, but is not limited to, examination of applications, publication in the Trade Marks Journal, and renewal of registrations. Any dispute concerning whether an act fee paid has been properly remitted may be referred to the Appellate Board for determination, subject to such procedures as are prescribed under this Act. The Registrar shall maintain detailed records pertaining to all act fees paid.

An applicant for registration of a trade mark shall be required to remit the prescribed act fee paid at the time of filing the application and subsequent dealings with the Trade Marks Registry, as determined by notification issued from time to time.
